## SONNET IX.

<margin>Francesco O.</margin>
**W**hen the planet that marks the hours,
Returns to dwell with the Bull,
Virtue falls from the flaming horns,
Clothing the world in a new color:
And not only that which opens to us outwardly,
Adorning the banks and hills with small flowers,
But within, where the light of day never reaches,
It makes the terrestrial moisture pregnant with itself:
**S**o that such fruit, and similar, may be gathered.
Thus she, who is a sun among women,
Moving the rays of her beautiful eyes toward me,
<margin>creates the</margin>
**C**reates thoughts, acts, and words of love;
But however she governs or turns them,
**F**or me, it is nonetheless never Spring.

**W**HEN THE planet—quite clearly shown in the preceding sonnet and explained by me as to what chain our poet was bound by, and how great the violence of lust is—in the present ninth sonnet, the process of love is declared with a beautiful similitude. This process only rests when it has achieved its desired end, which is not in words, but in deeds. He says, therefore, that it happens naturally: that in the month of April, by the warming rays of the sun, the moist earth, as if pregnant, produces and puts forth new color with various small flowers among the green grasses and diverse young trees. And it further appears as if she were pregnant and ready to give birth to such fruits as she has conceived within her depths. He shows that the same happens through the likeness

of his wandering beloved who, shining among other most beautiful women no differently than the sun does among the stars, directs the most splendid rays toward him with the sweet gaze of her lovely eyes. This wages war in his heart, producing thoughts, acts, and words of love. In this part, he shares a likeness with the beautiful color and joyful flowers of Spring. But regarding the fruit and the final effect of these amorous practices, he says that she is entirely unlike the Spring. Let us examine the beautiful comparison. WHEN THE sun, which is AND THE planet <margin>P</margin> that marks the hours: dividing them with equal distance according to its continuous and firm movements. The first inventor of the clock <note>original: *horologio*</note>, according to the common opinion of the Gentiles, was Anaximander of Miletus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher (c. 610–546 BC)</note>, but according to the true Christian philosophers, it was Ahaz <note>Refers to the "Sundial of Ahaz" mentioned in the Bible (2 Kings 20:11)</note>. RETURNS according to its usual annual course. TO DWELL WITH THE BULL: in the time of Spring <note>The sun enters the zodiac sign of Taurus in April</note>. VIRTUE: a certain power through the vigor of drying heat. FALLS: reaches the earth through the solar rays FROM THE FLAMING HORNS of the said Bull: which clearly signifies the month of April, when the sun already rises toward the head of Taurus, when the weather is all beautiful and cheerful. Therefore, although the Romans say Spring begins in Pisces—which would be past mid-February—this must be understood because at that time the cold has lost its vehemence and harshness. The sun, being closer, has already begun to boil with the enclosed moisture produced by winter, and even to sprout somewhat with its buds. But...

--- Page 25 ---
<meta>This page continues the analysis of Sonnet IX, specifically focusing on the astronomical timing of the poem—set in April when the sun enters Taurus—and comparing Petrarch’s descriptions of spring and Laura’s beauty to the classical poetry of Virgil.</meta>

After mid-April has passed, the sun is in the breast of Taurus <note>The constellation of the Bull</note>, which is a place in the [zodiacal] animals that is extremely hot because of its relationship to the heart. The earth, already well-warmed, is all in bloom, and as the sun ascends further toward the head [of the Bull], the earth becomes even more beautiful and delightful to look upon with its buds, various flowers, and small trees. We should not, however, understand this to mean that the sun had already reached the head of Taurus, because that would contradict the meaning in two ways. First, the poet intended to signify April; if the sun were in the head of Taurus, it would not be April, but around the middle of May.

Secondly, it would contradict the truth of the day, which he wishes to obscurely demonstrate: that it was the feast day of Saint George <note>April 23rd</note>. On that day, a beautiful festival was being held in Avignon where there were infinite and elegant women; while gazing among them and contemplating Lady Laura, it seemed to him that she surpassed all others in supreme beauty beyond any comparison. But in truth, he wished to follow the most excellent poet Virgil in this description of the season, in the first book of the *Georgics*, where he says:

->When the white Bull ascending with golden horns opens the joyful year,<-
->And the Dog, yielding to the opposing star, descends from his seat at the setting.<-

The text follows: **THAT**: which is the generative and productive power. **CLOTHES AND COVERS** in a vain dress. **THE WORLD**: the earth. **IN A NEW COLOR**: as a distinction from the past winter, in which the earth is not green and blooming as it is in spring. And the said power **DOES NOT ADORN** anew with various small flowers just the surface of the earth where there is greenery and blossoms. **WHICH** opens to us outwardly: that which we see in the said month of April on the surface of the earth; and he declares in his speech what it is that appears to us on the outside. **THE BANKS**: the rivers and the plains. **AND THE HILLS**: the hillocks and mounds, which places are commonly green and blooming. But the aforementioned power is the solar potency, which is hot and dry. **MAKES PREGNANT WITH ITSELF**: it impregnates with its power. **THE EARTHLY HUMOR**: the moisture enclosed in the earth which is cold. **WITHIN**: inside the bowels of the earth. **WHERE**: that solar power. **NEVER LINGERS**: it never delays in producing the fruit that has been impregnated and conceived. **WHENCE**: from which impregnated moisture such and similar fruit is gathered, by which that earthly moisture is impregnated by that solar power; and then he adapts his comparison to his beloved lady, showing her to be quite similar in terms of the fruit and the effect of love, saying: **THUS**: in a similar way. **SHE**: Laura. **WHO** is a sun among women: that is, like a sun. The sun is the most splendid among the other bright stars; so she is the most beautiful among other beautiful women, no differently than a lovely splendor. **MOVING**: the rays, the clear and splendid gazes like the rays of the sun. **OF BEAUTIFUL EYES**: which principally demonstrate the charm and gracious beauty that moves even the stones, similar to the solar power. **THOUGHTS**: which are first in the hearts of those in love. **ACTS**: which proceed from the thoughts of the heart, in that the person in love makes some gesture with the eye, or some other sign of the hand, or in another way. And words, which usually follow after such acts and gestures: and these three things correspond to the small flowers and the new color of spring. But how or in what manner it may be, I do not know. Perhaps Lady Laura governs those eyes with prudence, so that others do not notice. **SHE TURNS**: yet without such caution, she turns them elsewhere. Nevertheless, spring is never for me, insofar as I never gather such similar fruit as should finally follow if love were impregnated and conceived in the heart of my beloved according to the gracious gazes of her most beautiful eyes.

We should note, as said above, that Petrarch in this comparison and similitude wishes in part to follow Virgil only in the description of spring and not the [specific] day, likening Lady Laura to the sun and the gazes of her eyes to the rays of the sun that was in Taurus. The horns he mentioned are not meant to imply the sun was yet in the head of the Bull, but are in respect to the garments and headwear used by the women of Avignon and those regions on their heads, made in the likeness of coronets <note>Small crowns or headpieces</note>, which nonetheless appear to the women as elegant and noble.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
<insert>W</insert>**HEN the planet that distinguishes**: Messer Francesco imagines two suns: Phoebus <note>The sun god</note> in the sky and Laura on earth. He says that the one in the sky, which is the planet, when it enters the celestial sign of Taurus (which is around the 12th of April), brings spring and fills every land with flowers; but the second sun, which is placed in the eyes of Lady Laura—though it makes the said Messer Francesco rejoice—nevertheless has no end, nor did spring ever truly come for him <note>Meaning his love remains unfulfilled and stuck in a state of longing</note>.

# SONNET X.

**G**lorious column on which rests
Our hope and the great Latin name,
Which the anger of Jove <note>original: "Lira di gioue"; likely a variant of "Ira," meaning wrath, as the commentary explains it as a lightning bolt</note> has not yet turned from the true path
Through windy rain;
Here there are no palaces, no theater or portico,
But in their place a fir, a beech, a pine
Among the green grass on the beautiful nearby mountain,
From which one descends and climbs while composing poetry,
Lifting our intellect from the earth to the sky.
And the nightingale, who sweetly in the shade
All night long laments and weeps,
Fills the heart with amorous thoughts.
But such goodness you alone make truncated and imperfect,
My lord, because you are separated from us.

<margin>
FRANCIS
R.

**G**LORIOUS column:
Regarding the preceding tenth sonnet:
although it does not seem to
conform with the 
preceding amorous subject matter, it is
not, however, alien to it, insofar as 
lovers willingly seek solitary and delightful places to be able to use their thoughts and imagination regarding the practices and dealings of love with less hindrance, and also to have some refreshment for their weary spirits. Therefore, Master Francesco Petrarch having withdrawn somewhat outside of Avignon to a nearby and very solitary villa, before he returned to Italy and retired to Arquà, a Paduan village—and this to unburden <note>original: "sborarsi"</note> himself a little of his many troubles—he writes from that place this sonnet to Monsignore di Colonna, called by name (as said above) Master Giacomo <note>Giacomo Colonna, a bishop and close friend of Petrarch</note>, a generous man of great spirit and almost a sole bulwark of the splendor and Latin name against the annoying pride of those from across the mountains <note>original: "tramontani," referring to the French at the Papal court in Avignon</note>. For this reason, having first singularly praised the courage and constancy of the aforementioned Cardinal, he describes the pleasantness of the place where he was staying at that time, showing nonetheless that he is not without his usual amorous thoughts: and how he would have the greatest pleasure in that solitary and delightful state if he were not divided from the accustomed conversation of his Lordship. He says: GLORIOUS column: O Monsignore di Colonna, a most virtuous man: therefore glorious. But because we have written very deeply of glory in the second book of our work *On Exile* <note>original: "exilio"</note>, here it seems sufficient to follow the definition of it by Marcus Tullius [Cicero], who in the oration he gave to the Senate in the presence of Gaius Caesar for the reinstatement of Marcus Marcellus, says thus: "Glory is an illustrious and very public fame for many and great benefits that someone has performed for his kin, his country, or the whole human race." Well, then, did our poet call Monsignore di Colonna glorious, he being a man of most excellent virtue, liberal and beneficent toward everyone, and especially toward his homeland, insofar as he strove with every wit to bring the court of Avignon back to Italy. He continues: ON WHICH: in whose firmness and constancy the poet had respect for the name of the "Column" <note>A play on the family name Colonna, which means "column" in Italian</note>. RESTS: as on a most firm support, our hope: or the hope of me: and even the hope of all of us Latins; because it would then follow not by way of a conjunction, but as a clarification: The great Latin name: which could be said to be almost beaten to the ground regarding the Papacy in Avignon, if he alone with his great reputation had not sustained the dignity and majesty of the Italian name among those annoying and vain people. WHICH YET: which Latin name still. ANGER of Jove <note>original: "LIRA de Ioue"</note>: a heavenly bolt attributed by the poets to Jove. THROUGH windy rain: the wind mixed together with the rain, at which time the bolts fall into the air, generated by the violent impetus made by the winds in wanting to escape by force from the thick and surrounding clouds; that is to say, that the said Latin name [suffered] no strike from contrary and turbulent fortune. HAS NOT YET turned from the true path: as if to say: although you are in Avignon together with the court, you are nonetheless a true, upright Italian. Then, having praised him, what follows is the commendation of the pleasantness of the place where he was staying for his diversion. ¶ Here are no palaces, no theaters or portico: which things are accustomed to be in the largest and most famous cities: but there are in their place: that is, in the stead of them. A fir, a beech, a pine: which are...

...tall and straight trees: continually in full leaf. **AMONG** the green grass: of the meadows that are on the plain. **THE** nearby mountain: to that villa. And you can also note that perhaps not without reason has he named those three trees, because the fir—according to the opinion of the pagans—when it is struck by a bolt from heaven (that is, by lightning) signifies the death of the beloved: a gift <note>original: "donata"; this may refer to the lady as a gift from heaven, or a specific name in the commentator's circle</note>: which occurred not long after. **M. L.** <note>Likely the initials of a commentator, possibly Alessandro Vellutello or a similar scholar</note> Of the beech, the ancients used to make their arrows; and so that it might be known to many how much our poet was struck by the stinging arrows of love, it is clearly shown above. The pine is consecrated to the goddess of fraud and deceptions, and he finds himself more deceived by his love every day. Whence: from which mountain. **ONE** descends while composing poetry: one can descend very easily while making poetic verses and amorous rhymes. **AND** climbs: goes straight on his path to the plain; "climb" <note>original: "poggia"</note> is a term taken from sailors, who call it "going to *poggia*" when they have the wind straight and favorable right in the middle of the ship's stern. He says this to show that little mountain to be so easy and favorable that one can descend from there by the straight path without turning here and there as one usually does on rugged mountains. **LIFT**: the said three trees with their height. **OUR** intellect: looking up from the earth to the sky: thus he demonstrates that one should consider not only earthly and

<margin>T</margin>
low things: but also celestial and high things. And now that he has described the pleasantness of the place regarding the site, the greenness of the grass, and the shade of the very tall trees: **N**ow he describes the sweetness of the nightingale, saying the nightingale who laments for Tereus, his brother-in-law, because of the virginity he took from her. **AND** weeps: for the tongue that the said Tereus cut from her, so that she could not reveal to Procne, her sister, that she had been so shamefully forced by Tereus, her brother-in-law. **SWEET**-ly with a sweet song, in contrast to unpleasant laments and sorrowful weeping; in this, I say **I**n the shade: of the said trees. **ALL** the nights: the custom of nightingales who sing much better at night than during the day because of the cool air. **FI**-lls the heart with amorous thoughts: because the nightingale, making me remember with his sweetest song the unrestrained love of Tereus toward Philomela, I immediately remember my own love as well; and I think so much upon this that the heart remains entirely entangled by it. **BUT YOU** alone, my lord, who separates yourself from us: who remains divided from our company and domestic conversation, you truncate, diminish, and make imperfect and incomplete: as much good as I would have if I found you in such a place. And here note against the ignorance of the unlearned: Petrarch calls the Cardinal Colonna "Monsignore" in the singular, yet speaks of himself using "we": which all the ancients did, and even today is observed by all most learned men who wish to address someone as a singular person who is not merely singular, but

<margin>V</margin>
who has many like him. **H**owever, with suitable brevity, I will relate the story of Philomela turned into a nightingale; and of Procne her sister who became a swallow; and of the wicked Tereus made into a hoopoe bird; and also of the boy Itys, son of Tereus and Procne, changed into a goldfinch; for all these things are marvelous and beautiful. Pandion, king of the Athenians, had two daughters, Procne and Philomela. Procne, who was the elder, married Tereus, king of Daulia, a most warlike man and lustful, as was made manifest in the end. After Procne had been with her husband for five years, the desire came upon her to see her younger sister Philomela. Therefore, having found an opportune time, with sweet and flattering words she prayed Tereus her husband that he would grant her one of two favors: either that he let her go to see her sister, or that he arrange for her sister to come to her. Hearing this, Tereus immediately boarded a galley in person and went to Athens, where he arrived and was received magnificently by his father-in-law Pandion. As both a son-in-law and a king, after other honorable and customary words usually spoken at such times and places, he explained to Pandion his father-in-law the reason for his coming. While Tereus was modestly promising his father-in-law that he would soon return her to his presence, Philomela arrived according to her father's order to receive and honor Tereus, her brother-in-law. She was by nature so beautiful that she seemed a goddess, and then dressed most richly and adorned with most precious jewels, which kindled her natural beauty not a little. After she had made her paternal reverence according to filial duty and greeted her brother-in-law according to modest and usual custom: Tereus, who as soon as he had seen her was kindled with such love for her that he burned entirely, could hardly contain himself from seeking without delay to violently ravish her and satisfy his lustful and impious appetite. Yet with very great effort he restrained himself for the moment; in appearance, he began again with marvelous eloquence (which is usually sweeter in those who are in love) to pray Pandion that he would not deny such great consolation to his dearest daughter Procne. This was almost a prelude to the future misfortune. Nor was Tereus slow to depart; with the greatest speed, he placed Philomela in the galley and set out to the open sea. Like a victor and impious pursuer of his wicked vows, he did not know what to do with himself for his excessive joy. Keeping his eyes fixed on the graceful and angelic face of the enchanting Philomela, he was so stimulated by lust that the barbarian became almost insane; he could hardly contain his hidden joy or his impulses from reaching the final effect of his desired fury. But having forced the journey with sails and winds, once he arrived at his shores and everyone had left the ship, he did not lead Philomela to the royal city where Procne lived. Instead, he took her among the shadowy and densest forests where the stables of his herds were kept. In that place, the miserable Philomela, seeing where she had been led, turned pale with fear and nearly lost her senses. While she asked with tears where her sister was, Tereus, answering nothing to her demands, took her in his arms. Having locked himself inside a stable with her, and without any preamble declaring his detestable lust, he did not wait for an answer but forced that poor and solitary virgin according to his abominable dishonesty. Because she could use no other defense against the cruelty of that execrable barbarian, she cried out in a loud voice, calling for help now from her afflicted father, now from her wretched sister, and above all from the power of the great gods. At first, she was so overcome and shaken by trembling that, almost dead, she could not stand or even know where she was. ...the sword he had at his side, which Philomena, having seen it, was entirely comforted by, hoping he wished to kill her; and with a joyful face, she offered her throat, all the while with indignation cursing the cruel and nefarious Tereus and calling for help and vengeance upon King Pandion, her wretched father. But the wicked and ignorant tyrant, seeing her persevere in such a manner, seized her protesting tongue with tongs, and with the sharp sword that he had in his hand, having most cruelly cut it from the roots, he threw it to the ground with the bitterest wrath; nor did he stop until he had taken her by force several times. And finally, having left Philomena in that place under good guard, he returned to his royal city to his lady Procne, who without delay asked after her sister as someone most dear to her, and awaited her with wonderful desire. Tereus, with feigned groans, gave her to understand that she had fallen ill from the exhaustion of the sea voyage and died; and because in speaking of this he knew how to use pitiable tears, the deceived Procne easily believed it to be so without any doubt. Therefore, having performed the royal funeral rites for her by the custom of a **Cenotaph** <note>original: "Cenotaphio"; a funerary monument or empty tomb raised in honor of a person whose remains are elsewhere or lost</note>, she was in anguished and most bitter mourning for no small amount of time.

->**[Philomela’s Lament]**<-

From the marriage drawn from evil-doing,
You have confused everything: alas, that cry
I shall now use, for I am a warrior
Made so by my sister; and you can now
Boast: for in such a manner of yours
You are the husband of two: an enemy to me.
But why do you delay now, horrible beast?
I deserve great pain, which is why, if you are
My friend: take my soul from me quickly.
Give me death, hurry, for I tell it to you;
This alone is the exalted and nourishing glory
Which remains for you, impious traitor.
Why do you delay, then, to take the final palm? <note>Referring to the "palm of victory," here used ironically for the final act of murder</note>
Happy would I be if, before my grief
From this nefarious coupling, I had been killed
By you, so that without error
And without fault my divided shade
Might be separated from this light; but yet I hope,
If the supreme gods are not without laughter <note>Meaning: if the gods are not indifferent or mocking</note>
And are not all made a zero toward me,
If they can look upon our deeds,
You shall have punishment, wicked and fierce,
Whenever it may be; nor shall I cease to speak.
Casting away all shame, the whole deed
I will bring among the people; if to go among them
Is granted to me: and if indeed at the very most
I am kept hidden among the woods
So that I am made mute among the people,
Among the woods my tongue shall be loosened;
I will move the stones with my speaking
So that this fault shall not stay buried.
<margin>V</margin> Heaven and God will tell of it: if God can hear
Anyone in that place who could say these things;
Nor can you in any way prevent me
From daring to uncover your madness.

<margin>Z</margin> Twelve years had already passed since the time of the aforementioned committed wickedness, nor was anything more said of Philomena, nor was any other mention made than what is usually done for things dead and irrecoverable. But Philomena finally, her most noble wit awakened by the greatest grief—being most skilled in weaving—set herself with her own hands to weave a cloth of white silk with purple designs; and in that, with Greek letters, having figured and described her entire unhappy case, she begged one of the maidens left by Tereus as her guard—with signs, since she could not speak—that she should carry that cloth to Procne.

This was done by the simple and unsuspecting maiden, who did not comprehend what she was carrying. Immediately, Procne recognized the foul lust and thereafter also the horrible cruelty of her impious husband. At first, because of the immeasurable grief, she could say nothing, nor did any words worthy of such unheard-of monstrosity occur to her; then, entirely deliberating within herself to take vengeance for such injuries, she thought of nothing else but being able to punish the criminal outrage of her monstrous and abominable husband with a fitting punishment. Taking, therefore, the opportune time of the **Bacchanalia** <note>The festival of Bacchus/Dionysus, characterized by ritual madness and processions</note>, she went out by night from her royal palace under the pretext of wishing to honor the said festivity. Therefore, having prepared her person according to the rite and mystery of Bacchus, she covered her head with a garland of vine leaves <note>original: "pampinea"</note>, and her face with ivy leaves; her left hand sustained, in place of a shield, a deer skin; her right held the **thyrsus** <note>term: a staff tipped with a pine cone and entwined with ivy, carried by followers of Bacchus</note>. And in such a manner, running through the woods like a woman possessed—not so much by the breaths and spirit of the feigned Bacchus as by the stimulating furies of her immense grief—she arrived with the company of her trusted maidens at the hidden place where the wretched Philomena was locked up. And having broken the doors and pulled her out from there, and having put a similar habit upon her, she led her into the city, dismayed and astonished. But after she was in her palace, quite pale and almost out of her mind for the fear of seeing herself in such a place, Procne drew her aside—where she could be neither seen nor recognized by others—and took off that habit that had adorned her, and then with pitiable weeping, embracing her, [she called her] sister Philomena...

While the irate and furious Procne spoke these words with a pitiless soul and one most ready for any horrible vengeance, she saw her little son Itys coming toward her: at whose sight she was more firmly incited to wrath; and having already suddenly deliberated within her soul the wicked vengeance, looking at the wretched child with cruel and most atrocious eyes, she said:

> Ah, how similar you are to your impious father! / May you be the vengeance of him upon your mother.
> I see his face: his look, his way of walking / In such a way that every man must tell of it.

No longer did she speak, but prepared herself for his death: but then the child came to her and with a pleasant bow greeted her: and having thrown his little arms around her neck with childish flatteries and a laugh, he kissed her. Procne, overcome by maternal love, already began to set aside her terrible anger, and her eyes, despite herself, were bathed in many tears: and she was already moved to compassion, while looking anew at the face of her afflicted sister: and looking now at the boy, now at her, she spoke thus:

> Why does this one offer sweet flatteries,
> And she remains silent because her tongue was taken?
> Why does he raise the name of mother,
> While she cannot say "sister" even once?
> O daughter of the great King Pandion,
> Look at your wretched self, think and listen
> To whom you are married, and realize
> You have degenerated from illustrious names
> If you do not punish the treacherous thief.
> If you feel compassion, you show yourself quite base;
> Therefore, for every mercy shown to the fierce husband,
> Let a wicked deed be named for a thousand lustrums <note>A lustrum was a period of five years; she means the crime should be remembered for five thousand years</note>;
> Let your bold soul remember.

Having said this, without any other delay, the insane Procne dragged the wretched child Itys behind her, no differently than a lamb is usually dragged by an Arcadian wolf: or a fawn by a Marmaric lion <note>a lion from the Marmarica region of North Africa</note>: or a deer by a Gangetic tiger. Seeing death before his face, he began to stretch out his joined hands to her. "O my mother; O my mother!" he cried out with miserable weeping, wishing to embrace her neck with his extended arms. The merciless Procne, with a sharp sword and a mortal blow, struck him in the left side without turning her turbulent face and without changing her infuriated expression. Nor did Philomela rest; though the fallen boy was already passing from this life with anguished groans from such a wound, she took him by his curled and glowing hair and cut his throat with a knife. This done, both of them—stimulated by a similar fury—before the soul had entirely departed from the body, they cut him member from member. And so dismembered, and still trembling as if alive, they put him to the burning fire, part boiling and part roasting. And so that the wicked cruelty of the impious vengeance might correspond to the horrible enormity of the flagitious crime, Procne invited Tereus, her husband, to dine with her as if at a solemn and sacred banquet. To this, according to the Athenian custom which she had deceitfully feigned, no one else could be present except the husband and the wife. For this reason, the young men and maidens and everyone else were removed from that place. Tereus, having sat down together with the treacherous Procne in the royal seat of his ancestors, ate the prepared and seasoned flesh of his slaughtered son; and because he loved him alone marvelously above all other things, he asked that his Itys be brought to him. Then the impious Procne, unable to hide her infinite joy and happiness any longer, and wishing to be the messenger of his calamitous misfortune herself, replied to him that he had his Itys within him. Hearing this, Tereus looked around and still asked where he was. And while he thus asked and often called Itys by name, suddenly Philomela, who until then had been hidden, came out, enraged, disheveled, and bathed in the blood of the innocent boy. She threw his head—still dripping with blood—into the father’s face with a sign of infinite joy, grieving only for one thing: that her present pleasure could not be expressed with words suitable to such a case. Then Tereus, with a very great noise, having thrown down the table that was before him, rose up straight as if out of his mind and used these words:

...it was said he was king of the city of Daulia, located in the Phocian country: but such an error proceeded from the similarity of this name with the father Teres of Sitalces, who, many centuries after Tereus, was king of the Odrysians <note>The Odrysians were a powerful Thracian tribe</note>: as the most noble and most truthful historian Thucydides shows in the second book of the Peloponnesian War, saying thus: in that same summer the Athenians, who previously considered Nymphodorus of Abdera, son of Pythes, their enemy, made him a mediator and advisor for friendship. This man was very powerful with Sitalces, king of the Thracians, the son of Teres, the father of Sitalces: he was the first who, having subjugated a large part of the rest of Thrace, created the kingdom of the Odrysians: because part of the Thracians govern themselves as a community: and this Teres had no connection with that Tereus who had for his wife Procne, the daughter of Pandion, from the same Thrace: because the true Tereus lived in Daulia, which is in the country now called Phocis, which was at that time inhabited by Thracians: and in this country, that deed which is told of Itys was done by those women: and by many poets, in commemoration of the nightingale, they named that bird "Daulias" <note>original: "Daulias"; a poetic name for the nightingale, referring to the myth of Philomela and the city of Daulis</note>: and it is also to be believed that Pandion set such high esteem on the kinship and the union of his daughter more out of respect for the utility of both than for the journey of many days' travel all the way to the Odrysians. But Teres had that same name: and was the first king who ruled in the Odrysian land: whose son Sitalces the Athenians made their ally because they wanted the places that were in Thrace and to drive out King Perdiccas. These words are written literally by Thucydides: from which one can quite clearly understand how many things the poets, through some similarity, are accustomed to confuse.

<margin>To let go of the veil: Our most illustrious poet having returned from the villa to the city of Avignon: and having encountered M.L. <note>Madonna Laura, Petrarch's muse</note> who—not in tresses as she was formerly accustomed, but with a veil on her head—was returning from the church to her house, he writes the present canzone to her, where he modestly laments such attire of hers, and that she shows in her appearance no pity toward him, who loves her so much; although the said canzone has a form of rhyme dissimilar to the others, it is nonetheless quite beautiful and clear: which will be clearly understood in the explanation, directing it thus. **LADY** I did not see you. **To let go** the veil that you wore on your head. **Whether for sun, or for shade, or for heat, or for cold: AFTER** you recognized in me the great desire of our love. **WHICH EVERY OTHER WILL:** appetite. **Clears from me:** it</margin>

OF pity: of compassion: and this was because she had not yet understood the situation: so she looked at him purely without that intention which Petrarch <note>original: "Petrar."</note> took to understand for himself. BUT our blonde hair was then veiled: and similarly the loving gaze. IT WAS gathered into itself, looking down. THEN that love made you aware of me: after you noticed that I was in love with you. ¶ IF my life. The present 11th sonnet has a good and open conformity with the preceding one: because having in that one commended Madonna Laura for her honest bearing of her head and for the modest and continent gaze that gave no one cause to fall in love with her. Now it is shown that there is such gravity and almost veneration in that very beautiful face of hers: that he is ashamed and in no way dares to discover to her by mouth his loving and bitter martyrdoms <note>Petrarch often uses "martyrdoms" to describe the intense suffering caused by unrequited love</note>: and this because, being still young, he is ashamed to be esteemed as lascivious by such a lady. But what he did not have the courage to say to her by mouth, he signified through this sonnet, reminding her of old age when she will repent not having used the gracious fruit of her beauty in her youthful age: and therefore he speaks thus.

### SONNET 11

->If my life from the bitter torment<-
->Can so shield itself and from the anxieties,<-
->That I may see by virtue of my final years<-
->Lady, the light of your beautiful eyes extinguished,<-
->And the hair of fine gold turn to silver,<-
->And the leaving behind of garlands and green clothes,<-
->And the face turn pale, which to my harm<-
->Makes me fearful and slow in my lamenting;<-
->Yet love shall give me such boldness,<-
->That I shall discover to you my martyrdoms<-
->What have been the years and days and hours<-
->And if time is contrary to beautiful desires;<-
->It shall not be, that at least there does not reach my grief<-
->Some help from late sighs.<-

IF my life can so shield: defend itself from the bitter torment: and from the anxieties of love, dodging its blows. THAT I may see by virtue of my final years: of old age. O Lady, extinguished the luminous gaze of your beautiful eyes: and see. The Hair of fine gold: blonde like fine gold, become silver: gray and white like a piece of silver. AND see you. Leave the garlands which are granted to youth. AND GREEN clothes: which you use. AND the face turn pale: and see the color lost from your colorful face so as to be grave and worthy of reverence. ME. makes fearful: fearing to say things by mouth that might displease you. And slow: late because of such fear. In my harms: which I receive from being in love without fruit. LOVE shall yet give me such boldness: daring and confidence. THAT I shall discover to you: what have been the years, days, and hours. OF my martyrdoms: torments that I have received for your love. HERE there is the figure called <term>histeron protheron</term> <note>original: "histerō protheron"; a rhetorical device where the natural order is reversed, placing the last thing first</note> where the words that should be in front are behind: and those behind are in front, because first are the hours, then days, and then the years. AND if the time of old age. [Is] contrary to the beautiful desires of the effect of love. IT SHALL NOT BE: it will not happen: That at least some help of your late sighs: because of the sweet time having passed in vain in the past youthful age. Does not reach: does not arrive at my present grief: as if to say, you also being old will sigh: because when you were young and beautiful you did not succor the displeasure and melancholy that I presently receive because of you: but this may be late in respect to old age.

<margin>Antonio <note>original: "Anto."; refers to the commentator Antonio da Tempo</note></margin>
¶ *If my life from bitter torment.* <note>The opening line of Sonnet 11: "Se la mia vita dall'aspro tormento"</note> Master Francesco <note>original: "M. F."; refers to the commentator Francesco Filelfo</note> says that if he is able to endure the pains of love until old age, then he will finally be able to tell her his desires without suspicion. Note that hair is said to change from a golden color to a silver color when old age arrives and the head then becomes white.

## SONNET XII.

<margin>Francesco C. <note>original: "Fran. C"; refers to the scholar Francesco Filelfo, whose commentary was often paired with Petrarch's work</note></margin>
¶ *When among the others.* In the preceding two sonnets, he praised her hair, her eyes, and the color of her lovely face together with the movements of the head and the person of his beloved lady; now, in this present 12th sonnet, he praises and elevates with marvelous commendation the universal beauty of her face in general. He demonstrates that her beauty, without any comparison, surpasses the selection of all other graceful women. For this reason, he considers himself fortunate and thanks God for having made him worthy of such great honor, as it seems to him that attaining such a love is a thing of happiness; thus he speaks. *When Love comes from time to time*: at various moments. *In the beautiful face of this woman*: of Madonna Laura. *Among the other women*: finding herself together with other women; that is, when she, from time to time, is found with a joyful face and good will. Because at such a time the lady appears much more beautiful, and this is explained below: "the desire that makes me fall in love with her grows in my soul." *As much as each one is less beautiful than she*: insofar as she is more beautiful than any other. And for this very reason, I, Francesco Petrarch <note>original: "Fran. Petrar."</note>, *bless the place, the time, and the hour.* *That* where and when *my eyes looked so high.* That I, in gazing upon her, fell in love with such a high and exalted beauty. And speaking to myself I say: O my soul, you must greatly thank God that you were then in that place, time, and hour when you first fell in love with her. *Dignified*: considered worthy of *such great honor*, which is to be in love with such an excessive beauty, so that every thought is directed toward glorious things, despising everything that is prized by the common people; and he says: *The amorous thought that sends you to the highest good*: to happiness while you follow it, *comes*: proceeds from her. Insofar as you are in love with her, you think of nothing else but doing things for which you may be famous, so that you might please her. And he declares in what manner he is invited to that highest good by that amorous thought when he adds: *Valuing little what every man desires*: which he demonstrated above in the 7th sonnet. *The spirited grace*: the elegance of love. *Which to heaven*: to high and glorious things, as is said of Ulysses in Homer <note>original: "Vlyze in Home."</note> and Aeneas in Virgil <note>original: "Enea in Vir."</note>. *Guides you*: leads you. *By the right-hand path*: by the way of virtue and praiseworthy choices. And this is said according to the two paths figured by Pythagoras the philosopher in this letter: **Y**. The right branch of which was meant to be the path of virtue, and the left the path of vice <note>The "Pythagorean Y" was a common Renaissance symbol for the moral crossroads of life: the narrow right path leading to difficult virtue, and the wide left path to easy vice</note>. *Comes*: proceeds from her, insofar as she is the reason you strive to live gloriously. Concluding, he says: *So that I now walk proud with hope*: because I hope to obtain what I desire and achieve victory over the beloved lady. And victory and prosperity usually make a man proud and of great spirit through joyful happiness, by which our souls are marvelously prone to expand; whereas the displeasure of adverse and unhappy things causes the soul to shrink through affliction and become base in all those who, abandoned by reason, have submitted themselves to passion.

**W**hen among other women from time to time
**L**ove comes into the beautiful face of this lady;
**A**s much as each one is less beautiful than she,
**S**o much grows the desire that makes me fall in love.
**I** bless the place and the time and the hour,
**T**hat my eyes looked so high;
**A**nd I say: Soul, you must give great thanks,
**T**hat you were deemed worthy of such honor at that time.
**F**rom her comes to you the amorous thought,
**W**hich, while you follow it, sends you to the highest good,
**V**aluing little what every man desires;
**F**rom her comes the spirited grace,
**W**hich guides you to heaven along the right-hand path,
**S**o that I now walk already proud with hope.

<margin>Antonio <note>original: "Anto."</note></margin>
¶ *When among the other women from time to time*: Master Francesco <note>original: "M. F."</note> says that seeing Madonna Laura <note>original: "M. L."</note> at times among other women being the most beautiful, his love for her grows so much. Then he begins to bless the day he saw her and thank the hour that allowed him to look at his lady and love her. And he considers himself all the more required to thank his fortune and his good luck because from her comes every good example. *Valuing little what every man desires.* Here Master Francesco shows that he loved his Madonna Laura for her nobility and kindness, not for a dishonest <note>i.e., lustful or immoral</note> love, as he also says in several places.

<meta>This page continues the sequence of Petrarch’s *Canzoniere*, moving from the general praise of Madonna Laura’s beauty in the previous sonnets to the specific emotional weight of the poet's departure from Avignon. It introduces the second Canzone and the thirteenth Sonnet, focusing on the pain of physical separation.</meta>

<margin>Francesco <note>original: "Fran."; refers to Francesco Filelfo</note></margin>
<margin>H</margin>
**My weary eyes** <note>original: "OCchi mei lassi"</note> **was written by Petrarch: this second song <term>canzone <gloss>a complex Italian lyric poem</gloss></term> was written shortly before his departure from Avignon to return to Italy, which he had already desired for a long time. He demonstrates, therefore, alongside his great pleasure in repatriating to Italy, the singular displeasure he feels for the disjoining from his lady. He directs his speech to his fatigued eyes in this manner: My weary eyes, tired in the continual gazing upon my beloved: I PRAY YOU be cautious: awake and attentive. WHILE I turn you, as I turn you TO the beautiful face, praised above, OF that lady. WHO has killed us through feeling too many afflictions in gazing upon her in vain. BE therefore cautious and diligent, because Love already challenges you to wage war and give you trouble, insofar as you will no longer be able to see the beloved thing. Wherefore, because of this lack of confidence, I sigh, fearing that future afflictions will be even greater than the present ones, due to not being able then to see what they can see now. Because someone else might say: "what the eye does not see, the heart does not want," he will remove all of this thought from his side. He responds and says: DEATH alone can close to my thoughts THE amorous path that leads them TO the sweet port; that is, the quiet and tranquility OF their salvation. When I shall no longer think, nor have such afflictions anymore. He means to say: Love makes me think, nor can I ever do otherwise as long as life lasts. But my said thoughts will be led and conducted by Love until death, which will make my thoughts rest just as sailors, who have sustained many storms in the open sea, rest once they are led into port. Thus the amorous thoughts will always be within the heart. BUT your light, which is Madonna Laura, can hide in absence FROM YOU; eyes of mine, I say she can be hidden FOR less <note>original: "PER meno"; referring to a smaller distance or object</note>, meaning the minor intervention of the many days' journey from here to Italy. BECAUSE you were formed by God less whole and of lesser power than are the eyes of the soul—the human mind—through which we are said to be similar to God. Then, concluding, he demonstrates to them what they must do. THEREFORE, sorrowful ones, you my eyes, take now the end in this my departure. A brief comfort for such a long martyrdom that I shall have continually in my absence. And you will take this brief comfort by gazing at her. RATHER <note>original: "ANZI"; here meaning "before"</note> than the hours of your weeping are already near, or have come; because once I have departed, you will no longer be able to gaze upon her.**

### CANZONE II.

> My weary eyes, while I turn you
> Toward the beautiful face of her who has killed you;
> I pray you, be cautious:
> For Love already challenges you, for which I sigh.
> Death alone can close to my thoughts
> The amorous path; which leads them
> To the sweet port of their salvation:
> But your light can be hidden from you
> By a lesser object; because less complete
> You were formed, and of lesser power.
> Therefore, sorrowful ones, before they come,
> The hours of weeping, which are already near,
> Take now, at the end,
> Brief comfort for such long martyrdom.

---

<margin>Antonio <note>original: "Anto."; refers to Antonio da Tempo</note></margin>
**MY weary eyes while I turn you: Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> speaks to his eyes, comforting them to be alert while they look at Madonna Laura, because they are of lesser power regarding the object of Madonna Laura's eyes, which are like a sun; for the greater light obscures the lesser. DEATH can close: after he has spoken to the eyes, he says: that only death can make it so he does not think of his lady, and nothing else. It is as if he says that while he lives, his thoughts will follow her. But it can be [hidden] from you: that is, you [eyes] be alert and give yourselves joy and pleasure from your light: that is, from his lady.**

---

<margin>Francesco <note>Filelfo</note></margin>
**I TURN myself back: great are the afflictions of lovers when they see the beloved thing and cannot satisfy their desire. But certainly they are much greater and more troublesome when they distance themselves from her in such a way that they cannot even see her; because the feeding of the eyes provides relief.**

### SONNET XIII.

> I turn myself back at every step
> With my tired body, which I carry with great difficulty,
> And I take comfort then from your air,
> Which makes it go forward, saying, "alas, weary me."

On the long journey, and with my life [so] short;
I fix my feet, dismayed and pale;
And I cast my eyes to the ground, weeping.
**S**ometimes a doubt assails me in the midst of sad tears:
How can these limbs live far from their spirit?
**B**ut Love answers me: do you not remember
That this is a privilege of lovers,
Released from all human qualities?

...no small relief <note>original: "gerio," likely an abbreviation for "refrigerio"</note> to the inflamed desire: which is clearly demonstrated in the present 13th <term>Sonnet <gloss>a 14-line poem</gloss></term> by our enamored poet. Wherein, having already departed from Avignon to return to Italy, he declares with sweet and truthful speech the great anxiety he felt for his beloved lady in this manner. **I TURN MYSELF BACK.** With my weary body, which I carry with great pain: for the passion of the soul also affects the body. Back toward Avignon where my Lady Laura <note>original: "M. L."</note> was. **AT EVERY STEP:** that I take, I then take comfort from your air <note>Likely referring to the breeze or aura of the lady</note>, my sweetest Laura. **WHICH COMFORTS THE LABORS** of the said body. Woe is me: weary and anxious. **BUT THEN THINKING BACK**, I [reflect] on the sweet good that I leave behind in my distance, for you remain thus on the long journey of many days, which is quite bothersome in itself without any other mental distress. **AND TO MY SHORT LIFE:** not so much out of respect for my age, but because of my amorous troubles. **I, THUS AFFLICTED, FIX MY FEET, DISMAYED. OUT OF THE FEAR OF LOSING YOU, AND PALE AND WAN** due to the fear [where] the blood, having abandoned the exterior parts of the body, runs to the heart to strengthen and preserve the vital spirits. Thus, the said exterior parts, because of the said lack of blood, become pale: and if the lack is great, they remain beyond paleness, cold and with a trembling of the limbs: and in this state, if the blood does not return quickly, the man loses some limb, and sometimes dies: and as is the opinion of Ovid: "Love is a thing full of immense fear" <note>original Latin: "Amans, res est solliciti plena timoris" from Ovid's Heroides</note>. **AND I CAST MY EYES DOWN TO THE GROUND, WEEPING:** out of the displeasure of my troubled thoughts, and more expressly declaring the present distress: he raises a doubt which he immediately dissolves through Love’s answer, saying: **A DOUBT ASSAILS ME SOMETIMES IN THE MIDST OF THE SAD TEARS** that I shed: which is this: **HOW THESE LIMBS OF MINE CAN LIVE FAR** [and] distant from the spirit. **IN WHICH SOUL ARE YOU, MADONNA LAURA? BUT LOVE ANSWERS ME.** He responds to me and says: **DO YOU NOT REMEMBER:** do you not recall that this is a privilege: a particular law and constitution. **OF LOVERS RELEASED FROM ALL HUMAN QUALITIES:** as if he wished to say that the force and power of love is so great that, contrary to all other human conditions of the impossible, it makes [things] possible: which, being known to almost everyone through experience, I have not cared to confirm with other examples.

<margin>Antonio <note>Likely Antonio da Tempo, a 14th-century grammarian and commentator</note></margin>
¶ **I TURN MYSELF BACK AT EVERY STEP:** departing. Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> from Avignon where his Lady Laura was, composed this Sonnet, wherein he grieves much over the departure, as if his heart were lifted from his body; and he demonstrates a custom among true lovers that, when departing from their lady, they often turn back as long as they can see the place with their eyes. **DO YOU NOT REMEMBER.** That is, do you not remember that this is the privilege of lovers: saying that lovers live as if their spirit were separated from their body.

### SONNET . XIV .

**T**he little old man, white-haired and pale, moves
From the sweet place where he has spent his age,
And from his dismayed little family,
Who see their dear father failing.
**T**hence, dragging his ancient flank
Through the final days of his life,
As much as he can, he helps himself with good will,
**B**roken by the years and weary from the journey;
**A**nd he comes to Rome, following his desire,
To gaze upon the likeness of Him;

<margin>K</margin>
¶ **THE LITTLE OLD MAN MOVES.** Petrarch had already arrived in Italy and settled here in Milan at the time of the happy memory of the magnanimous prince Messer Galeazzo Visconti <note>Galeazzo II Visconti, a patron of Petrarch</note>, the renowned Lord of Milan, by whose most excellent highness he was well-regarded and much honored: therefore, from this most illustrious and abundant city—which has always been, as we see today, [full] of most beautiful women—he wrote the present 14th Sonnet to his beloved Lady Laura, showing that the same thing was happening to him now as happens to those who go to Rome to see the Sudarium <note>The Veil of Veronica, a relic showing the face of Christ</note>; although the Sudarium has much less resemblance [to the divine than Laura has to the poet's ideal].

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ *Moves the little old man, gray and white.* Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, just as he did in the preceding <term>sonnet <gloss>a 14-line poem</gloss></term> regarding his departure from Avignon, so in his return he did this other one, returning to Avignon. And he makes a comparison of his desire to the desire of one who goes to Rome to see the Holy Face and the Veronica, given with great devotion; thus he speaks of himself toward his lady as if she were a divine thing. Note that he says "little old man": because there is greater religious devotion in the old than in the young <note>original: "quia maior est religio in senibus quam i iuuenibus"</note>. *So, weary, sometimes:* he concludes for his purpose.

<margin>Francesco</margin>
¶ *Bitter tears rain down:* it can be clearly understood that the sonnets and moral songs were not written by Petrarch in the order in which they are found; because after returning to Italy from Avignon (whence he would never return to that country again, out of disdain because the Pope held his sister <note>Referring to a historical rumor that Petrarch's sister, Selvaggia, was a mistress to the Pope in Avignon</note>), we see clearly at the present 15th sonnet, and many others, that they were made in Avignon. Therefore, following the order I find, I say that lovers have little difference from the mindless and the mad; which our poet aptly demonstrates at present, being fiercely inflamed for Madonna Laura. When he saw her either laughing or turning her eyes toward him with a joyful gaze, he was always comforted, thereby adding wood to the fire; but seeing the contrary, he was entirely troubled with sighs and tears, thinking various fantasies and signs. Thus he begins: *Bitter tears rain from my face* with an anguished wind of sighs: they proceed from the bursting of the heart when it is burdened with too much...

### SONNET, XVI.

When I am entirely turned toward that part,
Where the beautiful face of my Lady shines;
And there remains in my thought the light,
Which burns and destroys me within, part by part;
**I**, who fear for my heart, which splits from me,
And see the end of my light <note>Original: "luce" - here meaning both the lady's eyes and the poet's life/vision</note> approaching;
Go away from her like a blind man without light:
Who knows not where he goes, and yet departs:
**S**o before the blows of death
I flee; but not so swiftly that desire
Does not come with me as it is wont to come.
**S**ilent I go; for dead words
Would make the people weep. And I desire
That my tears may be shed alone.

**Anto. M** <note>Likely a reference to a specific editor or commentator, possibly Antonio Mezzabarba</note>
</margin>

¶ **WHEN** I am entirely. This sixteenth Sonnet has a very good continuity with the preceding one: because having shown in that one how much fire and passion the smile and sweet gaze of the beloved lady ignited in his heart—and though at first appearance it seemed to offer some rest and refreshment—now similarly he says that the more he turns toward that place where she, being there, seems to shine through beauty, the more the thought of her destroys him entirely; so much so that through too much loving, his heart splits and he expects to die. Therefore, wishing to find a remedy for such great anxiety, he forces himself not to look at her so that he might be less inflamed. But he demonstrates that this is not enough, for he was already so captured by love that through the habit he had formed, nothing helped him; but being silent, he was entirely consumed. Which he inserts sweetly in this way, using those same words in different meanings. **WHEN** I am entirely: with my thought and my face turned toward that part. That beautiful face of M. L. <note>Madonna Laura</note> Shines: it shines out among other women because of her marvelous beauty and above all because of her lovely and graceful eyes. **AND** there remained in my thought the light: her lucid gaze. Which burns and destroys me: from too much loving, within the heart, part by part, following the various parts or powers of the soul. **I** who fear for my heart which splits from me: it divides itself from me due to too much distress. **AND** I see the end of my light: [I see] that the end of my life is near because of such pain, and I shall lose my life. **I** go away from her: to see if not looking at her might help me. Without light of reason and intellect, in the manner of a blind man: as the blind man, for lacking the light of physical eyes, knows not where he goes; so everyone conquered by passion—because they lack the mental light—knows not what they do or say. And persevering in the metaphor of the blind man...

¶ **THERE ARE animals.** Petrarch, for a long time before this 17th sonnet, could not be understood as an experienced hunter in the arena of love; because being much in love with My Lady Laura and being a hidden participant, he knew how to lead her into his nets, but only by loving her did he burn for her with desire. He had so little practical experience that he knew neither how to take nor to ask for that which would extinguish the fire in which he burned; these things he shows through a similitude of the bat and the moth, as will be manifested in the explanation of the sonnet. **THERE ARE** some animals in the world of noble sight: so high and sharp that they defend themselves against the sun, against the solar rays; as we see the eagle to be, whose sight is so sharp and strong and firm by its hot, dry, and <term>nervous nature</term> <note>In medieval physiology, "nervous" referred to the strength and sensitivity of the physical nerves connecting the eye to the brain</note> that looking straight at the solar body it is not dis-

And also the vulture has such sharp sight that, being very high in the air and many miles distant, it sees the fish far below the water of the sea, toward which it suddenly leads itself with admirable flight to seize it. Then he posits a second species of animals contrary to this: and says others do not come out of the place where they dwell except toward evening, and gives the reason for this: because the great light of the sun offends <note>In this context, "offends" means to physically hurt or damage the eyes</note> their sight, like the <term>bat</term> <note>original: "vespertilione"</note>; which, having very weak sight, cannot tolerate the light of the sun by day. <margin>O</margin>
¶ And he adds lastly the third species of animals, both similar and dissimilar to the two aforementioned species in this manner. And other animals experience the other power—that is, the power of fire—that burns. And this happens **with foolish desire**: they return and he shows what their desire is. Because they hope perhaps—by chance—to have joy and pleasure in the fire; he shows the cause that induces such animals: **because it shines**, that is, out of respect for the splendor of said fire. These are the moths which, having seen the light of a candle or a lamp at night, delighting in that splendor, fly around it and leave there their wings and often their lives. Some might understand this as the salamander, which flies to throw itself into the fire and the flames flee from it; and if the coals are touched by it, they are immediately extinguished, so that the salamander receives no harm from the fire, but rather its <term>satiety</term> <note>meaning its physical well-being or fulfillment</note> gains utility from the heat. We must therefore understand this as the moth, which is seen to be touched also by Dante when he says:

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Sonnet 17, focusing on the metaphor of the moth, before transitioning to the text and commentary of Sonnet 18. The previous page established the three types of animals—the eagle, the bat, and those with weak eyes—used to describe the poet's reaction to the "light" of his lady, Laura.</meta>

After these three species of animals, he returns to his own quality, saying that he is similar neither to the eagle that gazes fixedly at the sun, nor to the bat <note>original: "vespertiliõe"</note> that flees it: but to the moth: because just as the moth, through its imprudence, burns itself in the fire, so too does he burn with love because he does not know how to guide himself in his enamored state. And therefore, adapting the similitude, he says: **ALAS, I leave and place my position in this last rank** and order of the moths, and he assigns the cause: **FOR I am not strong enough to endure the light** and the eyes; and I gaze upon the radiance of this lady, My Lady Laura, just as the eagle is strong toward the light and the splendor of the solar rays—by which it is shown that the lover lacks the spirit. **And I do not know how to make shields for my defense** as the owl <note>original: "Barbã"; likely referring to the *barbagianni* or barn owl</note> does; rather, at a late hour, just as the bat <note>original: "vespertilione"</note> does. And from this he concludes the similitude of the moth for this reason: **MY destiny**, my fixed destination, leads me to see her. With my tearful, infirm, and weak eyes, I do not know how to do what I ought, neither by day in the likeness of the eagle, nor by night in the likeness of the bat—that is to say, neither openly nor secretly. **AND I well know that I go after**—following that beautiful face and the flashing gaze of My Lady Laura, which burns me because I love her too much, just as the fire does to the foolish moth.

<margin>Before.</margin>
**THERE ARE animals in the world of such a noble sort.** Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> recounts that there are some animals that have such strong vision that they radiate in the sun like the eagle, and others, unable to look at the sun, go out at night like the little owl <note>original: "noctula"</note>, and others who take delight in seeing the sun but cannot suffer it; and he says he is similar to these who do not wait for the light: and therefore when he goes to see his lady, he always goes to see her weeping, for he considers her to be his light. **I leave my place in this last rank:** that is, on earth.

**ASHAMED sometimes:** Since in the previous sonnet our Poet was shown to have no courage to follow his amorous war either openly or secretly, but that he only burned and consumed himself within himself, he now responds in the present 18th Sonnet to what might be an objection: namely, that if the beloved lady is a thing of such beauty as he seems to want to signify, why has he not made some singular work of her both in vernacular rhyme or in literary verses? Wishing to reasonably remove such an opposition and cast it entirely to the ground, he says this proceeds from the height and gravity of the subject matter, for which he does not find himself sufficient, neither regarding the invention <note>the "inventio," or the finding of ideas</note> nor the polished and elegant style. This is offered with singular praise for My Lady Laura in this manner: **ASHAMED:** I, sometimes, even though until now your beauty, O Lady, is silent through me in vernacular rhyme, I return, wishing from the very beginning to start writing of you and your beauty. **TO THE TIME when I first saw you:** which was on Good Friday <note>original: "venerdi scõ"</note>; and I saw you so graceful and beautiful. **THAT no other lady will ever be:** or will ever exist, who pleases me. **BUT wishing now no longer to be silent, I find a weight** regarding the intent of such material. **NOT for my arms:** for I do not feel myself powerful enough for it. **Nor a work to be polished with my file.** The tongue, as far as it is adorned with eloquence <note><term>elocutiõe</term>: the art of stylistic expression and choosing the right words</note>. **THEREFORE the intellect that gauges its strength:** becomes entirely frozen in the passion of wishing to speak of your beauty. And he proves this to be true by the experience he has had, saying: **I opened my lips many times** to speak of your beauty. **THEN my voice remained in the middle of my breast:** and he shows this to be a wonder with respect to the greatness and the excellence of the matter in this way: **BUT what sound:** what metrical eloquence could ever rise as high as your beauty deserves? And this is understood regarding speaking in rhymes; then he adds in literary verses...

<margin>Antonio da Tempo</margin>
**BEING ASHAMED** at times that he is still silent: the author says, Master Francesco tells his lady that every time he wishes to write of her, he returns to the first day he saw her so beautiful; because of which he finds the matter very excellent and of great weight for him, and many other times when he wanted to write of her, he was immediately overcome, his pen fell, and his intellect failed him.

<margin>Francesco Filelfo</margin>
**A THOUSAND** times: Few other things among mortals are found that clothe our wit as much as the flaming arrows of love. Although this could be shown to us through infinite examples and even reasons, the cleverness and prudence used in the present nineteenth sonnet by our aforementioned poet [is notable]. Since it seemed to him that he was sowing in sand and that neither in deeds nor in words was his love returned by My Lady Laura, he made a demonstration of loving another young woman, looking upon her amorously with his eyes; and she too, by her art in looking back at him with joyful eyes, did not show herself to be wild <note>The commentator suggests Petrarch used a "screen lady" to test Laura's feelings.</note>. When this reached the ears of My Lady Laura, and after she began to taste whether it were so, it seemed to her to be the truth of what she had first heard. She could not help but be somewhat troubled in her soul, as one who—although perhaps having no intention of consenting to Petrarch—nevertheless, according to the common law and vanity of women, did not dislike being courted and loved. Having noticed this thing, Petrarch—just as he had first imagined would follow—writes the present Sonnet to his beloved My Lady Laura. There, demonstrating that his whole heart is directed toward her and not toward any other, and astutely turning the truth, he advises her that another woman loves him, but that he disdains to love her just as My Lady Laura disdains to love him, as a thing low and unworthy of himself. He cautiously comforts her, saying that just as he drives his heart away from the love of any other woman for love of her, so she should be kind in receiving it into her grace, so that it does not lose its way from her as from its natural course. Should that follow, it would seem a fault to both: to him for inconstancy and impatience, and to her for capriciousness and stubbornness. And he would give even more blame to her, as she might have been ungrateful in not wanting to help him more than himself. Because the sonnet is quite clear in itself, I will not extend myself in further talk regarding the literal exposition, neither here nor elsewhere, except where there may be some doubt.

To every animal that dwells on earth,
Except for a few that hate the sun,
It is time to labor while it is day;
But after the sky lights its stars:
Some return home, and some nestle in the woods
To have rest at least until the dawn.
<note>Initial 'E' missing or cut off</note> And I, from the moment the beautiful dawn begins
To shake the shadows from around the earth,
Waking the animals in every wood,
Have no truce from sighs with the sun:
Then when I see the stars flaming,
I go weeping and desiring the day.
When the evening drives away the clear day,
And our darkness makes dawn for others:
I gaze pensively at the cruel stars,
Which have made me of sensitive earth:
And I curse the day that I saw the sun,
Which makes me in appearance a man nurtured in the wood.
I do not believe there ever grazed in a wood
So harsh a beast, either by night or by day,
As she for whom I weep in shadow and in sun;
And I am not tired by first sleep or by dawn;
For although I am a mortal body of earth:
Lo! my firm destiny comes from the stars.
Before I return to you, shining stars,
Or return down into the amorous wood,
Leaving my body, which shall be ground earth,
If I could see in her pity, which in a single day
Can restore many years; before the dawn
She could enrich me from the setting of the sun.
With her might I be from when the sun departs,
And no one see us but the stars,
Only one night; and may the dawn never come!

He then demonstrates his only desire, which is solely to be able, sometime before he dies, to find pity in the cruel Lady Laura. <sig>S</sig> ¶ We will note a few things briefly, and let this be the end: Petrarch says he is "made of sensitive earth" <note>original: "sensibile terra"</note> by the stars. That is, he is made sensitive in terms of the soul, and made of earth in terms of the body, which does not feel by itself, but through the power of the soul. This is not a Christian opinion, but a Platonic one; for Plato, following Pythagoras, held the opinion that souls were not created at the moment they descended into bodies, but that they were eternal, like the stars we see in heaven. From there, by divine will, they descended into the body created from our seed in the woman's womb. This soul vivified the body and made it sensitive. As long as a man lived virtuously in this life, his soul—once the allotted span of this life was finished, either in the body (if no other accident occurred) or out of the body (if it left before the due time by accidental or violent death)—would return to its original celestial place. Petrarch touches on this later where he says: BEFORE I return to you, shining stars. But if one had lived not according to reason, but according to passion, his soul would not return immediately to heaven, but would remain among the elements according to the quality of the sin, whether venial or mortal.

Those guilty of mortal and impious sins were punished in Tartarus, the deepest place in Hell. All others who, in sinning, had not been entirely wicked and impious, were punished in various places and with various penalties according to their sins. ¶ Lovers were punished in the manner described by Virgil in the sixth book of his *Aeneid* <note>Virgil's Aeneid, Book VI, lines 440–476</note> when he speaks with eloquence.

Recognizing therefore that Petrarch’s sin was one of lust <term>luxuria; here meaning excessive amorous passion</term> through amorous passion, he followed—as we have said—Plato and also our Platonic Virgil. Anchises looks on high and sets all apart
With clear order he first explains the heavens
And the earth, speaking of every part
And then the Elysian fields; and with his veil
The luminous lunar globe and of the sun
The resplendent stars, and without zeal
An inner nourishing spirit rules the whole
Worldly mass, infused through the limbs;

As long as they are not slowed by bodily error
Nor by earthly and mortal limbs
Dulled so that the soul loses its value.

Hence they have joy and pain

God calls all these souls, now cleansed,

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch's philosophical views regarding the soul, transitioning from the Virgil-inspired "amorous forest" to a critique of Petrarch's Platonic reasoning. It concludes the previous discussion and introduces the fourth major song (Canzone IIII) of the collection.</meta>

<meta>catchword: displeasure</meta>

naturally, some inclination toward virtue or vice is not by itself sufficient to make us good or even wicked; rather, habit and practice generate and preserve the habit of virtue in us, and similarly destroy it. And if anyone, persevering in the Platonic opinion mentioned above regarding the eternity of the soul, wished to say that the soul is divided into three parts—reason, concupiscence <term>concupiscentia; the faculty of desire</term>, and irascibility <term>iracundia; the faculty of anger or spiritedness</term>—since the soul is immortal, then according to this view Petrarch said that he never grew tired, neither in the evening nor in the morning. For although he was mortal in body, as a thing of the earth, his desire was nonetheless an immortal thing, being part of the soul which is immortal as a thing descended from heaven and from the quintessence <note>the "fifth element" beyond earth, water, air, and fire, believed to make up celestial bodies</note> from which all souls universally come. 

To this we can respond that even granting this false opinion, Petrarch’s statement would not be true; for those two parts—desire and anger—are attributed to the soul only so long as it is in the body, through the conjunction it has with it, and as things received from the body and not from heaven. But when the soul is outside the body, nothing remains but the superior and inferior reason, which is the proper celestial and divine thing. And through this reason, even while living, we possess free will so that we can trample upon and rule every other power and passion of the soul. Petrarch spoke in this part as a man in love; thus, we must hold him excused. 

**AND would not be transformed into a green wood:** he says this because of the fable explained above in the fifth sonnet regarding Apollo falling in love with Daphne, the daughter of Peneus, who was transformed into a laurel. **BUT I SHALL BE underground in a dry wood:** that is, in the place or house made of wood where the dead body is placed in the grave. **The day shall go full of tiny stars:** that is, it will sooner be the end of the world (which will be consumed by fire) than I can satisfy my desire; and this suffices for the present song.

<margin>Antonio</margin> **ANY animal that dwells on earth:** a moral sestina in which Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> shows himself to be the most unfortunate of all animals; he says that every animal has rest from the day's labors at least at night, while he remains in pain day and night. **I HAVE no truce from sighs with the sun:** as if to say, I am without rest just like the sun. **BEFORE I return to you, shining stars:** that is, before I reach the point of death. **AND WOULD NOT be transformed:** here he takes up the objection of the fable of Daphne, how she was transformed into a laurel in the arms of Apollo; and therefore he says: **AND would not be transformed into a green wood:** meaning his Lady Laura.

---

<margin>Francesco</margin> **IN the sweet time:** Petrarch intends in this fourth song to use lovely metaphors and fictions to describe almost the entire process of his amorous martyrdoms. He begins in this first stanza, in the form of an exordium <term>opening of a speech or poem</term>, to propose the things he intends to speak about, saying that he wishes first to sing through these present rhymes how he had lived free from every amorous passion in his early youth, before Love—who had not yet wished to frequent his dwelling, as if not deigning to enter such a philosophical soul—generated in him the fierce desire of such concupiscence. The beginning of this desire, though it was weak like a tender blade of grass, then grew little by little and took strength with great grief and labor. And he says he wishes to do this to vent somewhat the present fire; for in singing of such labor, the pain is usually diminished somewhat. Secondly, he says he wishes to follow the profound displeasure...

## CANZONE IIII.

> **I**n the sweet time of my early age,
> Which saw the birth, and still as if in grass,
> Of the fierce desire that grew for my own ill;
> Because by singing, grief becomes less bitter,
> I shall sing of how I lived in liberty,
> While Love was held in disdain in my dwelling;
> Then I shall follow how it grieved him
> Too deeply, and what happened to me because of it,
> By which I have become an example to many people;
> Although my harsh undoing
> Is written elsewhere, so that a thousand pens
> Are already tired of it, and in almost every valley
> Resounds the sound of my heavy sighs,
> Which grant credit to my painful life.
> And if here my memory does not aid me
> As it is wont to do, let my martyrdoms excuse it,
> And a thought that gives it only anguish.
