And makes me forget myself by force,
Holding that which is inside of me, while I [remain] the shell.

<margin>The displeasure that Love felt regarding the poet's freedom; and what happened to him as a result of such displeasure and disdain from Love, insofar as he was transformed into various things until he was made one.</margin>

A public example to many people. Although this harsh foolishness of his has been written by himself in many other songs, sonnets, epistles, and other works of his, so that not only the cities and the great courts, but almost every valley resounds with those very heavy sighs, through which one can easily believe his life to be afflicted by great pain through love. And so that others would not believe he had made the matter much greater than it actually was, he demonstrates the contrary: that because he had forgotten himself, he says much less than what truly was. Therefore, he shows it proceeds from the greatest torments he has in his heart, and that constant thinking he does of his beloved Madonna Laura, whose anguish allows him to think of nothing else, so that by force he almost forgets himself. And he declares that thought to be such that it has taken his heart and soul, and nothing has remained to him but the shell <note>the outer physical body as opposed to the internal soul</note> of his person.

<margin>Antonio <note>Refers to Antonio da Tempo, a 14th-century judge and poet who wrote an early commentary on Petrarch</note></margin>

# IN THE SWEET time of my first age
In this moral song, Master Francesco writes in how many strange forms he has come into the love of Madonna Laura. And first, he makes a prologue of what he means to say, saying "in the sweet time"—by which he means in the springtime, or perhaps in adolescence, in which he was fit for loving. Wherefore Master Francesco says in a verse of his that he writes in an epistle to Barbatus <note>Barbato da Sulmona, a close friend of Petrarch</note> concerning his love:

> That boy <note>Cupid</note> gave me, a boy, a wound with his point. <note>original: "Ille puer puero fecit mihi cuspide vulnus."</note>

<margin>Francesco Z. <note>likely Francesco Zabarella, a contemporary scholar</note></margin>
<margin>I SAY THAT From here he begins, after the aforementioned introduction, to narrate the beginning and process of his amorous thoughts, saying that many years had already passed before he ever knew how much the forces of love could do; and having already entered so far into amorous thoughts that his skin and even his hair seemed more like something other than a youth's; and having until that day persevered in such a way in an honest and continent life, habituated in chastity, so that as cold thoughts—enemies to concupiscence <term>concupiscientia; the faculty of worldly desire</term>—had made a glaze of diamonds and a very hard pavement around his heart, which in no way allowed him to slacken in such passion. Wherefore, neither did tears bathe him as they do lovers, nor for such reason was his sleep broken; he was even so alienated from such passion that it seemed a miracle to him when he heard of such troubles. He was in such a secure state when he was assaulted by Love that, as he later declares below, he could not defend himself nor prevail; but as he says to make the reader more attentive, he says through a beautiful comparison: "Alas, what am I? Now in love with such anxieties in this wretched servitude, compared to what I was when I was free and without such anguish." And he adds a saying of Solon the Athenian told to Croesus, King of Lydia, who, considering himself happy, was told by Solon that human happiness could not be judged until death, though it could be well [praised]</margin>

### SECOND STANZA

I say that from the day when the first assault
Love gave me, many years had passed;
So that I was changing my youthful appearance;
And around my heart frozen thoughts
Had made an almost adamantine <term>adamantino; diamond-like or unbreakable</term> glaze,
Which did not allow the hard affection to slacken.
Tears did not yet bathe my breast
Nor break my sleep; and that which was not in me
Seemed a miracle in others.
Alas, what am I? What was I?
The end praises the life, and the evening the day.
For that cruel one of whom I speak, feeling
That until then, even struck by his arrow,
I had not been pierced beyond the garment,
Took as his guide a powerful lady;
Against whom little ever availed me, or avails,
Wit, or strength, or asking for pardon.
The two of them transformed me into what I am,
Making me, from a living man, a green laurel;
Which in the cold season loses no leaf.

<summary>This page introduces the famous "Metamorphoses" canzone, where Petrarch describes his initial resistance to Love and his subsequent transformation. The commentary explains his transition from a state of chaste, "diamond-like" indifference to a total loss of self upon meeting Laura.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Petrarch's "Canzone 23," specifically detailing the various mythological transformations the poet undergoes—from a laurel tree to a swan, a stone, and a stag—as metaphors for his suffering and obsession with Laura.</meta>

...one could say that this man was either happy or miserable; a similar thing is said of the day, that in the evening one can say: "Today was a beautiful day," or the contrary. This means that a similar fate befell him, that after living so many years continently <note>original: "ꝑtinẽ" (pertinente/continente), referring to Petrarch's life before falling in love</note>, he finally fell so fiercely in love. This fact reveals the most excellent beauty of that lady, against whose amorous arrows no accustomed virtue was of any use. And therefore it is well added that, hearing that cruel Love with his arrows had made no wound on our poet—even though it had barely passed through his clothing—every movement of his regarding such a passion was very weak and without any heavy weight of concupiscence <note>desire or lust</note> in the company of his beloved Madonna Laura. Her power was such that against her, neither cunning, nor strength, nor humility could ever prevail—which are those three things through which, or at least through one of them, one usually seeks to obtain what they want in this life. And finally, he shows his first transformation, which he says was into a green Laurel, which keeps its leaves not only in summer but also in winter. This is drawn from the fable of Daphne, daughter of Peneus, who was converted into a laurel, as is narrated at length in the 5th sonnet. This demonstrates that his love was without the corruption of the flesh, however much it often grieved him; and as we have said, when Master Francesco fell in love, he was no longer a mere boy, but well advanced in his age. Nor should we wonder that he said at the beginning, "the sweet time of my first age," for he refers to all that time that had passed until the day he fell in love, which was "sweet" insofar as he had never before felt such anguish. This can be clearly understood in the words of the present second stanza.

<margin>Antonio <note>Antonio da Tempo, the commentator</note></margin>
**I SAY THAT from the day of the first assault.** Here Master Francesco says that before he fell in love with Madonna Laura, he had already been assaulted [by Love], as he mentions above in the second sonnet. At that time, he could not close [his heart], and this love seemed a strange thing to him, even in others. And seeing this, Love **TOOK** as his escort a powerful lady—that is, Madonna Laura—whom he could not contradict. And so Love and she transformed him into a green laurel, where he says: "Making me from a living man into a green laurel," out of respect for the name of his beloved <note>Laura's name plays on "Lauro," the Italian word for laurel</note>, which seemed to him to be fixed in his heart.

**NOT of Peneus: but of a more noble river;** that is, of power, above which river she was born. Wherefore he, out of love for her, went to dwell and stayed there continuously; therefore he says: **To become two roots; WHEREFORE I took on the color of a swan;** this is the nature of the swan, to walk along the banks and never rise high from the ground. **THEN I saw her again in another dress, alone;** this shows how Laura transformed herself and asked him if he loved Madonna Laura, and he told the truth. Whereupon, returning into herself, she changed him into a stone <note>original: "Saxo"</note>. And this often happens to lovers: to find themselves at times so dismayed that they remain like marble. Just as Medusa did, who changed into stone anyone who looked at her, speaking poetically. And if this is said of her, it was because of her great beauty. And for this reason, Master Francesco says that being a stone, if she returns him to his first state, he will never complain again. And he calls for her to return to making him weep. **WHEREFORE I cried out with paper and ink;** speaking in such a way: **THROUGH me, tired, upon the grass one day;** this shows how she fled from the prayers he made to her, so he returned to praying. **AND MAKE me a fountain at the foot of a beech tree;** he feigns being changed into a fountain to give the understanding that he did nothing but weep. **THE SOUL which alone was made noble by God;** he says this because of the loss of Madonna Laura. **AFTER Madonna Laura, moved by pity.** He says he had endured as much pain as was sufficient for his sin, as much as any good man ever did. **BUT let no wise man trust anything in the world;** He feigns still to be changed into flint <note>original: "silice"</note>, which is a fiery stone, to give the understanding that he remained burning and set on fire by the love of this Madonna Laura as before. And the poet Master Francesco says that in this changing into flint—that is <note>original: "hoc est"</note>, being so inflamed—he called for death to take him from this pain, to demonstrate that this love was of too much fire. **THAT one day while hunting.** He describes for his purpose the story of Actaeon, who, while watching Diana who was naked in a fountain, she threw water in his face and changed him into a stag, and thus he was torn apart by his own dogs, as Ovid says in the third [book] of the *Metamorphoses*. Thus Master Francesco, having seen his Madonna Laura in a fountain, naked as he says here—and because she felt shame that Master Francesco had seen her naked—he feigns being changed into a stag because he led a very solitary and wandering life, where he fled from all his friends. **SONG, I was not;** Master Francesco speaks to his song and touches upon a fable of how Jove rained down in the form of golden drops into the lap of Danaë, with whom he was in love. Ovid, book three of the *Metamorphoses*. And note that this above-mentioned commentary by Master Antonio da Tempo contains all these stanzas starting from that verse: **I Say that from the day of the first assault,** until that stanza that begins: **SONG, I was never that cloud of gold. WHICH then descended, etc.**

# STANZA III.

<margin>
WHAT I became. He continues with a pleasant ornament of words the transformation of himself into the laurel <note>The Italian text says "into Laura," a common pun in Petrarchan commentary conflating the lady with the laurel tree (Lauro)</note>: which, because it is clear in itself, needs no other note except that the river mentioned is called the **Sorgue** <note>original: "la Sorga"</note> and is located at the small village near Avignon where Madonna Laura was from. **The two roots** into which his feet were converted are understood as the two sources or the two springs from which the said river emerges. **THE TWO branches** into which his arms change: it is understood because the said river divides itself into two parts, hence when he says: **NOR yet does it freeze me.**

  *Nor yet does it freeze me*

<margin>
He touches upon a second transformation, how he, in the likeness of the King of the Ligurians <note>Cycnus, who was turned into a swan while mourning Phaethon</note>, was converted into a swan. We should therefore briefly note this fable: **Phaethon**, son of **Apollo** and **Clymene** (the wife of Merops), being there reproved in indignation by another boy named **Epaphus** (son of Jove and Io), who claimed that Phaethon was not the son of Apollo and that his mother deceived him because he was not born of such a great father; Phaethon, ashamed by such insulting words, first returned to his mother Clymene and...

  *The being covered then with white feathers*
  *At that time; when struck by lightning and dead lay*
  *My hope, which was mounting too high,*
  *For because I did not know where, nor when*
  *I might find it again; alone weeping,*
  *Where it was taken from me, day and night I went*
  *Searching from the bank and within the waters,*
  *And never then did my tongue fall silent,*
  *While it could [speak] of its malignant fall*
  *Whence I took, with my sound, the color of a swan.*

...with flattering words begged for the truth: since he heard from her by oath that **Apollo** was his father, in order to be better certified of this, he set out toward **Ethiopia** to the furthest East, going to the sea of the sun, his aforementioned father called otherwise Apollo. Having found him in the most splendid seat with the crown on his head, at first because of the excessive brightness he could not gaze upon him with fixed eyes; then, the sun noticing this, he took the crown from his head so as not to project so much splendor. Having made the boy come to him, he embraced him and, seeing him with paternal charity, asked him the reason for his coming. Having heard the story in detail, he replied that certainly he was his son and that his mother Clymene had told him the truth; and so that he should not doubt such a thing, he comforted him by telling him to ask for any grace he wished as a certainty of this, and he would grant it, binding himself of his own will with the oath of the **Stygian marsh** <note>The River Styx</note> of the underworld, which was irrevocable even to the gods. 

Then Phaethon, without thinking further like an inconsiderate boy eager for honor not worthy of himself, asked that he would grant him for one day the governance of his chariot with the four horses called **Pyroeis, Eous, Aethon, and Phlegon** (or otherwise Philezen), so named according to the qualities of the four parts of the day. Which request, although it was most sad to the sun, seeing the manifest destruction of Phaethon, after he had comforted him in vain with many persuasions that he should not wish to use such a favor, he gave the chariot and horses into his liberty. 

Phaethon, having then climbed into the chariot, was diligently instructed by his father about the whole path, and when he should follow it and what he should guard against; he directed the fierce and disobedient horses to the path, exiting from the eastern ocean toward the height of the sky. And although he, as a boy and unskilled, was not esteemed by the horses from the first moment either for weight or for knowing how to govern, yet in the ascent through the height of the difficult path he received no other harm. But after he had arrived on the plain of the highest sky, both through looking down at the deepest earth and through the headlong running of the most fierce horses, all pale with fear, he began to tremble in such a way that he could hardly hold the reins in his hand. Suddenly, when he reached the place of the Zodiac where the **Scorpion** was, fierce in its terrible aspect and form...

<summary>This page describes Petrarch's first two metaphorical transformations: first into a laurel tree (associating his love for Laura with the myth of Daphne) and second into a swan (mourning his "fallen" hopes like Cycnus mourning Phaethon). The commentary provides an extensive retelling of the myth of Phaethon to explain the poet's imagery of "mounting too high" and his subsequent "fall."</summary>

<sig>C</sig>

<margin>A</margin>
...frightened by the poisonous tail <note>A reference to the constellation Scorpio, which terrified Phaethon in the heavens</note>, then out of intolerable fear, as if he had lost his very self, he abandoned the reins; and he nearly fell from the chariot himself, overturned headlong. Once this was felt, the horses, as if now entirely free, immediately began—following the fierce impulse that spurred them—to run to the ultimate heights of the celestial spheres: now down below the moon and the places near the earth; now toward the north; now toward the mid-day <note>The south</note>; and now turning toward the west; now returning toward the east with sudden velocity. In such a manner, without any order or reason, they threw themselves here and there with hasty and headlong flight, so that all the elements began to burn from the sun’s heat. And not only the highest mountains, but also the plains and the lowest valleys, and even further, the rivers and the seas, together with the fish and all other animals, were all burning. Because of this, Tellus <note>The Roman goddess of the Earth</note>, the Goddess of the entire world, from deep within her palace at the center of the earth, already feeling the immeasurable heat of the solar flames, emerged somewhat at her own greatest peril. Putting her head out and placing her hands to her forehead so that she would not be harmed by the great blast and heat—after she saw everything burning—with the most bitter sighs and greatest anguish, she lamented to Jove <note>Jupiter, the King of the Gods</note> in this manner:

It serves as a commentary on the destructive power of uncontrolled passion, a theme central to the surrounding Petrarchan analysis.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the mythological narrative from page 23, where the goddess Tellus (Earth) pleaded with Jove (Jupiter) to intervene before the sun's chariot, driven by the inexperienced Phaethon, consumed the world in flames.</meta>

<page-num>24</page-num>
<sig>E</sig>

¶ These words, spoken with the greatest distress and even peril due to the many and horrible flames that overwhelmed her from every side, Goddess Tellus <note>The Roman personification of the Earth</note> withdrew her head as quickly as possible into the deepest parts of the earth. But Jove, seeing the manifest danger and moved by her words, demonstrated the total destruction and ruin of the entire world to all the gods and even to Apollo himself: if he did not immediately remedy such a great slaughter. As soon as he had ascended to the highest point of heaven—seeing that he could no longer find help from the dense clouds, which were already entirely dried up by the fire—he took his accustomed thunderous weapons and, thundering most harshly, threw a terrible lightning bolt at the head of Phaethon <note>The son of Apollo who attempted to drive the solar chariot</note>. Phaethon, already completely dazed and having lost his senses, was weeping loudly. Struck by this bolt, Phaethon fell suddenly head-over-heels, dead, from the great, overflowing, and burning chariot. Furthermore, the horses, out of great terror and the crash of the lightning-whirlwind—greatly frightened, stunned, and beaten—cast the yoke from their necks, broke their reins, and tumbled here and there. But Phaethon, thus wounded and dead, carried by the turbulent lightning to a distant part of the opposite world, fell, still flaming and burning, into the Po <note>The major river of northern Italy</note> in Lombardy; his body was finally found by the Naiads <note>Water nymphs</note> and was honorably buried by them. Apollo, his father, covered his face out of great grief and remained hidden for an entire day with bitter weeping, without providing the accustomed light to the universe—though in his place, the aforementioned fires of the disaster sufficed. ¶ His mother Clymene, together with her daughters, came from the direction of Ethiopia all the way to Lombardy. Once she found the tomb of her dead son, she stretched herself over it, weeping intensely. But even greater was the weeping of the daughters <note>The Heliades, sisters of Phaethon</note>, who for four months at the said tomb beat themselves with cruel shrieks. Finally, the eldest of them, named Phaethusa, while she was thus weeping, lamented that her feet had stiffened in such a way that she could no longer feel them. While her fair sister Lampetusa strove to come to her aid, she was stopped against her own will, as her feet had miraculously sent roots into the earth. The third sister, wanting to tear her shining hair with her hands, found leaves on her head instead. In almost the same moment, all seven of them—who were lovely and graceful girls—while trying to help one another with laments and mourning their present misfortune, were changed into very tall trees called by some *Oppi* <note>original: "Oppi"; likely field maples or a regional name for a type of poplar</note> and by others poplars. And because, while transforming, they continued to cry and call for their father's help, all those tears distilling from their eyes were hardened by the sun upon the branches and changed into amber, similar to that which has come down from there and is used by the women of Milan and Lombardy in this very time. ¶ Cycnus, King of the Ligurians and son of Sthenelus—who had a familial connection to Clymene—having heard of the atrocious death of the lightning-struck Phaethon, left his empire and came to the banks of the Po with bitter weeping, grieving over the event and cursing the unjust cruelty of Jove. He persevered so much in this bitterness of soul that his voice, from too much shouting, began to diminish and become thinner; his grey hairs transformed into white feathers, and his neck, thinned by too much melancholy, became very long. His arms changed into well-feathered wings, and finally, he turned into a water bird called a Swan <note>Cygnus</note>, named after himself. Out of fear of the lightning fire which he remembers killed Phaethon, he does not fly high but is constantly found near the water where he can defend himself from fire. Therefore, Petrarch <note>The famous Italian poet Francesco Petrarca</note> introduces this fable to represent the quality of his love: that he, similar to Phaethon, hoped for a lady higher than his merits <note>Madonna Laura, Petrarch's muse</note>, by whose love he is constantly deluded and falls low. And finally, what happened to the King of the Ligurians has happened to him: first, as the swan is always near the Sorgue <note>original: "Sorga"; the river in Vaucluse where Petrarch lived</note> for the love of Lady Laura; second, just as the swan is always covered in white feathers, so he has become grey-haired <note>original: "canuto"</note> from melancholy. Third, as the swan has a querulous and lamenting voice, so he does in his sonnets and songs, where he always complains and laments. And it is said that the swan has a louder and sweeter voice at the point of death than at other times; the philosophers say this occurs because at that moment all the vital spirits are gathered at the heart to comfort it, and thus, coming out together through the curved and long neck, they make a more resonant and sweeter sound.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s "Canzoniere" 23. The previous page concluded the transformation of the sisters of Phaethon into poplars and his cousin Cycnus into a swan. This page transitions from the mythological prologue into the poet’s personal experience of love and his own metaphorical transformations.</meta>

G **AND THUS ALONG THE BITTER.** <note>original: "E COSSI longo l'amate." The commentator likely misread the poem's "amare" (bitter) as "amate" (beloved).</note> Just as in the preceding stanza he dealt with the laurel <note>A reference to the transformation of Daphne into a laurel tree, symbolizing Petrarch’s beloved, Laura</note>, so in this present fourth stanza he continues the aforementioned transformation of himself into a swan. He signifies quite clearly his habit of often walking along the banks of the Sorgue <note>The river in Vaucluse, France, near Petrarch's home</note> to gaze longingly at Lady Laura, acting like the swan by casting toward her amorous words with the sweetest murmurs. We can also quite clearly understand here how his affair proceeded: that is, from the beginning Lady Laura looked at him with a modest and sweet face, as she had not yet realized that Master Francis <note>Francesco Petrarcha, the poet</note> was staring at her with any act of carnal lust. Master Francis, seeing himself being looked upon, led himself to believe that she was enamored with his long scholarly robes and his hood. Because of this, he moved forward more boldly and began to openly manifest his desire to her with signs and words, though he did not dare this without fear. Having heard this, she—as a worthy and modest woman—reproached him for his foolishness. Therefore, he concludes that because of this event, he was turned by her from a living man into nothing other than a stone, in that he was struck senseless by the words he heard.

## STANZA IV

> **T**hus along the bitter banks I went;
> That wishing to speak, I sang forever,

H **SHE SPOKE.** This continues the transformation described at the end of the previous stanza. Here he demonstrates how much Lady Laura was disturbed when she noticed his presumption in seeking to "wrestle" with her <note>A euphemism for sexual advances</note>. He touches upon the words spoken by her to him: namely, that she was not who he believed her to be. Perhaps she would not have said this if Master Francis had left behind his scholarly preambles and come to the facts; for women, even if they have unbridled desire, wish to appear as though such things are taken by force so that they may be esteemed as virtuous. Because Master Petrarch was much more practiced among books than in the <term>battles of Venus</term> <note>A classical metaphor for sexual intercourse</note>, he remained dismayed by such talk. He did not dare to do more than sigh and let himself be considered a <term>simpleton</term> <note>original: "moccicone," literally a "snot-nosed" fool or an idiot</note>, while she declared nonetheless that it would be more damaging to her than to him.

> **I** well believed that in her eyes

> And yet I speak of things manifest and well known.

<margin>Because for him: because he belonged more to her than to himself: and thus he clearly shows us that he would have willingly left "letters" <note>original: "lettere," referring to his scholarly pursuits</note> to use the "litter" <note>original: "letiere," a bed or carriage, implying he would trade his studies for physical intimacy</note>.</margin>

<sig>I</sig>
<margin>Francis</margin>
**C** I WELL believed: Now Petrarch, wondering to himself from whence it proceeded that Lady Laura, having heard his amorous request, was so bitterly troubled: says that in his opinion the cause was because in praying he humbled himself too much. This sentiment is drawn from the tragedy of Marcus Annaeus Seneca <note>The Roman philosopher and playwright; the quote is from his play *Phaedra*</note> where he says that he who prays timidly teaches how to deny <note>original: "qui timide rogat docet negare"</note>. Petrarch, believing that through humble speech he could acquire mercy from his beloved lady, not only did not acquire it, but was judged by her as unworthy of her grace. It seemed to her that he was a man of little worth who used timid and cowardly words when deeds were required. He says he learned this a long time afterward. He reveals that he wept so much for this error that through too many tears he was transformed into a fountain.

<margin>R. Francis</margin>
**C** THE SOUL which: It was not enough for Petrarch to have erred once through lack of skill, if he did not also demonstrate his imprudence a second time. He says, therefore, that having returned to the grace of Lady Laura—who, following the example of Christ, had inclined herself toward forgiveness—he wished to try again to see if his desire could be satisfied. Because of this, having called upon her with his usual humility for amorous consent, she was so troubled by this that she changed his punishment so that, according to the usual miracles <note>Refers to the poetic "miracles" of Ovidian metamorphosis</note>, he was transformed into a hard flint. Flint <term>silice: a hard, red stone that produces sparks when struck</term> is that red and hard stone which, when struck with a steel, sends forth sparks of fire. It is said that Battus <note>A shepherd in Greek mythology who witnessed Mercury stealing Apollo's cattle; he was turned to stone for his betrayal</note> was transformed into this stone by Mercury. This signifies the redness that appears in the faces of those who are ashamed of something they feel they have done wrong; and for this very reason, Petrarch said he became "Petrarca" <note>A play on the poet's name and the word *pietra*, meaning stone</note>.

**THE SPIRIT** : Contrary effects are all comprised within this song, because the four principal passions—joy and melancholy regarding present things (prosperous or adverse), and desire and fear regarding the future—are seen now in one place and now in another. This is quite manifest in the other stanzas. Having, therefore, recently made mention of his shame—which is the fear of infamy—which he held for many years for his presumption and boldness—which is a species of desire—he finally set aside all shame and took up his accustomed boldness. This grew even greater as he deliberated within himself to use words no longer, but if the opportunity were given to him, to want by every means to come to deeds. Therefore, while going about such a hunt, he found her one day as she was washing herself entirely naked in a fountain near the <term>Sorgue</term><note>The Sorgue is the river flowing from the Fountain of Vaucluse, where Petrarch lived.</note>, although the good lady herself felt no other heat than that of fire <note>referring to the fire of virtue or perhaps the heat of the day</note>. In whatever manner it was, <note>original: "M. Fran."</note> Master Francesco, as often tends to happen, perhaps lowering his sails <note>losing his nerve</note>, did not have the spirit to assault her; but he stood aside like a fool <note>original: "babion," literally a baboon or simpleton</note> to gaze at her, and in such a way to feed himself on wind. Then, Madonna Laura, having noticed this act, stood straight with her banner <note>original: "stendardo," likely a metaphor for her modesty or the water she used as a shield</note> between her legs and took the water with both hands and threw it in his face. At this, he, becoming like a dazed man in his flight, was transformed into a stag. This likeness is drawn from the transformation of <term>Actaeon</term><note>A hunter in Greek mythology who saw the goddess Diana bathing and was turned into a stag as punishment.</note>, which was as follows: Actaeon, son of Autonoe and grandson of Cadmus, the king and founder of Thebes, being a graceful and handsome youth, delighted in hunting above all other things. Given to this exercise, he sought to have brave dogs of every quality from all parts of the world. Having gathered a great multitude of them, he did nothing else night and day but attend to the hunt, in which he placed almost all his happiness, abandoning every other government and necessary study, not caring for any expense or other burden that might follow. But one day, having hunted much and it being midsummer with the sun most burning, he said to his servants that it was good—since they had taken many animals—to rest until the morning. This pleased everyone because of their fatigue, so they gathered the extended nets and each attended to his own pleasure. But Actaeon, who never knew how to be idle but always investigated the places where he estimated some beasts might hide, while the others satisfied their appetites in that way, set himself to walking through the great woods. There was a valley there called by the name Gargaphia, thick with very tall trees such as pines and cypresses, which was consecrated to the goddess Diana. At the edge of this was a very wooded and hidden place: a cave formed not by human art but by a natural skill, which on the right hand had a clear fountain with a flowery meadow around it. To this place the goddess Diana had just then come to rest, being also a little tired from the hunt and wishing, because of the excessive sweat...

...ready to wash herself: having given her bow and quiver to one of her nymphs, she immediately took off her shoes and stripped herself naked. Then her nymphs took up the water in certain vessels and threw it over her. ¶ And while the most chaste goddess was washing herself, Actaeon—who knew nothing of such things—went wandering along the bank through the woods and arrived, by his misfortune, at the place of this cave. As soon as the nymphs saw him entering, they beat their breasts with their hands out of fear and, crying out loudly, they covered the goddess Diana with their bodies so that Actaeon could not see her; for the goddess, just as she was of marvelous beauty, so too did she surpass the nymphs in height from the neck up. Diana, ashamed that she had been seen in such a way, became entirely crimson in the face. And although she was astonished, she nevertheless leaned to one side to avoid being seen; she even turned her face back and would have gladly had her bow in hand. But since she had nothing else, she took the water with both hands and threw it over Actaeon’s head, saying with anger:

->To have seen the goddess Diana naked,<-

Now you shall go telling, if you can:
->That to every age you shall be an example of this.<-

¶ Without any other threat used and without further delay, she transformed him into a stag. Then Actaeon, seized with fear, took to flight and ran faster than usual, so much so that he himself, not yet having realized his transformation, marveled that he was so light in his running. But as he fled in this manner, he came to a certain water, and there, stopping to drink, he saw his reflection. Understanding what had happened, he grieved immeasurably; and although he could not speak, his former intellect remained with him. Therefore, deeply afflicted within himself, he gave great groans and let out infinite sighs. He was hesitant between two choices: whether he should return to Thebes to his royal palaces, or dwell in the woods; on one side was the fear of wild beasts, on the other the shame of the citizens. But while he was thus in ambiguity, he was seen by his dogs, who, believing him to be a wild animal, all ran at him, barking fiercely. Actaeon, seeing himself in such peril and being unable to speak—though he would have gladly said to his servants, who were instigating the dogs to the prey, who he really was—took to flight. But it availed him little; for in a short space he was overtaken by his own dogs and most atrociously bitten in various places on his body. Actaeon’s servants also arrived there, and finding the stag kneeling on its front feet and moving its head here and there, asking for mercy with its eyes, they considered none of this. Instead, they continually egged on the dogs to the victory and looked around to see if by chance they might see Actaeon, their lord, in some part, so that he too might participate in the present pleasure. And they called out the name of the miserable Actaeon, who was already entirely torn apart. He made a sign with his head that it was he, wishing he were anywhere but there, seeing in others what he saw in himself. Finally, almost entirely mangled, after the dogs with their continuous biting put their muzzles right into his entrails and his heart, in such a manner was he killed by the wrath of Diana. Which would never have followed if Actaeon had held a greater concern for the government of his royal principality than for breeding beasts and feeding useless and harmful people <note>The commentator here adds a moralizing "museum label" interpretation: Actaeon's "dogs" represent the parasitic courtiers or base passions that destroy a ruler who neglects his duties for the sake of the hunt.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the various mythological transformations Petrarch undergoes. <margin>M</margin>
Or how she was, as the eagle flies above every other bird. ¶ Jove's forbidden falling in love with Danae was thus: Acrisius, king of Argos and son of Abas, having a daughter of singular beauty, was warned by the oracle that a son would be born of her by whose hands he would lose his life. Having heard this, Acrisius, wishing to prevent such a misfortune, locked his said daughter, named Danae, in a very high and strong tower; and as a guard, he placed there those most faithful to him, so that no one could have his said daughter. Once the fame of her marvelous beauty reached the ears of Jove, he immediately fell in love with her, burning within his desiring heart no differently than the flaming Mount Etna <note>original: "mongibello"</note>. For this reason, leaving the government of heaven and abandoning every other necessary care, he descended to earth to satisfy his amorous and fiery appetite. Having come to the place where the beloved girl was held locked away, he tempted the guards with humble prayers to let him enter or see the tower. When he saw that he could in no way achieve this through words, he decided to use an artifice by which he might easily deceive the guards and the guarded girl. Suddenly, having disappeared from their sight into the air with speed, and having risen without bringing other clouds, he transformed himself into a thick shower of gold. Raining in such a manner upon the bed of the well-guarded tower, he descended through the tiles into the lap of the lovely girl. She, watching that rain with great amazement and finding an unusual and supreme pleasure in the sight, not only did not move from the place where she sat, but with desire filled her lap with that rain until all that fallen gold—into which Jove had been transformed—returned to its former shape. Nor indeed was the girl upset that, after such an abundance of gold, she had a share of that thing which naturally pleases women much more than honey pleases flies, and which until that day had been forbidden to her by her suspicious father. Therefore, joining with Jove with amorous pleasure, she bore him Perseus. After Perseus had given no small demonstration of his virtue, he returned to Argos and showed his grandfather Acrisius—who did not wish to receive him—the head of Medusa, which transformed him into stone. This is what happens to those who, passing from this life, are in a state of perpetual coldness as far as the body is concerned.

<margin>IF THE HONORED: This 20th Sonnet was a response made by Petrarch while staying in Padua, a long time after the death of Lady Laura, to one Albertino Mussato <note>Albertino Mussato (1261–1329) was an early Italian statesman and poet, though the dates here suggest a historical conflation by the commentator</note>, a well-learned and eloquent man who had urged him for certain reasons to write some beautiful poem in verse. Responding to him, Petrarch says he can in no way do this because of the great distress of mind he has from the death of Lady Laura, whom he refers to under the name of the laurel <note>original: "lauro"</note>. He says that if the laurel—which cannot be struck by lightning <note>A common classical belief was that the laurel tree was immune to lightning strikes</note>—had not taken away his poetic crown (insofar as the melancholy given to him by her death was the cause of him neglecting his studies), he would have continued. These studies are given to the Muses, who are vilely abandoned by this age—and no less by this one—to attend to mechanical things and to profit. But because of that injury received from death, he says he has for a long time...</margin>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on mythological symbols, moving from the golden rain of Jove to the contest between Minerva and Neptune over the naming of Athens. ...thence was produced a green and leafy olive tree, all full of fruit. For this reason, after the matter was discussed and very diligently weighed in the council of the Areopagites <note>The high court of ancient Athens.</note>, it was judged that the miracle of Minerva ought to be preferred over the miracle of Neptune, just as peace is preferred over war. Thus, from the name of Minerva—called *Athene* in Greek—the city was named Athens; otherwise, it would have been named Posidonia from the name of Neptune, who is called *Poseidon* in Greek.

<margin>Anto. <note>Likely Antonio da Tempo, a 14th-century theorist and contemporary of Petrarch.</note></margin>
¶ IF THE HONORED Branch that protects: Master Francesco responds to someone who, according to the opinion of some, was Cardinal Colonna. The Cardinal had written to him saying he ought to write something in verse about a certain matter. Petrarch responds to him that if his coronation with the laurel had not been denied, he would have dedicated himself entirely to that most learned branch. That injury has kept him far from the inventor of the first olives: that is, from Pallas, goddess of civil sciences, who was the inventor of the olive. The laurel is said to "protect" from the wrath of heaven <note>original: "prescrivere l'ira del cielo"</note> because it is never struck by lightning from the sky. SEEK then: here Master Francesco says he should seek someone else to write, because he himself does not wish to write, being as if filled with indignation.

### SONNET XXI.

<margin>Q. Fran. <note>Likely referring to the commentator Francesco Quirinio.</note></margin>
> **L** ove was weeping, and I with him at times,
> From whom my steps were never far away;
> Observing, through bitter and strange effects,
> Your soul released from its worldly bonds.
> **N** ow that God has turned it back to the right path,
> Raising both hands with my heart to heaven,
> **I** thank Him, who benignly in His mercy
> Listens to the just prayers of humans;
> **A** nd if, returning to the life of love,
> To make you turn your back on beautiful desire,
> You found ditches and hills along the way,
> **I** t was to show how thorny is the path,
> And how alpine and hard is the ascent,
> **W** hence a man must climb to reach true valor.

¶ LOVE WEPT. Master Francesco wrote the present twenty-first sonnet to Master Cino da Pistoia <note>A famous Italian jurist and poet (c. 1270–1336) who was a friend of both Dante and Petrarch.</note>, who, having been in that age a most famous doctor of laws and very close to Petrarch, had recently departed this life and gone to heaven, according to Petrarch's view. He sends him, then, the present sonnet. I do not remember hearing who the messenger was. Directing his speech to Cino, he says that Love and he himself together, seeing that Cino's soul was dissolved and free from bodily ties, first wept for it because of the bitterness and hardship of such an end. But now that he sees the soul has gone to heaven, turned back by God to the right path, he humbly thanks God that He deigned, in His mercy, to benignly hear and grant the prayers and orations made for his soul. And because Master Cino had been a man not only in love himself, but had also done things common to his profession—for lawyers often, for money, make a "yes" out of a "no" and a "no" out of a "yes"—Petrarch adds, following the Platonic opinion <note>The idea that the soul descends from the stars and labors to return to its divine origin.</note>, that the return of the soul from this life to dwell in heaven is difficult. As I touched upon above in the third song, if in returning to the life of love and charity which he found in heaven he encountered some difficulty on the road, he should not marvel. This happened so that he would not let himself be conquered by the "beautiful desire" of worldly things. He says that all those ditches and hills show the way to go to heaven to be harsh, and likewise the climb to the blessed life is difficult and hard; and this is because virtue is most laborious to all those who are not well-habituated in it.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
¶ LOVE WEPT and I with him at times: by this, Master Francesco shows he had some promise or hope for his desire from his lady. Whence he says, "LOVE WEPT," speaking to her as a person of great cruelty who has now returned to loving him. <meta>This page transitions from the mourning of Cino da Pistoia to a thematic shift toward Petrarch’s relationship with his homeland (Florence) and his political hopes for Christendom. <margin>Fran. <note>Francesco Alunno, a 16th-century grammarian and commentator on Petrarch.</note></margin>
¶ **MORE THAN I.** <note>The opening of Sonnet 22.</note> No one fails to understand that love for one's fatherland has the greatest power. Petrarch also proves this because, although he was an exile and driven out along with his father, Ser Petracco of Ancisa, and however much he was poorly treated by his fellow citizens, he never found himself acting against his fatherland, nor did he ever rejoice in any of its adversities. On the contrary, when the Florentines were engaged in a great war against the Church while the Papal Court was in Avignon <note>The "Babylonian Captivity" of the Papacy (1309–1376).</note>, and were for this reason under interdict and excommunicated, he made a clear demonstration that this displeased him exceedingly. Thus, while that war lasted, he never rejoiced nor wrote any of his usual pleasant love poems in rhyme. Therefore, after peace was made and the Florentines were reconciled with the Church, he declares in the present twenty-second sonnet that he rejoices in this event just as sailors rejoice when they have escaped with their ship, which was in danger of being broken and submerged by the waves. Having come to safety on land, while still terrified, they kneel on the shore to thank God. Similarly, he rejoices like one who had the noose around his neck to be hanged and escaped. Thus he declares he has no less joy seeing the Florentine people having unbuckled and laid down the sword of war against his lord the Pope, who was in Avignon. Therefore, addressing all the courtiers who took pleasure in his amorous writings, he comforts them that they should now honor him modestly, commending himself by citing for his purpose the saying from the Gospel <note>A reference to Luke 15:7 regarding the joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.</note>.

¶ **THE SUCCESSOR.** The present twenty-third sonnet contains three things in which Master Francesco shows he takes no small delight. The first is that the King of France <note>Philip VI of Valois.</note> had set himself with a very great army in readiness to go against the Sultan of Babylon <note>Babylon here refers to Cairo/the Mamluk Sultanate.</note> to redeem the Holy Sepulcher. The second is that the Pope, who was Pope Urban V, was preparing to bring the Court back to Italy and return to Rome. The third is that Florence had—as is still its custom today—held a parliament and beheaded certain citizens and exiled others from the party hostile to the Church; thus the humble citizens struck down the "wolves" who were the robbers.

**O AWAITED in heaven.** This short song follows the first part of the preceding sonnet where mention was made of the preparation the King of France had made to make the passage <note>A "passage" (*passaggio*) was the standard term for a Crusade to the Holy Land.</note> against the infidels for the recovery of the Holy Sepulchre: and in summary, it encourages all faithful Italians generally to this most holy work. Beginning in this first stanza with an apostrophe to speak to the soul in a universal sense of all the devout, saying: "O Christian soul, blessed by the merits of your holy works and beautiful for being created in the image of God, you who are awaited in heaven for your reward: being you, by respect of baptism, clothed in human flesh but not burdened like the souls of the infidels by many sins; O soul, I say, beloved and obedient handmaid. **¶ PERHAPS THE DEVOUT.** Wishing in this second stanza, Petrarch, to better embolden all good Christians, demonstrates the reason why it occurred that God inspired the King of France to this <term>holy passage</term> <note>A "passage" (passaggio) was a common contemporary term for a Crusade to the Holy Land.</note>. **THERE IS A PART OF THE WORLD.** So that everyone may be more ready for this most devout undertaking, he also shows the furthest peoples of the North <note>original: "septentrione"</note> who are under the King of Denmark <note>original: "Datia"</note>, coming also most devoutly against their usual custom. Contrary to their habit, they are moved to devotion and come together with the Germans in this <term>passage</term> <note>A "passage" refers to a Crusade.</note>. Having thus demonstrated that the power of the Christians is very great, he manifests on the other hand the contrary regarding the infidels. Those who, passing through the Strait of Constantinople <note>original: "stretto di romania," referring to the Bosporus or Dardanelles</note> into Europe, taking and killing Christians, are not a people to be held in any esteem because they are without armor and do not know how to fight except with arrows.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s Canzone 28. The previous page concluded by describing how God has moved diverse nations—from the English to the Greeks—to join a holy crusade. Therefore, if you do not marvel when reading that Orpheus, with the sweetness of his song, moved even <note>original: "etiãdio"</note> the forests and the rocks to come and listen, and that Amphion, with the sound of his lyre <term>cythara: a stringed instrument similar to a harp or lute, used in antiquity to symbolize harmony and civilizing power</term>, moved stones to build the walls of Thebes by themselves—which signifies that they were most eloquent poets—then you will be much less surprised by how Italy and the Italian people will be awakened by the sound of this speech. O Petrarch, until such time as you take up the lance and arms for the love of Jesus! And then, concluding this stanza as confirmation, he says that never did ancient Italy—mother of the empire of the world and of every virtue—have causes as just and beautiful in any other age as she has at present.

->Until you take up the lance for Jesus:<-
->For, if this ancient mother looks at the truth,<-
->In none of her struggles<-
->Were there ever causes so beautiful, or so graceful.<-

<margin>C</margin> Who Orpheus was, and in what time he lived, has been narrated by us in the "Banquet" written to our very dear friend Tommaso Tebaldi <note>Thomaso thebaldo</note>. But as for the present: Orpheus, who is said to have lived at the time of the Argonauts, was the son of Oeagrus and Calliope. Having gone into the cave of Mount Pelion to visit Chiron the centaur <note>a mythological creature, half-man and half-horse, known as a wise teacher</note> together with King Peleus, father of Achilles—at the time when he was sailing in the company of Jason and the other Argonauts against Aeetes, King of Colchis—he was invited by the said Chiron to sing and play. Although Orpheus bore singular honor to Chiron, as was fitting for such a prince, he was nevertheless compelled by Chiron to descend into a trial of musical melody. Not only by the judgment of those standing around, but also by the express demonstration of the old Chiron, he excelled in such a way that even the wild beasts, the birds, the oaks, and the rocks moved from very distant places and came to the said cave only to hear the harmonic chords and the sweetest consonance of the young Orpheus. Afterward, when the Argonauts arrived at the island of Lemnos where Hypsipyle <note>Isiphile</note> reigned, Jason fell so much in love with her that he would have easily forgotten Colchis and the Golden Fleece; and similarly, almost all the other Greek princes attended to those same feasts with other women who were distressed by their dead husbands. Only Orpheus, with the sound of his clear lyre and his sweetest song, induced Jason and the other heroes to free themselves from the indissoluble bonds and the "snares of those hairs" <note>a poetic metaphor for the entrapment of love</note> which pull much more than a thousand winches, and they returned to the waiting galley to follow the glorious voyage. I could narrate many other infinite things through which the marvelous sweetness of the musician and poet Orpheus would be manifested. But let it suffice that, his most beautiful Eurydice having died from the bite of a venomous snake <note>original: "hydre"</note> and descended into the infernal circles like all other noble souls, Orpheus—who could not rest because of his desire and love for her—descended through the abyss of Taenarum <note>original: "tenero," referring to the traditional entrance to the Underworld in Greece</note> to the ultimate depths of horrible Tartarus. There dwelt Proserpina and Pluto, where the infernal furies were, and where the terrible Cerberus barked. And with such sweetness he opened his honeyed lips, always touching the sounding strings of his golden lyre, that all the infernal executioners were delayed in their pitiless mystery by the force of his song and sound. He constrained Pluto and Proserpina, against the custom of their inexorable judgment, to return to him his well-deserved Eurydice. He would have enjoyed her continually in this life with the usual pleasure if, at the final exit from the infernal gate, according to the promise he had made, he had not turned back with the impatience of love. This was the reason that, through his fault, his lady was lost again <note>This section of the manuscript contains a confusing or perhaps satirical reference to "the art of Poggio Bambalione," possibly a contemporary jab at a specific scholar or a corrupted reference to idle talk</note>. This led to his death because, while he devoted himself to boys and spoke as much as he could in contempt and disdain of women, he was stoned and killed by them with infinite rocks. Thus, that most eloquent voice, with which he had often made even the impossible possible, availed him nothing against the infuriated feminine impetus; and let this suffice for now.

<margin>B</margin> Amphion was the son of Jove and Antiope, who, having driven out Cadmus, the king and builder of the city of Thebes, possessed the Theban realm. He was a most worthy man and most excellent in music; according to the common opinion of learned men, he was the first inventor of the lyre, although some poets say it was first found by the god Apollo. Regarding this—as with Orpheus—having spoken at length in our "Milanese Banquets," I will not expand further at present except to say this: it is written by poets that the sweetness of Amphion’s playing was of such importance that stones, moving by themselves, built the walls around the aforementioned city of Thebes. This demonstrates that his eloquence was marvelous, for through it, all the crude and uncultured men willingly took up the labor of building the aforesaid walls.

Generous—no, but grateful and pious—
To avenge the merciless offenses
Alongside the glorious son of Mary?
What then does the enemy side hope for
In human defenses,
If Christ stands with the opposing host?

<margin>Francesco <note>Likely referring to the commentator Francesco Filelfo or the poet Francesco Petrarch.</note></margin>
"YOU WHO": In this sixth stanza, our poet directs his elegant speech to himself and to everyone like him who does not consume his leisure in sordid and mechanical arts <note>Manual labors or trades considered lower than the intellectual "liberal arts."</note>, but in sciences that are not adulterated or mercenary, but true and noble. Through these, the soul is nourished much more broadly than the body. He goes on to show that since fighting against the infidels is necessary for Italians—if they wish to be grateful and pious—victory is certain. Everyone should willingly be moved to join the present crusade <term>passaggio: literally "the passage," a common term for a crusade to the Holy Land</term>. He says: You, a man learned and erudite in ancient and modern histories, who, to enrich yourself, did not use robbery but a beautiful treasure of virtue and immortal glory, have read so many ancient and modern books, flying with your intellect and mental consideration even unto heaven. 

Furthermore, while living in the knowledge of how much Rome—from the time of the pagans ruling under Romulus until the time of Caesar Augustus when Christ was born, which was a period of seven hundred twenty-four years—was often generous and liberal in avenging injuries, not only her own but those of her friends and allies. This can be seen in what they did against the Carthaginians in the Second Punic War out of respect for the Saguntines, and again in the third and final war out of respect for Masinissa <note>A king of Numidia and ally of Rome whose grievances triggered the Third Punic War.</note>. Therefore, the aforementioned Rome, along with Roman Italy, must now be—I do not say generous, but—mindful of the benefits received; and also out of respect for her Creator, she must avenge the merciless offenses that Christians receive every hour from that rabble. This is especially true since Christ is on our side, for it is in His name and faith that the present crusade is undertaken. Therefore, he concludes that since God is found among the ranks of the Christians, the infidels can have no firm hope in any of their human forces. 

The three triumphs of Octavian Augustus were: first over the Illyrians; the second for the victory at Actium; the third over Cleopatra, Queen of Egypt.

## STANZA VII.

**S**et your mind on the reckless daring of Xerxes;
Who, to tread upon our shores,
Committed an outrage against the sea with new bridges.
And you will see, in the death of their husbands,
The Persian women all dressed in mourning black,
And the sea of Salamis dyed red.
And not only does this wretched ruin
Of the unhappy people of the East
Promise you victory,
But Marathon, and the mortal pass
That the Lion <note>Leonidas, the Spartan king at the Battle of Thermopylae.</note> defended with few people;

<margin>Francesco</margin>
"SET YOUR MIND": To better confirm the aforementioned statement, he clearly demonstrates in this seventh stanza the natural cowardice <note>original: "lignauia nãle," likely *l'ignavia naturale*</note> of the Eastern peoples. He first proves this through Xerxes, King of Persia, who crossed into Europe with five million men. So that he could pass more easily without too much delay, he built two bridges over ships—of which he had a thousand. One was above Constantinople in the strait that leads to the Black Sea called the Bosphorus. The other was over the Hellespont where Gallipoli is now, which is currently called the Strait of Romania. Beyond this, once he reached Mount Athos, now named...

<summary>This page uses Roman and Greek history to justify a new crusade, arguing that if Rome fought for its allies, it must now fight for Christ. It contrasts the historical military failures of Eastern empires, like that of Xerxes, with the inevitable victory of a Christian army backed by God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s Canzone 28. ->And a thousand others, which you have heard and read:<-
->For it is very fitting to incline toward God<-
->Both your knees and your mind,<-
->Who preserves your years for such great good.<-

...named the Holy Mountain <note>Mount Athos, known as 'Monte Santo' in Italian. The text refers to the canal Xerxes dug through the peninsula during his invasion of Greece.</note>, which stretches into the sea for a hundred miles, he [Xerxes] made such a cut at the foot of said mountain that he brought the sea through it and passed with his whole fleet, so that with greater speed he might suddenly overtake and overwhelm the fleet of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note>, which he heard was staying on the other side of the mountain. This man was finally defeated and broken at Salamis by the warning and singular prudence of Themistocles, the captain of the Athenians; with great difficulty and fear he fled back to Asia in a small fisherman's boat. And even before that, the army of his father Darius, which consisted of seven hundred thousand persons, had been broken by Miltiades at Marathon.

¶ The example he touches upon regarding Ilium, the principal city of Troy, I do not know how well it satisfies the present purpose, since that city was located in Asia and defended by Eastern peoples, while the army of the Greeks was from Europe. I will nevertheless say what I think about it according to what truth provides, which is much more doubtful than the Phoenix <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for something extremely rare or legendary.</note>. I shall begin from the origin of the injuries, because of which Asia and Europe became enemies to each other. After the Phoenicians had sailed amicably to Greece, according to the history of the most ancient historian Herodotus of Halicarnassus, they kidnapped the daughter of Inachus, king of the Argives, named Io. When a Greek embassy went to Phoenicia, demanding back the kidnapped girl and also the punishment of the kidnappers, they reported no other result than words; because of which all of Greece, indignant as if at a common injury, rose up. Jupiter, king of Crete, most powerful among all the Greeks, gave a large and mighty fleet to his captain, called by name or title Taurus. Having taken Europa, daughter of King Agenor, from the coast of Phoenicia, he returned with the said fleet and prey to the Cretan realm. And when the Phoenicians similarly demanded back the kidnapped Europa through their ambassadors, with restitution for damages, they received from the Greeks a similar response to the one they had previously given concerning the daughter of King Inachus. 

Nor were the Greeks then content with such vengeance, but they wished to be the authors of a second injury. Therefore, another much larger fleet was prepared under the captaincy and command of Jason, king of the Argives, against the realm of the Colchians. Having put the country to plunder, Jason brought Medea, daughter of King Aeetes, back with him to Greece. For which second injury, Priam, king of Troy—as the principal among all the Asian princes after the King of the Assyrians—thinking vengeance was permitted to him, set in order his son Alexander Paris and sent him with a valiant and great fleet to Greece. From there, having kidnapped Helen, he was the cause of the harsh and long Trojan War. Because immediately the Greeks, for vengeance of this, put in order ninety-six thousand four hundred and fifty men with one thousand two hundred and eighty-six ships <term>fuste: a type of light, fast galley</term>, and passed into Asia for the destruction of the Trojan empire, where they remained in siege for over ten years after many killings and routs on one side and the other. Finally, the attack and the effort were held against the city of Ilium, which—since the Greeks could never take it by force—they obtained, according to the words of Homer, through trickery and snares. 

¶ And let this be said according to the opinion of Herodotus and Homer; although some others want to show a completely contrary end with firm reasons: that the Greeks never achieved their intention, but departed with great shame; that Achilles was killed by Hector; and that Aeneas, Antenor, and Helenus were sent by the said Hector after the said war to acquire new realms as a reward for their good conduct and to amplify the Trojan name and empire. In which opinion are the Egyptians and Dio of Prusa <note>Dio Chrysostom, a 1st-century Greek philosopher who wrote a famous discourse arguing that the Trojans actually won the war.</note>. And thus we see this enmity and the peoples of Europe almost becoming natural enemies; for which reason it is no wonder if the Turks with such persistence and fury presently await the formidable army of Vladislaus <note>Vladislaus III of Poland and Hungary, who led the Crusade of Varna against the Ottoman Empire in the 1440s.</note>, the illustrious and most invincible king of Hungary and Poland.

¶ YOU will see, Italy, in this eighth and last stanza, following Petrarch’s usual manner: that concluding his moral songs <note>Canzoni</note>, he comforts his present song, telling it to go see Italy in his stead; which he says he cannot see, not so much...

> My Song; which from my eyes is hidden and withheld
> Not by sea, nor hill, nor river;
> But only by love, and its haughty light.

> The more it delights me, where it most inflames me:
> Nor can nature stand against habit,
> Now move: do not lose your other companions:
> For not only under veils
> Does love dwell; for whom one laughs and cries.

*...so much out of respect for some sea or hill or river, by which his eyes might be hindered, as for respect of love which keeps him enamored within his heart, gazing upon the luminous eyes of Lady Laura, showing that ingrained habit alone conquers natural virtue. And because he did not doubt that this song should reach Florence, he adds a few more amorous sighs, saying that not only in Avignon, under the horned veils <note>A reference to the "horned" headdress style fashionable in the 14th century, which Petrarch occasionally critiqued as being overly ornate.</note>, do amorous laughter and tears dwell: but also no less under Italian behaviors, and especially those of the Florentine women who polish themselves so gracefully.*

### SONG VI

> Green clothes, blood-red, dark, or purple
> No lady ever wore
> Nor twisted golden hair into a blonde braid
> So beautiful; as she, who strips me
> Of my will; and from the path of liberty
> Draws me with her, so that I cannot bear
> Any lighter yoke.

<margin>Francesco</margin>
**C GREEN** clothes. In this sixth moral song, Master Francesco shows that the beauty of Lady Laura is so great and marvelous that he—not without great reason, being a man and not a stone—fell in love with her in such a way that he is no longer master of himself. And therefore he says in this present first stanza that she does not appear beautiful like other women only if she is dressed in a certain single color: but in whatever color she is dressed, whether green or blood-red or dark or purple <term>perso: a dark, grayish-purple or indigo color often mentioned in medieval textiles</term>, never was a more beautiful woman seen than she, nor specifically with such beautiful hair that looks like threads of gold. For which reason he says it is no wonder if he has been stripped of his free will by such a goddess and drawn from his natural liberty into her power; although such amorous subjection is less heavy to him than any other servitude: because love is similar to madness, which whoever has it thinks himself wise and goes further than others.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
**C GREEN CLOTHES**, blood-red, dark, and purple. In this song Master Francesco praises certain singular beauties of his lady: and says that no woman ever wore any color of cloth who was more beautiful than she. *Any lighter yoke*: he means he knew no other lesser pain than that which he has for her. *Benign stars that became companions*: He praises the star under which his mother gave birth to him. *I know well that wanting to enclose in verses*: here the poet touches upon the immense beauty of Lady Laura as **Virgil** does in the *Aeneid*: <note>original: "Nam mihi si linguæ centum sint oraque centum."</note> "For if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths..." <note>A classic trope from Virgil expressing that even with a hundred tongues, one could not fully describe a subject.</note>

### STANZA II

> And if yet at times the soul arms itself
> to complain; to which comes failing
> Counsel, where the torment leads it to doubt;
> A sudden sight calls it back
> from its unbridled desire; which scrapes from my heart
> Every mad undertaking, and every disdain
> Makes her look sweet.

<margin>Francesco</margin>
**C AND IF YET.** The second stanza follows, which shows even more than the preceding one the power of love, saying that even if he—being in such passion and arming himself with the dictates of reason—deliberated within his soul to withdraw from the servitude into which he had fallen for lack of good counsel, he was immediately pulled back by the amorous torment into doubt of what he should follow: thus reason fights on one side and love on the other. But Lady Laura, suddenly seen by his unbridled desire, no differently than one who calls back <note>original: "rapella"</note> a runaway, pulls his soul back into her power in such a way that she completely removes from his heart every foolish undertaking he had previously made of not wanting to be subject to such love: and makes every such torment, which previously displeased him, become pleasing.

<margin>R</margin>
<margin>K</margin> **FOR AS much as for love**. This present third stanza demonstrates what is commonly said in the popular proverb: *He who endures, wins.* <note>The Italian proverb "chi la dura la vince."</note> He says he does not doubt that he will finally be avenged for all the pain and torment he has suffered in the past and will suffer in the future through the death of his beloved lady—until she, though pitiless, heals his heart which she herself mortified and made increasingly wretched. This "vengeance," in my opinion, will be that once he has eventually obtained that thing without which love never rests, he will play with her more with words than with deeds. He says this cannot fail to happen, provided his perseverance does not falter. This failure could happen by chance either through her pride and loftiness set against his humility, or through his own anger at seeing himself unesteemed by her; for these two things could easily turn his heart away from loving her further, since his accustomed humility brings him no benefit.

### STANTIA. III.

->*For as much as I ever suffered for love,*<-
->*And have to suffer still*<-
->*Until she who bit it heals my heart,*<-
->*She, a rebel to mercy who yet desires it;*<-
->*Let there be vengeance; provided that against humility*<-
->*Pride and anger do not close or lock*<-
->*The beautiful path, where I see her.*<-

<margin>L</margin> **BUT THEN and the day**. Now in this fourth stanza, he declares that it was not without great cause that he fell so deeply in love with her. There are some women who appear foul when wearing a certain color; but whichever of the contrasting colors she wears, she appears beautiful, and in such a woman nothing is lacking for the perfection of beauty—which he shows to be the case with Lady Laura. And so he says that on the first day he saw her—Good Friday, when she was dressed in black—and thereafter during the Easter feast days when he saw her dressed in white, having abandoned the awareness of chastity and continence, <note>Petrarch famously met Laura on Good Friday, April 6, 1327, in the church of Sainte-Claire in Avignon.</note> he immediately fell in love with her. This was no marvel, for she was "novel" <note>In the sense of being unique or extraordinary.</note> in a way he had never seen before; she was possessed of intellect and wit—no simpleton <term>gnocha</term> <note>Original: "gnocha," a derogatory term for a foolish or dim-witted person.</note>—and she possessed a striking physical presence. Thinking of this gives him the greatest passion. These three things were the root and beginning of his falling in love: but above all, her graceful beauty, in which our youthful age sees and mirrors itself. Without doubt, a man may be considered made of lead or wood if, upon seeing such a beautiful creature, he does not nourish himself and take delight merely in looking at her.

### STANTIA. IIII.

->*But then and the day; that I opened my eyes*<-
->*To the beautiful black and the white,*<-
->*Which drove me from where love ran;*<-
->*A new thing of this life, which pains me.*<-
->*They were the root; and that one, in whom our age*<-
->*Mirrors itself; who, seeing her, is not lead or wood,*<-
->*And who does not fear:*<-

<margin>M</margin> **TEAR**. Turning his thoughts to himself in this fifth stanza, and comforting himself with the hope of a good outcome—as something that reasonably ought to follow according to his desire—he speaks to the tear that falls from his eyes. He speaks of those tears that bathe his heart, which first felt his distress on the left side. <note>The "left side" refers to the heart, traditionally considered the seat of emotions and the first to be struck by Cupid's arrows.</note> He knows that no such restraint or pain was caused by his own desire; for naturally, the judgment falls in favor of the side that has reason, as I have against her who is in the wrong—as is the pitiless and cruel Lady Laura. Thus, if my soul sighs for her as one who has been injured, it is a worthy thing that she should also wash the wounds of said soul.

->*Do not turn me away from my desire:*<-
->*For the sentence falls in a just place:*<-
->*The soul sighs for her; and she is worthy*<-
->*To wash its wounds.*<-

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s Canzone 29. The previous page discussed the poet’s perseverance and his hope for "vengeance" through his Lady’s eventual mercy. Here, the commentator concludes the analysis of the final stanzas and the envoy.</meta>

### STANZA VI.

My thoughts have become estranged from me:
Such now that I grow weary,
The beloved sword turned back upon itself,
Nor do I pray that she might release me:
For all other roads lead straight to heaven,
And one does not aspire to the glorious kingdom
Certainly in a sturdier ship.

<margin>N</margin>
*¶ MY thoughts. "Too much love is indeed too much." Desiring to demonstrate this in this sixth stanza, Petrarch says his thoughts have now become estranged from his own self. Whereas previously he hoped to obtain the thing he loved and was full of joy, now, fearing he toils in vain, he is filled only with melancholy and displeasure. Because he is, as it were, weary of such thoughts, he says that Madonna Laura behaves toward him no differently than those who turn their <term>own</term> <note>The original uses the abbreviated form "ppria" for "propria."</note> sword against their own person—speaking here as lovers are accustomed to do when they are tormented and turn against themselves. He adds that he does not, however, pray for her to release him from his amorous suffering; for he who toils more deserves more. It is as if he were saying that if we wish to go by the straight path to heaven, we must go with many labors; for one cannot hope for such a kingdom, nor reach it, in a sturdier ship than that in which we labor greatly.*

### STANZA VII.

Kind stars, that were companions
At that fortunate side,
When her birth first dawned upon the world:
For she is a star on earth: and as the laurel leaf,
She preserves green the prize of integrity;
Where no lightning strikes, nor does any unworthy
Wind ever blow, to weigh her down.

<margin>O</margin>
*¶ KIND stars. Messer Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch, the poet.</note> continually strives with wonder to commend both the integrity and the beauty of Madonna Laura. Doing so in this seventh stanza, he praises her birth as having occurred under a very kind constellation. Though she was produced as beautiful as a star, she is also a preserver of honesty <note>The term "honesta" refers to moral integrity and chastity.</note> just as the laurel preserves its green leaves. And just as neither lightning nor wind harms the laurel, so too the prize and the praise of her integrity never fear being weighed down by the deeds or the ill words of others.*

### STANZA VIII.

I know well, that to wish to enclose in verse
Her praises, he would grow weary
Who set a worthier hand to writing.
What cell of memory is there, in which is gathered
All the virtue one sees, and all the beauty,
By him who gazes into her eyes, the sign of all worth,
The sweet key to my heart?

<margin>P</margin>
*¶ I KNOW well. Having touched upon the two qualities above—namely the integrity and the beauty of Madonna Laura—our poet wishes to conclude in this eighth stanza by saying that no man, however eloquent, could sufficiently comprehend her praises and commendations in his verses. This is because no memory would be sufficient to remember her great beauty, especially when gazing upon those flashing and gracious eyes where every kind of worth appears as a sign. He reasonably says these eyes are nothing less than the key to his heart.*

### STANZA IX.

As far as the sun turns, Love
Has no dearer pledge than you, my Lady.

<margin>Q</margin>
*¶ AS FAR as the sun turns. In these final two lines, which take the place of the refrain <note>Known as the "tornata" or envoy in a Petrarchan canzone.</note>, he concludes that in the whole world there is no woman more beautiful than she. For this reason, it can reasonably be said that she is the dearest pledge that Love possesses, as she appeared to others exactly as Petrarch demonstrates her to be when she is near him.*
