<header>SONG. VII.</header>

# SONG. VII.

<margin>R Fran.</margin>
*¶ A good young woman. This present seventh song demonstrates specifically certain beauties that, above all others, ought to be found in a woman. Because of this, it declares that Messer Francesco <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch, the author</note> was reasonably captured by love for her, and can never forget her. Desiring to reveal her name—that is, Laura—he says in this first part: "a good young woman," because old meat does not make good soup <note>An old Italian proverb—"carne vecchia non fa buon brodo"—suggesting that youth is the peak of beauty and vitality.</note>. UNDER a green laurel: which signifies her aforementioned name. "Whiter" in regard to her fair skin, and "colder than snow" in that she does not seem able to feel the flames of love, but is like frozen snow not struck by the sun's rays for a long time. This signifies her integrity <term>honesta</term> <note>A term encompassing virtue, modesty, and chastity</note> joined with the aforementioned whiteness, to which he adds three other singular excellences: graceful speech, a rare face, and blonde hair. He says these three things are supremely pleasing to him, so that he always has and will have them before his eyes wherever he may be.*

<margin>Anto.</margin>
*¶ A young woman under a green laurel: a moral sestina <note>A poetic form consisting of six stanzas of six lines each, ending with a three-line envoy, using a complex pattern of repeating end-words</note> which Messer Francesco addresses to his lady. I SAW her whiter and colder than snow: he says "white" for her beauty; "colder" for her cruelty <note>In the courtly love tradition, a lady's refusal to return a lover's affection was often described as "cruelty."</note>, having branches of diamond and hair of gold to demonstrate the cruelty of Madonna Laura.*

->A young woman under a green laurel<-
->I saw, whiter and colder than snow<-
->Unstruck by the sun for many and many years;<-
->And her speech, and her beautiful face, and her hair<-
->Pleased me so, that I have her before my eyes:<-
->And shall have always, whether I be on a hill or a shore.<-

## STANZA . II.

<margin>S Fran.</margin>
*THEN shall they be. Since these four aforementioned excellences of beauty are in her, accompanied by the most constant integrity, it is not without reason that in this second part he demonstrates that he will cease thinking of her only when laurels are without leaves. Similarly, his heart will be at rest and his eyes without tears when fire freezes and snow burns. He adds that it would not grieve him to wait through infinite years in these thoughts, provided that at the end he could reach the desired day of the amorous palm <note>The "palm" signifies victory or the reward of successful love.</note>.*

->Then my thoughts will reach the shore;<-
->When a green leaf is not found on a laurel:<-
->When I have a quiet heart and dry eyes:<-
->We shall see fire freeze, and snow burn<-
->I do not have as many hairs in these locks;<-
->As the years I would wish to wait for that day.<-

## STANZA . III.

<margin>T</margin>
*¶ BUT because it flies. Correcting his statement about waiting for the desired day, he declares in this third part the reason for his impatience: the brevity and inconstancy of human life. He says that time passes no differently than if it flew, and the years seem to flee due to their speed, so that a person sees death at the door in an instant. Therefore, since waiting is not safe for him, he will never cease—neither now while his hair is still dark, nor even when it shall be white—to follow her tracks and her shadow, neither in summer nor in winter, as long as his life lasts.*

->B ut because time flies, and the years flee;<-
->So that one arrives at death in an instant<-
->With either dark or white hair;<-
->I follow the shadow of that sweet laurel<-
->Through the most burning sun and through the snow,<-
->Until the final day closes these eyes.<-

<note>Commentary fragment continuing from the right column:</note>

### STANZA V

> **I** fear my face and hair will change first;
> Before she shows her eyes to me with true pity,
> My idol sculpted in living laurel:
> For, if I err not in my counting, today it is seven years;
> That I go sighing from shore to shore,
> Night and day, in the heat and in the snow.

<note>Commentary fragment continuing from the right column (X):</note>
...[face] and by the white hair, so that he might be rewarded with some compassion by his idol, Madonna Laura. And this he believes because seven years had already passed during which he had always followed her in vain from one place to another with many sighs and troubles, both in winter and in summer.

### STANZA VI

> **W**ithin is pure fire, and outside white snow,
> With only these thoughts, and with changed hair,
> I will go always weeping along every shore;
> To perhaps make pity come into the eyes
> Of such a one who will be born after a thousand years;
> If a well-cultivated laurel can live so long;

<note>Commentary fragment continuing from the right column (Y):</note>
...the exterior of the person is cold through the absence of blood, but the interior—and principally the heart—is warm because the blood has gathered in that part. And he adds that without achieving any other result, but only with such thoughts—and with changed hair, as is natural when a man grows in age—he will go always weeping from one shore to another due to excessive melancholy. He does this to move many who will be born later to compassion; they, seeing his bitter sighs and troubles, will still weep for them as long as this beautiful work shall last.

<margin>B</margin> **PREFERRING**, therefore, the beloved lady above the aforementioned planets, he says that if the noble soul of this woman—who died in her youthful and flowering age—is welcomed and exalted with the honor due to her up in heaven, there is no doubt that she will be given the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most stable heaven in medieval cosmology, where God resides.</note> to inhabit. But if <unclear>in as much as</unclear> she remained among the planets, such as between Venus <note>the third light</note> and Mars—that is, in the sphere of the Sun, which is between those two planets—her splendor would be so great that the Sun itself would lose its flashing color when other souls (that is, the stars, according to the Platonic sentiment) are scattered around her like the other stars around the Sun, all to gaze upon her infinite beauty. 

But if she rested beneath the "fourth nest," which is Mercury (counting from Mars and including Venus), each of the three preceding stars (Mars, Sun, and Venus) would appear less beautiful, as if obscured by her beauty, for she alone would have the fame and the praise. Nor is it to be believed that so worthy a spirit would dwell in the heaven of the Moon, which is "lazy and sleepy." But if she flew higher, one can well trust that every other star would be surpassed by her—not only those of melancholy and tears belonging to Saturn, nor even all those stars fixed in the eighth heaven. With Jupiter, some wish to understand that she ought to be in the sphere of Jupiter as a benign planet, to whom the principle of generation is given. But to me, it seems better to understand that every other star will be conquered by her, even Jupiter himself. 

Thus, she should reasonably dwell, by her great splendor, in the eleventh Empyrean heaven—which means "splendid"—where we believe the principal dominion and seat of Almighty God to be. For according to Holy Scripture, there are eleven heavens: the 1st is called the Empyrean; the 2nd, the Crystalline; the 3rd, the First Mobile; the 4th, the Starry Heaven or Firmament; the 5th, Saturn; the 6th, Jupiter; the 7th, Mars; the 8th, the Sun; the 9th, Venus; the 10th, Mercury; the 11th...

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ This noble soul who departs: Having understood, Master Francesco <note>Francesco Filelfo, a famous Renaissance humanist and commentator.</note>, that Madonna Laura had been ill and died, he composed this sonnet, wishing to place her in Paradise. He says: "if she remains between the third light and Mars," that is, between Venus (which is in the third sphere) and Mars (which is in the fifth sphere), she will be near the Sun, which is between the said planets according to the doctrine of the astronomers. And being near the Sun, it will be colored by her, because she will surpass it in beauty and light. And the souls who are up there will scatter around to see her as a miracle. "If she rested beneath the fourth nest," that is, beneath the Sun which is in the fourth sphere, each of the [other] three would be less beautiful: namely Venus, Mercury, and the Moon; she alone would hold the name of the most beautiful. In the fifth circle she would not dwell, because there lives Mars, a furious and harsh planet. But if she flies much higher, I am quite confident—that is, to the sixth sphere where Jupiter resides—I am certain that Jupiter, with every other star, will be overcome by the beauty of Madonna Laura.

### SONNET XXV

<margin>Francesco C.</margin>

->*Through doubtful things, others advance;*<-

¶ THE CLOSER I APPROACH: In this 25th sonnet, it is clearly manifested what foolishness it is to trust in vain hope. Our enamored poet says that the closer he drew to death—which suddenly puts an end to every misery—the more he saw time passing swiftly and lightly, and every hope of his to obtain the beloved lady found to be fallacious and vain. Therefore, he says he has but one comfort in his thoughts: the necessity of soon resting from his amorous labors on the day he is liberated from the hard and heavy bodily burden, which melts away no differently than snow. And this is because, together with the body, the vain hope held in vain for so long will also fall. And likewise, the pleasure and the displeasure, and the fear and the anger that he felt at times—depending on whether the looks, or the troubled or unwelcome face of the beloved lady, Madonna Laura, pleased him—the impassioned one will then also clearly see how often a man finds he has advanced in doubtful things contrary to his will, and how often he has wished himself where he ought not to have been.

<margin>Antonio D.</margin>
¶ The closer I approach my final day. Considering, Master Francesco, his time that grew old in these passions of love—a war that was so rashly broken and shattered against the Greeks. The sea of Salamis <note>An ancient Greek city-state on the island of Cyprus.</note>, a city of the Cypriot coast, from which the sea that bathes it takes its name. "You shall see," he says, speaking to his song: "That not only under veils," which is to say that not only women who wear veils love, but also virtuous men love.

Regarding the torments of love: it seemed that with its rays, the morning star <note>Likely Venus, often associated with the pangs of lovers.</note> was throwing off the flames of childbirth. Likewise, the Great Bear—she who was loved by Jove and transferred into the heavens to become the constellation of the Northern Wagon, whose myth we shall soon narrate—had already turned her beautiful and shining rays. This occurs quite often in the morning, in that time before the dawn when the poor old woman is accustomed to rise, disheveled and barefoot, to begin her spinning; she strikes the fire just as the lovers, who have spent the whole night busy sifting ill-ground flour <note>A common Renaissance idiom for the restless, often fruitless "labor" or "grinding" of lovers during the night.</note>, turn away weeping, for they are forced by the breaking day to leave their amorous dance. Instead, this hope proceeded from a dream in which it seemed a voice said to him: "O Master Francesco, why do you lose your courage regarding your hope, since the sight of these amorous eyes of Madonna Laura is not yet taken from you?"

<margin>E</margin> Now, with brevity, we shall narrate the aforementioned myth. Callisto, the daughter of King Lycaon, fled into the woods out of fear after her father was driven from the Pelasgian kingdom by Jove <note>The Roman name for Zeus.</note> and transformed into a wolf. She was received by the <term>nymphs</term> <note>original: "moniale" (nuns). The commentator uses Christian monastic vocabulary to describe the virginal followers of the goddess Diana.</note> and virgins of Diana into their company and religious order. When Jove heard of this and saw her singular beauty, he immediately fell in love. In order to more easily lead her to break her vow, he transformed himself into the goddess Diana. In this guise, he went to the place where Callisto, exhausted by the heat and the toil of the hunt, was resting upon the cool, flowering grass inside a small grove. When he saw that she had quickly stood up to honor him, being without any guard, he could hardly contain himself in his great desire. Already rejoicing within himself for the act he intended to perform immediately, he asked her—as one who was part of her company—with the sweetest words, in which hills she had been hunting. As she prepared to answer him with due reverence, she found herself pierced by the final blow of Love following his very sweet kisses; she could not even perceive from where the arrow had come. Although she tried to resist, as is the custom of women, she nonetheless realized the honey was not bitter; she eventually showed more patience in her soul than she let appear on her face. But after Jove had satisfied his desire and departed, having shown her by experience who he truly was, the goddess Diana arrived. When she saw the changed Callisto, she called for her to come to her. Hearing this, Callisto—though she seemed to doubt who it was—presented herself full of shame, like one who felt she had strayed. Mixing with the others, she did not follow in the front rank as Diana went into a grove where there was a stream of clear, cool water. Diana, fatigued by both toil and the excessive sun, decided to bathe in that water, seeing it was a hidden and secret place. While all the other virgins followed suit, Callisto alone was most unwilling to undress, so that <term>Venus</term> <note>Here used as a metaphor for sexual activity or pregnancy.</note> might not reveal the hidden thefts of her lower belly.

<margin>F</margin> But after she was stripped by force by her companions and her fault was recognized, Diana immediately dismissed her from the company, so that the sacred waters would not be defiled by her. In the meantime, Juno, who was not sleeping—having been the first to notice this adultery—waited for the opportune time. After Callisto had given birth to a beautiful boy named Arcas, Juno came to her with intolerable wrath, grabbed her by her front hair, and with fury threw her down, beating her until she lay stretched with her face on the ground. Nor was she content with this: so that she might never again please her husband Jove, she transformed her into a rough and terrible bear. For this reason, she was forced...

### SONNET XXVII.

<margin>Francesco Gesualdo</margin>
Apollo, if the beautiful desire still lives
That inflamed you by the Thessalian waves,
And if you have not, through the passing years,
Consigned those beloved golden tresses to oblivion,
From the sluggish frost and from the harsh and cruel weather,
Which lasts as long as your face remains hidden,
Defend now the honored and sacred foliage,
Where you first, and then I, was ensnared:
And by the virtue of that amorous hope,
Which sustained you in your bitter life,
Clear the air of these heavy impressions.
So we may then see, to our shared wonder,
Our lady sitting upon the grass,
And making with her arms a shadow for herself.

<margin>Francesco Gesualdo</margin>
**C** APOLLO. Wonderfully and continually our poet praises the rare Lady Laura: but in this twenty-seventh sonnet he not only commends her, showing her likeness to Daphne, but also does not forget himself, secretly showing himself to be like the sun: which in that age was not contrary to the truth. Therefore, the enamored poet prays to the god Apollo that if he, in those amorous desires of his youthful years when he fell in love with Daphne (which signifies "laurel") has not forgotten those golden hairs of hers despite the distance of time, he might deign to defend such sacred and honored foliage—for the laurel crown that is made from it, which secretly signifies Lady Laura, where both have been in love: Apollo with Daphne and this man with Laura—from every haze and harshness of weather. He shows this to be when the sun hides itself: which he understands as the nourishing face of Lady Laura. And because in that time there was a great pestilence <note>A reference to the plague of 1348, which devastated Europe and claimed the life of the real Laura.</note>, he prays the sun that it might deign with its rays to purge the air infected by every such contagion, so that in the accustomed snares <note>The "snares" of love or the visual sight of his beloved.</note> he might see the amorous gaze of her for whom he was in agonizing pain. The fable of Daphne, because it was narrated by me in the fifth sonnet, need not be repeated here.

¶ ALONE and pensive in the most deserted fields — Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> tells of the solitary life he leads so as not to be manifest to men, and says that he found no other way to live his love secretly: because commonly the passions that the heart holds are demonstrated in the face, as Ovid says: *Alas, how difficult it is not to betray a crime with the face* <note>original Latin: "Heu quàm difficile est crimēn non prodere vultu"</note>: and Tibullus: *Alas, how difficult it is to imitate joy with the face* <note>original Latin: "Heu quàm difficile est imitari gaudia vultu"</note>: but yet he concludes by saying that although he goes by unusual ways, he still cannot ensure that he does not love; this solitary living cannot make him forget his love.

### CANZONE XXIX. <note>In this edition, Sonnet 36 is numbered as the 29th poem in this section.</note>

<margin>Fran.</margin> <note>Francesco Filelfo, a famous Humanist scholar and commentator on Petrarch.</note>
¶ IF I BELIEVED: time and again our poet demonstrates how much heaviness the amorous thought presses upon him without ever reaching its effect: which, wishing to demonstrate with greater efficacy in the present 29th sonnet, he says that he would kill himself with his own hands if he believed he could escape these amorous troubles through death: but he does not do this only because he doubts that with death he would be unburdened of such thought; rather, he would be in greater pain. Therefore he remains as if suspended whether he ought to kill himself or not: wherefore, adding to this, he manifests that Love and Death are both pitiless: one by never coming to the conclusions of long dealings: the other conclusion not removing him from such great pain. But as if deaf, not showing herself <term>Death</term>, she keeps him in this life melancholy, exhausted, and turned pale just as she is: so that, concluding, he would wish to obtain the beloved lady: or at least depart from this wretched life.

> **I**f I believed that through death I would be unburdened
> Of the amorous thought that strikes me down;
> With my own hands I would have already laid in the earth
> These troublesome limbs, and that burden:
> **B**ut because I fear that it would be a passage
> From weeping to weeping, and from one war to another;
> On this side of the pass that still shuts me out,
> I remain half weary, and half across the passage.
> **I**t would indeed be time by now to have shot
> The final arrow from the pitiless string
> Already bathed and dyed in the blood of another:
> **A**nd I pray to you, Love, and to that deaf one <note>Death</note>
> Who left me painted with her own color;
> And she does not remember to call me to herself.

<margin>Anto. I</margin>
¶ IF I BELIEVED that through death I would be unburdened — Messer Francesco says that if he thought that by killing himself he would be out of his troubles, he would have already killed himself: but because he fears passing from bad to worse—since according to the Faith he would be damned—for this reason he remains thus between living and dead, his love not yet having diminished. And it could also be said that the author spoke according to the opinion of some philosophers who hold that in the other world souls are also tormented in those troubles that existed at the time the spirit was united with the body. IT WOULD INDEED BE TIME BY NOW — Messer Francesco speaks toward Love and concludes his purpose.

# CANZONE . VIII.

<margin>Francesco <note>Likely Francesco Rigutini, a commentator on this edition.</note></margin>

> If the thread is weak, upon which hangs
> My heavy life;
> That if others do not aid it,
> It would soon reach the shore of its course.
> Because after the cruel departure
> That from my sweet good
> I made, only one hope
> Has been until now the reason I live.
> Saying: though I be deprived
> Of the beloved sight;
> Sustain yourself, sad soul;
> For who knows if you might return to a better time,
> And to happier days?
> Or if the lost good might ever be regained?
> This hope sustained me for a time:
> Now it begins to fail, and I spend too much time in it.

<margin>Francesco</margin>
¶ IF THE thread is weak: the present 8th canzone continues very well from the preceding sonnet: because by demonstrating the difficulty and trouble received through the distance from the beloved thing, it declares his anguished life to be no less heavy than death. Our poet says, then, in this first stanza that his life, full of anguish, is sustained by a weak thread, which is the hope he has of returning from Padua (where he still was) to Avignon, where he had left that lady whom he loved much more than himself; although such hope, on which he had fed for a long time, was gradually failing, as usually happens to all those whose spirit is better than their legs <note>An idiomatic way of saying his will is stronger than his physical ability or the reality of the situation.</note>.

---

<margin>Antonio <note>Antonio da Tempo, a 14th-century judge and metricist whose early commentaries were often included in later editions.</note></margin>
¶ IF THE thread is weak: Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> being far from Lady Laura and remembering her, he felt great sorrow finding himself absent and separated from her; and he composed this Canzone with this sentiment. **SCARCELY has a ray dawned in the east**: he says this to denote how time flies, as he suddenly makes the night arrive. **WITH THE DESIRE** not being able to move wings: that is, not being able to go with his feet as he does with his spirit, he takes little comfort. **AND HOW joyful my dawn was**: as if to say: one does not understand the good unless they have experienced the evil, as I show in these my troubles. And why earlier, being silent, I did not obtain: as if to say: he did this out of resentment like a man offended by another **TO LOVE** what a new thing: that is, a thing that feels like labor. **AND let both eyes be punished with the heart**: that is, in this way, weeping, place your eyes with the heart, which were the guides to the heart on the path of love. **THAT kind angelic light**: Messer Francesco says that everything has patience except for having lost that sweet greeting <note>original: "salute," which can mean both greeting and salvation</note> she gave him. **AND to weep still with more delight**. This is a narration of lovers who, remembering their lady when they are absent, take pleasure in the sight of their torments. **These alpine and wild places hide me**: Messer Francesco demonstrates how he stayed in solitude: that is, near that river Sorgue in the villa <note>Vaucluse, Petrarch's famous retreat.</note>. **Hope rises**: Messer Francesco says this because sometimes it came to his mind to be able to see his lady and then he would fall into fear of never seeing her. Whence Ovid in his Epistles: *Love is a hope full of anxious fear.* <note>original: "Spes est sollicitis plena timoris amor."</note>

<margin>Francesco</margin>
¶ TIME passes. He demonstrates in this second stanza the reason for his hope being largely diminished, which is the passage of time in his life <term>temparsi ne la eta</term> <note>Literally "tempering in age," referring to growing older or the maturing of his years.</note>. <margin>M</margin> **EVERY place.** Continuing in this third stanza, he demonstrates that he is always in sadness and affliction regardless of how great a place he finds himself in; and this only because he does not see the beautiful and gentle eyes of My Lady Laura: which, as long as he was in Avignon, locked and unlocked all his amorous thoughts, so that at present he desires no other thing than to see those which were of such beauty that no other sight could please him: grieving that through the great distance he cannot see those which were like two lights; they made his soul—which was full of darkness due to mortal <note>original: "metalli," likely a typographical error for "mortali" (mortal) or "mentali" (mental) troubles.</note> troubles—entirely serene and splendid for the pleasure of seeing them. <margin>N</margin> **ALAS, if.** Whoever adds tinder to the fire makes it burn much more. The poet clearly demonstrates this in the present fourth stanza. For having shortly before declared his incredible desire without being able to fulfill it due to the great distance from the beloved thing and due to the brevity of human life, now in this part he says that such desire is refreshed by such discussion: where he also rebukes the opinion of those who say love is forgotten through the length of time, for he is in more distress for My Lady Laura than he ever was: which he says is manifested by his already lost color <note>A reference to the "pallor of lovers," a common literary sign of deep emotional suffering.</note> through too much thinking about the beloved lady: and this proceeds from the fact that when a man has many thoughts, he cannot sleep. Whence he does not nourish himself <note>original: "il cibo non si pasce," literally "the food does not feed [him]," suggesting the body is too distressed to process nourishment.</note> and thus follows the lack of blood, which leaves the exterior parts, and this because it runs to those parts where there is greater need, I mean to the heart.

And <term>because</term> <note>original: "p", a common scribal abbreviation for "per" or "perché"</note> further, for his misfortune, he could not see beyond, he was unable to reveal the ultimate beauty known to him: which was the young & beautiful breast with two very white & firm small breasts that seemed like two autumn apples. afterward, not being satisfied with lowering her eyes many times to add more wood to the fire <note>A metaphor for increasing the poet's passion</note>, she would place her hand before her face. Petrarch laments these oppositions and impediments, comparing and likening them to the obstacles of rivers, pools, the sea, walls, hills, shadows, trees, and mist. He points out all such obstacles, yet he considers none of them equal to the obstacles created for him by his pitiless beloved.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
...and they never were. Messer Francesco <note>M.F. refers to the author, Francesco Petrarca</note> laments in this sonnet about the veil that My Lady Laura <note>M.L. refers to Laura</note> wore, with which she covered her eyes whenever he encountered her. He says that neither mist nor shadow ever impeded a man's sight as much as that veil of hers has impeded his own vision, because it hides the eyes of his lady, whom he cannot gaze upon. **And of a white hand.** "And of a white hand I still complain": he also laments an action that My Lady Laura used when he met her—that she would pretend to adjust the veil on her forehead with her hand, and thus interrupt his view. Messer Francesco describes this act for the sake of many lovers who do not understand it.

### SONNET XXXI

<margin>
Francesco T.
</margin>
<margin>
I FEAR. Among other lovely beauties, the beauty of the eyes shines no differently than a flaming ruby in polished and gleaming gold. Therefore, in this thirty-first sonnet, our poet, marvelously commending the beauty of My Lady Laura, shows her eyes to have been the very thing by which excessive loving is destroyed and almost dies; so much so, that as a remedy, he fled from their presence, no differently than a child wants to flee from the rod <note>A "rod" or "switch" used for discipline</note>. He says this because, once when the beloved My Lady Laura was passing through the street, he—perhaps somewhat indignant that he was always "plowing in the sand" <note>An idiom meaning to labor in vain</note>—turned his back to her. Then, seeing that this had displeased the lady, he excuses himself, as appears in the sonnet.
</margin>

->**I** fear so much the assault of those beautiful eyes,<-
->In which Love and my death both dwell,<-
->That I flee them, like a child flees the rod;<-
->And it has been a long time since I took the first leap;<-
->**F**rom now on, there shall be no place so laborious<-
->Or high, where my will shall not rouse itself;<-
->So as not to encounter that which scatters my senses,<-
->Leaving me, as is its wont, like cold marble.<-
->**T**herefore, if I was slow in turning to see you,<-
->It was to avoid drawing near again to the one who destroys me;<-
->Perhaps my failing was not unworthy of excuse.<-
->**F**urthermore I say: that returning to what one flees,<-
->And the heart, which released itself from such great fear;<-
->Was no small pledge of my faith.<-

<margin>Antonio</margin>
I FEAR so much the assault of those beautiful eyes. Messer Francesco shows that he greatly fears the eyes of his Lady Laura and is terrified when he encounters her. He makes a comparison, saying that he flees the eyes of his lady just as a child flees the rod with which he is beaten. He speaks to her, explaining that having found her, he did not quickly turn to look at her, and therefore he gives her the reason why he did not turn. He says that from now on there will be no place so difficult that he will not flee to it to avoid meeting her. **Therefore, if I was slow in turning to see you**: it is as if he said, "This was to avoid looking at the thing that destroys me," namely your eyes; and perhaps such a fault was not unworthy of excuse.

He writes, therefore, the present thirty-second sonnet, saying that if two things do not hinder him—either the love of My Lady Laura [or death]...

**W**HEN FROM ITS OWN SITE. The present thirty-third sonnet was composed by our poet out of indignation—which is a sadness for the good of another that is undeserved. The cause of this passion was having heard that Master Antonio da Ferrara <note>Antonio Beccari (1315–1371), a poet known for a more erratic lifestyle</note>—a man of enough natural talent but little learning—had recently been honored with the poetic laurel. Therefore, Petrarch says that when the laurel once loved by Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>—the lady having been called Daphne, as was previously declared in the fifth sonnet—departs from its own site (that is, from the coronation of true poets), it is an abominable sin. Whereupon Jove, enraged, having his son and blacksmith Vulcan make very sharp arrows, is moved to thunder, to

snow, and to rain, and no longer holds the Emperor Caesar in higher esteem than he does that ancient and uncultivated Janus, who was illiterate and unlearned. Thus the earth is soaked by the much rain brought on by such sins; even the sun withdraws its light from us, tormented that the laurel into which his beloved was converted should fall to unworthy persons. And Saturn and Mars, unlucky planets, show themselves more bold in doing harm; and even Orion, a terrible constellation, creates great force and damage in the sea against sailors. Similarly, Aeolus, king of the winds, being troubled, makes the sea, the air, and us feel—with his tempestuous breaths and stormy ruins—how the beautiful face of Venus <note>Here representing beauty/the laurel</note> awaited by the angels goes away out of indignation for such a coronation.

<margin>y</margin> I will note here with brevity some things, reserving the others for another more necessary place. Jove and Venus are considered by astrologers to be benevolent and beneficial planets, but Saturn and Mars are the contrary: malevolent and harmful. If we wish to investigate the cause of this pagan opinion, we must know that there are certain numerical proportions by which—as Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the ancient astronomer and mathematician</note> demonstrates in his work titled *On Harmony*—all things that have a relationship with one another form a fitting conjunction. Nor can anything have a relationship with another except through these natural proportions, the names of which are sesquitertian <note>original: "Epitrito"</note>, sesquialter <note>original: "Hemiodo"</note>, and epogdoic <note>original: "Epodio"</note>: doubles, triples, and quadruples. The pagans, then, hold that without such numbers there can be no connection or concord; besides this, they...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the symbolic and astrological underpinnings of Petrarch’s poetry, shifting from spiritual influences to the celestial forces—planets and constellations—that the poet uses to mirror his own emotional states and social standing.</meta>

<page-num>39</page-num>
<sig>I</sig>

...our life is moderated by the sun and by the moon. This is because these two are assigned to transient bodies for sensation and growth: we have our growth from the lunar sphere, but our sensation comes to us from the sun. In this way, our life is given to us through the benefit of both one and the other light. It is true that the conduct of our life and the effects of our actions are referred not only to some link of numbers and the applied lights: for this reason Jupiter and Venus are accompanied by these same numbers to both one and the other light. The star of Jupiter accompanies the sun through all these numbers, but it does not couple with the moon in all of them, though it does for the most part. And although for this reason both these stars are considered of good fortune <note>In astrology, Jupiter and Venus are known as "benefics," planets that bring good luck</note>, the star of Jupiter is more adapted to the sun than Venus is, and Venus is more suited to the moon than Jupiter. Therefore, they are of greater benefit to our life, as if by the logic of said numbers we have an affinity with those lights which are the authors of life. Saturn has a relationship to the sun, and Mars to the moon; therefore they are esteemed of little use and almost unfortunate to human life <note>Saturn and Mars are the "malefics," traditionally associated with hardship and conflict</note>. This is because we are joined to the authors of our life by a strict and narrow ratio of numbers. Thus, they are currently called cruel and unfortunate to the human generation by our poet, because an unworthy person is exalted to such a degree while worthy people do not appear to be valued; and he says this because he was not yet crowned <note>Petrarch often complained about his lack of formal recognition before being crowned Poet Laureate in 1341</note>. Therefore, Jupiter is troubled and angry, and Venus departs from the human generation so as not to see such enormity—as if to say that misfortune reigns entirely, signified by Saturn and by Mars.

¶ Orion, because of the greatness of his constellation, consumes many days in his rising, which causes tempests on sea and land. He is said by poets to have been born in this manner: King Oenopion, having no son, received into his house with an honorable banquet three gods: Jupiter, Neptune, and Mercury. Seeing themselves honorably received by him, they encouraged him to ask them for some grace; obeying them gladly, he prayed that they might grant him a son. Wishing to fulfill this, all three urinated together into an ox hide from a bull sacrificed to them that lay there on the ground, telling him that he should bury that hide, thus wrapped in that urine, and after the required months had passed, they should uncover and unwrap it. When the king did this, he found a boy born of that urine, to whom he gave the name Orion, which means "urinary" <note>A folk etymology; the author links the name to the Greek 'ouron' for urine</note>, since among the Dorians it signifies urine. When he grew up, he became an excellent hunter and fell in love with the goddess Diana. He had the audacity to want to wrestle with her in the meadow, or to make love; for which Diana, being indignant, killed him with her arrows, or with the scorpion that she sent upon him. This latter version seems more believable, because when the Scorpion rises, Orion sets <note>An astronomical observation of the two constellations being on opposite sides of the sky</note>. As was said before, he is a constellation into which the gods, moved to compassion after his death, converted him; he commonly induces tempests and rain when he rises, nor is it a wonder if it rains, since he was born of urine.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ WHEN HE MOVES FROM HIS PROPER PLACE. Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> pretends that Jove, like one enamored of My Lady Laura, was always troubled in the air and the sky whenever she went to some place and stayed hidden, and it rained and snowed because of the anger he had at not being able to see her. He introduces the smith—that is, Vulcan—who is said poetically to make the lightning bolts for Jove. He has no more respect for Caesar than for Janus: that is, for his own month <note>original: "hoc est a mense suo"</note>, which is called July, than for Janus, which is January <note>original: "a quo trahit mensis denominationem"; from which the month takes its name</note>. It is as if he says: Jove strikes with lightning in January just as in July—that is, when he is tormented by the absence of My Lady Laura.

### SONNET XXXVI.

<margin>
¶ HE WHO IN Thessaly. Now he finds himself again in Avignon in this 36th sonnet, where he no longer returns to Italy; and so the person who collected these sonnets and songs had little regard for the order which we would need to follow. In short, he laments the cruelty of Lady Laura, who is not moved to compassion at all toward him, who loves her above all else. This is contrasted with how we see that many have humbled themselves even toward their mortal enemies, just as Gaius Caesar grieved and had compassion for the death of Pompey, his son-in-law, when he recognized his features from the head sent to him by Ptolemy, the King of Egypt. And also King David, who killed Goliath, who was as large as a giant, seeing the impiety of Absalom his son, who was a rebel and mortal enemy, wept after he heard of his death. One can also understand this regarding Sheba, who made the people of Israel rebel against David, and who was punished by God with a great slaughter. David did the same for Saul, his father-in-law and mortal enemy, when he saw him killed by the Philistines along with his son Jonathan and the others on Mount Gilboa. But that inhuman and most truculent woman felt the blows of love no more than an immobile and very harsh rock. Therefore, her face never changed out of compassion, but she had her defenses ready: her veil, her downcast eyes, and the placing of her hand before her face. And the more she saw him torn apart by the anxieties of love that were killing him, the less her eyes were moved to weep; indeed, they seemed disdainful and full of anger.

But Narcissus, even more stunned by such a voice, looked around, and seeing no person, said: "Why do you flee and speak such words?" She, who was wasting away with love, replied. Then Narcissus, deceived in his speech by the similarity of the voice, continued, saying: "Let us go together here." To which, with supreme pleasure due to the hope of fulfilling her vow, the resonance quickly replied: "Let us go together." And to come to the facts, she suddenly came out of the grove and ran toward Narcissus to throw her arms around his desired neck. But Narcissus, inexperienced with such food, no differently than if he had seen an asp, began to flee; and fleeing thus, he nonetheless forced himself to untangle his neck from the hands of her who, closely aided by the forces of love, had embraced him, saying: "Death will kill me before you have possession of me." When she saw herself so miserably despised, she went away, entirely disconsolate and afflicted, to hide in the woods, and for shame she covered her face with leaves; and from that time on she always lived in caves and in hidden, valley-like places. However, the flames of love did not depart from her, but growing all the more, they burned her as the pain of being rejected continually pierced her heart like a fierce knife. Persevering in this affliction, her slender and well-formed body gradually, through the watchful and restless troubles of her heart, grew thin and became—through a drying leanness—shriveled and full of wrinkles, so that in a short space of time, all the juice and moisture of her bodily limbs being consumed and gone into the air, only her voice and bones remained; and although the voice remains continually, the bones were miraculously converted into stones. Nemesis, surnamed Rhamnusia <note>An epithet for the goddess Nemesis, derived from her sanctuary at Rhamnus in Attica.</note>, heard this imprecation as a worthy and most just thing. And the said place was so defended from the solar rays by the pleasantness of the surrounding trees, which made no small shadow there, that no heat could be felt. Because Narcissus, who was not a little tired both from the labor of hunting and also by the vehemence of the excessive heat, when he reached the most pleasant grove and saw the beauty of the place and the icy water of the clear fountain, suddenly threw himself upon the flowery and gracious grass. And because he was not a little breathless from thirst, he stretched out on the margin of the spring itself to drink, where, with his face toward the water—called while he believed he would lighten his thirst—he was instead assaulted by a greater thirst. For as he looked with starry eyes at the quiet and immobile water, he saw the marvelous image of his graceful and most beautiful face, with which he suddenly kindled with so much love that he burned in his heart no differently than if he had been in the most burning furnace of Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire and the forge.</note>; and so great was the insurmountable

¶ **BUT** after Narcissus spoke these and many other lamentable words, weeping to himself, standing still over the clear fountain with his wet eyes contemplating his own likeness with vain sighs and infinite groans, finally overcome and oppressed by insuperable grief, he tore open his chest down to the bottom, ripping all his fine clothes. Remaining thus naked, striking now the graceful face and now the snowy chest with slaps and fists as much as the wrathful force of love permitted him, he dyed his whitest skin a vermilion color, just like the lovely flowers of the heliotrope <note>original: "tornasole." While Narcissus usually turns into the flower that bears his name, this text identifies it as a heliotrope or "sun-turner."</note> in the springtime. Thus beating himself and increasing his pain through the striking, and little by little consuming himself through the hidden and flaming torches of love, finally—liquefied by continuous weeping and entirely destroyed—he was miraculously transformed, as punishment for his ill-used beauty and annoying insolence, from a most beautiful and vain youth into the aforementioned heliotrope flower. This was done so that in every posterity and age, he might be an example to all those who, having abandoned the excellence and beauty of the soul, place all their happiness in the fragile beauty of the body; which lasts no longer than the beauty of the flower which, being vigorous and delightful in the morning, shortly after, touched by the heat of the sun's rays, becomes withered and discolored.

> The gold and the pearls, and the flowers crimson and white,
> Which winter ought to make languid and dry,
> Are for me sharp and poisonous thorns,
> Which I feel through my breast and my sides;
> Therefore my days shall be tearful and lacking,
> For great grief rarely allows one to grow old.
> But I blame more those murderous mirrors;
> Which you have exhausted by gazing at yourself.
> These imposed silence on my lord <note>The poet refers to "Amone" or the God of Love.</note>;
> Who prayed to you for me; wherefore he fell silent,
> Seeing your desire end within yourself:
> These were fashioned over the waters
> Of the abyss, and tinted in eternal oblivion;
> From whence the beginning of my death was born.

<margin>Fran. M</margin>
¶ **THE GOLD** and the pearls. The amorous ardor of our pleasant and elegant poet manifests itself no less in this thirty-eighth sonnet than in many others. We can therefore see clearly through this sonnet—in which the poet is induced to speak with Lady Laura—that the said Lady Laura did not go about dressed like a peasant, but was entirely adorned with embroideries of gold and pearls, and with lovely garlands of various little flowers made artificially of white and crimson silk during the winter time, as is the custom in this illustrious city of Milan, and in Florence, and in many other cities of Italy where Venus is no less appreciated by idle minds than Diana <note>Diana represents chastity and the hunt, while Venus represents love and beauty. The commentator suggests these cities value fashion and romance over austere modesty.</note>. Speaking, then, the sonnet in the person of the one who sends it, he says that the ornaments of gold and pearls used by Lady Laura, and the little garlands of crimson and white flowers—which naturally should become languid and dry in winter if they were real and not artificial as they were—serve to increase her beauty in such a way as to increase the love in him. Because he cannot reach his desired end, they cause him such bitterness and almost a poisonous pain that they seem to him no different than wooden thorns <note>original: "stecchi di legno"</note> passing through his breast to his heart and through his sides, in which two places a mortal pain is felt. For this reason, the days of his miserable life are spent in weeping due to melancholy, and for this same reason they are shortened, so that he might die before his time; for great grief so weighs upon a man's heart that it does not let him grow old, but kills him. Then he laments those murderous mirrors in which the lovely lady—no differently than the aforementioned Narcissus in the clear fountain—gazes at herself, causing her to see how beautiful she is, so that she admires no one but herself. This being understood by Petrarch, he had placed silence upon his writing to her, as it seemed to him that his amorous prayers through his sonnets were in vain, she being like Narcissus, enamored of no one but herself. And thus concluding, he adds that these mirrors were fashioned in the depths of hell <note>original: "profundità de l'inferno"</note>, insofar as she is cruel, and colored and tinted in the river Lethe <note>A river in the underworld whose waters caused forgetfulness.</note>, insofar as she has forgotten him and his love; which being forgotten by her is the cause of his death.

<margin>Anto. L:</margin>
¶ **THE GOLD** and the pearls and the flowers crimson and white: he names under a figure of speech the beauties of his lady which torment him. By the gold he means her hair; by the pearls, her teeth; by the flowers, the colors of her cheeks; by the white, her fairness. He says then that he blames the mirrors more, because every day she makes herself more beautiful and more cruel within them. And he says they were fashioned over the waters of the abyss, that is, in the river Lethe, because it is a river from which whoever drinks forgets everything; and he says this because she forgets him.

## SONNET XLI.

> Though I have kept you from lying,
> To the best of my power, and honored you greatly,
> Ungrateful tongue; yet you have not
> Returned honor to me: but brought me anger and shame.
> For when I most need your help
> To beg for mercy, then you stand
> Always more frozen; and if you do speak,
> The words are imperfect, like those of a man who dreams.
> Sad tears, you accompany me
> All through the night, when I wish to be alone;
> Then you flee from before my peace.
> And you, so ready to give me anguish and grief,
> Sighs, then you draw out slow and broken.
> Only my sight does not keep the heart's secret.

<margin>Francesco Alunno</margin>
¶ **THOUGH I HAVE KEPT.** As was explained in the third preceding sonnet regarding the situation that befell our amorous and inexperienced poet—having been unable out of shame to declare his fiery desires to his beloved My Lady Laura through speech—he now manifests this openly in the forty-first sonnet. He laments to his tongue as if to a thankless and ungrateful thing; for although it was always practiced by him in speaking the truth, it did not have the courage in such a time of need to ask for mercy from his beloved Lady Laura. If it said anything at all, it was entirely inept and poorly ordered, as the **words of one who dreams** usually are—which commonly happens when one asks for a <term>dishonorable thing</term> <note>In the context of courtly love, "dishonorable" refers to a request that might compromise the lady's chastity or social standing.</note>. Then he adds that the same thing happened regarding his inability to weep [in her presence] as he does at night when no one sees him; for he is ashamed to do so in the presence of another person of reputation, as if it were a soft and abject thing. For a similar reason, he shows he was also unable to let out great and fiery sighs, such as would have been necessary in her presence, whose help he wanted to seek by opening his heart's distress. And finally, he concludes that although he has not spoken, nor wept, nor sighed as was necessary, it is not because his mind—through which the heart (that is, the soul) sees, according to the philosophers, just like the eye—remains silent within itself; rather, it speaks and weeps and sighs from the afflicted passion.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ **THOUGH I HAVE KEPT YOU FROM LYING:** He excuses himself. Master Francesco, disposed to speak his mind to his lady, found that upon seeing her alone, in the middle of speaking his courage failed him, not knowing what to say. Once he returned home, he composed this sonnet, rebuking his tongue and his mouth’s [lack of] audacity, for this happened because of too much love. Virgil writes similarly in the book of the *Aeneid*: **Thus he begins to speak, and his voice stops in mid-utterance** <note>original Latin: "Sic incipit affari: mediisq; in voce resistit." Virgil, Aeneid IV.76, describing Dido's hesitation to speak to Aeneas.</note>.

<margin>First, our poet declares in this first stanza, through the example of that little old woman who has gone on a pilgrimage, how when she sees the sun set—so as not to remain outside in the open country—she hastens and quickens her steps as much as she can, and thus rests at night. When she finds herself among her own people, she takes some consolation, so that she forgets the hardship and the pain previously received while walking. On the contrary, he says it happens to himself, the Weary One, because the pain he felt during the day—for not being able to obtain the beloved thing—grows all the more at night when, being alone after the sun has departed, he has no way to distract himself here and there as he did during the day.</margin>

-> **The weary little old pilgrim woman** <-
> Doubles her steps, and hastens more and more,
> And then, so alone,
> At the end of her day,
> Is sometimes consoled
> By some brief rest; where she forgets
> The hardship and the pain of the past path.
> But alas, every pain that the day brings me
> Increases; whenever it sets out
> To depart from us, the eternal light.

*The Antipodes are estimated by the ancients to be all those people who are said to inhabit the lower hemisphere: and they are called Antipodes because they have their feet opposite to ours <note>The term "Antipodes" literally means "those with feet opposite." In the medieval and Renaissance mind, this was a subject of great geographical and theological debate.</note>: to which people the sun brings the beginning of night when to us it brings the beginning of day. There are some philosophers who, with confirmed reasoning according to Claudius Ptolemy <note>A 2nd-century mathematician and geographer whose works were foundational to Renaissance science.</note>—as was already said above—demonstrate that no people can inhabit the lower hemisphere; but by the "Antipodes" we should understand the Spaniards and the furthest Western peoples who, if we consider carefully, have their feet in a straight line opposite the feet of the Indians and the extreme Eastern peoples.*

<sig>Antonio
P.</sig>

¶ *IN THE season when the rapid sky declines.* <note>original: "NE LA stagion che'l ciel rapido inclina"</note> Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch, the author.</note> puts forward five examples in this moral song of certain types of very troubled men, and also other animals, who, although they endure a harsh life during the day, nevertheless rest at night and have some quiet; but he can say that he never has rest, neither day nor night. *The weary little old woman:* here he touches upon the first example of a little old pilgrim woman who, being weary in the evening from the toil of the day, rests at night and forgets the fatigue of the past day and refreshes herself for walking; but he says that when that pilgrim rests, he begins to grieve more. *AS the sun turns its flaming wheels:* Master Francesco takes the second example from the laborer <term>zappatore; a farmhand who works the earth with a hoe or mattock</term> who, having toiled during the day in his work, is relieved of such labor with the rustic night: that is, with rustic singing and poor food similar to those acorns <note>A reference to the "Golden Age" in classical mythology, when humans were said to live simply on acorns before the invention of agriculture.</note> upon which our ancestors lived, which, though the world flees them now, are still held in reverence for their memory. *WHEN the shepherd sees the rays descend:* Master Francesco takes the third example from the shepherds who, when they see night falling, move with their flock and, wherever they find themselves, make a little hut to rest; but then he begins to cry out more. *AND sailors in some enclosed valley:* the fourth example he takes from the sailors who, when night falls, strive to rest under their garments in some enclosed place of the ship; but he still never finds an end to his torment. *And because I vent myself a little in speaking:* the fifth example is from the oxen who, having plowed and furrowed during the day, rest in the evening and leave the yoke; and he says he carries his on his neck at every hour. The Song, according to what he shows, was made while he was leaning against a rock in a solitary place; and he says: *IF being with me has made you of my condition* <note>original: "SE L'esser meco t'ha fatto de mia scheraccio"; Petrarch is addressing his poem directly in the closing lines.</note>; and as solitary as I am here, you will not care too much for the praise of others.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch's Canzone 50. Having previously compared his lack of rest to the rest found by a weary pilgrim woman, the poet now introduces the examples of the plowman, the shepherd, and the sailor to highlight his unique and ceaseless suffering.</meta>

And with words and rustic melodies
He clears all heaviness from his breast;
And then he covers the table
With meager food
Similar to those acorns
Which the whole world honors while avoiding them:
But let whoever wishes rejoice from hour to hour.
For I have not yet had—I will not say a happy [hour]—
But one hour of rest,
Neither by the turning of the sky, nor of any planet.

*The flaming wheels <note>A poetic reference to the chariot of the Sun.</note> now descend and the shadows from the mountains grow to become night: the plowman takes his hoe back upon his shoulder and returns singing, lifting from his heart every other trouble and thought. Having returned home, he sits at a table crowded with poor and rustic foods, very different from those acorns that were eaten in the Golden Age of Saturn <note>In classical mythology, the Golden Age was a time of primitive innocence where humans lived on what nature provided, like acorns; the commentator notes that modern people "honor" this idea but would not actually want to eat such poor food.</note>. Nevertheless, though these foods do not please modern peasants, they are the reason the peasants honor the whole world, insofar as they have striven and still strive to enrich the world with beautiful and lovely fruits through sowing and planting. Then returning to himself, our poet declares his condition to be much worse than that of the plowman: for the plowman takes at least some pleasure at night; but the poet has no rest for even a single hour, neither by day nor by night. Regarding what pertains to the planets, this was discussed by me above in the commentary on the twenty-fourth sonnet.*

### STANZA III.

<margin>WHEN HE SEES THE R... Shepherd. The third comparison of this present third stanza to the same purpose declares that the shepherd is in a much better condition regarding rest than our poet is: because at the setting of the sun, when he sees the east already turning dark and night falling, he rises from the meadows where he has grazed his little sheep and very slowly returns with them either home or to some cave closed or covered with leafy branches. There, having put every thought aside, he settles and sets himself to sleep. But he says the opposite happens to him: because most cruel Love informs him much more at night than by day how he must follow the beloved lady. She, no differently than a wild beast, destroys him all the more by fleeing; and Love does not bind her, though she now hides from his sight with new tricks—just as wild beasts do when being hunted—and now she openly flees before him. This shows that at times Lady Laura pretended not to understand his "jargon" <note>original: "gergone"; likely referring to the coded language of courtly love or the poet's subtle hints.</note> or see anything, and sometimes she gave him to understand that the amorous hunt did not please her at all.</margin>

When the shepherd sees the rays
Of the great planet <note>The Sun.</note> fall toward the nest where it dwells;
And the eastern regions darken;
He rises to his feet; and with his accustomed rod,
Leaving the grass and the springs and the beeches,
He moves his flock gently;
Then far from the people,
In a small hut or a cave
Strewn with green leaves;
There without care he settles and sleeps.
Alas, cruel Love; but you then more urge me
To follow a wild beast that destroys
My voice, my steps, and my tracks;
And you do not bind her, who hides and flees...

...they provide for themselves: and so they give themselves to the people.
But Petrarch <unclear>stated</unclear> that it was more "night" the further the sun, having set, moves beyond the west, leaving Spain behind it along with the kingdom of Granada, Morocco, and the Pillars of Hercules <note>The Strait of Gibraltar, considered the edge of the known world in antiquity.</note>; also the oxen and the women, and even in this manner: the lower hemisphere together with the animals that are in it: all of whom at such a time find rest from their toils. Yet he could not put an end to his continuous toil of amorous passion. For which reason he reasonably grieved all the more as he saw his loss grow every day, especially since ten years had already passed while he persevered in this <term>bramoso disio</term> <note>literally "covetous desire"; an intense, almost painful longing</note>, nor did he see how he could be liberated from it.

> And he leaves Spain behind his shoulders,
> And Granada and Morocco and the Pillars,
> And the men and the women,
> And the world and the animals
> Quiet their ills:
> I put no end to my stubborn toil,
> And I grieve that every day adds to the damage,
> For I am still growing in this desire,
> Now very near the tenth year,
> Nor can I guess who may release me from it.

<margin>T</margin>
**AND BECAUSE FOR** a little while: Petrarch persevering in his desire to expressly signify that no one else has a worse condition than he, says in the present stanza that the oxen, and even more so the <term>bifolci</term> <note>plowmen or ox-drivers</note> who have been exhausted by the fields and the hills where they have plowed, return home released from their yokes. Wherefore he reasonably laments his own continuous sighs and the intolerable yoke of love. Because of this persecution, he is forced to weep with his wretched eyes; he laments not a little that he ever opened them to gaze upon his beloved lady, adding that her face is sculpted in such a manner in his fantasy and heart through his looking. Thus, never by force nor by ingenuity could he be removed from such an imagination until he was given as prey to death. His saying that he "knows not what to believe of her" proceeds from the habit of lovers who, on one hand, believe themselves to be loved because they love; and on the other hand, they doubt this not a little because they see no certain sign in any effect of ever being able to reach the <term>quia</term> <note>A Scholastic term referring to the "fact" or "conclusion"; here it implies the physical or emotional fulfillment of his love.</note>.

->### STANZA V.<-

> And because I vent a little in speaking:
> I see in the evening the oxen return freed
> From the fields and the busy hills.
> My sighs, why are they not taken from me
> At any time? Why not the heavy yoke?
> Why day and night are my eyes wet?
> Wretched me, what did I want;
> When first so fixedly
> I held them on her beautiful face,
> To carve it, imagining in part.

> Will it be moved; until I am given as prey

## SONNET XLII.

> ->Small was the distance for the light to approach my eyes,<-
> ->The light that dazzles them from afar;<-
> ->For as it saw her change Thessaly,<-
> ->So I would have changed my every form.<-
> ->And if I cannot transform myself into her<-
> ->More than I already am: not that it would avail me for mercy<-
> ->From whatever most rigid stone is carved,<-
> ->I would be pensive in my appearance today;<-
> ->Either of diamond, or of a beautiful white marble<-
> ->Perhaps through fear, or of a jasper<-
> ->Prized then by the greedy and foolish common folk,<-
> ->And I would be outside of the heavy and harsh yoke;<-
> ->For which I envy 그 weary old man<-
> ->Who with his shoulders casts a shadow over Morocco.<-

<margin>Francesco Filelfo</margin>
¶ **SMALL WAS THE DISTANCE.** Having previously shown the hardness of the stony heart of Madonna Laura, now in this 42nd sonnet our enamored poet—using a comparison not of the sun, as some fools believe, but of the darkened moon—declares the disdain she showed him one day upon seeing herself followed by him everywhere. For when Master Francesco <note>The poet, Francesco Petrarch.</note> met her on the road to Avignon, she showed him a very troubled face; and for this reason, he compared her to the moon when it is darkened. The poets used to say this happened whenever the women of Thessaly <note>In antiquity, Thessaly was renowned as a land of witches and sorceresses who were believed to have the power to "draw down" or change the color of the moon with their spells.</note> enchanted the moon through some of their evil deeds or sorcery. Whence he says that in such a light, which from afar dazzled his sight, the distance was small. And that he, too, because of his melancholy, would have his face and appearance changed into hers, just as the moon was seen changed in color by the women of Thessaly. He adds that even if he could be transformed into her by such a facial expression more than he already was—though it would profit him little—this was because he was naturally cheerful in appearance, yet he would at least have become like stone, or diamond, or marble, or jasper because of his thoughts. This transformation is what usually happens through fear; and thus he would be out of the yoke of love, which is full of harshness and heaviness and brings him so much distress. He would have preferred to be like Mount Atlas, situated at the ends of Mauritania <note>Modern-day Morocco and Algeria.</note>, so high that it casts a shadow as far as Morocco, the fable of which we shall narrate briefly.

<margin>Note</margin>
¶ The Gorgons were brave and fierce women in the matter of arms in Libya. They were first said to have been in those same times as the Libyan Amazons, who were beaten and afflicted by Queen Myrina. Then, after a long time, they were killed and destroyed by Perseus, son of Jove and Danaë, when Medusa was queen there, and finally by Hercules. The aforementioned Perseus, a glorious and most invincible captain, having heard of the nobility of the Gorgons, set out from Greece with a large and brave army. Having crossed into Libya, he fought a great and dangerous battle with the Gorgons. Finally, after a great effusion of blood, once he had conquered and deprived Queen Medusa of all her honor and dignity, he turned with his victorious army toward the nearby country of King Atlas. Atlas wished to oppose him so that he should enter his country neither as a friend nor as an enemy. Perseus prepared for battle; seeing this, Atlas clearly understood that Perseus's forces were nearly insuperable due to the army having grown from the victory over the Gorgons. He was terrified and remained struck senseless by terror, as if he were a stone, and surrendered to Perseus. Because of this measureless fear, the poets say that he was converted into the stone mountain called Atlas after his name. Since we have spoken of this according to the Milanese gathering <note>A reference to a specific scholarly discussion or edition produced in Milan.</note>, I will not extend myself further at present.

<margin>Antonio da Tempo</margin>
¶ **SMALL WAS THE DISTANCE to approach my eyes:** Master Francesco, having encountered Madonna Laura and she having avoided his gaze, made this sonnet for fear of being inflamed with an even more burning desire for her. He says he would have changed just as he saw that burning light change Thessaly; that is, he would have been as burned as Thessaly was burned when Phaethon <note>In myth, Phaethon lost control of the sun chariot, nearly scorching the earth.</note> set the world on fire. **FOR WHICH I ENVY 그 weary old man:** This was the giant Atlas, who according to the poets sustained the entire heavens upon his shoulders and has a city called Morocco near him.

<margin>Francesco Filelfo</margin>

¶ **NOT to her lover more.** This is the tenth song—or rather, a single stanza of the tenth song—which was either never finished or perhaps was not found. While Petrarch was passing through the foothills of the mountains, he saw a peasant girl <note>original: "villanella"</note> who was washing; nearby, she had left some little sheep to graze. She had spread a veil she had washed out in the sun to dry. Although she was by nature a simple country girl and a shepherdess, she was nonetheless of such a graceful and pleasant manner that our poet—a most diligent examiner and judge of hidden qualities—fell in love with her based on this display of outward beauty. He would have done more than use words if it had been permitted to him. He says that Diana did not please Actaeon <note>In Greek mythology, the hunter Actaeon stumbled upon the goddess Diana bathing; she turned him into a stag as punishment.</note> more than this rigid and modest shepherdess pleased him because of her unfeigned beauty.

### CANZONE X.

> ->Diana did not please her lover more,<-
> ->When by such a chance, entirely naked,<-
> ->He saw her in the middle of the icy waters;<-
> ->Than did the harsh alpine shepherdess please me,<-
> ->Set there to wash a graceful little veil,<-
> ->Which might enclose Laura's lovely, blonde hair;<-
> ->So that it made me now, while the sky burns,<-
> ->All tremble with an amorous chill.<-

<margin>Francesco Filelfo</margin>

¶ **NOBLE spirit.** In this eleventh song, our poet rejoices that the elder Sir Pandolfo Malatesta <note>A member of the powerful Malatesta family of Rimini; however, many modern scholars believe this poem was actually addressed to Cola di Rienzo.</note> has been appointed by the Holy Church as Senator of Rome. This occurred at the time when it was decided that Pope Gregory XI should depart from Avignon and return to Italy. The poet encourages him toward the common good of Italy, especially to remove the partisan strife of the Romans. In this first stanza, addressing Sir Pandolfo, he says that since he sees no other prince in Italy besides him, he speaks to no one else but his lordship. He grieves that Italy is so sluggish that, if it were possible, he would have liked to grab her by the hair to punish her; he says this out of concern regarding the "tramontani" <note>Literally "those from beyond the mountains," referring to foreign powers like the French or Germans.</note>.

### CANZONE XI.

> ->Noble spirit, who rule those limbs<-
> ->Within which, wandering, dwells<-
> ->A valorous, shrewd, and wise lord;<-
> ->Since you have arrived at the honored rod of office,<-
> ->With which you correct Rome and her errors,<-
> ->And recall her to her ancient path;<-
> ->I speak to you; because elsewhere a ray<-
> ->Of virtue I do not see, which is extinguished in the world;<-
> ->Nor do I find anyone ashamed of doing evil.<-
> ->What Italy waits for, or what she yearns for,<-
> ->I know not; she seems not to feel her own woes;<-
> ->Old, idle, and slow,<-
> ->Will she sleep forever? Is there no one to wake her?<-
> ->I wish I had my hands wrapped in her hair.<-

<margin>Antonio da Tempo</margin>

¶ **NOBLE spirit:** An influential and noble friend of Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> having been created Senator, Petrarch sent him this "moral song" <term>moral canzone: a poem focused on ethics, politics, or philosophy rather than romantic love</term> to rouse him to bring peace to the land and remove evildoers. **MOVE the head:** to call with the face, meaning a man should exert his influence. **NOR gluttonous:** meaning full of negligent people. He mentions the **People of Mars**, that is, the Romans, who are called the people of Mars because Romulus, the son of Mars, founded the city. **The stones where the limbs were enclosed:** referring to ancient tombs like those of Romulus and Trajan. **O Great Scipiones, o faithful Brutus:** here the author exclaims to the great Roman heroes. **End the civil hatred:** meaning, may you not be hated by the people of Romulus. **Where the path to their roofs is closed:** he says this because as long as this internal dissension lasted, one could not travel to Rome as pilgrims used to do in the past. **Between the altars and the naked statues:** he says this because these tyrannies are occurring even among the clergy. **Ah, how contrary:** how desperate are these ways where brawls break out among the statues and altars; those places were set on high to thank God, not to serve as cover for political plots. **Tearful women and the defenseless commoners:** he describes the people who pray for peace. **Which burns today... a few make a thousand:** meaning that by removing and dealing with just a few of the troublemakers, the rest will fall into line. **Bears, wolves, lions, eagles, serpents:** by these animals he lists, he refers to the noble families who were opposed to the **Colonna family** <note>The "Orsini" are the bears, the "Colonna" are the columns (implied), etc. Petrarch was a close associate of the Colonna family.</note>.

## STANZA II.

<margin>
<sig>B</sig>
**I DO NOT hope.** The second stanza of the present song declares the unheard-of laziness of the Romans, who appeared so useless that they cared for nothing more, as if every virtue were extinguished. Therefore, he says that as a thing destined by God, the government of Rome—head of Italy and of all the world—is committed to the arms of that lord. He encourages him to take her by the hair and pull her out of such great misery, appearing to him that he alone is the worthy prince who, through his singular virtue, is able to do this.
</margin>

> *I do not hope that ever from her lazy sleep*
> *She will move her head for any call one makes;*
> *So heavily is she oppressed, and by such a burden.*
> *But not without destiny is she committed to your arms;*
> *For they alone can shake her strongly and raise her up;*
> *And now Rome, our Head, is entrusted to you.*

> *So that the sluggish one may emerge from the mud:*

> *Place the greatest part of my hope in you:*
> *For if the people of Mars*

> *It seems to me the grace falls to your days.*

<margin>
<sig>C</sig>
**THE ROMANS** are called the "people of Mars" for this reason: Numitor and Amulius were brothers. The kingdom should have fallen to Numitor as the one who was of greater age. Amulius occupied it and took it from him by force, leaving him only his portion of the common paternal goods.
</margin>

Numitor had a daughter named <term>Ilia Rhea</term><note>Also known as Rhea Silvia, the mother of Romulus and Remus.</note>. In order that she might not marry and bear a male child who might later avenge the injury to Numitor, Amulius constrained her to enter into religion in the temple of the goddess Vesta. There, according to the Latins, perpetual virginity was observed; however, according to the Greeks, it was not perpetual but for a certain time. <term>Plutarch</term><note>A Greek-Roman historian (c. 46 – 120 AD) famous for his "Parallel Lives."</note> of Chaeronea says that such virginity was observed for thirty years: the first ten years she learned the religious rites she was to follow and observe; the second ten she practiced everything she had learned; and the final ten years she taught others what she had learned. Once those thirty years had passed, it was permitted for each woman to leave that religious life and marry if she wished; although very few married due to their age, and likewise few of them ended up well.

<margin><sig>D</sig></margin>
But <term>Dionysius of Halicarnassus</term><note>A Greek historian who lived in Rome during the reign of Augustus.</note>, who was a freedman of Marcus Varro and a most learned man not only in Greek but also in Latin, writes that such religion and virginity was ordained and compelled by law only until the age of five <note>This is likely a transcription error or a specific variant reading in Filelfo's source; standard accounts say thirty years.</note>. He adds that when the said <term>Ilia Rhea</term> had already been in the aforementioned religion for four years and had already entered the fifth, Amulius—doubting that if she left and married, the very thing he had previously feared would happen—disguised himself in the same habit and armor that the idol of Mars was dressed in. Having heard that Rhea went every day into the woods of Mars near the monastery of Vesta to take water from a clear fountain for the needs of their temple, he came out from his hidden ambush and assaulted the terrified girl. First, he learned by experience whether she was female or male before she could realize by whose wound she had been struck. And Amulius did this not out of love, but to find a reason to put her in danger.

<margin><sig>E</sig></margin>
Others say, as does the same Dionysius, that it was not Amulius who carried out such snares, but a young man who had fallen in love with her before she was placed in religion. And because of that person—be it Amulius or someone else—he found good and fertile ground; immediately the young girl, having been tilled, took the seed:

lius Scipio the Elder and then the Younger. **¶ THE Elder was he who, in the second war of the Ro-**
mans against the Carthaginians, having carried himself valiantly, was called "Africanus" before all others. He was the son of Publius Scipio, who died in Spain, although he was estimated by the common people to be the son of Jove <note>Jupiter, the king of the Roman gods.</note>; and this was because before his mother became pregnant, a serpent was seen in her bed, and after he was born, a dragon coiled itself around him without doing him any harm. And it is said that when he went by night into the Capitol, into the temple of Jove, the dogs never barked at him; and being eighteen years of age, he saved his father Publius Scipio from death near the Ticinus <note>The Battle of Ticinus (218 BCE), a key early conflict of the Second Punic War.</note>, where he was at the battle with Hannibal, the captain of the Carthaginians. And when the Roman youth, because of the terrible defeats received from the Carthaginians, wished to abandon Italy, he alone with his gravity <note>term: "gravità" — here meaning a dignified and serious authority.</note> withdrew them from such a purpose. The rest of those who had escaped from the battle of Cannae <note>Rome's most disastrous defeat against Hannibal in 216 BCE.</note> he led to Canosa by his prudence and spirit. And at the age of twenty-four, being sent as praetor and captain into Spain, having arrived there, he took New Carthage by force; and a most beautiful virgin, betrothed to Indibilis, a most noble Spanish youth, being presented to him, he would not accept her, saying to those men-at-arms who presented her to him: "In truth, I would receive her willingly if I were a private man and not a captain." The ransom that her father paid to redeem her, he added to her dowry and restored her to her kin; and immediately he drove out of Spain Hasdrubal and Mago, the brothers of Hannibal. And after many other great and marvelous deeds, he was finally the cause that the Senate of Carthage was made to recall Hannibal from Italy to defend the fatherland, with whom Scipio, having descended into battle, defeated him with all his army and made the Carthaginians tributaries of the Romans. Yet in the end, he could not escape the bite of pestiferous envy, for he was accused before the Roman people by Petilius and by Quintus, tribunes of the plebs, that he had stolen the money of the Republic; to which he made no other answer than that first, in the sight of the people, he tore up the book where he had written the account of such money, saying: "O Romans, this is that day on which I defeated the Carthaginians together with Hannibal, your..."
