<margin>H</margin>
¶ Publius Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus, who was later surnamed Africanus the Younger: he was the son of Lucius Aemilius Paullus and was adopted by the son of the aforementioned Africanus the Elder. He bore himself most valiantly in the battle against Perseus, the King of Macedonia, and performed many other brave deeds in Spain while serving as a legate <note>A high-ranking military officer or deputy.</note> to Lucilius in Africa under the commander Titus Manilius, where he was awarded the golden siege crown <term>obsidional crown</term> <note>The highest military honor, given to a commander who broke a siege.</note>. He later asked for the office of aedile <note>An official in charge of public buildings and festivals.</note> but was made consul before the legal age and without even asking for it. Having gone against Carthage, he took and destroyed it before six months had passed, and in Spain, he defeated Numantia by starvation. Later, having returned to Rome from an embassy given to him, because he replied to Carbo in the public assembly that it seemed to him Tiberius Gracchus had been justly killed, he was found the following morning in his chamber, murdered by the opposing faction with the consent of his wife, who was the sister of the Gracchi. It is estimated that nothing was found in his inheritance except twenty-two pounds of silver and half a pound of gold.

<margin>I</margin>
¶ Lucius Junius Brutus was the son of the sister of Tarquin the Proud; he had previously feigned being a fool <note>The name "Brutus" in Latin implies dullness or stupidity.</note> so as not to be killed as his brother had been, who was murdered by Tarquin for his riches. For this reason, he was called Brutus. Later, after the rape of Lucretia, seeing the opportunity, he conspired with Tricipitinus and Collatinus for the destruction of King Tarquin. Once the king and his sons were banished, Brutus himself was made the first consul. Having discovered that his own sons had conspired with the Aquilii and Vitellii to bring back the Tarquins, he had them whipped and beheaded. Later, coming to blows in battle with Aruns, the son of the king, they killed each other simultaneously.

<margin>K</margin>
¶ Gaius Fabricius was adorned with infinite virtues, and among others, that of integrity. Having gone to Pyrrhus to ransom prisoners, he refused to take an infinite amount of gold, nor would he accept lordship, even though Pyrrhus wished to give him part of his kingdom. To him, Fabricius replied: "This would not be useful to you, for if the people of Epirus get a taste of us both, they would rather be ruled by me than by you." We shall speak of him more nobly elsewhere.

### STANZA 4

<margin>Francesco Petrarch</margin>
> And if anything from down here is cared for in heaven;
> The souls, who are citizens up there,
> And have abandoned their bodies on earth;
> Pray you for an end to the long civil hatred;
> Because of which the people cannot find safety;
> Whereby the path to those dwellings is closed to them
> Which were once devout; and now in war
> Are made almost like a den of thieves,
> Such that the door is closed only to the good;
> And among the altars, and among the naked statues
> Every cruel enterprise seems to be plotted.
> Alas, how many diverse acts.
> Nor does an assault begin without the bells
> Which were placed on high to give thanks to God.

¶ AND IF ANYTHING FROM DOWN HERE: Because he had previously mentioned the souls of the Romans who were Gentiles <note>pagan Romans</note>, and consequently are in Hell, now in this fourth stanza he says the same of the Christian Romans who are in Heaven because of their most holy works. He signifies that even those souls, insofar as they have any care for these worldly things, we must believe that they pray to the aforementioned Lord, Master Pandolfo <note>Pandolfo II Malatesta (1325–1373), a condottiero and patron to whom this commentary likely appeals.</note>, that he might be the cause of ending all civil hatred and discord. Because of this discord, the way is not safe, and pilgrims do not go to Rome, which used to be a most devout place. Now it seems like a den of thieves, and there in the midst of the churches and altars, every cruelty and misery is committed. He says the "statues of the saints are naked" because all the ecclesiastical vestments and ornaments have been stolen—even robbed—and the bells that were placed in the bell towers to thank our Lord God ring all day long for the alarm of war and civil assaults.

<meta>Catchword: recent. This page continues the commentary on Petrarch's canzone "Spirto gentil," shifting from the historical examples of Roman virtue to the current desperate state of the city of Rome and its appeal to a new leader (likely Cola di Rienzo) to restore order.</meta>

<margin>M</margin> ¶ **The tearful women.** This shows the suffering and the desire of the laypeople of every sex and every age, and similarly of the religious; that is, the mendicant friars of Saint Augustine, Saint Francis, and Saint Dominic. In this stanza, he says that they all cry out seeking help from the aforementioned lord, revealing all their suffering and sorrows to the poor people. These sights would move to compassion any good soul, even one as cruel as the aforementioned Hannibal <note>original: "Hannibale anteditto"; referring to the Carthaginian general famous for his enmity toward Rome.</note>, urging him to punish those few heads of factions who are the cause of such a "fire" in that city which is the universal head of the Church of God. By doing this, peace will follow, and he will be greatly commended for such actions.

<margin>N</margin> ¶ **BEARS, wolves.** In this sixth stanza, he specifies who is the cause of so much evil, saying it proceeds from the Orsini <note>Symbolized by the "Bears."</note>, who together with the houses of Conti and Savelli and their other friends—making war even to their own detriment—and the Colonna family <note>Symbolized by the "Column."</note> are the cause of every scandal. He says, therefore, that the Romans (by whom he has been called to uproot all harmful men from their city) are in tears because of those people. He shows that for a very long time the "good Romans," by whom this city was built in that place, have been missing. Finally, he makes an exclamation to these present-day Romans as men who are haughty and without any reverence toward such a "mother" <note>Rome is personified as a mother.</note>. He adds that the aforementioned lord must be like a husband and father to her, considering that the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope, then residing in Avignon rather than Rome.</note> is attending to other work.

<margin>O</margin> ¶ **RARELY it happens.** To better incite him to the undertaking for the public utility of Rome, he says in this seventh stanza that Fortune—who is commonly accustomed to being contrary to high enterprises, as she bears hatred toward courageous deeds out of envy—is now made propitious and favorable to him, insofar as he has been elevated to such high office and government.

### STANZA V

**The tearful women, and the defenseless commoners**
**Of tender age, and the weary old men**
**Who hate themselves and their excessive life;**
**And the black little friars, and the gray and the white,** <note>The "black" are likely Dominicans, the "gray" Franciscans, and the "white" Carmelites or Cistercians.</note>

**Which today is all ablaze; by extinguishing**

**Which show themselves so inflamed shall be calmed;**
**Whence your works shall be praised in heaven.**

### STANZA VI

**Bears, wolves, lions, eagles, and serpents** <note>These animals represent the warring noble families of Rome: Orsini (Bears), Colonna (the Column mentioned next), etc.</note>

**For these, that noble lady weeps**

**More than a thousand years have already passed**
**Since those graceful souls were lacking in her**
**Who had placed her there where she was.** <note>Referring to the ancient Roman heroes who built the city's greatness.</note>

**Irreverent to so great and such a mother!**
**You are husband, you are father;**
**Every help is expected from your hand,**
**For the Greater Father <note>The Pope.</note> attends to other work.**

### STANZA VII

**Rarely it happens that against high enterprises**
**Injurious Fortune does not struggle,**
**For she agrees poorly with courageous deeds.**
**Now, clearing the path where you entered,**
**She makes me forgive her many other offenses,**
**Since at least here she disagrees with herself;**
**For as far as the world remembers,**
**The way was never opened to a mortal man**
**To win, like you, eternal fame.**

Which can be raised up—if I discern truly—
Into the state of the most noble monarchy.

*He was received in Rome with the joy of everyone, without fortune having opposed him, as if fortune itself had become a friend rather than an enemy. Therefore, the poet encourages him, since he has opened the way to achieve an eternal glory greater than anyone else ever desired in such an enterprise. Through such a work, he can direct the monarchy of the Romans in its current state, confirming his fame and glory by the best proof. Where the other ancient princes and Roman citizens helped that monarchy when it was in its growth and strength, Lord Messer Pandolfo <note>Pandolfo II Malatesta (1325–1373), a condottiero and ruler of Rimini. The commentator identifies him as the "Spirto Gentil" (Noble Spirit) Petrarch addresses.</note> will have saved it from death in its old age and ultimate impotence.*

---

# STANZA VIII.

<margin>P</margin>
<margin>
*UPON THE MOUNT. Concluding in this present eighth and final stanza, our Poet encourages the said song to present itself to the aforementioned Messer Pandolfo Malatesta, a senator in the Capitol, a knight honored by all Italians, and a lord of such charity, justice, and magnanimity that he cares much more for public affairs than for his own utility. He tells the song to say on his behalf—though he has never seen him except by reputation—how all the Romans, with many tears, ask him for mercy and help in their many tribulations.*
</margin>
<margin>S</margin>
Upon the Tarpeian mount <note>The Tarpeian Rock on the Capitoline Hill in Rome, a site of ancient symbolic importance.</note>, song, you will see
A knight whom all Italy honors;
Caring more for others than for himself.
Tell him: "One who has not yet seen you from nearby,
Except as one falls in love through fame,
Says that Rome at every hour,
With eyes wet and soft with sorrow,
Begs you for mercy from all seven hills."

# CANZONE XII.

<margin>Fran.</margin>
<margin>
*BECAUSE ON THAT FACE. In this present twelfth little song, composed in triplet rhymes <note>original: "rime di terzeto"; likely referring to the madrigal form or terza rima used here.</note>, our enamored Poet demonstrates what he clearly signifies in the third book of the "struggle and conflict of his affairs" <note>original: "affannato et conflicto de le sue cose"; a reference to Petrarch's Latin work 'Secretum' (De secreto conflictu curarum mearum).</note>. Namely, that he was much plagued by the love of the woman currently spoken of—it is not known who she was. This was a different woman than Lady Laura; and he was also of a younger age than when he was in love with Lady Laura (from whose love he never dissolved). He says, therefore, that when he was a youth and naturally inclined toward amorous pursuits, he was inflamed by love for a "pilgrim" girl <note>original: "peregrina giouene"; can mean a foreigner, a traveler, or a girl of singular beauty.</note> who seemed to him more honorable than any other. As he was hunting her and following her here and there, she made such a sign to him that he understood he was toiling in vain. Therefore, he withdrew at that time from such pursuits, returning to more useful works—namely, near the shadow of the Supreme Pontiff in Avignon. He was at that time about thirty-five years of age, which was the middle of human life <note>A common medieval trope, famously used by Dante: "In the middle of the journey of our life."</note>, when he somewhat withdrew from such love.*
</margin>
<margin>P</margin>
Because she bore the ensign of love upon her face,
A pilgrim girl moved my vain heart,
So that every other seemed to me less worthy of honor;
And following her over the green grass,
I heard a loud voice say from afar:
"Ah, how many steps you lose through the woods!"
Then I drew close to the shade of a beautiful beech,
All thoughtful; and looking around
I saw my journey was quite perilous,
And I turned back almost at midday.

<margin>Q</margin>
<margin>Anto.</margin>
*BECAUSE ON THAT FACE OF LOVE. In this little ballad, Messer Francesco feigns that while following his lady, it seemed to him he heard a voice telling him he was losing his steps, to make him understand that he was never to obtain anything from his Lady Laura.*

<margin>Francesco</margin>
THAT FIRE: In the thirteenth song <note>This refers to the poem "Quel foco ch’io pensai," which is Song 30 in modern editions of the *Canzoniere*.</note> presented here, although it seems to continue from the preceding tercets, we should not necessarily understand that our poet speaks of the same lady with whom he fell in love in Avignon during his youth, as was said from the beginning. Therefore, it is said that the fire of love—which seemed extinguished because the blood of his age was less warm—begins to refresh a new flame and torment in his soul. From this, he now clearly perceives that the embers (though it would be better to say "sparks") which are lit were never entirely extinguished, but only somewhat covered. For this reason, he reasonably says he fears that the "second error" of loving Madonna Laura <note>Original: "M. L."</note> may be worse than the first when he was in love in his youth (as mentioned in the preceding tercets), insofar as a relapse into an illness is more dangerous than being sick the first time. He says this seems so to him because of the many tears he sheds, which signify the displeasure of the heart that unburdens itself in this way. He says that in the heart, because of the abundance of blood and vital spirits <note>In medieval physiology, "vital spirits" were refined substances in the blood that governed life and emotion.</note>, there are "sparks" (meaning ignited blood) and the "tinder" (which is concupiscence <note><term>concupiscence: strong sexual desire or lust</term></note>), now much greater than ever before and increasing. He adds with wonder that the abundance of his weeping has been so great that it should have extinguished and killed any fire of love. Because it does not do so, it shows the fire of love to be immeasurable. Then, directing his speech to Love, he complains that Love wants to make him "distempered" <note>Unbalanced or dissolved.</note> between two contrary things: because the less he hopes, the more he falls in love upon seeing the lovely face of his beloved lady.

THAT FIRE which I thought was extinguished. Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch.</note> says that when he believed he was out of the hands of Love, he finds himself even more entangled within. He was never without some fire. "Two contraries distemper me"—that is, tears and fire.

<margin>**T**</margin>
And similarly he grieves over Love, who has led him into this vain hope for his mortal affliction. He concludes that the same thing happens to him that Solon—one of the Seven Sages of Greece—replied to Croesus, king of Lydia, a most powerful lord with greater treasure than could be found in any other. Namely, that no one in this present life can be called blessed as long as he lives. Rather, human happiness can be judged only after death. Solon the Athenian was a man most wise in that age; he wrote and gave excellent laws to the Athenians, which they had requested with marvelous desire. He had bound them with the strongest oaths to observe them for at least ten years. So that he would not be forced by the citizens to release them from such an oath while he was in Athens, and also to see the world, he departed from Athens for those ten years. He went, according to what Herodotus <note>Original: "Hero." refers to the Greek historian Herodotus.</note> says, first to Egypt to King Amasis—who, before anyone else, had added the island of Cyprus to his domain—and was received and honored most highly by him. Then he went to Lydia, to the most famous city called Sardis. As soon as King Croesus heard of his arrival, he received him in a friendly manner in his royal palace and honored him with most solemn banquets. But then, on the third or fourth day, Solon was led by the servants of Croesus, according to the king's command, to see his marvelous treasures. When Solon had looked upon their multitude and greatness with diligence, he did so without any admiration, considering them fortuitous and fleeting things. Croesus, seeing that he had placed all his happiness in the vanity of worldly things, asked for his opinion in this manner: "O Athenian friend, because of your fame which has reached our ears—that you are a wise man, and that you go through the world in this <margin>In Latin: traveling as a philosopher <note>Original: "in lat: che philosophando se"</note></margin> way, having come here to see many things—I wish to tell you that a great desire has come upon me to ask if, until now, you have seen anyone who surpasses all others in happiness." Croesus asked this question because he estimated himself to be the most blessed man in the world. Solon clearly understood this, and not wishing to be a flatterer like those who stood around the king, he replied that the happiest man he ever saw was one named Tellus of Athens. Marvelling at this answer, Croesus asked who this man was and why he esteemed him so happy. Solon replied: "This Tellus, having a good reputation in the city, had virtuous sons, and saw that he had grandsons, all of whom were living and good according to the human course. Furthermore, when the Athenians were at war with their neighbors at Eleusis, he brought his aid, broke the enemies, and died generously in battle. For this, he was publicly buried by the Athenians in that very place where he had fallen, and was honored excellently."

<margin>**V**</margin>
Having heard this, King Croesus, without further contradiction, asked Solon whom else after that man he had seen as most happy, it appearing clearly to him that Solon ought to name him. But Solon, who knew the inconstancy and mutability of fortune, did not answer with the king's name, but with Cleobis and Biton. These two, being of the city of Argos, were so robust of body that in the public games where strength is exercised, they always carried the prize. Among their other memorable deeds, they ultimately performed a work of immortal fame. The mother of these two most valorous youths was appointed to the priesthood of the goddess Juno. Her temple was forty-five stadia <note><term>stadia: an ancient Greek unit of distance; 45 stadia is approximately 5 miles.</term></note> outside the city, and it was necessary on that day, for the festival of the said goddess, for their mother to be carried in a chariot to the temple. As evening approached, the oxen had not yet come from the farm to pull the chariot, which caused the lady great distress. Hearing this, the two aforementioned sons, without waiting any longer, placed their mother in the chariot and, in place of the oxen, they...

<meta>This page continues the story of Solon and Croesus mentioned on the previous page. It serves as an exemplum (a moralizing example) to explain why the poet Petrarch feels his hopes for happiness in love were premature and misguided.</meta>

...placed the yoke upon their necks and led the chariot to the temple. While they were doing this, all those who were at the festival highly commended the gentle and pious nature of such sons. And the Argive women with one voice said: "Blessed is she who has given birth to such sons." Their mother, receiving wonderful sweetness from these things—both from their fame and from their service—prayed before the image of Juno that she might look upon her sons with the happiest thing a man can achieve. After this prayer, once the two youths had dined with great pleasure, they went to sleep with such joy that their sleep was eternal. This was esteemed from that age on as a most happy thing and acceptable to God. Therefore, the Argives <note>The people of Argos, Greece.</note> made statues of them and, as of upright and virtuous men, sent them to Delphi as a perpetual memorial.

<margin>X</margin>
¶ But Croesus, seeing that no mention was made by Solon of him—who would always be indicated as the most happy—was greatly troubled. He turned toward him and said: "O Solon, does our happiness then seem to you to be so cast aside as nothing? Are we unworthy of that of which you have made even the plebeian and common men worthy?" To which Solon replied: "O Croesus, you ask me about human affairs, which I believe I know; for every good of fortune is subject to envy and to the most turbulent movement and change. In a long life there are many things that a man would not wish to know. Since the term of human life is seventy years, in such a circuit of time there is so much change and variety that one day never resembles another in human affairs. Therefore, I tell you, O Croesus, that universally man is subject to misfortune. To me, you appear very rich and you are king of many men. But that which you ask, I cannot say is in you until I have heard that the end of your life was good and glorious. For the richest man is no more happy than he who lives from day to day, if until the end of his life he does not have the favor of fortune continually with him. Many men are very rich who are unhappy; many who have only a moderate living are happy." With these and many other words, demonstrating the need to consider the end of all things, he concluded that in no way could he or anyone else be named happy as long as he lived; for many appearing happy for a very long time are finally, through the mutation of fortune, found most unhappy. These words, although they were most true, greatly displeased Croesus, who was arrogant because of his prosperity. He did not hold Solon in the same esteem as before, but rather dismissed him, judging him a coarse and unlearned man because, not considering present goods, he said that one should look to the end of everything. Nor did Solon judge himself to be any less, even though he was not esteemed by King Croesus according to his virtue, considering that his own well-being was not located in the vain judgment of Croesus, but in the excellent works of his own intellect and learning.

<margin>X</margin>
¶ And not long after, Croesus proved by experience that what Solon had predicted was true. First, his only son, named Atys, who was to be the successor to his realm, was killed by his domestic friend Adrastus. Then, wishing to oppose the successes of Cyrus, King of Persia, he was defeated and taken in battle. Having lost his wealth and his lordship, he would have been miserably killed if the name of Solon had not succored him. For Cyrus, having deliberated by every means to have him burned, was present while Croesus was being led to the pyre. As Croesus passed before Cyrus, having seen him in such pride and pomp due to the marvelous successes of fortune, he remembered the admonition that Solon had once given him at the time when he esteemed himself most happy. Therefore, he cried out: "O Solon, Solon!" Hearing these words, Cyrus wanted to know what they meant. When Croesus narrated what Solon had once said to him, Cyrus—thinking on the variation of fortune and looking at Croesus as if in a mirror—decided that he should by no means die, and pardoned him entirely.

<margin>Antonio <note>Likely referring to Antonio da Tempo, a 14th-century commentator on Petrarch.</note></margin>

Hence Ovid says: "No one should be called blessed before death and the final funeral rites." <note>original: "beatus ante obitum nemo supremaq; funera debet." Then, following his theme and his despair of ever being able to effectively achieve his desire, he proposes some impossible things. These things, he says, would have to happen before his soul could be at rest—which is to say, never. Just as snows, which are white and cold by nature, would have to become black and warm; and the sea would have to stop its waves; and fish of every kind would be found on the Alps as in the sea; and the sun, which sets in the West, would have to set in Armenia in the East. In that land, from a single mountain source, two most noble rivers emerge: the Euphrates and the Tigris. So, all these things would sooner be possible than for Love or his beloved lady to accustom themselves to behave differently, so that he might continually be well, or at least be at peace with her sometimes. But it is as if they had made a pact against him; they are always contrary. He demonstrates that he has received and continues to receive such bitterness from Love and from the beloved lady that even if he were to receive some sweetness through a few pleasant words or a gracious act, he could not taste it—just as those who have lost their sense of taste find sweet things to be bitter. Thus, he concludes that he receives no pleasure at all.

¶ The Cheek. In this 45th sonnet, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> comforts and prays to Master Francesco da Carrara, the Elder, Lord of Padua <note>A patron of Petrarch and ruler of Padua from 1350–1388.</note>, that he should now—having entered his mature years—leave aside amorous thoughts, for which a man grows old and shortens his life. He urges him to give himself to rest and tranquility, saying that where previously, according to the various toils of love, he rested and turned his thoughts now on one cheek, now on the other, weeping for a love that was disobedient to him, he should now let his will rest in a single thought: that of not giving Love such mastery over himself.

With the other, close off from the left hand

...king who, as a cruel and inhuman figure, makes his followers turn grey and old. His other thought should be diligent not to let itself be overcome by the passions of the heart—that is, by any kind of <term>concupiscence</term> <note>Lust or strong worldly desire.</note>: which is all the more fervent as the vital spirits that are in the heart have more heat. > That it may purge every thought that afflicts the heart;
> Sweet in the end, and bitter in the beginning;
> And place [it] where pleasure is kept,

...these such passions, which are like messengers sent from external things to the heart, are false and deceitful and give one to understand now one thing, now another; and he shows the reason why he must do this, saying that old age is already approaching. He then adds a third thought, which says he should use [this remedy] no differently than if he were using some drink of a health-giving herb as medicine. And this is the purging by which the heart is afflicted; he shows that such a remedy, although in the beginning it seems bitter to men accustomed [to vice], yet in the end it provides sweetness because of the tranquility it induces in our souls. He adds that in this tranquility of soul he wishes to rest as well, so that he no longer has to fear <term>Charon</term> <note>The ferryman of the underworld in Greek mythology.</note>, the infernal ferryman, who signifies **Time**; and **Styx** signifies hatred, essentially the unpleasant time that always exists when the higher part of the soul is in distress.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
¶ **The cheek that was already tired from weeping** [refers to] an old cardinal, and according to the opinion of some, it was Cardinal Colonna. He asked advice of Master Francesco <note>Petrarch.</note> whether he should still remain in love, having always been most amorous. Master Francesco sent him a chalice, a cushion, and a breviary <note>A book of daily prayers.</note> with this sonnet as an answer: "Rest upon the one" (that is, on the pillow that whitens, meaning love). "With the other" (that is, with the breviary), "say your offices and prayers." On a day in August this falling in love began, on Good Friday, because he says "remember them how today you were on the cross" (that is, on such a day as today is).

<margin>Francesco</margin>
¶ **Because:** The present 14th Canzone is specifically a song for dancing <note>A ballata.</note>. Petrarch composed it while the husband of Lady Laura departed from Avignon and took the said lady with him. It contains three stanzas. In the first, he says that although the fault of her husband takes her away from him—she by whom he was first drawn to love—it does not, however, at all release him from his own will. He adds the reason in the second stanza, saying that his amorous snare was hidden between her will and her hair. Remembering still all the while her beautiful eyes, by which his heart froze as if stupefied, the splendor of those eyes being of such wonder that even in remembering them, the soul strips itself of every other desire and separates from the body. And so he adds in the third stanza how, having lost the two aforementioned pleasures—of being able to see her blonde hair and the beauty of those most virtuous eyes—he reasonably feels displeasure; yet neither through melancholy nor through death will he ever be untied from such love.

<margin>Antonio</margin>

### CANZONE, XIV.

> Because that which first drew me to love,
> Another's fault takes from me;
> From my firm will it does not yet turn me.
> Amidst the golden tresses was born the snare
> To which Love bound me;
> And from beautiful eyes moved the cold ice
> That passed into my heart
> With the power of a sudden splendor,
> Which of every other desire
> Only by remembering still strips the soul.
> Taken from me then is the sweet sight
> Of those blonde hairs, alas,
> And the turning of the two lights, virtuous and beautiful,
> Which with their flight saddens me:
> But because by dying well honor is acquired;
> Neither by death nor by sorrow
> Do I wish that Love untie me from such a knot.

¶ **Because that which first drew me to love.** Master Francesco says that although his lady deprives him of the gaze through which he fell in love, he will not for this reason turn from his desire. **Taken from me then**, that is <note>original: "idest"</note>, he is deprived of Laura's hair because after Master Francesco fell in love with her, she wore a veil, as appears above in a sonnet where he laments this, beginning "Leave the veil."

# SONNETTO XLVI.

**T**he noble tree, which I loved dearly for many years,
While its beautiful branches did not hold me in disdain,
Made my weak wit flourish
In its shade, and grow amidst my troubles.
**S**ince it made me certain of such deceits,
Turning from sweet to such pitiless wood,
I turned all my thoughts to a single aim,
Which always speak of their sad injuries.
**W**hat will he be able to say, who sighs for love,
If my new rhymes had given him
Another hope; and through her, he loses it?
**M**ay no poet ever gather from it, nor may Jove
Grant it privilege; and let it come into the sun's wrath,
So that every green leaf of it withers.

<margin>Francesco C.</margin>
¶ The noble tree: How much prudence or intellect they had who organized and ordered these sonnets and songs of our noble poet becomes more manifest every hour. This sonnet is intended to be among the last in this volume, as it was composed in Italy long after the death of Lady Laura <note>original: "M. L." or Madonna Laura.</note>, when Petrarch had already emerged from such passion. He says, therefore, in this 46th sonnet—understanding "The Laurel" to mean Lady Laura or any other beautiful woman fit for falling in love—that the laurel, which he was in love with for many years while she was alive, was the reason for sharpening his wit and making him greater regarding his amorous troubles. But after he was left without any further care for the deceits of love by the death of his beloved lady, he says he turned all his amorous thoughts toward speaking always of the harms received through them. And so he prays to God that no poet may ever gather from the laurel—that is, the pleasure of a woman—nor should Jove give it the privilege <note>In mythology, the laurel was privileged by Jove (Jupiter) to never be struck by lightning.</note> of not being struck by lightning. Instead, he prays it might wither from excessive heat so that it loses all beauty and youth, which is known to cause so many sighs in idle souls.

¶ Because he never received any fruit from his love, he thus prays to God that no poet may ever gather from the laurel—that is, the pleasure of a woman—nor should Jove give it the privilege of not being struck by lightning. Instead, he prays it might wither from excessive heat so that it loses all beauty and youth, which is known to cause so many sighs in idle souls.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ The noble tree which I loved dearly for many years. Master Francesco says that those rhymes he made in praise of Lady Laura, while she held his love dear, he has now collected to speak of his pains; whereby any other lover who had taken confidence and hope, only to lose it later through her hardness, will be able to curse her in the name of the laurel for her cruelty.

# SONNETTO XLVII.

**B**lessed be the day, and the month, and the year,
And the season, and the time, and the hour, and the point,
And the beautiful country, and the place where I was reached
By two beautiful eyes, which have bound me:
**A**nd blessed be the first sweet labor,
That I had in being joined with Love,
And the bow, and the arrows by which I was pierced;
And the wounds that go right to my heart.
**B**lessed be the many voices that I
Have scattered, calling the name of my lady,
And the sighs, and the tears, and the desire;
**A**nd blessed be all the papers,
Where I acquire fame for her: and my thought,
Which is only of her, so that no other has a part in it.

<margin>Francesco D.</margin>
¶ BLESSED. A small glance of amorous demonstration revives lovers from death to life, which Petrarch clearly manifests to us in the present 47th Sonnet. Having found himself at a dinner with Lady Laura, where she carried herself with a kindly look and gracious speech, he seems for this reason to be almost happy in the triumph of love. He blesses the time he fell in love with her, and also the place where he was captured and fell in love with her, and even his own labor and his entire tormented romance. And likewise, blessing all his sighs and weeping done for her, he also blesses all his writings made in her commendation, and ultimately, his every thought.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ Blessed be the day, the month, and the year. A literal sonnet <note>original: "textuale," referring to a poem where the meaning is clear and fundamental to the narrative.</note> in which Master Francesco blesses the day that he ever fell in love with Lady Laura, when he first saw her.

<margin>Francesco E.</margin>
**Father of Heaven.** The wolf shows a desire to become a monk <note>This metaphor suggests a predator—the poet's lower instincts—attempting to find spiritual discipline.</note>, which Petrarch demonstrates in this forty-eighth sonnet: because on Good Friday, finding himself moved to contrition and realizing he has wasted time on light and shameful things, he prays to God to deign, after so many of his labors and vanities, to illuminate his mind so that he might return to an honest and laudable life. He hopes that his infernal adversary <note>The devil.</note> might find himself deluded and shamed in his insidious hunt. Note the time: it was already the eleventh year from the beginning of when he first fell in love with Madonna Laura <note>original: "M. L."</note>, who then lived ten more years. He prays, therefore, to the eternal God to give him the grace to see himself clearly, and to put it in his heart to no longer attend to this vanity, showing the cruel nature of Love, which never humbles itself but rather shows itself more fierce the more one gives themselves to such passion. Therefore, he prays to God to have mercy on him and to lead his wandering thoughts back to the consideration of the passion of **Christ** <term>Christo</term> <note>The original uses the Greek-derived abbreviation "Xp̄o".</note>. This sonnet was intended to be in the second book, but no order is preserved here.

### SONNET XLVIII.

> **P**ather of heaven, after the lost days,
> After the nights spent in vain wandering
> With that fierce desire, which was kindled in my heart
> Beholding those acts so adorned for my harm,
> **M**ay it please You now with Your light that I return
> To another life, and to more beautiful enterprises,
> So that, having spread his nets in vain,
> My harsh adversary may be put to shame.
> **N**ow, my Lord, the eleventh year turns,
> Since I was subjected to the pitiless yoke,
> Which is most fierce upon those most submissive.
> **H**ave mercy <note>original: "Miserere"</note> on my unworthy suffering:
> Lead my wandering thoughts to a better place:
> Remind them how, on this day, You were upon the cross.

<margin>Antonio F.</margin>
**Father of heaven, after.** Messer Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch.</note> speaks to God, the supreme creator, grieving for his lost days and praying that He turn him back to Himself; he notes the time he has been in love and in what manner.

<margin>Francesco F.</margin>
**Turning your eyes: the present, 49th.** This sonnet was composed during his first amorous fires, where Petrarch shows that, having turned completely pale and being as if dead, Madonna Laura, with a lovely gaze mixed with sweet speech, made him as if resurrected. Thus, being greeted by her, he recovered his life. Therefore, he says he holds his life as a gift from her eyes and her angelic voice, being awakened by them no differently than a lazy animal is when it is struck. He adds that she alone is the one who can lock his heart through displeasure and unlock it through pleasure; and he concludes by being prepared to follow her every will.
**Turning your eyes to.** Having seen Messer Francesco looking very sad one time, Madonna Laura was moved by compassion and greeted him, for which Messer Francesco thanks her in this sonnet. He speaks of himself as a "lazy animal"—an apt comparison—and mentions "both keys," namely those of death and life <note>original: "mortis & vitæ"</note> or of humanity and cruelty.

### SONNET XLIX.

> Was an open gift from your beautiful eyes,

> From them I recognize my being, where I am:
> **F**or as a lazy animal is moved by a rod;
> So they awakened my heavy soul.
> **O**f my heart, Lady, you hold both keys
> **I**n your hand; and with this I am content,
> Ready to sail with every wind:
> For everything from you is sweet honor to me.

### SONNET LI.

**A**las, how ill-advised I was at first
On the day when Love came to wound me:
Who, step by step, then became the master
Of my life, and placed himself at the peak.
<margin>I</margin> I did not believe that by the force of his file,
Any point of firmness or of valor
Would ever be lacking in my hardened heart;
But so it goes for one who estimates himself above the truth.
From now on, every defense is late,
Other than to try whether, much or little,
Love regards these mortal prayers.
<margin>N</margin> I do not pray now—nor could it have any more place—
That my heart burn moderately;
But that she might have her share of the fire.

<margin>H</margin> <margin>
*Alas, how ill: In the present fifty-first sonnet, Petrarch demonstrates the habit of amorous desire <note>original: "cupiscētia amorosa"</note> which, by entering mortal hearts little by little, finally forms such a habit that in no way can a man untangle himself from it. He speaks of himself, saying that he did not have good diligence at the beginning in knowing how to guard himself from the wounds of love. Thus, step by step, he has become a servant of love and entirely subjected, adding the cause of his negligence: he shows it to have proceeded from ignorance, in that he did not believe love could do anything against him, as he seemed to himself to be valiant against all love's insidious forces. Whence he concludes that he can do nothing else against love, nor in any way can he do anything else against Lady Laura <note>original: "M. <margin>Antonio.</margin>
¶ ALAS, how poorly he perceived it at first: he grieved. Master Francesco <note>M. F. refers to Messer Francesco Petrarch</note> grieves that he had been so poorly perceived at the beginning of his falling in love, as seen in the text. That immeasurably: that is, <note>original: "nimio amore cor ipsius roditur"</note> his heart is gnawed by excessive love. Therefore, note, you lover, not to love except with measure; consider reason and do not care about burning with love. *Let it never fail in the hardened heart*—as if to say: I did not think that through her wounds she could ever turn my heart to love. *I do not pray now*—it can no longer have a place—as if to say: I do not pray now to burn only a little nor with measure, because I am already all fire; but I truly pray that she may have her part of it: that is, that she may burn for me just as I do for her.

<margin>Francesco I</margin>
¶ The Heavy Air: This present fifteenth canzone <note>This refers to Sestina I, "L’aer gravato," which is the 15th poem in some older arrangements of the collection</note> demonstrates through proper and beautiful similitudes and <term>metaphors|translatio</term> how our poet labors in vain. In this first stanza, wishing to show his weary heart entirely disposed to sighs, he tells you through a metaphorical comparison that the air, heavy with gathered vapors, and the mist rising from the earth, being surrounded and compressed by rabid and most turbulent winds, must necessarily soon convert into rain through resolution.

### CANZONE · XV · STANZA · I ·

-> The heavy air and the troublesome mist, <-
-> Enclosed around by rabid winds, <-
-> Must soon be converted into rain; <-
-> And already the rivers are almost like crystal; <-
-> And instead of the little grass through the valleys, <-
-> Nothing else is seen but hoarfrost and ice. <-

And already the rivers, made even by the aforementioned rain, have all frozen just as is customary in winter when the great cold arrives. And where the valleys used to be in spring and in the pleasant season adorned with little grass and lovely little flowers: now, as in winter, nothing is seen but hoarfrost and ice. This happens to lovers whose souls, when they obtain their desire, are all joyful like the spring. But insofar as things go to the contrary for them, they are melancholy and joyless like the winter weather.

<margin>Antonio.</margin>
¶ The heavy air and the troublesome mist: A moral sestina in which Master Francesco speaks under a figure and reduces everything to the purpose of crystal—that is, frozen rivers—by which the rivers appear proud in sight. This is from Virgil in the *Aeneid*: <note>original: "In fretta unde fluvii currunt"</note> "Speedily from where the rivers run." I must certainly pardon all the winds—that is, I must be content with every good and every evil that I have: she, for love of one who is in the midst of two rivers—that is, Cupid who binds us in the midst of two rivers—namely the Sorgue and the Rhône where Lady Laura <note>M. L.</note> was born. The winds: that is, the evil or the good.

### STANZA · II ·

<margin>Francesco K</margin>
¶ AND I IN THE: He adapts more clearly in this second stanza the preceding similitude to his own state, saying that within his heart—which, because of too much melancholy, is much colder than ice—there is such a mist and darkness from too many weary thoughts, similar to that which rises sometimes from these valleys of the region of Avignon; which valleys, as if they were rustic, neither receive nor cast out any amorous wind; and they are surrounded not by joyful and pleasant rivers, but by stagnant ones, as happens at the time of slow rain.

-> And I in my heart, far colder than ice, <-
-> Have such a mist of heavy thoughts, <-
-> Such as sometimes rises from these valleys <-
-> Locked away against the amorous winds, <-
-> And surrounded by stagnant rivers, <-
-> When slower rain falls from the sky. <-

### STANZA · III ·

-> In a short time every great rain passes; <-
-> And the heat makes the snow and ice vanish <-
-> By which the rivers appear proud in sight, <-
-> Nor did the sky ever hide such thick mist, <-
-> That, overtaken by the fury of the winds, <-
-> Did not flee from the hills and the valleys. <-

<margin>L</margin>
¶ IN A SHORT TIME. In this third stanza, continuing the similitude touched upon above, he demonstrates that natural rain ends sooner than his "accidental" rain, which proceeds from tears; and similarly, natural mist resolves sooner than his own, which proceeds from melancholy, which like a dark mist obscures the mind and the intellect, taking away every pleasure. He clearly manifests this in the following stanza.

### STANZA IV

But alas, it avails me nothing that the valleys flower;
Instead, I weep in the clear sky and in the rain,
And in the frozen and the gentle winds: <gloss>(that is</gloss>
May there one day be a time when my lady is without the ice
Within, and outside without her usual mist;
That I might see the sea, the lakes, and the rivers dried up.)

<margin>
¶ BUT ALAS. Similarly, adapting the preceding comparison, the author says in this fourth stanza that his weeping is continuous in both good weather and bad, in winter and in summer. He adds that Lady Laura will only be warmed by love and show a kind face to those who look upon her when the sea, the lakes, and the rivers are all dried up. This demonstrates that Petrarch had not the slightest hope for his love, neither in her words nor in her expression.
</margin>

---

### STANZA V

While the rivers descend to the sea,
And the wild beasts love the shady valleys;
That mist shall remain before those beautiful eyes,
Which gives birth to a continuous rain from mine;
And in her beautiful breast, the hardened ice,
Which draws such sorrowful winds from my own.

<margin>
¶ WHILE THE. The present fifth stanza declares the obstinate love of Petrarch alongside the persistent hatred or true disdain of Lady Laura. He says that as long as the rivers run to the sea—which is forever—and as long as the wild beasts love the shady valleys, which is
</margin>

their nature: Lady Laura will always show a face of disdain and anger, because of which he is forced by melancholy to weep. And she will always have a frozen breast toward him. For this reason, he is perforce driven to sighing.

---

### STANZA VI

I must indeed forgive all the winds
For the love of one which, between two rivers,
Enclosed me between the beautiful green and the sweet ice
In such a way that I later painted through a thousand valleys
The shade where I was: so that neither heat nor rain
Nor the sound of breaking mist troubled me.

<margin>
¶ I MUST INDEED. Petrarch demonstrates in this present sixth stanza that loving is a "sweet bitterness" <note>This refers to the common Petrarchan theme of "dolce amaro," where the lover finds a strange pleasure in his suffering</note> in that he himself enjoys his own misfortune. He says that he reasonably must forgive all other contrary winds for the love of that "windy" sighing through which he was amorously captured between the Rhône and the Sorgue <note>The two rivers near Avignon where Petrarch lived and encountered Laura</note> where Lady Laura resided. He adds that he took such
</margin>

pleasure in this that, through his writings, he has "painted" that shade where he fell in love across a thousand other valleys. Here, he modestly praises himself by signifying that the power of his writing is so great that he cares for nothing else.

---

### STANZA VII

But mist never fled before the winds
As it did that day; nor rivers ever for rain,
Nor ice, as when the sun opens the valleys.

<margin>
¶ BUT MIST NEVER. In the present final stanza <note>The "tornata" or envoy: a shorter concluding stanza typical of a sestina</note>, concluding the amorous inconstancy, he says that at no other time should he flee more than from that day when he fell in love, considering that nothing can achieve the like. He speaks of the rainy rivers and the ice when it wakes
</margin>

as spring arrives, while the solar heat, destroying the frozen rivers, makes the waters run with great fury.

<margin>16</margin> burden. Petrarch therefore says of himself—speaking of a time when he was near the Sorgue, traveling from Italy to Provence toward France—that he was on the left-hand side of the Tyrrhenian Sea, that is, the Tuscan Sea, so named after Tyrrhenus, the king who came from Lydia and lived in Tuscany. A very strange thing happened to him: while he was thinking of Lady Laura, whom he saw while passing through that village, he was so drawn by his imagination and had his eyes so fixed on his beloved that he did not pay attention to where he placed his feet. This was the reason that, while walking beside the Sorgue,

**Of whom I must write on so many pages:**
**Love, which was boiling within my soul,**
    **Out of the memory of those blonde tresses,**
    **Pushed me: where in a stream, hidden by grass,**
    **I fell, not at all like a living person.**
**Alone, where I was among groves and hills,**
    **I felt ashamed of myself; for to a noble heart**
    **That much is quite enough; and I needed no other spur.**
**At least it pleases me to have changed my style**
    **From eyes to feet: if only a kinder April**
    **Would dry the others, since they are wet.**
    <note>Petrarch is playing with the idea that usually his eyes are wet from weeping; here, his feet are wet from the river.</note>

the river, which was barely visible because of the grass growing in it, eluded him. His foot slipped in such a way that he fell inside; he says that although he was not seen by others, he nevertheless felt quite ashamed. And from what we can understand, he took a great tumble. He says, therefore, that he was ashamed of himself, reflecting later on his folly—that he was so overcome by such passion that he seemed entirely abandoned by reason. He remarks that feeling shame toward oneself is a very good punishment for a noble spirit. Finally, adding how he took at least one pleasure in this accident: that whereas before he used to bathe his eyes with amorous tears, now he has bathed his feet. He hopes that having his feet thus soaked might be the reason that another, similar April might pass: that is, within the year, he might dry his eyes by holding his beloved lady in his arms. Lydus and Tyrrhenus were brothers from the country now called Lydia; wishing to increase their dominion and glory according to the custom of the ancients, they decided that Lydus would remain to rule in their own homeland. Tyrrhenus, taking a great treasure with him and preparing a most powerful fleet, departed from Lydia and crossed into Italy, where he took the region of Tuscany, which was previously called Ausonia. He called it Tyrrhenia after his own name, and similarly the sea of Tuscany: that is, the lower sea, named the Tyrrhenian Sea, which even before then was called the Ausonian Sea, named after the son of Ulysses who was called Auson.

<margin>Antonio</margin>**IN** the Tyrrhenian sea on the left bank. Master Francesco, being in this place where he composed this sonnet, saw a laurel tree <note>The laurel tree is a constant symbol for Laura</note> and, as if driven to touch it in memory of Lady Laura, he ran without looking ahead and fell into a stream hidden by grass that he had not noticed. Here he describes that event: *it pleases me at least to have changed my style.* For previously his eyes, and now his feet, were bathed and wet—the latter by water, the former by tears. *May a kinder April dry the others.* <gloss>As if to say</gloss> <note>original: "quasi dicat"</note> an April more kind than the day he began to weep when he first fell in love (which was in April); may it dry the others: that is, his eyes, just as his feet can be dried.

### SONNET LIII.
**The sacred sight of your land**
    **Makes me draw groans from past ills,**
    **Crying out: "Rise up, wretch; what are you doing?"**
    **And it shows me the way to climb to heaven.**
**But with this thought another one jousts,**
    **And says to me: "Why do you go fleeing?**
    **If you remember, the time is passing now**
    **To return to see our lady."**
**I, who understand its reasoning then,**

<margin>Francesco S.</margin>**THE SIGHT.** In the present fifty-third sonnet, Master Francesco Petrarch responds here to Master Giovanni Boccaccio. Boccaccio—who had already been recalled from exile where he had previously been a rebel, together with Ser Petracco, the apostolic notary and Petrarch's father—was encouraging him to return to Florence. *I freeze within like a man who hears*
*News that suddenly strikes his heart:*
<margin>P</margin> *Then the first thought returns, and this one turns away;*

<margin>Antonio</margin> That is to say, the desire to return to Avignon to see Lady Laura: he did not know [which would win]; but in this way, he secretly showed that his mind was not yet settled, while showing himself to be fought over by these new thoughts of going to Florence—where, according to the encouragement of Boccaccio <note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), author of the *Decameron* and a close friend of Petrarch.</note>, he would have acquired great honor and glory—and of returning to Avignon. $\text{C}$ **The sacred sight of your land:** <note>original: "L'aspetto sacro de la terra vostra"</note> Master Francesco had been away many days and had not gone from the Sorgue to Avignon; many of his friends, wondering at this, wrote to him to ask the reason he did not go to them. He responds that there are two thoughts within him: one held him back, remembering past pain; the other urged him on to see his Lady Laura. "Not just once," but *Thousands and thousands of times* <note>original: "Sed milies & milies"</note>.

## SONNET LIII.

<margin>B</margin> *Well did I know that natural counsel*
*Never availed, Love, against you:*
*So many snares, so many false promises,*
*So much had I proven your ferocious claw:*
<margin>M</margin> *But newly (at which I marvel)*
*I will tell it as one who was affected by it;*
*And who noted it upon the salt waters*
*Between the Tuscan shore and Elba and Giglio.* <note>Elba and Giglio are islands off the coast of Tuscany.</note>
<margin>I</margin> *I was fleeing your hands, and on my way,*
*Tossed by the winds, the sky, and the waves,*
*I went as an unknown pilgrim;*
<margin>Q</margin> *When behold your ministers (I know not from where)*
*To give me to understand: that against one's destiny*
*He fares ill who struggles, and ill who hides.*

<margin>Francesco T.</margin> $\text{C}$ **WELL DID I KNOW.** As I remember mentioning above, Petrarch demonstrates in his third book titled *On the Secret Conflict of My Cares* <note>original: "de secreto del cōflitto de le sue cure"; usually known simply as the *Secretum*.</note> that he was very much given to the passions of love. This is clearly manifested in many other places and again in the present fifty-fourth sonnet, <note>The text labels it 53 in the heading but 54 in the commentary, a common numbering discrepancy in early editions.</note> where, while sailing in the Tuscan sea between Piombino, Elba, and the island of Giglio to go to Rome, he fell in love with a young woman who was on the ship. Nothing is known of who she was. He shows then, as an excuse for himself, that no natural reason or counsel prevails against love. Therefore, having many times experienced the deceptions of love, and having resolved not to attend to them anymore, he has newly fallen in love against his will. He concludes that no resistance is effective against the destiny of love.

*no resistance is effective against the destiny of love.*

<margin>Antonio</margin> $\text{C}$ **WELL DID I KNOW.** There is an opinion that Master Francesco, coming from France to Italy by sea, took port at Pisa. Before disembarking, seeing the shores, he remembered the other country where he had left his Lady Laura and wrote this sonnet addressed to Love, saying that Love leaves him alone neither near nor far, but rather pursues him. Elba and Giglio are two islands in the Tuscan sea. **When behold your ministers:** the ministers of Love are the thoughts and memories of love.

## CANZONE XVI.

<margin>L</margin> *Woe is me, for I know not where to turn*
*My hope, which has been betrayed many times:*
*For if there is no one who listens to me with pity,*
*Why scatter such frequent prayers to heaven?*
*But if it happens that I am not yet denied—*

<margin>Francesco V.</margin> $\text{C}$ **WOE IS ME.** In the present sixteenth canzone, Petrarch intends to demonstrate the suffering of the passion of love. He places the first stanza as a long introduction, showing first that his hope is uncertain, so that he does not know what he ought to hope for, having been many times deceived and betrayed by love. He seeks to make the listener well-disposed to hear him with pity.

->*Right and reason is that I remain here singing.*<- <note>original: "Drez & raison es qui eu ciant emdemori." This is a line in Old Occitan (Provencal) by the troubadour Arnaut Daniel, whom Petrarch admired and quoted here.</note>

<margin>Antonio</margin> ¶ Alas, I who do not know which way to turn: Remembering how Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> felt so failed by his hopes, he grieves and speaks to himself, saying these "wretched voices" are not heavy: meaning that these words and voices should end for him before he dies, addressed to my lord, that is, to Love. For he never began early enough. He means to say: I cannot begin to sing so early that it can match the weeping I have done; but even more so when, without lying—that is, a lady for whom I want to speak begs me to speak without falsehood—she remains with me so that day and night it torments me <note>term: "massanna" — an archaic term for troubling, exhausting, or grieving the spirit.</note>, that is, the love and that desire which I have so obstinately for L[aura]. The good that shows itself around me dazzles: that is, I do not understand more than what I perceive with my eye; and even if I come to discern it, the eye cannot remain focused with the intellect.

<margin>Francesco X</margin> ¶ Reason indeed. In the second stanza here, taking up the previous statement, he shows why it is reasonable that he sings, saying that having already sighed for a very long time, it is reasonable that at some point he passes from displeasure to pleasure. This <term>Platonic sentiment</term> <note>A reference to the *Phaedo*, where Socrates remarks that pleasure and pain are joined at the head like two bodies with one mind.</note> is such that Plato says pleasure and melancholy are like two branches growing from the same root, so that one cannot help but pass from one branch to the other: because the end of one is the beginning of the other. And he says he never began so early that he could, with laughter and pleasure, equal the weeping and displeasure he has sustained for so long, showing the desire he has to be able, with such singing, to offer some pleasure to his beloved lady, saying that if he could do this, he would consider himself blessed; but much more so if she begged him to do it, as is customary among lovers.

### STANZA II.

It is right indeed that sometimes I sing:
Since I have sighed for so great a time;
That I never begin early enough;
To equal so many sorrows with laughter.
And if I could make it so, that to her holy eyes
Some delight might be provided
By some sweet word of mine:
Oh, me, blessed above other lovers;
But even more, when I shall speak without lying,
Since my Lady begs me; for I wish to speak.

<margin>y</margin> ¶ Wandering thoughts. Now in this third stanza he begins his song, in which he shows the hardness of Lady Laura's iron heart, made in the likeness of <term>enamel</term> <note>original: "smalto." In medieval poetry, this refers to a hard, cold, or glassy surface, symbolizing an unyielding heart.</note>. He says he is not capable of being able to pierce inside it with his speech. Adding the reason for such great hardness, which is pride, in that she considers herself so beautiful: and of such worth that she does not deign to notice him: nor does she care for his speaking, as if this proceeds from some star of contrary influence which he cannot resist. From which he concludes that just as he, in such obstinate love, becomes hard and embittered: so also in his singing he cannot be anything but harsh, because words are the impression and the <note>original: "notte." Likely a scribal error for "note" (notes/marks).</note> signs of the things that are in the soul.

### STANZA III,

Wandering thoughts; that thus step by step
Have led me to reason so loftily;
See, that my lady has a heart of enamel
So strong, that I for my part cannot pierce within:
She does not deign to look so low,
That she should care for our words;
For heaven does not will it,
Against which, though struggling, I am already weary:
Wherefore, as in my heart I become hard and bitter;
So in my speech I wish to be harsh.

# STANZA .IIII.

What do I say? Or where am I? And who deceives me,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Other than myself and my own excessive desire?
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As the heavens have already passed from circle to circle,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;No planet condemns me to weep.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If a mortal veil dims my sight,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;What fault is it of the stars,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Or of beautiful things?
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;He stays with me, who day and night afflicts me,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Since the sweet sight and her lovely, gentle gaze
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Made me follow his pleasure to my own grief.

<margin>
¶ WHAT DO I SAY. Because he had previously mentioned that heaven did not want her to care for him—as if celestial influence were working against him—he now takes back those words and corrects himself. In this fourth stanza, he states the truth: that since he possesses reason and <term>free will</term> <note>original: "libero arbitrio"</note>, he is not forced to act by the heavens or by anyone else, but rather by his own passion and excessive lustful desire. This desire has effectively veiled the eyes of his mind, insofar as he does not employ the passage of reason and intellect. Thus, he concludes that his suffering does not proceed from any planet or star, but from his own <term>sensory appetite</term> <note>original: "sensitiuo appetito" — the part of the soul driven by feelings and desires rather than logic.</note>, by which he is tormented night and day, constantly remembering the sweet sight and gentle gaze of Lady Laura.
</margin>

# STANZA .V. AND LAST.

All things with which the world is adorned,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Came forth good from the hands of the eternal master:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But I, who do not discern so deeply within,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Am dazzled by the beauty shown all around me;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And if I ever return to the true splendor,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;My eye cannot stay firm;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;So infirm has it been made
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;By its own fault, and not by that day,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When I turned toward that angelic beauty
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In the sweet time of my early youth.

<margin>
¶ ALL THINGS. In the fifth and final stanza, he confirms what he said in the preceding fourth stanza: that no planet condemned him to weep, but rather his own passion. He says that God made all things good, and even more so created Man with mental excellence in His own likeness. However, being dazzled by the "veil" of bodily passion, the poet does not look deep within his mind where reason and intellect reside. Even when he begins to seek the help of reason, his passion overtakes him, and he cannot remain firm in listening to the teachings of reason. He concludes that he was not forced into this state by <note>Petrarch famously first saw Laura on Good Friday.</note> Good Friday <note>original: "venerdi sancto"</note> when he first saw Lady Laura, but rather by his own fault, as he allows himself to be conquered by a passion that he ought to restrain with the "bridle of reason."
</margin>

# CANZONE .XVII. STANZA .I.

Because life is short,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And my talent shrinks from the high undertaking,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I do not trust much in myself, nor in it;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But I hope that it may be understood
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;There where I yearn, and there where it must be:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;My grief, which I cry out while remaining silent.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Graceful eyes, where love makes its nest,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To you I turn my weak style,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Sluggish by itself, but great pleasure spurs it on;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And whoever speaks of you,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Takes from the subject a noble character;

<margin>
¶ BECAUSE LIFE IS. This song has nothing of the rustic or the unlearned vulgar style; rather, it is entirely graceful, filled with polished sentences and noble words. Directing it to his beloved Lady Laura more clearly than he had done before, he declares his burning desire and asks for mercy. He says, therefore, in the first stanza—using modesty in his speech—that although he might have intended to write a more extensive volume and with a more ingenious purpose, he nevertheless considered that human life is short and his talent, being weak, is not secure in such a noble undertaking...
</margin>

<meta>Catchword: ...of noble (di generosa)</meta>

<summary>Petrarch concludes his reflection on free will, admitting that his obsession with Laura is his own fault rather than a result of fate or the stars. He then begins a new poem, humbly dedicating his "weak style" to Laura's eyes while acknowledging the brevity of life.</summary>

</margin>
¶ **BECAUSE life is short.** <note>This begins the commentary on Petrarch's Poem 71.</note> Master Francesco directs this moral <term>canzone</term> <note>A traditional Italian song-form poem.</note> to his lady and to the text itself. *I trust neither it nor me much*: that is, life, because I do not know its end, nor his intellect, because it is exhausted by love. *Takes from the subject a noble character*: as if to say, you are the subject of the material I treat, and from such a noble subject, my speech takes on a similar character when speaking of you. *That I saw what thought cannot equal*: Master Francesco had seen some hidden thing in her, wherefore he says, *I know well that no one but you understands me.* *Perhaps my unworthiness then offends*: that is, I am unworthy of you. Because I look at you so readily, perhaps you hold me in disdain. *Now if this fear*: he speaks of the fear he has of offending her or making her indignant. *This would be a blessed passing*: that is, while looking at you. *Because in their presence.* ¶ *O hills, valleys, rivers, forests, fields*: here the poet calls as witnesses the places where he lived in solitude. *But if a greater fear*: that is, if he did not fear that worse might follow by dying by his own hand. *No certain path would restrain me*: as if to say, I would kill myself. But *whenever you turn to me*: that is, when you see me turn pale and lose my way when I see you, you recognize me by that act; for as beautiful as you are, those beauties are the cause of my turning pale. *Of the good that the soul feels from time to time*: that is, why do you deprive me of your eyes, which make my soul content? *Your mercy I feel in the midst of my soul.* *Your mercy* is placed appositively: as if to say, for this that I feel, I give thanks to you, saying: *Your mercy.* *So that out of a thousand, only one is found*: that is, what I have of you alone is found in me. *That the extreme of laughter equals the weeping*: as if to say, as much delight as I have had, I weep for just as much in the end. *Anguish and trouble flee at your appearance*: that is, when I see you, I remain without trouble or exhaustion, and when you leave, it returns to me. *Wherefore if any good fruit*: he speaks metaphorically, as if to say, if any beautiful work, rhyme, or sentiment comes from me, the subject of those things comes from you, and thus the honor is yours. *Song, you do not quiet me.* Master Francesco speaks to the song, invoking it, because in speaking of her, his soul is not in him but in her, and thus he invokes himself.

***

<margin>
Francesco Filelfo
</margin>
¶ **NOT BECAUSE I.** Responding to a silent objection in this second stanza: he says that although he recognizes that all his praise causes her displeasure—considering that as an act of love it brought her infamy—he cannot help but satisfy his own desire. This desire has existed since the time he first fell in love with her, showing that this was the beginning of all his troubled and restless state, for she might have said: "You go about showing through your praise that you are in love with me." He responds by saying that no one else understands, nor do they know who he is captivated by. He becomes cold as if he were dead when he gazes again upon her beautiful eyes.

### STANZA III.

<margin>D</margin>

¶ Therefore that I. <note>The commentator is referencing the first words of the third stanza: "Dunque ch'io."</note> He responds to another objection in this third stanza: for others might have been able to say: "If you burn with such a passion of love, not being of a more robust constitution, you ought to dissolve." Wherefore he responds that his not dissolving—being a fragile object and material receiving such a powerful fire—proceeds not so much from his own strength as from the fear that, freezing the veins and the exterior parts of the body, makes the blood flee to the heart, in which, thus warmed, life is maintained for him to give him more time to endure the intolerable heat of love. So fragile an object in so powerful a fire,
Is not my own strength that saves me;
But a little fear,
Which freezes the wandering blood through the veins,
And refortifies the heart, so that it may burn longer.
O hills, O valleys, O rivers, O woods, O fields,
O witnesses of my heavy life,
How many times have you heard me call for death?

### STANZA IIII.

<margin>E</margin>

Wherefore, directing his speech to the said pain, he laments that it leads him away from joyful and amorous speech and makes him say something less pleasing, showing that he has no quarrel with pain, but with love, of which he says he grieves. ...if she could see her own lovely eyes as he sees them, they would make her even more blessed and joyful, as much as one can possibly comprehend. He becomes entirely joyful when she looks back at him, or rather because she sees herself reflected in his eyes. And when he says he did not lament the pain nor yet of love: we should understand that he laments her, who does not reciprocate his love.

<margin>F</margin> ¶ IF YOU. He continues in the present fifth stanza by increasing the singular grace of the aforementioned beauty: and he says that if she could see her own aforementioned divine and incredible beauty as she sees him, she would have joy beyond measure, in such a way that the heart could not tolerate it—as one reads of many people who have died from immeasurable joy. And for this reason, his soul says that it gazes upon such beauty (which is perhaps somewhat removed from natural strength), for which reason he says his soul is blessed: it sighs and loves those flashing eyes which are like celestial lights. He shows that only to gaze upon them is he content to live, for otherwise life would be troublesome to him; he grieves that it is rarely granted to him to look back at them, and that even when he sees them, the opportunity to look at her longer is immediately taken away.

> *Lights of heaven; for which I give thanks*

> *Alas, why so rarely*
> *Do you give me that, of which I am never sated?*
> *Why do you not more often*
> *Gaze upon that one, whom love tears apart?*
> *And why do you strip me immediately*
> *Of the good, which from time to time the soul feels?*

->## STANZA VI<-

<margin>G</margin> ¶ I SAY THAT. Continuing in this sixth stanza with the preceding sentiment regarding the marvelous pleasure he feels through the noble gaze of her most splendid eyes: he says that by the grace of her looking back, he feels from hour to hour a singular sweetness, so that in that weeping <note>original: *piãto*</note> he forgets all other thoughts; nor does any other thought remain for him then except that of the most sweet gazing. For this reason alone does living please him, for otherwise he would wish to be dead. He grieves that this gazing lasts so little: for if it lasted longer, he would be in such felicity that others would be envious of him, and he might perhaps become proud because of it. He adds, following the <term>Platonic sentiment</term> <note>The idea that extremes of emotion inevitably swing to their opposites, or that earthly joy is always shadowed by sorrow.</note> touched upon above, that at the end of pleasure follows displeasure; he does not have so much delight when he gazes at her that he does not have even greater displeasure when she then denies him her most pleasant gaze. Therefore, he says that the weeping interrupts his <term>spirits</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirits" were subtle vapors that carried sensation and life through the body.</note> kindled with joy, and then he thinks only of his own troubles.

> <margin>D</margin> *I say, that from hour to hour,*
> *By your mercy, I feel in the midst of my soul*
> *An unusual and new sweetness,*
> *Which every other burden*
> *Of troublesome thoughts clears away then,*
> *So that of a thousand, only one is found there:*
> *That much alone, and no more, makes life pleasing to me:*
> *And if this my good lasted a while,*
> *No state could equal mine:*
> *But perhaps to another it would make him*
> *Envious; and such honor would make me proud:*
> *Therefore, alas, it is fitting,*
> *That the extreme of laughter be attacked by weeping;*
> *And interrupting those kindled spirits*
> *Return to me, and I think of myself.*

### STANZA VII.

**The loving thought,**
**Which dwells within you, reveals itself to me**
**In such a way that it draws every other joy from my heart.**
**Wherefore words and works**
**Issue from me then in such a manner, that I hope**
**To make myself immortal, though the flesh may die.**
**Anguish and trouble flee at your appearance;**
**And at your departure they return together:**
**But because the enamored memory**
**Closes the entrance to them afterward,**
**They do not spread from there to my furthest parts:**
**Hence, if any beautiful fruit**
**Is born of me, from you first comes the seed:**
**I for my part am almost a dry ground**
**Cultivated by you, and the merit is entirely yours.**

<margin>H</margin>
*¶ THE LOVING. In this seventh stanza he demonstrates what is perhaps true: that the constant thought he has regarding his love for her is the reason that he, in his writing, becomes immortal. This is because a joyful soul makes the intellect more graceful, as happens with the minds of lovers; feeling themselves often "at the hands" <note>original: "a le mane," a phrase suggesting being in the presence or under the influence of the beloved</note> of love, they receive such pleasure that they sing far better than nightingales. Thus it happens in every other passion: according to how a man is impassioned, so he speaks better. He adds that when he sees her, all anguish and all trouble flee from him; but when she departs, these return to his impassioned soul. However, they can do little harm because of the remaining memory of the beloved thing, which closes off the entry to sorrow. He concludes that the origin and seed of every good thing proceeding from his wit comes from her; through her love, his soul is led to a beautiful shore <note>original: "bel lito"</note>, whereas the good he would do by himself would be like a dry and sterile ground.*

---

### STANZA VIII.

**Song, you do not quiet me; rather you inflame me**
**To speak of that, which steals me from myself:**
**Therefore be certain of not being alone.**

<margin>I</margin>
*¶ SONG. He concludes in this eighth stanza <note>This is the "congedo" or "envoi," a short concluding stanza common in Italian lyric poetry</note> that which commonly happens to lovers: the more they speak of love, even if they complain of it, the more they catch fire from the amorous flames. He shows himself to be so inflamed by love for Lady Laura that in speaking of her, he is stolen from himself, in that he is no longer in his own power but in hers. Therefore he shows that he cannot put an end to his speaking through this song alone, but that it will be accompanied by the following song. This song belongs near the beginning of the book after the first introductory sonnet; but as has been said at other times, whoever collected these songs and sonnets had little brain, and observed neither order nor any method.*

**This is the sight that induces me to do good,**

**This alone distances me from the common crowd:**

*¶ MY NOBLE. This 18th song <note>Known in modern editions as Poem 72</note> follows immediately from the previous one. In it, by commending his beloved lady, our poet demonstrates the same thing he has done before: the immeasurable fire of his love toward her. He says, therefore, in the first stanza, in praise of her eyes, that there issues forth such a flashing splendor that it seems a sun; its light is sweet and joyful to human eyes. It is that light by whose great brilliance darkness is removed, allowing one to see heaven, not otherwise than how we see the eternal God through the light of truth. And he adds, as one who is enamored, that he believes entirely according to—*

> Both when winter scatters the frost,
