<margin>Anto.</margin>
**G**entle my lady, I see. In this moral song <note>A "canzone morale" is a structured poem dealing with philosophical or ethical themes</note> Messer Francesco speaks to Madonna Laura, showing himself more content than ever to love her because she is the incitement to every good. *The year rejuvenates itself*: that is, the springtime, which was the time he fell in love and which he calls his "first distress." *Where the eternal mover of the stars*: that is, in Paradise, from which God sent his lady to the world to show an example of His workmanship. *Love or fickle fortune*: he says that even a most fortunate lover never drank so many delights that he would not exchange them for a single glance from Madonna Laura. *And there alone with you remained Love*: that is, when I come to remember you, every other thought found in the mind departs, and only you and love remain in it. *How much sweetness in a while*: he says summarily that whatever pleasure any lover ever had from his lady is nothing compared to the glances he receives from her. *To my imperfection fortune is adverse*: that is, I have no perfect remedy for your love, because every other thing is contrary to me: I believe heaven proves this itself. *And the hand that so often crosses over*: He says "crosses over" because often, when meeting Messer Francesco, she would pretend to adjust her veil and place her hand before her face so as not to let herself be looked upon. *Comes from the eyes at the end, sweetly trembling*: he describes a gesture that many women often have, who, when turning their eyes or bowing, make a cheerful trembling motion that inflames love. *Song*: the poet speaks to the Song in that same "lodging": meaning that these Songs are written in the same style.

<margin>Fran. L</margin>
**I** think. In the second stanza, further exalting the beauty of this lady, he demonstrates that she is not a human work, but a divine one. And that through her, one understands how beautiful the other works of heaven must be. Thinking of this, the desire to die comes upon him, so that—by exiting this corporeal prison <note>A common Platonic metaphor for the physical body</note> because the path to heaven is closed to him—he might see the infinite beauty of the celestial works. But because he is moved more by what is closest to him, and by whose amorous passion he is most inflamed, he says that such a thought returned to the "accustomed war" of love. He thanks nature along with the day he was born, for which he was reserved for such a great good as being able to see her. He also thanks her, for whose love his heart was raised to such great hope; because until that day he saw her, he lay

### STANZA III.

<margin>M</margin>
<margin>
¶ NOR EVER. In this third stanza, he demonstrates what folly it is to trust in love, since love and fortune are both most inconstant and fraudulent. And the more one seems to love someone, the more he is deceived: because in the blink of an eye they make unhappy him who was before most happy. Therefore, he says his every rest fails so quickly—which he had hoped to enjoy by reaching the beloved object—just as every tree finally withers from the root. And directing his gaze to the lovely eyes of the beloved lady, he calls those "shining looks" "sparks," which is to say burning sparks, showing that only by looking does he seem to be blessed while living, insofar as every pleasure of his is kindled and inflamed there; feeling himself consumed and destroyed by this sweetest labor <note>original: "affanno," meaning the toil or suffering of a lover</note>, he says that being looked upon by such gazes, he seems to see—
</margin>

> Nor ever was a joyful state
> Given by Love, or fickle fortune,
> To those who were their greatest friends on earth,
> That I would not exchange for a single
> Turn of [your] eyes; from which all my rest
> Comes, as every tree comes from its roots.
> Lovely angelic sparks, beatifiers
> Of my life, where pleasure is kindled,
> Which sweetly consumes and destroys me;
> As every other light vanishes and flees
> Where yours shines;
> So from my heart,
> When such sweetness descends into it,
> Every other thing, every thought goes out;
> And love alone remains there with you.

—such splendor that every other light vanishes and flees. Similarly, when he feels that true sweetness, every other thought leaves the heart, nor does he think of anything else but his love for her.

### STANZA IV.

<margin>N</margin>
<margin>
¶ Fourth. The fourth stanza declares the infinite pleasure that Messer Francesco <note>M. F. refers to Francesco Petrarch</note> receives whenever he was gazed upon by Madonna Laura <note>M. L.</note> with some cheerful appearance. He says that if it were possible to gather in one place all the pleasure that all the lucky lovers who ever were successful in actually obtaining the beloved object ever felt, it would be nothing compared to the sweetness he feels when she occasionally looks at him with sweetness. He describes the attire of Madonna Laura, who was dressed in black and wore white veils on her head; saying that love "frolicked" in him signifies that he loved in vain, without any result, no differently than if Love were mocking him by feeding him on empty hope. And because it would seem that he had felt such sweetness contrary to what was deserved, he reveals that for this imperfection of his and his displeasure—insofar as his love is without result—and for this misfortune of his, he seems to have—
</margin>

> Whatever sweetness was ever
> Gathered in the hearts of fortunate lovers,
> All in one place it is nothing compared to what I feel,
> When you sometimes,
> Gently, between the beautiful black and the white,
> Turn your light, in which love frolics;
> And I believe that from my swaddling bands and cradle,
> For my imperfection, for adverse fortune,
> Heaven provided this remedy.
> The veil does me wrong,
> And the hand, which so often places itself between
> My highest delight
> And the eyes, from which day and night
> Great desire overflows to unburden the breast,
> Which takes its form from varied affection.

—lost the celestial influence from his very birth, which shared his pain with sweetness; and that merely being gazed upon by her at times with a grateful look is a remedy for his intolerable passion. For this reason, he reasonably complains of the way the beloved Madonna Laura covered her eyes with her veil, and sometimes by placing her hand across her face, between herself and the eyes of the lover.

<margin>M</margin> ...who stood in opposition: saying that he continually weeps for love of her, no differently than if his eyes poured out most abundant tears like rain. He does this because of the great desire he has for her and to vent the amorous fire of his heart, which—as if taking on various forms—is now joyful and now saddened; it seemed to him that she had shown him either a kind face or a harsh face. <margin>O</margin> <margin>P</margin> Therefore, he adds in this fifth stanza, more aptly than in any place above, how great was his desire to reach his "loving conclusions" <note>An idiom for the fulfillment or consummation of love.</note>. And he says that, realizing that the natural gift of his person—which is not at all rustic but quite handsome—is worth nothing in the eyes of Madonna Laura, he strives through study and virtuous praise to become pleasing and acceptable to her. He does not take pleasure in mercenary arts, nor in anything mechanical or base <note>The commentator emphasizes that Petrarch avoids "vile" manual labor or trade, focusing instead on the "liberal arts" befitting a gentleman.</note>; it seems to him that in regard to doing good he was prompt and ready, and on the contrary, slow to do ill. Such a reputation might easily help him with her, since she is of human and benign judgment—though perhaps Petrarch did not know that what women love is the "hardness of iron" <note>A cynical commentary note suggesting that women are more attracted to strength or stubbornness than to soft poetic virtue.</note>, which conquers every other excellent virtue. And finally, he demonstrates what he would want, saying that the end of his continuous weeping will come when her eyes tremble at the sweet end of love’s blows; and this is that ultimate hope which is desired by those who love courteously <note>term: "love courteously" (original: "amano cortesemente") refers to Courtly Love, a medieval European conception of nobly and chivalrously expressing love and admiration.</note>. And such an end Petrarch desired from Madonna Laura, and not from any other most beautiful woman; and he uses the present tense in place of the future, which he would have wished to have been present.

## CANZONE XIX. STANZA I.

<margin>Francis Q</margin> Since. The present nineteenth song <note>This refers to Canzone 73 in the standard numbering of Petrarch's "Canzoniere."</note> is adorned with graceful speech and shaped with noble elegance in keeping with the burning passion of love. Herein the poet, speaking the same sentiments as he did in the preceding songs, begins in this first stanza to show how great is his desire to manifest his pains to his beloved lady and to ask her for mercy; since he is almost predestined to that burning will.

> Since by my destiny
> That burning desire forces me to speak,
> Which has forced me to sigh forever,
> Love, who draws me to this,
> Be my guide; and show me the way;
> And temper my rhymes with my desire:
> But not in such a way that the heart dissolves.

*From excessive sweetness; as I fear*
*By that which I feel, where no other's eye reaches:*

<note>This concludes the first stanza of Canzone 73. Petrarch explores the paradox of how expressing his love, rather than providing relief, actually intensifies his passion.</note>

...[desi]re of love, which has always been spent in anxieties or in sighs, at present forces him to speak of his love: and for which reason he has such a desire that Love ought to guide him toward beautiful speech and be as a guide on his path, so that the rhymes might respond to his desire. But he does not wish them to be as "incendiary" as his immeasurable desire for love, because his heart would almost be unstrung by the excessive sweetness of such speech. He says he feels this within himself and almost sees it inside his heart, where others cannot gaze. And he gives the reason why he would not want the rhymes to be as fiery as his desire: because by speaking, he becomes more inflamed and more pierced by the arrows of love. And using modesty regarding himself, he says this does not proceed from his own wit, but from his burning desire, and he is therefore all the more frightened. In such a way, he shows himself to be so overcome by this passion that at times it seems to him the heat of natural reason is diminished: so that at the sound of his own speaking, he is entirely destroyed and consumed, no differently than if he were ice near the sun.

---

<margin>Anto.</margin> <note>Likely referring to Antonio da Tempo or another commentator whose views are being summarized.</note>
**S**INCE BY MY DESTINY: Our poet continues with this moral <note>A term used by Renaissance commentators to describe the thematic core or "message" of a stanza.</note> the speech concerning Madonna Laura. He says that since it is his destiny to speak of this, Love ought to guide him; and thus he invites Love to his favor "by that which I feel where no other’s eye reaches." This refers to the truth he wishes to treat, which no one but he can comprehend. "Now time abandons me" <note>original: "Hor m'abandona el tempo"</note>: it is so swift it leaves me in the hands of time, according to which it is necessary for me to speak. "Show me at least that I may say": He asks of himself that Love at least show him how to speak in such a way that if ever Laura, his "enemy," hears him, he might make her a friend through pity, rather than his own. "I say if in that age": Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> says summarily in this stanza that it is not fitting for him to seek other lands nor to travel through the world as those ancient Romans did to find and take the most beautiful and singular things that existed; for he says that he alone returns to the eyes of Madonna Laura, which is a solemn thing in the world. "As by the force of winds": He makes a comparison that just as two stars in the sky are a sign to sailors—that is, the Arctic and Antarctic poles in a storm—so the eyes of Madonna Laura are a guide to him in the tempest of love. "Alas, but much more is that which involves me": that is, what I take for myself that she does not perceive is much more than what she notices. "Tranquil peace without any anxiety": I say that when Madonna Laura laughs, an amorous act of peace moves in her eyes, similar to that eternal peace which is in heaven. "Without ever turning the supernal wheel" <note>original: "rota superna," referring to the celestial spheres or the sun.</note>: that is, that the day he first saw her might be eternal, so that the wheel of the sun might never move, nor should he care for anyone else or for himself. That is, that he should have no other thought but to contemplate her eyes. "Which Love encircles in my life": When the poet says that only that knot be loosened which Love encircles around his tongue "when the excessive light advances." "Human life": that is, Love should not constrain me to speak only of the eyes of Madonna Laura when she looks at me, for her gaze is that "excessive light" that surpasses my human sight; so that I might not be restricted to speaking of those eyes as I might say other things from which I would take boldness. "Song": The poet speaks to the song <note>The "Concedo" or "Tornata," the envoy at the end of a poem.</note> and says he already feels his pen tiring of speaking and writing so much of her, because in these four morals he has spoken of nothing but Madonna Laura and her beauties. But he says he does not yet feel tired of her, for my thoughts have much to speak of with me; and he gives us to understand that he wants to continue, but not in such a style.

this third stanza to exalt the insuperable beauty of Lady Laura, he says that where the ancient poets like Orpheus and Homer, and philosophers like Pythagoras, Democritus, and Plato, and makers of laws like Lycurgus and Solon <note>Solon and Lycurgus were the legendary lawgivers of Athens and Sparta, respectively. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch's Canzone 72 (historically often numbered 73), known as the second of the "Three Sisters" poems. The previous pages discussed the overwhelming power of Lady Laura's eyes; here, the author continues to analyze the fourth and fifth stanzas, focusing on the eyes as a navigational guide and a source of heavenly peace.</meta>

## STANZA 4

**J**ust as by the force of winds
A weary sailor at night raises his head
Toward the two lights that our pole always holds;
So in the tempest
That I endure for love, those shining eyes
Are my sign, and my only comfort.
Alas, but I steal <note>original: "enuolo"</note> much more from them,
Now here, now there, as Love instructs me,
Than what comes as a gracious gift:
And the little that I am,
Finds in them a perpetual rule <term>norma: a standard or model of behavior</term>:
Since I first saw them,
I have not moved a step toward doing good without them.
Thus I have placed them at my very summit;
For my own worth, on its own, is judged as false.

<margin>which has</margin>
**B**EHOLD BY FORCE. Through a beautiful simile in this fourth stanza, wishing to further exalt the beauty of the lovely eyes of Lady Laura, he says that just as the sailor at night in a sea storm—being quite weary not only from the excessive movement and tossing of the ship but also from too much waking—raises his head toward the sky to gaze upon the star of Callisto and Arcas her son <note>The constellations Ursa Major and Ursa Minor, used for navigation</note> above the arctic pole: this is so he may know where he is and how long remains until daybreak. So too, amidst his amorous anxieties and torments, he is accustomed to look upon the eyes of Lady Laura as his sign and his comfort. 

Adding that he is indeed weary and wretched because he cannot gaze at those shining eyes as much as he wishes; rather, it is much more that which he "steals" —now in this place, now in that, or at some banquet—than what is granted to him as a gift by Lady Laura. He acknowledges and shows that every nobility, knowledge, and virtue within him proceeds from those eyes which he has taken as his rule, saying that from the day he first saw them, he has never since left any footprint or trace of doing good without reflecting himself in them. In such a way, he has placed them above his head—where the <term>cogitative faculty: the part of the mind responsible for processing thought and reason</term> resides—since it seems to him that he is worth nothing by himself.

## STANZA 5

**I** could never
Imagine, much less narrate the effects
That those sweet eyes work within my heart.
All the other delights
Of this life I hold as far lesser:
And all other beauties fall behind.
Tranquil peace without any anguish,
Similar to that which is eternal in heaven,
Moves from their enamored smile.
If only I could gaze fixedly,
As Love gently governs them,
For just one day from nearby,
Without the heavenly wheel ever turning;
Nor thinking of others, nor of myself,
And let the blinking of my eyes not be frequent.

**I** COULD NEVER. Expanding in this fifth stanza upon the beauty of the aforementioned eyes, he says that such miraculous effects do these eyes produce in his heart, and such sweetness they provide, that every other delight is forgotten and considered trivial. He values no other beauty, for those eyes, with their joyful and gracious gaze, bring such consolation and rest to his heart that it seems to him like the tranquil peace of Paradise, which is eternal. 

In declaring his fiery desire, he says that he would gladly be able to gaze at them from nearby for one day under the "ceiling of the room" <note>likely referring to a private, intimate setting</note> and that this day should last forever, without the <term>heavenly wheel: the celestial spheres that move the sun and stars</term> ever turning. He wishes that he might forget not only external things but even himself, setting reason aside, so long as he could gaze at those most splendid eyes in his own way, with his own eyes held so steady that his blinking would be extremely rare. <meta>This page concludes the commentary on Petrarch's Canzone 72 (the second of the "Three Sisters") and begins the commentary on Sonnet 82 (traditionally numbered 55 in this edition), "I'o son gia stanco de pensar." The text focuses on the physical and psychological toll of unrequited love—specifically the "knot" that ties the lover's tongue and the physical exhaustion of the poet's body versus the tireless nature of his obsessive thoughts.</meta>

<margin>Alas, that.</margin>
**ALAS, THAT.** Seeing that he had asked for a bit too much previously, he says in this sixth stanza that he wishes he were at least allowed—whenever he occasionally finds himself with Lady Laura—to speak to her freely, and that his tongue were not tied by shame. If this could be, he would speak in such a way that Lady Laura would weep, moved to compassion. Wishing to show the reason for his inability to speak, he says this proceeds from the wounds of love struck into his heart; losing his courage, he becomes pale <note>original: "smorto"</note>. This happens because his request was improper; thus, fearing infamy, the blood rushes back to the heart, and therefore he appears pale because the blood is no longer at the surface of the body. Whence he says that this is the greatest blow he has received from love, for which he calls himself dead.

# STANZA 6

Alas, that desiring
  I seek what cannot be in any way,
  And I live on desire without hope.
  Only that knot
  Which Love ties around my tongue, when
  Human sight is surpassed by too much light:
  If it were untied, I would take courage
  To speak words so new in that moment
  That they would make anyone who understood them weep.
  But the wounds impressed
  Forcefully turn the bent heart elsewhere:
  Wherefore I become pale,
  And the blood hides itself, I know not where;
  Nor do I remain as I was; and I realize
  That this is the blow by which love has killed me— <note>The original text breaks here at the word "mor-" (short for "morto" or "dead"), acting as a transition to the next section.</note>

<margin>Song.</margin>
**SONG.** In the present seventh and final stanza, he concludes that his amorous desire toward Lady Laura is so great that although his hand grows weary from writing, his heart does not grow weary of the continuous thoughts he has of her. In this speech, the physical exhaustion is clearly demonstrated alongside the spiritual exhaustion a man receives when he is in love.

# STANZA 7

Song, I feel my pen already tiring
  From the long and sweet discourse with her:
  But my thoughts do not tire of speaking with me.

<margin>Francis.</margin>
**I AM ALREADY.** In the present 55th sonnet, the poet himself—marveling at his long perseverance in a love where he is not loved back—says with a lovely sentiment that he wonders how his thoughts toward her are not yet tired, even though he himself grows weary from the very act of thinking. He wonders why he does not kill himself to escape such pain and the weight of so many bitter sighs, and how his tongue and voice have not failed him in naming her day and night—she who had a most beautiful face, golden tresses, and flashing eyes. He also says he marvels, as if at something impossible, that his feet have not failed him from exhaustion while following her footprints everywhere she went, which commonly—

# SONNET 55

I am already tired of thinking how
  My thoughts of you are not tired;
  And how I do not yet abandon life,
  To flee so heavy a burden of sighs;
And how, in speaking of your face and hair,
  And of your beautiful eyes, of which I always discourse,
  My tongue and voice have not yet failed,
  Calling your name day and night;
And that my feet are not broken and weary
  From following your footprints in every place,
  Losing so many steps in vain;
And from where comes the ink? where the papers
  That I go filling with you? If I fail in this,
  It is the fault of Love, not a defect of art.

<margin>Francesco A</margin>
<margin>**THOSE BEAUTIFUL EYES.** In the present fifty-sixth sonnet, Petrarch says to his beloved that for his infirmity, the medicines of love are necessary, and not herbs, nor magic arts, nor even precious stones that come from across the sea <note>original: "oltra mare," likely referring to exotic gems from the East believed to have healing properties</note>. This infirmity proceeds only from her beautiful eyes, which have so removed him from every other love that the mere thought of their beauty makes his soul stay at rest. It only remains for his tongue to have the timely boldness to act as his guide: that is, the thoughts of his soul combined with his ingenuity would lack nothing. He continues with the praise of the eyes, through which he says Love gains victory over every man, and even more over himself, because those eyes are always in his heart with burning sparks; for this reason, he reasonably always speaks of their infinite beauty.</margin>

**THOSE BEAUTIFUL** eyes where I was struck. Master Francesco praises in this sonnet the eyes of Lady Laura and says that only the eyes by which he is struck could be the ones by which he might be healed, and not with other herbs or ingenuity. As Ovid says in his epistles: "Alas for me, for love is not curable by herbs" <note>original: "Hei mihi q̄ ammor non est medicabilis herbis." A quote from Ovid's *Heroides*.</note>. And he says that they have taken every thought from his mind and have left a single thought, that is, of his lady. "The guide" refers to that thought which leads the tongue; he means to say that his thought might well fail him, but not his will.

who at the time of King Agenor had been driven out of Syria by his forces and had occupied that island. There, together with his Cilicians and Phoenicians, having established a peaceful state, he reigned. And because the said Pygmalion was of marvelous genius in sculpture, he made with his own hands a girl of ivory <note>original: *eburnea*</note> of unheard-of beauty, which then, looking upon it as so beautiful, it seemed to him that he fell most ardently in love with her, in such a way that he could not contain himself from leading her in the "amorous dance"—perhaps as many as a thousand times. ¶ Some say this was not a fable, but the truth. Which is confirmed well enough by the testimony of Poggio Bambilione <note>Likely referring to the humanist Poggio Bracciolini (1380–1459).</note>, who says that while in England and having seen a girl most pleasing to him, and not being able in any way to have her, nor even to speak to her, he saw a plastered wooden image in which the figure and likeness of that girl was wonderfully represented; not once, but more than a hundred times he had carnal use of it. As for Poggio, since he confesses it himself, I say nothing; but as for Pygmalion, I estimate it to be a fable. This is especially because it is said that, being so in love with that image, he prayed to Venus to convert her into a woman and was heard; and then he had use of her and fathered a son named Paphos. It seems to me that Pygmalion making an ivory image signifies that, having seen that the Cypriot women were all lustful and immodest and none went as a virgin to a husband, he chose a young girl of a very small age—so that the "fig," having not yet ripened, would not be taken from him while small—and she was white and polished like ivory. Having accustomed her to his ways, although she was not yet of a suitable age, he liked her so much that he wanted to eat the fig half-ripe so that the winter frost would not take its vigor; let this suffice, as we shall speak of it more diffusely elsewhere. Thus, anyone can understand if Petrarch was "sending medlars" <note>An idiom meaning to speak nonsense or trifles.</note> when he spoke of such matters. And some fools, striving to turn the sun into darkness, want Lady Laura to be understood by some as Poetry, by others the Soul, and by others Virtue, and a thousand other frenetic and bizarre things. Although it displeases me to speak of such matters so openly.

<margin>Francesco G.</margin>
**With *If the beginning*:** At the start of this 60th sonnet, Petrarch shows the length of his infirmity <note>Love-sickness was often described as a physical illness in Renaissance literature.</note>, for he had already been in love with Lady Laura for fourteen years without ever being able to reach his desired goal. For this reason, he declares himself so exhausted by long sighs that he is as if dead, so that Laura can no longer help him—referring not only to her name but also to the "laura" <note>original: *l'aura*. A frequent pun in Petrarch’s work between the name Laura and the Italian word for a light breeze or "aura."</note> which is a cooling or moderate and pleasant wind. Nor can the "rezzo" <note>An archaic Italian term for shade or a cool, breezy spot.</note> help him, which is to say any shade that usually brings delight in hot weather. He says this happens only because of the multiplying and growing of his amorous desire. This proceeds because Love—with whom his thoughts of obtaining the beloved lady never find moderation—governs him so poorly that melancholy has made him waste away until nothing of his former self remains. Being thus subjugated by Love, he can never catch his breath. All of this comes from the labor he takes in rhyming about the beauty of his graceful but murderous beloved. He adds how much prudent lovers ought to observe, which is to conduct their affairs cautiously. Thus he says that as he fails and consumes himself for love day by day, no one notices it except himself and Lady Laura; for love of her, his heart is destroyed. He concludes that in such suffering he had barely led his life up to that day, nor did he yet know if he ought to live, since death was always approaching and his life was fleeing.

### SONETTO LX.

> If the end and the middle match the beginning
> Of the fourteenth year that I sigh;
> Laura <note>original: *Laura*. Here playing on the double meaning of the lady's name and the "aura" or breeze.</note> can no longer save me in the shade,
> So much do I feel my burning desire grow.
> Love, with whom thoughts never have a middle ground,

<margin>H</margin>
**With *I am so*:** There is no game so beautiful that it does not eventually become tedious. Demonstrating this in this 61st sonnet, our poet mentions how he has reconsidered his less-than-honest habit; since he was a most learned man, he should have attended to grave and glorious things, and not to love and light, youthful matters. He says it seems to him that he is entangled in sins by which he was weighed down, as if he had a most heavy bundle of wood <term>fascio antico</term> <note>literally "ancient bundle"; a metaphor for the accumulated weight of past sins and habits.</note> on his shoulders. He feared failing in such a way while living that he might fall into the hands of his enemy. We should understand this "enemy" not as the enemy of human nature <note>A common Renaissance euphemism for the Devil.</note>, but as the vicious habit which is the deprivation of virtue. This is bred in us when we practice dishonest actions for a long time; which being...

<meta>This page continues the theological and philosophical commentary on Petrarch’s spiritual struggle, transitioning from the myth of Pygmalion into a deep exploration of the "four graces" of scholastic theology and their relationship to Petrarch’s 62nd sonnet.</meta>

...being then generated within us with great difficulty and labor, we can eventually free ourselves from it. The "friend" who is said to have already come to him to free him from such servitude should be understood as the true **habit of virtue** <term>Habit of virtue: A disposition of the soul acquired through repeated good actions, making virtuous behavior natural and pleasant.</term>: which he says came to him unsought, but out of its own courtesy.

¶ For we must know that according to the theologians, there are four graces. The first is called **operating grace** <note>original: *gratia operante*</note>, when God, without any merit of our own, illuminates and excites us toward virtue; thus He operates in us. The second is called **cooperating grace** <note>original: *gratia cooperante*</note>, when, being thus illuminated and excited to desire to do good, God—seeing us willingly accept His grace and already attending to virtuous works—operates together with us. The third is named **persevering grace** <note>original: *gratia perseverante*</note>, when, having received from divine goodness not only operating grace but also cooperating grace, God grants us the perseverance to continue in good works. The fourth grace is called **saving grace** <note>original: *gratia salvante*</note>; for when we have received those three graces and are already habituated in solid and true virtue, we become, through divine grace, safe from every vice, and thus we acquire happy beatitude. 

He says, therefore, that the habit of virtue had already come to him in the form of the first grace (operating), by which he was illuminated out of his blind and lustful life. But because such grace found the "inn" closed and saw it was not willingly received, it flew away. Thus, he labors in vain, because one cannot, without the greatest and longest toil, withdraw oneself from the snares of love and from an intemperate habit. Nevertheless, he says he still hears as if a resonance of the voice of that friend in this life: that is, the admonition of **reason**, by which we are continually comforted to move toward virtue, unless vicious passion bars our way through the continuous and daily habit of wrongdoing. Therefore, in concluding, he demonstrates that he sees no remedy for his anguish unless operating grace—which proceeds from divine charity—lifts him from the lowest mud of vice as if he were a simple and light dove, and pulls him toward the rest of true virtue.

<margin>I</margin>
¶ **I AM SO TIRED.** The poet, Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch.</note>, shows himself going toward the perdition of his soul, having grown old in these sins of love; therefore he says, "My enemy," meaning the devil; then he imagines that a celestial voice called him back to the blessed life.
<margin>Antonio</margin>

**I HAVE NOT BEEN:** The petition of Petrarch, as understood in this 62nd sonnet, can be compared to the gallop of a mule, which lasts but a short time, however fast it seems at the beginning. Returning to his usual dance, he says that he has never grown tired of loving her, nor will he ever be tired as long as his life lasts. But his life is already hateful to him, in so far as he says he is tired of hating himself any longer and of wanting to always remain in his usual weeping, being already so exhausted that he is near failing. Therefore, he says he desires death as his rest, with the condition that the cause of his dying be written on his tomb, manifesting the name of Lady Laura as the one who made him die before his time. And yet, if she does not want this infamy of being considered homicidal and cruel, she should at least deign to satisfy him by being willing to meet him somewhat in secret, promising her not to do any offensive thing that might seem bitter to her; let her not believe anything but the truth, for she would be in error. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s spiritual and emotional struggle, moving from the philosophical definition of "graces" to a practical application of these concepts through the metaphor of a storm-tossed sailor in Petrarch’s 20th Song (traditionally known as Canzone 80 in the *Canzoniere*).</meta>

who, having understood the deed, composed this sonnet for Brizolo <note>Possibly a contemporary of the commentator or a misspelling of a name; the text suggests a person to whom the sentiment is addressed.</note>, saying to her that he will never be weary of gazing at her, but rather of hating and tormenting himself.

<margin>Francis</margin>
HE WHO IS DETERMINED. This present 20th song teaches us how foolish we are; for though we clearly see our wicked state and are able to remove ourselves from it, we do not do so. It is as if we have deliberately willed to be unhappy; even while we are able to find a remedy, we do not. He says, therefore, in this first stanza, speaking through a metaphor, that it happens to us no differently than to the sailor: who, having determined in his soul to spend his entire life sailing upon the deceptive waves—which appear to be calm, but in a small moment rise up into a great tempest—often finds himself sailing among these or those rocks in some small vessel <note>original: *piccol legno*, literally "small wood," a common poetic term for a boat.</note>, as if he cared nothing for death. Such a man cannot remain long in life; whereas, if he were wise, he would return to port in good time while the sail still catches the wind according to the direction of the rudder. In a similar way, a man should act while his appetite does not yet entirely rebel against reason.

## CANZONE XX. STANZA I.

->He who is determined to lead his life<-
->Upon the deceptive waves and among the rocks,<-
->Secure from death within a small vessel,<-
->Cannot be very far from his end:<-
->Therefore, it would be wise to retreat to port<-
->While the sail still trusts the helm.<-

<margin>Antonio</margin>
<margin>L</margin> HE WHO IS DETERMINED. In this sestina <note>A poem of six stanzas where the end-words of the first stanza are repeated in a specific rotating order in the following stanzas.</note>, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> speaks through the figure of one who is used to sailing and compares his entire being to the likeness of his life. The sail is **Reason**, which, just as a sail guides a ship, so reason ought to guide our life. "Sweet breeze <note>original: *Laura soaue*; a play on the name of Petrarch's beloved, Laura, and *l'aura*, the breeze.</note> to whose helm and sail": that is, Madonna Laura, with whom I fell so warmly in love, hoping to have more from her than I have, who then led me into a thousand rocks: that is, into a thousand anxieties. "And the causes of my sorrowful end": that is, not only did my torment show itself in my face, but I had long held it closed within my heart, this "blind vessel": that is, in this body. "And let my exile have a fair end": that is, that I may die in peace and tranquility. "Lord of my end and of my life": Master Francesco speaks here, offering prayers to God that He might convert him to the good path.

<margin>Francis M.</margin>
<margin>M</margin> SWEET BREEZE: Confirming the metaphor stated in this second stanza, he says it is the same for him as for the wind. Laura, while she is pleasant, is called the "helm" and the "guidance" of himself; when he disposed himself to enter the life of love, he was led by her no differently than onto rocks, into infinite passions and difficulties. He demonstrates that the cause of such a sorrowful end was not outside of himself, but within himself, insofar as he did not follow the admonition of reason but the impetus of unbridled passion, which is always the cause of all our anxieties and miseries.

## STANZA II.

->Sweet breeze, to whose helm and sail<-
->I committed myself when entering the life of love,<-
->And hoping to arrive at a better port;<-
->Then I was led among more than a thousand rocks:<-
->And the causes of my sorrowful end<-
->I had not only around me, but inside the vessel.<-

<margin>N</margin>
CLOSED FOR A LONG TIME: He continues in this third stanza, showing that for a long time he remained in this passion of love, so blinded in his reason that he could not use his light, as his sensory appetite was disobedient. He did not consider how he ought to conduct his life, whereby he was already diminished in his person as well as in his intellect, so that he was dying before his time. But being somewhat illuminated by the **operating grace** of God <note>Referencing the theological concept from the previous page where God initiates a turn toward virtue.</note>, he says he noticed his danger, no differently than one who would have been wrecked among the rocks if he had not noticed the port from afar.

## STANZA III.

->Closed for a long time in this blind vessel,<-
->I wandered without raising an eye to the sail,<-
->Which even before my day was carrying me to my end:<-
->Then it pleased Him, who brought me back to life,<-
->To call me so far back from the rocks<-
->That at least from afar the port appeared to me.<-

## STANZA IV

**L**ike a light at night in some port
I ever saw from the high sea ship or vessel,
Unless a storm or rocks took it from him;
So from above, with a swelling sail,
I saw the banners of that other life:
And then I sighed toward my end.

<margin>O</margin>
¶ LIKE A LIGHT. Although <note>original: *quantunque*</note> he was subjugated by love and thus given over to worldly vanity and inconstancy <note>original: *inconstantia mondana*</note>, he shows in this fourth stanza that he has been illuminated by the aforementioned operating grace. Having recognized his lack of good deeds, he is not unlike one who sails in a great storm <note>original: *tempesta*</note> and sees from afar a light in some port that serves as a signal to sailors so they may know how to reach a safe place—provided that high waves or some rocks <note>original: *schogli*</note> do not block the view of that light. This is similar to when unbridled passions take away the sight of reason from its use. And so he, having also seen from the consideration of worldly vanity and folly a sign of the other life, thinking of his present misery, has sighed for it like one who grieves for his current state.

## STANZA V

**N**ot that I am yet secure of the end.
For wishing to be in port by daybreak,
It is a great journey in so short a life:
Then I fear, as I see myself in a fragile vessel;
And more than I would wish, the sail is filled
With the wind that pushed me onto these rocks.

<margin>P</margin>
¶ NOT HOWEVER SECURE. And because <note>original: *perconciò*</note> he said he had recognized his ill-doing, he responds in this fifth stanza as if to a silent question: that although he has seen the said sign of the other happy life—meaning naturally when the soul is separated from the body—we should also understand it morally: when a man, having seen his vicious life, deliberates to withdraw from it and give himself to virtue, through whose practice a man in this life is called "happy." Yet, he does not yet feel secure in such a way regarding his end; for he believed he could easily withdraw from the troubles of love while alive, yet he finds himself caught by the most turbulent passions to which his life is given—far more than he would like. Thus, he finds himself among rocks in the midst of sensory difficulties.

## STANZA VI

**I**f I escape alive from the perilous rocks;
And my exile reaches a beautiful end;
How eager I would be to turn the sail,
And cast the anchors in some port;
Were it not that I burn like a lit piece of wood,
So hard is it for me to leave my accustomed life.

<margin>Q</margin>
¶ IF I ESCAPE. A habit already confirmed <note>original: *confermato*</note> can only be removed with great difficulty, as we said above. Petrarch demonstrates this again in this sixth stanza, saying that if he could emerge from such rocks and most laborious passions without being conquered and nearly killed by vice, and if he could reach some laudable end out of such an exile in which he finds himself—being banished from continence <note>original: *continentia*</note> and modesty like many others—he would willingly turn his sail and live in a different way than he has done until now. He would cast his anchor in some port of tranquility, steadying the state of his life. But this is difficult for him to do because he burns with love like a lit piece of wood <note>original: *legno acceso*; Petrarch uses the word *legno* to mean both his ship and a piece of burning timber</note>; therefore, leaving his accustomed way of living proves to be very troublesome for him.

## STANZA VII

**L**ord of my end and of my life,
Before I break my vessel among the rocks,
Direct the weary sail toward a good port.

<margin>R</margin>
¶ LORD OF THE. Finally, in this seventh and last stanza, he directs his speech to God, concluding with a prayer. He prays that He, as the one who has both death and life in His power, may deign to direct his will—which is what leads him in all he has done and does—toward some good port of virtue.

it was an error, but an error of the heart itself. In responding to this, Petrarch wants to show that the fault was theirs <note>referring to the eyes</note>, since love entered into his heart by way of them when, on Good Friday <note>original: *venerdi sancto*; Petrarch famously met Laura on April 6, 1327, which was Good Friday</note>, they paused to gaze upon Lady Laura; and from that hour onward, love has continually entered his heart as if into its own proper lodging. The eyes respond and readily concede it to be true that love entered the heart through their path; but they argue that the cause was the heart itself, because it held out hope to Master Francis <note>Petrarch</note>—who now dies like one deluded—that he would obtain the thing he loved. To this, Master Francis responds that their reasons are not valid: for if they had not first looked upon Lady Laura, being greedy for their own harm (insofar as they weep for it) and the harm of the heart (insofar as the heart grieves), the heart would not have been moved to love a thing unknown. Therefore, the eyes, not knowing how to argue further, say that his judgment is unjust, and that the blame belonging to the heart is being imputed to them, who have not failed.

The eyes respond <note>original: *Oculi respondent*</note>: "We opened the way for him." Master Francis replies: "I do not know how to speak to you." Again the eyes respond <note>original: *Iterum oculi respondent*</note>: "Now this is what saddens us more than anything else."

¶ I ALWAYS LOVED: Often, while Petrarch was at leisure—as can be understood in this 65th sonnet—he would go for his pleasure from Avignon to the Sorgue, which is a small river and also a village or castle of that name near Avignon toward Provence, where Lady Laura was born and lived when she was not in Avignon. He says he has always loved the Sorgue and still loves it strongly, and that every day he loved it more. To this place, he says he returns with frequent weeping when his heart is pierced by love, having resolved to love in the same manner as he did on that Good Friday morning when he first fell in love. Since from that point on, to better please Lady Laura, he removed from his heart every care that was not famous and illustrious. ...is to him like an example for doing good. Especially for the sake of pleasure, he would wish to be able to see all the aforementioned things together: the place, the time, the hour, and Lady Laura. These are "sweet enemies" because they bring him the sweetest distress; it would be almost impossible to see them all together and have his heart assailed by them with various pleasures. He turns his speech to Love, saying he is conquered by a great force: because he loves the place, he loves the springtime, and he loves the Good Friday dedicated to Lady Laura. He concludes that if he did not hope to eventually obtain the beloved object, he would undoubtedly fall dead from melancholy; however, the hope he has makes him desire to live and comforts him in such a way.

For her, his good deeds are the reason for his falling in love. But Master Francis marvels at the assault Love made upon him with many of its "enemies," which are the peace, wars, truces, and disdain of Lady Laura.

<meta>This page continues the line-by-line commentary on Petrarch’s "Canzoniere." Following the discussion of the eyes and the heart's blame on the previous page, the author now turns to Sonnets 66 and 67, focusing on the specific setting of Petrarch's suffering—a window—and the metaphor of the lady as a master archer.</meta>

<margin>Francesco X</margin>
¶ In the present 66th sonnet, Master Francis <note>original: *M. F.*; referring to Francesco Petrarca</note>, wishing to signify in how much distress he finds himself due to the blows of love, says that he bears great hatred toward a window of Lady Laura <note>original: *M. L.*</note> where she stood watching Petrarch. He observes that some women do this out of love—though they are very few—some out of idleness, and others out of vanity. She threw a good thousand arrows at him with her eyes, so that his love for her grew so much that he would have willingly wished, due to the excessive troubles of his heart, that some of those blows had been fatal. This is because it would have seemed to him a happy death, dying in such a joyful life; whereas remaining in this corporeal prison <note>a common Renaissance metaphor for the physical body</note> is the cause of infinite passions and malice. These evils, he says, cause him more pain because they will last as long as he lives. Then, speaking of his soul, he reproaches it as a wretched thing for not realizing it should depart this life after such a long trial, especially now that time cannot turn back, nor is there anyone to restrain it from its excessive distress. Then, adding the words he used against his soul, he demonstrates that he lives long enough who dies while life is pleasant and prosperous.

<margin>Antonio Y</margin>
¶ I shall always hold in hatred. Lady Laura had shown herself many times to Master Francis, whereby he remained more defeated than ever. Thus he complains of these acts and of the window that was the cause of many of his troubles. "For it is beautiful to die while" <note>original: *Ch’è bel morir, mentre*</note>: as if to say <note>original: *quasi dicat*</note>, one dies well when the mind is healthy. "In the earthly prison" <note>original: *Ne la pregione terrestre*</note>: that is <note>original: *i.*</note>, in this flesh. "Wretched" <note>original: *Misera*</note>: that which the soul should supply.

## SONNETTO LXVI.

**I** shall always hold in hatred the window,
From which Love once launched a thousand arrows at me,
Because some of them were not fatal;
For it is beautiful to die, while life is favorable.
**B** ut staying in this earthly prison
Is the cause, alas, of my infinite evils:
And it grieves me more that they are immortal with me,
Since the soul does not break free from the heart,
**W** retched thing; which should be aware
By long experience by now, that time
Is not something that turns back or that one can restrain.
**M** any times I have guided it with such words:
“Go away, sad one: for he does not depart too early,
Who leaves behind his more serene days.”

---

<margin>Francesco</margin>
¶ So soon as: Petrarch understood very well the nature of some foolish women who take pleasure when others fall in love with them. They do this not so much to do something that pleases them, but because they take pleasure in another's harm; these are women who have bizarre and fantastic heads, full of vanity. He speaks of this in the present 67th sonnet through a local simile: just as the archer, when he has released the bow and shot the arrow, immediately perceives from his shot whether it is to be little esteemed or if he should judge that it will hit the mark, so too she perceived that the blow from her murderous eyes was destined to pass through him to his innermost heart. Wherefore he says it is necessary that his heart, through such a wound, should overflow and shed eternal tears. Indeed, he seems to have understood her speech, for she had to say: "Alas, wretched lover, look at where his desire leads him; behold the present arrow by which Love wishes him to die." And as she sees now how grief restrains him, and also what her eyes (which are his enemies) continually do to him, all of this is not done to bring about his death—which would take him out of his pain—but to make him live in a longer agony.

## SONNETTO. LXVIII.

<margin>Francesco</margin>
*Since my hope is too long in coming* <gloss>¶ Since my [hope]. Time and experience provide the most prudent instructions for human life, as clearly shown in this 68th sonnet. Our poet, recognizing that he has placed his hope in vain—a light and deceptive thing—says that seeing his hope take too long, and considering that the passage of this life is short, he regrets not having realized this sooner so that he might have pulled back from such vanity with haste. Nevertheless, because it is better to start late than never, he says he flees backward with "weak arms" and even "lame," meaning he is as burdened by the passion of love as he ever was, no longer caring for such madness, even though he still carries signs of it in his face—having become pale and thin, and perhaps even aged by the melancholy taken from such an amorous encounter.</gloss>
*And the passing of life is so short;*
*I wish I had been aware at a better time*
*To flee backward, more than at a gallop:*
*And I still flee thus weak and lame*
*In one of my sides; where desire has twisted me,*
*Secure by now: but still in my face I bear*
*Signs that I took at the amorous encounter.*
*Wherefore I advise you who are on the way,*
*Turn your steps; and you whom love inflames,*
*Do not delay until the extreme heat:*
*For though I live; of a thousand, one does not escape,*
*My enemy was indeed strong*
*And I saw her wounded in the middle of the heart.*

Therefore, having experienced this, he advises all those who have not yet experienced as much as he has and who seek to fall in love, that they should turn their steps and their appetites backward; and also those who are already entangled in love, that they should withdraw and not delay so long that they are oppressed by the ultimate heat of love, saying that there are very few who can endure it as he did. He adds that no one should lead themselves to believe they can remain constant and not be overcome by love. He proves this by the example of Madonna Laura <note>original: *M. L.*</note>, who, although she was most chaste and of marvelous honesty, was not so much so that she did not also at times feel some arrows of love. It is no wonder, since a drop of water falling often on a stone eventually hollows it out. And "she alone is chaste," according to that same saying of Ovid <note>referring to *Amores* 1.8.43: *Casta est quam nemo rogavit*—"She is chaste whom no one has asked"</note>, "who is asked by no one," especially if money plays a role, which spoils every market.

<margin>Antonio A</margin>
¶ Since my hope is long. Master Francis <note>original: *M. F.*; Petrarch</note> grieves not to have realized his error in time, seeing his hope failed. Wherefore he advises "you who are on the way." Master Francis advises by the example of his lady that every lover should abandon the enterprise, because she, who was so cruel, he saw conquered by love. "Enemy," says the poet of his lady. "She was indeed strong," that is, rebellious.

...to live even a single day being without love; wherefore being so poorly content, Love soon appeared with disguised masks. And speaking of the first time he was lifted from youthful love but fell again into new snares: he says that he himself grieved and sighed as he was removed from that amorous life: and that it was much better to be in such servitude than in the new liberty. This demonstrates two things: one, that he was never entirely freed from the passion of love, but somewhat withdrawn; the other, that even when he did not seem to attend to love, he attended to some other passion, either avarice or vainglory or another of greater trouble. Now finally, having fully realized his poor counsel regarding attending to the love of any woman: he says he late perceived his own ill, and that with great effort he now pulls himself out as if from a most strong prison of amorous evil in which he had been involved by error.

**H Her hair was:** As I have said in other places, the same is confirmed by this present 70th sonnet: that no order was observed by whoever compiled this present work into a volume, but rather confused everything. Therefore, in this sonnet are described some singular beauties of Madonna Laura, through which he wishes to demonstrate that it was not without cause that he fell in love: wherefore beginning with her hair, he says that those, like threads of gold, were scattered to the breeze <note>The Italian "l'aura" means "the breeze," creating a constant pun on the name "Laura."</note>, which name he uses ambiguously out of respect for the lady, meaning not only a subtle and pleasant little wind but also Madonna Laura. And he follows by saying that those hairs, gathered into tresses, were knotted with great artifice, and she had charming and glowing eyes of marvelous splendor. And they were also most modest to look upon, and her aspect was humble and benign according to what he could understand from experience, if his judgment had not deceived him. Wherefore he shows it was no wonder if his chest, prepared like tinder for love, suddenly burned with the amorous flame. Furthermore, she did not walk like a rustic peasant girl, but as if she had an angelic form, and her way of speaking seemed like a divine voice. And concluding, he says that to his intellect she seemed a celestial spirit, and as for her beauty, she resembled a most splendid sun in the time she lived. And because someone might say: "But you, good man, now that she is dead, why do you still follow her with your love?" He responds with a beautiful simile: that when one is wounded by an arrow—just as he was by the arrow of Love—even though...

### SONNET. LXX.

**H**er golden hair was scattered to the breeze,
Which wound it in a thousand sweet knots;
And the charming light burned beyond measure
In those beautiful eyes, which are now so stingy with it;

And her face taking on the colors of pity—
I know not if it seemed true or false to me;
I, who had the amorous tinder in my breast:
**W**hat wonder, if I suddenly caught fire?

**H**er gait was no mortal thing,
But of angelic form; and her words
Sounded like something other than a human voice.

**A** celestial spirit, a living sun
Was what I saw; and if she were not such now,
A wound does not heal because the bow is slackened.

THEY WERE the golden hair <note>A reference to Sonnet 90, "Erano i capei d'oro," famously describing Laura's beauty</note>. This sonnet is a response to a man who had gone all the way to Avignon to see Madonna Laura, because he had heard her praised so much; and after he had seen her, he wrote back to Master Francesco [Petrarch] saying that she did not seem as beautiful to him as Petrarch made her out to be. <margin>Francesco</margin>
**THE BEAUTIFUL** lady. There are some who maintain that Petrarch wrote this seventy-first sonnet to Master Cino <note>Cino da Pistoia, a famous contemporary poet and friend of Petrarch</note>, who was mentioned in the 24th sonnet. They say that because one of Cino's beloveds had died and Petrarch saw him in great distress, he wrote this to console him. This does not seem right to me—that he would be comforting his friend toward death. Rather, as in the 24th sonnet, I do not wish to follow the opinion of the ignorant who are unaware of the war the Florentines had with the Church while the Papal Court was in Avignon <note>The "War of the Eight Saints" (1375–1378), a conflict between Gregory XI and a coalition of Italian city-states led by Florence</note>. This was when Bologna and the March [of Ancona] rebelled; nearly all the Church's lands made a league with the Florentines at the time they raised the standards that they and the Bolognese still use today, featuring these letters: LIBERTY <note>original: "LIBERTAS"</note>. Furthermore, the ten citizens who were in the magistracy <note><term>balia</term>: a temporary committee in Florentine government granted extraordinary powers during emergencies</note> at that time in Florence placed those arms over the gates for their descendants. These people of limited vision want our poet to have intended this for Master Cino here as well, but this only comes from the sentiment of the twenty-third sonnet preceding the one where he spoke of Master Cino. Therefore, just as in that place I did not follow what others claimed, but only the truth, so also now it seems to me that Master Francesco [Petrarch] directs these words not to Master Cino (of whom he will speak below), but to himself. He is saying that Madonna Laura—whom he mentioned in the previous sonnet and whom you, Petrarch, loved so much—has departed without being loved by us any longer; that is, she has left our human life. And according to what my judgment hopes, she has gone to heaven; this is proven by her manner of dying, which was neither frantic nor furious, but entirely sweet and gentle. And because she alone made you feel both sad and happy—as if she locked and unlocked your heart with two keys—now that she is dead, you must recover these keys yourself. That is, you must pull yourself out of such irrational passions, as it is time to do so given your age. You should do this as well as follow her footsteps by living with great self-control and virtue, leaving behind every earthly weight. I do not mean by killing the body, but by killing its passions, which he clarifies by saying: Since the passion of love has been laid down through her death (which was the heaviest burden you carried), you can now easily clear away the other passions to which you are not so naturally inclined. By doing this, you will be able to ascend to virtue—as if ascending to heaven—like a pilgrim climbing a difficult mountain. You must do this all the more because all created things must die in a short time, and so you must approach the pass of death in a way that your soul is light and free from worldly sins.

<margin>Francesco D.</margin> ¶ WEEP, ladies. In the present 72nd sonnet, Petrarch bitterly laments the death of Master Cino da Pistoia, who was mentioned in the preceding sonnet. Then, finally, he vituperates the Pistoiese who have lost such a citizen, despite the fact that through their warring factions—which for a long time existed between the Whites and Blacks, just as now between the Panciatichi and the Cancellieri <note>Refers to the violent political factions in Pistoia; the Whites and Blacks were 13th/14th-century factions, while the others were contemporary to the commentator</note>—they had made Master Cino an exile, and he lived with pleasure among those who ruled in Florence. <meta>This page continues the physiological and psychological analysis of love's effects on the body, specifically regarding paleness and blushing, as a transition into Sonnet 75. It focuses on the internal struggle between the poet's hidden thoughts and his inability to express them fully in verse.</meta>

...the bottom of the heart, however much others may place such a faculty in the brain; every other image that was previously in that place is pushed out, since the imaginative faculty and power is entirely directed toward the compression of the new image. Thus, the faculties of the soul—especially the sensitive and the heat-producing faculties—depart, so that the blood from the surface of the body retreats to the heart where the vital spirits reside. This leaves the limbs almost dormant, immobile, and cold because of the ceasing of the heat from that departed blood. But then, as the imaginative faculty gradually considers the presented image, it begins to understand that the object is not as it first appeared. Having left the first type of passion, which was like a fear of some pain, it turns to the second type of passion, which is proper **shame**: that is, the fear of disgrace, meaning to be called a "bad nuisance." This causes the blood—which had gone to reinforce the heart—to leave it once more and run back to the surface of the body, and especially to the face, as if to cover the external evil of infamy with its redness. Seeing this, it seems like a miracle, and thus it takes revenge for its past exile; for while it had gone to the heart, it had induced such paleness. For the stated reason, it shows that in both faces—his and hers—there appeared a pale color like death, because the vigor of the blood that previously showed them to be crimson was no longer in any part of them, nor in the extremities of the body, adapting what has been said to the two of them. He says that for this natural reason, he remembered the day he saw two lovers—that is, himself and Madam Laura—transformed into the aforementioned color: that is, from paleness, both becoming together what he alone is usually seen to be, namely pale, even though he has also stated the cause for the redness.

<margin>Antonio G.</margin>
¶ **When it reaches through the eyes to the depths of the heart**: the author, Master Francesco <note>Messere Francesco Petrarca.</note>, says that every time he remembers his lady and sees her, he becomes deathly pale; and seeing that color, his lady becomes similar. Thus, from the first miracle, the second is born, as the poet says, writing on this subject as Juvenal does: *One grape having been seen takes its livid color from the other.* <note>original Latin: "Unaque conspecta livorem ducit ab una." A reference to Juvenal's Satires (2.81), suggesting that one person "catches" a look or state from another, like a diseased grape affecting its neighbor.</note>

<margin>Francesco</margin>
¶ **If only I could.** That mental concepts are much fiercer than the words with which they can be expressed is clearly shown by our poet in the present 75th sonnet. There, directing his graceful speech toward the longing and most beautiful eyes of Madam Laura, he laments that he cannot encompass his thoughts in verse as well as he encloses them in his heart. He says that if he could do so, he would move every soul to compassion, however cruel it might be. He proves this to be true through the eyes of Madam Laura, to whom he says he is entirely manifest—both regarding the outward endurance of the body and the passion of the heart—no differently than if he were naked. He has been wounded by those eyes in such a way that no defense was of use to him, so they must clearly know this to be most true, even though he does not complain much with cries and tears...

## SONNET LXXVI.

**I** am by now so overcome by waiting,
And by the long war of these sighs;
That I hold hope and desires in hatred,
And every snare by which my heart is bound.
But the beautiful, graceful face, which **painted**
I carry in my breast, and see wherever I gaze,
Forces me back, so that into my first cruel **martyrs**
I am pushed again, quite against my will.
I erred then, when the ancient path
Of liberty was cut off and taken from me:
For one follows poorly what pleases the eyes.
Then the soul ran toward its own harm, free and loose;
Now, at the whim of another, it is forced to go—
That soul, which sinned only once.

<margin>Francesco H.</margin>
¶ **I am**. Few things in this life seem more bothersome to me than waiting. Our poet, wishing to show this in this 76th sonnet, says that he has waited so long to be able to fulfill his love for **Madonna Laura**—as he has always hoped and desired—that he is now exhausted. Thus, he hates hope and all such desires, and even every amorous bond by which his heart might be tied. Nevertheless, he says he is forced by the beautiful face of **Madonna Laura**, whose grace he always carries painted in his thoughts within his breast; and that face seems to repeat itself in his fantasy before his eyes wherever he looks. This has forcefully constrained him and pushed him back into those pitiless passions by which he was first tormented. He adds that the cause of all his misfortune was not having resisted the first assaults of love. Because of this, he allowed the <term>ancient path of liberty</term><note>The state of the soul before falling in love, governed by reason rather than passion.</note> to be cut off and taken from him. If he had not followed the pleasure of his eyes with his heart, he would not now be so tormented. From this it follows that where previously his soul was free from every bond of love, it now wants to fall in love and refuses to obey the <term>rational part</term><note>In Renaissance psychology, the part of the soul capable of logic and moral choice.</note>, obeying instead that part which is without reason. Therefore, because it sinned at the beginning, it is forced to follow the <term>sensitive appetite</term><note>The part of the soul that responds to physical senses and desires without the mediation of reason.</note> whether it wants to or not.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ **I am by**. **Messer Francesco** <note>Petrarch</note> shows how through long suffering his desire often becomes hateful to him; but the eyes of **Madonna Laura** constrain him to follow the enterprises of love if he saw her at the <term>ninth hour</term><note>Traditional time for the office of Nones, roughly 3:00 PM; often significant in Petrarch’s encounters with Laura.</note>, because at that hour the sun struck that part of her window.

## SONNET LXXVII.

Ah, beautiful liberty, how you have shown me,
By departing from me, what
My state was, when the first arrow
Made the wound from which I shall never recover.
My eyes then became so enamored of their own woes
That the bridle of reason is of no use there;
For they loathe every mortal work:
Alas, thus I accustomed them from the start.
Nor am I permitted to listen to anyone who does not speak
Of my death; for with her name alone
I go filling the air, which sounds so sweet.
Love spurs me toward no other place;
Nor do my feet take any other path; nor my hands,
As if any other person could be praised in my papers.

<margin>Francesco I.</margin>
¶ **Ah, beautiful**. The 77th sonnet declares what we feel every day through experience: that man never knows his own tranquil state and how great his liberty is until he lacks it. Before Petrarch was bound by the heavy and intolerable bond and chain of love, he did not know his own well-being or his rest. But now that he has been turned from a free man into a servant, lying under infinite torments, sighs, and anguishes, he remembers and grieves for his past rest. He directs his gaze toward his lost liberty, rightly calling it "beautiful," and notes that now, by its departure, he clearly recognizes what his past state was when he was wounded by the first arrow of an incurable wound. This blow was all the worse because his eyes took pleasure in their own harm and woes...

¶ SINCE YOU. The present 79th sonnet was written as a response by Petrarch to Messer Giovanni Boccaccio at the time when the latter was fiercely enamored of that lady against whom he finally wrote the *Corbaccio* <note>The *Corbaccio* was a bitter satirical work Boccaccio wrote later in life after being rejected by a widow</note>. Just as the sow teaches her piglets to eat in a disciplined manner while she herself keeps her snout and feet together inside the basin; so he, being "rotten with love," comforts Boccaccio so that he does not attend to such vanity, but only to virtue, through which man becomes happy. He says that since they both have many times seen through experience that all their amorous hope is fallacious and without effect, he must now raise his heart to a state of greater happiness following the Divine Good, which always delights more, considering that worldly life is like a meadow...

<margin>Francesco M.</margin>
**S**ince you and I have many times proven
How our hoping turns out to be fallacious;
Toward that highest Good, which never displeases,
Lift up your heart to a happier state.
**T**his earthly life is almost like a meadow,
Where the serpent lies among the flowers and the grass;
And if any of its sights please the eyes,
It is to leave the soul more ensnared.
**Y**ou therefore, if you seek to have a mind
Ever quiet before your final day;
Follow the few, and not the common people.
**W**ell may it be said to me: "Brother, you go
Showing others the way, where often
You were lost; and now more so than ever."

...which, although it appears green and flowery and full of various delights, has nonetheless hidden within it the serpent—the continual ambusher and enemy of human nature. Its sight, though it appears beautiful, is a false appearance intended to ensnare <term>inueschare</term> <note>Literally to catch with "birdlime," a sticky substance used to trap birds</note> and take our soul through wrongdoing. Therefore he comforts Boccaccio, and insofar as he wishes to have some rest and peace before he dies, he must now leave the customs of the stupid commoners <note>vulgo stolido</note> who estimate nothing else to be good except that which the appetite and unbridled sensuality are accustomed to delight in. And therefore he must follow the virtuous and the sane, whose number is fewer than that of the phoenixes. And such comfort was needed no less for himself than for Boccaccio; or, recognizing his own failing, he reproaches himself, in that he, wishing to show the way of good living to others—no differently than if he had lost it himself—does not choose it for himself.

**THAT** window. It is the habit of lovers to note and keep in their memory every act and sign of the beloved. Our poet clearly demonstrates this in this 80th sonnet, where, remembering the places and the house of Lady Laura where she used to sit, together with her manners and acts, he narrates the time of spring and Good Friday <note>Petrarch famously first saw Laura on Good Friday, April 6, 1327, in the Church of Saint Clare in Avignon</note> when he first saw her and fell in love with her. He mentions that window of Lady Laura’s house where, as she sat on one side, one of her eyes was seen, shining like the sun when it pleases her in the morning hour, and the other like the sun at the ninth hour <note>original: "nona"; the canonical hour of prayer, approximately 3:00 PM</note>. He describes how she sat now to my right and now to my left, perhaps according to how the summer sun warmed first one part and then another. And also that window where she used to sit because of the sun in that season, which offers its rays in the winter time when the days are short and the north wind <note>original: "tramontana"</note> strikes and beats the air, echoing with such passion. I let all these windows and places be and do not speak of them, together with that other window and place where my lady and beloved used to sit for a long time around the third hour <note>original: "terza"; approximately 9:00 AM</note>, all pensive: which is a sign in a woman of an idle mind and one inclined to create rumors, provided she could do so cautiously and without witnesses. And therefore, thinking, he reasons with himself how he might lead his soul in the darkness. I leave, then, these places along with all the others covered by the shadows and touched by the feet of her beautiful person. But certainly that thing which easily moves my eyes to weeping is Good Friday in the time of spring: where Love, like a hunter in a fierce pass, reached me, so that I could not escape. This cause refreshes my ancient wounds every year on that day; and similarly her face and her words, fixed deep in the center of my heart.

**THAT** window where the one sun is seen. Messer Francesco makes manifest what the things are that make him weep when remembering. He says first that there is a stone upon which Lady Laura, in summer, used to sit in the wind, which was above a window made in the manner of a door; therefore he says that above that window a sun sat—that is, his Lady Laura—in the wind because of the heat, alongside the other sun.

**ALAS, I WELL KNOW.** That the disease of love is dangerous can be understood no less in this 81st sonnet than in many others. In its meaning, Petrarch demonstrates that although he knew well that he had to die, and that no remedy can be given to death to keep it from coming with the greatest speed, he does not for all that turn away from amorous practices, even though they were without effect. Thus, with appetite and reason fighting together, in the end reason will remain the victor; and this proceeded not so much from his good disposition...

> The years carry them away; and I receive no deception,
> But a force much greater than magical arts
> The will and reason have fought

A velocity similar to a most rapid current abandons us: where time seems to promise us a very long life, it suddenly deceives us: for there is little reward for our much languishing. And though the day of death already echoed in his heart, he nonetheless did not cease, despite all these considerations, to be so stimulated by amorous passion that he did not stop weeping and shedding tears in his usual way. And amplifying what he had said regarding the knowledge of his very brief life, he says it is well known to him how the days, moments, times, and hours carry away the years of our life. And yet, the <term>sensitive appetite</term> <note>the part of the soul driven by desires and senses</note> and the <term>rational part</term> of the soul do not cease to fight together with a force greater than any magical art could loosen; and this such contention has already lasted fourteen years from the day he first fell in love with Lady Laura. Nevertheless, he says he hopes that in the end, reason will conquer the magical art: which proceeded from medicine and began at the time of **Zoroaster**, the first inventor of such falsehood. Plutarch says Zoroaster lived five thousand years before the Trojan War and was King of the <term>Bactrians</term> <note>an ancient civilization in Central Asia</note> and a great philosopher; against whom Ninus fought and killed him. According to our faith, he could not be so ancient, as Ninus fought him in the year three thousand one hundred and ninety-one from the beginning of the world.

**CAESAR** then. The present 82nd sonnet was written by Petrarch during the time he was in Padua with the Lord Messer Francesco da Carrara the Elder, who was a most prudent lord and a great lover of learned and excellent men. It having reached his ears that the brother of Petrarch—who was a monk and to whom Petrarch had written his *Bucolicum Carmen* <note>a series of Latin pastoral poems</note>—had recently died, the Lord went in person to Petrarch's room to visit him and also to console him, as is customary in such cases. Having entered the house as he usually did, he went toward Petrarch’s study; approaching it, he found it closed, and heard that Messer Francesco was playing a **lute** and singing a love song in a low voice. Hearing this, that Lord immediately turned back without saying anything, thinking to himself that Petrarch

> Caesar, after the traitor of Egypt
> Made him the gift of the honored head,
> Hiding his manifest joy,
> Wept through his eyes, as it is written;
> And Hannibal, when at his afflicted empire
> He saw fortune become so troublesome,
> Laughed among the tearful and sad people
> To vent his bitter spite.
> And so it happens, that every soul
> Covers its passion under a contrary cloak,
> With a look now clear, now dark;
> Therefore if sometimes I laugh, or sing;
> I do it, because I have no other
> Way to hide my anguished weeping.

must have heard nothing of the death of his said brother. Nor did he wish to be the messenger of such bad news. After his departure, Petrarch learned from those of his household the manner in which the Lord had behaved; thinking on this, after he clearly understood the whole fact, he offered him this sonnet without delay. In it, he demonstrates by the example of two most singular men, highly regarded in the judgment of that Lord—who were **Caesar** and **Hannibal**—that wise men must hide their passions and often make a demonstration of the total contrary; also out of respect...
