<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s poetry, specifically Sonnet 102, where the poet compares his own behavior to that of Julius Caesar and Hannibal. The previous page established the context of hiding one’s true emotions behind a false exterior.</meta>

...with respect to those standing around, saying that when the honorable head of **Gnaeus Pompey**, his son-in-law, was sent to **Caesar** as a gift by the traitor **Ptolemy**, King of Egypt, although Caesar secretly in his heart felt a singular pleasure that his enemy was dead, he nonetheless wept for him. And similarly, by contrast, **Hannibal**, captain of the Carthaginians, seeing that Fortune—which until 그날 had almost always been prosperous and favorable against the Romans—was becoming troublesome and unpleasant for the Carthaginian empire, found himself much troubled and afflicted by **Publius Cornelius Scipio** (who was later surnamed **Africanus** <note>Scipio was given this title after his victory over Carthage in North Africa</note>). For that reason, he was forced to depart from Italy and from the enterprise of Rome—which was already half-subjugated—to return to the defense of his homeland. While all the rest of the army was in melancholy and in tears because of the bad and unfortunate news, he, as if nothing were wrong, began to laugh and show a cheerful face, although within his heart he felt the most bitter displeasure. 

With the testimony of these two examples, the author adds a universal custom observed among wise and prudent men: saying that in such a way, the mind of these people covers every passion by demonstrating the opposite emotion. This is no different than one who hides under a cloak, showing a cheerful face when they are often full of melancholy, and similarly showing melancholy when they have consolation and some singular pleasure in their heart. Finally, he concludes that the lord <note>referring to the subject of Petrarch’s poem</note>, being most prudent, should not feel any surprise at his playing and singing amidst the sad and bitter news of the death of his brother; because he did not know any other way he could hide his anguished weeping and bitterness of heart except by making an outward demonstration of the contrary: such as in laughing, playing, singing, and similar pleasures.

¶ **Gaius Julius Caesar**, the unique light and glory in every virtue and excellence of the <term>Latin name</term> <note>a reference to Roman identity and heritage</note>, has been, in my judgment, most wrongly slandered by Petrarch in this sonnet. Although Petrarch—as can be understood from his other works—did this not as a historian or philosopher, but as an orator or <term>sophist</term> <note>someone who uses clever but fallacious arguments</note>, not caring to tell the truth as long as he could say something useful to his cause for his own excuse. We commonly see that all the Greek and Latin historians, who were serious and learned, have wonderfully commended the most humane nature and infinite clemency of Caesar. He always strove, through letters and intermediaries, to be a true and good friend to Gnaeus Pompey, but he could achieve nothing. Such was the intolerable pride and impious envy of Pompey that he chose rather to lose and die as an enemy of Caesar—with the greatest destruction of the Roman Empire—than to live in peace and remain honorable. Had he wished to behave amicably with Caesar, he would have forgotten the kinship they shared, for he had been Caesar's son-in-law, putting aside the power he had gained and the increase of his status through such affinity. 

Because I certainly believe that by divine judgment—as an ungrateful, envious, and wicked man grieving over the insuperable virtue and exaltation of the illustrious Caesarian name—Pompey was first broken, defeated, and undone in **Thessaly** <note>referring to the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BCE</note> with his greatest shame and cowardice. And then in the sea and port of **Alexandria**, by the command of the young King Ptolemy (to whom he fled as to a most faithful friend because of benefits received), he was most cruelly killed and then decapitated. He received that same merit and reward from his "obligated" friend that he himself had intended in his heart to give to Gaius Julius Caesar, his most unworthy father-in-law. Caesar, having first heard of his death, grieved most bitterly, as one who cared for nothing but doing good and being in all things most humane and merciful in his dealings. And immediately afterward, when the severed head was sent to him as a "most welcome" gift, along with Pompey’s own ring as greater testimony of the deed, he became entirely afflicted in his face with the most abundant shedding of burning tears. 

That noble soul could never have feigned such a thing with any artifice if he had not felt an icy grief within his heart. Wherefore, with words and signs used as an express and true signifies of his most bitter displeasure, he caused the presented head to be <margin>Q</margin> buried with many and most precious spices and scents <margin>R</margin> according to the custom of the heathens to be burned.

After he took to the field with marvelous pleasure for everyone, seeking a reason for new contention and war with the Romans, he laid siege to Saguntum, a city in Spain very friendly to the Romans and their ally; he subjugated it by force in the ninth month. Then, having crossed the Pyrenees mountains and then the Alps—always crushing those who opposed him—he first defeated Publius Cornelius Scipio (father of the first Africanus) at the Ticinus; then he defeated Sempronius Longus at the Trebia. And then, having crossed the Apennine mountains amidst heavy rain and storms, in the underlying marshes—due to staying awake too long for four days and three nights without any rest—while riding upon an elephant, he became blind in one eye. Later, having come through Tuscany to the Lake of Perugia <note>original: "lago di perusia"; modern Lake Trasimene</note>, he defeated the Roman army by ambush and killed the consul Flaminius. This loss was the greatest that the Romans received from Hannibal, except for that of Cannae, which was the absolute greatest; for in the battle of Cannae, some say thirty thousand Romans died, others thirty-five thousand, others forty thousand, and as many again among the allies and friends of the Romans. And also the consul Paullus, a man of great valor, most prudent and noble captain, was killed there. And while he certainly could have taken the city of Rome, Hannibal did not know how to follow up on the victory. Instead, he went into Campania, and his untamed and very robust army became sluggish and effeminate through excessive pleasures. Later, having set up camp near the city of Rome at a distance of three miles, on the day that the city had prepared to fight, the violence of the rain and storm was so immeasurable that he was forced to retreat. <margin>The year/author</margin> Although he was most prudent, he was nevertheless deceived several times by Fabius Maximus, rebuffed by Valerius Flaccus, and driven away by Gracchus and Marcellus. Finally, while he still expected to obtain total victory and the ultimate extermination of the Romans, a most powerful command came to him from the Senate and the people of Carthage that without any delay, with his whole army and whatever other power he could muster, he should return to the aid of Carthage. For otherwise, it had been brought to such extremity by Publius Cornelius Scipio (who was later surnamed Africanus) that it was altogether necessary to surrender. When this formidable and sad news was heard by the army, all were tormented and afflicted by heartfelt grief with infinite tears and weeping. Therefore, Hannibal, seeing this, although he himself felt a greater heartache, nevertheless showed a joyful face and began to laugh. This proceeded from the cause noted in the exposition of the sonnet above. And for now, let what pertains to this present part suffice. Just noting one thing: that the magnificent lord, Messer Francesco da Carrara named above, is said to have taken such pleasure in this sonnet that on that same day, he sent to Petrarch a beautiful silver comfit-box <note>original: "cofetiēra"; a container for sweets or spices</note> with five hundred ducats inside.

¶ **CAESAR**, since the traitor... Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, being asked by some of his friends what it meant that, while being so burdened by the love of his lady Laura, he many times now laughs, now sings, almost as if this laughing or singing proceeded from joy or from distress of heart; to which he responds by giving them two examples. One of Caesar who, being the enemy of Pompey, defeated him; Pompey fled to Ptolemy, King of Egypt, and the king, to do something pleasing to Caesar, decapitated him and sent the head as a gift to Caesar. Seeing the head of Pompey, Caesar wept, he being conquered more by blood <note>referring to their family ties through Julia</note> than by hatred and enmity. Some hold the opinion that he was actually happy, but that his weeping was feigned, as the Poet says here for this purpose. Similarly, Hannibal, with Carthage conquered and destroyed, mocking the variability of Fortune, laughed among the disconsolate. Similarly, Messer Francesco says that just as Caesar wept, feigning happiness, and Hannibal laughed, not showing his pain, in the same way I, by singing and laughing, quench the pain that burns my heart.

Lord Master Pandolfo <note>Pandolfo II Malatesta (1325–1373), a condottiero and patron of Petrarch</note> is advised that he should pursue the victory he obtained against the Orsini <note>A powerful Roman noble family; their name means "little bears," which often prompted animal-themed puns in poetry</note> in the month of May, so that it does not happen to him as it did to Hannibal. We speak of Hannibal in the next sonnet because, by not knowing how to follow his victorious fortune against the Romans, he was later forced by changing luck to return to Africa to help his homeland. Once he returned there, he was defeated by Scipio, leading to the oppression of his debt-burdened homeland. Afterward, as an exile, he first fled to Antiochus <note>Antiochus III the Great of the Seleucid Empire</note> and then to Prusias <note>Prusias I of Bithynia</note>, where, to avoid being handed over to the Romans, he killed himself with the poison he kept under the gem of his ring. Therefore, so that a similar misfortune does not befall the aforementioned lord, he [Petrarch] encourages him not to let the Orsini rest, but to follow up the victory so they do not regroup and gain greater strength against him. By doing this, he says that even after death, for thousands of years, he shall have honor and fame for such an action.

> Who find in May a bitter pasture <note>A reference to the Orsini "bears" finding defeat instead of food</note>
> It gnaws within; and it hardens teeth and claws,
> To avenge its losses upon us.
> While the new grief, then, pierces the heart,
> Do not put away your honored sword,
> Rather follow it where it calls you—
> Your fortune, straight along the path,
> Which can give you, even after death,
> A thousand and more thousands of years of honor and fame in the world.

<margin>Antonio</margin> **HANNIBAL CONQUERED** but did not know how to use it afterward: This sonnet was sent by Master Francesco [Petrarch] to a member of the Colonna house <note>The Colonna were a prominent Roman family and bitter rivals of the Orsini</note>, a captain of men-at-arms who had broken the Orsini, his enemies. He encourages him to pursue their destruction since he held the first victory, and not to delay, because he could later be conquered himself. He uses the example of Hannibal, who did not know how to use his victory after defeating the Romans at the place called Cannae. Wherefore it was said to him: <term>That master of the horse [said]: "You know how to conquer, Hannibal, but you do not know how to use a victory" <note>original Latin: "Ille magister equitum. Vincere scis Hannibal sed victoria vti nescis." The quote is traditionally attributed to the Carthaginian general Maharbal</note></term>. Hannibal then withdrew to Capua and so corrupted his army with gluttony and luxury that later Carthage was conquered and destroyed.

<margin>Francesco T.</margin> **T**HE EXPECTED. Many times Petrarch had encouraged Lord Pandolfo Malatesta (who is mentioned in the preceding sonnet) that, since he possessed a great and noble mind, he should wish to adorn it with eloquence and learning. Therefore, that lord, ignited by a singular desire for such study, applied himself in such a way that he became most learned, so that he not only understood but even wrote quite elegantly. Wherefore, in this 84th sonnet, Petrarch, commending him for a beautiful translation, says that now the expected virtue of eloquence and learning—which was flowering when his Lordship fell in love with such study—is now producing its desired fruit, as he already understands well and also writes ornately, the effect he hoped for having followed. This, he says, is the reason why he will write in praise of his name something of great exaltation for him; and that this will be a much more beautiful and lasting image than that which is carved from marble and similar stones. And this he proves by the memory and fame of four most noble men: these were Caesar (of whom we spoke before), Claudius Marcellus, Lucius Aemilius Paullus, and Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus (of whom we have written above at another time), saying that the memory of such men and their glorious fame does not endure in the world because of statues made of either metal or marble.

### SONNET 84.

> The expected virtue, which was flowering in you,

> Something by which your name may rise in esteem;
> For in no place is a living person

> Or Paullus, or the African were made such
> By any anvil or by hammer?

> In the long run; but our study is that
> Which makes men immortal through fame.

¶ **Marcus Claudius Marcellus** was a spirited man of great daring. This man, fighting hand-to-hand with Viridomarus, captain of the Insubrian Gauls, defeated and killed him and offered his armor to Quirinus <note>This refers to the *spolia opima*, the highest honor a Roman general could earn by killing an enemy commander in single combat</note>. And when the senate, through calumny, denied him a triumph, by his own deliberation he triumphed on Mount Alban. He was consul five times and took part in a great many battles. He was the first to see the back of the victorious Hannibal <note>Meaning he was the first to force Hannibal to retreat</note>: by whom he was later attacked in an ambush and, while fighting fiercely, was killed. Hannibal had his body burned most honorably and with great magnificence.

<margin>X</margin>
¶ **Lucius Aemilius Paullus**, father of P. Cornelius Africanus the Younger and son of 그 Paullus who was killed at Cannae, in the first consulship that he obtained after three rejections, triumphed over the Ligurians. He demonstrated well through his actions what he had said before when he was elected prefect; for with worthy indignation, I dare say, he did not thank the Romans at all for electing him, because he did not have as much need for the captaincy as the Romans had for a captain. In his second consulship, he defeated and captured Perseus, King of Macedonia and son of King Philip, for whose misfortune he wept: and to honor him, he had him sit by his side—and nonetheless led him in the triumph. And having four sons, he had previously given one in adoption to the house of the Cornelii and the other to the house of the Metelli. Of the other two, one died in the very days before the triumph. Yet he did not show any sign of displeasure. Instead, he said that he thanked Fortune most highly: for if there were any envy or indignation against the Roman people, he wished it to be vented upon his own head instead. For this reason, he was granted by the Roman people and the senate the right to wear triumphal robes during the circensian games. This man, who had filled the Roman treasury with infinite wealth, died in such poverty that it was necessary to sell his possessions to pay the dowry for his wife.

# CANZONE 21, STANZA 1

**N**ever do I wish to sing again as I was used to:
For others did not understand me; whence I had shame,
And in a beautiful dwelling I found only trouble.
Endless sighing avails nothing.
Already snow falls all around the Alps:
And already it is near day; wherefore I am awake.
A sweet, honest gesture is a noble thing:
And in a loving lady it still pleases me,
That she walks proud and disdainful,
Not haughty and stubborn.
Love rules his empire without a sword.
Let him who has lost the way turn back:
He who has no lodging, let him rest on the grass:
He who has no gold, or loses it;
Let him quench his thirst with a fine glass.

<sig>Z</sig>

->Sloth <note>The original "suria" likely refers to *lussuria* (lust) or *accidia* (sloth/apathy)</note> usually takes hold in the hearts of those who care for nothing except their throat and their belly. Because of this, the Pope no longer looked upon Petrarch with a kind eye, nor did he speak to him with the familiar and joyful speech he was accustomed to. Instead, he made it quite clear that Petrarch could expect nothing from him unless he was willing to go along with his unbridled pleasures. This situation was the reason why Petrarch composed this lovely and rare song <note>This refers to Canzone 105, "Mai non vo' più cantar com'io solea"</note>. He clearly demonstrated to the Pope how little he valued his disdain, signaling that he would depart from the court, as he did shortly thereafter.<-

<margin>Z</margin>
When he realized for certain that the wicked Pope had achieved his dishonest vice through the mediation of that vile brother of his, who finally became a monk: but descending to the brief explanation of this song, stanza by stanza. Beginning from the first, our poet, with many and varied proverbs, demonstrates the unstable variety of worldly things by way of insinuation in his opening; he does this so that only the Pope, understanding his meaning, might be discouraged from his lustful enterprise. And although he appears to speak of matters of love, this is not his primary intention. Rather, it is only what I first narrated: saying that he no longer wishes to sing in the usual manner, but in such a way that he wants the Pope to understand him. For until then, the Pope's mind had not grasped the gravity of the situation. Because of this, Petrarch felt scorned when the Pope, assuming he had found "soft ground" <note>An idiomatic way of saying the Pope thought Petrarch was an easy target or a pushover</note>, tried to tempt him regarding his sister. Petrarch felt this as a shameful insult, being disgraced that the Pope should consider him such a "pig" as to believe he would consent to such vileness. He adds that every immoderate passion is displeasing and becomes tiresome, just as the pleasure of too much rest does; conversely, continual melancholy is of no use. Wherefore, as he was already beginning to turn grey on every side—just as the Alps become white with snow—and having been too idle and doing nothing, like one who sleeps all night, he finally wakes up near morning. Just as he noticed the hidden traps of the Pope, he must no longer delay in such a manner, but must make a decision regarding his status. And if it is not fitting for any woman to be of only one manner—not only pleasant, but also honest—how much more is this required in a Pope? Furthermore, it usually delights the observer when a woman's gait does not seem proud and bizarre—like the beauty of Poggio Bambilione <note>Likely an archaic or local reference to a specific figure known for a haughty walk</note>—but rather somewhat high-minded due to her virtue and disdainful toward those who gaze at her lecherously. How much more would this be pleasing in the Supreme Pontiff? For the gait of that Pope was shown to be sometimes like a harlot and sometimes like an arrogant, bizarre man. And if you, **Mr. Donkey** <note>original: "Messer Lasino," a mocking nickname Petrarch uses for his target</note>, are in love, I remind you that love requires pleasance, not force; for a thing done by force is not worth a husk <note>A common proverb meaning something is worthless</note>. Therefore, if you have lost the path of honesty, turn back and turn away from vice. Or, like one who finds no inn on the road at night and rests upon the grass, if you must attend to amorous things and cannot have the woman you desire, take the one you can. Just as one who has no cup drinks from glass, if you cannot have the one you desire, take others that you can have. In such a way, with charming and most learned sayings and new proverbs, our Petrarch has partly reprimanded the Supreme Pontiff, partly signaled his intention to him, and partly instructed him on what he ought to do, should he still wish to pursue love.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
**I DO NOT wish to sing as I used to.** <note>original: "CMAI Non vo piu cantar come io solea," the opening line of Canzone 105</note> This song is obscure both in style and in meaning, and the mind of the author is poorly understood. However, from what can be gathered, it seems that Cardinal Colonna had sought to fall in love with My Lady Laura, seeing her so highly exalted by Master Francesco [Petrarch]. Whereupon she, having been advised by mediators, no longer wished to see Master Francesco, and indeed denied everything. Because of this, Master Francesco, having learned of the matter through secret ways, wished to write such a song so that it would not be publicly understood; for he was careful not to speak ill of such a great lord, especially since he had been his friend. Yet he continually bites at him regarding his purpose. Through many sayings, it is understood that this was his intention. *I gave it to St. Peter's guard:* that is, to his lieutenant, and this was the said Cardinal in the place of the Pontiff. *I hear that Phaeton fell into the Po and died.* <note>Phaeton was the son of Helios who lost control of the sun's chariot and was struck down by Jupiter</note> Phaeton was he who, not knowing how to guide the chariot of the sun, was struck by Jupiter's lightning and fell into the Po, and there he drowned. *He loosed the soul from the heart and shook it.* Master Francesco demonstrates that upon hearing such news of his lady being taken from him, he lifted himself entirely out of that love and put such amorous troubles behind him.

# STANZA II.

I gave them into the keeping of Saint Peter; but now no more, no:
Let him who can understand me; for I understand myself.
A heavy burden and a bad debt it is to maintain it.
As much as I can, I un-stone myself; <note>The original Italian "mi spetro" is a pun on the poet’s name, Petrarca, meaning he is "removing the stone" from his heart or freeing himself from his stony prison.</note> and I remain alone.
I hear of Phaethon, who fell into the Po and died:
And already the blackbird has crossed the river: <note>The "blackbird crossing the river" is an Italian idiom for escaping a trap or surviving a difficult period.</note>
Ah, come and see it now: I do not wish to:
A rock in the middle of the waves is no yoke,
Nor is birdlime <note>A sticky substance smeared on branches to catch small birds; here a metaphor for the traps of the court.</note> among the leaves: I grieve enough,
When an excessive pride
Hides many virtues in a beautiful woman.
There is one who answers the one who does not call:
Another, when begged, vanishes and flees.
Another melts at the ice:
Another desires his own death day and night.

<margin>A</margin>
**I GAVE into keeping:** In this second stanza, by narrating more clearly, the poet stings the Pope, whom he understands under the name of Saint Peter. He says he had given his sister <note>Petrarch’s sister, Selvaggia, was the subject of rumors involving the Pope; the commentator interprets the poem's "keeping" as Petrarch entrusting her or his honor to the Papacy.</note> into his "keeping," just as Christ entrusted the Church to Saint Peter. This was while the Pope was sending Petrarch as an ambassador to the King of France, the King of England, and similar places. But now he says he no longer wishes to grant him such guardianship, insulting the authority of this Pope who, by merely saying "let it be done" (*fiat*), thinks no one can contradict him. Therefore, Petrarch voluntarily removes himself from such subjection to return to a solitary life. He signifies which place he wishes to go by mentioning the Po river, as he later went to live in Milan with the magnanimous Lord Galeazzo Visconti. He intends to act like Phaethon of Egypt, who left the fires of Egypt and came to stay in Lombardy (whose story is found at length in Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*), showing by this his desire to spend his life in Lombardy—even though he eventually died in Padua. Then, so as not to be understood by others, he says the blackbird has passed the snare or the net; we should understand this to mean he will no longer be trapped by the Pope. He compares his own steadfastness to a rock that, although struck by waves from this side and that, does not move from its place. And just as birdlime is placed in the branches of trees to catch birds, so too through the Pope's flatteries and false honors many deceptions will come. And just as it is a defect in a woman to be proud and haughty, so too is the vice of lust and frivolity a defect in a Pope. He then adds other effects, such as answering those who do not call and not answering those who beg; others grow warm where they should be cold, and others continually seek their own death. These equal vices were either in that Pope or in those who surrounded him.

# STANZA III.

By proverb, "love the one who loves you" is an ancient saying.
I know well what I say: now let it go.
For it is fitting that one learns at his own expense:
A humble woman makes a sweet friend miserable.
One poorly knows the fig; <note>A metaphor for something that looks good on the outside but is rotten or empty inside.</note> to me it still seems
Wise not to begin too-lofty enterprises:
And in every country, there is a good place to stay.
Infinite hope kills others:
And I too was once in the dance.
That little which remains to me,
There will be someone who does not reject it, if I go to give it to him.
I trust in Him who rules the world,
And who shelters His followers in the woods;
That with a merciful staff
He may lead me now to pasture among His flocks.

<margin>B</margin>
¶ **Proverb:** Continuing in this third stanza, he clearly says that he perceived the Pope did not love him. Therefore, following the proverb, he shows that he will do the same, saying he has learned at his own expense. He explains that a man cannot be judged by appearances, just as one might see a woman appearing melancholy and believe she is humble, or judge a friend by his words or a "sweet" appearance when his heart is bitter. This is like the fig, which looks good on the outside but inside is worth nothing. He clearly adds that he does not care for a high status in the Papal court and will change his purpose, saying that since he sees himself deluded by too much hope, he will give himself to another lord. He believes God will not fail him even if the Pope fails him, even if he must live in the woods like a hermit.

### STANZA VI.

I weep and I laugh at my past losses,
Because I trust much in what I hear.
I enjoy the present, and I expect better:
And I go counting the years, and I am silent, and I cry out
And I nestle in a beautiful branch, and in such a way,
That I thank and praise the great refusal,
Which has finally conquered the hardened heart,
And has painted in my soul: I would have been heard,
And pointed it out with a finger, and has extinguished it.
I have been pushed so far forward,
That you yourself would not have been so bold.
Someone has wounded my side, and someone heals it,
Because of whom I write more in my heart than on paper
The one who makes me dead and alive;
Who in one moment freezes me, and warms me.

<margin>B</margin>
*¶ AT MY PAST. In this stanza, he shows more clearly to the Pope that he should never hope to achieve his intention, advising him that no pain could have been greater than to tempt him with such "merchandise." He says first that he sees clearly he has lost his time following such an ungrateful lord. And he grieves for these losses out of respect for the Pope, but laughs at himself for having so foolishly placed his hope in a man so ungrateful and lacking in recognition. He trusted in the Pope's false promises, but now he passes the time hoping for better elsewhere: now counting the wasted years, now silent in thought, now even crying out: "O foolish Francesco, what are you doing waiting for the Messiah?" <note>A proverbial expression meaning to wait for something that will never happen.</note> And so he lives in hope that is always like a green branch; therefore, he says he no longer cares about the "hat" <note>The Cardinal's hat.</note> which he saw was refused and denied to him by the Pope, insofar as he would not consent to give up his sister <note>original: "firocchia," a dialect term for sister. The commentator alleges the Pope offered a cardinalate in exchange for Petrarch's sister.</note>. He had always held this hope and affection; seeing that such a denial has finally led him to hope for it no more, he shows he is free from such anxiety. He has it as if painted in his soul that "I would have been heard by the Pope if I had been willing to consent," so that the choice to be a Cardinal rested with me. Therefore, I do not care, nor do I wish to be pointed at with a finger of infamy as a pimp for my sister, and be dead to my kin for such a reputation. And because I have said so much already, I will tell you further, lecherous Pope: watch that you do not have the boldness to seek out my sister. You have wounded my heart with a pain similar to a wound in the side that no one can ever heal, showing that he will never forget such a shame, any more than if it were written in his heart.*

### STANZA VII. AND LAST.

A new little angel, <note>Petrarch refers to his poem or a lady as a "nova angeletta."</note> clever on her wings,
Descended from heaven onto the fresh riverbank
There where I was passing alone by my destiny:
When she saw me without a companion and without an escort,
A snare, which she wove of silk,
She stretched across the grass, where the path is green:
Then I was caught: and it did not displease me afterward,
So sweet a light issued from her eyes.

<margin>F</margin>
*¶ A NEW little angel. Although the first sentence and the last stanza are put together with this song, it is not so much the substance of it as it is in praise of its elegance. He calls it a "little angel" not only because it is beautiful and angelic, but because it is the messenger of his mind and will to the High Pontiff; for "angel" in Greek means "messenger" in Latin <note>original: "nuncio." The commentator explains the etymology of the word angel (aggelos).</note>. And he says this song is entirely nimble and clever and awake, like a thing descended from heaven. Therefore, he is enamored with it just as if he were caught by a gentle and tenacious snare of silk among the green and pleasant grass, and it pleases him for the sweet beauty that comes out of this song, no differently than a most grateful light from eyes.*

<margin>Anto.</margin>
*¶ A NEW little angel, more clever than the others. In this little ballad <term>ballatina: a short poem intended to be set to music</term> Master Francesco shows how he returned to loving his lady, and feigns a little angel who set a snare for him, seeing him without escort and without company.*

<margin>Francesco</margin> **I** DO NOT see. The present sonnet .85. was composed by Petrarch in that same year that, shortly thereafter, Lady Laura passed from this life, which was the fifteenth year starting from the beginning when Master Francesco fell in love. He commends, as he has often done, the miraculous beauty of the lovely eyes of that lady, showing that through the war they wage against him, his heart is destroyed without any intermission of his troubles; and that now he is more in love with them than ever, in such a way that their great splendor dazzles his sight. <margin>H</margin> ¶ FORTUNATE. The lover notes every thing and every act in the beloved with a pleasant narration. The present .86. sonnet demonstrates this, in which Petrarch describes a noble act and manner that Lady Laura once performed in turning from the straight road of Avignon into another small street or alley on the left. In doing this, it seemed she gave him a side-long glance with a sweet look toward Petrarch; for this reason, Master Francesco writes the present sonnet to a pleasant, intimate, and amorous friend of his who saw what is described here while he was present. He therefore calls that place happy which was trodden by the feet of Lady Laura, who was his love, praising her eyes as the serene air: saying that it pleased him so much that he will always have it in memory and within his heart

### SONNET 86.

**F**ortunate more than any other ground,
Where I once saw Love plant his feet
Turning toward me those holy lights <note>meaning her eyes</note>,
Which make the air serene all around them.
**A** solid image of diamond would sooner
Waste away through time,
Than that sweet act should not remain before me,
Of which my memory and heart are so full.
**N**or will I see you <note>the ground where she walked</note> so many times,

**B**ut if love does not sleep in a courageous heart,
Pray, my Senuccio <note>Senuccio del Bene (c. 1275–1349), a Florentine poet and close friend of Petrarch.</note>, when you see him,
For some small tear, or a sigh.

as if she were in his presence. And he adds that whenever he passes that ground, he will bow down to see if the traces of that beautiful foot were still there from when Lady Laura turned at the bend of the road into the alley on the left. Directing his speech to the sonnet, he commands it to pray to his fellow lover Senuccio that, out of friendship and contemplation, he too might weep a little and let out a sigh.

### SONNET 87.

<margin>
Before.
¶ ALAS, how many times Master Francesco returns to the subject of the aforementioned glance and says that every hour that love enters his mind, he returns to that aforementioned place, always in that same air—that is, where she gave him that glance.

> Alas, how many times love assails me;
> Which between the night and the day are more than a thousand;
> I return where I saw the sparks burn,
> Which make the fire of my heart immortal,
> There I find peace: and I am led to such a state;
> That at noon, at vespers, at dawn: and behind my back
> I find them in my thoughts so tranquil;
> That of nothing else do I remember or care.

> Moves with the sound of clever words,
> To make a sweet serenity wherever it breathes;
> Almost like a noble spirit from paradise
> Always in that air it seems to comfort me;
> So that my weary heart breathes nowhere else.

<margin>
¶ ALAS, how many times. Through these few thoughts it is shown in this 87th sonnet that our amorous poet was accustomed to go very often where he might see Lady Laura. Wherefore, one day, having gazed at her to his heart's content and returned to his house, he immediately composed this sonnet where he says with wonder—and as one who is weary—that he is many times assailed in his heart by the love of that lady: adding that he had just then returned from that place where he had seen her, whose eyes were like sparks: and he does so in a way that they seem to burn. This also sets his heart on fire with immortal love, showing that every hour of night and day he rests in the love of his amorous imagination within those eyes, in such a way that he remembers nothing else. Nor does he take any other pleasure, nor can he keep himself from naming her, speaking of the pleasant and subtle little wind called the breeze <note>Again, the poet plays on "aura" (breeze) and "Laura".</note> moving from her clearest face with the sound of her sweet speech, like a noble and celestial spirit. And this, to bring about a sweet serenity in whatever place it usually breathes, seems always to comfort his heart in that district and neighborhood where she lived when he heard her speak; wherefore in no other place does it seem possible for his troubled heart to sigh except there.
</margin>

### SONNET 88.

<margin>
¶ PURSUING ME. If everything else were forgotten, Petrarch shows through the present 88th sonnet that the eyes of Lady Laura are fixed in his heart because of their infinite beauty. First, he says that he could never forget such a gracious glance. Comparing Lady Laura, then, to the sun because of the beauty of her most splendid eyes, he says that while he was in that lady's neighborhood (as was his habit) only to see her with his amorous and accustomed thoughts—similar to someone who expects the war of such passion—he turned toward the house of that lady and seemed to see, like a shadow, the air interposed between himself and her.
</margin>

> Love pursuing me to the usual place
> Hemmed in like a man awaiting war
> Who provides for himself and closes his ranks,
> I stood armed with my ancient thoughts:
> I turned, and saw a shadow, which from the side
> The sun printed, and I recognized on the ground;
> Her, who, if my judgment does not err,
> Was more worthy of an immortal state.
> I said within my heart, why do you fear?
> But that thought had not yet entered within,
> When the rays, in which I melt, were present.

...with her eyes shining like a sun. Because of this, he clearly understood that Lady Laura was worthy of divinity and an immortal state. And at this first sight—something supernatural and divine—he says he was entirely terrified, but then he returned to himself like a man illuminated by the rays that were already present from her eyes. This was not unlike being struck by the infinite light of a lightning bolt <note>original: "baleno"</note> when it thunders at that very same moment; he was illuminated by such light and at the same time greeted with a marvelous sweetness.

> Just as the thunder sounds with the flash:
> So was I struck by those beautiful, shining eyes,
> And joined at once by a sweet greeting.

<margin>Antonio</margin> ¶ Following Love's lead, Master Francesco had stopped at a corner near the house of his lady, and she, coming from elsewhere, came upon him from behind while the sun shone upon her shoulders. Master Francesco, seeing her shadow <note>original: "stampa," referring to her footprint or silhouette on the ground</note> on the earth, recognized it and was nearly stunned; as she reached him, she offered her greeting.

<margin>Francesco L</margin> ¶ THE lady. The present 89th sonnet—as well as the one preceding it, as can be understood by the subject matter—was composed by our poet in the early days of his amorous thoughts, when perhaps Lady Laura had not yet noticed that Petrarch was acting in earnest. It contains almost the same sentiment as the aforementioned sonnet. For he says, in short, that while he was sitting where Lady Laura was accustomed to pass, suspended in thought and reflecting on his amorous desires, the beloved Lady Laura passed before him. Because of this, he stood up straight to honor her; while he made an honored and beautiful bow with his head, his face became entirely pale from the sudden blow of love. And the noble and courteous Lady Laura, with a joyful and kind expression, turned toward Petrarch and greeted him with such sweetness that it would have humbled any angry or furious person even in their greatest lightning-strike of rage, and would have raised the dead. Therefore, after she had passed, Petrarch—who had lost himself because of that noble and almost divine gaze and that celestial and angelic speech—recovered and woke from his dulled senses. Examining in his heart that lightning-like glance together with the gracious greeting, he says he took such pleasure from it that from that day forward, he never felt any more sorrow.

<margin>Antonio</margin> ¶ She is very gracious, yet now haughty and proud, appearing at times both harsh and pitiless, and at other times level-headed and pious. Now she acts with modesty, now with charm, now with domesticity and gentleness, or on the contrary, she is disdainful and fierce. For this reason, Petrarch reasonably burns and is destroyed by her inconstancy, as he was always accustomed to being—turned this way and that as if by a wind. And he adds all her various ways, which he has carefully noted: her singing, her sitting, her turning around, her stopping, her looking at him, her speaking, her smiling, and her being troubled at times. He concludes that in such thoughts and anxieties, he is held continually by the imperial power of Love.

¶ SENUCCIO I want you to know. Master Francesco sends this sonnet to Senuccio, his friend, informing him of the life he was leading and how Love guided him. He calls Love "our lord" <note>original: "signor nostro"</note> because Senuccio was also a man in love.

### SONNET 91

**Here, where I am but half, my Senuccio**
**(Would that I were here whole, and you content)**
**I came fleeing the storm and the wind,**
**Which suddenly made the weather cruel.**
**Here I am safe: and I want to tell you why I**
**Do not fear the lightning as I used to;**
**And why I find my burning desire mitigated,**
**Though not extinguished, by my enemy.**
**As soon as I reached the amorous palace**
**I saw where sweet and pure Laura was born,**
**Who quiets the air and banishes the thunder;**
**Love in my soul, where she reigns,**
**Rekindled the fire and extinguished the fear:**

<margin>Francesco N</margin> ¶ HERE where. Writing the present 91st sonnet to that same Senuccio mentioned before, our poet signifies the pleasure he felt at having gone to the Sorgue <note>The Sorgue is the river at Vaucluse where Petrarch had a small cottage.</note> where Madam Laura was born. This pleasure, although great, he nevertheless shows to be much less than it would be if he were in his friend's company; for since a friend is half of one's heart and soul in their shared life, it seems to him that he is not "whole" without his Senuccio, but only "half." Likewise, he does not have complete joy. He shows first that due to his absence from Avignon (where his beloved lady was), he did not feel so much torment, but then shows how much his amorous desire was suddenly inflamed anew when he came to that little village and saw the place where Madam Laura was born. He concludes that the fire would be very great indeed if he were to look into her eyes, when the place alone has so fiercely rekindled it.

<margin>Antonio</margin> ¶ HERE where half. There having been some days of bad and cloudy weather in Avignon, Master Francesco retreated to the Sorgue where he had his residence near the house where his lady stayed. As soon as he arrived, he wrote this sonnet to Senuccio, informing him why he had departed. "To the amorous palace" <note>original: "amoroſa reggia"</note>: that is, the royal dwelling of his beloved. "What would I do then, looking into her eyes?": he says this as if to imply he would burn much more intensely.

that luxurious court, calling that city Babylonia: <note>Petrarch famously referred to the Papal court at Avignon as the "Babylonian Captivity," comparing its perceived corruption to the biblical city.</note> for it was just as Babylon was in the time of Herod: so then Avignon and the papal court were given over to every vice without any shame. He said he had risen and fled from there to escape melancholy and to live a longer life: and he stayed entirely for that time in that little village <note>Vaucluse, near Avignon.</note> as if in a solitary life, giving himself over to noble studies, <note>The "studia humanitatis" or humanities, which Petrarch helped pioneer.</note> not caring at all for common fame, and hoping to have a better life shortly. This followed soon after when he arrived in Milan, welcomed by the illustrious lord Master Galeazzo; <note>Galeazzo II Visconti, a powerful ruler of Milan and Petrarch's patron.</note> and putting every other base thought aside, he says he desires nothing but two people: the cordial love of my lady Laura and the constancy of the accustomed benevolence of my Lord Cardinal Colonna. The Cardinal, seeing that the Pope had not accepted Petrarch for the reason mentioned above, made a smaller outward show of love than he had previously used, although in his soul he carried a singular affection for him.

> I have fled to lengthen my life,
> Here I stay alone; and as love invites me,
> Now rhymes and verses; now I gather herbs and flowers,

> Always thinking; and this alone helps me:
> Neither do I care for the crowd, nor for fortune,
> Nor much for myself; nor for any base thing;
> Nor do I feel great heat within, nor without:
> Only two persons I ask for; and I would have the one

<margin>Antonio</margin>
**ON IMPURE BABYLON:** <term>M.F.</term> <note>Francesco Filelfo, a famous Renaissance humanist and commentator.</note> having departed from the court of Rome <note>Meaning the Papal court at Avignon.</note> because of the vices that reign there and because of the little profit made by virtue, and having returned to his solitary place—which some believe to be the Sorgue <note>The river at Vaucluse.</note>—he wished to specify in this sonnet the reason for his departure. He calls Rome "Babylon" because it is as full of similar errors as Babylon was. And *I would have the one*, that is, his Laura. *The other with a foot as it ever was firm*: this refers to one of the lords of the Colonna house who had been defeated by the Orsini. <note>The Colonna and Orsini were rival noble families in Rome; this note suggests a historical context for Colonna's "firmness" despite political setbacks.</note>

## SONNET 93

**IN THE MIDDLE.** With a graceful manner in this 93rd sonnet, he describes the act of <term>M. L.</term> <note>Madonna Laura.</note> sitting at the head of the table near a window through which the sun was entering. Master <term>Fr.</term> <note>Francesco Petrarch.</note> sitting next to that lady, wishes in short to demonstrate that she was much more beautiful than the sun, which also gazed longingly at her. Therefore, he says he saw <term>M. L.</term>, an honest lady of haughty appearance, in the middle of the table, and also the sun which illuminates the earth and the sky. When she noticed that the sun was gazing at her, she also turned with a joyful look toward <term>Petrarch</term>, as if she wished to say: "Look if your rival is beautiful! And yet I decide that in my mortar I shall make a sauce with your pestle, so you must still have patience." <note>This is a surprisingly earthy, metaphorical interpretation by the commentator, suggesting Laura prefers the poet over the sun.</note> Seeing this, Petrarch felt jealousy within, seeing himself as less beautiful than the sun; and he would still have been in that fear, were it not that seeing the sun realize that the face of my lady Laura was much more beautiful than its own, the sun felt great displeasure at being defeated by such beauty. Because of this, being much troubled, the sun covered its face for shame with a little cloud, which gave Petrarch the greatest pleasure, leaving him in such love without any other rival.

> In the middle of two lovers, honest and proud
> I saw a lady, and that lord with her, <note>The "lord" is Love personified.</note>
> Who reigns among men and among the gods;
> And on one side the sun; I was on the other.
> Since she noticed she was enclosed by the sphere
> Of a more beautiful friend; toward my eyes
> All joyful she turned; and I truly wish,
> That she were never more fierce toward me.
> Suddenly into joy was converted
> The jealousy, which at first sight
> For so high an adversary was born in my heart:
> Around his tearful and sad face
> A little cloud gathered;
> So much did being defeated displease him.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
In the presence of two lovers, one noble and honorable. <note>original: "IN MEZO de dui amanti honešta altera"</note> Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> had seen Lady Laura in a beam of sunlight that fell upon her, and he feigns that the sun was wooing her; as he approached, she turned around laughing. At that moment, the sun happened to be obscured. Therefore, the poet says that the sun hid itself for shame, having been surpassed by her. Some say <note>original: "aliqui dicũt"</note> that Master Francesco was on a balcony together with Lady Laura and the beam of the sun was hurting her eyes; as she withdrew toward Master Francesco, who was more in the shade, he feigns that the sun darkened itself.

<margin>Francesco</margin>
<sig>Q</sig>
<margin>¶ FULL OF. Very often Petrarch finds himself at the Sorga <note>The Sorgue river in Provence.</note>, which name signifies that river, and also the village where Lady Laura was born. Wherefore, in this 94th sonnet, marvelously commending the singular beauty of Lady Laura, he says his eyes felt such sweetness and pleasure on that day he first saw her, that afterward there was never a woman who pleased him. Thus, he would have gladly kept his eyes closed from 그날 on, so as not to see any other woman, so that in his visual imagination she would always be represented. He then adds how he often walked through the valley of the Sorga, always having his thoughts on Lady Laura.</margin>

### SONNET 94.

**F**ull of that ineffable sweetness
Which my eyes drew from her beautiful face
On the day when I would have gladly closed them,
Never to look upon a lesser beauty;
**I** left behind that which I most desire; and my mind
Is so accustomed to contemplating her alone,
That it sees nothing else; and whatever is not her,
By long-standing habit, it already hates and despises.
**I**n a valley closed on every side, <note>Vaucluse, from the Latin "Vallis Clausa," meaning "Closed Valley."</note>
Which is the refuge for my weary sighs,
I arrived alone with Love, pensive and slow:
**T**here, no women; but fountains and rocks,
And the image of that day I find,
Which my thought portrays, wherever I gaze.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
<margin>¶ FULL. Master Francesco demonstrates how he departed the following day—that is, the day after he received that gaze from Lady Laura—and went to Sorga, always keeping in mind that look he had from her; and he found her image there, just as when she turned so joyfully toward him.</margin>

### SONNET 95.

**I**f the rock, by which this valley is most enclosed,
From which its own proper name is derived,
Kept its face turned, by a shy nature,
Toward Rome, and its back toward Babel; <note>Petrarch uses "Babel" or "Babylon" to refer to Avignon, which he considered a place of exile and corruption.</note>
**M**y sighs would have a more kindly path
To go where their hope is alive:
Now they go scattered; and yet each one arrives
There where I send it, for not a single one fails:
**A**nd they are there so sweetly received,
As I perceive, that none ever returns;
With such delight they stay in those parts.
The grief belongs to my eyes; for as soon as day breaks,
Out of great desire for the beautiful places taken from them,
They give me weeping, and to my weary feet, exhaustion.

<margin>Francesco</margin>
<sig>R</sig>
<margin>¶ IF THE ROCK. In the present 95th sonnet, he again makes mention of the Sorga, and says in essence <note>original: "in snis" (in sensu)</note> that if the village of the Sorga—which sits in the narrowest part of that valley—just like that youth who is also called the Sorga, <note>A reference to a local personification or legend.</note> would turn its back to Babel (that is, Babylonia, which is Avignon), and if this were done out of natural distaste, and similarly out of natural pleasure for the Italians, his amorous sighs would reach his beloved lady (who at that time was at the Sorga) by a more kindly path. For she might have been perhaps more kindly toward him because he was Italian. Whereas now they do not go together, but scattered, some here and some there; however, because they are well received, none ever returns back, because she never answered him anything. Wherefore he grieves greatly that he cannot find himself in that same place.</margin>

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ IF THE ROCK. Master Francesco, finding himself in the aforementioned valley of Sorga, in which there was a very great rock from which the valley took its name—as if to say "Valley of the Rock" or similar <note>original: "val de saxo uel simile"</note>—and that rock blocking his view of where Lady Laura stayed, so that if he wished to see her he had to go atop the mountains: for this reason he made this sonnet and speaks to the said rock, complaining of it.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch's emotional state and his literary achievements. <margin>Francesco S.</margin>
**THE SIXTEENTH YEAR REMAINS** behind. In the present 96th sonnet <note>The commentator notes this as the 96th, though the text identifies it as the 116th.</note>, Petrarch’s long perseverance in his amorous torments is made clear. Sixteen years have already passed since the first day he fell in love with Lady Laura; although he was already turning gray, he did not for that reason withdraw from this useless enterprise. Rather, the closer he approached death, the more he burned with love. This being a bitter thing, it yet seemed most sweet to him, so much so that a thing harmful to both soul and body appeared to him most useful. He was so weary that he would have welcomed death to escape the dominion of adverse fortune, yet he also feared that the beloved lady might die before him. Then, adding the unstable counsel of lovers, he demonstrates that although he wished to leave Avignon <note>The seat of the Papal court in France, which Petrarch frequently criticized.</note> because he did not have what he desired from the beloved lady, he was still so bound that he did not know how to depart. He wished not to love, yet he could not wish for that, so conquered and seized was he by such passion. Therefore, being able to do nothing else, he did what he could, concluding that he is the same lover he ever was; and although a thousand tricks <note>original: "riuolte"</note> were played on him by the beloved lady, he still did not know how to leave Avignon to return to Italy. This signifies that the lady treated him with "the turn of the fox," showing him perhaps a kind face with signs of amorous hope, and then leaving him with nothing but the tail in his hand <note>A metaphor for being deceived or left with an empty prize.</note>.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
**THE SIXTEENTH YEAR REMAINS** behind. While Master Francesco was in this valley, he found himself of two minds: one wished to be near Lady Laura, the other did not. Established in such thought, he writes of the time he has been in love, which he states is sixteen years, and says that he fears death will arrive before his time, leaving his hope destroyed and preventing him from seeing the eyes of Lady Laura.

# SONNET 116.

> The sixteenth year of my sighs has fallen behind;
> And I move forward toward the end,
> And yet it seems to me that only just now
> Was the beginning of so much trouble.
> Bitterness is sweet to me; and my harm is useful,
> And living is heavy; and I pray that I may overcome
> Cruel fortune; and I fear lest death
> Should close those beautiful eyes that make me speak.
> Now here I am weary, and I wish to be elsewhere;
> And I would want to want more, and yet I want no more,
> and because I can do no more, I do what I can:
> And for ancient desires, new tears
> Prove that I am still the same as I used to be;
> Nor by a thousand turnings have I yet been moved.

<margin>Francesco T.</margin>
**A LADY MORE** than. This 22nd canzone <note>Marked as Canzone 12 in the header.</note> contains the commendation and praise of two faculties represented under the guise of a lady: the first is Poetry and the other is Eloquence. Master Francesco Petrarch was marvelously devoted to these studies from his childhood, so that it can truly be affirmed that he was the first to rescue such studies—which for hundreds of years had been not only depraved and corrupted through the ignorance of the Northerners <note>original: "tramontani," referring to non-Italian/barbarian influences</note>, but almost entirely dead. He resurrected them from death and restored them in great part to their ancient elegance. Having removed their obscurity, he conquered all the darkness and the monkish broth <note>original: "brodaglia fratešca," a derogatory term for the poor Latin and scholastic philosophy of medieval monks</note>. Beginning then in the first stanza: that a lady, namely Poetry, who surpasses the Sun in beauty because of her famous and glorious effect...

# CANZONE 12. STANZA 1.

> A lady much more beautiful than the sun,
> And more radiant, and of equal age,
> With famous beauty,
> While still young, drew me to her ranks:
> She, in thought, in works, and in words;
> Because she is one of the rare things in the world;
> She, through a thousand paths,
> Was always before me, graceful and proud:
> For her sake alone I turned back from what I was,
> Ever since I suffered her eyes near me:
> For her love I had set myself
> To a most laborious enterprise quite early
> Such that, if I arrive at the desired port,
> I hope through her for a long time
> To live, when others shall hold me for dead.

<margin>Antonio.</margin>
...and of light, and she is also always young like him, insofar as the poet, when he is most excellent, is every day more appreciated by excellent minds. He <note>The author of the commentary is likely referring to the personified spirit of Poetry or the Muse.</note> made Petrarch fall in love with her while he was still a mere young boy, showing the reason why he fell in love with her as an extraordinary thing in this world, regarding both the contemplative virtues and the grace of speech. Hence, she was always in his mind, no differently than if she had been before his eyes. This was the reason for lifting him out of the ranks of the ignorant commoners <note>original: "volgari"</note>, as he devoted himself early on to the study of doctrine and erudition, not caring for any hardship. He said that if he could reach the desired end of creating some beautiful work in verse—as he did with the *Bucolics* <note>original: "buccolica," referring to Petrarch's *Bucolicum carmen*</note> and the *Africa* <note>An epic poem in Latin about Scipio Africanus</note>, although he did not complete the latter—he hoped to live through fame for a very long time.

¶ A LADY MUCH MORE BEAUTIFUL THAN THE SUN. This moralizing work does not deal with love at all; rather, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> wrote it when he was crowned with laurel <note>Petrarch was crowned Poet Laureate in Rome in 1341.</note> in memory of the poetic crown and in honor of the sciences, to which he always devoted his effort; and she <note>Poetry/Philosophy</note> rises there in the manner of a lady. And he shows himself speaking with her, asking that she give him the laurel crown, to signify that he obtained such a crown through the sciences.
*She revealed herself to me, from which a chill was born in me*: that is, a zeal and appetitive love for them <note>the sciences/arts</note>. *I pressed myself to her feet*: he says this to signify that he began with the smallest things to arrive at the greatest. *But my adversary who disturbs the good*: that is, idleness and rest. *I wanted to say: this is an impossible thing.* Just as it is not possible that another lady should make my eyes more happy. But he says this because she had become aware of his love: *around and around my temples she wrapped*: meaning his coronation.

# STANZA II.

<margin>V ¶ THIS MY. Continuing the discourse of his life in this study: he says in this second stanza that for many years—all through his youth and even part of his more mature age—he used the study of poetry for amorous things regarding his rhymes; and his other writing in verse was nothing other than love, for which poetry seems the most suitable instrument. He says this happened to prove his constancy. And where he believed himself to be a good poet, it was not in fact true, insofar as he did not use poetry for glorious things but for low and lustful things; whereby he shows he did not first know her well or use her well. Seeing this now, he enjoys such a memory—not that he likes having done wrong, but only to recognize in his present good deeds his past wrongdoing, and that even now in old age she has revealed herself to him. This has induced such wonder that...</margin>
> This lady of mine led me for many years

The new excellence, not previously known, caused the blood to rush back to his heart, where he says a "chill" was born in him.

<margin>IT WAS RARE.</margin> *The fourth stanza demonstrates, contrary to what many believe—who say it is impossible for a man to be a good poet if he does not have it from nature—wherefore Petrarch responds that everyone who gives themselves to poetry in a short time falls in love with it and becomes as learned as they wish. But the reason for the few poets is greed: because seeing that such study is not esteemed useful by the common people <note>original: "vulgo"</note>, one more willingly gives oneself to law or medicine: or commerce: or similar gain as to one's master. But whoever hopes to be honored and glorious attends to such study: which makes man almost immortal and especially when eloquence is joined with it, for which he says his eyes should become more happy; and in such a way he prefers eloquence over poetry, which shows that he delighted more in prose than in verse, as is also seen through his works.*

Which was tied tight around my tongue
In the first embarrassment

### STANZA VII.

<margin>S</margin>
<margin>
**Just as.** Poetry responds in this seventh stanza to our poet, saying that both—that is, poetry and eloquence—make a man immortal: and that they are creatures of God, insofar as every science <term>science: "scientia," referring to any branch of organized knowledge</term> and every virtue proceeds from the divine light, and rebuking human negligence and misery because through their own defect no man is well-excellent in such a faculty: and that among the ancients these two faculties were highly prized and loved as beautiful and graceful, but now no esteem is held for them, and especially in the time of Petrarch, eloquence was entirely faded: because they delighted somewhat in poetry and in speaking in verse, although their verses were like the rhymes of the organ <note>original: "rime de lorgano," likely referring to mechanical, simplistic, or unrefined rhyming typical of medieval popular verse</note>: and thus eloquence was stripped bare and poetry was like a shadow. This being said, she also departing—insofar as the poet without eloquence is worth nothing—she crowned him with laurel, signifying in this way his coronation performed for him in the time of King Robert <note>King Robert of Anjou, who examined Petrarch in Naples before his 1341 coronation as Poet Laureate in Rome</note>.
</margin>

Just as it pleased our eternal Father;
Each of us two was born immortal:
Wretches, of what value to you?
It would be better if the defect were from us.
Beloved, beautiful, and graceful young women
We were for a time; and now we have come to such a state
That she flaps her wings
To return to her ancient dwelling:
I, for my part, am a shadow: and now I have said,
as much as can be understood by you in so short a time.
After her feet were moved
Saying, do not fear that I am moving away;
She gathered a garland of green laurel;
Which with her own hands
She wound round and round my temples.

THOSE PITEOUS. Petrarch wrote the present 97th sonnet in response to a moral song written in his praise by Master Antonio da Ferrara <note>Antonio Beccari (1315–1373), a poet known for his "frottola" style and his friendship with Petrarch.</note>. This occurred when Antonio heard by public rumor that Petrarch had passed from this life; in truth, Petrarch had suffered a very great illness, so severe that everyone despaired for him. Yet, in the end, he remained free of it. Once he was healed, reading the said song pleased him greatly, and as a grateful and kindly man, he responded without delay with this sonnet. In the sonnet, he first praises the wit of the aforementioned Master Antonio, as well as his affection and faith. He signifies to him that although his great infirmity put him in danger of death, nonetheless—because it was not yet granted by God that he should die—he escaped and is entirely free

<margin>Antonio</margin>
THOSE PITEOUS. In this sonnet, Master Francesco responds to a certain Master Antonio da Ferrara. Since Master Francesco had been sick unto death, Antonio composed a moral work as if he were dead, in which he invited all the sciences to weep for his death. Master Francesco, having been liberated, sent him this sonnet.

<margin>Francesco E.</margin>
NOW SEE. Petrarch directs this 23rd song to Love <note>Cupid</note> to induce and incite him against Laura. She, being most apt for the dances of love—both due to her youthful joy and also her bearing and the dress of her wandering person—was proud toward the empire of Love, in that she cared nothing for him. And she was pitiless toward the poet, in that she would not receive Petrarch into her lovely dwelling for any humble and sweet prayer made to her. He confesses, therefore, that he is in the power of that most cruel lady.

> Sits barefoot among the flowers and the grass,

<margin>
SEVENTEEN years. This 98th sonnet declares, like many others, the continuous and long perseverance of the amorous fire of Petrarch, who had already spent seventeen years in vain regarding the love of Madonna Laura. Now he was more inflamed than he had ever been, so that although his hair had changed and become gray, he had not changed his burning passion. He forgot that while he used to turn a head of red hair <note>A reference to Petrarch’s youthful appearance; he often wrote about the transition from "red" or "dark" hair to "white" as a marker of time's passage</note> upward, he now bowed that whitened head toward his shoes. He then laments much concerning the veil that the beloved lady wore on her head in the French fashion, it being a hindrance and obstacle that prevented him from gazing well into her eyes. He says he has the greatest desire to be able to look at them once in his own way, together with Venus <note>Meaning he wishes to look upon her with a reciprocal spirit of love and beauty</note>.
</margin>
<margin>Francesco F.</margin>

### SONNETTO.XCVIII.

**S**eventeen years the heavens have already revolved
Since I first burned, and never was I quenched;
But when it happens that I reflect upon my state,
I feel a chill in the midst of the flames.
**T**rue is the proverb, that one changes his hair
Before his habits <note>original: "vezo"; a variation of *vezzo*, meaning habit, vice, or custom</note>: and though the senses grow slack,
Human affections are no less intense;
This the wicked shadow of the heavy veil does to us.
**A**las, weary me: and when shall that day be
When, watching the flight of my years,
I may emerge from the fire and from such long pain?
**W**ill I ever see the day when, as much as I desire,
That sweet air of the beautiful, adorned face
May please these eyes, as much as is fitting?

...in the sweetest room of love.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
SEVENTEEN years have already revolved: the poet Messer Francesco describes how long he has been in love with Madonna Laura, and says that when he thinks of his being, he feels himself somewhat cooled. Through the slackening of the senses, it seems that I show myself somewhat weary of love, but not however cured.

---

<margin>
THAT LOVELY paleness. How much it pleases virtuous women—and not just those who are immodest—to be loved, our Petrarch clearly manifests in the present 99th Sonnet. This was written when he was sent as an ambassador by the Pope to the King of England <note>The commentator mentions the King of England, though historical records usually place Petrarch’s 1360 embassy to King John II of France in Paris; such geographical discrepancies are common in early commentaries</note>. Before he departed from Avignon, he went to visit Madonna Laura to take his leave with words worthy of both him and her. She, lowering her lashes along with her eyes—no less out of melancholy for such a departure than out of shame for his speaking—turned entirely pale in the face. This demonstrates that her heart was not a little refined by pity and compassion. Petrarch says, therefore, that the paleness of her face, which was previously troubled and before that smiling, was a sign of a reciprocal love from her toward him. So that, just as in Paradise nothing is hidden, so he, with his heart...
</margin>
<margin>Francesco G.</margin>

### SONNETTO.XCIX.

**T**hat lovely, wandering paleness, which the sweet smile
Covered with an amorous mist,
Offered itself to my heart with such majesty
That it met my heart halfway to my face.
**I** knew then, just as in Paradise
One sees the other; in such a way opened
That piteous thought, which others did not discern;
But I saw it, for I fix my gaze nowhere else.
**E**very angelic look, every humble act
That was ever seen in a woman in whom love existed,
Would be a disdain beside that of which I speak.
**S**he bent her beautiful, noble gaze to the ground;
And remaining silent, she said, as it seemed to me:
"Who takes my faithful friend away from me?"

¶ THAT beautiful, longing glance. Messer Francesco <note>original: "M. F.", referring to Petrarch</note>, while he stood once gazing longingly at Madonna Laura <note>original: "M. L."</note>, was led away by one of his servants who was passing by, spoke to him, and took him away from where she was. In the departure he made, he looked at Madonna Laura and saw her turn pale upon seeing him leave; and in that act he composed this sonnet, which seemed to say: "Who takes you from me? One who is my own dear friend."

## SONNET 100.

> Love, fortune, and my mind—which recoils 
> From what it sees and turns toward the past—
> Afflict me so, that I sometimes feel
> Envy for those who are on the other shore <note>A common metaphor for the dead who have crossed the river Styx</note>.
> Love destroys my heart; fortune deprives it
> Of every comfort; wherefore my foolish mind
> Grows angry and weeps, and thus in great pain
> It must always live, struggling.
> Nor do I hope that sweet days will return,
> But rather that what remains goes from bad to worse;
> And I have already passed the midpoint of my course.
> Alas, I see all my hope falling from my hands,
> Made not of diamond, but of glass;
> And all my thoughts breaking in the middle.

<margin>Francesco</margin>
¶ LOVE, fortune. In this present hundredth sonnet, he clearly demonstrates the continuous anxiety of those who have placed their vain study under the yoke of love—especially when they cannot obtain the thing they desire. Wherefore, appearing to themselves to be unfortunate, they are troubled in their minds and commit a thousand follies. Thus, he says he is afflicted by three things in such a way that he envies the dead. Of these three things: the first is Love, which destroys his heart. The second is fortune, which, being contrary to him, deprives him of all comfort. The third is his own mind, which, in respect to such love and such fortune, becomes foolish, inconsiderately growing angry with itself and weeping, and continually giving itself pain and torment. Therefore, seeing that time has passed uselessly regarding his desire and that he cannot return to the past, Petrarch hopes for even worse in the future, thinking that he has already passed more than half his life <note>original: "meza eta". Petrarch often reflected on reaching the midpoint of life, traditionally considered age 35</note> and seeing every fragile hope worsen, and every one of his thoughts being without effect. This sonnet, as far as can be understood, was composed by our poet in the early years of his falling in love.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ LOVE, fortune, and my—he says, Messer Francesco, that thinking of the good times past, he carries envy for those who are dead. Fortune: that is, my misfortune. But rather what remains goes from bad to worse: the poet says he doubts and fears that things will continue to decline. Alas, not of diamond, but of glass: because a diamond could not be broken by falling, but a glass certainly breaks and spills whatever is inside it, because it is a fragile thing and not solid like a diamond.

> Burning for her, who stands like a piece of ice,
> And leaves not a dram in me,
> That is not fire and flame,

the lady would be moved to compassion and would feel the amorous flame just as he does, and she would not make him suffer so, wandering now here and now there after her in vain, nor still weeping as he does; for she feels nothing of his love, as if she were sleeping or colder than ice.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ BECAUSE LOVE FORCES ME. <gloss>Commentary</gloss> **M. F.** <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch</note>, our poet, in this moral reflection on his own troubles, says that if the pain that torments him so were to "clothe" him—that is, if it made his outward appearance match his internal state—it would clearly show that he is burning within. Then he would feel that fire: that is, **M. L.** <note>Madonna Laura</note>. "Leave my pious leaves": that is, he would not go about so solitary and dispersed through the world. "Neither branch, nor flower, nor leaf." He says this because although a tree may have a rough bark, it can still produce good fruit; he says this of himself because he speaks so harshly in this song <note>Petrarch often referred to his "harsh" or "scattered" rhymes</note>, though he knows how to speak better. "One harms me and the other": that is, that weeping harms me; the other, that lamenting, does not harm her. "To another who is not shrewd": that is, I do not notice it, because I am juggling with it. "Sweet rhymes." **M. F.** at the beginning of his falling in love made rhymes in praise of **M. L.** "Who will ever shatter": that is, who will take away the hardness I have taken on through love so that I can speak in rhyme as I did before. "To want then to portray her": that is, to draw her out of the heart where I feel he <note>Love</note> paints her. "I am not powerful enough on my own." "In her face alone": as if to say she has no other joy but her own beautiful face. "You know well that so beautiful a foot": he speaks to that riverbank where **M. L.** passed many times to go toward Avignon <note>original: "vignoneta"</note>, sometimes making herself a seat there. He says this because in going from her house to the Sorgue River <note>original: "sorga"</note> which was nearby, she passed through meadows and would sit there at times. "O my poor little one, how rough you are": the poet speaks to his own song. "Rough": that is, crude and harsh.

## STANZA II.

> Because love forces me,
> And strips me of wisdom;
> I speak in harsh rhymes, devoid of sweetness.
> But not always on the bark,
> Does a branch, nor in flower nor in leaf,
> Show its natural virtue from the outside:
> Let Love and those beautiful eyes
> Look at what the heart hides:
> Where one finds rest in the shade.
> If the grief, which clears away,
> Should happen to overflow into tears or lamenting,
> One harms me, and the other
> Harms another, though I am not shrewd enough to see it.

<margin>Francesco R.</margin>
¶ BECAUSE LOVE. In the present second stanza, he demonstrates the same thing happening to his speech as he previously said of his thought: that by being too much in love, he loses his judgment and wisdom. Therefore, his rhymes are harsh and without any sweetness. He says this is not to be wondered at, using a beautiful simile: as it also happens with the bark of trees and in leaves and flowers, which do not show the interior virtue of the tree in their outward color. He then adds that this passion of his is known to Love, to whom he directs his speech, and who knows his heart is afflicted. Nevertheless, his eyes appear beautiful on the outside—that is, not afflicted or tearful—except when he is alone under the shade of some tree, or otherwise weeping and lamenting most strongly. This harms his body just as the internal passion harms his soul.

## STANZA III.

> Sweet graceful rhymes,
> Which in the first assault
> Of love I used, when I had no other weapons—

<margin>L</margin>
¶ SWEET RHYMES. He demonstrates in this third stanza the reason why he does not know how to speak as well at present as he used to at the beginning when he first fell in love. He says this is the intolerable passion of the heart...

*that much distress that takes away from him the knowledge as he said above, grieving so that it becomes in him no differently hardened than if it were an enamel* <note>original: "smalto"; here referring to a hard, glassy surface, symbolizing a heart so petrified by sorrow that tears cannot flow</note> *so that he cannot unburden himself in weeping: as he would wish, showing that he always holds the image of the beloved woman in said heart as if some noble painter, by constantly speaking of her, wished to portray her. <margin>M</margin> *¶ LIKE A Child. His inability to speak due to the distress of the heart is shown in this fourth stanza to be similar to that of a little child who, because his instruments are still weak and imperfect, however much he wishes, cannot express in speech what he has in his mental concept. Our Petrarch says that this also happens to him; for though he cannot speak as he desires, yet since silence is a burden, he resolves to speak in such a way that he may be heard by the beloved lady before he leaves this life through too much passion, commending the singular beauty of her face: of which he thinks so highly that he holds every other thing in contempt. Then he directs his speech to the bank of the Sorgue* <note>The river Sorgue in Vaucluse, France, near where Petrarch lived in Valchiusa (Vaucluse)</note> *where at that time Madonna Laura was staying, praying that she grant flight to his sighs, so that from there they might pass even to the ears of the pilgrim* <note>A poetic way of describing Laura as a heavenly visitor or a traveler on earth</note> *Madonna Laura: which, if the Sorgue will do, it will always be possible for everyone to speak of the great friendship that place will have brought to him.*

**W**herever I turn my eyes,
