### CANZONE XXV. <note>This is Poem 126 in the "Rerum vulgarium fragmenta," beginning "Chiare, fresche, et dolci acque."</note>

**C**lear, fresh, and sweet waters,
Where the beautiful limbs
She placed, who alone seems a lady to me;
Gentle branch, where it pleased her
(With sighs I remember)
To make a column for her beautiful side;
Grass and flowers, which her graceful
Gown covered
With her angelic breast;
Sacred and serene air,
Where Love with beautiful eyes opened my heart;
Give audience together
To my sorrowful, final words.

<margin>O</margin>
¶ WHEREVER I turn my eyes. He praises in this sixth stanza the beauty of the eyes of the beloved lady, which he shows to be of such splendor that they create a serenity in all the places where she, passing by, has gazed. He says the same of the grass and flowers, as if for each of those places she had placed her feet: thus the grass and flowers that have grown have their roots beneath those footprints. It seems to him that every flowery, green, and beautiful thing proceeds from the fact that Madonna Laura passed through there.

<margin>P</margin>
¶ O MY little poor one. This seventh and final stanza our Petrarch directs to his song, calling it by its true and proper name: "poor" in graceful sentiments and "crude" in polished speech. Because of this, he comforts it, telling it not to go to Madonna Laura, but rather to remain in those woods.

<margin>Hiero. Q</margin>
¶ CLEAR, fresh. There seems to be no doubt, as can be understood from the song above and this twenty-fifth one, that the place where Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch's full name was Francesco Petrarca.</note> had fled the plague <note>Petrarch famously fled the Black Death, which devastated Europe in 1348.</note> was near the Sorgue. <note>The Sorgue (Sorga) is the river at Vaucluse where Petrarch lived.</note> Describing it, then, in praise of Madonna Laura, speaking with himself, he remembers the places and the graceful acts, grieving for his fortune and much for the cruel lady, lamenting. Therefore, in this first stanza, he commends those waters where she, in the summer, was sometimes accustomed to bathe, and also the branch of the little tree where he saw her leaning; similarly the grass and flowers among which she used to place herself for pleasure in the heat; and thus also the air and serenity of that region: praying all the aforementioned things that they lend their ears to his present speech, which is much more ornate than the song above.

<margin>Ante.</margin>
Messer Francesco, praising the river where he had heard it said that Madonna Laura, being at the Sorgue, used to bathe in the summer because of the heat, speaks to those waters. *To make a column for her beautiful side:* that is, to lean against that trunk of the tree. *Give audience together:* he invokes them to hear him. *That Love might close these weeping eyes:* that is, that I might die weeping for love. *He could never in a more restful port:* He says that if he must indeed die thus, he could not die in any place where death would be more pleasing to him than in that one. *May that wild one return, beautiful and gentle:* that is, Madonna Laura. *Now earth among the stones:* that is, fragile as earth among stones, meaning among her cruelties or her pity, seeing that Love forces him to do so...

->Petrar.<-

...that she loves me. And she compels heaven <note>original: "faci forza al cielo"; a poetic expression meaning her prayers or presence are so powerful they move the divine realm.</note> because she is destined for chastity and modesty. *From the beautiful branches was descending*, write how, as she was sitting—meaning My Lady Laura—under a flowering tree, she was entirely covered by those flowers that were falling. *One rested on the ground and another on the waves*, meaning that river on which she sat when she had bathed. *If you had as many ornaments as you have desire*, our Poet, Master Francesco, speaks to his song metaphorically <note>original: "methaphorice"</note> as if to say: if you were adorned with worthy thoughts, you could be seen among people—that is, among learned men.

**IF IT IS.** In the eighth stanza <note>The commentator refers to this as the 8th stanza of the sequence, though it is the 3rd stanza of this specific poem.</note>, he prays to the aforementioned waters, branches, grass, and flowers that at least upon his death they might receive his body as a grave: because having such a hope, dying for love will be less painful.

### STANZA VIII.

> **I**f it is indeed my destiny,
> And heaven exerts itself in this,
> That Love should close these eyes with weeping,
> May some grace cover
> My wretched body among you,
> And the soul return to its own dwelling, naked.
> Death will be less cruel,
> If I carry this hope
> To that uncertain step:
> For the weary spirit
> Could never in a more restful port,
> Nor in a more tranquil grave
> Escape the troubled flesh and bone.

<margin>S</margin>
**TIME.** The ninth stanza demonstrates the vain hope of foolish lovers who, the more they see the lady is virtuous and no less obstinate in refusing to consent to amorous appetites, the more they are inflamed and the more they hope. Whence he says he still hopes that My Lady Laura will come toward him, gentle and kind, and that she will turn her soul toward him in loving him wonderfully: acting like the sail of a ship which, by contrary winds, turns in the opposite direction; as the wind changes, it returns to the right course. And so, he being dead and buried among the things mentioned above, he will be sought by that lady with no small desire.

### STANZA IX.

> **T**ime will perhaps yet come,
> When to her usual dwelling
> The beautiful and gentle beast <note>original: "fera"; Petrarch often uses the "gentle beast" or "wild deer" metaphor to describe Laura's elusive and untamed virtue.</note> returns,
> And there where she saw me
> On that blessed day,
> She turns her desirous and happy sight
> Seeking me; and with pity
> Seeing me already earth among the stones,
> May Love inspire her
> In such a way that she sighs
> So sweetly, that she obtains mercy for me,
> And compels heaven,
> Drying her eyes with her beautiful veil.

---

<margin>T</margin>
**FROM BEAUTIFUL.** In the tenth stanza, he describes an act that he saw one day of My Lady Laura: that while sitting on the flowering grass under a blossoming small tree, her tresses and her whole graceful and beautiful self were showered by fresh flowers in great abundance and quantity falling from the tree: now on her blonde hair and now in her lap. This gave her such ornament and loveliness that it would have surpassed any polished gold or whitest pearls: and thus she, and also the place around her, was so covered with flowers that it truly seemed to be the room where Love himself lived.

### STANZA X.

> **F**rom the beautiful branches was descending
> (Sweet in the memory)
> A rain of flowers over her lap,
> And she sat there
> Humble in such glory,
> Already covered by the amorous cloud:
> One flower fell on the hem,
> One on the golden tresses,
> Which were like polished gold and pearls
> To see them that day;
> One rested on the ground, and one on the waves...

### STANZA XI.
**H**ow many times I said
Then, full of fear:
"Surely this woman was born in paradise."
So burdened with oblivion
Her divine bearing
And her face, and her words, and her sweet smile
Had so divided me
From the true image;
That I said, sighing:
*How did I come here, or when?*
Believing I was in heaven, not there where I was:
From then until now I so love
This grass, that elsewhere I find no peace.

My sighs find a truce and I aid my sorrow.

A thousand different things, attentive and fixed;
I see only one lady and her beautiful face.

¶ **Whenever**. In the present 4th stanza he describes his boundless love: which is destroyed no differently than snow by the warming sun, yet in that face of the beloved lady, considering her beauty is almost divine: and then being far from her even as far as Milan: where at that time he found himself, he wept because of too much desire. ¶ **I NEVER SAW**. Through some beautiful similes, he describes in the 5th stanza the beauty of Lady Laura's eyes, first showing them to be similar to the planets when they appear clearest and most shining, as they usually are when the air is cleared after the night rain: or rather when at the break of morning they seem to flame. This demonstrates that at times Lady Laura had wept, and a little later, according to the instability of women <note>A common Renaissance trope regarding the changing emotions of a lady</note>, had shown her joyful gaze. And just as the sun when it rises in the morning is much more lovely than when it sets: similarly, when Lady Laura gazed back at him with some pleasant look, it seemed to him she was an oriental <note>rising</note> sun: but when she turned her eyes elsewhere, she seemed like the sun when it goes to its setting:

<margin>D</margin> **IF EVER.** Now in this 6th stanza, by the comparison of white and red roses, he describes the brightness of the face of Lady Laura mixed with a charming redness in her cheeks. By the "gold vessel" he means her blond hair, which has the likeness of gold. He clearly shows these three colors with expressive words, demonstrating that such excellences are the cause of his burning desire.

### STANZA VI

> If ever my eyes saw white roses mixed with red
> In a gold vessel, just then
> Plucked by a virgin hand;
> They thought they saw the face of her
> Who surpasses all other wonders
> With three beautiful excellences gathered in her;
> The blond tresses loosened over her neck,
> Where any milk would lose its contest <note>Meaning her skin is whiter than milk</note>;
> And the cheeks, which a sweet fire adorns.
> But if only the breeze should move
> White and yellow flowers a little through the hills;
> The place returns to my mind,
> And the first day, when I saw the golden hair
> Scattered upon Laura; for which I burned so suddenly.

<margin>E</margin> **EVERY ONE.** In the present 7th stanza, he shows it to be an impossible thing to be able to recount in such brief speech the excellence of the beauty of his beloved Lady Laura, just as it is impossible to count the stars or to shut all the waters in a small glass. He concludes that all his thought is in remembering her, no differently than if he had her before his eyes, in such a way that only her name—and no other that exists in the world—is ever in his mouth or in his sighs; but he always calls her as a thing most beautiful above all others.

### STANZA VII

> To count the stars one by one,
> And to shut all the waters in a small glass,
> Perhaps I believed; when in such a small paper <note>referring to the page of his poem</note>
> A new thought was born in me to recount
> In how many parts the flower of all other beauties,
> While standing by herself, is scattered by her light;
> So that I may never part from her:
> Nor will I do so; and even if I sometimes flee,
> She has blocked my steps in heaven and on earth:
> Because to my weary eyes
> She is always present: wherefore I am all consumed:
> And thus she stays with me;
> That I see no other ever, nor desire to see,
> Nor is the name of another in my sighs or calls.
<margin>(calls,</margin>

<margin>F</margin> **WELL YOU KNOW.** He concludes in this 8th and final stanza that all his speaking is nothing compared to his hidden and amorous thought; which thought regarding the beauty of the beloved lady is the very thing that, through sweet remembrance, keeps him alive. He adds that having distanced himself from Avignon <note>The city in France where the Papal court resided and where Petrarch met Laura</note> to Milan would have caused his death through continuous weeping, were it not for the comfort he takes in being always together with Lady Laura in his imagination, which is the reason he still lives.

### STANZA VIII

> Well you know, my song, that whatever I speak is nothing
> To my hidden amorous thought,
> Which day and night I carry in my mind;

> In such a long war <note>The "war" of his unrequited love</note> I do not yet perish:
> For the distance from my heart, weeping,
> Would have certainly killed me by now;
> But from here I take a delay of death.

<meta>This page transitions from the previous commentary on the poems concerning Lady Laura to Petrarch’s most famous political poem, Song 128 (labeled here as 28), "Italia mia." This song is a passionate appeal to the ruling lords of Italy to stop using foreign mercenaries and to end their internal warring.</meta>

# SONG XXVIII.

<margin>
This stanza, which serves as an introduction, addresses its speech universally to all of Italy regarding the Romans, the Florentines, and the Lombards. It states that although the author feels he speaks in vain—since no one will move against the Germans <note>original: "todeſchi"</note> who strike the Italians with mortal blows—he nevertheless wishes to demonstrate in this song the displeasure he feels at such a great injury. Then, turning his speech to our Lord God, he prays that He might deign to help the Romans, the head of the Catholic Church, and likewise all Italians, who were greatly harassed by those Germans; he shows himself eager to write what follows against the Germans.
</margin>

My Italy, although speech is in vain
For the mortal wounds
Which I see so frequent in your beautiful body,
It pleases me at least that my sighs be such
As the Tiber <note>original: "teuero"</note> and the Arno hope for,
And the Po, where I now sit sorrowful and heavy.
Ruler of heaven, I ask
That the pity which brought you to earth
May turn you to your beloved, noble country.
See, gracious Lord,
From what trivial causes such a cruel war arises;
And the heart that the proud and fierce Mars <note>The Roman god of war</note>
Hardens and locks,
Open it, Father, and soften it, and untie it:
There, make your truth
(however humble I may be) be heard through my tongue.

<margin>Anto.</margin> **MY ITALY.** Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarca</note> composed this moral song against the lords of Italy, who at this time were all at war, and he speaks toward Italy. *He hopes for the Tiber and the Arno:* that is, Rome and Florence, and Lombardy where I am at present. **You into whose hands fortune has placed the rein:** the poet speaks to the lords of the soldiers: *why are there so many foreign swords <note>original: "pelegrine ſpade"</note> here.* That is to say, it would be better to go against the barbarous and infidel peoples. *For in a venal heart, love:* that is, in soldiers of fortune <note>mercenaries</note> who sell themselves now to this one, now to that one. *Of whom, as one reads:* that is, the German people, whom Marius <note>Gaius Marius, the Roman general</note>, captain of the Roman forces, defeated and overcame, and he shed so much of their blood that, wanting later to drink from thirst, they could not drink the river water without drinking as much blood as water. *Of Caesar I am silent, who on every shore.* Caesar also conquered Germany, which is called Alamania. *It ruins the most beautiful part of the world:* that is, Italy. *Which spills blood and sells the soul near:* that is, causing soldiers to be led who sell their soul to others for money and spill their blood: *more broadly than any other anger compels you:* that is, silence incites and moves. *Is this not the ground I first touched:* he says to them that he intends to say in this, "Is this not my country and my dwelling?" so that by saying this they may be moved to pity and not keep it at war, for God's sake. *This lament:* that is, this thought. *After God, hope also that you show:* he says that first he hopes for rest from God, and then from you. *Lords, look how time flies.* The poet admonishes the said captains and warriors that they should consider their brief mortal life and spend their time in something other than harming their neighbor. *Song, I [send] you:* the poet instructs his song on what it must do.

## STANZA II.

<margin>
<margin>Fran. H</margin> **YOU WHOM.** In this second stanza, directing his speech to the Italian lords and princes, he rightfully reproaches them as ungrateful and without any compassion or charity toward the fatherland, for tolerating so many German soldiers who lead to the destruction of Italy. And he reproves the ignorance of those sluggish lords and princes who allow themselves to be flattered by the Germans and do not see their own ruin, seeing as there is never any faith <note>loyalty</note> in soldiers of fortune. Except in the victorious and magnanimous...
</margin>

You, into whose hands fortune has placed the rein
Of the beautiful lands,
For which no pity seems to constrain you,
What are so many foreign swords doing here?
Why is the green earth
To be painted with barbarian blood?
A vain error flatters you:
You see little, and yet you think you see much;

### STANZA III.

<margin>I</margin>
¶ NATURE PROVIDED WELL. Now in this third stanza, he confirms what was said before: that the Italians themselves lead the Germans into Italy. For in such a way nature provided for the Italian well-being by means of the Alps <note>The mountain range serving as a natural northern border</note> which surround it from the mainland, so that no power could harm it if our blind vision did not make us enemies of our own good. Because of this, once the Germans are led into Italy, they behave toward the Italians like wolves toward lambs. He adds, in contempt of those people, that these are the same Germans who were broken, defeated, and killed by Gaius Marius <note>A Roman general and statesman who held the consulship seven times</note>—barbarous men without law. This Gaius Marius, although he was from Arpinum <note>A city in Lazio</note> and born of very low status, became consul seven times through his industry and virtue. He was sent as a legate with Metellus, the Roman captain, against Jugurtha, the King of Numidia. Then, having returned to Rome with the intention of seeking the consulship, in order to obtain it more easily, he spoke many slanders against his captain. For this reason, he was made consul by the common people and given that same command held by Metellus. He won a victory over Jugurtha and led him, along with his two sons, bound before his triumphal chariot. In the following year, without even asking, he was made consul again. Coming to Lake Maggiore near Sesto, he defeated the Teutons and the Ambrones <note>Ancient Germanic and Celtic tribes</note> on two occasions; two hundred thousand of them were killed there. Continuing his consulship, and being offered a triumph, he said he did not want it until he had conquered the Cimbri, who had descended into the territory of Verona. Having gone against them, he fought them most fiercely and obtained the victory, killing one hundred and forty-four thousand of them. All these people were Germans.

> Nature provided well for our state,
> When she placed the shield of the Alps
> Between us and the German rage.
> But blind desire, stubborn against its own good,
> Has since so exerted itself,
> That it has brought the itch to a healthy body.
> Now within a single cage
> Wild beasts and gentle flocks
> Nest together, so that the better part always groans;
> And this is from the seed
> To the greater sorrow of the lawless people;
> Of whom, as one reads,
> Marius so opened the flank
> That the memory of the deed does not yet fade,
> When, parched and weary,
> He drank no longer water from the river, but blood.

> I say nothing of Caesar; who on every shore

For that the fury of his stubborn people 
Wins over us in intellect 
Is our own sin, and not a natural thing.

And their wills are full 
Already of the worst and ancient custom, 
Always an enemy of the truth. 
You will try your luck 
Among the few magnanimous ones, whom good pleases: 
Of them, who reassures me? 
I go crying peace, peace, peace.

...fierce in another thought just as if by fantasy <note>In Renaissance psychology, "fantasy" or "imagination" referred to the mental faculty of creating or recalling images in the mind's eye</note>; now he feared, now he hoped, and now he rejoiced; he felt melancholy for the desired thing. And as in his thinking he was varied, so also in his walking through this mountain: now through one [path], now through another, according as his various thoughts spurred him; and it delighted him much when he found some similarity in places to those where the power <note>original: "la forza"; likely referring to the site where he was first struck by the power of Love</note> was centered, as if he had found some solitary shore, some stream, or some fountain, or some valley between two small hills, often changing into various passions as his thought varied.

¶ THROUGH HIGH. In the 2nd stanza it is shown that the same thing happened to Petrarch that usually happens to every lover: that in order to be able to think better and more freely on the beloved thing, they willingly find themselves in solitary places, remembering past times and continual labors with various passions; and together with fear, still having some hope for the future of being able to obtain that which first escaped them, it appearing to them that they are dearer to the beloved lady than to themselves, inasmuch as they, to escape from labors and the bitterest displeasures, would desire death, and perhaps the beloved thing <note>the beloved woman</note> desires the life of such people; just as Petrarch gives us to understand that she, although she did not yield to him, was desirous of his life, showing [this...]

that in his heart, through contemplation, he took such <note>delight</note> from it that he would have desired nothing else through any sensory act; for it seemed to him that seeing her in all those places bore a resemblance to the regions of the Sorgue and of Avignon, and she seemed to him as beautiful as she was when he first saw her in her first flower <note>i.e., in the bloom of her youth</note>.

<margin>S</margin> **I HAVE HER MORE.** In the present 4th stanza, he demonstrates through remembrance the ways in which he used to see Madonna Laura in the time when he was in that region; that is, that at times he saw her bathing in summer, and at times sitting on the grass or leaning against the trunk of a beech tree like a most white goddess appearing in a cloud, far more beautiful than Helen, daughter of Tyndareus and Leda <note>In Greek mythology, Helen of Troy was the daughter of Leda and often cited as the standard of supreme beauty</note>: and that like a star whose radiant eyes covered her, no differently than the rays of the sun, showing himself to have been much more accustomed to finding himself in this fantasy the more he found himself in solitary places: and then, when he was taken from such an imagination and returned to himself, all the pleasure he had thus thought of changed into very bitter displeasure, seeing himself deprived of his accustomed delight in such a way that he remained cold as a block of ice.

<margin>T</margin> **WHERE NO OTHER.** The 5th stanza declares how Petrarch’s gaze was always toward the northern regions; for while staying in Lombardy, he looked toward the Alps and, seeing the Great Saint Bernard <note>A high mountain pass in the Western Alps</note>—a mountain higher than any other and not obstructed from being the most prominent peak among the other surrounding mountains—he said in his heart: "O wretched me, beyond that mountain in the lands of Avignon my sweet Madonna Laura is found." And he shed many tears, seeing the great distance of the path that lay between her and him, it seeming to him that perhaps in those parts he was still sighed for by her.

<margin>V</margin> **SONG, BEYOND.** The 6th and final stanza, as a conclusion, signifies that our enamored poet, although in body he was in Lombardy, was always in his imagination by the small river Sorgue near his beloved Madonna Laura, in that clear and joyous air and among those fragrant laurels <note>A pun on Laura's name, which Petrarch frequently associated with the laurel tree (Lauro)</note>.

### STANZA IIII.

**I** have many times (now who will believe me?)
In the clear water, and upon the green grass
Seen her alive; and in the trunk of a beech;
And in a white cloud, so fashioned, that Leda
Would have surely said her daughter was surpassed;
Like a star that the sun covers with its ray:
And the more in a wild
Place I find myself, and on a more deserted shore,
The more beautiful my thought shadows her forth:
Then when the truth clears away
That sweet error; right there I sit
As cold dead stone on living stone
In the manner of a man who thinks, and weeps, and writes.

### STANZA V.

**W**here the shadow of another mountain does not touch;
Toward the highest and most open ridge
An intense desire is wont to draw me;
Thence my losses to measure with my eyes
I begin; and meanwhile, weeping, I vent
The dense cloud of sorrow from my heart
Then, when I gaze and think
How much air separates me from that beautiful face,
Which is always so near to me and so far:
Then to myself, very softly,
"What are you doing, wretch? Perhaps in that place
Even now your absence is sighed for":
And in this thought the soul takes breath.

### SONNETTO CI.

<margin>Francesco X</margin>
<margin>
¶ SINCE THE In this hundred and first sonnet, which in itself is quite clear, he demonstrates the great displeasure Petrarch felt for having come from Avignon to Lombardy. He signifies that two comforts remained to him: one was the weeping that he frequently did, and in such a way he somewhat unburdened himself. The other was gazing upon the portrait of the noble person of Lady Laura made by Master Simon of Siena <note>original: "Symon da Siena"; this refers to the famous Sienese painter Simone Martini (c. 1284–1344), who painted a now-lost portrait of Laura for Petrarch</note>: who he says was a more noble painter than Zeuxis <note>A famous Greek painter of the 5th century BCE</note>: more than those two most noble sculptors Praxiteles and Phidias: by whom there are still two most noble marble horses with two naked youths, wonderfully proportioned and sculpted with singular skill and grace in Rome in the place called Monte Cavallo <note>Now the Quirinal Hill in Rome, where the ancient statues of the Dioscuri (the "Horse Tamers") stand</note>.
</margin>

**S**ince the path to mercy is closed to me;
Through a desperate way I am distanced
From the eyes, where (I know not by what deed)
The reward for all my faith was placed.
**I** feed my heart with sighs, for it asks nothing else;
And I live on tears, born to weep:
Nor do I grieve for this, because in such a state
Weeping is sweeter than others believe:
**A**nd I hold fast to only one image;
Which if not Zeuxis, or Praxiteles, or Phidias,
But a better master, and of higher genius <note>Petrarch suggests that the "master" who created Laura—God or Nature—surpasses the greatest artists of antiquity</note>
**W**hat Scythia <note>A region north of the Black Sea, used here to represent extreme cold</note> can assure me, or what Numidia <note>An ancient North African kingdom, used here to represent extreme heat</note>,
If, not yet satisfied by my unworthy exile,
Envy finds me out even thus hidden.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ SINCE THE PATH. In this sonnet the poet Master Francesco shows how he was in discord with his lady and had departed from Avignon and gone to the Sorgue where, staying there, he continually wept. *Than Zeuxis or Praxiteles or Phidias*: these were excellent sculptors, whose work is still found in Rome in a place called "the Horse." *What Scythia can assure me or what Numidia*: as if to say, no place, cold or hot, can assure me that I will not burn [with love] even being so hidden. Envy never wants to stay at peace and still goads me in my thoughts of love.

### SONETTO CII.

<margin>Antonio Y</margin>
<margin>
¶ I WOULD SING In the present hundred and second sonnet, the poet describes the marvelous sweetness he would feel if he found himself where he could see Lady Laura with that most beautiful face, white and crimson like white roses, and with those most white teeth that seemed like ivory, demonstrating the contrary passions of lovers who now sing and now heave sighs: now they have fiery desires, letting it be understood that Lady Laura is also in similar desires: and that she should not delay in repenting for not having pleased him when she could; he also touches upon the fact that although, through the most heavy troubles of love, he should reasonably desire death as desperate people usually do: nonetheless, for the pleasure he feels in this imagination of his, he is content to live.
</margin>

**I** would sing of love in such a new way;
That from her hard side a thousand sighs a day
I would draw by force, and a thousand high desires
I would rekindle in her frozen mind;
**A**nd I would see her beautiful face change often
And her eyes grow wet, and turn more piteously,
As does one who for another’s suffering
And for their own error, when it is no longer useful, repents;
**A**nd the crimson roses amidst the snow
Moved by her breath, and the disclosure of the ivory
That turns to marble anyone who looks at it closely;
**A**nd all that; because in this brief life
I do not regret myself; rather I glory
In being preserved for this later season.

<margin>Francesco</margin>
¶ I WOULD SING. The poet Master Francesco speaks as if someone were asking him if he had the spirit to mitigate the hardness of Lady Laura's heart with his verses, and he says that he would do this and all that follows. *And the crimson roses amidst the snow*: by the crimson roses the poet means the blushing color of Lady Laura making the white face turn pale for love of him; by the *ivory* he means her teeth, which were like ivory.

# SONNET 103.

<margin>Francesco <note>This refers to the commentator Francesco Filelfo, a 15th-century humanist</note></margin>
¶ IF IT IS NOT LOVE. In this 104th <note>original: "ciiij"; the text likely contains a printer's error, as it resides under the heading for Sonnet 103</note> sonnet, Petrarch clearly demonstrates through his own experience that no passion is more foolish or filled with more diverse and clashing contradictions than love. Because many people are used to defining love in a certain way, he wishes to declare the opposite, proving it by its effects. These effects are always harsh, or rather, more than death itself; and it is even worse because its fierce and intolerable torment seems sweet. Whereas a man should be content when he has what he wants, here it is the opposite: on one hand, he does not wish to remove himself from this passion (though he could if he truly wanted to), and on the other hand, he weeps and laments. Should someone say, "But I am in love despite myself and can do nothing else," Petrarch responds that if this were so, his will would count for nothing. He adds that love is like a continuous death and a "gracious ill," in which a man sometimes falls in love despite himself, and other times falls in love willingly; yet on the other hand, he is pained against his will. Man is caught in such errors and anxiety that he himself does not know what he wants. He takes pleasure in what he should not, and similarly, he takes displeasure in what should give him pleasure—like one who shivers in mid-summer and feels too hot in winter.

<margin>Antonio <note>Likely Antonio da Tempo, another early scholar of Petrarch’s work</note></margin>
¶ IF IT IS NOT LOVE. Master Francesco asks a question like a man doubtful of his own state, asking what it is that he feels—as if to say, "if it is not love, I myself do not know what it might be." This contains notable insights.

*If it is not love, what then is this I feel?*
*But if it is love, by God, what kind of thing and of what quality?*
*If good, whence comes the bitter, mortal effect?*
*If evil, whence is every torment so sweet?*
*If I burn by my own will, whence the weeping and lament?*
*If against my will, what does lamenting avail?*
*O living death; o delightful ill,*
*How can you have such power over me, if I do not consent?*
*And if I do consent, I grieve with great injustice:*
*Among such contrary winds, in a fragile boat,*
*I find myself on the high seas without a rudder,*
*So light in wisdom, so burdened with error,*
*That I myself do not know what I want;*
*And I shiver in mid-summer, while burning in winter.*

---

# SONNET 104.

<margin>Francesco A.</margin>
¶ LOVE HAS. The present 104th sonnet declares, through four similes, the destruction of Master Francesco’s heart. His thoughts were like a target set for the striking of arrows; and because of the lovely face of the beloved lady, which is like the sun, he consumed himself like snow placed before it; and because of his desire for her, he melted away like wax in the fire; and thirdly, because she was as haughty and proud as the wind, he was destroyed like mist. This all proceeded from her beauty, which included her beautiful singing and her polished speech—that is, her sharp and noble wit and intellect.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ LOVE HAS PLACED. The poet recounts the tearing apart that love performs on him. He makes a comparison that he is before love as a target is to an arrow, as wax is to fire, as snow is to the sun, and as mist is to the wind. For all these things are passive recipients of an active force, just as he is to love. Then he turns to speak to his lady.

*Love has placed me like a target for an arrow,*
*As snow to the sun, as wax to the fire,*
*And as mist to the wind; and I am already hoarse*
*Calling for mercy, Lady; and you do not care.*
*From your eyes issued the mortal blow,*
*Against which neither time nor place avails me;*
*From you alone proceeds (and it seems a game to you)*
*The sun, the fire, and the wind, which make me so.*
*My thoughts are arrows, and your face a sun,*
*And desire a fire: together with these weapons*
*Love pierces me, dazzles me, and destroys me;*
*And the angelic singing, and the words*
*With that sweet breath <note>original: "dolce spirto"; can also mean "sweet spirit"</note>, from which I cannot defend myself,*
*Are the breeze <note>original: "L'aura"; a characteristic pun on the name of Petrarch's muse, Laura</note>, before which my life flees.*

# SONNET 105.

> I find no peace, and have no war to wage;
> And I fear, and hope; and burn, and am like ice;
> And I fly above the heavens and lie on the earth;
> And I grasp nothing, and embrace the whole world.
> One has me in prison who neither opens nor shuts,
> Nor holds me as their own nor loosens the snare;
> And Love does not slay me, nor unchain me;
> Nor wishes me alive, nor draws me from trouble.
> I see without eyes, and have no tongue, yet I cry out;
> And I long to perish, and I beg for help;
> And I hate myself, and I love another:
> I feed on grief, and weeping, I laugh:
> Death and life are equally displeasing to me.
> I am in this state, my lady, because of you.

<margin>Francesco <note>Francesco Filelfo, a 15th-century humanist scholar whose commentaries often accompanied Petrarch's poems.</note></margin>
<margin>B</margin>
¶ I FIND NO PEACE. The contrary pains of amorous troubles are clearly demonstrated in this 105th sonnet. Because Petrarch loved My Lady Laura, and she sometimes showed him a kind face and spoke good words to him, she offered him some hope of his desired end, yet she could or did nothing further. Therefore he says that he "finds no peace" with her insofar as his desires are not fulfilled, yet he "has no war to wage" because she does not show herself to be an enemy. He fears not obtaining what he desires, yet he still has some hope. Thus he burns with desire and is cold with fear. Sometimes he feels confident and his spirit is lifted by a certain hope; at other times, as if he "lay on the ground," he loses heart. It seems to him no different to obtain her than if he "embraced the whole world," and then he finds nothing in his hands, feeling as though he has been mocked by his own hope. Then, manifesting the cause of such contradiction, he says that just as the heart might be in a prison that is neither closed nor open, so too is he in the power of the beloved lady. She neither grants him leave nor does what he wishes; she does not hold him as her lover, nor does she give him license to depart; she does not wish him dead, nor does she free him from his chains; she does not care for his life, nor does she pull him out of his distress. Because of this, he is so overwhelmed by passion that he cannot see as he would wish, nor speak as he ought. He wishes to die and yet asks for help to live. He hates himself and loves Lady Laura. Now he weeps, now he laughs, depending on whether he receives a gracious or a cruel look. He concludes that death displeases him because he still hopes to obtain her eventually, and yet life also displeases him when he loses that hope.

<margin>Antonio <note>Antonio da Tempo, a 14th-century judge and poet known for his work on Italian metrics and commentary.</note></margin>
¶ I FIND NO PEACE. Master Francesco speaks in this sonnet to his Lady Laura and presents several extremes regarding natural things. He says that he finds himself in these contradictions solely for the love of his lady; this is the literal meaning of the text.

¶ WHAT MORE. In this 29th canzone, through various and marvelous things found in diverse parts of the world, the troubled state of our enamored poet is demonstrated through charming similarities. Petrarch begins by showing himself to be like the Phoenix. This bird, having reached five hundred years of age, gathers various fragrant spices in the deserts of Egypt; having placed herself among them, she turns her eyes toward the sun and beats her wings so much that, from the heat of the solar rays, a fire is ignited in those spices. Thus she burns herself up among them. A short time after she has burned, a worm is born from her ashes, from which another Phoenix newly rises and thus recovers a new life. In a similar way... Petrarch, gazing at the face of Ma[donna]...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s poetry, transitioning from Sonnet 105 to the beginning of Canzone 135. The text provides a line-by-line explanation of the poet’s use of natural history and mythology to describe his love for Laura.</meta>

...Lady Laura, he dies from too much desire; then, by her showing him a somewhat cheerful face, he seems almost reborn through hope because of that sweet, gracious effect.

<margin>Antonio <note>Likely Antonio da Tempo, a 14th-century judge and grammarian who wrote early commentaries on Petrarch.</note></margin> ¶ **WHICH IS MORE DIVERSE AND STRANGE:** In this song, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> makes five comparisons between himself and certain strange things. The first is the **phoenix**, which is a bird unique in its species in the world; it lives for four hundred and sixty years and dwells in the East where the heat is great. Upon dying, it is renewed. He says he does the same, for in his will he is solitary like the phoenix; and as this phoenix, in renewing itself, turns toward the eyes of the sun and is burned, and from the remains that stay it is reborn, so he does the same, turning himself toward the eyes of My Lady Laura. Thus, in dying, he is renewed and born like the phoenix. **A stone so bold.** The second comparison is taken from the **magnet** <note>original: "calamita"</note> which is born in the Indian Sea and draws iron to itself; so he says that My Lady Laura’s eyes have such power over him that they draw him in their own way. **In the far West.** The third comparison the poet brings in is of the **basilisk**, which has such power in its eyes that it kills anyone who looks at it fixedly, and this is through the hidden power it has in its eyes; and so he says that he dies whenever his lady looks at him with those shining eyes. **A spring has Epirus.** The fourth comparison Master Francesco makes is to a spring found in Epirus <note>A region in Greece; this spring was famously said to ignite unlit wood but extinguish torches.</note> which is extremely cold, yet it ignites wood that is without fire, and extinguishes wood that already has fire within it. He says that he does the same: Love ignited his heart which was extinguished and without heat, but now that it is so, it remains inflamed and burns at every hour. **Beyond all our shores.** The fifth he takes from two springs that are in strange parts: whoever drinks from one lives a long time, and whoever drinks from the other dies laughing. **Love, who still guides me:** Master Francesco turns his speech to Love. **We see when the sun joins the Bull:** that is, when Spring begins, because that is the time of Spring, which is around the 13th of April. **Whoever might spy, little song:** the poet speaks to his song, which by itself avoids all other people—that is, the "L" <note>Referring to Laura</note> for whom he alone lives in solitude.

<margin>Francesco <note>Francesco Filelfo, the humanist scholar mentioned on the previous page.</note></margin> <margin>D</margin> ¶ **A STONE.** The second stanza demonstrates that the poet is so drawn by My Lady Laura—and his heart stolen by her with many cries and tears—just as iron is drawn by the magnet. In the Indian Sea, where there is a reef of such stone, it is often said to happen that iron nails are drawn and as if stolen from ships by the natural force of that magnet, so that the wooden vessels are accustomed to perish there; just as he also perishes from too many hardships.

<margin>E</margin> ¶ **IN THE FAR.** In the third stanza, he likens his beloved lady to that small beast found in the far regions of the West, which is named the **Catoblepas** <note>A mythical Ethiopian creature; the name literally means "to look downwards."</note>: which means "looks downward" because it carries its head to the ground. It appears that when one catches its gaze through the eyes of that beast, they receive no small injury of harm or pain, or even death. He says, therefore, that this happens to him with My Lady Laura; though she appears to be a beast not only gentle, but even angelic and innocent, when she is gazed upon by Master Francesco, she makes him die for love.

### STANZA II.

> By the stealing of my heart—which was once a hardened thing,
> And held me as one, though now I am divided and scattered:

> Flesh than iron—oh, my cruel fate!
> For being in the flesh, I see myself drawn to the shore
> By a living and sweet magnet.

To be, whatever gaze might turn toward her:
Provided that one does not look into her eyes;
The rest can be seen with safety:
But I, incautious and grieving,
Always run toward my own harm; and I know well how much
I have suffered from it, and how much I expect: but greedy
Will, which is blind and deaf,
So carries me away, that her beautiful, holy face,
And her lovely eyes will be the cause of my death,
Because of this innocent, angelic beast.

### STANZA IV

**T**here rises in the south
A fountain, which takes its name from the sun,
Which by its nature is accustomed
To boil at night, and to be cold during the day;
And it cools down so much,
The higher the sun climbs, and the closer it is:
So it happens to me myself;
Who am a fountain of tears, and a dwelling [of grief]:
When the beautiful, adorned light,
Which is my sun, moves away; and sad and alone
Are my eyes, and it is dark night for them;
I burn then: but if the gold,
And the rays I see appearing of the living sun;
All inside and out I feel myself change,
And I lie frozen, so cold do I become.

### STANZA V

**E**pirus <note>A region in northwestern Greece.</note> has another fountain;
Of which it is written, that though it is cold,
Every extinguished torch
It ignites, and puts out whichever it finds lit.
My soul, which was not yet
Attacked by the fire of love;
Approaching a little
To that cold one, for whom I always sigh,
Burned entirely; and a martyrdom
Like it was never seen by sun nor star:
For it would have moved a heart of marble to pity;
After she had set it aflame <gloss>it (be:</gloss>
Her frozen and beautiful virtue extinguished it.

***

**THERE RISES IN THE...** Similarly, in this fourth stanza, he compares Lady Laura's beauty to the sun, and himself to that "Solar Fountain" <note>This refers to the Fountain of the Sun at the Oasis of Siwa, described by ancient geographers like Herodotus and Pliny.</note> which Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, a Roman author and naturalist.</note> writes is in the southern parts: which boils so much more at night the further the sun is from it, and at dawn begins to cool down, becoming more frozen the higher the sun rises. He says, therefore, that the same thing happens to him: that the further he is from Lady Laura, the more he burns with the excessive anxieties of love; but when he is near her, due to excessive anxiety, he becomes cold as if stunned. The rest is clear.

**ANOTHER FOUNTAIN.** Persevering in this fifth stanza, he shows Lady Laura to be similar to that fountain in Epirus: which, being cold, extinguishes all the torches that are lit and ignites all those that are extinguished. So he says his beloved Lady Laura has done: for she, being of the coldest spirit and without any amorous flame, has ignited Petrarch’s soul with love for her—his soul which before that time was without the flame of love. And now, the heart being ignited, she extinguishes it, and being extinguished, she ignites it, according to how she gives a pleasant look; and when she did not show favor to him, she extinguished every fiery desire.

**THROUGH ALL...** In the present sixth stanza, he compares himself to two fountains that are in the Fortunate Isles <note>An ancient name for the Canary Islands; legends spoke of two springs there: one of laughter and one of tears.</note>; whoever drinks from one dies while laughing, but whoever drinks from the other escapes such misfortune. So he says it happens to him: that at times he takes such pleasure from some good sign of love he has seen in Lady Laura that he would burst with laughter; were it not that a little later—as is usually the case with the inconstancy of women, who have their brains in their heels <note>A dismissive Renaissance idiom for flightiness or lack of reason.</note>—his beloved lady, showing him a disdainful face, offers him such affliction that it made him weep, and thus pleasure was tempered with displeasure.

### SONNET CVI

May flame from heaven rain down upon your tresses,
O wicked one; you who from the river <note>The Rhône in Avignon.</note> and from the acorns <note>A reference to humble beginnings or perhaps the della Rovere family, though here symbolizing poverty.</note>

A nest of treachery in which is hatched
Whatever evil is spread through the world today,
A slave to wine, to beds, and to food,
In which lust performs its ultimate test.
Through your chambers young girls and old men

With bellows, and with fire, and with mirrors.
Truly you were not raised on feathers in the shade,
But naked to the wind, and barefoot among the thorns;
Now you live so that the stench of it reaches God.

¶ MAY FLAME FROM HEAVEN. In this sonnet, he curses and reviles a Florentine woman whose name is not known for certain, nor even what family she belonged to. Some say she was called Monna Contessina, and that she was from the house or family of the Medici <note>This is a historically dubious claim, as the Medici were not yet prominent in this way during Petrarch's time.</note>. This response so displeased Petrarch that in revilement of her he immediately wrote this sonnet. Because the poem is clear enough on its own, I will not expand further.

¶ GREEDY Babylon. In this 107th sonnet, the poet inveighs against the vices of Rome <note>Though the court was in Avignon, Petrarch and his commentators often used "Rome" to signify the Church or the Papacy's true rightful home.</note> just as in the sonnet written above; and he did so at the time he wrote (as one can consider) those letters without a title <note>Petrarch’s *Liber sine nomine* (Book without a Name), a series of letters criticizing the Papacy.</note> which are all against the vices of the Roman court, which in those times was in Avignon. The poet calls her Babylon to denote a greater fullness of error, because in Babylon every discord was first found to burn. When he says **new Sultan**, he wishes as if to prophesy that their temporal empire will yet be taken from them for their abominations. **A single seat will be made in Baghdad**, a place according to some in Florence, so-called; others say Rome, which pleases me more, because such things ought to be done in Rome rather than Florence, as Rome is the head of his seat; and this would do—

¶ **Greedy Babylon has filled her sack:** the poet continues his response against Rome, calling her Babylon to denote a greater fullness of errors. **But yet a new Sultan:** here the poet almost means to prophesy that the temporal state will be taken from her. **A single seat that shall be in Baghdad:** that is, under the canopy <note>A pun on "Baldacco" (Baghdad) and "baldacchino" (the ceremonial canopy used by the Pope).</note> where the Pope goes. **And her tower-keepers burned without as within:** they shall be burned by justice just as they burn within from sodomy and luxury. **Beautiful souls:** he means to say that it is necessary for the world to be renewed and return to the first age as it was in the time of Caesar Octavian, under whom virtue had such grace and beginning.

<meta>This page transitions from the political and moral critiques of the previous poems into a sequence of more introspective and lyrical pieces. It covers Sonnet 111, which uses the metaphor of a moth to describe Petrarch’s attraction to Laura, and the opening stanzas of Sestina 1 (Canzone 30), where Petrarch uses the imagery of the laurel tree to discuss his unyielding devotion.</meta>

# SONNET 111.

As sometimes in the warm season, 
A simple moth accustomed to the light 
Flies into the eyes of others for its own pleasure, 
Whence it happens that it dies, and others grieve: 
So I always run to my fatal sun 
Of those eyes, from which such sweetness comes to me; 
For Love does not prize the bridle of reason, 
And he who discerns is conquered by him who wills: 
And I see well how much they [the eyes] despise me; 
And I know that I shall truly die from it, 
For my strength cannot prevail against the anguish; 
But Love so sweetly dazzles me 
That I pity another’s annoyance and not my own harm, 
And blind, my soul consents to its own death.

<margin>**Jerome P.**</margin>
¶ AS SOMETIMES. With a most appropriate comparison, our graceful poet demonstrates his love in this 111th sonnet: he says how the moth is accustomed in the summer season to fly into the light of a candle, and as it becomes used to flying into the eyes of others it dies there: so he says it happens to him, going so often to see the eyes of Lady Laura; it is clear enough that it needs no other explanation.

<margin>**Antonio**</margin>
¶ AS SOMETIMES in the warm season. From a comparison, the poet Messer Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch.</note> likens himself to the moth, which is otherwise called a *zenzala* <note>original: "zenzala." While this usually means a mosquito in modern Italian, the commentator uses it here to describe a small, troublesome insect attracted to light or moisture.</note>, which is a troublesome little animal especially in summer, which is greedy for light so that, always running toward the light of the eyes, it comes to its own trouble; so he says it happens to him, going so often to see the eyes of his lady. And he who serves most is conquered by he who wills: that is, by Love who thus wishes to force reason.

---

# SONG 30.

To the sweet shade of the beautiful leaves, 
Thus fleeing a pitiless light, 
Which even down here burned me from the third heaven <note>The "third heaven" refers to the sphere of Venus, the planet of love, according to the Ptolemaic system of the universe.</note>, 
And was already clearing the hills of snow— 
The amorous breeze that renews the season; 
And herbs and branches were flowering through the slopes.

<margin>**Jerome Q.**</margin>
¶ TO THE SWEET. In this 30th song <note>This is technically Petrarch's first Sestina, a complex poetic form consisting of six stanzas of six lines each where the end-words repeat in a specific pattern.</note>, Messer Francesco speaks: having departed from Lady Laura because of the pain he had from her eyes, in the springtime he composed this song being in a solitary place; [the light] that even down here burned from the third heaven, that is, by the force of Love in which he reigns: because it is the place of Venus his mother, so honored by the supreme light: that is, by Phoebus <note>Phoebus Apollo, the sun god.</note> who loved the laurel out of respect for Daphne, as narrated above: he says that other trees change their condition from year to year except the laurel, because it is loved by Phoebus.

<margin>**Antonio**</margin>
¶ TO THE SWEET shade of the beautiful leaves. Having departed, Messer Francesco, from Lady Laura because of the pain he had from her eyes. In the springtime he made this moral song being in a solitary place. Which even down here burned from the third heaven: that is, by the force of love in which he reigns: because there is the place of Venus his mother, so honored by the supreme light: that is, by Phoebus who loved the laurel out of respect for Daphne as is read above in many places; and he says that other trees from year to year change their condition: but the laurel does not change: because it is a friend to Phoebus.

# STANZA II.

The world never saw such graceful branches, 
Nor did the wind ever move such green leaves, 
As they appeared to me in that first season; 
So that, fearing the burning light, 
I did not wish for the shade of hills as my refuge, 
But for the plant most favored in heaven <note>The Laurel, which was sacred to Apollo and symbolizes Laura.</note>.

<margin>**Jerome R.**</margin>
¶ NEVER SAW. In this second stanza he says he never saw such graceful branches: that is, such a graceful lady as Laura: and such is her splendor that he has not sought nor seeks another refuge: that is, any woman other than her.

S ¶ A LAUREL. In this stanza, one can understand it in two ways: either that the laurel with which poets are crowned <note>The laurel wreath was the traditional crown for poets and victors in antiquity, revived in the Renaissance.</note> turned him away from common opinion—that is, by following poetic studies—or truly that the virtue of Lady Laura, because he was in love with her, turned him away from many other enticements <note>original: "illecebritade," meaning charms or worldly temptations.</note>.

### STANZA . III.

> A laurel defended me then from the sky:
> Whence, often longing for its beautiful branches,
> Since then I have gone through woods and over hills:
> Nor did I ever find a trunk or leaves
> So honored by the light from above:
> That they did not change their quality with time.

---

<margin>
T ¶ THEREFORE. In this fourth stanza, he continues—either truly through poetry or through his love for Lady Laura—to always follow where it seems he is called by heaven: that is, by his destiny.
</margin>

### STANZA . IIII.

> Therefore, more firm ever from time to time,
> Following where I heard myself called from the sky,
> And guided by a sweet and clear light,
> I returned always devoted to the first branches,
> Both when the leaves are scattered on the ground,
> And when the sun makes the hills turn green.

---

<margin>
V ¶ WOODS. In this fifth stanza, the poet wishes to amend his love, saying that to the stones, fields, rivers, and hills, and all of creation that changes with time, he has asked for pardon so that he might flee those branches where he was ensnared <note>original: "inviscato," literally caught in birdlime, a sticky substance used to trap birds; a common metaphor for being trapped by desire.</note>.
</margin>

### STANZA . V.

> Woods, stones, fields, rivers, and hills,
> All that is created, time conquers and changes;
> Wherefore I beg pardon of these leaves,
> If, after the sky has revolved for many years,
> I fled the branches where I was ensnared,
> As soon as I began to see the light.

---

<margin>
X ¶ SO MUCH. <note>An ink blot on the original manuscript partially obscures this section.</note> In this sixth stanza, he says that the beauty of Lady Laura pleased him so much that he passed many hills—that is, time—to be able to fulfill his desire; but afterward, as he perceives the brevity of life, he takes <unclear>the path</unclear> of virtue: that is, toward heaven.
</margin>

### STANZA . VI.

> So much did that sweet light first please me,
> That I passed over great hills with much delight,
> To be able to approach the beloved branches;
> Now the brevity of life, and the place, and the time
> Show another path to go to heaven,
> And to bear fruit: not just flowers and leaves.

---

<margin>
Y ¶ ANOTHER Love. In this seventh and final stanza <note>The "commiato" or "envoi," a short concluding stanza common in Italian verse forms.</note>, he says that in order to ascend to heaven, he must love differently and hold to other paths than those held in the love of worldly women.
</margin>

### STANZA . VII.

> Another love, other leaves, and another light,
> Another climbing to heaven by other hills
> I seek (for it is indeed time) and other branches.

Z ¶ WHEN. In this 112th sonnet, the poet speaks to his lady, telling her how much sweetness he feels from her speech; then he speaks of her in the third person, describing how she comes to him in a vision all through the night. It seems he saw her seated in a garden, making a lap with her knees, and this is what he means when he says she sat "within"; he says this for the sake of propriety, not wishing to speak more plainly of her posture as she sat.

### SONNET CXIII

**N**or did I ever see the sun rise so beautiful,
even when the sky was most free of clouds;
Nor after rain did I see the celestial bow <note>The "celestial bow" is the rainbow.</note>
Vary its many colors through the air;
**A**s many as were the flaming transformations
On the day I took up the amorous burden,
That face, to which (and I am stingy in my speech)
No mortal thing could be compared.
**I** saw Love, who turned those beautiful eyes
So sweetly, that every other sight from then on
Began to appear dark to me.
**S**ennuccio, I saw him and the bow he stretched,
Such that my life was never safe again,
And yet it is so eager to see it once more.

<margin>
Hiero. A
¶ NOR SO. Master Francesco Petrarch writes this 113th sonnet to his companion Sennuccio <note>Sennuccio del Bene (c. 1275–1349) was a Florentine poet and close friend of Petrarch.</note> of whom mention was made above, and through a beautiful comparison he praises his Lady Laura, saying that he never saw the sun rise so colorful, nor the celestial bow vary in more colors after the rain, as the beautiful Laura was transformed on the day he began to follow her.
</margin>

<margin>
Anto.
¶ NOR SO BEAUTIFUL THE SUN. Master Francesco makes a comparison, saying that he never saw the sun rise so colorful, nor the virgin bow <note>The rainbow, often associated with Iris or the Virgin Mary in later interpretations.</note> of so many varied colors as his lady was transformed on the day he began to follow her; and he writes this sonnet to his most beloved Sennuccio.
</margin>

### SONNET CXIIII

**P**ut me where the sun kills the flowers and the grass,
Or where the ice and the snow conquer him.
Put me where his chariot is temperate and light:
And where those are who return it to us, or those who take it away:
**P**ut me in humble fortune or in proud;
In the sweet serene air, or the dark and heavy:
Put me in the night: in the long day or the brief:
In the mature age or in the unripe:
**P**ut me in heaven: or on earth: or in the abyss;
On a high hill, or in a deep and marshy valley;
A free spirit, or fixed to its limbs:
**P**ut me with obscure fame, or with illustrious;
I shall be what I was, I shall live as I have lived,
Continuing my three-lustrum <term>trilustre</term> <note>A "lustrum" is a period of five years; "trilustre" signifies fifteen years since he first fell in love with Laura.</note> sigh.

<margin>
Hiero. B
¶ PUT ME WHERE THE SUN. Master Francesco wishes to demonstrate to everyone in this 114th sonnet that he was always forced to love: and he speaks, saying: Put me where you wish in the East, in the West, or in the North, for I will always remain in love as I am now. "Free spirit" means either dead or alive. "Trilustri" are fifteen years.
</margin>

<margin>
Anto.
¶ PUT ME WHERE THE SUN KILLS. Master Francesco wishes to demonstrate to everyone that he was always forced to love, and speaks saying: Put me (that is, place me) wherever you wish: that is in the East or in the West or in the North, for I will always be in love as I am now. "Free spirit" means either dead or alive. "Trilustre" means of fifteen years.
</margin>

**O [SOUL] OF BURNING.** In this 115th sonnet, *Master Francesco* speaks, wishing to gain the favor of his lady. He says that if fortune willed that his rhymes were understood throughout the entire world—which he does for her love—they would have filled all four parts of the world. But since that is impossible due to the diversity of languages, at least Italy will hear them, which he describes most elegantly in a single verse.

<margin>
Antonio
</margin>
**O [SOUL] OF BURNING virtue.** *Master Francesco* says to the lady, wishing to gain her favor, that if his rhymes were understood as far away as he knows for her love, they would have filled all four parts of the world. But since that is impossible, at least Italy will hear them, which is divided by the Apennine mountains and surrounded by the Adriatic Sea and the Tyrrhenian Sea, and also toward France by the mountains. Thule <note>original: "tyle"; a mythical northern land representing the edge of the world</note> is a river in the west; the Ebro is in the east.

## SONNET 115.

> O noble soul, adorned and warm with burning virtue,
> For whom I write so many pages;
> O once the sole and complete dwelling of honesty,
> A tower founded on high valor and steadfast;
> O flame; O roses scattered in a sweet fold
> Of living snow, in which I mirror and refine myself;
> O pleasure, from which I lift my wings toward that beautiful face,
> Which shines above all that the sun warms;
> Of your name; if my rhymes were understood
> So far away; if I could fill Thule and the Bactrus <note>The Bactrus (modern Balkh River in Afghanistan) represented the eastern edge of the known world</note>,
> The Don, the Nile; Atlas, Olympus, and Calpe <note>Calpe is the Rock of Gibraltar, the southern limit</note>,
> Since I cannot carry it into all four
> Parts of the world; that beautiful country shall hear it;
> Which the Apennines divide, and the sea and the Alps surround.

---

<margin>
Hieronymo
D
</margin>
**WHEN THE WILL.** In this 116th sonnet, the poet narrates what happens to him when his will is transported by desire and by hope, which are the "sighs of lovers." Then he understands his soul, and she appears so troubled that he remains lost and conquered by it. But "cold": he says that nevertheless, sometimes when he was so lost in hope, she showed herself to be merciful.

<margin>
Antonio
</margin>
**WHEN THE WILL:** Here the poet narrates what happens to him when he is transported by desire and by hope, for those are the sighs of lovers; then he understands his soul and she appears so troubled that he remains lost and conquered. But "cold": he says that even sometimes when he was so lost in hope, she showed herself to be merciful.

## SONNET 116.

> When my will, which with two burning spurs <note>The "two spurs" are often interpreted as Desire and Hope</note>
> And with a hard bit leads and governs me,
> Transgresses from time to time the usual law
> To make my spirits content in part;
> It finds one who reads the fears and the darings
> Of the deep heart within the mind;
> And sees Love, who corrects his undertakings,
> Flashing in her troubled, piercing eyes:
> Wherefore, like one who fears the blow
> Of angry Jove, it draws back;
> For great fear curbs great desire:
> But cold fire and fearful hope
> Of the soul, which shines through like glass,
> Sometimes her sweet sight makes serene.

**NOT THE TICINO.** To demonstrate that *Master Francesco* loved Lady Laura ardently, he says in this 117th sonnet that there is no river nor tree that could extinguish a single spark of his burning, except that river where he had planted the "Laurel" <term>Lauro: a pun on Laura’s name and the poetic laurel</term> by the Sorgue <note>A river in Provence where Petrarch lived in Vaucluse</note>; thus he shows how he has grown to plant the laurel so deeply within himself, and this is for the love of the said Lady Laura.

As much as a beautiful river, which always weeps with me
With the small tree, which I adorn and celebrate in rhymes
This one relief I find against the assaults
Of Love; wherefore it is necessary that I live armed
In this life, which passes with such great leaps:
So may the beautiful laurel grow on the cool bank;
And let him who writes down the weeping, and the graceful and high thoughts
In the sweet shade to the sound of the water.

### CANZONE, XXXI.

From time to time the angelic figure
And the sweet smile become less harsh to me,
And the air of the beautiful face
And of the graceful eyes less dark.
What are these sighs doing with me now,
Which were born of grief,
And showed outwardly
My anguished and desperate life:
If it happens that I turn my face in that direction
To quiet my heart,
I seem to see Love
Upholding my cause; and giving me aid:
Yet I do not yet find the war finished,
Nor every state of my heart tranquil:
For the more my desire burns me,
The more hope reassures me.

### SONETTO. CXVIII,

What are you doing, soul? What are you thinking? Will we ever have peace?
Will we ever have a truce? Or will we have eternal war?
What will become of us, I do not know: but in that which I discern
In her beautiful eyes, our suffering does not please her.
What use is it, if with those eyes she makes for us
Ice in summer, and fire when it is winter?
Not she; but he who governs them <note>Petrarch refers to the god of Love governing Laura's eyes</note>.
What is this to us, if she sees it, and remains silent?
Sometimes the tongue is silent: and the heart complains
With a loud voice, and with a dry and happy look
One weeps, where others looking on do not see it.
For all this the mind does not find peace <margin>stagnates:</margin>
Breaking the grief, which gathers and stays within her
For a wretched man does not believe in great hope.

<margin>Anto. E</margin>
¶ **NOT THE TICINO, THE PO.** <note>original: "NON thesin po"; a reference to the opening of Sonnet 117 listing rivers that cannot extinguish his fire</note> To demonstrate that **Master Francesco** <note>Petrarch</note> loved ardently: he says in this sonnet that there is no river nor tree that could extinguish a spark of his heat except that river and 그 laurel he had planted upon the bank of the river Sorgue <note>The Sorgue river in Vaucluse, where Petrarch lived</note>. "So may [the laurel] grow" demonstrates that he had planted that laurel himself.

¶ **FROM TIME:** In this 31st song, it seems that our enamored poet had received some good response from his beloved **Lady Laura**, and for joy he makes this noble and amorous ballad. "If it happens that the face [turns]": that is, toward Avignon where **Lady Laura** was: because he made this song when he was at the Sorgue.

<margin>Anto. F</margin>
¶ **FROM TIME to time:** It appears that **Master Francesco** had received some good word from his lady for which he makes this ballad in demonstration of his joy. "If it happens that": that is, toward Avignon where **Lady Laura** was.

<margin>Hiero.</margin>
¶ **WHAT are you doing, soul.** In this 118th sonnet, **Master Francesco** speaks with his soul, asking if he is ever to have peace: then she responds and he asks her again, and again she responds: "in her beautiful eyes our suffering does not please her." That is to say, she does not look willingly upon our suffering. "Not she," says the soul: that is to say, it is not her but Love who rules her. He weeps inside and shows himself happy outside, breaking his heart. The soul says it does not find peace, breaking the grief that gathers within her: it stagnates <note>The marginal "gna" completes "stagna" (stagnates/pools)</note> through the lamentation of the heart. The soul says it finds no peace breaking that grief that gathers in her with that lamenting: because through that she does not hope to find mercy: namely, from **Lady Laura**.

<margin>Anto. G</margin>

"In her beautiful eyes our suffering does not please her": as if to say, she does not look willingly upon our suffering.

H

¶ NO DARK. In this 119th sonnet, Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch</note> makes two graceful comparisons: one of himself, where he compares himself to a pilot fleeing a storm; the other of My Lady Laura’s eyes, which overcome the rays of the sun. Then, looking back to Propertius <note>Sextus Propertius, a Roman elegiac poet</note>, he describes Love as not seeing (blind) but equipped with a quiver, and not being naked—meaning that he cannot see the parts that are hidden for shame—and there he saw all his subject matter, of which he speaks or writes.

# SONETTO. CXIX.

*No tired pilot ever fled from the dark*
*And stormy sea wave into port,*
*As I flee from the dark and turbid thought,*
*Where the great desire spurs and inclines me;*
*Nor did divine light ever overcome mortal sight*
*As my own was overcome by that haughty ray*
*Of the beautiful, sweet, gentle white and black,*
*In which Love gilds and sharpens his arrows.*
*I see him not blind, but with a quiver;*
*Naked, except for what shame veils,*
*A boy with wings, not painted, but alive.*
*From there he shows me what he hides from many:*
*For bit by bit within those beautiful eyes I read*
*All that I say of love, and all that I write.*

<margin>
Antonio
</margin>
¶ NO DARK and stormy sea wave. Master Francesco makes a comparison of himself to a pilot fleeing a storm. He makes a second comparison to the eyes of My Lady Laura, which overcome his own eyes, just as the ray of the sun overcomes human vision, as he shows me. From there: that is <note>original: "i." for "id est"</note>, from her eyes.

# SONETTO. CXX.

<margin>

¶ THIS HUMBLE beast. In this 120th sonnet, Master Francesco describes his own doubtful state, in which My Lady Laura keeps him in uncertainty between fear and hope; she has the heart of a tiger or a bear in regard to her cruelty, but he still hopes to win her through her virtue.

*This humble beast, a heart of tiger or of bear,*
*Who comes in human likeness and an angel's form,*
*In laughter and in tears, between fear and hope,*
*Turns me so that my every state is in doubt.*
*If she does not soon receive me or release me;*
*But still, as she is wont to do, holds me between two,*
*By that which I feel going through my heart like snow,*
*Sweet poison, Love, my life has run its course.*
*My fragile and weary virtue can no longer*
*Suffer so many changes now.*
*For in a moment it burns, freezes, blushes, and turns white,*
*Fleeing, it hopes to end its sorrows;*
*Like one who fails from hour to hour:*
*For he can do nothing, who cannot die.*

<margin>
Antonio
</margin>
¶ THIS humble beast. Master Francesco speaks of his doubtful state in which My Lady Laura keeps him in uncertainty: that is <note>original: "idest"</note>, in doubt; she keeps me between two: that is, between fear and hope; a heart of tiger or bear: here it stands appositively <note>A grammatical term meaning the tiger/bear heart is another way of describing the "humble beast"</note>. Fleeing, it hopes to end its sorrow: that is, that virtue, by fleeing, hopes to escape from suffering.

# SONETTO. CXXI.

<margin>
Hieronymo
K
</margin>
¶ GO, WARM. Master Francesco speaks in this 121st sonnet to his own sighs: saying that they must penetrate the cold heart of My Lady Laura and break the ice that surrounds her, praying that she might have compassion for him, for that beautiful gaze does not extend to my torment, which she does not see.

*Go, warm sighs, to the cold heart:*
*Break the ice that resists pity;*
*And if a mortal prayer is heard in heaven,*
*Let death or mercy be the end of my sorrow.*
*Go, sweet thoughts, speaking out...*

Of that where the beautiful gaze does not reach:
If indeed her harshness, or my star <note>In Renaissance thought, one's "star" refers to their astrological destiny or fate.</note> offends us
We shall be out of hope, and out of error:
It can well be said for you, perhaps not fully,
That our state is restless and dark;
Just as hers is peaceful and serene.
Go secure now, for Love goes with you:
And wicked fortune may well diminish;
If I recognize the air by the signs of my sun <note>Petrarch often uses "his sun" as a metaphor for Laura.</note>.

### SONETTO.CXXII.

**T**he stars, the sky, and the elements in competition
All their arts, and every extreme care
Placed in the living light, in which nature
Mirrors itself, and the sun which elsewhere finds no equal.
**T**he work is so lofty, so graceful, and new;
That mortal gaze is not secure in her;
So much does it seem that love, and sweetness, and grace
Rain beyond measure from those beautiful eyes.
**T**he air struck by their sweet rays
Is inflamed with honesty; and becomes such
That it greatly surpasses our speech and thought.
**N**o base desire is felt there;
But of honor and of virtue. Now when was
Lowly sorrow ever extinguished by supreme beauty?

### SONETTO.CXXIII.

**N**ever were Jove and Caesar so moved
To strike with lightning the one, the other to wound;
That pity would not have extinguished their rages,
And shaken both from their accustomed arms.
**M**y lady was weeping; and my lord <note>Refers to the personification of Love.</note> willed that I be there
To see her, and to hear her laments,
To fill me with sorrow, and with desire,
And to search through my marrow and bones.
**L**ove painted that sweet weeping for me,
Rather, he sculpted it, and those sweet words
He wrote within a diamond in the middle of my heart
**W**here with firm and clever keys
He still returns often to draw out
Rare tears, and long and heavy sighs.

---

<margin>Antonio da Tempo</margin>
**G**O FORTH <note>Original: "CITE," a truncated form of "Uscite."</note> warm sighs. Master Francesco speaks to his sighs, saying that they must penetrate the cold heart of My Lady Laura and break the ice that surrounds her, praying that she might have compassion for him regarding that where her "beautiful gaze does not reach": that is, to my torment which she does not see.

<margin>Hieronymo Squarciafico</margin>
**T**HE stars, the sky. In this 122nd sonnet, Master Francesco, as one entirely conquered by love, gracefully says that if all the stars together with the elements and all their influence and art combined, they could not make a more beautiful woman than his Lady Laura. And in the end, he says that her rays of love come to conquer every other thing: and everything, in respect to them, becomes base.

<margin>Antonio da Tempo</margin>
**T**HE stars, the sky, and the elements in competition. Master Francesco exalts his lady as a divine thing; specifically, he says that the heavens used all their power to create her. "O when was ever": <note>original: "quasi dicat nunquam"</note> as if to say "never." "Surpasses our speech and thought": that is, the thought of your beauties exceeds my ability to write.

<margin>Hieronymo Squarciafico</margin>
**N**EVER WERE. In this 123rd sonnet—it being the common custom of lovers to describe every act of their beloved ladies—Petrarch does so in this sonnet because, My Lady Laura’s mother having died and Master Francesco having seen her weeping so sweetly, he made this sonnet and the three following ones about that weeping, saying how Love willed that he should be there to see her: weeping long and heavy sighs that make me weep when I remember them. Caesar and Jove <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods, and Julius Caesar.</note> would have had pity on her weeping: and he says that when he remembers it, he weeps out of pity.

<margin>Antonio da Tempo</margin>
**N**EVER were Jove or Caesar so moved. My Lady Laura’s mother having died, and Master Francesco having seen her weeping so sweetly, he made this sonnet and the three following ones about that weeping, saying how Love willed that he should be there to see her.
