...to see her weep. Long and heavy sighs that make me weep when I remember them; he says that Caesar and Torquatus <note>Original: "Tor". Likely refers to Titus Manlius Torquatus, a Roman consul known for his sternness; the poet suggests even the harshest men would be moved by Laura's grief.</note> would have had pity for her weeping. He willed to see her and hear her laments: that is, the aforementioned Love willed that I be there to see her. Rare tears and long sighs: as if to say, sometimes remembering them I weep out of pity.

## SONNET 124.

<margin>Hieronymo Squarciafico</margin>
¶ I SAW. In this 124th sonnet, the poet continues narrating the weeping of My Lady Laura and says that aside from that weeping, every other thing seems as nothing to him. A sweeter harmony <term>harmony: original "concento," referring to a musical blending of voices</term> and a concordance of many voices: of such sweetness: that is, because of that weeping.

<margin>Antonio da Tempo</margin>
¶ I SAW on earth. The poet continues narrating the weeping of My Lady Laura and says that aside from that weeping, in everything else he sees nothing. A sweeter harmony and a concordance of many voices. Of such sweetness, namely because of that weeping.

*I saw on earth angelic manners,*
*And celestial beauties unique in the world,*
*Such that remembering them delights and pains me:*
*For all I gaze upon seems dreams, shadows, and smoke.*
*And I saw those two beautiful lights <note>referring to her eyes</note> weep,*
*Which have a thousand times made the sun envious;*
*And I heard words said with sighs,*
*That would make mountains move and rivers stand still.*
*Love, wisdom, valor, pity, and sorrow*
*Made, through weeping, a sweeter harmony*
*Than any other usually heard in the world;*
*And the sky was so intent on that harmony,*
*That one saw not a leaf move on a branch;*
*Such sweetness filled the air and the wind.*

## SONNET 125.

<margin>Hieronymo Squarciafico</margin>
¶ THAT ALWAYS. In this 125th sonnet, the poet still continues as one who could not forget the weeping he had seen from his My Lady Laura, so that speaking he says he often remembers it with great delight. Then when he says "the head," he describes the appearance in which he saw her weeping. Ebony is a black wood and an oriental wood; he calls her lips "red roses" and takes "pearls" to mean her teeth.

<margin>Antonio da Tempo</margin>
¶ THAT ALWAYS bitter. The poet continues speaking of that weeping which he says he often remembers with great delight. "The head" describes the appearance in which he saw her weeping. Ebony for the eyebrows; ebony is an oriental wood. He calls the lips "red roses" and for the teeth, "pearls."

*That ever bitter and honored day*
*Sent her living image so deep into my heart,*
*That no wit or style will ever be able to describe it;*
*But often I return to it with my memory.*
*That bearing adorned with every noble pity,*
*And the bittersweet lamenting that I heard,*
*Made me doubt if she were a mortal woman or a goddess*
*Who made the sky clear all around.*
*Her head of fine gold, and her face warm snow;*
*Ebony her eyebrows and her eyes were two stars,*
*From which Love did not draw his bow in vain;*
*Pearls and red roses, where the gathered*
*Sorrow formed burning and beautiful voices;*
*Sighs were flame, and tears were crystal.*

## SONNET 126.

<margin>Hieronymo Squarciafico</margin>
¶ Fixed deeply within himself was our poet's memory of the weeping of My Lady Laura, which she did for the death of her mother; as he has said in the two other sonnets written above. In this 126th sonnet he still continues with that weeping, saying that in every place where he looks he seems to see that most sweet act of My Lady Laura weeping: saying that truly Love was with him.

<margin>Antonio da Tempo</margin>
¶ WHEREVER I TURN. The poet wrote these four sonnets wherein he continues with the theme of the weeping.

*Wherever I place my weary eyes, or turn them*
*To quiet the longing that drives them,*
*I find one who paints a beautiful lady there*
*To make my desires forever green.*
*With graceful sorrow she seems to breathe*
*A deep pity, which grips a noble heart;*

Beyond the sight, she adorns the ears, and creates
Her living voices, and her holy sighs.
**L**ove and truth were with me to say that those [beauties]
Which I saw, were beauties unique in the world
Never seen before beneath the stars:
**N**or were such pitiful and sweet words
Ever heard: nor such beautiful tears
**D**id the sun ever see fall from such beautiful eyes.

### SONNET 127.

**I**n what part of heaven, in what Idea <note>referring to the Platonic "Idea" or perfect form</note>
Was the example from which Nature took
That beautiful, graceful face, in which she wished
To show down here how much she could do up there?
**W**hat nymph in the springs, what goddess in the woods
Ever loosed hair of such fine gold to the breeze?
When did a heart gather so many virtues in itself?
Though the sum of them is guilty of my death.
**H**e looks in vain for divine beauty
Who never saw the eyes of this lady,
How sweetly she turns them.
**H**e knows not how Love heals, and how he kills,
Who does not know how sweetly she sighs,
And how sweetly she speaks, and sweetly she laughs.

### SONNET 128.

**L**ove and I, so full of wonder,
Like one who sees an incredible thing,
Gaze upon her when she speaks or laughs,
Who resembles only herself and no other.
**F**rom the beautiful serenity of her tranquil brows
My two faithful stars <note>meaning Laura's eyes</note> sparkle so,
That there is no other light to inflame or guide
One who resolves to love loftily.
**W**hat a miracle it is when, among the grass,
Like a flower she sits; or when she presses
A green turf with her white breast?
**W**hat sweetness it is in the bitter season
To see her go alone with her thoughts
Weaving a circle <term>circle: original "cerchio," meaning a garland</term> for her clear and curly gold [hair].

### SONNET 129.

**O**h scattered steps; oh wandering and ready thoughts;
Oh tenacious memory; oh fierce ardor,

---

Speaking of the weeping of My Lady Laura, saying that wherever he looks he seems to see this sweetest act of weeping. "Love and the truth": as if saying it is true that Love was with me.

<margin>Hieronymo Squarciafico</margin>
¶ **IN WHAT PART.** In this 127th Sonnet, out of wonder at the beauty of My Lady Laura, the enamored poet asks a question, saying: in what place could Nature have found this so beautiful a likeness? He follows the Platonic opinion which holds that our souls take their likeness in heaven: and this is shown quite clearly, beyond the works of Plato, by Cicero in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations* <term>Tusculan Disputations: a series of philosophical books by the Roman orator Cicero exploring the soul and human suffering</term>.

<margin>Antonio da Tempo</margin>
¶ **IN WHAT PART.** The poet asks a question out of great wonder as to where heaven could have such a beautiful example when it formed his lady. "He knows not how Love heals." Note this last instance: it is a most sweet thought to have an "Idea" of a woman—a thing of the imagination—even before she is created and made.

<margin>Hieronymo Squarciafico</margin>
¶ **LOVE. In this 128th Sonnet**, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> tells how he often stopped with Love to contemplate the actions of his lady, especially when she sat in a meadow making herself a garland for her hair: and he does not wish to compare her to any mortal thing.

<margin>Antonio da Tempo</margin>
¶ **LOVE AND I SO FULL.** Master Francesco narrates how he often stopped with Love to contemplate the actions of his lady, especially when she sat in a meadow. "A green turf": a green turf is a globe of earth with grass around it. "A circle": that is, a garland for her hair. And he does not want to compare her to any mortal thing because he says she was a divine thing.

<margin>Hieronymo Squarciafico</margin>
¶ **OH STEPS.** In this 129th Sonnet, the poet invokes all the labors he ever suffered in loving his lady, and the past souls who have loved, who remain to see his grief: "O gentle souls." He uses an apostrophe to the souls; that is, addressing any gentle soul in the world who might look upon what his grief is like.

HAPPY: one hundred and thirtieth sonnet. The poet praises the place through which his beloved Lady Laura passed every morning: namely, through a garden where a stream was in the middle, in which she washed her hands, and he says that he bears great envy toward it. And he takes his quality from the living light, as if to say: "you are bright because of her similar face."

As long as I am consumed by good desire,
May it not displease her that I sigh for her.

### SONNET CXXXII. <note>Modern numbering: 164</note>

N ow that the heavens and the earth and the wind are silent,
And the wild beasts and the birds are restrained by sleep.
Night leads her starry chariot in its circuit,
And in its bed the sea lies without a wave;
I see, I think, I burn, I weep; and she who uncurls me
Is always before me, to my sweet pain:
War is my state, full of anger and of grief;
And only by thinking of her do I have some peace.
Thus, from a single clear and living fountain
Flows the sweet and the bitter, on which I feed;
A single hand both heals and pierces me:
And so that my martyrdom does not reach the shore;
A thousand times a day I die, and a thousand I am born;
So far am I from my salvation.

### SONNET CXXXIII. <note>Modern numbering: 165</note>

A s her white foot through the fresh grass
Moves her sweet steps with dignity;
A virtue, which opens and renews the flowers all around,
Seems to issue from her tender soles.
Love, who ensnares only graceful hearts,
Nor cares to try his strength elsewhere:
From her beautiful eyes such a warm pleasure rains;
That I care for no other good, nor crave other bait.
And with her gait, and with her gentle gaze,
Her sweetest words are in accord,
And her mild, humble, and measured actions.
From these four sparks—and yet they are not the only ones—
Is born the great fire in which I live and burn:
For I have become like a nocturnal bird in the sun.

### SONNET CXXXIIII. <note>Modern numbering: 166</note>

I f I had remained firm at the cave
There, where Apollo became a prophet;
Florence would perhaps have her poet today,
Not just Verona, and Mantua, and Arunca:
And because my land does not produce rushes <note>original: "non s'ingiunca" — meaning "is not covered in rushes," a metaphor for lack of poetic cultivation</note>

<margin>Hieronymo</margin>
¶ **As her white [foot].** This 132nd <note>referring to the previous sonnet 133</note> sonnet is quite easy, so I will not expand too much upon it. In it, the poet says of his Lady Laura how the grass flowered for joy at being trodden by her feet as she walked. And not only that, but he narrates nearly all the amorous gestures he saw in her, through which the poet was rekindled in his love.

<margin>Hieronymo</margin>
<margin>Z</margin>
¶ **If I had.** In sonnet 134, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> wishes to demonstrate that if he had followed his studies, he would have been crowned with the laurel <note>The "poet laureate" crown</note>. He says this through circumlocution <note>a roundabout way of speaking</note>. By Mantua he means Virgil; by Verona, Catullus; and for Arunca he takes Lucilius, who was a satirical poet. The text is clear.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ **If I had remained firm.** Master Francesco wishes to demonstrate that if he had followed his studies, he would have been crowned with the laurel, and he says this through circumlocution: Mantua, namely Virgil; Verona, Catullus. Hence Ovid says: **"Mantua rejoices in Virgil, Verona in Catullus."** <note>original: "Mantuā virgilio gaudet veronā Catullo"</note> For Arunca, he takes Lucilius. By the "cave" he means the one under Mount Parnassus <note>Home of the Muses</note>, which is that rock **from which flows the Helicon spring.** <note>original: "Ex quo manat fons helicon"</note>

<margin>Hieronymo</margin>
<margin>A</margin>
¶ **WHEN.** In sonnet 135, Master Francesco describes a charming gesture of Lady Laura which, upon seeing it, made him languish: and when he wished to speak, she sometimes bowed her head and began her speech with a little sigh. And by "thread" <note>original: "stame"</note> he means the thread of human life spun by the three sisters named by the poets as the Parcae <note>The Fates of mythology</note>.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ **When Love [to] the beautiful eyes.** Master Francesco describes a most charming gesture of Lady Laura which, upon seeing it, made him languish. And when he wished to speak, she sometimes bowed her head and began her speech with a little sigh. And "thread"—that is, that which is spun by those sisters whom the poets call the Parcae by contradiction <note>A common medieval etymology: "Parcae" comes from "parcere" (to spare) because they spare no one</note> because they spare no one. They are three: namely, Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos.
<margin>B</margin>

<margin>Hieronymo</margin>
¶ **LOVE SENDS ME.** Sonnet 136, in which the poet narrates the promises that Love makes to him and the hopes in which he holds him regarding the season—that is, toward his old age.

<meta>catchword: ¶ Joined</meta>

**Anto.** ¶ LOVE SENDS me. The poet tells of the promises that love makes to him and the hopes in which it keeps him. *Toward the season: that is, toward old age, which is natural* <note>original Latin: "versus senectutem que natura est"</note>.

**Hiero.** ¶ FULL OF a wandering. Sonnet 137 <note>Modern numbering: 170</note>. In which Master Francesco speaks of what happens to him at times when he decides to speak his mind to Lady Laura regarding a thought that reigns in him; and yet he sees a ray of pity in her eyes.

**Anto.** ¶ FULL OF a wandering. In this Sonnet, Master Francesco speaks of what happens to him at times when he decides to speak his mind to Lady Laura regarding a thought that reigns in him, and he sees yet a ray of pity in her eyes.

**Hiero.** ¶ MANY TIMES. Sonnet 138 <note>Modern numbering: 171</note>. O how many times what our enamored poet writes in this sonnet usually happens to lovers: that when they believe they will speak to their lady and have everything well-composed in their mind, then when they come to the act itself, they do not know how to utter a single word that is good, because the gentle sight of the beloved lady’s eyes at the end frightens him; and this is seen quite clearly in everyone.

<margin>D</margin>
**Anto.** ¶ MANY times already from the beautiful. Master Francesco reveals how many times he has had the spirit and the resolve to speak to Lady Laura, seeing her so gentle in appearance; but her eyes at the end frighten him and take away such thought, and he adds a notable point through which she understands this is because of too much loving and very great passion. *Fioco* means hoarse <note>original: "rauco"</note>.

**Hiero.** ¶ LOVE HAS joined me. Sonnet 139 <note>Modern numbering: 172</note>. Master Francesco shows how love has brought him to counsel himself for the better, not wishing to complain anymore because by complaining his pain grows every hour. The Rhine is a river which runs through Germany <note>The Rhine river</note>; another small one of the same name also runs through Bologna <note>The Reno river in Italy</note>. He concludes saying that however hard and cruel she may be, he will not stop loving her and sighing and hoping for her.

> From the moisture of that rock; another planet
> I must follow, and from my field reap
> Burrs and thorns with the hooked scythe.
> The olive is dry; and turned elsewhere
> Is the water that derives from Parnassus <note>The mountain home of the Muses; a symbol of poetic inspiration</note>,

### SONNET. CXXXV. <note>Modern numbering: 167</note>

> When Love inclines those beautiful eyes to the earth,
> And gathers the wandering spirits in a sigh
> With his hands; and then releases them in a voice
> Clear, sweet, angelic, and divine;
> I feel a sweet robbery committed on my heart,
> And my thoughts and desires so changed within,
> That I say, "Now these shall be my final spoils,
> If heaven destines such an honorable death for me":
> But the sound, which binds the senses with sweetness,
> With the great desire of being blessed by hearing,
> Restrains the soul ready to depart.
> Thus I live; and thus she winds and unwinds
> The thread of the life that is given to me,
> This lone Siren of heaven among us.

### SONNET. CXXXVI. <note>Modern numbering: 168</note>

> Love sends me that sweet thought,
> Which is an old confidant <note>original: "secretario"</note> between us two;
> And comforts me, and says that it was
> Never, as now, ready for that which I crave and hope.
> I, who sometimes lies, and sometimes truth
> Have found in his words,
> Do not know if I should believe him; and I live between two,
> Neither "yes" nor "no" sounds whole in my heart.
> In this, time passes; and in the mirror
> I see myself approaching the contrary season <note>His old age</note>
> To his promise and to my hope.
> Now let it be as it can: I am not the only one growing old:
> My desire does not vary with age.
> I do fear a brief life; for little remains.

-># SONNET 138<-

**M**any times already from that beautiful human face

To assault with honest and clever words

**T**hen her eyes make my thought vain:
Because all my fortune, all my fate,

He who alone can do so, has placed in her hand:
**W**hence I could never form a word,
That could be understood by any but myself;
So has love made me trembling and hoarse:
**A**nd I see well now; that kindled charity <note>In this context, "charity" refers to an intense, burning love.</note>
Binds the tongue of others, and steals away the spirits;
Who can say how he burns in a little fire.

-># SONNET 139<-

**L**ove has caught me between beautiful and cruel arms
Which kill me wrongly; and if I complain
My martyrdom doubles: wherefore, as I am accustomed,
The best thing is that I die loving, and keep silent;
**F**or she could make the Rhine <note>original: "rhē"</note>, whenever it freezes,
Burn with her eyes, and break every hard rock;
And she has a pride equal to her beauties,
That she seems displeased by the pleasure of others;
Nothing can I take away by my own wit.

<margin>M.F. Anto.</margin> ¶ *Love has caught me* relates how love has caught him and advises him that it is for the best not to want to complain anymore because by complaining his pain increases every hour: the Rhine <note>original: "el rhē"</note> is a very cold river in the North. In the end, Master Francesco concludes that however hard and cruel she may be, he will not stop loving her and sighing while hoping in her.

<margin>Hiero. F</margin> ¶ *O Envy*: Sonnet 140. Because Master Francesco had been spoken ill of to his lady out of envy, he speaks in this one of envy, calling it by name. ¶ *O Envy*: and he concludes that it may do as it pleases, for he will always want to love her.

¶ *O Envy, enemy of virtue.* Because Master Francesco had been blamed to his lady through envy and ill had been said of him, he speaks in this of envy calling it by name, O Envy: and concludes that it may do as it pleases, for he will always want to love her anyway.

<margin>Anto. G</margin> ¶ *Admiring the sun* <note>original: "Mirādo El sol"</note>. Sonnet 141. This sonnet is quite literal <note>original: "textuale"</note>, in which Master Francesco speaks of the eyes of My Lady Laura <note>original: "M. L."</note> and says that at times, looking at her, it seems to him that his soul falls from his body to go to her between two contraries, that is, sweet and bitter; or you could say between frozen desires or kindled desires, as he says below, or between sad or joyful pleasures. Such fruit is born of such a root: that is, from the eyes of My Lady Laura. And the more one repents: that is, those sad ones who are many repent of the ancient enterprises they undertake in love.

<margin>Anto.</margin> ¶ *Admiring the sun*. This sonnet is literal, in which Master Francesco speaks of the eyes of his lady: and says that at times, looking at her, it seems that his soul departs from the body to go to her. Between two contraries, that is, sweet and bitter: or you could say between frozen desires and kindled desires as he says below, or you could say between joyful thoughts and sad thoughts. Such fruit is born of such a root, that is, from the eyes of his lady or from love. And the more one repents: that is, those sad ones who are many repent of the ancient enterprises they undertake in loving.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ **G**eri, when sometimes. Messire Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> writes this sonnet to a friend of his named Geri regarding the life he led with his lady and the way he lives in his love, advising him also to do the same: That the head of Medusa was a woman who, because of a rape committed in the temple of Diana, was changed into a monster with snakes for hair, and her horrible sight changed those who looked at her into stone. "Before such a one as our lord uses," he says, "before the wings," to give us to understand that love reaches a man in every part.

<margin>Hieronymus S.</margin>
¶ **G**eri. In this most elegant sonnet, 147, which he writes to a friend of his named Geri, he describes the life he led with his lady and the way he lives in his love, advising him also to do the same. And he says that sometimes, because of his gazing at her, she turns her eyes all disdainfully toward him, so that it seems she wishes to deprive him of all light. But he, with his weeping, humbles himself so much that by force she is compelled to pull back her disdain. So that by this she will seem, in seeing her, not otherwise than the head of Medusa, who because of the rape committed in the temple of Neptune <note>The commentators disagree: Antonio cites Diana, while Hieronymus cites Neptune, following the more common version found in Ovid.</note> became very deformed with snaky hair, so that whoever saw her became marble. This fable is narrated above and is touched upon extensively by Ovid in his *Metamorphoses*.

<margin>Hieronymus</margin>
¶ **PO** well. This sonnet, 148, which Petrarch composed while sailing along the river Po; and being somewhat unfortunate. He says that nothing could set him at rest so well, even if he denied it: because although the vile "bark" <term>bark: the "scorza" or outer shell, meaning the physical body</term> took the body away, the spirit that hides within does not care for its power, without alternate "poggia" and "orza" <term>poggia and orza: maritime terms for leeward and windward; here used to mean steering or maneuvering</term>; he means to say that without wandering or being led astray, he held his soul toward his Laura from the window. And he asks the Po, king of the other rivers, imitating Virgil in the first book of his *Georgics*, who says "Eridanus, king of the other rivers." <note>original: "Eridano de li altri fiumi re" — Eridanus was the ancient mythical name for the Po River.</note>

## SONNET CXLV

A thousand slopes in one day and a thousand streams
Love has shown me through the famous Ardennes; <note>The Forest of Ardennes, which Petrarch traveled through in 1333 during a period of political unrest.</note>
Who for his followers feathers the feet and the hearts,
To make them go flying alive to the third heaven. <note>The third heaven is the sphere of Venus, the planet of love.</note>
**I**t was sweet to me to have been there alone and unarmed,
Where armed Mars strikes and does not even signal;
Like a ship without a rudder and without a mast,
A vessel in a sea full of heavy and shunned thoughts.
**Y**et arrived at last at the end of the dark day,
Remembering whence I come, and with what wings,
I feel a fear born of too much daring:
**B**ut the beautiful country and its delightful river <note>The Rhone river, near Avignon where Laura lived.</note>
With a serene welcome reassures
The heart already turned back, where its light dwells.

## SONNET CXLVI

**L**ove spurs me and at one time pulls the reins:
Reassures and frightens me; burns and freezes;
Welcomes and disdains; calls me and drives me away,
Now holds me in hope and now in pain.
**N**ow high, now low he leads my weary heart:
So that my wandering desire loses the trail;
And his highest pleasure seems to displease him,
My mind is full of such a novel error.
**A** friendly thought shows her the ford—
Not of water, which is resolved through the eyes—
To go quickly where she hopes to be content:
**T**hen, as if a greater force releases her from there,
She must follow another path, and to her own regret,
Consent to her long death and to mine.

Because she hopes to deprive my life of light;
I show her mine so full of true humility,
That by force she pulls back all her disdain.
**I**f it were not so, I would go not otherwise

### SONNET 148.

Po, you may well carry away the shell
Of me with your powerful and rapid waves:
But the spirit, which hides within:
Cares neither for your strength, nor that of another:
Which, without alternating, steers a steady course
Straight through the breezes toward its favorable desire,
Beating its wings toward the golden branch <note>The laurel, representing Laura</note>,
It overcomes the water, the wind, the sail, and the oars.
King of the others, proud and lofty river,
Who meets the sun when it brings the day,
And in the west abandons a more beautiful light;
You go away with my mortal part upon your horn <note>A classical poetic reference to river gods often depicted with horns</note>
The other, covered with amorous feathers,
Returns flying to its sweet dwelling.

### SONNET 149.

Love among the grass stretched a graceful net
Of gold and pearls under a branch
Of the ever-green tree <note>The laurel</note>, which I love so much
Though it has more sad shadows than happy ones.
The bait was the seed, which he sows and reaps,
Both sweet and bitter; which I fear and crave:
The nights were never, since the day Adam
Opened his eyes, so sweet and quiet:
And the clear light, which makes the sun disappear,
Flashed all around, and the cord was wound
Round the hand that surpasses ivory and snow;
So I fell into the net, and here I have been caught by
The charming gestures, and the angelic words,
And the pleasure, and the desire, and the hope.

### SONNET 150.

Love, who inflames the heart with burning zeal,
Holds it constrained by frozen fear;
And which might be greater makes the intellect doubt:
Hope or fear, the flame or the frost.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ **P**o, you may well carry. Regarding sailing. Messire Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> composed this sonnet while traveling along the Po in Italy and speaks to the river, saying it can well carry his body, but not his mind.

<margin>Hieronymus S.</margin>
¶ **L**ove among the grass. In this 149th sonnet, lovers many times recall the manner in which they first fell in love, just as our poet does here. Saying that love stretched a graceful net under a laurel: which he takes to represent Lady Laura. And he says he loves her much though he has had more melancholy than joy from it. The bait was the seed—that is, the beautiful look of Lady Laura—and he says he craves her even though he is terrified. And he says, returning to his beginning, that when he fell in love, he saw his splendor like a lightning bolt that darkened the sun, and so he fell into the net; and here with her beautiful eyes, gestures, and manners, he was captured by love.

<margin>Hieronymus Q.</margin>
¶ **L**ove who inflames. In this 150th sonnet, the excellent poet describes his no small amorous passion through the opposition of things. He says then that Love inflames his heart with a burning zeal—"zeal" being synonymous with "devotion" according to Servius the Grammarian <note>A famous 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note>. This kind of opposition is usually called <term>cacozelia</term> <note>original: "cacozelia"—here used to describe a rhetorical style involving contradictory terms like fire and ice</note>. Note this in Virgil: the victors fall just as if they were the vanquished; the others not conquered but for themselves. If they are not conquered, as other examples could be brought forth: so our poet notes these types of opposites very well. Burning day and night—this is because lovers usually have greater passion at night than by day; and he rightly says that his intellect, which he carries at the peak, although he spreads his wings in vain: that is, such thoughts profit him nothing.

<margin>Hieronymus</margin>
¶ **I**f the sweet Good. The poet excellently describes the passion of lovers in these sonnets of his: but among the others, he expresses it in this 151st sonnet: because it is the custom of lovers that every glance of their beloved young ladies kills them; and they always exalt whatever they say, it seeming to them better and better said than could ever be spoken. And this I have experienced myself with my Epirotina <note>A reference to a woman from Epirus, possibly Squarzafico's own beloved</note>, who with her sweet speech...

<margin>Hieronymo S. <note>Likely Hieronymo Squarciafico, a 15th-century editor and commentator of Petrarch.</note></margin> free myself.

¶ **LOVE, nature.** In this following sonnet, our poet praises his beloved Madonna Laura as much as possible, as he has done in many others. He says that although by nature she is humble—meaning not of noble birth <note>Petrarch often plays with the contrast between Laura’s modest origins and her spiritual nobility.</note>—every virtue reigns in her. And he says she is turned against him in such a way that he ought to hope for nothing from her. Nature holds her, says the poet, with a noble snare; everything else is distasteful to her. And so his spirit from hour to hour leads him toward death. And he concludes well: unless death pulls back the reins, he will realize too late that all things in this world are vain, those very vanities in which he used to live.

<margin>Hieronymo T.</margin>¶ **THIS phoenix.** In this following sonnet, Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> calls his beloved a golden phoenix; and truly a phoenix, for just as that bird is unique in the world, so he considered his Madonna Laura to be alone in beauty and every other virtue. He describes her among women wearing a necklace <term>monile</term> <note>A decorative collar or necklace, often associated with status or symbolic purity.</note> about her neck of such integrity that he had never been able to see the like in others. It was in the form of a diadem which made all the heavy air around her become thin and clear. This means nothing else than that amidst the crowd of vices that then reigned in those parts—due to the court of those Popes who were there <note>A critique of the papal court at Avignon, which Petrarch famously called the "Babylon of the West."</note>—she alone lived purely. *Purple garment.* He says the red color of the purple, which was a royal garment, was sprinkled with a celestial hem; that is to say, he could extract nothing from her but the scent of her beauties; and because of this, it seemed her chastity remained reserved in her lap while she had flown to heaven.

<margin>Antonio.</margin>¶ **THIS phoenix.** Messer Francesco describes the dress around the neck of Madonna Laura; and says it is a necklace, that is, the chains of pearls and gold that women wear in Italy.

<margin>Hieronymo V.</margin>¶ **IF Virgil.** Our poet did not know in what way he could praise his Madonna Laura more, except by wishing to take away the fame
<meta>The catchword "la fama" indicates the first words of the following page's commentary.</meta>

*I tremble in the hottest sky, I burn in the coldest,*
*Always full of desire and of suspicion;*
*Just as a woman in a simple dress*
*Might hide a living man, or under a small veil.*

### SONNET 151

*If the sweet look of this lady kills me,*
*And her soft, clever little words;*
*And if Love makes her so powerful over me*
*Only when she speaks, or when she smiles;*
*Alas, what will happen if perhaps she turns—*
*Either by my fault, or by wicked fate—*
*Her eyes away from mercy; so that she trusts me*
*To death there, where she now assures me?*
*Therefore if I tremble and walk with a frozen heart*
*Whenever I see her expression changed,*
*This fear is born of ancient trials;*
*A woman is a changeable thing by nature:* <note>original: "Femina e cosa mobil per natura." A reference to Virgil's famous line "Varium et mutabile semper femina."</note>
*Whence I know well, that a state of love*
*Lasts but a short time in a woman's heart.*

### SONNET 152

*Love, nature, and the beautiful humble soul,*
*Where every other virtue dwells and reigns,*
*Are sworn against me: Love strives*
*That I should die completely; and in this follows his style.*
*Nature holds her with such a noble*
*Snare; that there is no strength that can endure it:*
*She is so shy, that she does not deign to dwell*
*Any longer in this weary and base life.*
*Thus the spirit from hour to hour fails*
*Those beautiful, dear, honest limbs*
*Which were the mirror of true grace;*
*And if Love and pity do not pull the reins;*
*Alas, I see well in what state these*
*Vain hopes are, by which I used to live.*

# SONNET 153.

**T**his Phoenix <note>The phoenix was a mythical bird that lived for centuries before burning itself and rising from the ashes; in Renaissance poetry, it often represents a unique, incomparable woman.</note> of the golden plumage
Around her beautiful, white, and noble neck
Forms without art so dear a necklace <term>monile</term> <note>A decorative collar or necklace.</note>:
That it sweetens every heart, and consumes mine:
**I**t forms a natural diadem; which lights up
The air around; and from there the silent flint
Of love draws a subtle liquid
Fire, which burns me in the frostiest winter.
**A** purple robe with a sky-blue hem
Sprinkled with roses veils her lovely shoulders;
A new fashion, and beauty unique and alone.
**F**ame places and hides her in the fragrant and rich bosom
Of Arabian mountains;
Who flies so loftily through our sea.

# SONNET 154.

**I**f Virgil and Homer had seen

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Petrarch's poetry, specifically focusing on the conclusion of Sonnet 155 and the full texts of Sonnets 156, 157, and the beginning of 158. <margin>Antonio</margin>
In the oration which he [Cicero] made for the poet Archias <note>Cicero’s *Pro Archia Poeta* is a famous defense of literature and the fame that poets grant to great men.</note>, where he speaks in praise of poets: that when Alexander the Great had reached the tomb of the brave Achilles, sighing, he called him fortunate to have had Homer as a great herald and writer of his deeds. Our Petrarch does not disagree, placing his own praises [of Laura] between those of Virgil and Homer, saying that it was given to him by fate from heaven to praise his Madonna Laura, and that these fates are fixed for everyone; although she is worthy of being praised by Orpheus and Virgil, and for this reason he fears that he diminishes a great part of her praise.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
**ALEXANDER** having arrived: in the said singular act of Alexander performed at the tomb of Achilles, saying that he found one who wrote of him so loftily, and this was Homer. Messer Francesco [Petrarch] returns to his Madonna Laura, saying that she would have been more worthy of any other style [of poetry].

Deformed star: that is, by destiny it was given to me to write of her.

**NOURISHING** sun. In this 156th sonnet, our poet returns once more to praising his beloved Madonna Laura, asking the sun to love her holy name, which he takes from the leaves [of the laurel], and says there has never been one like her in the world since our father Adam committed his and our evil [the original sin]: which was the beginning of the human generation until the end of her day. He then invokes the sun, saying: And you, sun, still flee from her sight, casting shadows upon the hills; he speaks to the sun for the love of Daphne, which in Greek means laurel, with whom he was in love as written above <note>In myth, Apollo (the Sun) loved Daphne, who was transformed into a laurel tree to escape him.</note>. He then concludes with his own sun: that is, his Laura, who dwelt where the sun set, whom Messer Francesco saw by force; and he rightly says it grows in his heart while he speaks of it, and therefore says he dwells with her.

**NOURISHING** sun, that... ## SONNET CLIX

Just as eternal life is to see God,
    Nor is more desired, nor is it permitted to desire more;
    So seeing you makes me happy
    In this brief and fragile life of mine:
Nor did I ever see you yourself so beautiful
    As now; if the eye speaks truth to the heart
    Of my sweet and blessed thought;
    Which overcomes every high hope, every desire:
And if it were not for her flight being so swift;
    I would ask for nothing more: for if some live
    Only on scent, and such fame gains belief;
Others satisfy the taste and touch with water or fire,
    Things deprived of every sweetness;
    Why not I with your divine sight? <note>Petrarch argues that if some legendary creatures live on air or elements, he can live purely on the sight of Laura.</note>

## SONNET CLX

Let us stay, Love, to see our glory,
    Things proud and new beyond nature:
    See well how much sweetness rains upon her:
    See the light that heaven shows on earth:
See how much art gilds, and pearls, and adorns
    The chosen attire, never seen elsewhere;
    Who sweetly moves her feet and eyes
    Through this shaded cloister of beautiful hills.
The green grass, and the flowers of a thousand colors
    Scattered under that ancient and black holm-oak,
    Pray that her beautiful foot presses or touches them;
And the sky with lovely and bright sparks
    Kindles around and rejoices in the sight
    Of being made serene by such beautiful eyes.

<margin>Hieronimo Z.</margin>
¶ THE ship passes. <note>original: "PASSA la naue." This refers to Sonnet 189 in modern editions.</note> In this 158th sonnet, our enamored poet uses the simile of a ship to represent his amorous passion: he says, therefore, by likeness to his love, that he is in a small ship in which the sails were broken; which signifies nothing else but him being almost desperate in his love; and each oar represents a prompt and wicked thought. As for the storm, it signifies nothing else but the contrary winds of a rain of tears. Here the poet says he is so distressed as to never have been able to know his straight path, and therefore says "the two sweet accustomed signs are hidden from me": that is, the memory of things past, the understanding of the present, and the guidance by which he begins to despair of the port: that is, of ever knowing how to return to a state of virtue.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ THE ship passes. Master Francesco [Petrarch] likens his mind to a ship that is in a sea storm, just as he is in the storm of love. Regarding the sail, he takes "reason" as the sail, because a ship without a sail is like a man without reason. "Hidden are my two sweet accustomed signs": that is, the eyes of My Lady [Laura]. "I began": that is, to come to the end of my desire.

<margin>Hieronimo A.</margin>
¶ A WHITE [doe]: <note>original: "VNA candida." Refers to the sonnet ending at the top of this page, modern 190.</note> by a wandering and beautiful simile in this 158th sonnet, our amorous Master Francesco recalls having once seen his My Lady Laura, comparing her to a white doe which he intends to represent her chastity. "Upon the green grass with two golden horns." "Between two rivers": <note>Likely the Rhône and the Sorgue in Avignon.</note> this he says for her beauty which was desired by many, and though she was indeed wealthy, she was not of a low lineage; because, as has been mentioned in many places above, his Madonna Laura was not of a high noble nation, but by her virtues she deserved every great praise. Oh, how poorly understood our poet is in several places; and this is because many who do not know what they are saying, having not seen his works, find fault with him here.

# SONNET 162.

The gentle breeze <note>The word "L’aura" (the breeze) is a recurring pun on the name of Petrarch’s beloved, Laura.</note>, which clears the hills
Awakening the flowers throughout this shaded woods,
I recognize by its sweet spirit;
Through which it is necessary that I rise in pain and in fame.
**T** o find a place where my weary heart might rest,
I flee from my native, sweet Tuscan air:
To bring light to my troubled and dark thoughts,
I seek my sun <note>Referring to Laura as the "sun" who illuminates his life.</note>; and I hope to see her today:
**I** n whom I experience sweetnesses so many and such,
That Love by force leads me back to her;
Then she so dazzles me, that my escape is too slow.
**I** would ask not for weapons to flee, but wings:
But Heaven grants that I perish by this light;
For from afar I am consumed, and up close I burn.

# SONNET 163.

From day to day I go changing my face and my hair:
Yet I do not spit out the sweet baited hooks,
Nor do I break free from the green and limed branches <note>A metaphor for being trapped like a bird on branches coated in sticky "birdlime."</note>
Of the tree <note>The "Arbor" or Laurel tree, another symbol for Laura.</note>; which cares for neither sun nor frost.
**W** ithout water the sea, and without stars the sky
Shall be, before I do not always fear and desire
Her beautiful shadow, and before I do not hate and love
The deep amorous wound, which I poorly hide.
**I** do not hope ever to have rest from my suffering
Until I am unboned, unnerved, and stripped of flesh;
Or unless my enemy <note>Laura, often called his "sweet enemy."</note> should have pity on me.
**E** very impossible thing might happen first;
Than anyone other than death, or she, should heal the blow;
Which Love with her beautiful eyes impressed upon my heart.

The serene breeze; which among green leaves

The first wounds so sweet and deep;

Which disdain or jealousy keeps concealed from me;
And the hair, now wrapped in pearls and gems,
Which then was loose; and more golden than polished gold:
**W** hich she scattered so sweetly,

<margin>Right Column Commentary</margin>

<margin>General Commentary</margin>
He is consumed from afar and burns up close. The noble poet does not forget to praise Italy here, calling its air gentle and that of France <note>original: "Frāza"</note> troubled and dark, just as in those heroic verses he makes in praise of Italy, where he says that he left the clouds behind him and the serene air was upon his face.

<margin>Antonio Brucioli</margin>
**THE GENTLE BREEZE.** As Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> was going from Tuscany to Avignon, being already near that land, he composed this sonnet in a small grove where a bit of wind was blowing.

<margin>Hieronymo</margin>
**FROM DAY TO DAY.** The burning love that our enamored poet had was great and intimate, as can be seen in many places of this work of his: but he manifests it quite clearly in this 163rd sonnet. He says that although his hair is changing, turning white due to old age, he does not for this reason leave his love; rather he says that the sea will be without water or the sky without stars before he stops, and he never hopes to be released from such love until he is undone, just as dead bodies are dissolved.

<margin>Antonio Brucioli</margin>
**FROM DAY TO DAY. Master** Francesco says that although he changes his face, he does not change his will or thought; and he says this under the figure of the tree reached at its highest happiness. Against the sun's force... <note>This section notes Laura's influence on the poet's steadfastness.</note>

<margin>Hieronymo</margin>
**THE SERENE BREEZE. Our Master Francesco made** this 164th sonnet because, finding himself in a place where the wind struck him in the face, which proceeded from the grove where his Lady Laura was, the breeze <note>aura</note> which signifies her name reminds him of her: because they sound with that same name. Then he turns to her tresses, saying that she used to keep them loose when she was more of a girl, and now she has them gathered up; and because of her face and likewise because of her hair, he has kept it in jealousy, though he has not shown it.

<margin>Antonio Brucioli</margin>
**THE SERENE BREEZE. Being Master Francesco in a place** where the wind struck him in the face, he made this sonnet: because of that breeze <note>aura</note> he remembers Lady Laura, because they have the same name: *then loose and more golden than polished gold*: he says this remembering the hair of Lady Laura, for as she grew in age she made braids, gathering her hair together and binding it in their fashion.

**O** beautiful hand, that squeezes my heart,
And in a small space shuts up my life;
Hand where every art and all their studies
Nature and Heaven placed, to do themselves honor;
Of five pearls <note>A metaphor for the fingernails or tips of the fingers.</note> of oriental <note>In this period, "oriental" referred to the highest quality or luster, as the finest pearls came from the East.</note> color,

<margin>Hieronymo Ruscelli</margin>
**O BEAUTIFUL hand.** It seems a great prize to lovers when they can have some trifle <note>original: "fraschuza"</note> that belongs to their beloved ladies; and the more love there is, the more that thing becomes dear to them, as is shown in this 167th sonnet by our enamored poet, Master Francesco Petrarch, who is completely overjoyed by a glove of his beloved Madonna Laura that he had found. First, he praises the beautiful hand as much as possible, for which Laura possesses the glove, because such a beautiful hand covers it. Second, he says he never saw sweeter spoils <note>The glove is treated as a "spoil of war" or a trophy taken from the beloved.</note>. Then he says he would willingly have as much of her beautiful veil. Finally, he concludes that he cannot keep it because it is a theft; so it shows that our poet, even in his own little basin, would have willingly fished <note>A colloquial metaphor suggesting the poet would have gladly kept the "stolen" item without guilt if he could have gotten away with it.</note> without having a conscience about it.

<margin>Antonio Brucioli</margin>
**O BEAUTIFUL hand.** Messer Francesco having found a glove of Madonna Laura that she had forgotten upon a table, he made this sonnet and speaks to that glove, which had a decoration of pearls around it.

**T**he serene eyes, and the starry brows;
The beautiful angelic mouth full of pearls <note>Metaphor for teeth.</note>
Full and of roses <note>Metaphor for lips.</note> and of sweet words,
**W**hich make others tremble with wonder;
And the brow, and the hair, which to see them
In summer at midday conquer the sun.

<margin>Hieronymo Ruscelli</margin>
**NOT ONLY.** Our poet continues in this 168th sonnet on the subject of the above sonnet, describing some properties of this glove. It seems here in this one and the following that he has already restored <note>Returned the stolen item to Laura.</note> the glove. He says not only the hand makes war on him, but also the arms; and Love sets a thousand snares for him every day, and none in vain because of her heavenly dress and her angelic mouth always full of pearls and roses; and because of the brow and the hair that in mid-summer at noon conquer the sun, so bright they are to his eyes.

<margin>Antonio Brucioli</margin>
**NOT ONLY THE ONE.** He continues some properties of the glove; and says not only that hand from that glove, but the other and even the arms are there to torment him.

<margin>If only his Madonna Laura <note>Petrarch’s idealized muse and beloved.</note> had wished for him to believe it. But what is worse is to see him love and languish for her and not believe it. This is a common habit that Petrarch describes here: that the more beautiful women are, the less they believe the passions of those subject to them. For he says well that Madonna Laura sees him burning indeed, but cares little for it; so many of his rhymes have already been spread abroad that they could inflame more than a thousand people; yet she is not moved to pity.</margin>

<margin>Anto.</margin>
**Alas, that I burn.** <note>original: "L'Asso ch'io ardo." Likely a variant of "Lasso," an exclamation of grief.</note> Master Francesco says in this Sonnet that he burns with his torments, and he is not believed by the one he wishes would believe; then he turns and speaks to her. **A cold tongue and two beautiful closed eyes**; that is, after our death.

<margin>Hiero.</margin>
¶ **Soul that diverse.** <note>The opening of Sonnet 172: "Anima che diverse cose tante."</note> This sonnet, number 172, is truly most elegant. In it, our poet, appealing to his soul, examines his conscience very well; saying: "O soul, who saw and felt all my thoughts as they were made, who perceives well the words that I have spoken, for better or worse, for love—would you now wish that I had never found myself in love with this woman who seems to be dead?" Because he continues by saying he does not find her burning lights [eyes]. With such a life as that of Madonna Laura, one should not be able to err in the "brief journey" that is our life. He tells his heart to direct itself to heaven through the "mist"; that is, through the calamities and miseries of this world. Following the honest steps of his beloved Madonna Laura.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
¶ **Soul that diverse.** Master Francesco, thinking on the harshness of Madonna Laura, asks a question of his soul, asking how much it would wish not to have died in order to have seen Madonna Laura in the world; and then he turns to his heart, telling it to turn to heaven, seeing his lady is of such a will that he must follow her and her steps and her examples.

### SONNET 173.

> ->Sweet angers, sweet disdains, and sweet peaces,<-
> ->Sweet evil, sweet toil, and sweet burden;<-
> ->Sweet speech, and sweetly understood<-
> ->Now filled with sweetness, now full of sweet torches.<-
> ->Soul, do not complain, but suffer and be silent;<-
> ->And temper the sweet bitterness that has offended us<-
> ->With the sweet honor you gained from loving her.<-
> ->To whom I said: you alone please me.<-
> ->Perhaps there will yet be one who, sighing, might say<-
> ->Tinged with sweet envy: he sustained much<-
> ->For a most beautiful love in his time;<-
> ->Another: O fortune, enemy to my eyes?<-
> ->Why did I not see her? Why did she not come<-
> ->Later, or why was I not born sooner?<-

<margin>Hiero.</margin>
<margin>¶ **Sweet angers.** In this 173rd sonnet, he declares himself content to be so in love with Madonna Laura. Calling everything about her sweet and mild. Her angers, disdains, and peaces have been sweet. The poet responds to a silent question that could be put to him, saying: "Even though I have suffered passion for her, and though my soul might rest by complaining of this," he responds that he must suffer and temper the bitterness with the sweetness of having had so much good in the face of her to whom he said, "You alone pleased me." He can well have endured these martyrdoms. Perhaps our poet also believes that through his polished writing in rhyme, he deserves (as he has indeed done) that some of those who come after will say: "Master Francesco sustained much for love." For his love, I would have willingly seen such a beautiful young woman for whom he sighed so much; and for this, I would wish I had been born earlier, or that she had stayed until later so that I could have seen her.</margin>

<margin>Anto.</margin>
¶ **Sweet angers.** Master Francesco speaks to the toils he suffers in his love and calls them most sweet because they are his only care in the "ice" <note>likely a metaphor for Laura's coldness or the poet's isolation</note>: that is, the "vile laurel" <note>A pun on Laura's name and the laurel tree (Lauro).</note> which always stays green: until I am weakened and stripped of flesh: that is, until I die or she has pity on me.

<margin>Hiero.</margin>
¶ **If I ever said.** <note>original: "Dissi mai."</note> Song XXXII. In which, as can be understood from the poem itself, Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch).</note> composed it because it had been reported to Lady Laura that he had said he did not love her as much as was believed, and that he had shown by certain outward acts that he loved another. This being told to Lady Laura, she took it very badly, and showed herself very angry toward Master Francesco. He, seeing her so enraged, composed this song and sent it to her; in this poem, with many oaths, he says he never said such a thing. Swearing first by his love, without which he would die, the song is quite easy to understand in itself; for this reason, I will not expand further on explaining it, as it would be a waste of time.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
¶ **If I ever said:** so that I might fall into her hatred. Master Francesco wrote this song regarding a matter of which he had been accused to his Lady Laura, from which sayings arose to his shame; and he swears that those were never his words. **If I ever said it, her golden arrow.** The golden arrows <note>original: "l'aurata quadrella."</note> are the arrows of love with which he inflames lovers, and the leaden arrows are those arrows of love that freeze the soul, turning the heart away from loving. **Nor ever more sweet or pious:** that is, Lady Laura; **the clear sun nor his sister**, that is the moon, who were children of Latona <note>A reference to the twins Apollo and Diana.</note>, as if to say neither by day nor by night.

<margin>Hiero.</margin>
<insert>S</insert> ¶ **If Love said.** This is explained in the fable of Daphne, which was mentioned above. Ovid says in that fable <note>In the "Metamorphoses," Apollo loves Daphne because of a gold arrow, while she flees him because of a leaden one.</note> that Love carries two arrows in his bow: one has a golden tip and this grants love; the other is lead at the tip and that drives it away. And so he says if he ever said this, let all the leaden ones be shot into Lady Laura and the golden ones into him.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
¶ **HE WELL believes.** Master Francesco grieves in this amorous song over the anger of Lady Laura which had turned against him for the reason we touched upon in the above-written song, that he believed he had her...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s Canzone 32, "S'i' 'l dissi mai." The previous page established the context: Petrarch is defending himself against accusations of infidelity or speaking ill of Lady Laura. This page provides specific biblical typologies—Pharaoh, Jacob, and Elijah—to illustrate themes of stubbornness, faithful service, and spiritual ascent.</meta>

**C** **P**haraoh was the King of Egypt who, while persecuting the Hebrews who had fled Egypt, reached the shore of the Red Sea. Moses struck the waters with his rod and they divided so much that they passed through on dry land; Pharaoh, wishing to follow them, was submerged and suffocated in the waters.

**E** **A**S PHARAOH PERSECUTED. This touches upon a story from the Old Testament: Pharaoh, being obstinate in his persecution of the chosen people—that is, the Hebrews—suffered infinite adversity and was finally submerged in the depths of the sea along with all his people. **So sweet a light that makes me return** <note>original: "Si dolce albor che vinto mi redeit"</note> that is, the speech of Lady Laura; **but I did not say it.** Since the poet Master Francesco <note>Petrarch.</note> has sworn that these were not his words, he returns to a contrary sense of hope, as follows. And then he says: **Ill does he who so quickly forgets such faith.** <note>original: "Mal fa che tata fe si tosto oblia"</note> Notable. He means to say: it is a shame to forget such love and faith that exists between us. **Let truth conquer then;** Master Francesco speaks toward Love and continues: **You know everything in me**, meaning, you, Love, are the witness of everything. **For Rachel I have served, and not for Leah.** Here he touches upon a story from the Old Testament concerning Jacob, who served Laban, the father of Rachel, for seven years to have her as his lady; when the seven years were finished, the father first wanted to give him Leah, who was Rachel's sister. As he did not want anyone but Rachel, he was obliged to serve another seven years. **His chariot a chariot of fire.**

### STANZA V.

<margin>Before.</margin>
**B**ut if I did not say it, who so sweetly opened
My heart to hope in my youth,
Let her still steer this weary little boat
With the rudder of her innate pity;
Nor let her change, but be as she was,
When I could do no more
Than lose myself;
Nor should I lose more.
Ill does he who so quickly forgets such faith.

<margin>Jerome V</margin>
*THAT I LOST MYSELF. This clearly denotes that he is in love with no one else but her, that is, Lady Laura.*

### STANZA VI.

**I** never said it; nor could I say it
For gold or for cities or for castles:
Let the truth conquer then, and remain in the saddle;
And let the lie fall defeated to the ground.
You know everything in me, Love: if she spies it,
Tell her what you must:
Thrice blessed I would say,
And four times and six;
He who, having to languish, died sooner;

*THAT I NEVER SAID IT. Master Francesco says: I love no other except you, Lady Laura, nor could I ever say such a thing for all the gold or the cities in the world. He says he has served for Rachel and not for Leah. Jacob, the son of Abraham <note>Jacob was actually the grandson of Abraham and son of Isaac; the commentator likely uses "son" in the broader ancestral sense.</note>, went to Laban to have Rachel as his wife, and to have her he served seven years; afterward, Laban gave him her sister, who had weeping eyes, so that he had to serve another seven years, which made fourteen, so that he might have Rachel. This is why he says he served for Rachel and not for Leah. In the second "Triumph of Love," he says: "seven and seven years for Rachel he served."*

---

### STANZA VII.

<margin>X</margin>
**F**or Rachel I have served, and not for Leah:
Nor with another would I know how
To live; and I would endure,
When heaven calls us back,
To go with her
In the chariot of Elijah.

*Of ELIJAH we shall speak briefly of his whole life: because Elijah has not been mentioned elsewhere. Elijah the Tishbite was a most worthy prophet in his time, and he shone with many miracles like a burning fire, and his words were like torches. He went by command of the Lord to Ahab, King of Israel, who had abandoned the commandments of the Lord and served Baal. He predicted a great famine in Samaria for three years, for which reason he immediately fled and hid himself within a brook; there for three years he was fed by a raven. Afterward, when the brook dried up, he stayed in the city of Zarephath, and there for the widow he made the flour and oil multiply; he also resurrected her son Jonah <note>According to Jewish tradition, the son of the widow of Zarephath whom Elijah resurrected was the future prophet Jonah.</note> who was dead. While he was praying in the presence of King Ahab, the heavens gave rain and a storm; he then had four hundred and fifty [prophets of Baal] killed...*

<margin>Jerome</margin>
¶ **I WELL BELIEVED.** Master Francesco <note>Petrarch.</note> laments in this amorous song of the lyre of Lady Laura that he has encountered the same obstacle we touched upon in the previous song: he believed he had almost lost her favor, and he sought by many means to return to her grace. Therefore, if he wanted a glance from her, it was necessary for him to "steal" it. He says he believed his life would pass as it used to, without using any more schemes to obtain even a single look from his Laureate Lady. Therefore, he speaks to Love, marvelling that at such an age Love makes him become a thief—that is, making it necessary to steal every little glance from his lady, without which glance he could no longer live. And he says: would to God she had shown herself this way in his early years, for then he would not have cared for her as he did.

## CANZONE XXXIII.

**I** well believed I would pass my time henceforth,
As I had passed these years before;
Without further study, and without new schemes:
But now that from my Lady I do not obtain
The accustomed help; to what a state have you led me,
You see it, Love, you who teach me such an art:
I know not if I should be indignant;
That in this age you make me become a thief
Of the beautiful, graceful light;
Without which I could not live in such distress:
Would that in my first years
I had taken up the style I must now adopt:
For in youthful failing there is less shame.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ **I WELL BELIEVED** to pass my time henceforth. Master Francesco laments, seeing that because of the words opposed to him—of having spoken ill of his Lady Laura—he had lost her grace; so if he wanted a look from her, he had to steal it. **She was so courteous to me at the beginning.** That is, at the start when I began to love her. **In the manner of a man who has no riches of his own.** [A good comparison.] **I become injurious and persistent.** That is, to have some look from her. And he compares his desire to a poor man when he is fasting, who uses every persistence to feed himself. So he says that being starved of the sight of Lady Laura, he would do anything to see her. **He runs even to the angelic sparks.** That is, to the eyes and the gaze of Lady Laura. **Where less guard is kept over what I crave.** That is, her eyes and gaze. **Strange food** and **Miraculous Salamander.** <note>The salamander was a mythical creature believed to live within fire without being consumed.</note> The salamander is an animal that lives in the fire, and so Master Francesco lives in the amorous fire of his lady. **Hence and thence nourishment for a short life.** That is, the merit of the gaze of his Laura, by which he says he lives if he pursues it so as not to die. **If another lives on her own without her feeling it.** That is, if I live on the sight of her beauty without any harm to her, she ought to be quite content. **To search lands and sea from every shore.** That is, when I approach to try to see her, she—who knows—knows. <note>original: "ella chi po sape"</note> Which is to say: no one else knows. **Quiet my frail and famished spirits.** "Famished," meaning servants and subjects. **One lives on scent there by the great river.** By the Nile, there are people <note>The mythical 'Astomi' or 'Apple-Smellers' mentioned in medieval lore.</note> who live on the scent of flowers. **Act by your hand so that I do not die merely by craving.** That is, make me die quickly without always craving as I have done. **Now that my studies are tedious even to myself.** Because I can no longer remain hidden. **She who with her power leads me to the end.** That is, with the power you [Love] give her. **And for the sin of another I ask pardon.** That is, for the sin of Lady Laura, or rather for my own, for I ought to turn my eyes away. It is as if he says: I should not care...

Like a man, whom not his own riches

### STANZA III.

**F**or I have already sought more than a thousand ways,
To try without them <note>The eyes of Lady Laura.</note>, if a mortal thing

So from her beautiful face

C</margin> **WHO knows it not** — Stanza five, where he says his love is so known to all that everyone must know what he lives on and that he has always lived on the love of My Lady Laura from the first day until this one: searching through land and sea from every shore—that is, as far as one can travel—to see her. Thus he lives on love, just as those people live on scents on the bank of the river Nile, of whom we spoke above <note>original: "quelle gente... che viuano di odore". This refers to the Astomi, a legendary race of people who had no mouths and survived solely by smelling fruits and flowers.</note>.
<margin>D</margin>

**HIDDEN flame.** Sixth stanza, where he says his love grows so much from day to day that he can no longer hide it. He turns, responding to a silent question that one might ask: "Who can believe this love is so great?" [He answers] "I know it because you saw well how suddenly I burned." I have now become such that I pity myself. He then exclaims at his fate and at the vain things of this world. And that this lovely light <note>Laura's beauty.</note> is so dear to his heart: a hope so tenacious that it holds him thus mute and bound. And this is the fault of love, but the loss is his own.

<margin>E</margin> **THUS from loving well.** Stanza VII, where he says that for well-bearing torment and for the sin of another <note>Laura’s cruelty or indifference.</note> he asks pardon; and then wishes that he had not turned his sight from the beautiful eyes of My Lady Laura, nor closed his ears to the sweet words of his lady: and so great is his love that even yet he does not repent of it. And he concludes that it is good to die, because through that one comes to escape from grief: and here he touches upon the opinion of Epicurus <note>The Greek philosopher Epicurus; the commentator suggests that the idea of death as a release from suffering aligns with Epicurean thought.</note>.

---

> From the day that I first saw those beautiful eyes,
> Which made me change my life and habits,
> To search land and sea from every shore.
> Who can know all human temperaments?
> One lives on scent there by the great river <note>The Nile.</note>:
> I here, with fire and light,
> Quiet my fragile and hungry spirits.
> Love (and I wish to tell you)
> It is unbecoming of a lord to be so stingy.
> You have the arrows and the bow:
> Work with your hand, do not let me die merely longing;
> For a beautiful death honors all of life.

## STANZA VI.

> A hidden flame is more burning; and if it still grows,
> In no way can it longer be hidden;
> Love, I know it; for I feel it at your hands.
> You saw well, when I burned so silently:
> Now I pity myself for my own cries,
> Which go about annoying both neighbors and those far away.
> Oh world, oh vain thoughts,
> Oh my harsh fortune, where does it lead me:
> Oh from what lovely light
> In my heart was born that tenacious hope;
> Whereby she binds and presses him,
> She who, with your power, leads me to the end.
> The fault is yours; and mine the loss and the pain.

## STANZA VII.

> Thus from loving well I bear torment;
> And for another’s sin I ask pardon;
> Or rather for mine; for I should have turned my eyes
> From too much light; and to the sound of sirens <note>The sirens of mythology, whose songs lured sailors to their doom; Petrarch compares Laura's voice to this irresistible danger.</note>
> Closed my ears: and yet I do not repent
> That my heart overflows with sweet poison.
> I still wait for the release
> Of the final blow, which gave me the first:
> And it will be, if I judge rightly,
> A kind of mercy to kill quickly,
> Since he is not disposed
> To do anything else with me than what he is accustomed:
> For he dies well, who dying escapes from sorrow.

### STANZA VIII.
**My Song, I shall stand firm in the field:**
**For it is a dishonor to die fleeing;**
**And I reproach myself**
**For such laments; so sweet is my fate,**
**Grief, sighs, and death.**
**Servant of love, who read these rhymes,**
**Well the world has nothing that equals my suffering.**

---

### SONNET CLXXIIII.
**R**apid river; that from an alpine vein
Gnawing around, from which you take your name <note>original: "rodendo" (gnawing/eroding). The commentator notes a popular etymology linking the river Rhone (Rhodano) to the Italian word for gnawing (rodere).</note>
Night and day with me desirously you descend
Where love leads me, and nature leads only you;
**V**attene—go on ahead: your course is not slowed
Neither by weariness nor sleep: and before you return
Your due to the sea, wait fixed where you see
The grass most green, and the air most serene:
There is that living and sweet sun of ours;
Who adorns and brings flowers to your left bank.
Perhaps (oh, what I hope!) my delay grieves her.
**K**iss her foot; or the hand beautiful and white:
Tell her; let the kissing be in place of words:
The spirit is willing; but the flesh is weak. <note>original: "Lo spirito e pronto; ma la carne e stanca." A reference to the words of Jesus in Matthew 26:41.</note>

---

### SONNET CLXXV.
**T**he sweet hills; where I left myself
Departing, from where I can never depart;
Go before me, and always upon me is
That dear burden, which love has entrusted to me.
**W**ith myself I often marvel at myself;
That I still go ever onward; and yet have not moved
From the beautiful yoke shaken many times in vain:
But the further I distance myself, the closer I approach.
**A**nd like a deer wounded by an arrow
With the poisoned iron inside its side
Flees; and the more it hurries, the more it hurts,
**S**o I with that arrow in my left side;
Which consumes me, and partly delights me;
With grief I melt away; and I grow tired of fleeing.

---

<margin>F</margin>
**Song.** Eighth and final stanza, in which he speaks to his song, telling it that he will stand strong in the field: that is, in loving, and that it seems a dishonor to him to die fleeing. He says he reproaches himself for his weakness in having so many laments. He then turns to the reader of these rhymes, saying the world has nothing that can equal his suffering.

<margin>Hiero. G</margin>
**Rapid river.** The poet wrote this 174th sonnet upon the river Rhone. This Rhone, according to some, is so named because it gnaws <note>original: "pche rode"</note> around its banks. He prays that it should go to find his lady, because it runs near where Lady Laura stayed. He prays it to kiss her foot or her beautiful white hand, and that such a kissing will be to her in place of a greeting. The Rhone is a river of Transalpine Gaul <note>The region of France across the Alps from Italy.</note>; it is named after a castle. it comes from the Alps, not far from the source of the Danube and the Rhine, and with a continuous course descends into Lake Geneva <note>original: "lagho lemano"</note>. From there it passes through France and runs through the middle of the city of Avignon.

<margin>Ante.</margin>
**Rapid river that from.** This sonnet was written by the poet upon the river Rhone, so called because it gnaws around its banks. He prays that it should go find his lady because it flows near where she stayed. He also prays that it should kiss her foot or her white hand and that this kissing will be to her in place of a greeting <note>original: "en vece .i. loco salutationis"</note>.

<margin>Hiero. H</margin>
**The sweet hills.** This 175th sonnet is graceful and easy. Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> wrote it while departing from his Lady Laura to come to Italy. In the manner of lovers, he shows he always has her before his eyes together with those mountains where he had seen her and where he had left her. He makes a comparison of himself to a wounded deer: which, after it feels itself wounded, hastens to flee, but by fleeing quickly it only grows more tired from the pain. He says he does the same because of the wound which love has given him.

<margin>Antonio</margin> ¶ **OF SWEET hills.** Master Francesco <note>referring to the author, Francesco Petrarca</note>, departing from his Lady Laura to come to Italy, wrote this sonnet where he demonstrates that it always seemed to him that he had those mountains where he had left Lady Laura before his eyes. He makes a comparison of himself to a wounded deer which, once it feels itself struck, hastens to flee, and by fleeing quickly becomes exhausted by the pain; so he says it happens to him.

<margin>Hieronymo</margin> ¶ **NOT FROM the Spanish.** This 176th sonnet is most elegant, in which Master Francesco, through beautiful introductions, gathers the four parts of the world and says that in it there is no more beautiful woman than his Lady Laura. Thus, she is as alone in beauty as the phoenix is alone among birds—which Pliny, in describing it, can hardly believe exists. **What right-hand raven or what left-hand crow:** sings my fate. Among the ancient augurs <note>priests who interpreted the will of the gods through the flight of birds</note> it was a bad omen when the raven flew from the right side and the crow from the left; as Meliboeus says in the *Bucolics* of Virgil <note>original: "Bucolica di Virgi." referring to Virgil's Eclogues</note>, namely that many times the crow had flown to him from the left side. The Parcae <note>the Fates</note> are three: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, who spin human life according to what the poets write. He says that so many are the amorous thoughts he has for Lady Laura that they will make his temples flower before their time—that is, make him become old.

### SONNET CLXXVI.

<margin>Antonio</margin> ¶ **NOT FROM the Spanish.** Searching every part of the sea. In this sonnet, Master Francesco, by way of introduction, gathers the four parts of the world and says that in them there is no woman more beautiful than his own. And she is alone like the phoenix. Let my fate sing, or whichever Fate winds the spindle: the Parcae are the goddesses who spin human life. From the flowering of the temples before their time: that is, making me grow old before my time.

<margin>Hieronymo</margin> ¶ **WILL spurs me.** This sonnet is quite easy, in which Master Francesco tells of the various things that destroy him in his love, wherein the heart is sweetly ensnared. He then describes the time in which he fell in love, which was in the year one thousand three hundred twenty-seven. The poet was then twenty-three years old. We shall speak of this fully in the *Life*; so there is no need to say more of it here.

# SONNET CLXXVIII.

**B**lessed in dreams, and content to languish,
To embrace shadows, and follow the summer breeze,
I swim through a sea that has no bottom or shore;
I plow the waves, and build in sand, and write in the wind.
**A**nd I gaze at the sun so much that its splendor
Has already extinguished my power of sight;
And a wandering and fugitive doe
I hunt with a lame ox, sick and slow.
**B**lind and weary to everything but my own harm,
Which I seek, pulsating, day and night;
I call only upon Love, and my Lady, and Death.
**T**hus for twenty years—a heavy and long suffering—
I have traded only in tears, and sighs, and sorrow;
Under such a star I took the bait and the hook. <note>Petrarch uses the "lame ox" and "writing in the wind" as classical metaphors for performing an impossible or futile task.</note>

# SONNET CLXXIX.

**G**races that heaven destines to a few;
Rare virtue, not belonging to the common folk;
A mature mind beneath blonde hair,
And in a humble woman, high divine beauty;
**A** singular and rare elegance;
And the singing that is felt within the soul;
A celestial gait; and a lovely, ardent spirit
That breaks every hardness and humbles every height;
**A**nd those beautiful eyes, which turn hearts to stone,
Powerful enough to brighten the abyss and the night,
And take souls from bodies to give them to another;
**W**ith speech full of sweet and high intellects;
With sighs softly broken—
By these wonders I was transformed. <note>The "wonders" or "magi" here refers to the enchanting qualities of Laura that transformed the poet’s very being.</note>

# SONG XXXIIII.

**B**efore three days had passed, a soul was created in part
From its care for lofty and new things,
And to despise that which many prize;
This soul, still uncertain of its fatal course,
Alone, pensive, young, and free,
Entered a beautiful forest in the first spring.
**A**nd to a tender flower born in that forest
The day before, and its root in a place
That no free soul could approach:

***

<note>This section serves as a general summary of Sonnet 178.</note>
...his dear and beloved Lady Laura: therefore Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarca</note> describes the things of this love of his, finding them all to be in vain; and he sees himself remaining entirely deceived like a man who sows in the sand. He calls himself blind and slow to everything except his own harm, because he well perceives his own languishing, which is vain; therefore he rightly says he calls upon the name of his lady and death, as lovers do; and twenty years had already passed since he had fallen in love.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ BLESSED in dreams and content to languish. Master Francesco writes how in this love of his he finds all his hopes to be in vain and remains failed like a man who sows in sand. "I trade only in tears and sighs and sorrow"—that is, I conduct myself in trade <note>original Latin: "mercor mercaris," meaning to trade or deal in goods</note>.

<margin>Hieronymo M.</margin>
¶ GRACES. Sonnet 179, in which the poet writes what the image was that transformed him, making a man into a laurel <note>A play on the name "Laura" and the "Lauro" (laurel tree)</note>, which was the figure of Lady Laura herself. He takes her as the laurel, and as one can see in this sonnet, he praises her greatly, as he has always done in every place where he has spoken of her.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ GRACES that to few— Master Francesco writes what the image was that transformed him into a laurel from a man.

<margin>Hieronymo</margin>
¶ BEFORE THREE DAYS were passed: this song is quite obscure and difficult; it almost seems that he himself does not want to be understood. He proceeds only with circumlocution and metaphor, so that it is no easy thing to be able to guess the mind of our enamored poet. Thus, so as not to stain myself or play at guessing, I will put here briefly, according to my judgment, the argument of this song as far as can be understood. It seems that our poet, Master Francesco, not long before he fell in love with Lady Laura—which was on the day of Good Friday, as has been said many times—had confessed and come to contrition for his sins.

sins: And therefore he says "before three days the soul was created in part": <note>This refers to the opening line of Petrarch's Canzone 214: "Anzi tre dì creata era l'alma in parte."</note> because one says the soul is "recreated" when it turns from evil to good. Thus, just as the soul was disposed to things that are not vain, alone and released within the first true [springtime] in the wood of laurels: that is, in the love of Lady Laura <note>A frequent pun in Petrarch's work: *Lauro* (laurel) and *Laura*.</note> from the time of spring, for at that time he began to fall in love with her, which takes away his liberty: that is, to write for the love of a lady in the green wood of laurels for love of her.
