<margin>N</margin>
Another interpretation can still be given which pleases me much more, which intends to signify our three first ages such as infancy, childhood, and youth: because Petrarch was no more than twenty-four years old when he fell in love, and Lady Laura could have been fourteen years old. And this is signified when in the second stanza it says: "a tender flower born in that wood the day before its youth," which signifies the childhood of Lady Laura: no person could approach her without falling in love with her. So, reader, take whichever explanation pleases you more.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
*SONG: Before three days the soul was created in part.* <note>Original: "Anzi tre dì creata era l'alma in parte."</note> This song is quite obscure: but as far as can be understood, Master Francesco had come to contrition for his sins shortly before he took knowledge of Laura: therefore he says "before three days the soul was created in part" because he says the soul is created anew when it returns from evil to good. Just as it was disposed to things not vain, alone and released within the spring in the wood of laurels: that is, in the love of Lady Laura from the time of spring, for in that time he began to fall in love with her and take liberty: that is, writing for the love of a lady. To the green wood: that is, the wood of laurels for love of her: but alas, now he sees: as if to say: I shall die of it. "If I still find her with you in a better part": that is, in heaven. Now here in part are my new questions: here Master Francesco concludes.

<margin>Hieros O</margin>
*NOBLE. Sonnet 180.* in which Master Francesco extols his lady Laura as much as possible: and describes the nature and the unique qualities gathered in the person of Lady Laura.

> That there were forms of snares so new,
> And such pleasure hurried my course;
> That losing liberty was a prize.
> Dear, sweet, high, and weary prize;
> That quickly turned me to the green wood,
> Where fate led me astray in mid-course,
> And I have since searched the world part by part:
> Whether verses, or stones, or juice of new herbs
> Might one day return my mind to be free.
> But alas, now I see that the flesh set free
> Will be that knot; where its greatest prize is,
> Before ancient or new medicines
> Heal the wounds I received in that wood
> Thick with thorns; where I have such a part,
> That I emerge limping; and entered there with such a great course.
> Full of snares: and a hard course of thorns
> I must finish; where a light and free
> Foot would be needed, and healthy in every part.
> But you, Lord: who have the prize of mercy
> Reach out your right hand to me in this wood:
> May your sun conquer my new darkness.
> Watch my state amid the new charms
> Which, interrupting the course of my life,
> Have made me a dweller of a shadowy wood:
> Return to me, if it can be, free and released
> My wandering companion [the soul]. And may the prize be yours,
> If I still find her with you in a better part:
> Now here in part are my new questions;
> If any merit lives in me, or is entirely run out,
> Or the soul is set free, or held back in the wood.

Old fruit upon the youthful flower,
And a joyful soul within a pensive aspect,
Her destiny <note>original: "pianeta," literally "planet," referring to one's astrological fate</note> has gathered in this woman;

# SONNET CLXXXI.

*All day I weep; and then at night when*
*Wretched mortals take their rest,*
*I find myself in tears; and my evils redouble:*
*Thus I spend my time in weeping.*
*In sad humor I consume my eyes,*
*And my heart in pain; and I am among the animals*
*The last indeed, for the arrows of love*
*Keep me at every hour banned from peace.*
*Alas; for even from one sun to the other,*
*And from one shadow to another I have already run the greater part*
*Of this death, which is called life.*
*Another’s fault more than my own hurts me:*
*For living pity, and my faithful help* <note>Referring to Laura</note>
*Sees me burn in the fire; and does not aid me.*

# SONNET CLXXXII.

*Once I desired with such just complaint,*
*And in such fervent rhymes to make myself heard,*
*That a fire of pity might be felt*
*By that hard heart, which freezes in midsummer;*
*And the impious cloud, which cools and veils it,*
*Might be broken by the breeze of my burning speech;*
*Or make that woman come to be hated by others,*
*Who hides those eyes from me, which destroy me with their beauty.*
*Now I seek not hate for her, but pity for myself:*
*For that I do not want; this I cannot do;*
*Such was my star, and such my cruel fate:*
*But I sing of her divine beauty:*

<margin>Hieronymo P</margin>
**ALL** day. In this 181st sonnet the poet describes his cruel and passionate way of living under the passion of love. "Alas, from one sun to the other": <note>original: "lasso che da luno a laltro sole"</note> it is as if he says: I have already passed more than halfway through my life.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
**ALL** day I weep and then. Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> describes his cruel and passionate living under the passions of love. "Alas, from one sun to the other": as if he says: I have already passed more than half of my life.

<margin>Hieronymo Q</margin>
**ONCE** I desired. The poet continues in this 182nd sonnet that to be pleasing to his Lady Laura he has written infinite rhymes: so that she might be moved to pity to love him: but she makes no beautiful acceptance of him: because she hides those eyes from him where he is destroyed. And then he says "I seek that which I do not want, this I cannot do": <note>original: "cerco quello chio non uoglio questo non posso"</note> as if he says: I hate this: that is, pity. "Such was my star": <note>original: "tal fu mia stella"</note> as if he says: this is by destiny and my misfortune.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
**ONCE** I desired with just complaint. Master Francesco follows by saying that to be pleasing to his Lady Laura he has written infinite rhymes so she might be moved by pity to love him: but she makes no beautiful acceptance because she hides those eyes from him: where he is destroyed. And then he says "I seek that which I do not want, this I cannot do": as if he says: I hate this: that is, pity. "Such was my star": as if he says: this is through his bad destiny and misfortune.

<margin>Hieronymo R</margin>
**AMONG** whatever. In this 183rd sonnet Master Francesco makes a comparison, saying that Lady Laura does this to other women: wherever she finds herself, she is like the sun among the stars, which when it begins to appear, takes away the sight of the other stars. He says then that it seems Love says to him every time: "This woman you see on earth, let your living always be beautiful and virtuous": because those who are truly in love make themselves virtuous, guarding themselves from vices so as not to displease their ladies. And after she is taken from the earth, one will see the heavens, the moon, and the other things he names all troubled, and his genius and words will fail him. So that it can be considered...

> *That when I am shaken free from this flesh;*
> *The world may know how sweet my death is.*

---

<margin>
**Anto.** ¶ AMONG however many graceful. Master Francesco makes a comparison, saying that Lady Laura does to the other women among whom she finds herself what the sun does to the stars, which then takes away man's sight, and his intellect and words by comparison.
</margin>

### SONNET CLXXXIII.

> *Among however many graceful and beautiful women*
> *This lady arrives, who has no equal in the world,*
> *She is accustomed with her face to do to the others*
> *That which the day does to the lesser stars.*
> *Love seems to speak into my ears*
> *Saying: as long as she appears on earth*
> *Life will be beautiful; and then we shall see it troubled,*
> *Virtues perish, and my kingdom with them.*
> *As if nature from the sky took the moon and the sun,*
> *From the air the winds, from the earth herbs and leaves,*
> *From man the intellect and words,*
> *And from the sea took back the fish and the waves;*
> *So much and more will things be dark and lonely,*
> *If death closes and hides her eyes.*

---

<margin>
**Hiero.** ¶ THE singing. In this 184th sonnet, Master Francesco writes what the little birds do in the time of May at dawn <note>original: "l’aurora"</note>; he describes it quite elegantly. She whose face is like snow is compared to the discernment of that dawn, which he equates with his Lady Laura. He says that he rises at that hour many times, and in that hour has seen his Lady Laura. By the "dawn" he understands Tithonus <note>In mythology, the aged husband of Aurora, the goddess of the Dawn</note>, who was the husband of the Dawn; and the sun that leads the Dawn.
</margin>

<margin>
**Anto.** ¶ THE new singing and the weeping. Master Francesco describes how he used to rise and wake himself always at dawn out of reverence for Lady Laura; "combing the white fleece of her old man," the old man: that is, Tithonus. That "making the stars" and this "making him disappear": that is, the sun and Tithonus who leads the dawn.
</margin>

### SONNET CLXXXIIII.

> *The new singing and the weeping of the birds*
> *At the break of day make the valleys resound,*
> *And the murmuring of liquid crystals*
> *Down through clear, fresh, and swift streams.*
> *She whose face is snow and hair is gold,*
> *In whose love there were never deceits nor faults,*
> *Wakes me to the sound of amorous dances,*
> *Combing the white fleece of her old man.*
> *Thus I wake to greet the dawn,*
> *And the sun that is with her; and even more the other sun, by which I was*
> *Dazzled in my early years, and still am.*
> *I have seen them both on a certain day*
> *Rise together at one point and in one hour;*
> *The one making the stars appear, and the other making him disappear.*

---

<margin>
**Hiero.** ¶ WHENCE he took. In this 185th sonnet, Master Francesco praises his Lady Laura point by point. He says it has already been twenty years since he fell in love with her, and concludes by saying he finds peace in her eyes: because he is quite happy.
</margin>

<margin>
**Anto.** ¶ WHENCE Love took. Here Master Francesco asks a question: from where Love took the origin of the beauties of Lady Laura; from where the pearls in which he breaks and restrains: by the "pearls" he means her teeth. From which angels she moved and from which sphere: he says this because Laura sang angelically.
</margin>

### SONNET CLXXXV.

> *From where did Love take the gold, and from what vein,*
> *To make two blonde tresses? and from what thorns*
> *Did he pluck the roses? and on what shore the frosts,*
> *Tender and fresh, and gave them pulse and breath?*
> *From where the pearls, in which he breaks and restrains*
> *Sweet words, honest and rare?*
> *From where so many beauties, and so divine*

### SONNET CLXXXVI.

<margin>Q</margin>**Q**uat destiny of mine, what force, or what deceit
leads me back unarmed to the field
where I am always conquered; and if I escape from it,
I shall marvel at it; if I die, the loss—
<margin>D</margin>Loss? Not at all, but gain; so sweet remain
the sparks in my heart, and the clear flash
that dazzles it and destroys it, and in which I am consumed;
And I am already burning in the twentieth year. <gloss>(and more)</gloss>
<margin>S</margin>I feel the messengers of death; whenever I see
the beautiful eyes appear, and flash from afar:
Then, if it happens that they approach me,
<margin>V</margin>Love anoints and pricks me with such sweetness
that I cannot rethink it, let alone speak it:
For neither wit nor tongue reaches the truth.

<margin>Anto.</margin><gloss>WHAT destiny of mine, what force. Antonio. The poet Master Francesco questions himself as to what thing it is that always draws him to see his lady by whom he is always conquered: so that neither wit nor tongue reaches the truth: as if he were to say: I do not have enough wit to comprehend it.</gloss>

### SONNET CLXXXVII.

<margin>L</margin>**L**ovely and pensive, accompanied and alone,
Ladies, who go talking along the way;
Where is my life, where is my death?
Why is she not with you, as she is accustomed to be?
<margin>L</margin>We are happy through the memory of that sun,
but grieved for her sweet company,
which envy and jealousy take from us—
envy, which grieves at another's good as if it were its own ill.
<margin>C</margin>Who puts a bridle on lovers, or gives them law?
None to the soul; to the body, anger and harshness:
this is now felt in her, and at times in us.
<margin>M</margin>**M**ut often the heart is read upon the brow;
thus we see her high beauty grow dark,
and all her eyes bedewed with tears.

<margin>Hiero.</margin><sig>X 4</sig><gloss>LOVELY AND pensive. Sonnet 187, which Master Francesco made to certain young ladies who were companions of Lady Laura: where he asks them, saying where was his life and his death <note>Petrarch often refers to Laura as both his "life" and his "death," representing the joy and suffering she causes.</note>: and why that time she was not with them as she used to be at other times: and he says within himself that they answered him: who could ever place a bridle or law on lovers: as if to say no one: because as Virgil says: what is there that wicked love does not dare? <note>original: "che cosa e che non ardisca l'improbo amore," a reference to Virgil’s Eclogues or the Aeneid, "Improbus Amor, quid non mortalia pectora cogis!"</note></gloss>

<margin>Anto.</margin><gloss>LOVELY AND pensive. Having seen, Master Francesco, once, the companions of Lady Laura without her, he made this sonnet and asks them where his Lady Laura was. And they answer him: "Who puts a bridle on lovers or gives them law?" As if to say: no one.</gloss>

### SONNET CLXXXVIII.

**Q**uando the sun bathes his golden chariot in the sea,
And our air and my mind grow dark;

<margin>Hiero.</margin><gloss>WHEN the sun. In this sonnet 188, as is common for lovers, our poet shows that they speak to themselves: therefore describing the night: when the sun tends toward its setting and goes, according to some, into the Ocean sea: then with Love and with my lady, I argue with myself: just as those do who build castles in the air; so do lovers, as our poet has demonstrated here and in many other places.</gloss>

<margin>Anto.</margin>
**WHEN** the sun. Master Francis <note>Francesco Petrarca</note> relates: what his rest was like when the sun bathes his laurelled chariot in the sea; that is, when evening falls because the sun, when setting, falls into the Ocean sea. With Love, with my lady, and with myself I quarrel; that is, I cry out and struggle. Then comes the dawn and the breeze <note>Original: "l'aura," a pun on Laura's name</note> darkens at daybreak; that is, it becomes day. The sun leads me, which burns and amuses my heart; he says this because he always remains in the darkness of weeping.

<margin>Hiero. Z</margin>
**IF** one Sonnet 189. In which the poet says to his lady those things which should move her to compassion and penance for him; and all the things he writes are the reasons why he dissolves in his love.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
**IF** one faith. In this sonnet Master Francis speaks to his lady to move her to penance for his suffering, and says if a loving faith and all the things he writes are the reasons that I dissolve; that is, loving you, the sin and the fault are ours, but the damage is certainly mine.

<margin>Hiero. A</margin>
**TWELVE** ladies. Sonnet 190, in which our poet describes how he once saw his Lady Laura in a boat with some ladies who were not ladies but stars, he calls them, in the midst of a sun which was Lady Laura; then he also saw her in a triumphal chariot. And he says do not believe that Jason ever plowed the waves in such a ship when he went for the golden fleece; which fleece everyone desires because it well says "where today everyone wants to clothe themselves"; then I saw his lady singing not human but celestial things. The inventor of the ship was Argus, and of the chariot, Automedon <note>Automedon was the charioteer of Achilles, often cited in classical literature as the archetypal driver.</note>.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
**TWELVE** ladies. Master Francis had seen Lady Laura with other ladies in a garden, and leaving it, she crossed a small river by boat, then she climbed upon a chariot to return home; wherefore he wrote this sonnet for them and says she appeared like a sun among ten stars. "The shepherd for whom Troy still grieves"; that is, Paris when he brought Helen from Greece.

> With heaven, and with the stars, and with the moon
> I relate a distressing and hard night;
> **T**hen, weary, I speak to one who does not listen, and I relate
> All my labors one by one;
> And with the world, and with my blind fortune,
> With love, with my lady, and with myself I quarrel.
> **S**leep is banished; and of rest there is none;
> But sighs and laments until the dawn,
> And tears, which the soul sends to the eyes.
> **T**hen comes the dawn and the dark breeze <note>Original: "l'aura," punning on Laura</note>
> Leads in the daybreak; but the sun that burns and delights my heart
> Can alone soften my pain.

### SONNET CLXXXIX.

> If a loving faith; a heart unfeigned,
> **A** sweet languishing; a courtly desiring;
> If honest wills kindled in a noble fire,
> If long wandering in a blind labyrinth;
> **I**f every thought is depicted on the brow,
> Or in broken voices hardly understood,
> Now hindered by fear, now by shame;
> If a pallor tinted with violet and love;
> **I**f holding another more dear than oneself;
> If sighing and weeping evermore,
> Feeding on grief, on anger, and on anguish;
> **I**f burning from afar, and freezing up close,
> Are the reasons why, in loving, I dissolve;
> Yours, lady, is the sin, and mine shall be the loss.

### SONNET CXC.

> **TWELVE** ladies honestly weary,
> Or rather twelve stars, and in the midst a sun
> I saw in a happy and solitary boat,
> The like of which I know not if any other ever plowed the waves:
> **I** do not believe Jason carried a similar one
> To the fleece, which today every man wants to wear,
> Nor the shepherd <note>Paris</note>, for whom Troy still grieves;
> From whom these two made such a clamor in the world.
> **T**hen I saw them in a triumphal chariot;
> And my Laura with her holy, modest gestures
> Sitting apart, and singing sweetly;
> **N**ot human things or a mortal vision:

### SONNET 191.

> <margin>P</margin> Never was a sparrow so solitary on any roof,
> As I am; nor will one be in any woods:
> For I do not see that beautiful face: and I know no
> Other sun, nor do my eyes have any other object.
> <margin>L</margin> To weep always is my highest delight;
> To laugh is pain, my food is wormwood and poison,
> The night is agony, and the clear sky is dark to me,
> And my bed is a hard field of battle.
> <margin>I</margin> Sleep is truly, as men say,
> The wall of death; and it steals the heart
> From that sweet thought which keeps it alive.
> <margin>S</margin> Only blessed and happy land in the world,
> Green banks, flowery shaded shores,
> You possess her, and I weep for my beloved.

<margin>Hieronymo B</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
¶ NEVER A SPARROW. Master Francis <note>Petrarch</note> makes a comparison between himself and a sparrow in this sonnet 191, which sparrow is a very solitary little bird. And "hard field of battle" refers to the bed, because of the thoughts regarding that sweet jousting: because he often dreamed of being with his Lady Laura. And he calls sleep the brother of death; then, concluding, he praises the land of his lady Laura.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ NEVER A SPARROW. Master Francis makes a comparison between himself and a sparrow, which is a solitary bird. And the bed is a "hard field of battle," that is, because of the thought of love, the kinsman of death, which steals the heart from that sweet thought, because he often dreamed of being with his lady. "Only blessed and happy land in the world": he turns his speech to the land where his lady was, and he was not.

### SONNET 192.

> <margin>A</margin> Breeze <note>Italian: "Aura," a pun on his lady's name, Laura</note>, that surrounds those blond and curly locks,
> And moves them, and are moved by them
> So softly; and you scatter that sweet gold,
> And then gather it and ripple it in beautiful knots;
> <margin>T</margin> You stay in her eyes; from which amorous wasps
> Sting me so that even here I feel it, and I weep;
> And wavering I seek my treasure;
> Like an animal that often shies at shadows;
> <margin>C</margin> For now I seem to find her; and now I realize

> For now what I crave, now what is true I discern.
> Happy air, with the beautiful living ray
> Remain, and you, running and clear stream:
> Why cannot I change my journey with yours?

<margin>Hieronymo C</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
¶ BREEZE THAT. Master Francis being once in a certain place where he saw his Lady Laura placed in the wind because of the heat with her hair loose: seeing her, Master Francis made this sonnet speaking to the breeze <note>Laura</note> like an "animal that shies at shadows": like a skittish horse. "Happy air": the poet speaks to the place where he composed the sonnet and where he had seen Lady Laura.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ BREEZE THAT. Lady Laura being once placed in the wind because of the heat with her hair loose, Master Francis, seeing her, made this sonnet speaking to Laura: like an "animal that shies at shadows": like a skittish horse. "Happy air": the poet speaks to the place where he made the sonnet and where he had seen Lady Laura in the aforementioned place.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Sonnet 193, where Petrarch describes the internal presence of Laura. It then provides the full text and dual commentary by Hieronymo Squarciafico and Antonio da Tempo for Sonnets 194 and 195, and the beginning of 196. ...in his heart the name of Lady Laura, for whom he constantly weeps and remains in thought. He says this metaphorically <note>original: "sotto figura"</note>, showing that Love had planted a laurel tree inside his heart; and that with the liquid that rains from his eyes, he keeps it adorned and green. "To discharge <note>original: "vomer," likely a variant of "vome," meaning to pour forth or vomit</note> from the pen with sighs from the side"—"discharge" meaning to cast out—I find her at my breast, where whoever I may be, I find pity at my breast.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ **LOVE** with the hand. This sonnet is literal, and the poet says that he finds the name of Lady Laura so fixed in his heart that he constantly weeps and remains in thought. He says this metaphorically, showing that Love had planted a laurel within his heart and that from the liquid that rains down from his eyes, he keeps it adorned and green. "To discharge from the pen with sighs from the side." "Discharge" <note>original: "vomer"</note>, that is, to throw out, as in the Latin "to vomit" <note>original: "uomo vomis"</note>. Such I find her at my breast, or wherever I may be, I find pity at my breast.

<margin>Hieronymo E</margin>
¶ **I SANG.** Sonnet 194. In which Master Francis <note>Petrarch</note>, his lady being disdainful, says that he still wishes to suffer every bitterness because his weapons do not carry those of Lady Laura: his weapons were his rhyming and his poetizing in praise of his lady; therefore he says the point of disdain breaks: because through this she was not mitigated.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ **I SANG.** Master Francis shows his lady to be disdainful; and says that he still wishes to suffer every bitterness because his weapons did not fear any disdain from her: his weapons were his rhyming and poetizing in praise of his lady; therefore he says points of disdain are scorned because through this she was not mitigated.

<margin>Hieronymo F</margin>
¶ **I WEPT.** The poet speaks now to the contrary, saying that after his lady has become humble instead of proud, and where she used to hide her face from him, she now shows it to him; and therefore he says that he wants to sing in the place of weeping. "Not laurel or palm or tranquil olive"—by the laurel he means the bitterness of love, and by the olive, peace and humility.

### SONNET 195.

<margin>I</margin> **I** wept; now I sing: for the celestial light
That living sun <note>Laura's eyes</note> does not hide from my eyes;
In which honest love clearly reveals
Its sweet power, and its holy custom.
<margin>O</margin> **O**nce it used to draw such a river of tears
To shorten the web of my life;
That neither bridge, nor ford, nor oars, nor sail,
Nor wings or feathers could help me escape.
<margin>S</margin> **S**o deep it was, and of such a wide vein
Was my weeping, and so far the shore,
That I reached it with thought only with difficulty.
<margin>N</margin> **N**ot laurel or palm, but tranquil olive
Pity sends me; and the time clears;
And wipes away the weeping; and still wishes that I live.

<margin>I</margin> **I** was living content with my lot,
Without tears and without any envy

<meta>This page continues the text of Sonnet 196 and begins Sonnet 197. For if another lover has more favorable fortune;
A thousand pleasures are not worth one torment.
**N**ow those beautiful eyes, for which I never repent
Of my pains, and of which I do not wish to lose even one;
Such a fog covers them, so heavy and dark,
That the sun of my life is almost extinguished.
O, Nature, merciful and fierce mother—
Whence comes such power, and such contrary desires
To create things, and then unmake so many graceful ones?
**F**rom a living fountain <note>Petrarch refers to God as the "living fountain" of all creation</note> all power is gathered:
But how do you permit it, O Highest Father,
That others strip us of your dear gift?

<margin>Antonio</margin>
*I WEPT, now I sing. The poet now speaks to the contrary, saying that since his lady has turned from proud to humble: and where she used to hide her face from him, now she shows it; instead of weeping, he wants to sing. "No laurel or palm or tranquil olive"—he says his lady no longer sends him the laurel or palm: by the laurel or palm he means bitterness or harshness, and by the olive he means peace and humility.*

<margin>Hieronymo G</margin>
*I LIVED. In this 196th sonnet, Master Francis <note>Petrarch</note> laments that his lady is still disdainful; and is so stingy with him regarding her eyes: and he recounts what the pleasure of his life was before she deprived him of her sight. He then turns his speech to the Highest God, saying: O Highest Father, how do you allow this, that I should be deprived of your celestial gift? That is, being able to see her beautiful eyes.*

<gloss>I LIVED. In this 196th sonnet, Master Francis laments that his lady is still disdainful; and is so stingy with him regarding her eyes: and he recounts what the pleasure of his life was before she deprived him of her sight. He then turns his speech to the Highest God, saying: O Highest Father, how do you allow this, that I should be deprived of your celestial gift? That is, being able to see her beautiful eyes.</gloss>

<margin>Antonio</margin>
*I LIVED by my fate. Master Francis intended to say that his lady is still disdainful and is so stingy with him regarding her eyes: and he recounts what the pleasure of his life was before she deprived him of her sight: but you do not permit it, O Highest Father <note>original: "loquitur poeta versus deum" — the poet speaks toward God</note>. "Of your dear gift"—that is, of the eyes, which were a celestial gift.*

### SONNET CXCVII.

**A**lexander the Victor was conquered by anger;
And he was lesser in this regard than Philip:
What use to him were Pyrgoteles or Lysippus <note>Pyrgoteles was a gem engraver and Lysippus a sculptor, both favored by Alexander the Great</note>
Who only carved him; and Apelles <note>The most famous painter of antiquity</note> who painted him?
**A**nger drove Tydeus to such fury;
That as he was dying, he gnawed on Melanippus <note>A gruesome scene from the story of the Seven Against Thebes, where Tydeus eats the brains of his enemy</note>.
Anger had made Sulla not just bleary-eyed <note>original: "lippo" refers to someone with bleary or inflamed eyes</note>
But entirely blind; and in the end, it extinguished him.
**V**alentinian knows that anger leads
To a similar pain, and so does he who died of it,
Ajax, who was strong against many, then against himself.
**A**nger is a brief madness, and he who does not restrain it
Is in a long madness; which often leads its possessor
To shame and sometimes even to death.

<margin>Hieronymo H</margin>
*ALEXANDER THE VICTOR. Master Francis in this 197th sonnet describes through examples how much evil there is in anger. And he wrote it to Master Giacomo da Carrara, Lord of Padua <note>A close friend and patron of Petrarch</note>: who was a most worthy man and a great friend of Petrarch; who, having become angry against two of his nephews, was killed by them while at the table; so the poet, seeing him very angry, wrote the said sonnet saying that Alexander, son of Philip, son of Amyntas, who was the victor in every war, was conquered by anger: and for this reason he was less than Philip his father, who was not so conquered by anger, because as Justin says at the end of the ninth book, Philip often feigned anger and overcame it: and Alexander was very prone to it: as he showed toward Clitus and Callisthenes. So that*

<note>original: "Capaneo"</note> Through Capaneus misfortune was brought to him: out of rage he gnaws the head <note>The text refers to the myth of Tydeus at the siege of Thebes, who gnawed the head of his enemy Menalippus</note>: where Pallas <note>The goddess Athena</note>, seeing such cruelty, hid her face behind her shield. He says then that Sulla <note>Roman dictator known for his bloody proscriptions</note> was not bleary-eyed <term>lippo<gloss>bleary-eyed or suffering from eye inflammation</gloss></term> in this anger: that is, Sulla, blind with rage, in one day on the Capitoline caused twelve thousand Romans to be slaughtered. As Suetonius writes, he killed his own worms out of the rage he had for the disease of lice <note>Sulla was said to have died of phthiriasis, a gruesome infestation of lice or maggots</note> that his flesh continually cast out. Valerius Maximus also, in the chapter on anger, says that he killed himself out of rage caused by the pain of Sulla. It follows then with Valentinian, who was Emperor of the Romans and was very wrathful, and his anger harmed him greatly, and for this, writers have greatly disapproved of him. Although Ausonius, through many of his epigrams, attributes no small praise to him. Ajax son of Telamon, the strongest among the Greeks, being unable to have the arms of Achilles—for which he had contended with Ulysses—as Ovid writes, killed himself with that very sword that Hector once gave him. Euripides in one of his tragedies says that once, because of the great hatred he bore for Ulysses, finding himself among the flocks in the Greek camp, he killed many cattle with his sword, believing he was fighting those of Ulysses. And when he realized his error, he killed himself: because it is well concluded that anger is a brief madness, and for those who do not restrain it, beyond the shame, it leads them at times to death.

Nor do I fly only from my secret and my rest; 
But more from myself and my own thoughts: 
Which, following them, sometimes I take flight. 
**T**he common people, my enemy and hateful to me 
(Who would have ever believed it?) I seek as my refuge;

### SONNET 200.

**A**las; love carries me away where I do not wish; 
And I well perceive that the bounds of duty are overstepped: 
Hence to her who sits as monarch in my heart, 
I am much more troublesome than I am wont to be: 
**N**or did ever wise pilot watch from a rock 
A ship laden with precious goods, 
As much as I always guard my weak boat 
From the blows of her hard pride. 
**B**ut a tearful rain and fierce winds 
Of infinite sighs have now driven it: 
For it is a horrible night and winter in my sea, 
**W**here it brings trouble to others, and to itself pains and torments, 
And nothing else, already conquered by the waves, 
Stripped of sails and of rudder.

### SONNET 201.

**L**ove, I err and I see my error: 
But I know it as a man who burns and has the fire within him: 
For the pain still grows; and reason fails 
And is already almost conquered by the martyrdom. 
**I**t used to curb my hot desire, 
So as not to disturb that beautiful, serene face: 
I can no longer: you have snatched the reins from my hand 
And the soul, despairing, has taken courage. 
**T**herefore if it ventures beyond its usual style; 
You know it, since you so kindle and so spur it, 
That it tries every harsh way for its salvation; 
**A**nd better the celestial and rare gifts know it, 
Which you have in yourself, my lady: now do so that she feels it less 
And pardons her own faults to herself. 
<note>Petrarch asks Laura to forgive the "faults" of his soul—his over-persistent love—because her own beauty is the cause of them.</note>

**A**LAS: LOVE. Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> accuses himself of the importunity <term>importunità<gloss>the quality of being bothersome or overly persistent in making requests</gloss></term> that he uses against his lady, saying that love forces him. *Hence to her who sits as monarch in my heart*: monarch, that is, Lady Laura, whose star is in his heart alone.

**L**OVE, I. Master Francesco speaks in this 201st sonnet to Love, still regarding his importunity: *and the soul, despairing, has taken courage*. Love, and *let her pardon her own faults to herself*: that is, do not take another revenge.

<margin>Antonio Brucioli</margin>
**L**OVE, I. Master Francesco speaks to Love, still excusing himself for his importunity: *and the soul, despairing, has taken courage*. Note: "the lover." *And let her pardon her own faults to herself*: that is, do not take another revenge.

<margin>Hieronimo Malipiero, Book R</margin>
**T**HE SEA DOES NOT HAVE. A song which is quite happy for its solitary similes; it describes the great passions he bore for love; and that he never hopes to see the last evening: that is, the end of his love. And it follows that since he fell in love he has never had peace: by following the song it will be easily understood.

<margin>Hieronimo Malipiero, Book S</margin>
**R**OYAL NATURE. <note>Refers to the next sonnet, 202</note> In this sonnet the Poet describes an act performed by the Emperor Albert <note>Though the commentator writes "Alberto," historical records and Petrarch’s own letters identify this emperor as Charles IV, whom Petrarch met in Avignon in 1346 or 1351.</note> who, being in Avignon where the court of Rome was at that time, and there being a certain solemnity where many ladies were, and praising Lady Laura above all: he had her come to him to kiss her forehead. Master Francesco received displeasure from this and it did not please him, and for this he made the said sonnet.

<margin>Antonio Brucioli</margin>
**R**OYAL NATURE. The Emperor having kissed the beloved of Master Francesco at a feast according to the custom of that country, he wrote this sonnet speaking of him and praising him as a lord of singular wit because he recognized the most beautiful lady. *The sweet and strange act filled me with envy*: that is to say, "this act pleased me and did not please me."

<margin>Hieronymo T</margin>
**THE AIR, the dawn: A Song** in which he describes the spring, then grieving through many stanzas, following his diverse sorrows which he suffered during his long love for his Lady Laura.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
**THE AIR, the dawn.** The Poet says that he feels so drawn by love that every morning at dawn he wakes and must return to his accustomed singing of his lady, and from this he cannot abstain. "She stands with harsh alps at the dawn": a comparison. "And I felt them at the first opening of flowers" because love won and shot him in the spring "at the final need": "O wretched soul." Master Francesco speaks here to his own soul. "And they make the asps enchanted by their notes": Asps are poisonous and deaf animals <note>The "deaf asp" is a common biblical and medieval metaphor for those who refuse to hear the truth or, in this case, the lover's pleas.</note>.

<margin>Hieronymo V</margin>
**THAT I HAVE prayed to love. Sonnet 203.** <note>The text labels this ccij, but it refers to Sonnet 203, "Lasso, ch'i' ardo".</note> In which he excuses himself if he cannot fully write of his pain. And the faith of love holds him: and he cannot deny it nor wishes to deny it. But the will cannot follow what reason curbs. Nonetheless, many times it overruns to where his desire leads him.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
**THAT I HAVE prayed to love.** Master Francesco speaks to his lady, yet excusing himself to her if his love oversteps what is due by being too importunate: "You should say, 'Piteous without disdain.'" He tells her that she should speak these words to herself regarding him.

<margin>Hieronymo X</margin>
**THE HIGH lord. Sonnet 204.** In which he says that love has given him such a lady to love that he cannot hide from anyone that he is truly in love: and therefore he says it is of no use to him to flee nor to make a defense: for "one wound burns and pours fire and flame"—this one is his own; the other belongs to Lady Laura.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
**THE HIGH lord:** Master Francesco speaks to Lady Laura and tells her how love has struck him with two arrows: one of mortal gold, the other of rays of pity for himself.

<margin>Hieronymo Y</margin>
**BEHOLD.** In this sonnet, the Poet follows the manner of those in love—

---

Nor did any field or slope ever have so much grass,
as my heart has thoughts each evening.
From day to day I hope now for the final evening
that separates the waves from the living earth in me,
And lets me sleep on some slope:
For no man under the moon ever suffered
so many troubles as I: the woods know it,
for I go seeking alone day and night.
I never had a tranquil night:
But went sighing morning and evening,
since love made me a citizen of the woods.
Truly, before I find rest, let the sea be without waves
and the sun shall have its light from the moon,
and April flowers die on every slope.
I go consuming myself from slope to slope
pensive by day; then I weep at night;
nor have I ever stayed, except as the moon <note>This implies he is as restless and ever-changing as the moon.</note>.
Swiftly, as I see the evening darken,
sighs [break] from my breast, and from my eyes come waves
to soak the grass and to shake the woods.
Cities are enemies; the woods are friends
to my thoughts; for through this high slope
I go venting with the murmur of the waves
through the sweet silence of the night,
such that I wait all day for the evening;
for the sun to depart and give place to the moon.
Oh, were I now with the lover of the moon <note>Referring to the myth of Endymion, the beautiful youth beloved by the moon goddess Selene/Diana.</note>
asleep in some green woods,
and she, who makes evening for me before vespers,
were to come with her and with Love to that slope
to stay there alone one night;
and the day stayed, and the sun were always in the waves.
Over hard waves by the light of the moon,
Song born by night in the midst of the woods,
you will see a rich slope tomorrow by evening.

<meta>This page continues the Renaissance commentary on Petrarch’s *Canzoniere*. The previous page discussed Petrarch’s departure from Avignon and his longing for Laura while at the Sorgue river. Here, the commentators Antonio and Hieronimo discuss Petrarch’s journey to Rome for the Jubilee of 1350 and his interactions with the Visconti family in Milan.</meta>

Antonio ¶ **EVIL presses me.** <note>original: "Il Mal me preme," referring to Sonnet 244</note> This sonnet is a response. Because "the path is long and the time is short," he means the path is long regarding celestial matters.

Hieronimo <sig>B</sig> ¶ **TWO Roses.** Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> wrote this sonnet when his lady <note>Laura</note> was arriving in Florence while traveling to Rome for the Jubilee <note>The Holy Year of 1350, a major pilgrimage event</note>. Following her, Messer Francesco arranged to go to a place belonging to friars called "Paradiso" <note>The monastery of Santa Maria del Paradiso near Florence</note> outside of Florence, where there was an old governor of that place who was a relative of Messer Francesco. Knowing of his love, he picked two roses from the garden and divided them between him and her, saying the following words.

Antonio ¶ **TWO Roses.** Following his lady to the indulgence in Rome, and having arrived in Florence, Messer Francesco went to see the city and went to a monastery called "Paradiso" outside the city of Florence. There was an old governor of that place, a relative of Messer Francesco, who, knowing of his love, picked two roses from the garden and divided them between him and her, speaking the words that he recites.

Hieronimo <sig>C</sig> ¶ **THE BREEZE.** <note>original: "L’aura," a frequent pun on the name Laura</note> The poet wrote this sonnet shortly after the one written above, when Lady Laura was feeling a bit ill: such was the love he bore her that he prayed to God to let him die sooner than her.

Antonio ¶ **THE BREEZE.** Messer Francesco praises his lady and prays to God to send death to him before it reaches her.

Hieronimo <sig>D</sig> ¶ **IT WILL SEEM.** <note>original: "Parra," referring to Sonnet 248</note> He writes this sonnet, in my opinion, to Messer Bernabò, Lord of Milan <note>Bernabò Visconti, a powerful and sometimes cruel ruler of Milan who was a patron of Petrarch</note>. While Petrarch was in Milan, he spoke every time of this lady of his, Laura, and of her great beauty and virtue. The aforementioned Lord Bernabò told him that she could not be as beautiful nor of such virtue as he made her out to be in his verses. Therefore, Petrarch says that to many it will seem the opposite, but let such people come to see her, and once they have seen her, they will say his praise had been **low** <note>Meaning his poetry actually understated her true beauty</note>.

---

Not that the frost adorns with new flowers.
Now little grasses and flowers laugh along the slopes;
It cannot be that that angelic soul
Does not hear the sound of loving notes.
If our wicked fortune is of greater strength;
Weeping and singing our verses,
And with the lame ox we shall go chasing the breeze <note>A reference to a proverb about futility; Petrarch puns on "l’aura" (the breeze) as Laura</note>
In a net I gather the breeze and on ice I sow flowers,
And in verses I tempt a deaf and rigid soul;
Which prizes neither the force of love nor its notes.

### SONNET CCIII.

I have prayed to Love, and I pray again,
That he excuse me to you, my sweet pain,
My bitter delight; if with full
Faith I bend away from my straight path.
I cannot deny it, Lady, and I do not deny
That reason, which restrains every good soul,
Is not overcome by desire; hence he leads me
Sometimes to a place where I follow him by force.
You, with that heart which heaven illumines
With such clear genius and such high virtue,
As much as ever rained down from a benign star;
You ought to say, piteously and without disdain:
"What else can he do? My face consumes him;
He because he is greedy, and I because I am so beautiful."

---

### SONNET CCIV.

The high Lord, before whom it is of no use
To hide, nor flee, nor make defense;
Had kindled my mind with a beautiful pleasure
With a burning and amorous arrow.
And although the first blow was sharp and mortal
Of itself; to advance his enterprise,
He has taken an arrow of pity;
And here and there he pricks and assails the heart.
One wound burns, and pours out focus and flame;
The other, tears, which grief distills
Through my eyes because of your wicked state:
Nor for two fountains does a single spark
Slacken of the fire that inflames me;
Rather, through pity, desire increases.

### SONNET 205.

Look at that hill, O my weary, wandering heart:
There we left her yesterday; she who for some time
Had some care for us, and felt pity for it;
Now she would draw a lake from our eyes.
Return you there; for I am content to be alone:
Try; if perhaps there might yet be time
To diminish our sorrow; which has grown until now;
O sharer and foreteller of my misfortune.
Now you; who have placed yourself in oblivion,
And speak to the heart as if it were still with you,
Wretched and full of vain and foolish thoughts:
For at the departure of your greatest desire
You went away; and it remained with her,
And hid itself within her beautiful eyes.

### SONNET 206.

Fresh, shady, flowery, and green hill;
Where now she sits, sometimes thinking and sometimes singing,
And there she gives witness of celestial spirits,
She, who takes fame away from all the world;
My heart; which wished to leave me for her,
And acted with great wisdom, and more, if it never returns;
Goes now counting where by that beautiful foot
The grass is marked, and by these eyes it is moistened.
He draws close to himself, and says at every step,
"Alas, if only he were here: that miserable man for a little while,
Who is already weary of weeping and of living."
She laughs at it, and the game is not equal;
You are paradise, I a stone without a heart,
O sacred, adventurous, and sweet place.

### SONNET 207.

Evil presses me, and the worse terrifies me:
To which I see such a wide and level path;
That I have entered into a similar frenzy,
And with harsh thoughts I rave with you:
Neither do I know if I ask God for war or peace,
For the loss is heavy and the shame is wicked:
But why languish further? Let of us be
That which is already ordained in the highest seat,
Though I am not worthy of that great honor,

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ **IT WILL PERHAPS SEEM** <note>original: "PARRA forse ad alcun," referring to Sonnet 248</note> to some. Master Francesco responds to an objection that could be made to him about his writing of Lady Laura: it is a thing to weary Athens, Arpino, Mantua, Smyrna, and the one and the other lyre. That is <note>original: "hoc est"</note> Demosthenes the Athenian, Tully <note>Cicero</note> of Arpino, Virgil of Mantua, Homer of Smyrna, who were all singular and most eloquent men. "The one and the other lyre" speaks of Virgil and Homer, one of whom had the Greek language and the other the Latin.

<margin>Hieronimo E</margin>
¶ **WHOEVER WISHES.** <note>original: "CHI vol," referring to Sonnet 248</note> This sonnet is made on a similar subject to the one written above; Master Francesco, seeing that he had not said enough, made this other one, which requires no other explanation: because the argument of the first is the declaration of the second.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ **WHOEVER WISHES TO SEE HOW MUCH.** <note>original: "CHI vol veder quantunq"</note> Master Francesco invites anyone who wishes to see the power of nature to come and see Lady Laura: but if he delays longer, he will have cause to weep forever: as if to say <note>original: "quasi dicat"</note>: he will grieve at not having gone to see her, having heard her named so much as a divine thing.

<margin>Hieronimo F</margin>
¶ **WHAT FEAR.** <note>original: "QVAL paura," referring to Sonnet 249</note> Master Francesco grieved, remembering much of the day that he departed from his lady: because he left her full of anxieties, and he imagines in his mind how she was, and grieved that he often dreamed of her; and may it please God that the dream is in vain <note>that it is not a premonition of her death</note>.

And may it please God that it is in vain: that is <note>original: "idest"</note> that it may not be true.

<margin>Hieronimo</margin>
¶ **I USED TO**. <note>original: "Solea," referring to Sonnet 250, "Solea lontan in sonno" (I used to, far away in sleep)</note> Many times through dreams we are made certain of our circumstances: just as in this sonnet our Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), the poet</note> shows, saying that his Lady Laura appeared to him in a vision to tell him not to hope to see her on earth again. Master Francesco was at that time in Parma, as can be seen by one of his letters written by his own hand on a leaf of his <term>Virgil</term> <note>Petrarch’s famous personal copy of Virgil, now in the Ambrosian Library, where he recorded the date of Laura's death</note>; I have seen it in the castle of Pavia. Later it was printed. He was made certain of her death through letters from a very close friend of his named Ludovico, whom he calls "Socrates" in many of his letters, verses, and rhymes. I say this on the authority of Donato Albanzani <note>A friend of Petrarch and a scholar</note> in the commendation he makes in Petrarch's <term>Bucolics</term> <note>A collection of Latin pastoral poems</note>. Here, in my judgment, begins the <term>Vita Nuova</term> <note>Literally "New Life"; here the commentator uses the term to describe the second part of the songbook, written after Laura's death</note>; that is, what he composed after the death of Lady Laura.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ **I USED TO BE FAR AWAY**. Master Francesco speaks here of an obscure vision that came to him while he was away from her; as he reveals in a letter, at that moment he was in Parma. "Do you not remember": here Lady Laura speaks; "then I did not wish it": that is, she says she did not want it.

<margin>Hieronimo</margin>
¶ **O WRETCHED**. <note>original: "O misera," referring to Sonnet 251</note> This sonnet is on a similar subject to the one above; he asks about the cruel vision and speaks with wonder, saying: "Can it be that she died before her time?" Lady Laura was thirty-five years old, and entirely embittered, he says he marvels that it has not been told by more voices. And not only because of the aforementioned letter does he pray to God and Nature that they not allow it; and yet hope helps the afflicted, as he shows. And if she is dead, he prays to God that He make him die soon as well.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ **O WRETCHED**. Master Francesco says, still regarding that obscure vision: "She has indeed gone out of the beautiful inn"; <note>The "beautiful inn" refers to the body as the dwelling of the soul</note> that is, "I pray that if she is dead, I may also die soon," and in this note—

# SONNET 212

Whoever wishes to see how much Nature
And Heaven can do among us, let them come to gaze upon her;
For she alone is a sun, not only to my eyes,
But to the blind world, which cares not for virtue.
And let them come soon; because death steals
The best first, and lets the wicked stay;
This lady, awaited in the kingdom of the gods,
A beautiful mortal thing, passes away and does not last.
He will see, if he arrives in time, every virtue,
Every beauty, every royal manner,
Joined in one body with miraculous temperance;
Then he will say that my rhymes are mute,
My intellect overwhelmed by the excessive light:
But if he delays longer, he will have cause for eternal weeping.

<margin>**I AM IN DOUBT.** In this as well, the amorous poet speaks of the death of his Lady Laura: now thinking of death, now of life, sometimes weeping and sometimes singing, he passed through his wavering opinion. And venting his grief, he said to himself: "Can it be that that holy face no longer gives me its light?" and in such thoughts our poet lived in doubt: now of life, now of death, thinking that he knows not if she is in heaven or on earth: and he says he is, by comparison, like one who rides along a perilous path. <term>Hieronimo</term> <note>The commentator Girolamo Squarciafico</note> **I**</margin>

# SONNET 212 <note>Though numbered 212 in this edition, this is Sonnet 214 in modern editions, "Qual paura ho."</note>

What fear I have, when it returns to my mind
That day when I left my Lady
Heavy and pensive, and my heart with her; and there is nothing
That I think of so willingly and so frequently.
There I see her again, standing humbly
Among beautiful women in the manner of a rose
Among lesser flowers, neither happy nor sorrowful,
Like one who fears, and feels no other ill.
She had laid aside her usual grace,
Her pearls, and garlands, and cheerful clothes,
And her laughter and song and sweet, human speech.
Thus in doubt I left my life:
Now sad omens, and dreams, and black thoughts
Assail me, and may it please God that they be in vain.

<margin>**O SWEET** glances. In this sonnet he calls upon the beauties of Lady Laura: and this is almost as if he were certain of her death: it is the proper custom of lovers to remember all the acts, all the ways, and all the words they have seen in their beloved ladies, just as our poet does here; and concluding that he had many times gone away from her, sometimes on horseback by land and sometimes by ship; that is, by water. <term>Hieronimo</term> **O**</margin>

<margin>**O SWEET** glances. Master Francesco calls upon the beauties that were in Lady Laura, saying now: "Will the day ever come when I see her again?" And "never far": now he goes by horse, now by ship: he says this because of his departure, as needing to leave, he had to go by water or by land. <term>Antonio</term></margin>

<meta>This page continues the Renaissance commentary on Petrarch’s sonnets, specifically focusing on his premonitions of Laura’s death. ...to many she seemed beautiful. The poet notes a principle of physics <note>original: "physica opinione"</note> which only the Philosopher <note>A standard Renaissance reference to Aristotle.</note> mentions in his *Problems*: the question is why a young person who performs the actions belonging to the elderly dies sooner. The solution is that nature used up the strength in the youth before their old age, and in such a person, nature's forces fail sooner than in others. Therefore, it follows well in Petrarch: that God must have taken her to heaven to make her a star, because in Lady Laura so much wisdom was demonstrated in her youth that she deservedly died before her time. Lamenting at the end, he says his work is a "vile fable" <note>likely meaning a "common story" or "humble composition"</note> completed: that is, to be able to write more in the middle of his years when his time is finished.

<margin>Hier. Q</margin>
THE EVENING. It seems this sonnet was made by our poet during the time Lady Laura was alive, and it says what is customary for lovers who are happy in their loves—they usually desire the night to better lead the amorous dance, and they hate the dawn which takes them away from their loves. This was for him a source of distress; as he was unhappy in love, the night always redoubled his sorrows more than the morning, when the dawn provides another kind of solace.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
THE EVENING. Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374)</note> writes that the nature of tranquil lovers is to love the evening; and he says he does the opposite, because he loves the dawn: for at the breaking of the dawn, one sun <note>Laura</note> rises for the other <note>the poet or the world</note>.

<margin>Hiero. R</margin>
COULD I BUT TAKE REVENGE <note>original: "FAR potesse io"</note>. Sonnet 212 <note>This refers to Sonnet 211 in modern numbering, "Voglia mi sprona."</note>. Similarly made while his Lady Laura was living, in which our Poet greatly grieves that he cannot take vengeance for the acts which his beloved did to him: who, as is common with these young women, shows herself to her lovers and then suddenly hides; and thus his afflicted thoughts leaped to his heart in the manner of a lion.

### SONNET CCXV.

O sweet glances, o clever little words
Will the day ever come when I see and hear you again?
O golden locks, with which Love binds my heart,
And thus captured, leads it to death:
O beautiful face given to me by harsh fate;
For which I always weep and never rejoice
O sweet deception, and amorous fraud;
To give me a pleasure that brings only pain:
And if sometimes from those sweet, lovely eyes,
Where my life and my thoughts reside,
Perhaps some honest sweetness comes to me;
Suddenly, so that all my good is scattered,
And to move me away; Fortune now readies horses, now ships;
Fortune, who always offers herself to my harm.

### SONNET CCXVII.

I still listen; and hear no news
Of my sweet and beloved enemy;
Nor do I know what to think of her, or what she says to me;
So much do fear and hope support my heart.
To have been so beautiful once harmed another; <note>A likely reference to historical or mythological figures whose beauty led to tragedy, such as Helen of Troy.</note>
This woman is more beautiful than others, and more modest,
Perhaps God wishes to take such a friend of virtue
From the earth, and make her a star in heaven;
Or rather, a sun: and if this is so, my life
My short rests and my long troubles
Have reached their end; oh, harsh departure
Why have you placed me far from my own ruin?
My brief story is already finished;
And my time completed in the middle of my years.

<margin>Hiero. Q</margin>
¶ **I have sought.** How much our enamored poet loved the solitary life is well demonstrated in the book he composed *On the Solitary Life* <note>original: *de vita solitaria*</note>: so he rightly says in this 222nd sonnet: and the woods and fields bear witness to it: if my wish were fulfilled: that is, if he did not desire any more to return to his own country, he would still have the beautiful country of Avignon and the Sorgue river, where he went to live nearby to lead a solitary life.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
¶ **I have always sought.** In this sonnet, Master Francis <note>Francesco Petrarca</note> demonstrates what kind of life he has always maintained, and takes the woods and fields as witnesses. *To see my beautiful treasure in the mud*: that is, his lady born in the "mud," which is to say in a village or a lowly place. And where he says "solitary life," he touches upon an opinion of the philosophers who say *a solitary man is either a god or a beast* <note>original: *homo solitarius aut deus aut bestia est*</note>.

<margin>Hiero. R</margin>
¶ **Under such a star.** Sonnet 213. Here our poet continues in the praises of his Lady Laura: and he cannot forget her. He says, then, that he saw in her eyes such honesty and sweetness that for their sake he has always despised every other sight. He does not wish for any other woman to be able to equal her: not only in her own age, but even in those past: and because of this, he gives the example of Helen, who was the final ruin of the Trojans. Helen was the daughter of Tyndareus and Leda, first kidnapped by Theseus and—because she was a girl—she was returned and later married to Menelaus. Then she was kidnapped by Paris: because of which kidnapping Troy was ultimately destroyed. Then follows the example of Lucretia the Roman: who, having been raped by Sextus Tarquinius, killed herself in front of her father and husband. Polyxena, who was the daughter <note>The commentary cuts off; Polyxena was the daughter of Priam, King of Troy.</note>

How often in a moment they both open at once,
The one sun and the other, like two dawns,
So similar in beauty and in light;
That even heaven falls in love with the earth;
As it once did then, when the first branches
Turned green; which have a root in my heart
For which I always love another more than myself.
Thus two contrary hours make of me:
And it is right that I long for the one who calms me;
And fear and hate the one who brings me distress.

### SONNET CCXIX.

If only I could take vengeance on her,
Who destroys me with her looking and speaking,
And then, to add to my pain, hides and flees,
Concealing from me those eyes, so sweet and yet so cruel:
Thus, little by little, she consumes and flees
My afflicted and weary spirits;
And in my heart, like a fierce lion, she roars
At night, just when I ought to be resting.
The soul, which death chases from its home,
Departs from me, and, freed from its bond,
Goes straight to her: who threatens it.
I truly marvel: if at any time;
While it speaks and weeps to her, and then embraces her,
She does not break her sleep; if she hears it.

### SONNET CCXX.

Upon that beautiful face, for which I sigh and long,
My eyes were fixed, desirous and intense;
When Love held out—as if to say, "What are you thinking?"—
That honored hand, which I love second <note>Petrarch refers to Laura's hand as the second most beloved thing after her face.</note>,
My heart was caught there, like a fish on a hook,
Whereby one comes to do good through a living example;
But it did not turn my occupied senses toward the truth:
Like a new bird caught on a lime-twig on a branch <note>A "lime-twig" refers to a traditional method of catching birds using sticky glue (birdlime) smeared on branches.</note>:
But my sight, deprived of its object;
As if dreaming, tried to make its way,
Without which its well-being is imperfect:
My soul, between the one and the other glory of mine,
Felt I know not what new celestial delight.
And what strange sweetness was felt.

### SONNET CCXXIII.
Under such a star I saw two beautiful eyes,
->All full of honesty and sweetness;<-
->That near those graceful nests of love<-
->My weary heart scorns every other sight.<-
Let no one be compared to her, who is most prized
->In any age or on any foreign shores:<-
->Not she who, with her wandering beauty, brought<-
->To Greece such woes, and to Troy its final cries;<-
Not the beautiful Roman <note>Lucretia, whose suicide after being raped by Sextus Tarquinius led to the founding of the Roman Republic.</note>; who with the blade...

The daughter of Priam <note>Polyxena</note>, with whom Achilles was in love; wishing to have her as his wife, he entered the temple of Thymbraean Apollo thinking he would marry her, but he was killed by Paris as revenge for his brothers whom Achilles had slain. There follows then Hypsipyle, who was deceived by Jason. The history is quite clear in the fifth book of Statius’s *Thebaid* <note>A 1st-century Latin epic poem.</note>, as is the story of Argia by the same author. Thus the poet wishes to place his Lady Laura above all these women. And because he concludes well that she is a great glory to him. But because she arrives "late," she soon goes away; this is because his Lady Laura did not live at the time of the most exalted poets.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
¶ **UNDER SUCH a star.** The poet speaks of the beauties of Lady Laura. He says "woes to Greece" because of Helen, whom Paris abducted. "Not the beautiful Roman," that is, Lucretia, who, after being violated by the son of Tarquin, killed herself with her own sword <note>original: *proprio gladio se interfecit*</note>. Polyxena, daughter of Priam, King of Troy; Hypsipyle, who was deceived by Jason; Argia, who was the wife of Polynices—all of whom were most beautiful women.

<margin>Hiero. S.</margin>
¶ **WHICH WOMAN.** <note>Referring to the next sonnet, 224.</note> He intends in every way in this 224th sonnet to praise his Lady Laura above every other woman, not so much for her beauty as for her other virtues, such as wisdom, worth, and courtesy. He says all these things are contained in the eyes of his Lady Laura, whom he calls his enemy—an "enemy" only in that she does not wish to consent to his desires. Thus it follows that through her, one can understand how honor and fame are acquired, and how beauty is well-joined with honesty. He then praises her speech and the beauty of her eyes, which completely dazzled him, saying that these are acquired by nature and not by art.

¶ WHICH

Opened her chaste & disdainful breast:
Not Polyxena, Hypsipyle, & Argia <note>Three tragic heroines of Greek mythology known for their sacrifice, beauty, or loyalty.</note>.
This excellence is a glory (if I am not mistaken)
Great for nature, and for me a supreme delight:
But what of it? It arrives late; & suddenly it departs.

### SONNET . CCXXIIII .

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ WHICH LADY. Here the poet exalts the eyes and the beauties of My Lady Laura and invites the women who follow to become famous by gazing into her eyes and mirroring themselves in the conduct of his lady, telling them that in this way they will acquire the means to rise to glorious fame.

Which lady seeks after glorious fame
For wisdom, for valor, for courtesy;
Let her gaze fixedly into those eyes of that
Enemy of mine, whom the world calls my lady.
How honor is acquired, how God is loved,
How <term>chastity</term> <note>original: "honesta"</note> is joined with grace,
There it is learned, & which is the straight path
To go to heaven, which expects & longs for her:
There the speech, which no style can equal,
And the beautiful silence; & those holy manners,
Which human wit cannot explain on paper.
The infinite beauty, which dazzles others,
Is not learned there: for those sweet lights
Are acquired by fortune, & not by art.

---

### SONNET . CCXXV .

<margin>Girolamo T.</margin>
¶ LIFE IS DEAR. He writes in this sonnet an event that happened to his lady: having once been asked by a matron what was the dearest thing a woman possesses, she replied that it was she who does not allow herself to be deprived of her honor. Therefore he says he does not marvel at Lucretia <note>A legendary Roman noblewoman who took her own life to preserve her honor after being raped.</note> and for this reason he wishes his Laura to surpass her: and to prove this he invites all the philosophers and therefore concludes that she rises in flight above the others in fame.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ LIFE IS DEAR. The poet writes this to an excellent lady who had asked him what was the dearest thing for a woman, and he responds to her question & calls her "mother" as a sign of honor, reverence & love. Change the order: take the contrary. Nor of Lucretia who pierced herself with a sword after being raped: let all the philosophers come, says the moral poet Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, disparaging that act of Lucretia, for her internal grief should have been enough without killing herself; this is the opinion of Augustine in the book <term>The City of God</term> <note>original: "libro de ciuitate dei"</note>.

Life is dear, & after it, it seems to me
True <term>chastity</term> <note>original: "honesta"</note> is what exists in a beautiful woman.
Reverse the order: & things were never dear
Or beautiful to my mother <note>Likely referring to the woman who asked the question, as noted in the commentary.</note> without chastity:
And whoever allows herself to be deprived of her honor;
Is no longer a woman, nor alive: & if, as before,
She appears in sight; such a life is harsh & wicked
Far more than death, & of more bitter pains:
Nor did I marvel at Lucretia;
Except that she had need of a
Blade to die, and that grief alone did not suffice.
Let all the philosophers who ever were come
To speak of this: all their ways will be low,
And we shall see this one lady rise in flight.

---

### SONNET . CCXXVI .

<margin>Girolamo V.</margin>
¶ VICTORIOUS TREE. In this sonnet Master Francesco invites his lady under the figure of the Laurel: which he calls victorious & triumphal because the emperors, when they triumphed, went crowned with those leaves; similarly the honor of the poets, because just as the laurel is always green, so their fame always lasts. He then says that his lady, whom he takes for the Laurel, cares for no worldly thing, neither for the <term>birdlime of love</term> <note>A sticky substance used to catch birds, here a metaphor for the traps of desire.</note> nor for his other restraints, because none of these things have power against her...

Victorious triumphal tree,
Honor of emperors & of poets,
How many sorrowful & happy days have you given me
In this brief mortal life of mine?

**THE VICTORIOUS TREE.** *Messer Francesco also speaks and invites his lady under the figure of a Laurel. "True lady" <note>original: "Vera donna"</note>: she is so called from "to rule" <note>Latin: "à dominor dominaris dicitur." <margin>Girolamo X.</margin>
**I GO THINKING.** *Canzone XXXVII <note>Commonly numbered as Canzone 264 in modern editions.</note>. In which Messer Francesco, considering his soul and how his mind has been spent on vanity and transitory things, begins in this moral song to rebuke himself by way of a dialogue. He composed it after the death of My Lady Laura <note>Modern scholars debate this, as the poem reflects a spiritual crisis that may have begun while she was alive.</note>. And he says that after he noticed his end was nearly at the close of his life, he asked God for enough intellect so that he might remove himself from these common opinions; and he says, correcting himself of his error, that he still sees the mercy of God standing with open arms to receive him and anyone else who amends themselves. He sees this through many examples, yet he still fears not a little for his own state.*

->### CANZONE XXXVII.<-

> I go thinking, and in my thought a pity
> For myself assails me so strongly,
> That it often leads me
> To a different weeping than I was accustomed to;
> For seeing every day the end drawing nearer,
> A thousand times I have asked God for those wings
> With which our intellect raises itself
> From this mortal prison to heaven.
> But up to this point, nothing relieves me—
> No prayer, nor sigh, nor weeping that I make:
> And so by reason it must be:
> For he who fell on the way while being able to stand,
> Is worthy of lying on the ground against his will.
> Those merciful arms,
> In which I trust, I see still open:
> But fear gripes my heart
> Because of other examples, and I tremble at my state;
> For others spur me on, and I am perhaps at the end.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Antonio</margin>
**I GO THINKING** *and in my thought it assails me. Messer Francesco, considering his soul and that his mind has been spent on vanity and transitory things, begins in this moral poem to rebuke himself, grieving for the time lost. One thought speaks with the mind and says... Messer Francesco feigns two contrary thoughts that fought in his mind. From the*

*other side, a thought both sweet and bitter. He sets down the words and the effect of the other thought. "And I fear that a tomb may close us both," meaning that it might last until death. "As many as are born near him," it seems that it "adduce," "addugo," or "addigge," that is, it "removes." "Like a man who dreams": a comparison adapted to the poet's words. "Anger in the middle of the forehead where others may see it," that is, my soul is understood in my facial expression. "Now as I believe, at the time of departure": namely, near the end of my life. "Song, here I am": he concludes the lady <note>the "Lady" addressed at the end of the poem</note> and speaks of death.*

<margin>Girolamo Y.</margin>
**THE ONE THOUGHT.** *Here in this second stanza the dialogue begins, and he feigns Reason speaking to Sensuality, saying that it is no longer time to attend to transitory things. And because he is passing time with great dishonor to himself, he exhorts him, saying:*

->### STANZA II.<-

> One thought speaks with the mind, and says:
> What do you still long for? From where do you expect help?
> Wretch, do you not understand
> With how much dishonor to you the time passes?

### STANZA V

> But that other will, of which I am full,
> seems to blight all others born near it:
> And part of the time flies;
> Because writing of others, I do not care for myself:
> The light of those beautiful eyes, which consumes me
> Sweetly in its serene warmth,
> Holds me back with a bridle,
> Against which no wit or strength avails me.
> What does it profit then, though I fully coat
> My little boat <note>A common metaphor in Renaissance poetry representing the soul or the poet's life journey.</note>, since among the rocks
> It is still held by two knots?
> You; who from the others, who in diverse ways
> Bind the world, completely untie me;
> My Lord, why do you not take
> This shame from my face at last?
> For like a man who dreams,
> Death seems to be before my eyes
> And I would make a defense, and I have no weapons.

<margin>B</margin>
¶ **BUT THAT OTHER.** In this fifth stanza, the poet continues in wanting to excuse his error for the love of My Lady Laura, because writing of her he seems not to care for any other thing because her shining eyes held him with such a bridle that he cared for nothing else. And from that, neither strength nor wit could distract him, because he says figuratively that his **little boat**—that is, his mind—is held within the rocks with such **knots** <note>The "two knots" are traditionally interpreted as Love (for Laura) and Glory (literary fame).</note> that it cannot be untied so easily. And for this, he prays to God that He might take this such shame from his eyes so that he may be cleansed.

### STANZA VI

> What I do, I see, and the truth does not deceive me,
> Though poorly understood; rather, love forces me;
> For the path of honor
> Is never followed by one who trusts love too much:
> And I feel from time to time coming to my heart
> A graceful disdain, harsh & severe;

<margin>C</margin>
¶ **WHAT I DO.** The sixth stanza in which he wishes to correct his error, saying he sees that which the truth does not deceive him in: but love forces him, and he always feels coming to his heart amorous thoughts which drive out every other thought because he concludes and that...

<summary>Petrarch struggles with his desire for posthumous fame and his love for Laura, metaphors he describes as "knots" and a "bridle" preventing his spiritual ascent. He concludes by acknowledging his error while admitting he lacks the strength to resist the "force" of love.</summary>

### STANZA VII

I do not know what span of time was granted me by heaven,
When I first came into the world
To suffer the harsh war,
Which I knew how to wage against myself:
Nor can I foresee the day that closes life
Through this bodily veil;
But I see my hair 
Changing, and every desire within me shifting.
Now that I believe myself to be near the time
Of departure, or not far from it;
Like one whom loss makes alert and wise,
I go rethinking where I left the journey
From the right hand <note>original: "mā destra." This is a classical and biblical metaphor for the path of virtue and salvation.</note>; which leads to a good port:
And on one side stings
Shame and grief, which turn me back;
On the other, a pleasure 
So strong in me by habit does not release me,
That it even dares to bargain with death.

SONG. A beam in a loom around which the cloth is wound.</note> of his cloth—that is, the shuttle that weavers use—and his short cloth <note>A metaphor for the remaining time in his life.</note> is almost finished. ### STANZA VIII

Song, here I am, and I have a heart much colder
With fear than frozen snow,
Feeling myself perish without any doubt;

A great part now of my short cloth:
Nor was a weight ever so heavy
As that which I sustain in such a state:

## CANZONE XXXVIII.

<margin>**Hiero.**</margin> <note>Girolamo Squarzafico was a 15th-century scholar whose commentaries helped make Petrarch’s work accessible to Renaissance readers.</note>
¶ *What should I do. Canzone 38, in which the poet asks advice of Love, saying that it is now truly time to die since his beloved is dead, who has carried away his heart; and if he wished to follow it, he would have to cut short these wicked years, which was not permitted to him because he can no longer see her here, and waiting is a burden: because all his joy has been carried away with her departure, and through her death all his happiness has been taken from him and everything has turned to weeping.*

*What should I do? What do you advise me, Love?*
*It is indeed time to die;*
*And I have delayed now longer than I would wish.*
*My lady is dead, and has my heart with her;*
*And wishing to follow it,*
*I must interrupt these wicked years.*
*Because I never hope to see her*
*On this side; and waiting is a burden to me.*
*Since all my joy*
*Is turned to weeping by her departure:*
*Every sweetness of my life is taken away.*

<margin>**Anto.**</margin>
¶ *WHAT should I do. The poet asks advice of Love. "What wit or words": he turns his speech toward the world. "This handful of such great hope": Note, lover, that you feed yourself on wind. "Her invisible form is in paradise": he places her as having ascended into heaven. "More than ever beautiful and graceful lady": he writes as he imagined her in his mind. "To see her who is now so near the truth": "her" meaning his lady; "so near the truth" meaning near to God, to whom all things are present. "A long time on the path to follow her": that is, if I do not die soon. "Put a curb on the great grief": these are words that Love spoke within his heart.*

### STANZA II.

<margin>**Hiero.**</margin>
*The poet instructs his song to flee the bright sky and the green.*
¶ *LOVE, you feel it. The second stanza, in which the poet says to Love: you feel well what I mean, and therefore here I grieve, although I know that my ill weighs upon you and pains you, because for both of us the ship has been broken upon a rock, and for both of us the sun was darkened in an instant, so that I have neither wit nor words by which I might declare my suffering; and then he turns as one despairing to the world, and calls it blind for having lost Lady Laura, and ungrateful for not having recognized her when she was alive, because he says it ought to weep with him for the good it possessed and has now lost with her.*

*We have wrecked the ship;*

*Ah, blind, ungrateful world,*
*Great cause you have to weep with me:*
*For whatever good you possessed, you have lost with her.*
