You well know with what celestial bearing she lived on earth; I grieve for myself, and let pity come to you—not for her who is dead, because she has ascended to heaven and has left me in war <note>The "war" refers to the poet's internal struggle and the pain of earthly life without his beloved.</note>. And I desire to go soon to see her, and this is what Love knows, so that I do not break the knot of my life <note>The "knot" is a metaphor for the soul's connection to the body; he refrains from suicide only because Love speaks to him of her.</note>.

<margin>P</margin> **PLACE A BRIDLE.** In this seventh stanza, the poet rebukes himself and speaks in the voice of Love, saying he realizes that too much love carries him away through excessive will. Because through excessive wanting, one often loses heaven, where his beloved Laura is. It seems to him that she is dead, but she laughs to herself and sighs for him: she laughs because of the fame he has given her through his verses, and she sighs because of his excessive pain, which carries him toward illicit things <note>The commentator suggests that wallowing in earthly grief can lead the soul away from the path to heaven.</note>. Note, however, that blessed souls cannot truly be saddened, but the poet has spoken according to the things of the world and not according to the celestial.

<margin>Q</margin> **FLEE THE.** In this eighth and final stanza, he speaks to his song, telling it that it should flee every cheerful color because it speaks of sorrow. Where there are songs, it should not approach, but rather go where there are tears.

<margin>Hiero.</margin> <note>Likely a reference to the commentator, possibly Hieronymo.</note>
<margin>R</margin> **BROKEN is the high column.** Messer Francesco <note>A familiar way of referring to Francesco Petrarca.</note>, in this sonnet number 230, laments the death of Monsignor the Cardinal Colonna and the death of his lady Laura. Therefore, he rightly says that the "high column" and the "green laurel" are broken, both of which gave shade to his weary thoughts. He grieves because not for all the gold in the world could he recover them. But if it was so predestined, what more can be done but weep—to always have the head bowed in weeping? He concludes morally that our life, which appears so beautiful in the view of a single morning, is easily extinguished.

## SONG XXXIX.

Love, if you want me to return to the old yoke, <note>The "old yoke" refers to the state of being in love, which Petrarch views as a form of servitude he endured for twenty-one years.</note>
As it seems you are showing another
Wondrous and new trial;
To tame me, you must first conquer
My beloved treasure found in the earth,
Who is hidden from me, whence I am so impoverished;
And the wise, modest heart,
Where my life used to dwell:
And if it is true, that your power is
So great in heaven, as they say,
And in the abyss; (because here among us
what you are worth and then [some],
I believe every noble person feels)
Take back from death what she has taken from us;
And replace your banners in that beautiful face.

Replace within that beautiful face the living light,
Which was my guide, and the sweet flame,
Which still, weary, inflames me,
Though it is extinguished; now what will it be when burning?
And never was a stag or doe seen
With such desire to seek a spring or river,
As I seek that sweet custom,
From which I have already had much bitterness and expect more,
If I understand myself and my longing well;
Which makes me wander in thought alone;
And go to a place where the path is missing;
And with a tired mind
To follow a thing that I never hope to reach.

Now I do not deign to come at your call:
For you have no lordship outside your kingdom.
Make me feel that gentle breeze <note>original: "aura gentile" – a characteristic pun on the name "Laura".</note>
Outside, just as it is still felt within;
Which was powerful enough
By singing to quiet scorns and rages;
To clear the stormy mind,
And sweep away every dark and vile mist
And raised my style
Above itself, where it cannot go now.
Equal my hope with my desire;

<margin>Hiero. S</margin> <note>Likely Hieronimo Squarciafico, a 15th-century editor and commentator of Petrarch.</note>
¶ **LOVE, If you want.** In this thirty-ninth song, the poet shows, after the death of Lady Laura, that Love wants once again to make him fall in love with another woman, and this is [what he means by] "taming me": but first you must conquer [her], and therefore he rightly says that Love should find his beloved treasure in the earth: because nothing else can make him fall in love again except his first love, in whose sight his life dwelt: and if it is true as they say that your power is in heaven and in the abyss, make her rise again and there replace your banners in her; then I will always be of your troop.

<margin>T</margin>
¶ **REPLACE within.** In this second stanza, the enamored poet continues, remembering the beautiful face of Lady Laura: which was his guide and kept him alive, and even remembering it inflamed him, and therefore he rightly says to Love—how does he want him to fall in love once more, she being dead? And by comparison to a stag and a doe: saying that never did they so willingly seek a fountain or river as he sought to see the beautiful face of his Lady Laura.

<margin>V</margin>
¶ **MAKE ME feel.** In this third stanza, the poet continues speaking to Love, [asking] that he make him feel—that is, see—his Lady Laura: as much outside as he feels her within; she who, when he saw her, made him forget his other passions and cleared his heart, and took everything from his heart, so much so that his speech was nothing if not of magnificent and noble things; otherwise, Love, you employ your forces in vain by not returning Laura to me, whom the earth covers.

Y ¶ **FROM THE GOLDEN SNARE.** In this fifth stanza, the poet continues by telling Love that he cannot be untied from his first love for Lady Laura. He is so entangled in it that he cannot leave that sweet sight for any other woman, even though she is dead. Her memory kept his mind "green"—more than if it were made of laurel or myrtle, whose leaves are always green—just as she did while living. There was no lack of noble subject matter for his poetry; but since death has taken her (the very death he once feared to escape), he cannot find any other love to weave a second snare. Thus, Love has lost his weapons against the poet, for he can no longer be captured by any other woman.

### SONNET CCXXX.

*The burning knot, in which from hour to hour*
*I was held fast for twenty-one whole years,*
*Death untied; nor have I ever felt such a weight*
*Of grief: nor do I believe a man can die of sorrow.*
*Love, not wishing to lose me yet,*
*Had another snare stretched out among the grass,*
*And another fire kindled with new fuel,*
*Such that I would have escaped from it only with great difficulty.*
*And were it not for my great experience*
*With my first sufferings, I would have been caught and burned.*

<margin>
A ¶ **THE SOULS.** In this stanza, the poet continues his speech against Love, saying that by the promise of heaven, he cannot be bound to any other than his one love. He is not like others who bind themselves now to one woman and now to another; but his first love was so great that he still cries and weeps for it. Exclaiming against Love, he asks: what divine judgment was it that he, having been born first, was not the first to die? "Thus, Love, I fear you no more, because every woman has fallen from my heart as I remember my Laura."
</margin>

<margin>
B ¶ **DEATH.** In this eighth and final stanza concluding his song <term>canzone: a structured Italian lyric poem</term>, he says that death has delivered him from Love. She who was once his beloved has gone to heaven, leaving his life free but sad because of the pain he feels at her death.
</margin>

<margin>
C ¶ **THE BURNING KNOT.** Sonnet 230, in which he says briefly what he said in the aforementioned song: that Love was trying to make him fall in love with another woman. But he belonged entirely to Lady Laura, even though she was dead. He had already been held by that love for twenty-one years, and his grief was so great that he believes a man cannot die from the pain of the soul. He touches here upon what one reads in Titus Livius <note original: "Tito Liuio">Livy, the Roman historian.</note>: that there were two women who, in the time of Hannibal, received news that their two sons were dead. When one of the sons later returned, his mother died of joy. It is a medical opinion <note>Refers to Renaissance "Galenic" medicine regarding the movement of "vital spirits."</note> that we can die more readily from great joy than from grief; this happens because of the great "overflowing" that the veins make toward the heart, which ends up extinguishing it. This does not happen in grief; rather, the veins restrict themselves, and the man suffers with the sickness of the soul and the body. Yet he did not have...
</margin>

<summary>This page concludes Petrarch's poetic defiance of Love following Laura's death, asserting that his twenty-one years of devotion make him immune to new attractions. The commentary includes a fascinating Renaissance medical explanation of why humans can die of joy but tend to linger in suffering when experiencing grief.</summary>

> *And things present, and those past*
> *Give me war, and those future still:*
> *And remembering, and expecting, pierce my heart*
> *Now from here, now from there, so that in truth:*
> *Were it not that I have pity on myself:*
> *I would already be out of these thoughts.* <note>He implies he would have committed suicide to escape his mental anguish.</note>
> *If ever my sad heart had any sweetness,*
> *It returns before me; and then on the other side*
> *I see the winds troubled for my sailing;*
> *I see a storm in the harbor; and my pilot now tired;* <note>original: "fortuna in porto" — "Fortuna" here refers to a sea-storm. The "pilot" (nocchier) represents his reason or his soul.</note>
> *And masts and shrouds broken,*
> *And those beautiful lights, that I was used to gazing upon, extinguished.* <note>The "beautiful lights" (lumi bei) are Laura's eyes.</note>

<sig>Hiero. D</sig> **LIFE flees.** In this 232nd sonnet, which is highly moral: the poet describes how fleeting our life is; and when he remembers past things they cause him such distress that if it were not for the pity he has for himself, he would kill himself to escape so many pains. All of this proceeds from the great afflictions given to him by the death of Lady Laura.

<sig>Anto. E</sig> **LIFE flees.** He says how fleeting our life is. *I would already be:* that is, I would have killed myself. *I see a storm:* that is, the death of Laura. *My pilot:* that is, love.

---

### SONNET CCXXXIII.

> *What are you doing? what are you thinking? why do you still look back*
> *At the time that can never return,*
> *Disconsolate soul, why do you go on*
> *Adding wood to the fire where you burn?*
> *The soft words and the sweet glances*
> *That one by one you have described and painted;*
> *Are taken from the earth: and it is (as you well know)*
> *Untimely and late to seek them here:*
> *Oh, do not renew that which kills us:*
> *Follow no more the wandering, deceptive thought;*
> *But one firm and certain, that guides us to a good end.*
> *Let us seek heaven, if nothing here pleases us:*
> *For ill for us was that beauty seen,*
> *If alive and dead it had to take our peace.*

<sig>Anto.</sig> **WHAT are you doing, what are you thinking:** Messer Francesco speaks to his soul and she responds to him. *Do not renew:* that is, do not refresh the pain of love for Laura. <gloss>Regarding "do not renew": here the soul begins to respond.</gloss>

<sig>Hiero. F</sig> **GIVE me peace.** <note>Squarzafico appears to be referencing the theme of the next sonnet here.</note> A similar sentiment is found in this 233rd sonnet to the one above; he speaks in the manner of lovers to his thoughts, which want to give him peace and no longer bother him more than he was already bothered by the death of his Lady Laura, to whom every one of his thoughts returned.

---

### SONNET CCXXXIIII.

> *Give me peace, oh my harsh thoughts:*
> *Is it not enough that love, fortune, and death*
> *Make war around me and at the gates,*
> *Without finding other warriors within me?*
> *And you, my heart, still as you were,*

<sig>Anto.</sig> **GIVE me peace.** Messer Francesco speaks to his thoughts and asks them for peace, because they remained in his mind; saying that enough was done by what death did: the memory of that blow. The "blow" was when he was first wounded [by love], from which so many torments followed. <gloss>It is necessary that it leads to the end.</gloss>

<margin>I</margin>
Disloyal to me alone; you who, having been seen as guides,
Go receiving, and have become a consort
Of my enemies so prompt and light:
In you Love stores his secret messages;
In you Fortune displays all her pomp,
And Death the memory of that blow,
Which the remainder of me must break:
In you wandering thoughts arm themselves with error:
Because for every ill of mine I blame you alone. <note>This concludes Sonnet 233, where Petrarch addresses his own thoughts or perhaps his heart as "disloyal" for harboring the painful memory of Laura’s death.</note>

## SONNET CCXXXIIII.
My eyes, our sun is obscured;
Rather, she has ascended to heaven, and there she shines:
There we shall see her again: there she awaits us;
And perhaps our delay <note>i.e., his continued life on earth</note> grieves her.
My ears, those angelic words
Sound in that place where there is one who understands better:
My feet, your reach does not extend there;
Where she is who used to keep you in motion.
Therefore, why do you wage this war against me?
I was not the cause of our losing
The sight of her, the hearing of her, or finding her on earth;
Blame Death; or rather, praise Him;
Who binds and looses; and in a moment opens and shuts;
And after weeping makes others happy. <note>The "Him" refers to God, the one who "binds and looses" (a reference to the keys of Heaven).</note>

## SONNET CCXXXV.
Since that serene, angelic sight
By sudden departure has left the soul
In great sorrow and in dark horror,
I seek by speaking to loosen my pain.
<margin>P</margin>
Just grief certainly leads me to lament:
He knows it, who is the cause; and Love knows it:
For my heart had no other remedy
Against the troubles with which life is full.
Death, your hand has taken this one <insert>remedy</insert> from me,
And you; who cover, and guard, and now have with you,
O happy earth, that beautiful human face.
Where do you leave me, disconsolate and blind;
Since the sweet, and loving, and gentle
Light of my eyes is no longer with me?

<margin>Hiero.</margin>
<margin>G</margin>
*<term>MY EYES</term>. He demonstrates in truth a great love toward his beloved Lady Laura: in this 234th sonnet, speaking to his eyes, saying that his sun was obscured to the world: but as far as reason is concerned, she had ascended to heaven and there <note>original: "ibi"</note> she shone far more beautiful than before: where he still hoped to see her again. She awaited him and was even pained by his delay. He then turns to his physical faculties, telling them that they should not wage war against him if they can no longer hear or see her as they used to; let them blame death for this, or rather in truth let them praise Him <note>God</note>, as the one who in a moment binds and looses all the things of the world.*

<margin>Anto.</margin>
*<term>MY EYES, obscured</term>. Master Francesco speaks to his eyes, ears, and feet, saying that each has lost its function: that is, the eyes to see his lady, the ears to hear her, the feet to seek her out. And he says this because his lady is dead and has gone to paradise. "Praise Him": that is, God.*

<margin>Hiero.</margin>
<margin>H</margin>
*<term>SINCE that angelic sight</term>. He says in this 235th sonnet that since his lady is dead, he seeks by speaking to ease his sorrows. "This one" <note>original: "Questu[n]" - likely a contraction for 'this one remedy'</note>, namely this remedy and comfort. "Since the sweet": that is, it kills me as well.*

<margin>Hiero.</margin>
<margin>I</margin>
*<term>IF love [gives] new counsel</term>. In this 236th sonnet, Master Francesco laments the love of his lady; he says that if Love does not give him some counsel—and this is because of the grief over her death—it will be necessary for him to die of sorrow as well: wherefore he says that more than ever his Laura comes to his heart, as he often remembers her and her glory, but it pains him not to be able to see her.*

<margin>Antonio</margin>
*IF Love [does not bring] new counsel. Master Francesco laments the love of his lady and says that if Love does not give him some counsel, he will necessarily die of grief. Whereby clearer than ever she shines through the heart. He says that more than ever his Laura shines through to his heart and not to his eyes, because he often remembers her and her glory, but he cannot see her.*

<margin>Hieronymo</margin>
*IN her happy [age]. In this 237th sonnet, the poet describes what age his lady was when she died and how long he has loved her up to this point after she has died. Alas, why does my mortal [part]: that is, why do I not also die, to make myself more burdened with pains.*

<margin>Antonio</margin>
*IN her most beautiful age. In this sonnet, Master Francesco writes what age his lady was when she died and how long he has loved her up to this point after she has died. Alas, why does my mortal [part]: that is, why do I not die yet. To make myself a heavier burden to myself: <note>original: "idest piu carco de pene"</note> that is, more loaded with pains.*

*IF THE Lamenting. He says in this 238th [sonnet] that through any of these things: that is, either the lamenting of birds or the sighing of the breeze through the leaves that rustle where he was writing of love, it seems to him that he hears his Laura; then he recounts what it seems to him she says to him there where I sit <note>original: "idest la doue sedeua"</note> that is, there where he sat. Who made my days <note>original: "idest fecero"</note> that is, they made. Alas, why do you consume yourself before your time: here his lady responds and comforts him.*

### SONNET CCXXXVI.

If Love does not bring new counsel,
By force it will be necessary that I change my life:
So much fear and grief afflict my sad soul,
That desire lives, and hope is dead;
Whereby it becomes terrified and discouraged.
My life entirely, both night and day, weeps,
Tired, without a pilot in a breaking sea,
And on a doubtful path without a trusted escort.
An imagined guide leads it,
For the true one is underground—or rather, is in heaven;
Whence clearer than ever she shines through to the heart;
But not to the eyes, for a sorrowful veil
Denies them that desired light,
And makes me change my hair so prematurely. <note>Petrarch refers to his hair turning gray or white from the stress of his mourning.</note>

### SONNET CCXXXVII.

In her most beautiful and flourishing age,
When love is accustomed to have the most power in us,
Leaving her earthly shell on the earth,
My vital breeze <note>A characteristic pun on the name "Laura" and "l'aura" (the breeze/breath).</note> departed from me;
And living, and beautiful, and naked, she ascended to heaven;
From there she rules me, from there she compels me.
Alas, why does the last day—which is the first of the other life—
Not strip me of my mortal [flesh]?
So that, just as my thoughts go after her,
So the soul, light, unhindered, and happy,
Might follow her, and I might be out of such great anguish.
Whatever is delayed is truly for my harm,
To make myself a heavier burden to myself.
Oh, what a beautiful death it would have been three years ago today! <note>This marks the third anniversary of Laura’s death on April 6, 1348.</note>

### SONNET CCXXXVIII.

If the lamenting of birds, or green leaves
Moving softly in the summer breeze,
Or the hoarse murmuring of clear waves
Is heard from a flowering and fresh bank,
There where I sit pensive of love, and write;
She, whom heaven showed us and earth hides,
I see, and hear, and understand that she still lives,
Responding from so far away to my sighs.
"Alas, why do you consume yourself before your time?"

### SONNET CCXXXIX.

> Never was I in a place where I saw so clearly

### SONNET CCXL.

> How many times to my sweet retreat
> Fleeing others, and if it may be, myself,

> Breaking the nearby air with sighs.

> Seeking with thought the high delight;
> Which death has taken, for which I often call her.

> Now I have seen her upon the fresh grass
> Treading the flowers like a living lady,
> Showing by her look that she pities me.

<margin>Hieronimo</margin>
¶ NEVER [was I]. Sonnet 239. Hieronimo writes: Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch</note> writes that walking one day through woods and valleys thinking of his lady, he happened to find himself upon a hill from which he saw below the city of Avignon, and below in the valley he saw the little village where his Lady Laura was: and that place was flowering with many herbs, waters, and *plenty* of shade: he says this place is dedicated to Venus just like Cyprus, which island is dedicated to Venus by the poets, and there was her most marvelous temple, about which Cornelius Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian</note> writes much.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ NEVER was I in a place where. Walking one day through woods and valleys thinking of his lady, he happened to find himself upon a hill from which he saw all of Avignon and below was a flowery little valley: with plenty of water and shade: and so about this place he made this sonnet: "In Cyprus had": he speaks of Cyprus which is an island dedicated to Venus. "But you, well-born one": He turns to speak to his lady.

<margin>Hieronimo N.</margin>
¶ HOW many times. In this 240th sonnet the poet says that returning to his solitary place he had walked weeping and sighing, set in harsh paths to find his lady: and he says that it seemed to him he saw her from hour to hour in the form of a goddess above the river Sorgue where he used to live, as we will clearly state in his Life.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ HOW many times has my heart. Here he says that returning to his solitary retreat: he had walked weeping and sighing and set in harsh paths to find his lady: and he says that it seemed to him he saw her now in the form of a goddess upon the river Sorgue: where she used to go.

<margin>Hieronimo O.</margin>
¶ SOUL. What the poet has said in many other sonnets he returns to say here in this 241st sonnet, in which the soul of his Lady Laura speaks: who appeared to him in sleep, and he, through great love, thanks her for the vision.

**Hieronimo:** "DISCOLORED." <note>original: "DISCOLORATO"</note> Our poet turns his speech against death in this Sonnet 242, reproaching it for having discolored the most beautiful face that was ever on earth and for having released the most noble spirit—more kindled with virtue than any other. Therefore he rightly laments her death, which in a moment took all his good from him, so that everything he sees and hears becomes a source of annoyance to him. Yet then he comforts himself saying that if he could describe her light as heaven sees it, he would be warmed by love even if his heart were made of wood.

### SONNET 242.

**D** eath, you have discolored the most beautiful face
That was ever seen, and extinguished the most beautiful eyes;
You have released a spirit more kindled with burning virtues
From the most graceful and beautiful knot. <note>original: "nodo," a common Petrarchan metaphor for the body binding the soul.</note>
**I** n a moment you have taken all my good from me:
You have placed silence upon the most sweet accents
That were ever heard; and left me full of laments.
Whatever I see is a burden to me, and whatever I hear.
**M** y Lady truly returns to console such great sorrow,
To where pity leads her back,
Nor do I find in this life any other help;
**A** nd if I could retell how she speaks and how she shines,
I would kindle with love—
I do not say a man—but the heart of a tiger or a bear.

**Hieronimo:** "SO BRIEF." <note>original: "SI BREue"</note> Sonnet 243, in which he laments the brevity of time and that his lady is dead, meaning medicine no longer avails his grief. Love, he says, has left him and keeps him on the cross; for although Lady Laura is dead, he says she can appear to him, but he cannot endure her great light. For this reason, he blesses the hours of his falling in love.

### SONNET 243.

**T** ime is so brief, and thought so fast,
Which brings my Lady back to me, though dead,
That the medicine for my great pain is short-lived:
Yet while I see her, nothing harms me.
**L** ove, who has bound me and keeps me on the cross,
Trembles when he sees her at the door
Of my soul, where she still kills me, being so skilled,
So sweet in sight, and so soft in voice.
**L** ike a lady coming to her own dwelling, she comes proud,
Chasing from the dark and heavy heart
All sad thoughts with her serene brow.
**T** he soul, which cannot sustain such great light,
Sighs and says: "Oh, blessed be the hours
Of the day when you opened this path with your eyes."

**Antonio:** "Time is SO brief": Master Francesco says that his thought is so fast in imagining Lady Laura that he is not sufficient to find a remedy for his grief, which is so great. "Like a lady in her dwelling": here he identifies his heart as the dwelling of Lady Laura, into which she often comes. "Of the day that you opened this path with your eyes": that is, the path that leads into his heart.

# SONNET CCXLIIII.

Never did a pitying mother to her dear son,
Nor a wife, burning with love, to her beloved spouse,
Give with so many sighs, or with such concern
In an uncertain state, such faithful counsel;
As she gives to me; who, looking upon my heavy exile <note>The poet refers to his earthly life as a "heavy exile" from the divine presence and from Laura.</note>
From her eternal high retreat,
Often returns to me with her accustomed affection,
Her brow adorned with a double pity,
Now as a mother, now as a lover: now she fears; now she burns 
With an honorable fire; and in her speech she shows me
What I should flee or follow in this journey,
Relating the misfortunes of our life,
Praying that my soul does not delay its rising:
And only while she speaks, do I have peace or truce.

<margin>R</margin>
<sig>R</sig>
> NEVER. Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> makes a comparison in this sonnet 244 between a mother’s love toward her dear son and a wife’s toward her husband, saying that no mother ever counseled her son, nor wife her husband, as well as his Laura counseled him when he was in an uncertain state. Therefore he rightly says that now as a lover and now as a mother she fears and burns with so many things concerning his life, praying that his soul no longer delays, for only when she speaks does he have peace or truce—that is, through her counsel.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
> NEVER a pitying mother. Master Francesco makes two comparisons: first of the love of a mother toward a dear son; second of a wife toward her husband. He says that neither of those ever counseled a son or husband as well as his Laura counsels him in his uncertain state.

# SONNET CCXLV.

**I**f that sweet breeze of sighs <note>original: "aura" – a recurring pun on the name Laura</note>,
Which I hear from her who was my 
Lady here; now she is in heaven, yet it seems she is still here,
And lives, and feels, and walks, and loves, and breathes,
**I**f I could bring it back; now what warm desires
I would stir by speaking; so solicitous and pious
She returns to where I am, fearing lest on the way
I grow weary, or turn back, or wander to the left or right:
**S**he teaches me to go straight to heaven; and I, who understand
Her chaste allurements and her righteous prayers
With their sweet, pitying, and low murmur;
**M**ust govern and bend myself according to her,
Because of the sweetness I take from her words:
Which would have the power to make a stone weep.

<margin>
Hiero.
S

<sig>S</sig>
> IF THAT Laura: It seems the poet does not know how to pull himself away from these dreams of his, and this is because of a great passion of love. Thus in this 245th sonnet he says that if he could in any way bring back the sighs of Laura—who was once his lady on earth and is now in heaven—it seems through the sighing she does on earth that if he could bring back those warm desires, she would come to see him wherever he might be. Petrarch truly dreams of attributing human passion to blessed souls: but speaking as a lover, he may be forgiven.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
> IF THAT sweet breeze. Master Francesco says that if he could in any way bring back Laura through the sighs she draws for him when she comes from heaven to visit him, it would rekindle every person with warm desire.

...of his Sennuccio and of his death, wishing him to ascend to heaven to the third sphere—which is the heaven of Venus where lovers dwell—and asking that he greet others on his behalf. Guittone, who was from Arezzo <note>The text says "of Calabria," but Guittone d'Arezzo was a famous Tuscan poet; this may be a geographical error by the commentator or a specific historical reference to his travels</note> and was among the first to write in rhyme; and then, after he greets Guittone, he should greet Messer Cino, and Dante, and our Franceschino, and all that company.

> Remembering her beautiful face and her holy works.

Messer Cino, who was from Pistoia and a great doctor of law, also wrote many rhymes for love which are read even to our day; and then he greets Dante, who was the supreme poet and wrote many moral songs for his Beatrice; then Franceschino, his very dear friend, with all the rest of the company of lovers. Franceschino was a great singer of rhymes and was a great friend of Petrarch, as is shown in the *Triumphs*; finally, he charges him to tell his lady in what troubles and sorrows he lives for her.

<margin>Anto.</margin> **SENNUCCIO** my good friend. A great friend of Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> had died, and he speaks to him in this sonnet, placing him in the third heaven: that is, in the sphere of lovers where Venus resides. And he prays that he should greet Guittone, Messer Cino, and Dante, who were his contemporaries, and Lady Laura.

<margin>Hiero. V</margin> **I HAVE.** In this 247th sonnet, the poet writes that, having climbed a small hill from which one can see Avignon with effort <note>original: "da forza"</note>, looking into the valley where his Lady Laura was born, he speaks against his miserable life. He says she is in heaven and he goes searching for her everywhere, and to this every plant and every thicket bears witness; then, for further emphasis, he says that even the waters that drip there know how great his pain is.

<margin>Anto.</margin> **I HAVE** filled all this air with sighs. Master Francesco, having climbed the mountain that looks toward Avignon and into the valley where Lady Laura was born, composed this sonnet and recounts his miserable life. There is no thicket nor stone that does not bear witness to his bitter life, as attested by the plants, stones, and thickets.

**THE SOUL.** Master Francesco says through circumlocution <note>An indirect or roundabout way of speaking</note> in this 248th sonnet how his lady, through her death, has ascended to paradise; and he says he begins to wake up, realizing it was for the best that she did not consent to his desires, and for this she is in glory and he is praised for his virtue.

-> My soul’s flame, beautiful beyond the beautiful, <-

<margin>Anto.</margin> **THE SOUL'S** flame, beautiful beyond the beautiful. Master Francesco says through circumlocution how his lady, through death, has ascended to paradise: which is her rightful country. "Before my time" means she departed before him, as if to say that although she deserved to be in paradise, she went too soon because he remained behind.

### SONNET CCXLIX.

> As the world goes: now it delights and pleases me
> that which most displeased me: now I see and feel;
> That to have salvation I had torment,
> And a brief war for eternal peace.
> O hope, O desire always fallacious,
> And for lovers a hundred times more so:
> O how much worse it was for her to make me happy,
> She who now sits in heaven and lies in the earth.
> But blind love and my deaf mind
> Misled me so; that to go by living
> Force I had to, where death was.
> Blessed is she; who to a better shore
> Turned my course, and the wicked burning desire
> Coaxing she restrained, so that I do not perish.

<margin>Hieronymo Y</margin>
**AS THE world goes:** This is a Horatian sentiment <note>Referring to the Roman poet Horace</note> that Petrarch places in this 249th sonnet: that the world has always been a certain way. Therefore, he says well "now it delights me." And now he fears what used to please him and likes what he once most disliked; for this reason, he often sees that where he believed he would have pleasure, he had torment. Therefore, he rightly says hope is fallacious, and then speaks of his Laura, who by coaxing his love led him to an end he was not seeking <note>meaning she guided him toward spiritual salvation rather than earthly lust</note>.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
**AS THE world goes.** Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> praises the way he sees the world going. Discerning that it was worse for him to have achieved his intent with his lady. "So that he does not perish": that is, die.

### SONNET CCL.

> O happy Tithonus <note>In Greek mythology, the mortal husband of Eos (Dawn), who was granted eternal life but not eternal youth</note>, you know well the hour

<margin>Hieronymo Z</margin>
**WHEN I SEE.** Master Francesco says in this 250th sonnet how in the morning, when he sees the dawn <note>Petrarch uses "l'aurora" as a pun on "Laura"</note> departing—which the poets imagine, as we touched on above, goes to sleep with her old husband Tithonus—at that hour the poet remembers his Laura, as they share nearly the same name. And then he speaks to Tithonus, saying that the parting of his dawn from him is not as bitter as that of his Laura: because his dawn returns every night to see him, but his Laura never returns.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
**WHEN I SEE from heaven.** Master Francesco saw how in the morning, when he sees the dawn departing—whom the poets imagine goes to sleep with her old husband Tithonus—at that hour he remembers his Laura, as they share nearly the same name. And then he speaks to Tithonus, saying that the parting his dawn makes from him is not as bitter as that of his Laura: because every night she returns to him, and his lady never returns.

<margin>Hieronymo A</margin>
IF I HAD. Master Francesco shows in this 252nd sonnet that, having sent the rhymes he had composed to some of his companions—who, as they deservedly ought, praised them—and having received as a response the good judgment they had of his rhymes, he grieves that he had not written them more ornately. He says he can no longer do so because she for whom he sang is dead. Certainly, he says in excuse, that at that time he sought only to unburden his sorrowful heart of his love, and not to acquire fame through his writing.

...if he were to recount his sorrows, it would break the very stones. "Divine" is said of a thing deified and honored by virtue. "Who weeps inside": that is, the soul and the love within me. Truly we are dust and shadow.

<margin>Hieronimo C</margin>
**TRULY** the desire. He says this because of the various [thoughts].
**MY THOUGHTS USED TO**. Master Francesco speaks to himself in this 254th sonnet and says that by seeing his lady, all his thoughts were in her, who was his object; but since she has gone to heaven, perhaps up there she speaks and hears and feels as she used to, and grieves that she died so soon. He says she has returned to heaven from where she first came, touching upon the <term>Platonic opinion: the philosophical belief that human souls or "forms" exist in heaven before birth and return there after death.</term> that our every form is first in heaven, from where such beauty without example proceeded.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
**MY THOUGHTS USED TO.**
Master Francesco speaks to himself and says that while his lady was living, his thoughts were in her, who was his object: but after she went to heaven, he says that she looks back, perhaps from up there, and speaks, hears, and feels as she once did. And he grieves that she died so soon and returned to where she came from: that is, from heaven, where she proceeded with such beauty without example.

<margin>Hieronimo D</margin>
**I USED TO.** Master Francesco says in this 255th sonnet, excusing himself for the error of which he formerly accused himself: that is, for being captured while My Lady Laura was living. He speaks against the goddess <term>Fates: in mythology, the Parcae (Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos) who spin and cut the thread of life.</term> who so quickly broke the thread in which the life of his lady was wound. Wherefore death was pleasing beyond our custom: that is, it pleased him to die, which is beyond the common human habit that death should be pleasing.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
**I USED TO ACCUSE MYSELF.** Master Francesco says that he now excuses himself for the error of which he was once accused: that is, of being captured while My Lady Laura was living. He speaks against the goddesses, the Fates, who so quickly broke the spindle with which the bond was twisted that held him captured; so sweetly was the arrow made. Wherefore death pleased me beyond our custom: that is, because of that arrow it pleased me to die: which is beyond human usage that death should be pleasing.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s "Rime sparse," specifically transitioning from the poet's reflections on his "virtuous prison" to the miraculous coexistence of beauty and virtue in Laura, and his subsequent despair after her death. The commentary is provided by Hieronimo Corso (Hiero.) and Antonio Brucioli (Anto.).</meta>

<margin>Hiero. E</margin>
¶ **TWO great enemies.** <note>original: "DVE gran nemiche"</note> Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> writes in this 256th sonnet about impossible things: that virtue could coexist with beauty. He says this because usually, when a woman is beautiful, she cannot also be chaste; therefore, he says that Virtue and Beauty were two enemies. It is a great miracle that they resisted conflict while being together, as they are opposites and enemies; yet, according to him, they were both found in Lady Laura. And "if I am slow to follow"—meaning I remain behind so that I do not die—this will be the reason that, by necessity, I shall make her immortal.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
¶ **TWO great enemies.** Messer Francesco writes of virtue and beauty, saying it seems a great miracle they were joined, being two opposites and enemies. That is, that a modest heart was found joined with such great beauty as was in Lady Laura. And "if I am slow to follow," that is <note>original Latin: "idest"</note>, I remain behind her who is not dead in fame. "Not die": this will be the reason that perhaps I will make her immortal.

### SONNET 256.

->Two great enemies were joined together,<-
->Beauty and virtue <term>Honestà: in this context, it refers to moral integrity and feminine chastity.</term> with such peace,<-
->That the holy soul never felt rebellion<-
->After they were joined to stay with her:<-
->**A**nd now by death they are scattered and disjointed;<-
->One is in heaven, which glories and boasts of it;<-
->The other is underground, covering those beautiful eyes,<-
->From which once came so many arrows of love.<-
->**T**he gentle gesture, and the wise, humble speech<-
->Which moved from a high place: and the sweet gaze<-
->Which wounded my heart and still marks it;<-
->**T**hey have vanished: and if I am slow to follow,<-
->Perhaps it will be that her fair, noble name<-
->I shall consecrate with this weary pen.<-

<margin>Hiero. F</margin>
¶ **WHEN.** <note>original: "QVANDO"</note> In this 257th sonnet, Messer Francesco says that he is now weary of life, remembering the past days, and that she for whom he burned is extinguished. I rouse myself from whatever reminds me of her, and because of this, he says he envies every "extreme fate" <note>likely meaning those already dead or in the worst possible misery</note>. For this reason, he cries out to his fatal star and to fortune for having placed him in such a lowly state of living without his Lady Laura.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
¶ **WHEN I.** Messer Francesco says that he is now weary of being alive, remembering the past days. The main verb appears at the end: "I rouse myself." "O always sweet for me": that is, when he fell in love and when his Laura died, which happened in different years; but it falls on the same hours and days of the same month, as is noted in the life of the poet. <note>Laura reportedly died on the same day and hour that Petrarch first saw her: April 6th.</note>

### SONNET 257.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s "Rime sparse" (Songbook) following the death of his beloved Laura. It focuses on the poet's profound sense of loss and his envy toward the elements and entities that now possess her—the earth, the heavens, and the blessed spirits—while he remains in the physical world, haunting the places they once shared near the Sorgue river.</meta>

Where are the beauties gathered in her,
That for a long time made me desire them?
Where is the gentle shade of the human face,
That gave peace and rest to my tired soul,
And where all my thoughts were written?
Where is she who held my life in her hand?
How much the miserable world lacks, how much
To my eyes that shall never be dry.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
To be reduced to a little dust and whose heart does not cease to weep.
¶ **WHERE** the brow. <note>original: "OVE la fronte"</note> The poet asks a tearful question, remembering his lady, and asks where her beauties are, now turned to dust. "There where," that is <note>original Latin: "i." for "id est"</note>, there in that shadow of the human face.

### SONNET 259.

->How much envy I bear you, greedy earth;<-
->Who embrace her whom I am forbidden to see;<-
->And deny me the air of that beautiful face;<-
->Where I found peace from all my war:<-
->**H**ow much I bear to heaven; which closes and locks away,<-
->And has so eagerly gathered into itself,<-
->The spirit loosened from those beautiful limbs,<-
->And so rarely opens itself for others:<-
->**H**ow much envy to those souls, who now<-
->Have her holy and sweet company;<-
->Which I always sought with such longing:<-
->**H**ow much to pitiless and hard death;<-
->Who, having extinguished my life in her<-
->Stays in her beautiful eyes, and does not call me.<-

<margin>Hiero. H</margin>
¶ **HOW MUCH.** <note>original: "QUANt."</note> Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> speaks in this 259th sonnet of bearing envy toward four things that cause him grief: the first is the inability to see his lady because of the earth, which he calls greedy because it destroys and corrupts our bodies. The second is the heaven where she has ascended. The third are the blessed souls who keep her in their company. The fourth is death, which has been the cause of every evil.

<margin>Anto.</margin>
¶ **HOW MUCH** envy: Messer Francesco speaks against four things that are the reason for hiding his lady. First the earth where she was buried. Second the heaven where she had ascended. Third the souls who keep her in their company. Fourth death which has been the cause of all his pain.

¶ **VALLEY.** Before Lady Laura died, Messer Francesco had in the valley of the Sorgue a little hill upon which he often went: and looked toward Avignon where his lady was. Therefore in this sonnet he speaks to those places and then to that hill.

**Hieronymo**
**K**
*I LIFTED UP MY. Sonnet 261. In which Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> describes his thought reaching the place where he was before; he no longer finds her [Laura] on earth, for she had ascended to heaven into the sphere of Venus, which is the realm of love’s inclination. He imagines that Lady Laura speaks to him, saying that he will also be in that place with her, "unless I am deceived," and to know that "I am she who gave you so much war" while she was alive. My "blessing" where I am in heaven is such that the human intellect could not comprehend it; as the Apostle Paul says, celestial goodness is such that it cannot descend into the human intellect, nor would it even be possible for it to be understood. He says at the end that he stayed with her only a short time, for upon waking from his fantasy, he found himself as he was before.*
</margin>

<margin>
**Antonio**
*I LIFTED UP MY thought. Master Francesco imagines himself having ascended in thought to the third heaven <note>The sphere of Venus, traditionally associated with lovers</note> and there having seen Laura and spoken with her. "A little more" <note>referring to the final line of the sonnet</note> notes the deep, intrinsic quality of the thought.*
</margin>

# SONNET 261.

> I lifted up my thought to a place where she was,
> whom I seek and do not find again on earth;
> there, among those whom the third circle <note>the sphere of Venus</note> encloses,
> I saw her again, more beautiful and less proud.
> She took me by the hand and said: "In this sphere
> you shall yet be with me, if desire does not stray;
> I am she who gave you so much war,
> and completed my journey before the evening.
> My blessing cannot be contained by human intellect.
> I wait for you alone, and that which you loved so much,
> my beautiful veil <note>her physical body</note>, which remained down there."
> Ah, why did she fall silent and open her hand?
> For at the sound of words so merciful and chaste,
> I nearly remained there in heaven.

*LOVE WHO WITH ME. Master Francesco imagines in this 262nd sonnet and says he remembers how Love stayed with him in the good times—that is, when Lady Laura was alive—and he used to wander along these banks with Love, speaking of his passion. He calls as witnesses the flowers, leaves, grasses, shadows, and sweet laurels, the enclosed valleys and the high, sunny hills. Turning then to the nymphs and the inhabitants of the woods, he tells them they know how he once lived there in contentment, and how now, because of the lady's death, he remains gloomy and sorrowful.*
</margin>

<margin>
**Antonio**
*LOVE WHO WITH ME. Master Francesco speaks to Love and tells of the pleasure he had through him before Laura's death; then he speaks to the witnesses of his solitary life, recounting his pains.*

# SONNET 262.

> Love, who in the good times stayed with me
> among these banks, friends to our thoughts;
> and to settle our ancient accounts,
> you went along, reasoning with me and the river;
> flowers, leaves, grasses, shadows, caves, waves, sweet breezes,

> haven for my amorous labors,
> and for my many and heavy fortunes:
> O wandering inhabitants of the green woods,

> my days were so bright; now they are so dark,
> like Death, who makes them so. Thus in the world
> each person has his fate from the day he is born.

Beautiful soul, released from that knot
Than which nature never knew how to weave one more fair;
From heaven, turn your mind to my dark life,
Turned from such happy thoughts to weeping.
The false opinion is removed from my heart,
Which for a time made your sweet sight
Bitter and hard to me: now, entirely safe,
Turn your eyes toward me, and hear my sighs.
Look at the great rock, from where the Sorgue rises;
And you will see one who, alone among the grass and waters,
Feeds only on your memory and on grief.
The place where your dwelling lies, and where
Our love was born, I wish for you to abandon and leave,
So you do not see in your own [people] that which displeased you.

<gloss>I pray everyone to look at the rock where the Sorgue <note>The river at Vaucluse, Petrarch's retreat</note> is born, and see me, who feeds myself only on your memory and my own sorrow.</gloss>

That sun, which showed me the right path
To go to heaven with glorious steps,
Returning to the Highest Sun, in a few stones
Enclosed my light, and its earthly prison;
Wherefore I have become a wild animal,

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the classical and mythological geography mentioned in Petrarch’s poetry, specifically focusing on the transition between Sonnets 265, 266, and 267. It provides historical and geographical context for Lake Avernus and the River Styx before moving into the poet’s lament over his inability to adequately describe Laura’s beauty in his later years.</meta>

Dis <note>original: "dite"; referring to the Greek "Hades" or the Roman "Dis Pater," used here to mean the underworld</note> signifies sadness, and for this reason the gods feared to swear by it, because sadness is contrary to the glorious and blessed ones. Avernus is a lake in Campania at the edge of Baiae, much celebrated by writers and especially by poets for the antiquity of the Sibyl, traces of whose oracle still seem to remain. Nearby are baths with sulfurous odors, and it produces black fish which, because of the stench, cannot be eaten. According to what some believe, Ulysses was killed in that place. Elpenor <note>one of Ulysses' companions</note>, by the power of magic verses, summoned the souls of the underworld and took counsel from them. Similarly, Aeneas, after the death of Misenus, descended with the Sibyl to the underworld; and even to the present day it is shown by the inhabitants. I have seen it and have entered many steps into the said cave. And therefore the poet calls it, together with the Styx, an infernal place.

<margin>Anto. <note>Antonio Brucioli</note></margin>

Avernus and Styx: Avernus is a river in the underworld; Styx is a swamp in the underworld.

¶ SHE. Sonnet 267, where our poet, in love, says that for love he changed the Arno for the Sorgue; <note>The Arno is the river of Florence; the Sorgue is the river of Vaucluse, near Avignon</note> that is, having left his native place and gone to live in France for her love, rather than living free and content in Italy with his poverty. This was not the case in Avignon, because he had to stay with Cardinal Colonna or other great prelates. He says this was of no value because she has willed her holy beauty to another life, for which he destroys and wastes away, becoming thin. He has tried many times to capture her beauty for the world, but wanting to follow that path, he lacks the courage, the talent, and the art.

### SONNET 266.

I thought I was nimble enough on my wings,
Not by their own power, but by the power of the one who spreads them
To go singing as an equal to that beautiful knot; <note>referring to his bond of love for Laura</note>
From which death releases me, but Love binds me:
I found myself far more slow and fragile at the task
Than a tiny branch which a great weight bends;
And I said: he who climbs too high is bound to fall;
Nor is that well done by man, which heaven denies.
Never could the pen of genius fly,
Nor a grave style, nor a tongue, to where nature
Wove a flight for my sweet restraint: <note>referring to Laura</note>
Love followed her with such marvelous care
In adorning her, that I was not worthy
Even of the sight: but it was my fortune.

### SONNET 267.

She, for whom with power I changed the Arno for the Sorgue,
Serves riches with honest poverty;
Turned her holy sweetness into bitterness;
From which I once lived, but now I destroy and waste away.
Since then, I have tried several times in vain
To paint her high beauties for the age to come,
Singing of them so that the souls might prize them;
But I cannot embody her beautiful face with my style,
Her praises are never of another, but strictly her own;

## SONNETTO CCLXVIII.
**The high and new miracle, which in our days**

**THE HIGH and new.** In this 268th sonnet, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> speaks through <term>circumlocution</term> <note>a roundabout way of expressing a thought</note> as a lover who writes of his lady, who by a miracle had appeared to the world; and he wishes that by writing, he might paint her for those who come after him. **THE HIGH and new.** Master Francesco speaks through circumlocution of how Love wishes him to write of his lady, who was that miracle appearing to the world at the summit—that is <note>original: "idest"</note> at the high point of her virtues.

**ZEPHYR.** Master Francesco wrote this 269th sonnet during the time of spring, remembering that it was at that time he had fallen in love. And through elegant words, he describes the story of Procne and Philomela, of which enough was said above in the commentary of Filelfo <note>Francesco Filelfo, a famous 15th-century humanist scholar</note>. He knows well that all animals rejoice at such a time; he alone must grieve, remembering that at such a time he was captured by love for his Lady Laura.

He says that perhaps this little bird carries a similar pain, just as he does for having lost his sweet consort, just as he has lost his beloved lover. And then concluding, he says that his wicked fortune wills that he go on weeping...

**THAT nightingale.** In this 270th sonnet, Master Francis <note>Francesco Petrarch</note> makes mention of a nightingale: which went about singing day and night near his house, and he says that it was perhaps similar to him, who goes about weeping for his spouse.

*And all night it seems to accompany me,*

*For I have no one but myself to complain of:*

<margin>Girolamo V.</margin>
**NOR BY.** Master Francis wishes to show in this 271st sonnet his great sorrow; and through four things which usually most gladden the sight and the heart of man, he has shown it; and being unable to be gladdened because of his great sorrow, he says that his living is tedious <note>Italian: "noia"; implying a weariness of life</note> to him, and for this reason he calls for his end, to see her in the other life, whom it was best not to see in this world.

### SONNET CCLXXI.

*Neither through the serene sky wandering beautiful stars;*
*Nor through the tranquil sea coated ships <note>original: "legni spalmati"; refers to ships with pitch-coated hulls ready for sailing</note>;*
*Nor through the countryside armed knights;*
*Nor through beautiful woods joyful and swift beasts;*
*Nor fresh news of an expected good;*
*Nor the words of love in high and ornate styles;*
*Nor among clear fountains and green meadows*

*Nor anything else will ever reach my heart;*
*Since she knew how to bury it with herself,*
*Who alone was light and mirror to my eyes.*
*Life is a weariness to me, so heavy and long;*
*That I call for the end because of the great desire*
*To see again her, whom it was best not to see.*

<margin>Girolamo X</margin>
**PASSED.** This sentiment which Petrarch says in this 272nd sonnet to all men—it could be said that to everyone, in truth, the time has passed and one cannot be of a single will; and remembering the first time, they grieve. Therefore, he says well, grieving that his refreshment <note>original: "refrigerio"; comfort or relief from the heat of love's passion</note> has passed to her for whom he wept and wrote; and he says she has carried away his beautiful mantle to the earth and to heaven; he takes the soul for the one and the body for the other; he desires still for his love to be among those blessed souls.

### SONNET CCLXXII.

*Passed is the time now, alas, that for so long*
*I lived with refreshment in the midst of the fire:*
*Passed is she for whom I wept and wrote:*
*But she has indeed left me my pen and my weeping.*
*Passed is that face so graceful and holy:*
*But in passing, those sweet eyes have fixed themselves in my heart—*
*In my heart, once mine, which following her departed*
*To her, who had wrapped it in her beautiful mantle.*
*She carried it away under the earth and into heaven;*
*Where now she triumphs, adorned with the laurel,*
*Which her unconquered honesty deserved.*
*Thus, dissolved from my mortal veil,*
*Which by force keeps me here, would that I were with them*
*Away from sighs, among the blessed souls.*

### ### SONNET CCLXXIII.
My mind, which, foretelling your losses,
In happy times was already pensive and sad,
If intently in that beloved face
You sought rest from future troubles:
<margin>A</margin> From the gestures, the words, the face, the clothes,
From the new pity mixed with sorrow,
I could well say, if you were fully aware,
"This is the last day of my sweet years."
<margin>what</margin> What sweetness was that, oh wretched soul?
How we burned at that moment when I saw
The eyes which I was never to see again?
<margin>when</margin> When to them, as to two most faithful friends,
Leaving in their care the most noble burden <note>original: "salma"; here referring to the weight of his soul or his very life</note>
I left my dear thoughts and my heart.

### ### SONNET CCLXXIIII.
All my flowering and green age
Was passing; and I already felt the fire cooling
Which burned my heart, and it had reached the place
Where life descends, which in the end falls:
<margin>G</margin> Already my dear enemy <note>a recurring term Petrarch uses for Laura to describe the "war" of unrequited love</note> began to take security
Little by little from her suspicions: and turned into a game
My bitter pains with her sweet honesty:
<margin>P</margin> The time was near where Love meets
With Chastity; and it is given to lovers
To sit together and speak of what meets them.
<margin>M</margin> Death felt envy for my happy state,
Or rather for my hope; and met her
Midway, like an armed enemy.

### ### SONNET CCLXXV.
It was now time to find peace, or a truce
From such great war; and perhaps it was on its way;
If not that he turned back those happy steps;
<margin>C</margin> He who equals our inequalities <note>Death, who makes all people equal regardless of status</note>:
For as mist vanishes in the wind,
So her life suddenly passed away,
She who once guided me with her beautiful eyes,
And now it is necessary that I follow her with my thought.
<margin>P</margin> There was little time left to delay, for years and gray hair

---

<margin>Girolamo X</margin>
¶ **MY MIND.** The mind is usually for the most part foretelling of our future evils; this our poet shows most elegantly in this 273rd sonnet, in which, speaking to his mind, he says it was foretelling of its losses, especially in that time when it sought repose from its future troubles. This was seen through the gestures, the words, and the clothes of Lady Laura: you could perceive it because the mind always told him that he would see her on earth for only a short time; and he remembers the last day when he saw her, and even now that beauty remains fixed in his heart.

<margin>Girolamo Z</margin>
¶ **ALL.** In this 274th sonnet, Master Francis <note>Francesco Petrarch</note> suggests that he was approaching the time when it would have been permitted to speak with his lady. As their years grew, he would not be held in suspicion even if he had spoken with her; for this reason, he says that his "dear enemy" began to feel secure. He says it was already near the time when Love and Chastity meet together—the age when a man and a woman can reason together about their past loves—but Death felt envy for his happy state, and in such a season, it caused his beloved to die.

<margin>Girolamo A</margin>
¶ **TIME.** In this 275th sonnet is a similar matter to the one above. He says that it was now time to find peace or a truce from his labors, and this opportunity came to him shortly before his beloved died. But like the mist that vanishes in the wind, so the sight of his lady vanished. There was little more time to wait for the season when hair changes with age, when they could have told each other of all their past labors; they would not have had a single thought that was not honorable <note>original: "honestade"; referring to chaste, platonic affection</note>.
¶ Tranquillo.

The commentary by Girolamo emphasizes the "envy" of Death in stealing away this long-awaited period of tranquility.</summary>

Their habits <note>meaning their way of life and interaction</note> were changing: so that no suspicion
Would arise from talking of my sickness <note>his lovesickness</note> with her,
With what honest sighs I would have told her
My long labors: and now from heaven
She sees, I am certain; and she still grieves with me.

<margin>Hieronimo B.</margin>
**T**ranquil. Sonnet 276. In which Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, repeating that love had first shown itself sweet to him and because of that he never believed he would have such a long storm as he had from Laura's eyes: which had pierced his heart and in which he used to take joy: but envious death took those beautiful eyes from him; whereas if he could have lived to see them grow old, the very sight would have changed his face and the color of both their hair: that is, from a state of sadness he would have become happy.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
**T**ranquil harbor. Continues the previous theme. Master Francesco says that as he was beginning to be accepted by his lady, the aforementioned death has taken this pleasure from him. "Changed faces" <note>original: "Cangiati volti"</note> means they had both grown old.

### ### SONNET CCLXXVI.

> **T**ranquil harbor love had shown
> To my long and turbulent storm;
> Among the years of honest mature age;
> Which strips away vices and clothes one in virtue and honor.
> **A**lready my heart shone through her beautiful eyes,
> And my deep faith was no longer a burden to them.
> Ah, wicked death, how ready you are to uproot
> The fruit of many years in so few hours!
> **I**f only I could have reached that point while still living, where, having laid down
> Into those chaste ears while speaking
> The ancient burden of my sweet thoughts:
> **A**nd she would have perhaps responded to me
> With some holy word, sighing,
> Our faces changed, and both our heads of hair <note>original: "coma"; referring to their hair turning grey with age</note>.

---

<margin>Hieronimo C.</margin>
**A**t the falling. Master Francesco represents in this 277th sonnet the death of Lady Laura: a plant uprooted by force by iron and wind, scattering its high leaves to the earth. He saw another which Love chose as its object—which was the laurel that he loved for the name of his Laura: a subject within me as to the material he writes, along with Calliope and Euterpe. Calliope is one of the nine Muses: the Muses are the nine daughters of Jove and Memory; she is named Calliope from the glory that arises from the speech of poets. Euterpe is named for the pleasure <note>original: "volunta"</note> that the listeners take from the teaching <note>original: "amsistramento," likely "ammaestramento"</note> of honest things.

### ### SONNET CCLXXVII.

> **A**t the falling of a plant, which was torn up;
> Like one that iron or wind uproots;
> Scattering its noble spoils upon the ground,
> Showing to the sun its withered roots,
> **I** saw another; which Love chose as its object,
> A subject within me for Calliope and Euterpe;
> Which seized my heart, and made its own dwelling there
> As ivy creeps through a trunk or a wall.
> **T**hat living laurel; where high thoughts
> And my burning sighs used to make their nest,
> Which never moved a leaf of those beautiful branches;
> **A**t the translation to heaven in that its faithful dwelling
> It left roots; wherefore with heavy accents
> I still call out; and there is no one who answers.

---

<margin>Hieronimo H.</margin>
**M**y days. In this 278th sonnet Master Francesco laments the extreme speed of time, which is so great that the human mind cannot comprehend it, as he demonstrated in the penultimate Triumph <note>The Triumph of Time</note>: and here he says it is swifter than any stag: stags, according to what Pliny writes <note>referring to Pliny the Elder's Natural History</note>, leaving aside the other parts of their nature and saying only those which suit our purpose here: that after they have grazed upon two herbs, which are *Aros* <note>Cuckoo-pint</note> and *Sesile* <note>Meadow-saxifrage</note>, the mothers exercise their fawns.

### ### SONNET CCLXXVIII.

> **M**y days swifter than any stag,
> Fled like a shadow; and saw no more good
> Than the blink of an eye; and a few serene hours
> Which I keep, bitter and sweet, in my mind. <meta>catchword: (than</meta>

**W**retched world, unstable and arrogant,
You are entirely blind; whoever places his hope in you:

Who is already earth, and joins no bone to nerve.

With her beauties every hour she makes me fall more in love:

### SONNET CCLXXIX.

<margin>
Hieronimo E.

Returning Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> to his solitary refuge, all the while traveling, he makes this 279th Sonnet in which he shows how he approaches that place where he wished to lie dead; that is: "I have served the lord," meaning Love. "Now I go weeping": that is, for the death of Laura.
</margin>

**I** feel my ancient breeze <note>original: "l'aura" — a frequent pun on the name Laura</note>; and the sweet hills
I see appearing; where the beautiful light was born;
That held my eyes, while it pleased heaven;
Desirous and happy, now it holds them sad and moist.
**O** fleeting hopes, o foolish thoughts:
The grasses are widowed, and the waters are turbid
And empty and cold is the nest in which she lay;
In which I wished to lie living and dead,
**H**oping at last from those sweet feet,
And from her beautiful eyes that have burned my heart,
Some rest from so many labors.
**I** have served a cruel and meager master,
Who burned me as long as I had my fire before me;
Now I go weeping for her scattered ashes.

---

### SONNET CCLXXX.

<margin>
Hieronimo F.

"And this is the nest." Concerning Laura: the first time that Master Francesco came to the tomb of his lady, he made this 280th sonnet; he always returns to the place: that is, to the Sorgue <note>original: "Sorga," the river at Vaucluse</note> where she was born, or rather to the tomb where she was buried.

But.
</margin>

**A**nd this is the nest; in which my phoenix
Put her golden and purple feathers;
Who held my heart under her wings;
And still draws out words and sighs?
**O** first root of my sweet ill,
Where is the beautiful face, from where that light came,
That kept me living and happy in burning?
You were unique on earth, now you are happy in heaven,
**A**nd you have left me here wretched and alone,
Such that, full of grief, I always return to the place,
Which I honor and cherish as consecrated through you,

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the "Canzoniere," specifically focusing on the transition from the poems of life to the poems written after Laura's death. Although the user indicated the source language was Latin, the text is written in Renaissance-era Italian, which has been translated here into English. The catchword "la prima" refers to the first lines of the following section.</meta>

<margin>Hieronymus G.</margin>
**NEVER.** In this 281st sonnet, our Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch, the author</note> says that his eyes will never again see tranquility of soul, nor in those verses—where Love once used to shine—does it seem that he has destroyed them with his own hand. For this reason, he could not overcome any earthly desire in the world; and by "Love," he means the Nature that had made her <note>Laura</note> so well-proportioned. In the end, he laments that he could not show greater eloquence in praising her, as she died before her time.

<margin>Antonius</margin>
**NEVER shall they see.** Master Francesco says that his lady will never see him without weeping. He mentions "other work," meaning work that would have treated her death differently.

<margin>Hieronymus H.</margin>
**STANDING.** This 40th song <note>Canzone 323 in modern editions</note> describes the poet’s six visions of the death of his Lady Laura. This song, because of its varied style of writing, is considered no less difficult than it is elegant. Before we come to its declaration, we shall say a few things so that the poet’s mind may be better understood. Vitruvius writes in the second book of *On Architecture* <note>An ancient Roman treatise</note> that Socrates—who was reputed by the Delphic Apollo <note>The Oracle at Delphi</note> to be the wisest of all men—said, with no less learning than prudence, that he wished all human minds were windowed <note>The "Socratic window" was a common Renaissance metaphor for transparency of the soul</note>, so that no evil thing could be hidden within, but everything would be open, unable to show one thing for another as we see many people do many times. Therefore, the poet, not wishing to proceed by simulation, wanted to show openly that he was in love with a woman who truly existed: Lady Laura. He does not wish to speak in riddles as many have fantasized—some saying he spoke of Poetry, some of Fame, some of Our Lady <note>The Virgin Mary</note>. He shows that these people understand little and have not seen his works; for in his letters, he shows he was in love with a woman named Laura. Similarly, in his *Bucolicum carmen* <note>Petrarch's Latin pastoral poems</note>, he describes his falling in love and the death of his Laura; and likewise in his metric epistles, in the first one:

Seeing dark night around the hills,
From whence you took your last flight to heaven,
And where your eyes were once accustomed to bring the day.

### SONNET . CCLXXXI .

<margin>M</margin>
**N**ever shall my eyes see, dry and tearless,
With the parts of my soul at peace,
those verses where Love seems to sparkle,
And Piety <note>original: "pieta," which can mean both pity and religious devotion</note> seems to have constructed them with her own hand;
<margin>S</margin>
**D**riven, once unvanquished, to earthly struggles,
That now so much sweetness distills from heaven;
So that to the style which death has severed,
You have brought back my straying rhymes.
<margin>D**
**I** believed I would show you another labor
From my tender leaves: and what fierce planet
Envied us both, O my noble treasure?
<margin>C</margin>
**F**or it hides and forbids you to me before your time;
Whom I see with my heart, and honor with my tongue;
And in you, sweet sigh, my soul finds rest.

### SONG . XL .

<margin>S</margin>
**S**tanding one day alone at the window,
Whence I saw things so many and so new,
That I was almost tired just from looking;
A wild beast <note>likely a doe or hind representing Laura</note> appeared to me on the right hand,
With a human face fit to make Jove burn with love,
Chased by two hounds, one black, one white <note>These represent Day and Night, or the passage of Time</note>,
Which bit both the flanks
Of that noble beast so fiercely,
That in a short time they led her to the pass,
Where, enclosed in a stone <note>the tomb</note>,
Bitter death overcame great beauty,
And made me sigh for her hard fate.
<margin>I</margin>
**T**hen, upon the high sea, I saw a ship
With silken shrouds, and a sail of gold,
All composed of ivory and ebony;
And the sea was tranquil, and the breeze was gentle,
And the sky was as it is when no cloud veils it,
The ship laden with rich and honest merchandise;
Then a sudden storm
From the East so disturbed the air and the waves,
That the ship struck against a rock.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s Canzone 323 ("Standomi un giorno"), following the previous page's discussion of the "Socratic window" and Vitruvius's architectural metaphors for the human mind.</meta>

In his first letter, which he wrote to Barbato <note>Barbato da Sulmona, a close friend and confidant of Petrarch</note>, he openly says that he had been in love with Lady Laura. And therefore, the poet says—wishing to describe her death—that while standing one day alone at the window (that is, thinking in his mind, for he takes the window to mean the mind, which window we have demonstrated above through the authority of Vitruvius), he contemplated the death of his Lady Laura. He depicts this through six figures in this way: first, he says that while standing one day at the window (which is his mind, as we said above) and thinking of various and strange things until he was almost tired of it, a graceful beast appeared. This beast signifies Lady Laura, who was chased by two hounds <note>term: veltri; swift hunting dogs, likely greyhounds</note>, one black and the other white, which bit her side so hard that they led her to death. By the hounds, he means day and night, which is the passing of our lives; hounds are very fast dogs that catch beasts in the chase and then, through their cruelty, kill them. For this reason, he says they led Lady Laura to her death, and thus they extinguished such great beauty with a bitter death; he still sighs for her, remembering such a hard fate.

<margin>Before.</margin>
# **S**TANDING one day.
Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> fakes in this moral work five visions <note>Though the text says five here, the poem traditionally contains six; the commentator may be grouping them or miscounting</note> that appeared to him as a sign of the death of Lady Laura. Chased by two hounds, one black and one white: he says one black and one white to represent dark time and light time <note>Night and Day</note>. *The high riches second to no other, indeed first of all.* And *from its shadow came such sweet songs* refers to the singing of Lady Laura, *clothed in purple* with a *head of gold* because of her tresses. Whereupon the *heart burned with pity and love*: that is, because of her death, later *stung in the heel by a small snake.* The heel is the lower part of the foot.

<margin>Hieronymus R.</margin>
# **T**HEN.
In this second stanza, he places his other vision, in which it seemed to him he saw on the high sea a beautiful ship, which had ropes of silk and a sail of gold, and the ship was fashioned of ivory and ebony—which is an oriental wood, black and very solid, where woodworms do not take hold. This ship is Lady Laura with her beautiful ornaments. For this ship, the sea was tranquil and the breeze and the sky were very mild, showing no sign of a storm: this represents his early falling in love, when everything seemed very favorable and easy. But the end was the opposite, which he attributes to fortune; he saw a storm coming, and fortune, with a wind, caused that beautiful and adorned ship to strike a rock—that is, the sudden death that overtook his lady, which caused a heavy grief to be shown in his heart.

<margin>L</margin>
-> Oh, what heavy sorrow: <-
-> A brief hour oppressed, and a small space hides <-
-> The high riches second to no other. <-
-> **I**n a new little grove the holy branches <-
-> Were flowering with a young and pure laurel; <-
-> Which seemed one of the trees of paradise; <-
-> And from its shadow came such sweet songs <-
-> Of various birds, and so much other delight; <-
-> That I was entirely divided from the world: <-
-> And as I gazed at it fixedly <-
-> The sky changed around it: and, dark in appearance, <-
-> It struck it with lightning, and from the root <-
-> That happy plant <-
-> Was suddenly uprooted: wherefore my way is sad: <-
-> For a similar shadow is never regained. <-
-> **A** clear fountain in that same wood <-
-> Rose from a rock; and fresh and sweet waters <-
-> It spread, murmuring softly. <-
-> To that beautiful, secluded, shady, and dark seat <-

# **I**N a.
In this third stanza, he describes his third vision, representing his Lady Laura as a pure laurel tree flowering in a grove, which to see it seemed like one of the holy trees of paradise. And from its shadow came various songs of birds—that is, the sweet and mild words of Lady Laura. And therefore he says that those who gazed at it were entirely "killed" to the world, for in many places he has said that he could think of no other thing except his Lady Laura. Then he says the sky changed around that tree, and striking it with lightning, suddenly broke it; because of this, his sight is sad due to the death of his lady, whom he can no longer regain on earth.

# **C**LEAR.
In this fourth stanza, he describes his love and the death of his Lady Laura by way of a fountain, which is his fourth consideration. He speaks of a mild fountain which was situated in a beautiful spot, referring to the Sorgue fountain <note>The Fontaine de Vaucluse near Avignon, where Petrarch lived</note> near Avignon.
