<meta>This page continues the line-by-line commentary on Petrarch’s "Canzone delle visioni" (Song of Visions), moving from the fourth vision of the fountain to the final visions of the phoenix and the dying lady. It follows the previous page's discussion of the "graceful beast" (the deer) and the ship.</meta>

...of which we shall speak at length in the life of Petrarch. By "the fountain," he means Lady Laura, and he says that neither shepherds nor ploughmen <note>original: "bifolchi"; literally ox-drivers, here used to represent common or vulgar people</note> approached it, for no base person could draw near to her. He uses "ploughmen" to mean low-born people. But nymphs and muses approached her, who sang—that is to say, everyone who saw her praised her. Here, the poet, along with the others, feels afflicted the more sweetness he took from her. I saw a cave open, which is death, which rose from the earth; he still feels the pain of it. Only by remembering her is he terrified, wondering how there could have been such great sweetness on earth.

> Neither shepherds nor ploughmen drew near,
> But nymphs and Muses, singing to that tune.
> There I sat; and when
> I took the most sweetness from such harmony
> And such a sight, I saw a cave open
> And carry away with it
> The fountain and the place: from which I still feel grief,
> And the mere memory terrifies me.

---

<margin>M</margin> **A STRANGE phoenix. Stanza**
The fifth stanza, in which he represents his Lady Laura as a phoenix. We have spoken of the nature of the phoenix a little earlier. He says this phoenix appeared to him clothed in purple with a head of gold: which represents the adornment of his lady. He calls her a phoenix because, just as the phoenix is unique, so she was solitary in her beauty and virtue, such that no other in the world was like her. For this reason, he says that when he sees her coming, one can see an immortal and celestial figure. She went through the woods—which is this world—and he always thought she was immortal until the aforementioned hour when he saw her striking herself <note>literally "uprooting the laurel," though the commentary focuses on the bird's self-destruction</note> and the phoenix turning its beak upon itself and dying. From her death, he concludes he felt no small measure of pity.

> A strange phoenix, both its wings
> Clothed in purple, and its head in gold,
> Seeing through the wood, proud and alone,
> A celestial and immortal form
> I first thought; until it reached the uprooted laurel
> And the fountain that the earth steals away:
> Everything flies toward its end:
> For watching the leaves scattered on the ground,
> And the broken trunk, and that living water dried up,
> It turned its beak upon itself;
> As if in disdain; and in an instant vanished:
> Wherefore my heart burned with pity and love.

---

<margin>N</margin> **AT the end. This sixth stanza and final vision**
which the poet creates in this, his moral song. He says he saw, walking among the grass and flowers, a graceful and beautiful lady, who was Lady Laura. He never thinks of her without burning with love and trembling with fear; although she was humble in herself, toward Love she was proud and haughty. She had on her back a white garment, so well woven of gold and snow that they seemed joined together; because of the subtle workmanship, one could not be distinguished from the other. Then he saw her upper parts wrapped in a dark cloud, and a little snake <note>original: "angue"</note> bite her in the heel, and because of that, she died like a plucked flower. Truly, nothing in the world can last except for weeping and sorrow. When he says "stung in the heel," he touches upon the myth of Orpheus, which happened in this way:

> At last I saw among the flowers and the grass
> A lady walking, pensive, so graceful and beautiful;
> That I never think of it without burning and trembling:
> Humble in herself, but proud against Love:
> And she wore a garment so white,
> So woven; that gold and snow seemed joined:
> But the highest parts
> Were wrapped in a dark mist:
> Stung then in the heel by a little snake;
> Like a plucked flower she fades;
> Joyfully she departed, and more than secure.
> Alas, nothing but weeping lasts in the world.

> Song, you may well say:
> "These six visions for my lord
> Have made a sweet desire for death."

---

<margin>O</margin> **¶ Orpheus was the son of the river Oeagrus**
and of the nymph Calliope. Having Eurydice as his wife, and she having died from the bite of an asp, he descended to the dark houses of Pluto to get her back. He received her back under the law that he should not look back; but because he did not keep the pact, he lost her. He gave... <note>The text cuts off here, leading to the catchword "diede" on the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s "Canzone delle visioni" (Canzone 323), specifically concluding the mythological parallels before moving into Canzone 61 (modern 324) and Canzone 62 (modern 325). The previous page discussed the visions of the phoenix and the lady.</meta>

...gave himself because of that to boyish love <note>The text refers to the myth that after losing Eurydice, Orpheus rejected the love of women. In Renaissance commentary, this was often interpreted as a "puerile" or immature turning away from the natural order.</note> where he was killed by the Thracian women. While they were in a frenzy <note>original: "ī solutiōe"; likely referring to the Dionysian madness of the Maenads</note>, they cut off his head, which was of no use to him despite his beautiful and sweet singing. They threw the head along with the lyre into the river Hebrus; it drifted into the sea and reached the island of Lesbos. After it was cast onto the shore by the waves, a serpent began to lick the blood from his face. Before it could be reached by Apollo and Latona (the children of Jove), it was transformed into stone. There are many who do not attribute all these aforementioned visions to Madonna Laura.

### CANZONE . LXI.

**L**ove, when my hope was flowering,
And the reward for all my faith:
She was taken from me, from whom I expected mercy;
Oh pitiless death, oh cruel life:
The one has placed me in sorrow,
And has harshly extinguished my hopes:
The other holds me down here against my will;
And her, who has departed;
I cannot follow; for she does not allow it:
But yet, always present
In the midst of my heart my lady sits:
And what my life is, she herself sees.

<margin>Jerome</margin>
¶ SONG, you can. Where it is shown through the "A" <note>referring to the initial letter of the poem</note> to his song, and he tells it that these aforementioned visions have created in his lord a new desire to want to die.
¶ LOVE, when my hope was flowering. Master Francesco <note>original: "M. F."; refers to Francesco Petrarch</note> laments against Love for his hope which failed him through the death of his lady, and he grieves as much for his own life as for her death because he cannot follow her.

### CANZONE . LXII.

**I** cannot be silent; and I fear my tongue may produce
An effect contrary to my heart;
Which would wish to do honor
To its lady, who hears us from heaven.
How can I, if you do not teach me, Love,
Equal divine works with mortal words;
And that which another
Humility, gathered within itself, covers?
The noble soul had still been but a short time
In the beautiful prison from which it is now released,
At the time I first became aware of her:
Whence I immediately ran
(For it was April of the year and of my age)
To gather flowers in those surrounding meadows,
Hoping to please her eyes so adorned.

<margin>Jerome Q</margin>
¶ I CANNOT be silent. This sixty-second song which the poet made is no less elegant than the other, in which he similarly laments the death of his Madonna Laura. He says that it is impossible for him to be silent, and that he fears his tongue is not sufficient to give her that honor which he has conceived in his heart; he wishes to honor her who has ascended to heaven and hears him from up there. And how can he do this if you, Love, do not teach him—you from whom everything proceeds—for with mortal words one cannot equal divine things. That noble soul of his lady had been on earth only a short time when the poet was taken by her; he says it was in the month of April, as we have said above, and will say more extensively in his life <note>referring to a biography of Petrarch often included in these editions</note>.

<margin>Ante.</margin>
¶ I CANNOT be silent. In this moral [song] Master Francesco continues lamenting the death of his lady and excuses himself that he cannot be silent, even though he fears that speaking might offend his lady. "In the beautiful prison from which she is now released" refers to the flesh, which is the prison of the soul. "The walls were of alabaster and the roof of gold"—the poet figures her limbs and her person. By "alabasters" he means her body; by "golden roof" he refers to her hair. "The ivory door" for her teeth; "the sapphire windows" for her eyes. "Crowned with gold," before which a column—he says this because her forehead held itself up and governed at a nod, and his thought was recognized in a single glance. Jupiter, Apollo, Polyphemus, and Mars—as if to say all these are less powerful than she. And "joyful," i.e., happy. "In oblivion," i.e., to forget. I was on earth and my heart in paradise out of respect for Madonna Laura when a lady, quite prompt and secure like Fortune, came to speak to him. "The day she was born the stars were"—that is, Fortune speaks to Master Francesco about the birth of his Laura, and says that Madonna Laura was born under happy planets, namely Jupiter and Venus. And "wicked lights" and...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s "Canzone delle visioni" (Canzone 323). The previous page concluded the discussion of the phoenix and the lady's death, and this section moves into a detailed architectural allegory of Laura’s body, drawing on classical sources like Pliny the Elder.</meta>

...bitterness <note>original: "felle," referring to the bitter influence of planets</note>: that is, Mars and Saturn were dispersed and had no power in heaven. "A distant cloud displeased me": Master Francesco speaks of the death which he portrays in that cloud. "And now on all fours" <note>original: "carpone," meaning to move on hands and knees</note>: that is, a gentle progress. "He reached his third flowery age": that is, youth, which is the third age—the others being infancy and adolescence. "Earthly prison": that is, her body. Having said this to its "turning wheel," he recites what fortune did. "Song": the poet speaks to the song and concludes the poem.

***

<margin>Jerome R. <note>likely Jerome Ruscelli, a famous 16th-century editor of Petrarch</note></margin>
THE WALLS were. In this second stanza, the poet portrays the beautiful limbs of his Lady. He says the body was of alabaster, which is a stone that is very solid and transparent. By the "roof of gold," he means her beautiful hair. The "ivory door" refers to the teeth. By the "sapphire windows," he intends the eyes crowned by laurel. The sapphire is a stone that is very comforting and of a sky-blue color; it preserves the limbs and comforts the sight, and it stanches nosebleeds if one touches the temples with it. It often loses its virtues through the carnal act. "Before a crystalline column": he refers to the high forehead, which is as radiant as crystal and transparent as glass, in which he could see every thought written at a single glance.

<margin>S</margin>
THE alabaster of which he says the body of Madonna Laura is made: according to Pliny in Book 36 <note>Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History*, a standard reference for Renaissance scholars</note>, this stone originates around the city of Thebes in Egypt. They make jars for ointments from it because it is believed that they are best preserved therein. Therefore, I believe that in Holy Scripture we read that the Magdalene had a jar of alabaster full of the precious ointment. It is white and transparent; it also originates in Damascus in Syria, but the most esteemed is that from Carmania. One cannot make objects larger than ointment jars, small plates, and cups. Glass and the crystal, of which he says the forehead of his Madonna Laura is made...

<margin>T</margin>
GLASS originates in the regions of Syria called Phoenicia, near Judea, between the roots of Mount Carmel. Regarding its first invention: they say that merchants arriving there with a ship were preparing food on the shore; having no stones to support their pots, they used blocks of nitre <note>original: "vetro," though Pliny specifies nitre/soda</note> from the ship. When the fires were lit, the nitre mixed with the sand of the shore and melted, creating a shining stream of noble liquid. They say this was the first discovery of glass. In the time of the Emperor Tiberius, we read that a tempering of glass was found that made it flexible, but they destroyed that workshop so that the value of bronze, silver, and gold would not diminish. In the time of Nero, also, two small cups were seen... calling them "petrotidi" <note>likely *pteroti*, or "winged" cups with handles</note>, costing six thousand sesterces. Crystal originates elsewhere: where the winter snows freeze deeply, which is why by the Greeks it is
->called<- <note>The text cuts off, but refers to *krystallos*, meaning "ice"</note>

> **T**he walls were of alabaster, and the roof of gold;
>    The door of ivory, and the windows of sapphire;
>    From where the first sigh
>    Reached my heart, and the last shall reach it:
>    From there the messengers of love issued, armed
>    With arrows and with fire: so that of them,
>    Crowned with laurel,
>    Even as I am now; I tremble just remembering.
> **O**f a beautiful square diamond, never diminished,
>    One saw in the center a high throne,
>    Where the beautiful lady sat alone;
>    Before her a column
>    Of crystal, and within every thought
>    Was written, and shone through so clearly,
>    That it made me glad, and often made me sigh.
> **T**o the stinging, burning, and shining weapons;
>    To the victorious green banner;
>    Against which in the field
>    Jove, and Apollo, and Polyphemus, and Mars lose;
>    Where the weeping is always fresh and green,
>    I saw myself arrive: and being unable to help myself,
>    I let myself be led away as a prisoner:
>    So that now I know neither the way out, nor the art of it.
> **B**ut just as a man sometimes: who weeps and departs,
>    Sees something that charms both eyes and heart,
>    So she, for whom I am in prison,
>    Standing at a balcony;
>    Who was the only perfect thing in her day:
>    I began to gaze with such desire;
>    That I put myself and my suffering into oblivion.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the various visions in Petrarch's "Canzone delle visioni" (Canzone 323). The previous page discussed the physical allegory of Laura as a magnificent building made of alabaster and gold, citing Pliny the Elder’s descriptions of precious stones.</meta>

...is to be preferred over that of India, although it grows in many other places, as Pliny says in the final book of his *Natural History*. <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author, wrote an encyclopedic work that was a primary source for Renaissance knowledge of nature.</note>

<margin>V</margin>
**THOSE pungent [thorns].** In this third stanza, the poet shows that his weapons were not powerful against Lady Laura—that is, in attempting to corrupt her chastity. This is signified by the color green, just as he says in his *Triumphs*. Their victorious banner on a green field was a white ermine <note>The ermine was a symbol of purity because it was believed it would rather die than soil its white fur.</note> wearing fine gold and topazes around its neck. He says that Jupiter, Apollo, Polyphemus, and Mars would not have been enough to overcome her. Who Jupiter, Apollo, and Mars are should be well known to everyone, and therefore we will say no more of them here. Polyphemus was the son of Neptune and was a Cyclops—that is, he had one eye, which was put out by Ulysses, as the poets write of him, and especially Virgil in the third book of his *Aeneid*. The poet says all these were less powerful than his lady; because of her, he allowed himself to be led away, and from such a prison he knows not how to escape, neither through herbs nor through art. Instead, he remains like a man who sees something that delights his heart and eyes, and to see it he suffers everything. So he says he does for his Laura, who keeps him in prison. Standing at a balcony, he began to gaze at her so fixedly that he has forgotten everything else for her sake.

<margin>X</margin>
**I WAS on earth.** In this fourth stanza, the poet says that from this world he contemplated the things of paradise where Lady Laura was. By the "balcony" mentioned above, he means heaven; and through that contemplation, he forgot every other thing. Out of the wonder of such contemplation, he stood outside of himself as if he had been made of marble. In this passage, he imagines Fortune speaking to him, as if his lady were taking counsel with her, because everything in the world turns at Fortune's request. Fortune tells him to keep his eyes fixed on her—or rather on Lady Laura—just as the eagle keeps its eyes fixed on the sun. <note>It was a common medieval belief that eagles were the only creatures that could look directly into the sun without being blinded.</note> Thus he held his eyes on her, as was said before regarding her divinity; she told him the truth.

### STANZA IV.

> **I** was on earth, and my heart in paradise,
> Sweetly forgetting every other care.
> And my living form
> I felt turn to marble, filled with wonder,
> **W**hen a lady, quite prompt and secure,
> **A**ncient in years, yet youthful in face,
> **S**eeing me so fixed
> **I**n the expression of my brow and lashes,
> **S**aid to me: "Take counsel with me,
> **F**or I am of a different power than you believe;
> **A**nd I can make people happy and sad in a moment,
> **L**ighter than the wind;
> **A**nd I rule and turn everything you see in the world.
> **K**eep your eyes, like the eagle, on that sun:
> **L**end your ears to these words of mine."

<margin>Y</margin>
**THE DAY that she.** In this fifth stanza, which the poet writes here in the persona of Fortune, he wishes to prove—by the influence our bodies receive from the heavens—that at the birth of Lady Laura, she could not be anything but pleasing. Yet she was not lustful, because the star of Venus was opposite to that of her father, Jupiter <note>original: "Gioue." In astrology, Jupiter and Venus are the "benefics" or lucky planets.</note>, which together produce wonderful effects among us. He says that these two stars then held the ruling parts of the sky. And the other stars that induce sad effects were dispersed, so as to make her birth happy and beautiful. He says the sun never appeared more beautiful, and the air and the earth rejoiced together; and the sea was at peace with the rivers, seeing such a fortunate birth brought into the world as was that of Lady Laura. But the stars were not so friendly to her that a distant cloud did not displease her; she feared it would turn into weeping, unless pity were turned toward her in heaven.

### STANZA V.

> **T**he day she was born, the stars were there,
> **T**hose which produce happy effects among us,
> **I**n high and chosen places,
> **O**ne toward the other turned with love.
> **V**enus and the father <note>Jupiter</note> with kind affections
> **H**eld the ruling and beautiful parts;
> **A**nd the wicked and cruel lights...

<margin>Z</margin>
**AS SHE came.** This is the sixth stanza in which Fortune says that the world was not worthy of having her. She was a wonderful thing, new to the sight, and most holy.

...sweet and sharp <note>original: "dolce & acerba"</note> toward vices, yet most holy and sweet toward the virtues. She appeared to the sight like a **white pearl** set in fine gold. To further praise his lady, the poet speaks of her infancy, when she moved on the ground with her hands because her tender legs could not yet support her. This is what he means by **on all fours** <term>carpone<gloss>crawling on hands and knees</gloss></term>; and afterwards, they walk with trembling steps as they grow a little more, so that as she went, everything she passed became gentle. She caused all her companions to flourish through her beauty, and she was such that she calmed the winds and the storms. He speaks now of the age when children begin to speak, and how she first moved her tongue in a manner very different from others, clearly showing to the blind world how great a blessing it possessed within her.

<margin>A</margin>
¶ **THEN growing.** The poet continues, still in the persona of Fortune, who tells him how she grew in virtue as she grew in time. Having reached her **third age** <term>third age<gloss>In the Renaissance "Ages of Man," this typically refers to "Adolescentia" or youth, the bloom of life between childhood and maturity</gloss></term>, which is youth, such beauty is seen in her—full of grace—that he believes the sun, which sees all things, never saw another like her. Her speech was sweet and gentle, with eyes always full of modesty. Her virtues are so many and of such a kind that all tongues would be struck mute in trying to speak of her, because one could never say so much that there was not still more to say. And for this reason, she was taken so soon from this life.

<margin>B</margin>
¶ **HAVING SAID THIS.** Fortune gave a turn to her wheel, which never stands still, and with that turn our life—that is, our good and our evil—is revolved. Because of this turn, the poet says he has already desired to die for many years out of love for his lady. He then concludes the song by saying that sharp and cruel death could not have killed a more beautiful body than that of Madonna Laura.

### SONNET CCLXXXII.

**N**ow you have done the utmost of your power,
O cruel Death: now you have the kingdom of Love
Impoverished: now the flower of beauty
And the light you have quenched, and enclosed in a small grave.
**N**ow you have despoiled our life, and shaken it
Of every ornament, and of its sovereign honor:
But fame, and merit, which never die,
Are not in your power. Hold the naked bones:
**F**or the other part Heaven holds, and in its clarity,
As if in a more beautiful sun, it rejoices and glories,
And she shall be in the memory of the good forever.
**M**ay your heart, in such a great victory,
New angel up there, take pity on me,
As your beauty here conquered my heart.

May your heart: he speaks to her, saying she should have pity on me, so that your heart may be conquered since I am left without you, just as your beauty conquered my heart.</margin>

### SONNET CCLXXXIII.

**T**he breeze, and the scent, the refreshment, and the shade
Of the sweet laurel, and its flowering sight,
The light and rest of my weary life,
Has been taken by she who unburdens all the world,
**A**s the sun is to us, if its sister shadows it:
So my high light has vanished from me.
I ask death for help against death,
With such dark thoughts does love encumber me.
**Y**ou have slept, beautiful lady, a brief sleep:
Now you have awakened among the chosen spirits,
Where the soul enters deep into its Creator:
**A**nd if my rhymes have any power,
Consecrated among noble intellects
Your name shall be here in eternal memory.

<margin>THE BREEZE and the scent, the refreshment: he says figuratively <note>original: "sotto figura"</note> how death has taken every comfort from him. Just as the sun: a comparison. I ask death: that is, I also ask and desire to die.</margin> <margin>Antonio.</margin>

<margin>Hieronymo C</margin>
*NOW YOU have done. In this 282nd sonnet, the poet speaks angrily against Death, saying to it: Death, now you have truly done as much as you can do; and your power could do no more, since you have killed my Lady Laura. Because you have impoverished the world of beauty—for nothing more remains in it similar to her—and that great beauty you have enclosed in a small grave. And also because of her, the kingdom of Love is impoverished. Then he turns and says: O Death, what do you believe you have done? Her fame and her merit are not dead, for you have no power over them. So, you hold the naked bones; Heaven holds the rest, which rejoices and glories in her. May your heart: the poet speaks to her, saying: let pity for me thus conquer your heart in its great victory, just as your great beauty conquered my heart here on earth.*

<margin>Antonio.</margin>
*NOW you have done the utmost of your power: the poet speaks to Death, saying that it has no greater force than to be able to kill such a person as she was.*

<margin>Hieronymo D</margin>
*THE LAUREL and the scent. The poet speaks figuratively in this 283rd sonnet, saying that death has taken from him all his comfort, which is Laura, who was the light and rest of his life. Thus death has taken my light from me, just as the moon, through an eclipse, comes to obscure the sun, which is its brother. The poets call the moon the sister of the sun and the daughter of Jupiter and Latona—a most apt comparison. Then he says he asks for help against death: that is, he wishes to die himself, and this because of the sacred thoughts he had of Lady Laura. Then he turns to her, saying that her living was like a brief sleep in the world. But your name—if my rhymes have power as I hope—will be so consecrated that your name will be an eternal memory, as I believe has happened.*

¶ **The last weary one <note>original: "L'Vltimo lasso"</note> recalls. Master Francesco** <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch, the author</note> in this 284th sonnet remembers the last look that Madonna Laura <note>M.L.</note> gave him, after which he never saw her again; therefore he rightly says "weary," which is a sign of pain in my happy days: which were indeed few because of the brief life of Madonna Laura. ### SONNET CCLXXXIV.

**T**he last (alas!) of my happy days,
Of which I have seen few in this brief life,
Had arrived; and my heart became lukewarm snow,
Perhaps a premonition of sad and black days.
**A**s one who already has sick nerves and pulses and thoughts,
Whom a domestic fever <term>domestic fever|a recurring or "household" fever, such as a low-grade malarial chill</term> must assail,
So I felt myself, not knowing that the end
Of my incomplete joys was coming so lightly.
**T**hose beautiful eyes, now clear and happy in heaven
With the light from which salvation and life rain down,
Leaving my own eyes here, miserable and beggarly,
**S**aid to them with chaste and novel sparks:
"Remain in peace, o dear friends;
*never more here; but we shall see each other elsewhere.*"

<margin>**Hieronymo F**</margin>
¶ **O Day, o hour. Master Francesco accuses** in this 285th sonnet the stars which have been contrary to his love: then he returns again to that look of which we spoke above. Because she who gave it to him is dead, he will never be content again, so that, coming to his senses, he recognizes his losses. O how sick and vain are our beliefs! We believe we are doing one thing and another comes to pass, and thus the wind carries many away. Already Master Francesco says the opposite of what I desired was ordained in heaven: that my holy good, where I lived, was to be taken from me, and in her sight was written the opinion of fate. Here the poet touches upon how death is ordained for everyone—what they must do—and how it cannot be otherwise, though this is contrary to our faith <note>The commentator notes the tension between the classical concept of inescapable Fate and Christian free will or providence</note>. But before his eyes, a veil was placed that did not let him recognize what we now clearly see.

<margin>**Antonio**</margin>
¶ **O Day, o hour. Master Francesco accuses** the planets that have been so contrary to him: and then returns again to that look Madonna Laura gave him upon departing from him. "To lose a part, not all" <note>original: "Perder parte non tutto"</note>—that is, he thought she would be away for a time, not forever; that is, he did not think she would die.

### SONNET CCLXXXV.

**O** day, o hour, o last moment,
**O** stars conspired to impoverish me,
**O** faithful look, what did you want to tell me
As I departed, never to be happy again?
**N**ow I know my losses; now I feel it:
For I believed (ah, vain and infirm beliefs!)
To lose a part, not all, upon departing.
**H**ow many hopes are carried away by the wind!
**F**or already the contrary was ordained in heaven,
To extinguish the soul-light by which I lived;
And it was written in her sweet-bitter sight.
**B**ut before my eyes a veil was placed,
Which made me not see that which I saw,
To make my life suddenly more sad.

### SONNET CCLXXXVI.

> That lovely, sweet, dear, modest gaze
> Seemed to say: "Take from me what you can,
> For you will never see me here again,
> Once you have moved your foot from here, slow to move."
> **I**ntellect, swifter than a leopard,
> Yet lazy in foreseeing your own sorrows,
> How did you not see in her eyes

> But He who bound us here dissolves the knot,

<margin>Hieronymo G</margin>
¶ **That lovely gaze.** Master Francesco <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch, the author</note> remembers that beautiful look, which was the last his lady ever gave him. He speaks of this in Sonnet 285, and again in this one, recalling that the lovely, sweet, dear, modest gaze truly seemed to say to him: "Take from me what you can, for once you depart from here, you will see me no more." He says "slow to move" <note>original: "tardo"</note> concerning his feet, because lovers cannot bear to be pulled away from the sight of their beloveds; therefore he rightly says "slow." He then turns to his own intellect and calls it "swifter than a leopard." We shall speak of the leopard later, but he means: "In all other things you are swift, yet you were lazy in recognizing your own coming sorrows." O my slow intellect! He speaks to his own wit, which did not perceive what is now plainly seen: because in this last look, the eyes of Madonna Laura <note>M.L.</note> appeared more brilliant than usual. As for the leopard, they are extremely fast and are born of the Panther; they are marked with black spots. This beast abounds in Africa and Syria. Whoever wishes to understand more of this should read Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist</note> in the eighth book of his *Natural History*.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
* It seemed that they <note>Laura's eyes</note> said: "Look at me well, because heaven wants us, and your life must grow old here."

¶ **That lovely gaze.** Master Francesco returns to speaking of the aforementioned look that she gave him at his departure, and he writes what he felt she was saying in her mind and what it signified. **"Silently sparkling beyond their usual custom"**: he says it seemed to him that Madonna Laura's eyes spoke thus to his own. **"And yours, to cause you grief, wills that it grow old"**; here the poet predicts his own old age. "Yours": that is, your heaven <note>original: "el vostro cielo"</note>.

### CANZONE XLIII. STANZA I.

<margin>Hieronymo H</margin>
> **I** used to, from the fountain of my life,
> Distance myself, and seek lands and seas,
> Not by my will, but following my star;
> And I always went (such help love gave me)
> Into those exiles; how bitter it was, he saw,
> Feeding my heart on memory and hope:
> Now, weary, I raise my hand and surrender my arms
> To my pitiless and violent fortune,
> Which has deprived me of such sweet hope;
> Only memory remains to me;
> And I feed my great desire only on this one,
> Whereby my soul becomes weak and hungry.

¶ **I USED TO, from the fountain.** In this 43rd moral canzone, our enamored poet manifests his way of life while Madonna Laura was alive. He says that his life was destined not to stay still, but to search through lands and seas; not because he loved such a thing, but by destiny. To this point, he notes in his letters <note>Petrarch's *Epistolae familiares*</note> that once his farmhand said to him: "As I see it, you will always go wandering and I do not believe you will ever be rich." Petrarch follows this by acknowledging the truth of the proverb: "A rolling stone gathers no moss" <note>original: "sasso spesso rivoltato non fa fango," literally "a stone often turned does not make mud"</note>. Here he touches upon his first exile: for his father, Ser Petracco (as we shall say in his *Life*), was made an exile, and because of that exile he came to Avignon, where he saw Madonna Laura. He says his heart fed on memory, remembering her, and on hope, for he always hoped to possess her. Since she is dead, he "surrenders his arms" to his pitiless fortune which has deprived him of such a great good, and he feeds his great desire only on her memory, which leaves his soul fragile and hungry.

<margin>Antonio</margin> ¶ **I used to, from the fountain of my life.** <note>original: "Solea dala fontana," though the OCR mistakenly reads "fortuna." This is the opening of Canzone 331.</note> In this moral song, Master Francesco reveals his way of living while Madonna Laura was alive, comparing himself to a courier. A comparison: Of how Death makes my sad heart bare. Then, he notes that by dying on earth she was reborn in heaven: note the moral purpose <note>original: "proposito morale"</note> that by dying well we are reborn in heaven <note>original: "bene moriendo renascimur in cœlo"</note>. Lest he should have moved elsewhere while wandering, he returns to that same look he received when departing from her.

<margin>Hieronymo</margin>
<margin>I</margin>
¶ **Like a courier.** In this stanza, our poet makes a comparison in this manner: Just as it happens to a courier who travels, who—if he lacks food because of the weakness of his body—cannot travel as well as when he is well-fed, so that he is forced to slow his pace. So he says, adapting the comparison to his purpose, that his weary life lacked the dear nourishment that was Laura. And through her loss, every pleasure flees from him like dust or mist before the wind. And thus, lamenting, he says it is by my destiny.

### STANZA II.

> **L**ike a courier on his way, if food is lacking,
> He is forced to slow his pace,
> Diminishing the strength that made him go fast,
> So, lacking in my weary life
> That dear nourishment, which was bitten away
> By her who makes the world bare and my heart sad,
> The sweet becomes bitter, and the beautiful pleasure troublesome
> To me from hour to hour: wherefore the journey
> So short I hope not to finish, and I fear.
> Like mist or dust in the wind
> I flee, so as to be a pilgrim no longer:
> And so let it go, if such is my destiny.

<margin>K</margin>
¶ **NEVER.** In this third stanza, he continues by explaining that through the death of his lady, he has recognized the fragility of the world, so that this mortal life never pleased him. Love, with whom he often speaks, knows this well and is a good witness. He responds to a doubt that might be raised: "You, Master Francesco, did not say this at the beginning of your love." He replies that if life ever pleased him, it was because of her who was his light and mine; who, dying here on earth, was reborn in heaven. Then he says he was ill-advised in his state for not noticing the signs: because Love, under the beautiful brow of Madonna Laura, showed him that because of her death he should be sad and disconsolate. Whereas shortly before her death, he considered himself blessed through her alone.

### STANZA III.

> **N**ever did this mortal life please me,
> (Love knows it, with whom I often speak of it)
> Except for her, who was its light and mine.
> Since, dying on earth, she was reborn in heaven,
> That spirit by which I lived; to follow it
> Would be lawful, and my highest desire.
> But I have reason to grieve always, because I
> Was ill-advised to provide for my state,
> For Love showed me under that beautiful brow—
> To give me different counsel—
> That such a one died already sad and disconsolate,
> Who shortly before found death to be blessed.

<margin>L</margin>
¶ **IN THE EYES.** In the fourth stanza, the poet continues regarding the love he held for his Lady Laura; therefore he says truly that in the eyes where his heart used to dwell—and it lived there until harsh fate grew envious of such rich pleasure as the sight of Lady Laura was, and banished it—he says that Love, with his own hand, had described with pity what was to happen to him. And then would have been his beautiful death, when she died, so that his... <note>The commentary breaks off here at the bottom of the page.</note>

> **I**n the eyes where my heart used to dwell,
> Until my harsh fate grew envious,
> And banished it from such a rich dwelling,
> With his own hand Love had first described
> With letters of pity that which would
> Soon come from my so long desiring.

> In dying I did not die, my life remaining together,

Having put living into exile, now he says his hopes are all scattered: for it has come to pass that death has caused a little earth to press upon his treasure, which was his lady. <note>The "little earth" refers to the mound of a grave.</note>

### STANZA V.

**I**f my meager intellect had been
With me in my need, and if no other beauty
Had turned it elsewhere, leading it astray;

And could have gone before her

<margin>M</margin>
> ¶ **IF IT HAD BEEN.** The fifth stanza, in which the poet says what he stated above: that if his intellect had been with him in his time of need, he would have easily recognized that he was losing time following My Lady Laura; but her beauty caused this distraction in him. We can also say he refers to the final act of which we spoke in Sonnet 288: and this is because he says he would have read that he had reached the end of his lady’s life; though before she died, if he had more time, he could have gone to see her seat prepared for her in heaven: though he will follow her later, but with "different hair," meaning he will be older.

**S**ong, if you find a man living quietly in his love;
Tell him: die while you are happy:
For death at the right time is not a sorrow, but a refuge;
And he who can die well should not seek delay.

<margin>N</margin>
> ¶ **SONG.** The last stanza, which is the sixth, in which in his customary manner he speaks to his song, telling it that if it finds anyone who is peaceful in love, it should tell them to die while they are happy, because death then is not a sorrow but a refuge; and he who can die a "good death" <note>A "good death" in this context implies dying at the peak of happiness or in a state of grace.</note> ought not to delay any longer.

**WHERE IT IS** led. Stanza III. Our poet grieves not a little, remembering the things he previously wrote which were joyful and full of sweet love, and what he is obliged to write at present; for he sees well where his amorous style is led: that where before he spoke with a cheerful heart, now he is obliged to speak of weeping. He no longer feigns fables <note>The "fables" refer to the conventional, often idealized mythological metaphors used in love poetry.</note> nor can he speak of anything other than weeping, and this because of the death of his My Lady Laura.

### STANZA III.
Where is my amorous style led?
To speak of anger; to discourse of death.
Where are the verses, where have the rhymes joined,
That a noble heart heard, pensive and joyful?
Where is the storytelling of love at night?
Now I speak not, nor think of anything but weeping.

---

<margin>R</margin>
**ONCE FOR ME** it was. Stanza IV. In which, wishing to increase the weight of his sorrow further, he says that never in the time when his lady lived—and she who always desired his weeping <note>Petrarch often suggests that Laura’s coldness or "honesty" in life provoked his poetic tears of unrequited love.</note>—however bitter it was, it was full of sweetness. Now, weeping for love is more bitter to him than death: because he no longer hopes to see that honest and joyful gaze: which gaze was a high subject for his humble rhymes.

### STANZA IV.
Once weeping was so sweet to me with desire,
That it seasoned every bitter style with sweetness;
And it made me stay awake all the nights:
Now weeping is more bitter to me than death:
Never hoping for the honest and joyful gaze,
A high subject for my humble rhymes.

<margin>S</margin>
**A CLEAR** sign. Stanza V. In which he says that love had placed a limit on his rhymes: that is, according to how his My Lady Laura looked upon him; and therefore he says that he goes about changing his style with his thought, and prays again to love, to whom he turns his speech, that he might withdraw from such painful verses.

### STANZA V.
Love placed a clear sign on my rhymes
Within those beautiful eyes; and now he has placed it in weeping,
Remembering with grief the joyful time:
Whence I go changing my style with my thought,
And praying again to you, pale death,
That you might rescue me from such painful nights.

<margin>T</margin>
**SLEEP** has fled. Stanza VI. In which the poet says that sleep has fled from his cruel nights: which know how to treat of nothing other than death; and just as he has already said his style has been converted into weeping: so that my style in the kingdom of love is now as sad as it ever was joyful.

### STANZA VI.
Sleep has fled from my cruel nights,
And the usual sound from my hoarse rhymes;
Which know not how to treat of anything but death:
So is my singing converted into weeping.
The kingdom of love does not have so varied a style;
For it is now as sad as it ever was joyful.

<margin>rV</margin>
**NO ONE** ever lived. Stanza VII. He returns again to remembering the life of his lady: saying that no one ever lived more joyful than he when his Laura was alive: nor now does anyone lead more sorrowful days or nights: as his sorrow doubles, his style doubles: because living in hope he had anguish of mind: and now that she is dead, he weeps for himself.

### STANZA VII.
No one ever lived more joyful than I:
No one lives more sadly, both days and nights;
And doubling the sorrow, the style doubles,
Which draws such tearful rhymes from the heart.
I lived on hope: now I live only on weeping;
Nor against death do I hope for anything but death.

He weeps: nor does he hope for anything other than that through death he might quiet what she has done to him by dying: that is, that by dying he will escape from thoughts, pains, and troubles.

<margin>X</margin>
**DEATH** has slain me. Stanza VIII says what was said above: that only death—which has already "slain" him in this life through the loss of his lady—is the only power that can, by actually killing him, allow him to return to see the joyful face of his Laura. Her love made the sighs and weeping he performed for her feel joyful. He mentions the "breeze" <note>original: "laura," referring to the wind/air</note> and the rain; these were sweet to his rhymes when his "chosen thoughts" helped him compose his amorous poetry.

<margin>Y</margin>

This is the specific order of his <term>double sestina</term> <note>A complex poetic form where the ending words of one stanza are repeated in a specific pattern in the next.</note>: to continue his speech from the conclusion of the previous verse. He says that if he had a style as piteous as Orpheus had <note>In Greek mythology, Orpheus descended into the underworld to retrieve his wife Eurydice using the power of his music.</note>, he could take his Laura back from death. We have narrated the fable of Orpheus quite completely above. Furthermore, if he could do this, he would live more joyful than ever. But since this cannot be, he asks that one of these nights—in which he crafts these hard thoughts—might close his eyes, which have become two fountains for weeping: that is, let them make him die.

He says: "I do not hope to have anything else from you, Love." Therefore, he says he is moved to pray to Death to take him, in order to make him joyful; because he cannot be otherwise unless he is with her, for whom he sings, and in the singing of his rhymes, he weeps.

¶ **GO, sorrowful rhymes.** He speaks to his rhymes in this 287th sonnet, and sends them to the tomb of his lady Laura. # SONNETTO. CCLXXXIX.

**I** saw among a thousand women one such,
   That an amorous fear assailed my heart
   Looking at her in images that were not false
   Equal in appearance to the celestial spirits.
**N**othing in her was earthly, or mortal:
   As if she cared for heaven and nothing else.
   The soul; which burned for her so often, and froze;
   Longing to go with her, opened both its wings:
**B**ut she was too high for my earthly weight;
   And shortly after she vanished entirely from my sight:
   Thinking of which I still freeze and grow numb.
**O** beautiful and high and shining windows;
   Through which she who makes many people sad,
   Found the way to enter into such a beautiful body.

<margin>
Girolamo

A

I

</margin>
"I SAW among a thousand." Our graceful poet returns to his accustomed love; although in many sonnets he has done so, in this sonnet he does not forget to return to the <note>original: "notte amorose" - likely a typo for "note amorose" or "amorous notes/verses"</note> amorous verses: therefore he rightly says that "among a thousand I saw one" such that seeing her, an amorous fear seized him; for he was gazing at her, and not in a false image, for she was equal to the celestial spirits. There was nothing in her that was of the world, for all was immortal. His soul, which often rose for her; <gloss>it was "alse," which means cold,</gloss> was cold for her as Ovid says: that the breast of the lover was colder than ice. This was at the time she died: therefore he says his thought had gone too high for the earthly weight he possessed. "O beautiful and high and shining windows" are those of paradise <note>He refers to her eyes, which in the poetic tradition were the "windows" to the soul and the entrance for both Love and Death.</note>. Where she who "makes many people sad"—that is, Laura—makes many people sad because she was loved by many for her virtues; and he says he "finds the way to go into a beautiful body": that is, to go where she is in paradise.

<margin>Antonio</margin>

"SHE returns to my mind." In this 290th sonnet, Messer Francesco remembers his lady many times through his great imagination: and he says she cannot be banished from him by <term>Lethe|The river of forgetfulness in Greek mythology</term>, which signifies oblivion; rather she presents herself to him just as he first saw her in her "flowering age," and she seems to him to be all lit with the rays of her star, which is the star of love: for it signifies nothing other than the star of Venus. In his first meeting she appears to him, and at other times he sees her gathered in herself, so that in his sleep he cries out, "She is indeed my Laura, and she is not dead, but rather alive." And as a gift he asks her to speak to him; sometimes it seems she responds and at other times she seems to stay silent, so much so that he tells his mind it is deceived.

of that time in that year when he says she died. <term>Madonna Laura|Petrarch's muse and beloved</term> died during such a great universal plague, in which a third of all people died; <term>Boccaccio|Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), author of the Decameron and a close friend of Petrarch</term> makes significant mention of this plague in the prologue to his "one hundred stories," and the poet mentions it in various places in his works, and especially in the first epistle of his volume of *Letters on Familiar Matters*. <term>Lethe|In Greek mythology, the river of forgetfulness in the underworld</term>, which we mentioned above, is a river that poets place near the underworld; and just as the souls there taste of it and forget everything, so it is in truth. <margin>G</margin>
¶ THIS OUR FLEETING. Messer Francesco, in this 291st sonnet, says that all beauties were never gathered into one body as they were in that of Madonna Laura. Therefore, he rightly says that "this our fleeting and fragile good" is nothing but shadow and wind, as we have said. These many beauties existed in her time to cause him pain. But he says, comforting himself, that Nature makes one person rich and puts the others in poverty; that is, that he alone possessed or recognized such beauty, while others did not recognize it as he did. And here it appears that Madonna Laura did not have a husband; but we shall nonetheless stick to our first opinion. But her beauty, he says, was so "covered" <gloss>that is, modest or hidden</gloss> that the "foolish world"—meaning the common people—hardly noticed it. And it soon vanished through death. But I still, says Petrarch, contemplate her even though she is in heaven. And he wishes that of all beauties that were, are, and shall be, none can be equal to her.

¶ THIS OUR FLEETING. Messer Francesco says that all beauties were never in one body in this world except in Madonna Laura, and that no age ever had such beauty; it soon vanished because she died.

<margin>Girolamo</margin>
<margin>H</margin>
¶ O TIME. The poet exclaims in this 292nd sonnet against the volatility of time; and he says everything in this world is fleeting and fickle, and he, as an experienced man, knows it well, and he rebukes himself for the deceptions of the world. Note the moral: Nature has given to us mortals, because time is swift, the eyes of the intellect, so that we ought to recognize the fragility of the world and not place our hope in it. So, having recognized this, he says it is now time to turn to a more secure place—that is, to celestial things which are not transitory.

## SONNET .CCXCIIII.

**D**eath, you have left the world without a sun,

<margin>Girolamo I</margin>
¶ **T**hat which in fragrance. In this [Sonnet] 293, Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> greatly praises his Madonna Laura; and it is almost a marvelous thing where, with so many beautiful inventions, he found ways to exalt her. He says she was more fragrant to the world than all the aromatics that come from the East: and for this reason, France <term>the West|In the original "Ponente," referring to Avignon/Vaucluse in the West compared to the spice-bearing East</term> has held the prize of an excellence more fragrant than all others, which is Madonna Laura. Following this, he calls her "sweet laurel," saying where every beauty and every other burning virtue used to dwell: and I saw this standing in her shadow; but God willed to withdraw her into heaven as a thing worthy of that place, and to make her a star, as has already been said.

<margin>Antonio</margin>
¶ **T**hat which in [fragrance]. Messer Francesco says how God took Laura from the world to make heaven more beautiful, and he says this through <term>circumlocution|A roundabout way of speaking</term>: "that which in fragrance," because Madonna Laura was in the West; he wishes to exalt that country above the East.

<margin>Girolamo R</margin>
¶ **D**eath, you have left. Sonnet 294, in which Messer Francesco, crying out to Death who, by taking Madonna Laura, has left the world without a sun—that is, without the beauty of women, because none was like her. And for this reason he rightly says that Love is cold, because there is no one else so worthy of being loved as Laura was; blind and unarmed, having lost his "sun," as we said, and being disarmed because he allowed her to be taken without ever getting her back. Thus, courtesy is in exile because of her, and honesty is at the bottom; and he grieves for this sun, although the human race should also grieve: because without her, it is a meadow without flowers and a ring without a gem. And while she was alive, the world did not know her; but he knew her well, who has remained to weep. And heaven is made beautiful by his weeping because it has the glory of possessing her for whom so much is wept.

<margin>Hieronymo Squarzafico L</margin>
¶ **I RECOGNIZED** how in this 295th sonnet Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> says that he cannot in any way equal with his rhymes the celestial virtue of his Laura. Thus, all his words have been eclipsed by the grace of Lady Laura. Her celestial form, her virtues, her immense beauties, and her lofty forms could not be understood by him; these immortal things were not equal to his low sight. Therefore, whatever he ever wrote or spoke of her before <note>Petrarch refers to his poetry written during her lifetime</note>, for which he now offers prayers to God, though it was a small spark, it was full of infinite abysses, meaning the world's ignorance. He did what he could because one's style cannot extend beyond one's talent <term>ingegno</term>. He makes a comparison to a person who wants to look through the rays of the sun and finds their sight deceived; because of the splendor of the solar rays, they see less. In this same way, he was blinded by seeing the great beauty of his Laura.

### SONNET CCXCV.

> **I** recognized, as much as heaven opened my eyes,

<margin>Hieronymo Squarzafico M</margin>
¶ **Sweet my dear.** It appears in this 296th sonnet that Master Francesco, although Lady Laura <note>abbreviated as M. L. in the original</note> was dead, wishes to lament to her because she had not come to him in a dream as she used to. Therefore he asks why her pity has been so slow that he has not seen her in a dream as was his custom; he asks her to make him worthy of her visit. Because of this, he has been without any relief <term>refrigerio</term> and cannot imagine why this is so. He marvels at this because up there in heaven there is neither anger nor disdain which would cause her to stay away. And since she was once a mortal being here on earth, a merciful heart is usually moved by the torments of others; and therefore he says Love lives in his kingdom. So then, Lady Laura, you who see him from the outside and the inside, come and wish to make me content with your vision.

<margin>Antonio da Tempo</margin>
¶ **Sweet my dear.** Master Francesco had spent several nights without dreaming of his Laura, and in this sonnet he prays that she might go to comfort him with her shadow <note>original: "ombra", referring to her spirit or ghost</note>.

> ¶ ON the food of which the lord. In this 298th sonnet, in which (as in the preceding one) our poet does two things: one is his own lamenting, the other is the comfort which Lady Laura gives him. He says she appeared to him and consoled him at his bed. From the food of sorrow and of thoughts of which his lord—which is Love—so abounds, because a lover is never without thoughts, which are always mixed with pain: and therefore he says that with sorrow and with tears his heart nourishes itself: and for this he often trembles and becomes pale thinking of the great sorrow he carries for love: but if such is his love that there was never one like it, or truly that never was anyone as enamored of so beautiful a lady as Laura: she appears to him consoling him at his bed and there upon the edge sits pityingly for his comfort; and with her hand, which he has already desired so much, she wipes his tearful eyes and pours forth such a sweetness that never was another like it felt. And she sets forth her words that he should no longer weep, for he has wept enough, and for his greater comfort concludes that he might be as alive as she is alive.

> ¶ THINKING BACK. The poet demonstrates in this 299th Sonnet that it is a great marvel that he does not die, thinking back on what he has lost, which heaven honors today. It is read in many examples that the blessed souls do honor to another soul ascending to the celestial homeland: therefore he says that heaven honors [her]: that is, in her departure. <margin>Hiero. R</margin> ¶ **LOVE DRIVES**. In this 301st sonnet, he speaks of the love and the great pain for his lady: they have pushed his tongue to lament for her, of whom he should no longer complain. But the tongue, which is always used to speaking of her for whom I sang and burned with love: she should now comfort me, being in heaven. And so love and pain push him to lament wrongly—especially seeing her so familiar with me <note>Petrarch refers to his visions of Laura visiting him from heaven.</note> in order to console me. And indeed, I console myself with this, especially for her glory, for I say that I would no longer wish to see her in this world, which he calls a "hell" <note>original: "ifer no" / "inferno"</note> due to the great tribulations within it. And he sees her more beautiful than ever, raised in flight with the angels at the feet of My Lord Jesus Christ, who is our Lord.

### SONNET 301.

<margin>S</margin> Love and grief pushed where they should not go,
My tongue was led to lament itself,
To speak of her for whom I sang and burned,
Which, if it were true, would be a wrong,
For my wicked state should be much quieted
By that blessed one, and the heart should be consoled
Seeing her make herself so familiar
With him <note>Meaning God or Christ.</note> whom she always held in her heart while living.
<margin>E</margin> And indeed I grow quiet, and I console myself;

Rather I wish to die, and live alone:
<margin>C</margin> For more beautiful than ever, with my inner eye,

<margin>Hiero. S</margin> ¶ **THE CHOSEN ANGELS**. I do not know how much higher our poet could praise his Lady Laura than he does in this sonnet, saying that all of heaven was struck with wonder at her immense beauty. He recounts what the blessed said among themselves: "What light is this? What new beauty was this that lived down in the wandering world?" In this high place, in all this age, there has never been such a beauty as this which has ascended here today. Where Laura, seeing such glory, is content to have changed her lodging—that is, life—for her good living. She is compared with the most perfect ones, and she even turns back, wondering if he <note>Petrarch</note> follows her. And what more? He waits for nothing else but to go where she is, she whom he has always so desired. And he, who turns his every thought to heaven, seems to hear her tell him to hasten to come up there to her.

Compares herself even with the most perfect;
And from time to time she turns back
**L**ooking to see if I follow her; and it seems she waits;
Wherefore I raise all my desires and thoughts to heaven
Because I hear her praying that I might hurry.

¶ **LADY WHO JOYFUL.** The poet speaks to his lady who has gone to paradise, saying she stays joyful with our Beginning (which is God) and there, as your soul requires, you are placed for your good works on a high throne: and adorned with a thing finer than either purple <note>original: "purpura"</note> or pearls; he calls her by excellence a rare and lofty wonder <note>original: "mostro", here meaning a marvel or portent</note> of beauty among all other women for whom he has filled so many pages and not without tears. ### SONNET 303.

**L**ady, who joyful with our Beginning
You stay, as your soul’s life requires,
**S**eated on a high and glorious throne,
And adorned with something other than pearls or purple;
**O** lofty and rare wonder among women,
Now in the face of Him who sees all,
**Y**ou see my love and that pure faith,
For which I shed so many tears and so much ink;
**A**nd you feel that toward you my heart on earth
Was such as it is now in heaven; and I never wished
Anything else from you but the sun of your eyes.
**T**herefore, to amend the long war,
For which I turned from the world to you alone,
Pray that I may come soon to stay with you.

<margin><margin>Hiero. V</margin>
¶ **MY SACRED LAURA.** In this 304th sonnet, the poet returns again to that which he has said many times: that Laura appeared to him in sleep, and that he takes courage to tell her of the pain he has felt and feels; and in such a way he tells her that in life he would not have had the courage to say it. And he begins from the first look when he fell in love, which was the beginning of such a long torment that lasted twenty-one years. And then he follows most minutely from day to day and hour to hour to tell his amorous passions, and My Lady Laura speaks.</margin>

### SONNET 304.

**M**y sacred Laura breathes so often
Upon my weary rest: that I take courage
To tell her of the pain that I have felt, and feel:
Which, while she lived, I would not have dared.
**I** begin from that amorous look:
Which was the beginning of so long a torment:
Then I follow, how wretched and yet content,
From day to day, from hour to hour, love has gnawed at me.
**S**he remains silent: and painted with pity
She gazes fixedly at me; sometimes she sighs,
And adorns her face with virtuous tears;
**W**herefore my soul, overcome by grief,
While weeping it then grows angry with itself,
Released from sleep, it returns to itself.

¶ **EVERY DAY.** This 305th sonnet varies little from the others written above, saying that every day seems like more than a thousand years until he goes to find his My Lady Laura; and he calls her a faithful and dear guide because through her he never lapsed into any vice. She leads him to a better life in which he will have no labors, and so great is the desire he has to follow her that he began to count the days and the years since he had her, or rather, since My Lady Laura died.</margin>

### SONNET 305.

**E**very day seems more than a thousand years to me,
Since I follow my faithful and dear guide;

*¶ WHEN MY GENTLE. This is the 44th moral song of our poet, which is a dream; it is composed as a dialogue in which he imagines that his Lady Laura has come to comfort him with a branch of palm and one of laurel. By the one, that is the palm, he signifies victory; the laurel signifies her name, as is seen further below, or truly an imperial sign because emperors are accustomed to be crowned with it, or truly because he was a poet who would similarly be crowned with it. He sets down the words of the poet who asks her where she comes from, with her answer that she has moved from heaven only to console him.*

### STANZA II.

**I**n deed and in words I thank her
Humbly, and then I ask: Now, from where
Do you know my state? And she: the sad waves
Of weeping, of which you are never satisfied,
With the breeze of sighs across such a distance
Pass to heaven; and they disturb my peace;
Does it displease you so greatly,
That I have departed from this misery,
And reached a better life;
Which should please you; if you loved me,
As much as your appearances and your writings showed.

<note original: "da con la sua risposta...">He responds with her answer. And when he asks, "How do you, Laura, know my plight and my state?" she replies that the wretched weeping and his praises for Laura have been carried up to heaven. These sighs of yours are such that they disturb my peace; for, loving you as I do, I cannot have peace hearing you lament. And through a question she says to him: "Does it displease you so much that I have left this life and reached a better life, which is that of paradise?" And if you loved me as you have already shown through your writings, you ought to rejoice and not grieve for me.</note>

### STANZA III.

**I** reply: I weep for nothing other than myself;
For I am left in darkness and in martyrdom,
Always certain of your ascent to heaven,
As of a thing that a man sees from up close.
How would God and nature have placed
In a youthful heart such great virtue,
If eternal salvation
Were not destined for her good deeds?
O rare among souls,
Who lived so loftily here among us,
And who then suddenly flew to heaven.

<margin>B</margin> I reply. The third stanza in which the poet provides his response, saying that the weeping he does is not because I grieve for your peace. I say that I weep for nothing other than myself, having remained here without you in darkness and in martyrdom <note>Petrarch uses "martyrdom" here to describe the intense psychological and spiritual suffering of his earthly life without Laura</note>; but as for your ascent to heaven, I was always certain of it, just as a man is certain of a thing when he has it close at hand. He wonders how God and nature—which are essentially one thing—could fail to take her. Here the commentator notes the theological terms <term>natura naturans</term> <note>Latin: "Nature naturing," referring to God as the creative source of all being</note> and <term>natura naturata</term> <note>Latin: "Nature natured," referring to the created universe and its laws</note>; but the poet does not intend to speak in such a complex way. He simply means that nature would not have placed such virtue in her if eternal salvation had not been destined for her. The manner of this is difficult for us to understand. O...

### STANZA IIII.

**B**ut what else can I do but weep forever,
Wretched and alone, for without you I am nothing?
Would that I had been extinguished at the breast or in the cradle,
So as not to experience the trials of love.
And she: why do you still weep and waste away?
How much better it would be to lift your wings from the earth,
And to weigh mortal things,
And these sweet, fallacious idle-talkings of yours
With a just scale;
And follow me, if it is true that you love me so much,
Gathering now one of these branches.

<margin>C</margin> But what else can I do. The fourth stanza in which the poet returns to his first theme, saying: what shall I do if not weep forever? Because, as has been said many times, he says he is nothing without his lady. He says that when he thinks on it, he wishes he had been extinguished and died; he wishes he had not waited so long, but had been snuffed out at his first milk in the cradle, rather than dissolving himself in pains and tears. He recognizes it would be better for him to leave mortal things behind. And these are the words of Lady Laura.

**I** wanted to ask, I responded then,
What those two branches mean to signify?
And she: you answer yourself,
You, whose pen so honors one of them.

<margin>D</margin> I WANTED to ask. The fifth stanza in which the poet responds to his Laura: I wanted to ask you what those two branches signify. and she responds to him: you answer yourself. ### CANZONE XLV. STANZA I.

<margin>Q</margin> uel <note>That</note> ancient my sweet cruel lord
Being summoned before the queen,
Who the divine part
Holds of our nature, and sits at the summit;
There, like gold that is refined in the fire,
I represent myself burdened with grief,
With fear, and with horror,
Like a man who fears death and asks for justice.
And I begin: My Lady, my left foot
I placed as a youth into this man’s kingdom:
Where nothing but anger and disdain
Did I ever have; and so many and such diverse
Torments I suffered there,
That in the end my infinite patience
Was conquered, and I held life in hatred.

...nor from the Stoics <note>The Stoics were ancient philosophers who emphasized virtue and reason over emotion; here the commentator suggests the definition of justice isn't purely from their school.</note>. Justice is a silent agreement discovered for the aid of many, so that justice having been defined: we come to the declaration itself. And there, before that Justice—prior to whom good men prove themselves no differently than gold in the fire—he presented himself, speaking against Love as it happened. He went into Love's kingdom, in which he never gathered anything but disdain and anger; and in the end, his constancy could not be so great that it was not defeated, so that he holds and carries his own life in hatred.

<margin>
**H** THUS my time until now has passed. The second stanza: in which Petrarch laments having so consumed his time by following this love, because he has always lived in pain and despised every honest pleasure. And this was only to serve this flattering love; and no genius with words as ready as his own can show his state, nor how many just complaints he says he has made against this ungrateful love for these troubles of his. From Love, he has had little [honey] mixed with much gall; and even if he did receive some noble and pleasant look, he received so many opposites that they were like a very bitter gall mixed into that little honey. As he says in the *Triumphs*: "a little sweetness satisfies much bitterness." <note>Original: "uno poco dolce molto amaro appaga."</note> Thus, with the false habits of the prow, his life was always in pain and torments because Love’s amorous troop pierces him; where...

## STANZA . II .

Thus my time until now has passed
In flame and in pain; and how many useful and honest
Paths I despised, and how many celebrations,
To serve this cruel flatterer.
And what genius has words so ready
That could describe my unhappy state,
And my many, so grave, and so just
Complaints against this ungrateful one?
O little honey, much aloe with gall:
In such bitterness has he accustomed my life
With his false sweetness,
Which drew me to the amorous troop;
Who, if I am not mistaken, was
Disposed to lift me high from the earth;
And he took me from peace, and placed me in war.

<note>Annotation related to the closing lines of Stanza II</note>
If it had not been for love alone, he had the spirit to raise himself so high from the earth—that is, with his genius to describe loftily some distinguished deed or divine things—whereas love took this intention from him where he would have had peace, and constrained him to love where he always had war.

<margin>
**I** THESE have made me. Third stanza: in which our author confesses his sin, saying: "Look, high queen, what this cruel love has done to me." It made it so that I loved God less than I should have, and cared much less for myself than I ought. For a lady, who was Laura, I placed every other thought into disregard; and he cannot excuse himself from this, because Love himself was his counselor, always sharpening his youthful desire in his desire to stand strong in love. He hoped, by staying under Love's yoke, to have rest; but indeed that yoke is harsh and fierce, and the opposite of all he hoped for is found. And he asks himself, wretched, why he did not use the other gifts given to him by heaven; so now that he is changing his hair <note>A metaphor for growing old or turning gray.</note>...
</margin>

## STANZA . III .

These have made me love God less
Than I ought; and care less for myself:
For a lady I have placed
Equally in disregard every thought;
Of this, he alone has been my counselor,
Always sharpening my youthful desire
On the cruel whetstone; whence I
Hoped for rest from the harsh and fierce yoke:
Wretched me, to what end [was] that clear, noble genius,
And the other gifts given to me by heaven?
For I am changing my hair;
Yet I cannot change my obstinate will;
Thus this cruel one, whom I accuse,
Entirely strips me of my liberty;
Who has turned my bitter living into a sweet habit.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch's Canzone 360, an allegorical legal battle where the poet sues the god of Love before the court of Reason. ...nor does he yet notice that his obstinate will still deprives him of freedom, and he accuses this cruel love which, through love, has put this into practice.

<margin>**He made me seek.**</margin> Fourth stanza <note>The OCR reads "Statia quattatne," likely a corruption of the Italian "Stanza quarta."</note> which follows the poet as he gives his reasons. He was made to seek diverse countries; Petrarch wandered much through the world, as shown in his juvenile and senior letters <note>Original: "epistole giouenile & senile." These refer to Petrarch's collected Latin correspondence, the *Epistolae familiares* and *Seniles*.</note>. Therefore, he speaks of the things found while traveling, and in every place he walked he found a thousand snares—whether we take this to mean love or simply his physical body. [He mentions] winter in strange months, such as in Germany and Britain where he traveled, where winter came upon him before its time. In these foreign parts, he was never without the toil caused by his enemy, who is Laura. If he did not die before his time despite such great hardships, it was for no other reason than divine mercy, and certainly not because of this tyrant [Love], who feeds on his pain and suffering.

## STANZA .IIII.

> He made me seek desert lands,
> Wild beasts, and greedy thieves, and prickly thorns;
> Harsh people and customs,
> And every error that entangles pilgrims;
> Mountains, valleys, marshes, and seas, and rivers;
> A thousand snares stretched in every part;
> And winter in strange months,
> With present danger and with toil:
> Neither he, nor that other enemy of mine [Laura],
> Whom I fled, left me for a single moment:
> So that if I have not reached
> A bitter and hard death before my time;
> Celestial piety has care
> Of my health, not this tyrant;
> Who feeds on my grief and on my harm.

<margin>**Since I was his.**</margin> Fifth stanza, in which the poet continues lamenting about Love, saying that since the time he was made his servant, he never had a single hour of peace, nor does he hope to have one. This is because of the pain he has received from him; and the proof of it is found in his nights, in which he should have slept, but because of love he lamented instead. In this way, sleep was taken from him so that he can no longer have it, not even through herbs that might help. This is all for the love of Laura, who can never be removed from his soul by any means. His thoughts have grown so much that this love has power over him as a master, whom he calls *donno*, which in the Spanish language means "lord" <note>The commentator notes the use of the term *donno* (lord/master), which Petrarch likely adapted from Spanish or Provençal for the sake of the rhyme.</note>. He used that word for the harmony of the verse. He says that at every hour the *squilla* <note>A *squilla* is a small bell, specifically the vesper bell that rings in the evening.</note> rings—which is a bell—as it is called in the villages.

## STANZA .V.

> Since I was his, I had no quiet hour;
> Nor do I hope to have one; and sleep is banished
> From my nights, and no longer can they
> By herbs or by incantations draw it back:
> By deceptions and by force he is made lord [*donno*]
> Over my spirits; and then there is no bell [*squilla*],
> Wherever I may be in some village,
> That I did not hear; and he knows that I speak the truth:
> For no woodworm ever gnawed old wood,
> As this one gnaws my heart, in which he nests,
> And challenges it with death:
> From here are born the tears and the sufferings;
> The words and the sighs,
> Of which I am wearying myself, and perhaps others:
> You judge, you who know me and him.

And therefore he rightly says "wherever I may be in some village," so that there was never an hour that he did not hear it. Love knows well that he speaks the truth, for no woodworm ever gnawed wood as love gnaws him. It nests in his heart so that death has already challenged him through great passion. And from here are born the tears and the sighs of which I am wearying myself—and perhaps even others, hearing me lament so much, are weary. So you, Queen [Reason], who know us well, judge and give this sentence.

## STANZA VI.

My adversary with bitter reproaches
Begins: "O Lady <note>Love addresses Reason, who acts as the judge in this allegorical trial.</note>, hear the other side;
For the truth, from which he departs,
This ungrateful man shall hear without flaw.
In his early youth, he was given to the art
Of selling little words, or rather, lies;
Nor does he seem ashamed,
Having been taken from that boredom for my delight,
To complain of me; for I kept him pure and clean
Against the desire that often seeks his own harm:
Wherefore he now grieves,
In a sweet life which he calls misery,
Having risen to some fame
Only through me, who raised his intellect,
Where, by his own power, he would never have risen."

<margin>M</margin>
**My adversary.** Sixth stanza: in which is placed the response that Love made to him. It says that the adversary—Love—with a bitter and reproachful murmuring, began to say from the other side: "Do not make such a judgment, Lady, but choose to hear the other side," because he who hears both sides can judge better. Because this ungrateful man departs from the truth, Love began his response with indignation. Thus, to this ungrateful man who has complained so much of me, saying that he never had any good in my kingdom—in which I honored him—[I say] that in the beginning when he came to me, he was given to the art of selling words and lies; that is, to practice in the law courts <term>corte forense</term> <note>Love is mocking Petrarch’s early training in law, suggesting it was a dishonest profession compared to poetry.</note>. For Petrarch, as he himself writes in many places in his letters, studied civil law <term>rason ciuile</term>, and perhaps in the beginning he went through the palaces of justice acting as an advocate with his father, Ser Petracco. And it seems this ungrateful man is not ashamed that I took him out of such annoyance and removed him from that art for my pleasure, and have since kept him in a happy life, which he—not being ashamed—calls misery. For this life, I say he has risen to some fame, because previously he was a total servant [to law]; and this is through the love of Lady Laura, who first began to excite him to write elegant verses, prose, and rhymes.

## STANZA VII.

"He knows that the great son of Atreus <note>Agamemnon.</note>, and the noble Achilles,
And Hannibal on your bitter earth,
And the most famous of all <note>Likely Scipio Africanus.</note>,
Another distinguished in both virtue and fortune;
As his stars ordained for each;
I allowed to fall into the vile love of handmaidens:
While for this man, from a thousand
Excellent and chosen women, I selected one;
The likes of whom will never be seen under the Moon,
Even if Lucretia were to return to Rome;
And I gave her such sweet speech <note>Original: "idioma."</note>,
And a singing so soft,
That no low or heavy thought
Could ever endure in her presence.
These, with him, were my 'deceptions'."

<margin>N</margin>
**He knows that the great son of Atreus.** Seventh stanza: in which Love rebukes the poet using four worthy men to show he treated the poet better than he deserved. Therefore, he rightly says: "O high Queen <note>Addressing Reason.</note>, this ungrateful man knows that the great son of Atreus, who is Agamemnon, and the noble Achilles, and Hannibal on your bitter earth, and the most famous of all—all of whom were taken by the love of handmaidens <note>Love is contrasting Petrarch's noble love for Laura with the historical heroes' attractions to slave girls (e.g., Achilles and Briseis).</note>—we will speak of these at the end of the stanza. And for this man, from a thousand beautiful and graceful women, I chose one, and I chose her such that her equal will not be found under the moon." This is to praise Laura further and to further confound the poet. He says even if Lucretia <note>The Roman model of virtue.</note> returned to Rome, [she would not compare]. By "sweet speech," he means he gave her a way of speaking so honest and soft, with such gravity, that no person could have an unvirtuous mind toward her; for immediately upon hearing her sweet speech, everything [dishonest vanished]...
