<meta>This page continues the defense of Love against the Poet's accusations in the trial before Reason. Following the previous page, where Love argued he rescued the Poet from a mundane legal career, Love now compares the Poet’s "suffering" to the legendary struggles and loves of great historical and mythological figures like Agamemnon, Achilles, Hannibal, and Scipio.</meta>

...no dishonest thought ever fell from her mind. And when he says that even if Lucretia were to return to Rome—for one reads of the great eloquence of Lucretia, who incited her husband and her father, together with Brutus, against **Tarquin the Proud** <note>Tarquinio Superbo, the last legendary king of Rome, whose son's assault on Lucretia led to the birth of the Roman Republic.</note>—even if Lucretia were to be brought back to life, she would not be as eloquent as Laura. Thus, these have been my "arts and deceits" about which he has so loudly complained. Let us now briefly explain the histories touched upon above.

<margin>O</margin> $\P$ Both Agamemnon and Menelaus were the sons of Plisthenes, although some hold that their father was Atreus; they descended from the lineage of Jove. Agamemnon was the prince over all the Greeks in the **siege of Troy**; after the destruction of the city, returning to his homeland with infinite spoils, his wife Clytemnestra—who had been enjoying herself while he was away with many Trojan captives—conspired with Aegisthus the priest <note>In classical mythology, Aegisthus was Agamemnon's cousin, not a priest, but the commentator here identifies him as such.</note>, who was consorting with her, and had Agamemnon killed. Thus, the women he took were his servants, whom the poet calls handmaidens.

<margin>P</margin> $\P$ Achilles is called "great"; indeed, he was great for being celebrated by every writer more than any of the other Greeks. He was the son of Peleus, King of the island called Aegina, located opposite the Morea <note>The Peloponnese peninsula in Greece.</note>. He was raised by **Chiron the Centaur**, and by him made learned in Astrology, medicine, and music. Dressed in women's clothing, he was sent to stay with the daughters of Lycomedes on the island of Scyros, where he remained for some years without being recognized. From him and the maiden Deidamia was born Pyrrhus. Later, taken away by the cunning of **Ulysses**, he went with the others to the siege of Troy and showed his incredible strength. Because of his prowess, he killed Hector and many other sons of Priam. Later, in the temple of Apollo Thymbraeus—which he had entered to take Polyxena, daughter of Priam, as his bride—he was killed by Paris and Deiphobus. $\P$ The love for the handmaiden of whom the poet speaks was Briseis, mentioned by **Ovid** in his third epistle; she is called a handmaiden because she was his captive.

<margin>Q</margin> $\P$ The other was **Hannibal** of Carthage.

<margin>R</margin> Truly, he loved Italy, which is our land. He was the son of Hamilcar. After crossing into Italy and taking Saguntum in Spain, he was victorious over the Romans everywhere—at the Ticinus, at the Trebbia, at Lake Trasimene, and at the village of Cannae in Apulia—with a very great effusion of blood. In the end, he was defeated in his own homeland. But first, at the castle of Salapia in Apulia, he was so subjugated by a meretricious love that he could hardly be excused. As our author says in his book *On the Remedies of Both Good and Bad Fortune* <note>original: "de li remedij de luna: et laltra fortuna"; referring to Petrarch's *De remediis utriusque fortunae*.</note> when speaking of this: "Look how much power this Love has—that which so many hard souls and so many bitter breasts could not conquer or restrain in its course, a vile woman has restrained and captured for her love."

<margin>S</margin> $\P$ The other is **Scipio** (though some say Alexander the Great). I say it is Scipio, who was the son of Publius Scipio, whom he saved from death in the Battle of Ticinus. This was one of his first deeds. After the defeat suffered at Cannae, Rome was not abandoned because of him; he drew his sword against Metellus in his own house, and without regard for his rank as a military tribune, he forced him and the others through fear to swear not to abandon their fatherland. At twenty-four years of age, he went to Spain where his father and uncle had been defeated and killed by the Carthaginians. On the first day, he took New Carthage (today called Cartagena). When Hannibal was recalled out of fear, Scipio crushed him and made Carthage tributary to Rome. Later, having returned to Rome, he was made an exile without guilt by the tribune Petilius. As **Seneca** says, it was necessary that either Scipio harm liberty or liberty harm Scipio; he judged it better to bear the injuries of his fragile fatherland. But before his departure, he fell in love with one of his handmaidens, as **Valerius Maximus** testifies in the sixth book, seventh chapter, in his ninth example. His wife Emilia, noticing this, always kept it secret; she did not want the man who had won so many victories to be known for such infamy. Thus, after his death, she freed the servant and married her off, so that it could never be said her husband had been involved with a mere slave. So, even he was captured by the love of a handmaiden.

### STANZA.XI.

<margin>V</margin>
<margin>$\P$ To say. Stanza 9, in which it seems Love wishes to conclude his plea, although he does not finish. To say at the end, without wandering further: the great service I have done for him by being in my kingdom. I withdrew him from a thousand dishonest acts, for by no pact could any ill-done thing ever please him. I made him be a "shy youth": that is, one who avoids common things, and is shameful <note>In this context, "vergognoso" or shameful refers to the medieval virtue of "shamefastness"—a modest, sensitive moral conscience.</note> in his every act. Aristotle does not wish for shame to be counted among the virtues of the body, as Petrarch seems to want here, although many hold his opinion; however, Aristotle maintains it. And I made him a liege man: "liege" <term>liege: "ligio," a legal term for a vassal bound to serve only one lord</term> is a legal term that refers to one who serves only one lord, just as Petrarch was subject only to Madonna Laura. Having done this, I made him similar to her, so that one sees how much of the extraordinary and the noble <note>original: "pellegrino & gentile"</note> he possesses. From her and from me he had nothing vain, which he calls "phantasms"—these are false opinions that often appear, especially to melancholics. Thus, he has not been so full of errors as he has accused us, blaming us in the manner you have heard. Thus, he has returned to greatness in every way, even if at times he had something that was not to his liking. And of this, the proud man laments and repents.</margin>

And to say at the last the great service;
From a thousand dishonest acts I drew him:
For never by any pact
Could a vile thing please him:
A shy and shameful youth in act
And in thought, since he was made a liege man
Of her, who impressed another footprint
Upon his heart, and made him like herself.
Whatever he has of the extraordinary and the noble,
He holds from her and from me, whom he blames.
Never was a nocturnal phantasm
So full of error as he is toward us:
He who later, by grace,
Knew us, and God, and the people:
Of this the proud man laments, and repents.

### STANZA.X.

<margin>X</margin>
<margin>$\P$ Further. This tenth stanza, to further aggravate the sin of ingratitude, says that everything surpasses what I have already said. Above the heavens I had given him wings to fly: and this is through his wisdom which flew above the heavens. For as **Sallust** <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus, a Roman historian; Love refers to the prologue of his "War with Catiline" regarding those who live like cattle.</note> says, those who die like cattle leave no memory of themselves. Thus, the knowledge I gave him, by which he makes a ladder to go to his God: and that this is the truth, he himself does not dispute, because he has spoken of it through his rhymes.</margin>

Further (and this is what surpasses everything)
To fly above the sky I had given him wings
Through mortal things;
Which are a ladder to the Creator, for him who values them well:
For whoever gazes steadily at the good, how many and what
Were the virtues in that hope of his,
From one appearance to another
He could rise to the high First Cause;

...me. And now, as a reward for such a great gift, he has consigned me to oblivion, just like that lady who ought to sustain him, or the well-being of his fragile life.

<margin>Y</margin> **At the end. The final stanza.** Both of them turned toward the seat of justice: the one, who is Petrarch, with a trembling voice; the other, who is Love, with a loud and harsh voice. Each says the judgment should be in his favor, and they say: "O noble lady, we await your sentence." And she, smiling at them, said: "It pleases me well to have heard this dispute of yours, but more time is needed for so great a case."

<margin>Hieronymo Z</margin> **He tells me.** The poet expresses a sentiment that everyone should consider as a meditation on their own life: that his faithful mirror and his changed skin <note>original: "cangiata scorza," a metaphor for his aging body</note> make him clearly realize he is old and his agility is much diminished. His mirror tells him this, for it does not hide the truth. He says in one of his own letters that in his youth he was very physically agile. Thus, it is necessary to obey nature—that is, to bear old age in peace—and there is no need to contend with her, for time is the force that compels us. Just as water extinguishes fire, so he wakes from a heavy and long sleep and, because of this, notices the great velocity of our human life.

<margin>Hieronymo A</margin> **I fly.** A sonnet in which the poet says he often flies with wings to heaven—that is, rising through meditation—because his treasure, which is Laura, is there. Sometimes, seeing her with a heart full of love, a "sweet frost" <note>original: "dolce gelo," a classic Petrarchan oxymoron describing the shivering of a lover</note> ensnares his heart for her sake. Because of her, he loses his color. She says to him: "I love you and I honor you now, because your habits have changed along with your hair" <note>referring to his graying hair and the spiritual maturity that comes with age</note>. He says she leads him to the Supreme God, and bowing, he prays that he may remain to see both faces: that of God and that of Laura. God responds to him that if his destiny is firmly fixed—that is, when you are well-confirmed in grace—then it will be the time for perpetuity here. Thus, staying on earth for twenty or thirty years does not seem pleasing to him; this waiting is too long for him. To us mortals, the term would seem long, but to God it is nothing, for a hundred years is like the blink of an eye.

¶ I fly with wings. The poet imagines how he often finds himself in heaven with his thoughts to converse with his lady, and he imagines how he prays to God and how God responds to Master Francesco <note>original: "Meser Francesco," referring to Francesco Petrarch</note>.

### SONNET CCCIX.

<margin>
Hieronymo B.
¶ DEATH. A sonnet in which the poet laments the death that has taken Laura from him; so he says death has extinguished his sun—that is, Laura—who through her beauties used to dazzle his eyes. Those eyes, which were once so firm that no person could look directly at them because of her radiance, have now become earth. Thus, that place where he felt cold and heat—that is, in loving her—is gone. All his actions are extinguished, such that he asks for the laurels <note>original: "lauri," a pun on the name Laura and the poet's laurel crown</note> which now have become oaks and elms. This is to distinguish them, because oaks and elms are hard woods that are used more than others for burning; or perhaps he places them as something base in comparison to Laura. It could also mean that now his thoughts are most base compared to the time his lady was alive. He says indeed that it is good for her to be dead to see her bliss, and he grieves for it in part; for while she was alive, she made his thoughts sometimes fearful and other times bold. So Laura is no more, she who still warms and freezes his thoughts, even though they are old; he says this because of love, for one time more than another we are warmer toward the things we love, and sometimes colder. Through these diversities, his intellect was made sharper. Yet it was sweet as far as his life went, and for this he thanked God, whom he adores, who governs and rules everything with a mere glance. And so, returning to himself from his thought—which through elevation he had fixed on the high things of heaven, as said in the previous sonnet—he says his weary life is full to bursting.
</margin>

**M**eath has extinguished that sun which used to dazzle me,
**A**nd in darkness are my eyes, once whole and firm;
**T**arth is she from whom I had my cold and heat;
**S**xtinguished are my laurels, now oaks and elms.
**I** say I see my good, and in part it pains me.
**T**here is no one to make my thoughts both fearful
**A**nd bold, nor one to freeze or warm them,
**N**or one to fill them with hope or brim them with grief.
**O**ut of the hands of him who stings and soothes, <note>Petrarch refers here to Love/Cupid</note>
**W**ho once made such a long slaughter of me,
**I** find myself in a liberty both bitter and sweet;
**A**nd to the Lord, whom I adore and whom I thank,
**W**ho governs and sustains heaven with a mere glance,
**I** return, weary of living—not merely satiated.

### SONNET CCCX.

<margin>
¶ Love held me. Sonnet 310. In which it is understood that, remembering his past life, the poet grieves greatly for himself and reproaches his own ill-living. He was already twenty-one years old, and Laura could not have been more than fourteen or fifteen; so when he wrote this sonnet, the poet was forty-four years old, and at that time Lady Laura died. For he rightly says that during that time he remained happy in the fire—that is, in love—and gripped in the grief which was always full of hope. Regarding hope, we shall say what Hesiod <note>A Greek poet; the commentator likely refers to the myth of Pandora's jar where hope remains</note> says at the end of the sonnet, which shall serve as a declaration for all the places where it is mentioned, since his lady Laura is dead and ascended to heaven; and he remained there ten more...
</margin>

**L**ove held me burning for twenty-one years,
**H**appy in the fire, and in grief full of hope.
**S**ince my lady, and my heart together with her,
**A**scended to heaven, ten other years of weeping have passed.
**N**ow I am weary, and I reproach my life
**F**or so much error, which has almost extinguished
**T**he seed of virtue; and my final parts <note>referring to his soul and his final days</note>
**T**o you, High God, I devoutly render,
**P**entant and sad for my years so spent,
**W**hich ought to have been spent in better use:
**I**n seeking peace, and in fleeing hardships.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the late poems of Francesco Petrarch’s "Canzoniere." Following the previous discussion of his grief for Laura, the text now shifts toward a more explicitly religious and penitential tone. Petrarch reflects on his age—specifically his decision at forty-one to renounce carnal desires—and prepares for his own death by turning his focus from his mortal "sun" (Laura) to the eternal "King of Heaven."</meta>

...ten other years only for his memory of being in love. The poet writes in one of his epistles through which he shows the entire progress of his life, stating that by the age of 41 years he never again knew a woman carnally: nor did he care for them as if he had never seen a woman again. Thus he rightly says he is now tired of his past life and reproaches himself for the great error in which he had been, through which he had almost lost the "seed": that is, the way of knowing how to lead himself back to all the virtues. So, turning to God, he says he devotedly surrenders these final parts of his life to Him: that is, by no longer wanting to live as he had lived. He says he is repentant and sad for his ill-spent years, which he should have used for better things, such as seeking peace and fleeing troubles. He prays: "Lord, who has enclosed me in the search of the world, pull me out safe so that by my deeds I may not be damned; I know my failure and I confess it, I do not excuse myself." Let us now say what we promised above.

> Lord, who has enclosed me in this prison;
> Pull me out safe from eternal harms:
> For I know my fault, and I do not excuse it.

<margin>D</margin>
¶ Hesiod writes in his *Theogony*: that Prometheus, having ascended to heaven with the help of Pallas <note>The goddess Athena, often associated with wisdom and the intellect</note> to breathe life into the clay statue <note>original: "statua lutea"</note> he had made, took all the virtues and placed them in a very well-sealed chest. He entrusted it to Pandora, warning her that she must not open it for any reason. Jupiter, seeing this, sent Mercury in a transformed shape to Prometheus’s house. Not finding him home, Mercury was able to persuade Pandora, telling her that the chest was full of treasure. She took it and opened it, and all the virtues flew back to heaven: except for Hope, which remained at the bottom of the chest. Because the chest was closed while the others escaped, she could not flee. Thus, hope is the only thing we hold in this world, and upon it we feed.

<margin>Antonio.</margin>
"HE HELD ME, love, burning for twenty-one years." Master Francesco describes how he loved her for 21 years while Laura was alive, and 10 years after her death. The "eternal harms" are the pains of Hell.

<margin>Hieronymo.</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
"I GO." In a similar theme to what was written above, the poet grieves for his lost time because he did not spend it in better exercise than in loving mortal things. He laments that he did not take flight despite having wings: that is, having the intellect <note>The "wings" represent the human soul’s capacity to rise toward divine understanding</note> through which he could recognize the nature of his actions. He then turns to God, saying: King of Heaven, who is invisible and immortal, who sees my defects, succor this my soul <note>original: "aiata," likely a variant of "anima," soul</note>. Through Your grace, fulfill its defects: so that if he lived in war and tempest, he may die in peace. If his staying in this world was in vain, may his dying be honorable through Your mercy. May he spend the few days of life remaining to him well, and at his death, may Your hand be ready to receive him, because in You alone he has hope.

<margin>Hiero.</margin> <note>Commentary on the end of Sonnet 312</note>
Sweet is her noble manner in which every courtesy clearly shines with supreme honesty. And for this, he calls her the flower of virtue and the fountain of beauties; her happy gaze was capable of making the man who saw her happy: and that gaze was also stern in restraining whoever was so bold as to ask of her that which is honestly denied—referring to dishonest things. She was also ready to comfort his life, and this "beautiful variation" of hers was the root of this salvation of his, which otherwise would have gone, for he would have come to a bad end.

# SONNET CCCXIII.

<margin>S</margin> **S** happy spirit, who so sweetly
Turned those eyes brighter than the sun;
And formed the sighs and the words
Living, which still sound in my mind:
<margin>G</margin> **G** I once saw you burning with honest fire
Move your feet among the grass and violets
Not like a woman but as an angel is wont;
Of her, who now is more present to me than ever:
<margin>L</margin> **L** Whom you then, returning to your Maker,
Left on earth, and that sweet veil,
Which by high destiny came to your lot.
In your departing, love departed from the world,
And courtesy; and the sun fell from the heaven,
And death began to become sweet.

<margin>Hiero.</margin> <note>Commentary on Sonnet 313</note>
<term>SPIRIT</term> — the poet speaks to the soul of his Madonna Laura, calling her "happy spirit," who when she was alive so sweetly turned those eyes which were brighter than the sun, and formed those sweet words and the sighs of love so sweetly that even now, while he is alive, they sound in his ears; and this is because of his remembering them. Here the poet uses "spirit" for "soul" according to Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, who discussed the nature of the soul and spirit</note>: they are similar in essence but different in name. Petrarch says: "The ardor of an honest fire." And he says this because of the love that moved her feet among the grass and violets; she did not move like a woman, but her walking was like an angel's, and through these many elegant acts of hers, she is more than ever in his mind. He turns his speech to Laura, saying: "You have returned to your Maker and have left your sweet veil on earth": that is, the body <note>A common poetic metaphor for the physical body as a temporary covering for the soul</note>, which was so beautiful that I say it was given by lot through destiny. What more praise can be given to her than what he attributes here: that when she departed from the world, love departed with her, and not only love, but courtesy. "The sun fell from the heaven"—this is a metaphor for her beauty; he uses the sun for the falling of heaven to describe her death: and because of her dying, death began to become sweet: that is, such were her beauties that death in her could not be cruel or bitter, but sweet.

---

# SONNET CCCXIIII.

<margin>D</margin> **D** Ah, lend a hand to the troubled intellect,
Love, and to the tired and fragile style,
To speak of her who is made immortal;
And a citizen of the celestial kingdom.
<margin>D</margin> **D** Give to me, Lord, that my speech may reach the mark
Of her praises, where by itself it does not rise;
If virtue, if beauty had no equal
In the world; which was not worthy to have her.
<margin>R</margin> **R** He responds: "As much as heaven and I can do,
The good counsels, and the honest conversation;
Everything was in her, of which death has deprived us."

<margin>Hiero.</margin> <note>Commentary on Sonnet 314</note>
<term>AH, LEND</term>. Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> asks for help in this 314th sonnet from Love, that he might lend a hand to his troubled style—and well-troubled because of the death of his Laura. And he prays God to give him help for this tired and fragile speech: "tired" from grief and "fragile," that is, humble, in wanting to speak of that Laura who is made immortal by her virtues and made a citizen of the celestial kingdom. "O Lord Love, give me of yourself so that I may reach the mark of her praises," for without his help the intellect cannot rise by itself. That is, he says "I want to go so high" since there was no equal to her whom I praise...

<margin>Hieronymus I</margin>
**W**ANDERING <term>vago</term> <note>The Italian "vago" can mean wandering, charming, or longing; here the commentator interprets it as "forestiero" (stranger/wandering).</note> our poet, as if sorrowful: & for his grief he speaks to a wandering little bird. "Vandering" here he takes for "stranger," which little bird used to go singing around his house thus at the setting of the sun: and at sunrise or in the evening Petrarch always delighted in the solitary life: so that speaking as one impassioned to this little bird he says to it: O wandering little bird that from here goes singing, or rather your song is of sorrow because it tells, weeping, of your past time; this is because the night and the winter, which are both contrary to you, you see them suddenly at your side: just as you, little bird, know your troubles, so I wish you could know mine; for knowing them, you would come into the lap of this disconsolate one that I, Petrarch, am. Many times men speak of various passions to non-intellectual things as if they wished to share their cares with them, just as Petrarch does at present. And he says: coming into my lap you would share with me your sorrowful woes: but I know not, Petrarch continues, if the parts would be equal: because she for whom you weep is perhaps [still] alive. And from me, death & heaven are so stingy with her that I can no longer see her. He says "death" because it holds her back from him; but the season of this time is not so pleasing to me: because of the memory of the sweet years in which I used to see my lady at such a time, therefore he said "less pleasing": and so also remembering the years as much sweet as bitter. And this such remembering invites me to reason with you, little bird. This, dearest reader, is the sonnet declared above, and the last one answered for all reasons. So that having now arrived, I, Hieronymus Squarzafico of Alexandria <note>An Italian humanist and editor active in the late 15th century.</note>, rejoice and grieve that at the instance of the printers with great speed I have followed in explaining all that Philelpho <note>Francesco Filelfo (1398–1481), a famous humanist scholar whose commentary Squarzafico was completing.</note> had left out, which was from the sonnet that begins *Flame from heaven rain upon your tresses* <note>Sonnet 136, one of Petrarch's "Babylonian" sonnets criticizing the Papal court.</note>. I, as I have said, have followed until this end: and so I rejoice for having reached the finish. I wish then, because of the great haste that was necessary for me to use for the brevity of wanting to write for the printers—and this I have wanted to write at this end for my excuse—to do as Phidias <note>A famous ancient Greek sculptor.</note> did with the statue of Minerva, who at the end wanted to sculpt his own face: and in such a way that without the destruction of the work it could not be removed.

## SONNET CCCXV.

**W**andering little bird, that goest singing,
Or rather weeping for your time gone by,
Seeing the night and winter at your side,
And the day behind your shoulders and the gay months.
**I**f as you know your heavy troubles
So you knew my similar state,
You would come into the lap of this disconsolate one
To share with him his sorrowful woes.
**I** know not if the parts would be equal,
For she whom you weep for is perhaps alive;
Of whom death and heaven are so stingy to me.
**B**ut the season and the hour, less pleasing,
With the memory of sweet years and bitter,
Invites me to speak with you in pity.

### SONNET CCCXX.

And it seems to me from hour to hour to hear the messenger
That my lady sends to me, calling me to herself;
Thus inside and out I go changing;
And in not many years I have become so diminished,
That I hardly recognize myself anymore:
I have banished all my usual way of living:
I would be happy to know the "when":
But still the time should be near.
O happy that day, when leaving the earthly
Prison <note>Petrarch often refers to the physical body as a "prison" for the soul.</note>, I leave broken and scattered
This my heavy, and frail, and mortal garment <note>The "garment" is a metaphor for the flesh/body.</note>;
And from such thick darkness I depart
Flying so high in the beautiful serenity,
That I may see my Lord and my lady.

<margin>Hieronymus L.</margin>
This sonnet is connected with the one above because it shows the poet soon expects to follow his dear lady, since he is so changed from his former state by her death; and he calls that day happy in which, leaving his body to the earth, he goes to heaven to see the divine majesty and his Lady Laura.

<margin>Hieronymus</margin>
*It seems to me from hour to hour*: the poet says that until now he has been so impassioned that he wishes he were dead, and it seems like a thousand years until he is called and hears the messenger sent by his Lady Laura. *Leaving the earthly prison*: that is, this body which is the prison of the soul. *That I may see my Lord and my lady*: that is, God and his Lady Laura.

## PRAISE TO THE VIRGIN MARY.

Beautiful Virgin, who, clothed in the sun,
Crowned with stars, to the highest Sun <note>The "highest Sun" refers to God.</note>
You were so pleasing that he hid his light in you;
Love drives me to speak words of you;
But I do not know how to begin without your aid,
And his, who out of love placed himself in you.
I invoke her; who always answered well
Anyone who called upon her with faith.
Virgin, if to mercy
The extreme misery of human things
Ever turned you, incline yourself to my prayer;
Succor me in my war,
Though I be earth, and you the queen of heaven.

<margin>Hieronymus M.</margin>
*Virgin*. This is a praise <term>laude</term> which our graceful poet made to the blessed Virgin Mary: and it was placed at the end of these sonnets of his to give everyone to understand how devoted he was to the queen of the heavens. I speak of her without whom we would all be deprived of celestial goods. It is a most elegant and no less pious work, through which he recommends himself to her as much as he can, because he knew that whoever desires grace and does not resort to her, his desire "wishes to fly without wings," as Dante says <note>A reference to Dante Alighieri’s *Paradiso*, Canto XXXIII.</note>. He begins then: *O beautiful Virgin who are clothed in the sun* and are crowned with stars by the highest Sun, which is God. He says what Saint John writes in the Apocalypse: that there appeared in heaven a great sign, a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon was under her feet, and on her head she had a crown of twelve stars <note>Revelation 12:1.</note>. Thus, O Queen of Heaven, the love I bear you makes me sing this praise, but without your help I cannot begin; likewise without the help of God, who loving you placed himself in you, because you, a Virgin, gave birth to him who was God. Thus I invoke you, that I may always know I have your...

**W**ise Virgin, and one of the beautiful number

## STANZA III.

**V**irgin pure, in every part whole,
Daughter and mother of your noble birth,
Who illuminates this life, and adorns the other:
Through you, your son, and that of the highest Father <note>In Christian theology, Christ is the son of Mary (humanly) and the son of God the Father (divinely).</note>,

He then calls her the "window of heaven," just as it is written in one of his books. O Virgin, who are so shining and proud, come to save me when I pass from this life, which are the final days. You, blessed Virgin, among all other earthly persons were chosen: and you were also the one who returned the weeping of Eve—who was our first mother—into joy: he says "of Eve" because of the eating of the forbidden fruit <note>The apple from the Garden of Eden.</note>, through which sin the entire human generation fell into misery from which they could not be lifted without the birthing of Mary. "Make me," the poet says to her, "that I may be worthy of the grace of your son." O blessed without end: who, as we have said above, are crowned in the supernal kingdom.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch's "Canzone alla Vergine." The previous page concluded the commentary on Stanzas II and III, which focused on the Virgin's wisdom and her role as a shield for the afflicted. This page covers Stanzas IV, V, and the beginning of VI.</meta>

# STANZA IIII.

> Holy Virgin, full of every grace;
> Who through true and highest humility
> Ascended to heaven, from where you hear my prayers;
> You gave birth to the fountain of mercy,
> And the sun of justice; which clears
> The age full of dark and thick errors;
> Three sweet and dear names you have gathered in yourself:
> Mother, and daughter, and spouse <note>A theological paradox frequently cited by Petrarch: Mary is the Mother of Christ, the Daughter of God the Father, and the Spouse of the Holy Spirit.</note>;
> Glorious Virgin;
> Lady of the King, who has untied our bonds,
> And made the world free and happy;
> In whose holy wounds
> I pray that my heart might find true peace <note>original: "beatrice," a play on the name Beatrice, meaning "she who makes blessed" or "bringer of joy."</note>.

<margin>P</margin>
¶ Holy Virgin, Stanza IIII. In which he says what we say every day in the salutation of this Virgin: that she is full of grace. Through her highest humility, she ascended to heaven where she listens to his prayers and gave birth to God, who is the fountain of mercy. And this was through her great humility, because as Augustine says, and also Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and mystic known for his intense devotion to Mary.</note> in one of his sermons, the humility of Mary pleased God more than her virginity. She was humble in her actions and her character, just as she showed herself by saying: *Behold the handmaid of the Lord* <note>original Latin: "Ecce acilla [ancilla] dei." This is Mary's response to the Angel Gabriel at the Annunciation (Luke 1:38).</note>. And in the psalm <note>The Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55).</note>, God looked upon the humility of his handmaid: for this, all generations shall call me blessed. Not only did she give birth to the fountain of mercy—which in God is supreme—but also to the sun of justice, which alone clears the world that is full of hard, sad, and dark errors. You, Virgin, have three names gathered in you that no other woman can have, for you are the glorious virgin, mother, daughter, and spouse. You are the Lady of Him who is Christ, who has untied all our bonds; for we could not be saved without his coming.

---

# STANZA V.

> Virgin alone in the world without example;
> Who enamored heaven with your beauties;
> To whom there was none similar before, nor after;
> Holy thoughts, merciful and chaste acts
> Made a sacred and living temple for the true God
> In your fertile virginity.
> Through you my life can be joyful;
> If to your prayers, O Mary,
> Sweet and pious Virgin,
> Where sin abounded, grace abounds <note>A reference to Romans 5:20: "But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound."</note>.
> With the knees of my mind bowed,
> I pray that you be my guide,
> And straighten my crooked way to a good end.

<margin>Q :</margin>
¶ Virgin alone. Stanza V. Note the poet’s other titles of honor for our Lady, which cannot be attributed to anyone but her; nor can such epithets be used for another. For he says that you alone are a virgin without example, because we can compare no other virginity to hers. Her beauties were such that heaven fell in love with them, which resulted from her virginity and humility, in which no other's virtue has ever been or will ever be equal. Her thoughts were holy, chaste, and merciful. For this reason, she was made fertile by the true God and gave birth while remaining a virgin. So, through you, O Mary, my life can be joyful if you attend to your prayers, pious Virgin; you who through your merits will supply what is lacking in my failings. And so, with the knees of his mind bowed, he prays that she be his guide and that she straighten his crooked path toward a good end.

---

> Trusted guide of every faithful pilot,
> Consider in what a terrible storm
> I find myself, alone without a rudder;
> And I already hear from nearby the final cries:
> But still my soul trusts in you—
> A sinful soul, I do not deny it...

<margin>R</margin>
¶ Bright Virgin. Stanza VI. In which the poet calls her "bright": and shining among all others in this world, just as her hymn says <note>Referring to the hymn *Ave Maris Stella*.</note>. She is the guide and star of the tempestuous sea—by which he means the world—and the guide of every faithful pilot—by which he means those who believe rightly. He prays that she take note of the terrible tempest in which he finds himself, this because of the entanglement...

The previous page discussed the Virgin's humility and her role as the Mother of God.</meta>

...contemplation of his sins and now the final cry <note>original: "strida," referring to the lamentations or the "death-rattle" of those passing away</note> of his neighbors, that is, of his contemporaries who have died. But yet my soul trusts in you, as much as it may be a sinner, and I do not deny it. But Virgin, I pray you that the enemy of human nature <note>A common epithet for Satan.</note>, who is his enemy, does not laugh at him. And to better show that she ought to help him, he reminds her that:

> Virgin: but I pray you,
> That your enemy does not laugh at my misfortune;
> Remember, that our sinning made
> God take, to save us,
> Human flesh in your virginal cloister;

*Christ took flesh and willed to die for our sin: and this to redeem it.*

---

### STANZA VII.

<margin>S</margin>
**VIRGIN, HOW MANY.** Seventh stanza, in which he confesses his errors. He speaks, grieving for the tears and the flatteries which he has already cast away in vain for the fleeting things of this world. He says they were in vain because they were not without his own pain and distress from the hour he was born; he has always gone wandering here and there, as we have written elsewhere. He says this since the time he was born "on the bank of the Arno." 

Here it should be known that Petrarch was not actually born on the bank of the Arno, but was born in Arezzo in the *Borgo dell’Orto* <note>The "District of the Garden," a historic neighborhood in Arezzo where Petrarch’s birthplace still stands.</note>, as he himself writes in his first epistle to his "Socrates" <note>Petrarch’s nickname for his close friend, the Flemish musician Ludwig van Kempen.</note>. It is true that his family was from Incisa <note>Incisa in Val d'Arno, the ancestral home of Petrarch’s father, Ser Petracco.</note>, which is on the bank of the Arno, and he substitutes one place for the other. His distress was caused by "mortal beauty," that is, by Laura, whose beauty and pleasant words clouded <note>original: "offuscarono," meaning dimmed or darkened the spiritual light of the soul.</note> his whole soul. So, holy Virgin, do not delay any longer in giving me help, because my days run faster than an arrow, and know that I only await death.

> Virgin, how many tears I have already shed,
> How many flatteries, and how many prayers in vain,
> Only to my own pain, and to my heavy loss!
> Since I was born on the bank of the Arno,
> Searching now this side, and now that,
> My life has been nothing but trouble.
> Mortal beauty, gestures, and words have
> Entirely clouded my soul.
> Sacred and nourishing Virgin,
> Do not delay, for I am perhaps in my final year:
> My days, swifter than an arrow,
> Amidst miseries and sins
> Have gone, and only death awaits them.

---

### STANZA VIII.

<margin>T</margin>
**VIRGIN, SUCH.** In this eighth stanza, the poet cannot help but remember his Lady Laura, even in the midst of such deep contrition. He says, "O Virgin Mary, such a one is now earth who was Laura," who while she was living kept his heart always in weeping. She did not know even one of his thousand ills, and even if she had known, the same result would have followed. This is because the love he bore her was so great that he could never have left her, for she was every desire of his heart. 

He says she was "death" to him because he desired to possess the beloved thing, and that desire was death to his soul (since the soul is said to die through sin). And to her, she brought "ill fame," that is to Laura, for having been the cause of his honor being neglected. Therefore, you, Lady:

> Virgin, such a one is earth: and has placed in grief
> My heart, which while living she kept in weeping;
> And of a thousand of my ills she knew not one;
> And had she known it, yet that which happened
> Would have happened: for every other desire of hers
> Was death to me, and to her ill fame.
> Now you, Lady of heaven; you our Goddess <note>The use of "Goddess" (Dea) for the Virgin Mary is a characteristic of Renaissance Humanism, blending classical poetic language with Christian devotion.</note>,
> If it is permitted and fitting to say;
> Virgin of high senses
> You see everything, and that which no other
> Could do, is nothing to your great power:
> Put an end to my sorrow,
> Which shall be honor to you, and salvation to me.

--- Page 306 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Francesco Petrarch’s "Canzone alla Vergine" (Song to the Virgin), specifically following the discussion of the Seventh and Eighth stanzas. The commentator is transitioning into the theological implications of calling Mary a "Goddess" and moves into the analysis of Stanza IX.</meta>

...of heaven & our Goddess, if it is fitting to call you Goddess—as that is a name from ancient idolatry or pertains only to the divine essence—but let "Goddess" be understood as "Divine": you, through your most profound and elevated sentiments in infinite height, see and know all: therefore, putting an end to my sorrow (which no one else could do) is nothing compared to your many virtues. By doing so, you will have the honor of having recovered my soul, and likewise, I shall have my salvation.

<margin>
**V** VIRGIN in whom. Stanza IX. In which the poet returns, as if to repeat what he has already said, regarding how he lacked the preeminence to give praise to such a great Virgin. So he says he has all his hope in her and prays, as he has already done, that she might wish to help him in his great need. He says she should not look at his errors or leave him at the final step <note>The "final step" (extremo passo) is a common Renaissance metaphor for the moment of death.</note>. To further show that she ought to help him, he says she should not look at him, but at Him who deigned to create him. Regarding the soul, he means what the Master of Scholastic Histories <note>Referring to Peter Comestor, a 12th-century theologian whose *Historia Scholastica* was a standard textbook.</note> says: that He created all things [at once], except for man, whom He fashioned later. Therefore, Genesis says in the person of God: "Let us make man in our image and likeness" <note>original: "faciamo l'hō a la imagine et similitudine nostra"</note>. He created the soul afterward, so it is well said: "do not look at him, but at Him..."
</margin>

## STANZA IX.

**V**irgin, in whom I have all my hope,
Who can and will help me in my great need;
Do not leave me at the final step:
Look not at me, but at Him who deigned to create me:
Not at my own worth, but at His high likeness,
Which may move you to care for a man so low.
Medusa <note>In Petrarch's poetry, Medusa often represents his obsession with Laura, which "petrified" his soul and turned him away from God.</note> and my own error have made me a stone
Dripping with vain humors;
Virgin, fill my weary heart
With holy and pious tears;
So that at least this final weeping may be devout
Without earthly mud;
As the first was not empty of shame.

...who deigned to create him. One could also bring forth the opinion of those who believe that souls were all created from the beginning and later infused into our bodies. But we, as those who are hurried by the printers <note>A fascinating glimpse into the life of a 16th-century commentator being rushed by a publishing deadline.</note>—as we said in the last sonnet—shall pass over all these things. He says that his own value did not deserve this—that the immense God should grant him such a benefit as to create him—but for this reason, let His "high likeness" (since He created and fashioned him in His own image) move you to care for a man so low. Like Medusa, who dazzled everyone with her terrible aspect, his errors have made him a stone dripping with "vain humors," which are the things of this world. So, Virgin, I pray you to fill my weary heart so that this may be my final weeping: a devout one at the hour of death, not entangled in these worldly things as was my first cry.

<margin>
**X** HUMAN VIRGIN. Stanza X. In which he continues recommending himself through praises to the Virgin Mary. He asks the enemy of pride that their common origin <note>Meaning their shared humanity, as Mary was a human woman and Christ took human form through her.</note>—which is humility—might induce her to have mercy on him, and especially that his heart may be humbly contrite. Here the poet praises his own devotion, noting that if he is accustomed to loving such a small piece of mortal and fleeting earth as his [beloved's] body, and in loving it, he trusts to have hope and help from her. It can also be understood in another way: for the love of Laura; that if he has willed to love with such great faith, as I have said, a fleeting body...
</margin>

## STANZA X.

**V**irgin, human and enemy of pride,
Let love for our common origin induce you
To have mercy on a contrite, humble heart:
For if I am accustomed to love a little piece
Of mortal, fleeting earth with such wondrous faith;
What ought I to do for you, a noble thing?
If from a wretched, miserable, and vile state
I rise again through your hands,
Virgin; I consecrate and purify
To your name my thoughts, my wit, and style,
My tongue and heart, my tears, and my sighs.

<margin>
...mortal love that was given to Laura: he ought to do so in loving you, O Virgin, who are so noble that more cannot be said. Therefore, O Virgin, if this miserable and low state of his is taken away—that is, if it is dried up through <term>your intercession</term> <note>Intercession: the act of a saint or the Virgin Mary praying to God on behalf of a human.</note>—so that if this is done, he consigns to you every thought, talent, and style of his, his tongue, his tears, and his sighs. Thus he prays that you would wish to help him.
</margin>

Guide me to the better ford;
And accept with favor my changed desires.

<margin>
☞ THE DAY. Stanza XI and the last of the song and of the book: in which the poet says his time is approaching, and it cannot be far off. For this reason, he prays to the Blessed Virgin that she might wish to help him: because you, O Virgin, are the only one who can recommend us to your son, God, for the sake of our conscience; which, at the <term>moment of death</term> <note>original: "articulo de la morte"</note>, often wavers because of worldly things that one must leave behind. Thus, I pray that you would wish to recommend me to your true Son, who is Man and God, so that in the end he may receive my spirit in peace. And not without reason has the poet said at the end of this praise—or song to the Virgin—that she should recommend him to her Son: because all graces proceed from Him, and no person can better obtain them than she, as <term>Bernard</term> <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and mystic famous for his devotion to the Virgin Mary.</note> says: "O man, you have a secure recourse to God by way of his mother, who stands always before her Son; and the Son before the Father." ✠ The mother shows the Son the breast and the nipples with which she suckled him; the Son shows the Father his side with the wounds: so that no refusal can ever be made to them.
</margin>

### STANZA XI AND LAST.

The day draws near, and cannot be far;
Time runs so fast and flies,
O unique and lonely Virgin,
And the heart is pricked now by conscience, now by death:
I recommend myself to your true Son,
True Man, and true God;
May he receive my final spirit in peace.

## SONG BY MASTER FRANCESCO
## PETRARCH RECENTLY RE-
## DISCOVERED.

**THAT**, which our nature has most worthy within it,
On this side of the Good through which the human essence
Is distinguished in part from the animals—
That is, intellectual knowledge—
Seems to me a beautiful, a valiant indignation,
When it extinguishes the great flames of malice,
Which already with a thousand adamantine tongues,
With voices of steel, sounding and strong,
Could greatly praise that of which I speak.
Nor do I come to speak ill of it,
But to tell some part of it to discerning intellects;
I say that many deaths
Are a small price for such a joy, and so new;
So few are found today
Who truly believed that the seed was dead;
And it stayed gathered within itself,
All thoughtful, a gentle spirit
Full of the indignation that I went seeking.
It stayed hidden so secretively,
That I said to myself: "Alas, when
Will this harsh and vile time ever end?"
He sees the oppressed and miserable people
Reached to the extreme, and did not see his course
Appear from here or there, from any part,
Thus Saturn,

## CANZONE.

**N**ew beauty in noble dress
Turned my heart to the amorous company,
Where pain is endured, and beauty is hoped for;

Since a bridle was placed on my wandering thought

Are the sparks of love, because they burn my heart.

## THE SAME FATHER MARSILIO
## to the Magnificent and Generous <term>Master</term> <note>original: "Messer."</note> Marino

> **H**ow much power does virtue have, Sublime Marino,
> And the primary subject of every good writer;
> That I am constrained to love one I have never seen,

# <term>FATHER</term> <note>original: "PRE" (Prete). A title for a priest.</note> MARSILIO UMBRO OF FOSSOMBRONE TO THE MAGNIFICENT LUDOVICO BARBARIGO, HEALTH AND GRACE.
-> .D. <note>original: "D." Abbreviation for "Dedicavit," meaning "He dedicated this."</note> <-

**N**o common and small praises, magnanimous Ludovico, should be attributed to the first inventor of <term>letterpress printing</term> <note>original: "letterale impressione." Marsilio is praising the invention of the printing press, which was still a relatively young technology (about 70 years old) at the time of this publication.</note>: when one openly recognizes such a marvelous discovery to be truly judged as divine rather than human: if we are willing to diligently consider the many exquisite occurrences in such a ministry, and the supreme and redundant utility it brings us. But what work is so excellent, or what invention so awakened, that it is not made lacking and consumed by the swiftest and irreparable time? Or even corrupted and depraved by the malignant and negligent ignorance of those who administer it? For the misery of our age is entirely intent on vile gain: and greedy for a bargain that is not good, neither prizing nor wishing to weigh the immense labors and excessive expenses that are usually necessary in this and other <term>professions</term> <note>original: "exercitij."</note>. And because of this, it is no wonder if we see almost no human art anymore administered truly and with sincere faith. Wherefore with you, most studious zealot of all our perfection, and most ardent cultivator of the illustrious virtues, I charitably grieve; and not without intimate and loving anxiety do I torment and exhaust myself that such a vice and corruption has not only entered into every <term>mechanical trade</term> <note>original: "mecchanico exercitio."</note>, but has also miserably fallen upon literary study and the Latin faculty. Although some, most diligent in every language and today most accurate in printing, have striven with diligent care and consumed labor to obviate and provide for such a calamity, nonetheless the evil is so strengthened and so widespread everywhere that the wound has now become almost incurable. It is rare that any book in any faculty printed from those first times past can be found, whether in Latin or in the <term>vernacular</term> <note>original: "volgare," referring to the Italian language.</note>, that is not diminished, incorrect, and depraved: and quite different from its ancient copy and primary origin, as can easily be seen by daily experience.

I, in my little studying and not too frequent reading, since I began to have some knowledge of letters, have continually experienced this. But much more so now that—constrained not so much by daily living as by the natural instinct of not being born for myself alone in the world—I have condescended to the request and instance of <term>Messer</term> <note>A title of respect.</note> Bernardino Stagnino, who most desires perfection in every such work, to have to correct, as far as my weakest strengths extend and can supply, the books to be printed daily in his workshop. Even though there is little intelligence in me and less sufficiency in such a task, nevertheless, trusting in the overabounding and infinite grace of the Eternal Father, we have assumed such a weight, hoping with whatever charity and diligence of ours to satisfy for the most part that which comes into our hands; for to do so entirely would be almost impossible if one did not intervene with some universal and supreme authority.

Therefore, having already been established in this ministry, the first works that occurred to us were the vernacular things of the most distinguished and your most familiar poet, <term>Messer Francesco Petrarca</term> <note>Petrarch (1304–1374), the famous Italian poet and scholar.</note>, with his commentaries. These were so incorrect that it was difficult to discern whether they should properly be judged as formal work, or fragments, or rather an inextricable confusion; especially the commentaries on the *Triumphs*. To speak of those on the sonnets and songs would be a great folly, even though <term>Filelfo</term> <note>Francesco Filelfo (1398–1481), a famous Renaissance humanist who wrote popular but sometimes criticized commentaries on Petrarch.</note>, a man most erudite in his time, partially commented on them—though I for one do not believe it.

But truly the opposite can be said of the most excellent physician and most completely practiced in every doctrine, <term>Messer Bernardo Illicinio</term> <note>Bernardo Ilicino (c. 1430–1492), a Sienese physician whose commentary on Petrarch's *Triumphs* became the standard Renaissance interpretation.</note> of Siena: who with such faith and integrity, with such erudition and perspicacious intellect, has explained and easily cleared up those same *Triumphs* for us. He has used such quality (not despising others, however) as any other interpreter, whether of the vernacular or of Latin; for running through all this work of his, one will find nothing other than a severe impugning of vices; a glorious exaltation of every virtue; most faithful <term>Greek and Latin history</term> <note>original: "greca & latina historia."</note>; every liberal art; moral and natural philosophy; and finally, all our true and supreme theology with such graceful and flowery speech. I dare to affirm that he has preserved no less doctrine and eloquence in the <term>Tuscan language</term> <note>original: "thoscana lingua," meaning Italian.</note> than <term>Cicero</term> in Latin or <term>Demosthenes</term> in Greek ever professed. And would to God that his primary copy and original <term>archetype</term> <note>The author's original manuscript.</note> could be had, which I would hope to see again in its pristine dignity and perfection.

<meta>This page continues the dedicatory letter from Marsilio Umbro to Ludovico Barbarigo. Having lamented the poor state of current printing, Umbro now describes his editorial process, citing the specific scholars and manuscripts he consulted to restore Petrarch's text to its original quality.</meta>

...not accurately restored. Nevertheless, I have forced myself to compare many <term>Petrarchs</term> <note>Meaning copies or editions of Francesco Petrarca’s works.</note> together, varying in form and printed in various times and places: and from those, I have chosen the oldest and least incorrect. Among the others, I chose one very good one belonging to the Magnificent Messer **Marino Sanuto**, a gentleman of our times (as everyone knows) who is most curious about every <term>ephemeral</term> <note>original: "Ephimerico." Refers to passing events or daily records; Sanuto was famous for his massive diaries recording daily Venetian life.</note> word or memorable deed, and most abundant in almost infinite books. Likewise, I used another from my most affectionate Magnificent Doctor, Messer **Lodovico Venier**, who is no less observant of natural and learned humanity than he is skilled in pontifical and imperial laws. I also used another Petrarch, no worse than the aforementioned, from the Magnificent Messer **Bernardo Grimani**, a marvelous spectacle of virtue in our days: in whom not only does a very learned Latinity redound in his magnificence, but a rare probity and <term>Socratic politeness</term> <note>Refers to a refined, philosophical, and humble way of conducting oneself, modeled after Socrates.</note> shines not a little in such a youthful age.

And so, running through now one and now the other, and matching their readings together, I have labored to restore the much-diminished elegance and almost antiquated gravity of the most worthy interpreter, faithfully reintegrating it in many parts. This was necessary because sometimes we found an entire page left out; and often many verses; almost infinite words removed; and likewise the meanings spoiled and corrupted: the histories cheated; and the cited sentences neither healthy nor original. Whence, afterward, it was necessary in many places to play the part of **Oedipus** <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for solving difficult riddles or deciphering corrupted texts, referring to Oedipus solving the riddle of the Sphinx.</note> and almost entirely flee to the proper source, and redirect and restore those to their good and healthy intellect. I have done this as far as my few books and low intelligence—along with the very short time squeezed out by the printers—have permitted us. For after my priestly and scholastic occupations, I was forced every two days to have the corrected <term>quire</term> <note>original: "quaderno." A gathering of folded sheets of paper for the printing press.</note> ready, which would have required me to attend to no other business.

Whence, if some errors should offend you while reading, Magnificent Messer Ludovico, know that some occurred through the inadvertence of the workers; some also were overlooked by me as they were looming and undiscussed, because I was unable to draw a good meaning from them myself. However, praise God, we have brought this work to such perfection that I hope its understanding will be very easy for everyone, and much clearer and more manifest than any other printed many years ago. 

But because, Magnificent Patron, very often some are found (as **Apuleius** says) so stubborn and of such a pernicious nature that they would rather misinterpret even praiseworthy works and often claim they are blameworthy, than sincerely consider the true intent of the authors or simply seek to understand them. Whence it seemed quite expedient and necessary for me to run and draw near to your excellent and, among all, most gracious magnificence. For I hope that under your favored support and all-encompassing sufficiency, I may be able to safely bring these new labors of mine and <term>wakeful little lucubrations</term> <note>original: "euigilate lucubratiuncule." Scholarly works produced by staying up late at night by lamplight.</note> into the light; and likewise freely flee the biting of the envious and detractors, or at least patiently tolerate it. This will easily happen for me if these works are accepted by you and understood as secured by your healthy and perfect judgment. 

Therefore, let your greatness not disdain to pleasantly accept the first small gift, though very tiny, from me, your most humble servant, as a sign of my most inclined affection toward your most noble nature and lordly customs. I pray always to Divine Clemency that, through its infinite goodness, it may preserve your magnificence in every grace and completely satisfy your best desires, to which I continually recommend myself.

## ¶ A certain memorandum about Laura, written by Francesco Petrarch’s own hand, found in a certain <term>Virgil Codex</term> <note>Petrarch’s personal copy of the works of the Roman poet Virgil, which he used as a diary for his most private thoughts.</note> in the library at Pavia.

**L**aura, illustrious by her own virtues and long celebrated in my poems, first appeared to my eyes during the first period of my youth, in the year of our Lord 1327, on the sixth day of the month of April, in the church of Saint Clare at <term>Avignon</term> <note>A city in France which was the seat of the Papacy at the time, often criticized by Petrarch for its corruption.</note> at the morning hour. And in that same city, in that same month of April, on that same sixth day, at that same first morning hour, in the year 1348, that light was withdrawn from this light <note>A poetic way of saying Laura died.</note> while I happened to be in Verona, alas, unaware of my fate. The unhappy news, however, reached me through a letter from my friend Louis in the same year, on the nineteenth day of May. That most chaste and beautiful body was laid in the place of the <term>Friars Minor</term> <note>The Franciscan Order.</note> on the very evening of the day of her death. I am persuaded that her soul indeed (as <term>Seneca</term> <note>A Roman Stoic philosopher.</note> says of Africanus) has returned to the heaven from whence it came. It seemed right to write this down with a certain bitter sweetness as a sharp memory of this event, in this place especially which often returns before my eyes: so that I may reflect that there should be nothing more in this life to please me. Now that my greatest bond is broken, this frequent looking upon these words and the consideration of this most fleeting age should warn me that it is time to flee from <term>Babylon</term> <note>original: "Babilone." Petrarch frequently used "Babylon" as a metaphor for the worldly vanity and corruption of the papal court at Avignon.</note>. This will be easy, by the preceding grace of God, for one who thinks sharply and manfully of the superfluous cares, vain hopes, and unexpected ends of the past time.

---

## ¶ A fragment of a certain letter by the same Francesco Petrarch to Giacomo Colonna, Bishop of Lombez.

**W**hat then? Do you say that I have invented the beautiful name of "Laura" for myself so that there would be someone for me to speak about, and because of whom many would speak of me? Do you claim that, in truth, there is no "Laura" in my soul except perhaps that <term>poetic laurel</term> <note>The "Laurel" (Laurus) refers to the crown of poets; Colonna was suggesting Laura was a fictional symbol for Petrarch’s literary ambition rather than a real woman.</note> for which my long and tireless study bears witness? And that regarding this living Laura, by whose beauty I seem to be captured, you claim all my sighs are faked and manufactured? In this one thing, I wish you were joking! Would that it were a pretense, and not a madness! But believe me, no one can pretend for long without great effort. To labor to appear insane for no reason is the highest insanity. Furthermore, while we who are healthy can imitate the gestures of illness, we cannot fake true paleness. To you, my paleness and my labor are well known.

# PROLOGUE

## To the most illustrious Duke of Modena, the divine Borso d’Este, here begins the exposition of the *Triumphs* of the most famous poet Francesco Petrarch, by Bernardo Ilicino, student of medicine and philosophy.

**P**UBLIO Cornelius Scipio <note>Scipio Africanus (236–183 BC), the Roman general who defeated Hannibal. He was Petrarch’s ultimate hero of Roman virtue.</note>, the most illustrious leader, defined no victory as greater and no triumph as more singular than conquering oneself in those things desired by the sensual appetite. For this reason—although he was joined in singular friendship to Masinissa, King of the Massylii, due to many exceptional favors received from him—he did not wish to ratify the marriage vow given to Sophonisba <note>A Carthaginian noblewoman. Masinissa fell in love with her, but Scipio insisted she be surrendered as a prisoner of war to Rome, leading her to commit suicide to avoid capture.</note> during the pressure of the siege of Cirta against reason. He judged it more fitting to return Masinissa to himself and to a higher self-knowledge than to condescend to his most ardent amorous desire. 

This was certainly a distinguished deed, most fitting for a Roman man: to refuse to secure his best friend from errors in any way other than he would himself. To wish to achieve such supreme and singular glory, nothing was judged more useful than to openly recognize the necessary transition that every human must make from the first day they are procreated on earth; the weakness of our intellect cannot transcend further in its discourse. Understanding this ancient priority and the wisdom of the Delphic Apollo perfectly—although the first precept and institution is attributed to Thales of Miletus <note>An early Greek philosopher (c. 624–546 BC), often cited as the first to say "Know thyself."</note>—it was expressed as: **Know thyself.** <note>original: "Nosce te ipsum." This Socratic/Delphic maxim is the foundation of the moral philosophy presented here.</note>

This same wisdom, having flowed like a great sea through small streams into the narrow pools of modern intellects from its ancient integrity, the most excellent and famous poet Francesco Petrarch wished to prepare. Under a graceful and wondrous poetic veil, he polished the path for those who, with a sincere soul, wish to enter into an understanding of themselves. And just as it seems a man moves step by step until he reaches his final, unchanging stability, so our poet gracefully introduces six glorious triumphs, designating each as superior to and dominant over the last. In these, the clearest understanding of every state of man is placed and revealed. 

Wishing therefore, according to the excellent golden maxim of <term>Plato</term> <note>The author refers to the idea from Plato's "Republic" or "Laws" that humans are not born for themselves alone, but for their country and friends.</note>, not to have been born for myself alone, but—just as I have received great fruit from the labors of others—to likewise repay those who come after us, I decided, as far as the weakness of my talent extends, to explain the intention of this glorious poet in the aforementioned *Triumphs*. I certainly judge this to be useful: both for the admirable doctrine enclosed within them (which will now be more common) and also because I hope such an example and such a work will perhaps ignite some noble mind. Once I have roughed out the work, a mind of greater height may polish it perfectly with a file and plane. Thus, the excellent, great, and singular dignity of the poet shall receive the most fitting praises, as he most justly deserves.

For this reason, having diligently and with good examination considered to whom I should primarily direct these nightly labors, no one else occurred to me with more reason than your **Most Illustrious Lordship** <note>Referring to Borso d’Este (1413–1471), the first Duke of Ferrara and Modena, known for his patronage of the arts.</note>. This is both because the subject of the work is, in my judgment, an extraordinary matter, and also because, since it treats "Triumphs," no one else can offer a better judgment than one who has always reported a triumph from every one of his works, both internal and external. This, in my opinion, your Lordship has achieved, having always gloriously overcome every operation of Fortune with a strong and unbroken soul. To you, therefore, the triumph is suited; to you alone is reserved the judgment in determining triumphs. 

May your aforementioned Most Illustrious Lordship not disdain the pure faith of your servant. But when some rest interposes itself amidst the great and most urgent cares of your government, may it not displease you to read this work. For although, due to the greatness of your intellect, nothing is said here that is hidden or unknown to you, you will at least find the sincerity of the faith of me, your servant, with a most ardent desire to see and hear that you are always happy in our century and blessed in the future.

<summary>Bernardo Ilicino opens his commentary on Petrarch’s "Triumphs" by dedicating the work to Duke Borso d’Este, framing the poems as a guide to self-knowledge and moral victory. He argues that Petrarch’s six triumphs reflect the human journey from earthly passion to eternal stability.</summary>
<keywords>Bernardo Ilicino, Borso d’Este, Petrarch, Triumphs, Scipio Africanus, Sophonisba, self-knowledge, moral philosophy, Renaissance humanism, Nosce te ipsum</keywords>

--- Page 318 ---
<meta>This page continues the prologue by Bernardo Ilicino. Having introduced the moral example of Scipio Africanus on the previous page, Ilicino now transitions into the formal academic structure of his commentary on Petrarch’s "Triumphs," adhering to the medieval and Renaissance tradition of the "accessus ad auctores" (introduction to the authors).</meta>

It is a universal opinion, approved by the ancient and best expositors, that at the beginning of books several things must be diligently considered; if we wished to report all of them in the present work, we would sooner fall into superfluity and obscurity than achieve clarity for the book. Therefore, out of those many, we shall strive to explain only four for our purpose. The first: what the subject and matter of the book is. The second: its utility. The third: the name of the book and the author. The fourth and last: its division. It seems that **Servius Honoratus** <note>A 4th-century grammarian famous for his commentary on Virgil.</note> teaches us this at the beginning of his work and elucidation of **Virgil**; and the great philosopher **Averroës** <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> in the preface to the *Natural Hearing* <note>The *Physics* of Aristotle.</note>.

Regarding the first, I say the intention and subject is the human soul under the consideration of its transition, variety, respect, and relation to human works and the judgment of those works given by men. For this understanding, it must be considered that our soul has no operation of its own; rather, it communicates each one with the body, and thus they must be attributed only to the "composite man" <term>composite man: the philosophical concept that a human being is a single substance made of both soul and body, rather than just a soul using a body.</term> of soul and body. The Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> writes this opinion in the first and second book *On the Soul*, where he says:

> To say that the soul gets angry is as if one were to say that it weaves or builds. <note>original: "Dicere autem animam irafci fimile eft ac fi aliquis dicat eam texere aut edificare."</note>

From which it follows appropriately that, according to the different bodily disposition, human works are also diversified. Wherefore **Galen**, the illustrious physician, attributes different customs to different complexions in his signs. For this reason, the moral philosophers—and **Aristotle** at the end of the first book of the *Ethics*, and **Cicero** in the first book of *On Duties*—define two principles of operation: namely, the sensitive appetite and the intellect (or rather, reason). According to which one dominates the other, so are the operations suited to men multiplied. These principles are also continually in conflict with each other, as the Apostle clearly describes in **Romans** 7 and **Galatians** 5, where he says:

> I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind... and the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. <note>original: "Video aliā legem ī membris meis repugnantem legi mentis mee & caro concupifcit aduerfus fpūm: spūs aduerfus carnem."</note>

And therefore, just as the bodily parts increase and dissolve through the physical course of life, so too is the soul variously affected to produce different effects. Since life is divided into two general parts—namely, youth and old age—for this reason, youthful operations derive from the first part and elderly operations from the second; of which the first are deservedly attributed by men to appetite, and the second to reason. But when, through the consumption of the bond of the **substantific humor** <note>Also called "radical moisture," a medieval medical concept of the vital fluid that sustains life; its depletion causes aging and death.</note>, our soul can no longer maintain itself in its bodily home, a single operation is attributed to it, which is to divide itself. This division—according to the opinion of **Tullius** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, of **Aristotle** in *On Death and Life*, and of the Christian religion—is nothing other than death.

The philosophical opinions on the process of the soul are in agreement up to this point; but from here onward they disagree greatly. For some, like the **Epicureans**, asserted that the soul is no more, but is totally annihilated. Others said that it remains and, after its departure from the body, immediately flies to heaven, as was the view of **Plato** (although he spoke of this article in various ways, as we shall see in the *Triumphs of Fame*). But **Pythagoras**, submitting it to a more rigorous justice, made it subject to infernal purgation, through which it might pass to the delights of the **Elysian Fields** <note>In Greek mythology, the final resting place of the souls of the heroic and the virtuous.</note> until such time as it wished to return into other bodies, as **Virgil** openly demonstrates in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*. 

From this opinion **Aristotle** and a great part of the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> deviated, positing only one intellect, not according to a place separate from it, but by its incorruptible nature. The **Stoics**, likewise proving that virtue is the highest good, held the soul to be truly immortal, referring all its care and state to divine government. Certainly all the aforementioned opinions erred, but they were excusable errors; for only the knowledge of the truth depends on the First Truth and True Light, the Divine Word illuminating every man who comes to dwell in the world. And therefore, the supreme Divine Majesty, in whom error never falls, determines through the sacrosanct **Catholic faith** that the soul is preserved after its separation. According to the distribution of justice, it is placed in various locations according to different merits until the day of the universal judgment, which the eternal judge **Christ** must perform, as the prophet **David** foretold in Psalm 95, saying:

> He shall judge the world in equity and the people in his truth. <note>original: "Indicabit orbem terre in equitate & populos ī ueritate fua."</note>

And in Psalm 75 he says from
heaven <note>The catchword at the bottom of the page is "calo" (heaven), indicating the start of the next page.</note>

<summary>Bernardo Ilicino outlines the four-part structure of his commentary and argues that the human soul's operations are tied to the body, moving from youthful appetite to elderly reason. He surveys various ancient philosophical views on the soul's immortality before affirming the Catholic doctrine of the Last Judgment.</summary>

<keywords>Aristotle, soul and body, sensitive appetite, reason, death, Epicureans, Plato, Pythagoras, Catholic faith, Last Judgment, Bernardo Ilicino, Petrarch's Triumphs</keywords>
