<meta>continuity: This page continues the introduction to the commentary on Petrarch's "Triumphs" by Bernardo Ilicino. The previous page discussed the soul's nature and the "composite man." Here, the author shifts to the theological certainty of the Last Judgment and introduces the symbolic structure of Petrarch's six poems as an allegory for the human experience and the soul's journey toward eternity.</meta>

From heaven, You made judgment heard: the earth trembled and was still when the Lord arose in judgment to save all the meek of the earth <note>original: "caelo auditum fecisti iudicium: terra tremuit & quieuit cum exurgeret in iudicium Dominus & saluos faceret omnes mansuetos terre" — Psalm 76:8–9.</note>. Isaiah likewise spoke in the fifth chapter, saying: *The Lord of hosts shall be exalted in judgment: and the holy God shall be sanctified in justice.* <note>original: "Exaltabitur Dominus exercituum in iudicio: & deus sanctus sanctificabitur in iustitia" — Isaiah 5:16.</note> Malachi wrote the same in the third chapter when he said: *I will come to you in judgment: and I will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and perjurers;* <note>original: "accedam ad vos in iudicio: & ero testis velox maleficis & adulteris & periuris" — Malachi 3:5.</note> but Solomon certainly expressed it more clearly than any other prophet in the third chapter of Ecclesiastes when he said: *God shall judge the just and the impious: and then shall be the time for every matter;* <note>original: "Iustum, & impium iudicabit deus: & tempus omnis rei tūc erit" — Ecclesiastes 3:17.</note> the same is proven by the text of the Erythraean Sibyl <note>A legendary prophetess of Greek antiquity, often cited by medieval Christians as having predicted the Last Judgment.</note>, Ezekiel in the thirty-fourth chapter, Daniel in the seventh, and the Gospel text of Matthew in the twenty-fifth. To cite these at greater length would be to offer unnecessary testimony for a matter that is not in doubt. At the presence of this Judge, the resumed bodies shall be assigned places suitable for the vital works that preceded them, as the Apocalypse teaches us, saying: *for their works follow them.* <note>original: "opera enim illorum sequuntur illos" — Revelation 14:13.</note> 

However, even though there is a vast difference among the aforementioned opinions—except for the Epicurean view <note>Epicureans generally believed the soul was mortal and died with the body, a view Ilicino rejects here.</note>—they all agree that there must be a great distance and a long space of time from the day the soul is separated until its reunion with the body, whether according to Pythagoras, or Plato, or according to the Faith. Hence, in such a state, it seems two qualities apply to it. One is that praise and fame should be attributed to it for the virtuous works practiced during life while it was with the body. The other is that since every effect and product in the world decays through the length of time, it seems even such praise and fame must eventually be darkened, according to the sentiment of Solomon in the third chapter of Ecclesiastes when he said: *All things have a time, and all things under heaven pass away in their proper spans;* <note>original: "Omnia tempus habent & spatijs suis transeunt vniuersa sub celo" — Ecclesiastes 3:1.</note> the soul also passes from this state—which is a finite measure, since every movement is finite and its time is its measure, as Aristotle demonstrates in the fourth book of the *Physics*—to an everlasting and infinite distance. Once the soul is led there, our intellect can no longer consider its state, for it is not capable of understanding it.

Considering, then, this transition of the soul, our most distinguished poet <note>Petrarch.</note>, with artful grace and a learned poetic veil, established and composed six **Triumphs**. The **first** pertains to the soul which, through the strong inclination of the body, descends to act according to the dominion of the senses; he feigns "Love," by which he means the <term>sensory appetite: the part of the soul driven by physical desires and feelings rather than reason.</term> triumphing over men in the time of youth. In the **second**, he introduces "Reason" triumphing over Love, which he presents under the veil of **Madonna Laura**; this naturally occurs at the time of manhood and old age, when the sensory delights have declined along with the natural heat that was their instrument. In the **third**, he adds "Death" triumphing over Laura—that is, over rational action. In the **fourth** place, "Fame" triumphs over Death, because even though a man can no longer act for himself, he nonetheless compels and moves others by his example to act virtuously; thus he is continually celebrated in praise, and his name becomes clearer. In the **fifth**, "Time" triumphs over Fame, since its length corrupts every mortal thing. Finally, "Eternity" triumphs over Time; as we cannot distinctly comprehend this, yet must follow it after the Universal Judgment as its beginning, the glorious poet demonstrates it to us in the **sixth Triumph**.

---

¶ Having thus explained the universal subject of the book, it is now appropriate to descend to see what utility the present doctrine contributes. If the sentiment of all moralists is true—that virtuous operations, or virtue itself, is the supreme good—and if that which leads by the right path to the possession of such a good is defined as "useful," then certainly nothing can be shown to be more useful to us than the present doctrine. For who will there be who, having recognized the ignobility of human enticements and understood the excellence of acting reasonably, does not submit his unbridled appetite to moderate reason? Who will there be who, having understood the nature of death, does not become brave in undergoing dangers for the defense of justice and the opposition of injury? Who will there be who, through fame acquired...

O healthy and admirable doctrine, therefore, which leads men from the stormy sea of worldly tribulations with perennial fame to the celestial homeland.

---

### Regarding now the third point which I said above should be clarified, namely the name and title of the book: *The Book of Triumphs by Francesco Petrarch begins*; which is in itself easy to understand; for a "triumph" among the Romans was nothing other than a public procession <term>pompa<gloss>a solemn, ceremonial procession</gloss></term> at the entry of those who, after conquering provinces, brought victory back to their homeland. In these processions, the conquered prisoners and the images of the subjected cities preceded the triumphing leaders and the soldiers crowned with laurel; it is in the likeness of these that our excellent poet has ordered his moral triumphs.

### This Francesco Petrarch was, therefore, Florentine by origin, although born in Arezzo in the year of our era 1304, on the first day of August. His father resided in that city at that time, having been sent into exile by his Republic. Thereafter, before a year had passed, having been recalled together with his mother by a special grace to a villa of hers called Lancisa, situated above Florence, he completed his childhood. And having reached the eighth year of his age—knowing his family to be of honest and ancient stock, though not of very high or honored station—he could not bear to see his father exiled in such a manner. He therefore persuaded his father that they should depart from Italy; and thus, after wandering for eight years in Pisa, the father, at the persuasion of his son, moved to Transalpine Gaul <note>The region of France across the Alps from Italy.</note> to the city of Avignon on the Rhône. At that time, the Roman Court <note>The Papal Court, which resided in Avignon during the "Babylonian Captivity" (1309–1376).</note> resided there, and he remained for some time in that city and in Carpentras, a city near Avignon, where he learned Grammar, Dialectics, and Rhetoric. 

He kemudian went to Montpellier to apply himself to Civil Law <note>The study of Roman and secular legal systems.</note>, where he studied for four years, and in that place, hearing the fame of the schools of Bologna, he went to Bologna, where for three more years he toiled at said studies. During this time, returning to Avignon to visit his dearest parents whom he loved exceedingly, it happened that one day on Good Friday—which that year was the sixth of April—going according to custom out of devotion to the churches, he met in the church of Saint Clare a young girl born in a village very close to the city called Graveson. Though of honest parents, she was named Lauretta, a name much used and given in those parts. He immediately fell in love with her, and loved her for twenty-one years during her life and ten years after her death; she was called first Lauretta and then Laura by him for the sake of better resonance; and he himself, through his celebrated works, remained famous among mortals. 

Having therefore loved her for about a year, and being already thirty-three years of age <note>The text reads "xxxiii" (33), though historical records usually place Petrarch's age around 22 at his mother's death and 24 at his father's.</note>, his father and mother died. Knowing the malice of men to be so great that the sacred and venerable authority of the laws was corrupted—and being unable to patiently tolerate what was not just, nor being able to provide a remedy by himself—for both these reasons he withdrew from his legal studies, giving himself over to the care of poetry. Returning to Arezzo, where his sublime virtues began to be recognized, his acquaintance and friendship were desired by many most excellent men, among whom was Master Giacomo Colonna, a Roman citizen of great reputation and Bishop of Lombez <note>original: "Vescouo Bomborienses o vero Bōbergiense"</note>, with whom he saw Gascony and parts of France with the greatest delight.

Not less <margin>Not less</margin>

Master Giovanni, Cardinal Colonna, was certainly no less dear to him than to his own brother <note>Petrarch's brother, Gherardo, also served the Colonna family.</note>: with whom he lived happily for many years, being much loved and esteemed by him. During this time, seized by a praiseworthy desire to see all of France, he departed for Germany <note>original: "la Magna"</note> and put his plan into effect. Having completed this pilgrimage and returning to Italy, he arrived in Rome and Naples to visit Robert, who at that time was King of Naples. While in Rome, he was graciously received by Stefano Colonna, father of the aforementioned Master Giacomo and Master Giovanni, and he stayed with him for a long time. 

Later, returning again to Avignon and being displeased by the customs of the Roman court—which was located there in those times—he withdrew to live in a solitary valley named Vaucluse <term>Clusa<gloss>From the Latin "Vallis Clausa," meaning "Closed Valley"</gloss></term>, where there was a most pleasant spring called the Sorgue. In that place, he wrote the greater part of his works, both in the vernacular and in Latin. Most notably, he wrote the *Africa* <note>An epic poem in Latin about the Second Punic War.</note>, which was widely circulated and highly praised by the learned. For this reason, he was invited during those times by King Robert in Naples, by the University of Paris, and by the Senate in Rome to be crowned with the laurel. Being requested by all and greatly desiring it himself, he finally, by the advice and persuasion of Cardinal Giovanni Colonna, was crowned with the laurel in Rome; an event which caused him much more envy than glory. 

While Master Francesco was living in Italy during these times, he stayed sometimes in Parma with the Lords of Correggio and sometimes in Verona, so that he was very well known and most dear to all the lords of Italy—especially to the illustrious and exalted Galeazzo Visconti, then Count of Pavia and Lord of Milan, and also to the powerful and magnanimous Lord Jacopo di Carrara. Jacopo, understanding that Master Francesco delighted in a clerical and religious life, gave him a canonry in Padua so that he might keep him nearby. After holding this for two years, and after the death of the said Lord Jacopo, Petrarch returned again to France. 

Finally, as he was now approaching old age and almost reproaching himself for having moved between so many different places, he decided to settle in his final home. Thus, having returned to Italy in the territory of Padua with a most dear friend named Lombardo, he built a comfortable dwelling in a place called Arquà <note>Now known as Arquà Petrarca.</note>. In that place, continually applying himself to his studies, he composed many works, among which were the excellent *Triumphs*. Being already seventy years of age, on the 28th of August, 1374, he was seized by a paroxysm of epilepsy <term>morbo comitiale<gloss>Historically called the "comitial disease" because it was considered an omen that could suspend the "comitia," or public assemblies, in Ancient Rome</gloss></term>, by which he had been much vexed in preceding times. As his declining strength could no longer overcome the illness, he was forced to succumb; and so that worthy and generous soul departed from the world. I do not doubt that, through his greatest nobility and singular virtue, he receives a reward in the celestial homeland from the Just Judge, who just as He never leaves any fault unpunished, likewise never permits any good deed to go unrewarded.

---

### The Division of the Book

Having now completed the three parts of our introduction, it remains to descend to the fourth and last part, which is the general division of the book. This present work is divided principally into six parts, just as it was shown before that there are six variations which our soul generally undergoes according to worldly understanding. 

In the first of these, Master Francesco determines the dominion of the sensitive appetite <note>The realm of physical desire and emotion.</note>, which, according to poetic fantasy, he personifies in the figure of Cupid. In the second, he treats the sovereignty of Reason, which he portrays through the person of Madonna Laura. In the third part, he describes Death, the third variation attributed to the soul. In the fourth, he adds Fame, which is attributed to the soul by men after death. In the fifth, he shows how the length of Time obscures the aforesaid fame. In the sixth and last, he demonstrates that Eternity follows the universal divine judgment. 

The first part begins: *In the time that renews my sighs.* 
The second part begins with that chapter: *When at one place and at one time here.* 
The third in that chapter: *How many already in mature and bitter age.* 
The fourth in that chapter: *In the heart full of most bitter sweetness.* 
The fifth in that chapter: *From the golden dwelling with the dawn before.* 
The sixth and last in that chapter: *After I saw no thing under the sky.* 

It remains, therefore, that through these preludes of ours, matters have been shown quite clearly...

## CHAPTER ONE

**M**aster Francesco <note>The author, Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), one of the most influential poets of the Italian Renaissance.</note> describes the lord of the senses, feigning that Cupid triumphs over mankind in this manner: that is, by considering how the ancient Romans, whenever they triumphed, were placed upon chariots and led to the temples of the gods, where they consecrated their spoils. Thus, he feigns that Love is first carried upon a chariot, triumphing through the world, and finally led to the temple of the mother goddess Venus: a place truly suited for such a triumph. Secondly, just as the one who triumphed proceeded adorned in various robes, so Master Francesco attributes to Love the specific qualities that befit him. In the third and final part, just as the triumphing general led untamed prisoners bound before him, so Master Francesco describes those men who were bound and conquered by love following his triumph as subjects; just as conquered and subjugated kings and leaders preceded the triumpher, and the low-born prisoners followed him. Thus Master Francesco describes Jove <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods in Roman mythology.</note> before the chariot as the most exalted god celebrated by the ignorant people of antiquity, and all the others following after the triumph. The poet divides this entire subject into four equal chapters, which we will explain particularly in their proper places according to their specific details. As for the first chapter, in it Master Francesco primarily describes the time, specifically the hour in which he feigns to have seen these visions, pretending to sleep and expressing the qualities which are all provocative of sleep. He says, therefore, that at the time when his amorous sighs were renewed by the sweet memory of the first day he fell in love—which was the beginning of his labors of love—the sun was already warming both horns of the Bull: that is, it was the month of April or March, where the sun had already passed the first half of the degrees of the sign of Taurus and had entered the second, which is what he means by "one and the other horn." And he adds, not without great and natural reason, that the particular hour of his sleep was the dawn, saying that the maiden of Tithonus <note>Aurora, the goddess of the dawn, who in myth was the wife of Tithonus.</note> at that hour proceeded chilled to her accustomed stay, with her routine unchanged. Whence he says:

<margin>FOR a clearer understanding of the two preceding tercets <note>A tercet is a poetic unit of three lines.</note>, it is necessary to understand according to the rules of philosophy and astrology: that the eighth celestial sphere being divided into five zones, the middle one, through which the sun passes, is named the Torrid Zone. Its entire circumference is divided into twelve equal parts, where each, being adorned with notable stars, receives a different name for itself. Wherefore the first is called: Aries [The Ram]; the second Taurus [The Bull]; the third Gemini [The Twins]; the fourth Cancer [The Crab]; the fifth Leo [The Lion]; the sixth Virgo [The Virgin]; the seventh Libra [The Scales]; the eighth Scorpio [The Scorpion]; the ninth Sagittarius [The Archer]; the tenth Capricornus [The Goat]; the eleventh Aquarius [The Water-Bearer]; the twelfth and last Pisces [The Fish]. Thereafter, each of the aforementioned twelve parts of the sky is divided into thirty distinct parts, each of which is called a degree. And every degree is then divided into sixty parts called minutes, and every minute into sixty other parts called seconds; which division of minutes and seconds is also attributed to the hours. And imagining these twelve parts to be situated in an oblique circle called the Zodiac, in such a way that imagining in that zone three parallel circles: one is in the middle called the Equinoctial; the other toward the Antarctic pole called the Winter Solstice; and the other toward the Arctic called the Summer Solstice. The sun is found under each of these at different times of the year. Wherefore in March or September it is found under the equinoctial line, as we shall say in the third chapter of this triumph; and in the month of June it is found under the circle of the Summer Solstice; and in the month of December it is found under the circle of the Winter Solstice. The sun, running in its own sphere directly under the twelve parts, returns to the same point in the time of one year.</margin>

### THE TRIUMPH OF CUPID

the [twelfth] point from which it began to move. In this path, it is said to have traversed all twelve signs. Thus, the sun enters the first degree of Aries and its first minute on the eleventh or twelfth day of March, according to the proportion of hours that exceed the perfect 365 days of the year. It stays for approximately 24 hours and one-third per degree. From this, it appears manifest that whenever the sun is in the sign of Taurus, it falls in the month of April or May. Secondly, **Master Francesco** writes that the particular hour of his dream was the dawn, saying that "the frozen girl of Tithonus was running to her usual dwelling." <note>original: "la fanciulla di Titõe gelata." Petrarch uses this mythological metaphor to describe the cold early morning light.</note> Here it is to be understood that it pleased the poets for Aurora <note>The goddess of the Dawn.</note> to be the daughter of Titan and the Earth. Indeed, the dawn is nothing other than a brightness and splendor preceding the face of the sun; and because the sun is the son of Hyperion, son of Titan, son of Heaven, son of Ether, son of Erebus, son of Demogorgon, he is often named after his grandfather by the ancients; therefore, Aurora is said to be the daughter of Titan. But she is called the daughter of the Earth because, our sight being drawn to the origin of whatever thing rises in that part of the sky, it also seems to rise from the earth. The "girl of Tithonus" is the name the poet gives to Aurora in this place because Tithonus, brother of Laomedon, King of Troy (according to what Ovid writes in the 13th book of the *Metamorphoses* <note>The text cites book XII, but the story of Memnon and Tithonus is found in book XIII.</note>), though some others say he was his son, was loved and snatched away by Aurora. He, asking for long life from Aurora, obtained it—so much so that after the death of his son Memnon, he was turned into a grasshopper. Because of his great old age and the immutable age of Aurora (who is described by poets as a young girl), **Master Francesco** rightly calls her the "girl of Tithonus." He consequently describes the hour of dawn as being "frozen and cold" for two reasons: first, because of the coldness of the night which has continued until that hour; second, because as the heat of the sun's rays approaches, the coldness is pushed back by the arrival of its opposite, a process called by philosophers <term>antiparistasis</term> <note>A philosophical concept where a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as cold air feeling sharper just as the sun begins to warm the earth.</note>. Thus, gathered into itself, the cold becomes more intense. I said from the beginning that it was not without reason that **Master Francesco** chose the hour of dawn and no other for his dream, as he wishes to demonstrate that his vision is true. According to the opinion of the singular philosopher Albertus Magnus in his book *On Sleep and Waking* <note>original: "de somno & vigilia."</note>: just as the radial light of the stars communicated to the material elements produces a quality for which the elemental virtues become instruments and ministers, so the celestial and abstract intelligences of the angels influence our souls with their intrinsic virtues. Using these within us with their own effect as instruments—sometimes through phantasms and images, sometimes in the manner of a teaching doctor, and sometimes by their own essence—they demonstrate to us things that are true: whether present, past, or future. And because for such a vision it is necessary for the organs and instruments of the internal senses to be purged of superfluous vapors, and since this cannot happen unless digestion is complete (because fumes continually ascend from the stomach to the brain), it is necessary—if one is to see true things or foresee them in sleep—that it be the morning hour, in which the fumes elevated from food are totally dissolved. For this reason, Macrobius, in the *Dream of Scipio* <note>original: "de sõnipionis" referring to the "Somnium Scipionis."</note>, established that there are five species of dreams: the first is called the *phantasm* <note>An apparition or "nightmare" occurring between waking and sleep.</note>; the second is the *insomnium* <note>A dream caused by physical or mental distress, having no prophetic value.</note>; the third is the *somnium* <note>An enigmatic dream that requires interpretation.</note>; the fourth is the *visio* <note>A prophetic vision of an event that later comes true.</note>; and the fifth and last is the *oraculum* <note>An oracle, where a parent or authority figure appears to give advice.</note>. Thus, it remains a clear enough argument by which Master Francesco can show his vision to be true, being made in the hour of dawn, in which true and certain visions are demonstrated to mortals. Having thus described the time and the hour in the preceding verses in which he saw these visions, Master Francesco then adds how he was sleeping, expressing the causes by which he was occupied by sleep: saying that passion and indignations, amorous laments, and likewise the season and the time had led him to sleep, in which state the weary heart rests and relaxes its every bundle of thoughts and deeds. And he adds that in such a sleep he saw a very great light upon the grass: that is, because in the time of spring the surface of the earth is all filled with green, although it can also be adapted to mean that by "the grass" he intends the place where he had laid himself down to sleep. In that light was very heavy and bitter pain with little solace and pleasure, and that which was there was slippery and with very heavy consequence. Wherefore he says:

<margin>C. For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, one must know that sleep is defined as nothing other than a binding of the primary senses.</margin>

-> Had led me back to the enclosed place; <-

> There among the grass, already faint from weeping,
> Overcome by sleep I saw a great light,
> And within much sorrow with brief joy,

<margin>First, regarding the withdrawal of the vital spirits back to their own source. Therefore, the primary sensory power is an internal faculty called "common sense": because it commonly renders judgment on all particular sensations. This faculty is situated according to—</margin>

—the philosophers and physicians in the first ventricle of the brain. From there, a path exists through which the motive and sensory spirits <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids that carried signals through the nerves.</note> generated in the brain spread through the body, giving the limbs the functions of feeling and moving. When this path is blocked, it induces sleep. This power is said to be "blocked" when it is filled by smoky evaporations or cerebral moisture, which happens either when there is a superfluity of food, or when physical or mental exercise reigns in our body. Internal moisture also descends to this place when moisture is increased in our limbs by an external cause, or when the retentive power of the brain is weakened by external or internal causes. From this, it appears clearly that **Master Francesco** was compelled to sleep at that time: first, because of the season and the hour in which moisture is most increased in our bodies, making a person more inclined to sleep; for as **Virgil** writes in the second book of the *Aeneid*: "The falling stars invite sleep." <note>original: "Suadentque cadentia sydera somnos."</note> Likewise, since the distress of love, indignation, and anger are each causes that dissolve and ignite the vital spirits, the governing power of our bodies is necessitated to produce sleep for the restoration and refreshment of those same spirits.

¶ Secondly, **Master Francesco** said: *That the weary heart puts down its every burden.* This is to follow the distinct and separate operations according to three locations: the rational and intellectual in the brain; the concupiscible <note>The "concupiscible" faculty relates to desires and emotions like love or longing.</note> in the heart; and the natural in the liver. Just as they were divided by location, so he attributed different operations to them. Therefore, by giving every concupiscible appetite to the heart, and as that appetite settles in sleep, the heart "puts down" every burden of its thoughts into that enclosed place of operations.

<margin>D</margin>

Lastly, **Master Francesco** adds that he saw a "great light." Because light is the object of the power of sight, nothing is visible by itself unless it is truly light, or <gloss>or of</gloss> a participant in light. Since the sensory appetite is clearly visible through its operations, and especially through carnal desire, **Master Francesco**, wishing to describe these things appropriately, says he saw a "very great light." Afterward, **Master Francesco** adds what he saw inside this light: saying he saw a leader, most powerful and victorious, triumphing in the likeness of those for whom triumphal chariots were established for their glory and honor by the ancient Romans; those who acted with virtue were conducted to the Capitol, the head and fortress of the Roman Republic. Thus he says:

> I saw a victorious and supreme leader,
> Just like one of those who to the triumphal
> Capitol lead a chariot with great glory.

<margin>¶ Among the other orders of triumph described in the histories of the Latin language that are found as evidence for the preceding verses, let it suffice to mention the one observed in the triumph of Scipio Aemilianus after having—</margin>
<margin>Oy sa m</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
<margin>B</margin>

—destroyed Carthage, as written by **Appian of Alexandria** in the *Third Punic War* <note>Appian's *Punica*, specifically describing the triumph of Scipio Aemilianus in 146 BCE.</note> in this form: <note>The following is a translation of the Latin passage quoting Appian.</note> Wreathed with garlands, all with trumpets playing before them, they led chariots filled with spoils; wooden towers were carried, presenting models of the captured cities; then came inscriptions and images of the things they had achieved. Then gold and silver, partly in raw masses, partly marked or stamped with figures of this kind. Furthermore, there were crowns which cities, or allies, or the army had given to the soldiers as a reward for virtue. White oxen and elephants followed them. After these came the leaders of the Carthaginians or Numidians captured in the war. Lictors <note>Officers attending Roman magistrates.</note> preceded the general, dressed in purple robes, with a crowd of lyre players and trumpeters in the Etruscan style of procession; these, girded and wreathed with golden crowns, went forward singing and playing in their order. They call these "Lydians," and I can easily believe that the Etruscans took their origin from the Lydians. In the middle of them, someone dressed in a robe reaching the ankles, shining with gold fringes and bracelets, performed various gestures; by mocking the conquered enemies, he provoked laughter on all sides. After a great quantity of incense and perfumes, the general followed, surrounded [by his men], who was in a gilded chariot...

# THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

...and shining with many-colored marks, white horses carried him, wearing on his head a golden crown adorned with stones and gems. Here, wearing a purple garment tucked up according to ancestral custom, interwoven with golden stars, in one hand he bore an ivory scepter, and in the other a laurel, which the Romans would carry as a sign of victory. With him were boys and girls, and nearby on either side his young kinsmen; finally followed the writers, attendants, and shield-bearers who had accompanied the army. Lastly, the army followed the chariot, divided into troops and ranks. The soldiers, wreathed in laurel and carrying laurel in their hands, had badges of merit attached to them; according to their conduct, some wore laurels, others were attacked with wit <note>original: "salibus", referring to biting or "salty" humor used to mock those who failed to live up to military standards</note>, and some were marked with infamy. With a similarity little different from this, **Master Francesco** <note>Petrarch</note> affirms he saw the love of men triumphing in this manner, truly a most powerful and victorious leader. This is because, according to the opinion of the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the fourth book of the *Ethics*, it is more difficult to resist pleasure than the first natural movements, even though those are not in our power. Whence he says: *For it is more difficult to resist pleasure than anger*, as **Heraclitus** says <note>original: "Difficilius enim est resistere voluptati quam irae vt heraclitus inqt"</note>. By this opinion, it is clearly understood how great the force of this strong and furious affection is. The poet continues then by expressing the operation that he seemed to perform upon seeing this most just prince: he speaks by accusing the laziness of the age in which he lived, saying that since men in his time were already so depraved—not just because they did not act in such a way that they might justly come to triumph with honor, but because their souls were entirely empty of valor and virtue and full of pride and arrogance—and such a triumph was not customary to be seen, yet ardently desiring to learn new things, it seemed to him that he diligently raised his eyes, tired by amorous weeping and heavy with sleep, to look at and understand this new and wonderful spectacle, to clearly and aptly know who the triumpher was and over whom he triumphed, having no other delight or pleasure than to feed his intellect always with new knowledge. Whence he says:

<margin>Heraclitus mentioned in his [treatise] on peace...</margin> <note>The marginal note is abbreviated and likely refers to Heraclitus’s views on the strife and harmony of opposites.</note>

F

¶ It seems perhaps to some that—since men always have free choice <note>term: "arbitrio libero" - Free Will. The commentator is addressing the tension between human choice and the "power" of Love or the stars.</note> in their actions, as this same **Master Francesco** affirms in that moral song, *Thinking of you* <note>original: "Tuo pensando", referencing Petrarch's Canzone 264</note>, when he says while the body is alive: *You had the bridle in the power of your thoughts* <note>original: "Hauiui el freno in bailia di pensieri tuoi"</note>; and it being also a universal conclusion of the theologians in the second book of the *Sentences* <note>The standard medieval theological textbook by Peter Lombard.</note> and of the Peripatetics <note>term: Peripatetics - the followers of Aristotle, so named because they walked while teaching.</note> in the second book of the *Physics* and in the *Ethics* of **Aristotle**—the ages are unjustly reproached by him in this place. Rather, only the men produced in those ages should be blamed by the poet. To them, it is answered that it is a true thing that our soul is superior to every bodily inclination; whence even **Ptolemy** affirms in the *Tetrabiblos* <note>original: "quadripartito", the primary ancient text on astrology.</note>:

->I, who am not accustomed to such a sight<-
->Because of the tedious age in which I find myself,<-
->Empty of every valor, full of every pride:<-
->The haughty habit, unaccustomed and new,<-
->I gazed upon, raising my eyes heavy and tired,<-
->For I experience no other delight than learning.<-

*Because the wise man shall rule the stars* <note>original: "Quia sapiens dñabitur astris"</note>. Nonetheless, man being always inclined toward the flesh and bodily delight because of the contagion of original sin—as is written in the second book of the *Sentences* at the 30th distinction—and the intellect often being taken captive by the forces of the senses through the strongest bodily inclination; and there being also the dominion of the celestial bodies over inferior ones, whose proper complexion is conformed to that of the stars, where the philosopher says in the prologue of the *Meteorology*: *This inferior world is of necessity continuous with the superior motions, so that all its power is governed from there.* <note>original: "Est autem ex necessitate continuus iste mundus inferior superioribus lationibus: vt omnis virtus ip sius inde gubernetur."</note> Therefore, the ages can justly be blamed in which unhappy, depressed, and ignoble constellations reign, just as they did in the time of **Master Francesco** compared to those that ruled in the time of the glorious **Romans**. 

Petrarch then adds the appearance and properties of the triumpher, saying that he is a naked boy placed upon a chariot of fire, fierce and cruel in sight, armed only with a bow and a quiver placed at his side full of arrows, against which no helmet or shield is of any use. Upon his shoulders extend two large wings, varied and distinct in a great number of different colors. He then leads an innumerable prey of prisoners, divided into three different conditions and effects: because some were only captured in battle, some others wounded by the sharpest darts, and some others totally killed. And thus this most ferocious leader was guided by four snow-white horses which, pulling, preceded the chariot. Whence he says:

->CHAPTER THREE<-

# CHAPTER THREE

**I** saw four steeds whiter than snow;
Upon a chariot of fire, a cruel youth
With bow in hand and arrows at his sides;
**A**gainst which neither helmet nor shield avails:
Upon his shoulders he had only two great wings
Of a thousand colors, and all else was naked:
**A**round him were innumerable mortals,
Some taken in battle, and some slain,
Others wounded by stinging shafts.

A great and excellent concept our famous and admired poet <note>Petrarch</note> has enclosed under the veil of the preceding verses, the clear meaning of which must be understood: that whenever the <term>sensory appetite</term> <note>the part of the soul driven by feelings and desires rather than logic</note> through figurative "love" holds dominion over a man instead of reason, the human property of discursive reason is lost, and the man is made common with the beasts. This can be understood from **Aristotle** in the discourse of the seventh book of the *Ethics*, the first of the *Politics*, and the prologue of the *Metaphysics*. From these sources, it is seen 

<margin>G</margin> how just as those animals, through their instincts, cannot hide their actions, so too a man stripped of his mind—his concepts and appetites—makes them manifest to anyone who looks at him. And thus "naked," he sits upon the fire of carnal <term>concupiscence</term> <note>intense sexual desire or lust</note> and immortal passions, and the unbridled desire for the beloved object. He has no armor of reason to defend himself, but only arrows from himself and a bow, whose force is not limited by any distance. Instead, it reaches and arrives at any place and any object where there is something that provides delight to the lascivious senses. He also wears the wings of swift instability, varied in as many colors as there can be causes for carnal delights.

<margin>H</margin> This appetite is then guided by four very white steeds—and certainly for good reason. For the natural law of the principles of our works is perverted; that is, the <term>intellectual</term> and the <term>sensory</term>. Those things which the intellect commands, the sensory should obey. Where these were once firmly established by the four primary virtues called "cardinal," they are now oppressed by the four contrary vices. These operative principles of ours are the two main parts of the soul: the intellect (divided into intellect and will) and the sensory (divided into the <term>concupiscible</term> <note>the faculty of desiring good</note> and the <term>irascible</term> <note>the faculty of resisting obstacles</note>). Of these divided members, the first is established through **Prudence**, the second through **Justice**, the third through **Temperance**, and the fourth through **Fortitude**. And so, conversely, when appetite demands it, it leads man in his actions into: imprudence, injustice, intemperance, and audacity <note>recklessness</note>. Therefore, the poets have appropriately described such men as being turned into stones or into ugly animals. These four vices are thus the four horses of the chariot of Love, which are reasonably portrayed as very white. For just as whiteness is a color that scatters <note>original: "disgregatiuo", referring to how intense white light can overwhelm or blind the eyes</note> the sight of man, so too these four vices scatter and corrupt the human mind. 

Next, our poet attributes, not without moral sentiment, three distinct generations of prisoners: those only wounded in battle, those captured, and those killed. To understand this, it is necessary to know that mortals desire sensory delights or objects in three ways. The first is through the "first movements" which arise naturally; by consenting to these, one takes sensory pleasure. One does not remain in them, however, but men pull back from them, constrained by reasonable discourse. These are the ones who are properly "wounded" by love, whose wound is healed by the true knowledge of oneself. The second group consists of those who, through powerful and immense concupiscence—even though they clearly recognize they are in error—cannot nonetheless reject the object of delight and lasciviousness. These are called "incontinent" by the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the seventh book of the *Ethics*; because, though they know the desired object should be fled from, they are nonetheless forced by great concupiscence to follow it. Thus, not persisting in reason, they are "captured in battle" by the superior appetite represented as Love. The third and final way is of those whose reason is entirely exterminated and obscured, and who are overcome without any consideration of even the smallest pleasure. These Aristotle calls "intemperate," truly "slain" by the arrows of love. Of such a person, who would not rightly judge him dead? He has fallen into a more miserable state than death. The proof of this is known through a far less unhappy disposition of man. Aristotle says in the third book of the *Ethics*: "Death is more choice-worthy than a safety found in flight" <note>original: "Eligibilior enim est mors salute fuge"</note>. And **Quintus Curtius**, introducing **Alexander**, says: "It is better to die than to be a commander by another's leave" <note>original: "Mori prestat quam precario imperatorem esse"</note>. Persuaded by this truth, how many glorious Romans, ancient foreigners, and ancient women...

It classifies the victims of love into three categories—wounded, captured, and slain—based on Aristotelian definitions of self-control and moral failure.</summary>

<header>CHAPTER ONE</header>

# CHAPTER ONE

*Toward whom my wit and strength availed little or avail now: asking for pardon*
*And the two <note>Likely referring to Love and the beloved, or Love and the poet's own desire</note> transformed me into what I am,*
*Making me from a living man into a green laurel,*
*Which loses no leaf through the cold season.*

This you shall know: no longer through the report of others. It was, then, in this time that **Master Francis** <note>Petrarch</note> was nearby: for being one of those who are "ahead of their time"—that is, before Love comes of its own accord—they lead themselves into a state much worse than death. **Master Francis** also says this state is a "fasting of tears" <note>Italian: *digiuno di lachryme*</note> to demonstrate the immense passion and most heavy torment of lustful men. Because their appetite is disordered, and they intensely desire the objects they love, they weep whenever they cannot possess them. And then, even when they do possess them, they are not free of tears because of the fear of losing them, seeing and understanding that they cannot possess them with justice. 

Wherefore **Cicero** <note>Roman statesman and philosopher, 106–43 BCE</note> rightly says these words in the *Paradoxes* <note>The *Paradoxa Stoicorum*</note>, wishing to express such an effect universally: **"By Hercules, I have never considered the money of those people, nor their magnificent houses, nor their power, nor their commands, nor those pleasures to which they are most closely bound, to be among good things to be sought. For I saw that men overflowing with these things still especially desired those very things in which they abounded. Indeed, the thirst of greed is never filled nor satisfied; and not only are they tormented by the lust for increasing what they have, but also by the fear of losing it."** <note>Original Latin: "Nunquam Hercule pecunias istorum... sed etiam amittendi metu."</note> For this reason, love is rightly always "fasting of tears" and empty: since it is never satisfied, but always shows itself to be more famished.

<margin>M</margin>
**Master Francis** now brings forward, to begin the recitation of examples of men conquered and overcome by carnal appetite, a shadow <note>a spirit or ghost</note> unknown to his sight. He introduces this shadow calling him by name and showing him the amorous martyrs of those who were acquired only through love. The poet feigns to respond with wonder, asking by what cause it happened that he was known by that shadow, and yet he did not recognize the shadow in return. To this question, the shadow replies that this happens for the reason expressed above: namely, because of the great bonds and the darkened, misty air in which the lewdness of men lives. But he affirms that in life he had been his friend and was born with him in a Tuscan land. By these words, the poet affirms he recognized his friend; and to speak with him, he says they both sat down in a temperate and pleasant place, prepared to understand one another. Whence he says:

<margin>M</margin>
<margin>**Master Francis** preserves in these verses the style and custom used whenever poets wish to recite a history, or something resembling a history: they introduce a third person, whom they make direct the words of the one whose history they wish to recite. Just as **Homer** introduces **Ulysses**, at the end of his wandering, reaching Phoenicia and King **Alcinous** of that province, making him tell all his maritime errors. Similarly, **Virgil** introduces **Dido** at the end of **Aeneas's** voyage, making Aeneas recount the whole history and destruction of **Troy**. Thus, at present, our poet introduces a shadow.</margin>

A shade somewhat less sad than the others
  Came toward me; and called me by name,
  Saying, "This is what one acquires through loving."
Whereupon I, wondering, said, "Now how
  Do you know me, when I do not recognize you?"
  And he: "This happens to me through the bitter burdens
Of the bonds I carry; and the dark air
  Contends against your eyes: but a true friend
  I am to you; and with you I was born in Tuscan land."
His words, and the old way of speaking,
  Discovered what his face had hidden from me:
  And so we sat ourselves in that open place.

This was done to have cause to speak with him and have him recite a portion of the men conquered and subjugated by amorous appetite. But who this shadow might be, the poet does not describe, nor is it necessary for the understanding of the book; however, some wish to say it was **Master Angelo di Bostozzi da Retio** <note>Angelo di Costanzo or a similar contemporary scholar</note>, a most learned man and much respected in the Roman court.

TRIVMPHVS AMORIS

### THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

Then afterwards, and not without reason, **Master Francis** <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch, the author</note> describes the air as being dark where Love triumphs, lacking moral clarity and individual feeling. For no darkness or blindness is greater than that of the intellect. Therefore, wishing to lead the people to true intellectual recognition, the Savior says in **Saint John, chapter 12**: "Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you: for he who walks in darkness does not know where he goes" <note>Original Latin: *ambulate dū lucē habetis ne tenebre vos comprehendant: nam qui ambulat in tenebris nescit quo uadat*</note>. To this same opinion, the consideration of moral philosophers also conforms; because light is a quality fixed in celestial bodies, whenever they are removed from any work, it is necessary that such an effect be seized by shadows. And therefore, man is naturally produced for the contemplation of celestial things, as described in the first distinction of the second book of the *Sentences* <note>A reference to Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*, a standard medieval theology textbook</note>; and **Ovid in the first book of the *Metamorphoses*** confirms this same thing in these verses, saying: "While other animals look down toward the earth, he gave to man an uplifted face and ordered him to gaze at the sky and raise his upright countenance to the stars" <note>Original Latin: *Pronaque cū spectent aīalia cetera terrā. Os hoī sublime dedit: caelūq uidere iussit: & erectos ad sydera tollere vultꝰ*</note>. **Dante Alighieri** also attests to this same thing gracefully in the 14th <note>The text says 18th, but the quote is from Purgatorio 14</note> Canto of the *Purgatorio*, saying: "The heavens call you and circle around you, showing you their eternal beauties, and yet your eye gazes only at the earth; wherefore He who discerns all things strikes you." <note>Original Italian: *Chiamaui il ciel: & intorno vi si gira mōstradoui le sue bellezze eterne ma lochio vostro pur a terra mira. Vnde ui batte chi tutto discerne*</note>. For this reason, then, the appetite governs and preserves the reason so that it no longer considers the things of heaven, but remains on earth and operates on earth in dense shadows and most horrendous darkness; which worthy opinion **Master Francis** himself approves in that sonnet, *Gluttony, sleep, and cushiony idleness*, when he says: **AND THEY** have extinguished every kind light of heaven, through which human life is shaped. F."; referring to the author, Francesco Petrarch</note> saying that within a short space of time, he would understand it for himself through the operation or arrangement of the "knot" <note>A metaphor for the binding power of romantic obsession</note> which was being prepared, and to which he was to be tightly bound. This knot was of such a nature that his hair would change color <note>i.e., he would grow old</note> before such a knot could ever be loosened from his free neck and from his feet, which until then had been rebellious toward the processes of love. <margin>As we said above, it is not without great and artful judgment that our poet describes himself at the aforementioned time as not recognizing this triumphant figure nor his company. This is because, as **Livy** writes in the *History of the Second Punic War*: "Human natures are such as to lighten the guilt of each person" <note>original: "Ingenia humana sunt ad cuique leuandā culpam"</note>. For this reason, whenever a man is ensnared in some indecency, he attends to the errors of other men with much greater diligence; he estimates, by comparing himself to those who are more vicious than he, that he can not only excuse himself but even praise himself. This follows the sentiment of the most holy **Jerome**, who speaks on this subject in this manner: "It is a cheap enough good for those seeking their own praise to make others appear vile, for they think they are praised through the disparagement of others" <note>original: "Vilius satis bonū est suā laude querentiū alios viles facere: qm aliorū vituperatione se laudari putant"</note>.</margin>

Therefore, whenever a man submits his appetite to reason, he is free and attends to the understanding of worthy objects and of grave and serious things. According to how reason leads us, he abandons the other operations of those who are not conformed in sentiment. But those who, on the contrary, are conquered and overcome by the sensory appetite, only intend to recognize those who are stained with a similar mark, so that with a similar example they can excuse themselves for their errors, believing it to be enough for them. From this, that sentence of **Tully** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> in the first book of *On Duties* is verified, which says: "For it happens, I know not how, that we perceive more in others than in ourselves if any fault is committed" <note>original: "Fit enim nescio quō vt magis in alijs quā nobisipis cernamus: si q̄d delingtur"</note>. And therefore, **Master Francis**, having been in the age of his adolescence until the day he fell in love, was always devoted to speculative operations <note>Intellectual study and philosophy</note>. By pretending to have seen this vision at that time, he appropriately affirms that he did not yet recognize Love in the fleshly appetite. # THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

This happens because some people possess such little intelligence that they do not acknowledge anything that cannot be understood by our five external senses. And because they feed only on worldly things, they are rightly named after the world. These, then, are the ones who know love more than others. Therefore, the poet adds the origin of love's birth, saying he was born of idleness and nourished by human lust, and then maintained by the sweetness and pleasantness of thoughts; finally, he was deified by foolish and vain people. In his "canonization," whatever lustful desire exists leads its life with the greatest harshness and most cruel bitterness. Wherefore he says:

<margin>X</margin>
->*He was born of idleness and human lust,*<-
->*Nourished by thoughts sweet and soft,*<-
->*Made lord and God by vain people.*<-
->*Some are killed by him; others with more heavy*<-
->*Laws lead their lives harsh and bitter*<-
->*Under a thousand chains and a thousand keys.*<-

¶ For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known that according to the opinion of **Job** in the second chapter <note>actually Job 5:7</note>, and of **the Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note> in the first book of the *Politics*: just as every animal is produced for some specific function, so too God produced man naturally for exercise and labor. Whence Job says: <term>For the bird is known for flight, but man for labor</term> <note>original Latin: "Auis enim ad volatum scitur: hō autē ad laborem"</note>. This opinion conforms to that of Genesis in the third chapter, when after the ruin and fall of our first parents, God said to Adam: <term>In the sweat of your brow you shall eat your bread</term> <note>original Latin: "In sudore vultus tui vesceris pane tuo"</term>. Because man can justly exercise himself in two ways—one with the mind alone, the other with both mind and body—there are two types of life defined: one called the **contemplative life** and the other the **active life**. One is given only to mental exercise and the other to the corporal, as is written at the beginning of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics</note>. Whenever the perverse order of human actions distracts a man and he deviates from his nature—giving himself over to idleness, especially of the intellect—he fails to exercise himself toward the knowledge of things. From this comes our happiness; but when we turn from it, lustful desire is derived and born, which men call and name Love.

<margin>Y</margin>
¶ It is nourished thereafter by the sweetness and pleasantness of thoughts. Whenever something occurs that brings sadness to the soul, or is necessary for the sustenance of human life—because there is a natural desire in every created thing to perpetuate itself as much as it can, as is written in the first book of the *Physics*—it is necessary to work in a fitting way to drive away the soul's distress and acquire what is needed for daily living. Because of this, the mind ceases to focus on such an object <note>meaning, when we are busy, we do not dwell on passion</note>. Therefore **Ovid** wrote in the book *The Remedies for Love* that the prohibition of idleness and a scarcity of food were among the remedies to be used against love. Wherefore **Crates the Theban**, a famous and distinguished philosopher, used to say often on this subject, as **Laertius** wrote: <term>Hunger settles love</term> <note>original Latin: "Amorem sedat fames"</note>. And because sometimes men do not want to force themselves to resist such delicious incentives, they say—as if thinking this were a sufficient excuse for their errors—that love is a divine madness which men cannot resist, as **Seneca** clearly writes in his eighth Tragedy (which is the ninth in order). Wherefore he says:

> *A great force of the mind and a seductive heat of the soul*
> *Is Love; it is born of luxury and idleness,*
> *Nourished by happy and good fortune;*
> *Which, if you cease to cherish and feed it, falls*
> *And quickly, being extinguished, loses its strength.*
> <note>translated from the Latin quote from Seneca's "Octavia"</note>

> *And in the Hippolytus, which is the fourth in order, he said:*
> *Lust feigned that Love was a god,*
> *Favoring shameful slavery, so that it might be more free.*
> *It added the title of a god to its madness to deceive.*
> <note>translated from the Latin quote from Seneca's "Phaedra/Hippolytus"</note>

<margin>Z</margin>

Since the nature of the soul is such that it was created immortal and cannot exist without some kind of life, its "greatest death" is its alienation from the life of God in the eternity of punishment. **Solomon** also said in the first book of *Wisdom*: <term>The mouth that lies kills the soul</term> <note>original Latin: "Os quod mētitur occidit aiām"</note>, and **Ezekiel** 18: <term>The soul that sins, the same shall die</term> <note>original Latin: "aia quae peccauerit ipsa morietur"</note>. Finally, the **Apostle Paul** in 1 Corinthians 15 said: <term>the sting</term>...

### CHAPTER ONE

### CHAPTER ONE

*The sting of death is sin.* <note>original: "Stimulus aut mortis pctm̄ est." A reference to 1 Corinthians 15:56.</note> This, then, is that which leads wretched mortals through a thousand hardships and bitterness, always with weeping and laments, to their final breath under an infinite number of dangers and certain adversities. For this reason, <term>Plautus</term> <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BC), a Roman playwright famous for his comedies.</note> appropriately wrote in the comedy ***Asinaria***: *O Libanus, how miserable is the man who loves!* <note>original: "O libane ut miser est hō qui amat"</note> and in the other comedy called ***Curculio*** he said: *One must go where ungrateful love commands* <note>original: "Eundū est quo īperat ingratus amor"</note> and a little further below: *Secret love is an evil; it is pure loss.* <note>original: "Malū est clandestinū amor: damnū autē merum"</note>

Most excellently, then, our poet describes love leading men under the heaviest hardships, and even killing them by placing them in a state that should be chosen far less than the death of the body, according to the Gospel sentence of **Matthew** in the tenth chapter. There, testifying of Christ speaking to the disciples, he says: *Do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can cast both soul and body into hell.* <note>original: "Nolite timere eos qui occidūt corpus:āiam autē non possunt occidere: sed poti⁹ timete eū qui potest & āiam & corpus mittere in gehennā"</note> This also follows the opinion of the Stoics which **Augustine** reports in the ninth book of the *City of God*, saying: *The Stoics say it is worse to lose those things by which the nature and safety of the body are maintained than to commit those things by which justice is violated.* <note>original: "Stoici male se dicunt haec amittere: quibus natura corporis salus: & incolumis habetur: quā illa cōmittere: quibus iusticia violatur."</note> This "violation" is nothing other than sin, which is generated and committed only by the dominion of the sensory appetite over reason, when accessory and instrumental things are desired as if they were primary goals.

Wherefore **Augustine**, in the *Book of Eighty-Three Questions*, defining sin, said: *Sin is to use things that should be enjoyed, and to enjoy things that should be used.* <note>original: "Peccatū est vti fruendis & vtendis frui." Augustine's famous distinction: we should "enjoy" God (the end) and "use" the world (the means).</note> In this definition, it is clearly understood that just as the soul is the end of the body—as written in the second book of *On the Soul* and the seventh of the *Politics* <note>References to Aristotle.</note>—and the body itself is ordered toward the soul, so too corporal pleasures must be such that they direct the soul toward the objects established for it according to its two primary universal powers: namely, intellect and will. The first of these is directed toward the Supreme Truth, and the other toward the Supreme Good. When these are attained, the soul finds itself in its ultimate end and rest, which is its supreme and naturally desired happiness. Now, since **M. F.** <note>Messer Francesco (Petrarch).</note>, by means of the shadow's report, has described who this triumphant figure is, he consequently brings forward the examples of those men who were conquered by such appetite, submitting their reason and its use to him. The first of these he places as **Julius Caesar**. Although he had performed many most glorious works for the Roman Republic, he was nonetheless constrained in Egypt by the charms of **Cleopatra** to postpone every duty and take carnal delight in her. Because of this, the poet adds that it is appropriate to write that Caesar was conquered, even though he was the ruler of the world. ### THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

<margin>C. For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, one must know that among the Romans, there were two ways to acquire children. One was through natural propagation—a work most natural among all others, as is written in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de aīa" - referring to Aristotle's treatise *De Anima*.</note>.</margin>

Her <note>Cleopatra</note> desire to rule caused her to quickly poison the weary one; after his death, her other brother, Ptolemy, was substituted by the work of **Pompey**. It happened that after the death of Pompey, **Cleopatra** became an adherent to **Caesar**. After he died, she turned to **Mark Antony**, whom she led to be intensely in love with her through her charms. She was promised the empire of Rome as a reward for her unchaste pleasure. Finally, when dissension and war arose between **Octavian** and **Antony**, and Antony was defeated and driven to death by desperation, Cleopatra attempted to capture the young Octavian just as she had captured Caesar and Antony. But he would not consent to her lasciviousness, intending to save her for his <term>triumph</term> <note>A civil ceremony and religious rite of ancient Rome, held to publicly celebrate and sanctify the success of a military commander.</note>. Ultimately, in despair, she had her veins opened and applied serpents to them, being forced to die. Nevertheless, it is said by some others that Cleopatra died because she was forced by Antony to drink the poison which she had previously forbidden him from taking.

In the second place, **Master Francesco** <note>The poet Petrarch.</note> introduces the example of **Octavian Augustus**. Although he loved less blamefully, he was nonetheless driven by carnal desire and sensory appetite. The poet says the one who followed was the "son" of Caesar, who had loved more justly, having obtained through pleas his beloved and most desired consort, **Livia**. Whence he says:

->**The other is his son; and yet he loved**<-
->**More justly; he is Caesar Augustus**<-
->**Who took Livia, while pregnant, from another.**<-

The other way <note>referring back to the margin note about acquiring children</note> is through <term>adoption</term>, which according to the opinion of **Gellius** in the fifth book of *Attic Nights* <note>original: "noctibus Atticis"</note> is declared to be done when, with the authority of the <term>praetor</term> <note>A Roman judicial officer.</note> interposed, the one adopting pronounces the adopted one to be his son, with the natural father consenting. If the father were already dead, this pronouncement is not called "adoption" but <term>arrogation</term> <note>original: "arrogatione" - the legal adoption of a person who was already legally independent (sui iuris).</note> of the "arrogated" son. Octavian was, therefore, the son of **Julius Caesar** not by nature but only by adoption. By the origin of his ancestors, he was a citizen of Velletri, the son of **Gaius Octavius**. Thus, after the death of Caesar, having been instituted as his heir and having agreed with **Mark Antony** to take revenge for his adoptive father, he drove **Brutus** and **Cassius** (the killers of Caesar) to a desperate death. Then, having come into dissension with Antony and defeated him, he alone held the empire of Rome. During his rule, Octavian loved various women. Ultimately, having repudiated **Scribonia**, he loved **Livia Drusilla**, who was the wife of one of his soldiers named **Tiberius Nero**. At that time, she was pregnant by the said Tiberius Nero. Although he could have obtained her by force, he did not wish to act proudly in that matter. Instead, turning to pleas and humbly offering them to Tiberius, he finally obtained his dear Livia, whom he joined to himself as his legitimate wife.

Next, **Master Francesco** adds the third example, **Domitius Nero**. Although he was a most cruel man—as our **Tranquillus** <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, the Roman biographer.</note> demonstrates, and even more clearly **Cornelius Tacitus**—he was nonetheless still constrained by the carnal appetite for women. Whence the poet says:

<margin>D. Nero Domitius took his surname from Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus due to his primary origin; he followed the character of his grandfather Domitius and his father Domitius. He was the sixth Emperor of the Romans, to whom the Empire came:</margin>

->**Nero is the third, pitiless and unjust:**<-
->**See him go, full of wrath and disdain.**<-
->**A woman conquered him, though he seems so robust.**<-

This happened because when **Claudius**, the fourth Emperor, had his wife **Messalina** put to death for violating her marriage vows, he took as his wife **Agrippina**, the mother of **Nero**. Loving her quite intensely, he also adopted Nero as his son. Agrippina, desiring the empire first for herself and then for Nero, poisoned the same Claudius (as **Tacitus** writes). Upon his death, two children remained: a male named **Britannicus**, younger than Nero, and a female named **Octavia**. Agrippina and Nero took control of the empire. Once Nero was established in the palace, his injustices, his most cruel deeds, and his immense ingratitude soon became known and manifest. ## CHAPTER ONE

played the lyre and also sang: activities that were totally unsuitable for the son of an emperor. Britannicus obeyed Nero, and in his song, he recounted his entire miserable state, which moved the people to great compassion. Nero, having recognized this and fearing that with the favor of the people Britannicus might one day recover the empire, had him poisoned. He did it in this manner: while dining one morning with Nero, Britannicus, who was accustomed to drinking water, <margin>H</margin> had Nero prepare certain poisoned ice-water. Nero assigned this to the man who performed the <term>credence</term> <note>The practice of a servant tasting food or drink to prove it is not poisoned.</note> for Britannicus, who was aware of this treason. Then he had the water given to Britannicus hotter than usual; after it was tasted by the servant, Britannicus asked for ice to cool it. The servant, as if acting without premeditation, immediately poured the poisoned water (which he had ready there) mixed with the other. Upon tasting it, Britannicus immediately fell dead upon the table. <margin>F</margin> Seeing this, those standing around immediately understood the wicked treachery, even though Nero said in his excuse that Britannicus was accustomed to falling in that way due to the "falling sickness" <note>original: "morbo comitiale" - an old term for epilepsy.</note>. 

Nero was also cruel and unjust toward Octavia, whom he had taken as his wife out of consideration for the Roman people; for he first repudiated her without any cause, then exiled her, and ultimately, without any fault of hers, he had her put to death by accusing her of a lack of chastity. He likewise killed his wife Poppaea Sabina and Statilia Messalina, whom he had also kept as wives. He killed many Roman citizens, and among the others, he killed his teacher Seneca. So that his cruelty would not bypass his own blood, he killed Claudia Antonia, his own daughter, because she did not want to [marry him after the death of her mother] <note>The text here contains a slight historical confusion regarding Agrippina; Nero famously murdered his mother Agrippina first, then later Antonia for refusing to marry him.</note> Agrippina. To fulfill every kind of <term>parricide</term> <note>The murder of a parent or close relative.</note>, he caused nearly two-thirds of Rome to burn. Despite his many injustices and cruelties, he nevertheless intensely loved another woman, Poppaea Sabina, who was first the wife of one Crispus Rufus, then of Otho, and finally of Nero. One day, being angry either by design or out of pure fury, he killed her with a kick. 

Further on, our poet recites the fourth example, that of Marcus Aurelius <note>original: "Marcoantonio" - here referring to Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, the philosopher-emperor.</note>, truly most worthy and excellent in studies and letters; but like those mentioned above, he was conquered by worldly appetite. The poet says that although his breast and tongue were full of philosophy, he was nonetheless constrained by Faustina to follow the triumph of love with the others. Thus he says:

<margin>G</margin>
> See the good Marcus, worthy of every praise;
> His tongue and breast full of philosophy:
> But still Faustina keeps him here in check.

In this place, there are two things to consider for the understanding of the preceding verses. One is that, according to the writings of Julius Capitolinus <note>One of the supposed authors of the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note>, there were two Marcus Antoninus "Pius" emperors of Rome. The first was born in Transalpine Gaul and descended from Titus Aurelius Fulvus; his mother was Arria Fadilla and his wife was Annia Faustina. He was a most eloquent man, beautiful of body, honest in character, and pleasant in appearance; merciful, learned, and observant of agriculture. Born under Domitian, he later succeeded Aelius Commodus in the empire; because of his light, the Senate compared him to Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, known for his piety.</note>. But the poet does not mean this man. 

The other was Marcus Aurelius Antoninus the Pious, a Roman by origin, born on the Caelian Hill, the son of one Annius Verus and Domitia Lucilla. He was a most excellent man in character, most learned in natural philosophy, and to be placed before all other princes in sanctity, justice, and piety. He studied grammar under one Euphormion, music under Geminus Commodus, <margin>I</margin> and eloquence under Alexander the Greek and under Oroso, Proculus, and Pollio in Latin. Marcus also had several teachers in natural philosophy, among whom were Commodus of Chalcedon and Sextus of Chaeronea, the grandson of Plutarch. He succeeded the previous Antoninus in the empire, of whom he was also the son by adoption. He took as his wife Faustina, the natural daughter of his adoptive father Antoninus. She was so beautiful that, according to what is written of her, it was believed some divine quality was mixed with her mortality. Thus, for perpetual memory, the sculptors of those times left her image figured in gold, silver, and on armor for posterity. And just as Faustina was beautiful, so was she unchaste; she was not content with a single adulterer. Among others, the most well-known were Ventidius, Orphitus, and Tertullus, the latter of whom was even found at dinner with her by Marcus. This page consists of a masterful Renaissance woodcut illustrating the **Triumph of Love** <note>original: "Trionfo d'Amore"</note>, the opening sequence of Petrarch’s allegorical poem. 

At the heart of the composition, the winged god **Cupid** <note>original: "Amor"</note> stands atop a pedestal placed upon an ornate triumphal chariot. He is depicted in his traditional guise, wielding a bow and aiming his arrows at the multitude below. The chariot is drawn by two spirited horses through a vast procession of figures. These figures represent famous lovers and victims of passion from ancient history, mythology, and the Bible, all subjugated by the power of Love.

<margin>In the foreground at the bottom right, a seated figure—representing the poet Petrarch—is shown observing the grand procession.</margin>

The entire scene is framed by a sophisticated four-part decorative border. This border is adorned with intricate floral motifs and classical architectural elements, typical of high-quality early Italian printing.

# CHAPTER ONE

**M**aster Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> describes the dominion of the senses, feigning that Cupid triumphs over men in this manner: that is, by considering how the ancient Romans, whenever they triumphed, were placed upon chariots led to the temples of the gods where they consecrated their spoils. Thus, he imagines Love being carried in triumph through the world upon a chariot, and finally being led to the temple of his mother, the goddess Venus—a place truly suited for such a triumphant figure. Secondly, just as the one who triumphed proceeded adorned in various robes, so Master Francesco attributes to Love the specific qualities that befit him. In the third and final place, just as those who triumphed led untamed prisoners bound before them, so Master Francesco describes those men who were bound and conquered by love following his triumph as subjects. Furthermore, just as conquered kings and leaders preceded the triumpher while common prisoners followed him, so Master Francesco describes Jove <note>Jupiter, king of the gods</note> before the chariot as the most excellent god celebrated by the ignorant ancient people, with all others following after the triumph. The poet divides this entire subject into four equal chapters, which we shall explain in their proper places according to their specific details. Regarding the first chapter, Master Francesco primarily describes the particular time and the hour in which he feigns having seen these visions, imagining himself to be asleep and describing the conditions that induce sleep. He says, therefore, that at the time when his amorous sighs are renewed by the sweet memory of the first day he fell in love—which was the beginning of his labors of love—the sun was already warming both horns of the Bull <note>The sun was in the zodiac sign of Taurus, indicating springtime</note>. This was in the month of April or March, when the sun had already passed the first half of the degrees of the sign of Taurus and entered the second; this is what he means by "one and the other horn." He adds, not without great and natural reason, that the specific hour of his sleep was at dawn, saying that the "girl of Tithonus" <note>Aurora, the goddess of Dawn, who in mythology was the consort of Tithonus</note> in that hour proceeded chilled to her accustomed dwelling, her habits unchanged. Whence he says:

---

<margin>¶ For a clearer understanding of the two preceding tercets, it is necessary to understand according to philosophical and astronomical rules: that the eighth celestial sphere is divided into five zones. The middle one, because of the sun's path, is named the Torrid zone. Its entire circumference is divided into twelve parts, each of which, being adorned with notable stars, receives a different name. Thus, the first is called Aries, the second Taurus, the third Gemini, the fourth Cancer, the fifth Leo, the sixth Virgo, the seventh Libra, the eighth Scorpio, the ninth Sagittarius, the tenth Capricornus, the eleventh Aquarius, and the twelfth and last, Pisces.</margin>

> **I**N the time that renews my sighs
> Through the sweet memory of that day,
> Which was the beginning of such long martyrdoms,
> The sun was already warming both horns
> Of the Bull, and the girl of Tithonus
> Ran chilled to her ancient dwelling.

---

Thereafter, each of the aforementioned twelve parts of the sky is divided into thirty distinct thirtieth-parts of its own, each of which is called a degree. And every degree is then divided into sixty sixtieths called minutes, and every sixtieth into sixty other sixtieths called seconds; this division of minutes and seconds is also attributed to the hours. And imagining also these twelve parts to be situated along an oblique circle called the <term>Zodiac (the path of the sun through the constellations)</term> in such a way that one imagines three parallel circles in this zone: one is in the middle, called the <term>Equinoctial (the celestial equator)</term>; another toward the Antarctic pole, called the <term>Winter Solstitial (the Tropic of Capricorn)</term>; and the other toward the Arctic, called the <term>Summer Solstitial (the Tropic of Cancer)</term>. The sun is found under each of these at different times of the year. Thus, in March or September it is found under the equinoctial line, as we shall say in the third chapter of this triumph; in the month of June it is found under the Summer Solstitial circle; and in the month of December it is found under the Winter Solstitial circle. The sun, traveling in its own sphere directly under the twelve parts, returns to the same point in the span of one year.
