## THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

...tenth point from where it began to move. In this path, it is said to have traversed all twelve signs. The sun therefore enters the first degree of Aries and its first minute on the eleventh or twelfth day of March, according to the proportion of hours that remain beyond the 365 complete days of the year. It remains there for about twenty-four hours and one-third per degree. From this, it appears manifest to us that whenever the sun is in the sign of Taurus, it falls in the month of April or May.

Secondly, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> writes that the particular hour of his dream was dawn, saying that the "frozen girl of Tithonus ran to her usual dwelling." Here it is to be understood that it pleased the poets for Aurora <note>the Dawn</note> to be the daughter of Titan and the Earth. This is because the dawn is nothing other than a brightness and splendor preceding the face of the sun. And because the sun is the son of Hyperion, who was the son of Titan, who was the son of Heaven, who was the son of Aether, who was the son of Erebus, who was the son of Demogorgon—the sun is often named after his grandfather by the ancients. Therefore, Aurora is said to be the daughter of Titan. But she is called the daughter of the Earth because, as our sight is drawn to the horizon, whatever rises in that part of the sky also appears to rise from the earth.

But the "girl of Tithonus" is what the poet calls Aurora in this place. Tithonus was the brother of Laomedon, King of Troy, according to what Ovid writes in the twelfth book of the *Metamorphoses* <note>original: "methamorphoseos"</note>; but according to others, he was his son. He was loved and carried away by Aurora. Asking for long life from Aurora, he obtained it, so much so that after the death of his son Memnon, he was transformed into a <term>cicada</term> <note>a cricket or grasshopper; used here to symbolize extreme, shriveled old age</note>. Because of his great old age, and because of the unchanging age of Aurora—whom the poets describe as a young girl—Master Francesco deservedly calls her the "girl of Tithonus." 

He consequently describes the hour of dawn as being frozen and cold for two reasons. First, because of the coldness of the night which has continued until that hour. Second, because as the heat of the sun's rays approaches, the coldness gathers itself together due to the arrival of its opposite, a process called by philosophers <term>antiparistasis</term> <note>the intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite, such as cold becoming more intense just before heat arrives</note>. Thus gathered within itself, the cold becomes more intense. 

I said at the beginning that it was not without reason that Master Francesco chose the hour of dawn for his dream and no other, as he wishes to demonstrate that his vision is true. According to the opinion of the singular philosopher Albertus Magnus in his book *On Sleep and Waking* <note>original: "de somno & vigilia"</note>: just as the radial light of the stars communicated to the material elements produces a likeness to which the elemental powers become instruments and ministers, so the celestial and abstract intelligences of the angels influence our soul with their intrinsic powers. The soul uses these alongside its own effects as instruments; sometimes through phantasms and images, sometimes in the manner of a teaching master, and sometimes through its own essence, they demonstrate to us true things—whether present, past, or future. 

And because for such a vision it is necessary for the organs and instruments of the internal senses to be purged of superfluous vapors, this cannot happen while digestion is taking place, because fumes continually ascend from the stomach to the brain. Therefore, it is necessary that if one is to see true things or foresee them in a dream, it must be in the morning hour, in which the fumes raised by food are totally dissolved. Thus Macrobius, in his *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* <note>original: "de somnio Scipionis"</note>, established that there are five species of dreams: the first is called <term>fantasma</term> <note>an apparition or nightmare</note>; the second, <term>insomnium</term> <note>an ordinary dream caused by daily cares</note>; the third, <term>somnium</term> <note>an enigmatic dream requiring interpretation</note>; the fourth, <term>visio</term> <note>a prophetic vision of a future event</note>; and the fifth and last, <term>oraculum</term> <note>an oracle or revelation from a higher authority</note>. This remains a clear enough argument by which Master Francesco can show his vision to be true, having occurred at the hour of dawn in which true and certain visions are demonstrated to mortals.

Having thus described the time and the hour in the preceding verses in which he saw these visions, Master Francesco adds how he was sleeping, expressing the causes by which he was occupied by sleep. He says that passion, disdains, and amorous tears, and likewise the season and the time, had led him to sleep—in which state the weary heart rests and relaxes its every burden of thoughts and works. And he adds that in such a sleep he saw a very great light upon the grass; this is because in the time of spring, the surface of the earth is all filled with green, although it can also be adapted to mean that by "the grass" he intends the place where he had laid himself down to sleep. In that light was a very heavy and bitter grief with little solace or pleasure, and that was slippery and accompanied by a very heavy game. Wherefore he says:

<margin>
NOW, for a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known that sleep is defined as nothing other than a binding of the primary sense.
</margin>

->Love, disdains, and tears, and the season<-
->Had led me back to the enclosed place;<-

# CHAPTER ONE

<margin>...not for the revocation of the animated spirits to their own principle. And therefore, the primary sensory power is an intrinsic virtue called the common sense <note>term: "senso comune" — a medieval psychological concept of a faculty that processes and combines data from all five senses</note>: because it commonly renders judgment on all particular sensations. This virtue is situated, according to philosophers and doctors, in the first ventricle of the brain: from which there is a path through which the motor and sensory spirits generated in the brain spread through the body, giving the members the operations of feeling and moving. When this path is blocked, it induces sleep. This path is said to be blocked when it is filled by smoky evaporation or cerebral humidity. Vapors rise to this place when either a superfluity of food or excessive bodily or mental exercise reigns in our body. Intrinsic humidity also descends to the said place, or when it is multiplied in our members by an extrinsic cause: when the retentive virtue of the brain is weakened by an external or internal cause. From this it appears manifest that Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> was constrained to sleep at that time: first because of the season and the hour in which humidity most multiplies in our bodies, making it more convenient for a man to sleep: for as Virgil writes in the second book of the *Aeneid*: "The setting stars urge sleep" <note>original: "Suadentque cadentia sydera somnos"</note>. Likewise, although the distress of love, indignation, and anger are each causes of resolving the vital spirits and setting them on fire: thus the governing virtue of our body is necessitated to produce sleep for the restoration and refreshment of those same spirits.</margin>

*Where the weary heart lays down every burden:*
*There among the grass, already faint from weeping,*
*Overcome by sleep I saw a great light,*
*And within it much sorrow with brief joy,*

<margin>D</margin>
¶ Secondly, Master Francesco said: *Where the weary heart lays down every burden.* To follow the distinct and separate operations according to three locations: namely, the rational and intellectual in the brain; the concupiscible <note>desiring or emotional</note> in the precordia <note>term: "pcordij" (precordia) — the region around the heart, then believed to be the seat of emotions</note>; and the natural in the liver. Just as they were divided by location, so different operations were attributed to them. Therefore, giving every concupiscible appetite to that of the precordia, when that part settled in sleep, the heart laid down every burden of its thoughts in that enclosed place of operations.

Finally, Master Francesco adds that he saw a great light: because light is the object of the visual power such that nothing is visible by itself unless it is truly light or a participant in light. Therefore, since the sensory appetite is manifestly visible through its operations and especially through carnal desire, Master Francesco, wishing to describe those things appropriately, says he saw a very great light. Afterward, Master Francesco adds what he saw inside this light: saying he saw a most powerful and victorious leader, triumphing in the manner of those for whom triumphal chariots were established for their glory and honor by the ancient Romans—those who, by operating with virtue, were conducted to the Capitol, the head and citadel of the Roman Republic. Whence he says:

<margin>Now he knows</margin>
*I saw a victorious and supreme leader,*
*Just like one of those who to the Capitoline*
*Leads a triumphal chariot with great glory.*

<margin>¶ Among the other orders of triumphing described in the histories of the Latin language for the evidence of the preceding verses, let it suffice to refer only to what was observed in the triumph of Scipio Aemilianus after the destruction of Carthage, written by Appian of Alexandria in the *Third Punic War* in this form: Crowned with wreaths, all with trumpets sounding before them, they led chariots filled with spoils; wooden towers were also carried, displaying models of the captured cities; then came writings and images of the deeds that had been performed; then gold and silver, partly in raw masses, partly marked or impressed with figures of this kind. Furthermore, there were crowns which, for the sake of virtue, the cities, allies, or the army had given to the citizens and soldiers. Then followed white oxen and elephants; after these, the leaders of the Carthaginians or Numidians captured in war. Before the commander went the lictors <note>attendants of Roman magistrates</note> dressed in purple robes with a crowd of lyre-players and trumpeters in the likeness of an Etruscan procession; where, girt up and crowned with golden wreaths, they went forward in their order, singing and playing; these they call Lydians—as I would easily believe the Etruscans took their origin from the Lydians. In the midst of these, someone dressed in a floor-length robe with fringes and bracelets shining with gold made various gestures; insulting the conquered enemies, he provoked laughter everywhere. After this, a great quantity of incense and perfumes surrounded the commander, whom in a gilded chariot...</margin>

# THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

And white horses, shining with many markings, drew him, wearing a golden crown on his head adorned with small stones and gems. Here, girded in a purple garment woven with golden stars in the ancestral fashion, he carried an ivory scepter in one hand and laurel in the other—which the Romans displayed as a sign of victory. With him were boys and girls on both sides, and nearby were his young kinsmen; and finally the scribes, servants, and shield-bearers who had followed the army. Finally, the army followed the chariot, divided into troops and battle lines. The soldiers, crowned with laurel and carrying laurel in their hands, were joined by marks of merit, so that according to these customs they might bear some with praise and others they might mock with wit; and some they might mark with infamy.

Therefore, with a similarity that differs only slightly from this, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> affirms that he saw Love triumphing over men in the manner of a truly most powerful and victorious leader. This is because, according to the opinion of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the second book of the *Ethics*, it is more difficult to resist pleasure than to resist the primary natural movements, even though those are not in our power. Whence he says: "For it is more difficult to resist pleasure than anger," as Heraclitus says <note>original: "Difficilius n. est resistere voluptati quam iræ vt Heraclitus inqt"</note>. By this opinion, it is clearly understood how great the force of this strong and furious affection is. The poet continues by expressing the effect he seemed to experience upon seeing this most just prince. He speaks by accusing the laziness of the age in which he lives; for since men in his time were already so depraved that they not only failed to act in such a way that they might justly come to triumph with honor, but their souls were entirely empty of value and virtue and full of pride and arrogance—such a triumph being unusual to see—nevertheless, ardently desiring to learn new things, it seemed to him that he must diligently raise his eyes, tired from amorous weeping and heavy with sleep, to watch and understand this new and wonderful spectacle, to know clearly and aptly who the triumpher was and over whom he triumphed, having no other delight or pleasure than to feed his intellect always with new knowledge. Whence he says:

<margin>
My hands are...
In the hand of the Lord
</margin>

<sig>F</sig>

> I, who am not accustomed to such a sight
> Because of the tedious age in which I find myself,
> Empty of all valor, full of all pride:
> This haughty habit, unusual and new,
> I gazed upon, lifting my eyes heavy and tired;
> For I feel no other delight than learning.

It perhaps seems to some that since men always have free will over their actions—Master Francesco himself affirming this in that moral song, *Thinking of you, the thought assails me*, where he says while the body is alive: *You have the bridle in the power of your thoughts*—and it being also a universal conclusion of the theologians in the second book of the *Sentences*, and of the Peripatetics in the second book of the *Physics* and in Aristotle’s *Ethics*, that he unjustly reproaches the "ages" in this place; rather, only the men produced in those ages should be blamed by the poet. To those people, it is replied that it is true that our soul is superior to every bodily inclination; whence Ptolemy also affirms in the *Quadripartitum*: <term>A wise man shall rule the stars</term> <note>original: "Quia sapiens dñabitur astris" — a famous medieval maxim suggesting that while stars influence the physical body, the rational soul can overcome them</note>. Nevertheless, man being always inclined toward the flesh and bodily pleasure due to the contagion of original sin—as written in the second book of the *Sentences* at the 30th distinction—the intellect is often held captive within the power of the senses by the very strong bodily inclination. And let there also be the dominion of the celestial bodies over the inferior ones, whose proper complexion is conformed to that of the stars; whence the Philosopher says in the prologue of the <term>Meteorology</term> <note>Aristotle's work on natural science</note>: <term>Moreover, this inferior world is necessarily continuous with the superior motions, so that all its virtue is governed from there</term>. Therefore, he may justly blame the ages in which unhappy, depressed, and ignoble constellations reign, just as they did in the time of Master Francesco compared to those that dominated in the time of the glorious Romans.

Petrarch then adds the appearance and properties of the triumpher, saying that he was a naked boy placed upon a chariot of fire, fierce and cruel in sight, armed only with a bow and a quiver placed at his side full of arrows, against which no helmet or shield is of any use. Upon his shoulders extend two great wings, varied and distinguished by a great number of different colors. Then he led an innumerable prey of prisoners, divided into three different conditions: for some were only taken in battle; others were wounded by very sharp arrows; and others were totally killed. And this most ferocious leader was thus guided by four very white horses which went along pulling the chariot. Whence he says:

# CHAPTER THREE

> **F**our steeds more white than snow;
> Upon a chariot of fire a cruel youth
> With bow in hand and arrows at his sides;
> **A**gainst which neither helmet nor shield avails:
> Upon his shoulders he had but two great wings
> Of a thousand colors, and all else was naked:
> **A**round him were innumerable mortals,
> Part taken in battle, and part slain,

<margin>G</margin> **O**ur illustrious and admirable poet has enclosed a grand and excellent concept beneath the veil of the preceding verses. The clear understanding of this must be sought: when the sensual appetite—represented here as Love—holds dominion over a man’s reason, the human property of rational discourse is lost, and the man becomes common with the beasts. This can be understood from Aristotle in the discussion of the seventh book of the *Ethics*, the first of the *Politics*, and the prologue of the *Metaphysics*. Just as the actions of beasts, driven by instinct, cannot be hidden, so too does a man become "naked" regarding his concepts and appetites, making them known and manifest to whoever looks upon him.

And so, naked, he rests upon the fire of carnal concupiscence <term>concupiscence: strong sexual desire or lust</term> and immortal passions and the unbridled desire for the beloved thing. He has no armor of reason to defend himself, but only arrows from himself and a bow, whose force is not limited by any distance, but reaches and arrives at any place and <margin>H</margin> from any object where there is something that offers delight to the lewdness of the senses. He also wears wings of swift instability, varied in as many colors as there are causes for carnal delights.

This appetite is then guided by four very white steeds—and certainly with good reason. For when the natural law of the principles of our works is subverted—that is, the intellectual and the sensual, where the intellect should command and the sensual should obey—those parts which were once stabilized by the four primary virtues called "cardinal" <note>Prudence, Justice, Temperance, and Fortitude</note> are instead oppressed by the four contrary vices. These living principles of ours are the two main parts of the soul: the intellect is divided into intellect and will, and the sensual into the concupiscible <term>concupiscible: the faculty of the soul that desires pleasures</term> and the irascible <term>irascible: the faculty associated with anger or the drive to overcome obstacles</term>. The first of these members is stabilized by Prudence; the second by Justice; the third by Temperance; and the fourth by Fortitude.

Conversely, when appetite leads a man in his actions, it brings him to Imprudence, Injustice, Intemperance, and Audacity. Therefore, poets have fittingly described such men as either turned into stones or into brute animals. These four vices are the four horses of the chariot of Love, which are reasonably depicted as "very white." For just as whiteness is a color that scatters and weakens human sight, so too these four vices are dispersive and corruptive to the human mind.

Next, our poet attributes, not without moral sentiment, three distinct generations of prisoners: those only wounded in battle, those taken, and those slain. To understand this, it is necessary to know that there are three ways in which mortals desire sensual delights or their objects:

1.  The first is through the "first movements" which arise naturally. By consenting to these, one takes sensual pleasure, yet does not dwell in them; rather, men pull back from them, constrained by rational discourse. These are the ones who are properly "wounded by love," whose wound is healed by the true knowledge of oneself.
2.  The second belongs to those who, by force of an immense concupiscence, even though they clearly recognize they are erring, cannot nonetheless repudiate the object of delight and lewdness. These are called "incontinent" by the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the seventh book of the *Ethics*; though they know the desired object should be fled, they are nonetheless forced by great concupiscence to follow it. Thus, failing to persist in reason, they are "taken in battle" by the superior appetite represented as Love.
3.  The third and final way belongs to those in whom reason is entirely exterminated and obscured, and who are overcome without any consideration for anything but the smallest pleasures. These Aristotle calls the "intemperate," who are truly "slain" by the arrows of love. Of these, one might justly judge that they are worse than dead, having fallen into a state more miserable than death. Aristotle says in the third book of the *Ethics*: "For death is more to be chosen than the safety of flight" <note>original: "Eligibilior enim est mors salute fuge"</note>. And Quintus Curtius, introducing Alexander, says: "It is better to die than to be a leader by another’s whim" <note>original: "Mori prestat quam precario imperatorem esse"</note>. Persuaded by this truth, many glorious Romans, foreign men, and women...

<header>THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE</header>

Of those whose fragile nature should have inclined toward delights, many chose rather to die than to consent to what reason denied should be done; it would be far too long to recount them all. Truly dead, then—and worse than dead—are all those who, neglecting themselves, consent without any resistance to the blameworthy flatteries of the appetite. Because of these works, the eyes of reason are bound by this Love, and so the poets depict him veiled; and also Master Francesco <note>Messer Francesco: Petrarch (Francesco Petrarca), the author of the poem being commented upon.</note> affirms him to be blind, as he describes below the unjust exchange made by Clytemnestra, who left Agamemnon for Aegisthus <note>In Greek mythology, Clytemnestra murdered her husband Agamemnon after taking Aegisthus as her lover; this is used here as a classic example of reason being overcome by lust.</note>. The poet then recounts that he was seized by a most burning desire to hear and understand news of this "Duke" <note>Duke: Here referring to Cupid/Love as the leader of the procession.</note> and of so many people whom he, conquered by himself, led. He says that he placed himself among them so much that he was on the verge of falling into their number, and of being of their company from then on. Thus, standing in this kingdom of this king who is always fasting and void of tears <note>original: "digiuno & vacuo di lachryme." This suggests a realm of suffering where tears are either constant or where the ruler, Cupid, is mercilessly unmoved by them.</note>, he looked to see if he might recognize anyone among such a great people and so large a multitude. And furthermore, he affirms that he recognized no one, so much had they been changed by death or by a cruel, fierce, and bitter prison. Thus he says:

<margin>I</margin> Not without wonderful and worthy artifice has our poet described in the preceding tercets <note>tercets: stanzas of three lines, the building block of the *terza rima* rhyme scheme used by Petrarch and Dante.</note> that he first recognized no one in that company, and secondly, that this king is always "fasting from tears," and that he himself was nearly "dead" like the others. For the understanding of this, it should be known that before Master Francesco loved Lady Laura, he was tempted to love another woman, the record of whom never came to light because that love was not celebrated by him except in a confused way. Thus, by resisting such temptation, he remained continent. And the more he considered the state of those in love, the more it seemed to him hard and harsh, and in no way to be followed by any grave or prudent judgment. He shows us this openly in this place, but it is known more clearly in this madrigal <note>madrigal: a short lyrical poem, often set to music.</note> when he says:

> Eager to hear news, I set myself further ahead
> So much so that I was among those
> Whom Love has divided from life before their time.
> Then I pressed myself to look back, if anyone
> I might recognize in the thick throng
> Of the king always fasting from tears.
> I recognized no one there: and if any there were
> Known to me, they had changed their appearance
> Through death or through a cruel and fierce prison.

> Because the face of Love bore the banner,
> A wanderer moved my vain heart,
> Who seemed to me more worthy of honor than any other;
> And following her over the green grass,
> I heard a loud voice from afar say:
> "Ah, how many steps you lose through the woods!"
> Then I pressed myself into the shade of a beautiful beech,
> All thoughtful, and looking around,
> I saw my journey was quite perilous,
> And I turned back almost at midday.

¶ This same thing he explains even more clearly in that moral song <term>canzone: a complex Italian verse form used for serious or philosophical subjects</term>: **IN THE SWEET TIME OF EARLY YOUTH** <note>original: "Nel dolce tempo de la prima etade." This is the opening line of Petrarch's *Canzone 23*.</note>: In the second stanza where he says:

<margin>K</margin> ¶ Since Master Francesco was superior to the first assault of love, and in this place, by feigning to be in that first time, he appropriately describes himself as not recognizing that multitude. This is because men who are conquered by their sensory appetite have their nature transformed; they are different in their actions from continent men, from whom they deviate and hide. Furthermore, reasonable men willingly separate themselves from them. Therefore, to demonstrate this natural division, Master Francesco affirms in this place that he recognized absolutely none of them. But later, in the second—

> Love gave me, many years had passed,
> Such that I was changing my youthful appearance,

It was at this time, then, that Master Francesco <note>Messer Francesco: Petrarch (Francesco Petrarca), the author of the poem.</note> was captured. For he is one of those who are ahead of their time: that is, before love comes of its own accord, they lead themselves into a state much worse than death. Master Francesco also says this state is "fasting of tears" to demonstrate the immense passion and gravest torment of lustful men. For since their appetite is disordered and they intensely desire the objects of their love, they weep whenever they cannot possess them. And even when they do possess them, they are not at all free of tears, due to the fear of losing them, seeing and understanding that they cannot possess them rightfully. Hence Cicero, in the *Paradoxes* <note>original: *Paradoxa Stoicorum*, a work by the Roman philosopher Cicero exploring Stoic principles.</note>, wishing to express such an effect universally, says these words: <note>original: "Nunquam Hercule pecunias istorum: neq; tecta magnifica: neque opes neque iperias: neque eas qbus maxime astricti sunt voluptates i bonis rebus aut expetēdis cōduxi. Quippe cum viderem hoīes circunfluentes his rebus ea tamen maxime desiderare qbus abundarēt. Neque eni vnquam expletur neque satiatur cupiditas sitis; neque ea solum q habent libidine augendi cruciantur: sed etiam amittendi metu."</note> "By Hercules, I never considered the money of those men, nor their magnificent houses, nor power, nor commands, nor the pleasures to which they are most bound, as good things or things to be sought. For I saw men overflowing with these things still greatly desiring those very things in which they abounded. For the thirst of desire is never filled nor satisfied; not only are they tortured by the lust for increasing what they have, but also by the fear of losing it." Therefore, for this reason, Love is rightly always "fasting of tears" and empty: because it is never satisfied, but always shows itself to be more famished.

**Master Francesco now introduces—to begin the recitation of examples of men conquered and overcome by carnal appetite—a shadow <note>shadow: A ghost or spirit of a deceased person.</note> unknown to him by sight. He brings it in so that it may call him by name and show him the amorous martyrdoms of those who are acquired only through love. He feigns to respond with wonder, asking by what cause it happened that he was known by that shadow, and yet he did not recognize the shadow. To this question, he adds that the shadow responds that this happens for the reason expressed above: namely, because of the heavy bonds and because of the darkened and misty air in which the lewdness of men lives. Yet the shadow affirms that in life he was his friend and was born with him in a Tuscan land. By these words, the poet affirms he recognized his friend; and to speak with him, he says that they both sat down in a temperate and pleasant place, prepared to understand one another. Whence he says:**

<margin>
Master Francesco follows in these verses the style and custom which is that whenever poets wish to recite a historical story in the likeness of a history, they introduce a third person. They have this person direct the words of the one whose history they wish to recite. Just as Homer introduces at the end of his wanderings Ulysses arriving in Phoenicia <note>Phaeacia in the original Homeric text, though often confused or generalized in early commentaries.</note> before Alcinous, King of the province, and has him recount all his maritime errors. Similarly, Virgil introduces Dido at the end of Aeneas’s voyage, to whom he has Aeneas recount the entire history and fall of Troy. So at present, our poet introduces a shadow.

->### THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE ###<-

<margin>M</margin> Following this, and not without reason, Master Francesco <note>Messer Francesco: Francesco Petrarch, the author.</note> describes the air as being dark where Love triumphs, without any moral or singular feeling. This is because no obscurity or blindness is greater than that of the intellect. Thus, wishing to lead the Judeans to true intellectual recognition, the Savior says in Saint John, chapter 12: **"Walk while you have the light, lest darkness come upon you; for he who walks in darkness does not know where he goes."** <note>original Latin: *ambulate dū lucē habetis ne tenebre vos comprehendant: nam qui ambulat in tenebris nescit quo uadat.*</note> The considerations of moralists are also in agreement with this same sentence; for since light is a quality attached to celestial bodies, whenever a person moves away from them, it is necessary that such an effect be overtaken by darkness. Therefore, man is naturally produced for the consideration of celestial things, as described in the first distinction of the second book of the *Sentences* <note>A reference to Peter Lombard's *Sentences*, a standard medieval theological textbook.</note> and by **Ovid in the first book of the *Metamorphoses*.** Ovid affirms this same thing in these verses, saying: **"While other animals look down toward the earth, He gave to man an uplifted face, and ordered him to see the sky and to raise his eyes erect to the stars."** <note>original Latin: *Pronaque cū spectent aiālia cetera terrā. Os hoi sublime dedit: cælumq: uidere iussit: & erectos ad sydera tollere vult.*</note> **Dante Alighieri** also attests to this same point gracefully in the 17th canto of the *Purgatorio*, saying: **"He calls you to the heavens, which circle around you, showing you their eternal beauties, yet your eye gazes only at the ground. Whence He who discerns all strikes you."** <note>original Italian: *Chiamaui al ciel: e intorno vi si gira mostrādouxu le sue bellezze eterne ma lochio vostro pur a terra mira. Vnde ui batte chi tutto discerne.*</note> By this, therefore, the appetite governs and preserves reason so that it no longer considers the things of heaven, but stays upon the earth and acts upon the earth in dense shadows and most horrific obscurity. Master Francesco himself approves this worthy sentence in that sonnet, **"Gluttony, and sleep,"** <note>Petrarch’s Sonnet 7: *La gola e 'l sonno e l'oziose piume*.</note> when he says: **"And every kind light from heaven is extinguished, through which human life is shaped."** <note>original Italian: *ET ESSI spento ogni benigno lume Del ciel p cui sin forma humana uita.*</note> Whereupon, fittingly after his silent confession and self-accusation, Master Francesco writes that he recognized the spirit because he was shaped like him, according to the sentence of **Seneca** in his tragedies, which says: **"He who is ashamed of having sinned is almost innocent."** <note>original Latin: *Que pænite peccasse pene est inocens.* From Seneca's *Agamemnon*.</note> Therefore, out of this respect, they sat down together.

<margin>O</margin> The shadow <note>term: shadow <gloss>ombra</gloss> — a common term in Renaissance literature for the spirit or soul of a deceased person.</note> began to speak in this manner to Master Francesco: "When I considered in times past the disposition of your works and your condition, I judged for certain that you ought to be among us; for your appearance provided an infallible omen even from your tender years and your youth." To these words the poet adds that he replied it was true, and that his actions showed it from the beginning; it would indeed have followed, except that the "amorous troubles" frightened him so much that he left the arduous and difficult undertaking—for which, however little time it lasted, he still carried his chest and clothes bitterly torn. Nevertheless, some texts are found in which it is written that the *shadow* carries his chest and clothes torn, directing these words to that spirit rather than saying them regarding himself—an interpretation that seems appropriate to me. And therefore Master Francesco adds that, having heard that shadow’s fated reproach of his amorous struggles (or rather the great complaint of his first Cupid-like assault), according to the texts, the spirit followed by saying: **"O my son, what flame is lit?"** Master Francesco adds these words because he did not understand them then; but later they were fixed so firmly in his head that certainly no letters were ever carved in marble of greater or more lasting solidity. Whence he says:

> And he began: "It is a long time that I thought
> I would see you here among us, for from your early years
> Your look gave such a presage of you.
> And it was quite true; but the amorous troubles
> Frightened me so, that I left the enterprise:
> But I carry my chest and clothes torn."
> Thus I spoke: and he, when he had heard
> My answer, said smilingly:
> "O my son, what a flame is lit for you!"
> I did not understand it then; but now so fixed
> Do I find his words in my head,
> That never was anything written more firmly in marble.

<margin>P</margin> Now that the shadow has expressed to Master Francesco a kind of silent prophecy of the love that would overcome him, he adds how he was stirred by the novelty of the sight of the triumph. Whence the mind becomes ready and prepared to understand it, and the tongue swift as its servant; he asked who this was who triumphed, and who were the people following him in the triumph. Some texts are also found that say "but because of the new age, which is bold and ready, it makes the tongue and the mind"—a sentence that is still tolerated. For as the tender age of youth is inexperienced, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> says in the first book of the *Ethics*, and since every man naturally desires to learn, as is written at the beginning of the *Metaphysics*, for this reason young people have tongues ready to ask, and the

## CHAPTER THREE ##

<margin>Q</margin>
The mind is naturally inclined to attend to and learn unusual things. The shadow therefore responded to the question of Master Francesco <note>Messer Francesco: Petrarch, the author of the poem.</note> by saying that within a short space of time he would understand it for himself through the operation or arrangement of the "knot" which was being prepared: and to which he was to be tightly bound. This knot was of such a nature that he would sooner change the color of his hair than have that bond ever loosened from his free neck or from his feet, which until then had been rebels against the progress of love. However, to satisfy his request, the shadow adds that he is content to say who they were. And first, he speaks of the triumphant one, the greatest of all: he who, as we see, strips others of their liberty and life. Thus he says:

> And because of my youth, bold and quick,
> Between my mind and tongue I asked him:
> "Tell me, by your courtesy, what people are these?"
> "In a short time you yourself shall know,"
> He replied, "and you shall be one of them;
> Such a knot is being made for you, and you know it not.
> And sooner shall you change your face and hair
> Than the knot of which I speak shall be untied
> From your neck and from your feet, still rebellious.
> But to fulfill your youthful desire,
> I will tell of us, and first of the greatest,
> Who thus strips us of life and liberty."

<margin>R</margin>
As we said above, it is not without great and artful judgment that our poet describes himself at that time as not recognizing this triumphant one or his company. He introduces the shadow to prophesy that in a short time he will know it clearly for himself. This is because, naturally, as Livy writes in the second Punic War: **"Human minds are prone to lightening their own guilt."** <note>original Latin: *Ingenia humana sunt ad cuique leuandā culpam.*</note> Because of this, whenever a man is entangled in some obscenity, he attends with great diligence to the errors of other men; he thinks that by comparing himself to those who are more vicious than he is, he can not only excuse himself but even be praised. This follows the sentiment of the most holy Jerome, who speaks on this subject in this form:

<margin>S</margin>
**"It is the mark of quite low men, seeking their own praise, to make others seem low; for they think they are praised by the disparagement of others. And because they cannot please by their own merit, they wish to please by comparison to those who are worse."** <note>original Latin: *Viliū satis boiū est suā laudē querentiū alios viles facerē: qm aliorū uituperatione se laudari putant. Et qm pprio merito placere non possunt: placere uolunt in cōparatione peiorū.*</note> Therefore, whenever a man subdues his appetite to reason, he is free to attend to the understanding of worthy objects and of grave and serious things. According to what reason leads us to, he abandons the actions of those who are not conformed to this state. But those who, on the contrary, are conquered and overcome by their sensory appetite, only intend to recognize those who are stained with a similar mark, so that by such an example they can excuse their own errors, believing it to be enough for them. This verifies that sentence of Tully <note>Cicero</note> in the first book of *On Duties* which says: **"For it happens, I know not how, that we see more in others than in ourselves if any fault is committed."** <note>original Latin: *Fit enim nescio quō ut magis in alijs quā nobismetipsis cernamus: si qd delinqtur.*</note> And because Master Francesco had been, in the age of his adolescence up until the day he fell in love, always given to speculative works <note>Intellectual or philosophical study.</note>, and imagining himself at this time to have seen this vision, he appropriately affirms that he did not yet recognize love in the fleshly appetite. Thus, the shadow appropriately begins to reveal the triumphant Love to him in this form, saying: "Master Francesco, this powerful youth and most excellent leader is harsh and bitter as you can perceive, but you will understand it much better when he is lord over you, just as he is at present over us." He calls the method "love," which in its appearance is a gentle child, but over a span of time it casts away all pleasantness and becomes a fierce and <unclear>most dismal</unclear> old man. Alas, he who tries it and has been pierced by it knows it, and you yourself shall know it before a thousand years have passed, though I announce it to you even now. Thus he says:

> "This is he whom the world calls Love;
> Bitter as you see, and you shall see better
> When he shall be your lord, as he is ours:
> A gentle child, and a fierce old man.
> He knows it well who tries it; and let it be clear to you
> Before a thousand years; even now I wake you to it."

<margin>T</margin>
It is a true and ready opinion that Love is only called and known "by the world." It should be noted that among authors, especially in the Gospel text, men given to bodily delights are often denoted by the term "the world." Thus it is written in the first chapter of John: **"He was in the world, and the world knew him not."** <note>original Latin: *In mundo erat & mundus eum non cognouit.*</note> And this happens...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s *Triumph of Love*, specifically interpreting the lines describing the nature and origin of Love. # THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE #

<margin>X</margin> ¶ This occurs because some people possess such little intelligence that they do not admit anything exists which cannot be grasped by our five external senses. And for this reason, feeding only on the things of the world, they are deservedly named by him [Love]; these, then, are those who know love more than others. And therefore he adds the origin of its birth, saying it was born of idleness and nourished by human lust, and then maintained by the sweetness and suavity of thoughts: finally deified by foolish and vain people. In this canonization, some are killed by him, while others—under the gravest laws and held by a thousand chains and a thousand keys of indissoluble concupiscence <term>concupiscence: an intense worldly or sexual desire that distracts from the spiritual</term>—lead their lives with the greatest harshness and most cruel bitterness. Hence he says:

<margin>¶</margin> ¶ For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, one must know that according to the sentiment of Job in the second chapter, and of the Philosopher <note>The Philosopher: Aristotle, the standard academic reference of the time.</note> in the progression of the first book of the *Politics*: just as every animal is produced for some proper function, so also man is naturally produced for exercise and labor. Hence Job says: "For a bird is known for flight, but man for labor" <note>original Latin: *Auis enim ad volatum scitur: hō autē ad laborem*</note>. Conforming to this sentiment is that of Genesis in the third chapter, when after the ruin and fall of our first ancestors, God said to Adam: "In the sweat of your face shall you eat your bread" <note>original Latin: *In sudore vultus tui vesceris pane tuo*</note>. Since man can justly exercise himself in two ways—one with the mind alone, the other with both mind and body—they define two types of life: one called the contemplative life and the other the active life; one given only to mental exercise and the other to physical, as is written at the beginning of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note>. Therefore, whenever the perverse order of human actions distracts man and he deviates from his nature, giving himself over to idleness—especially of the intellect when it is not exercised in the knowledge of things (from which our happiness follows)—lustful desire is derived and born from that very laziness, which by men is called and named "Love."

<margin>y</margin> ¶ It is then nourished by the sweetness and suavity of thoughts: because whenever something occurs that offers sadness to the soul, or is necessary for the sustenance of human life—as it is the natural desire of every created thing to perpetuate itself as much as it can, as is written in the first book of the *Physics* <note>Aristotle's *Physics*.</note>—it is therefore necessary to act in a suitable way to drive away the soul's distress and acquire the daily necessities of life. Because of this, the mind ceases to focus on such a goal [Love]; thus Ovid wrote in the book *The Remedy of Love* <note>original: *Remedia Amoris*</note> that the prohibition of idleness and the scarcity of food were among the remedies to be used against love. Hence Crates of Thebes, a clear and distinguished philosopher, often used to say on this subject, as Laertius wrote: "Hunger settles love" <note>original Latin: *Amorem sedat fames*</note>. And because sometimes men do not wish to use their strength to resist such delightful incentives, almost as if judging this a sufficient excuse for their errors, they said love was a divine fury <term>divine fury: the idea that love is an irresistible madness sent by the gods, used here as a critique of those who refuse to control their passions</term> which could not be resisted by men, as Seneca clearly writes in the eighth tragedy (which is the ninth in order). Hence he says:

# CHAPTER ONE

"The sting of death is sin." <note>original Latin: *Stimulus aut mortis pctm̃ est*. A variation on 1 Corinthians 15:56: "The sting of death is sin."</note> This, then, is that which—through a thousand hardships and bitternesses—leads wretched mortals always with tears and lamentations to their final breath, under an infinite number of perilous and most certain adversities. Regarding this, Plautus <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BC) was a Roman playwright famous for his comedies.</note> appropriately wrote in his comedy *Asinaria*: "O Theban, how wretched is the man who loves!" <note>original: *O tibane vt miser est hō qui amat*</note>. And in another comedy called *Curculio*, he said: "One must go where ungrateful love commands" <note>original: *Eundū est quo īperat ingratus amor*</note>; and a little further below: "Clandestine love is an evil; it is pure loss" <note>original: *Malū est clandestinū amor: dānū autē merum*</note>. Most excellently, then, our poet <note>Petrarch</note> describes how love leads men under the heaviest hardships, and even kills them by placing them in a state which ought to be chosen far less than the death of the body, according to the Gospel sentiment of Matthew in the tenth chapter. This passage, testifying to Christ speaking to the disciples, says: "Do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can send both soul and body into Gehenna" <note>original: *Nolite timere eos qui occidūt corpus: aiām autē non possunt occidere: sed potiꝰ timete eū qui potest aiām: & corpus mittere in gehennā* (Matthew 10:28).</note>. This also follows the sentiment of the Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that emphasized virtue and rationality over emotion.</note> which Augustine relates in the ninth book of the *City of God*, saying: "The Stoics say it is worse to lose those things by which the nature of the body is kept safe and sound, than to commit those things by which justice is violated" <note>original: *Stoici male se dicunt hæc amittere: quibus natura corporis salua: & incolumis habetur: quā illa cōmittere: quibus iusticia violatur.*</note>. This is nothing other than sin, which is generated and committed only through the dominion of the <term>sensory appetite</term> <note>the part of the human psyche driven by physical feelings and desires rather than reason</note> over reason, when accessory and instrumental things are desired as if they were the primary goals. Hence Augustine, in his *Book of Eighty-Three Questions*, defining sin, said: "Sin is to use what should be enjoyed, and to enjoy what should be used" <note>original: *Peccatū est vti fruendis & vtēdis frui*. St. Augustine argues we should "enjoy" God but "use" the world to get to Him; sin flips this order.</note>. In this definition, it is clearly understood that just as the soul is the end goal of the body—as is written in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's *De Anima*</note> and the seventh book of the *Politics*—and the body itself is ordered toward the soul, so too must bodily pleasures be such that the soul directs them toward the objects established for it according to its two primary universal powers: namely, the intellect and the will. The first of these is directed toward the Highest Truth, and the other toward the Highest Good. When these are attained, the soul finds itself at its ultimate end and rest, which is its highest and naturally desired happiness. Now, since <term>Messer Francesco</term> <note>Petrarch</note> has described through the report of the shade who this triumphant figure is, he consequently brings forward the examples of those men who were conquered by such appetite, submitting their reason and its use to it. The first of these he sets down as Julius Caesar: who, although he had performed many most glorious works for the Roman Republic, was nonetheless forced in Egypt by the lusts of Cleopatra to postpone every duty to take carnal delight in her. For this reason, he adds that it is fitting to write that Caesar was conquered, even though he had been the ruler of the world; because, just as he had received glory from those whom he had conquered, so should the glory belong to the one who was the victor over him. Whence he says:

The desire to reign caused [Cleopatra] to be poisoned in a short time. After she died, through the work of Pompey, her other brother Ptolemy was substituted. | <margin>C</margin> For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, one should know that among the Romans there were two ways to acquire sons. One was through natural propagation—an act most natural above all others, as is written in the second book *On the Soul* <note>original Latin: *de aīa*—referring to Aristotle's treatise *De Anima*.</note>. The other way is through adoption, which, according to the opinion of Gellius in the fifth book of *Attic Nights* <note>original Latin: *noctibus Atticis*—Aulus Gellius (c. 125 – after 180 AD) was a Roman author known for this compilation of diverse notes on grammar, philosophy, and history.</note>, is declared to occur when, with the authority of the praetor interposed, the one adopting pronounces the adopted one to be his son, with the natural father consenting. If the natural father were already dead, this pronouncement is called "arrogation" <note>A legal process in Rome for adopting someone who was not under the authority of a father (sui iuris).</note> rather than adoption. Octavian, then, was the son of Julius Caesar not by nature but only by adoption; for by his ancient ancestry, he was a citizen of Velletri and the son of Gaius Octavius. Therefore, after the death of Caesar, being appointed his heir and having agreed with Mark Antony to take vengeance on his adoptive father, he drove Brutus and Cassius (the killers of Caesar) to a desperate death. Then, having come into dissension with Antony and having defeated him, he held the empire of Rome alone. <br><br> <margin>A</margin> While in power, Octavian loved various women. Although he could have obtained her by force, he did not wish to use it. Instead, turning to prayers and offering them humbly to Tiberius, he finally obtained his dear Livia, whom he joined to himself as his legitimate wife. Next, Master Francesco adds the third example: Domitius Nero. Although he was a most cruel man—as our poet <note>Petrarch</note> shows, and even more clearly Cornelius Tacitus—he was nonetheless also driven by the carnal appetite for women. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the Roman emperors and famous figures in Petrarch’s "Triumph of Love." Following the discussion of Nero, the text moves to Marcus Aurelius (referred to here as Antoninus), his wife Faustina, and later to the Greek tyrants Dionysius and Alexander.</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

I know of the doctor who was put to death so that Faustina’s body could be bathed in his blood, through which she was first restored to health. <note>This refers to a legendary medical treatment for Faustina the Younger, wife of Marcus Aurelius, who was said to be infatuated with a gladiator; the "cure" supposedly involved bathing in the gladiator's blood.</note> Nevertheless, the son born afterward to Faustina was Commodus Antoninus, who demonstrated by his dishonorable behavior that she had committed adultery, as he was far more similar to a gladiator in his character and deeds than to Antoninus Pius. <note>Marcus Aurelius is frequently called "Antoninus" or "Antoninus Pius" in medieval and Renaissance texts, though he was the adopted son of the original Antoninus Pius.</note> Although Antoninus was often urged to separate from Faustina, it is believed that because of the immense benevolence he felt for her, he responded in this way: that when women are separated, their dowries must be returned—and Faustina’s dowry was the Roman Empire. <note>A famous historical anecdote: since Marcus Aurelius gained his claim to the throne through his marriage to the daughter of the previous emperor, divorcing her would symbolically mean returning the Empire itself.</note>

<margin>H</margin>
He demonstrated this same benevolence after her death. For while Antoninus was traveling through the Roman Republic to face the kings of the East, and while Faustina was in Cilicia at the foot of Mount Taurus in a place called Halala, she died. Hearing of this, Antoninus suffered the greatest grief. In praise of Faustina, he prayed to the Senate—who had previously decreed her the title of **Augusta**—that they should deify her and count her among the divine. The Senate likewise condescended to do this to please Antoninus. Secondly, to resolve the contradiction that seems inserted into these verses—namely, how Antoninus could be a philosopher and yet <term>incontinent</term> <note>original: "incontinente" — here meaning lacking self-control over his passions or love.</note>—it must be known that just as our life is divided into the active and the contemplative, so too is **philosophy** divided into **active** and **contemplative**. In the case of contemplative philosophy, there is no contradiction if the appetite is depraved, because speculative science only concerns the perfection of the intellect and not the will. However, active philosophy cannot be compatible with a malicious will, because it was instituted solely to keep the will perfect. Thus, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> says at the beginning of the second book of the *Ethics*: *Since, then, the present work is not for the sake of contemplation, like the others—for we are not studying so that we might know what virtue is (since then there would be no utility in it), but so that we might become good—it is necessary to look at actions and how they ought to be performed.* <note>original: "Cum igitur præsens opus..." from Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note> And in the first book, speaking of what the disposition and quality of a listener of moral philosophy should be, he says for our purpose: *But he who still follows his passions will hear such discourses in vain and without profit. For the end is not knowledge, but action.* <note>original: "Qui uero adhuc..." from Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note> Therefore, although Marcus Antoninus Pius was a philosopher by nature and most learned, he was nonetheless overcome by carnal appetite. And if anyone else should say that the poet described Antoninus as a moral philosopher—which he seems to show when he says that not only his tongue but his breast was full of philosophy (which denotes the source of his actions)—the answer is that the practical habit of moral philosophy can exist without the action, but one cannot be called a **perfect philosopher** because of it, as perfection requires not just the habit but the work that derives from it. This is what happened to Antoninus when he looked upon his Faustina with too much delight.

Consequently, our poet narrates two other examples as great arguments for how much infirmity exists in our souls, saying that after Marcus Antoninus followed two timid and suspicious tyrants: namely, **Dionysius of Syracuse** and **Alexander of Pherae**. He affirms, however, that the former received a fitting satisfaction and result from his great and unreasonable fear. Thus he says:

<margin>I</margin>
<insert>
-> Those two full of fear and suspicion, <-
-> One is Dionysius, and the other is Alexander; <-
-> But that one’s fear brings a worthy effect. <-
</insert>

It is a very great misery and a low state indeed when men, through disordered greed, make themselves more like brute animals than maintaining their manly and worthy nature. Just as they were deprived of such excellence by immoderate appetite, so were these two aforementioned tyrants. Being entirely subjected to the unregulated desire to rule—where they could have been free lords by ruling justly—they instead constrained themselves into a prison, becoming much worse than slaves. As Cicero writes in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations* and the second book of *On Duties*, Dionysius of Syracuse was a man of sharp and industrious intellect, moderate in his daily food and wine, but by nature unjust and malignant. Although he was born of honorable parents and had many relatives and attendants, he seized dominion over the Syracusans. Furthermore, because he did not trust public spaces, he granted audiences only from a small tower, and from that same spot, he conducted the business of his kingdom. He also had two daughters; while they were young, he had them shave him. But when they reached adulthood, he did not trust them to shave him with a blade. He only permitted them to "shave" him using glowing coals. <note>Dionysius I of Syracuse was famously paranoid; the detail about his daughters using hot nutshells or coals to singe his beard appears in Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*.</note> However, his love was directed toward many objects, yet it was never firm because of his fear. For according to the Greek custom, he was defiled by the shameful venereal delight of youths. In the seventh book of the *Ethics*, <note>original: "septimo de Lethica" referring to Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*</note> this is shown to be against divine, human, natural, and political law. In this love, fear was more powerful than pleasure. For one day, while playing ball, he gave his knife and cloak to his most beloved youth to hold. Another member of the household jokingly said to Dionysius that he had entrusted his life to the boy. The youth laughed at these words. Because of this, Dionysius had both of them beheaded. Yet, he afterward bore the death of his beloved page so impatiently that he wished to die without remedy. He also loved two other women: one named Aristomache of Syracuse, the other Doris of Locris. Nevertheless, whenever he wished to join one of them at night, he would not lie down until he had searched the entire room to see if anyone was hidden there. 

Just how much "delight" and "joy" he truly had, he demonstrated to his close friend Damocles. Dionysius placed Damocles in his own seat so that he might experience the falsely believed sweetness of power. While Damocles was positioned in the tyrant's place at the table, surrounded by all the apparent luxuries, Dionysius had a shining and sharp sword tied above his head, held only by a single thin horsehair. <note>This is the famous "Sword of Damocles" anecdote, illustrating that a ruler lives in constant mortal peril.</note> When Damocles saw this sword, he renounced the position and begged Dionysius for permission to leave, well understanding how dear and great the anxiety is in the souls of those who rule unjustly. Thus, with more mature judgment, he preferred a private life of peace and quiet over any public office. 

Alexander of Pherae was constrained by a similar or even more beastly fear. Though he ardently loved Thebe, his dear and lawful wife, he would never go to bed with her until he had sent men to search her jewel boxes to see if anything was inside. Likewise, he tried to see if she was carrying a blade on her person with which she might harm him. He even had an armed barbarian walk before him—a man who bore the "stigmata" or marks of excessive vice and infidelity. After a long time, the woman could no longer tolerate these beastly actions and unheard-of cowardice, and she ultimately had him killed—a reward, without a doubt, suited to the effects of such fear. 

Next to these figures, our poet <note>Petrarch</note> recounts the story of the great Trojan Aeneas, who, after the fall of Troy, wept for the death of his wife Creusa, the daughter of Priam, beneath the rock of Antandros. He could not otherwise fulfill his duty to her with funeral rites in Troy, as she had vanished in the ruins, as Virgil writes. When Aeneas departed with his father Anchises and his son Ascanius, he later arrived in Italy and took the love intended for Turnus—namely Lavinia, the daughter of Latinus, King of the Latins. This same Turnus took the life of Pallas, the son of Evander. <note>In the *Aeneid*, Pallas is the young prince whose death at the hands of Turnus leads to Aeneas's final vengeful duel.</note> Evander had been the king of Arcadia first, and then of that part of Italy where the city of Rome stands today. He had come to live there at the persuasion of his mother Nicostrata, after having killed his father in Arcadia.

After he had wandered for about seven years through various seas, he finally arrived at the mouth of the Tiber. There, in that place, he was graciously received and welcomed by Evander, the king of that country. Since Evander had a son named Pallas, who was of a generous and magnificent spirit, he formed a singular friendship with Aeneas at this time. 

Now, King Latinus, king of the Latins—persuaded by his wife Amata, although others say it was Pallas’s daughter Pallantia—had promised his daughter Lavinia in marriage to Turnus, the son of Daunus, king of the Rutulians. It happened that a swarm of bees settled upon a laurel tree which stood above the tower of Laurentum, the city and capital of Latinus's kingdom. Seeing this, Latinus asked the augurs <note>priests who interpreted the will of the gods through signs</note> what such an event was meant to signify. They replied that this demonstrated the will of the gods: that a son-in-law of a foreign nation would arrive, and his name would spread as far as the ocean. Because of this, they advised him to abstain from giving Lavinia to Turnus as a wife. 

Latinus, having understood their answer, went to the oracle of Faunus, his father, to perform a sacrifice and ask further about the augury. Faunus replied in the same manner: that he should abstain from the marriage with Turnus and wait for his fated <note>original: "fatale," meaning destined by the Fates</note> son-in-law. Latinus returned to the palace, and while he was reflecting on the answer he had received, the ambassadors of Aeneas reached him, asking on his behalf for peace and safe passage. Latinus understood their embassy and asked about their origin. Having considered their condition and well-remembering the entire augury, he replied that he was not only content to grant the things they asked, but beyond that—insofar as it might please him—he wished to enter into an alliance with Aeneas and give him his daughter Lavinia as a wife. Aeneas accepted this offer, and thus it followed: because of this, Turnus, feeling himself bitterly insulted, moved a great war against Latinus and Aeneas. In this war, because of the friendship already contracted between Aeneas and Evander, Pallas came to the aid of Aeneas against Turnus. One day, while proceeding to battle, this Pallas was attacked and killed by Turnus. Therefore, Aeneas took Turnus’s love from him by taking Lavinia, whom Turnus intensely loved; and Turnus took Evander’s son by killing Pallas in the battle, who was Evander’s most beloved child.

<header>CHAPTER ONE</header>

# CHAPTER ONE

The people of Megara one day through deceit killed Androgeus <note>the son of King Minos of Crete</note>; when this was understood, his father Minos was moved to great anger and resolved to take full revenge for his son. Therefore, having gathered his armies and proceeded against them with a heavy siege, he conquered both peoples in a short time. Now, while Minos was maintaining the siege, his wife Pasiphae fell into such bestial nature—as Ovid writes—that she fell in love with a bull without any restraint. Determined to have her union with it, she sent for Daedalus, who in those times was a most ingenious craftsman, and explained her desire to him. Daedalus fashioned a wooden cow similar to one that the bull in the herds seemed most inclined to follow. Then, he killed that cow and stretched its hide over the wooden one, and inside he enclosed Pasiphae; in this way, he induced the bull to satisfy her bestial and immoderate lust. From this it followed that Pasiphae became pregnant and, in time, gave birth to the ferocious monster known as the Minotaur. 

Having learned of this outcome, Minos had the same Daedalus build the Labyrinth, where he shut the Minotaur away. For this reason, among the other laws imposed after his victory over the Athenians and Megarians, the heavy conditions of peace required that at certain times they had to send a man to the Minotaur to be devoured by him. When these people heard the harsh and bitter law imposed upon them, they decided to proceed by lot to the election of the one who was to be the food of the Minotaur. It so happened that once the lot fell upon Theseus; because of this, he was fully prepared to fulfill the bitterness of the law. He arrived in Crete and presented himself to Minos. 

Minos had two very beautiful daughters: one named Ariadne, the other Phaedra. Because Ariadne was the elder, and having seen that Theseus had a most beautiful body, she immediately fell in love with him. Therefore, having arranged to speak with him in secret, she agreed with him to save him from the Minotaur if he would take her as his wife and marry her sister Phaedra to Hippolytus; to which Theseus consented. Thus it happened that Ariadne taught him how to overcome the Minotaur and also how to exit the Labyrinth. Theseus then killed the Minotaur, and returning with victory to Athens, he took Ariadne and Phaedra with him. 

But having arrived on the journey at the island of Chios—as Ovid testifies—or Naxos—as Lactantius writes—he left Ariadne there while she was asleep and departed with Phaedra. Once he arrived in Athens, he took Phaedra as his legitimate wife. Later, he accompanied his most singular friend Pirithous into the underworld to recover Proserpina. In his absence, Phaedra fell in love with Hippolytus <note>her stepson</note> and, being in love, she requested carnal union with him. Hippolytus, as reason dictated, refused her. Because of this, Phaedra at that time turned all her benevolence into the most cruel hatred toward Hippolytus. When Theseus returned to Athens, she first accused Hippolytus to Theseus, saying that he had wanted to violate her. Upon this report, the infuriated Theseus drove him away into exile, doing everything to ensure he would die. Afterward, because of his departure, Phaedra felt such grief that she killed herself with Hippolytus's own sword—or she hanged herself, as Servius testifies. And truly, she took worthy revenge on Hippolytus, whom she caused to stay wrongly in exile; and on Theseus, whom she made the minister of his own grief; and on her sister Ariadne, whom she deceived by taking away her husband.

<margin>P</margin>
¶ Afterward, our worthy poet interposes a most just and excellent sentiment regarding the false accusation made by Phaedra against the most chaste Hippolytus, saying that it often happens that men, in accusing and blaming others, condemn themselves. And besides this, he adds that he who takes delight in deceiving others should not complain if he then suffers the same from others. Hence he says: 
->He blames another who condemns himself;<-
->And he who takes delight in practicing fraud,<-
->Must not lament if another deceives him.<-

<margin>Q</margin>
¶ It is a fitting thing that any law, whether natural or written, be common not only to those who are subjects but also to the prince, he being defined as the living law <note>original Latin: "lex animata"</note> and the guardian of justice. Just as it is written in the fifth book of the *Ethics* <note>referring to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics</note>, and because every man is the prince of his own works and especially of his own judgment; for this reason, the first law and rubric <term>Digest: quod quisque iuris</term> <note>a Roman law principle stating that a person should be bound by the same law they apply to others</note> obliges everyone to that same sentence by which he judged anyone else should be bound.

<margin>R</margin>
¶ Wherefore, regarding this, Cicero most excellently admonishes us in the *Tusculan Disputations*, wishing to demonstrate how great an error it is to rebuke another for one's own vice, saying: "For it is the property of folly to see the vices of others and forget one's own" <note>original: "Proprium enim stultiti est aliorum vicia cernere suorum obliuisci"</note>. Therefore, returning to the example of our poet, the malignant Phaedra was worthily accusing herself when she was blaming Hippolytus to Theseus. One can also see through these same verses how the poet reproves Ariadne, and in what way he responds to the great lament which she made on the island of Chios after she woke and no longer saw Theseus, saying that she wrongly complained of having been deceived by Theseus, since she herself had defrauded Minos and procured the death of her brother, the Minotaur.

->Petra. BB<-

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch's *Triumph of Love*, moving from the backstory of the Minotaur to the specific figures of Theseus and Hercules as examples of great men conquered by passion.</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

<margin>Q</margin> ¶ Next, My Master Francesco <note>The author refers to the poet Francesco Petrarch</note> introduces the example of Theseus by bringing his shadow forward to show him to us. He says: behold the "famous one," that is, Theseus, who, despite all the many praises attributed to him, is led captive between two sisters—namely Phaedra and Ariadne. They are truly "dead" in the fire of concupiscence <note>intense sexual desire</note>. One of them "enjoys him," namely Ariadne, who fell in love with him first; and he "enjoys the other," namely Phaedra, whom he took as his lawful wife after leaving Ariadne. Thus the poem says:

> I saw the famous one with so many of his praises
> ->Led captive between two dead sisters,<-
> ->One enjoys him, and he enjoys the other.<-

<margin>R</margin> ¶ For the understanding of the preceding verses, one must know this place primarily because the poet calls Theseus "famous." Because of his supreme and singular virtues, he deserved to be numbered among the "Herculeses" <note>a term used here to mean "great heroes"</note>. Indeed, he neglected nothing through which a man might achieve praise or fame; there was nothing he did not attempt, and no attempt that did not yield a good result. Thus, first, together with Hercules and by the command of King Eurystheus, he overcame Oreithyia and Antiope, queens of the Amazons—a victory that was certainly bloody and glorious in that time. Secondly, he extinguished the immense pride of King Creon of Thebes, who forbade the burial due to the dead bodies in the cruel battle of Eteocles and Polynices; this deed was truly to be judged religious and pious. Thirdly, he overcame the most ferocious bull sent by Eurystheus to the fields of Marathon, which was disturbing the land of Attica and bringing it almost to ruin. He killed Sciron and Procrustes, bandits who forced their prisoners upon a rock to worship them, or rather to wash their feet while they were intent on the task; not realizing his great treachery, he would suddenly cast them into the sea. He abducted Helen. He killed the Minotaur. He accompanied Pirithous to the underworld. Finally, he peacefully brought the Athenians, who were dispersed in many places, back to Athens. Ultimately, having driven away Hippolytus in anger and fury solely based on the simple report of Phaedra—and Hippolytus, being much loved by the Athenians, was sent into exile for his own revenge, where he died miserably—it therefore seems that the text of the second verse is more appropriate when it says: *Led captive between two sisters in death.* For after Ariadne's departure, who wept and lamented loudly, it happened by chance that on that day Bacchus, the son of Jove, passed by that island. Seeing such lamentation, he approached the shore and saw Ariadne crying; moved to compassion for her, he took her with him and took her as his wife. She outlived Theseus and saw his exile and his death, which was a singular joy for her as a matter of revenge; just as Theseus similarly made himself glad at the death of Phaedra for his revenge, and that of Hippolytus, after she confessed her error to him. Thus, Theseus was led captive between two sisters "in death": one enjoys him, namely Ariadne, who saw him forced to die in exile; and he enjoys Phaedra, who, by killing herself, avenged the double injury against him.

There are nonetheless some other texts that say: *Behold the famous one with his many praises / Led captive between two wan sisters / And he enjoys the one and the other / He who is with him is that powerful Hercules.* In this version, it is not necessary to understand Ariadne and Phaedra as the two sisters, but rather Hippolyta and Menalippe, sisters of Queen Oreithyia. The poet appropriately calls them "wan" <note>original: "smorte," meaning pale or deathly-looking</note> to show the exercise of arms in which the Amazons uniquely practiced. Reasonably, from this exertion, a mortification of color <note>paleness</note> comes to the face. This interpretation is consistent with the one found in the *Triumph of Fame* when My Master Francesco says of Menalippe and the others that "to conquer them was glory to the great Alcides <note>another name for Hercules</note>; for one had the one sister, and Theseus the other." For this reason, it is clearly shown that according to the diversity of the texts, the passage can be explained in different ways. 

And not without reason, our worthy poet, continuing according to the first and more common text, adds the example of the most mighty Hercules after Theseus. There was never any physical labor so great or difficult that Hercules did not overcome it in the first encounters. Yet he was conquered and subjugated solely by the sensory appetite of love. The poet says that "he who was fierce"—that is, with Theseus—was that fierce and powerful Hercules whom Love captured; and certainly, it was a great marvel. Thus he says:

> He who is with him is that powerful and strong
> ->Hercules, whom love captured,<-

<margin>T</margin> ¶ It is difficult knowledge to know who Hercules properly was, because "Hercules" does not signify the identity of one man, but is a surname <note>or title</note>; for whoever performed...
