<header>CHAPTER ONE</header>

# CHAPTER ONE

¶ Because he possessed a certain great strength, he was called Hercules, which in the Greek language means "robust" <note>original: *robusto*; the etymology links the name Herakles to strength or the glory of Hera</note>. According to Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar</note>, there were three men surnamed Hercules: the Theban, the Argive, and the Libyan. But the one who is most well-known above all others was the Theban, the son of Jove and Alcmene, the wife of Amphitryon. As Plautus writes in his first comedy <note>The play *Amphitruo*</note>, he introduces Amphitryon having gone out against the Teleboans to avenge the death of his father-in-law's brother; Jove took on his form, and Mercury took that of his servant Sosia, and Jove lay with Alcmene by means of this deception.
<margin>V</margin>
¶ This Hercules first fell in love with Deianira, daughter of Oeneus, King of Calydon. Since she had been promised as a wife to Achelous, the river-god of Calydon, Hercules, driven by her beauty and by love, fought with Achelous. As Ovid writes, Hercules first overcame him in human form; then, when Achelous turned into a serpent; and finally, when he became a bull. Because of this, Hercules became the husband of Deianira, his beloved mistress. Secondly, Hercules loved Iole, the daughter of Eurytus, the excellent King of Oechalia. He was driven to love her so ardently and without measure that, laying aside all his ferocity and leaving behind the glorious trophy of the Nemean lion's skin, and even abandoning his most powerful club, he stood in the midst of the royal maidens to divide and distribute the wool among them and spin with them. Omphale of Lydia also brought him back to this same lowly exercise. Therefore, love rightly took and bound him, and partially obscured his fame in the chapter on famous men. Next, the poet brings forward Achilles, the son of Peleus, King of Thessaly <note>The text says Etholia, likely a scribal error for Thessalia</note>, and of the nymph Thetis, or water goddess, saying that the other was Achilles,
<margin>X</margin>
who, following love, had many doubtful and dangerous outcomes. Thus he says:

<margin>To understand the loves of Achilles, which Master Francesco commemorates in these verses, it is primarily to be known that Thetis, wife of Peleus, was his mother.</margin>
->And the other is Achilles,<-
->Who had in his love a very sorrowful fate.<-

As one of the water goddesses and the daughter of Nereo the sea god, Thetis had long foreseen the abduction of Helen that would be carried out by Paris, and that this would stir up a war between the Greeks and the Trojans. She saw that if her son Achilles went there, he was destined to die. For this reason, she dressed him in female clothing and sent him into the care of King Lycomedes to live among his daughters. It happened that the King, seeing him as a very pleasing girl, made him sleep with Deidamia, his most noble daughter, assuming Achilles was a maiden. From this, natural appetite led them to take amorous pleasure in one another, and they were intensely compelled to love. Through this kindness and amorous intimacy, Deidamia became pregnant by Achilles and in time gave birth to Neoptolemus, who was later surnamed Pyrrhus. 

When the Trojan War subsequently followed, the Greeks learned from the oracles that Troy could not be taken without the presence of Achilles. They searched for him diligently, and having finally been found by Ulysses, he proceeded with the others to the siege of Troy. There he loved Briseis, who had fallen to him as his share of the spoils. When Chryseis, the prize of Agamemnon, was returned to her father because of the prophecy of the priest Calchas—with Achilles and the other Greeks insisting on this—the indignant Agamemnon took his beloved Briseis away from Achilles. Achilles was moved to such anger and disdain by this that he no longer wished to take up arms against the Trojans. He persisted in this hardness and obstinacy until Patroclus, his unique and most beloved friend, was killed in battle by Hector. Then, because of this death, Achilles continued the fight and killed the most mighty Hector in battle. 

Later, a truce occurred between the Greeks and the Trojans. Achilles went into Troy to the temple where the funeral rites for Hector were being performed. There he saw Polyxena, a most beautiful maiden and the sister of Hector, who was weeping bitterly. Achilles fell in love with her and made his desire known to her mother, Hecuba, promising her the removal of the siege of Troy if she would give him Polyxena as a wife. While he was in the grip of this love, it happened that, departing from his purpose of not fighting, he one day killed Troilus in the Trojan battle, who was the son of Priam and Hecuba, and the brother of Polyxena. For this reason, Hecuba, planning to avenge her two sons, sent word to Achilles that he should come to her, as she wished to grant him Polyxena. Achilles, having heard the message, was more incited by his extreme love than restrained by true reason. Immediately, without armor and without company except for his sword and Antilochus, the son of Nestor, he went into Troy. When they arrived at the temple of Apollo, they were eventually cut down and cruelly killed by Paris. And thus the unhappy Achilles experienced the harsh fate of love. 

Next, our poet Master Francesco narrates a pair of lovers fervently in love with one another, saying that two others followed equally behind Achilles: one being Demophoon and the other Phyllis, worthy lovers and a most excellent pair. Thus he says:

<header>THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE</header>

<margin>y</margin>
¶ **Demophon** was the son of **Theseus** and **Phaedra**. Having gone with the other Greeks to the Trojan War, and departing from there after the fall of Troy to return to his homeland, he was driven by the fortune of the winds to Thrace. There, he was kindly received by **Phyllis**, the daughter of **Lycurgus** <note>original: *Lycurgo*; in Greek mythology, Lycurgus was a king of Thrace</note>—son of Dryas, son of Hippolytus, son of Orion, son of the Cretan **Jove**—who ruled in that province. While he stayed there for some time, news reached him of the death of **Mnestheus**, the Duke of **Athens**. Hearing this, and desiring to recover his kingdom, he took his leave of **Phyllis** for a time and returned to **Athens**. Having taken power there, he ruled in peace for a long period. In this stay, he exceeded the deadline he had given to **Phyllis** for his return; because of this, she became desperate and, driven by the commands of love, she hanged herself by the throat. According to some others, however, as she was about to throw herself into the sea, she was turned into an almond tree <note>original: *amândola*; a common mythological trope where Phyllis becomes a leafless almond tree that blossoms when Demophon finally returns and embraces it</note> out of the compassion of the gods. Later, when **Demophon** returned to Thrace to see his beloved Phyllis again, he heard the news of her death, and he wept for her as much as was fitting for a most faithful lover. After recounting Phyllis and **Demophon**, our poet introduces another pair of lovers: that is, **Jason** and **Medea**, saying that of the other two who followed, one was **Jason** and the other **Medea**, who had followed love and him through many different places and countries. And as much as she had been cruel and wicked to her brother and father upon her departure, she became even more troubled and fierce <note>original: *fella*; meaning treacherous or cruel</note> toward Jason, believing herself to be undoubtedly more worthy of his love, especially for the great favors she had bestowed upon him. Wherefore the poet says:

->that other is **Demophon**, and she is **Phyllis**<-

<margin>z</margin>
¶ **FOR** a proper understanding of the preceding verses and the history contained within them, one must know that **Pelias**, King of Thessaly and son of **Neptune**, had received an oracle stating that he would be near death when, while he was sacrificing, a man should come to the temple with only one foot covered and the other bare. It happened that while he was intent on the sacrifice to his father, his nephew **Jason**—who was his kinsman, being the son of **Aeson**, who was the son of **Tyro**, a nymph and daughter of **Salmoneus**, King of **Salamis** (who was also the mother of Pelias)—was fishing in a river and taking his pleasure there. He heard the sound of the sacrifice and, wishing to attend and hurrying there, he left one shoe on the bank of the river. Thus, barefoot on one foot, he came to the temple. Seeing this, Pelias remembered the words of the oracle and recognized that his death was near. Wishing to secure the kingdom for his own son **Acastus**, and fearing that **Jason** might occupy it because of his great popularity with the people, he said to **Jason** one day that it seemed to him that to acquire fame, Jason should go to conquer the Golden Fleece. This was on the island of Colchis. Pelias believed Jason would never return because of the great and insurmountable dangers that stood guard over the Golden Fleece: such as the bulls that vomited terrifying flames, which it was first necessary to conquer, then put under the yoke to plow the earth, and then sow in it the teeth of a fierce dragon. He would then have to overcome the dragon itself; and though the bulls spat fire, from those sown teeth would ultimately be born armed men, all of whom he was forced to kill. Only after their death was complete victory obtained. **Jason**, therefore, disposed to follow his uncle's persuasion without delay, prepared himself and set out to sea. He arrived at the island of Colchis, where at that time reigned a king called **Aeetes** <note>original: *Oetes*</note>, who had a daughter most learned in magic <note>original: *in magicis*</note> named **Medea**, and a small son called **Absyrtus** (or **Aegialeus**, according to some). When **Jason** arrived before **Aeetes**, he explained the reason for his coming and his desire to conquer the Golden Fleece. **Aeetes**, seeing his presence and judging him a most worthy youth, told him many times not to put himself in such manifest danger. To move him from his purpose, out of compassion, he made him wait many days, during which time—as a liberal king—he hosted him splendidly at banquets in the presence of his daughter **Medea**. It happened through this regular company that **Medea**, seeing how beautiful he was of body, fell in love with him. Whereupon, having arranged to speak with him in secret, she agreed to give him a glorious victory provided he take her as his wife; and she prepared the remedies for him.

> That one is **Jason**, and that other is **Medea**,
> Who followed Love and him through so many towns;
> And as much as she was wicked to her father and brother,
> So much more was she troubled and fierce toward her lover:
> For she believed herself more worthy of his love.

# CHAPTER ONE

Jason went to the fierce battle: in which he was eventually the victor. Having obtained the golden fleece, Jason resolved to depart and return to Thessaly. It then seemed to Medea that they should flee in secret; and so, having ordered the flight, she took all her father’s riches and with them entered Jason's ship. And so that her father, wishing to follow her, might be delayed further, she took Absyrtus, her little brother, and cut him limb from limb, leaving a part of him at certain intervals on the ground, scattered from the city to the sea, and then they departed. Arriving then in Thessaly, Medea primarily restored youth to Aeson <note>Jason's father</note>. Whereupon the daughters of Pelias likewise requested that she perform the same effect for their father; she told them that they should open his veins so that the blood of old age might flow out. When they did this, they led him to his death; and thus she deceived them so that the kingdom might succeed to Jason. Medea then became pregnant by Jason and gave birth to two sons. At this time, having come to be hated by him, he repudiated her and took as his wife <term>Creusa</term> <note>Also known as Glauce, the daughter of Creon</note>, daughter of Creon, King of the Corinthians. This being deeply displeasing to Medea, she prepared her sorceries and feigned sending her sons with gifts to win the favor of their stepmother. Those gifts were a crafted fire contained in a small casket; which, as soon as Creusa opened it, immediately set her and the queen on fire. Although the children escaped through her art, she later killed them out of revenge in the presence of Jason. When Jason tried to strike her, she fled to Athens and married Aegeus, to whom she bore a son named Medus. At this time, Theseus returned to Athens; she, wishing to poison him, was forced to flee. Returning then to Thessaly, she reconciled with Jason, and they returned together to Colchis where they recovered the kingdom and returned it to the now-aged Aeëtes, who was an exile, and they lived with him. Next, Master <term>Francesco</term> <note>Petrarch, the author of the poem being commented upon</note> recounts the example of Hypsipyle, saying how Hypsipyle came after Medea, grieving over the barbaric love of Jason directed toward Medea, by which he was occupied, though she loved him exceedingly. Wherefore, he was reputed to be the son of shepherds; and he exercised the pastoral office, during which time, while pasturing the royal flocks in the Idaean forest, and sometimes when the bulls fought among themselves, Alexander <note>Another name for Paris</note> always honored the victor who remained with a crown of victory: through which thing he came to the fame of being a most just judge. Therefore he was nicknamed by everyone Paris: that is, "equal" <note>The text suggests a pseudo-etymology where "Paris" is linked to the idea of parity or equality in judgment</note>. It happened then at that time
<margin>T</margin> that Peleus, son of Aeacus and father of Achilles, took as his wife Thetis, daughter of Nereus: to whose wedding Jove had all the gods and goddesses invited, except for Iris <note>original: "Iris"; the author likely means Eris, the goddess of Discord</note>, the goddess of discord. Wherefore she, indignant and wishing to disturb the wedding, seeing Juno, Venus, and Pallas [Athena] there, took a most beautiful golden apple on which she wrote these words: *Let the beautiful apple be given to the most beautiful* <note>original: "Pulchrũ pomũ pulchriori det̃"</note>; and she threw it into the midst of the three who were sitting at the table. Having then taken the apple and read the writing, they immediately came into dissension, each judging the apple for herself and affirming herself to be the most beautiful. Whereupon, to end this dispute of theirs, they submitted themselves to the judgment of Jove, praying him to decide their difference. But Jove, not wishing to judge between them—Juno being his wife and sister, and Venus and Pallas his dear daughters—remitted them to the judgment of Paris, who at that moment, from excessive exercise in hunting, was sleeping in the Idaean forest. He then commanded Mercury that, together with the three goddesses, he should appear to Paris in a dream and explain their question to him. Mercury performed Jove's command: after whose proposal, each goddess presented herself naked to Paris at his request, and offered him the greatest gifts if he would pronounce the sentence in her favor. Thus Juno offered him greater wealth than had ever been in the world; Pallas, greater wisdom; Venus, then, the most beautiful woman. Paris then, having seen the naked goddesses, as in truth Venus was the most beautiful, so he judged her far more worthy of the apple than the others. And it being then at this time, shortly after Jason had gone to acquire the golden ram <note>The Golden Fleece</note>, and having landed with Hercules and the other companions on the Trojan shore, they were dismissed with great threats by King Laomedon, father of Priam, who then ruled the province haughtily.
<margin>V</margin> Which thing they took as a most grave injury. Returning to Thessaly, they prepared armies and came to Troy; they took it and gave it to ruin, and killed Laomedon. And they gave Hesione <note>original: "Exiona"</note>, his daughter, as a prize to Telamon <note>original: "Thalamone"</note>, King of Salamis, because he was the first who entered the city. King Priam was absent when Troy was destroyed by the Greeks, having gone to recover a certain territory which at that time had rebelled against the king. Whereupon, having heard the news of the capture of Troy, abandoning the enterprise, he returned to the place where he rebuilt the city anew, which was arranged and composed with more strength and beauty than it had been before. Afterward, he sought to recover Hesione from the Greeks, consigning every other injury to oblivion; but not being heard by them—rather, they insulted his messenger Antenor in word and deed. Priam convoked a great number of Trojans, to whom he proposed what should be done regarding the injury done to them by the Greeks. To which he was answered by Hector, Helenus <note>original: "Helenor"</note>, and Cassandra, his children, and by Protheus, a Trojan knight, that he should abstain from war. But Paris, now recognized as the king's son and living at the royal court with great honor and reputation, explained his dream and the promise of Venus, giving counsel that armies should be sent to Greece so that some beautiful woman might be taken, according to the promise of the gods; it would be an easy thing to recover Hesione in exchange for her. This opinion pleased Priam; wherefore, having prepared ships, he commanded that Paris, together with Aeneas, should be the captain of the fleet <note>original: "classe"</note> and go to Greece to seize, above all, some worthy woman. They departed from Troy according to Priam's command, and with prosperous winds they landed on the island of Cythera, from where news reached Helen of this arrival and of the beauty of Paris. Wherefore, moved by a most ardent desire to see him, under the pretext of going to the sacrifice of Venus, she departed from Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> and arrived in Cythera. And having come into the temple, as did the Trojans, Paris and Helen, looking fixedly at one another, each judged the other most beautiful. Then Paris, judging their spirits to be in accord, returned to the ships and took up arms; and having returned to the temple, they led the beautiful Helen by force to Troy. Then the Greek nation, hearing of this prize taken by the Trojans, considered it a most grave injury and deliberated to take revenge. Wherefore, having prepared a great supply of ships and a vast multitude of armies, they came against Troy, in which war many kings and princes of the Greeks died, and the Trojans were totally destroyed; such that the world was deservedly turned upside down, as our graceful poet <note>Petrarch</note> has described. Next, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> introduces the nymph Oenone and Menelaus, saying how after Helen followed Oenone and Menelaus: of whom one lamented Paris, and the other grieved for Helen. Wherefore he says:

# Hear then the lament among the other sorrowful women,
# Oenone for Paris, and Menelaus
# For Helen;

<margin>G</margin>
With good reason and great justice, a person laments when they have received great ingratitude. Oenone grieved for Paris: because, while he was still in the pastoral life, he found Oenone in the woods. She loved him with pure faith and simple benevolence, and she felt as if she were Prometheus <note>Petrarch's commentator likely uses Prometheus here as a metaphor for a creative or life-giving force</note> amidst the barrenness of the place, showing him liberality and courtesy. However, as soon as he was restored to royal dignity, he paid for every benefit received from her with oblivion. Despite such great ingratitude, Oenone's flames of love did not diminish in any part; they continued as long as the life of Paris lasted. When his life ended, theirs likewise failed. For after he was killed—either by Ajax, as Dares <note>Dares Phrygius, a supposed witness to the Trojan War</note> says, or by Philoctetes, as Dictys of Crete <note>Another legendary chronicler of the Trojan War</note> clearly writes—as soon as Oenone saw his body, she lost her mind from grief and died, as Dictys himself affirms. <margin>H</margin> With similar ingratitude, Menelaus, son of Atreus (or of Plisthenes, according to other opinions), experienced the same after showing such immense benevolence to Helen. For the fleeting beauty of the lecherous adulterer <note>Paris</note> had more power over her than the praiseworthy and conjugal love of her affectionate husband. To these two, our worthy poet <note>Petrarch</note> adds a third example: Hermione and Orestes, saying that following the laments of Oenone and Menelaus, Hermione continued to be heard loudly calling for her beloved Orestes. Wherefore he says:

# And Hermione calling for Orestes;

<margin>I</margin>
In this place, it is necessary to know—for the understanding of the preceding example—how Orestes, son of Agamemnon and King of Mycenae, took a cruel and horrendous vengeance upon Clytemnestra, his mother, for the death she arranged for Agamemnon, his father. Having been accused by Menelaus before the lords of Greece, who said he was unworthy of the crown for such a crude sentence expressed against his mother, he was ultimately acquitted and crowned King of Mycenae through the effort and judgment of Mnestheus, Duke of Athens. It was ordained at this coronation that, in order to live in peace with Menelaus, he should take as his wife Hermione, the daughter of Menelaus and Helen. By doing this, Orestes developed a very great love and singular benevolence, which was born between them as most beloved companions <note>The original uses "fratelli," which can mean brothers/siblings, but here refers to their close bond as cousins and spouses</note> and spouses. It happened then, after a short time, that Pyrrhus, son of Achilles, passing one day through the kingdom of Orestes, saw Hermione; whereupon he was suddenly and strongly enamored by her beauty. For this reason, using industry and effort, he kidnapped her and took her away with him. At this time, Orestes had become furious <note>driven to madness by the Furies</note> because of the ghost of his mother, who appeared before him continually, armed with serpents and fire. Because of this, he could not attend to her rescue, for which reason Hermione wept loudly and called for Orestes. But later, through the work of Pylades, son of Strophius the Phocian—his most singular friend—Orestes was led to the temple of Diana on the island of Colchos <note>Historically identified as Tauris in this myth</note> and was restored to his former health. Departing from there and returning to his kingdom, he came upon the road to the island of Delos, where Pyrrhus was to sacrifice to Apollo. Having corrupted Machareus, the priest of the temple, with money, Orestes killed Pyrrhus; thus he recovered Hermione and returned with her to Mycenae. Next, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> recounts the amorous example of Laodamia, wife of Protesilaus of Thessaly, saying that just as the preceding Hermione called her beloved husband Orestes, so also did Laodamia call her beloved spouse Protesilaus. Wherefore he says:

# And Laodamia her Protesilaus

<margin>K</margin>
Laodamia, as Ovid writes in his *Heroides* <note>original: "amorose epistole"</note>, was the daughter of Acastus of Thessaly. Likewise, Protesilaus was the son of Iphiclus <note>original: "Isiphilo"</note>, also of Thessaly. While he was preparing with the other Greeks to go on the expedition of the Trojan War, Laodamia, as he entered the sea, stood upon the Thessalian shore to watch him and speak to him until he departed. But once the sails were granted to the wind, Laodamia followed him longingly with her sight as long as the distance allowed the ship to be seen. But once it vanished from her eyes and nothing appeared but water, Laodamia, out of excessive love and fear, fell to the ground as if dead. Afterwards, she spent all her days weeping and always calling for her Protesilaus. He, on the first day he came into <unclear>the sight of the</unclear> Trojans, while performing marvels of arms to everyone's wonder, was killed by the hand of the most powerful Hector, to his great glory.

# THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

<margin>L</margin>
The glory attributed to him by the remaining Greeks: and in this place, some others add that after Protesilaus <note>The first Greek hero to die at Troy</note> died, having been carried back to Thessaly: as soon as Laodamia saw his body, she threw herself upon it and died, following the example of Evadne, the daughter of Mars and wife of Capaneus of Thebes. This seems to be the origin of the fiction written by Ovid and the companionship shown by Virgil in the sixth book <note>The *Aeneid*</note> saying: "Evadne and Pasiphae; Laodamia goes as their companion" <note>original: *Euadnemque & pasiphaen: his Laodomia it comes*</note>. Wherefore, Laodamia is rightly described as searching and weeping for her Protesilaus. Consequently, he introduces the example of Argia, the most faithful and beloved wife of Polynices of Thebes, saying that after Laodamia followed Argia, a much more faithful wife to Polynices than the greedy Eriphyle was to her husband Amphiaraus: wherefore he says:

<margin>¶ II</margin>
For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it is necessary to repeat how Oedipus, son of Laius, King of Thebes, having been destined at his birth

->**And Argia to Polynices much more faithful,**<-
->**Than the greedy wife of Amphiaraus;**<-

by his father to be devoured by the elements <note>or "beasts," likely a reference to exposure</note>: he was carried by servants into a forest. In that place, out of pity, he was not killed; but with his tendons <term>nerui</term> <note>referring to the ankles, hence his name "Oedipus" or "Swollen-foot"</note> pierced, he was hung from a tree. From there, hearing his crying, a shepherd belonging to Polybus, the King of Corinth, came to him; and having untied him, he raised him. Thus, as Oedipus grew up, he was considered the son of Polybus. Having learned the truth in time, he disposed himself to search for his father and mother. When he asked the oracle, he received the answer that near Phocis he would find his father and would take his mother as his wife. Oedipus decided to test this answer: and so he came to those people, whom he found to be in dissension—the citizens against the peasants. He decided to lend his favor to the peasants; and in this conflict came Laius to quiet the battle. Oedipus, not knowing him, killed him. Not seeing anyone else thereafter whom he recognized as his father, he thought himself deluded by the oracle. Therefore, as the son of Polybus, he came to Thebes, and there, as the price of the kingdom, he was given his mother Jocasta as his wife. Later, when Polybus died in Corinth, they elected Oedipus as their king. When they sent ambassadors to him, Oedipus then understood clearly the manner of his arrival in Corinth. Hearing this, and having learned from the servants of the arrival of her son, Jocasta looked at the tendons of his feet; seeing that they had once been pierced, she knew Oedipus to be her son. Oedipus likewise understood that he had killed his father Laius and lain with his mother Jocasta; wherefore, out of grief, he condemned himself to everlasting darkness and plucked out his eyes.

<margin>M ¶</margin>
In this time, Oedipus had fathered two sons with Jocasta: namely, Eteocles and Polynices. These sons, seeing their father blind and despising him, took the kingdom on the condition that each of them should reign for one year. Eteocles, therefore, having reigned his time, did not want to return the kingdom to Polynices; instead, he sought to seize it. Thus, Polynices was forced to flee. In his flight, he arrived by night, tossed by winds and water, in the city of Argos, belonging to King Adrastus, King of the Argives, where he rested under the portico of the palace. At this same time, Tydeus, son of Oeneus, King of Calydon, having inadvertently killed his brother Melanippus while hunting, also fled that same night and arrived at Argos. Being drenched like Polynices, he took refuge under that same portico, from which there arose a dispute and a fight between them. Adrastus, hearing their dissension, came to see what it might be; and finally, seeing these two young men fighting together, he made peace between them. Observing that Polynices was covered in a lion's skin and Tydeus in a boar's skin, and thus knowing their origins, he gave Deiphile as a wife to Tydeus and Argia to Polynices. After these marriages, Adrastus decided that the kingdom should be requested back from Eteocles for Polynices. He sent Tydeus to demand it, but Eteocles would not consent to the request; instead, he prepared an ambush for Tydeus's return and commanded that he be killed. But Tydeus bravely defended himself, killing a great many of them and forcing the others to flee. Having returned to Argos,

<margin>N</margin>
the embassy was explained; and having told of Eteocles's deceit, Adrastus, Polynices, and Tydeus gathered their armies to retake the kingdom of Thebes by force. In this assembly was Amphiaraus, son of Oecles, a prince in the kingdom of Argos. Being required to go on this expedition, he asked the oracle what would happen to him; the oracle replied that if he went, he would surely die there. Because of this, Amphiaraus hid himself and made his hiding place known only to his wife Eriphyle, daughter of Talaios, son of Iasius. Adrastus, searching for Amphiaraus for a long time, delayed the siege because of his absence. It happened one day that Argia wore around her neck a beautiful necklace <term>monile</term> <note>The Necklace of Harmonia, a cursed piece of jewelry forged by Vulcan</note>, which Vulcan had once given to Hermione <note>Harmonia</note>, the wife of Cadmus, son of Agenor...

# CHAPTER ONE

<margin>O</margin>
The grandson <note>The text mentions Agenor, the King of Phoenicia; Polynices was his descendant through Cadmus</note> of Agenor, King of Phoenicia, possessed a gift <note>The Necklace of Harmonia, which was cursed</note>. Seeing Eriphyle and her desire for it, he said that if she wished for him to give it to her, she must reveal the hiding place of Amphiaraus <note>Amphiaraus was a seer who knew he would die at Thebes and thus hid to avoid the war</note>. The most faithful Argia, hearing these words and desiring the success of her husband's expedition, was content to give it to her; and so she gave it. Eriphyle then betrayed Amphiaraus. Once he was found, the Argives proceeded to the siege of Thebes, where in the end Amphiaraus, Tydeus, and Polynices were killed. By the command of the most cruel King Creon, their bodies were left without burial. Hearing of this, the most faithful Argia, not frightened by the cruel edict, wished to offer the final tears and the final funeral pyre to her husband. Departing from Argos one night, she arrived at Thebes together with Antigone, the sister of Polynices. Alone, with only the help of a small torch, turning over the wounded corpses, she finally found her dear Polynices. Washing him with her tears and kissing him a thousand times with sobs, she made for him such a funeral pyre as was possible for her. Hearing of this, Creon had her captured and cruelly put to death. From this, it remains quite manifest how greedy Eriphyle should be called, and how faithful the unhappy Argia was. The first was Venus, the daughter of Coelius <note>Uranus</note> and of the Day <note>Dies</note>, to whom is specifically attributed the girdle called the *Cestus*, which is involved in conjugal love, where she is found distinct from the other love of women; and by this one, the ancients understood the planet Venus. ### TRIUMPH OF LOVE

<margin>V</margin>
But Mars loved Venus. Mars was the son of Juno, born of her alone because she ate a flower found in the Olenian fields <note>A reference to Ovid’s *Fasti*, where Juno, jealous that Jupiter birthed Minerva from his head, conceives Mars with the help of a magical flower provided by Flora</note> on the advice of Flora, the wife of Zephyr. This happened after Jupiter had produced Minerva alone from the striking of his head, as Ovid shows in his book *The Fasti*. One day, while Venus was embracing Mars, their adultery was revealed to Vulcan by the Sun. Out of indignation, Vulcan threw invisible chains around his bed, and in one stroke he caught Mars together with his lady, Venus. Having bound them thus, he showed them to all the other gods. However, releasing them later at the prayers of Apollo, Mercury, and Neptune, Venus—seeking revenge against the Sun—led all his daughters into the practice of prostitution <note>Venus cursed the lineage of the Sun (Helios) because he was the one who spotted her affair with Mars. This curse affected his descendants, including Pasiphae and Phaedra</note>. Mars, as was said, was the son born of Juno and dedicated to the practice of war, and for this reason, he was judged by the ancients to be the god of battles. Hence, he is fittingly described in this place by our poet <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch</note> as "bound" <note>original: "cincto"</note>: surrounded by iron at his feet, arms, and neck, either because of the chains of Vulcan or truly to denote that such a habit is common for one who proceeds to battle and desires to remain the victor and superior. Messer Francesco next narrates, saying that after Venus and Mars followed Pluto and Proserpina, who were together in a place remote from the others, and they loved each other fervently. Whence he says:

->**And Pluto, and Proserpina apart.**<-

<margin>Y</margin>
For a clear understanding of the preceding verse, it should be known that Pluto, the son of Saturn and his lady Ops, was reputed by the ancients to be the god of hell and king of the city of Dis. Being in hell, as Ovid writes, while the giant Typhoeus was struggling to shake off the weight of Sicily <note>original: "Trinacria," an ancient name for Sicily</note>, Pluto saw some light enter hell because of that shaking. Fearing that his kingdom might be occupied by the presence of light, he went out to see the foundations of the island. While he was near Syracuse, Proserpina—the daughter of Jupiter and Ceres, queen of the island—had gone out with other girls into the meadows to gather flowers. Pluto encountered her, and seeing her beauty, he suddenly fell in love. Approaching her, he seized her and joyfully took her with him to hell. When her mother Ceres heard of this, she set out to search for her throughout the whole world. Finally, not finding her, she learned from the testimony of the nymph Arethusa <note>A nymph of a fountain in Syracuse who claimed to have seen Proserpina in the underworld</note> that she had descended to hell. Being the goddess of grain, and unable to recover her daughter, she denied grain to the whole world. Because of this, many complaints were brought to Jupiter. In the end, he judged that Ceres should restore grain to the world, and her daughter Proserpina should inhabit half the time with her mother Ceres and the other half with her husband in hell. For this reason, Messer Francesco rightly said he saw her and Pluto "apart." Next, Messer Francesco brings forward the example of Juno, saying: "See, O Messer Francesco, the jealous Juno, as she follows the amorous triumph." Whence he says:

->**See jealous Juno,**<-

<margin>A</margin>
Juno, as the ancient writers liked, was the daughter of Saturn, King of Crete, and of his lady Ops. Although she was born in the same birth with Jupiter, she nevertheless came into the world before him; and she was Jupiter's lady and sister. Juno was appropriately written to follow the triumph of love because of the immoderate and improperly directed benevolence she bore toward Jupiter, and for this reason, she was nicknamed "jealous." This was deserved, since Jupiter almost never had a love that she did not discover and find through her own watchfulness, to which jealousy drove her. For this reason, the poets write that many loved by Jupiter were transformed by her from their human nature. <margin>B</margin> Chiefly, the daughter of the river Inachus <note>Io, whom Juno turned into a cow</note> was turned into a cow. Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, King of Arcadia, was also turned into a bear by Juno, and then by the mercy of Jupiter, she was taken up into heaven and turned into a star <note>The constellation Ursa Major</note>. And the nymph Echo was transformed into the reflection of the final accent of the human voice. Semele, daughter of Cadmus, was embraced by Jupiter through the works of Juno <note>Juno tricked Semele into asking Jupiter to appear in his full divine glory, which incinerated her</note>. And ultimately, Athamas, son of Aeolus, and Ino, also the daughter of Cadmus and his lady, were made insane by Juno solely for having nursed Bacchus. Next, our poet adds the example of Apollo, saying that after the jealous Juno followed the blond Apollo, who once used to despise the immature age of Cupid and the practice of shooting arrows; this thing gave him such a shock and so much agitation in Thessaly. Whence he says:

->**and the blond Apollo;**<-
->**Who used to despise the age and the bow,**<-

# CHAPTER ONE

->Who afterwards gave such a downfall to Thessaly.<-

<margin>He was the son of Vulcan, the first son of Heaven; the poet does not mean this one</margin>
because to him is attributed nothing except the invention of the virtues of herbs. The other was the son of Jove and Latona, the daughter of Coeus <note>The original text says "Celio," likely referring to the Titan Coeus</note>, the son of Titan. This one, then—as Ovid writes—since the earth had produced various and enormous serpents due to the moisture of the deluge, killed one especially great and horrendous serpent called Python with his arrows. Because of this victory, in his pride, he judged that the bow and the practice of archery were suitable for no one other than himself. For this reason, Cupid was indignant at seeing his power despised by Apollo. One day, while Apollo was looking at Daphne, the daughter of the river Peneus in Thessaly, Cupid struck him with a golden arrow and Daphne with one of lead. Thus it happened that Apollo was intent only on following her, and she on fleeing from him. One day, therefore, as Apollo was overtaking her in the race, she commended herself to the gods that they should not permit her to lose her virginity. Being heard by them, she was converted into a laurel tree. Seeing this, Apollo ordained that it should be an honored tree with many privileges: such as being untouched by lightning, and also being the glory and emblem of emperors and poets, as the illustrious Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> himself demonstrates in those sonnets, namely: *Glorious column on which one leans*; *If the honored branch that preserves*; and *Victorious and triumphant tree*. Besides these privileges, he made it worthy of being forever green. This same Apollo also loved Leucothoe, daughter of Orchamus, son of Achemenides; he was so intensely seized by her love that sometimes he neglected to illuminate the world. After she was killed by her father, and being unable to offer her any other benefit, he turned his rays toward her and converted her into a frankincense branch. He also loved Clytie, another of his beloveds, though he later despised her because it was through her doing that Leucothoe was killed, she having revealed to her father Orchamus the love of Apollo and their amorous delights. Finally, regarding this chapter, our poet adds a group of them under a general enumeration, as all the gods described by Marcus Varro have remained subjects of Love. Then he introduces Jove, saying that he proceeds bound by a thousand snares before the chariot, as the most worthy prisoner. Hence he says:

> What should I say? I pass them in one step:
> All of Varro's gods are prisoners here;
> And laden with countless snares
> Jove comes chained before the chariot.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it should be understood that Marcus Varro, a notable Roman citizen, wrote a book on the "Select Gods" for the instruction of the Roman Republic. There he shows that the ancients proposed a divinity, either a god or a goddess, for almost every human act and operation, who would direct and lead each person to their proper end, as Saint Augustine writes in the fourth book of *The City of God* <note>original: "Aug. iiij. de ciuitate dei"</note>. From this, the poet, wanting to show that this Love had appropriately conquered them, says "all the gods of Varro," meaning those described by Varro were prisoners in that place, especially Jove. For the understanding of this, it should be known that the name of Jove was attributed by the ancients to the god who governed the entire universe, denoted by them as the father of gods and men.

<margin>F</margin>
¶ There were, then, three who were each named Jove. The first was, according to what Leontius <note>Likely Leontius Pilatus, a 14th-century translator and source for Boccaccio and Petrarch</note> writes, Lysania of Arcadia. Because he reduced the rough and inexperienced Athenians to a political life and instituted legitimate marriages for them, they called him Jove; he was the son of Heaven and Day. There was another Lysania, also an Arcadian King of the Athenians, so similar to the first that they are currently taken as the same person. The second was Pericles the Athenian prince, who was called by many "Olympic Jove," and our Messer Francesco does not mean either of these at present.

<margin>G</margin>
The third and last Jove for our purpose was the Cretan Jove, son of Saturn and Ops. According to what Ovid writes of him, he was ensnared in innumerable traps of love. First, he fell in love with Io, daughter of Inachus, and he took her in the form of a cloud. Second, he loved Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, whom he obtained by transforming himself into a woman <note>Specifically, he disguised himself as the goddess Diana to approach her</note>. Third, he loved Europa, daughter of King Agenor, whom he possessed in the figure of a Bull. Fourth, he loved Semele, daughter of Cadmus, and he had his way with her by pretending to be Beroe, her nurse. Fifth, he loved Danaë, daughter of Acrisius, King of the Argives, whom he reached by transforming himself into a shower of gold. Sixth, he loved Asteria, daughter of Coeus, with whom he consorted by converting himself into an eagle. Seventh, he loved Leda, wife of Tyndareus, with whom he lay in the figure of a swan. Eighth, he loved Antiope, daughter of Nycteus, King in Lesbos, and wife of Lycus, King of Thebes, with whom he joined in the form of a Satyr—whose figure was a man from the waist up and a goat from the waist down, including the forehead.

->EXPOSITION OF THE SECOND CHAPTER.<-

<margin>H</margin>
**J**UST AS naturally every customary thing leads human minds to negligence, so likewise that which occurs outside of custom draws the mind to great wonder. Therefore, as the philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle</note> says in the second book of *On the Heavens*: just as the body cannot be moved by those things that often happen to it, so the soul and the mind do not move except for that object which presents itself anew. This wonder is often the cause of very great effects, as **Plutarch** writes in the *Life of Paullus Æmilius*: that because of the unusual eclipse of the moon, the **Macedonians** were terrified, thinking the gods were angry against them. And by contrast, **Paullus**, showing the **Roman** soldiers by natural reason that this was a customary effect of nature, kept them without fear. Whence they remained superior in battle and possessed a complete victory. **Aulus Gellius** also writes of **Socrates** in the second book of *Attic Nights* that he

<margin>I</margin>
sometimes stood firm and immobile from one sunrise to the next; which occurred whenever his mind was fixed on some new and excellent speculation. This same natural disposition, then, follows our glorious poet <note>Petrarch</note>, who after having demonstrated in the first chapter what the state and habit of the sensitive appetite is, and having described part of the men and gods who have been overcome by this love, and having affirmed that he himself was not yet subjected to it. Now, at the beginning of this second chapter, he describes himself as being drawn to such great wonder that he stood like a man who, by such affection, cannot speak; but being silent, he waits for counsel from others on what he should do in his future works. In this chapter, therefore, **Messer Francesco** <note>Petrarch</note> intends by a universal argument and subject to treat and describe a greater number of lovers, and beyond this to number himself among those captured and subjected to the powerful [Love], and to explain those passions which his tenacious affection produces in him. He describes himself as being led to this state with a silent and reasonable excuse. For he affirms he marvels greatly at the sight of the men and gods whom he saw captured by this powerful Duke <note>Love</note>; whereupon, thinking himself to have come into that same pressure, he became discolored and pale, because the thought had already fallen upon him that he must suffer similar punishments when constrained by similar passions. And in this consideration, he says that he saw at his side a beautiful, purest young girl <note>Laura</note> who, although it was believed she had manfully defended herself at other times against armed and robust men, was captured and conquered and totally bound; wherefore he made no defense, but rendered himself prisoner. By this fiction, **Messer Francesco** intends to make his excuse: which is that the sensitive appetite in men is awakened when some delightful object is perceived through the external senses. When reason denies possession of it, human frailty strives to excuse itself with some example from others, by which it seems to him that it is permissible to act in that same likeness—estimating that the more common the error is, the lesser the fault must be. Wherefore, the poet writing that he had so beautiful a girl, and seeing himself in the midst of so many enamored men as he describes in this first triumph, it did not seem inconvenient that he should not resist this love, but rather consent to it, not by industry, but by inadvertence, as we shall say in the proper place. Common custom being of such force that, although it may be an error, yet sometimes it is transformed into a just operation, as the text of the legal consultants says in the law *Barbarius Philippus* <note>original: "Barbarius philippus ff de officio presidis," a reference to the Digest of Roman Law (D.1.14.3), which discusses a case where a common error creates a legal right</note>. For this reason, the poet having presented so many and such worthy enamored men, it seems that having consented to love, he too is worthy of pardon. He continues, then, and introduces himself as being drawn to great wonder by the preceding sight of...

# CHAPTER ONE

at the sight of so many worthy and so excellent prisoners, saying that his heart was so full of wonder that he stood like a man who, constrained by most intense affection, cannot speak; but remains silent and waits for counsel from others, where he judges himself insufficient to know how to make it public. Whence he says:

<margin>L</margin>
<margin>Messer Francesco <note>M.F. refers to the author, Francesco Petrarch</note> describes a worthy and natural sentiment in the preceding verses, saying that because of great wonder he is unable to speak and waits for the counsel of others, not being fit to take it for himself. For the understanding of this, it should be understood as the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> writes in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>Latin: "De Anima"</note>.</margin>

> My heart was so full of wonders;
> That I stood like a man who cannot speak,
> And is silent, and only waits for others to counsel him;

The philosopher writes that souls are contained within one another just as the triangle is contained within the quadrangle; that is, the imperfect soul is the potential, virtue, and accident of the superior and more perfect soul. From this, according to what he writes in the seventh book of the *Politics*: Every inferior virtue works and moves by the precept and command of the superior power. Similarly, it is necessary that it cease its operations when it is not moved by the superior power. Secondly, it should be understood that the intellect, according to what is written in the sixth book of the *Ethics*, is divided into the practical and the speculative. The practical intellect pertains to the deliberative part, because regarding those objects pertaining to the speculative intellect—and those things that cannot be performed by us—no one deliberates. Whence the philosopher says in the third book of the *Ethics*: *No one deliberates about eternal things, nor about those things that always exist in the same motion, whether by necessity, or nature, or for some other cause, such as the rising or the turning of the stars; nor about those things that happen by chance; nor even about all human affairs. For example, no Spartan deliberates about how the Scythian republic might best be governed. For these things cannot be acted upon by us.* <note>original Latin: "De eternis aut nemō consultat. neq. de his que in motu semper eodem modo existunt siue de necessitate: siue natura: siue ppter aliam cām ueluti de ortu: siue conuersione syderu neq. de his que sunt a fortuna: sed neq. de humanis oībus. Nā quēadmodu scitharū respublica optime gubernet nemo lcedemonius consultat. Hec enim per nos agi non possunt."</note> And beyond this, it is also appropriate that the practical part depends on the simple speculative part; and not the contrary, because no one can act well who does not understand, but one can certainly understand without acting, distinguishing the action from the intellection. From this it follows that whenever our intellect is totally fixed on the intellection of an object, and especially when it considers it with admiration, all the parts of the soul inferior to it are lulled to sleep, except for the natural ones, which naturally and by absolute necessity continue their operation for the preservation of the man; these, even where the other powers are bound in sleep, are further strengthened and increased. By this, one can clearly understand how gracefully the poet has described his inability to speak or even to counsel himself, these inferior virtues being bound by the fixation of the intellect upon that object which he considered with such wonder. Being then in such a state, Messer Francesco then introduces the shadow <note>the spirit of a friend guiding him</note> as a sort of fire or refreshment and aid, to speak these words to him: "O Messer Francesco, now what are you doing? Now what are you gazing at? Now what are you thinking, and what is this sloth and tardiness of yours? Now, do you not know that I am of the amorous crowd, and it behooves me to follow where Love pleases, in the amorous triumph? And you no longer ask nor seek to know what follows further, as if you remained satisfied only with the sight of the preceding prisoners." And he adds that he replies to the shadow, saying: "O my dear brother, you know my being and my disposition; whence you must know the love which has already so inflamed me that the act of asking and reasoning is delayed by the desire for knowledge." Whence he says:

<margin>M</margin>
> When my friend, whom you know, said: What are you gazing at?
> What are you thinking? Do you not well know that I
> Am of the crowd, and it behooves me to follow?
> Brother, I replied, you know my state,
> And you must know the love that has so inflamed me,
> That the work is delayed by the desire;

<margin>For clearer evidence of the preceding verses, it should be understood that a natural effect is defined as this: whenever several equal things are proposed to the will as objects, it directs itself toward none of those choices but remains suspended in its act. Just as they write in the [treatises] of the cognition of things, through which one would never understand any particular thing if it were not determined by...</margin>

singular accidents and phantasms <note>mental images or impressions</note>; in the likeness of which one places the hungry appetite that does not move when it is in the midst of several different foods equally desired by it. # THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

particular objects, because the will does not determine itself toward any one of them.

<margin>O</margin>
¶ Hence, just as a body moves more slowly in a multitude and tumult—according to the opinion of Quintus Curtius <note>A Roman historian known for his history of Alexander the Great</note> who says: *Haste in a tumult is slow* <note>original: "Festinatio in tumultu tarda est"</note>—so it also happens to the mind, because it moves to understand more slowly the greater the number of intelligible objects. This is because the intellect naturally desires to understand perfectly that which it intends to understand: a thing which cannot happen with the speed and multitude of objects. This is as Livy writes in the second Punic War, introducing Fabius Maximus speaking to Paulus Aemilius, to whom he said at the end of the oration: *Haste is improvident and blind* <note>original: "Festinatio improuida est & ceca"</note>. For this reason, therefore, our graceful poet <note>Petrarch</note> describes himself as lingering and dazed, seeing such a multitude of people, and desiring to know who they all were. Next, Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> adds that the shadow <note>The guide or spirit accompanying the narrator</note>, having noticed his ambiguity, manifests his desire to him: that is, that he yearns to know who was another group of people following the Triumph of Love. Furthermore, the shadow offers to tell him, provided that speech is not hindered, beginning by saying: Messer Francesco, that great and excellent man revered and honored by everyone; that is Pompey, and together with him he has his Cornelia, who weeps and laments over the vile and ungrateful Ptolemy, the unworthy King of the province of Egypt. Whence he says:

<margin>P</margin>
¶ Messer Francesco demonstrates quite gracefully how variable the state of lovers is when he says the shadow wishes to recount who the other lovers are, provided it is not contrary to his speech; because this disposition is manifest, he passes on to narrate the examples. Pompey, therefore—to whom, for his supreme and singular virtues, was attributed

> And he said to me: I had already understood you in silence:
> You wish to know who these others also are:
> I will tell you, if the telling is not forbidden to me.
> See that great man, whom every man honors,
> He is Pompey, and he has Cornelia with him,
> Who over the vile Ptolemy laments and weeps.

the surname "the Great" <note>Magnus</note>—was a most excellent man in the Roman Republic. After Cornelius Sulla died, he was the head and prince of the Sullan faction; whereas Julius Caesar, being of the faction of Marius, these two in the Roman Republic were always contraries and enemies. Through many passages of time, having finally reached the Battle of Pharsalus, Pompey was defeated; fleeing from there into Egypt, he was put to death by Ptolemy through the hands of Lucius Septimius and Achillas, most audacious men.

<margin>Q</margin>
¶ Pompey thus loved Cornelia, daughter of Lucius Scipio Africanus, a woman who had first been the wife of Gracchus; and he loved her in such a way that even until the last breath of life he followed her, and in her arms he was cruelly killed by the aforementioned men. The poet next writes that he was honored by every man, first to demonstrate his excellence, and second because never did so many peoples serve any prince voluntarily as they did Pompey. Whence, in the war which he waged against Caesar, he first had almost all the Roman nobles; second, the Greek peoples of the islands of the Aegean sea: that is, from Corcyra, Athens, and Pontus; furthermore he had those of Britain, those of Syria, those of Cilicia, of Phoenicia, those of Achaea, of Sicily, and Italy; he had the Asians, King Deiotarus, Cotys of Thrace, and Ariobarzanes of Cappadocia.

<margin>R</margin>
¶ And further he had the Gauls, Germans, Thessalians, Macedonians, and many other peoples and princes, as the civil commentary <note>Likely referring to Caesar's *Commentarii de Bello Civili*</note> demonstrates, all of whom followed Pompey in his enterprises. Finally, he adds that Ptolemy was vile, and certainly he is right; for through his own pusillanimity and fear of Caesar, and for not having had the proper gratitude toward Pompey for the benefits received from him in his kingdom, that most vile king commanded that Pompey be killed. Not recognizing in himself any virtue by which he might please Caesar, he wished to ingratiate himself with the gift of the head of that man whom he ought to have defended, and for whom he ought to have placed his own life in danger infinite times. This gift was accepted by Caesar just as the vileness and perfidy of that ungrateful, vile, and faithless occupier of the kingdom of Egypt deserved. Next, Messer Francesco introduces the example of Agamemnon, saying that after Pompey followed that great Greek king, who had also been defeated and subjugated by powerful love. Whence he says:

# CHAPTER ONE

**The other further off, that is the great Greek,**

<margin>S</margin>
¶ Regarding the understanding of the preceding verse, there are various interpretations. Some understand this "great Greek" to be Philip of Macedon <note>The father of Alexander the Great</note> because of the love he bore for Larisse, with whom he fathered Arideus (who held the kingdom after Alexander the Great). He also loved Cleopatra, the sister of Attalus, for whom he repudiated Olympias, the mother of Alexander. Beyond this, he most justly loved Alexander, whom he made King of Epirus, making him his son-in-law and depriving his brother-in-law Arybbas of the kingdom. Others believe it is not Philip, but his son Alexander, who was stained by a similar blemish as his father. For besides his royal dignity, he loved Hephaestion, his most beloved and immodest friend; he also loved the beautiful Barsine, by whom he fathered a son named Hercules; and likewise, he loved Thalestris, Queen of the Amazons, and in addition to these, Queen Roxana. 

Nonetheless, while always deferring to better judgment, I believe our poet intended in this place the King Agamemnon, son of Atreus (or of Plisthenes, according to some others). For although the others were great through their dominion over lands, Agamemnon was greater through his dominion over souls, having been elected commander over so many leaders, princes, and kings at the destruction of Troy. One should not consider a lord to be greater who has a larger number of servants by legal servitude than one who has a larger multitude of voluntary servitude. Furthermore, Philip or Alexander did not celebrate love beyond the fulfillment of a simple venereal act, whereas Agamemnon did: for love, he took Briseis away from Achilles, and it was also rumored that out of a personal passion of love, he brought Cassandra, daughter of Priam, to Mycenae to make her queen. Therefore, it certainly seems there is no doubt our poet described Agamemnon in this place. 

Immediately after Agamemnon, he adds the example of Aegisthus and the unfaithful and adulterous Clytemnestra, saying: "O Master Francesco, see Aegisthus and the impious and cruel Clytemnestra," through whom you can clearly see how love is senseless and blind. Whence he says:

<margin>T</margin>

> **The King sees Aegisthus and the impious Clytemnestra;**
> **Now you can see love, if it is indeed blind.**

<margin>V</margin>
To understand the preceding verses, one must know that when Agamemnon had gone on the expedition to the Trojan War, Clytemnestra, his lady and the daughter of Jove and Leda, fell in love with Aegisthus, the son of Thyestes, who at that time was a priest of the temple. Having committed adultery with him for a long time, and the city of Troy having already fallen into ruin, and Agamemnon returning with victory to Mycenae, she reckoned that upon his arrival she could no longer satisfy her insatiable lust. For this reason, she plotted to have him killed, and having conspired with her adulterer Aegisthus, she brought the wicked and nefarious deed to its conclusion. 

It is true that authors speak differently regarding how he died. Some say that Aegisthus, with several conspirators, arranged for Agamemnon to be killed while he was at a banquet in the temple. Seneca, however, in the tragedy titled *Agamemnon*, says that Clytemnestra, being angry because Agamemnon had brought Cassandra with him, plotted to have him killed in this way: when he returned dressed in the clothes of Priam, she told him and begged him to return to the dress of his homeland. When Agamemnon consented, she had a garment made which had no opening for the head to pass through to the shoulders. When it was given to him to put on, while Agamemnon was searching for the opening and was entangled in it, the adulterer Aegisthus arrived and killed Agamemnon. Love was indeed blind for Clytemnestra to prefer a vile priest to a most excellent king, renowned for the beauty of his body, his virtue, his soul, and his intellect, and most abundant in the goods of fortune. 

Conveniently, after Clytemnestra, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> introduces the example of Hypermestra, daughter of Danaus (son of the ancient Belus, King of Upper Egypt). For as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> writes in the second book of *On the Heavens*: "Opposites placed near one another shine more brightly" <note>original: "Opposita iuxta se posita magis elucescunt"</note>. Thus he narrates that after the impious and unfaithful Clytemnestra followed Hypermestra, saying: "See, O Master Francesco, another faith, another conjugal love," by seeing Hypermestra. Whence he says:

<margin>X</margin>

> **Another faith, another love, see Hypermestra;**

<margin>✳</margin>

For Aegyptus had fifty sons, and Danaus had fifty daughters. Because of this, Aegyptus asked Danaus if he would be pleased to give the daughters as wives to his sons; but Danaus...

Therefore, the sons of Aegyptus went to Argos and besieged Danaus in such a way that he was forced to succumb. From this, he took the course of consenting to their will, thinking at once of how to avenge himself and escape the danger. For this reason, she was imprisoned by Danaus and held so long that Lynceus finally took vengeance for his lady and his brothers by killing Danaus with a cruel punishment, which was assigned to him by the gods with great reason for his impiety. the spring to drink. Wherefore Thisbe, seeing her and being filled with fear, began to flee, and in her flight, her veil fell, which she—being more intent on fleeing than on gathering it—left on the ground. When the lioness later departed from the spring and found Thisbe's veil on the ground, she nuzzled it, and in sniffing it, stained it with blood and went away. By this time, Pyramus had arrived near the spring, and finding the bloodied veil, which he knew very well belonged to Thisbe, he immediately estimated that she must have been devoured by some most atrocious beast. Wherefore, judging himself to have been the cause of her death, he did not wish to live any longer without her. And for this reason, drawing his sword with grief and fury, he threw himself miserably upon its point. He had not yet breathed his last breath when Thisbe arrived, returning to the spring. Finding her beloved Pyramus in such a sad and unhappy state, and knowing that such misfortune had occurred only because of her, she wished to die herself together with him. Whereupon, with that grief which was fitting for such a case, she threw herself in despair upon the remainder of the naked sword which protruded from Pyramus's body. In such a fashion, the burning love of these two most fervent lovers came to an end. So that a perpetual memory of this might remain, the gods decreed that the mulberry tree, which previously produced white fruit, should forever after produce bloody and black fruit—similar in effect but different in manner. Our graceful Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> adds another pair of lovers, saying in the name of the shade: "O Messer Francesco, see beyond Pyramus and Thisbe, Leander in the sea and Hero looking out from the window." ¶ The dominion and nearly the entire monarchy of the world at the time of Caesar was divided among three men <note>The First Triumvirate</note>: C. Pompey, Julius Caesar, and Marcus Crassus. Because of various Roman dissensions—Caesar having succeeded to the faction of Marius and Pompey to that of Sulla—the Roman Senate established a plan to keep these two powerful men joined together with a bond of affinity and love: that Pompey, although he was much older than Caesar, should take Julia, Caesar's daughter, as his wife. Although she was a young girl of tender age, and Pompey was quite mature in years, she nonetheless loved him most ardently and with great faith. Then, one day, while Pompey was together with the other officials of Rome at the public assemblies generally called the <term>comitia</term> <note>The Roman people’s assemblies for elections and passing laws</note>, celebrating with joy at a sacrifice in the temple, the priest in charge of killing the victim struck it, and as the animal thrashed about in its pain, it stained and spotted Pompey’s white robe with blood in several places. Because of this, he sent the robe to his house by way of a servant. The servant encountered Julia, who was pregnant, in the hall of the residence. She, seeing her husband's bloodied robe and believing her dear Pompey had been killed, fell to the ground in grief before the servant’s feet without asking a single question, and died as she breathed her last. This death was the cause of grave troubles and most bitter losses, not only to Rome and her husband Pompey, but to the whole world. <note>Julia’s death in 54 BCE broke the family tie between Caesar and Pompey, leading directly to the Roman Civil War</note>

<margin>O</margin>

Having up to this point demonstrated the effective power of this commanding appetite through the examples of the pagans—for whom it seems such behavior was permitted with more excuse—the poet now brings forward those of the Jewish people, who, because of the great familiarity they had with God, should presumably have resisted it. Great joy rushed to father Laban, and the arrival of Jacob was announced to him. Being beyond measure joyful at this, Laban went to meet him and, embracing him, asked the reason for his coming. To which Jacob replied that he had come only to serve. Laban then said that he should name the price for his work, for otherwise he would not suffer him to serve for nothing, being his nephew. Jacob replied that he was <margin>R</margin> prepared to serve him seven years if, in return, he would give him Rachel as his wife. This pleased Laban, and they harmoniously confirmed the pact. Wherefore, after the seven years were finished, Jacob asked Laban for his Rachel. Laban replied that he was most content and, the wedding being prepared, he had Jacob marry Rachel. <margin>S</margin> However, that night, in going to bed, in place of Rachel, her sister Leah was sent to sleep with Jacob, with whom he joined in marriage. Then in the morning, when the light appeared, Jacob realized that in that night he had lain with the sister Leah—who was bleary-eyed <note>The original Italian "lippa" translates to bleary-eyed or having rheumy eyes, following the biblical description of Leah in Genesis 29:17</note> and deformed—and not with his beautiful and beloved Rachel. Because of this deception, he complained loudly to Laban. But he, in his <margin>T</margin> excuse, replied that it was not the custom in that country to give the younger daughters in marriage before the elder. But if he still wanted Rachel, he should stay in his service another seven years, at the end of which he would grant her to him. This seemed an easy choice to the loving heart of Jacob; and setting aside every injury, he consented to stay and serve Laban another seven years. When these were finished, he finally obtained his so greatly desired Rachel as his wife. Next, <term>M. F.</term> <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch, the author of the poem</note> exclaims in the person of the narrator, continuing the demonstration of these examples, saying: "O lively and potent love, which not only continues, but indeed multiplies and grows in times of trouble. Now look." Messer Francesco then points to his [Jacob's] father Isaac and his grandfather Abraham, how he leaves all his delights with only Sarah <margin>V</margin> behind, disregarding them to fulfill the divine commandment. ¶ Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should primarily be known that the designation of "great fathers" or "patriarchs" attributed to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had its origin from God speaking to Moses in the unburnt bush, as it is

written in Exodus in the third chapter when He said: "Go and gather the elders of Israel and say to them: The Lord God of your fathers appeared to me, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob." <margin>X</margin> This same thing was later confirmed by Jesus Christ in Saint Matthew in the 22nd chapter and Saint Luke in the 20th, when He spoke to the Sadducees who denied the resurrection: "That the dead truly rise, Moses showed regarding the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." <note>Original Latin: "Quod vero resurgant mortui Moyses ostẽdit secus rubū sicut dicit dñm deū Abraam deū Isaac deū Iacob"</note> Hence, just as Jacob is designated a "great father" by the poet, so too Abraham and Isaac deserved to be called so. Secondly, it is to be understood regarding Isaac that after Sarah his mother was taken by death in the city of Arba in the land of Hebron in the region of Canaan, he never allowed himself to take any consolation whereby he might soothe such great sadness and grief conceived by the death of Sarah, until he was constrained by the potent love of Rebecca his wife. She was procured for him <margin>☞</margin> by a servant of Abraham who asked for her from Bethuel, having first sworn to Abraham upon his body that he would not give to Isaac any wife born of the generation of Canaan. Bethuel was Isaac’s cousin, being the son of Nahor, brother of Abraham, son of Terah. When Isaac was joined to Rebecca, he loved her so intensely that immediately all the sorrow he had held for the death of Sarah ceased, as it is written in Genesis in the 24th chapter. Regarding Abraham, it is to be noted as Genesis testifies in the 12th chapter, that God having commanded Abraham to depart from the land of Haran and go to the place He would show him—which was the Promised Land inhabited at that time by the generation of Canaan—he obeyed the divine commandment. Then, after departing and dwelling upon Mount Bethel, a common and miserable famine came upon that region, by which Abraham was forced to go into Egypt. Because he loved Sarah supremely, and knowing that adultery was a most grave sin among the Egyptians, he feared being killed by them. To avoid being an adulterer with Sarah <note>The author suggests that if the Egyptians knew she was his wife, they would kill him to take her legally, whereas if they thought she was his sister, they would merely court her</note>, he begged her to consent to a lie and say she was not his wife, but only his sister. Thus love constrained the great Abraham to lie; which lie is not only determined to be a sin by theologians, but is also <term>eziandio</term> <note>An archaic Italian term meaning "even" or "also"</note> blamed by the moralists. Wherefore the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the fourth book of the *Ethics*: "A lie is in itself wicked and worthy of blame." <note>Original Latin: "Mendacium est per seipsum improbum ac vituperatione dignum"</note> He adds:

Wherefore, being more confirmed in his amorous pursuit through lying with Bathsheba, he commanded Uriah, who was then in Jerusalem, to return to the armies. By Uriah's own hands, he wrote back to Joab that he should expose Uriah so far forward in the battles to danger that he would surely die. Joab did as David had written to him; thus, while holding the siege at a city called Rabbah, the people of that land came out one day against the Israelites, and many of them—and among the others, Uriah the Hittite—were killed. When David heard this news, he immediately took Bathsheba as his wife. But later, having his error made known to him by Nathan <note>The prophet Nathan</note>, who proposed to him the case of the rich man who deserved death for having many sheep yet stealing the single lamb of a poor man, David judged that man worthy of death. Nathan replied that he was that rich man, and Uriah the Hittite was that poor man. Wherefore, on behalf of God, he announced to him an eternal curse. David, repentant, wept seven days upon the ground until the son whom Bathsheba had birthed died.

### THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

To fulfill his carnal appetite, he <note>King Solomon</note> had seven hundred queenly wives and three hundred other concubines, among whom were Egyptians, Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Sidonians, and Hittites. He loved them so immoderately that he allowed himself to be led into idolatry. Thus, to please the Sidonian women, he worshipped 
<margin>C</margin> the goddess Ashtoreth <note>Original: "Astherthen," the Phoenician goddess of fertility and love</note>, who was cultivated and venerated by that nation; and to console the Ammonite women, he worshipped Moloch, the idol of the Ammonites. Consequently, his fame was deservedly obscured, and it was called into doubt whether he had ever possessed any true intelligence in former times. Next, the poet <note>Petrarch</note> introduces the example of the furious and wicked love of Amnon, son of David, saying: Master Francesco, see that man—that is, Amnon—who here in a single indivisible moment both loves and defames Tamar, his sister. And see afterward how she, with great disdain and sorrow, laments to Absalom—her brother by both mother and father—regarding the injury done to her by Amnon. Whence he says:

> See him who in one moment loves and defames;
> See Tamar, who to her brother Absalom,
> Disdainful and grieving, makes her complaint.

<margin>D</margin> For a clearer understanding of the preceding lines, it should be understood that David had two children by the same woman, Absalom and Tamar, each of whom was most beautiful in their own way. David also had another son, Amnon, by a different woman. It happened, as written in the eleventh and twelfth chapters of the second book of Kings <note>Modern 2 Samuel 13</note>, that the aforementioned Amnon fell in love with his sister Tamar. Loving her ardently and keeping silent out of shame, he believed he could lead her to his desire; because she was a virgin and inexperienced in the flames of love, he was driven by this to fall ill. Seeing this, Jonadab—son of Shammah and brother of David <note>Actually David's nephew</note>, a prudent and cautious young man—asked him the cause of his illness. After various answers, Amnon finally told him the cause of his malady was Tamar, with whom he was strongly in love. Asking for help, Jonadab advised him to pretend to be gravely ill and ask David for Tamar to minister to him, so that he might then do his will with her. 

The advice of Jonadab pleased Amnon, and he put it into execution. Faking a condition much more grave than it was, when David visited him, Amnon asked as a favor that he grant him Tamar as his nurse. David did not suspect his son's wicked thought; therefore, he freely consented to the request. When Tamar arrived to care for her brother Amnon, as soon as she entered the room, he commanded everyone else to leave. Once they were alone, Amnon told Tamar he wished her to lie with him. But Tamar, recognizing the sin, resisted; she would not consent to his will but told him with sweet and discrete words that he should ask David for her as a wife, so he might possess without sin what he now sought to abuse through urgency. 

Amnon, however, stimulated by amorous fury and ignoring her true excuses and healthy warnings, set aside words and used force; thus, he lay with her not without violence. Immediately after his wicked desire was fulfilled, all the love he had improperly felt turned into hate, and she was <margin>E</margin> alone. Tamar, having received this injury, lamented to her brother Absalom. He took this grievance heavily but, prudently hiding his intent, prepared a most splendid banquet one day during the sheep-shearing season. Inviting all the King’s sons and his brothers, he invited Amnon with them. When they had all arrived, Absalom, for the sake of common vengeance for himself and Tamar, had Amnon killed. Thus did Amnon suffer the fitting penalty for the terrible sin committed against his sister, whom he could have justly enjoyed with delight. 

Next, the poet introduces the example of the very strong Samson, saying: Master Francesco, look a little beyond Amnon and see Samson, whom <margin>F</margin> you know was much stronger; yet Samson places his head in the lap of the unfaithful Delilah, his enemy. Whence:

> A little before her, see Samson,
> Far stronger than wise: who for trifles
> Lays his head in the lap of his enemy.
