# CHAPTER TWO

A swarm of bees had already created honey there; he took a portion of the honeycomb and ate it, and gave another part to his father and mother, but he did not reveal to them where he had obtained it. Afterward, Samson's father arranged a banquet for him, according to the custom of seven days. The citizens of Timnah <note>Original: "Thánata," the city where Samson found his first wife</note> chose thirty men to keep Samson company. One day, Samson said to them: "I want to propose a riddle to you. If you solve it for me within the seven days of the feast, I will give you thirty linen shirts and thirty changes of clothes; if you do not solve it, I want you to give the same to me." They replied that they were content and told him to propose the riddle. Samson then proposed it in this form: **Out of the eater came meat, and out of the strong came sweetness.** <note>original: "De comedēte exiuit cibus: 7 de forte egressa est dulcedo." This refers to the honey Samson found inside the carcass of a lion he had killed.</note> Those of Timnah, considering these words and being unable to interpret them in any way, went to his wife, saying: "Persuade your husband Samson to explain the riddle he proposed; otherwise, we will burn your house and your family." The girl, being terrified and weeping, begged Samson to manifest the hidden meaning he had proposed. After much resistance, Samson opened his heart to her, and she later revealed it to those who had asked. When the seventh day came, they solved the riddle, saying: **What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?** <note>original: "Quid dulcius melle: qd leone fortius."</note> And Samson said that if they had not plowed with his heifer <note>A biblical metaphor for his wife</note>, they never would have solved the proposition. He became quite indignant with the woman and returned to his father's house, having first paid for the shirts and garments which he took from thirty men he killed at Ashkelon. After this departure, Samson's father-in-law, seeing him indignant with the daughter, married her to another young man of the land who was joined to him in close friendship.

Then, after a certain time had passed and Samson's anger had cooled, he returned to Timnah to see his wife. Going to the father-in-law's house and wanting to enter the usual chamber, he was entirely prevented by the man, who said that he had married her to someone else, assuming Samson was still angry. Samson, hearing these words, said: "Now I am entirely excused if I do damage to the Philistines," and he departed. Since it was the time when the grain was dry, Samson took three hundred foxes <note>original: "volpiz"</note>, tied fire to their tails, and let them loose in the middle of the Philistines' fields. Running through the country, they burned all the grain. When the Philistines heard this and knew what Samson had done, they ran to the father-in-law's house and burned it down with him and all his substance and family inside. Hearing this, Samson—moved by the love he once bore his bride—resolved to take revenge. Staying in a cave called Etam, he did much and diverse damage to the Philistines. Therefore,
<margin>H</margin> 
the armed Philistines came into the land of Judah to capture Samson. The tribe of Judah, understanding the will of the Philistines and wishing to receive no further damage from them, promised to deliver Samson into their hands bound. Thus, three thousand of them went to the cave to bind him; he consented to this, first making them swear that they themselves would not kill him once he was bound. Leading him away in this manner, and having arrived at a place called the Jawbone <note>original: "maxilla," referring to Lehi</note>, the Philistines revealed certain ambushes and wanted to kill him. But seeing this, he broke the bonds and took up the jawbone of an ass, and with it he killed a thousand of them; the others he forced to flee.

Afterward, Samson came to a land named Gaza, where he saw a prostitute and went in to be with her. When the Philistines learned of this, they locked him in the land, keeping watch. But rising at midnight to depart and finding the gates locked, he took them upon his shoulders and carried them to the top of the mountain in the valley of Hebron. Finally, Samson loved a woman called Delilah <note>original: "Dalida"</note>. When the Philistines learned of this, they promised infinite gifts if she would arrange for Samson to be captured and fall into their power. She, moved by greed, asked Samson what was the cause of his great strength. Samson answered her several times but kept the truth hidden, and thus the Philistines were deluded. Wherefore Delilah, with a great abundance of tears, prayed to him again that he would 
<margin>I</margin> 
tell her the truth. Samson, moved by her feigned affection, said that all his strength was located in his hair. Therefore, one day Delilah, making more fuss over him than usual, had Samson lie in her lap to sleep. Then Delilah took scissors and cut off his hair. Consequently, when he was afterward assaulted by the Philistines, no longer having his accustomed strength, he remained a prisoner. They gouged out his eyes <note>original: "abacceinarō"</note> and he lived in such misery until his hair grew back. When Samson felt his strength returning, one day while a sacrifice was being celebrated in the temple—where all the people of the Philistines had gathered—he was kept by a column. Samson approached it and, embracing it, broke it. Thus, the temple fell, and he killed himself and the people for his revenge.

# THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

*He, although he was engaged in the practice of arms—where minds intent on great things are usually most distant from carnal lusts—was nonetheless seized by love to such an extent that he met his death. *For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known—as written in the Book of Judith—that after Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonosor," the King of the Neo-Babylonian Empire</note>, King of the Assyrians, had conquered a king named Arphaxad, his pride grew. He determined to subjugate the entire world to his empire. For this reason, he called Holofernes, the prince and duke of his armed forces, and commanded him to go to war, sparing no kingdom nor omitting any, no matter how strong or well-fortified the city. Holofernes did as the King commanded; he first took all of Cilicia and Mesopotamia, and from there, arriving in the fields of Damascus, he struck such terror into the minds of the neighboring peoples that they all confessed through their ambassadors that they wished to be his subjects.*

*Hearing this news, the children of Israel were greatly afraid. They first made preparations with God through the priest Eliakim <note>original: "Helischim"</note>. Afterward, they fortified the city with walls and provisions, especially upon the mountains and difficult places. In addition to this, so that Holofernes would not pass through and destroy Jerusalem and the Temple, they made other worthy and excellent provisions. When this became known to Holofernes, he was greatly angered. He asked the Moabites and those from the region of Ammon about the conditions, status, and strength of the people of Israel, marvelling that they alone among all the eastern peoples wished to resist him. He was answered by Achior, the leader of the Ammonites, who recounted the entire history of the children of Israel. He told him that they were of such a condition that if they had angered their God, he [Holofernes] could easily conquer them; if not, and if their God defended them, he would seek to subjugate them in vain.*

*Holofernes, enraged by these words, told Achior to leave and go to the children of Israel to see if any god was more powerful than Nebuchadnezzar; let him be defended by them, and if Holofernes captured the city, he would kill Achior along with them for his prophecy. Immediately, he commanded his servants to take him to Bethulia, a city of Israel, and leave him there. As the servants led Achior to Bethulia according to Holofernes' command, certain slingers <term>fundibulari (soldiers armed with slings)</term> came out from the land against them. There, having tied Achior to a tree, the servants fled; and the children of Israel, coming upon him, untied him and led him into Bethulia.*

*While Holofernes established the siege at Bethulia, and the people heard Holofernes' intentions from Achior, everyone grew fearful and began to weep and offer prayers to God. In the meantime, while Holofernes was organizing the battle, he found that Bethulia had its water source outside the gates. This water entered Bethulia through a system of conduits, which he immediately ordered to be cut, leaving Bethulia without water. Seeing this, the people decided*

| ¶ To understand the preceding verses, one must primarily know what is written in the Book of Esther: that King Ahasuerus was a powerful and esteemed king who ruled from Lower India even unto Ethiopia. Between these extremes were one hundred and twenty-seven provinces subject to him. This man had a most beautiful wife named Queen Vashti, with whom he was most fervently in love. Thus it happened that in the third year of his reign, Ahasuerus held a most splendid banquet for the princes of Persia and Media, and for the governors of the other provinces. To this banquet he also invited all the people of his capital city, called Susa, and decreed that this feast should last seven days according to their ancient custom. <margin>R</margin>
¶ And on the seventh day, King Ahasuerus being more cheerful than usual, commanded his eunuchs to introduce Queen Vashti to him. When they came to her, they explained the King’s will, to which she replied that she did not wish to go. For this reason the King was enraged, especially because he wished to show her beauty to the people. He took counsel from the seven leaders of Persia and Media, who were named Carshena, Shethar, Tarshish, Admatha, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, as to what should be done with Queen Vashti for not having obeyed him. Memucan replied that his judgment was that, lest the other women of Persia and Media be induced by her example to disobey their husbands—and moreover, because the queen had offended not only the king but all the princes present at the banquet—she should be deprived of her kingdom and no longer be admitted to the king’s presence, but another should be put in her place. This sentence pleased Ahasuerus, and he put it into execution. Because his eunuchs knew that if the King did not find another woman for a short space of time, he would not be able to restrain himself regarding Queen Vashti due to the immense love he bore her, they commanded Hegai <note>original: "Egeo," the keeper of the women</note>, the first eunuch, to search the kingdom for young maidens whose beauty would satisfy the king. Searching, therefore, he found in a city called Susa a most beautiful Hebrew girl without parents named Esther, who was governed only by her paternal uncle whose name was Mordecai. When she was led before the king and compared with all the others, she pleased Ahasuerus more than any other. For this reason, he established her as queen, and immediately his memory of the beauty and the intense love he bore for Queen Vashti began to fail and disappear in a short time. Secondly, it is to be known that not without reason during life it is commonly said:

> Just as one nail is driven out by another, so is love expelled by love. <note>original: "Sicut clauus clauo truditur ita amor amore pellitur." A common medieval proverb used to describe how a new passion cures an old one.</note>

And Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch, the author of the poem</note> affirms this to be the best remedy for love: to untie oneself from one knot by binding oneself to another. For love gives rise to a delight which leads a man into a habit, which then turns into nature, according to the opinion of Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher famous for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> in the first and seventh books of the *Physics*. And that which is natural always remains in the same uniformity, as Aristotle writes in the second book of the *Ethics*. For whenever a man has only one object of love, he always fixes his imagination solely on possessing that one. But when he then turns to another, he sets aside the first; for it is impossible for one mind to be intent upon two objects of love with equal goodwill, as is shown in the eighth book of the *Ethics*. And just as a river diminishes when diverted into several different streams, so by accumulating several different desires, the first ones always become more weakened. Afterward, Ahasuerus brings our poet to the example of Herod, the grandson of Herod of Ascalon, saying: Messer Francesco, do you wish to see in one heart and soul more varied contradictions—that is, weariness and delight, sweet and bitter? Now look at the fierce Herod, whom love and cruelty have besieged together. See also how he burns first with anger and pride against Saint John the Baptist, and then how he gnaws at himself and grieves through penance; and in vain he calls back for him because John does not hear him, Herod having had him put to death. Wherefore he says:

<margin>T</margin> The Tetrarch of Galilee <note>Herod Antipas</note> loved most exceedingly Herodias <note>original: "Herodiana"</note>, the wife of his brother Philip, Tetrarch of Iturea and the region of Trachonitis. For this matter, he was several times rebuked by John the Baptist. Wanting to withdraw from her because of John’s warnings—owing to the love and reverence he bore for John—the false Herodias, with feigned tears, so troubled Herod that he put <term>Saint John</term> in prison. 
¶ It then happened at this time that the anniversary of Herod's birth was celebrated, for which Herod, according to his custom, ordered a famous banquet to be prepared. In this banquet, the daughter of Herodias <note>Salome</note> having danced gracefully and having pleased Herod, he told her to ask for whatever she desired and affirmed with an oath that he would give it to her. When the young girl heard the king's offer, not knowing what to ask, she went to her mother to ask for advice. Herodias replied, telling her to ask for the head of <term>John the Baptist</term>. The girl returned to the banquet and asked Herod for what her mother had commanded. Herod was greatly disturbed because he feared and loved John the Baptist; yet, so as not to make the girl sad, he had John the Baptist's head cut off and given to her, which she immediately gave to her mother. Afterward, Herod, bearing this excess most painfully and repenting of the error committed, many times in vain—remembering John’s holy admonitions and prayers—called out for John the Baptist. There is also another interpretation concerning the preceding verses, and perhaps one no less fitting: that is, that the poet intends to speak of Herod of Ascalon <note>Herod the Great</note>, son of Antipater, procurator of Judea. How great his ferocity was is shown not only by the Gospel text of Matthew in the second chapter, but also by the killing of his own sons: Alexander, Aristobulus, and Antipater. Regarding this, Augustus deservedly said: "I would rather be Herod's pig than his son." <note>original: "se uole piu presto essere di Herode porco che figliuol"; this is a play on the Greek words for pig (*hyn*) and son (*hyion*).</note> His death was judged to be a clear vengeance for the bereaved fathers and mothers of Bethlehem. This man had a wife whom he loved intensely named <term>Mariamne</term> (or Ariane). One day, Salome <note>original: "Salonia"</note>, the sister of Herod, told him that her husband had lain with her <note>meaning Mariamne</note>. Because of this, he was infuriated and immediately killed the woman and his brother-in-law. Afterward, he took such grief for his dead wife that he almost entirely lost his senses; he wept for her always, in every place and at every time. But she, being dead, did not answer him; according to this interpretation, that last verse was meant: **Calling for MARIANNE, who does not hear him.** Next, the poet adds the example of three most singular women, saying:

¶ Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should primarily be known that <term>Procris</term> was the daughter of Erichthonius, son of Vulcan, and the wife of <term>Cephalus</term>, son of Aeolus. She loved her husband exceedingly, and Cephalus loved her so much that he no longer cared for Aurora <note>the Goddess of the Dawn</note>, who had anciently been his lover. Because of this mutual love, Aurora was moved to great anger; out of disdain, she told Cephalus to stop loving Procris, for if he knew what she knew, he would regret having her as a wife. Cephalus, becoming suspicious because of these words and wishing to test the chastity of his wife, transformed himself and took the habit of a merchant. By offering her great gifts, he made a pact for her virtue. When Cephalus realized her resolve wavered, he revealed himself. Procris felt such great shame that she suddenly fled into the woods and spent much time there with Diana. But having later returned to Cephalus through his prayers, and he still practicing the hunt, Procris gave him her Spear and the hound which Diana had previously given to her. As Cephalus often practiced the hunt, one day being exhausted and calling out for <term>Laura</term> <note>a play on the breeze (*Aura*) and Petrarch's beloved Laura</note> for refreshment, it was reported to Procris by a peasant that Cephalus was waiting for a nymph. She, then, to see what it was, followed him another day. While Cephalus, according to his custom, stopped and called for "Laura," Procris placed herself among the thick bushes and began to move toward him. Hearing this and thinking it was some wild beast, he threw the spear and struck her to death.

Secondly, one must understand the very great testimony and argument for love and benevolence written by **Cicero** in the third book of the *Tusculan Disputations* concerning **Queen Artemisia** <note>Artemisia II of Caria, famous for her extraordinary grief</note> and the love she bore for her beloved husband, **Mausolus**. He was the King of Caria, who, after a long time spent with his worthy and beloved Artemisia, came to his death. After his end, she showed no fewer signs of benevolence than she had in life. Thus, after the dutiful—even exuberant—tears, and also through her perpetual widowhood, she had a marvelous tomb constructed for him in the region of Halicarnassus, which was deservedly numbered as one of the <term>Seven Wonders of the World</term>. Nor was she content with a single architect; setting aside all greed, she brought in **Scopas**, **Bryaxis**, **Timotheus**, and **Leochares** <note>original: "iocare"</note>, the most singular builders in all of Greece, for the construction. Truly, this was to be judged a notable sign of love. But certainly much greater is what she did after the burning of the funeral pyre and after the collection of the ashes of her beloved husband Mausolus. For judging every other vessel and tomb to be unworthy of them—except for that breast where the flame of love was always burning—she took those ashes, and having mixed them with liquid, she drank them. And with her
<margin>About Deidamia</margin>
tears she buried a part of him every day, until at once the tears, the ashes, and her life failed her. In the third and final place, one must see how, appearing not much inferior to this, **Deidamia** is to be judged. She was the daughter of **Lycomedes**, to whom her mother **Thetis** had sent **Achilles** dressed in women’s clothing <note>Thetis hid Achilles among women to prevent him from going to the Trojan War</note>. Having slept with her and she having become pregnant with **Pyrrhus**, she was prepared never to change her love after Achilles' departure. She never again wished to consent to another new husband, but determined that as long as she lived, she would feed her mind on his memory. After his death, she mourned his fortune, rendering no less honor to him in her widowhood than she had received pleasure from him in life. Just as the poet has described three excellent women of singular and praiseworthy love in the preceding verses, so in the following ones he describes three other most wicked women whose appetite was not only disordered but highly to be blasphemed and rebuked, saying: "O Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, see three other bold and wicked women: namely, **Semiramis**, **Byblis**, and **Myrrha**." And see how each of them seems to be ashamed of their crooked path, which was not only unpermitted but entirely prohibited. Whence he says:

<margin>Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should primarily be known—as **Trogus** writes—that **Semiramis** was the wife of **Ninus**, King of the Assyrians. He, having begun to subject kingdoms by means of war and to treat them according to his will, tried to subdue the Egyptians. Leading his armies against them, he was wounded by an arrow in battle and died. He was succeeded by Semiramis and his son, **Ninus**. She was singular in her rule; thus, she not only maintained what remained to her dead husband but added Ethiopia and India <note>original: "Lindia"</note> to her kingdom, as we shall say in the *Triumph of Fame*. Nevertheless, there was such an itch of lust in her regarding the venereal act that she cast aside the proper chastity of women with many men. Beyond this, she committed the wicked incest with her son Ninus; and to excuse herself for such wickedness, she added to the sin a law that in the venereal act every license should be permitted. A truly abominable thing, conforming more to a bestial nature than a human one. In the second place, it must be understood that **Byblis**, daughter of **Miletus** (son of the Sun), was not different in her wound. For as **Ovid** writes in the tenth book of the *Metamorphoses*, her brother **Caunus** being most beautiful of body, she fell fervently in love with him. Being unable to restrain her unbridled desire, she revealed her appetite to him. Caunus, having understood, discreetly rebuked her for such an error, and to remove every cause, he left her and went to live in other lands. But Byblis, still standing in her fierce purpose, followed him through various regions, such as Lelegian Caria and Lycia. Nevertheless, Caunus never wavered from his reasonable constancy.</margin>

And not knowing in what way she could fulfill her beastly appetite because of the great impropriety which she rightly judged in this desire, she turned entirely to despair and to killing herself. A nurse of hers, recognizing this great passion and distress, comforted her and promised her help, and moreover, arranged a work suited to her will. For one day when Cinyras was alone, she told him that a noble young girl was in love with him and greatly desired to sleep with him, but by no means wished to be seen by him. Cinyras, having heard her proposal and not suspecting the wound of his daughter, consented to do as the nurse had requested. Whereupon she, giving herself to the service, managed it in such a way that Myrrha lay several times with her father, to the point that she became pregnant with Adonis, who was later loved by Venus according to the poets. Then, after no great delay of time, Cinyras, recognizing the deception of Myrrha, became almost furious; wishing to strike her, she fled. He followed her as far as Arabia and Sheba <note>original: "Sabea"</note>, where, having reached her, he struck her with a knife in the belly, from which she died; and the son, Adonis, fell to the ground from the wound. was converted into a tree, from whose cracks in the bark she then gave birth to Adonis. Messer Francesco says: "See, here are those," namely Lancelot, Tristan, and the other wandering knights, around whom—due to the follies already described regarding them—it is necessary that common men yearn for them; and with them see also Guinevere and Iseult, and the other lovers of the aforementioned description. <margin>F</margin>
For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it should be understood that the Lord of Rimini, of the House of Malatesta, had two sons: one named Gianciotto <note>original: "Anciotto"</note> and the other Paolo. Gianciotto took as his wife a most beautiful young woman named Francesca. When she saw her brother-in-law Paolo, who was very handsome, and he looked upon her, seeing her no less beautiful and noble, they secretly fell in love with one another. Nonetheless, such was the restraint of each of them that neither dared to reveal it to the other, but they only made certain signs that naturally tend to be produced by such a desire. It then happened that, following their permitted intimacy and their family relation, one day the two secret lovers remained alone together. Following the custom of nobles, they began to read for pleasure; they happened to pick up a book called *Galeotto* <note>Referring to the Old French Lancelot-Grail cycle; "Galeotto" (Galahaut) was the go-between for Lancelot and Guinevere</note>, written and composed by a certain Master Galeotto, which contained the story of the love between Queen Guinevere <note>original: "Gineura"</note> and Lancelot <note>original: "Lancilotto"</note>, her most faithful lover. Having reached a place in their reading where a kiss given by Lancelot to Queen Guinevere was described, love and the efficacy of those words had such power that Paolo took courage; drawing near to his Francesca, he kissed her, while she was trembling and making an amorous gesture. This act served as a means for each lover to discover how great their flame of love had been and with what difficulty it had been hidden. From that hour forward, it was the cause of their love reaching its desired conclusion. After some time, either through their own inadvertence or by chance, the husband Gianciotto noticed their behavior. He kept such a diligent watch over their proceedings that one day he caught them in the very act of love. Moved to great anger and immeasurable fury, he took a knife and rushed upon them; as they were one on top of the other, he cruelly killed them both with a single blow. Thus, the most noble bride Francesca and his brother Paolo, through this death, gave cause to be celebrated by poets in their poems during these times. Having finished the discourse of the shade, Messer Francesco consequently describes what became of him through its words; this is the principal conclusion he intends for this second chapter, where he wishes to show that he himself was also captured by love, and this by means of a graceful young girl, pure in soul like a very white dove. Whence the poet says that—considering the restraint, the learning, the arduous cares of kingdoms, the ferocity of spirits, and the other singular qualities of those men he had recounted, who were nonetheless conquered by love—he already despaired of himself and feared he might come to similar sufferings. And like one who is judged to die, while the sentence is read and the trumpet announces silence, who continually thinks of his final step, weighing the pain and bitterness of it, even though he is not yet oppressed by the executioner <note>original: "spicvlatore"</note>: so the poet affirms that he thought of what martyrdoms he would be forced to suffer when he fell in love. While he wandered in this thought, out of fear of the future evil that seemed already prepared for him, pale and colorless, he saw a most pure young girl at his side. Although he had believed he could defend himself like a robust man, expert and wrapped in armor, he was nonetheless conquered and overcome by her presence. Whence he says:

## CHAPTER TWO
->24<-

->To defend myself from a man covered in armor;<-
->With words and with gestures I was bound;<-

These words are understood to mean that women possess men, since beautiful women are naturally desired objects for men for the procreation of children; for this reason, as soon as they appear before our eyes, they are desired by the appetite. But this appetite can be either upright and blameless, or reprehensible. It is upright when one desires women for the sake of a natural end, which is lawful marriage. But it is reprehensible when they are desired only for carnal delight, which is, as we said above, an original inclination <note>original: "originale inclinatione," referring to the theological concept of the bent toward sin inherited from Adam</note> toward such acts solely through the sin of our first parents.

<margin>H</margin>
It happens, therefore, that when beautiful women are seen by men of gravity and prudence, some pleasure is taken in the sight of them; seeing them a second and third time, they look upon them again with delight. Through this continued looking, desire is secretly kindled to such an extent that they realize they cannot refrain from seeing them again without great difficulty and distress. In this state—especially if they have received some sign of mutual goodwill—even though they know their desire is not reasonable, they begin to argue with themselves and cite examples of other men caught in a similar snare <note>original: "laccio irretiti"</note>, through which they are confirmed in their love. This process, then, led our Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, after having first described so many other men in love, to be inadvertently captured himself by that pure girl. By this capture, he, along with the others, had fallen into a most wretched state, according to the judgment of Seneca in the book *On the Happy Life*, who says:

<margin>I</margin>
Pleasure comes to a most shameful life, and indeed the unhappy are not without pleasure; rather, they become so because of pleasure itself <note>original: "Voluptas ad vitam turpissimam venit & quidem infelices non sine voluptate: immo ob ipsam voluptatem fiunt."</note>.

Similarly, Archytas of Tarentum <note>A Greek philosopher and mathematician, a contemporary of Plato</note> used to say:

No more deadly plague has been given to men by nature than bodily pleasure, since God gave man nothing more excellent than the mind: nothing is so hostile to this divine gift as pleasure <note>original: "Nulla capitalior pestis hominib9 a natura data est quam corporis voluptas cum qua nihil prestabilius mēte Deus dedisset homini: nihil huic tam divino muneri est tam inimicum quam voluptas."</note>.

Moving forward, one must understand the great diversity of opinions that are celebrated at the present time regarding what this girl, with whom Master Francesco says he is in love, is meant to represent. For many do not agree that she was an earthly woman, because he testifies in that fourth song, **GREEN CLOTHES** <note>The canzone "Verdi panni, sanguigni, oscuri o persi"</note>, that no other object is a more fitting means of reaching the kingdom of eternal life than that of his love, where he says at the end: "since I saw her, all other paths to heaven have been made straight for me." And one does not aspire to the glorious kingdom in a sturdier ship; a thing which can in no way be understood as referring to an earthly woman. The second reason is that he says in many places that he loves that same girl who Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> loved, who was turned into a tree. And especially in that sonnet, "Apollo, if the beautiful desire still lives," where he says: **DEFEND NOW** the honored and sacred foliage <note>The laurel tree/Daphne</note>, where you first and then I were ensnared; this same thing he affirms in that first sestina, **TO EVERY ANIMAL** that dwells on earth, where he says at the end of the sixth stanza: "And that she would not be transformed into a green wood / To ever escape my arms, as on the day / That Apollo followed her down here on earth." From this, it seems necessarily to follow that this meaning cannot be verified in a mortal woman. The third and final reason is that Master Francesco, in his other Latin works, most highly blames all those who have fallen into this error <note>The "error" of carnal love</note>, especially in the *Eclogues* and in *On the Remedies of Both Fortunes*. There, where poets and philosophers—and especially Plato—condemn and mock this kind of vanity, it seems he would have to rebuke himself if he had loved an earthly woman so intensely. And therefore some say the beloved was the Christian religion; some say Penitence; others Science in general; some only Poetry; some Moral Philosophy; some the Soul; and some others the Mother Mary. Although each of the aforementioned opinions has a very serious author behind it, we certainly 

<margin>K</margin>
affirm that the beloved of Master Francesco was Lauretta, a truly mortal woman, of whom we spoke above in our discourse on his life. [He] demonstrates in several places, especially in the *Triumph of Chastity*, how he transforms himself into her; just as he asserts in the present chapter. This transformation <term>transformation</term> <note>The Neo-Platonic idea of the lover becoming the beloved</note> is nothing other than [an effect] through work and through will. And through this operation, **Master Francesco** <note>Petrarch</note>, following the example of Laura virtuously, was in such a way led to the highest good <term>highest good</term> <note>the *summum bonum* or ultimate happiness</note> and glorious kingdom of virtue. There is no efficacy if one were to say that a man led to happiness no longer removes his soul from it—as **Plato** said in the ***Phaedrus***—in order to possess inferior things. For Plato only asserted this when there was a continuous rule of reason over appetite <term>appetite</term> <note>the sensory desires or passions</note>. But during our life, reason and appetite being the principles of our operations—as is written in the first [book] of **the *Ethics*** <note>Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics*</note> and in the first of ***On Duties*** <note>Cicero’s *De Officiis*</note>—and because the faculty of choosing is free within us, for this reason, sometimes reason dominates, and sometimes the sensory appetite. And therefore, sometimes men are brought down from high considerations to the lowest, and from the lowest they then ascend to the heights. That such variations were in **Master Francesco** is clearly shown in those three sonnets: **FATHER of heaven, after** <note>original: "PADRE del ciel doppo," Sonnet 62</note> <margin>O</margin> **the lost days.** The sixteenth year remained behind; he says: **Seventeen years has the sky already turned.** <note>original: "diceſepte anni ha gia riuolto il cielo," Sonnet 122</note> From which it is not inconvenient if **Master Francesco** asserts that he is pulled by Laura to the highest good, and then he will depart from that through the force of the sensory appetite. The other way is according to the opinion of speculative theologians and philosophers, who assert the highest good is to know God. And because He is his own essence and cannot be [directly] known, it is necessary to understand Him by proceeding from effects to that first cause. From which, the more this perfection is an effect, the more readily it invites us to divine knowledge. # THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

...and if anyone should say that **Master Francesco** <note>Petrarch</note> often says **Lady Laura** is a divine thing and therefore not an earthly lady: we respond that this is a custom of poets. When they wish to praise someone supremely, they say either that they are truly divine or descended from the gods, just as **Virgil** affirms in the *Eclogues* <note>The *Bucolics*</note> when he says in praise of **Octavian**: *Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven.* <note>original Latin: "Iam nova progenies celo dimittit alto"</note> And also, if others should say the poem of Master Francesco is unworthy because he spoke of an earthly woman—the contrary of which is affirmed by him and by others—we respond that this objection is frivolous. This is because, principally, a most virtuous lady is a worthy subject for a poem; and even if she were not, the poem is rendered worthy by its invention, purpose, and words. Otherwise, it would be necessary to concede that all the poems of the comic writers and many orations of the orators were unworthy.

<margin>R</margin>
Therefore, without further delaying our speech, let us conclude that the pure maiden whom our Master Francesco took [as his subject] was Lady Laura, a truly mortal woman produced naturally in this way. But if in this place anyone should judge me an insolent, ungrateful, and stubborn son for being at odds with and almost contrary to the opinion of the venerable memory of the eminent doctor **Master Piero da Montalcino**, our father—who in his exposition of the sonnets of Master Francesco to **Filippo Maria**, the late happy Duke of Milan, says and affirms that our poet’s muse was "Lady Poetry"—I respond to this that I would be too worthy of grave censure if in any small part I attempted to refute the opinion of him from whose person I have received my being according to every understanding, dignity, and comfort. Wherefore, confirming his most worthy imagination, I say that between his opinion and mine there is no contradiction. For he, as was appropriate to his gravity, learning, and clear genius, wished to follow the moral sense <term>moral sense</term> <note>the allegorical or symbolic meaning of a text</note> in explaining it; but the lowliness of my intellect did not allow me to fly so high. Therefore, leaving him to sit upon the mountains in heaven, I intend to proceed according to my own strengths, following only the literal sense <term>literal sense</term> <note>the historical or surface-level meaning</note> down on earth. Thus, since my father and I have different intentions regarding the same subject, every contradiction is removed according to the doctrine of the rules of logic <term>dialectical norms</term>. Master Francesco then adds most elegantly, demonstrating the nature of those who err by not recognizing their own failings, but only becoming aware of them when they are manifested by others. Therefore, he introduces the shade <note>a spirit or ghost</note> who, smiling at him, says: "O Master Francesco, you can now speak for yourself and recognize the enamored spirits; for you are now, together with all the rest of us, subject to the flames of love and are stained with the same pitch." <note>A metaphor for being involved in the same difficult or "sticky" situation</note>

<margin>S</margin>
As we said at the beginning, the poet skillfully describes himself from this point forward as knowing the enamored spirits by his own sight, because he is no longer divided from them. He is constrained to excuse his error by bringing in the example of others, as is the nature and custom of all those who, while making some resistance with reason against appetite, are in the end entirely 
<margin>T</margin>
subjugated by that appetite. Our Master Francesco, having been placed in such a state of love, describes separately within himself the propensity of lovers, reciting what he became after he realized he had fallen in love. Wherefore he says that, principally, he had joined the number of those to whom the pleasure and contentment of others is much more painful than their own misfortune—especially being in the presence of the one who had ensnared him while he was in peace and tranquil liberty. Wherefore he says:

> And as it seems I truly recall,
> My friend drew closer to me,
> And with a smile, to give me more pain,
> He said into my ear: "Henceforth you are permitted
> To speak for yourself with whom you please,
> For we shall all be stained with the same pitch."

<margin>V</margin>
The meaning introduced by the preceding verses of our poet is a most well-known thing. For its clarity, one must know that when a man is truly in love, because of his intense desire for the beloved thing, he does not comprehend that any of his own passion is damaging to him. Instead, he only takes displeasure at the delights of others, judging every other happiness of lovers to be his own torment when seeing them; and seeing them prosper in love, he thinks they have a much better fortune in love than he does.

> I was one of those whom it more displeases
> To see another's good than his own ill,
> Seeing the one who had taken me in liberty and in peace:

### CHAPTER THREE

<margin>X</margin>
¶ [The author] introduces next the second effect of love in which the poet finds himself, saying that although he realized it late after his injury, he understood that only Lady Laura caused him pain and death through her beauty, whereby he burned with love, jealousy, and envy. Hence he says:

> **And how late after the damage do I understand;**
> **From her beauties my death was made,**
> **Burning with love, jealousy, and envy.**

<margin>y</margin>
<margin>
¶ As Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> shows clearly enough in the preceding verses, it is a nearly universal custom of lovers that at the start of their falling in love, they think they have supreme pleasure and delight in the beauties of the ladies they love, for then they consider nothing further. But after they are ensnared in the snares of love, they then realize they have competitors; whence jealousy and the fear of losing the goodwill of their beloved immediately arise from their love. Regarding this, Ovid writes excellently: *Love is a thing full of anxious fear* <note>original Latin: "Res est solliciti plena timoris amor"</note>. Nor are the unhappy lovers troubled by this passion alone, but also by envy: for when they recognize that some sweet and amorous pleasure is granted to other lovers, either by their beloved or other women, so much envy arises in their hearts that whatever other trouble occurs to them may well be judged much smaller.
</margin>

¶ The poet then recounts another effect which arises from love: an insatiable will to possess and to see the desired beloved <term>manza|An archaic Italian term for a sweetheart or mistress</term> and to always hear talk of her. He excellently compares lovers to the appetite of sick men who always desire those things which, while offering little pleasure to the taste, cause great detriment to their health. Since they are deaf to other reasoning and blind to different objects, and totally numb to other pleasures, they only follow their desire through so many doubtful and dangerous outcomes that if it ever happens they are released from such love, they tremble with fear and shame whenever they remember their past life. Our Master Francesco describes this happening to him after his imprisonment <note>Referring to the "captivity" of love</note>. Hence he says:

> **I did not turn my eyes from her beautiful face,**
> **Like a sick man, greedy for such a thing**
> **Which is sweet to the taste, but harmful to health.**
> **To every other pleasure I was blind and deaf,**
> **Following her through such doubtful steps**
> **That I still tremble whenever I remember it.**

<margin>
Concerning the clearer understanding of the preceding verses, one must know that there are two dangerous paths by which wretched lovers are lost, especially those from whom gravity and moderation are expected due to some excellent dignity. One is the danger to the body, and the other is the danger to one’s reputation <term>fama|In this context, it refers to one's social standing, honor, and public name</term>. Oh, how many hardships they suffer in the rigid and turbulent nights of winter just to hear a single word from the beloved!
</margin>

How many [hardships] in scouting the entrance to go speak with her; how many [dangers] from the mutual enmities of lovers coming to the sword. How much sleep is lost. How many illnesses are contracted. How many cold spells, rains, snows, hailstorms, and windstorms are finally tolerated with patience. Oh, who is there who can fully explain the infamy that is acquired: the many follies, the wickedness, the undignified detours that are taken, the tears that are shed against constant virility, the young and effeminate grooming of the body, the many lusts that are contemplated—whence not only men but even faint-hearted and base women should rightly deem them infamous. Therefore, Master Francesco rightly trembled when he considered these dangers prepared for him, which he felt were procured for him by the great love he bore for Laura. He also well recognized that the sweetnesses of love, however much sweetness they gave to the taste, were nonetheless totally contrary to the health of both body and soul. The will, confirming itself and almost forming a habit in amorous desire through the sensory delight, generated a custom from which remorse is then impossible, or at least very difficult. [The author] introduces next another effect of love, which is a continuous affliction of the mind with a disdain toward oneself and a varied defense which lovers make when it seems they receive injury in their love: which is to separate oneself from human company and live in solitude to test oneself and consign the injuries received from love to oblivion—which thing is the greatest stimulus and increase of desire and of...

The commentator compares the lover's irrational desire to a sick man's craving for harmful food, emphasizing the damage done to one's reputation and health.</summary>

# THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

...sorrow and returning to his accustomed martyrdoms: saying that from the day he fell in love, he always kept his
eyes cast down, looking at the earth: and they were wet from the tears shed in grief: and his heart was filled
with thoughts: and for his solitary dwelling, he chose infinite rivers, mountains, and woods: stones: deserts: uncultivated and 
uninhabited forests. Wherefore he says:

->**From that time I had my eyes moist and downcast**<-
->**The heart pensive, and a solitary dwelling;**<-
->**Springs, rivers, mountains, woods, and stones**<-

<margin>B</margin>
The well-known and manifest reasons for the solitary state of lovers are understood chiefly by those who have been ensnared by similar traps. The poet describes one of these in the aforementioned verses, namely, to consign amorous injuries to oblivion; and this is found almost universally in all lovers. The other reason is to flee the blame they feel they incur for their effeminate deeds, especially when they are men of some <term>gravity|the quality of being serious, dignified, and authoritative</term>; for such men, whose minds are usually occupied with excellent things, are often distracted by such lascivious desires, just as our author affirms he has done entirely. Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> consequently narrates another effect of love: not a universal one, but one specific to men of letters, saying that he would tear up all the papers he filled with ink in praise of Lady Laura, accompanied by a great abundance of tears and sighs for the memory of past slights; and then, compelled by powerful Love, he would prepare, rule, and write just as many again. Wherefore he says:

->**From then on I sprinkle so many papers**<-
->**With thoughts, with tears, and with ink:**<-
->**So many I tear, prepare anew, and write**<-

<margin>C</margin>
It is the custom and nature of excellent wits to always exercise themselves in works that are laudable, especially in scholastic studies. When love joins with such high-mindedness, the man chiefly practices poetic studies, as they are more conforming and more suited to cooling the amorous flames from which poems often proceed. Through these, one seeks to acquire goodwill or to move the beloved to compassion; yet when the poets see themselves moved to anger and desperation, they tear them up, and then for the same reasons they compose them again, just as happened to our poet, who sometimes,
<margin>D</margin>
to satisfy his appetite for vengeance, would tear up his works in vain, and then, conversely, would write them again. The poet next introduces a general effect of amorous hope and fear, whose swift variety clearly demonstrates how much bodily <term>consumption|the wasting away of the body, often linked to melancholy or illness in the Renaissance</term> follows. He says that from the day he fell in love, he knows what happens within the "cloister" of love, and how quickly a man moves from hope to fear. Thus, he who well understands the nature of love can clearly see on the lover's forehead the disposition of the soul within, which can be read openly in that place. Wherefore he says:

->**From then on I know what is done in the cloister**<-
->**Of Love, and who fears, and who hopes,**<-
->**For one who knows how to read the omen on the forehead,**<- <note>original: "mostro". While literally "monster," in this poetic context it refers to the outward sign or "prodigy" of the internal state.</note>

<margin>E</margin>
In the preceding verses, he expresses a natural reason for the <term>macilentia|leanness or wasting away of the body</term> and <term>mestitia|deep sadness or melancholy</term> of wretched lovers: which is the mortification of the vital spirits by their inward burning. From this follows a general consumption of the 
body, one part of which comes from the fear of losing the beloved object, and the second from the continuous movement of those spirits. Most frequent is the wrath of lovers, by which the spirits become inflamed, whereby the forehead becomes melancholic and the face wrinkled in such a way that one can clearly perceive the soul within to be seized by great and singular displeasure.
<margin>F</margin>
It is not without reason that lovers have fallen into such a state as our graceful poet has described, for which they must lament. Therefore, Master Francesco adds an amorous lament which arises from a universal opinion among lovers: that it is never possible for their beloveds to love them in the same way they are loved. Wherefore they always accuse them of obstinacy, cruelty, and hardness—especially our Master Francesco, who truly experienced that Laura did not wish to consent to his pleasures. As he affirms in the subsequent chapter, he saw this graceful and most cruel beast, Laura, go her way, caring nothing for his pains nor his singular sorrows, proud in her appearance through her own virtue.

# CHAPTER TWO

natural and mental [qualities], and furthermore she showed herself no less proud for having ensnared and captured Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> with her beauty and excellent gifts, making him a subject to the empire of love: wherefore she carried away his <term>spoils|the clothing or armor taken from a defeated enemy in war</term> in the likeness of ancient beasts of burden <note>original: "iumenti"</note>. And besides this, he adds that he is deprived of all hope, because Love—in whom he trusted—was forcing everyone else, but trembled and was terrified of her. Nor did Love show any daring or strength in defense of the wretched lover; rather, if he ever wanted to show her favor, he flattered and deceived her, while he cruelly flayed the lover along with all other lovers in a similar state. From this it happened that there was no one who could constrain Laura in any part; but solitary and remote, free and unattached, she proceeded far from the banners of love, not only a rebel against him but bold and haughty. Wherefore he says:

<margin>G</margin>
->**And I see that graceful and fierce woman go her way,**<-
->**Caring nothing for me, nor for my pains,**<-
->**Proud of her virtue and of my spoils.**<-

->**This lord who forces the whole world**<-
->**Fears her, wherefore I am without hope;**<-
->**For I have neither daring nor strength for my defense,**<-

->**To walk alone, away from the banners of love.**<-

It is a consistent thing that whenever lovers love intensely and are constrained by most ardent desire, they must try by every means to see if they are equally loved in return. This is because it is only through mutual and reciprocal love that they can reach that intended goal they seek; without it, every appetite and will of theirs is in vain. However, it may be that in loving, one does not desire carnal union, as happened to Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, as he clearly shows in that sonnet *Among the other ladies from time to time* <note>Sonnet 218</note> and in that other one, *When Simon reached the high concept* <note>Sonnet 77, referring to the painter Simone Martini</note>. Nevertheless, it is impossible that one does not desire mutual benevolence and reciprocal love,

<margin>H</margin>
without which—where there is no disordered hope—it is impossible for the amorous concept to be maintained. Having therefore Master Francesco tried the mind of Laura in various ways to find this, and being unable to gain any certain confidence from her, he describes himself in the preceding verses as being almost deprived of all hope. He adds next a universal custom of lovers (but much more so among discreet and grateful men), which is to always highly praise, extol, and adorn their beloved with every virtue. Our poet optimally observes this in this place, and by highly expressing the dignity of Laura, he conforms to those continent lovers who, as long as they recognize some singular quality in their beloved, patiently endure all amorous martyrdoms. Continuing from the superior verses, he says this Lady Laura is a total rebel and fugitive from love in every gesture: her walk, her smile, her disdain, and her words. In comparison to other women, she is like the bright sun among the lesser stars, which it obscures with its greater light and splendor. And besides this, such is the brightness and beauty of her hair—whether gathered in tresses and bound with gold, or truly dispersed in the wind—and the celestial, lovely, and unfailing light of her beautiful eyes, which inflames him so sweetly that, considering their excellence, he said: "I am content to burn." But these are only gifts of nature which deserve most ample praise. Therefore, who could ever adequately explain the graceful, angelic, and sweet customs and the sublime virtues of her soul? Certainly, my style would be as follows in wanting to extol those: like a tiny stream compared to the sea, wishing for its water to make the sea overflow. For truly these singular parts of Laura are new, never before seen in the world with such perfection, nor even to be seen more than once. This is because it is impossible for such a perfect being of the soul to be found in another person, and also because there cannot be another gathering of the particular causes of her beauty. This follows the judgment of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the second book of *On Generation* <note>original: "de generatione"</note>: that an effect cannot return in a similar way, nor can there be two effects of every-way similarity. Wherefore he says:

<header>THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE</header>

# THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

<margin>F</margin>
It is the natural appetite of all men, in whatever action they perform, to wish to receive commendation and praise for it, and especially in those two areas where the examination of judgment and the freedom of choice concur. From these, when one judges and chooses rightly, much honor seems to follow. Since the judgment and choice of love are of this quality, it is the universal custom of all lovers, while their amorous desire lasts, to highly praise and extol their beloved. Therefore, <note>Petrarch</note> **M. F.** <note>original: "Messer Francesco"</note>, not deviating from this custom, has reported the aforementioned praises of his lady Laura, through which he might be able to justly excuse himself for how much he was reproached for this love at that time. Furthermore, he provides an effective and fitting response to anyone who, out of some passion, might condemn his beloved. **M. F.** then narrates the conclusion of his state together with a lover’s exclamation, saying that from what was narrated above, he found himself caught in the snares of love while Laura remained free and entirely rebellious. Crying out, he says: "O unjust star that guides and conducts my actions; I call to her continually day and night, and she not only does not yield to my voice, but hardly ever stops to listen to me." Wherefore he says:

> And truly she is a sun among the stars,
> A singular bearing of her own,
> Her smile, her disdain, and her words.
> Her tresses gathered in gold, or scattered to the wind;
> The eyes, which, lit with a celestial light,
> Inflame me so, that I am content to burn.
> Who could ever equal in speech her gentle, noble manner
> And her virtue,
> Where my style is like a small river to the sea:
> New things, and never seen before,
> Nor ever to be seen again more than once,
> Where all tongues would be silent.

<margin>R</margin>
<margin>L</margin>
For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it is necessary to know <note>original: "sapere"</note> that many most learned men—such as Cicero in his book *On Divination*, Virgil in the *Aeneid*, Ovid in the *Metamorphoses*, Seneca in his *Tragedies*, and many others as we shall say in the *Triumph of Fame*—wished that every effect produced in this world were produced by a <term>fatal disposition|the idea that events are predetermined by fate or the stars</term>. However, they held differing opinions on what "fate" was. Some said it was a connection of causes ordered among themselves back to the first cause, which is the immutable Divine Will; Cicero seems to affirm this opinion in the cited book. Some others said the cause of the necessity of effects was the stars and the celestial bodies, and that the Divine Will might not be the efficient cause but the final cause; such was the view of the astrologer Posidonius, Nigidius Figulo <note>A Roman scholar and astrologer</note>, and our **M. F.**, as he shows us in this place. But he is clearer in that sonnet: *If the star in heaven has power over us / as much as some believe: it was under such a star I was born.* And in that other: *The evil <note>original: "M AL." refers to 'Il mal'</note> presses me: I fear the worst,* where he says: *But why complain more of us? / That chord is already struck in the high seat,* and in many other places which we omit as they are not necessary now. For this reason, **M. F.**, attributing the effects to the bodies above, then laments against Laura and reproaches her, saying: "O unjust star." **M. F.** proceeds even further in his exclamation, describing another effect of love: the way lovers console themselves when they have recognized the hardness and harshness of the amorous life, eventually reducing themselves to patience because so many men are bound by love, even those who were reputed to be gods. He says: "O harsh law of love, though it be crooked, bitter, and heavy, yet it must be observed with patience because it is universal and ancient, not only among earthly men." He even adds to this the heaven of those whose virtues and works caused them to be reputed as gods by us. Wherefore he says:

> Thus I find myself captured and she free;
> And I pray day and night (O unjust star)
> And she hardly listens to one in a thousand.

<margin>M</margin>
**MESSER FRANCESCO** does not depart with this sentiment from the venerable authority of the laws, which constrain men to obey them, however much <note>catchword: "tung ne" / "although"</note>

> Harsh law of love: but though it be unjust,
> It must be obeyed, for it joins
> Heaven to earth, a universal and ancient thing.

It explains that the "harsh law of love" is an inescapable force affecting both mortals and gods alike.</summary>

# CHAPTER THREE

However harsh, sharp, and difficult they are to endure—as is clearly shown by the text in the law *prospexit* <note>A reference to the *Digest* of Roman Law regarding how seeing the similar misfortunes of others can provide a form of legal or emotional relief</note>—when one recognizes a similar passion in others, one is almost silently invited to have patience. Next, **M. F.** <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch</note> adds many varied effects of love <margin>N</margin> besides those already narrated, which wretched lovers experience. He says that now that he is in love, he knows how the heart separates itself from the body, and how it often makes war, truce, and then peace with his beloved; and also how sometimes the pain and passion are covered and hidden, even though there is a very sharp sting within the soul. Wherefore he says:

<margin>O</margin>
<margin>V</margin>
<margin>¶ We said at the beginning, according to Plato's division of the souls, how the vital soul <note>In Renaissance philosophy, the 'vital soul' was responsible for life and heat, centered in the heart</note> resided in the heart, whose operations are assumed to be primary. Therefore, as the concupiscible soul <note>The 'desiring' part of the soul associated with appetite and attraction</note> separates from us and joins—</margin>
> Now I know how the heart separates from itself;
> And how it knows to make peace, war, and truce;
> And to cover its pain when it is stung.

<margin>P</margin>
—joining with their beloveds, lovers find through proven experience how, neglecting all care for themselves, they have placed their own joy inside the bodies of the beloved ladies. They also know by experience how quickly they make war with them when they see some sign of contempt, or—what is much more painful to them—when it seems that the ladies look more lovingly upon another lover than upon themselves. And they also experience how, in their most fervent anger, some memory of past sweetness returns, so that they immediately bend to make a truce; then, unable to resist the desire, they conclude a peace within themselves, especially when some piteous look from the beloved intervenes: a small tear, a sigh, or some sweet word of good promise or reasonable excuse. He consequently narrates another effect of love which often occurs in the disposition of loving, saying that he knows how the blood vanishes in an instant, and then spreads all through the cheeks when it happens that fear or shame seizes the lovers. Wherefore he says:

<margin>Q</margin>
<margin>X</margin>
<margin>¶ From the aforementioned accident of love, one can understand that no class of men experiences as many causes of fear and shame as wretched lovers do, through which, according to the opinion of philosophers and physicians—</margin>
> And I know how in an instant the blood vanishes;
> And then spreads through the cheeks;
> If fear or shame happens to follow it.

<margin>R</margin>
—the aforementioned accident follows. For whenever something fearful occurs, nature recalls its protection—which is the blood and the spirits—to the heart to make its final defense in that place <note>This was the contemporary medical explanation for why people turn pale when afraid: the blood rushes inward to protect the core</note>. On the contrary, in shame, the spirits are ignited by the internal commotion and spread to the outer surface, from which that ruby-red color appears. He then introduces three other effects of love contained in a contradiction, which truly never leave those who are constrained by intense amorous desire and love with great fervor: saying that he knows how the serpent stays hidden among the flowers, and how lovers always wake and sleep in ambiguity between two contrary thoughts, and likewise how one languishes and dies many times a day even without ever dying. Wherefore he says:

<margin>S</margin>
<margin>¶ One can place certain faith in Messer Francesco, as he testifies that the troubles of love are hidden and revealed by slippery delights and unstable pleasures; for it is commonly experienced that under the happy welcomes—</margin>
> I know how the snake stays hidden among the flowers;
> How one always sees and sleeps between two;
> How without languishing one dies and languishes.

—of the beloved, under broad promises, and even under their unmerited courtesies, there are many deceits and many betrayals. There is much loss of time, reputation, and substance; likewise, many pains proceed from this, either by leaving present sweetness or by desiring it beyond measure after tasting it. And from this one can further know how much stability there is in amorous hope: how quickly it turns to fear; how, as a man decides on one side, he is immediately pulled by the other; and how the fantasy is so fixed that not only in wakefulness, but also in sleep, contrary images appear to the imagination.

# CHAPTER TWO

<meta>image quality: clear; catchword: Suole</meta>

They deceive themselves, even thinking they please when they are being torn apart in some mockery: however much they follow their beloveds with such dispositions. And away from their presence, they may arrange and deliberate words and deeds among themselves, even intending to make their martyrdoms <note>In this context, 'martyrdom' refers to the extreme emotional suffering of a lover</note> known and to ask for mercy; yet when they later find themselves before her face, their hearts grow cold: their boldness flees, their tongues become tied, and their actions are delayed. As **M. Fr.** <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch</note> demonstrates in that sonnet: *Many times already from the beautiful human face* <note>original: "PIV volte gia dal bel fembiãte humano"; Petrarch's Sonnet 173</note>; and also in that other one: *Because I have guarded you from falsehood* <note>original: "PER chio habia guardato di menzogna"; Petrarch's Sonnet 49</note>; whereby lovers can appropriately be called "stunned" and "frozen." Next, **M. F.** adduces how great the force of love is, and how variously he calls himself afflicted by different martyrdoms, saying that he knows in what way love roars and lords over lovers, and how it drives away all reasonable action from itself: in how many various manners and different ways the heart is melted in the burning desire of love. Wherefore he says:

<margin>y</margin>
<margin>¶ He can clearly understand how great the force of love is, in whose desire it reigns; because among all the sensory delights, none has more efficacy, nor does any so confound the empire of reason.</margin>
> I know how love roars over the mind,
> And how it drives out all reason from there;
> And I know in how many ways the heart is destroyed,

<margin>y</margin>
If, therefore, any sensory delight almost cuts off the freedom of our will, as Cassiodorus explains, saying: *for a deceitful mind does not follow the command of judgment, but rather unfolds its own pleasures* <note>original: "animus enim dolosus non arbitriũ feqtur imperatiũ sed fuas potius explicat voluptates"</note>. Much more greatly is carnal desire—which is in men by natural inclination and also by perverse choice—apt to dominate reason: whence one experiences as many different kinds of pain as there are incentives of the venereal appetite. Next, **M. F.** adds another effect, which is the softness, inconstancy, and ready volatility of man when, in making choices, he submits himself to the judgment of the senses, saying that he knows with how small a rope a loving and noble soul is bound and caught when it does not have the weapons of reason to help it defend itself from the assault of the senses. > A noble soul, when it is alone,

> And I know how it now threatens, and now strikes;
> How it robs by force, and how it steals;

The common praises attributed to beloved women ensnare them in the traps of love no differently than a simple bird might find itself entangled in birdlime on a branch; wherefore such a desire ignites in their hearts that every other care is sent into oblivion. F.** adds the instability of the amorous state: from which is born doubtful hope, heavy pain, certain bitterness, and the clear experience of amorous perfidy, saying that he knows how unstable the wheels and foundations of this love are: the hopes are doubtful and for the most part deceptive, the pain is certain and inseparable, and how the promises made by love are totally void of faith. # CHAPTER THREE

O hot sighs: o nightly songs expressed from the deep heart out of pain and bitterness. Truly blessed is he who never felt the flame or spark of love: oh, how many times the wretched and afflicted lovers, wishing to lament and having already continued their speech for some time, suddenly fall into silence out of fear, so that their beloveds might not know they are complaining of them. O wretched life, in which one is not even permitted to lament one's own wicked pains; to whom, if ever a reason for even the slightest laughter occurs, long and most cruel weeping immediately follows. Wherefore, truly—just as our graceful poet well compares—lovers know, whenever they seem to taste the greatest sweetness, that it is like honey poured around and mixed with wormwood <note>Wormwood (Latin: *absinthium*) is a bitter herb used here to symbolize the bitterness hidden within the "sweetness" of love.</note>: which thing having been experienced as true testimony in the preceding verses, our **M. F.** <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch</note> has related it to us.

<margin>L</margin>

## EXPOSITION OF THE THIRD CHAPTER.

<margin>M</margin>

**A**ncient usage and frequent custom it was among the Romans that, when triumphing, they would proceed through Rome to a most beautiful end—usually some appropriate temple—where they could consecrate the spoils taken in war to the gods. Following this similarity, our <term>Messer Francesco</term> <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the author of the *Triumphs*</note> in this third chapter intends to lead Love to the temple of his mother Venus on the island of <term>Cythera</term> <note>A Greek island legendary as the birthplace of Venus and a symbol of carnal love</note>: a place truly suited and pleasing to the <term>sensitive appetite</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the part of the soul driven by physical senses and desires</note>. In the same manner, he leads <term>Laura</term> in the following triumph to Rome to the Temple of Chastity, where it was fitting to pass with such virtue. Later, when the glorious poet intends for Death, Fame, Time, and [Eternity] universally to wander through the world, he does not assign them a determined place, but says only that they have been seen on earth—until the sixth Triumph, that of Eternity, where he attributes Heaven as its place, which alone is suited to such direction and measure for spirits after God. 

And because, as we said at the beginning, **M. F.** intends to speak universally in this triumph of the sensitive appetite, he silently demonstrates the solution to a question which might be raised according to this opinion: namely, whether the desire for learning and science is blameworthy or notable. In responding, he establishes a foundation that whenever a power is not directed toward its proper object and its perfection, then such work should not be praised. If, therefore, we speak of poetry and rhetoric, it is undoubtedly said that the appetite for them is perverse; for in none of these notices is there any acquisition of a necessary truth. Whence our intellect can only become accustomed to their office, which is to recite what has already been said, or rather to veil and hide it under new fictions. For this reason, the Romans several times banished rhetoricians and poets from Rome, as <term>Suetonius Tranquillus</term> <note>A Roman historian (c. 69 – after 122 AD)</note> affirms in his book *On Grammarians*, expressing the edict in these words:

> In the consulship of Gaius Fannius Strabo and Marcus Valerius Messalla <note>161 BC</note>, the praetor Marcus Pomponius consulted the Senate regarding what words had been spoken concerning philosophers and rhetoricians. Regarding this matter, they decreed: that Marcus Pomponius the praetor should take heed and see to it, if it seemed useful to the Republic and to his own good faith, that they should not be in Rome. After some time had passed, the censors Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus and Lucius Licinius Crassus likewise said: "It has been reported to us that there are men who have instituted a new kind of discipline, to whom the youth flock in schools; they have taken the name 'Latin rhetoricians.' There, all the young men sit idle all day long. Our ancestors established what they wished their children to learn and what schools they should follow. These new things, which happen contrary to the custom and manner of our ancestors, neither please us nor seem right. Therefore, it seems necessary to show our opinion both to those who hold these schools and to those who are accustomed to go there: that they do not please us."

Plato also wrote that poets should be totally separated from a well-instituted Republic, as <term>Augustine</term> writes in the second book of *The City of God*. Whence he himself in the sixth book, alleging <term>Varro</term> <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar</note>, adds to this purpose: "From which Varro says: a greater fellowship ought to be ours with philosophers than with poets; for the former wrote for utility, while the latter truly wrote for the sake of pleasure." But if someone were to say that rhetoric is for the defense of the oppressed and the opposition of the unjust—which pertains to the supreme virtue of justice, and thus makes rhetoric similar to it—to this, <term>Cornelius Tacitus</term> <note>Roman historian and orator (c. 56–120 AD)</note> responds gracefully in his book *On Famous Orators*, saying: "I protect the status of each person for their security more by their innocence than by eloquence." And as it is said, all eloquence is superfluous where there is the duty and appropriate disposition of the judge. But if we pass to the others, which alone are in the number of honorable goods (excepting Theology), we likewise say that if they...

<margin>N</margin>
These sciences are desired as the highest end according to the notion of **Averroes** <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was an influential Al-Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> in the prologue of his *Physics*, thinking that through the knowledge of these things, man becomes happy in this world. However, desiring them as such would be an error, because according to **Solomon** in *Ecclesiastes*, "all these things are vanity." As **Lactantius** <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was an early Christian author who advised on the limits of pagan philosophy.</note> says in the third book of *Against the Nations* in chapter 27: wherefore **Jeremiah** appropriately said in the ninth chapter: *Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom* <note>original Latin: "Non gloriet sapiens in sapientia sua"</note>; and Solomon in *Wisdom* in the thirteenth: *For all men are vain in whom there is no knowledge of God* <note>original Latin: "vani sunt aut̃ omnes hoies qb' nõ subest scientia dei"</note>; to which purpose the sentiment of **Hosea** in the fourth chapter is in agreement, saying: *There is no truth, and there is no mercy, and there is no knowledge of God in the land* <note>original Latin: "Non est veritas & non est misericordia non est scientia dei in terra"</note>. Our <term>Messer Francesco</term> <note>Petrarch</note> also demonstrates this to those who follow such things with the aforementioned intention. Therefore, the poet in these *Triumphs*, as a religious Christian, wishes to blame every object except God which is sought as a principal end. For this reason, he subjects the desire for worldly sciences and especially the study of poetry to the sensitive appetite; and because he himself was seized by a similar will, he introduces himself as following the Triumph of Love with this company, together with **Socrates** and **Laelius**. He does this to show, through the person of Socrates, that he desired knowledge of moral philosophy—which Socrates brought down from heaven to earth, as **Cicero** affirms in the beginning of the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*. And through the person of Laelius, he intends to show that through the benevolence he bore for **Scipio** (similar to that of Laelius), he followed the doctrine of poetry and composed the *Africa* in praise of Scipio—through which work, as we said at the beginning, the poet was crowned with laurel. That he had these desires for the aforementioned doctrines is not only shown in the aforementioned book *On the Conflict of His Cares* <note>The *Secretum*, Petrarch's imaginary dialogue with St. Augustine.</note>, but he clearly explains it in that song, *A lady much more beautiful than the sun* <note>The canzone "Una donna più bella assai che’l sole."</note>, where he says he was enamored first of poetry and then of philosophy, in addition to his desire for **Laura**. Therefore, <term>Messer Francesco</term>, being placed under the dominion of the sensitive appetite, and with the nerves of free will cut and severed and its foundations overturned, says that he immediately came into the notice and familiarity of all his fellow-servants. Although at first he was quite wild and remote from worldly desires and delights, he saw and knew for himself all their punishments and amorous martyrdoms, and with what art and ingenuity each lover had been led to that amorous and divine condition. Wherefore he says:

# CHAPTER THREE OF THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE.

<margin>P</margin>
It is a fitting and reasonable thing, as we said at the beginning, that men have better understanding and notice of those similar to themselves than of those who are dissimilar and different. Therefore, being subject to love like the others, <term>Messer Francesco</term> reasonably affirms that he knows each of the other enamored souls no longer through an interpreter, but through his own knowledge. Beyond this, he says he has notice of the manner, the art, and the ingenuity by which men are led under the amorous yoke, as one who has had true experience. He then narrates, saying that after he had become a friend to all the other enamored spirits in such a form, he turned around to see if among them he might recognize someone famous, either through modern or ancient writers, who showed themselves to be in love with human science or another object, regarding which he might exercise his teaching and observation. He adds that he saw **Orpheus**, who loved only **Eurydice**; when she died, he was constrained by the love he bore her to go even unto hell to ask **Pluto** for her; and then, having lost her through his own fault, he often called her back in his final cries. Wherefore he says:

> was quickly tamed, together with all
> my unhappy and wretched fellow-servants:
> and I saw their labors and their mournings;
> through what twisted paths and with what craft
