<gloss>Having received the <term>cythara</term> <note>A stringed instrument similar to a lyre, associated with Apollo and the power of poetic music.</note> from Mercury, he fell in love with the nymph Eurydice, whom he made his wife after attracting her favor with his music. One day, while Eurydice was wandering on the banks of the river Hebrus...</gloss>

*One day **Aristaeus** <note>In mythology, a minor god of agriculture and beekeeping.</note> came upon her; he had been in love with her for a long time and wanted to take her. But she, realizing this, began to flee. In her flight, while treading in a meadow, she was bitten by a serpent; from that bite, she died quickly. Orpheus, then, hearing the miserable fate of his beloved Eurydice and knowing every other effort would be in vain, took up his lyre and with it descended to the underworld. Having placated all the Furies and the infernal gods with it, he finally obtained his beloved Eurydice from **Pluto** and **Proserpina** on this condition: that until he returned to see the stars, he should never turn back to look at her. Whereupon Orpheus proceeded in such a manner until he was about to exit the underworld; having reached the edge, compelled by his immense love for Eurydice, he turned back to look at her to see if she followed him. For this reason, forced by the observance of the pact, he lost her again. He then resolved never to want another woman, and in his songs and poems he always persuaded men to remain free and not entangle themselves in the marital knot. Because of this, he came into such hatred among women that they conspired against him; and one day, while he was sacrificing to **Bacchus**, he was attacked, killed, and torn apart by the women. His head together with his lyre were thrown into the river Hebrus; which, through the force of the waves, reached the island of Lesbos. When a serpent wanted to devour it, it was turned into stone by his father **Apollo**. Therefore, these things are attributed to Orpheus according to poetic fantasy; but in truth, he was a very ancient poet who delighted much in poetry, especially in singing of love.* <margin>S</margin> <margin>T</margin> <margin>V</margin> *Next, <term>Messer Francesco</term> <note>Petrarch</note> adds three other poets: namely, Alcaeus, Pindar, and Anacreon, saying that each of these illustrious poets celebrated this poetic study and, for the most part, sang of love. Wherefore he says:*

<gloss>REGARDING THE understanding of the preceding verses, it is to be understood that Alcaeus was a most excellent Greek poet and a well-known and famous citizen in his republic for his learning, as **Tully** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), often referred to as "Tully" by Renaissance scholars.</note> writes in the fourth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*.</gloss>

*He composed almost every one of his poems against tyrannical life and against the immoderate love of youths; in which works he wrote so elegantly and with such learning that he deservedly achieved this: that a golden lyre was given to him by the public, as **Quintilian** writes in the tenth book of the *Education of the Orator*. Pindar likewise, according to the aforementioned Quintilian, was such a singular and worthy poet that if he had wished to observe gravity of subjects in his poems and not go wandering through such wantonness, he would have been considered quite equal to **Homer**. Pindar, then, loved a youth exceedingly; and one day, while he was in the <term>Gymnasium</term> <note>A place for both physical exercise and intellectual discussion in ancient Greece.</note> resting his head upon the youth's chest, he expired while sleeping, as **Valerius** writes in the ninth book and twelfth chapter; truly a great kindness of fortune to make him die in that place which he had desired more than any other rest. Similarly, Anacreon, as Tully writes in the previously cited book, turned all his study to speaking of love; wherefore, not wandering through the spacious sea of delights, but having led his Muses only into the amorous port, Tully rightly says of him: "Anacreon's entire poetry is indeed amatory; it is evident that Ibycus of Rhegium burned with love most of all; and we see that the loves of all these men were lustful" <note>original Latin: "Anacreontis quidem tota poesis est amatoria: maxime vero omnium fragrasse amore rheginum ibicum apparet: atque horum omnium libidinosos esse amores videmus."</note>. Therefore, he was deservedly numbered in this place by our poet along with the others. After these, <term>Messer Francesco</term> describes some other <margin>Y</margin> Latin poets who, besides the study of singing of excellent things in history and natural knowledge, also wrote of and celebrated love, saying how he saw **Virgil**; and it seemed to him that he had around him a company for pastime and pleasure—namely, **Ovid**, **Catullus**, **Propertius**, and **Tibullus**—which company he more willingly chose in the world for his practice and study than others for which he was very well-suited. # THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

<margin>A</margin>
¶ Just as it can be known through the poems of the aforementioned poets, each of these was an excellent and glorious writer, and each celebrated a certain graceful maiden as his beloved. One of these was Virgil, as is noted in the second book <note>The commentator likely refers to the "Lydia," a poem traditionally but perhaps incorrectly attributed to Virgil in the Renaissance.</note> concerning **Lydia**, an illustrious woman whom he showed to be his most cherished beloved. Ovid—as is read especially in the book without a title <note>This refers to Ovid’s *Amores*, which was sometimes titled *sine titulo* in medieval and Renaissance manuscripts.</note>—celebrated **Corinna**; Catullus celebrated **Lesbia**; Propertius celebrated **Cynthia**, whose real name was **Hostilia**; Tibullus celebrated **Plania**, although he named her **Delia** <note>In Latin, "planus" corresponds to the Greek "delos," both meaning "clear" or "plain."</note> as is written in their elegies. This is the universal custom of all poets to make similar celebrations. Thus the poet Gallus celebrated **Lycoris**, whose true name was **Cytheris**; Horace Flaccus made his **Lalage** eternal. Dante celebrated **Beatrice**, and Messer Francesco <note>Messer Francesco (M. F.) refers to the author, Petrarch.</note> celebrated **Laura**.

<margin>B</margin>
Messer Francesco then adds the most learned **Sappho**, saying how a young Greek woman proceeded equally with these noble poets, singing of love; she possessed a sweet, elegant, and rare style found within the female nature. Wherefore he says:

> I saw Virgil; and it seemed he had about him
> Companions of high genius, and of leisure,
> Of those whom the world once willingly chose.
> One was Ovid, and the other was Tibullus,
> The other Propertius, who sang of love
> Fervently, and the other was Catullus.

¶ Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should be understood that Sappho the poetess was from the island of Lesbos. If her origin matches her spirit, she was truly born of noble and generous parents. She, therefore, set aside humble feminine tasks and with the greatest diligence gave herself to poetic study, in which she became so perfect that she not only deserved to be numbered among the other poets, but also, to her glory, an excellent statue was constructed and erected in her name in Mytilene. From there she became quite well known and famous in that province. Just as she was endowed by nature with outstanding talent, so too by choice was she afflicted by a most powerful love. Loving a young man named **Phaon**, and he not returning her love, she composed a graceful poem to entice him to her favor in a varied style and diverse poetic nature, which then deserved to be called the **Sapphic style** <note>A specific meter in classical poetry characterized by a particular rhythmic pattern.</note>. Messer Francesco then explains many excellent men who were his contemporaries, who gave themselves to many kinds of study and some to love, saying he had seen them on the green and flowery slope of the sciences and the practice of letters. The first of these was **Dante** and his **Beatrice**, and **Cino da Pistoia**, a most famous <term>legal consultant</term> <note>Cino was a renowned jurist as well as a poet.</note> with his **Selvaggia**, who followed the most outstanding men described below. Wherefore he says:

> A young Greek woman, side by side
> With the noble poets once singing;
> And she had a style of her own, graceful and rare.

<margin>C</margin>
¶ In this place, the reason is quite manifest, and it serves as an excuse if a more particular exposition of the aforementioned examples is not given; for it is a very recent thing that one should have knowledge of men in two ways: one through physical sight, the other through the record left to us by writers. Therefore, one cannot say that through any of the said ways the introduced examples are totally known or that a full and particular account of them can be given. First, because they preceded Laura in age and by a long span of time; secondly, because history can only be understood by a few, and not very much can be grasped from it. But one can well consider each of them generally through the testimony of Messer Francesco as having been learned and excellent men, starting with Dante:

> Thus now here, now there gazing,
> I saw on a flowery and green slope
> People who went along reasoning of love.
> Behold Dante and Beatrice; behold Selvaggia
> And Cino da Pistoia; with Guittone d’Arezzo,
> Who seems to feel resentment at not being first.

> As every man saw; and then there was a troop

> Great master of love, who to his own land...

<margin>D</margin> [The commentator] speaks of Dante and likewise of Master Cino <note>Cino da Pistoia, a famous jurist and poet.</note>, of Guido Bonatti <note>The text mentions "Guido Bonato," a famous astrologer, though Petrarch often associates with Guido Cavalcanti in this context.</note>, the worthy astrologer; Guido Cavalcanti the philosopher; and Sennuccio <note>Sennuccio del Bene.</note>; of Peter of Alvernia: of these, there are works that have come to our knowledge. Of the others, we confess to not having more ready knowledge, wishing to be ascribed to ignorance rather than to temerity <note>A humble disclaimer by the commentator regarding his lack of information on some of the more obscure Troubadours.</note>, not deviating from the modest opinion of those who, even regarding what they certainly believe they know, do not affirm it without fear. Let it suffice then for our purpose that Dante, together with the other narrated examples, took more delight and pleasure in worldly studies than was convenient: not yet separating himself from amorous delights: especially since man is always subject to the sudden contingency of death: which the poet deplores in his friend Thomas: saying that this mortal life which so pleases men is nothing other than a dream of the foolish and of sick <term>romances</term> <note>In this context, the commentator defines "romances" as simple chronicles or popular tales rather than modern novels.</note>: which in the Gallic tongue signify the annals and brief memories made of occurring things. Being therefore Master Francis <note>Petrarch.</note> also linked with these studious companions: like a just man, he still condemns himself in this same way, saying that not only for the sake of Laura was he constrained to follow the triumph of love, but also for this other worldly desire for earthly sciences: wherefore he says: that being a little outside the common road, he saw Socrates and Lelius <note>Petrarch’s nicknames for his closest friends, Ludwig van Kempen (Socrates) and Lello di Pietro Stefano (Lelius).</note> with whom he was constrained to proceed in various places and with these to search various mountains and countries and open all his desires to them. And he adds that he believed he could never part from these friends, there being such a wealth of most excellent men that no mortal tongue, whether in prose or in verse or in rhyme, could sufficiently explain it: he greatly desired never to find himself separated from them. Wherefore he says:

<margin>O</margin> O what a pair of friends, whom neither in rhyme,
Nor in prose, nor in verses could one adorn enough,
As they are stripped of all virtue <note>original: "virtu nuda," meaning they are the very essence of virtue without need of ornament.</note>.
<margin>C</margin> With these two I searched diverse mountains
All three of us always going under one yoke:
To these I opened all my wounds.

<margin>F</margin> With high concept and artful grace, Master Francis describes in these verses for which studies he had been more desirous than was proper. Where it is to be understood principally that by the most worthy authors in the Latin tongue it is described—especially by Saint Jerome—where the paths of the process of our life are. One is that of virtue: which is harsh and mountainous and difficult: and the other is that of worldly pleasures and delights: which is open, flat, and with ease...

# THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

...ease, one proceeds through it. This is why to Hercules, in his infancy or childhood, [two paths] were shown and given to choose from; he chose the path of works <note>The "Choice of Hercules" is a classic allegory where the hero chooses the difficult path of Virtue over the easy path of Pleasure.</note>, leading him to the possession of the glory of fame. This [easy] path belongs to hypocrites, among whom are even numbered those who give themselves to studies, as Virgil demonstrates in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*, saying: "Then thus the prophetess began to speak, child of the blood of gods, Trojan son of Anchises: the descent to the underworld is easy; night and day the door of gloomy Dis stands open. But to recall one's step and escape to the upper air: this is the task, this is the labor; few have been loved by impartial Jupiter, or have been carried to the heavens by glowing virtue." <note>original Latin: "Tum sic orsa loqui vates fate sanguine diuū. Tros anchisiade facilis descensus auerni..." from Virgil's Aeneid, VI.125-131.</note> Messer Francesco <note>Referring to the author, Francesco Petrarch.</note> expresses this same sentiment in that sonnet, *Gluttony, sleep, and idle pillows*, when he says at the end: "What desire for laurel, what for myrtle? Philosophy, you go poor and naked, says the crowd intent on base gain. You will have few companions on the other path; therefore I pray you the more, O gentle spirit, do not abandon your magnanimous undertaking." Wherefore Messer Francesco says: that already through the practice of grammar he was a little way out of the common road of the vernacular speakers when he saw Socrates—that is, moral doctrine. This is because Socrates, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> writes in the *Metaphysics*, Diogenes Laertius in his *Life [of the Philosophers]*, Isidore in the *Etymologies*, and Cicero in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, set aside all other cares to give himself solely to the contemplation of good and excellent customs. And Lelio—that is, Cicero's book *On Friendship*—through which he became a lover of the African virtues <note>The virtues of Scipio Africanus, the Roman general.</note>. In order to be able to celebrate those virtues, he gave himself to poetic study. Wherefore he later composed the *Africa*, where he describes the deeds of Scipio; this work, filled with poetry and morality, was the cause for Messer Francesco of a most singular fame and glory, as we said at the beginning. And therefore, adding to this, he exclaims that for this reason nothing could separate him from this abundance of friends, whom no tongue could adequately praise, neither in rhyme, nor in prose, nor in Latin verses, if naked virtue is to be properly esteemed. There are nonetheless some texts which say: *Just as the knot of virtue is esteemed*, which are also tolerable. For the understanding of this, one must know that man is a "companionable animal," as is written in the first book of the *Politics* <note>Aristotle’s Politics, describing man as a "political animal" (zoon politikon).</note>. Thus many have said that friendship is not a virtue, nor is it with virtue, nor does it even deserve praise, since it arises from natural effects and not from acquired merit, as is written in the second book of the *Ethics*. But Cicero demonstrates this to be false in his book *On Friendship*, as does Aristotle in the eighth book of the *Ethics*, where he says: "For friendship is a virtue, or is accompanied by virtue." <note>original Latin: "Est enim amicicia virtus vel cū uirtute."</note>

->Neither time nor place can ever<-
->Divide me from these; as I hope and desire;<-
->Even to the ash of the funereal pyre;<-

<margin>G</margin> ¶ Since virtuous men are highly praiseworthy, and since friendship is a virtue—or is with virtue—especially regarding these two men, namely Socrates and Lelio, praise is appropriate for them. The poet says, then, that with these two friends—by whom he means these two disciplines, namely poetry and moral philosophy—he circled diverse mountains—that is, diverse and various investigations—by his own will with them. Under the same yoke of scientific difficulty, he always proceeded together with them in such studies, and to them he opened all his wounds and his disciplined feelings. For this reason, he affirms that the pleasure he took in such company was so great that he hopes and desires never to be separated from them until his body is turned to ash inside the funereal pyre made for him according to the ancient custom. To understand this, one must know what Herodian <note>A Greek historian who wrote about the Roman Empire.</note>, a most grave and Greek author, writes when treating the funerals of the Emperor Severus.

<margin>H</margin> ¶ He writes that the Romans were accustomed to construct an image of the deceased body in the likeness of how he was when alive, and to make it in the form of when he was sick; for some time, they kept it in that form, pretending afterwards that it had died. Then the relatives on one side and the women on the other would come to weep and perform other ceremonies used in those times. Afterwards, the most noble of the relatives carried it out upon a bed adorned with the richest cloths of gold, silver, silk, and wool, according to the condition of the deceased. The true body was carried outside of Rome to the place of burial, where a quadrangular pyre <term>pyra: a funeral pile for burning a corpse</term> was built entirely of combustible wood. As it rose upward, it proportionately diminished in size, and in the middle, the body was placed along with the image. And after the body was placed there and burned, and the ashes collected and put into a very small urn, they had performed their due funeral rites. And when they wished to show that a good man had been deified <term>deification: the act of making someone a god</term> at his death, they placed an eagle—which was considered the bird of Jove—at the very top of the pyre; the eagle, feeling the heat of the fire, would fly away and...

And nevertheless, he adds that of her alone he thought: and of her his heart was in continual desire, yet he could never pluck nor possess branch nor leaf: nor any other delight: although [the laurel] was provided, the roots of his beginning and the foundation of all his works were wicked and bitter <note>A pun on "Laura" and "Lauro" (laurel). And because no scientific habit can have its perfection without philosophy. Just as Cicero specifically proves regarding eloquence in his *Orator* to Brutus when he says: <term>But the orator is most greatly elevated and aided by the discussions of Plato and other philosophers; for from them, as if from a forest of words, all abundance is drawn.</term> <note>original Latin: "Sed ex platonis & aliorū p̃horū disputatiōibus orator maxime exaggeratus est..." from Cicero's Orator, 3.12.</note> And he adds: it is established for the sake of grace that it can be better understood that the eloquent man we seek can exist [only] with philosophy. Therefore he says that the poet has plucked and obtained the crown of Laurel together with Socrates and Lelio, having described moral and natural philosophical sentences under the poetic veil. And for this reason, in this place, one can clearly understand that Messer Francesco’s love for the Laurel was distinct from his beloved Lady Laura, the former being placed here as a sign and memory of her. Nor can it be said that he was merely in love with poetry, of which the laurel reminds him. For Messer Francesco writes that he is most learned in poetry, yet nevertheless, he burns continually for love, as he shows in that sonnet: <term>I am already weary of thinking:</term> <note>original Italian: "Io son già stanco di pensar."</note> as he says at the end: that if he erred in the praises attributed to his beloved Laura, this fault and this error should be excused by the cause of love, and not by the effect of the poetic art that was within him.

<margin>L</margin>
¶ The poet then adds what end the miserable lovers met: into what place of love they were led: and besides this, what effect he saw intervene from love: and in what way he was captured by the chastity of Lady Laura, saying: that although he, because of his obstinate desire and Laura's will, often chose to lament, like a man who languishes and weeps for being offended by the ingratitude of love by justice; nevertheless, the vengeance which he saw made before his eyes—seeing Love being overcome by the chastity of Laura—was a curb and an effective argument for him that he should never complain of this. Which vengeance and the pressure of Love is a matter for "cothurni" <note>cothurni: Buskins or boots worn by ancient Greek tragic actors, here signifying a high, tragic, or heroic style of writing.</note>—that is, for heroic verses and also for a grandiloquent style—and not for elegies and low verses used by foolish poets. For it is arduous and difficult to be able to persuade others of this: that he who is reputed a god by the crude, uncultured, foolish, and depressed minds (incapable of reason contrary to their opinions) is defeated, captured, and bound only by the simple determination of a virgin. And he adds that before he sings of this pressure—which will be in the *Triumph of Chastity*—he first wishes to recount what Love did to him and to the other prisoners: and then say what he sustained from others. This work, although recited by Messer Francesco, is not primarily his own but that of Homer or Orpheus, most famous Greek poets, each of whom had first written of the punishments that arose from following love, and also the glory acquired by whoever most manfully resisted him. Whence he says:

# THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

<margin>M</margin>
¶ Regarding the rational understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known that Messer Francesco <note>Messer Francesco: Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the author of the poem.</note> is shown lamenting over Laura because, while the <term>sensory appetite</term> <note>sensory appetite: The physical or carnal desires, as opposed to intellectual or spiritual love.</note> dominates the bodies of men, they always take it as an injury when carnal delight is denied to them by those they love. However, once that burning passion and fire is consumed and reason has resumed its lost strength, they then hate and blame their past life, praising the constancy of their beloved and affirming that they have received their salvation from them. Whence, Messer Francesco most excellently describes how, although he often used to complain about Laura’s behavior, seeing afterward how much he had regulated his appetite through her example—and how that appetite was excited toward eternal salvation—it seemed reasonable to him not only to complain no longer, but to always praise Laura most highly.

> Like a man who is offended; that which with these eyes
> I saw, is a bridle to me so that I never grieve more.

¶ Messer Francesco next introduces what the enamored spirits finally did, saying that, following behind the flight of the purple feathers of the winged steeds which guide the chariot of Love through a thousand harsh and difficult places and through a thousand wide ditches, at last Love arrived in the kingdom of his mother Venus. On this journey, the heavy chains were never—I do not say shaken off—but even loosened; instead, being pulled by force through forests and mountains and other inaccessible and uncultivated places, with their clothes and flesh torn, almost no one knew in what state or in what world they were. <margin>O</margin>
¶ Our Messer Francesco writes gracefully in these verses. Before a man has reached the end of his warring desire, there are torments, hardships, and small sufferings that are endured every hour while the soul is held within the power of lascivious appetite. In this place of execution, this amorous will is so tenacious that in no part does it diminish the intense and burning desire for love; rather, the mind becomes confused, not knowing how to limit itself or make any determined choice. This is because on one side it is forced by the inflamed will to possess its beloved object, and on the other side it is pulled back by the bitterness, harshness, and difficulty it sees in having to obtain it. Therefore, a man always remains suspended and hanging between being happy and miserable, appearing to be submerged by affection and raised up by hope. Messer Francesco aptly shows this contrariety and disposition in that sonnet, *Gazing at the sun of those beautiful serene eyes*, where he says at the end: *Through these two mixed opposite extremes, now with frozen desires, now with burning ones, one stands thus between misery and happiness.* <note>original: "Per questi extremi duo contrarij mixti hor con voglie gelate: hora cõ accese: stassi cosi fra misera 7 felice." This refers to Petrarch's Canzoniere 173.</note> Therefore, appropriately, before arriving at the kingdom of Venus

Messer Francesco describes the particular place where Love, having arrived together with his innumerable company of prisoners, wished to triumph and consecrate the spoils of his victory, saying that where the Aegean Sea <note>original: "mare egeo"</note> sighs and appears to weep, there is situated a most delicate and pleasant little island, much more so than any other washed by the sea or illuminated and warmed by the sun. In the middle of it is a sunny, pleasant, and most placid hill, flowery and green, named Cythero <note>Cythero: Mount Cythera on the island of the same name, legendary birthplace of Venus.</note>, where sacrifices were made to Venus. On this island, the waters are so sweet and the breezes so mild that all sadness and perturbation of the soul in that place is removed far from the minds of men. This island and region pleased Venus for her habitation, and it was consecrated to her in that time when the true God was not known through the mystery of the Incarnation. He commanded Theseus and the mariners that, should he escape such a punishment, upon his return they should change the signals and the sails from black to white in demonstration of victory. Theseus then, having arrived in Crete, by the favor of Ariadne killed the Minotaur, escaped the Labyrinth, and survived such a harsh fate. However, through immoderate joy, forgetting his father's instructions, on his return he did not change the sails but came toward Athens with the same ones. Seeing this from afar, Aegeus—who every day waited upon a promontory for the return—affirming his son to be dead, threw himself into the sea out of great grief. For this reason, it has ever since been called the Aegean Sea. This sea, therefore, by its position, is for the most part exposed to the Eastern and Southern winds and is often gravely stirred by them. Whence, as the waters rise by their fury and return in droplets, the poets feigned that the Aegean still sighs and weeps for the falsely believed death of Theseus, its son. Secondly, it is to be noted that the island called Cythera, by its location suitably removed from the extremes, is a temperate place, much closer than any other region or country to the temperance of the air, which was chosen by Venus. Because she is the goddess of delights, she took much pleasure in the temperament of the air. This island was attributed to Venus by writers rather than the region under the equinoctial line <note>The Equator.</note>, which according to the opinion of <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Avicenna (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were standard in European universities.</note> in the first sentence of the first book of the <term>Conciliator</term> <note>The "Conciliator Differentiarum Philosophorum" by Pietro d'Abano (1257–1315), which attempted to reconcile the contradictions between Greek and Arabic philosophy/medicine.</note>, difference 67, is the most temperate region. This is first because of the universal opinion of all, and secondly because poetry and writing about Venus first began in Greece, and that other region was not known due to its distance. Therefore, they attributed Cythera to Venus and sacrificed to her in that place while the announced truth of the Incarnation was not yet elucidated by the prophets through the coming of Christ; which thing <term>Zephaniah</term> <note>Sophonia in the text.</note> predicted should happen concerning her and all the other gods, saying:

an uninhabitable place: because it is always found in extreme intemperance. For this reason, from the **vernal equinox** <note>The spring equinox, around March 21st.</note> when the sun is in **Aries** <note>The sign of the Ram.</note> to the **autumnal equinox** when the sun is in **Libra** <note>The sign of the Scales, around September 23rd.</note>, the sun always stays above the hemisphere; it illuminates it and never sets. Conversely, from the autumnal equinox to the vernal one, the sun never illuminates it, and thus there are six months of day and six months of continuous night. Therefore, this island is positioned almost directly toward India in its site. It also follows that joy and secrecy must necessarily be brief, because that joy depends—as an effect—upon amorous hope. Since the cause is brief and unstable, it is necessary that the effect be of the same nature, according to the principles of the natural philosophers, especially **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to late medieval thought.</note> in the eighth book of the **Metaphysics** <note>original: "Methaphisica"</note>. From this brief and fleeting joy follows sorrow and repentance, just as happened to the kingdom of Troy because of the abduction of Helen by Paris, as was said above. Because of this, the Trojans were killed, imprisoned, and dispersed; the noble city of Troy was completely ruined, even though in the beginning it greatly pleased Priam, Paris, and the other Trojans to have taken Helen from the Greek nation under the hope of recovering **Hesione** <note>original: "Exione"; the sister of Priam whose earlier abduction by the Greeks was the justification for Paris taking Helen.</note>. Tarquin was forced to live miserably in exile and die unhappily. Likewise, the aforementioned Appius Claudius, the decemvir, being forced by amorous appetite, gave an unjust **judgment** <note>original: "snia," abbreviation for "sententia."</note> against Virginia, daughter of Virginius, adjudging her the slave of a man named Claudius, as we shall describe more clearly in the account of the trial. # THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

Indeed, I step out into the sight of green, which is a color that gladdens man because it arises from vital principles in which all living things participate, according to "the Philosopher" <note>Aristotle, the standard authority for medieval and Renaissance science.</note> in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de anima"</note>. For he says: **"For living things, to live is to be."** <note>original: "Viuere viuentibus est eē [esse]"</note>. Consequently, at such a time, the spirits gather together as ministers of natural operations. In places of such quality, these operations find a more joyful and pleasant release. Likewise, in the summer time, if one can counter the exhaustion and natural weakness that follows the heat of the air through the means described, men would be even more satisfied by the **venereal operation** <note>Sexual activity, named after Venus.</note>. Finally, even in winter, if its rigid cold could be tempered, the same would occur. For it is the opinion of **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the primary medical textbook of the era.</note> in the first part of the first book, and of **Galen** <note>A 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> in the second book of the **Art of Medicine** <note>original: "tegni," from the Greek "Technē," referring to Galen's *Ars Medica*.</note>, that every operation, whatever it may be, becomes more perfect and intense through balance rather than through imbalance.

Therefore, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, regarding the location, has described those properties suitable for sensory delight. Following the description of the place, he adds the hour and the season appropriate for love. He says the season and time in which Love wished to triumph was when, after the equinox, the day becomes superior to the night—and when **Procne** <note>original: "Progne"; in Greek myth, she was turned into a swallow.</note> returns with her sister **Philomela** <note>original: "Philomena"; turned into a nightingale.</note> to her sweet exercise of singing and visiting our Italian regions. Exclaiming and lamenting the instability of human fortune, the poet says that Love wished to triumph in that place and hour because it demands a greater tribute of hot tears from the eyes of wretched lovers. Thus, he clearly saw and knew to what servitude, what torment, and what death those who incautiously consent to fall in love are headed. Hence he says:

<margin>I</margin>
->It was the season when the equinox<-
->Makes the day the victor, and Procne returns<-
->With her sister to her sweet business,<-
->O unstable faith of our fortunes!<-
->In that place, in that time, and in that hour<-
->Which demands a larger tribute from the eyes,<-
->He whom the common folk adore wished to triumph;<-
->And I saw to what service, and to what death,<-
->And to what torment he goes, who falls in love.<-

For a clearer and more efficient understanding of the preceding verses, one must know that as the sun travels obliquely through the circle of the **zodiac** <note>The belt of constellations through which the sun, moon, and planets appear to move.</note>, passing from one parallel circle to another, it reaches the summer or winter solstice. It is necessary that twice a year the sun finds itself under the equinoctial line: once when it enters **Aries** <note>The Ram (the start of Spring).</note> and the other when it enters **Libra** <note>The Scales (the start of Autumn).</note>. In the first equinox, as the sun moves toward the summer tropic of **Cancer**, the day remains superior to the night in its duration. Since the sun travels along the circle beyond the equinoctial line toward the summer parallel, the sun must remain above our hemisphere for more than twelve hours. The further it moves from that line toward the aforementioned circle, the longer our day becomes. Conversely, when it approaches the opposite circle, it travels a smaller arc in our hemisphere, thereby increasing the length of the night.

Master Francesco says, therefore, that the time in which he saw Love triumph was when, after the equinox, the day already begins to be greater than the night, and when Procne (the swallow) and her sister (the nightingale) return to their
<margin>K</margin>
sweet custom of visiting us and giving us their sweet songs—that is, in the time of **Spring**. Here it is to be understood, according to the poetic description, that Procne and Philomela were sisters and daughters of **Pandion**, King of Athens. Pandion gave Procne in marriage to **Tereus**, King of Thrace, who, according to the promise of kinship, while staying in Pandion's house, fell in love with Philomela, his sister-in-law, because of her beauty. One day, being in his kingdom and remembering Philomela, and being unable to resist the hidden flames any longer, he departed and arrived in Athens, where he was graciously received by Pandion, who asked him the reason for his visit...

Consequently, Master Francesco does not deviate in anything from the custom of the ancient triumphant Romans, for whom a triumphal arch was built for eternal memory, where all the deeds and effects of the conqueror were sculpted, as is still manifest in the present times in the city of Rome through the triumphal arches of Constantine and Lucius Septimius <note>Septimius Severus</note>. Thus he principally narrates how, on the columns and above on the architrave and pediment, were sculpted errors, dreams, and pale, faded images; and beneath the bases were designated false opinions and infinite self-deceptions. <meta>This page continues the moral and philosophical analysis of Petrarch's "Triumph of Love," moving from the tragic examples of lust (like Tereus) to a broader discussion of how desire deludes the mind, affects the physical body, and subverts the natural order of reason.</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

The mind of lovers does nothing but falsely imagine those things they desire to be their salvation; and though they take supreme pleasure in them, they nonetheless lead to eternal harm and the distress of those in love. Furthermore, just as they desire to joyfully possess their beloveds, they also imagine that they themselves are desired and "possessed" by those they love. How false this is was shown clearly enough in the preceding chapter, where the effects of love were demonstrated. From this false opinion, errors subsequently follow and multiply, according to the teaching of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the first book of the *Physics*, where he says: <note>original: "dato uno inconvenienti plura contingunt"</note> "Given one absurdity, many others follow." And in the first book of *On the Heavens*, he said: <note>original: "Si quis enim modicum fuerit transgressus a veritate recedens: fiet longe plus decies milies"</note> "If one has strayed even a little, departing from the truth, it will eventually become ten thousand times greater." This happens because the mind is confounded by burning desire. 

<margin>N</margin> Thus, confirming the sentiment of Phaedra written by Ovid in the *Heroides*: <note>original: "Iuppiter esse pium statuit quodcumque iuvaret"</note> "Jupiter decreed that whatever brought pleasure was pious." This was shown in effect, and a similar decree was sanctioned by Queen Semiramis when, being in love with her son Ninus, she made such excess legal by law. How many others besides these, seized by such unrestrained desire, have neglected and abandoned elderly fathers, sick mothers, and small children? They have neglected public duties and cast aside private ones. How many false judgments are made, how many truths are confounded, how many virtues are exterminated, and how many prohibited acts are put into execution? 

And following this, because of continuous and fixed obsession, they do not only think of the same thing while awake, but in sleep the images and <term>intelligible species</term><note>In medieval psychology, these are the "mental portraits" of objects stored in the mind.</note> return along with <term>phantasms</term><note>Mental images produced by the imagination.</note>, and [this causes a reaction] in the internal faculties. Thus, what one desires while awake is also seen in sleep. From this continuous mental exercise, there arises the mortification and paleness of the body, due to the great <term>resolution of the spirits</term><note>The "spirits" were believed to be thin vapors that carried life and heat through the body; here, intense thought "uses them up," leaving none for the skin's color.</note>. 

<margin>O</margin> Since these spirits are of the nature of light, they can no longer bring color to the outer surface. For this reason, the flesh remains pale and dull. Therefore Ovid concluded in the *Art of Love* that paleness was a color suited to Cupid. Whence he says: <note>original: "Palleat omnis amans color hic est aptus amanti"</note> "Let every lover turn pale; this is the color proper to a lover." 

He then adds, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, the images situated within the arch, saying that on the stairs inside, by which one ascended to its true summit, was sculpted a slippery and weak hope in the midst of a weary rest and a restful toil. The nature of the steps of the stairs was such that the more one climbed them, the more one found oneself at the end to have descended. 

<margin>P</margin> Whence he says:

<margin>For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, one must know that nothing can be solid or permanent which is violent, as is the universal opinion of natural philosophers, especially Aristotle in the second book of "On the Heavens."</margin>

-> And slippery hope upon the stairs; <-
-> And harmful gain, and useful loss; <-
-> And steps where he who climbs most, descends the furthest. <-

And world: certainly, in my opinion, no violence can be greater than that by which our soul is constrained to follow corporal delight. For this reason, it is necessary that the hope founded upon them be slippery and fallacious, as the man has no foundation of reason. From this then arises a "weary rest," because when a man has greatly exercised himself with both mind and body and has not obtained or possessed his desired pleasure, it is necessary that he rest, according to the teaching of the Philosopher in the first book of *On Sleep and Waking*, who says: <note>original: "quonuncunque est aliquod opus secundum naturam cum excesserit tempus in quo possunt aliquid facere necesse est eos languescere & illud non facere"</note> "Whenever there is any work according to nature, when the time in which they can do something has passed, it is necessary for them to grow weary and cease doing it." In this rest, much more exhaustion and distress result, since to lovers every moment seems totally lost which is not spent in the acquisition of the beloved thing. 

And just as, by continuing in this will, every rest of the lovers is exhaustion, so conversely, toiling seems to them a supreme rest and placid quiet, because they hope to possess what they seek. In that, they rest themselves, because love and desire took away from them every cause of difficulty, as Cicero testifies in the *Orator to Brutus*, saying: <note>original: "Nihil difficile amanti puto"</note> "I think nothing is difficult for a lover." And in such amorous operations, one proceeds by steps where he who climbs higher finds himself in a lower place in the end, having always descended. This condition is acquired for three evident reasons: first, by the nature of man; secondly, by the preservation of reputation; thirdly, by the quality and consistency of the senses. Cicero writes appropriately in the first book of *On Duties*, and Aristotle at the end of the first book of the *Ethics*, that the nature of man according to his perfection is that reason should rule and appetite should obey. Because of this disposition, the Philosopher says in the prologue of the *Metaphysics*: <note>original: "Humani genus arte & rationibus vivit"</note> "The human race lives by art and reason." <margin>Q</margin> Cicero, in the first book of *On Duties*, says: "Man, because he is a partaker of reason <note>original: "Homo enim quoniam rationis est particeps"</note>, through which he discerns consequences, sees the causes of things, and is not ignorant of their progress or their preceding causes; he compares similarities and joins and annexes future things to present ones, easily seeing the course of his whole life and preparing the necessary things to govern it." It is from this most excellent use of reason that man is called a "rational animal." This is also what Cicero concludes in the *Paradoxes* <note>The *Paradoxa Stoicorum*, a work where Cicero explains Stoic ethical principles</note> where he says: **"Pleasure, which claims the most advocacy, is not to be counted among good things. And as it is greater, so much more does it move the mind from its seat and state."** <note>original: "Voluptas quae patrocinii plurimum defendit in rebus bonis habenda non est. Et aque quo est maior: eo magis mentem ex sua sede et statu demovet."</note> The more a man indulges in carnal delights, the further he distances himself from his most perfect nature. Secondly, the same becomes manifest through the second reason, for it is clear that the more one rises into amorous pleasures, the more a man shows himself to become effeminate and to turn away from virility.

<margin>R</margin> For this reason, such a man is considered most vile by men of virtue and fame, obscured and unworthy of praise; this often produces the greatest changes in those men. Thus, the kingdom was taken from Sardanapalus <note>The last king of Assyria, often cited in literature as a symbol of decadence and effeminacy</note> because his military captain, Arbatus, was disgusted by such a king due to his many effeminate and lewd behaviors. We descend, then, through the third reason: that as one rises in carnal delights—which is the nature of the senses and the bodily disposition, especially in venereal pleasure—the more pleasure one takes in that act, the less powerful the man becomes to continue taking it. Hence, Cicero says in *On Old Age*: **"Lust in youth delivers an exhausted body to old age."** <note>original: "Luxuria in iuuentute effetiū corpus tradit senectuti"</note> And Avicenna <note>A Persian physician and philosopher whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe</note> at the end of the third book, in chapter twenty, says: **"Sexual intercourse empties the substances of the final digestion <note>In medieval medicine, this referred to the final stage of nutrient processing that created vital fluids</note>, which brings weakness; similar evacuations do not bring such weakness because it empties the substance of the spirits <note>The 'vital spirits' believed to animate the body</note> in great quantity due to the delight; and because they delight more, they fall further into weakness."** Thus it appears manifest how much of the substantial parts, the spirits, and the virtues are dissolved in the act of pollution; therefore, beyond the harm and weakness that follows, no greater foolishness can be committed. For as Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> says in the second book of *On Duties* against the prodigal: **"Nothing can be more foolish than to act so that you cannot continue to do for a long time what you do willingly."** <note>original: "Nihil enim potest esse stultius quam quod libenter facias curare ut id diutius facere non possis"</note> This is precisely what happens to those who take too much pleasure in the venereal act. This same disposition can also be attributed to the other senses, as they are constituted in a certain and determined proportion and measure, as is written in the second book *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's *De Anima*</note>.

<margin>S</margin> Therefore, it appears clearly through the reasons introduced above that the "ladders of love" are of such a nature that he who climbs higher upon them finds himself in the end to have descended further. Next, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> brings forward six other sculptures, as if they were seen on the Arch of Love, saying that besides "weary rest" and "restful toil," he saw sculpted the harmful gain of lovers and their most useful losses; and he saw nearby that their dishonor and infamy were bright and well-known, while their glory was black and overshadowed; and he also saw the treachery of amorous loyalty and the faith of the deceits committed for love. Wherefore he says:

<margin>T</margin> <margin>Although it is the poet's intention to universally blame the dominion of the sensitive appetite, he nevertheless often seems to limit himself to detesting venereal desire, in which lovers think and judge nothing to be so useful to them as possessing their beloveds; how harmful this is to them is not very difficult to understand.</margin>

->**Weary rest and restful toil.**<-
->**Clear dishonor, and glory dark and black**<-
->**Treacherous loyalty, and faithful deceit:**<-

Who could properly recount how many possessions and lordships decline because of the negligence that follows love? How many useless expenses are made to satisfy beloveds? What prodigality is shown toward that end in banquets? How many superfluous expenses on dogs, horses, and birds? How many gifts are inadvertently made only to appear liberal? These things, were it not for amorous desire, would be regulated according to the condition and state of the owner. From this, it follows that if the imagined gain of lovers is harmful, then the "loss" they feel at totally losing their beloveds is actually useful, according to the universal rule written in the *Topics* by the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>, which says: **"As the opposite is in the opposite, so is the proposition in the proposition."** <note>original: "Sicut oppositum in opposito: ita propositum in proposito"</note> This sentiment is usurped by legal scholars in the first law regarding the office of the one to whom jurisdiction is mandated. From this, one takes the argument of its universal truth.

<margin>V</margin> With these properties, then, another is connected: that the infamy and shame of lovers is well-known. Because they are in the eyes of the multitude and act against reason, they are blamed by the good (because injustice is offensive to them) and are even reviled by the wicked, because it seems to the wicked that the errors of other men are a sufficient excuse for their own fail—

# THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

...mind. And if it happens that in times past a man has always acted virtuously, yet afterwards falls into even one tiny error, all his preceding virtuous deeds and past glory are obscured. And this occurs not only because of vices arising from choice, but even from those that occur almost naturally, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the third book of the *Ethics*: **Fury corrupts the best man.** This most especially happens through carnal love, which is judged to be an effeminate thing, such that men in love are said to have drunk from the fountain of Salmacis. <note>In Greek mythology, the fountain of Salmacis made men weak and effeminate.</note> Hence Cicero, in the first book of *On Duties*, mocking this sluggishness of men, says by comparing them to Salmacis: **"Salmacian spoils without sweat or blood."** <note>original: "Salmacida spolia sine sudore & sanguine." This refers to achieving "victories" through soft, unmanly means rather than true effort.</note> It is also well known how much treacherous loyalty and how many faithful deceptions occur among lovers; for simple lovers sometimes think that once they have promised to love each other unitedly, if they turn away from this purpose, they are treacherous and disloyal.

<margin>X</margin>
O ignorant mind! O blind and clouded intellect! How much treachery do men commit toward their most faithful wives just to be "faithful" to their mistresses? How many women also break their marriage vows to their husbands for fear of being unfaithful to their lovers? O unjust loyalty! O crooked maintenance of faith! On the contrary, how truly faithful is that deception, and how just and reasonable is that "treachery," when—recognizing their own state—women and men break the faith they previously promised to their disordered appetite. O, how faithful would that woman be who, having promised her faith to a lover, instead led him into the hands of her husband! Whereupon, if he were appropriately corrected, he might afterwards abstain from such love. Likewise, the man who, by breaking his promise to his mistress, returned to the faithful examples of a most chaste wife: truly, these should be judged not as perjurers or traitors, but as most faithful. Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> then introduces three other images sculpted on the arch of love, which are universally shown to be present in the battles of love, saying that besides the other images mentioned above, he saw that **Anxious Fury** was the worker there, and **Lazy Reason** was drowsy; in the midst of these, he saw a **prison** which is reached by a wide, open, and easy road, but where one finds the exit narrow, difficult, and blocked when searching for a way out. Thus he says:

<margin>y</margin>
<margin>
It was the opinion of the ancients, as shown in the tragedies and by Leonardo of Arezzo <note>Leonardo Bruni, a famous humanist scholar</note>—who is most learned in our times—in his letter to Mario the Sicilian, that love was a divine fury sent by Cupid into the minds of men.
</margin>

->Anxious fury and lazy reason:<-
->A prison entered by open roads,<-
->From which one departs through narrow ways with great difficulty:<-

Through this fury, lovers were driven to many perverse and intense actions. Speaking according to this opinion, the poet <note>Petrarch</note> presents this "fury" as the agitator of amorous minds in which reason is totally asleep. But if we speak according to the judgment of Cicero in that paradox, **All fools are insane** <note>original: "Omnes stultos insanire"</note>—which we believe to be a more fitting opinion—Messer Francesco means that in those who, through ignorance and lack of restraint, allow themselves to be overcome by lewd appetite, it is necessary that the mind becomes furious through too much anxiety. Consequently, reason and intellect become sluggish, fall asleep, and are veiled. Because of this, man is locked in the prison which is reached via the broad and wide way of carnal delights and worldly pleasures or comforts. Wishing to exit this prison, one finds the way most narrow and almost totally cut off, so that it is nearly impossible, or certainly not easy, to return to liberty. This is according to the judgment of Augustine in his *Book of Confessions*, where he says:

> For from a perverse will, lust is made; and while one serves lust, habit is formed; and when habit is not resisted, necessity is made; by which, as if by linked rings—which they call a chain—a harsh servitude held me bound. <note>original: "Ex voluntate.n.peruersa fit libido & dum libidini seruit fit consuetudo: dum uero consuetudini non resistitur fit necessitas qbus tanquam a nullis sibimet inexis quos catenam appellant tenebat me dura seruitus"</note>

<margin>z</margin>
Likewise, Cicero proves in the previously cited *Paradoxes* that he is a slave who, entangled in pleasures, continually follows the sensory appetite. This judgment is testified to by the infallible truth of Christ in the seventh chapter of Saint John, who says when speaking to the Jews: **"For everyone who commits sin is a slave to sin."** <note>original: "Omnis. n. qui facit peccatum seruus est peccati."</note> He, therefore, who is a slave in another’s power—and one is in another’s power most especially through a vicious habit—can only with great difficulty return to full liberty by his own effort, as Aristotle clearly demonstrates in the third book of the *Ethics*. For this reason, the poet appropriately says that the prison of love has its exit at a steep, narrow, broken, and inaccessible path. Messer Francesco next adds what the life of lovers is like after they have been...

### CHAPTER FOUR

Having been led inside the loving prison, the author says that inside this jail there is nothing but a mixed crowd and clouded confusion, from which a most certain pain, an uncertain happiness, a doubtful hope, and a fleeting sweetness are never separated. Hence he says:

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it is to be understood that the minds of afflicted lovers are confused in two ways: one is that in their actions they always seek the pleasure of others—namely, their beloveds. Since that pleasure is often uncertain or unknown, they do not know what to choose or what to do.</margin>
> The descent is quick at the entrance, the exit is steep;
> Inside is a turbid confusion, and a mixture
> Of certain sorrows, and uncertain joys.

How many times do they perform many actions only to please their beloveds, which nevertheless displease them greatly? Then, trying to fix it by doing the opposite, they likewise find they have caused further displeasure. Thus, they become confused, ignorant, and stunned with the heaviest grief, having experienced the joy they just held—thinking they were pleasing their beloveds—to be a most uncertain thing. The other way they are confused is when they turn somewhat to the consideration of themselves; seeing their misery, their state, and the difficulty of separating themselves from it, they are overwhelmed with shame and grief. They prove to themselves by certain experience that if they ever had any joy, it was unstable and fleeting, wherefore they deplore their past life within themselves, just as the poet <note>Petrarch</note> does in that sonnet: *I go weeping for my lost time.* And in that other: *Love held me burning for twenty-one years.* In the first sonnet and in *Beautiful Virgin.* <note>These are references to Petrarch’s *Canzoniere*, specifically poems 364, 365, and 366, which express his late-life regret.</note> The poet then concludes by comparing the harshness, the trouble, and the punishments of the prison of love, saying that never—even under the sun's greatest height or most direct gaze, when all impediment of clouds is removed—did incense flames boil so much, nor did these five islands of Vulcan vomit so much fire. These islands are: Lipari, Ischia, Hiera, Mongibello, and Strongyle. He means that the place of the loving prison boils as fervently as these, and anyone who goes there by their own choice is very bold, risks much, and exposes themselves to a strong danger. Hence he says:

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, one should know that as Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century geographer.</note> writes in *The Wonders of the World* and Pliny in his book of *Natural History*, there are islands in the Sicilian sea formerly named the Ephestie <note>From the Greek *Hephaistos*, god of fire.</note>...</margin>
> Vulcan, Lipari, or Ischia never boiled,
> Nor Strongyle or Mongibello, like that place,
> Where anyone who comes risks themselves greatly.

<margin>C</margin>
...the nature of which is to throw flames of fire over the surface of the earth, especially when facing the rays of the sun. Therefore, the island of Vulcan, formerly called Hiera <note>Greek for "Sacred."</note> and later given its current name simply because it was consecrated to Vulcan, contains within it a very high mountain that burns almost continuously; at night its light shines from quite far away. The island of Lipari was named after King Liparus, who lived there much earlier than Aeolus. Strongyle <note>The modern island of Stromboli.</note> was the island considered the palace of Aeolus, because by its smoke the inhabitants can know within three days—according to the diversity of the smells—which winds are about to blow over the earth. Ischia is an island a little more remote than the others, similar to them because of the eruption of flames, and very well known today for the events occurring there. Mongibello <note>Mt. Etna.</note> is in Sicily, and is more famous than any of these for its burning, and its fire appears most manifest. Various opinions have existed regarding this burning: for some said these places were the descent into Hell, and that Pluto, near that place, had snatched Proserpina away to the underworld. But according to Trogus, as reported by Justin in the fourth book of *Foreign Wars*, which does not seem to disagree with the opinion of the natural philosophers: Sicily is a cavernous region. Because of its site, the nature of the earth is almost sulfurous. Therefore, the winds, trapping themselves in those hollows and clashing together in that flammable earth, ignite by their own force and generate flames—both because of the nature of fire which always ascends, being very light, and also by the force of those winds which drive the fire before them. For this reason, the whole mountain of Etna is abundant with fire, as Virgil excellently describes it in the *Georgics*, saying: **"We have seen Etna surge with its furnaces broken, and balls of flame and molten rocks rolling."** <note>original: "Vidimus undante ruptis fornacibus Ethnam. Flammarūq; globos liquefactaq; voluere saxa." - Virgil, *Georgics* 1.472-3</note> And those other islands mentioned above contain a similar nature. For this reason, one can easily understand how much fervor and boiling there is in the souls of those driven by immense desire and by the...

### THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

...through the unbearable hardships which they do not hesitate to subject themselves to for the sake of amorous appetite. He continues then by saying how, once the enamored spirits reached that most turbulent prison, they were tortured by Love, saying that in that place they were all bound in various and contrary kinds of punishment, in ice and in fire and in everlasting darkness, where each one, calling in vain for mercy for their painful martyrdoms, had already become hoarse. Whence he says:

<margin>D</margin> **How many are the contrary crosses** <note>The author uses 'patibuli' (gallows/crosses) to describe the psychological instruments of torture lovers endure.</note> upon which wretched lovers afflict themselves is shown quite clearly in the section above; because, since the dominion of our works is placed only in seeking the delights of the senses, the causes of the lovers' affliction are as many as there are delightful objects. From this, the light of the active intellect is extinguished, insofar as it only follows sensory judgment and does not deliberate concerning the choice of objects placed before it; rather, it remains numbed and almost consumed by reason, according to the opinion of Cicero <note>The author refers to Marcus Tullius Cicero as 'Tullio.'</note> in his *Rhetoric*, who says: *Talent is like iron, which unless exercised is covered in rust.* <note>original: "Ingeniū est sicut ferrū quod nisi exercitē rubigīe tegitur."</note> By this, it is manifest that it is a consistent thing that lovers bound in the prison of love live always in everlasting darkness. Finally, Messer Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch, the author of the poem.</note> concludes the end of the chapter in which he affirms that he, along with the other prisoners, had been enclosed within the amorous prison for many years, saying that once led to that prison, he lived for many years where, because of the immoderate martyrdoms he sustained, he always wept in his solitary dwellings for the Sorgue <note>The river in Provence near Petrarch’s home in Vaucluse.</note> and for the Arno <note>The river of Florence, representing Petrarch’s Tuscan heritage.</note>—one out of natural affection for his homeland, and the other for his accustomed study. During this time, he was always desiring and longing for his former liberty, which nonetheless he could not achieve through all the excellence of the Tuscan wits; because he was exiled from himself, having suspended the use of reason. He found only one remedy to slacken his so intense suffering somewhat: to go about thinking and imagining great and memorable things through the exercise of his study. In this thought, he was especially moved by his wandering sight, which the desire to know and understand made most prompt and light to look back and see if anyone had ever loved, and who had been the beloved or the lover. And in this looking, he first, through the natural compassion he bore for those foreign souls, seeing them brought to such a state, melted just as snow dissolves when exposed to the hot rays of the sun. And so great was this multitude that, wishing to look at all of them, it happened to him as to one who gazes in a short time upon a long, ornate, and well-composed painting, where as his feet move forward, his eyes often return backward, judging that because of its greatness and the multitude of perfect figures, he had considered it imperfectly in such a short time. Whence he says:

> **T**here we were bound in ice and in fire
> **A**nd in everlasting darkness, where in vain
> Each one calling for mercy was hoarse.

---

<margin>E</margin> **Our Messer Francesco being led** into that state where the other wretched lovers are found, had found a very suitable remedy both for himself and for his so bitter suffering. For whenever a man directs his mind to consider some outstanding example in that cause, the soul is called back from thinking of the beloved women; and furthermore, a man is awakened to great things, which, if he wishes to perform them, it is necessary to cast away effeminate and base cares. Nonetheless, for all this, Messer Francesco could not achieve his former liberty through the industry of the wits of Val d'Arno—that is, the Tuscan wits—taking the part for the whole <note>A literary device called synecdoche, using the Arno valley to represent all of Tuscany.</note>, where it is to be understood that in such—

> **T**here, while sighing for the Sorgue and the Arno,
> I stayed many years, and dreaming of liberty;
> Nor could I, through the wits of Val d'Arno,
> **F**or I was placed in exile by myself;
> Only one remedy did I have in that state:
> Gazing upon great and memorable things;
> **I** turned my wandering sight to every side,
> For the desire to know is so prompt and light;
> To know who and when one had loved.
> **G**azing, I was turned to snow in the sun
> By so many spirits, and so bright in the dark prison;
> Almost like a long painting in a brief time:
> **T**hat the foot goes forward, and the eye turns back.

# CHAPTER FOUR

<margin>F</margin>
Italy, by its very location, has a reputation for producing more climatic wits <note>The author refers to the theory of "humors" and "climates," where a region's geography was thought to dictate the intelligence and temperament of its people.</note> than any other region in the world: both through the practice of letters and through trade, and even through the practice of arms. Regarding this, Vegetius <note>Publius Flavius Vegetius Renatus, a 4th-century Roman military theorist.</note> writes in his book *On Military Matters*: "the captain of the people should be Italian and the combatants Spanish" <note>original: "il capitano de la gente vole esser italico & icombatenti Hispani"</note> if one wishes to well-constitute an army within the Italian nation. Furthermore, the Tuscans are said to be the most acute and expert in practical affairs, which is necessary for them because of the sterile state of their land in comparison to other parts. And among the Tuscans, the people situated along the Arno <note>The river flowing through Florence and Pisa.</note> have a reputation for greater subtlety of wit than other Tuscans in comparison, specifically regarding matters pertaining to political life. Because of the competence of the Tuscans—which the Poet <note>Petrarch.</note> understands primarily through his own modesty—he could not, however, shield himself from the harsh blows and arrows of Love, nor find a remedy for them once he was subjected to them. Nevertheless, he employed that action which was appropriate for a foreign and noble soul, even though it might seem almost the opposite to hide the property of the thing—that is, he felt compassion, as is the nature and custom of all noble men. This was demonstrated by Virgil <note>Publius Vergilius Maro, the Roman epic poet.</note> through the persona of Dido when she said: *Not unacquainted with misfortune, I learn to help the wretched.* <note>original: "Non ignara mali miseris succurrere disco." A famous line from the Aeneid, Book 1.</note>

<margin>G</margin>
### EXPOSITION OF THE FOURTH CHAPTER.

<margin>H</margin>
**I**t being a natural thing that the intellect, devoted to the cognition of things, is always thirsty for the understanding of them; and the more difficulty arises concerning them, the more the human desire is kindled to comprehend them solely through the work of the irascible virtue. <note>In medieval psychology, the "irascible virtue" or power was the part of the soul that drives one to overcome obstacles and pursue difficult goals.</note> From this it follows that sometimes one desists sooner because of the fatigue communicated to the body, which then (through the senses) cannot provide for the soul so that man might be satisfied by the total comprehension of the objects. Our poet affirms this happened to him at the beginning of this present fourth chapter. For, having been led inside the most fervent prison of Cupid, and having no other remedy than to look at and consider great and memorable things—which were in that place in such a great multitude—he found that in wanting to diligently comprehend them all, it happened to him as it does to one who, in a short time, must view a very long painting. Where, as his feet proceed forward, he turns his eyes back to take a more distinct knowledge of the preceding pictures. Hence, already despairing of being able to know everything, he gave himself to looking diversely here and there at things so great and so worthy that, had he wanted to recite them in this *Triumph*, he would have occupied too much time. Through this search for knowledge, he had become tired, but not sated with seeing so many things which he would have desired to report in his book like the others. There was also, besides the aforementioned exhaustion of the soul, a multitude of thoughts in considering the actions of those who had been most offended by Love: who was most affected by fortune, who had received the most from others, and who had acted most nobly. And thus, thinking diversely, Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch.</note> says that he was totally rapt by the consideration of two enamored spirits <note>This likely refers to Paolo and Francesca, the famous tragic lovers also featured in Dante's Inferno.</note> who passed before him, weeping and lamenting the force and the Roman laws, and the constancy of the administrator <note>The "administrator" here refers to the legal or social forces that separated the lovers.</note> by which it was necessary that their amorous knots be broken by death, since they wished to keep their sudden and inadvertent promise of faith to one another. He then continues the narration of many other worthy spirits who were detained in the prison of Love, which he intends as the particular subjects of this fourth and final chapter of the *Triumph of Love*. Whence, beginning his introduction, the poet speaks thus:

#### CHAPTER FOUR OF THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE.

<margin>5</margin>
> Tired now of looking, yet not sated,
> Now here, now there, I turned my gaze,
> Seeing things for which the time to remember is brief.
> My heart went from thought to thought: when
> All to itself it drew two who, hand in hand,
> Passed by, sweetly conversing.

<margin>I</margin>
**T**here is nothing that has compassion and displeasure for the desires and troubles of others except for man, because he is by nature a "friendly and civil animal," <note>A reference to Aristotle's definition of man as a "political animal" (zoon politikon) in his Ethics and Politics.</note> as is openly written by the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> in the first book of the *Ethics* and the *Politics*. Therefore, when something occurs that at first appears harmful to our fellow man, a natural compassion and mercy results in us because of the common obligation which Cicero writes in the first book of *On Duties* is naturally between...

# THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

...among men, from whom our Messer Francesco <note>Messer Francesco refers to Francesco Petrarch, the author of the poem.</note> does not deviate. Seeing two amorous spirits weeping, and moved by natural compassion, he turned entirely toward them, desiring to understand the cause of their amorous suffering. He says that the foreign language of their speech was unknown and obscure to him, but his interpreter <note>In the context of the poem, the "interpreter" is often understood as Love himself or the guide showing Petrarch the vision.</note> had made it manifest and clear to him. Moved toward them because of their strange clothing, and having recognized how one of them was a great friend to the Roman name <note>original: "nōe latino"</note> while the other appeared harsh and hostile, he turned to the benevolent one and called him by name. He entreated him by his two closest bonds of affection—namely by Scipio Africanus <note>The Roman general who defeated Hannibal and was a close ally of Masinissa.</note> and by Sophonisba of Carthage <note>A Carthaginian noblewoman whom Masinissa loved, but who was forced to commit suicide to avoid being taken as a Roman prisoner.</note>—saying: "[Masinissa], let it not trouble you to speak with me for a while and answer those things which I shall ask you." Thus he says:

<margin>K</margin>
The poet clearly demonstrates in the preceding verses how much the power of friendship can do to intervene and obtain a request, having asked Masinissa by the names of Scipio and Sophonisba, whom he had loved uniquely. Because of this, Masinissa turned to listen and engaged in a long discussion with him. The text adds that Messer Francesco, having a natural desire to know of the events occurring before him, asked and prayed Masinissa to listen. Masinissa, drawn to great admiration that the poet had so well known the two objects of his affection, asked him who he was, saying that he would willingly listen since the poet had so well discovered and identified his two most singular loves. Thus he says:

->Their graceful, strange attire caught my eye,<-
->And their foreign speech, which was obscure to me;<-
->But my interpreter made it clear to me.<-
->After I knew who they were, I approached<-
->Them: for one spirit was a friend<-
->To our name; the other was impious and harsh.<-
->I went to the first: "O ancient Masinissa,<-
->By your Scipio, and by her,"<-
->I began, "let not what I say trouble you."<-

<margin>L</margin>
Messer Francesco describes a very great humanity in the preceding verses, showing that Masinissa was already prepared to grant his wish and ask who the author was. Therefore, the poet adds his response with modesty and great reverence, keeping his own identity silent and demonstrating great humility. He adds the reasons why he did not deserve to be known by Masinissa, saying: "O Masinissa, my little being does not deserve nor sustain having such a great man know it, for a small flame cannot produce a great light from so far away"—a response truly suited to a prudent man. Continuing further, he says: "O Masinissa, your most excellent fame reaches throughout the whole world in such a way that many equals who never saw you, nor will ever see you, are joined to you by a beautiful knot of love and friendship. I pray you to tell me: if he who proceeds in triumph before us guides and keeps your love in peace, what a pair are you and Sophonisba! You certainly seem to me one of the faithful and rare things to have happened in the world, considering the effects of love you displayed in your lives." Thus he says:

->He broke in and said: "I would willingly know<-
->Who you are first, since you have so well<-
->Spied out both of my affections."<-

<margin>M</margin>
Messer Francesco clearly demonstrates in the preceding verses how much modesty one should have and how much reverence one should show toward those greater than oneself. He adds how Masinissa, having heard and understood the courteous response of the author, wished to grant his request. Starting to speak and narrate the manner of his falling in love, he continues by saying that Scipio had been the cause of the breaking <note>original: "corruptiōe."
