# CHAPTER FOUR

### CHAPTER FOUR

The custom of true friendship: which is to justify the undertaking of friends even if they are sometimes the cause of displeasure and annoyance. Thus, in the person of Masinissa, Messer Francesco <note>Messer Francesco refers to the poet, Petrarch.</note> says: "Although your tongue has been so quick to call my name, demonstrating that you must already know my thoughts through yourself, yet to vent the grief of a sad friend and the bitterness resulting from the death of my beloved Sophonisba, I am content to speak and fulfill your wish. Having, therefore, placed and located all my heart, soul, and goodwill in that supreme man, Scipio Africanus <note>The Roman general who defeated Carthage; he was a close ally of Masinissa but forced the separation of the lovers for political reasons.</note>, such that I hardly and with difficulty grant Laelius <note>Gaius Laelius, Scipio's historical best friend.</note> the first rank in such friendship: wherever the Roman banners were under his leadership and auspices, I was always near them, dedicated and allied to the Romans. In which expedition, fortune was always his favorer; but certainly not as much as his supreme valor deserved, of which his soul was truly more full and distinguished than any other man. Wherefore, after the Roman arms were spread with great honor and glorious victory through the extreme west in Mauritania and the city of Cirta <note>Modern-day Constantine, Algeria; it was the capital of the Numidian kingdom.</note>: as you see, in that place love reached us and joined us. And certainly with such sweetness and delight that no amorous flame ever burned with equal sweetness in any other enamored hearts, nor do I believe it can burn in future times. But alas, how few were those nights in which such pleasure was tasted; rather, they were very brief and scarce, and of little delight. For while we were led in vain to the marital yoke and legitimate bonds—which were no false excuses for our passion—they were shattered and broken: because he who alone was worth more than all the rest of the world, namely Scipio Africanus, parted and separated us lovers with his wise and holy words; which, as he [Petrarch] writes in the life of Scipio in the book *On Illustrious Men* <note>original: "De viris illustribus," a famous work by Petrarch containing biographies of great leaders.</note>, says:

> For a wall covers the body from the enemy, or a rampart separates it, or iron protects it; nothing else defends and separates the soul from pleasures except virtue. <note>original: "Corpus enim ab hoste vel murus tegit vel vallum separat vel tuetur ferrum animum a voluptatibus nihil aliud defendit ac separat nisi virtus."</note>

And he cared nothing, nor did he heed our many inflamed sighs. Nevertheless, although he acted and did this in a way that gave me cause to grieve—and even now I wish to—I still saw in him a clear and burning virtue by means of which he did not consent to my pleas. For truly he is blind who does not see the light of the sun, which I judged to be less than the virtue of Scipio.

<margin>N</margin>
And it is quite true that a great and rigorous justice is a most heavy offense to lovers: for being against the just amorous appetite, such a justice prohibits it entirely. Therefore, such a just friend and such upright counsel as Scipio was, was like a hard and bitter rock to the amorous enterprise. And especially because, although by age he was a brother and equal to me, nevertheless by honor he was a father to me and by love a son. For this reason, it was necessary to obey him, though with a sad, grieving, and afflicted heart, and with a face mournful and intensely troubled. From this it followed that my dear and beloved Sophonisba and bride died; for seeing herself brought into Roman power, she chose to die rather than serve <note>Sophonisba committed suicide by drinking poison to avoid being led through Rome as a captive in a triumphal parade.</note>. In which death I myself was the minister of my own great grief, because of the fierce spirit <note>original: "predatore," perhaps implying her spirit "captured" his better judgment.</note> which was the soul of Sophonisba; through her most ardent pleas, by which, not wishing to offend, I offended myself. I sent her the poison with as much pain and bitterness as I know and feel by experience; and she believes it, and you yourself can consider if you have ever felt even a spark of love. Wherefore, from such an excellent bride, the only heir that remained to me was only bitter weeping. Although she was my every good and every hope, nonetheless I chose to lose her rather than ever fail in the faith promised to her or to my most excellent Scipio.

<margin>O</margin>
Consider then, Messer Francesco, if you find anything notable and worthy similar to this in this company: for there is much more left of the work and the things to consider than there is of the day or the time in which the mind toils at such work." Wherefore it says:

->**Y**our tongue being so ready with my name<-
->**P**roves, said he, that you know it through yourself;<-
->**M**ut I shall speak to vent my sad soul.<-
->**H**aving placed all my heart in the supreme man<-
->**S**o much that I barely grant the prize to Laelius.<-

<margin>
It is no wonder if our **Messer Francesco** <note>Petrarch</note> narrates the present history contained in the preceding verses and the following more copiously and diffusely than the others: because of the singular affection he had for the name of Scipio, wherever any of them intervened with some action.

...his deeds, nor did he speak with such passion that he could not withdraw from the conversation. From this, one gained a modest acquaintance: almost every tiny gesture of the present story has been given and reported. Nevertheless, to show even more particularly what information pertains to the preceding verses, one must primarily know that such was the mutual benevolence between Scipio and Laelius <note>Gaius Laelius was the closest friend and advisor to the Roman general Scipio Africanus; their friendship was a classical archetype of loyalty.</note> that neither wished to perform any worthy thing without the other. Hence, Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> says in the second book of the Punic War: <note>original: "Scipionemque sine Laelio nihil maioris rei volebat ducere"</note> "Scipio wished to undertake no matter of great importance without Laelius." Therefore, the poet appropriately describes Masinissa as hardly granting to Laelius the prize for Scipio’s benevolence.

Secondly, it is to be understood that after Scipio Africanus, in the Second Punic War, had broken and defeated the two brothers of Hannibal—namely Hasdrubal and Mago—at Gades <note>Modern-day Cádiz, Spain.</note> and had already subjected all of Spain <note>original: "Hispania"</note>, he turned his attention toward occupying Africa. Knowing that it would be useful to provoke the friendship of Rome, he deliberated going in person to persuade Syphax, king of the Masaesyli <note>The text reads "limas fily," likely a corruption of "Masaesyli," a powerful Numidian tribe.</note> in the region of Numidia, located at the extremity of the western habitable land. Whereupon, at that same time, he encountered Hasdrubal, son of Gisco, a Carthaginian sent by his senate for the same purpose. Finding that the Carthaginians heard of Scipio's coming and knowing the great self-restraint of the man, in order to more easily obtain their intent and avoid an evident danger, they offered to the said Syphax a noble girl as a wife: the daughter of the aforementioned Hasdrubal, whose name was Sophonisba. She then so altered the mind of Syphax that, although he had been allied with the Romans through Scipio, he nevertheless separated himself from their friendship and took the side of Carthage. Whereupon it happened that Masinissa, a king in the same region and Syphax’s capital enemy, allied himself conversely with the Romans. In which habit:

# CHAPTER FOUR

By habit, having come to know the singular virtues of Scipio Africanus, Masinissa’s love for him was joined in a bond of perfect friendship. For this reason, after being sent by Scipio along with Laelius against Syphax <note>Syphax was the king of the Masaesyli in western Numidia, who had defected from Rome to Carthage.</note>, they defeated him and his kingdom through their virtue, and rendered him a prisoner of the Romans. It happened then that, having captured Cirta—the metropolitan city and capital of the kingdom of Syphax—as Masinissa was ascending to the royal palace, Sophonisba <note>The daughter of the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal Gisco and wife of Syphax.</note> came before him. With piteous gestures and humble, flexible words, she prayed that he might be pleased to honor her in such a way that she, being Carthaginian and an enemy of the victorious Romans, would not fall into their power. This could not be done except by means of her death; she begged him most insistently that he should kill her there with his own hands. Masinissa heard her humane and piteous words and, immediately taken by her beauty, inadvertently not only promised her what she had asked, but even took her as his wife. Afterward, he reported what he had done and promised to Scipio, as Livy writes in the tenth book of the Second Punic War <note>original: "Li. in de. ij. bello punico libro decimo." Livy's actual account of this is in Book 30.</note>. Scipio did not confirm or assent to these 

<margin>P</margin>
things promised and performed by Masinissa, but responded in this form and with these words: 

> I believe, Masinissa, that seeing some good in me at the beginning in Spain, you came to join in friendship with me, and later in Africa, you committed yourself and all your hope to my faith. However, there is no virtue among those for which I seemed desirable to you in which I have gloried as much as temperance and the control of lusts. I would wish that you too, Masinissa, would add this to your other exceptional virtues. Believe me, there is not so much danger for those of our age from armed enemies as there is from the pleasures surrounding us on all sides. He who has bridled and tamed them by his temperance has achieved a much greater honor and a greater victory for himself than the victory we have over the defeated Syphax. What you did strenuously and bravely in my absence, I have both gladly remembered and found out; as for the rest, I prefer that you reconsider it yourself and blush at my words. Syphax was defeated and captured under the auspices of the Roman people; therefore, he himself, his wife, the kingdom, the land, the towns, the people who inhabit them—finally, whatever belonged to Syphax—is the prize of the Roman people. Even if his wife were not a Carthaginian citizen, even if we did not see her father as the commander of our enemies, it would be proper for me to send her to Rome. Let the Senate and the Roman People <note>original: "S.P.Q.R." (Senatus Populusque Romanus)</note> have the judgment and decision over her, for she is said to have alienated a king who was our ally and driven him headlong into arms against us. Conquer your spirit; beware lest you deform many good qualities with one vice, or corrupt so many types of merit with a fault greater than the cause of the fault.

<margin>Q</margin>
¶ Therefore, Masinissa, having heard the just, grave, and rigorous response of Scipio, and knowing that by not handing over Sophonisba as a prize along with the other prisoners he was failing in his faith to the Romans—and if he did hand her over, he would break his promise to Sophonisba by consenting to her being led as a prisoner in a triumph—he took a hard, bitter, and lamentable path. This was to send her a little poison, telling her that if she wanted him to keep his faith to her, she should drink what he had sent. Sophonisba took the poison in her hand and replied to the messenger that she willingly took the gift sent by Masinissa, but that only one thing distressed her: that she was married at her own funeral and death. Having said these words, she drank the poison, which was the cause of death and liberty for her, and of grief and tears for Masinissa. Finally, it is to be noted that the poet rightly introduced Masinissa saying to Scipio that he had been a father to him in honor and a son in love, in addition to being a brother in years. For no greater obligation can be attributed than to a father, since no greater bond can be born from anyone, nor can so many benefits be received as from a father, according to the opinion of Cicero in the *Paradoxes* <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, Roman statesman and philosopher.</note>. For the father, by generating, gives being, provides nourishment, and establishes one in private domain and public honors. For this reason, Aulus Gellius in the second book of *Attic Nights* <note>original: "Gellio. ij. lib. de no. acti." refers to Noctes Atticae.</note> reports that Taurus the Athenian philosopher concluded that in private places where natural procreation has its place, the father ought to precede the son, even if the son holds a public magistracy. This is taught not only by nature but also by divine law, numbering it as a commandment in the Holy Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>. And consequently, if greater affection is shown to good children than to any other earthly thing, not only natural example but the experience of those who have them 

<margin>R</margin>
testifies to it. And Aristotle, in the first book of the *Ethics*, confirms this, attributing so much to children that he asserts one cannot be happy in any way without them. Afterward, Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch (Francesco Petrarca).</note> adds what became of him having heard and understood the narration made by Masinissa, what he also heard Sophonisba say and how he responded to her words, and finally what followed after the conversation, saying:

->Petrar.<-

# THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

<margin>T</margin>
<note>The letter 'T' likely refers to the "Triumphus," the title of the poem being commented upon.</note>

...as he understood how much fortune had opposed the love they had shared, and how in such a short space of time such great benevolence ended with such a bitter conclusion, he became full of pity for their unfortunate circumstances. His heart melted with compassion no differently than if it had been snow exposed to the hot rays of the sun. And while staying in this state, he heard Sophonisba say toward Masinissa: "O Masinissa, this Latin man who is here, Master Francis <note>original: "Meser Francesco," referring to the poet Petrarch himself, who appears as a character in his own vision.</note>, does not in truth displease me on his own account. But I am in a firm and steady purpose to hold all of his people in hatred."

And the poet adds his response to the aforementioned words, saying that he told Sophonisba: "By now it is no longer the time to preserve hatred against the Italians; therefore, put your heart in peace. Know that your Carthage fell twice by the hands of us Italians and was humbled; the third time, it was entirely given over to ruin." Then Master Francis relates what Sophonisba answered to his reproach of her Carthage, saying that she replied: "O Latin, the enmity is not to be diminished nor the praise lowered because of this reproach of yours. For if Africa wept in those wars, Italy certainly did not laugh, given the many slaughters of Romans and Italians carried out by the Carthaginians, for whose testimony I cite your own histories; read those." And having said this, the poet concludes that Masinissa, his own dearest friend and the friend of Sophonisba, separated from him, placing himself into the great throng of enamored spirits in such a way that he was divided from his sight. Whence he says:

<margin>T</margin>
¶ FOR A CLEARER understanding of the aforementioned verses, one must know that between the Romans and the Carthaginians there were three wars. The first began because, while the Messinese and Syracusans were making war in Sicily, those of Messina implored help from the Romans, and those of Syracuse asked it of the Carthaginians. In this war there was much variety and many different victories; in the end, by the virtue of Quintus Lutatius Catulus <note>A Roman consul who won the decisive naval Battle of the Aegates Islands in 241 BCE.</note>, having defeated six hundred ships of the Carthaginians at the Aegates Islands, the Romans were superior. Peace was made with this condition: that Sicily, Sardinia, and all the other islands which are in the middle between Italy and Africa should remain as the dominion of the Romans.

The second war began when Hannibal was nine years of age. Being led by his father Hamilcar to the altar to swear perpetual hatred against the Romans, and Hamilcar having later died, Hannibal kept the oath he had made. Therefore, while there was a city in Spain named Saguntum allied with the Romans, Hannibal laid siege to it and captured it, from which the second war followed. In this war, the Roman Empire was almost extinguished, and the walls of Rome saw the camps of the African enemies. Finally, through the virtue and work of Scipio Africanus, Hannibal was overcome, and the Carthaginians were constrained to ask peace of the Romans. They granted it to them with the very harsh conditions of paying money, grain, and warships, and the return of their fugitives and the loss of Spain, as Titus Livy <note>original: "Tito Linio"</note> openly writes at the end of the tenth book of the third decade.

The third and final war had its origin because, Carthage having always been an enemy of the Romans and having already returned to being more powerful than ever, the Senate held a council on what should be done with her. Marcus Cato <note>Cato the Elder, famous for the phrase "Carthago delenda est" (Carthage must be destroyed).</note> judged that she ought to be entirely undone. But Scipio Nasica <note>Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum, who argued that Carthage should be spared to keep Rome disciplined by a common threat.</note> gave the opinion that she should be maintained, so that by removing the obstacle to the Romans, they would not create dissension among themselves. The Senate, then, seeing the contrary opinions of such grave and excellent men, took the middle path; and having created as consuls Titus Ma. and Cato the Censor... <note>The text ends mid-sentence as it moves to the poetic stanzas.</note>

> I was full of pity, thinking of the brief
>   Space allowed to the great fire of two such lovers;
>   To the sun, my heart seemed made of snow.
> When I heard it said as I passed forward:
>   "This man certainly does not displease me for his own sake;
>   But I am firm in hating them all."
> "Put your heart, O Sophonisba, in peace," I said,
>   "For your Carthage at our hands
>   Fell three times, and at the third it lies."

>   If Africa wept, Italy did not laugh;
>   Ask your own histories about it."
> Meanwhile, our friend and hers placed himself,
>   Smiling with her, into the great throng,

# CHAPTER FOUR

...first, they sent [the consuls] against the Carthaginians to execute their harsh decrees, or else to take Carthage by force. The consuls thus arrived in Africa and primarily told the Carthaginians that they must burn their warships and only keep their merchant ships. Because the Carthaginians desired to live in peace, they agreed to burn the ships. The consuls then commanded that all defensive and offensive weapons be handed over to them, and again the Carthaginians were content to obey the Romans. Once the arms were surrendered, the consuls commanded that they must go and live wherever they pleased, provided they were eight miles away from the
<margin>V</margin> sea, because they wanted to ruin Carthage. Hearing the harsh edict made by the consuls, the Carthaginians turned all their penance into desperation and rage, and they all decided together to defend themselves unto death. When the Roman Senate heard of their disposition, they decided two things: one, seeing it was almost fated <note>original: "fattale," meaning destined by fate</note> that the house of Scipio should overcome Carthage, they made Scipio Aemilianus consul until the war's end—he was the natural son of Paulus Aemilius and the adopted son of Lucius Scipio, son of Scipio Africanus. The other decision was that if Carthage were taken, it should be burned and turned into ruins. Thus, in the course of time, Scipio having captured Carthage, it fell according to the Roman decree. In those wars, so many Romans and Latins died that it was difficult to judge whether one should laugh more at the victories achieved or weep for the many excellent leaders and outstanding Romans who died. For this reason, Master Francis <note>The poet Petrarch</note> introduces Sophonisba as having a universal enmity and not a personal hatred for individual Latin men—a sentiment worthy of and suited to a great and excellent soul.

Next, Master Francis relates another example of love in which he demonstrates the great power of a miraculous restraint of lovers and a most singular fatherly pity and courtesy. He says that after Masinissa's departure, it happened to him <note>To Petrarch, the narrator of the poem</note> as it does to one who rides through uncertain and hostile terrain, who, out of fear of sudden assaults, stops at every step and looks back to see if his path is safe. This is a well-known effect: the thought of the journey ahead shortens and cuts away the perceived distance. For so great was the multitude of enamored spirits that at every
<margin>X</margin> turn of his eyes, the poet saw new things, which he stopped to grasp because of his desire to know who each one was, in what fire they burned, and with what harsh punishment. And proceeding thus, he saw on the left hand one who had gone off the common path, walking like one who diligently searches for something which, once found, brings both joy and shame; and he gave his beloved bride to another—truly a supreme love and a new courtesy. In this admirable exchange, the bride herself seemed to be both happy and ashamed of the change. Thus all three spirits proceeded together—that is, the first and second husband and the changed bride—talking sweetly of their tender love and sighing over the kingdom of Syria <note>original: "Soria"</note> taken from them by the Romans under the consulship of Scipio Africanus. Therefore he says:

<margin>A</margin>
...I should have waited, but that spirit <note>referring to King Seleucus I Nicator</note>, having heard that sound and the Latin speech <note>original: "idioma latino"; here referring to the Italian vernacular used by the poet Petrarch</note>, was completely troubled in his appearance; yet he restrained himself and stopped, showing himself to be reconsidering the ancient war and the heavy enmity he had with the Roman people. Beyond this, almost appearing to be a diviner of Master Francesco's <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the author of the poem</note> wish, he began to speak and said: "Know, Master Francesco, that I am Seleucus, the ancient King of Syria; and this is my son Antiochus, who had a great war with you." And he adds, excusing him: "But reason has no place in one's actions against force, neither in the affections of the mind nor even in physical dispositions." Continuing, he says of this other woman: "First she was my wife and then she was his, whom I gave to him only to save him from the death to which his amorous desire was leading him. The gift made by me among us was lawful, not being prohibited by any law. Know that her name is Stratonice; from which you can see how our fate is indivisible. By this effective sign, one understands how tenacious and strong our love is." It is seen also through this other effect: that she was content to leave the kingdom and return from being a queen to a private citizen. I, likewise, was content to divide myself from every sweet delight by parting from Stratonice. And Antiochus was content to abandon his life and every pleasure to demonstrate how much his generous soul was to be esteemed—a quality of a well-mannered and noble soul. Certainly, if it had not been for the arrival and help of the learned and noble physician <term>Erasistratus</term> <note>a famous Greek anatomist and royal physician</note>, who most excellently perceived the cause of his illness, his life would have ended in death in the flower of his years. In conclusion, the pious father Seleucus brings forward the excuse of his beloved son, saying that he almost ran to his death by loving and keeping that love silent. Thus, to love was a necessity for him, considering that it came from Cupid as if from a deity; but to keep this love secret was indeed his own singular virtue, as was the fatherly piety that succored him by granting him his beloved and noble Stratonice as a bride. Wherefore he says:

> I drew myself toward those three spirits, who were huddled
> Together to follow another path;

> Troubled in his look, held himself back a little,

> My son, who had a great war with you;

> I my delight, and he his life,
> To make each other worthier than himself.
> And were it not for the discreet help..."

<margin>B</margin>
Our graceful poet has described the history narrated here so extensively and clearly that, by reading the verses, anyone can sufficiently understand it for themselves. Re-summarizing it more quickly than explaining it, I say primarily that Seleucus was King of Syria and Antiochus was his son. Seleucus, having taken the beautiful Stratonice as his wife after the death of Antiochus' mother—a woman equal to him in origin and excellence of soul, but different in years—Antiochus, his firstborn, fell most intensely in love with her. Since his desire seemed inappropriate to him, he decided he would rather die than manifest it in any way. Whereupon, agitated by agony and constrained by amorous desire, he fell into a very great and mortal illness. Having become very close to death, Seleucus had a great number of doctors called for his cure. These doctors, not knowing any cause for such a heavy sickness in him, remained in suspense and did not know how to act for his...

# CHAPTER FOUR

> Of the noble physician; who well perceived
> His age in its flowering was finished.
> **K** eeping silent, loving, he almost ran to death,
> And love was force, and silence was virtue;
> My true pity; which came to his aid.
<note>These lines refer to the Greek physician Erasistratus, who discovered that Prince Antiochus was dying not of a physical ailment, but of secret love.</note>

For his health, it happened by chance that one of them called Erasistratus <note>Erasistratus of Ceos (c. 304–250 BCE), a famous anatomist and royal physician</note>, holding his arm in hand and searching for the pulse, just then Queen Stratonice presented herself before Antiochus. At the sight of her, his pulse grew vigorous by its own power and became stronger, showing a very great variation; afterward, as soon as she had departed, Antiochus returned to his own great weakness. Then, when the queen appeared another time in the presence of Antiochus, the pulse had the same effect. Because of this, Erasistratus clearly recognized that Antiochus was in love with his stepmother. Wherefore, as Appian of Alexandria <note>Appian (c. 95–165 CE), a historian who chronicled the Roman wars</note> writes, Erasistratus judged that if he told Seleucus suddenly <note>original: "ex abrupto"</note>, he perhaps would not have consented to give him his beautiful Stratonice as a wife; for this reason, with great ingenuity, he compelled him to do so for the sake of Antiochus's health. 

Whence he said thus to Seleucus: "Your Antiochus must necessarily die, for I have discovered him to be in love with my wife, whom I would not grant to him for anything; therefore it is inevitable that he shall soon meet his death." Seleucus, hearing these words, out of pity for his son and believing a heavy sorrow was coming to his heart, piteously turned to Erasistratus and begged him greatly for the life of his son, that he might grant him his dear wife, offering him very great gifts as compensation. Erasistratus says: <margin>C</margin> "Woe to me, Seleucus: you burden me to give my wife to Antiochus, who is your son; and yet, you would not consent to give him Stratonice if he loved her as he loves mine." Seleucus replied: "Would to the gods it were so! So that for the health of my own son I should have to burden no one else but myself." Then Erasistratus, having heard what Seleucus had offered him, revealed the truth: how Antiochus was in danger only for the sake of the love he secretly bore for Queen Stratonice. Whereupon Seleucus, diligently inquiring of his son if this were so, found through his modest confession that what Erasistratus had told him was true. Therefore, by the shared will and consent of Seleucus, Antiochus and Stratonice were wed; she who was first the wife of the father became the bride of his son, Antiochus.

Secondly, it is to be understood that this Antiochus had a most cruel war with the Romans <note>referring to the Roman-Seleucid War (192–188 BCE)</note>, and the cause was this: that Ptolemy Philopator <note>Ptolemy IV, King of Egypt</note>, a most worthy king, having died and left his children as wards under the protection of the Romans, Antiochus turned his mind to occupying Egypt. He did this especially because he saw it was very rich in treasure and abundant in people; furthermore, Hannibal the Carthaginian, who had recently been put to flight by Scipio Africanus and was staying with him, made him much bolder. For this reason, the Romans, justly taking up the defense of the orphans, went to war with Antiochus. They appointed as consul Scipio Asiaticus <note>original: "Scipione Affiano"; the text likely means Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus</note>, the brother of Scipio Africanus, with Africanus himself as his legate, so that Antiochus would well understand that the Romans had no less confidence in the victor Scipio than he had in the defeated Hannibal. 

Thus, the Romans fighting with Antiochus near Mount Sipylus, between Syria and Egypt, Antiochus was defeated and relegated to Cilicia beyond Mount Taurus. From there, in the small part of the kingdom left to him by the grace of Rome, while reigning he used to thank fortune and the Romans for having diminished his royal cares, thoughts, and anxieties, leaving him only such a part of the kingdom that his mind was intent only on its preservation and not its expansion.

The poet then narrates how, Seleucus having finished his speech, his mind and words were removed at once; he departed so quickly that Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> could barely return his greeting before he was gone. And he adds that after that shadow departed from his eyes, he stood heavy with thought regarding the aforementioned words, sighing with compassion. While remaining very fixed in this thought, he says he heard a voice—that is, a sharp phantom—speaking to him: "Master Francesco, you remain too long suspended in one single thought, considering how many and diverse things you have to narrate, especially knowing how swift and brief time is." Whereupon, awakened by this voice and looking about, he says that Xerxes, King of Persia, never led so many armed men into Greece as the number of enamored spirits he saw after Seleucus, so that his eye could not endure such a diverse multitude of objects. This multitude was varied in language and speech, and varied in regions and homelands, so that out of a thousand, Master Francesco recognized only one; but of those few he knew, he will provide the history in this poem of his. Whence he says:

**FOR A clearer understanding of the multitude of the armed followers of Xerxes, it is to be understood that Xerxes was the son of Darius, King of Persia, who was appointed king by the neighing of a horse, as Trogus <note>Gnaeus Pompeius Trogus, a Roman historian of the 1st century BCE</note> and Justin <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, who famously abridged Trogus's works</note> write and refer to in the first book of *The Extreme Wars*. Darius, then, having waged war against the Greeks, and that war continuing until his death, Xerxes succeeded him in the kingdom. Artabazanes <note>original: "Archemenes"</note> was set aside by the judgment of their uncle Artaphernes <note>original: "Arisferne"</note>, even though he was the elder brother; but he was born at the time when Darius was a private citizen and not yet king. Xerxes therefore wished to follow the war begun by his father, whence he first came into Greece with six hundred thousand people. There he was defeated and driven out on land by Leonidas the Spartan with only six hundred companions in the narrow pass of Thermopylae <note>A famous battle in 480 BCE where a small Greek force held back the massive Persian army</note>, and by Themistocles in the maritime battle <note>The Battle of Salamis</note>. Afterward, returning again to Greece with an equal army, he was forced by Cimon, son of Miltiades the Athenian, by land and by sea, to return to Persia with great shame. From this one can conclude how vast was the number of men led in the war of Xerxes, it being one million and more than four thousand. The poet <note>Petrarch</note> also says, not without natural reason, that his eyes could not bear the sight of such a multitude of enamored spirits; because since the judgment of common sense and the other internal faculties must conform with the external senses, there arises from the exercise of the organic members a natural weakness, through which the operation of sensing is no longer produced. Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, having stated in the preceding verses that he wished to tell the stories of those few spirits captured and conquered by love whom he had known among such a multitude, consequently begins to narrate them, saying that the first was Perseus, about whom he wished to know how Andromeda, the black virgin, had pleased his eyes and her hair in the regions of Ethiopia. Whereupon the horrible monster came out of the water in a great fury to devour Andromeda. With Cepheus present, Perseus killed it and took Andromeda as his wife. Andromeda had previously been promised to Phineus, the brother of Cepheus; because of this, while the wedding of Perseus was being celebrated, Phineus tried to kidnap her. Solinus writes in *The Wonders of the World* <note>original: "de mirabilibus mundi"; a 3rd-century geographical work</note> that the sea monster that was to devour Andromeda was so large that its rib was certainly forty feet in length, and its height well exceeded that of an Indian elephant. This was made known by Marcus Scaurus, a prominent Roman citizen, during the time of his aedileship <note>An elected office in Rome responsible for public games and buildings</note>, when he brought it among other things to Rome from the aforementioned rock known as the "Chains of Andromeda." <margin>P</margin> For clearer evidence of the preceding verses, it should be known that Ovid writes in the 14th book of the *Metamorphoses* that on the island of Cyprus there was once a youth named Iphis who deeply loved a girl named Anaxarete. But she, totally despising his intense love, would never even listen to, let alone grant, any of his prayers or words. Because of this, Iphis, in despair and judging it a much lesser evil to die than to suffer in such a way, took a noose and with it hanged himself by the throat before her door. When the servants of the house heard the banging against the door, they went out and found the youth hanging; once they cut him down, they carried him to the house of his already widowed mother. After she performed the maternal rites, the funeral was honorably led to the burial; as the procession moved in pomp, it happened to pass before the house of the cruel Anaxarete. She, hearing this—more by the justice of powerful Cupid than out of love or compassion for the wretched Iphis—went up to the highest windows of her palace to see the miserable deceased who was to pass by. No sooner had she seen him than she was turned into the harshest stone. For good reason, the poets remain silent about the great multitude of others who killed themselves for love. Among these, although the poet warns us of the contrary, it is worth mentioning a youth dressed in a religious habit who, not too long ago in the city of Siena, followed the example written above. This man loved a girl who, though of humble birth,

Finally, one day he asked her what he should do to end his martyrdoms; she replied that he should hang himself. Once he heard this answer, he immediately put it into effect. <margin>R</margin> An amorous tale: telling how he saw those two companions whom the force of love made inseparable and eternal, namely **Halcyone and Ceyx**, who are accustomed to make their nests upon the seashore in the most pleasant and sweet times of winter. Wherefore he says:

> *Halcyone and Ceyx, upon the seashore*
> *Making their nests in the sweetest winters.*

¶ **CONCERNING** the knowledge of the preceding verses, it should be understood that **Ceyx** was the son of **Lucifer** <note>In this context, Lucifer refers to the "Morning Star" (the planet Venus), the father of Ceyx in mythology, rather than the fallen angel.</note>, King of Trachis <note>original: "Tarchuria"</note>, who was the son of Jove. Ceyx took as his wife **Halcyone**, the daughter of **Aeolus**, King of the Winds. Now, Ceyx wished to go to the oracle of Apollo 

<margin>T</margin> to ask for some guidance. Being unable to go by land because of the war of Phorbas <note>A legendary king of the Phlegyans who robbed pilgrims on the road to Delphi.</note> blocking the way, he chose—though against the advice of his wife—to go by sea. While Ceyx was sailing, a terrible storm arose, through which his ship was broken in a short span of time and he was drowned. Halcyone, who had remained at the royal palace, offered prayers every day to **Juno** for the well-being of her beloved husband. But Juno, weary of so many tears and so many cries from Halcyone, and wishing to rid herself of this annoyance, had the harsh death and shipwreck of her husband Ceyx revealed to her. As **Ovid** writes, this was done through a servant of Sleep called **Morpheus**. Having clearly understood the death of her husband in her dream, Halcyone was moved by the greatest grief and came to the seashore. When the body of her dear husband was by chance washed ashore by the waves, as soon as she saw him, she suddenly threw herself into the sea. Because of this, the gods were moved to great compassion—especially Lucifer, the father of Ceyx. The dead body and the living Halcyone, amorous spouses who had lived in delight, were transformed into the Halcyon birds <note>Kingfishers</note>. These birds, through the ancient memory of their affection, are accustomed to nest, dwell, and fly over the seashores. And as **Saint Ambrose** testifies in his book *The Hexameron* <note>original: "exameron"; a treatise on the six days of Creation</note>, confirming the opinion of Ovid in the eleventh book of the *Metamorphoses* <note>original: "methamorphoseo"</note>: while these aforementioned birds hatch their young on the seashore, they provide nourishment for a period of fourteen days. During this interval, the sea stays quiet and never receives any storm; therefore, sailors call those days "Halcyon days." Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> next adds another example and amorous case of **Aesacus**, son of King Priam and the nymph Hesperia <note>original: "Eperia"</note>, saying that beside those two (Halcyone and Ceyx), he saw Aesacus standing all thoughtful, searching for Hesperia his lover, resting now upon a rock, now entering beneath the water, and now flying high. Wherefore he says:

<margin>V</margin> > *Beside them, I saw thoughtful Aesacus stand,*
> *Seeking Hesperia; now seated on a rock,*
> *And now beneath the water, and now flying high.*

¶ **FOR** a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known that **Aesacus**, according to what **Ovid** writes in the eleventh book of the *Metamorphoses*, was the son of **Priam**, King of Troy, and of **Alexirhoe**, daughter of the river Cebren. This Aesacus was born in secret and raised on the shaded Mount Ida; having become a handsome and courageous youth, no less so than his brother **Hector**, he despised the city and urban affairs. He gave himself to the woodland and pastoral life, delighting in wandering through shaded mountains and pleasant valleys. While living this life, he happened one day upon a very beautiful nymph called **Hesperia**, and upon seeing her, he was immediately inflamed with love. Following her as she fled, it happened that in her swift flight, the wretched girl incautiously stepped on a serpent with her foot, by whose bite she died instantly. Aesacus, unable to endure her death because he had been the cause of her bitter end, decided he no longer wished to live. In despair, he threw himself from a high mountain or steep cliff into the sea. In his fall, he was transformed by **Thetis** into a bird called a <term>diver bird</term> <note>original: "smergo"; likely a cormorant or merganser</note>. This bird still preserves the desire to die, for it often plunges itself beneath the waters, now flying high and now throwing itself down, always seeking to drown itself. Master Francesco next adds the example of the most cruel **Scylla**, saying: "I saw, after Aesacus and Hesperia, the cruel daughter of **Nisus** fleeing and flying from the presence of her father." Wherefore he says:

For this reason, he came to the battlefield, as **Ovid** writes at the beginning of the eighth book of the *Metamorphoses*, laying siege to the principal city of the kingdom of the Megarians called **Alcathous** <note>Alcathous was the name of the citadel of Megara, named after its legendary builder.</note>, where **Nisus**, an ally of the Athenians, reigned. Now, this Nisus had a single golden lock among his hair, which possessed a magical property: as long as Nisus did not lose it, he could never lose his kingdom. He also had a daughter named **Scylla**, who was beautiful of body but savage of soul. Sometimes, for her own pleasure, she would go atop a tower where **Apollo** had once rested his sweet lyre while flying through those parts; because of this, a soft harmony could still be heard echoing from the stones of that wall. Having ascended the tower one day to view the armies, she saw Minos fighting in the midst of the fields, and she fell ardently in love with him. Seeking to please him and fulfill her illicit desire, and knowing the nature of her father's golden lock, she cut it off while he slept. Running swiftly with it, she came to Minos and gave it to him, begging him to take her as his wife. But Minos, seeing the wound inflicted by the unfaithful daughter and being a most just man, would not fulfill her unseemly request; instead, he commanded her to leave him. Seeing herself a rebel to her father and cast out by Minos, and not knowing where to turn, she wandered until she and Nisus were transformed into birds. As can still be seen today, they maintain a deserved enmity for such a great betrayal <note>In mythology, Nisus was turned into a sea-eagle and Scylla into a bird called the 'Ciris,' forever pursued by the eagle.</note>. Being faster than any other in running, she established this law: that whoever wished to win her as his bride must compete with her in a race. If he surpassed her in running, she would become his wife; but if he were surpassed, he must then lose both his head and his life. It then happened that **Hippomenes**, son of Megareus and grandson of **Neptune**, who was a most beautiful and well-mannered youth, fell in love with the beautiful Atalanta as soon as he saw her. # THE TRIUMPH OF LOVE

Regarding the sea gods: This Glaucus <note>A fisherman turned sea-god mentioned on the previous page</note> loved a maiden named Scylla, daughter of Phorcus. However, Circe—the queen of Mount Circeo near Gaeta and daughter of the Sun—was in love with him. Because Circe saw that Glaucus prized Scylla much more than he did her, she became enraged against Scylla. She placed certain poisons in a beautiful spring where Scylla was accustomed to wash herself. Thus it happened that one day, when Scylla returned to bathe in that spring, she was transformed by Circe’s witchcraft into various and horrible forms. Because of this, she threw herself into the sea, where, through the influence of Glaucus, she was established as a sea goddess. Yet Glaucus, recognizing the wickedness of Circe, <margin>F</margin> forever after called her a cruel beast and a most bitter lover. Next, the poet brings forward another example, that of Picus and his wife Canens. He says that after Glaucus, he saw Canens and Picus—the latter once a king of the Latins, but transformed by Circe into a bird <note>The woodpecker, or *picus* in Latin; the original text notes "uccello del suo nome"</note>. <margin>G</margin> ¶ For the understanding of the preceding verses, it is necessary to know that Picus was the son of Saturn and the father of Faunus, as Ovid writes in the fourteenth book of the *Metamorphoses* <note>original: "metamorphoseos"</note>. He took as his wife the most noble maiden Canens, daughter of Janus and Venilia. She deserved equal praise for the beauty of her body and the sweetness of her song. It happened then that Picus, who loved her deeply, went out one day to hunt in a forest where Circe was also accustomed to frequent. Seeing that he was exceedingly beautiful of body, she fell intensely in love with him. She then conjured a phantom wild boar to appear before Picus; out of a desire for the prey, he followed it into the densest part of the forest. Circe was hidden in that place, and revealing herself, she stepped before him and intensely begged him to be pleased by her person, showing him that she was the daughter of the Sun. Picus, who was devoted only to his beloved Canens, replied that as long as his wife lived, he never wished to be joined to another woman. Circe, agitated by great sorrow and moved by great anger at this response, immediately transformed him into the bird of his name. Upon hearing of this, Canens died of great grief, weeping by the banks of the Tiber. Next, Master Francis <note>Petrarch</note> narrates two other examples, saying that after Picus, he saw the weeping of Egeria; and afterward, he recognized how, in place of her bones, Scylla hardened into stone, and how she became the infamy of the Sicilian sea. # CHAPTER FOUR

### **And she holds the naked blade in her left hand:**

<margin>O</margin> In this scene, we see Canace and Macareus, who loved each other improperly and took illicit pleasure together. Canace found herself pregnant, and after the proper time, she gave birth to a son. She gave the child to a servant to carry secretly to a nurse to be raised, so that her crime would be hidden from her father, Aeolus <note>In mythology, Aeolus was the keeper of the winds</note>. However, while the child was being carried away and was near Aeolus, the infant began to cry. Hearing the cry, Aeolus called the servant back and finally discovered the sin of his children. Enraged, Aeolus commanded that the child be given as food to wild beasts, and he sent a knife to Canace, commanding that she use it upon herself as a just punishment. Having received it, and holding it in her left hand, she wrote to Macareus—who had fled from their father's hands—praying that after her death he would deign to collect her remains and those of her child and place them in a tomb. Next, the poet adds the example of Pygmalion, who, hating women and refusing for any reason to take a wife, made an ivory statue. He fell so deeply in love with it that day and night he prayed to Venus <note>The goddess of love</note> that she would make the image come alive so that he could take her as his wife. Finally, Venus granted his wish. Thus the poet says:

### **Pygmalion with his living lady;**
### **And a thousand others whom I saw singing**
### **By Castalia and Aganippe on both banks;**

<margin>P</margin> ¶ For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, one must first know that Pygmalion was the son of Cilix, who was the son of Agenor. Being a most spirited youth and considering that the glory of his ancestors had reached even to the furthest sea <note>The original text uses "lastrico mare," perhaps a corruption of a specific sea name</note>, he set out to acquire fame and honor for himself. He prepared a fleet and came to Cyprus, where, after fighting several battles, he finally emerged as the victor. Once Pygmalion had peaceful possession of that kingdom, he found much decadence among the women of the island. Because of this, he decided to live entirely without any woman. But because he was a clever and singular sculptor, and since the desire for women is a natural inclination for everyone, he remained firm in his purpose but carved an ivory image of a most beautiful woman. He looked at her often and took great delight in her, eventually falling in love. Because of this, he most devoutly prayed to Venus many times that she should animate his statue and return her to him as a living woman. Venus consented and heard Pygmalion’s prayers. One night, while he lay silently with his statue, he felt it grow warm and move in some places. Marveling at this, he looked more closely and finally realized she was alive. Becoming overjoyed beyond measure, he lived ever after with her in the sweetest happiness until the final days of his life.

<margin>Q</margin>

<margin>R</margin> ¶ Secondly, it should be understood that Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> says he heard a thousand singing at Castalia and Aganippe because he wishes to describe, in a general and quiet way, all the loves sung about by poets. This is because each of these two springs is consecrated to the Muses <note>The nine goddesses of the arts and sciences</note>, and the writing of such effects is commonly <note>original: "vt plurimum"</note> observed by poets. These poets were especially abundant and famous in Boeotia, where the Castalian spring is located. It took its name from the nymph Castalia; while she was walking one day on Mount Parnassus, Apollo <note>The god of light and poetry</note> wanted to seize and violate her. She fled, and as she ran with Apollo pursuing her, she finally threw herself into that spring to preserve her virginity. Ever after, the spring retained her name. Finally, Master Francesco concludes the Triumph of Love with this chapter, saying that he ultimately saw in the prison of love how Cidippe was tricked by an apple. Wherefore he says:

He took a golden apple upon which he wrote these words: "I, Cidippe, swear by the immortal gods that I wish to be the wife of Acontius." Having written this, he sent it to her as a gift. Seeing the letters, the girl read them aloud, and by reading them, she came to swear that she wanted to be Acontius’s lady. For which reason...

# EXPOSITION OF THE TRIUMPH OF CHASTITY.

<insert>N</insert>O thing among human perfections is found whereby man is known to have a nature different from the wild beasts, except for the rational soul, when the use of that soul is turned toward acting according to the highest and most excellent virtue. And although the soul, by its nature, inclines toward such actions, it is nonetheless sometimes removed from its proper end by the delight it receives from the senses. For this reason, if a man recognizes himself—through the two natures of which he is composed—as being similar to plants, beasts, and birds, and yet having the power of free will, he can say he is able to conform to any of these similar objects by losing the form of the others. And truly, he should be called by the name of that nature to which he most conforms by his own choice. Therefore, if he prizes sensual sweetness more than intellectual operation, he truly deserves to be called "bestial"; whereas if he chooses the pleasure and joy of the intellect, he is not only to be called "angelic," but truly divine. 

This is because just as divine wisdom never errs in its operation, so too the habit of human virtue is of such perfection that, where it is established, it never permits any evil to happen or be done. Wherefore Aristotle, defining virtue in the second book of the *Ethics*, says: **"Virtue is that which, being well-disposed, brings perfection and makes its work good."** <note>original: "Virtus est que bene se habens pficit: & opus eius bonum reddit"</note> Augustine, in his book on *Free Will*, writes: **"Virtue is a good quality of the mind by which one lives rightly and which no one uses badly."** <note>original: "Virtus est bona qualitas mentis qua recte viuitur qua nemo male utitur"</note> And finally, in the seventh book of the *Ethics*, the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> concluded that men made perfect through heroic virtue are divine. 

For this reason, our most illustrious poet, Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, having determined in the preceding Triumph the dominion of the sensual appetite—which was defined above as the first state of the soul in which the soul finds itself operating during the time of youth—and having shown how many evils and inconveniences follow from it, now treats in the following Triumph the dominion of reason and intellect. This corresponds to the state attributed to the soul when it rests in the time of manhood, in which men commonly have the proper knowledge of themselves. He shows how many excellences and singular parts result in a man when he obtains victory within himself against the sensual appetite. This universal argument is gracefully described to us by Messer Francesco with a marvelous poetic veil in the present Triumph, introducing Laura as Reason, just as he had previously taken Love to represent Lascivious Appetite. 

The poet narrates then that Love, having made an assault against Lady Laura with horrendous fury, was defeated by her, for she was wise and clever, shielding herself from his blows. She finally conquered him and placed him under her rule. Thereafter, Love—thus conquered and bound, just as he had previously triumphed over men and led them to the island of Cythera <note>The mythical island of Venus</note>, consecrating the stolen spoils to his mother—was led by Laura and her company to Rome, to the temples of Chastity and Modesty, where she also left the palms and spoils of her victory in honor. 

On this journey, the poet introduces her having visited Scipio Africanus <note>The Roman general who defeated Hannibal</note>, who lived in his villa at Liternum <note>original: "castello da linterno"</note> where he was a voluntary exile, solely out of disdain conceived against his homeland for the ingratitude of having allowed him to be accused of the embezzlement of funds <note>original: "repetunde pecunie"</note>. Thus, with equal consent, they both proceeded with the other companions to the aforementioned temples. Oh, truly glorious triumph! Oh, singular and health-giving victory, in which he is conquered without blood—he who, with so much anguish, produces so many weapons, deploys so many armies, and sheds so much blood whenever he gains victory over men. 

Beginning now to descend to the text, Messer Francesco starts by consoling those who, in their youthful age, were constrained by some delight and submitted to this appetite. Here he silently answers a hidden question: whether young people who are conquered by this appetite should be deprived of hope and eternally grieve for their error and the sin committed. To this he responds "no" for two reasons: the first, because even the gods and great men have been...

## CHAPTER FOUR

<insert>M</insert>en considered most excellent in the world, having been captured and subdued by this appetite <note>The "appetite" refers to sensual desire or passionate love</note>, can hardly endure it with patience. For an unwary youth, disarmed of prudence and counsel by a lack of experience, it is a great consolation when he sees men of greater dignity placed in the same state to which he has been miserably led. 

The other reason is that men, considering their past life and how the time gone by was spent in vanity, turn themselves entirely to the moral and political life, whereby the shame of past errors is taken away. For repentance is of such great power that it renders a person entirely innocent of every sin committed; because one can return to repentance through the freedom of our human will at any time while life lasts. For this reason, one must never despair over the errors of others, but call them back to a better life and more just actions. By doing so—according to either human or divine laws—one finds pardon for sin, just as Christ expressed in Saint Matthew, in chapter 18 <note>The source text cites chapter 17, but the dialogue occurs in Matthew 18:21–22</note>, when he replied to the question of Saint Peter where the text says: *“Lord, how many times shall my brother sin against me and I forgive him? As many as seven times?” Jesus said to him, “I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven.”* <note>original Latin: "Domine quotiens peccauerit in me frater meus dimittam ei vsq; septies . dixit illi Iesus non dico tibi vsq; septies sed vsq; septuagies septies ."</note>

I say then that our poet, giving a beginning to this second triumph <note>The Triumph of Chastity</note>, says that this same reasoning comforted him. Having seen in one same place and at one same time the height of the gods and of men—who were so excellent they were reputed divine in the world—tamed and subjugated, he took an example from their state. Their harm and misfortune resulted in his own benefit and profit, allowing him to console his own cases and sorrows and to suffer them patiently. He expresses the cause, saying that if Phoebus <note>The sun god Apollo, often depicted as being mastered by Love</note> and Leander of Abydos <note>The youth who famously drowned in the Hellespont while swimming to reach his beloved Hero</note> are wounded by the same bow and the same arrow—of whom one was reputed a god and the other a pure man and mortal like others—and also seeing in the same snare Juno the goddess and Dido, that most excellent and mortal lady (who surrendered herself to death for the love of Sychaeus <note>Dido’s first husband; Petrarch famously defended the historical Dido, who committed suicide to remain faithful to her dead husband rather than for Aeneas</note> and not for that of Aeneas, as is commonly said), he should not grieve without measure and moderation. For he was conquered by love while a youth, unwary and disarmed. 

Furthermore, he should not lament if his beloved (and then enemy) <note>Referring to Laura, who resisted his advances to preserve her virtue</note>, whom he loved without any order, was not constrained by tenacious Cupid, considering how grave an error would have followed from such an effect. And he adds the second reason that occurred to him, saying that another cause occurred which brought no small sorrow: he recognized that this Love, through the operation of Reason—represented by My Lady Laura—had fallen into such lowliness, into so miserable a state and so deprived of the weapons of flight, that moved and overcome by compassion, he wept bitterly for it. Whence he says:

Our Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the author of the *Triumphs*</note> so gracefully offers hope for his youthful error in the preceding verses, and the way in which he reasonably excuses it seems well expressed in our prelude. Similarly, who Phoebus, Juno, and Leander were, and by what appetite they were seized, was also demonstrated above in the preceding Triumph <note>The "Triumph of Love," which comes before Chastity in Petrarch's sequence</note> according to the necessary requirements. Therefore, for the understanding of the preceding verses, it remains only to know who Dido was and in what way she was tied in the same snare along with Juno. 

On this, it should be known that Dido was the daughter of Belus, the son of Phoenix, King of Phoenicia. Being a very beautiful girl, she was given in marriage by Belus to Sychaeus, who was a priest of Hercules. Because he was extremely wealthy, he was murdered for greed by Pygmalion, his brother-in-law <note>In most accounts, Pygmalion was Dido's brother, but the text here refers to him as her "cugnato" or brother-in-law</note>, and his treasure was stolen. Since Dido did not know the misfortune that had befallen her husband Sychaeus, he appeared to her several times in a dream, revealing the wickedness of her brother Pygmalion. For this reason, Dido took great care and diligence to seek out if this were true; and having found and recognized the truth, she conspired against her brother with all those to whom Pygmalion was hateful. Having prepared ships, she stole all her brother's treasure and, together with a great number of people, arrived without hindrance in Africa. 

Having arrived there, she was asked by those of that country to settle in those parts. She consented and made a pact with them to buy as much land as she could surround with a bull's hide. By cutting the hide into very tiny strips, she enclosed a great quantity of land with it. There she built the city which she named Carthage from the word for "Charter" <note>The text suggests an etymological link between "Cartha" and "Carthage"</note> and later called its citadel Byrsa <note>A pun on the Greek word *byrsa*, meaning "hide"</note>. <meta>Continuing from the previous page, the author finishes the backstory of Dido's flight from her brother Pygmalion and her arrival in Africa to found Carthage, setting the stage for the discussion of her character's treatment by Virgil versus the historical truth.</meta>

->TRIUMPH OF CHASTITY<-

Having arrived in Carthage where he was received by Dido and greatly honored: she stayed with him for some time, during which Virgil feigns that Dido fell in love with Aeneas and that during a hunt, in a cave, she took carnal pleasure with him—which is entirely false. Indeed, Aeneas came to Italy many years before Dido was born; for according to Trogus <note>Gnaeus Pompeius Trogus, a Roman historian from the time of Augustus</note>, whom Justin <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, who epitomized Trogus's work</note> cites, Carthage was built seventy years before Rome. Nevertheless, Virgil makes use of this fiction for two universal reasons. The first is that, wishing to imitate Homer—just as Homer introduces Ulysses as having arrived in Phoenicia to King Alcinous to recount all his maritime wanderings—so Virgil describes Aeneas as having come to Carthage and Dido as the most suitable place, and he has him recount to her the entire destruction and the war of Troy. The other reason is to further glorify the Romans by placing every virtue in Aeneas, from whom they are descended; and beyond this, he describes him as so handsome that he could have drawn to concupiscence even a <margin>F</margin> most chaste soul, such as that of the excellent Dido. Consequently, in praise of continence, Virgil describes him as unwilling to consent to the allurements of Queen Dido, but remaining upright and constant in the will of the gods. Ultimately, he exalts the Romans by showing, through the curses Dido made upon Aeneas’s departure, how great the difficulty was in overcoming powerful Carthage. From this graceful and artful fiction of Virgil’s, those who are little practiced in poetic inventions have taken the argument, saying that Dido killed herself out of grief for Aeneas’s departure. From the aforementioned true history of Dido, therefore, an answer can appear to a doubt that arises in this place: that is, if Queen Dido was caught in a snare together with Juno, she should not be numbered among the companions of Laura <note>Laura is Petrarch's muse and the symbol of Chastity in this poem</note>; and if she is deservedly among Laura’s companions, she should not be caught with Juno in a snare. To this, it is answered that Dido deserves to be seen in both qualities: for Juno is described as conquered by love only because she desired simple sensual pleasure from Jove, unregulated by any reason; Dido likewise desired this during the life of her husband Sychaeus, and thus was appropriately subject to love. But thereafter, wishing rather to die than to act against the justice of her country’s laws—and being a free queen, refusing to be a subjected bride—through this just and reasonable act, Dido deserved to accompany Laura, who demonstrates to us the dominion of reason. By this, our stated intention from the beginning is clearly proven true: that <margin>G</margin> Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> does not mean only carnal appetite by "love," but every sensory delight and lascivious desire. And through Laura, he describes not only chastity, but every work regulated by virtue. Finally, it should be known that Messer Francesco, in weeping for the misery of love, does not intend to show that he regrets the victory of reason; but rather to make understood how great the efficacy of virtuous works is against vices when a man, recognizing himself, departs from them and gives himself to virtue. Or rather, he describes himself weeping to demonstrate that when a man overcomes his appetite, he weeps for the state and misery of his lost life. Having thus described this reasonable cause for hope, he consequently describes what the sudden and swift movement of appetite against reason was, figured as Love and Lady Laura, saying that he saw Love moving with all his arguments against Lady Laura. He speaks of her with no other comparison than that of two fierce lions rising in battle, or two burning lightning bolts descending from the air with no less fury, which, wherever they strike, make every other obstacle fall, whether in heaven, on earth, or in the sea; and to this, Messer Francesco adds that he saw her likewise to be ready and much swifter than winds, air, or vapors. Whence he says:

# CHAPTER ONE

GG v

> Moving against her, of whom I speak;
> And she much swifter than flame or winds

among the prey. Lightning is also one of the most powerful atmospheric phenomena <term>impressioni aeree</term><note>The author uses the Aristotelian term for phenomena occurring in the "middle region" of the air, such as rain, wind, or lightning.</note> among all others. Therefore, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the third book of the *Meteorology*, when a hot and dry exhalation rises into the middle region of the air and is trapped inside clouds—which are condensing into water due to the intense cold of that place—this exhalation, surrounded by the clouds and feeling the conflict of opposites, seeks an exit. Thus, finding none, it violently bursts through the cloud. And because this exhalation is composed of diverse and irregular parts, it moves the earth lightly, and in this movement, it penetrates the air (which does nothing to stop it) and shatters whatever it encounters on the ground; sometimes it even forces the waters of the sea to open to their very depths. With similar or even greater violence, human appetite sometimes moves impetuously. For this reason, according to the judgment of physicians, when men are seized by such appetite, they are said to be "furious" <note>From the Latin *furiosi*, meaning driven to a state of madness or uncontrollable rage by passion.</note>. 

However, in this commotion, reason moves itself and its defense much faster than winds or vapors. Vapors are very subtle bodies, slightly denser than air but thinner than clouds (though clouds are nothing more than denser vapors which, rising to the second region of the air, condense there). From these come rain, hail, snow, dew, and frost. Wind is nothing other than air moving impetuously through the mixing of dry exhalations drawn with speed by the celestial bodies from the cavities and pores of the earth—as the Philosopher seems to intend in the second book of the *Meteorology*. Both wind and vapor, as seen by experience, move with great velocity, but the will is certainly much faster in choosing the actions to be done, which are then regulated by reason. To understand this, one should note the judgment of the Philosopher in the seventh book of the *Ethics*, who says that the will does not move without the intellect roaming through thought, as Aristotle proves in the third book of *On the Soul* and Saint Thomas in the first part of the second book, question six, article one. To this purpose, Augustine also says: <note>original: "Amamus quidem inuisa incognita autem nequaquam"</note> "We may indeed love things that are unseen, but things that are unknown, not at all." 

Therefore, the intellect always prepares a universal proposition for the will, which is that "all good must be followed and all evil must be fled," because the desiring power is regulated by reason. Then, in the other proposition—called the "minor" by logicians—which contains the particular object toward which the will must rise with a choice, the will limits itself either to following that object if it is good, or fleeing it if it is evil. Thus, just as in speculative matters the conclusion is known immediately once the minor premise is introduced, so in practical matters, once the minor proposition is proposed, the will immediately rises to choose. And because no corporeal thing moves as fast as the powers of the soul, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> says that when these powers are well-disposed, they are swifter than vapors or winds. Master Francesco then explains the efficacy and the great disturbance of the soul that occurs when men are brought to deliberate on whether they wish to be obedient to lustful appetite or, by subduing it, obey reason. This deliberation is most difficult according to the judgment of Tully <note>Cicero</note> in the first book of *On Duties*, who says: <note>original: "in primis autem costituēdum est quos nos & quales esse uelimus & in quo genere uite quae deliberatio est omnium difficillima:"</note> "First of all, we must decide who and what we wish to be, and what kind of life we should lead; this deliberation is the most difficult of all." 

Therefore, he describes through a simile the fierce assault made upon Lady Laura after the movement of love, saying that the sound and tumult of the heavy and doubtful assault of love made upon Laura was much greater than that of Mount Etna when it is most shaken by the giant Enceladus, or the roar of the rushing waters of Scylla and Charybdis <note>The famous whirlpool and sea monster of the Strait of Messina in Greek mythology.</note> even when they appear most angry—so much so that one despairs of ever being able to return to or truly explain such a horrendous thunder. Thus he says:

> Not so great nor so terrible a sound
> Does Etna make, even when most shaken by Enceladus,
> Nor Scylla and Charybdis, when they are angry;

> That no greater way was found in the first move

The giants moved together in war against the gods and against <term>Jupiter</term><note>Jove</note>, where they were struck by his lightning. Although by their great power they did not die, the highest name of <term>Etna</term> was turned upon <term>Enceladus</term>; and over <term>Typhon</term><note>Tipheo</note> he placed the island of <term>Inarime</term><note>OCR "isrime"; Inarime is a classical name for Ischia</note>, which today is named <term>Ischia</term>. From this, the poets add the fiction that these giants often struggle to lift such a heavy weight from their backs, and in doing so, they shake the entire earth. <term>Scylla</term>’s identity was explained quite a bit earlier in the Triumph of Love, where it was said she is a whirlpool whose fury is clearly shown by <term>Virgil</term> in the first book of the *Aeneid*, when speaking in the person of Aeneas to his companions, he says:

<margin>L</margin>
> You have approached Scylla's rage and her deep-sounding
> rocks; you have experienced the Cyclopean stones: recall your courage and dismiss
> sad fear; perhaps one day it will be a joy to remember even these things.
<note>original: "Vos a scylleam rabiem penitusque sonantes accestis skopulos: vos & cyclopea saxa experti reuocate animos mestuq; timorem mittite forsan & hec olim meminiisse iuuabit."</note>

<term>Charybdis</term> also, according to the opinion of <term>Ovid</term> and <term>Isidore</term>, is a whirlpool very near <term>Scylla</term> of the same disposition and nature, which seems to take delight in submerging ships. Thus <term>Ovid</term> calls her *greedy Charybdis* <note>original: "avidam caribdim"</note>. The fable told about her is that Charybdis was a most greedy prostitute who, as <term>Hercules</term> was passing by, he killed and threw into that place which is today Charybdis. From this, it still appears in the present times that she strives to steal ships and other vessels. But in truth, just as Scylla is a cavernous place where the winds, becoming trapped, cause those regurgitations in which ships perish, so it also happens with Charybdis, as narrated by those who have seen the places. Next, <term>Messer Francesco</term><note>Petrarch</note> feigns the state of those who were in the company of Love, and similarly those who followed Laura, as they saw the assault begin, saying that everyone retreated to an elevated and high place to better see and comprehend the end of the vigorous battle. Already the horror of the bold undertaking had—not without great wonder—turned their hearts and eyes into enamel. Thus he says:

> Each one for himself retreated to high ground
> To see better, and from the horror of the undertaking,
> Their hearts and eyes were made of enamel.

<margin>M</margin>
Not without reason does our Poet describe the men retreating to high ground whenever Love battles with <term>Lady Laura</term>. This is because it is necessary for men to be drawn toward high contemplation to demonstrate the immortal soul; from which conclusion it follows that sensory delights are repugnant to human perfection. Where immortality is not presupposed, the opposite must be granted. In this consideration, the poet excellently compares their eyes and hearts to enamel. Just as the features made in enamel and the eyes painted upon it are always uniform and never turn elsewhere, so those who are seized by great wonder or fixed contemplation fix their eyes upon an object from which they do not move, and their hearts upon a thought from which they do not separate. Thus, by this disposition, they truly become similar to enamel—that worthy and delightful mixture which goldsmiths use to enamel their figures on gold and silver vessels. He next adds <term>Messer Francesco</term>'s description of the habit and armor of Love and his sudden assault. He says that the victor over gods and men (recounted earlier in the previous Triumph), who came primarily to offend <term>Laura</term>, had already taken the bow with his left hand and the arrow with his right. Having placed it upon the string, he had drawn it back to his ear like a strong and skilled archer. In this manner, still having the burning sparks in his face—from which he himself still burns and torments whenever he remembers the prison and the snares of love—never did a light leopard run to the crossing of a fleeing deer, whether free in the forest or in the service of man (unburdened of its chain and loosed), that would not have seemed sluggish, slow, and utterly late in comparison to Love, so prompt and light did he come solely for the sake of wounding <term>Lady Laura</term>. Thus he says:

> That victor who was first to the offense;
> In the right hand the arrow, in the other the bow.
> And he had already stretched the string to his ear.

<margin>N</margin>
Whenever any dexterity, agility, or lightness is understood in any subject, it is fittingly compared to the leopard. For, according to <term>Pliny</term>, it is generated by the mixture...
