<margin>A mixture of the leopard and the lioness, or rather the lion and the leopardess; because of this it is a most ferocious animal and thirsty for blood, and because of its ferocity it becomes swift, and therefore it follows its prey not by running but by leaping. If it does not catch it in three leaps, it abandons it, turning its anger against its own laziness. Wherefore Master Francesco intends</margin>

to show the speed of the <term>appetite</term><note>Here meaning "passion" or "desire"</note> in moving against <term>reason</term>; he fittingly says it moved like a leopard. Nevertheless, some texts find in the last verse "with living sparks." From which "I am all on fire," which does not, however, vary the meaning. The poet then introduces what his disposition was, seeing Love have so furiously assaulted Lady Laura in such a way, saying that he was involved in a great contradiction, because on one side he was fought by the desire that Love might succeed, in order to have such sweet, pleasing, and suave company as was Laura: on the other side, it seemed to him a painful, hard, and unbearable thing that such an excellent woman should perish and be stripped of her dignity. Wherefore he says:

> Desire fought in me against pity:
>    For such a companion was sweet to me:
>    Yet it was hard to see her perish in such a way.

<margin>Elegantly in these verses Master Francesco demonstrates a natural disposition of men which resulted in us after the sin of the first parent <note>Adam</note>. Wherefore according to the sentence of the theologians in the second book of the <term>Sentences</term> at the 24th distinction</margin>

our soul contains within itself two principal parts, as we also said above—namely, <term>reason</term> and <term>sensuality</term>. Reason has two other parts: one through which it looks toward the knowledge of superior and eternal things; the other through which it directs itself to the proper use of temporal things. Thus it happens that whenever any object presents itself to the will, sensuality induces one toward bodily pleasure and reason calls one back to the propriety of use: from which is born, in every wayward choice, the remorse of conscience because reason contradicts sensuality. This is exactly what <term>Master Francesco</term><note>Petrarch</note> says happened to him, which in this place and in that song he affirms when he says: *I go thinking, and in my thought I am assaulted.* <note>Petrarch’s poem "Io vo pensando," Canzoniere 264</note> There, he explains this connection: first the effects of one thought of such <unclear>intentions</unclear> being in him, and then the other. And therefore the theologians say that they are always linked together as <term>Adam, Eve, and the serpent</term>, understanding by Adam the superior parts of reason, by Eve the inferior parts, and by the serpent the sensuality. 

The poet then adds a golden sentiment along with the gesture that Laura made for the defense against the assault of Love, saying that the virtue and excellence of the soul—which never separates itself from the good—demonstrated well through Lady Laura how much one wrongly blames others for what they themselves leave behind by approaching vice. For Laura, having been assaulted by Love with no other favor and no other help than her own will, never did a fencer so excellently or with such dexterity dodge a wound or a blow thrown at him, nor even did a wise pilot ever turn his ship into port with such speed and cunning to flee from the rocks, as a swift defense and a fearless and honest protection covered the beautiful face of Laura, and withdrew it from the amorous blow, which is fatal and bitter to those who experience and await it. Wherefore he says:

> But virtue, which never leaves the good,
>    Showed well at that point how greatly wrong
>    Is he who abandons her and then complains of others.
> For never was a fencer so skillful
>    At dodging a blow; nor a pilot so quick.

<margin>It is customary by natural human weakness that when men allow themselves to slip into any lewdness, they do not blame themselves for their excuse, but some blame the power of the stars, some the predestined order of future things, some others the disposition of objects...</margin>

In defining this in the seventh book of the <term>Ethics</term>, <term>Aristotle</term> says: <term>The continent person is the same as the one who is steadfast in reason.</term> <note>original Latin: "Continens idem est & constans in ratione."</note> <margin>D</margin> Wherefore, when a man is fixed and habituated in continence, when these libidinous appetites reach him, he does not consent to them. Master Francesco then describes Love's arrows as being golden to conform to the sentiment of <term>Ovid</term> in the first book of the <term>Metamorphoses</term>, who attributes two kinds of arrows to Love: some are made of gold, through which sensory delights are pursued, and others are leaden arrows, from which those same pleasures are fled. Nor is Ovid distant in this from the sentiment of the <margin>E</margin> metaphysicians and logicians, who maintain that contraries can arise regarding the same subject, just as <term>Aristotle</term> affirms in the *Postpredicamenta* and the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*. These golden arrows, then, are all in the pleasure of amorous beauties and kindled by the burning flames of desire <margin>F</margin> that are born in us when, according to sensuality, we desire fleshly delights. Our poet then adds a comparison, feigning how much anger Laura was moved to after she saw that Love’s assault against her had failed. THE TRIUMPH OF CHASTITY

# THE TRIUMPH OF CHASTITY

<margin>To his daughter born in childbirth also...</margin>
->**Against him who breaks through every breastplate.**<-
<note>This line is quoted from Petrarch's "Triumph of Chastity," referring to Cupid, whose arrows are said to pierce any armor.</note>

He called her Camilla: it happened, therefore, in those times that the aforementioned peoples subjected to him conspired against Metabus <note>Metabus was a legendary king of the Volscians and father of Camilla</note>: for which reason he was forced to leave the kingdom and go into exile. Wherefore, in his sudden and necessary departure, he had no time to carry anything with him except his little daughter Camilla. Being thus pursued in his flight, he came to a river which had grown and become very large that same day because of the rain. <margin>G</margin> Metabus, seeing this and his flight being a contrary accident, and not being able to swim with the little daughter, and expecting that if he waited he would fall into the hands of his enemies, took a difficult course of action. This was that, having wrapped the little girl in bark, he tied her to a spear <margin>H</margin> which he happened to have carried in his hand. Then, after vowing her to Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt and protector of virgins</note>, he threw the spear across the river together with the little girl tied to it. Metabus then, swimming to the other side of the river, found that his daughter, through the work of Diana, was unharmed. Taking her and having given most abundant thanks to Diana, he went with her to live in the woods and solitary, sylvan places. There, as Camilla grew, she determined to preserve her virginity for Diana; wherefore, giving herself to the woods, to the frequenting of hunts, and to the exercise of arms, in a short time she became excellent in such actions and famous for her excellence. Having repudiated all the loves of young men and all marriages, she was finally recalled and established as queen in her kingdom. Afterwards, when Aeneas came to Italy from the destruction of Troy, making war against Turnus, king of the Rutuli, for the love of Lavinia (daughter of King Latinus), she joined Turnus's side because of their proximity. In fighting against the Trojans, she waged great war against them, among whom she killed a priest named Chloreus <note>Original text: "corebo", likely referring to Chloreus from the Aeneid</note>. Finally, fighting one day with a Trojan named Arruns, <margin>I</margin> she was wounded by him in the breast, from which she came to her death and expired, as Virgil demonstrates well enough in the eleventh book of the *Aeneid*.

Secondly, it is to be known that according to Trogus and Justin <note>Roman historians Pompeius Trogus and Justinus</note> who report it in "On Foreign Wars," there were two young men in Scythia: one named Plenos and the other Scolopitus. By a conspiracy of their nobles, they were driven from the kingdom; wherefore it happened that as they fled, a very great multitude of Scythian youths followed them. Having arrived then in the region of Cappadocia, they took and occupied a very wide country in that place. But in a short space of time, because they caused trouble to the neighboring provinces, they were finally punished by those neighbors and all were killed. The women of these men, seeing that through the deaths of their husbands a perpetual loss was brought upon them, took up arms and not only defended their borders, but also waged great war against other peoples. Many of these they submitted by force to their lordship. These women still did not wish to marry others so as not to diminish their number; they would go at certain times to have relations with their neighbors and stayed with them until they felt themselves pregnant. Then they would return to their kingdom where, if they gave birth to males, they killed them, and if females, they nourished them. To these girls, as was the custom, they would burn the right breast in infancy so that they would be more unencumbered in <margin>K</margin> battle for the hand using the sword and the spear, proceeding only with the left breast intact.

Third and lastly, it is to be noted that Julius Caesar, being the father-in-law of Pompey, was by nature very mild and clement. Only in the Battle of Pharsalia, which he fought against the Pompeians, did he deviate from his usual spirit and custom; for when the soldiers were already in battle formation <margin>L</margin> to fight, he commanded them that they should only be intent on wounding and giving death to their enemies, and nothing else during the battle. But he always conducted himself as an excellent leader and a most strong soldier, and finally remaining superior and fatigued by so much killing, as Florus writes <note>Lucius Annaeus Florus, a Roman historian</note>, more out of a sense of sorrow than true desire, crying out the other word to the knights, he said: <note>original: "parcite ciuibus"</note> "Spare the citizens."

Concluding, therefore, that none of these aforementioned examples had even a drachm of true value in comparison to Laura. Truly and rightly, no such great victory can be worthily compared to that in which a person overcomes their own appetite, as was expressed above regarding Masinissa by the judgment of Scipio Africanus. Nor indeed were these same people ever so cruel or ardent against their enemies as Lady Laura was against the conquered Cupid. Having therefore met and defeated that strongest athlete, Cupid, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> now begins to narrate the company of the armed combatants who were with Laura in this glorious victory, saying that together with her were armed her bright and singular virtues—truly a noble and glorious troop—which, combining two by two...

It transitions into a description of the personified virtues that accompany Laura in her "Triumph."</summary>

<page-num>35</page-num>
->CHAPTER ONE<-

# CHAPTER &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; FIRST

...but they proceed with equal rank to the first two that were at the front and the vanguard: one was Honesty; the other, Shame. These were certainly a most excellent pair of divine virtues which made her worthy and proud among other women. Thereafter followed, close and bordering them, Wisdom and Modesty, which were subsequent to a fixed and firm habit and delight within the soul, and a Perseverance, for which—as an end—praise, honor, and most excellent glory were reserved. Near these were other virtues: a most gracious and beautiful Welcome, together with a prudent Insight, with which were granted a simple Purity and an abundant and joyful Courtly Grace, along with a very great fear of infamy and an most ardent desire for honor. With these, finally, were seen together wise and meditated thoughts, grey with experience though in a youthful age <note>The "grey thoughts in a young age" refers to the concept of *puer senex*, a youth who possesses the wisdom of an elder</note> (to which such wisdom seems by its own nature to be repugnant), and that rare harmony seen in the world: namely, a supreme beauty joined with an integral and inviolable chastity. Whence he <note>Petrarch</note> says:

<margin>
M
¶ Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> describes a wonderful, most true, and singular doctrine in the preceding verses. For their understanding, one must know that whenever reason governs a man, appetite is subjected to it; within him reigns a universal prudence and justice, which are the foundations in which all other virtues are joined. Speaking of this prudence in the fifth book of the *Ethics*, Aristotle says: <note>original: "Videtur prudentis esse viri bene cōsulere posse circa illa que sibi bona & vtilia sunt."</note> *It seems to be the mark of a prudent man to be able to deliberate well about those things that are good and useful for himself.* And he concludes shortly thereafter, saying: <note>original: "Quāobrem & vniuersaliter prudens esset cōsulatiuus."</note> *Wherefore the universally prudent person would be one who is capable of deliberation.* And of justice, he writes thus in the fifth book of the *Ethics*: <note>original: "Hec itaq; iusticia uirtus quidem est perfecta: nō simpliciter: sed ad aliū & ob hoc excellentissima virtutum videtur esse iusticia: neq; hesperus: neq; lucifer ita mirabilis: sic in prouerbio dicimus omnes simul virtutes iusticie inesse."</note> *Thus, this justice is indeed perfect virtue, not simply, but in relation to another; and for this reason, justice is seen as the most excellent of virtues: neither the evening star nor the morning star is so wonderful; as the proverb says, all virtues are found together in justice.*
</margin>

> Armed with her were all her
> Bright virtues; oh glorious band;
> And they held each other two by two by the hand.

<margin>N</margin>

From which it follows: that from this foundation every virtuous action has its origin. Therefore, the poet first recounts in this place those virtues that spring from this foundation: those which suit a man considered in his own right, and not as part of a civil society. From these, glory and honor are attributed to him, which are the extrinsic rewards of virtue, as is written in the fourth book of the *Ethics*. Afterward, he adds other virtues according to which a man acts when he is established in political life through his natural sociability. From this, it is understood that no part of him is separated from duty, as Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> teaches in the first book of *On Duties*, where he says: <note>original: "Nulla n. vite pars ne que publicis neq; priuatis neq; forensibus neq; domesticis in rebus: neq; si tecū agas quid: neq; si cum altero contrahas vacare officio debet."</note> *No part of life—neither in public nor private affairs, neither in the forum nor at home, neither in one's own concerns nor in dealings with another—ought to be free from duty.* Now, descending particularly to demonstrate, according to the precepts of moral philosophy, how each of the aforementioned virtues recounted by Master Francesco derives from the universal fountain of prudence and justice, it must be understood principally that from them is born Honor (*Honestade*). According to Tully in the first book of *On Duties*, this is acting appropriately according to the disposition of the place, the time, and the persons with whom a man must converse. Therefore, Aristotle says in the fourth book of the *Ethics* that not every gift is liberality, but only when it is done when it is necessary, where it is necessary, and to whom it is necessary. Considering this Honor, the Supreme Pontiffs, following the authority of Cicero in the fourth book of *On Duties*, sanctioned the chapter *non debet* <note>A reference to Canon Law regarding consanguinity and affinity</note>, which says: <note>original: "Nō debet reprehensibile iudicari si scōm varietatem temporū statuta quoq; variantur humana."</note> *It should not be judged reprehensible if human statutes also vary according to the variety of the times.* For prudence is the right rule of our actions...

<page-num>54</page-num>

->CHAPTER FIRST<-

<margin>S</margin>
...a most profound fear of infamy and an intense desire for honor, which is a most certain sign of virtue and is desired by excellent men as the highest good. This is according to the opinion of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the first book of the *Ethics*, who, speaking of the diversity of opinions regarding what happiness consists of, says: "Refined men fit for action are led by honor" <note>original: *Elegantes autem viri a rebus agendis apti honore ducuntur*</note>. Such habits, protected by purity and faith, derive from that foundation of justice, as Cicero writes in the first book of *On Duties*: "The foundation of justice is faith" <note>original: *Fundamentum autem iustitie est fides*</note>. From these virtues, at whatever age, diligence is born, along with "grey thoughts" and a mature spirit, especially in youth, as they are most desirous of glory and honor. This is shown by Livy in his history of the Second Punic War, through the speeches of Quintus Fabius Maximus and Scipio Africanus, when the Roman Senate consulted on whether the army should cross into Africa. In such actions, as one reads in the first book of the *Ethics*, no defect should be attributed to age, but only to character. Thus, men are called "young" or "old" according to their age but also according to their actions. Mature and "grey" thoughts are so named by analogy; for just as the elderly are slow in their physical movements, so too—by always applying good examination and premeditation—they are never hasty in offering their judgment or putting it into practice. This duty is described by Tully <note>Cicero</note> in the first book of *On Duties*, where he says: "In all matters, before you begin, careful preparation must be employed" <note>original: *In omnibus autem negocijs priusquam aggrediare adhibenda est preparatio diligens*</note>. This sentiment is confirmed by the Philosopher in the sixth book of the *Ethics*, saying: "One should act quickly on good advice, but deliberate slowly" <note>original: *Oportet quidem velociter operari bene consilia: consultari autem tarde*</note>. Ultimately, these excellent virtues give birth to a concord which is found most rarely among mortals: namely, the union of physical beauty, modesty, and constancy of mind. For the desire for the union of man and woman is so natural—as is written in the first book of the *Politics* and in the *Economics*—that even if physical beauty is absent (which greatly delights the senses and the mind according to the prophetic sentiment: "You have delighted me, Lord, in your handiwork" <note>original: *Delectasti me domine in factura tua*; Psalm 92:4</note>), man can hardly restrain himself from falling into obscene lust. Therefore, when beauty is also present, the libidinous appetite is much more greatly kindled and inflamed, making it a matter of the greatest difficulty and power to maintain both the beauty of the body and the integrity of the soul. Truly, then, from the laudable dominion of reason over the enticing and detestable appetite, a glorious troop of virtues, or singular affections, or ineffable kindnesses are born. Next, Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> adds the greatest excellence and affection shown by this outstanding army in coming against and resisting Love, saying that Laura, together with these worthy and singular virtues, proceeded in such an admirable way against Love—with such favor from heaven and the blessed souls—that he <note>the personification of Love/Cupid</note> could not endure the sight of the magnitude and weight of such a worthy and excellent object. Whence he says:

> Such she came against Love, and with such favorable
> Support from heaven and from noble souls,
> That he could not endure the weight of her gaze.

<margin>T</margin>
For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it must be understood—according to the opinion of Cicero in the first book of *On Duties*, Aristotle in the second book of *Physics*, and the prophet David in the Psalms—that the heavens and all

<margin>V</margin>
material things are ordered for the use of man as their final purpose. From this, it is an apparent argument and an effective conjecture that when man maintains himself in his natural perfection, the heavens (by divine will) are favorable in all his works. Thus we read of Joshua, in the fifth <note>actually chapter 10</note> book of *Joshua*, that the heavens stood still to lend him the light of the sun to achieve a complete victory over the Amorites <note>term: *Amorrei*, a biblical people often symbolizing enemies of the faithful</note>. Similarly, the sea obeyed Moses, opening for the Hebrews and closing upon the Egyptians, as is written in *Exodus*, the fourteenth chapter. > A thousand victorious and bright palms.

<margin>👉</margin>
Just as by the rules of war it is determined that the victor carries off a triumph and the honored spoils of the prisoners he has taken; so it happens that if he himself is conquered by another, it is considered appropriate that the past victories are no longer spoken of to his praise, but to that of the victor who is no longer conquered. Whence, just as above the conqueror and master of the world, Caesar, was subject to Love and all his glories passed to him; so all the forces of the appetite, which was once subjugated by reason, are extinguished and deleted: the leadership of every work is attributed no longer to the appetite, but solely to the intellect. Messer Francesco next demonstrates by comparison and example how sudden and strange the <unclear>loss</unclear> of Love is judged to be, almost contrary to all possibility, saying that his fall did not seem as sudden and strange to Hannibal—considering that he had obtained so many great and glorious victories against the Romans, and had been in possession of Italy for so long, knowing himself also to have the highest skill in the military art—and yet seeing himself first forcibly recalled from Italy. Secondly, that Scipio <note>Scipio Africanus, the Roman general who eventually defeated Hannibal</note> cared nothing for him nor wanted peace with him; and finally, that he was surpassed and conquered by that young man at such a tender age before Carthage. Similarly, the Philistine Goliath did not feel such great wonder nor such fear when the first stone thrown by David with his sling struck him in the forehead—especially having previously seen the entire army of Saul, King of Israel, flee before him. And likewise, Cyrus, King of Persia, was not so stupefied when he saw himself first a prisoner <margin>Z</margin> and then led to death by the hands of the widow Tomyris <note>Queen of the Massagetae, who according to legend defeated and beheaded Cyrus the Great</note>—a queen of Scythia deprived of her son—as it seemed strange to Love to see himself entirely conquered and bound by Lady Laura.

He therefore reached the Alpine mountains which mark the boundary of Italy, and having broken through them by the force of fire and vinegar <note>A famous legend from the historian Livy, claiming Hannibal cracked Alpine rocks by heating them with fire and pouring cold vinegar over them.</note>, he descended into Italy. Having come between the Po and the Ticino rivers, he encountered Publius Scipio, the father of Scipio Africanus. Fighting him in that place, he defeated and conquered him. In that battle, Scipio certainly would have been killed if it had not been for the virtue of Africanus who, although of tender age—being about eighteen years old—manfully defended his father in the midst of the armed enemies, giving a sign of how he was destined to be the salvation of the Roman Republic. Hannibal then passed into the kingdom of Apulia, where the consuls Paullus Aemilius and Terentius Varro were sent against him. Fighting them at Cannae, he made the slaughter of the Romans so great that even his own iron-hard heart could no longer endure the horror of the blood shed in the Latin name; satiated with killing, he was forced to say to his army: "Spare the sword" <note>original: "parce ferro"</note>. So many were killed in that battle that he sent two pecks <note>A "moggio" or peck was a dry measure of volume.</note> of rings to Carthage, having pulled one ring from each of the fallen. Because of this, the Romans were reduced to such cowardice that they no longer consulted on how to defend the Roman Republic, but how to abandon it. 

In the midst of this great public sorrow, the excellent virtue of Scipio was awakened. Primarily in the house of Caecilius Metellus, with sword in hand, he forced everyone present to swear an oath to defend the fatherland, and offered himself as consul and defender of Rome against Hannibal. Whence, having taken command of the armies, he first recovered Spain and then passed into Africa to besiege Carthage. Finding the city nearly exhausted of treasure and people, the Carthaginians were forced to recall Hannibal from Italy for the safety of Carthage. As soon as he returned, he had a meeting with Scipio; seeing that Scipio was only twenty-eight years old, Hannibal was greatly marveled and, having watched him somewhat silently, he then requested peace. Scipio denied it and told him to prepare to fight, in which battle
<margin>D</margin>
Hannibal was defeated and forced to flee, and the Carthaginians were forced to surrender.

In the third place, it is to be known as it is written in the first book of Kings in the seventeenth chapter <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Samuel 17.</note>, that while Saul, King of the Jews, was making war against the Philistines and had many times been successful through his virtue, one day from the Philistine side there came into the war a giant of mixed race <note>The text uses "spurio," likely referring to Goliath's status as a champion or perhaps a "mongrel" outside the standard lineage.</note> whose name was Goliath. He was of such immense and measured strength that he alone could resist ten thousand combatants. Because of him, the Jewish people were so terrified that at his presence alone everyone fled to the camps, nor did they dare to join battle against the Philistines for any reason out of fear of Goliath. There were at this time in Saul's army three sons of Jesse: one named Eliab, the second Abinadab, and the third Shammah. Besides these, Jesse had a tiny son who was in Bethlehem guarding the flocks, whose name was David. At this time, Jesse sent David to visit his brothers and sent them some provisions. When David reached the army and approached his dear brothers, he heard a proclamation on behalf of the king that whoever fought with Goliath would have Michal, his beautiful daughter, for a wife, along with a part of the kingdom and a great treasure for a dowry. He also saw at that very hour, because Goliath had come into the field, all the Jews fleeing to the camps. David asked about both matters, and it was answered that this was happening because no one wanted to fight the giant. Whereupon David, marvelling, went to the king and asked for permission to fight. He told Saul not to distrust him because of his young age, for a few days before he had killed a bear and a lion that had wanted to devour his cows. It pleased Saul that David should fight. In the fourth and last place, it seems more convenient to recount a little of the origin of Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Great, the founder of the Achaemenid Persian Empire.</note>. It should be understood that as the kingdom of the Medes had come by succession to Astyages, the grandfather of Cyrus, he saw one night in a dream that from his only daughter a vine grew forth, the branches of which overshadowed all of Asia. Astyages then asked the Soothsayers <term>Arioli</term> <note>From the Latin "harioli," meaning diviners or priests who interpret dreams and omens.</note> what the dream might portend. They replied that this signified that a grandson was to be born to him who would rule the East and govern the whole kingdom of the Medes. Because of this, the terrified Astyages did not want to marry his daughter to any prince or king, but gave her to an ordinary private citizen whose name was Cambyses. She became pregnant and in time gave birth to a son. When Astyages learned of this, he sent for the child and gave him to a captain named Harpagus, ordering him to take him away and kill him. Harpagus, having received the infant and fearing that after the death of Astyages, if the kingdom passed to the daughter, she might take revenge on him for killing the child, did not want to put him to death. Instead, he gave him to one of the king's shepherds to be exposed <term>exponesse</term> <note>The practice of "exposure"—leaving an unwanted infant in the wilderness—was a common trope in ancient founding myths.</note> and devoured by wild beasts. Thus the shepherd carried out what Harpagus had commanded him, and returned to his hut where, finding his wife, he related the harsh fate of the little child. That same wife of the shepherd had also just given birth; therefore, she piteously begged her husband so much to go back for that child, as she wanted to see him, that he, overwhelmed by his wife’s prayers, returned to the very place where he had exposed him. Arriving there, the shepherd found that a bitch <note>This reflects a legend recorded by Herodotus; the name of the shepherd's wife, Spako, meant "bitch" in the Median language.</note> was nursing him with her milk and defending him from wild beasts and birds. Seeing the bitch so compassionate, he himself was moved to mercy. Thus, picking up the child, he carried him to the hut to his wife, and the bitch followed him all the way inside. Once the woman received the child in her arms, she loved him so intensely for his graceful appearance that she then begged her husband to expose their own [stillborn] son to the beasts in place of Cyrus, and to raise Cyrus in place of their son. As the fortune of Cyrus would have it, the shepherd consented to the woman. When Cyrus had grown, it happened one day that while playing with other children of his age—as is their custom and exercise—he was chosen as their king. He then harshly punished and beat them, as befitted a royal office, whenever they were in default. Consequently, a complaint was made by the children's fathers to Astyages, whereupon Astyages sent for Cyrus and asked if it were true as had been complained of him. Cyrus, hearing the words of Astyages, replied with a constant face that since he was king, it was his right to do so. Astyages, marveling at the response as well as his constancy, and considering also his age and the features of his body, and having heard the report of the shepherd whom he had questioned about Cyrus's origin, recognized at last that this was his grandson. He judged that because he had been made king by the children, the portent of his dream had already been fulfilled. Therefore, feeling secure, he proceeded no further against Cyrus; but for Harpagus, because of his disobedience, he gave him his own son to eat <note>Astyages famously punished Harpagus by serving him the flesh of his own son at a banquet.</note>. Cyrus, having reached the years of manhood and being most excellent in feats of arms, went to Persia to prove his supreme and singular virtues. There, Harpagus, seeking to avenge himself for the sorrow of his eaten son, wrote to Cyrus the whole process of his life: how Astyages had given him up to be killed, and how he had escaped death, and how because of this his own son had been eaten. Therefore, he encouraged him to take revenge on Astyages, and for this purpose—if such were his intention—he offered to grant him passage through Media. That same night that he received the letters from Harpagus, Cyrus saw in a dream one who admonished and exhorted him to the same effect. He therefore decided to undertake the enterprise. For this reason, having gathered all the citizens of Pasargadae <note>original: "Presopoli", referring to Pasargadae or Persepolis.</note> and having taken a servant as a companion according to the admonitions of the gods, whose name was Sybare, he made them all take up axes and they went with him to cut down a forest. Thus established in such height, Cyrus decided to attempt to subject the northern parts to his empire, wherefore he resolved to move war against the Scythians. Having prepared a great number of armies, he crossed the river Araxes and entered Scythia. At that time, a widowed queen named Tomyris reigned over that province; seeing that Cyrus and the Persians had come against her in Scythia, she immediately sent her only son, named Spargapises, to the defense of the region. Cyrus, hearing this and knowing that the Scythians were not accustomed to wine, had tables prepared throughout the camps and filled them with the finest foods and sweetest wines; then, having set certain traps and going to battle, he feigned flight. To the Scythians, it seemed they were the victors, especially seeing the camps left without any guard by the Persians. Finding the tables prepared, they set themselves to eating and drinking. Because they were unaccustomed to wine, they all became intoxicated in a short hour. Cyrus, taking the opportunity and revealing the ambush, returned to the field where, finding the Scythians sleeping from drunkenness, he killed nearly all of them along with Spargapises, the son of Queen Tomyris. Having heard this news and recognizing Cyrus's fraud, Tomyris disposed herself to take revenge with similar fraud.

<margin>C</margin> For this reason, she personally took up arms and, having restored a massive army, stationed it behind certain mountains that enclosed a valley. Then, with a few people, she stood before Cyrus, where she continually fled from him, feigning fear until she led him into the valley where she had hidden the army around the mountains. As soon as Cyrus arrived, she gave the signal for everyone to reveal themselves; the Scythians, manifesting themselves, proceeded courageously against the Persians. In the short hour that the battle lasted, Cyrus was killed with his entire army of two hundred thousand men, in such a way that not even a messenger survived to carry the news to Persia. Afterwards, by command of the Queen, Cyrus's head was taken and placed in a wineskin filled with blood, and she said to him: "Satiate yourself with the blood, Cyrus, for which you have always shown such a great thirst." This was truly a memorable vengeance, as our Master Francesco <note>Petrarch (Francesco Petrarca), whose poems this manuscript likely comments upon.</note> testifies. He adds nearby another disposition of men who, turning from a life of lewdness and dishonesty, return to just and reasonable living; saying that Love <note>Cupid/Desire</note> stands like one who is healthy and, by his own defect and disorder, becomes diseased in an instant, so that in a moment he is dismayed by fear and secretly grieves, appearing like one who wipes some shame from his eyes with his hand. In such a way, and in an even worse state, he remained: for fear, anger, grief, and shame were all at once in his face and his image, in such a way that he raged and seethed within himself. The sea makes much less horror when it is most stirred by contrary winds; similarly, Inarime <note>The island of Ischia, where the giant Typhoeus was said to be buried.</note> makes less noise when the giant Typhoeus cries out, or Mongibello <note>Mount Etna.</note> when Enceladus sighs. Whence he says:

<margin>I</margin> —this desire is not fulfilled, or when after its attainment, a man receives the deserved correction according to justice. Thus, they roar and lament among themselves so much that Typhoeus wails no more under Inarime <note>Inarime is an ancient name for the volcanic island of Ischia.</note>, nor does Enceladus sigh more under Etna. ### CHAPTER ONE

...the daughter of Phorcys <note>original: "Phorcho." In mythology, a primordial sea god.</note>, King of distant Hesperia <note>The "Western lands," often associated with the edge of the world in Greek myth.</note>. She was so beautiful that, beyond her other charms, she possessed golden hair. Neptune fell in love with her and took carnal pleasure with her in the temple of Pallas Athena. For this reason, the goddess was outraged and turned all of Medusa’s hair into serpents, which resulted in her becoming monstrous instead of beautiful. Furthermore, she acquired the property that whoever looked her in the face suddenly turned to stone. Perseus, therefore, the son of Jove and Danae, of whom we spoke above, having heard the fame of Medusa, decided to fight her. He borrowed the crystal shield from Pallas and, covering himself with it to oppose Medusa, she looked into it and, seeing her own deformity, was stunned, allowing Perseus to cut off her head.

<margin>O</margin>
Near this, just and prudent men have a column of jasper, in the center of which is a chain made of cold topaz and the hardest diamond. Regarding its meaning, it should be noted that by the jasper we ought to understand the repression or reduction of the "hot humors," such as blood and choler <note>In medieval medicine, these "humors" or bodily fluids were thought to govern temperament; heat was associated with anger and passion.</note>, and the effects that arise from them, such as anger and carnal pleasure. Thus, when these two primary affections—which mainly arise from the sensory principle—are repressed and taken away by dominant Reason, men are worthily made similar to a column of noble jasper. From this same disposition is derived the unbreakable chain of diamond and topaz; that is, the hardness and constancy found in such men against carnal pleasures and delights. Just as among gems and metals the diamond is the most constant and hardest, so too is temperance signified by the topaz. According to Pliny and Dioscorides <note>Pliny the Elder and Dioscorides were famous ancient authorities on natural history and medicine.</note>, the nature of the topaz is to prohibit any boiling, even of scalding water. This "chain" of temperance and hardness was once used among women, but today it is no longer used because it has been submerged in the Lethean river; that is, the aforementioned virtues are put aside and forgotten due to the lasciviousness of the present times.

<margin>B</margin>
Thus, Lethe, according to what the poets write, is a river that surrounds the underworld, where Charon the boatman stays and carries souls to their appointed places. As they cross the river Lethe, they no longer remember anything that happened in the present life, as is the clear and expressed opinion of the Philosopher <note>A standard medieval reference to Aristotle.</note> in the third book of the *Ethics*. Master Francesco <note>Petrarch.</note> then follows by saying that after the victory of Laura and the overthrow of powerful Cupid, he finally saw him bound and treated with such suffering that it was truly appropriate for a thousand other revenges, even if more had been desired, at which sight he saw himself very satisfied and content. Hence he says:

> *I saw him bound, and treated with such shame,*
> *That it sufficed for a thousand other wrongs;*
> *And I, for my part, was content and satisfied.*

<meta>This page continues the allegorical commentary on Petrarch’s "Triumph of Chastity." While the previous page focused on the physical symbols of virtue (like the shield of Medusa and gemstones), this page shifts to a philosophical and mythological explanation of why the Muses—the traditional goddesses of inspiration—are insufficient for describing the highest forms of virtue. It transitions into a catalog of famous virtuous women, starting with Lucretia.</meta>

->TRIVMPH OF CHASTITY<-

# THE TRIUMPH OF CHASTITY

> Not Calliope, nor Clio with the other seven. <note>original: "Non calliope, & clio con l'altre sette." Petrarch begins this section by stating that the traditional Muses are not enough to describe the purity of the women he is about to name.</note>
> But of some I shall speak, who on the summit
> Of true virtue stand, among whom...

Those who followed the rule of reason alone are recounted here as certain virgins and youths. This is to demonstrate that within their fragile age and nature, there is a greater difficulty in resisting carnal appetite. From this, one can easily conclude that if they resisted, then other men, with much greater reason, can repress this lustful appetite. Therefore, he silently accuses and rebukes the laziness of those who claim the forces of this "delightful incentive" <note>A euphemism for sexual desire or passion.</note> are so great that they cannot be resisted in any way. He shows that fragile women, through a regulated will alone, have overcome and extinguished it.

<margin>S</margin> Secondarily, it should be known that the Muses, according to Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an influential scholar who wrote an encyclopedia of the Middle Ages.</note>, are the daughters of Jove and Memory. The poets imagined them, according to Macrobius in his commentary on the *Dream of Scipio* <note>A famous Neoplatonic text that describes the universe as a series of celestial spheres.</note>, because they represent the harmony resulting from the eight celestial spheres and the specific voices or sounds of each of the eight; between these individual sounds and the universal harmony, the number reaches nine. This was the opinion of Aristoxenus, the musician and philosopher, which Cicero approves of in the *Dream of Scipio*. Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher who argued the soul was a "harmony" of the body.</note> does not deny in the second book of *On the Heavens* that the celestial spheres made sound and harmony together.

However, Fulgentius <note>A late Roman mythographer who gave allegorical meanings to ancient myths.</note> had another interpretation regarding the Muses, understanding them as the nine necessary stages that concur in the learning of the sciences. By explaining their names, he declares what they are meant to signify. Thus:
1. **Clio**, who is the first, is interpreted as the **thought of learning**.
2. The second, **Euterpe**, means **delight**.
3. The third, **Thalia**, signifies **capacity** <note>The ability to hold or understand information.</note>.
4. The fourth, **Melpomene**, is understood as **meditation**.
5. The fifth, **Polyhymnia**, demonstrates **much memory**.
6. The sixth, **Erato**, is interpreted as **invention** <note>The ability to find new ideas or arguments.</note>.
7. The seventh, **Terpsichore**, signifies **delectable distinction** <note>The ability to categorize and tell things apart clearly.</note>.
8. The eighth, **Urania**, signifies the **celestial**.
9. The ninth and last, **Calliope**, is understood to be the **best voice**.

Thus, one sees among these Muses an admirable order contained in respect to their goal, which is the acquisition of human knowledge. First, one needs the desire to learn; second, to find delight in it; third, to be capable of such intelligence; fourth, to meditate on what others have learned; fifth, to commit it well to memory; sixth, from those acquired habits, to make new inferences and inventions; seventh, to distinguish one habit from another; eighth, to direct the intellect toward high and celestial speculations; and ninth and last, to recite, compose, and debate those things well. 

But the poets—and our Master Francesco [Petrarch] in this place and in the *Triumph of Fame*—understand the Muses according to other intentions, because they attribute different qualities to them. Therefore, they invoke them variously according to different subject matters and different acts.

<margin>T</margin> Thus, **Clio** is invoked whenever poets recount past deeds of every kind of virtue that have been neglected for some time. **Euterpe** is called upon to make the poetic song fruitful when, after the beginning is made, it has been interrupted for some reason. **Thalia** is requested whenever one treats of playful comedies; **Melpomene** for mournful tragedies. But **Terpsichore** is prayed to when the poet wishes to show intense affection regarding the poem. **Erato** is invoked in various and sweet elegies, and the excellent **Polyhymnia** is required when singing of the glorious deeds of arms. **Urania** is appointed to give favor to the singing of celestial things, and lastly, the outstanding **Calliope** is called back for the other worthy and grand style—otherwise called the **heroic style** <note>Epic poetry, such as that written by Virgil or Homer.</note>—in which some worthy and excellent history is recounted.

<margin>S</margin> **Apollo** then sits in the midst of these Muses; he can be invoked indifferently in any diverse subject matter. This diversity and the office of the Muses was briefly expressed in these verses:

> Clio, singing of deeds, brings back past times.
> Euterpe urges the pipes with sweet-speaking breaths.
> Thalia rejoices in the playful speech of comedy.
> Melpomene proclaims mournful things with a tragic cry.
> Terpsichore moves, commands, and increases the feeling of the lyre.
> Bearing the plectrum, Erato dances with foot, song, and face.
> Polyhymnia signifies all things with her hand and speaks through gesture.
> Urania examines the pole, the movements, and the stars.
> Calliope commits heroic poems to books.
> Residing in the middle, Phoebus [Apollo] embraces them all.

These Muses, then, were not sufficient to be able to recount the story of the sacred and blessed virgins who, in their times, had accompanied Laura through their modesty. Therefore, having offered his excuse, Master Francesco begins afterward to narrate the virgins whom he saw at the summit of true virtue, saying that among them, on the right hand, the first was the Roman **Lucretia** <note>A legendary figure in Roman history whose suicide, following her rape by the king's son, sparked the revolution that established the Roman Republic.</note>.

<summary>This page explains the allegorical significance of the Muses as both stages of intellectual learning and patrons of specific poetic genres, ultimately arguing they are insufficient to describe the supreme virtue of the women following Petrarch's Laura.</summary>

# CHAPTER ONE

<margin>Lucretia, on the right hand, was the first;</margin>
<margin>V</margin>

**C** Regarding the information in the preceding verse, it should be known that Lucretia, the mirror and light of Roman chastity <term>pudicitia: a Roman virtue representing modesty and sexual virtue</term>, was the daughter of Spurius Lucretius Tricipitinus and the wife of Tarquinius Collatinus, the son of the brother of the noble Tarquinius Priscus. It happened then that while Tarquinius the Proud, the seventh king of the Romans, was at the siege of the city of Ardea—which was near the castle of Collatia <margin>X</margin> where Lucretia resided—the aforementioned Collatinus and Sextus Tarquinius, the son of Tarquinius the Proud, were in the army. These young men began talking together one day about the constancy and chastity of Roman women. Collatinus, for many reasons, proposed that his Lucretia was superior to all others, and likewise the other young men did the same for theirs. Therefore, they all agreed to go and put it to the test and see the chastity of their wives for themselves.

Going first to the house of Tarquinius, they found the royal maidens enjoying themselves with their peers and dancing. They then arrived in Collatia, where they found Lucretia, who was deeply intent on her wool-work <note>Working with wool was considered the highest domestic virtue for a Roman noblewoman.</note>, which was then a most dignified feminine exercise. She was without any elegant adornment on her person, for which reason, by the universal judgment of all, Lucretia was judged the most perfect of all.

Collatinus then received the young men and honored them in his house. Sextus Tarquinius fell in love with Lucretia, even though he was joined to Collatinus by close kinship. He proposed in his mind to fulfill his desire by violence if he could not obtain it otherwise. For this reason, not many days later, after they had returned to the camp, Sextus departed the lodgings by night, driven by fury, and came to the house of Lucretia, by whom he was graciously received as a relative of her husband. After everyone in the house had gone to sleep, Sextus rose from his bed and went to Lucretia’s chamber armed. Finding her alone, he told her to consent to his will or he would kill her. But Lucretia, choosing to die rather than consent, always moved to defend herself. Finally, the infuriated Sextus told her that if she did not consent, he would kill her along with one of his slaves and then say he had killed them both after finding them together in adultery.

Lucretia, seeing the wicked intention of Tarquinius and that he was ready to put into action what he had said, and knowing that this would leave a great infamy upon her and her family, chose to consent to the adultery, and then demonstrate with her death the violence done to her body and her soul; and so she did.

After Sextus had departed from her, Lucretia sent for Lucretius her father and for Brutus Junius and Collatinus her husband. They had already heard the rumor of Sextus's violence and her intention to kill herself. To console her, as Livy writes in *From the Foundations of the City* <note>original: "Ab Urbe Condita," the monumental history of Rome by Titus Livius.</note>, Collatinus entered and, seeing her weeping, said: "Is all well, Lucretia?" To which she replied: "Far from it, for what can be well with a woman when her chastity is lost? The tracks of another man, Collatinus, are in your bed. <margin>Y</margin> However, only the body has been violated; the soul is innocent. Death shall be my witness. But give me your right hands and your word that the adulterer shall not go unpunished. It is Sextus Tarquinius who, as an enemy instead of a guest, came last night armed with force against me and himself; if you are men, he has stolen a fatal joy from here. You shall see what is owed to him; as for me, though I absolve myself of the sin, I do not free myself from the punishment; nor shall any unchaste woman live by the example of Lucretia." <note>original: "Satin lucretia: cui ella cosi rispose. Mi ni me qd eni salu: est mulieri amissa pudicitia: vestigia uiri alieni Collatine in lecto tuo sunt ceterum corpus est tantū uiolatum: aīus infons: mors testis erit: sed date dextras fidemque haud īpane adultero fore Sextus ē Tarqunus q hostis pro hospite pore note ui armatus mihi sibiq si uos uiri estis pestiferum hinc abstulit gauiium. Vos uideritis qd illi debeatur: ego me si peccato absoluo supplicio non libero: nec ulla ipudica Lucretia esempio uiuet."</note>

And having said these words, she stabbed herself in the breast with a knife in their presence and killed herself. Of her manly spirit and supreme chastity, Valerius Maximus writes in Chapter 6 of Book 6, saying these words: "Lucretia, the leader of Roman chastity, whose masculine spirit by a malign error of fortune was allotted a female body, having been forced by violence to suffer ravishment by the son of King Tarquin the Proud, after she had deplored her injury with the gravest words in a council of her kinsmen, killed herself with a blade she had brought hidden in her garment. By her bitter death, she became the cause for the Roman people to exchange kingly rule for consular power." <note>original: "Dux romane pudicitie lucretia cuius uirilis aīus maligno errore fortune muliebre corpus sortitus est a Tarqni regis supbi filio p uim strupru pati coacta cū grauissimis uerbis iniurs suā in concilio necessariorum deplorasset ferro se qõ veste tectum attulerat iteremit caq; tam atoso iteritu iperīu cõsulare pregio p mutādi populo Romano fuit."</note> For the conspiracy of Brutus, Lucretius, and Collatinus began there, which finally resulted in Tarquin the Proud and his sons being driven from Rome into perpetual exile, where he died miserably.

But some in this place are accustomed to bring against Lucretia the reasoning that Augustine writes in the first book of *The City of God* <note>St. Augustine (354–430 AD) famously debated the morality of Lucretia's suicide, arguing from a Christian perspective against self-killing.</note>: namely, that if Lucretia was chaste, she should not have killed herself; and if she was not chaste, she should not be praised. To which we respond that Lucretia was chaste, because chastity is a virtue of the soul. Even though the body may be in another's power, the soul should not be stained by the body's blemishes. <margin>Z</margin> And if chastity were lost through a failure of the body, it would not truly be a virtue of the soul, but of nature; for which no person would ever be praised, as is the opinion of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> in the second book of the *Ethics*. And Lucretia killed herself afterwards, as she testified, so as not to appear to have consented to that which her soul had always...

It includes a philosophical defense of her suicide against St. Augustine's critiques, arguing that virtue resides in the soul rather than the physical body.</summary>

<margin>A</margin> REGARDING the knowledge of the preceding verses, it is to be understood that Penelope was the daughter of Icarius, King of Laconia, and the wife of Ulysses, son of Laertes, King of Ithaca, and of Anticlea <note>The original text uses "Autholia," a common variant or error in early modern texts for Anticlea, the mother of Ulysses.</note> his wife. After Penelope had already had a son by Ulysses named Telemachus, he departed and went to the Trojan wars. Because of this, while there was certainty of the death or return of all

But the most constant Penelope, frightened by the long uncertainty and terrified by the hard fate of her mother-in-law, decided to wait for her husband Ulysses until she heard some certain news of him. While she was thus in this purpose, being much harassed by many lords and by her father to take another husband—and especially because, since Laertes had departed and gone to his villa, many of her suitors <term>proci: the group of noblemen seeking to marry Penelope</term> had occupied the palace—Penelope, fearing that her chastity might be violated and also that they might lay snares for Telemachus, with great prudence discerning her choice, asked them for a deadline to wait for Ulysses only as long as she thought necessary to finish a cloth which, according to the custom of royal women, she had begun. Truly, then, these two women broke the bow and arrows of love, casting aside all its wicked sweetness to maintain themselves under the scepter of commanding virtue and reason. But one must with great reason in this part deplore the accidental delay of the production of things; for it happened that in our times there appeared (and by the heavens was taken away from those same times) a most worthy example of virtue, in no part inferior to Lucretia or Penelope: namely, the worthy and excellent lady Honorata Orsini <note>Original: "Vrsina"</note>, who was the wife of a gentleman from Siena, truly noble in spirit and manners, named Giacomo di Saracini. <header>CHAPTER ONE</header>

# CHAPTER ONE

Sonnets and triumphs: no other person ever expressed them with more sweetness of voice, with more gentleness and accents, with more pleasing expression or better action up to this day than has come to our notice. Whence I certainly do not doubt that if the honored lady was born in the time of Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch), the 14th-century poet whose "Triumphs" this text comments upon.</note>, she would have been honored by this triumph. Therefore, having died in her time, this unique and most excellent lady at the age of 22 years—and honored in heaven according to her merits—these words were inscribed upon her tomb in Siena by the universal judgment of learned men:

> ->Honorata Orsini, the glory of girls, the splendor of matrons, the honor of spouses, the example of beauty and the peak of virtues: she is buried in this very small sacred place.<-
<note>original: "Honorata Vrsina puellarũ decus: matronarum splendor: coniugum honor forme exemplum cumulusq; virtutũ: hoc perexiguo conditur sacro."</note>

From this, without doubt, if Lucretia and Penelope, having by their works broken the arrows and the bow of love, Lady Honorata would have overturned the chariot with all its wheels; for which reason she is rightly described in their company. Nevertheless, there occurs <margin>D</margin> in this place a reasonable doubt: for what reason is Penelope introduced by the poet in the *Triumph of Chastity* rather than Julia, or Portia, or Artemisia, or Argia, or Hypsicratea <note>These are all famous women from classical antiquity noted for their devotion to their husbands.</note>? Each of these was introduced above in the *Triumph of Love*; yet each of these bore no less affection for her beloved husband, nor lived less chastely than Penelope did with Ulysses (whose fidelity the poet Lycophron even makes suspect). Hence it seems that either Penelope should be assigned to the *Triumph of Love*, or those others should be numbered in the *Triumph of Chastity*, so that there does not appear to be this distinction between them and Penelope—especially by the authority of Valerius Maximus <note>A 1st-century Roman author who wrote a collection of historical anecdotes.</note>, who describes them all in the same chapter concerning the "faith or love of wives toward their husbands." To this doubt, it is answered that not without reason and marvelous artifice has our Master Francesco described these women under these different triumphs. This is because, as we said from the beginning, by "Love" he understands not only carnal pleasure, but every transgression made by the force of the sensitive appetite; nor by "Chastity and Purity" does he understand only abstinence from the venereal act, but every operation that proceeds from true judgment given by reason. Otherwise, Master Francesco could not defend himself from partiality, having attributed those women above to Love and Penelope to Chastity. According to this very true foundation, then, I say that a woman acting justly should only do those things that are appropriate to her according to her own nature regarding domestic and political life. These are many, as Aristotle writes in the *Economics*, in the first book of the *Politics*, and the eighth of the *Ethics*. Among these feminine laws, we will presently refer to three, adducing the formal words of the Philosopher <note>A standard medieval and Renaissance way of referring to Aristotle.</note>, by means of which our doubt will be quite clearly solved. The first law is to care for and preside over the things of the house which are acquired by the husband from the outside. Whence the Philosopher says:

> ->Therefore, let the woman encourage herself in these things; and let her proceed to preside over matters praise-worthily. For it seems indecent to a man to know those things which are within the house; but in all other things, let the woman strive to obey.<-
<note>original: "Se igitur ipsam in his animet mulier: pergatque laudabiliter rebus preesse. Nam viro quidem indecens videtur ea scire que intrandes sunt. in ceteris vero omnibus parere mulier contendat."</note>

The second law is that the woman should not meddle in public cares, nor seek to do anything that belongs to the husband. Whence Aristotle adds:

> ->Not daring anything concerning the Republic, nor handling any of those things which seem to pertain to the marriage; and thus let her deliberate in such a way that she follows the husband's opinion, understanding that it is not as shameful for a man to do any of the things that are at home as it is for a woman to seek those things which are outside.<-
<note>original: "Non audens quicquam de rep. nec tractans quicquam eorum que ad connubia spectare videntur: atque sic una deliberet ut sententiam viri sequatur intelligens non ita turpe viro esse quicquam eorum que domi sunt facere sicut mulieri quæ foris perquirere."</note>

The third and last law is that the woman must patiently and with a comforted soul endure all the adversities that happen to her in respect to her husband. Whence the Philosopher continues:

> ->Furthermore, if she had lived with a fortunate man, her virtue would not have been so greatly illustrated: it is truly no small thing to use favorable circumstances well; yet to endure adverse ones moderately is to be esteemed much greater. For in great calamities and injuries, to do nothing basely is the mark of a lofty soul. One must pray, therefore, that no such thing happens to the husband; but if any adversity happens to him, the woman ought to think that from this, the best praise will come to her if she conducts herself rightly.<-
<note>original: "Præterea si cum fortunato vixisset viro non usque adeo virtus eius illustrata esset: non est sane parum secundis rebus bene vti: attamen aduersis moderate perferre multo maius est estimandum. Nam in magnis calamitatibus & iniurijs nihil abiecte facere celsi est animi: Precandum est igitur ne quid tale accidat viro: quod si quid illi accidat aduersi putare debet mulier hinc optimam sibi laudem: si recte se gesserit prouenturam."<-

Whenever, then, a woman lives together with others according to these three laws, then she can deservedly be assigned to the life according to reason. But when she deviates from these, it can be said she was led not by reason, but by intense appetite and a swift and unpremeditated will. Penelope, then, having always been conforming to the aforementioned laws and never having departed from them in any way...

## TRIUMPH OF CHASTITY
<term>Triumphus Castitatis</term>

...where Ovid demonstrates that she [Penelope] optimally followed these precepts in caring for what pertained to her: leaving the other cares of the kingdom to her husband; and patiently enduring that distress which was born in her because of his absence. For this reason: just as the philosopher <note>Aristotle, often referred to simply as "the Philosopher" in this period.</note> in the *Economics* <note>A work on household management attributed to Aristotle.</note> highly praises Penelope along with Alcestis, the wife of Admetus; so too our poet <note>Petrarch (Messer Francesco).</note> deservedly ascribes her actions to reasonable conduct. For this reason, it evidently follows that each of the other aforementioned women—guided not by reason but by inflamed will—were attributed to the *Triumph of Love*.

Hence, it was not the duty of Hypsicratea <note>The wife of King Mithridates VI, known for following him into battle dressed as a man.</note> to proceed armed into the armies, but rather to remain in the royal palace and await the fortune of Mithridates and preserve herself for it. Similarly, Artemisia <note>Queen of Caria, who built the Mausoleum for her husband Mausolus.</note> was not persuaded by any reason to make a sepulcher of her own body for Mausolus; rather, such a work proceeded only from the irascible power <note>In medieval psychology, the "irascible" faculty governed passions like anger and extreme grief.</note>. Argia likewise, drawn by impatience, contributed to the funeral of Polynices not premeditated tears, but those expressed through excessive disdain and grief. Similarly, Portia <note>The wife of Brutus; legend says she committed suicide by swallowing hot coals after his death.</note> would have more justly wept and lamented the death of her Brutus in her chamber than, with such impetus and fury to live no longer, to have taken and swallowed hissing coals. Julia <note>The daughter of Julius Caesar and wife of Pompey.</note> is to be excused more than any other, seeing as only the fear which is almost naturally inherent in the hearts of women led her to death.

But certainly, reason dictated in that case that she should wish to understand what had happened to her beloved husband Pompey, and thus conform herself according to the outcome of fortune <margin>G</margin> and endure with a great soul if any disaster had befallen her spouse. Thus, there appears a most sufficient reason why these singular women, united in conjugal love, were separated by our poet in honor and in praise and placed in different triumphs. And one responds to Valerius <note>Valerius Maximus, a Roman historian often cited for moral examples.</note> that a just thing—which matrimonial benevolence can justly perform—can be demonstrated according to the sentiment of the Philosopher in the fifth book of the *Ethics*.

Next, our Master Francesco <note>Petrarch.</note> adds the example of Virginia the Roman, a worthy and outstanding maiden, and of Virginius, her excellent and unhappy father; saying that after Lucretia and Penelope, he saw Virginia, and near her, her fierce father armed with iron, with piety, and with disdain: through which he caused the condition and state of both Rome and his beloved daughter Virginia to be changed. Whence he says:

And besides this, they gave them power to make new laws, which, having been examined and approved, they added others to them. They constituted the "Laws of the Twelve Tables" because they were inscribed on twelve tables. Since the authority to interpret the laws also rested with these ten men, they held nearly half the dominion of Rome and used it as such.

Among these men elected by the Roman people was one Appius Claudius. ...considering that to do violence to her would have been too offensive to the Roman people, he [Appius Claudius] conspired with one of his freedmen, a most audacious man named Marcus Claudius, that he should kidnap her when she passed through the street, claiming she was a fugitive slave. Once seized, she was to be brought to the tribunal so that the judge might award her to him. One day, this Marcus carried out what Claudius had commanded. When Virginia took that path, she was assaulted; the women accompanying her offered help and raised such a great clamor that a large crowd gathered, including her husband <note>The text mentions a "marito" (husband), but historically she was betrothed to Lucius Icilius.</note>. Once the dispute was understood, it was announced and brought before the judge, who pronounced a sentence intending to delay the matter until the following day. 

In the meantime, news of this kidnapping reached Virginius, who immediately set out and came to Rome. But he did not arrive before Claudius, having appeared the next day, gave sentence that she was the slave of that Marcus Claudius. Hearing this, the father, Virginius, begged Claudius for the grace that, in the presence of such a judgment, he might speak to Virginia and her nurse in private, so that having heard the truth from them, he might more easily consent to give her up. The perverse judge consented to the request made by Virginius. For this reason, having pulled Virginia aside, he said: "My daughter, by the only way granted to me, I return your liberty to you." Taking a knife in the presence of the judge, he stabbed her in the breast; she, intrepid, seemed to offer herself voluntarily. To the Romans <margin>K</margin> who were present, this seemed an excessively unhappy and miserable spectacle. 

When the cause was understood and the iniquity of Claudius was finally recognized, the people conspired together and deposed those <term>Decemvirs</term> <note>The Decemviri were a ten-man commission established to codify Roman law, but they became tyrannical.</note> from their magistracy. Afterward, Claudius, by just vengeance, was shackled and led to prison, where he died with great hardship and much misery. And the wicked freedman Marcus Claudius fled; out of fear, his goods were confiscated, and he was condemned, as was just, to eternal exile. From this, it is manifest that through the deed of Virginius, his beloved daughter was first restored to her liberty (however unhappily), and the Roman Republic likewise was restored from the occupation of those Decemvirs. 

Immediately following this, the poet narrates the example of the immense constancy of the German women, who by a cruel and most bitter death saved their "barbaric honor," worthy of praise and sublime glory. Wherefore he says:

¶ Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known that at the time of Marius, the Cimbri and the Teutons <note>The "tedeschi" or Germans.</note> and other nations subject to the northern regions conspired against the Roman name. To fight against them with stronger spirits and without any hope of flight, they decided that their women, children, and belongings should follow them upon wagons. While descending into Italy in this manner, the Romans sent Gaius Marius against them to resist. He first encountered the Teutons near <term>Aquae Sextiae</term> <note>original: "acque Sextili"; modern Aix-en-Provence.</note>, fought with them, and defeated them, turning them to flight. Afterward, proceeding against the Cimbri <margin>M</margin>, he likewise broke them near the Salmidian field <note>Likely referring to the Battle of Vercellae.</note>. Their women, more concerned for honor than their husbands who would not follow them, decided to die gloriously in their own defense. 

And so, gathered together upon the wagons, they courageously awaited the Romans. They then considered that this situation could lead to the staining of their chastity. Thus, they concluded it was much better to bargain with the Romans than to resist in such a way. They requested to speak to Marius, from whom they asked the favor—not to follow their husbands who had so vilely fled, nor to save their children or wealth—but only that they be permitted to go to Rome and there become <term>nuns</term> <note>The author uses "mõache" (nuns) to explain the Vestal Virgins to a contemporary audience.</note> with the others in the Temple of Vesta. When Marius denied them this, they resolved to preserve the liberty of their children and their own chastity by the only way they could. Therefore, imitating Virginius, they killed their children that same day; and the following night, they all hanged themselves by the throat, leaving nothing of themselves to the Romans but their dead bodies. Consequently, Messer Francesco [Petrarch] introduces Judith, saying that he then saw the wise, most chaste, and courageous Judith following with the others in the Triumph of Laura. Wherefore he says:

The first is Theoxena <note>The text spells this "Theofena." She was a noblewoman of Thessaly whose story is recorded by the Roman historian Livy.</note>, daughter of Herodicus, a prince of Thessaly. Here it must be understood that Herodicus and Archo <note>The text reads "Archofus," likely a corruption of Archo.</note>, his daughter, were married by their father to two other lords who matched them in virtue and origin. Philip, the son of Demetrius and King of Macedonia <note>Philip V of Macedon (reigned 221–179 BCE).</note>, had both of their husbands killed. After only one small child remained to each of them, it happened that Archo took another husband, a prince also in Thessaly named Poris. After being with him for some time and bearing him several children, she died. Thereupon Theoxena, her sister—who had resolved her mind to maintain perpetual widowhood—was moved by love for her nephews. So that they would not fall under the power of another stepmother (there being no law prohibiting it at the time), she likewise married Poris. During this time, Philip of Macedon, having occupied and largely destroyed Thessaly with grave tyranny, issued an edict by which the son and nephews of Theoxena were condemned to death. He commanded that every remnant of his enemies and rebels must die. Hearing this, and judging that Philip would have them searched for and brought into his power, Theoxena told Poris her husband that she wished to kill them all with her own hands first. Poris, terrified, told her not to do it, and that he wanted to flee and place them in the care of some of his most faithful friends. Immediately, to put his words into effect, he prepared a ship, pretending he wanted to perform certain sacrifices at the harbor. Then, at night, putting the lady Theoxena, the children, and the stepson aboard, he set sail to depart from Thessaly. When they had moved some distance away, contrary winds rose at sea, by which Poris was delayed and could no longer proceed in any way. In the morning, as day broke, the harbor guards whom Philip had stationed saw this ship struggling against the winds at sea. Seeing that it appeared to be fleeing, they immediately boarded their galleys and went toward it, not knowing who it was but intending to capture it. Seeing this, Poris and Theoxena recognized their grave danger and continually exhorted and helped the sailors so that they might escape. But when they saw the waves were against them and the enemy galleys were already near, Theoxena took poison and put it in a cup, and she took a sharp knife. Turning to her son and nephews, she said: *Death alone can provide vengeance and safety for us all; indeed, the cup and the sword are the paths to death.* <note>original Latin: "Mors sola uindictam salutemque nobis omnibus prestare potest: ad mortem uero poculum: gladiusque sunt uie."</note> She exhorted them to die with powerful words, though they hesitated for a time out of fear. Theoxena, greedy for their liberty and having no other way to save them...

<margin>Q</margin>
The other—who is also a suitable subject for the poet—was Hippo, a most ancient Greek maiden. Although her homeland and origins are unknown, one can easily conjecture that she came from an excellent lineage and a land where virtue was highly prized. One day, while walking near the seashore, she was kidnapped by pirates and carried off to various other countries. While this maiden was on the journey, she heard the pirates discussing their desire to take their "amorous pleasure" with her. Knowing she could not resist this except through death, and choosing not to stain her modesty <note>The text uses "pudicitia," referring to the Roman virtue of feminine chastity and sexual honor.</note>, she decided to prefer death over her life—which she then judged to be most miserable. Therefore, having approached the edge of the galley, she took a leap and threw herself into the sea, choosing to end her wretched life in the water among the fish rather than allow her modesty to be corrupted among cruel pirates. But if anyone in this place should say that she went to her death in vain for the sake of her virginity—since physical violence and the corruption of the body do not take away the virtue of the soul, as we said above regarding Lucretia...

<margin>R</margin>
To this it is answered that the reasoning is not the same for Hippo and Lucretia. No motive could have moved Hippo to consent to the will of the pirates other than fear of death or carnal pleasure, both of which would have corrupted her spirit. But Lucretia was moved by neither; she only wished to avoid a perpetual infamy, which would have followed if she had been killed and found together with that slave <note>Sextus Tarquinius threatened to kill Lucretia and a slave and lay them together to make it look like she was caught in adultery.</note>. And therefore Lucretia was deservedly forced to consent to Sextus Tarquinius, and Hippo was deservedly forced to jump and die in the middle of the sea rather than consent to the pirates.

Having been brought before the priest to hear the sentence and suffer the punishment of fire established by Roman law, she—on the other hand—knew her own integrity. Recognizing this as an infamy and having no way to clear her name, she turned with great confidence to the goddess Vesta, whom she had served purely, praying that she would not allow her minister's innocence to be oppressed and hidden. She took a sieve and, in the presence of the priest, said these words: "Vesta, if I have always used clean hands in your sacrifices, I pray that you let me draw water from the Tiber with this sieve and carry it into your most sacred temple." After finishing her prayer, with great hope and faith, she went to the river, took the water, and carried it in the sieve up to the temple. Thus, she was deservedly not only exonerated, but became a saintly figure of wonder to all of Rome.
