The messengers were denied their request by the neighbors, as the Romans were still despised and lived in a pastoral manner. Whereupon Romulus, recognizing that it was necessary either to abandon the city or to find women through industry, and wishing to maintain the city for the future, instituted certain games and spectacles. He built a theater and sent out a proclamation that everyone could come to watch safely and freely. It happened that a great multitude of men and women gathered to see them, especially the Sabine virgins. Romulus, then, when it seemed the right time, proceeded into the middle armed together with his people. They seized all the unwed virgins, doing violence to no others; having retained them, he gave them as wives to his newly-made Romans. Among this number was one far more excellent than the others named Hersilia, who was assigned to Romulus as his wife. 

<margin>X</margin>Regarding this, Ovid says at the end of the *Metamorphoses*: *His wife wept for him as lost, when royal Juno commanded Iris to descend to Hersilia along her curved path and thus deliver her mandates to the widowed queen: "O glory of Latium, O pride of the Sabine people, most worthy to have been the wife of such a great hero before, and now to be his consort [as the god Quirinus]. Cease your weeping, etc., if you care to see your husband again."* <note>original: "Flebat ut amissum coniunx cu regia iuno Irin ad Hersiliam descendere limite curuo..." Ovid describes the deification of Romulus and Hersilia’s subsequent grief and elevation.</note> Since this abduction had sparked a great war between the Sabines and the Romans, one day while they were actually fighting—the battle being very cruel—Hersilia, as the leader of the other Sabine women, proceeded with them into the midst of the armed fathers, brothers, and husbands. With just and reasonable prayers, they pacified them, reconciling them in such a way that many of the Sabines came to stay and live in Rome. Certainly, it was not possible to act with more reason; for it would have been necessary to break faith either with fathers and brothers or with husbands if they had acted otherwise, both of which would have been against their duty. Justly, therefore, the writers of the Latin language who record the Roman origins do not omit Hersilia in any way, she having conducted herself so worthily and with such justice.

He tells the ignorant common folk—who are unaware of poetic artifice and believe, through the description of Virgil, that Dido killed herself for the vain love of Aeneas—to be silent, as that story is entirely alien to the truth. <margin>Y</margin>Because it was made quite clear above at the beginning of this Triumph how Dido, out of love for her husband and not for Aeneas, proceeded to her death; for what reason Virgil was excused for having feigned that Dido had fallen in love with Aeneas; and for what quality she had been bound to Juno; and also why she was described in terms of <term>pudicitia</term> <note>A Roman virtue representing a woman's sexual honor and fidelity to her husband.</note>; therefore, at present, it is not necessary to repeat her history, but only to praise her for having preferred to die free rather than live bound under the laws of the marital yoke, by which she would have been deprived and stripped of all her dominion. She also showed no fickleness regarding the love of her late husband, which was a thing judged as a great disgrace in those times.

While the divine office was being celebrated, Emperor Otto <note>Otto IV</note>, along with many other barons, came to the church. Upon his arrival, because Bellincione was a notable citizen of Florence, he was placed at the Emperor’s side to answer his questions. Looking upon that multitude of exceedingly beautiful women, Otto praised each one; however, he affirmed that Gualdrada surpassed the others in beauty. Turning to a fellow soldier, he asked who that virgin might be. Bellincione, who was her father, replied: "Sacred Majesty, whatever this girl may be, she will give a kiss to Your Serenity if you so desire and if I command it." <margin>A</margin> Gualdrada, who was not far off and heard the words of her father, was suddenly overcome with a virtuous blush and said to Bellincione: "My father, never promise to anyone that which is not in your power; however, be certain that I would sooner pass this knife—which I now draw naked—through the middle of my breast before any man other than the one you give me as a husband shall touch my flesh." And with a modestly troubled expression, she sat down. The Emperor was exceedingly pleased by her constant virginity, for which reason he immediately called a noble youth who was in his presence named Guido <note>Guido Guerra I</note>, a man suitable to her in status and origin. He joined them together as spouses in that very place and hour, and from his own money, he gave Gualdrada a very great dowry. But later, spurred only by the memory of her beauty and unable to keep from showing it, it was said that he pressured her father to arrange things so that Otto might take amorous pleasure from her. There are, nonetheless, some other men of no small authority who say there was a girl born in Florence of honorable parents who, due to the plague that occurred in the year 1348, remained very wealthy after nearly all her relatives died. For this reason, she disposed herself to serve God and fled to a monastery of holy life and excellent reputation located along the Arno above the Ponte Vecchio on the slope called Saint George, solely for the purpose of escaping marriage. <margin>B</margin> It happened then that a hermit of great reputation for holiness and goodness, being at that monastery as a spiritual father and being young, saw her beauty and asked her for carnal relations; beyond this, he used some force upon her. Because she had not yet reached the time of making her profession <note>The formal vow taken by a nun</note>, and seeing the iniquity of the hermit, she returned to her house and took a husband against her original will and intent, believing that in such a life she could still live without offending God. Certainly, Boccaccio, in the book *Decameron*, recounted this truth under a noble veil when he composed the novella of Alibech and the young hermit Rustico <note>A famous and humorous story from Boccaccio's third day, here given a moralizing historical interpretation</note>. 

Now, Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> adds the end of Laura's procession, the location having been determined. He describes how he, with his company and this triumph, had arrived at Baia in the time of the mild winter; and passing from that place between Mount Barbaro and Lake Avernus—where the Cumaean Sibyl once lived—he came inside the castle of Liternum <note>original: "dalinterno"</note>. This was the home of the great and excellent man called the African <note>Scipio Africanus</note>, so named because he was the first to open the vital parts of Africa with the sword, recovering Spain, recalling Hannibal, and subjugating Carthage. Finding the aforementioned Scipio there, and looking upon one another, and seeing the style of his glorious story <note>referring to Petrarch's poem "Africa"</note>—not esteemed in any part by the sight of common men—it pleased everyone. In that comparison, no physical beauty was considered superior; rather, that truth was held to be more beautiful which, in its works, was more chaste. Wherefore he says:

<margin>
¶ What land Baia, Mount Barbaro, and Lake Avernus in the Kingdom of Puglia <note>modern Campania</note> are is quite manifest in these present times; likewise, how the Sibyl lived in that place is clearly shown in the sixth book of Virgil's *Aeneid*. Similarly, the castle of Liternum is known to have been near where the city stands today.
</margin>

> Beat against Baia, which in the mild winter
> He reached on the right hand, and climbed onto firm land.

# THE TRIUMPH OF CHASTITY

<margin>D</margin> *The city of Gaeta is well known through the writers of the Latin language. It remains, therefore, for the understanding of the preceding verses, to know that Scipio Africanus <note>Scipio Africanus (236–183 BCE) was the Roman general who defeated Hannibal. Despite his service, he was later accused of corruption by political rivals and went into a self-imposed exile.</note> went to live in that place. Having conquered Carthage and returning to Rome, although he had always been most abstinent regarding the property of others, he was nonetheless accused by Attius Petilius and forced to give an account of his administration in Africa. Because of this, Scipio, feeling indignant, went to the Capitol; there, stripping himself bare, he showed the people the wounds he had received in Africa. He said that he had acquired nothing but those wounds and his surname <note>The title "Africanus" was granted to him as a "property" or honor resulting from his victory.</note> from the victory in Africa. After this act, departing from Rome in indignation, although he had been acquitted by the people, he went into voluntary exile to live in the villa of Liternum <note>original: "Linterno." An ancient town on the coast of Campania where Scipio spent his final years.</note>. Secondly, it should be understood that the poet describes Laura going to find Scipio with worthy artistry; by this, he intends to show that Scipio always acted with such reason that he is deservedly described as being equal to Lady Laura, so much so that she does not disdain to go and find him even in that place where he was hidden.*

-> Passing on, they went straight to Liternum. <-
-> In such a narrow and solitary villa <-
-> Was the great man, who is named for Africa <-
-> Because he first opened the way there with the sword. <-
<gloss>Here is the noble news of the honor won from the enemy</gloss>
-> Unfailing to the eyes, he pleased all; <-
-> And the most chaste one there was the most beautiful: <-

---

<margin>E</margin> *Finally, it should be noted that this company, with their honor, style, and conversation, was not judged merely by the eyes; for any thing other than virtuous action greatly diminishes in dignity the more frequently it is looked upon. Only virtue and reason are those things which, the more they are contemplated, the more they produce delight in the soul. The poet then recites what Scipio did, and how he joined this company, saying that it did not displease him to follow in a triumph that was not his own. This is because, if the universal opinion of men and their cruelty is not entirely in vain, he alone was born for empires and triumphs. Thus, this company, together with Scipio, arrived at Rome and went to the pious temple which the worthy Sulpitia <note>Sulpitia was a Roman matron chosen as the most virtuous woman in Rome to dedicate a statue of Venus Verticordia, intended to turn the hearts of women toward chastity.</note> built, so that the foolish and insane flame of love might be extinguished in the minds of men. From that shrine, they then passed to the Temple of Chastity <note>original: "pudicitia." The Temple of Pudicitia Patricia in Rome was reserved for noblewomen of the patrician class.</note>, through which chaste and most honest desires are kindled in noble and gentle souls that are not low or common. Thus he says:*

-> In following the triumph of another, it did not displease <-
-> Him, who (if belief is not vain) <-
-> Was born solely for triumphs and for empires. <-
-> Thus we arrived at the sovereign city <-
-> At the temple first, which Sulpitia dedicated <-
-> To extinguish from the mind the insane flame: <-
-> We stopped at the temple then of Chastity; <-
-> Which kindles honest desires in a noble heart, <-
-> Not of common folk, but of the patricians. <-

---

<margin>F</margin> *Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known primarily that Messer Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch), the author of the poem.</note>, being a just man, although he was most affectionate toward Scipio, says that this triumph of reason and chastity was not his own. This is because a thing which is common to many people should not be made the property of any single individual. However, Messer Francesco adds, to the great praise of Scipio, that it pleased him to follow in this triumph <unclear>where we ought</unclear> to understand that <unclear>being</unclear> this a triumph of <unclear>reason</unclear>, he wished in his life <unclear>to describe</unclear> himself as acting so justly that he did not have to follow anyone, but went as an equal with whoever was found triumphing in this triumph. There are, nonetheless, some texts that say: "In the triumph I know not, following did not displease him," where the meaning is easy, and much humanity is attributed to Scipio. But the first verses have a more credible meaning. There are also some others who say that Scipio felt it beneath him to follow this triumph, having been born only for triumphs, and that Messer Francesco said this to demonstrate the excellence of Scipio, who did not deserve to follow any other person.*

# CHAPTER ONE

<margin>G</margin> You will continue to demonstrate the ingratitude of the Romans by feigning that Scipio did not wish to follow Laura, going to Rome instead because of the anger he felt toward the Roman people. Secondary to this, it should be understood that when the Romans wished to build a temple to Venus <note>This refers to the Temple of Venus Verticordia ("Venus the Changer of Hearts"), established to turn the minds of women from lust toward chastity.</note>—so that the Roman women might be confirmed in the habit of chastity—the decree of the Decemviri <note>A commission of ten men in the Roman Republic tasked with special administrative or legal duties.</note> mandated that they appoint a woman as the architect of such a grand building. They arrived at this selection by choosing one thousand women from the total number in Rome; from those thousand, they chose one hundred; from the hundred, they chose ten; and from those ten, they selected one. This final choice was entrusted to the judgment of the women themselves. By their universal judgment, they chose Sulpicia—the daughter of a patrician named Servius and the wife of Fulvius Flaccus—with no less glory for her chastity than that possessed by Lucretia. Having been elevated to such honor, she brought the building to its proper completion with great praise for herself, to the contentment of the men, and to the supreme joy of the Roman women. Immediately afterward, our poet, **Messer Francesco** <note>Petrarch.</note>, in observance of Roman triumph customs, describes Laura being led to the Temple of Modesty <term>Pudicitia: The Roman personification of feminine virtue and sexual modesty.</term> to consecrate the spoils she gained in the war of love. He says that Laura proceeded together with Scipio (not, according to the first interpretation, to Rome itself), and having passed to the Temple of Modesty, she displayed her victorious spoils there; likewise, she laid down and consecrated her dear and precious leaves <note>A poetic play on "Laura" and the laurel ("Lauro") leaves, symbolizing both her name and her physical beauty being dedicated to a higher virtue.</note>. Hence he says:

<margin>H</margin>
> There the beautiful victress displayed 
> The glorious spoils; there she laid down 
> Her victorious and sacred leaves;

Our **Messer Francesco** has described no small praise for Scipio and Laura in the preceding verses, having depicted them proceeding equally as they arrived in Rome at the Temple of Chastity and Modesty. Here we may understand that Scipio and Laura were such that they deservedly preceded all others in righteous action. Furthermore, he has shown them to possess such continence and observance that, while each deserved the highest rank in their own right, he nonetheless rendered honor to both: Laura having visited Scipio, and Scipio having accompanied Laura. By mutual consent, they arrived in Rome at the temples most appropriate for them, where Laura consecrated the spoils obtained through her previous deeds and the dear leaves of her own limbs to inflexible chastity and virtue. **Messer Francesco** then adds that, after Laura had made her consecration, the Tuscan youth also left and placed his beautiful wounds under the guard of modesty, so that he might not be suspected by his common enemy <note>The "common enemy" refers to Cupid, or the universal temptation of lust.</note>. Hence he says:

<margin>I</margin>
> And the Tuscan youth, who did not hide 
> The beautiful wounds that made him above suspicion; 
> Placed them in the guard of the common enemy.

FOR the understanding of the preceding verses, one should know what **Valerius Maximus** <note>A Roman historian (1st century CE) known for his collection of "Memorable Deeds and Sayings."</note> writes in his fourth book, chapter five: that long ago, before there was any city in Tuscany, there was a youth of marvelous beauty named **Spurinna**. He saw and realized that all the women of the region were intensely in love with him. Because of this, he knew he was an object of envy for their husbands and fathers. Being himself most continent and recognizing that his beauty was an incitement to lust for all the women, he deliberated that he would rather have deformity bear witness to his faith and continence than have his beauty lead to the passion and failings of others. Therefore, he covered his beautiful face—and especially his mouth, which most invited women to lust—with wounds and scars, becoming so deformed that every suspicion generated by him in the minds of the people was deservedly driven out and removed. He concludes finally at the end of this chapter and triumph by saying that, together with the Tuscan youth, he saw many other men, among whom he recognized the Greek **Hippolytus** and the Hebrew **Joseph**. Hence he says:

<margin>K</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
> With several others; and the name of some 
> Of them was told to me, as my guide knew them; 
> Who had made a clear renunciation of love, 
> Among whom I saw Hippolytus and Joseph.

Who **Hippolytus** was, and how he reasonably resisted the furious mind and insane will of **Phaedra**, was made quite clear above in the *Triumph of Love*. It remains now, for the understanding of the preceding verses, only to know how **Joseph** was the son of the patriarch **Jacob**...

# THE TRIUMPH OF CHASTITY

<margin>He who triumphed:</margin> **[Joseph] who triumphed:** as is written in Genesis chapters 37 and 39, having seen in a dream that while he and his brothers were harvesting grain, their sheaves bowed down to his sheaf; and likewise the sun, the moon, and eleven stars bowed to him. He recounted what he had dreamed to his brothers, at which they were moved against him with great anger and envy, judging by this that he intended to rule over them. One day, therefore, while they were guarding the flocks, Joseph brought them food. Seeing him from a distance, they said among themselves: "Behold, the dreamer! Now let us go and kill him." Proceeding against him, the nine brothers wanted to put him to death, but one of them named Reuben, moved inwardly by brotherly love, said to the others—hoping to save him from such fury—"My brothers, let us not stain our hands with the blood of our brother. But since there is a dry cistern nearby, let us put him inside; and so we shall escape this atrocious homicide." Reuben's counsel pleased each of the others. Having brought him to the cistern and already stripped Joseph to put him inside, certain Ishmaelite merchants passed by. Thinking it a good plan to see Joseph sold, they agreed on a price and sold him for thirty pieces of silver <note>original: "trenta dinari"</note>, in a figure and prefiguration of the sale of the immaculate lamb, Christ Jesus, just as the prophet Amos predicted in the second chapter and Zechariah in the second <note>The text cites Zechariah 2, but the quote is from Zechariah 11:12.</note>, saying: *And they weighed out for my price thirty pieces of silver.* <note>original: "Et appenderunt mercede meã triginta argenteos."</note> The Ishmaelites, then taking Joseph, went with him to Egypt, where they sold him to Potiphar, an official <term>Eunuch: Here used as a title for a high-ranking court official, not necessarily a castrated male.</term> of Pharaoh, who, seeing Joseph was handsome of body and pleasant in appearance, placed him over all his affairs, leaving him the entire governance of his house. One day, when Joseph had returned home and no one else of the family was there, Potiphar's wife pressured and requested him for lustful pleasure. Since he did not consent nor wished to consent, and she was doing him violence, he finally fled from her, and in leaving, he left his cloak behind. Seeing herself thus rebuffed by Joseph, when Potiphar returned home, she said to him weeping: that Joseph had wanted to violate her, and that she had cried out and he fled, leaving his cloak in his flight. Potiphar believed the woman and therefore had Joseph imprisoned. While there, Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker were also imprisoned. Both dreaming one night, Joseph interpreted their dreams: for the baker, his death; and for the <margin>Interpretation</margin> cupbearer, his restoration. Following this, Joseph gained great fame as an interpreter. This led subsequently to Pharaoh’s dream of the full and empty ears of grain, and of the fat and thin cows. Joseph interpreted this to mean there would be seven years of fertility and seven others of great sterility. Because of this, Pharaoh placed Joseph in charge of the accumulation of grain. Consequently, after the famine came upon the whole world, it happened that Jacob and his sons went to Egypt to bow before Joseph; thus the dream was verified, as the history of Genesis relates. Joseph having acted so justly in every thing—whether through continence, clemency, piety, holiness, or learning—he has for this reason been deservedly numbered in the triumph of our **Messer Francesco.** <note>Petrarch.</note>

->EXPOSITION OF THE THIRD TRIUMPH: DEATH.<-

<margin>Mortality</margin> **WHATEVER** thing is produced into being through natural generation or any other transformation within the heavens, it is seen through certain experience to fail. Nature has especially subjected human nature to this deficiency, so that through many various channels, death is distilled into the bodies of men. For this reason, they are deservedly named "mortals" among all other living creatures. Nor can one escape this law through any work, however worthy or excellent: for whoever is born into the world must of necessity die once. Such is the flow from human origins, ever since our first parents, through disobedience, experienced the harshness of divine laws. But infinite goodness is always disposed in every just sentence not to separate mercy from justice. Although death was instituted as a punishment for the transgression of His commandments, He did not wish that the angelic nature—<margin>The Soul</margin> the principal and most worthy part of man—should fail; rather, only the body which it sustained should be that which turns to nothing. Death, then, is only the separation of the soul from our body, by which means human operations are totally ceased and taken away. Wherefore the poets, considering this natural continuation and necessary disposition of man—in which the soul first joins the body, and through that union proceeds into being, and finally...

It establishes the philosophical framework for the poem, moving from the soul's life within the body to its inevitable separation and return to its divine origin.</meta>

->CHAPTER ONE<-

# CHAPTER ONE

the soul is separated from it <note>This continues the thought from the previous page regarding the soul leaving the body.</note>: and therefore the poets feigned that **Clotho**, **Lachesis**, and **Atropos** <note>The three Fates of Greek mythology who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life.</note> were the ministers of the Maker, through whom this natural process is described. Having therefore our **Messer Francesco** <note>Petrarch, the author of the *Triumphs*.</note> already described two states of the universal soul in which it finds itself while united in life with the body—namely, the dominion of the sensitive appetite in the time of youth, and the dominion of reason in the time of manhood and old age—he consequently describes the third state, which is its universal separation from everyone, called **Death**. In this, he intends to demonstrate two things by universal argument: the first is that every man, however perfect in virtue, is subject to death and to the natural changes that precede it.

<margin>P</margin>
Thus he silently admonishes men to be bold against death and not to fear it, according to the opinion of **Averroes** <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> in the prologue to the *Physics* when he says:

> And when one sees that death occurs from the necessity of the form or of matter, then one will necessarily be bold. <note>original: "Et cū viderit quod mors cōtigerit ex neceſſitate idee ſiue materiæ tunc erit audax ex neceſſitate."</note>

The other purpose is to persuade us of the immortality of the soul, which he demonstrates by introducing **Laura** speaking with him in a dream, and asking her about the quality of death; this he does in the second chapter. When, therefore, Messer Francesco introduces this in the first chapter, he follows the opinion of **the Philosopher** <note>A traditional title for Aristotle.</note> in the first book of the *Physics*, who says that things are resolved and corrupted into those same principles from which they had their generation and being. Astrologers then say a celestial revolution is finished when the celestial bodies return to that same point and similar position in which they were at the beginning of their movement. He introduces **Laura** returning to her own domicile <note>Heaven, the soul's true home.</note>, from which she had departed and wandered through the world, finally arriving in Rome to consecrate the glorious spoils of her victory. From there, having reached the end of her worthy works, it was fitting that she return to her first origin. In this return, encountering **Death**, the poet cautiously instructs us to remember our first principle—which the Holy Catholic Church demonstrates to us on the first day of Lent as being only ash and earth, and according to what the Holy Scripture testifies in the first chapter of **Genesis**. Messer Francesco says, then, that Laura, having had the glorious victory over the powerful **Cupid** with her noble and excellent company, and returning to **Vaucluse** <note>Petrarch's home in France; the text uses "Caue sons," a corruption of "Chiusa" or "Vaucluse."</note> along the journey, she encountered Death. Death, manifesting herself, challenged her and said she wished to make her die entirely. Laura, responding as befitted her excellence, made Death lay down her ferocity, and they continued their reasoning together with the response that belongs to a just, prudent, and religious soul.

<margin>Q</margin>
In the end, Laura consented to die. After describing the death, the poet recounts the great weeping and fitting lamentation of the neighboring women who were joined to Laura in honest friendship. Giving, therefore, a beginning to this third **Triumph**, Messer Francesco compares it to all the others of the ancient Romans, saying: however many triumphs there ever were in the ancient age of the city of Rome during the time of the Republic <note>literally "the political living."</note>, or of nature in the time of the Emperors, where the glorious **Quirinal Hill** flourished. And likewise, however many there were under him who did not distribute silver but a bloody river for his soldiers to drink <note>Likely a reference to Julius Caesar or a similar military leader known for bloody victories.</note>, or under the monarch who took the name of "Greatness" from every other lord <note>Augustus Caesar.</note>, who wished to describe the entire universal world; however many prisoners were also led under his empire along the **Sacred Way** to the **Capitoline Hill**, they did not give as much glory and honor to their possessors as love alone increased the merit of praise for Laura, she being his prisoner, through whom she led a triumph in such a manner. Whence he says:

All were turned from little to nothing;
This one of whom I speak is such a white swan <note>Petrarch refers to himself or perhaps a specific virtuous soul (like Laura) as a swan, a symbol of purity and poetic grace.</note>

<margin>
VARIOUS NOTES: Our most illustrious poet has described a worthy matter in the preceding verses. Regarding this, it is primarily to be understood: as we said at the beginning in the *Triumph of Love*, that whenever those who received a triumph were in their proper act of triumphing, they always proceeded along the **Sacred Way** via the **Lata Way**; routes specifically designated for the triumphal army. Thus triumphing, and with that order which was mentioned above in the triumph of Scipio, they came finally to the **Quirinal Hill**, which was the Capitol and the fortress of Rome. Secondly, it is to be understood that among all the princes who are ever read to have ruled, there was never any who justly deserved to be named **Monarch**, except for **Octavian** <note>Augustus Caesar.</note>: because he alone possessed the entire universal world in supreme tranquility and peace, which is the proper work of a monarch. This aforementioned Monarch having succeeded Caesar, and after the death of Hirtius and Pansa in the Battle of Modena, remained the sole protector of the Roman Republic. Finally, as **Tranquillus** <note>The historian Suetonius.</note> writes, being already in peaceful possession, he triumphed for an entire three days, where he brought back the Dalmatian, Asiatic, and Alexandrian triumphs. Besides these, Octavian had almost innumerable honors and triumphs from the peoples who peacefully submitted to him, such as the Scythians, the Smarigli <note>Likely the Sarmatians.</note>, the Indians, Parthians, and other nations, so that as **Lucius Florus** writes, the whole world converged under him: some through victory, some through treaty. Therefore, Octavian deservedly took the name and even the greatness of status and lordship from all other princes who ever were. Having therefore established Octavian in the monarchy, he decided to see how many men he commanded. For this reason, he issued a command in every place that the number of living men should be recorded. This is testified by the Gospel in Saint Luke in the second chapter, where it says: **"In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered."** <note>original: "In diebus illis Exijt edictum a Cesare Augusto vt describeretur vniuersus orbis."</note> In the third and last place, it is to be noted: that he who gave his men a drink from a bloody stream was **Gaius Marius**, originally from Arpinum. He went against the Cimbri and Teutons, as we clearly said in the next triumph. Since they were camped above certain small rivers of clear water, and the Romans were in great need, and finally his soldiers, exhausted by exercise and the weather, told him they should leave the field and return to a place where there was water so they could drink. Marius denied them with a copious speech, showing them the water upon which the enemies were lodged. He said: "You are seven men: look at the water." Through these words, the Roman soldiers flared up in such a fury that immediately taking up arms and proceeding to the battle, they made so great a slaughter of the enemies that those small streams rose with their blood, so that later Marius and all his others, the fierce and bitter battle being finished and a complete and great victory obtained, wished to drink, and they drank no less blood from those streams than they did water. This thing our famous poet **Master Francesco** <note>Petrarch.</note> writes and affirms in that song: **"My Italy, although speaking is in vain."** <note>original: "ITALIA MIA BENCHEL PARLAR SI AINDAR NO." One of Petrarch's most famous political poems.</note> Where he says: "WELL PROVIDENCE..."

### THE TRIUMPH OF DEATH

NATURE PROVIDED our state with the shield of the Alps as a defense between us and the German rage; <note>The "German rage" refers to the historical invasions of Italy by Germanic tribes across the Alps.</note> but blind desire, acting against its own well-being, has been so clever that it has brought a scab <note>A metaphor for corruption or plague</note> upon the healthy body. Now, behind a cage, wild beasts and tame flocks huddle together, where the best always groan; and this is for the greater sorrow of the lawless people. As we read, Marius opened their flank so wide that the memory of the deed still lingers on our tongues: when, parched and weary, he drank no more water from the river than he did blood. <note>original: "quando affetato & stancho non piu beue del fiume acqua che sangue". This refers to the Roman general Gaius Marius, whose soldiers were so thirsty during the battle against the Teutones that they fought to reach a river, which then flowed with the blood of their enemies.</note> Under Gaius Marius there were also many, specifically three triumphs: that of Jugurtha, the most powerful king of Numidia; the triumph over the Cimbri; and the triumph over the Germans. From these, he brought back the greatest glory and honor; and a massive multitude of prisoners followed him to the Capitoline Hill, he having been consul seven times. To conclude, however, all these triumphs were of little or no value in comparison to that of the excellent Laura, which she received for her victory over Cupid. Consequently, the poet demonstrates by comparison how great Laura's innocence was, saying: that as Lady Laura returned to her place of origin, her beautiful face was so adorned and white that any swan—though it is the whitest of animals—would have appeared like a crow in comparison to her. And in this state, with a moderate and most sweet gesture, with a gentle but troubled look, the glorious and most honorable victress Lady Laura, turning toward the sunset, followed the curved Tyrrhenian shore, sounding with the crashing of waves against its hard rocks. Wherefore he says:

> There was never a swan that did not seem a crow
> Beside that angelic and benign fair face;
> And thus, with a sweet gesture, she turned back,
> The honorable victress, toward the sunset,
> Following the Tyrrhenian shore, sounding and curved.

<margin>C</margin> REGARDING the understanding of the preceding verses, it is to be understood that Lady Laura, being naturally of a most beautiful body, represents in this triumph the dominion of Reason. Since innocence is the foundation of every work that proceeds from Reason, her innocence is symbolized here by whiteness, as we said above. Therefore, the poet appropriately says that no swan is so white that, in comparison to the beautiful face of Laura, it would not appear as a very black crow. Secondly, it should be known that Laura is shown returning with a "troubled" look; for it is the natural habit of reasonable people to appear troubled in their aspect whenever they must repress 
<margin>D</margin> lustful appetite. In the third place, it should be noted that Laura "turning toward the sunset" can have two true meanings. Either by "sunset" he means the land of France, to which she was returning from Rome along the Tyrrhenian shore (and as one travels there, it always seems one is proceeding toward the West, France being mostly situated in the West); or truly, by "sunset" he can mean the end and the death of Lady Laura. This second interpretation seems more fitting to me, as the poet affirms that Lady Laura found death at the end of this journey. The poet describes Laura, in this return, following the Tyrrhenian shore—or according to another reading, returning by the Tyrrhenian shore via the sea, just as she had come to Baia by sea. This is even more appropriate, as the "shore" can represent the sea due to the nature of her arrival. Here it should be understood that the sea, according to the natural philosophers and Aristotle in the second book of the *Meteorology*, <note>original: "Aristote. nel secondo de la metau." referring to *Meteorologica*</note> is nothing other than the congregation of water which surrounds the earth, as it was named at the beginning of its creation in the book of Genesis. This congregation of seas is principally divided into two names: one is called the Ocean and the other the Mediterranean. The Ocean is that which, following the spherical shape, surrounds the earth; it receives other specific names according to different parts of the earth, such as the Atlantic, the Indian, the British, and many others. But the Mediterranean is so named because it opens the earth from the extremity of the West between the mountains of Calpe <note>The Rock of Gibraltar</note> and Abyla—called thus by Solinus <note>A 3rd-century Roman geographer</note> and the cosmographers—and flowing, it reaches the Eastern regions. From there it turns toward the North, and so it appears to divide and determine Africa, Asia, and likewise Europe. This sea is also called by many names according to the particular regions it flows past; wherefore, at its entrance, it is primarily called the Gaditanian [Strait of Gibraltar], then toward the...

# CHAPTER ONE

Following the shore of the land on the left, it is called the Iberian, Balearic, and Spanish sea. Next follows the Gallic sea, which ends at Provençal territory. Then comes the Ligurian sea, and after that the Tyrrhenian sea, which is otherwise named the Ionian and the Lower sea. Following that is the Sicilian sea, which extends as far as the sea of Crete; but on the right shore, the Mediterranean is principally called the Moorish sea. Then the Libyan—or truly the African—and proceeding toward the south, one finds the Cyrenaic sea; then continuing to the Cyprian or Syrian sea; and entering the land, the Gulf of Cilicia follows, joined then by the Pamphylian sea, which is also contiguous with the sea of Crete. Somewhat from the northern part begins the Illyrian and the Adriatic—otherwise called the Upper sea. Proceeding then from the Cretan sea toward the East follows the Archipelago <note>The Aegean Sea</note>, which, extending toward the north, narrows into very tight straits, today called the Strait of Gallipoli and formerly the Hellespont. Then follows the sea called the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>, which again narrows where it is called the Bosphorus, upon which strait is situated the city of Constantinople. Finally follows the Great Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>, which spreads toward the north and east beyond the strait of Constantinople, where on the right shore of the east it is called the Euxine Point, and on the left it is named the Scythian sea. It also has more specific names from the islands, whence it is named Abydean, Rhodian, Cyprian, Carpathian, and many other various names, which we will omit, seeking rather its location than its name, especially having recounted the entire flow of the Mediterranean sea.

<margin>E</margin>
It remains therefore manifest that if anyone wishes to return from Rome to France, it is necessary to follow the straight path along the coast and the Tyrrhenian sea. Afterward, Messer Francesco <note>Messer Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch), the author of the poems being commented upon</note> describes specifically the place where he was born and where Laura returned, saying that she—who today is a naked spirit and returned to a little earth—was the one for whom he primarily chose to do good and pursue his studies. She returned with the greatest honor from her war, having conquered her great and powerful enemy, Cupid, who with his wits brings down and dominates the entire world, to the place of Gravesons <note>A village in Provence</note> which is situated where the Sorgue and Durance, those graceful little rivers, join their turbid waters in the larger vessel of the Rhône. This place was once, to him, both an Academy and a Parnassus. Whence he says:

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>As we said from the beginning: Madame Laura was born in Gravesons, a village enclosed between those two rivers, namely the Sorgue and the Durance. Messer Francesco affirms that this place was his Academy and Parnassus to show that he wrote moral philosophy here together with poetic things, since the Academy was the place which Plato chose for his studies.</margin>

->Where the Sorgue and Durance in a larger vessel<-

->She, for whose sake it first pleased me to do well;<-
->**R**eturning with honor from her war,<-
->Joyful, having conquered the great enemy<-
->Who with his cunning brings the whole world down.<-

There, the philosophers would gather and dispute philosophy. Parnassus is likewise the mountain consecrated to Apollo and the Muses, upon which it is said anyone who writes poetic fantasies dwells, as Persius affirms.

<margin>G</margin>
Secondly, the poet affirms that Laura returned to this place, she who had become a naked spirit and little earth. We say this to demonstrate that man is constituted of two principal parts: namely, body and soul. Of these, the body being corruptible, in a short space of time it turns into earth; while the soul remains a naked spirit, being subtracted from all corruption. As it is the principal part, man is very often named for it; this naming did not originate from the common folk, but the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> describes it in the fourth book of *Physics*, and Augustine confirms it in the eighth book of *The City of God*, alleging Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>, where he says:
> Your grandfather, O Asclepius, the first inventor of medicine, to whom a temple is consecrated on the mountain of Libya near the shore of the crocodiles, in which his earthly man lies; for the rest, or rather the whole man, if he is a man in the better sense of life, has returned to heaven. <note>original Latin: "Avus tuus o Asclepi medicine primus inuentor cui templum consecratum est in monte lybiæ circa littus cocodrilorum in quo eius iacet mundanus homo : reliquus enim uel potius totus si est homo in sensu vitæ meliori remeauit in cælum"</note>

# THE TRIUMPH OF DEATH

...great glory and a singular triumph, being joyful in her appearance. This is truly with good reason: for whenever men, through reason, resist lustful appetite and finally make it subject to her—delighting themselves greatly in virtuous works—they demonstrate great joy and ultimate gladness. This is especially true because they see themselves placed in such a state that they no longer fear being troubled by carnal desires; for thus, their will is confirmed by the dominion of reason, according to the opinion of *Augustine in the ninth book of the City of God, where he says:*

> For the disturbance of passions that rules over the foolish and wicked is governed by the wise and good in such a way that they would rather not have it than have to conquer it. <note>original: "Perturbatio enim passionum quae stultis malis dominatur: a sapientibus uero & bonis ita regitur: ut malint eam non habere quam uincere."</note>

*Master Francesco* <note>Francesco Petrarch, the author of the poem</note> adds afterwards that *Laura* used certain weapons and instruments of war to subjugate *Love*. He says that she carried no other weapon into battle than a chaste, modest, and pure heart without stain, and a beautiful face, adorned and not neglected, with a multitude of modest thoughts far removed from any lewdness; and finally, a wise and moderate way of speaking, entirely a friend to true virtue. Whence he says:

->Not with other weapons than a chaste heart,<-
->And a beautiful face, and modest thoughts,<-
->With wise speech, and a friend of virtue.<-

<margin>A</margin> According to sacred and moral teachings, man can use no other weapon or sword more suited to dominating appetite than these which our excellent poet has described in these verses. Regarding the understanding of these, one must know—according to the evangelical doctrine of *Matthew*—that there are universal commandments upon which every divine, natural, and written law depends: namely, to love God with all one’s heart and mind, and one's neighbor as oneself. Whence he says in *chapter 22*, introducing Christ affirming it thus:

> You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength: this is the first and greatest commandment. And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets. <note>original: "Diliges dominum deum tuum ex toto corde tuo... in his duobus mandatis uniuersa lex pēdet & prophetae."</note>

Whence Saint Paul, seeing that love is presupposed in each of these commandments, says that charity is more worthy than faith and hope. Whence in *1 Corinthians 13*, he says:

> And now abide faith, hope, and charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity. <note>original: "Nunc aut manet fides spes & charitas: haec tria: maior autem horum est charitas."</note>

Therefore, through these commandments, sin is avoided and appetite is mastered, according to the definition of sin given by *Augustine in his book against Faustus the Heretic*, where he says:

> Sin is a word, deed, or desire against the law of Christ. <note>original: "Peccatum est dictum aut factū aut concupitū contra legem Christi."</note>

These precepts, therefore, presuppose the purity and cleanliness of the heart. Whence Christ says in Saint *Matthew, chapter 5*:

> Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God. <note>original: "Beati mundo corde: quoniam ipsi deum uidebunt."</note>

And likewise *Isaiah* in the first chapter, speaking in the person of God, shows that prayers and sacrifices are not acceptable to Him when the soul and its actions are stained by some earthly effect; whence he says:

> When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you; and even though you make many prayers, I will not listen. Your hands are full of blood. <note>original: "Cum extederitis manus uestras: auertam oculos meos a uobis... Manus enī uestre sanguine plene sunt."</note>

On the contrary, the cleanliness of the body <note>meaning the "temple" of the person</note> in the sacrifice to God is shown to be greatly cherished, as *Malachi* also writes in the first chapter, speaking in the person of God against the Jews. He says He no longer wishes to receive sacrifices from them because their hands are polluted, while in every place a clean and immaculate offering is presented to His holy name. Whence he says:

> I have no pleasure in you, and I will not accept an offering from your hands. For from the rising of the sun to its setting, my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense and a pure offering are sacrificed and offered to my name. <note>original: "Nō ē mihi uolūtas in uobis... Ab ortu enim solis usq; ad occasum magnū ē nomē meū... oblatio munda."</note>

This offering and sacrifice is now nothing other than the heart and the mind of men, as the prophet *David* testifies in *Psalm 50* <note>modern Psalm 51</note> when he says:

> The sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; a broken and a humbled heart, O God, you will not despise. <note>original: "Sacrificiū deo spiritus cōtribulatus cor contritū & humiliatū deus non despicies."</note>

<margin>B</margin> Whence it appears manifest that the first weapons against appetite are fittingly placed in a modest heart. This operation also requires the delight of the soul, so that the outward appearance is joyful and decorous in accordance with its righteousness; whence *Christ* instructs us in *Saint Matthew*, saying:

> But you, when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face. <note>original: "Tu aut cum ieiunas unge caput tuum & faciē tuā laua."</note>

Modest thoughts and wise words also contribute to this effect. For whenever a man consents to a lewd thought within himself and delights in it, he sins according to the judgment of Christ in *Saint Matthew, chapter 5*, where he says:

> He who looks at a woman with lust has already committed adultery in his heart. <note>original: "Qui uiderit mulierē ad cōcupiscēdū iā mechatus est in corde suo."</note>

And that wise words are necessary for this state is aptly written in *chapter 12 of Matthew*, when Christ said:

> For every idle word, you shall give an account. <note>original: "De omni uerbo ocioso redditu-ri estis."</note>

It aligns her "weapons"—purity, modest thoughts, and wise speech—with biblical mandates from Matthew, Paul, and the Prophets regarding the sanctity of the heart.</summary>

# CHAPTER ONE

...you shall give an account on the day of judgment. <note>original: "ti estis rationem in die iudicij," likely completing "reddituri estis..."</note> Therefore, it is a very well-known thing that Lady Laura used those weapons against powerful Cupid; that one ought to use them is demonstrated by the moral law, which is not a difficult thing to understand. Whence, regarding the pure heart, the soul, and the joyful countenance that follows, Aristotle writes in the first book of the *Ethics*, speaking on what the disposition of one who wishes to follow the commandments or moral precepts should be: *Indeed, one who is still a follower of his passions will listen in vain and to no purpose, since the end is not knowledge, but action.* <note>original: "Sequax vero adhuc affectibus existes inaniter & inutiliter audiet: quum finis sit: nō cognitio: sed actio:"</note> Then, affirming the same regarding the avoidance of [immoral] thoughts, he adds in the same book: *Furthermore, he is not good who does not delight in good actions.* <note>original: "Non est preteres bonus qui bonis operationibus non delectatur."</note> Whence it follows: when a man delights in good works, he always holds others in the highest contempt. Aristotle likewise demonstrates a similar disposition regarding wise speech. Whence in the sixth book of the *Politics* he says: *For obscenity of words must be forbidden in cities; for from the license of speaking basely follows also the license of acting basely.* <note>original: "Prohibenda enim est in ciuitatibus obscenitas verborum: nam ex turpiter loquendi licentia sequitur & turpiter facere:"</note> Here one clearly sees the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> conforming to this sentiment in the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter fifteen, where he says: *Bad company corrupts good character.* <note>original: "Corrumpunt enim bonos mores colloquia mala."</note> Concluding, then, it remains well known that with these weapons alone, appetite is conquered and made subject to the empire of reason; the poet then conforms to the aforementioned sentiment. He adds, saying how in that place there was to be seen a great miracle: the invincible weapons of Love were broken—that is, the tenacious bow and the piercing arrows. And a much greater marvel was to see there some who had been killed by him and some others who were taken alive, such as Achilles, Pyrrhus, Leander, Antony, Julius Caesar, Augustus, and Hannibal, and many others. Whence he says:

> It was a new miracle to see here
> The weapons of Love broken—bow and arrows;
> And some dead by him, and some taken alive.

<margin>
**C**
Human nature, though perfect in its origin, has been so depraved by its own greed for earthly delights and carnal pleasures that it has given itself almost totally to following the judgment of the senses.
</margin>

Therefore, it is deservedly judged a very great miracle, as the poet writes in the preceding verses, when men abstain from carnal appetite and follow their right judgment of reason. He himself testifies to this in that sonnet *Gluttony, sleep, and idle feathers*, where he says: *And every benign light of heaven is extinguished, through which human life is informed, so that it is pointed out as a miraculous thing by whoever wishes to make a river spring from Helicon.* <note>A reference to Petrarch's Sonnet 7, lamenting the decline of philosophy and poetry in a materialistic world.</note> And this is seen to be a particularly great disposition among the common people, who, the more they multiply in number, the more they deviate from the use of reason, according to what the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> writes in the third book of the *Rhetoric*, where he says: *The greater the crowd, the smaller the intellect.* <note>original: "Quanto maior populus tanto minor intellectus."</note> He then adds, describing the number, the state, and the outward appearance of Laura and her excellent companions, returning from the victory achieved against Cupid. They were gathered in a beautiful little company, and they were few, because few are those to whom the merit of true glory is communicated through their works; but truly, of those few, each by herself seemed worthy of a singular history and a most famous poem. Whence he says:

<margin>**D**</margin>
> **T**he beautiful lady and her chosen companions,
> **R**eturning from the noble victory,
> **W**ere gathered in a beautiful little company.
> **F**ew they were, because true glory is rare;
> **B**ut each by herself seemed well worthy
> **O**f a most clear poem and history.

<margin>

Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it is primarily to be known how Master Francesco does not deviate in these verses from the sentiment of Paul the Apostle, narrating that the chosen persons are worthy of glory.
</margin>

Here it is to be understood that God observes a certain order in the justification of men: first predestining them, secondly calling them through the second and particular vocation; when they consent to this with their free will, He then sanctifies them, and ultimately honors and magnifies them. Therefore the Apostle said in the eighth chapter <note>Romans 8:30</note>: *Moreover, those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.* <note>original: "Quos autem predestinauit hos & vocauit & quos vocauit: hos & iustificauit: quos autem iustificauit: illos & magnificauit."</note> Secondarily, it is to be understood that those people who proceed with reason...

<header>THE TRIUMPH OF DEATH</header>
<meta>Catchword: [justifica]tion thus</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF DEATH <note>Though titled "Triumph of Death," the content describes the "Triumph of Chastity," specifically the banner of the ermine. In early editions, these sections were sometimes grouped or mislabeled.</note>

...in their works for two reasons to be worthy of poem and history: one so that they might deservedly have praise for their practiced virtues; because by their example anyone who had knowledge of them might be moved to do well, whereby they might regulate themselves in their course of life, according to the definition of history given by Cicero in the book *On the Orator*, who says: *History is the witness of times, the teacher of life, the life of memory, the light of truth.* <note>original: "Historia est testis temporum: magistra vitae: vita memoriae: lux veritatis." Cicero, *De Oratore*, 2.36.</note> Lastly, it is to be noted that the poet says those women are few; because true glory is rarely communicated, in order to conform to the Sibylline sentence cited above written by Virgil in the sixth [book of the *Aeneid*], and also to the truth of Christ in Saint Matthew: *For many are called, but few are chosen.* <note>original: "Multi eni sunt vocati: pauci vero electi." Matthew 22:14.</note> But if anyone in this place should ask a reasonable question: whether Lucretia <note>A legendary Roman heroine who chose death to preserve her honor.</note> and the others listed in the company of Laura were chosen by God, having lived according to reason without violating any law of nature or scripture. The response to this is according to the doctrine of Saint Thomas [Aquinas] in the *Prima Secundae*, question 11, article 1: <note>original: "prima secondo a la. q. c. al. xj. art." refers to the *Summa Theologiae*.</note> that in the right of disposing justification for the executions of justice, they were chosen by a general election, through which God desires the salvation of everyone. The other [type of election] is not sufficient for special election; because it is necessary that for this particular election, besides human justification, there also concurs infused justice, which comes only from God and from His incomprehensible will, as the Apostle [Paul] shows in Romans 4 when he says: *For if Abraham was justified by the works of the law, he has glory, but not before God.* <note>original: "Si eni abraam ex operibus legis iustificatus est habet gloria: sed non apud deum." Romans 4:2.</note> Wherefore Lucretia and the other companions of Laura were justified by legal justification, insofar as it pertains to acting justly according to virtuous nature; because these women were a law unto themselves according to the Apostle to the Romans who says: *For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature those things which are of the law, not having such a law, they are a law unto themselves.* <note>original: "Cum eni gentes: quae legem non habent naturaliter ea quae legis sunt faciunt: einusmodi legem non habentes: ipsi sibi sunt lex." Romans 2:14.</note> And so, concluding on "dispositive justification," Lucretia and the others were justified within themselves. 

Master Francesco [Petrarch] then gracefully and fittingly adds an ensign for this worthy and glorious company, saying that their noble and victorious ensign was of a pure white ermine with a noble and adorned collar of gold and topaz in the middle of a green field; which banner, spread to the wind, preceded Laura and the others. Wherefore he says:

<margin>R</margin>
<margin>To understand the preceding verses.</margin>
> Their victorious ensign was
> A white ermine in a green field;
> With fine gold and topazes reigning at its neck.

It is to be known principally that the universal purpose of banners and ensigns in wars and armies is to distinguish the leaders and show the variety of the ranks; so that by means of them, the soldiers or knights know where they must return to give aid to their own and provide for the needs of the confused and mixed battle. For this reason, banners serve in the distinction of other signs, which the intellect uses for the cognition of its meaning. Therefore, that sign is said to be most proper which is most conformed to the thing signified by it. For this reason, I do not doubt that among all signs, no other could be found more fitting to be indicated than the ensign of Lady Laura, which signifies the full dominion of reason over appetite. 

Wherefore, just as green signifies the proper disposition of vital principles, so too in this dominion, a man directly disposed to the blessed life through virtuous action—according to morals and according to faith—is prepared to receive divine grace, through which one lives eternally. And likewise, a man is similar and conformed to the ermine when reason dominates appetite; because by its nature, that little animal first consents to fall into the hands of those who follow it and to die rather than stain its whiteness. Whence those who seek ermines, as they see them come out of their hiding places and go to pasture, then place mud and other filthy matter over the openings [of their dens]. Thus, when it is chased by the hunter, fleeing to its lair and finding the outside polluted, it stops and allows itself to be taken, choosing to die rather than stain its great purity. It would be a long history to recount how many noble saints and how many martyrs first consented to receive death rather than lose their innocence, simply indicating that reason should be disposed to act in such a way. In this innocence and disposition, man is also very similar to gold, which in every test made of it always becomes more refined and perfect. And likewise, just as the topaz prohibits every boiling [of passion] and pollution, so...

-># THE TRIUMPH OF DEATH<-

...decreed as a punishment for the sin of our first parents <note>referring to Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden</note>: which, although according to Macrobius in his commentary on the *Dream of Scipio*, it is distinguished by a universal division—that is, into natural and violent—nevertheless, at present it is taken only in a general sense, and as common <term>to one and the other: meaning both natural and violent death</term>. This death, however it may occur, is certainly the "last of all terrible things" according to Aristotle in the third book of the *Ethics*. For this reason, even the humanity of Christ felt fear of it, as one reads in Saint Matthew in chapter 26, in Saint Mark in chapter 14, and in Saint Luke in chapter 22. 

The poet <note>Petrarch</note> appropriately compares this [fear] to the fury of the giants, the greatness of which the mind can only comprehend through judgment and reflection. For this reason, Ovid, in the fifth book of the *Metamorphoses*, writes that the gods fled to Egypt for fear of Typhoeus and the other giants, and in that place transformed themselves into diverse forms. The same Ovid also describes the giants as having fought against the gods in the Valley of Phlegra, which, according to Solinus in his *Wonders of the World*—and also other cosmographers—is located in Macedonia. They believed that in that place, through their great strength, they could overcome the gods and occupy the kingdom of heaven. 

However, in this passage, various opinions converge regarding the nature of the giants. Some say, on the authority of Macrobius in the *Saturnalia*, that the giants were not men of greater height than those who live today, but were merely an impious and cruel people who denied the power of the gods. From this, poets took the occasion to invent the story of the giants fighting the gods in the Valley of Phlegra. Others reject this opinion based on the authority of Holy Scripture: in Genesis chapters 6 and 10, and in the First Book of Kings <note>modern 1 Samuel</note> chapter 17, where it is affirmed that Nimrod and Goliath were giants due to their excessive size. Josephus also, in his *Antiquities of the Jews*, affirms that the giants were of immense size, although he does not provide a well-proven cause for their generation. Cicero, too, in his book *On Old Age*, seems to affirm the [metaphorical] nature of giants when he says:

<margin>N</margin>

> For what else is dying like giants battling the gods, if not resisting nature? <note>original: "Quid enim est aliud mori giga[n]tum bellare cu[m] dijs nisi repugnare nature."</note>

Therefore, it seems very appropriate for the poet to compare death to the fury of giants. Finally, Death is wrapped in a dark robe, black with horror. Wherefore Statius, in the eighth book of the *Thebaid*, describes Death with these verses:

<margin>O</margin>

> But if wars call for other new strengths to be fashioned, Calliope, and a greater Apollo extends the lyre to me; then for the peoples who of their own accord demand their fatal hour, the dark day moves away, sent forth from the shadows of the Styx. Death enjoys the sky and, flying, covers the warrior field, inviting men into her black gaping maw. She chooses nothing common, but only what is most worthy of life; rushing down, she marks with her serpent the funerals of those most distinguished in years and spirit. And now, for those wretched ones, every task of the Sisters <note>The Fates (Parcae)</note> is cut short, and the Furies have snatched the threads from the Fates. <note>original: "Sed si bella uocant alias nouas fingere uires... & furie rapueru[n]t litia parcis."</note>

This point is seen very clearly: <term>M. F.: Messer Francesco (Petrarch)</term> in his verses has conformed closely to Statius. Having thus encountered Madonna Laura, Death adds the words that the poet says she expressed toward Laura and her companions. He says that Death moved toward Laura and said: "O lady, you who go through the world proud and adorned with youth and beauty, and know not when the end of your life shall be: know that I am she whom you mortal men—a people truly deaf to hearing and blind to seeing the objects of your salvation, and for whom the darkest night falls before the setting of the sun—call so fierce, importunate, and cruel. And furthermore, know that I, with my piercing sword of the finest edge, have brought to their final end the Roman people, the Trojans, the Greeks, and other barbarian and foreign nations. When men think of me least and are least attentive, I then reach them and strike down and set aside their vain and infinite thoughts. Now, at present, while living delights you greatly, I have directed my course, intending to take you from life before Fortune places or commits any cause of bitterness or trouble into your sweet, wise, and pleasant thoughts." Wherefore he says:

# CHAPTER ONE

> I have brought the Greek people to their end,
> and finally the Trojans: the Romans
> with my sword, which pricks and cuts;
> and other barbarian and strange peoples;
> and arriving when others do not expect you,
> I have interrupted a thousand vain thoughts.
> Now toward you, when living is most delightful,
> I direct my course forward; so that fortune
> may put some bitterness into your sweetness.
<note>These lines are from Petrarch's *Triumph of Death*, where Death speaks to Laura, the poet's beloved.</note>

In Matthew, chapter 24 <note>original: "al. xxiij capi."</note>, it is said: *Therefore you also must be ready, for you know not the day nor the hour when the Son of Man is coming* <note>original: "Ideo & uos estote parati qa nescitis diem neq; horam qñ filius hoïs venturus est"</note>. But the reason for this is given in Deuteronomy, chapter 32, where the text speaks in the person of God: *I shall kill and I shall make to live: see that I am alone and there is no other god besides me* <note>original: "Ego occidã & ego uiuere faciã: uidete ꝙ ego sim solus & nō sit alius deus ꝓ ter me"</note>. Since death and life are immediate effects proceeding from God, it is therefore impossible for them to be understood by the human intellect when they arrive. For this reason, Solomon, in Ecclesiastes <note>The text says "ecclesiastico al. xiiii," likely a slip for Ecclesiastes 9</note>, confirming this same sentiment, says: *I saw under the sun that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the learned, nor favor to the skilled, but time and chance, for man does not know his end in all things* <note>original: "Vidi que sub sole nec uelocium esse cursum: neq; fortium bellum: nec sapientiū panē: neq; doctorū diuitias: nec artificū gratiā sed tēpus: & casum que i omnibus nescit homo finem suum."</note>.

<margin>R</margin>
Secondly, it must be understood that the poet <note>Petrarch</note> with great reason calls the human multitude a "deaf and blind people." Deaf to the moral doctrine of the moralists, the warnings of the sacred canons and most just laws, and the sermons and persuasions of the most holy doctors of theology; but blind to the stupendous miracles of God worked through His saints, to the miraculous order of the universe, and to the knowledge of human frailty. From this follows, through greed and the dominance of appetite, the night of the obscurity of sin and the darkness of the intellect before the evening of the coming of death. This is shown to us by Christ in Saint Matthew, chapter 6, when he says: *The lamp of your body is your eye: if your eye is single, your whole body will be bright; but if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark* <note>original: "Lucerna corporis tui e oculus tuus: si oculus tuus fuerit simplex: totū corpus tuū lucidū erit: si autē oculus tuus fuerit nequā: totum corpus tuū tenebrosum erit."</note>.

<margin>S</margin>
*If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great will that darkness be* <note>original: "Si ergo lumē quod in te est tenebre sunt ipse tenebre quante erunt."</note>. Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> next demonstrates that the Divine Goodness has the greatest care and diligence for the salvation of our souls, by introducing Death telling Laura that he had directed his course toward her before fortune had put any bitterness into her sweet heart. Here it must be understood, according to the opinion of the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the first book of the *Ethics*, that the blessed and the wise are subject to the blows of fortune, by which they may be removed from a state of bliss. Whence Aristotle says: *Great and many things, if they are prosperous, make life more blessed. For they are both fitting with honor, and their use is good and virtuous. But if they are adverse, they crush and stain the blessed one. For they bring sadness and impede many operations* <note>original: "Grandia uero & multa si prospera sunt beatiorem uitā efficiunt... Si aut aduersa beatum conterunt qdem atq; inqnant. Nā & tristitiam afferunt & operationes multas ipediunt."</note>. And therefore, death being given by God as an inevitable punishment for the sin of our first parents—as written in the first part of Genesis—Augustine confirms it in his book *On the Faith to Peter*, and Ecclesiasticus, chapter 39, describes it saying: *Fire, hail, famine, and death: all these were created for vengeance* <note>original: "Ignis: grando: famis & mors omnia haec ad uindictam creata sunt."</note>. Death transfers itself into each person whenever God sees humans brought to the disposition necessary for eternal bliss; then He permits death to take them from the earth, so that being found in such a state of innocence, they may ascend to heaven. There they are totally exempt from the grave perils of the present life, for which reason it is fittingly said that no one can be called "saved" while they dwell in the world, according to the sentiment of Christ in Saint Luke, chapter 10, when He said: *Salute no one by the way* <note>original: "Nemine per uiam salutaueritis." This is a theological interpretation of the command to travel quickly.</note>.

<margin>T</margin>
Finally, it is to be noted that not without reason does Master Francesco say Death expressed to Laura that his flight had already been directed at her when living most delighted her. For it is good to die when life begins to delight; that is, when the soul is absolute and free from passions, and when a person takes delight only in themselves and their own good deeds. Dying in this disposition, the soul is without any doubt assumed into supreme bliss, which is the universal object of human desire, according to what the philosopher writes in the first book of the *Ethics* and Augustine in *The City of God*, who says: *For it is certain knowledge of all that all men want to be happy* <note>original: "Omnium enī certa scientia omnes hoīes se beatos esse uelle."</note>.

<margin>❦</margin>
It was fitting, then, for Laura to die at that time, since then living was most delightful to her. Master Francesco then adds the response of Laura, after she had thus heard Death speak to her, expressing these words: "O Death, in these excellent companions of mine, do you have no...

<margin>A wise and fitting response for a most excellent soul: our poet has described it as being that of Laura. For its understanding, one must know that death is of such a nature that once it has occurred, it can never return to the same individual; which the Apostle to the Hebrews in chapter 9 testifies when he says: **It is appointed for man to die once.** <note>original: "Statutum enim est homini semel mori."</note> Since Lucretia and Penelope <note>figures of ancient virtue and chastity</note> and Laura's other companions were already dead, they were for this reason totally withdrawn from the right and power of death. Likewise, Laura was subject to death in only a small part; being only subjected by the nature of the earthly body, while the soul remains absolute after dying according to the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "i. ii. de aĩa"</note>, Virgil in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*, and Cicero in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, along with the authority of all the sacred writings. **Mo** <note>This "Mo" likely serves as a section marker for the commentary by Bernardo Ilicino</note> And in these words he silently describes the pain of well-disposed souls when some person dies whose actions were the cause of following virtues more fervently: but these excellent men, considering that our rest is not in the present life, have the habit of desiring—like Madonna Laura—that through their death they might attain another life, one no longer subject to death; where they despise every earthly joy. And therefore the Apostle in Hebrews 13 says: **We have no lasting city here, but we seek one to come.** <note>original: "Non habemus hic ciuitatem manentem: sed futuram inquirimus."</note> And speaking of himself to the Philippians in the first chapter, he wrote: **I desire to be dissolved and be with Christ.** <note>original: "Dissolui cupio & esse cum Christo"</note> This is demonstrated in effect by the philosopher Cleombrotus of Ambracia, who (as Cicero writes in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations* and Augustine in the first book of *The City of God*), having read Plato's book on the immortality of the soul, through the desire to possess that life, threw himself from a wall to die, and died.

<margin>Therefore, death is nothing other than a separation of united parts—that is, soul and body—of which the soul remains unchanging while only the body is that which fails. Wherefore Cicero, in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, speaking on this subject regarding death, says: **For death is like a departure through the tearing apart and separation of those parts which, before death, were held together by some union.** <note>original: "Est enim interitus quasi discessus ex segregatiōe direptus earum partium: quae ante interitum iunctione aliqua tenebantur."</note> Wherefore, because of this, death is a singular grace for souls freed from sins when it comes upon them to lift them from the earth. Without fear, and without any pain."

¶ Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should be understood that Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, under the graceful fiction of the person of Death, intends to demonstrate a natural consideration and a fitting reasoning that men engage in every hour when they consider death to be an effect which naturally occurs to living things. This is as Socrates affirmed to the one who said to him, "The Athenians have condemned you to death." To which he replied: **And nature has condemned them.** <note>original: "Et illos natura."</note> By this, he showed that death can in no way be escaped. When reasonable men see this necessity, they always consider it, according to the sentiment of Plato in the *Phaedo* (transcribed by Tully <note>Cicero</note> in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*), which says: **The whole life of philosophers is a contemplation of death.** <note>original: "Tota eniz philosophorum vita cōmendatio est mortis." Note: "cōmendatio" is likely a scribal variant for "commentatio," meaning study or preparation.</note> From this, they always strive to persuade themselves to endure it patiently. This is especially true when the conscience is light; then the mind has no fear of <term>Aeacus</term>, <term>Minos</term>, and <term>Rhadamanthus</term> <note>the three judges of the underworld in Greek mythology</note> according to the pagans, or of the rigorous divine justice according to the Christian religion. Nor does one have grief over past evil deeds. Therefore, through this, one passes into the other life with a joyful soul and pleasant hope, because only the remorse of conscience and sin is what makes death seem difficult. This is the sentiment of Paul the Apostle in the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 15 (alleged once before in the *Triumph of Love*), where he says: **The sting of death is sin.** <note>original: "Stimulus autem mortis peccatum est."</note>

<margin>B</margin>
And for this reason, considering old age to be a troublesome age—whence Virgil, in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*, writes of it being at the entrance to hell, saying: **Before the porch itself and in the very jaws of Orcus, Grief and avenging Cares have set their beds; and pale Diseases dwell there, and sad Old Age.** <note>original: "Vestibulum ante ipsum primisq; i faucibus orci Luctus: & vltrices posuere cubilia curæ. Pallentesque habitant morbi tristisque senectus."</note> Because of this, righteous men desire to die in their youth, so that by overcoming natural forces with virtue, they do not stain their souls through extreme weariness and great impatience. Thus, dying in this state of youth with the purity of their conscience, they acquire the greatest glory, honor, and reward before God (the rewarder of all good works) and singular fame before the world, being always praised and commended as virtuous men. Having up to this point introduced Death as having finished her words, Messer Francesco now brings in the response of Laura, which is fitting for a sincere, wise soul and a friend of God. He says that after Laura had heard Death and the reasons alleged by her for why she should consent to die, and also her worthy offers, she replied: "O Death, just as it pleases that Lord who stays in heaven, and from there rules the universe and tempers every excess according to need, I consent to dying. And therefore, according to His will, you shall do with me what is done to others by natural law." Whence he says:

**A**s it pleases the Lord, who stays in heaven,
And from there rules and tempers the universe,
You shall do with me what is done with others.

<margin>C</margin>
¶ It is a manifest thing in the narrated response of Lady Laura that not only are modesty and prudence preserved—prudence in accepting death, and modesty in wishing herself to be equal to others—but also religion and reverence for divine commandments and civility. Beyond this, it confutes certain senseless and heretical opinions. Here it should be understood principally (as Lactantius writes in the first book of the *Divine Institutes*) how Pythagoras and Diagoras denied entirely the existence of the eternal God...
