<header>THE TRIUMPH OF DEATH, PART IV</header>

# THE TRIUMPH OF DEATH, PART IV

<margin>D</margin>
**G**od is often viewed through an erroneous opinion similar to that of the fool; of whom the prophet says in Psalm 52: *The fool has said in his heart, there is no God.* <note>Psalm 52:1 (or 53:1 in modern Bibles).</note> Some others, such as the Epicureans <note>Followers of Epicurus who believed gods were uninvolved in human affairs.</note> and Democritus, said that God was idle and performed no work in the affairs of this world. Beyond these, as Averroes <note>An influential Islamic philosopher from Spain known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> writes in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*, some imagined the sky itself to be God and the "prime mover," from which every effect in the world must proceed. There were also the Egyptians and other idolaters who perversely imagined the nature of God. Therefore, not to go on at length, it is well known that our poet <note>Petrarch</note> in the preceding verses has elegantly refuted these errors. The truth he expresses is primarily demonstrated by the prophets, approved and declared by the philosophers, and later celebrated by the pagan poets.

Firstly, regarding the heavens being the dwelling place of God, the prophet David says in the Psalm cited above: *God looked down from heaven upon the children of men.* <note>original: "Deus de celo prospexit super filios hominum."</note> And in the second book of Exodus, the text speaking in the person of God says: *You have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven.* <note>original: "Vos vidistis que de cælo loquutus sum vobis."</note> Likewise, Isaiah in chapter 66 demonstrates this, saying: *Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool.* <note>original: "Cælum est mihi sedes: & terra scabellum pedum meorum."</note> This same sentiment is confirmed by Aristotle in the first book of *On the Heavens* when he says: *Reason seems to testify to appearances, and appearances to reason. For all men have a common estimation of these things, and all attribute the place above to God—both barbarians and Greeks—whoever thinks there are gods; as they fit the immortal to the immortal.* <note>original: "Videtur autem ratio & apparentibus..." Aristotle argues that the universal human instinct to look upward when thinking of the divine is evidence of truth.</note>

<margin>E</margin>
And in the little book *On the World* addressed to Alexander <note>A text attributed to Aristotle in the Middle Ages, though now usually considered "Pseudo-Aristotle."</note>, speaking of God, he says: *He has obtained the highest and primary seat for himself; for which reason he is called the Most High, and according to the poet, he resides on the supreme summit of the universe.* This same fact is confessed by Virgil in the tenth book of the *Aeneid*, where he writes these verses for this purpose: *The home of almighty Olympus opens, and the king of gods and men calls a council to the starry seat, from where, on high, he looks upon all lands, the Trojan camp, and the Latin people.* <note>original: "Pandit̃ itereã domus oĩpotẽtis olympi..." Virgil describes Jupiter presiding over the world from the heavens.</note> Nor does Ovid depart from this true and common opinion at the beginning of the *Metamorphoses*; where, having spoken of the works performed by God, he adds: *After he unrolled these things and took them from the blind heap [of chaos], he bound the things separated by location in harmonious peace. The fiery power of the vaulted and weightless heaven flashed out and chose the highest place for its citadel.* <note>original: "Quæ postq̃ euoluit..." Ovid describes the creation of the cosmos from Chaos.</note>

It remains manifest, then, that God's seat is in heaven—not, however, by a restriction of space, since God is incorporeal, nor by a partial designation or definition of a single point, since he is present at every point in the world and present in every place—but only because the intuitive enjoyment of the blessed is in heaven.

Similarly, regarding divine governance, heretical wickedness is confounded. In this cause, I shall pass over the sacred doctors of theology, most especially Augustine in the third book of *On the Trinity* and his *Literal Commentary on Genesis*, and likewise leaving aside the Gospel text of John in the first chapter and the beginning of Genesis, and not worrying about Isidore in his book *On the Supreme Good* or Isaiah in chapter 49. Instead, it shall suffice only to refer to the authority of the pagans, from which it is understood that the most high God governs whatever thing exists in this world.

Aristotle, primarily to Alexander in the book *On the World*, says: *For in truth, God is the Savior and father of all things, whatever and however they happen in this world.* And he adds: *For all passions, both those in the air and those upon the earth and those in the water, are truly said to be the works of God. And according to the naturalist Empedocles, all things that are, and shall later be, proceeded from him.* And in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*, speaking of God, he says: *From this principle depend the heavens and all of nature.* Cicero also says in the sixth book of the *Republic* for this purpose: *For there is nothing to that primary God*

<margin>F</margin>
*who rules the whole world, among all things that happen on earth, more acceptable than the gatherings and assemblies of men joined by law, which are called states.* <note>original: "Nihil est enim principi illi deo..." This is from the "Dream of Scipio," a famous passage on the soul and the cosmos.</note> Through these words, it is clearly seen that Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> attributes the beginning of this universe to God. And Pliny does not depart from this opinion. Hence, in his *Panegyric* to the Emperor Trajan, he says: *The elders, O Conscript Fathers, established well and wisely that just as with the conduct of business, so should the beginning of speaking start with prayers, because men should begin nothing properly or providently without the work, counsel, honor, and auspices of the immortal gods.*

Livy also writes the same in the third book of *From the Founding of the City*; where, after Appius Claudius <note>A Roman official famous for his tyranny and the tragedy of Virginia.</note> was imprisoned through the work of Virginius, as we said above, he says: *They grumbled at last that there are gods, and if their punishments for cruelty come late, they are nonetheless not light.* And in the speech of Pontius Herennius to the Samnites, he writes: *Since nothing is left of human law when facing a more powerful force, I shall flee to the gods as judges of intolerable pride and I shall pray.* He affirms the same in the ninth book of the *Second Punic War* in the speech of the Locrians against Pleminius, introducing the example of Pyrrhus when he plundered the temple of Proserpine. Caesar himself contests this in the *Gallic Commentaries* where he says: *the immortal gods, to bring heavier grief for their sins, sometimes grant [prosperity to wicked men]...*

<header>CHAPTER ONE</header>

# CHAPTER ONE

...ever more lasting and long-enduring. But the aforementioned plurality of gods is finally reduced to one single principal ruler, as Virgil aptly demonstrates in the first book of the *Aeneid*, when he introduces Venus speaking to Jove after the loss of Aeneas:
> O you who rule the affairs of men and gods with eternal commands and terrify them with your lightning. <note>original Latin: "O qui rex hoiu~que deu~q; æternis regis impiis & fulmine terres." This is a famous address to Jupiter from Virgil's Aeneid, Book I, line 229.</note>

Finally, Averroes, in the second book of his *Physics*, while conceding that nature acts toward a determined end, concludes that God has care and concern for all things in the world. He adds that the eternal God, who dwells in heaven, rules and tempers—that is to say, as the poet says—the entire world from that place. Secondly, it should be understood that Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> introduces Laura as consenting to death only according to the divine will, and not absolutely by her own choice. For it is prohibited not only by the Christian religion to desire or perform the act of dying before it is the will of God, but also by the noble philosophers. Among others, Pythagoras, in the precepts he gave to his disciples, said: <sig>G</sig>
> Know that one must not depart from one's station except by the command of the general. <note>original Latin: "Scitote naque discedendum no~ esse de statione nisi iussu imperatoris." This metaphor compares life to a military post that one cannot abandon without orders from the commander (God).</note>

And Cicero, in *The Dream of Scipio*, introduces Paulus Aemilius responding to Scipio (who wanted to kill himself to reach the possession of those goods he saw his father enjoying) by saying:
> For unless that God, whose temple is all this which you behold, has freed you from the prison of the body, the entrance hither cannot be open to you. <note>original Latin: "Nisi enim cu~ deus is cuius est hoc te~plu~ oẽ quod conspicistis te corporis custodiis liberaurit: huc tibi aditus patere no~ potest." A key Stoic argument against suicide.</note>

And in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, he describes the same effect thus:
> For that ruling God forbids us to depart hence without his order. <note>original Latin: "Vetat enim nobis dominans ille deus in iussu hinc suo nos demigrare."</note>

But if some cause arises by which it is known that it pleases God that a man should die, then everyone ought to rejoice that through death he is lifted from the earth. As in the same book, Cicero adds:
> When indeed God himself has given a just cause—as then to Socrates, and often to many like Cato—then, by my faith, let that wise man depart joyfully from these shadows into that light; yet let him not break the bonds of his prison. For the laws forbid it; but let him go out as if called and released by a magistrate or some lawful power, even so by God. <note>original Latin: "Cum uero ca~m iustam deus ipse dederit... Nec tame~ illa vincula carceris ruperit." Mentions Socrates and Cato as examples of those whose deaths were seen as divinely sanctioned or noble.</note>

A sentiment truly worthy, not only for a pagan unexperienced in the Christian religion but fitting and appropriate for even the most holy person within it. Laura, therefore, consented to die, as befits a most prudent soul, once the divine will had ordained it—that is, as a holy, religious, and devoted mind. The poet gracefully admonishes everyone in the preceding verses to act according to her example. But if someone here should say this sentiment is invalidated by the authority of the Church, which defines Samson as being saved despite killing himself violently, the answer is that his killing was permitted by God and approved to take vengeance for Him and for Israel against the Philistines. The text in the Book of Judges shows this, where it almost always says of Samson's actions:
> The spirit of the Lord rushed upon Samson. <note>original Latin: "Irruit spiritus domini in sansone." Refers to Judges 14:6 and similar passages, justifying Samson's final act as a divine mandate rather than simple suicide.</note>

Thus, he did not deviate from the divine will, although he inflicted death upon himself in such a manner. Now that the poet has described Laura’s consent to die and the presence of Death and her will to kill her, he turns the narrative to the state of mortality. He shows that man, however virtuous and glorious he may have been in life, is nonetheless required to obey death. Likewise, through silence, he implies that Laura was counted among the great crowd which he saw after her response—those who had died upon the face and surface of the world. <sig>H</sig> He says that as soon as Laura had answered Death, he saw from across a great number and such a crowd of the dead that the entire countryside—stretching from India to Cathay, and from Morocco to Spain—was full of them. It was incomprehensible and unspeakable by human tongue, whether in prose or in verse. There one could see the bodies of those who in the present life were esteemed happy: that is, kings, emperors, and popes. Nevertheless, today they are stripped of their limbs, miserable in spirit, and beggars of external riches, according to common opinion. Whence he says:

<margin>

Refers to Romans 5:12, explaining the theological origin of death through Adam.</note>

-># THE TRIUMPH OF DEATH<-

<unclear>Just</unclear> as sin entered into this world through one man, and through sin, death: so death passed into all men, in whom all have sinned. <note>original Latin: "Quem in hunc mundum peccatū ītrauit..." This is a reference to the Epistle to the Romans 5:12, establishing the theological origin of death.</note> This is confirmed by Augustine in the book *On Vices and Lusts* and in the transcript of *On Faith to Peter*, as well as in the decree *De consecratione*, distinction four, in the chapter *Firmissimes*.

<margin>I</margin>
> There were those who were called happy:
> Popes, rulers, and emperors;
> Now they are naked, poor, and beggars.

where it says: "Hold most firmly and do not doubt in any way that every human who is conceived through the sexual union of man and woman is born with original sin." <note>original Latin: "Firmissime tene: z nullatenus dubites..." A standard theological citation regarding the universality of the Fall.</note> For this reason, all men who were ever born are subject to death, except for those whom the Christian religion affirms are reserved until the Day of Judgment as witnesses to the divine incarnation. <note>This likely refers to figures like Enoch and Elijah, who in tradition were taken up to heaven without dying.</note> Neither worldly wisdom, nor any royal or papal dignity, nor any other status can free us from this death;

<margin>K</margin> because before divine justice there is no acceptance or partiality toward specific persons, just as the Apostle writes to the Ephesians in chapter six, when he says: "There is no respect of persons with God." <note>original Latin: "Acceptio personarū non est apud deū," from Ephesians 6:9.</note> Therefore, in that great crowd of the dead were gathered the popes, emperors, and kings who were considered happy by the common people, but who later became quite beggarly and miserable. It was reasonable that the entire countryside was full, from India to Cathay <note>an archaic name for China</note>, from Morocco to Spain—that is, the extremes and the middle of the world which the poet intends to describe through these locations. This is not because they are diametrically opposed, but because by "India" he means the southern part; by "Cathay"—which although it is in India, is nevertheless at its furthest extremity toward the East—he means the eastern region. Similarly, by "Morocco," which is a western region being situated toward Mount Atlas, he means the West; and by "Spain" he means the North, as it is located quite close to that direction. <note>The commentator is mapping Petrarch's geography to the four cardinal directions: South, East, West, and North.</note>

<margin>L</margin> Therefore, since these four places signify the principal regions of the world, the crowd that lay upon this plain was rightfully large. Afterward, the poet justly cries out and rebukes the blind and intense greed of men, and the labor so uselessly lost in acquiring possessions and kingdoms, hoping they might be a cause of peace when in fact they are a source of continual distress and perturbation of the soul. He says: "O mortals, entirely blind and heedless, too greedy for fleeting and transitory things! Where are the riches and treasures possessed by secular and ecclesiastical princes now? Where are the splendid gold vases and those of purified silver? Where is the multitude of horses? Where are the precious gems? Where are the ornate and most wealthy scepters? Where are the gleaming crowns? Where are the purple colors? <note>Purple was the traditional color of imperial and high-ranking status.</note> Where are the joyful beds? And finally, where are the mitres, the reverences, the prayers, and the submissions once made to them by an almost infinite number of men?"

<margin>M</margin> O truly miserable and unhappy is he who places his hope in a mortal thing! Indeed, having placed it there, it is with great reason and justice that he is deceived in the end. O worldly ones, entirely deprived of all light, what does it profit you, or what utility does the immense labor and intolerable suffering bring to acquire reputation and dominion? For in a short space of time, you will all return to your ancient earth and original mother, and your name will hardly be found mentioned among men. I pray you, tell me—you who with the greatest industry and diligence attend to your studies, desires, and operations—if even one among a thousand of your ancient, finished labors is profitable, or if they are not all instead vanities and shadows? Tell me also what value or what firmness and stability is gained by subjugating countries, kingdoms, and the regions of others, and making barbarian nations and strange peoples pay you tribute, when they always have their souls inflamed toward your harm, death, and ruin? Especially when pursuing vain and dangerous enterprises where lands and treasures are acquired with blood; whereas truly, a life fed only on simple bread and water in a vessel of wood or glass is found to be much sweeter and more peaceful than that of gems, gold, and delicate, exquisite foods. Finally, the poet concludes that rather than continuing such a long subject as this, it is time to return to his earlier work. Whence he says:

<margin>N</margin> How health-giving, how true, and how holy is the rebuke given by our excellent poet in the preceding verses; each person can understand it for themselves better than it can be... <note>The sentence breaks off as the commentary transitions back to the verse.</note>

> Where are the riches now? Where are the honors?
> And the gems, and the scepters, and the crowns,
> The mitres with purple colors?

# CHAPTER ONE

> Wretched is he who places hope in mortal things,
> (But who is there who does not?) and if he finds himself
> Deceived in the end, it is only right.
> O blind ones, what does so much labor profit you?
> You all return to the great ancient mother <note>The "great ancient mother" is a poetic reference to the Earth, where all bodies are buried.</note>;
> And your name is hardly to be found.
> Of a thousand labors, is there even one useful one?
> So that they are not all revealed as vanities;
> Let him who understands your studies tell me so.
> What is the value of subjugating so many lands,
> And making foreign peoples tributary
> With minds always inflamed to their own harm?
> After perilous and vain undertakings,
> And acquiring lands and treasure with blood,
> One finds water and bread far sweeter,
> And glass and wood, than gems and gold.
> But to follow such a long theme no further;
> It is time for me to return to my primary work.

No tongue can fully explain: for this is most just in itself, and in every part founded upon divine law and Christian doctrine. For its understanding, it is principally necessary to know that at its first questioning—where are the honors, riches, gems, scepters, and crowns, the mitres and purple colors of past princes?—no other answer can be given than that which Solomon writes: namely, "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity." <note>original Latin: "vanita di vanitata ogni cosa e vanita," referring to Ecclesiastes 1:2.</note> This is taught to us not only by Ecclesiastes at the beginning, but experience in our own times clearly demonstrates it to us. We have seen the deaths of such singular popes: Eugenius, Nicholas, Calixtus, and Pius <note>Popes Eugenius IV (d. 1447), Nicholas V (d. 1455), Calixtus III (d. 1458), and Pius II (d. 1464).</note>—the light, glory, and honor not only of the magnificent and exalted city of Siena, but of all Italy and the Christian name likewise. Similarly, that most serene King Alfonso of Aragon, <note>Alfonso V of Aragon (d. 1458), a great patron of Renaissance learning.</note> certainly the equal of any prince, whether Latin or Greek; the most illustrious Duke Filippo Maria, <note>Filippo Maria Visconti (d. 1447), Duke of Milan.</note> in spirit and liberality not inferior to Alexander; and likewise the most glorious Francesco Sforza, <note>Francesco Sforza (d. 1466), who succeeded the Visconti as Duke of Milan.</note> a duke so worthy and excellent in every virtue that he rendered himself superior or equal to the Greek Epaminondas. Similarly, finally, Leonello and Borso d'Este, <note>Brothers who ruled Ferrara; Leonello (d. 1450) and Borso (d. 1471).</note> most just dukes, in whom the prudence of Fabius, the strength of Caesar, the long-suffering of Sertorius, the dexterity of Marcellus, and the good fortune of Cornelius Sulla were seen to be held fast in a just dominion.

Secondly, it is to be understood that one may rightly be called wretched who has placed
<margin>O</margin> hope in earthly or mortal things. For hope is a virtuous habit suitable only to men. Concerning this, the poets write that when the gods returned by the command of Jove to their own realms—either up in heaven or below in hell—only Hope remained in the world and among living men. This is because neither those above nor those below can hope in any way: the former possess every good, and the latter are condemned to eternal punishments. From this opinion the sacred theologians do not deviate in the third book of the *Sentences*, <note>Refers to Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*, the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> saying that in the heavenly homeland there is not properly faith or hope as a virtue, because it is no longer enigmatic or speculative, but a clear and open vision of things to be believed and hoped for. Therefore, hope is, according to the Master of the Sentences in the cited book at the 26th distinction, a virtue by which spiritual and eternal goods are hoped for and expected with confidence. From this it appears manifest that the true object of hope is firm, immobile, and exempt from all variety and change. For this reason, a mortal object is repugnant to the essence of hope; therefore, he who expects and only desires such a thing is deprived of true hoping, and thus is truly wretched. Since happiness is attained by means of hope, it is quite reasonable that anyone who esteems and prizes fragile and fleeting things as stable and permanent should find himself deceived in the end. 

There are nonetheless some texts which say: "Wretched is he who places hope in mortal things; but who does not
<margin>P</margin> place it there? And if he finds himself deceived in the end, it is a great reason." Where the poet used a graceful and silent rebuke, consistent with the text of Solomon in Wisdom when he says: <term>Blessed is the man who has not gone after gold: who is he, and we will praise him?</term> <note>original Latin: "Beatus vir qui nō abiit post aurū: quis ē hic & laudabimus eū," from the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 31:8.</note> This sentiment and these verses can be held as primary. In the third place, with great reason, all those are to be called blind who labor so much for the acquisition of temporal goods; because in a short time, man returns to his first origin, which is the earth—a thing which the Scripture manifests at the beginning...

Having previously discussed the universal law of mortality, the commentator now uses classical and biblical examples to illustrate how Earth is our final mother and why worldly power is a source of vanity and strife compared to the peace found in poverty.</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF DEATH

<margin>Q</margin> In the beginning of Genesis, it is said: *God formed man from the mud of the earth* <note>original Latin: "Formauit Deus hoiem ex limo terre"</note>; which earth is truly our mother. As proof of this, Livy testifies in the first book of *From the Founding of the City* that after Tarquin the Proud <note>The legendary seventh and final king of Rome.</note> had conquered the Gabii, his sons went to the oracle at Delphi <note>The text uses "Adelphos," the Greek word for brothers, to refer to the sons of Tarquin.</note> to ask which of them should succeed to the kingdom. On this journey, they also took with them Junius Brutus. When the oracle responded that he would rule in Rome after Tarquin who first kissed his mother, Brutus pretended to fall to the ground and kissed it. The sons of Tarquin, not understanding the hidden meaning of the response, hurried back to Rome to kiss their literal mother. And so it followed that when Tarquin was driven out of Rome, the first consul elected by the Romans was Brutus, and he succeeded to the Roman dominion. Thus, one can rightly argue that the earth is our ancient mother, to whom we return when the name that was so glorious in life is almost totally extinguished.

<margin>R</margin> How vain human works are when devoted to the possession of temporal goods is sufficiently shown by Solomon, as we said above at the beginning of Ecclesiastes: *Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. For what does a man have from all his labor which he toils at under the sun?* <note>original Latin: "Vanitas vanitatum & omnia vanitas. Quid enim habet homo de uniuerso labore suo quod laborat sub sole." Referencing Ecclesiastes 1:2-3.</note> And there he affirms of himself that he had enjoyed all worldly delights, and yet they were to him nothing but vanity and affliction of spirit. Among such activities, the most damaging is that by which one acquires more dominion; for according to what the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> writes in the first book of the *Politics*, there is always a natural enmity between master and servant. Therefore, he who acquires more servants only multiplies his mortal enemies.

<margin>S</margin> Lastly, it should be noted how much sweeter and quieter the life of joyful poverty is than that of gems and gold. Solomon shows this in the fifth chapter of Ecclesiastes when he says: *Better is a handful with rest, than both hands full with labor and affliction of the soul.* <note>original Latin: "Melius est pugillus cū requie: quã plena vtraq; manus cū labore & afflictione animi." Referencing Ecclesiastes 4:6.</note> Similarly, Seneca, in his fourth letter to Lucilius, approves this sentiment, saying: *Great riches are poverty settled by law. For he who gets along well with poverty is rich.* <note>original Latin: "Magnæ diuitiæ sunt lege composita paupertas. Nā qui cū paupertate bene conuenit diues est."</note> Solinus <note>A 3rd-century Roman geographer.</note> also says the same in *The Wonders of the World*: *For Cornelius Sulla was called "fortunate" rather than actually being so; the oracle of Delphi judged only Aglaus of Psophis truly happy, who, as the owner of a poor plot of land in the narrowest corner of Arcadia, was found never to have crossed the boundaries of his father's field.* <note>Solinus recounts this to show that the happiest man was not the Roman dictator Sulla, but a poor farmer who never left home.</note> Countless other authorities and examples could be cited to prove this proposition, which we will omit for now as unnecessary evidence in a well-known case. Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch.</note> then descends to the observation of a loving custom of faithful lovers, which is to observe every act of their beloveds and to celebrate and extol them to increase their fame and honor. After having described Laura consenting to death, and deplored human misery, and rebuked intense greed, he returns consequently to narrating the passing of Laura and the actions of those standing by. He says that the final hour of the worthy and glorious life of Madonna Laura had already arrived, along with that doubtful step of death, from which the whole world rightly trembles. Many excellent ladies, all her neighbors and close friends, had come to visit her and stood there intently to see if Laura's death would be merciful. And in this state, contemplating the end of our life—which everyone must necessarily face only once—death plucked the golden hair from Laura’s fair head, her blessed soul dedicated to wearing in heaven the eternal laurel crown granted by God to blessed souls. Thus he says:

At the first hour on the sixth day of April, I entered the labyrinth: nor do I know how to exit it. <note>Petrarch famously fell in love with Laura on April 6, 1327, and she died on the same date in 1348. He often refers to his obsessive love as a "labyrinth."</note> Thus it is no wonder if he [Petrarch] grieved bitterly, since that same day brought him the affliction of Laura's death and the memory of the beginning of his love; he returned to his laments, seeing himself deprived of such sweetness.

<margin>H</margin>
Secondly, it is to be understood with what powerful and effective reasoning the poet says that it was a debt to the world and to the age then passing that he should be cast out of life before Laura. Here it must be considered that often a composite thing is denoted by its most noble part: just as when we say "man is intelligent and knowing" only because the soul knows and understands, according to the doctrine of the philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle</note> in the fourth book of the *Physics*. Therefore, the world being defined by Aristotle in his book *On the World* <note>original Latin: "Mundus est aggregatū ex cælo & terræ: & his quæ infra hæc sunt," meaning "The world is an aggregate of the heaven and the earth, and those things which are beneath them."</note> in this form: because of this, he often says the world has produced a single effect that has come from the disposition of the heavens: and especially the <term>generation and corruption</term> <note>The medieval scientific terms for birth/creation and death/decay.</note> of things, which proceeds to us from heaven solely through the operation and movement of the sun. Hence the philosopher says in the second book of the *Physics*: "The sun and man generate man" <note>original Latin: "Sol & homo generant hominem."</note> and in the second book of *On Generation*: "The motion of the sun in the circle of the Zodiac brings us toward generation and leads us away [to death]." Therefore, there being one and the same cause for generation and corruption, it was a fitting thing that **Master Francesco** <note>Petrarch himself.</note> having been generated first, should also be "corrupted" [die] before Laura—especially since time is the cause of corruption, as is written in the fourth book of the *Physics*. It was also a debt that Master Francesco should depart first because, being older, he was less powerful to resist the causes of physical change than the youth of Laura; thus he should have reached death sooner.

The poet returns again to narrate the words which the women who came to Laura's funeral spoke; they reasoned in their weeping, saying that while the women stood with great sadness and affliction around the most chaste bed, they said crying: "Alas for us now, if in Laura’s body virtue, grace, and beauty are dead; now what will become of us? Who will ever see again in a woman more lovely acts, perfect signs, and gestures of the finest character? Who will ever again hear a speech full of wisdom and modesty similar to Laura’s? Who will there be who ever understands the sweetness of her song, which was full of such delight that it showed itself to be like the angels?" Wherefore he says:

**Virtue is dead, and beauty and courtesy:**
**The beautiful women around the chaste bed**
**Sadly said: "Now what shall become of us?**
**Who shall ever see in a woman a perfect act?**
**Who will hear speech full of wisdom,**
**And song full of angelic delight?"**

<margin>I</margin>
The poet demonstrates quite clearly in this <term>womanly lament</term> <note>original: "muliebre lamento," a traditional poetic scene of mourning.</note> how reasonably the women discourse, arguing that if Laura—in whom there was such excellence of beauty and virtue—was dead, they could not hope for well-being for themselves. And also, Laura being as it were their rule and example for living, and she being gone, they did not know how to judge what should become of them in the future. Thus, we can understand from these verses that the greatest and most singular praise was attributed to Laura by our poet. 

Then our graceful poet adds that a disposition of the blessed souls was granted to the spirit of Lady Laura, saying that the spirit—already <term>solitary</term> <note>original: "romito," literally "hermit-like" or self-contained.</note> within itself and encompassed by all worthy and singular virtues—had, through its departure from that beautiful breast and most noble body of Laura, returned a very great serenity and light to that part of heaven which was above Laura’s house. Wherefore he says:

**The spirit, departing from that beautiful breast,**
**With all its virtues solitary within itself,**
**Had made the sky serene in that quarter.**

# THE TRIUMPH OF DEATH

Since serenity is nothing other than the presence of a most lucid object, it is therefore appropriate that Laura’s departure—being herself luminous—made that part of the heaven where she ascended to supernatural glory serene by her presence. Consequently, the prior disposition through which Laura's soul had become luminous—that is, her being without sin—meant that none of the adversaries of human nature <note>The "adversaries" refers to demons or fallen angels who were believed to haunt the deathbeds of sinners to tempt them to despair.</note> had such audacity that they appeared with their dark sight to Laura until death had totally completed its assault. Hence he says:

-> None of the adversaries was so bold; <-
-> That they ever appeared with a dark gaze, <-
-> Until death had finished its assault. <-

<margin>L</margin>
For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses: it is important to know that after the angelic nature sinned before God—whereupon the rebel angels were submerged in the deep hell—and man was created for the restoration and possession of those eternal seats, the demon always bore the greatest envy toward man. As Augustine <note>Saint Augustine (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian theologian.</note> writes in the last chapter of *The City of God*, where he says:

> Juno did not envy the Trojans (from whom Rome takes its fleshly origin) or the Roman arts as much as these demons (whom some still think are gods) envy the eternal seats for all of mankind. <note>original Latin: "Non tam Iuno troianis: a quibus Roma carnalem ducis originē: artes vľ iuidisse Romanis q̄ isti demones quos adhuc deos putat: oī generi hoīum sedes iuident sempiternas."</note>

<margin>M</margin>
From this it happens that, in order to harm man when he finds himself in the agony of death, the demon appears, bringing to his memory all his sins and demonstrating them to be such that he could never deserve mercy from God. He strives to lead the soul to desperation and thus deceive it, for such is always his nature; as the same Augustine writes in the third book of the aforementioned work, chapter seven, saying:

> For the demons, always most watchful to deceive, have done what they could. <note>original Latin: "Nā demones semp ad decipiēdū uigilantissimi q̄ potuerūt fecerunt"</note>

It is therefore the highest praise of Laura that no sin was found in her through which the demon could take the opportunity to appear to her and attempt to deceive her. The poet then adds how, after long weeping and suppressed fear, the ladies who were such friends to Laura reacted, saying that having set aside their weeping and cruel lamentation, and likewise the same fear, each of them was intent on the beautiful face of Laura; and they held their eyes fixed upon it, and were made secure, not by comfort, but by desperation. Hence he says:

-> After the weeping and the fear were set aside, <-
-> Each one was intent only on the beautiful face, <-
-> And made secure through desperation. <-

<margin>N</margin>
It is a fitting thing that when a person sees no more way to escape a thing they greatly fear, they eventually become secure <note>In this context, "secure" means certain or resolute, having moved past the agitation of fear into the stillness of the inevitable.</note> regarding it, just as happened to Laura's companions, who, seeing her dead, had come to despair of themselves and regarding their own way of living because of the necessity of death.

<margin>O</margin>
Hence, on this subject, Quintus Curtius <note>A Roman historian, likely the author of a history of Alexander the Great.</note> says:

> Necessity also sharpens cowardice, and desperation is often the cause of hope. <note>original Latin: "Ignauia quoq; necessitas acuit: & sepe despatio cā spei est."</note>

From which, with a similar sentiment, Virgil <note>The famous Roman poet, author of the Aeneid.</note> writes in the second book of the *Aeneid* when he says:

> The only safety for the conquered is to hope for no safety. <note>original Latin: "Vna salus victis nullā sperare salutē."</note>

Therefore, the poet deservedly describes those already mentioned as having become secure through desperation. He then describes her final end, and what the transition of the consumed Laura was like after her strength was weakened, saying that the soul, content to die, went from this life to the next in peace: not like a flame that is extinguished by force and violence, but which by itself consumes and dissolves, just like a clear and sweet light whose nourishment <note>i.e., the oil in a lamp</note> fails; and in this dissolution, she always preserved her clear character, firmness, and perfection of intellect until the end. Hence he says:

-> Not like a flame that by force is spent, <-
-> But which by itself is consumed: <-
-> The content soul went away in peace, <-
-> In the manner of a sweet and clear light <-
-> Whose nourishment fails little by little, <-
-> Holding to its usual custom until the end. <-

<margin>P</margin>
Messer Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the author of the poem.</note> excellently compares the triumph of Laura to the failing of the light's nourishment, wanting to show that there was no violence in her ending, but only a natural dissolution. Here it is to be understood that the principles of our life—as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC).</note> says in *On the Cause of the Length and Brevity of Life*, and Avicenna <note>A Persian physician and philosopher (c. 980–1037 AD) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook.</note> in the first book of the first part—are natural heat and radical moisture <term>Radical Moisture: a medieval medical concept describing the fundamental fluid of the body that acts as fuel for life's "natural heat"; death occurs when this fluid is exhausted.</term>. From which man is the subject and matter of the heat, which continually from the day of our birth is resolved... <note>The text ends here as a catchword for the next page: "is resolved" or "is dissolved."</note>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch's "Triumph of Death," specifically concluding the analysis of Chapter One regarding the physical state of Laura’s body and the philosophical nature of dying, before transitioning to Chapter Two, which addresses the immortality of the soul.</meta>

# CHAPTER ONE

The body dissolves and turns to earth according to the course of our age: its dissolution is inhibited only so long as the natural heat acts upon the fluid influx of food. For this reason, Hippocrates <note>Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BC), the ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> said in the first section of the *Aphorisms*: "Those who are growing have the most innate heat; therefore, they require the most nourishment." <note>original Latin: "q crescũt plurimũ habent inatũ calorē plurimo ergo indigent nutrimento."</note> If it is not nourished, the body is consumed. When the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>The "radical moisture" was a medieval medical concept representing the finite, vital fluid every human is born with; its exhaustion resulted in death.</note> is depleted and dissolved, life ends; just as when the oil that feeds the flame is gone, that light is immediately extinguished.

<margin>Q</margin>
Finally, the poet turns his prose to narrate the appearance of Laura’s dead body, saying that it held no paleness, but was white in the likeness of pure snow that falls upon the mountains without the force of storms or winds. She seemed to be resting, as sometimes happens to people who have become weary from great exertion. Thus, once the spirit was divided from her, that which foolish men call "dying" seemed like a sweet sleep and a gentle slumber, so that without any doubt, death—when considered in Laura’s face—demonstrated itself to be beautiful. As he says:

<gloss>
How great Laura's beauty was can be well known from the preceding verses, since the darkness and horror of death, when placed and set within her beautiful face, demonstrated and appeared to be a beautiful thing. Only that beautiful body remained, white due to the <term>mortification of the spirits</term> <note>The withdrawal of the "vital spirits" believed to animate the flesh.</note>, whereas the natural whiteness of the flesh usually appears vivid and ruddy. Truly, it seemed like a gentle sleep.

> **P**ale, no; but whiter than the snow
> That falls without wind upon a lovely hill;
> She seemed to rest like a weary person.
> **A**s if a sweet sleep were in her beautiful eyes,
> The spirit having already departed from her,
> It was that which the foolish call dying:
> **D**eath appeared beautiful in her beautiful face.

That which foolish, unlearned, and coarse men call "dying" is misunderstood; for in truth, "dying" occurs while life lasts, but once life is finished, one no longer "dies." And therefore Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), Roman statesman and philosopher.</note> appropriately says in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: "You have sleep as the image of death, and you put it on daily." <note>original Latin: "Habes somnum imaginez mortis: eãq; quotidie induis."</note> But Seneca explains this much more extensively in his first letter to Lucilius when he says: "Whom can you show me who places any value on time, who weighs the worth of a day, who understands that he is dying daily? In this we are deceived: that we look forward to death; a great part of it has already passed. Whatever of our age is behind us, death holds." <note>original Latin: "Quē mihi dabis: q aliquod precium tempori ponat... mors tenet."</note> Finally, Augustine in the fifth book of *The City of God*, defining life in chapter eleven, amply demonstrates how ignorant all those are who call the end of our life "dying," saying: "This life is a disposition of the dying and a succession of the dead." <note>original Latin: "Vita hæc est di sitio morientiũ: e successio mortuorum."</note> From this it is manifest that when death reaches men, at that point all power of dying is totally finished. Most famous is that golden maxim: "When we are born, we begin to die; when we die, we cease to die." <note>original Latin: "Cum nascimur mori inci- pimus: cum vero morimur desinimus mori."</note>
<margin>S</margin>

## EXPOSITION OF THE SECOND CHAPTER OF THE TRIUMPH OF DEATH

<margin>T</margin>
**H**uman nature—however much it may be perfect in every part regarding bodily beauty, excellence of intellectual habits, glory, and honor—is surrounded by and subject to natural variations and to death, as has been sufficiently said by our excellent poet in the preceding chapter. But because that preceding section shows nothing further regarding the third state of the soul—which is to remain simple and naked by itself after its separation from the body—the poet in the present chapter intends to describe this immortality of the soul by gracefully feigning the testimony of the soul of Lady Laura. Here, by a universal argument, he intends to prove the difficult doctrine of the eternity of our souls, which is denied by the <term>Epicureans</term> <note>Followers of Epicurus, who believed the soul was material and perished with the body.</note> and by those who affirm that nothing can exist beyond that which is perceived by the senses. Having done this, he intends to clear every doubt that might have arisen concerning his love and Laura’s continence, not deviating from the custom of grateful lovers who primarily desire no blame for their beloveds, and secondarily always strive to acquire for them glory, praise, and commendation. And because in the state of the "nakedness of souls" neither fiction nor lies can exist, he introduces Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch, the author.</note> asking about his past love, and whether she was ever disposed to please him or if her will ever conformed to his. Concerning this question, he writes.

She smiled, as was appropriate and fitting for a soul in a state of grace worthy of a response; therefore, this recitation falls into the form of a dialogue. To this end, the poet describes falling asleep, and in his sleep, Laura appearing to him and inviting him to reason with her. In this discourse, one sees the aforementioned intention clearly expressed. He says, therefore: that the night which followed the horrible event of Laura's death—which extinguished the sun of all beauty and virtue on earth and returned it to heaven—he remained like a blind man, having held her as his guide and his virtuous path. The sweet summer frost was already spreading through the air, which together with the white Aurora, <margin>V</margin> daughter of Tithonus, <note>In Greek mythology, Aurora (the Dawn) was the lover of Tithonus. Her appearance signifies the time just before sunrise when dreams were traditionally thought to be true.</note> is wont to lift the veil of falsehood from confused dreams. At this hour, then, the soul of Laura appeared in the form of a lady resembling the season of spring. She appeared crowned with oriental gems, and departing from a thousand other crowned souls, she came toward Master Francesco. Reaching out her hand like a gentle sigh, she said: "O Master Francesco, recognize her who first turned your steps from the common path of the unlearned masses as soon as your youthful heart became aware of her." Having said this, pensive and with a grave and modest look, she seemed to sit upon the bank of a clear stream where a beautiful green Laurel <note>A play on Laura's name (Lauro), symbolizing both the poet's beloved and the laurel crown of poetic fame.</note> and a leafy beech tree provided shade. Whence he says:

---

<margin>X</margin>
<margin>
Our Master Francesco has enclosed a wonderful understanding within these verses, founded upon a solid basis of reason. To understand this, one must know that the poet primarily feigns having seen this vision on the night following the funeral of Madonna Laura to denote a sense of probability: for where the mind has been fixed during the day considering some object, it is consistent that the same phantoms return in a dream at night. Whence Cicero, demonstrating this opinion in the sixth book of *On the Republic*, says: "It happens for the most part that our thoughts and speeches produce something in sleep such as Ennius writes of Homer, namely what he most often used to think and speak of while awake." <note>original Latin: "Fit enī fere ut cogitationes sermonesq[ue] nīi pariāt aliq̃d ī somno tale: quale de Homero scribit Enni[us] uidelicet q̃ sa pissime vigilās solebat cogitare & loqui."</note> But if Master Francesco describes having had thoughts or speech concerning Laura on the day of her death—to whom he then describes dreaming of her that night—anyone who has ever felt a spark of benevolence can clearly understand that it is truly indicative that his natural powers were so relaxed by thinking and reasoning of her that he was compelled to go to sleep. Secondary to this, the poet describes having dreamed in the hour of the morning, and he aptly declares why: so that it might be clearly understood that from his dream every veil of obscure meaning and false presentation was removed. The cause of this effect was demonstrated at length above at the beginning of the book through the doctrine of Albertus; <note>Likely referring to Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who wrote extensively on the nature of dreams.</note> and similarly, the reason why Aurora is called the girl or daughter of Tithonus was expressed in that same place. In the third place, it is to be understood that Master Francesco says Madonna Laura was like the season of spring; he intends to say that just as spring is more beautiful, healthier, and more temperate than any other time—according to the opinion of Hippocrates and Galen <note>Ancient medical authorities; Galen (129–c. 210 AD) expanded on the works of Hippocrates.</note> in the third part of the *Aphorisms*—so too was her beauty.
</margin>

## CHAPTER TWO

76

Petrarch describes the beauty of Laura and her serenity as superior to all other souls taken up into heaven; to Master Francesco <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the author of the poems being commented upon.</note>, she appeared most excellent in the company she kept. He describes Laura next as being crowned, distinguishing her from a thousand other crowns to explain the teachings of theologians, who assert that to every righteous soul in the celestial homeland is attributed a crown, according to the teaching of Paul the Apostle to Timothy in chapter four, where he says:
> I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day. <note>original: "Bonum certamen certavi: cursum consummavi fidem servavi: in reliquo reposita est mihi corona iustitię: q̃ reddet mihi dñs ĩ illa die iustus iudex"</note>
And likewise, the holy Church Militant sings in the Office of Martyrs and Confessors, in the Offertory, to commemorate the holy prize of their crown:
> O Lord, you have placed a crown of precious stones upon his head. <note>original: "Posuisti dñe sup caput eius coronā de lapide precioso." From Psalm 21:3.</note>
Laura was therefore crowned with oriental gems and accompanied, because of her excellence, by a thousand other crowns—that is, by a thousand other righteous, crowned souls. Lastly, he says that she extended her hand and said, "Recognize her who first turned your steps from the public path." Here, Master Francesco shows that Laura was not only the reason he was called back from the study of civil law <note>Petrarch’s father forced him to study law at Montpellier and Bologna, a pursuit he abandoned for poetry after his father's death.</note>—as he himself affirms in that song, *That old, sweet, cruel lord of mine*—but also from the wide path of vice, which is so named by Christ in the Gospel of Saint Matthew, chapter seven, when he says:
<margin>A</margin>
> Enter through the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the way is spacious that leads to perdition, and many are those who enter through it. <note>original: "Intrate per angustā: q̃a lata porta & spatiosa uia est q̃ ducit ad p̃ditiōē: & multi sunt q̃ intrāt p̃ eam."</note>
As he affirms in that same song and in many sonnets. Therefore, she invites him to recognize her anew now that she is beatified, having stripped away the heavy garment of her earthly limbs and arrived at the celestial homeland. There, all change ceases, and every sensual inclination is removed and fails; the soul is directed only to contemplate its ultimate end, to possess, love, and enjoy it. Therefore, with great reason, she calls him back to recognize her, as she has changed from a mortal state to an immortal one, from the temporal to the eternal, from misery to beatitude, from the doubtful storm to the most certain and invisible joyful tranquility. To lead him to this recognition to which Laura calls him, she makes him sit down, to demonstrate that not by sudden movement, nor by sudden will, nor by swift exercise, but gravely, thoughtfully, and with long-term and mature examination, must a person proceed to the understanding of the celestial homeland and the state of blessed souls. Just as in every good work, a person must persevere until the end, as Christ says in Saint Mark chapter thirteen and Saint Matthew chapter twenty-four:
> But he who perseveres until the end shall be saved. <note>original: "Qui auit p̃seuerauerit usq; in finem hic saluus erit."</note>
And besides this, through the resting of the body, the soul becomes prudent, as "the philosopher" <note>A common medieval and Renaissance reference to Aristotle.</note> attests in the sixth book of the *Physics* <note>The quote actually appears in Aristotle's Physics, Book 7.</note> when he says:
> By sitting and resting, the soul becomes prudent. <note>original: "Sedendo aĩa & quescendo fit anima prudens."</note>
From this, the reason remains manifest why Laura compelled Master Francesco to sit. The poet, having thus described his situation, acted with wonder that she should suggest he might not recognize her, saying that he, in the likeness of a man who speaks while weeping, said: "O my Laura, how do I not recognize you, who are my divine soul? Certainly, I see that you are she; therefore, for this reason, I pray you only to tell me if you are dead or truly alive." Wherefore he says:

-> "How do you not recognize your divine soul?" <-
-> I answered like a man who speaks and weeps, <-
-> "Tell me, I pray, if you are dead or alive." <-

<margin>B</margin> Concerning the understanding of the preceding verses, two things occur for consideration. One is the great affection and the fixation on the phantom held in the mind of Master Francesco regarding the person of Laura; it seemed to him that he saw her alive, while on the other hand, there were the images of death. Thus, in the dream, he remained ambiguous as to whether Laura was alive or dead. The other concept we should have is why Master Francesco asks her if she is alive or dead, not because the state of the soul after death was unknown to him, but according to poetic custom, to narrate the immortality of the soul through the person of a third party. To this recitation, he appropriately introduces Laura first, because she had been described above as so virtuous that a lie could not fit within her; as the philosopher says in the fourth book of the *Ethics*:
> Falsehood is in itself mean and blameworthy. <note>original: "Est enĩ mēdaciū p̃ seipsum ĩprobum ac vitupatiōe dignū." Reference to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics.</note>
Thus, untrue words were not compatible with Laura's singular virtue. Secondly, it was suited to Laura because she was dead, and through experience, she had proven and understood that immortality. Third and last, because by Laura he understands "Reason"; no one else can speak better of immortality than Reason, as that judgment is removed from the senses and is comprehensible only by Reason. He adds next that Laura responded to his question, showing that he preferred to understand those things...

To understand this more clearly, if one wished to follow the holy theological doctors—especially Saint Thomas in his *Summa contra Gentiles*—it would be a very long and difficult inquiry. Furthermore, the Christian religion presupposes immortality as an article of faith. However, if we only cited our patrons and advocates following the theologians in this cause, it would be a thing entirely alien to any just legal judgment. Therefore, wishing to bring forth some evidence regarding the eternity of our soul, and setting aside the theologians for this part, we shall build our foundations only upon the opinions of the highest philosophers <note>term: philosophers (original: "phi" or "philosopho"). In the medieval and Renaissance periods, "The Philosopher" almost always refers specifically to Aristotle.</note>, the authority of the prophets, and the examples of the pagans. ¶ Aristotle, then, the supreme philosopher, having diligently considered all the natures and properties of things, determines in the end that <term>corruption</term> <note>In philosophy, "corruption" refers to the process of a thing breaking down or ceasing to exist in its current form.</note> occurs in substantial things because they participate in <term>prime matter</term> <note>The most basic, formless substance from which all physical things are made.</note>. Whence, defining it in the seventh book of his *Metaphysics*, he says: "Matter is that through which a thing is able to be and not to be." <note>original: "Materia ē p̃q̃ res p̃t eẽ & nō esse."</note> And in the first book of the *Physics*, he writes: "I say that prime matter is the first subject of each thing, from which something is made." From these definitions, the Philosopher infers in the first book of *On the Heavens* that the heavens are incorruptible, because they have no subject or matter from which they could be made. To this purpose, Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were essential to Western thought.</note> also says in the first book of the *Physics*: "From this it is declared that the super-celestial bodies have no matter at all; for then they would be generable and corruptible; for nothing else is the cause of generation and corruption but prime matter." From this foundation, then, a first reason arises for the soul being incorruptible: it is absolute and exempt from all matter and corporeal corruption; therefore, it cannot suffer corruption, being alien to the principles of it. This is understood not only by the authority of Anaxagoras—who affirmed the soul was immaterial, unmixed, and impassible—but it is clearly seen by the operations that proceed from it. For where the body is sometimes intensely afflicted, the soul is in great joy; and conversely, while the body is in luxuries, the soul feels the heaviest distress. And furthermore, the soul understands

<margin>G</margin>
abstract and universal things, and discourses upon non-sensory objects; which could not be the case if its power were fixed to any corporeal organ or member. ¶ The second reason has its origin in the doctrine of the Philosopher in the first and fifth books of the *Physics*, where he says that every action and transformation is always between contrary terms, saying: "All [philosophers], therefore, make the principles contraries." <note>original: "Oēs igit̃ pricipia cõtraria faciūt."</note> Whence, if the soul naturally came to not-being by its own essence, it would be necessary for it to be alterable, as alteration is the precursor to corruption. The first reason demonstrates this to be false, because according to the Philosopher in the first book of *On Generation*, the first contrary qualities—among which is alteration—namely, Heat, Cold, Dryness, and Humidity, are inseparable <term>accidents</term> <note>Properties that can change without the thing itself changing essence, though here they are described as bound to physical matter.</note> of matter and elemental bodies. Indeed, Averroes in the second book of the *Physics*, in the fifteenth commentary, says these accidents are not separated from prime matter, and thus he calls them "essential accidents." Nor is it effective if someone should assert that our soul is corrupted by the corruption of the human body,

# CHAPTER TWO

<margin>H</margin>
...which is its proximate subject: just as other accidents <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that can change without the substance itself changing—like the color of an object.</note> relate to other natural, substantial forms. This is not through its own corruption, but through simple cessation. For the soul, when compared to our body, acts as the formal, efficient, and final cause—as written in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de aīa", referring to Aristotle's *De Anima*.</note>. For this reason, it is an antecedent to the body in perfection, nobility, and independence. Consequently, it follows that the soul cannot receive any corruption from the body, since it does not depend on the body for its existence or preservation; rather, the opposite is more likely and more reasonable. ¶ And the third reason comes from the opinion of the Philosopher <note>The "Philosopher" almost always refers to Aristotle in this period.</note> in the first and second books of *On the Heavens and the Earth* and in the third book of *On the Soul*, where he affirms that God and nature produced nothing in this world in vain, saying:
> God and nature do nothing in vain. <note>original: "Deus & natura nihil frustra faciunt."</note>
And in the second book of *Physics*, he says a thing is produced in vain if it cannot achieve the end for which it was originally ordained, saying:
> The sign of what is vain is when a thing is said not to exist for the sake of that for which it was intended; just as walking is for the sake of relief, but if a walker does not achieve it, we say he walked in vain and the walking was useless. <note>original: "Signū aut quod vanum est: qm dī: quum non sist ppter quod aliud illius cā: vt ambulare depositiōis cauſa est. Si uero non fiat ambulanti frustra dicimus ambulaſſet: ambulatio vana."</note>
Therefore, since our two universal powers—namely intelligence and will—were created for the pursuit of the First Truth and the Supreme Good, and since these two objects cannot be possessed in the present life (as experience teaches us, alongside the authority of the doctors), it is necessary to concede either that these two powers were created in vain by God or nature, or that there is a state after this life in which the soul, released from the body, can attain them. This attainment is clearly impossible if the soul does not remain immortal forever after this life.

<margin>I</margin>
¶ The fourth and final reason is based on the intent of the Philosopher in the booklet *On Good Fortune* <note>original: "libello de bona fortuna".</note>, where he considers it a great impropriety to concede that God is unjust; and therefore he denies that the care of the goods of fortune lies within Him, saying:
> For if we say that God cares for the goods of fortune, we would make him an unjust judge. <note>original: "Si enim bona fortunæ deuū curare dixerimus ipſum prauū iudicē faciemus."</note>
Therefore, if the soul were mortal, it would be necessary that all divine justice be perished, or that the order of nature and its delights were totally outside of divine government. For it is clear by experience that many men live according to the law of moral nature and yet are continually met with most unhappy outcomes. Conversely, some prosper for whom every law is perverse; and likewise, we see some from the very beginning of their birth are more or less suited to the operations of the intellect. Therefore, if the existence of the soul belonged only to the present life, all divine reverence would have to be removed, since God would be either unwilling or unable to balance these excesses.

<margin>K</margin>
But this falsehood was taken away not only by the opinion of the ancient Romans, but by public law, as the text speaks in the law of the *Digest* concerning justice and law, saying:
> Just as there is religion toward God, so also toward the fatherland and parents. <note>original: "Veluti erga deū religio: ſic & patriæ & parentibus."</note>
Let these four reasons concerning the immortality of the soul suffice for our purpose out of the many that could be brought forward. Consequently, we will add for greater evidence some authorities conforming to our true and reasonable proposition. ¶ Aristotle, then, principally in the second book of *On the Soul*, speaking of our intellectual soul in comparison to others, says:
> One separates this from that as the perpetual from the corruptible; <note>original: "Separaū aut hoc ab hoc tanq̄ ppetuum a corruptibilitate"</note>
which same opinion Plato shared, who—according to Cicero, Eusebius, and our poet <note>Petrarch.</note>—is to be preferred above every other philosopher. Augustine also testifies to this in the ninth book of the *City of God*, chapter nine, saying these words:
> For Plato, when dealing with human affairs, said that the Merciful One made mortal bonds for them. He thus judged that it pertained to the mercy of God that men are mortal in body, lest they be held forever in the misery of this life. <note>original: "Plato enim cum de humanis agere: inqt ipſe miſericors mortalia illis vincula faciebat... ne ſemp huius uitæ miſeria tenerentur."</note>

<margin>L</margin>
¶ Cicero, likewise, in the *Dream of Scipio* and the seventh book of *The Republic*, introducing the elder Scipio speaking to the younger Africanus, says, confirming the same purpose:
> But so that you, Africanus, may be more eager to protect the commonwealth, know this: for all those who have preserved, aided, or enlarged their fatherland, there is a certain and defined place in heaven where the blessed enjoy eternal time. <note>original: "Sed quo ſis affricane alacrior ad tutandam rempu ſic habeto. Omnibus q̄ patriam conſerua-rent; adiuuerint auxerint certum eſſe in cælo & definitum locū; ubi beati æuo ſempiterno fruantur."</note>
And beyond this, how much he affirmed this same opinion can be well known through the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*. And here again, he affirms the same when he says that excellent men are deified through their works, as is seen in several places in the *Metamorphoses*, and especially in the ninth book, introducing the death of Hercules, and in it Jupiter says these words:
> Vulcan's power is only over the part he took from his mother; but that which he drew from me is eternal and exempt from death, and I shall receive it into the celestial realms. <note>original: "Nec niſi materna vulcanum parte potentē / Idq̄ ego defunctum terris cæleſtibus oris: / Sentiet: æternū est & me: q̄ traxit & expers / Accipiam. / At qui im mune necis: nulla q̄ domabile flāma." The quote describes how the mortal part of Hercules (from his mother) is burned away, but his divine part (from Jupiter) remains.</note>

# TRIUMPH OF DEATH

...the soul must be subject to divine justice: and from this, it receives penalties and merit according to the works performed in life. He <note>Likely referring to the poet Virgil, whose *Aeneid* was often read as a source of theological truth in the Renaissance.</note> writes in this form:

| | |
|:---|:---|
| Even when life leaves at the final light, | They pay the penalties: some are spread open |
| Not all evil leaves the wretched, nor entirely | To the empty winds; for others, the infected crime |
| Do bodily plagues depart; it is utterly necessary | Is washed away under a vast whirlpool, or burned out by fire. |
| That many things, long ingrained, grow in wondrous ways. | Each of us suffers his own spirit; then through the wide |
| Therefore they are worked by punishments, and for old evils | Elysium we are sent; and we few hold the joyful fields. |

<note>original: "Quin & supremo cum lumine vita reliquit..." This passage from Virgil's *Aeneid* (Book VI) describes the purification of souls after death, a concept the author uses to bridge classical myth with Christian purgatory.</note>

<margin>N</margin> ¶ This true sentence is also proven by the holy testimony of the divine prophets: who, being equally inspired by God, pronounced to the people as much as they understood of Him. Hence, the prophet David primarily shows in Psalm 70 that the soul is reserved for resurrection when he says: *How many tribulations, many and evil, you have shown me: and turning, you gave me life: and from the abysses of the earth you led me back again.* <note>original: "Quātas ostendisti mihi tribulationes..." refers to Psalm 71:20 in modern numbering.</note> Micah also says in the 7th chapter: *I will wait for the Lord my savior: my God will hear me: my enemy shall not rejoice over me; though I have fallen, I shall rise when I sit in darkness.* <note>Micah 7:7-8.</note> Ezekiel, in chapter 37, aptly demonstrates the reservation of souls and how they must reunite with bodies, saying: *Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. Behold, I will send spirit into you and you shall live: and I will give you sinews, and make flesh grow over you: and I will stretch skin over you: and I will give you spirit and you shall live: and you shall know that I am the Lord.* <note>The famous "Vision of the Valley of Dry Bones."</note> But if someone should say that God does not infuse the souls of the dead, but creates new ones to pour into the bones of the bodies, this would be erroneous: and the prophet himself would argue against it; for they would not be the same men as before, nor would they recognize Him as God through the miracle any more than the men who died before. It would also be a contrary opinion to the other prophets, who make special mention of "numerical identity" <note>A philosophical term meaning the exact same individual, not just a similar one.</note> in the resurrection. Job also held this hope, and therefore said: *I know that my redeemer lives: and on the last day I shall rise from the earth. And again I shall be surrounded by my skin and I shall see God my savior.* <note>Job 19:25-26.</note>

¶ Finally, in this matter, the worthy authority of the great philosopher Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a dominant figure in medieval science and theology.</note> certifies us; who, in his first book *On the Soul*, says that he has seen experience of our soul being mobile after it has departed from its body—a point which is greatly doubted among philosophers. Hence he says: *But that which seeks to destroy this doubt is what is asserted by the most ancient Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with hermetic philosophy and magic.</note> and now by divine incantators: namely, that spirits (whom they call angels or demons) and souls stripped of their bodies are moved from place to place; the truth of which we have also experienced in magical arts.*

<margin>O</margin> ¶ Lastly, the examples of the Gentiles <note>The non-Christian Greeks and Romans.</note> regarding the observance of laws, the erection of statues, sumptuous funerals, and piety toward the gods, testify to nothing other than the hoped-for and certified nature of human souls. Let us therefore conclude together with our poet <note>Petrarch.</note>: that Laura is alive; and those men who are in the world are dead until the final day of their present life, according to the opinion of Cicero in *The Dream of Scipio*, who says: *Indeed, they truly live who have flown out from the chains of the body as if from a prison. Your life, however, is death.* <note>original: "Immo uero uiuunt..." From Cicero's *Somnium Scipionis*, a key text for Renaissance views on the soul.</note> Augustine, in the 9th book of *The City of God*, chapter 4, says: *It is much more credible and probable that men are miserable as long as they live.* From this, we can rightfully affirm that death extinguishes a "living death" and gives birth to eternal life. Since Laura has answered the poet that she is alive, and he, placing indubitable faith in her, asks no further on this part; rather, he turns his words to another question, saying: "O Lady Laura, tell me: if at the end of this other serene [path] called life, is dying such pain and punishment as is commonly thought, since you know it through proof and experience?" Hence he says:

¶ The third and final [suffering] is a mental pain, seeing oneself forced without any remedy to be led before that eternal judge who, at that time, administered justice so rigorously: upon whose grace alone one's merit depends, and not upon any other work. For these reasons, death is said by men to be a most heavy penalty. Afterward, Messer Francesco <note>The author uses "M.F." for Messer Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch), the poet of the *Triumphs*.</note> recounts the worthy and excellent response of Laura to his question, saying that she said: "O Messer Francesco, as long as you follow the judgment of the common crowd and its false opinions, you can certainly never be happy. Therefore, I assure you that death is the end of a narrow and dark prison to noble souls who are devoted to the knowledge of celestial things. But to the others, who have placed all their care and desire in the mud of earthly things, death is only annoyance and disdain. And even more beyond this, I tell you that my dying—which at present is so annoying and troublesome to you—would bring you joy and pleasure if you felt even one of a thousand parts of as much joy and gladness as I feel." Wherefore he says:

<margin>S</margin>
> She replied: "While you follow after the common crowd,
> And its blind and harsh opinion;
> You can never be happy.
> Death is the end of a dark prison
> For noble souls; for others it is a burden;

> And now my dying, which so troubles you,
> Would make you rejoice, if you felt
> The thousandth part of my joy."

¶ For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, one must primarily know that the nature of our soul—not only according to theologians and the Christian religion but also according to the opinion of the philosophers—is divine. This truth is first written at the beginning of Moses's Genesis in the person of God:
> Let us make man in our image and likeness. <note>original: "Faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram." Refers to Genesis 1:26.</note>
This sentiment is in keeping with the colorful imagination of the poets who, in their fictions, say: that after Prometheus had formed man, being led and conducted into heaven by Minerva so that he might take for the completion of his work whatever most delighted him; he, seeing the light of the sun, lit a torch from it, judging every other thing less worthy. Applying it to the breast of his unformed body, he introduced the soul into man, as Ovid testifies in the first book of the *Metamorphoses*. And so he became alive. How true this sentiment is, and what light the poets mean, is declared by Plotinus the Platonist, whom Augustine refers to in the tenth book of *The City of God*, chapter two, saying:
> Plotinus the Platonist does not doubt that our intellectual soul—which dwells in celestial seats—has no nature above itself except that of God, who created the world by whom she herself was made; nor is the blessed life and the light of the intelligence of truth provided to her from anywhere else above. <note>original: "Plotinus Platonicus animam nostram intellectualem..." Here, the author uses Augustine’s commentary to bridge Neoplatonic philosophy with Christian thought.</note>
Hence the sentiment is in harmony with the Gospel itself where it is said:
> He was the true light which enlightens every man coming into this world. <note>original: "Erat lux vera quæ illuminat..." Refers to John 1:9.</note>
Cicero also writes this same thing in the *Paradoxes*, demonstrating the soul to be of a divine nature when he says:
> Since either God or nature, the mother (so to speak) of all things, has given you a soul—than which nothing is more excellent nor more divine—will you so cast yourself down and prostrate yourself that you think there is no difference between you and a four-legged beast? <note>original: "Tu cum tibi siue deus..." From Cicero’s *Paradoxa Stoicorum*.</note>
The Philosopher <note>Standard medieval/Renaissance shorthand for Aristotle.</note> affirms this same thing in the seventh book of the *Ethics*, and also the first book of the *Politics*.

<margin>T</margin>
¶ And Socrates often used to say, in confirmation of the aforementioned sentiment:
> A man perfected through wisdom is nothing else than God breathed into a human body. <note>original: "Homo perfectus per sapientiam nihil aliud est: quam Deus in humano corpore conspiratus."</note>
By these authorities, it can be well-known and manifest that the ancient philosophers did not doubt in any way that our soul must be divine. Thus, for this foundation:

<margin>V</margin>

One can clearly understand death to be the end of an obscure prison to noble souls, and a burden to others who have placed all their care and delight in the mud; for the knowledge of which it should be known that...
