# TRIUMPH OF DEATH

<margin>X</margin>
Know that "noble" <note>The Italian "gentili" refers to people of noble spirit or refined character, rather than "gentiles" in a religious sense.</note> souls are those who, through some action, make themselves similar to their origin, according to the opinion of the Philosopher <note>Standard medieval/Renaissance shorthand for Aristotle.</note> in the sixth book of the *Ethics*, where, speaking of bestial vices, he recounts one who had beaten his father: and being rebuked, he replied: "He himself also beat his own father," and pointing to his young son, he said: "And he, when he is a man, will beat me, for that is natural to us." <note>original: "Et ipse patrē verberauit suū: & puerū filiū ostēdēs inquit: & hic cū vir erit verberabit me nā id nobis gētile est."</note> Noble souls, therefore, desire to conform to their beginning, and to be released and simplified from this form of the earthly body, to remove themselves from the care and possession of mortal things. ¶ Whence also Augustine in the ninth book of the *City of God* says to this purpose: "If, therefore, the more one is like God, the nearer one becomes; there is no other distance from Him than unlikeness. To that incorporeal, eternal, and immutable one, the soul of man is more unlike the more it is desirous of changeable temporal things." <note>original: "Si ergo deo quāto similior: tāto fit q̄sq; p̄pinquior. Nulla est ab illo alia longinquitas q̄ eius dissimilitudo..."</note> And in the divine Plato, in the booklet on the immortality of the soul <note>Likely referring to the *Phaedo*.</note>: demonstrating the joy of noble souls when they approach death—wherefore they distance themselves from the body—he says to this purpose: "It is indeed a well-worn truth, sung by all, that our life is a kind of pilgrimage; those who have lived tamely, modestly, and moderately, departing with a brave soul as if singing a song of triumph <note>term: "peana" (paean) — a Greek song of praise or triumph, specifically a hymn to Apollo after a victory.</note>, approach the debt of nature." <note>original: "Tritū si qdē & ad oēs decantatū vitā nostrā peregrinationē quandā eē..."</note> For this reason, then, Solon the Athenian said, as Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> writes in the book *On Old Age*, that he did not want his friends to weep at his death, nor suffer any grief because of it. Whence the poet Ennius was also accustomed to say: "Let no one honor me with tears, nor perform my funeral with weeping." <note>original: "Nemo me lachrymis decoret: neq; funera fletu faxit."</note> Judging death to be the joy and sweetness of the soul, as Tullius writes in the same book. This, then, is the custom

<margin>Y</margin>
of worthy and noble souls. And the divine Scipio Aemilianus, as Tullius writes in *The Dream of Scipio*: just as he saw in a dream his father Paulus Aemilius, having heard from the elder Africanus the disposition of that eternal life, he said: "I beseech you, most holy and excellent father: since this is life, as I hear Africanus say: why do I linger on earth? Why do I not hasten to come here to you?" <note>original: "Queso p̄r sanctissime atq; optime: qm haec est vita... qd moror in terris qn huc p̄pero ad vos venire."</note> And just as worthy souls rejoice at the coming of death, so conversely do those who care for the things of the world, which are properly called "mud," being things that rot in a very short space of time. From this it appears manifest that a similar judgment can be rendered concerning other things as is given to that thing which is considered most noble in the world: namely money, which is most vile, being exchanged for all the most filthy things, as Aristotle writes in the fifth book of the *Ethics*; and Augustine in the fifth book of the *City of God* against the opinion of Varro; and the divine Christ instructs us in Saint Matthew, chapter five <note>Actually Matthew 6:19.</note>, that one should not care for these earthly riches, saying: "Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal." <note>original: "Nolite thesaurizare vobis thesauros in terra: vbi erugo & tinea demolit̄r..."</note> From this, joy and gladness spring only from the possession of things that please; and grief and annoyance from the loss of them. For this 

<margin>Z</margin>
reason, as men are constrained by death to leave the world where they have placed their care, it is reasonable that they are saddened when they come to die. ¶ This diversity of desires Pythagoras affirmed to Leon, Prince of the Phliasians, when he asked what the name "philosopher" implied; to whom he replied, as Tullius writes in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, in this form: "Pythagoras is said to have replied that the life of men seemed to him similar to the marketplace <note>term: "mercatum" — here referring to the great festival gatherings or fairs held during the Panhellenic Games.</note> held with the greatest apparatus of games celebrated by all of Greece. For as some there sought glory and the nobility of the crown with exercised bodies; others were led by the desire for buying or selling; there was a certain kind of them, and that the most noble, who sought neither applause nor profit, but came for the sake of seeing, and studiously observed what was done and how. So we, as if in a crowded marketplace, having set out from one city—that is, from another life and nature—into this life, some serve glory, others money; rare are those who, holding all other things as nothing, studiously look into the nature of things; these he called students of wisdom, that is, philosophers." <note>original: "Pythagorā autē respondisse fertur similē sibi videre vitā hominū & mercatum..."</note> By this desire, then, to understand and speculate upon the 

<margin>A</margin>
natures of things, men make themselves more similar to God; because according to the Philosopher in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*, God is properly called the "Intelligence of intelligences." ¶ Concluding, then, Laura <note>In the poem, Petrarch's deceased beloved, Laura, appears to him in a vision to explain the nature of death.</note> says justly that M.F. <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch.</note> would have rejoiced if he had felt only one of a thousand parts of the sweetness she had achieved through death in the celestial homeland. She adds—M.F. says that Laura, having spoken as he reported above, and while always keeping her eyes fixed on heaven, at last fell silent, until he, asking her again, said to her: "It is a thing of great wonder that there was no pain in death. Oh Laura, according to the common opinion of men, Sulla, Marius, Nero, Mezentius, and Gaius <note>Gaius Caligula.</note> with their devised tortures—and likewise the intense and sharp pains of the side, and of the stomach, and the burning fevers which follow death—make it seem truly not sweet, but much more bitter and harsh than any taste of wormwood." <note>term: "assentio" (absinthe/wormwood) — a plant used as a metaphor for extreme bitterness.</note> Whence he says:

# CHAPTER TWO

->Thus she spoke, her eyes fixed toward heaven<-
->Devoutly; then she placed into silence<-
->those rosy lips, until I said:<-
->Sulla, Marius, Nero, Gaius, and Mezentius;<-
->Sides, stomachs, and burning fevers make<-
->death appear more bitter than wormwood.<-

<margin>B</margin>
Through these verses, the poet intends to demonstrate the great bitterness found in death: both because of the harsh torments given to men, and also because of the natural sufferings that often precede it. Thus, from the time of the Roman Republic, he introduces as examples Sulla and Marius of Arpino <note>Lucius Cornelius Sulla and Gaius Marius, rival Roman generals whose civil wars were famously bloody.</note>, most famous Roman citizens but most cruel to many other citizens, as is evident from history. These men, therefore, because of the cruelties they practiced in dealing death to others, made death seem most bitter. The same is true of the cruel Nero—according to Cornelius Tacitus and Suetonius Tranquillus—and Gaius Caligula, the fourth Roman emperor. It almost seems they nourished themselves on the troubles and hardships they inflicted upon men. To these was also compared Mezentius <note>The commentator here conflates the mythical Mezentius from the *Aeneid* with the historical Maxentius, who was defeated by Constantine at the Milvian Bridge in 312 AD.</note>, the son of Maximian, at the time when Constantine, son of Helena and 29th emperor of the Romans, reigned. By the fury of the Praetorian soldiers, he was called Augustus at Rome—a most cruel man and a great persecutor of the Christian name—but he was later defeated and killed by Constantine near the Milvian Bridge near Rome. This same effect of death’s bitterness seems also to be produced by "colic pain," commonly called "pain of the side" <note>The "side" refers to the flank or lower abdomen.</note>, as it is most intense. For according to the opinion of Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age; his *Canon of Medicine* was a standard European textbook.</note> in the 16th [section] of the third [book], that pain occurs most often due to thick "windiness" <note>Gas or flatulence, which medieval medicine believed caused severe internal pressure.</note> trapped in the intestine called the colon by doctors. As it surges back and forth seeking an exit, it produces the most grave suffering in a man, as experience teaches us. It also sometimes arises from excessive dryness of the body, and especially natural excess caused by too much exercise, the heat of the air and of food, or by the poor flow of choleric humor <note>Yellow bile, one of the four humors.</note> to the intestines. Thus the "expulsive power" <note>The body's natural ability to evacuate waste.</note> is weakened, and thick, viscous phlegmatic humors are generated, which cling tenaciously to the intestines. When nature tries to struggle against them, the most grievous pain arises.

<margin>C</margin>
Ultimately, [these pains] are also generated by an <term>abscess</term> <note>original: "apostema"—a swelling or internal gathering of purulent matter.</note> contained in the intestines because of matter flowing through the veins and pathways to the weakest places, of which nature takes less care and concern. Therefore, in whatever way this illness arises, it always produces most intense and grave pains. In this way also, the stomach is sometimes the cause of harsh suffering, because according to Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a millennium.</note> and Avicenna in the 13th [section] of the third [book], the stomach is a member full of nerves; thus it is rendered very sensitive, as nerves are the medium and instrument of the sense of touch, according to the opinion of doctors and philosophers in the book *On the Soul*. Many causes of pain, therefore, come to the stomach: namely, a material "bad complexion" <note>An imbalance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile).</note>, whether simple or compound, or indeed with matter flowing into that place; likewise an abscess, or a "solution of continuity" <note>A medical term for a break in the tissue, such as a wound or ulcer.</note>, ulceration, windiness, nausea, hiccups, and the destruction or weakening of the appetite, and many other illnesses that are the causes of bitter twisting and most grave pains.

<margin>D</margin>
How many troubles even fever brings and gives to men can be well known by its definition written by Avicenna at the beginning of the first [section] of the fourth [book], where he says: <margin>E</margin>
> Fever is an extraneous heat kindled in the heart, arising from it by means of the spirit and blood through the veins and arteries into the whole body. <note>original: "Febris est calor extraneus accensus ī corde proueniens ab eo mediantibus spū & sanguine per venas & arterias in totum corpus."</note>

And Galen, in the first part of the *Aphorisms*, shows the bitterness of fever with briefer words, saying:
> Fever is when natural heat is changed into a fiery one. <note>original: "Febris est calor naturalis mutatur in igneum."</note>

And Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus, a 9th-century Jewish physician and philosopher whose work on fevers was highly influential.</note> in *On Fevers* affirms that fever surpasses all other illnesses in its misery, since from it come not only restlessness, alienation of the mind, excessive wakefulness, and immoderate thirst and other troublesome accidents, but it also hinders and makes imperfect all other human operations. These natural sufferings and these pains are the reasons why, together with the other torments which men inflict, death is judged by the common people to be most bitter. Having had our Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch, the author of the poem.</note> pose the aforementioned objection to Laura, he now describes a response from her, as worthy and fitting as truly becomes her excellence, saying: "Master Francesco, I cannot deny, and do not deny, that the struggle and the martyrdom which precedes death does not hurt most bitterly; and even more than this, a man is troubled by agony and the fear of eternal damnation, knowing he has offended God, who is an inflexible judge after the sentence is given. But tell me truly, comforting the soul..."

<header>THE TRIUMPH OF DEATH</header>

# THE TRIUMPH OF DEATH

...in the mercy of God; and giving to the heart—which perhaps feels weary within itself—some comfort of salvation or hope. For what is death in truth but a most brief sigh? Thus he says:

> I cannot deny (she said) that the suffering
> Which precedes dying brings strong pain;
> But more to be feared is the dread of eternal loss.
> But provided that the soul takes comfort in God,
> And the heart, which is perhaps weary within itself;
> What else is death but a brief sigh?

<margin>F</margin>
Truly worthy and singular was the response of Lady Laura <note>Laura is the idealized subject of Petrarch’s poetry; here she speaks from beyond the grave.</note>. Certainly, nothing better or more fitting could be said. As Augustine says in the first book of *The City of God*: it is not the diverse manner or the varying way of dying that makes us blame death, but only that which follows death. Thus, he judges the variety of ways of dying to be irrelevant to its "evil." He says: *For what does it matter by what kind of death this life is ended, since he whose life is ended is not compelled to die again? Since for every mortal, amid the daily accidents of this life, countless deaths are in a way contained—as long as it is uncertain which nature of things is to come—I ask whether it is holier to suffer one death by dying, or to fear all deaths by living.* <note>original: "Quid enim īterest quo mortis genere uita ista finiatur..."</note> And he adds: *A death is not to be considered bad if a good life preceded it; for nothing makes death bad except what follows death.* <note>original: "Mala mors putandā non est: quā bona uita precessit..."</note> For this reason, he concludes in the fifth chapter that the holy martyrs surpassed the Curtius, Decius, and Scaevola families <note>Famous Roman heroes known for self-sacrifice.</note> in patiently enduring the death given to them by others rather than inflicting it upon themselves. This constancy, nonetheless, they clearly showed—as far as their limited knowledge allowed—by not fearing death. Marcus Atilius Regulus did so at Carthage; Theramenes among the thirty tyrants of Lacedaemonia; Charidemus of Athens before Darius; and Theodorus before Lysimachus. When Lysimachus threatened to have him killed on a cross, he replied—as Cicero writes in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations* and Valerius in the chapter on free speech: *I pray you, threaten those horrors to your purple-clad courtiers. To Theodorus, indeed, it matters nothing whether he rots on the ground or on high.* <note>original: "Istis queso ista horribilia minitare purpuratis tuis..."</note> Besides these, many others cared little for the Punishment that precedes death, being armed with the hope that was born of their country's laws. 

He adds, through the person of Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch himself, the author of the poem.</note>, a proof and testimony of Laura within herself: how the soul is not disturbed at the final step by passions, provided it is strong and directed toward eternal salvation. He introduces Laura continuing her words: "Oh, Messer Francesco, the true proof of my words: know that I already had the final step of this our life near at hand. Although my body and flesh were fragile and infirm, my soul was nonetheless ready. When I was in this state, I heard someone say with very sad and grieving words: 'O wretched lover of Messer Francesco,' who, one by one, counts the days of Laura’s illness; and each of those days seems like a thousand years to him, so much does he desire to see her again every hour. Nonetheless, she is led to such a pass that they shall never again meet together on earth. Truly wretched is he, who—searching almost every land..."

<margin>G</margin>
"...searching the sea and every one of its shores, has always kept the same custom: only thinking and speaking of her, and always writing of her." Having heard him speak thus, I turned toward the place where the sound of the words came from. Looking back, I saw the one who had often helped me to love you <note>Likely referring to a personification of Virtue or Reason.</note>, and held me back from amorous fury, whom I quickly recognized by both her face and her speech. For she had often comforted me before my death; now, grave and wise, she brings great delight. Thus he says:

<margin>H</margin>
To more clearly understand the learned and elegant sentiment contained in the preceding verses, one must primarily know that it is the custom and nature of "pilgrim souls"—those who, having put aside the filth of the sexual act, only intend toward amorous pleasure that is not separated from joyful honesty—that when they see two similar lovers, they strive with words and deeds to maintain them in such amorous exercise.

> I had already reached my final step,
> My flesh was weak, yet my soul was still ready,
> When I heard a voice say in a sad and low tone:
> "O wretched man, who counts the days,
> and to whom one seems a thousand years; he lives in vain,
> for they shall never meet again on earth;
> and he searches the sea and all its shores,
> and always keeps one style, wherever he may be;"

## CHAPTER TWO

> He thinks only of her, or speaks of her, or writes.
> At that hour, in that place from which the sound came,
> I turn my languid eyes; and I see her
> Who impelled us both, and restrained you.
> I recognized her by her face and by her speech,
> Which has often already comforted my heart—
> Now grave and wise, then virtuous and beautiful.

...this exercise: just as Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> shows in that sonnet, **Two fresh roses gathered in paradise**; and this happens especially when there is some excellence of genius in the beloved, whereby he composes in praise of the beloved some graceful work which brings delight and pleasure to other lovers as they read it, as happened with Master Francesco through his sonnets and his moral songs <term>canzoni morali: a structured form of Italian lyric poetry dealing with serious themes</term>. And although this custom belongs to every country, it is practiced even more in France, where men show themselves to be more amorous than in any other province. For this reason, Master Francesco's love was most pleasing to many, so much so that in those times there was a rumor that Pope Benedict XII and Pope Clement VI both consented and gave dispensation so that our famous poet Master Francesco might be granted church benefices <note>An ecclesiastical office providing an income</note> and yet still be allowed to have Laura as his lady.

<margin>I</margin>
This love of the poet was, therefore, among others, most dear to a noble lady of Avignon—though many say this lady was Laura’s nurse. To me, this does not seem likely, because it is almost contrary to nature that in a soul so lowly—as that of Laura’s nurse must have been, since such a task belongs to the lowest people—and especially because Laura was of humble origin, born in that village called **Graveson**, such a lofty concept should take hold as maintaining in honest and laudable love two most singular lovers. According then to the consistency described above, where he said that the women who came to visit Laura in her sickness were all her friends and neighbors, I say that a noble lady in the city of Avignon greatly desired this benevolence and connection of souls between Laura and Master Francesco. And therefore, whenever Master Francesco received some amorous injury from Laura, he showed that he wanted to be troubled and depart entirely from this love; whereupon Laura became even more hardened. Then this noble lady, with virtuous persuasions, would restrain Master Francesco, telling him not to depart from Laura’s love, and by blaming Laura for her hardness, she would urge her toward some gratitude; thus their preceding angers were nothing other than a restoration of love. Having then this knowledge, Master Francesco wants to demonstrate that our soul is superior, even in death, to all bodily passions when it is fortified within itself with due confidence in God.

<margin>K</margin>
Where it must be understood that love, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the fifth book of the *Ethics* and the second of the *Topics*, is a passion of the concupiscible power <note>The faculty of the soul relating to desire</note>. According to Augustine in the thirteenth book of *The City of God*, love is the first and principal foundation of all other desires. Where he says: *All passions of the soul are caused by love. For love, gasping to possess what is loved, is desire; but having and enjoying it, it is joy.* <note>original: "Omnes animi passiones ex amore causantur. Amor enim inhians habere quod amatur cupiditas est: id autem habens: eo quæ fruens letitia"</note> Thus, a person is moved by nothing so much as by the memory of the object loved, just as Master Francesco describes in that sonnet **Of the martyred Rhine and the left bank**; for which reason, Master Francesco having been reminded by that lady during the death of Laura—and he loving her as much as virtue permitted, as he shows in the verses immediately following—not being moved in any part, nor his soul hanging in suspense for any worldly pleasure, it can easily be concluded that no other passion could alter her except for her beloved lover moving her. Whence it is manifest that the upright and ready soul, although the flesh is fragile, is not disordered in death but remains the master of every passion. And for this reason, the poet having recounted that he had recognized the noble lady Laura, and remained comforted by her because she had become wise, grave, and prudent—where in life, being still virtuous and beautiful, she also comforted him—therefore he recounts no further that his words caused any change. Next, Master Francesco adds the other proof made by Laura, through her testimony, that in death there is no pain, since it has been shown that the soul can remain superior to any sensory affection; saying that Laura, continuing, said: "O Master Francesco, know further what I have already told you: that when I was in my most beautiful state of youth and beauty, and in that age which you showed was most dear to you in words, gestures, and deeds—whereby because of that beauty you have given many cause to talk—my life was then almost bitter and troublesome to me because of..."

# THE TRIUMPH OF DEATH

I speak of that sweet and gentle death: which, due to our depraved nature, is very rarely experienced by mortals. For in that transition of mine, I was much more joyful than one who returns from exile to a sweet and long-desired homeland. Except that compassion and pity for you alone gripped my heart, because you remained in the misery of the world. Whence she says:

->And when I was in my most beautiful state,<-
->In my greenest age, most dear to you,<-
->Which has given many cause to speak and think;<-
->Life was little less than bitter to me<-
->Compared to that gentle,<-
->And sweet death; which is rare to mortals:<-
->For in all that passage of mine I was more joyful,<-
->Than one who returns from exile to a sweet home;<-
->Except that pity for you alone gripped me.<-

<margin>L</margin> Our poet describes two notable effects achieved by Laura in the preceding verses. The first follows the law of friendship and its properties established by Pythagoras <note>Ancient Greek philosopher famous for his mathematical and mystical theories</note>, confirmed by the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the eighth book of the *Ethics*, by Cicero in his book *On Friendship*, and by Seneca in his sixth letter to Lucilius where he says: **For no possession of any good is pleasant without a companion.** <note>Original Latin: *Nullius enim boni sine socio iocunda possessio est.*</note> Therefore, Laura, having pity and compassion for Master Francesco, desired a state for him similar to her own, through which he might be outside of worldly misery. The other effect is her rightful rejoicing at her passage from this life to the other, like those who return from exile to their homeland. And truly this is with good reason, as this life of ours is nothing other than a sea of turbulent storms. Whence Cicero deservedly writes these words in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: *If we hang in suspense, tortured and driven by waiting and longing: by the immortal gods, how pleasant will that journey then be, which once completed, no care, no anxiety will remain!* <note>Original Latin: *Quod si expectando & desiderando pendemus animis cruciamur & agimur: prob dij immortales quam illud tunc iter iocundum esse quo confecto nulla reliqua cura: nulla sollicitudo futura sit.*</note>

<margin>M</margin> Socrates understood this disposition no less clearly; for being imprisoned by the Athenians because he detested their idolatries, he did not want any patron or advocate to defend him in his cause, nor did he offer any plea to the judges. But he chose to remain in free defiance. And on the last day of his life, just as Cicero writes in the same book, while disputing the state of the soul, he said there were two paths and two courses for all souls departing from bodies. Whence Cicero adds: *For those who have contaminated themselves with human vices and given themselves entirely to lusts, by which, as if blinded by domestic vices and crimes, they have stained themselves—where they have conceived inexpiable frauds for violating the republic—to these a certain path is secluded from the council of the gods. But those who have kept themselves pure and chaste, and who have had minimal contagion with bodies, and have always withdrawn themselves from them and imitated the life of the gods while in human bodies: to these an easy return is open to those from whom they set out.* <note>Original Latin excerpt from Cicero’s reporting of Socrates’ final dialogue</note> Cicero also confirms this same point in the *Dream of Scipio*, introducing Paulus Aemilius showing his son Scipio (and grandson by adoption of the Elder Africanus) that the path of virtue is the only one that recalls our souls to heaven, saying: *But thus, Scipio, as this grandfather of yours, as I who fathered you, cultivate justice and piety; which is great toward parents and kin, but greatest toward the homeland. Therefore that life is the way to heaven and to this gathering of those who have already lived and, released from the body, inhabit that place you see.* <note>Original Latin: *Sed sic scipio vt auus hic tuus...*</note>

<margin>N</margin> Death is therefore not to be mourned; which Julius Caesar—according to what Sallust writes in the *Catiline Conspiracy* and Cicero in his oration against Catiline—estimated to proceed either by necessity of nature or as the end and rest of our labor and misery, and not to be a punishment attributed by the gods to men. And therefore those who are healthy never died against their will, but those who are strong often willingly provoke death. It is then truly an exile of the soul to dwell in the body, especially according to the opinion of Plato, who holds that our souls are not newly created, but are eternal, and descend from heaven into bodies as soon as matter is prepared for their reception. Whence they fittingly rejoice when, released from those bodies, they return to heaven. Our poet has quite gracefully described up to this point the nature of souls, the disposition of death, and the glory that follows victorious deeds. Now, as we said at the beginning of this chapter, he wishes to show through the report and testimony of Laura the process of his love, which was not reprehensible but followed a tolerable custom, wishing to remove any doubt if anyone had conceived the idea that he had loved Lady Laura in a less than virtuous manner.

<margin>O</margin> And therefore he introduces himself asking if, in truth, in the temple when...

# CHAPTER TWO

Whether, when she was alive, she was ever disposed to have compassion for him, saying: "Ah, Lady Laura, my singular lady, I pray you by that sincere and unsullied faith that I bore you during your lifetime—which then, as I believe, was manifest to you, but is now much more known to you in the face of the divine essence <note>The nature of God, in which the blessed are said to see all truth</note>, which sees and knows every outcome—that you tell me if Love ever generated in your soul any thought of being pitiful toward my amorous martyrdom, without however abandoning your high, worthy, and reasonable pursuit of true virtue. For sometimes your sweet distains and sweet angers, and even the sweet peaces written in your beautiful eyes, held me and my desire perplexed, hanging in long hesitation." Whence he says:

<margin>¶ Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known that Master Francesco, according to the opinion of theologians, asserts that Lady Laura must know his faith in the face of Him who sees everything—that is, in the divine essence. This is something that the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, a famous medieval theologian</note> says in the first book, distinction 35, following the opinion of Augustine in his *Literal Commentary on Genesis*, and Saint Ambrose in his third book *On the Trinity*. Every thing is present to God, both past and future in respect to the world; an opinion which Aristotle also affirms in the book *On Good Fortune*.</margin>

> **"A h, Lady," I said, "by that faith,**
> **Which was, I believe, manifest to you then,**
> **And now more so in the face of Him who sees all,**
> **D i d Love ever create a thought in your head**
> **To have pity on my long martyrdom,**
> **W i t h o u t abandoning your high, virtuous endeavor?**
> **F o r your sweet distains and sweet angers,**
> **The sweet peaces written in your beautiful eyes,**
> **H e l d my desire in doubt for many years."**

...good fortune; whence because in God, through His all-encompassing simplicity, essence, being, knowledge, power, and other divine attributes are one pure and same thing—that is, God Himself—for this reason, created things always shine in the divine essence in the likeness of objects that form their images within a mirror. Whence, as Augustine says in the ninth book of *The City of God*: **He is the true God with whom alone, in whom alone, and from whom alone the rational and intellectual soul is blessed.** <note>original: "Verus deus est cum quo solo: in quo solo: & de quo solo anima rationalis & intellectiua beata est."</note> Since God alone is the food and nourishment of the soul in the blessed life, the souls are always intent upon Him, always looking toward Him, and always fixed in Him. And by comprehending the divine essence according to their capacity, they also comprehend the images and likenesses of created things that shine within it.

¶ Master Francesco then adds Laura’s reply to his question, which is fitting and truly appropriate for a soul placed in heaven, saying: that as soon as he had finished his words, he saw the flash of Laura's sweet smile, which was once his comfort and the sole restorer of his afflicted spirits. Then, beginning with a soft and piteous sigh, she began to speak: "Master Francesco, I declare to you that never in life was my heart separated from you by goodwill, nor shall it ever be divided in the future. But knowing the heat of your amorous flame, I tempered and cooled it at times with my face, showing it as troubled. This was because, to save you in your restraint and me in my modesty, and our common reputation in its fresh esteem, no other way could be found more secure or more easy. And for this, you must not think that I was not always full of pity for you, just as a mother is not to be judged less pious even though she very often punishes her dear son with harshness."

¶ "How many times," I said within myself, "how much this Master Francesco loves me! Or rather, he does not love with measure, but burns; wherefore it is necessary that I protect us only to flee common infamy." But certainly, it was a difficult and wretched task: for he who craves a result but nevertheless fears to act makes a poor provision—just as happened to me, who greatly desired that you should love me, yet feared that your love might in some part produce a scandal. And therefore, through such foresight, I said within myself: "Now, let Master Francesco look only upon the outward appearance, but let him by no means see the inner disposition of my soul." And this caution was what constrained you and turned you from your purpose, just as a bit turns back a horse that wanders. And know also from me truly, that more than a thousand times, anger and indig...

### THE TRIUMPH OF DEATH

...thus my face was painted outwardly while love burned me within and destroyed my heart: nonetheless, never because of this loving you did my desire and its fire overcome reason or discourse. But after I saw you were angry, overcome by amorous grief: then I directed toward you my eyes full of sweet gestures and kindness, saving at once your own life and our common honor. And you also know that if your passion was very sharp and powerful, 
<margin>S</margin>
I moved my voice and my brow to kindly offer you safety: now in a fearful sight, now tearful and sorrowful. These, therefore, were my devices and arts with you: now welcoming you kindly, now showing you disdain: which thing you openly know, because you have sung of it in many places. And in the end I used this great variety because I saw at times your eyes so heavy with tears and pregnant with grief that I truly said: "this man has run to the end of his life if I do not offer him help," for I recognized it by his signs. And therefore I then provided you with a virtuous help and laudable comfort. And then I saw you had at your side the spurs of security <note>the "spurs" of excessive confidence or passion</note>, so that I said to myself: "here a harder bit <note>term: "morso" (bit or bridle), a common metaphor for moral restraint</note> is needed to hold him back." Whence, among these contraries—now hot, now cold, now white, now crimson, now sad, now glad—I have led you safely, though weary, even to this point. Whence within myself, I enjoy it, I rejoice, and I glory in it. Wherefore he says:

<margin>T</margin>
<margin>Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses: it is to be known principally that it is quite compatible with the observance of virtue to take delight in bodily beauty: for the Author of Nature is a non-erring intelligence. This natural agent <note>Nature or God as the creator</note>, whatever it may be that immediately produces such an effect in the world, did not intend to produce it as an object of the visual power without that power being able to delight in its comprehension. Wherefore Cicero in the first book of the *Duties* <note>original: "De Officiis"</note>, approving this sentiment, says and affirms that due care and diligence should be given concerning the form and cleanliness of the body. And Virgil in the fifth book, showing this same thing, says: "Virtue is more pleasing when it comes in a beautiful body" <note>original: "Gratior et pulchro veniens in corpore virtus"</note>. It is added: wherefore love is not reprehensible, provided the soul does not lapse into obscene lechery. Thus, Laura being benevolent toward Master Francesco, and Master Francesco loving only her beauty—as he demonstrates in that sonnet "When among the other women from time to time"—for this reason, desiring no further venereal act together, they did not depart from virtuous operation.</margin>

->CAPITVLO SECVNDO<-

# CHAPTER TWO

That I saw your eyes at times so full
Of tears, that I said, this body is 
At death’s door if not helped: I see the signs:
Then I provided honest help:
At other times I saw such spurs at your side;
That I said, here a firmer bit <note>term: "morso" (bit/bridle), a metaphor for moral restraint</note> is needed.
Thus hot, crimson, cold, and pale,
Now sad, now happy, until here I have led you
Safely; for which I rejoice, though weary.

...paradoxes <note>original: "radoxe," likely completing the word "paradoxe" from the previous page</note> that these things are snares for human liberty: but when used and measured with due method, they do not prejudice the free soul. Conveniently, then, as to the understanding of the verses: Lady Laura, becoming troubled at times with Master Francesco to repress his eager will to see her, should not be considered less pious for seeking to avoid infamy; for according to the sentiment of Solomon in the Proverbs: to chastise children denotes greater love, saying:

*He who spares the rod hates his son.* <note>Latin original: "Qui parcit virge odit filium suum." See Proverbs 13:24.</note> And so, whoever does not pull back his friend from improper things certainly does not love him. Wherefore Lady Laura is supremely to be commended, who so worthily, according to the necessary dispositions, knew how to accommodate him even when it was necessary to greet him with her own voice. As he himself testifies in this place, and in that sonnet *Perseguendomi amor al loco usito* <note>Sonnet 214: "Love pursuing me to the usual place"</note> and in that madrigal *Volgendo gli occhi al mio nouo colore* <note>Madrigal 52: "Turning her eyes toward my new color"</note>. Wherefore this removes the opinion of anyone who imagines that, beyond a virtuous love, there was a disordered appetite in Master Francesco. 
<margin>X</margin>
¶ Master Francesco then narrates what he responded to Lady Laura, not deviating in this response from the custom and nature of a lover, in whom a very great jealousy is always inherent, saying that with fear and not without tears he spoke. "Lady Laura, your words would bear great and sweet fruit for all the faith I have carried for your excellence, if only I believed them to be as true as you say." Whence he says:

And I, "Lady, this would be a great fruit
Of all my faith, if only I believed it";
I said trembling, and not with a dry face.

¶ O unhappy, hard, and miserable condition of lovers! They are so very ardently oppressed in loving that, while loving their beloveds, they can never persuade themselves that they are loved by them in return. And the reason is this: that being always disposed to do everything indiscriminately at every hour for the pleasure of their beloveds, for this reason, whatever is denied to them, they undoubtedly estimate to be a diminution of love and benevolence. And that which is sometimes done for their own salvation, they, miserable and afflicted, repute as an injury, just as the poet demonstrates quite clearly in these verses.

<margin>Y</margin>
¶ Master Francesco consequently narrates the response made by Laura to his words, showing her somewhat troubled in appearance and reasonably so, saying: "O wicked, incredulous man of little faith! If what I have told you were not known to me or if it were not true, what reason would I have that would induce me to affirm it so? I do not wish to be silent if your person pleased me in the world: but this I say well, and I confess to you: that that sweet and amorous knot of benevolence which you had around your heart always pleased me and delighted me supremely. And it also pleased me—if in understanding the voices of mortals I hear the truth—the beautiful name of glory and fame which you acquired for me long ago and ever since with your poetic speech. Truly know that for this I requested nothing else in your love nor desired but one thing only: a certain observance and measure. And this alone was then what was lacking; because while you wanted to show me in tearful and sad acts the disposition of your soul (which I always understood and saw), you opened and showed your closed heart, making it very well known to the whole world. Wherefore because of this, I hide and conceal my own soul. For which thing even today you are angry and distressed: but except for this difference between you and me, there was always such a harmony as love is accustomed to join, provided it is tempered by worthy virtue. And know also: that in us there were almost equal amorous flames, at least when I perceived your intense fire; but one [you] revealed them, and I, who was the other, hid and concealed them. And it likewise happened that at times you were already hoarse from crying for mercy, when I within myself remained silent; because shame and fear made my great and burning desire appear tepid and small; but truly pain does not decrease by suppressing it."

I hope that the third sphere of heaven <note>The sphere of Venus, the planet of love, which was believed to influence human passions.</note> led him and raised him to as much love as could have been produced anywhere, had it remained unmoved and stable. Wherefore even this light comes to part us, and therefore if you have anything to say to me, study to be brief; and with what little time remains, strive now to dispense your words." ### [COMMENTARY]

The reason is: because if Master Francesco the poet were so far away, he might have turned elsewhere to love another woman. Whereby Laura would have become obscure and unknown: through which words we ought to understand two things. One: that the desire for fame is a laudable, worthy, and natural thing that men desire most highly. Which thing Themistocles the Athenian demonstrates, as Tully <note>The Roman orator Cicero</note> writes in the *Oration for Archias the Poet*: who being in the theater where there were many singers, and asked which voice pleased him more than any other, replied: that one by which his praises were sung. Likewise Alexander of Macedon <note>Alexander the Great</note>, only through the desire for glory, prohibited any other sculptor than Polyclitus, Apelles, and Pyrgoteles from painting or sculpting the royal image: fearing lest by the lack of skill of others his fame might be diminished. Understanding this same thing, Virgil introduces Venus in the first book of the *Aeneid* only to console herself for the loss of Aeneas through the glory and fame that was to follow him. And therefore the Romans were accustomed to exposing themselves to the gravest danger and certain death without any delay, only for the statues and insignias and their standing through fame. From this, Solomon, well understanding that fame is a good and desirable thing, said in Proverbs at chapter 22:
> "A good name is better than much riches." <note>original Latin: "Melius est nomen bonum quam divitiae multae."</note>

And Cicero, in the first book of *On Duties*, says that to acquire good fame and opinion, one must teach this caution:
> "A certain reverence must therefore be employed toward men, both toward the best and toward the rest. For to neglect what everyone thinks of him is not only the mark of an arrogant man, but also of a dissolute one." <note>original Latin: "Adhibenda est igitur quedam reuerentia..."</note>

Wherefore, if Laura had desired fame in this regard, her appetite was not perverse nor alien to nature; next, because it seems that the union of souls and friendship depends in great part on proximity, habit, and union: as it seems the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> teaches us in the eighth book of the *Ethics*, saying:
> "For places do not [divide friendship...]" <note>original Latin: "Loca enim non dis-"</note>

<margin>E</margin> This is the source of the saying that "silence breaks many friendships." <note>A common medieval proverb derived from Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics.</note> Therefore, Laura felt grief that she was not born near Messer Francesco, especially since she was born in a rural village. She believed that if her origins had not been a "contrary quality" <note>meaning her humble social standing or provincial birthplace</note>, Messer Francesco would have sung her praises even more firmly. Indeed, he was often criticized by many for attributing such great fame to Laura, as is noted in the sonnet **PARA** *Perhaps to someone who [criticized] praising her* and that other one, *He who with infinite prudence and art.* <note>Petrarch’s Sonnets 247 and 248, where he defends his poetic devotion to Laura against those who thought her unworthy of such high style.</note> Thus, it is likely that the poet had to restrain himself somewhat due to the persuasions made against him. On the other hand, Messer Francesco tacitly praises himself and credits his own learning with the power to make Laura worthy of such honor. And truly he is right, for in him is demonstrated how much power human <term>genius</term> <note>the innate creative power of the mind</note> can have in the <term>Tuscan idiom</term> <note>the Italian vernacular of Florence and surroundings, which Petrarch helped establish as a literary language</note>. And for great reason, he describes himself as not having responded to those words, so that by either confirming or contradicting them he would not fall into the error of either praising or blaming himself. But he says that by these words, he was raised and inflamed to a great love by the third sphere.

<margin>F</margin> At this third point, one must understand the celestial spheres. According to the natural philosophers and astrologers, there are eight; however, according to the theologians, they are greater in number, as written by **Nicolaus de Lyra** <note>a famous 14th-century Franciscan teacher</note> at the beginning of his commentary on Genesis. The first, starting from the proximity of the Earth, is the sphere of the Moon. The second is that of Mercury. The third is that of **Venus**. The fourth is that of the Sun. The fifth is that of Mars. The sixth is that of Jupiter. The seventh is that of Saturn. The eighth is that of the Fixed Stars. Each of these, through the properties of its planet, produces various effects. For our purpose, the third sphere of Venus, among other effects, produces the "concept of love," according to the opinion of **Andalo di Negro** <note>original: "Andalo dalbumasari," a 14th-century astronomer and teacher of Boccaccio</note> and all other astrologers. Not only does it have power over the act of physical love, but also over all other amorous incentives that produce such desire. It also generates many other varied effects which we will omit for now, as they are not very relevant to our intention.

<margin>G</margin> Finally, with great artistry, the poet says this sphere raised him to as much love as it would have if it had remained motionless and stable. Here it must be understood that it is the universal opinion of astrologers and philosophers that the celestial bodies influence our bodies, especially through the light of the sun which reflects off them. Since every influence has more power when it is direct <note>original: "recto"</note> rather than at an angle <note>original: "obliquo"</note>, and furthermore, the longer it lasts, the more efficacy and intense effect it produces. For this reason, he demonstrates the intensity and greatness of the love to which he was raised; because if the sphere of Venus were motionless and stable, its aspect over us would be direct while above our hemisphere, and it would influence us continuously without varying or slanting due to its continuous circular movement. Therefore, in this state, it would likely produce the most intense effect possible.

<margin>H</margin> Finally, Messer Francesco adds the disposition and habit of all those men who bow to the truth and remain quiet when presented with the aforementioned reasons. He affirms first that he is totally satisfied regarding the love Laura bore him. Secondly, he shows through his words that an extremely burning desire to die was kindled in him, saying: **"O Lady Laura,** however many martyrdoms and pains I ever suffered in life and in the world while loving you, your sweet and pious speech has made them seem a light and pleasant thing. But it only weighs on me, and seems most heavy, to live any longer without you. Therefore, I desire to know from you at this your departure—and at the end of our conversation—am I to follow you by dying soon, or truly much later?" To this question, he continues, Laura (already moved, in his opinion) said to him: **"Messer Francesco, you will live on the earth a long time without me."** Wherefore he says:

<margin>According to common opinion; or rather according to the truth of the desire that should be in us. Messer Francesco stayed a very long time on earth after the death of Laura, as he lived twenty-six years before he came to his death.</margin>

> Whatever I ever suffered, sweet and light
> I said, your sweet and pious speech has made for me;
> But living without you is hard and heavy to me;
> Therefore I would like to know, my Lady, if I...

> "Am I too late to follow you, or in good time?"
> She, already departing, said, "In my belief,
> You will remain on earth without me for a long time."
<note>original: "Son per tardi seguirui, o se per tempo: / Ella gia mossa disse, al creder mio / Tu starai n terra senza me gran tempo." These lines are from Petrarch's Triumph of Death, where the spirit of Laura speaks to the poet.</note>

</center>

As we said from the beginning, Messer Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the famous Italian poet and scholar.</note> was born in the years of the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, 1304, and died in the year 1374; thus he came to live seventy years. And during this time, being twenty-three years of age, he fell in love with Laura in the year 1327, on the sixth day of the month of April, as he himself testifies in that sonnet: *Will spurs me, Love guides and perceives me*, which we cited previously. Messer Francesco loved her for twenty-one years, as he affirms in that sonnet: *Love held me burning for twenty-one years*. Then, Laura dying on that same day, the sixth of the month of April, as has been recounted above, Messer Francesco came to be forty-four years of age at the death of Lady Laura. From then until the seventy years that he lived, there remained twenty-six years; truly, to a soul desiring heaven and the blessed life, a long and troublesome and very great time.

## EXPOSITION OF THE FOURTH TRIUMPH, OF FAME.

<margin>K</margin> **N**OTHING contained within the celestial spheres is regarded with as much care and admiration as human action, through which the fragile and falling nature of man is changed from a slippery and transitory state to the eternal. Nor is this wonder of the mind born without cause; for although the influence of the heavens, the preparation of the elements, and the disposition of the earth produce such varied and marvelous effects, they do not change from their custom or instinct which they have always naturally maintained. But man—who by his mortal property is earthly and fleeting—once established through his own action alone, converts himself from unstable to immortal and celestial. This is the effect that should reasonably draw our understanding into great confusion; thus, that habit is worthily deserving of praise which confirms a man in such a state and condition, because it is necessary for that to be outside the dominion of Fortune, the power of the heavens, and the order of nature. For each of these causes produces great variation in us; just as such habitual perfection reasonably draws us to wonder, so also it should lead us to desire and to love of itself.

<margin>L</margin> Running through all the things that can be possessed by us, only virtue is understood to be that which establishes and confirms us in such a degree of excellence. For bodily beauty and health, dominions and empires, a great number of children, a multitude of servants, the quantity of riches, the greatness of possessions, the liberty of one's country, and bodily delights are in one small moment taken from us and cut off. And even if these things were never altered by Fortune or the heavens, they still cannot proceed where the will of the possessor goes. O outstanding, then, excellent and divine virtue! She alone is the one who places men in a tranquil and secure state; she makes them masters, she makes them strong, she makes them rich, she makes them free. She gives them unchangeable and everlasting pleasures; she accompanies them by night and by day, in theaters and in solitude, in delights and in dangers. She makes them famous while living; she withdraws them from death and establishes them as divine.

<margin>M</margin> Thus, Plautus wrote appropriately in *Amphitruo* <note>A comedic play by the Roman playwright Plautus.</note> as follows: *Virtue is the best prize; virtue surpasses all things: certainly through virtue, liberty, safety, life, property, parents, homeland, and children are protected and preserved. Virtue has all things in itself; all good things are present for the one who possesses virtue.* <note>original: "Virtus premium est optimum: virtus omnibus rebus anteit: profecto virtute libertas. Salus: vita: res: parentes: & patria & prognati tutantur & seruantur. Virtus in se oia habet: oia ad sunt bona quem penes est virtus."</note> Indeed, who was there ever in whom divine virtue lived that did not tolerate the adverse influences of heaven and the calamities of the earth with a strong soul? And what is even more worthy of praise: who did not restrain human prosperity with gravity and prudence? Indeed, what things remain unattempted where virtue is found, where human perfection has been able to shine in some part? Truly, as Curtius <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, a Roman historian.</note> writes: *Virtue leaves nothing unattempted.* <note>original: "Virtus nil intentatum omittit."</note> And Ovid in the fourteenth book of the *Metamorphoses* said: *On the path of virtue, no way is impassable.* <note>original: "In via virtutis nulla est via." A common medieval paraphrase suggesting virtue overcomes all obstacles.</note> She has found the nature and simplicity of our first Author <note>referring to God</note>; she has demonstrated the number of the heavens, the courses of the planets, the mixing of the elements, the natural principles, the origins of seas and rivers, the generation and corruption of things, the divine sciences, the nature of man, and immortality. This [virtue]...

<meta>This page transitions from the biography of Petrarch into a philosophical and literary commentary on his "Triumph of Fame." It argues that while death ends physical life, virtue creates a lasting "fame" that allows the soul to live on in memory and in heaven.</meta>

<page-num>18</page-num>

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>N</margin> It teaches how to distribute to each person what is their own; it reveals public governance and private actions; it shows how to follow its own path; and in what way vices, poverty, pain, and death are to be overcome. Regarding this purpose, in the *Second Punic War*, Titus Livius <note>Livy (59 BC–AD 17), the Roman historian whose work "Ab Urbe Condita" includes the history of the wars with Carthage.</note> writes: **"Persistent virtue nevertheless conquers all."** It truly conquers, and most of all it conquers death; for men live famously when, dying in the body, they live in heaven with a soul distinguished by virtue. And among men, they are glorious and honored through fame. Therefore, Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the Roman statesman and orator.</note> in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, wishing to express that life comes from virtue despite death, says: **"No one has lived too short a time who has performed the perfect duty of perfect virtue."** This is confirmed by Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC–AD 65), the Stoic philosopher and dramatist.</note> at the end of his tragedies, where he says: **"Now if glorious virtue is carried to the Stygian shadows, live as brave men."** Likewise, Titus Livius in the fifth book of the *Second Punic War*, introducing Lucius Martius, a distinguished Roman knight, after the death of Gnaeus and Publius Scipio in Spain, describes him exhorting the soldiers in his name in this form: **"I would wish that you, soldiers, do not pursue them with laments and tears as if they had perished. The Scipios live, and shall live, by the fame of their deeds; but as often as the memory of them occurs, you should see them as if they were urging you on and giving the signal to enter battle."** From this exquisite and singular gift of most excellent and sublime human virtue, its reward and fruit are born; which, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), whom medieval and Renaissance scholars often called simply "The Philosopher."</note> in the fourth book of the *Ethics*, is the honor and glory attributed to men either in life or in death.

<margin>O</margin> Cicero, in his oration *Pro Marcello*, thus defines glory: **"Glory is the illustrious and widespread fame of great services, whether toward one's fellow citizens, one's country, or toward the whole human race."** And Virgil <note>Publius Vergilius Maro (70–19 BC), author of the Aeneid.</note>, to confirm this previously introduced opinion, brings in Hercules in the tenth book of the *Aeneid* to console him for the death of Pallas, the son of Evander, demonstrating that death should be little esteemed provided that fame follows virtuous action, saying:

> Each has his own day; time is brief and irreparable for all.
> This is the work of virtue: to extend one’s fame through deeds.
<note>original: "Stat sua cuiq; dies breue & irreparabile tempus / Omnibus est vitæ: sed famam extēdere factis / Hoc uirtutis opus."</note>

Therefore, after inevitable death has removed virtuous action from the earth by separating the soul from the body, glory and fame extinguish death and renew a life in the world no longer subject to the various contingencies of death. Since our Master Francesco <note>Petrarch.</note> in the preceding Triumph demonstrated that death dominates and triumphs over earthly life and virtuous actions as far as the present life is concerned, <margin>P</margin> he now declares in our present Triumph the fourth state of life, which is the glory and fame attributed to men through the virtuous and just actions proceeding from it while the soul was united with the body in the world. When posterity wishes to resemble their predecessors, they are immediately moved by fame and glory arising from worthy and elegant works. Thus, just as death had extinguished those lives in the first ancestors, so fame, by obscuring death, makes them reign in the memory of the living.

<margin>Q</margin> Because according to the description of Fame given by Virgil in the fourth book of the *Aeneid* and by Ovid <note>Publius Ovidius Naso (43 BC–AD 17), Roman poet known for the Metamorphoses.</note> in the twelfth book of the *Metamorphoses*, it is truly the rumor and popular talk that is described rather than true fame. Virgil says:

> Fame is an evil, than which no other is swifter.
> She thrives on speed and gains strength as she goes.
> Small at first from fear, she soon lifts herself into the air,
> Walks on the ground, and hides her head among the clouds.
> Mother Earth, provoked by the anger of the gods,
> Brought her forth last (so they say) as a sister to Enceladus,
> Swift of foot and with tireless wings.
> A huge and horrific monster: for every feather on her body,
> There is a watchful eye beneath (marvelous to tell!),
> As many tongues, as many sounding mouths, as many pricked-up ears.
> By night she flies midway between heaven and earth through the shadows,
> Screeching; she does not close her eyes in sweet sleep.
> By day she sits as a guardian, either on the peak of a high roof
> Or on tall towers, and she terrifies great cities.
> She is as tenacious a messenger of lies and perversity as she is of truth.
<note>original: Virgil, Aeneid IV, 174-188.</note>

And Ovid, in the cited place, to demonstrate this same common talk, says:

> There is a place in the middle of the world, between the earth, the sea,
> And the celestial regions, at the boundaries of the threefold universe.
> From here, everything that exists is seen, however far away,
> And every voice penetrates to hollow ears.
> Fame holds the heights and chose her home in the highest citadel;
> She added countless openings and a thousand windows to the roof,
> And closed the thresholds with no doors.
> It lies open night and day; the whole house is of sounding brass.
> It hums throughout, echoing voices and repeating what it hears.
> There is no rest, no silence in any part;
> Yet there is no clamor, but the murmurs of a low voice.
<note>original: Ovid, Metamorphoses XII, 39-49.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the "Triumph of Fame" by explaining how virtue allows humans to overcome death through lasting glory. It cites classical authorities like Cicero, Livy, Virgil, and Ovid to define fame both as the reward for virtue and as a pervasive, legendary force.</summary>

¶ Therefore, Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch (1304–1374), the author of the *Triumphs*.</note> does not intend to treat this kind of "fame" here. As the aforementioned poets make clear, that kind of fame belongs only to the living in this present life. His intention, instead, is to describe that fame of praise and glory which follows after death, resulting from some worthy and virtuous action performed during life. This is the fame celebrated by historians, poets, and writers, so that those who follow through the passage of time may be moved by such examples. We read of this in the case of Themistocles <note>An Athenian general and politician.</note>, as we mentioned above regarding the fourth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: when he walked in the forum every night and was asked why he did not sleep, he replied that he was kept awake by the triumphs of Miltiades <note>The hero of the Battle of Marathon; Themistocles was inspired by his predecessor's glory.</note>. Similarly, Scipio Africanus said his soul was set on fire for virtue every hour when he saw the statues and images of his Roman ancestors. ¶ Wherefore, as Livy writes in the fifth book of the *Second Punic War*: when Scipio Africanus went to Spain as consul after the death of his father and uncle to recover the armies, he spoke to his knights at the end of his first oration, saying (to our point):

<margin>R</margin>
> "Only you, soldiers, favor the name of Scipio and the offspring of your generals. As if from cut branches growing back, lead the old soldiers as a new army; lead a new general across the winter quarters into the land with many brave deeds. I hope from you that, just as you now recognize in me the likeness of my father and uncle—in my face, expression, and the features of my body—so I shall return to you an image and example of my character, faith, and virtue, so that each man may say that General Scipio has lived again or been reborn for him." <note>original: "Vos modo milites fauete nomini Scipionis..."</note>

¶ To wish to achieve this glory and everlasting fame, no action is more suited than to despise and flee from it. Thus, Fabius Maximus <note>A Roman general famous for his delaying tactics against Hannibal.</note> says to Paulus Aemilius, as Livy writes:

<margin>S</margin>
> "He who spurns glory shall have true glory." <note>original: "Qui gloriā spreuerit ueram habebit"</note> And Saint Augustine says in the sixteenth chapter of *The City of God*: "To one who possesses virtues, it is a great virtue to despise glory." <note>original: "Habenti uirtutes magna uirtus est cōtemnere gloriam."</note>

These authorities clearly demonstrate that a man should only intend to act virtuously, and not for the wind or the gossip of the common people. Therefore, the poet [Petrarch], intending to treat this stable and lasting glory, primarily describes himself as "freed from sleep" <note>The poet "wakes up" to signify the transition from the dream-like Triumphs of Love and Death to the historical reality of Fame.</note>. This demonstrates the present subject and the material of the Latin language, whereas in the preceding *Triumphs* he described himself as sleeping through a "graceful fiction," through which he clouded his most moral and learned meaning. Messer Francesco says, then, that having heard the reasoning of his beloved and dear Lady Laura, the sweet accents of her words—full of a "bitter sweetness"—still resonated in his heart. Only he prizes and esteems this conversation, for nothing else is so loved by him. Since at the end she had said that he would be on earth without her for a long time, he adds what he wanted to say: "O days of my life, miserable, late, and slow," and other things pertaining to lamentation. For he was to be deprived of her company for such a long span of time, even as he saw her depart from him happily, going into the midst of those beautiful, holy, and most chaste souls. Wherefore he says:

# CHAPTER ONE

<margin>T</margin>
*To understand the preceding verses, one must know that with great likelihood our Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> says that the accents of Madonna Laura’s words resonated in his heart with bitter sweetness. This is because, as we said above, the strong affections of the mind and the intense effects experienced while awake usually return in the same way during sleep. Thus, since Laura was dead and this image remained in his intellect, and then she appeared to him in his dream having wept with him, he felt in those words a sweetness tinged with the bitterness of the memory of her death. Furthermore, his sweetness had turned bitter because she had said at her departure that he would remain a long time on earth without her. Thus, the consolation he received from the immortality of the soul and the glory she receives after leaving the world was taken away by the long delay of the time of possession which he desired. For this reason, he was provoked with great reason to accuse and blame his slow progress through life, and also to express other matters of the soul, such as her praying to the Most High God that this time should be*

### THE FOURTH TRIUMPH: FAME

**I**n my heart, full of bitterest sweetness,
The final accents of that discourse still resonated,
Which alone I crave, and prize, and desire;
And I wished to say: "O my sad and slow [years],"
And many other things: when I saw her, happy,
Departing among beautiful, shining souls.

<margin>A</margin>
*shortened. And here it is described that in this state of will, he saw her depart and go away among most beautiful and lucid souls. Then he woke up; and reasonably so, first because the hour in which he was was quite suited to the ending of sleep, the sun having already risen above the hemisphere. Secondly, because it is a natural effect that at the hour when one seems to see terrible things or things of grief in a dream, one must wake up due to the sudden alteration made in the body by the recall of the vital spirits <term>vital spirits: in medieval physiology, these were subtle fluids believed to carry life and sensation through the body</term> to the heart, as they naturally return to that place as if to the beginning and the fortress of our whole body. For this reason, the hour of waking comes; and here Master Francesco, having heard at the end the words of Madonna Laura which had brought the greatest bitterness, describes himself being awakened by them as if by an object of fear and grief. He then describes the particular hour and what he, being awake, could see following this death, saying that already at that hour the sun had taken the black and humid bandage of the night from the face of the hard earth—which night is the rest of weak and mortal people. At this hour, sleep had barely departed, and with it the vision of her who still opens and closes his heart with the keys of love, when he saw another worthy and most noble war begin. Thus he says:*

<margin>V</margin>

> Already the sun had the humid and black bandage
> Taken from the hard face of the earth,
> The rest of the weary mortal folk;
> Sleep, and she who still opens and closes
> My weary heart, had barely departed,
> When I saw another war begin.

<margin>X</margin>
*Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should be understood that the poet calls the night a "humid and black bandage" because night is nothing other than an obscurity caused by the absence of the sun. Since the day is serene, lucid, and white due to the sun's presence, night must likely be compressed by contrary qualities due to its absence, according to the doctrine of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the second book of the Physics.*

<margin>α.</margin>
*In the second book of the Physics, while speaking of privative causes, he says: "Furthermore, the same thing is the cause of contraries; for that which, when present, is the cause of something, we sometimes say that its absence is the cause of the contrary. For example, the absence of the pilot is the cause of the ship's sinking, whereas his presence was the cause of its safety." <note>original Latin: "Amplius autē idē contrariorū est cā: qđ. n. pñs cā cuiuspis est: id & absens nōnūq̄ cām eē cōtrarii dicim⁹. vt gubernatoris absentia subuersiōis nauis: Cuius pñtia cā erat salutis."</note> But the night is said to be humid primarily for a similar reason, the day being dried of vapors by the heat of the sun. Secondly, because in the night those vapors multiply which are quite humid by nature; and besides this, the moon has more power being*

<margin>X</margin>

Afterward, **Master Francesco** invokes the help and favor of **Polymnia**, one of the nine Muses, and of **Minerva** to express the great concept he had seen of the glorious deeds of the ancients, saying: **"O Polymnia, I pray that you must help me, and you, Minerva, may you accompany my style, which undertakes to seek out diverse shores, parts, and regions, and to narrate the men and worthy gestures and glorious deeds performed in the middle parts and at the edge of the world where the sun bathes in the ocean, rising in the morning and setting in the evening."** Hence he says:

Since Polymnia—whose name is also interpreted as "much memory"—is designated to narrate clear deeds and notable histories, and as he must now treat of these, **Messer Francesco** appropriately invokes*

For this reason, she is said to be the wisdom of Jove, having had her origin in his head. Therefore, she was proposed and dedicated by the ancient poets as the goddess of wisdom and of doctrines. Accordingly, since **Master Francesco** must treat of those who have remained bright and famous in the world through wisdom, he appropriately invokes Minerva for this, as she presides over doctrines and studies.
<margin>C</margin>
*¶ Secondly, it should be understood that **Master Francesco** says his style seeks out the middle and extreme parts where the sun bathes in the morning and evening to demonstrate the different placement of the Ocean sea that surrounds the earth. When the sun rises over our hemisphere, it appears that the sun comes out of the Ocean sea; and likewise, when it returns in the evening, it appears that it similarly bathes in the Ocean. Thus, such a comparison is drawn by our poet.* Afterward, **Master Francesco** adds, saying that he saw many noble and excellent people proceeding together under the banners of a very great and admirable queen, whom everyone loves for her own sake, and everyone reveres and honors. <margin>D</margin>

<margin>E</margin>

# CHAPTER ONE

All praise consists in action. <note>original: "Laus omnis in actione consistit"</note> Through this, fame, by compelling others to act justly and according to virtue, leads man to his ultimate end of beatitude; thus it governs him so excellently that it rightly deserves to be named "queen." This is because everyone marches for her, everyone reveres her with praise, and everyone fears her. Indeed, there is no one so devoted to luxury and vice that they do not desire a good reputation and do not strive to shake off <term>excutere</term> all infamy from themselves. Hence, for this reason, everyone must fear her. Many examples could be brought forward to prove this sentence, but let the example of **Lucretia** suffice alone: she whom neither the flatteries nor the violence of **Sextus Tarquinius**, nor threats of death, could sway; only the fear of infamy constrained her to fulfill his wicked desires. Afterward, wishing to show that her soul remained pure before **Brutus**, **Collatinus**, and **Lucretius**, she courageously killed herself, as was said above. The poet then narrates what this queen looked like in appearance, saying that to look upon her, she truly seemed a divine, admirable, and stupendous thing. Whence he says:

<margin>F</margin>

<margin>G ¶ In this verse, **Master Francesco** <note>Petrarch</note> does not separate himself from the opinion of the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the first book of *On the Heavens* <note>original: "de celo"</note>, saying that fame appears to be a divine thing. It should be understood here that Aristotle affirms in that passage that the first quality suiting divinity is perpetuity and invariability. Thus the philosopher says: *For indeed this divine name was declared by the ancients, receiving the proof of always being.* <note>original: "Et enim nomen hoc divinum enunciatum est ab antiquis semper esse suscipiens demonstrationem"</note> Therefore, a thing participates more in divinity the more it contains these dispositions within itself. Thus, since fame extends itself over a very long time, it seems to contain something of divinity within itself. However, **Master Francesco** did not say that it *was* divine, but that it *seemed* so, because in truth it does not last forever, as he demonstrates in the subsequent triumph <note>The Triumph of Time</note>; but it certainly exceeds many ages of men, for which reason it is reputed by them to be divine. He adds that this queen had on her right hand a great Roman who caused great ruin in France. Whence he says:</margin>

of Julius, returning from Apollonia to Italy and being assisted by **Cicero**—even though he was but a youth—he was sent by the Senate with the consuls **Hirtius** and **Pansa** against **Mark Antony**, who was besieging **Decimus Brutus** in Modena. <margin>K ¶ **Drusus** was the son of **Tiberius Nero** and **Livia Drusilla**.
