# CHAPTER ONE

After Tarquin was driven out, the first of the consuls <note>This refers to Lucius Junius Brutus, the founder of the Roman Republic.</note> had his own sons, Titus and Tiberius, beheaded because they, along with other young men, had conspired to restore the King to Rome, from which he had been exiled to Torquato. Finally, while fighting against Aruns, the son of Tarquin, they killed one another; thus the glorious soul of Brutus, the father of Roman liberty, pursued Aruns even to hell, as Lucius Florus <note>A Roman historian who wrote an epitome of Roman history.</note> narrates. There was another Brutus <note>Marcus Junius Brutus, the assassin of Julius Caesar.</note> who restored liberty when he killed Julius Caesar alongside Cassius. Having been defeated by Augustus and Marc Antony on the fields of Philippi, he died by his own hand. Plutarch wrote extensively about him, and Tully <note>The common medieval and Renaissance name for the orator Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> praised him in many places. There were others of this family worthy of memory, but these two hold the highest place. Following this, he mentions some others, where he says:

<margin>V</margin>

> Then the good peasant who made the river red
> With fierce blood; and the old man who held Hannibal
> In check with delay and with counsel.

Some wish to understand this through a common fable without a known author, which says a peasant killed a King who had besieged Rome, though they do not say who it was at that time, only that he deserved to have a statue in Rome in the same dress he wore when he was victorious. This is entirely fabulous. Instead, it can be understood as referring to Gaius Marius <note>A Roman general and statesman of humble origins.</note>, born of a Sybilla <note>Likely a reference to Marius’s mother or an obscure legend; historically, Marius was known for his humble, "peasant" upbringing in Arpinum.</note> in Arpino, who, being most expert in arms, triumphed over Jugurtha, the King of Numidia, and later achieved victory over the Cimbri and Teutons who wished to occupy Italy. The "red river" can be understood as the Rhone, where he defeated the Cimbri, or the *Aquae Sextiae* <note>Modern-day Aix-en-Provence.</note> where he defeated the Teutons, where the color of the water was deservedly changed by the blood.

<margin>X</margin>

The old man who checked Hannibal with delay and counsel was Fabius Maximus, who reigned <note>In this context, "held office" as Dictator.</note> at the time of Hannibal. By not giving him the opportunity to fight, he wore down Hannibal's youthful ardor; and so, through his patience, he deserved to be called the "Cunctator" <note>The Delayer.</note> and the vindicator of the Republic. As the poet Ennius says: *One man, by delaying, restored the state for us.* <note>original: "Unus homo nobis cunctando restituit rem."</note> He was consul five times during the Second Punic War, in which he was the shield of the city of Rome and of all Italy, which was vexed by the wounds inflicted by Hannibal the Carthaginian. But no less beneficial was the deed of Claudius, who killed Hasdrubal. Whence:

<margin>Y</margin>

> Claudius Nero, who presented the head of Hasdrubal
> To his harsh and ferocious brother,
> Such that he made him turn his back in grief.

In this same battle, the consul Claudius was positioned against Hannibal, and his colleague Livius Salinator was against Hasdrubal, so that the two Carthaginian armies would not join together, for that would have been the end of the Romans. Therefore, Claudius secretly departed from Hannibal, leaving a part of his army behind, and was quietly received by his colleague. He came to blows with Hasdrubal—who was unaware of this—near Fossombrone at a river called the Metaurus. There, fifty-six thousand Carthaginians died. Claudius, returning to his own army, carried the head of Hasdrubal with him and had it thrown into Hannibal's camp. Hannibal did not know of Claudius's departure or return until he saw the head of his dead brother, and then, with great sorrow, he retreated to the furthest part of Italy.

<margin>Z</margin>

Then followed others: Mucius and Horatius. Mucius was a young man of excellent spirit. While Rome was besieged by Porsena, the King of Chiusi in Tuscany, he went alone into the enemy camp. Intending to kill the King, he instead killed the secretary who was paying the soldiers' wages. Having recognized his error in the presence of the King, he placed his hand upon the fire, burning the hand that had erred. When the King saw such endurance, and was then shrewdly warned that there were many others prepared for the same task of killing him, he determined to make peace with the Romans.

<margin>A</margin>

Horatius, called Cocles <note>Meaning "One-Eyed."</note>, as Porsena was nearly entering Rome with the Tuscans, stood alone in resistance on the bridge called the Sublician. He resisted long enough for the Romans to be able to cut down the bridge, and then he threw himself into the water. Thus, by swimming, he liberated both himself and his fatherland from the enemies. Whence the poet says:

<margin>B</margin>

> Mucius, who burned his own erring right hand,
> Horatius alone against all of Tuscany;
> For neither fire nor iron can harm virtue.

Because it is not enough merely to guard oneself against evils, but it is also necessary to remove suspicion, Valerius—later called Publicola <note>Meaning "Friend of the People."</note>—having built a house in an eminent place...

# CHAPTER ONE

While with my eyes I searched here and there,
I saw him there with the hostile spoils:
And the dictator Aemilius Mamercus

And several others of humble nature,
Rutilius, with Volumnius and Gracchus, and Philo,
Made noble and high through the virtue of arms.

These I saw among the noble blood of Ilus <note>Ilus was the mythical founder of Troy; the Romans claimed descent from the Trojans through Aeneas.</note>,
Mixed with the clear and beautiful Roman blood;
For whom neither my style nor any other is enough.

<margin>N</margin> He then narrates having seen two Pauls and Marcellus. There were two Pauls called Aemilii: the first, Lucius Paullus Aemilius, together with Gaius Atilius, led the troops against the Cisalpine and Transalpine Gauls; he triumphed over Illyricum, now called Slavonia <note>The region along the eastern Adriatic coast.</note>, and was later consul with Marcus Terentius Varro. Due to the recklessness of his companion at Cannae, a village in Apulia, while fighting courageously against Hannibal, he was killed. The other Paul was his son; he conquered Liguria, today called the Riviera of Genoa. Later, after sixty-eight years had passed, as consul he defeated Perseus, King of Macedonia, which he reduced to the form of a province, and led him captive in his triumph. This triumph involved so much plunder that the procession of it lasted three days.

<margin>O</margin> ¶ Marcus Marcellus: as we have said, at Clastidium <note>A town in Cisalpine Gaul, modern Casteggio.</note> he killed with his own hands Viridomarus, King of the Gauls, and having taken Milan, he triumphed over them. Clastidium is a city on the bank of the Po; he dedicated the *spolia opima* <note>original: "spoglie opime"; the "rich spoils" taken by a Roman general who killed the opposing commander in single combat.</note> there to Jupiter Feretrius. He was the first who taught how to make Hannibal flee near Nola; he later passed into Sicily and captured Syracuse. And in his fifth consulship against Hannibal, being with few people—as Livy and Valerius narrate—having gone to scout a place suitable for a camp, that glorious captain was ambushed; he who had gloriously fought thirty-nine times with banners flying, surpassed in this only by Caesar, who fought fifty times. Whence he says:

I saw two Pauls; and the good Marcus Marcellus,
Who on the bank of the Po near Clastidium,
Killed with his own hand the great rebel.

<margin>P</margin> ¶ Turning back, the poet narrates having seen the first four Kings of Rome. First, Romulus, the founder of Rome, who with arms subdued some neighboring peoples; he killed Acron, King of the Caeninenses, whence he first carried the *spolia opima*, and having made peace and shared the command with Titus Tatius the Sabine, after organizing the senators, he was killed by them, as Livy and Plutarch explain in great detail.

<margin>Q</margin> ¶ It was necessary, as Lucius Florus says, that the impetus of Romulus and military violence be mitigated; therefore succeeded Numa Pompilius, a religious man, who for his goodness and justice was called by the Sabines to the kingship of Rome. He composed the minds of the Romans, previously accustomed to battles, and submitted them to religion; but because the Romans seemed too effeminate under him...

<margin>R</margin> ¶ ...there succeeded after his death Tullus Hostilius, a warlike man; he awakened the Romans and fought many battles; he tore apart Mettius Fufetius <note>The dictator of Alba Longa who was executed for treachery by being pulled apart by two chariots.</note>, destroyed Alba, and moved all the noble families to Rome.

<margin>S</margin> ¶ Next succeeded Ancus Marcius, born of a daughter of Numa Pompilius, a man worthy in peace and war; he conquered the Latins, destroyed some lands, and moved many to inhabit Rome, which he enlarged; he also built the city of Ostia on the coast; he died a natural death, having reigned twenty-three years. These were the first four Roman kings. Whence he says:

And turning back I still see
The first four kings who held in Rome
The first, second, third, and fourth seats:

<margin>T</margin> ¶ He then calls Cincinnatus "with the unkept hair" <note>original: "inculta chioma"; a reference to his simple, rustic life as a farmer.</note> who, while the consul Minucius was besieged by the peoples called Aequi, was created Dictator and was found plowing; and so, wiping off the dust—as Livy says—he took the dictatorship; and after fifteen days, triumphing, he laid it down, "so much did the triumphant farmer hasten back to his interrupted work" <note>original: "tan' ad intermissum opus festinaret triumpha'lis agricola"; a quote from the historian Florus emphasizing Cincinnatus's lack of political ambition.</note>. Later he had Spurius Maelius, a seditious man, killed by Servilius Ahala in the presence of the people, as Maelius was seeking to oppress Roman liberty.

<margin>V</margin> ¶ Fabius Rutilianus <note>Known to history as Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus.</note> was there, who was left in Samnium with the army by Papirius Cursor with the command that he should not fight until the Dictator returned. Fabius, master of the horse <note>original: "maestro de le genti darme: & cauallo"; the Magister Equitum, the second-in-command to a Dictator.</note>, seeing the infinite opportunities due to the absence of the dictator and the enemy's lack of preparation, attacked and won. When Papirius returned, he had him summoned for having acted against military discipline; whence Fabius fled, hoping more in the clemency of the Senate.

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

...who, fleeing the severity of Papirius <note>Lucius Papirius Cursor, a Roman dictator known for his strictness and military discipline.</note>, went to Rome. Papirius suddenly followed him, seeking to punish Fabius <note>Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus, who had engaged the enemy against orders.</note>. With great difficulty, he granted a pardon, giving him up to the tears of his father and the prayers of his relatives, the Senate, and the Roman people. Fabius was indignant that he should be punished for a victory, but it would have helped him little if the Dictator had not faced so many intercessors. He later triumphed three times over the Apulians, the Samnites, and finally over the Gauls who were joined with the Tuscans. ¶ Together with him is joined Lucius Metellus, who was consul several times, dictator, and then Pontifex Maximus <note>The high priest of the Roman state religion.</note>. When the Temple of Minerva was burning, where the Palladium—that is, the statue of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena; the statue was a sacred relic believed to guarantee the safety of the city that held it.</note> which was the fate of every kingdom—was kept, he was moved by religious devotion. Entering the midst of the fire, he freed and preserved the Palladium. This is the "noble burden" of which the poet speaks, and from this event Metellus became blind. Whence it is said:

<margin>Y</margin>
| | |
|:--- | :--- |
| ¶ Atilius Regulus deserved great praise | |
| for defeating Carthage many times, but | **And Cincinnatus with his unkempt hair.** |
| much greater was the glory he | **And the great Rutilian with his noble disdain,** |
| acquired by keeping his faith <note>original: "fede"; referring to his oath or word of honor.</note>. Being | **And Metellus, sightless with his noble burden.** |
| captured, he was sent to Rome as an | |
| ambassador from Carthage under oath | |

<margin>Z</margin>
so that the Romans would return the Carthaginian prisoners in exchange for retaining Atilius Regulus. Although the Senate was content with such a condition, he was of the contrary opinion, pretending to have been poisoned <note>A strategy to ensure the Romans would not feel guilty for letting him return to his death.</note>. He did not want his homeland to suffer the damage of restoring so many prisoners just for his sake. Nevertheless, he did not wish to fail his oath, and so he returned, knowing well what cruel punishment he would endure, and how he was afterwards tormented and killed most cruelly. He was famous for both winning and dying deservedly. ¶ Beside him was Appius the Blind, who became blind because he was the cause of the sacrifices of Hercules—which had been celebrated by ancient succession by the family of the Potitii—being transferred to the humble and vile ministry of slaves. He dissuaded Rome from making peace with Pyrrhus, King of the Epirotes; thus he was the reason why Manius Curius Dentatus recovered the past losses. Pyrrhus was forced to leave Italy, never being able to see Rome because of Appius’s counsel. Whence it is said:

<margin>A</margin>
->**Atilius Regulus, so worthy of praise**<-
->**Both in winning and in dying; and Appius the blind;**<-
->**Who made Pyrrhus unworthy of seeing Rome,**<-

¶ With him was another Appius, whom he calls the "spur of the people." We can understand this to be that Appius who was created consul during the sedition between the senators and the people regarding the tribunitian law. He alone resisted the will of the people in defense of the Senate. The senators could hardly restrain him from deciding the matter with arms, calling the gods as witnesses that the consul did not fail the Senate, but the Senate failed the consul. Later, sent as consul against the Volscians, he treated the army so proudly that, to spite the consul, they allowed themselves to be defeated and put to flight, refusing to fight. Realizing this, he withdrew the people to a safe place and first had the heads of the centurions who had fled cut off, and then executed every tenth man-at-arms <note>The practice of decimation.</note>. He was later accused before the people and deposed from his magistracy the following year. In that case, he fatigued the whole Senate more than ever in any other matter; nor could he ever be persuaded to change his dress or relax his austerity. But, overcome by infirmity before the case was determined, the end of the judgment could not be seen. This man was the "spur" and stimulus of the people, though almost all the Appii were bitter enemies of the commoners. ¶ Next were two Fulvii. The first was Quintus Fulvius, who took vengeance on Capua, which had rebelled to join Hannibal. Having taken the city, he brought out the nobility and senators and killed them. While he was doing so, letters came from the Senate saying he should show mercy; he did not read the letters until he had finished killing those who remained. ¶ The other was called Fulvius Nobilior, the consul. He defeated the Aetolians and many peoples of Epirus and Cephalonia who had favored Antiochus, King of Asia, against the Romans, and he triumphed for this victory. ¶ Gnaeus Manlius Vulso succeeded Lucius Scipio in the provinces after Antiochus was defeated. Hearing that the Galatians <note>original: "gallo greci"; Gauls who had settled in Hellenistic Asia Minor.</note> were powerful among those peoples in Asia—being a mix of Gauls and Greeks who had made a part of Asia their own and were a great terror to other lords—he moved his armies against them. In a short time, he almost wiped out their seed as they fled to Mount Olympus; he killed more than seventy thousand and took many prisoners. Manlius triumphed over these, having previously defeated Brennus, the captain of that people. ¶ Flaminius, son of the Flaminius who died at Lake Perugia <note>Lake Trasimene.</note>, was sent against Philip, King of Macedonia, father of Perseus. Philip was defeated by Paulus Aemilius, who conquered and routed him so thoroughly that he struggled even to obtain peace.

->CAPITVLO PRIMO<-
<note>Chapter One</note>

MM ii

# CHAPTER ONE

...peace with many conditions, among which was that Greece should have no impediment from him nor should he have any claim over it; to which he restored its ancient liberty and customary laws, and then declared the Greek country free. Whence it says:

> And another Appius, a spur to the people with him;
> Two Fulvii, and Manlius the Volscian, and that Flamininus;
> Who conquered and freed the Greek country.
<note>Titus Quinctius Flamininus famously declared the "Freedom of the Greeks" at the Isthmian Games in 196 BC after defeating Philip V of Macedon.</note>

<margin>F</margin>
Among the others was Virginius, stained with blood for this reason: as there was great strife between the <term>plebeians (common people)</term> and the senators over the creation of new laws, it was decided to elect ten men <term>Decemviri</term> who would have summary power in judgments. Among these was Appius Claudius, who fell in love with Virginia, the daughter of Lucius Virginius (who at that time was away on an expedition against the Sabines). Being unable to have her by any other means, Appius had one of his partisans named Marcus Claudius claim her as his slave before his own tribunal. The father, recalled from the army and unable to otherwise free his daughter from shameful servitude, took a knife from a butcher and with it killed Virginia, his daughter. With that bloody knife, he went to the army; moved by this, they came to Rome and seized the Aventine Hill. Thus it was necessary to drive out those ten men—whom he calls tyrants—and so through Lucius Valerius and Marcus Horatius, Virginius and the others were reconciled to the Senate. Whence it says:

> There among the others was Virginius, stained
> With the blood of his daughter: through whom from those ten
> Tyrants the impious dominion was taken.

<margin>G</margin>
How much love citizens should have toward their fatherland was shown by Decius, the colleague of Torquatus, in the battle against the Latins and Sabines. Having a vision that the gods of the underworld and the Earth demanded the captain of one or the other army, he chose to die voluntarily for his country <note>This ritual of self-sacrifice was known as *devotio*.</note>. His son followed him in the battle against the Samnites, Gauls, and Tuscans, dying in the same manner; and as if it were an inheritance, the grandson followed the footsteps of his grandfather and father. Whence against Pyrrhus of Epirus, he chose to die for his country in the same way. These three Decii were generous with their blood.

<margin>H</margin>
Afterward were two brothers, Publius and Gnaeus Scipio, sent to Spain against Hasdrubal and Mago. For eight years, with victory and great benefit to the Romans, they performed great deeds in Spain; but while striving to put an end to that long war, through the treachery of the Numidians and the flight of the Celtiberians, both consuls were killed within the span of thirty days.

<margin>I</margin>
There was a young man named Lucius Marcius, of supreme spirit and outstanding virtue, who gathered the remains of the two broken armies. While comforting them with his words, a flame miraculously appeared around his head, which gave so much hope to the Romans that they responded, assaulted the enemies, and captured the camps of Hasdrubal and Mago. Thus Marcius sustained the weight of two consuls, and with a very great slaughter of enemies and the safety of the Romans, he preserved Spain and the Republic and the Roman state in this manner. Whence it says:

> And generous with their blood were three Decii;
> And two great Scipios, whom Spain crushed;
> And Marcius, who sustained both their places.

<margin>K</margin>
Next were two sons: one was Lucius Scipio Asiaticus, brother of Scipio the Elder and son of the Publius Scipio mentioned above who died in Spain. Being sent to Asia against Antiochus <note>Antiochus III the Great, the Seleucid King.</note>, he brought back victory and a triumph, and also earned the right to be called "Asiaticus" for the victory in Asia.

<margin>L</margin>
The other was Scipio Nasica, son of the Gnaeus Scipio mentioned above, who by his virtues deserved to be judged by the Senate as the "best man in Rome." Thus he welcomed the statue of Cybele, mother of the gods, brought from Phrygia, until her temple was built. He fought against the Cisalpine Gauls and against the Boii (as those people are called) and brought back a triumph. Later, as a private citizen, he was the author of the death of Tiberius Gracchus, a seditious man, which was of great benefit to the Roman Senate. These men each seemed to approach the stature of their fathers. Whence it says:

> And as each seemed to approach his own [father's] stature:
> Asiaticus was there, and that perfect one
> Whom the good Senate alone chose as the best.

<margin>M</margin>
Deservedly he adds that Gaius Laelius was together with the Cornelii Scipiones, because he was a great friend of the elder Africanus, with whom he served in war and did great deeds. He was also consul and lived with the highest reputation; but

### TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>N</margin>
Metellus did not seem to be such a friend; who in life seemed divided from Cornelius <note>referring to Scipio Aemilianus, of the Cornelii family</note> but in death showed himself to be reconciled. ¶ Whence it is to be known that Metellus, surnamed the Fortunate <note>Latin: *felix*</note>, was a rival of the virtue of Scipio Aemilianus and was at odds with him only for the sake of honor and ambition. Thus, when Scipio died, Metellus grieved in the senate and commanded his sons to honor the body of Scipio; so, while alive, he chose to be a rival of his virtue, but loved him in death. This man was surnamed <term>Macedonicus</term> <note>a title given for his victory over Macedonia</note> because he triumphed over Macedonia. He was a consul in Spain where he performed many feats. He had four sons, three of whom he saw become consuls, and one who held a triumph before his death. Among these were Metellus <term>Numidicus</term>, who fought against Jugurtha, and Metellus <term>Creticus</term>, who conquered Crete. These four sons carried their dead father to the tomb. Therefore, the poet M.F. says that the "seed" <note>meaning his progeny or sons</note> was near the father, which he placed under the earth. Whence he says:

->And Laelius was close to his Cornelius;<-
->Not so that Metellus, upon whom Fortune<-
->Smiled so much that he is called the Fortunate:<-
->Living, their minds seemed divided;<-
->In dying, he reunited them: and with the father<-
->Was his seed, which placed him beneath the earth.<-

<margin>O</margin>
¶ The poet recognized Vespasian by the shape of his body and his "square shoulders," just as Suetonius describes him. This man was an excellent emperor; he triumphed with his son Titus over Jerusalem, as Josephus mentions. After his death, he left two sons: Titus and Domitian.

<margin>P</margin>
¶ He was succeeded by Titus, his true son and a successor who was a man adorned with every virtue and most liberal; but as envious Fortune quickly deprives men of their governance, he died a short time after his father: <note>original: *fœlix breuitate imperij*</note> "fortunate in the brevity of his rule."

<margin>Q</margin>
¶ He was succeeded by his brother Domitian, a most wicked man; and in this period, the succession did not follow the others, but rather those who had come to the Roman Empire through the election of the senate or through adoption. Just as after Domitian, Nerva was elected emperor by the senate; a good, moderate, and just man, he died after sixteen months of his rule and left as his successor Trajan, his adopted son. Trajan was Spanish by nationality and most worthy; he subjugated Dacia and reacquired Armenia which had been taken by the Parthians, and he reduced Assyria, Mesopotamia, and Arabia to provinces. After many glorious works in peace and war, he died in Asia at the noble city of Seleucia.

<margin>R</margin>
¶ Hadrian, adopted by Trajan, visited almost all the provinces subject to the Romans, settling their affairs. He was a most literate man and a lover of learned and virtuous men. He was most learned in the Greek and Latin languages, arithmetic, geometry, painting, and astrology, and most skilled in the military arts, which he restored after they had declined. He died at Baiae at the age of seventy years, five months, and seventeen days; he reigned for twenty-one years.

<margin>S</margin>
¶ Antoninus Pius succeeded him as his adopted son, a most merciful man who focused more on preserving the empire than increasing it. Because he loved his citizens, he used to say that he would rather preserve one citizen than kill a thousand enemies. This sentiment was also held by Scipio. He died at the age of seventy-two according to Eusebius, or seventy-seven according to Eutropius.

<margin>T</margin>
¶ He left Marcus Antoninus <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>, his adopted son, who was most learned. He fought only one battle against certain peoples of Asia, and in the third year of those wars, he triumphed. He was most merciful to his people and wrote that the state would be happy if it had chosen an adopted son rather than leaving the empire to Lucius Antoninus Commodus, his natural son, who was most wicked and was finally strangled in his house by his own people.

<margin>V</margin>
¶ But he would have done much better to adopt one like Theodosius, who succeeded to the throne about 240 years after him. Between them, there were many emperors: Alexander, Aurelian, Diocletian, Constantine, and many others; but—

<margin>X</margin>
Theodosius was the last <note>referring to the last emperor of a united empire</note>. He was a religious man; in his time lived Saint Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine, and the poet Claudian. ¶ He died in Milan, and after his death, the world began to fail from its ancient institutions and good customs, and the Roman Empire fell into ruin. Whence he says:

<margin>Y</margin>
¶ Shortly thereafter, the poet relates having noticed some worthy and most glorious men who were overshadowed by the splendid fame of their successors. These whom he names were all Kings of Alba; among whom was the first founder of Alba Longa, Iulus Ascanius, the son of Aeneas. ¶ Atys was an Alban king who ruled for twenty-four years.

<margin>A</margin>
¶ Numitor was the father of Rhea Silvia, the mother of Romulus and Remus, and the brother of Amulius.

->Then Vespasian, and by his square shoulders<-
->I recognized him, in the manner of a man who strives,<-
->With his Titus, for high and graceful works;<-
->Domitian was not there; whence he felt anger and shame:<-
->But there was the family that, through the path<-
->Of adoption, rises to the great empire:<-
->Trajan, and Hadrian, Antoninus, and Marcus.<-

*At last Theodosius, not sparing in good deeds,*
*Was the final mirror of virtue*
*In that order, I say; and after him*

<margin>B C D</margin> ¶ The son of Procas: he was driven out by his brother and was restored to the kingdom by his grandsons <note>Referring to the myth of Numitor, restored by Romulus and Remus</note>. ¶ Silvius, so named because he was born in the forest <note>Latin: *silva*</note>, after whom all the other Alban kings were called "Silvii." ¶ Procas was the father of King Amulius and Numitor. ¶ Capi Silvius reigned for 27 years and 11 months. ¶ The "New Latinus" is distinguished from the father of Lavinia, which New Latinus succeeded Aeneas Silvius. <margin>E F G</margin> ¶ Agrippa reigned for 40 years. ¶ And Tiberinus and Aventinus: the first, having been drowned, caused the Tiber to be named after him; the other, being buried there, gave an eternal name to the Aventine Hill—although there are various opinions regarding these names. *A little apart, I was not yet aware*

*But it was covered by the shadow of others.*
*There was he who placed the foundations*
*Of Alba Longa on that wandering mountain;*

*And Capi, and the old and new King Latinus,*

<margin>H</margin> ¶ Not without mystery does the poet pretend that he did not notice these ancient kings of Italy because of their great antiquity, but a sign was made to him. And so he saw Saturn, driven out by his son Jove from Arcadia, who came to Italy where he reigned with Janus; and because he taught that rough people to sow grain and plant and similar things, after his death he was worshipped as a god.

<margin>I</margin> ¶ Picus, the son of Saturn and husband of Pomona, the goddess of fruit, was loved by Circe and by her changed into a woodpecker <note>Italian: *pico*</note>, as the poets imagine, because that king made much use of the augury of that bird. <margin>K</margin> ¶ Faunus, the son of Picus, took his sister Fauna as his wife; he killed her when he found she had drunk wine, and for the love he bore her, he had her worshipped as a goddess and ordained sacrifices. <margin>L</margin> ¶ Janus, the most ancient king of Italy, first established temples to the gods and sacrifices; it was during his time that Saturn came to Italy. He was depicted with two faces, and later with four, and was worshipped as the god of every beginning. ¶ Camilla, the daughter of Metabus, king of Priverno in the Volscian land, was raised with military customs; she came to the aid of Turnus against Aeneas. She was most chaste and, as Virgil narrates, was killed by Arruns. <margin>M N</margin> ¶ Turnus, the son of Daunus and Venilia and king of the Rutulians and Ardea, fought with Aeneas for the love of Lavinia, the daughter of Latinus; although he was a very strong man, he was killed by him, having first himself killed Pallas, the son of King Evander. The poet narrates this. Whence he says:

*I did not notice: but a sign was made to me;*
*And as if in a doubtful nocturnal gaze*
*I saw those who had less strength and more wisdom:*
*The first Italian kings: there were Saturn,*
*Picus, Faunus, Janus; and then not far off*
*I saw Camilla and Turnus walking pensively:*

<margin>O</margin> ¶ Then he gathers some most worthy men of diverse nations, whom he narrates having seen first: that great Carthaginian, Hannibal, who did not forget the oath made to his father to always be an enemy of the Romans. He passed into Italy with his army and first broke <note>defeated</note> P. Scipio the consul, and then Tiberius Sempronius with that same army. He broke Scipio again at the Trebia; later he lost an eye on the plain of the Arno, which at that time was a swamp, due to the excessive cold. At Lake Trasimene <note>OCR: *pufia*</note> he defeated Flaminius, and at Cannae, Paulus Emilius and Terentius. <margin>P</margin> ¶ Varro was delayed by Fabio Maximo, made to flee by Marcellus, and finally recalled by Scipio to Africa. He was overcome by him, after which he fled to Antiochus; and when peace was made between the Romans and Antiochus, he went to Prusias, king of Bithynia, where he took his own life by poison <note>Italian: *auenento*</note> so as not to fall into the hands of the Romans. ¶ Next he saw Philip of Macedon, the father of Alexander, who similarly was blind in one eye, having been wounded by an arrow in battle. He defeated the Athenians, Illyrians, Molossians, Greeks, Cappadocians, and Thracians; he defeated the Dardanians and several other peoples. Thinking to go against the Persians, he was killed with a knife by Pausania, a youth, in the midst of Alexander his son and Alexander his son-in-law (the husband of Cleopatra his daughter) during a wedding, not without suspicion of the consent of Olympias, the mother of Alexander, and of the son himself, about whom Justin writes excellently with brevity. And Xanthippus the Lacedaemonian. <margin>Q</margin>

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>R</margin>
Having been made captain of the Carthaginians, he <note>Xanthippus of Sparta</note> captured Marcus Atilius Regulus, the Roman general. When returning to his homeland, the Carthaginians sent a ship after him; out of suspicion and fear of his virtue and wisdom, they put him to death. Thus, they repaid his fine service with the height of ingratitude. ¶ Gylippus was a similar Spartan: sent by his citizens to Sicily to help Syracuse against Catania (which was favored by the Athenians), he was victorious three times. Having killed the Athenian general Lamachus, he liberated the city from siege. When the battle moved to the sea, he won twice and captured 130 ships. Their captain, Nicias, bringing back a thousand talents of booty, kept thirty for himself without giving a reason; for this, he was sent into exile by the severe justice of the Spartans, and died there. He then joins these men together, where he says:

->And because glory reaches every part:<-
->I saw beyond a stream a great Carthaginian<-
<note>Hannibal, the famous general of Carthage who invaded Italy</note>
->Whose memory still stings Italy;<-
->One eye he had left in my country<-
->When the Tuscan river was stagnant in the cold weather<-
<note>The Arno river; Hannibal lost an eye to infection while crossing the marshes of Etruria</note>
->So that he was a strange sight to behold:<-
<margin>S</margin> ->Atop a great elephant, a one-eyed leader<-
->He looks around him, and I saw King Philip<-
<note>Philip V of Macedon, who fought Rome and also lost an eye</note>
->Similarly darkened on one side.<-
->I saw the Spartan Xanthippus there,<-
->Who did a fine service for ungrateful people;<-
->And from the same nest came Gylippus.<-

<margin>S</margin>
¶ How much care the ancients took in seeking glory is clearly shown by poetic fables. Even Hercules, who was not only a man superior to us but, trusting in his own strength, also descended to the underworld. According to the authority of Varro, there were sixty-four different men named Hercules; but one, the son of Jupiter and Alcmene, was greatly celebrated above the others. This is the one who, as a small child in his cradle, strangled two serpents; he killed the lion, defeated the Hydra, and the Erymanthian boar; he defeated Achelous and Antaeus; he made the horses of Diomedes of Thrace eat their master; he held up the sky, went to the underworld and dragged Cerberus out by force; and performed many other trials exceeding thirty in number.

<margin>T</margin>
<margin>V</margin>
¶ Although twelve principal labors are cited, he also killed the centaur Nessus. Later, on Mount Oeta in Thessaly, he wore a shirt dyed in the blood of Nessus, who had been wounded by Hercules' poisonous arrows. It was sent by his wife Deianira, who believed it was a charm to make Hercules love her (as Nessus had told her as he died); thus he died and was buried by Philoctetes. After his death, he was worshipped. Aeneas, as Virgil and Livy narrate, came to Italy and fought with Turnus, killing him. He took Lavinia, daughter of King Latinus, as his wife. But as Virgil narrates in Book VI, he also went to the Stygian realm—that is, the underworld—with the Sibyl. Afterwards he returned and was victorious in Italy, as has been said. His death is quite uncertain, but it is generally held that he drowned in the river Numicus. After this, he was worshipped and called "Jupiter Indiges." Many trials are told of Theseus. He tamed the Corinthian, Geryon, Sciron, and the Minotaur. He went to the underworld to kidnap Proserpina with Pirithous. Some say he returned, others say not; it is a mythical matter. But the truth is that he wanted to kidnap Proserpina, daughter of the King of the Molossians <note>The commentator rationalizes the myth into a historical event</note>, by whom he was captured and later liberated by Hercules. He did many things, as Plutarch describes extensively in his *Life*. Ulysses, son of Laertes, was one of the Greek captains. He did many things at Troy: he brought Achilles to the army; he killed Dolon and Rhesus, King of <margin>X</margin> Thrace. He took the ashes of Laomedon and also took the Palladium from the citadel of Troy. In the end, with his great cunning and prudence, he overcame Troy. He wandered ten years by sea, escaped the cruelty of Polyphemus, the tempest of Scylla and Charybdis, the frauds of the Sirens, and the ferocity of the Laestrygonians, as Homer narrates. He went to the underworld; then, having returned to Ithaca, he could not escape the oracle which predicted he would be killed by his own offspring. Thus, he was killed by Telegonus, his son whom he had with Circe. These are the ones the poets say went to the Stygian realm, that is, the underworld. Whence he says:

<margin>Y</margin>
¶ There was in Tuscany a man named Dardanus from a land called Cortona <note>original: "Coito" - likely an error for Cortona, the traditional Italian origin of the founder of Troy</note>, who was the son of Jupiter and Electra. He went to Phrygia and was a leader there or founded the city of Troy; hence the Trojans are called Dardanians after him, and the province Dardania.

->I saw those who went to the Stygian realm:<-
->Hercules, Aeneas, Theseus, and Ulysses,<-
->To leave such a trace of fame behind here.<-

# CHAPTER ONE

<sig>MM iii</sig>

<margin>Z</margin>
Dardanus: his son was Erichthonius, from whom was born Tros, the Trojan king, after whom Troy is named. He had two sons: Ilus and Assaracus. From Ilus, the fortress of Troy took the name Ilium <note>named after the "Ilian rock"</note>. This Ilus was the father of Laomedon, the father of Priam, who among many sons had Hector, a man of greatest strength and moderation. Hector killed Patroclus and many times withstood the onslaught of the Greeks, afflicting them greatly; in the end, he was killed by Achilles. Old Priam lived so long that after the death of fifty sons (whom he is said to have had), he saw his homeland taken by enemies and was then miserably killed by Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles. Therefore the poet <note>Petrarch</note> says that he lived too long, for had he died sooner, he would not have seen such misery. Among many, he specifically mentions having seen Hector, Priam, Dardanus, and Tros. Hence he says:

-> That Hector with his father, who lived too long; <-
-> Dardanus, and Tros, and other heroes I saw <-
-> Renowned for themselves: but more for those who wrote of them. <-

<margin>4</margin>
<margin>¶ Note well the great undertaking of the Greeks against the Trojans, in which there were many strong heroes. Among them was Diomedes, the son of Tydeus and friend of Ulysses. He was very useful to the Greeks. After the fall of Troy, he returned to Argos; but out of shame for his wife Aegiale, who had committed adultery, he fled to Apulia and built a land called Argoripa (later Arpi), where he lived.</margin>
<margin>B</margin> ¶ Achilles was the son of Peleus, raised by Chiron. Led to the Trojan conquest, he easily proved himself the strongest of all. He killed Hector with his own hands. Having seen Polyxena, he fell in love with her; while seeking her hand, as had been arranged, he went to the temple of Apollo Thymbraeus to join in kinship with Priam and end the siege. There, Paris treacherously attacked and killed him. He was buried at the Sigeion promontory of Troy. <margin>C</margin> ¶ The great Atridae: these were Agamemnon and Menelaus, sons of Philisthenes (though reputed to be sons of Atreus). After the captivity of Troy, Agamemnon returned home where he was killed by his wife Clytemnestra and her adulterer, Aegisthus. <margin>D</margin> ¶ Menelaus, having reclaimed his Helen, was much tossed by storms but finally returned to his homeland and died in peace. <margin>E</margin> ¶ The two Ajaxes: one was Telamonian Ajax, who was the strongest in the Greek army. After the death of Achilles, he contested with Ulysses for the succession of Achilles' armor; having lost, he went mad and killed himself, <margin>F</margin> as Ovid narrates in the 14th book of the *Metamorphoses*. The other was Ajax Oileus, a very fast and strong man; while returning home near the Caphareus promontory, he was overcome by a storm and drowned, also struck by lightning through the wrath of Pallas <note>Athena</note>, as the poets say. It is these men the poet <note>Petrarch</note> intends by saying:

-> Diomedes, Achilles, and the great Atridae; <-
-> The two Ajaxes; <-

<margin>G</margin>
<margin>¶ There was a city in Boeotia called Thebes, built by Cadmus the Phoenician while searching for his sister Europa, who had been kidnapped by Jove. Having been commanded by his father Agenor not to return without her, he founded this city.</margin>
In this city was a king, among others, called Oedipus, who had two male sons: Eteocles and Polynices. As we have said above in the first *Triumph of Love*, they divided the lordship so that they would reign for one year each. Thus, Polynices went into exile for the first year. One evening he arrived in Argos, going to Adrastus, the king of that city. Tydeus of Calydon had also arrived there, having imprudently killed his brother Menalippus. While at the king's gate, the two came to a great contention and anger, so much so that their fighting was heard and reported to the king. Coming there to pacify them, the king saw Polynices wearing a lion's skin and Tydeus a boar's skin. That king had two daughters: one Argia, the other Deiphile. He had received an answer from an oracle: <note>original: "Setigerumque suem: & fulvum adventare leonem"</note> "That a bristly boar and a tawny lion would arrive," to whom he should give his daughters. Thus he gave Argia to Polynices and Deiphile to Tydeus. Afterward, there was such love between Tydeus and Polynices that they deserve to be counted among the greatest of friends. <margin>H</margin> ¶ After the year passed, Polynices sent Tydeus as an ambassador to his brother to demand the return of the lordship. Eteocles proudly denied it, and so seven captains gathered: Adrastus, Tydeus, Polynices, Amphiaraus, Capaneus, Hippomedon, and Parthenopaeus. They all died at Thebes except for Adrastus, who fled. The brothers Eteocles and Polynices killed each other. Capaneus was killed while scaling the walls, and Amphiaraus was swallowed by the earth. The others died in battle, and of this the poet makes mention, saying:

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>I</margin> ¶ There were certainly women in Scythia called Amazons, strong and warlike, who lived without men and performed great deeds in arms. After the death of Queen Marpesia <note>original: "mathesia"</note>, she was succeeded by Orithyia, who was distinguished for many virtues and principally for perpetual virginity. These Amazons were of such terror that by the command of Eurystheus,

-> Tydeus and Polynices, <-
-> Enemies first; then such faithful friends; <-
-> And the bold and unhappy company <-
-> That fell at Thebes; and that other, which at Troy <-
-> Accomplished much, I believe; but more is said of them. <-

Hercules, as if it were an almost impossible task, came to subdue them. At that time, Orithyia was away on a military campaign outside her homeland, and so Hercules captured two sisters: Hippolyta, whom he gave to Theseus, and the other, Menalippe. When Orithyia returned, she crossed into Greece to recover her sister Hippolyta, but she was defeated 

<margin>K</margin> by Theseus and the Athenians. ¶ After her death, she was succeeded by Penthesilea, who came to the aid of the Trojans; although she arrived somewhat late, she gave many proofs of her valor. In the end, she was killed by Achilles along with her army, and those few who remained were killed by neighboring peoples and died without heirs <note>original: "itestate" (intestate)</note>, so that in a very short time the empire of the Scythian Amazons—of whom Petrarch here makes mention—failed. Thus he says:

<margin>L</margin> ¶ And because the poet had mentioned these famous women, he deservedly adds Cyrus, who was defeated by Tomyris, Queen of Scythia, as is a well-known fact among historians. Above, quite extensively in the *Triumph of Chastity*,

-> Penthesilea, who caused the Greeks great trouble; <-
-> Hippolyta and Orithyia, who reigned <-
-> There near the sea where the Tanais <note>original: "dannoia" (The River Don)</note> enters: <-

we have narrated how Cyrus, son of Cambyses and Mandane, appointed by heaven to the empire of the Medes, drove his grandfather Astyages from his lordship and in a short time subjugated all of Asia and part

<margin>M</margin> of the East. But having crossed into Scythia against Tomyris, he was defeated and killed by her, along with 200,000 Persians, using the same artifice by which he had previously defeated her son. ¶ The head of Cyrus was cut off and placed

<margin>N</margin> into a wineskin of human blood with these words: "Cyrus, Cyrus, you thirsted for blood; drink blood." <note>original Latin: "cyre cyre sanguine sitisti: sanguine bibe"</note> Therefore Petrarch says that he was more greedy for blood than Crassus was for gold. ¶ This Crassus, a most powerful Roman citizen, went against the Parthians out of greed for accumulating gold, because he had heard they were wealthy. Because he attended only to accumulation, he, his son, and his army were destroyed, and the glorious Roman standards fell into the hands of barbarians. Crassus’s head was cut off and, sent to the King of the Parthians, it was filled with molten gold <note>original: "fittilato" (melted/cast)</note>, and it was said to him: <term>Still you thirsted for gold, drink gold</term> <note>original Latin: "anchora aurum sitisti aurum bibas"</note>. Therefore, the poet rightly says that greed was bitter to both: to the former for blood, to the latter for gold. Thus he says:

For some, the veil of envy is removed only by death—envy being the enemy and constant companion of virtue among the living—and then virtue shows itself more lucid and resplendent. ¶ For this reason, I do not doubt that Marcus Attilius Regulus <note>A Roman general famous for his honor; he returned to Carthage to face execution rather than break his word.</note> returned to the Carthaginians and shortened this
</margin>

*briefest life in some small moment in order to live eternally in the mouths and monuments of posterity. This same impulse drove various and diverse enterprises: the Fabii, Scipiones, Decii, Marcelli, and so many other famous Romans and foreigners. Recognizing this under an excellent allegory, the poet portrays Death—after she has triumphed over Laura—departing, and Fame succeeding her. Fame alone is what draws man out of the grave and preserves him alive in continuity. Deservedly, in the preceding chapter, he calls her a queen who appeared as a divine thing, possessing such power that the dead, through her potency and force, live almost eternally. He then adds that this Queen Fame, who appeared as a divine thing, has Caesar and Scipio at her right hand. But which of them was closer was difficult to judge. Of these two most famous and excellent men: one was a servant only of virtue and not of love; the other was a servant of both. For Scipio, in following virtue, had always been a stranger to love. But Caesar had observed both love and virtue in his time. Thus he says:*

¶ Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, one must primarily know that Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> places this distinguished and excellent company on the right hand of Fame—those whom he describes below—to demonstrate that they are more worthy of fame than those men who gave themselves only to literary leisure, even though these others are also worthy of honor.
</margin>

*Because a greater notice, memory, and discussion of the former always remains in the world, while in the others a number of virtues are always found secondarily. It is also to be understood that since Master Francesco wishes in this Triumph only to describe the deeds of virtue, it is not necessary to report every act of history as the writers of the Latin language do in order. For they observe every minimal gesture, many of which are worthy of neither praise, nor fame, nor commendation. Therefore, it is enough for us to report only those which we have noticed as having proceeded from virtue or excellence, especially in deeds of arms. This seems to be the intention of the poet when, in the third and final chapter of this Triumph, he says: "I could not pull myself away from such a sight, when I heard it said: turn your mind to the other side, for honor is well-earned by things other than arms." Thus, men have acted in such a way that fame of them has deservedly remained in the world. The reason is because it belongs to a single discipline to determine opposites, as the famous proposition goes: **The science of opposites is one and the same.** <note>original: "Oppositorum eadem est disciplina." This is a common philosophical maxim in the Middle Ages derived from Aristotle.</note> Likewise, it is appropriate to be brief to conform to the order of the poet, who often commemorates only the name, and sometimes only a single gesture among many. In the third and final place, it is to be noted that it is first necessary to narrate the deeds of Caesar and Scipio, then to show such conformity between them that there is great reason for it to be difficult to judge which one should precede the other in fame. ¶ Julius Caesar, then, was the son of Lucius Caesar and Aurelia, most honorable Roman citizens. Having reached the age of sixteen, he was left without a father. Being of a kingly nature and most pleasing appearance, he was very hateful to Lucius Cornelius Sulla, especially because Caesar was joined to Marius by close affinity; for Julia, his paternal aunt, was the wife of Marius, and the son of Marius born of her was his cousin. For this reason, Sulla several times wanted to have him put to death. Consequently, Caesar was forced to live in hiding-places and ransom himself with money from Sulla's knights, who sometimes found him hidden. Having been for some time under this persecution, at last one Mamercus Emilio and one Aurelio Cotta, his kinsmen...*

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

His influential and benevolent friends obtained a pardon for him from Sulla; although Sulla said to them, as <margin>Plutarch</margin> writes: "You are fools if you do not see many Mariuses in this boy." <note>original Latin: "Vos amentes estis: nisi in hoc puero multos ispiciatis marios." Gaius Marius was Sulla's great rival; Sulla correctly predicted that Caesar would eventually overturn his own political order.</note> Caesar, then being exempt from the ban and edict of Sulla, left Rome and went to Britain <note>Likely a transcription error or authorial mistake for Bithynia in Asia Minor, where Caesar famously spent time at the court of King Nicomedes.</note> to the king of the island of Pharmacusa. He was taken by pirates, with whom he stayed about thirty days in captivity with only one doctor and two chamberlains. Ransomed later for money, he set out to pursue them and take revenge; and finally, having taken the city of Pergamon, he seized all the pirates and executed them by the throat, just as he had often jokingly predicted he would do while he was in prison with them. After Sulla died and the Roman Republic began to be disturbed, Caesar returned to Rome where Marcus Lepidus almost held the leadership. Although Lepidus wanted Caesar to share in all his fortunes, Caesar did not wish to consent, but rather to rule for himself and govern in public administrations. From there he attained many honors for himself, such as Aedile, Praetor, Priest <note>Pontifex Maximus</note>, and Consul. Chiefly regarding military expeditions, having been Praetor, Further Spain fell to him as a province, beyond the River Baetis. Going there briefly and successfully, he settled it by subjecting the Callaeci and the Lusitanians to Roman rule as far as the ocean. Returning later to Rome when it was time to elect new consuls, Caesar wished to seek the consulship and, on the other hand, to triumph over the Spaniards. But because it was necessary for one who triumphed to remain outside Rome for a time, and for one who sought the consulship to be present in the Senate house, Caesar ultimately gave up the triumph because of this conflict and sought the consulship. At this time, the government and the care of Rome were committed and totally reduced to Marcus Crassus, G. Pompey, and Julius Caesar. By the duty of his consulship, Caesar went against the Gauls and Germans; at that time, Marcus Crassus and G. Pompey were re-elected consuls. Crassus proceeded against the Parthians and was killed by them, and his armies were lost in Mesopotamia. Now Pompey, who had a deep-seated enmity with Caesar due to ambition, seeing himself left alone in Rome, strove as much as he could to diminish Caesar in every honor and reputation. From this it happened that Caesar, having conquered and subjugated the Gauls, the Germans, the Saxons, the Bulgarians <note>Likely the Belgae; the author uses the contemporary term "Bulgari" for northern tribes.</note>, and the other peoples described in his *Gallic Commentaries*, returned toward Rome and asked the Senate for a second consulship and an extension of his command. This request was denied by the Senate through the work of Pompey, Cato, Marcus Bibulus, and Marcus Marcellus. Beyond this, by the authority of the consul, he was ordered while still on his way that before he crossed the Rubicon—a river situated above Rimini—he should disband his armies and come to Rome as a private citizen. Furthermore, the Senate granted command to Pompey along with certain legions that were reserved at Luceria. When this determination of the Senate was announced, one of Caesar’s centurions named Curio <note>Historically a Tribune of the Plebs, though the text identifies him as a soldier.</note> replied in Caesar's name that he was content to observe what the Senate had disposed for him and to release his men if Pompey did the same. Since the Senate would not accept this, and Caesar did not wish to beg for his command, Curio put his hand to <margin>I</margin> his sword and, pulling it out, said: "This sword indeed shall extend it" <note>original Latin: "Hic ensis quidem prorogabit"</note>, and departed. At this time Caesar had already reached the Rubicon, returning from Gaul; there he stopped on the bank and thought to himself whether he should pass further. While his soldiers marveled and asked why he stopped, Caesar, pointing to the bridge, said: "If we cross this little bridge, soldiers, all things must be done by arms." <note>original Latin: "Si hunc ponticulum transierimus milites omnia armis agenda erunt."</note> Finally, while still in doubt, there appeared in the air a form of a very large man who took a trumpet from one of the army and crossed the river, sounding it from the other bank. Then Caesar, seeing this, said: "The die is cast; let us go where the portents of the gods and the iniquity of our enemies call us." <note>original Latin: "Iacta est alea: eamus quo deorum ostenta e inimicorum iniquitas vocat."</note> And he crossed the river. Having not agreed on peace with Pompey's ambassadors at Ravenna, he came to Rimini that same night. After taking it, he took Osimo and the whole March; from there he came to Corfinio, where Domitius Ahenobarbus was in garrison. Domitius, fleeing out of fear, was taken by Caesar's soldiers and brought to Caesar with a great quantity of gold. But Caesar released Domitius and Actius Varro (who had been taken by Mark Antony) and all of them with great liberality, so that he might appear moderate no less in money than in the lives of men. <margin>R</margin> When Caesar's actions were heard of in Rome, Pompey departed and rode to Capua; and Lentulus the consul, out of fear, fled with part of the senators to Pompey. But Caesar, knowing of the flight of the consul and the senators to Pompey, departed from Corfinio and went to follow them. Because of this, Pompey fled to Brindisi where Caesar besieged him, and finally forced him along with the senators to flee to Epirus at Durrës. Caesar took Brindisi, and then returned to Rome to settle and pacify the city and the remaining senators, whom he humbly prayed would join him in defending the liberty of the Roman Republic. And having thus settled Rome...

## CHAPTER TWO

He departed from Rome and went to Spain against Petreius and Afranius <note>Marcus Petreius and Lucius Afranius were generals under Pompey the Great who commanded his forces in Spain.</note>, whom he finally forced to lay down their arms. During this time, he was frequently urged by his soldiers to fight, even under the pretext of not fighting when it pleased him. Nevertheless, he did not change his mind, but said to them: *“It is no less the mark of a general to overcome by strategy than by the sword.”* <note>original Latin: "Non minus iperatoris est consilio superare qg gladio."</note> Continuing his victory, he took the city of Marseilles and returned to Italy. I believe Caesar then appointed new consuls: namely, Lucius Caesar and Publius Servilio; and having settled the affairs of Italy, he turned entirely to pursuing Pompey. Departing from Brundisium, he sailed successfully to Pharsalia; from there he went to Epirus, where, after fighting several times by land and sea with Pompey’s forces, he finally forced Pompey to flee to Thessaly, where he ultimately overcame and defeated him. Because of this, Pompey fled to Egypt, where, by the command of Ptolemy, he was killed by the hands of one Lucius Septimius, or according to <margin>L</margin> Appian, by Photinus and one Achillas, a most daring man. Caesar, therefore, not knowing of Pompey’s death, came to Egypt; once he learned of it and saw the head, the arm, and the ring of Pompey, he wept. After many deeds, Caesar fought with Ptolemy and defeated him near Alexandria in a place called the Delta; the king, while fleeing, drowned in the Nile. ¶ At this time, Pharnaces, the son of Mithridates, trusting in the discord and dissension of the Romans rather than his own power, went to occupy Cappadocia. Hearing of this, Caesar came against him and, fighting with him near a land called Zala, or rather Zela, Caesar overcame him and put him to flight with such speed that he subsequently occupied the entire region of Pontus as well. King Deiotarus and the other tetrarchs of Syria, Bohemia <note>Likely a transcription error for Bithynia.</note>, Cappadocia, and Armenia were also subdued, so that he rightly used to say he had conquered before he had even seen the enemy. After Caesar returned to Rome and pacified the province of Italy, he decided to go against the remnants of the Pompeians, who at that time were mostly gathered in Africa. There were Marcus Cato, Lucius Scipio, Considius, and Gnaeus and Sextus Pompey (the sons of Pompey the Great), who, together with Juba of Numidia and his prefect Saburra, thought they could quite easily resist <margin>M</margin> Caesar. ¶ When Caesar arrived in Africa, he fought many battles with them, in which Gnaeus, the son of Pompey, was defeated and killed by Caesar’s prefect Didius. Sextus fled to Sicily; Considius was killed by the Gaetulians; and Accius Varro and Scipio were forced by Caesar to surrender. Juba met a violent death, having himself killed by a servant, and Cato committed voluntary suicide, having given it to himself in Utica <note>Cato the Younger famously committed suicide to avoid living under Caesar's tyranny, becoming a symbol of Stoic liberty.</note>. Afterward, returning to Rome, Caesar triumphed for four days, carrying upon triumphal chariots the likenesses of his won battles. First, he triumphed over the Gauls, carrying as emblems the Rhine, the Rhone, and the Ocean; then he triumphed over the Egyptians, carrying the Egyptian laurel, the Nile, Queen Arsinoe, the dead Achillas, and Photinus, as Florus and Appian write. He triumphed in the third place over Pharnaces, where he displayed him fleeing, with the inscription above: *I came, I saw, I conquered.* <note>original Latin: "veni: vidi: vici."</note> Finally, there was the African triumph, where he displayed Petreius dying of hunger, Scipio falling into the sea, and the great Cato tearing out his own <margin>N</margin> intestines. In this triumph, it was understood that he had twice subjugated Spain. ¶ Having then become perpetual dictator, and having in part oppressed the liberty of the Roman Republic, he was finally cruelly murdered in the Senate house in the presence of the Senate by Brutus and Cassius, where they gave him twenty-three dagger wounds. Receiving these at the end of his life, he wished to preserve his noble modesty and wrapped himself in his mantle so that he might fall more decently to the earth. Having thus come to the end of his life, it should not be overlooked that amidst such turbulence of war and so great a weight of deeds, and in so many diverse fortunes, he attended to his studies in such a way as his writings, worthy commentaries, and letters show us, so that he may rightly be said to have been a fellow student of Cicero under Posidonius. Hence Quintilian, in the tenth book of the *Education of the Orator*, says these words of Caesar: *“Truly, if Gaius Caesar had only devoted himself to the law courts, no other of our men would be named as a rival to Cicero; there is such force in him, such sharpness, such passion, that it appears he spoke with the same spirit with which he fought.”* <note>original Latin: "Caius vero Cesar si tantum foro uacasset: non aliis ex nostris contra Ciceronem nominaretur: tanta in eo uis est id acumen ea concitatio vt illum eodem animo dixisse: quo bellauit appareat."</note> One can therefore clearly understand with what reason Julius Caesar is placed by our poet <note>Referring to Petrarch, whose poem "The Triumph of Fame" this text accompanies.</note> as the first to precede all others in fame.

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

A very large serpent was found with his mother in her bed; and while he was still a small child, though he was seized by a terrifying dragon, he suffered no harm. Furthermore, when he went to the Capitol at night, the dogs stationed there as guards did not bark at all. By these signs, it was rightly judged that Jove <note>Jupiter, the king of the Roman gods.</note> looked after him no differently than his own son. 

When Hannibal the Carthaginian had entered Italy, crossed the mountains, and led his forces into Lombardy near the city of Pavia, the Romans sent Publius Scipio (the father of Scipio Africanus) against him to defend and protect the Roman Empire. Scipio <margin>P</margin> Africanus had also gone with him. As the two armies fought and Publius was being overcome in the battle, young Scipio—then eighteen years old—threw himself into the midst of the most crowded soldiers; he manfully defended his father from them and brought him back safely to the camp. 

Wherefore, as Livy <note>Titus Livius, the famous Roman historian.</note> writes, Africanus provided a nearly certain omen that, having saved the life of the consul, he was destined to be the savior of the Roman Republic. This followed other disasters inflicted by Hannibal upon the people of Rome: specifically the defeat of Sempronius at the Trebbia, that of Gaius Flaminius at Lake Trasimene, and the memorable slaughter at Cannae <note>Three of Rome's most devastating defeats during the Second Punic War (218–216 BCE).</note>. These losses moved Quintus Metellus to propose fleeing Rome—not only to abandon the city, but even Italy itself—solely out of the immense fear conceived from Hannibal's fury. 

While they were consulting about this flight in the house of Quintus Metellus, the young Scipio said that this was not a matter for consultation. Stepping into their circle, he turned toward Metellus and said: **"I swear by my country that I will not desert it, nor will I allow any other Roman citizen to desert it. I demand of you, therefore, Caecilius Metellus, that you do not abandon our homeland. Let all others present know that this drawn sword is against anyone who does not take this oath."** <note>original Latin: "Ego iuro p patriam non deseram: neq; alium ciuem Romanum deserere patiar. Expostulo igitur cecili metelle vt via res patriã nõ relinquere. Cæteri q̃ adestis qui non iurauerit in se hunc gladium strictum esse sciat."</note> 

In this affliction of the Roman Republic, as no other defender offered himself, the command was unanimously granted to Publius Cornelius Scipio and Publius Clodio by Quintus Fabius (son of Fabius Maximus), Publius Bibulus, and Appius Pulcher—the remaining tribunes of the first, second, and third legions. Having received this command with great wisdom and strength, and administering the remnants of the armies left after the slaughter at Cannae, Scipio led them safely through Hannibal’s own camps to Venosa. 

To better understand our subject, it is necessary to recount the history of the Second Punic War a bit further back. We say that for six years Hannibal had been nearly in control and possession of Italy. Meanwhile, Gnaeus and Publius Scipio were in Spain, where they had fought successfully against the Carthaginians, defeating Hasdrubal (son of Gisgo) and Mago (Hannibal’s brother) and their armies. At this time, Hasdrubal (son of Hamilcar and brother of Hannibal) was coming from Carthage with his armies to cross into Italy and join him. 

The Scipios, hearing of this and seeing that if such a junction occurred the Roman Empire would be totally destroyed, chose to oppose him in Spain to prevent or delay him, even though they knew it meant their manifest ruin and death. They divided their army: part went against Hasdrubal Barca, and part remained against Mago and Hasdrubal son of Gisgo. It so happened that, being divided in this way, they were overcome by the Carthaginians, and within thirty days both Scipios were killed. 

Because of this, such great fear arose in the minds of the Romans that no one could be found who wished to be the leader against the Carthaginians. Scipio, then twenty-four years old, was neither terrified by Hannibal’s previous victories nor frightened by the recent deaths of his father and uncle. He offered himself as the defender of the Roman Republic against the Carthaginians. Made Proconsul by the Roman people, he went to Spain, where he took the remains of the Scipios’ armies (which had been preserved by the virtue of Lucius Marcius, a most brave Roman knight). With these, in a short time, he conquered both Nearer and Farther Spain. On the same day he arrived at New Carthage <note>Cartagena, Spain; the headquarters of the Carthaginian empire in the region.</note>, which was the armory of the Carthaginians in Spain, he fought and won. This was no small <margin>Q</margin> help to the Romans and a most heavy loss to the Carthaginians. 

In the capture of this Carthage, there was brought before Scipio, among other prisoners, a very beautiful maiden. When he asked who she was and what her status was, he learned she was of noble origin and, among other things, the betrothed of a prince of the Celtiberians named Luceio. Therefore, Scipio sent for him, as he was then serving with the Carthaginians. When Luceio came into his presence, Scipio, knowing that he loved his bride immoderately, returned her to him, saying these words: *"I, a young man, speak to you as a young man, so that there may be less [formality in this]* 
->conversation<-"
<note>original Latin: "Iuuenis iuvene appello ut minor sit huius sermonis"</note>

### CHAPTER TWO

<note>This passage translates a speech Scipio gave to a Spanish prince, often called Allucius or Luceius in historical texts.</note>
"There is a natural restraint in our conversation. When your fiancée was called for by our soldiers and brought to me, and I heard that she was dear to your heart—a claim her beauty made easy to believe—I wished to show that I support your love. If I were allowed to enjoy such things, especially in the playfulness of youth or in a lawful and happy love, and if the affairs of the Republic did not occupy my mind, I would want you to grant me forgiveness for loving a bride so intensely. Since she is yours, I favor your love. Your fiancée has been with me just as she would have been with your own parents-in-law or her own parents; her modesty has been preserved for you so that she could be given to you as a gift, inviolate and worthy of both me and you. I bargain for only this one reward for this gift: that you be a friend to the Roman people." 

Because of this, it happened that when Luceius <note>original: "Luceo"; usually identified as Allucius, a prince of the Celtiberians.</note> saw such great courtesy, he became a very close friend to the Romans, from which they reaped the greatest fruit. Immediately, the father and mother of the aforementioned girl gave Scipio a very large quantity of gold. Once he had received it, he called Luceius to him once more and, giving it all to him, said: "In addition to the dowry you are to receive from your father-in-law, let these gifts from me be added as a wedding portion." <note>original: "Super dotez quam accepturus a socero es hæc tibi a me dotalia dona accedant."</note>

<margin>R</margin> As the war continued, after he had defeated and driven out Hasdrubal Barca near Baecula <note>original: "Bottula"</note>, and Mago at Gades <note>Modern Cádiz.</note>, and the other Hasdrubal, and had completely expelled the Carthaginians from Spain, Scipio set his mind on dominating Africa. From there he returned to Rome and, being made consul by the favor of the people, he took the armies and, crossing into Africa, came to Carthage. Because Carthage had suffered many disasters in Spain and had constantly been forced to supply and reinforce Hannibal in Italy—which had left them exhausted of both strength and men—it became necessary for Hannibal to be recalled from Italy to come and defend the walls of his homeland. 

When Hannibal arrived, he wished to have a conference with Scipio. Where they discussed peace, Scipio denied it; and finally, in battle, Hannibal was overcome and defeated. Forced to flee, Hannibal reached King Antiochus in Syria, whom he stirred up to wage war against the Romans. Meanwhile, Scipio, having imposed the conditions of peace upon Carthage after his victory, returned to Rome and triumphed for it. As the war with Antiochus continued, the Romans wished to show that they had no less hope in the victor Scipio than Antiochus had in the defeated Hannibal; therefore, they elected Scipio consul against Antiochus. But to honor his younger brother, Lucius Cornelius Scipio, he did not want to accept the consulship himself; instead, he had his brother elected and went as his legate <note>original: "collega"; historically, Scipio served as a deputy to his brother to provide him with prestige.</note>. Arriving in Syria, he easily defeated Antiochus. Hannibal fled to Prusias, the King of Bithynia, where Scipio pursued him until he finally forced him to take poison, and he died.

<margin>S</margin> When the two brothers later returned to Rome, they brought back nothing for themselves from so many victories except their surnames: one called "Africanus" and the other "Asiaticus." 

**ULT**imately, when Scipio Africanus was forced by Aulus Petillius <note>original: "Aclio petilio"; refers to the tribunes who accused Scipio of corruption.</note> to show the accounts of his administration, he went to the Capitol. There, he bared his chest and showed the wounds received in the wars and said he had brought back nothing else from Africa except that very surname; upon which he was immediately acquitted. However, because of the great ingratitude he saw shown to him, he departed from Rome and went into voluntary exile at the villa of Liternum <note>original: "Linterno"</note> in the Kingdom of Naples. Dying in that place, he asked his wife as a favor that she not allow his body to be brought back to Rome. 

Even though the mind of Scipio Africanus was involved in so many and such dangerous deeds, he did not neglect learning; instead, having become a student of Panaetius <note>A Stoic philosopher who lived in Scipio's household.</note>, he proved himself no less an excellent philosopher than a military captain. Not without reason does our Master Francesco <note>Petrarch (Francesco Petrarca), the famous humanist poet and biographer.</note> say that it is difficult to judge which of these two exceeds the other in fame or is superior. For if Caesar conquered more peoples, Scipio tamed the fiercest (especially according to what Vegetius <note>A Roman writer on military matters.</note> writes in his book *On Military Matters*). If Caesar acquired greater dominion for the Roman Republic, Scipio liberated it from graver peril. If Caesar was liberal, Scipio was most merciful. If Caesar was a most illustrious orator, Scipio was a distinguished philosopher. If Caesar ruled the Roman Republic, Scipio ruled men's souls, being universally elected consul by the people for the African war, even with the Senate opposing him. If Caesar is attributed more charm for having been a lover, Scipio is given more credit for continence for having resisted such love. Finally, if Caesar is attributed with speed, the same is granted to Scipio, considering they died at a similar age: Caesar at fifty-six years and Scipio at fifty-five. And if Caesar was active closer to his death, Scipio began his deeds at a better hour <note>referring to his early heroism at eighteen.</note>. Therefore, this case remains deservedly doubtful, confused, and undecided.
