# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<meta>Digitized by Google watermark in lower right</meta>

Messer Francesco [Petrarch] next adds the order and progression of those who were described and celebrated as famous, saying that after such a beautiful and glorious beginning, a multitude was shown to him, armed with virtue and valor, in much the same way and likeness that the ancient Romans once processed to the Capitol in former times via the *Via Lata* or the *Via Sacra*. <note>The Via Lata (Broad Way) and Via Sacra (Sacred Way) were the traditional routes for Roman Triumphal parades leading to the Capitoline Hill.</note> And he adds that he saw them all coming in that order which he describes, and each one wore their name written upon their brow—those who remained most beloved by glory in the world. Wherefore he says:

> And then there was shown to me,
> After so glorious and beautiful a beginning,
> A people armed with iron and with valor;
> Just as to the Capitol in ancient times
> Sometimes by the Sacred Way, or by the Broad Way.
> They all came in that order of which I speak;
> And upon the brow of each was read
> The name most friendly to glory in the world.

<margin>T</margin> ¶ Regarding the understanding of the aforesaid verses, it should be known that Messer Francesco says this noble and glorious people were "armed with valor," and truly with good reason: because having all practiced themselves in war, they deservedly armed their outer limbs with iron; yet they also armed themselves within their hearts with virtue and valor, which is nothing other than the "fury" that serves the arms, as Virgil writes in the first book of the *Aeneid* when he says: "Fury supplies arms." <note>original: "Furor arma ministrat." In this context, 'fury' refers to a righteous, channeled martial energy.</note> This fury is an ignition of the spirits that give life to the virtue of fortitude. Hence the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the fourth book of the *Ethics*, speaking of this by the authority of Homer: "Virtue follows fury." <note>original: "Virtutem imittetur furori"</note> And according to the new translation, he says: Wherefore Homer says: "He cast strength into the mind; and elsewhere: he stirred up force and spirit through which an impulse [comes] through the ears, and the blood boiled up." <note>original: "Robur animo iniecit: & alibi vim & animum concitauit qua per aures ipetus: & efferbuit sanguis."</note> Thus, by the one armor and the other, they proceeded into war armed with valor and iron.

<margin>V</margin> ¶ Secondly, it is to be understood that Petrarch says these men proceed in that order which he describes because he judges that one or the other of them ought to precede in fame just as he was doing and describing. Finally, the manner in which those who triumphed at the Capitol came by the Sacred and Broad ways was demonstrated and described far above, at the beginning of the *Triumph of Love*. The poet then consequently narrates whom he saw following Caesar and Scipio in fame, saying that while he stood intent on the noble conversation and murmur <note>original: "bisbiglio"; the soft sound of many voices talking at once.</note> made of these famous men, and also on their faces and presence, and their acts and works: I saw a nephew and a son come, who was without any other equal in the world; they followed the first two: namely, Caesar and Scipio Africanus. Wherefore he says:

> I was intent on the noble murmur,
> On the face, on the acts: and of those first two
> One was followed by the nephew, and the other by the son;
> Who alone, without any equal in the world, was;

<margin>X</margin> ¶ For a clearer notice of the preceding verses, it should be known that—as we said above in the *Triumph of Love*—among the Romans, sons were acquired in two ways: namely, by nature and by adoption. Therefore, these two described here by the poet were not the natural nephews or sons of Scipio or Caesar, <margin>Y</margin> but only by adoption. ¶ It is to be understood that Scipio Africanus had a son named Publius Cornelius Scipio, who was of an infirm body and powerless in the exercise of arms; in his youth, he was captured by Antiochus and restored to his father; hence he was very much a "degenerate" <note>Meaning he fell short of the high standards of his ancestors.</note> compared to his father’s virtues, as Valerius [Maximus] writes. This man, therefore, having no son, adopted as his son Scipio Aemilianus, the natural son of Lucius Aemilius Paullus, and placed him in the family of the Cornelii; thus he became the nephew <note>The Italian 'nipote' can mean grandson or nephew; here it refers to Aemilianus being the 'grandson' of the elder Scipio by adoption.</note> by adoption of Scipio Africanus. Scipio [Aemilianus] then, nephew of Scipio and natural son of Lucius Aemilius primarily—as Plutarch writes in the *Life* of his father Paullus—having gone with him in the armies against Perseus, King of Macedonia, in the age of his youth: in that battle in which Perseus was defeated and conquered, he gave himself so sharply and with such persistence to the pursuit of the enemies that he did not return to the Roman camp until after midnight had passed, to the great grief and fear of his father Aemilius and the whole army. Having obtained the victory...

## CHAPTER ONE

After the victory of [Aemilius] Paulus and his return to Rome with his son, at which time the Spaniards, incited by the fury given to them by the barbarians of Africa, moved war against the Romans. Whereupon the Romans sent Scipio there, who in a short time won the war to the honor of the Roman Senate; and where, in single combat near a city called Intercatia, he defeated a barbarian challenger. <note>Intercatia was a town of the Vaccaei in Roman Spain; the "barbarian challenger" refers to a famous duel Scipio fought against a giant Spanish warrior.</note>
<margin>Z</margin>
When that city was later stormed by the Romans, Scipio was the first to scale its walls. ¶ At this same time, the city of Carthage had become powerful again after the peace made by Scipio Africanus <note>This refers to Scipio Africanus the Elder, who defeated Hannibal in the Second Punic War.</note> so that the Romans, fearing a new war as Appian of Alexandria writes, wanted to give them new terms of peace. Among these was this: that they should abandon Carthage and rebuild it at least seven miles from the sea. For this reason, the Carthaginians not wishing to consent, the Third Punic War broke out. To this war, the Romans sent the consuls Titus Manilius and Cato the Censor; Scipio went there as a tribune under the auspices and consulship of Manlius, where he practiced himself so worthily with prudence and strength in arms that one Phameas, prefect of the Libyans—who lived continually in the woods and did not permit the Roman soldiers to lead any provisions into the camp—was yet bold enough to proceed into battle to come out against Scipio. During the war, one day through the imprudence of Consul Manlius and the sedition of the tribunes, the Romans were defeated in battle; wherefore part of them fled to a ruined mound and farmhouse where they were surrounded by Hasdrubal, son of Gisco <note>Hasdrubal the Boetharch; the text distinguishes him from the Hasdrubal defeated in the previous century.</note>. Hearing this, Scipio, although he saw the greatest danger and his soldiers were somewhat terrified, spoke these words to them:

> When things are beginning, one must use prudence and counsel; but when so many excellent citizens are in peril, one must use audacity and indeed an admirable kind. <note>original: "Rebus inchoantibus prudentia & consilio vti oportet: periclitantibus vero tot optimis ciuibus audacia & quidem admirabili vtēdū est."</note>

<margin>A</margin>
Then, proceeding spiritedly against the Carthaginians, he finally led his Romans safely back to the fields. ¶ As this Punic war continued, the Romans declared that the destruction of Carthage was fated to the name of the Scipios, for which reason they created him consul without revocation until the war was finished. Scipio then, leading the armies himself, conquered Carthage within six months and turned it to ash. Then followed the Numantine War, in which the Romans sent the consul Tullus Hostilius Mancinus; he, having been defeated by the Numantines with great shame and loss, meant that no Roman was bold enough to look any Numantine in the face, nor could any tribune, legate, or consul be found to take up the command. Scipio, as Livy writes in the 58th book of his 5th decade, and as Lucius Florus recites, offered himself in the Senate to carry out whatever kind of provincial duty was commanded of him. For this reason, having been committed to the task, he primarily punished the effeminate soldiers of his armies, then attending to the war, he finally forced the Numantines to surrender. Because of this victory, the Roman commander rose to great glory. Scipio was later sent by the Senate on an embassy to Syria, Egypt, Asia, and Greece; on this expedition, he proceeded with only two servants, as Cicero commemorates in the sixth book of *The Republic* and Pliny in *On Famous Men*. And at this time, Gaius Gracchus having been killed by Scipio Nasica, upon Scipio's return, the people were pleased to hear his opinion; he judged that Gracchus had been justly killed, at which sentence the people created a tumult. Scipio boldly said:

> Let those be silent for whom Italy is a stepmother, not a mother, whom I sold under the crown. <note>original: "Taceant quibus Italia nouerca est: non mater: quos ego sub corona vendidi." This refers to the many Roman citizens who were actually former slaves or foreigners; "sold under the crown" refers to the ancient practice of placing a garland on the heads of captives sold at auction.</note>

Having been made Censor in time, and given one Mummius <note>The text reads "Anumio," likely a corruption of Lucius Mummius.</note> as a colleague, Scipio, accusing his colleague's laziness in the Senate, said:

> Would that you, my colleague, had seen, or not seen. <note>original: "Vtinā collega vidissetis aut nō vedisse."</note>

Finally, taking up the cause of favoring the Agrarian Law primarily promulgated by Fabio Ambusto and Ancus Marcius Coriolanus, he was found dead one day with his head wrapped up. ¶ Also while living, Scipio was of such continence beyond his exercise of arms
<margin>B</margin>
that he left only 22 pounds of silver and half a pound of gold as an inheritance to his descendants. Justly, therefore, this younger grandson followed the fame of his grandfather, Scipio Africanus. Octavian Augustus, natural son of Gaius Octavius, was of ancient origin from Velletri; his family was brought to Rome by Lucius Tarquinius Priscus and designated into the patrician order by Servius Tullius—the former being the fifth and the latter the sixth King of the Romans. This man, in the fourth year of his life, lost his father. Wherefore he was adopted as a son by Julius Caesar, having at the age of twelve praised his dead grandmother Julia very eloquently. Having grown up, he took the *toga virilis* <term>toga virilis</term> <note>The "toga of manhood" assumed by Roman boys upon reaching maturity.</note> during Caesar's African triumph and was honored by him with military insignias and ornaments; and although he had not been in battle due to the defect of his age, he was nonetheless made a soldier by him, succeeding later upon the death of Julius Caesar. Since it appeared to the Roman people that they had returned to their former liberty, for this reason, the Senate at first favored him...

->### THE TRIUMPH OF FAME <-

...death at the hands of Brutus and Cassius, the assassins of Caesar. From this, the civil wars were renewed. Mark Antony, the consul, and Marcus Lepidus, Caesar’s master of the horse, wanted to put them to death to avenge Julius and, beyond this, to keep the Republic oppressed in the same manner that Caesar had done. It then happened that the Senate declared Antony an enemy of the Republic; while he was in Cisalpine Gaul, he held Decimus Brutus under siege. Consequently, the last consuls went against him: namely, Hirtius and Pansa, accompanied by Gaius Octavian, who was seventeen years of age. When the armies drew near, they finally came to battle near the city of Modena. That fight was so bitter and so cruel that although Antony was routed and fled, Pansa nevertheless remained dead on the battlefield, and Hirtius died within a few days from his wounds. Whereupon Gaius Octavian, having conducted himself manfully in this battle and being entirely covered in the blood of his enemies, saw the standard of the eagle in the hand of a signifer <note>A standard-bearer in the Roman legions.</note> who was dying of his wounds. Having no other way to save it, he carried it upon his shoulders back to the camp. He alone remained to possess the victory; as a result, with the two consuls dead, three armies were joined into one under the leadership of Octavian. It followed that after this victory, the Senate attributed more glory to Decimus Brutus than they did to Octavian. Indignant at this, he made peace with Mark Antony through the mediation of Lepidus. Returning to Rome with their armies, they established the magistrate of the Triumvirate, which was assumed by Marcus Lepidus, Mark Antony, and Octavian. At this time, Brutus and Cassius, the assassins of Caesar, were in Macedonia. When Antony and Octavian heard they had gathered their armies, they resolved to go against them. Having put this into execution and arrived in Greece, they fought the first battle. In this, Brutus so overcame Octavian that he was barely able to reach the other wing where Mark Antony was.

<margin>e</margin>
Then, the second battle was prepared. While the conflict was underway, Cassius had already taken Octavian's camp; because of this, his cavalry, intent on plunder, began to scatter without any order. Seeing this, Cassius believed they were fleeing out of fear and because they had been broken. Therefore, he fled with a few others and hid himself on a hill. Being reduced to such a state, he sent one of those soldiers to see what had happened to Brutus after his own flight. This messenger being slow to return, Cassius imagined he had been captured. In despair, he gave his sword to one of his servants and had himself killed. Brutus, on the other hand, seeing that his friend Cassius had fled <note>Brutus actually thought Cassius was dead or defeated; the text here focuses on the confusion of the battlefield.</note>, took his sword and killed himself. Thus they left the complete victory in the hands of Antony and Gaius Octavian. Afterward, Octavian sought out Brutus, and having found his body, he had the head struck from the corpse to be carried to Rome and placed at the foot of the statue of Caesar. In this victory, Octavian used much cruelty, especially toward many Roman nobles, whom he afflicted with insulting words and put to death. When he was begged by one of them to at least allow him burial after he was dead, he replied: 
> That is now in the power of the birds. <note>original: "Iam ista in volucrum est potestate." A famous, cold response attributed to Octavian by Suetonius, implying the body would be left for vultures.</note>
Returning afterward to Rome, Octavian faced even more civil wars, for Lucius Antony, brother of Mark Antony, trusting in his brother’s place in the triumvirate, prepared snares for the ruin of Octavian. Therefore, Octavian went against him and followed him as far as Perugia, where, not without many battles, he finally forced him to surrender. He then proceeded in the fourth place against Sextus Pompey. Although the war lasted a long time due to many actions taken in Africa and Spain, Octavian ultimately remained the victor. During these times, Octavian had equally divided the empire with Mark Antony, with Mark Antony reigning in the East and Octavian in the West; furthermore, Octavian had given him his sister Octavia as a wife.

<margin>D</margin>
Mark Antony fell in love with Cleopatra, Queen of Egypt, and to please her, he repudiated Octavia. For this reason, Octavian was indignant and made war against Mark Antony. Antony arrived together with Cleopatra with a very great fleet near Actium and the island of Lefkada. Octavian went to meet them there, where they fought boldly, as is clearly shown in the eighth book of Virgil. <note>Referring to the description of the Battle of Actium on the shield of Aeneas in the *Aeneid*.</note> In the end, Octavian was the victor, and he forced Antony to flee with his army, ultimately following him until Antony took poison. Having thus overcome every enemy in this course of civil wars, Octavian returned to Rome, where with great justice and singular modesty he organized the Republic and the subjugated provinces and dominions. Octavian did not only exert himself in these civil wars and emerge as the victor, but by his own hand he won the Dalmatian and Cantabrian wars; through his legates and ministers, he conquered Aquitaine, Illyricum, Cisalpine Gaul, Dacia, the Germans, Suebia, and Sugambria. He defeated many other nations and princes and triumphed three times, as we have said. He was most learned in Latin and Greek literature.

-> ## CHAPTER ONE <-

He held the complete monarchy of the world; nevertheless, in such great excellence and dominion, he never permitted anyone to call him "Lord" <note>Augustus preferred the title *Princeps* (First Citizen) to avoid the appearance of being a king or dictator</note>, as Suetonius Tranquillus writes. Finally, having possessed the whole world in peace for many years, he died in the month of August at the age of seventy-six. Therefore, considering his illustrious deeds, Octavian, the father <note>original: "padre Cesare," likely a typo or shorthand for "Pater Patriae" or referring to his status as the successor to Caesar</note>, can deservedly follow Caesar in the second place of fame. Next follows **M. F.** <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch</note> regarding the noble Scipios, saying that after them followed two fathers accompanied by three sons together, who wished to block the passage of Italy with their bodies against armed enemies. Of these sons, one went ahead, and two followed after. And the last of the three sons was the first among all those praised. Whence he says:

<margin>
Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it is primarily to be understood what the genealogy is among these Scipios described here by the poet. Wherefore Publius Cornelius Scipio and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio were brothers descended from the same father, called "Scipio" <note>The name "Scipio" means "staff" or "wand" in Latin</note> because when he was a young boy, his father, being

> *Of armed enemies with their own limbs,*

old, used to walk through Rome leaning on Publius Cornelius Scipio, whom he adopted as a son: Publius Scipio Emilianus <note>The commentator here is clarifying the complex family tree of the Scipios to explain Petrarch's poetic phrasing</note>. But from Gnaeus Scipio was born only Scipio Nasica, with whom the genealogy ended. Secondly, it should be known that when Hannibal had descended into Italy and had defeated Publius Scipio at the Ticino <note>The Battle of Ticinus, 218 BCE, where Scipio was saved by his son, the future Africanus</note>, he [Publius] decided to cross into Spain where his brother Gnaeus was, who was laying siege to a city called Hibera. At this time, Hasdrubal came from Carthage wanting to aid that city and then pass into Italy. Whereupon the Scipios fought with him and overcame him, by which thing almost all of Spain came under the dominion of the Romans. It followed then that they sent from Carthage to Spain Mago Barca and Hasdrubal, sons of Gisco, with another very powerful army. Publius Scipio, crossing the Ebro river, made resistance and defeated and conquered them near Liturgium, where fifteen thousand Carthaginians died, and fifteen thousand were taken prisoner, along with thirty-six military standards. The Scipios then conquered another Carthaginian army near Munda, where among others, thirty-nine elephants died. Finally, the Carthaginians having restored their armies and wanting to send Hasdrubal Barca into Italy so he could join his brother Hannibal, the Celtiberians failed the Romans and allied with the Carthaginians. Whereupon one of their leaders named Indibilis, with seven thousand infantry, came to join the Carthaginian army. Therefore, Publius Scipio decided to assault them by night or by day wherever he found them. He took one part of the army and left the other with Titus Fonteius in the camp. In the end, he clashed with the Numidians, with whom he was fighting when the African armies arrived; ultimately, he was defeated and killed. Hearing then of the death of his brother, Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio, judging it disastrous for the Romans if Hasdrubal passed into Italy, decided to oppose him. Being there with a much smaller army, after several eruptions and assaults, on the thirtieth day of fighting since Publius Scipio had died, he was defeated and killed. Over these men, Lucius Marcius remained <note>A Roman eques who took command after both generals fell</note>; as we said above, exhorting the Roman soldiers in such great sorrow, he assaulted the Carthaginian camps by night. While the Carthaginians were weighed down by their previous fatigue, the Romans killed thirty-eight thousand, took a great quantity of them, and totally destroyed their camps. There, among other things, they took the shield of Hasdrubal, where his own image was sculpted, which weighed one hundred and thirty-eight pounds of silver. This shield was sent to Rome, where it provided no small recreation to the Romans in such great public grief conceived for the death of the consuls. <margin>F</margin> Lucius Cornelius Scipio left no more notice of himself than having, together with his brother Scipio Africanus, defeated and overcome Antiochus, King of Syria, near Mount Sipylus, and with him the already broken and weakened Hannibal. Wherefore, by this victory, he then subjugated all of Asia to the Romans, from which he took the surname "Asiaticus." Having returned later to Rome and triumphed over Antiochus, it happened that on the anniversary of his triumph, someone wanted to put him in prison for certain sums of money, which his poverty did not allow him to repay. But Tiberius Gracchus, tribune of the plebs, although he had a heavy enmity with him and with his brother Africanus, nevertheless freed him, saying it was not an honor for the Roman Republic that—

-> ## THE TRIUMPH OF FAME <-

<margin>G</margin> On that same day, he who had led the enemies of the Roman people into prison the year before was himself released from custody; this occurrence was an honor to Scipio and a testimony to his merit and virtue. ¶ Although it appears that **Scipio Nasica** <note>Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica, a cousin of Scipio Africanus</note> gained little recognition or fame in the practice of arms—having only manfully captured Delminium, the capital and metropolis of the Dalmatian region, during his consulship—he nonetheless left a great reputation for his other outstanding and singular virtues. For this reason, while he was still a young man and prohibited by law from the dignity of the office of quaestor, he was judged and confirmed by the Senate to be the most virtuous of all the men in Rome. Shortly thereafter, having been named consul by Gaius Gracchus <note>The text likely refers to a different historical chronology here; Nasica was consul in 162 BC and 155 BC, while Gracchus was active later</note>, he resigned the magistracy because it was against the religious omens <note>original: "auspicio"</note>. This act was no small testament to his self-restraint, especially since he threw to the ground all the statues erected by others in the Forum, indicating that such things belonged to private praise rather than to the common utility, which alone should be extended in public to the common society to confound all pride. <margin>H</margin> He also refused his own triumph. He was a most eloquent and famous legal expert <note>original: "iurisconsulto"</note>; thus, he deservedly rose to great fame. ¶ Finally, the confirmation of all his excellence was found in the **Sibylline books** <note>A collection of oracular prophecies consulted by the Roman state in times of crisis</note>, which stated that Hannibal would never leave Italy until the **Mother of the Gods** <note>The goddess Cybele, known as the Magna Mater</note> was brought to Rome and received by the hands of the man who was the most perfect of all Romans. They sought her out from Attalus, the King of Asia, who held her; hearing the desire of the Romans, he freely gave her to them. When she was finally brought to the harbor of Ostia on the Tiber, the Romans sent Nasica along with all the Roman mothers and matrons. When the Asian priests gave the statue into Nasica’s hands, he then gave it to a woman named **Claudia Quinta**; and thus, with the greatest devotion and triumph, they led her to Rome to the Temple of Victory. Now, returning to the poet’s purpose, the aforementioned notice says that **M.F.** <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch</note> writes that the two fathers—namely Publius Cornelius and Gnaeus Scipio—wished to block the path of the enemy with their own bodies. This is according to what **Cicero** <note>original: "Tullio"</note> writes in the *Paradoxes* <note>original: "ne le parado." referring to *Paradoxa Stoicorum*</note>, saying: <note>original: "Qui iduo propugnacula belli G. N. & . P. Scipiones: quos corporibus suis carthaginensium aduentum itercludendum putauerunt."</note> "Those two bulwarks of war, Gnaeus and Publius Scipio, who thought the arrival of the Carthaginians should be blocked by their own bodies." They came with three sons: namely Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus, Lucius Scipio Asiaticus, and Scipio Nasica. The last of the sons—that is, Scipio Africanus—went ahead, and two followed after. And justly in the deeds of arms, the last in age (Africanus) was the first among those praised by fame. Nevertheless, some say the last in the practice of arms—namely Nasica—was the first among those praised by the Senate, being judged the best by public determination. That interpretation is valid, but in our judgment, the first explanation is more consistent with Petrarch, who describes him proceeding equally alongside Caesar in the Triumph of Fame. The poet then consequently introduces **Claudius Nero**, who followed the Scipios like a shining <term>pyropo</term> <note>A brilliant red gemstone or a fiery alloy of gold and bronze</note>, who with his counsel, foresight, and even with his hand and arms, arrived at Italy’s moment of greatest need. This was Claudius Nero, who, quiet and silent by night, saw the River Metaurus come by his labor to purge the Roman fields and countryside of a pestilential and ruinous seed <note>The "seed" refers to the Carthaginian army led by Hasdrubal</note>. Truly, in this operation, he possessed most sharp-sighted eyes to see it and swift wings to fly and execute the task. Whence it says:

> Then flashed like a fire-stone
> He who, with counsel and with hand,
> Served Italy in her greatest need;
> I speak of the sword; who, silent by night,
> When he saw the Metaurus, came to purge
> The good Roman fields of the evil seed,
> Having eyes to see and wings to fly;

<margin>I</margin> ¶ Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should primarily be known that the name <term>pyropo</term> is a general term and signifies anything shining presented before our eyes, but it especially denotes a very bright gem of a red color. <margin>K</margin> It is also a mixture of gold and brass, which is said to be extremely brilliant. ¶ Secondly, it must be understood that during part of the eleventh year and part of the twelfth year of the **Second Punic War**, after the death of the Scipios in Spain, **Hasdrubal** <note>Hannibal's brother</note> crossed into Italy to join Hannibal, who was in the Kingdom of Naples. At this time, two consuls were elected: **Livius Salinator** and **Claudius Nero**, who divided the provinces by lot.

# CHAPTER TWO

<margin>L</margin> **Claudius** [Nero] was sent to oppose **Hannibal**, and **Livius Salinator** to oppose **Hasdrubal** <note>Hasdrubal Barca, Hannibal’s brother, who was bringing reinforcements from Spain</note>. While Claudius was engaged in his expedition, Hasdrubal, who was in the field at Piacenza, wrote to Hannibal regarding his status and his desire to join him, intending only the destruction of the city of Rome. It happened that this messenger was captured and the letters intercepted. When Claudius had them interpreted by African prisoners, he recognized Hasdrubal's plan and the manifest ruin of Rome if he did not provide a remedy. Wherefore he immediately sent Hasdrubal’s letters to Rome and wrote to the Senate that they should send Salinator as quickly as possible to oppose Hasdrubal, and so it was done. Without any new movements in his own camp, he took about six thousand chosen combatants and departed by night. With great speed, he arrived in Lombardy <note>The author uses "Lombardia" to refer generally to Northern Italy, where the Battle of the Metaurus took place</note>. In this place, he joined his colleague and revealed his plan: to assault Hasdrubal by surprise and unawares so that he could not join with Hannibal. ¶ Beyond this, <margin>M</margin> on the evening before the battle, an excellent opportunity was offered to the Romans; for Hasdrubal, seeing that his messengers did not return, imagined what had occurred. Therefore, he broke off the siege of Piacenza and at night set out to cross the river **Metaurus**. But, not knowing the fords, he delayed until daybreak with much exhaustion and disorder in his army. In the morning, therefore, the Roman consuls, being prepared and in position, assaulted Hasdrubal. Fighting fiercely with him, the Romans were ultimately superior. In this bitter battle, eight thousand Romans died, and fifty-eight thousand Carthaginians <note>Ancient sources often provide high casualty figures; modern estimates for the Carthaginian dead at Metaurus are typically lower, around 10,000 to 20,000</note> along with their leader Hasdrubal, while five thousand remained prisoners. Having thus obtained this victory, on the night following the day of the battle, Claudius departed from Lombardy and on the sixth day returned to his camps at the edge of the kingdom <note>Referring to the southern front in Apulia where Hannibal was stationed</note>, carrying the head of Hasdrubal. He had the head thrown into Hannibal’s camp. When Hannibal saw it, he said no more than that he now recognized the [ill] fortune of the Carthaginians. Deservedly, then, **Claudius Nero** had eyes to see and wings to fly, judging so well and so quickly coming to the aid of the Roman Republic in its greatest peril. Afterward, he brings forward **M. F. Quintus Fabius Maximus**, saying that as Claudius Nero moved forward, a great old man, excellent in virtue, followed happily behind him, who with singular skill and prudence held Hannibal at bay in arms. For this reason, throughout his consulship, he prohibited Hannibal from winning. Whence he says:

<margin>N</margin> ->And a great old man followed close behind;<-
->Who with skill held Hannibal at bay.<-

<insert>
¶ **Quintus Fabius Maximus**, a most noble Roman citizen. When Hannibal the Carthaginian had crossed into Italy, he defeated three consuls—namely Publius Scipio, Titus Sempronius, and Gaius Flaminius—and
</insert>

exterminated their armies in many parts. After Hannibal had passed into the territory of Apulia, Fabius was elected consul by the Romans and sent with the armies against Hannibal. Seeing Hannibal exulting in his previous victories and the majority of his own Romans terrified, and considering also that Hannibal was so far from Carthage that it was necessary for him to waste away before help or aid could reach him, Fabius decided not to fight, but only to defend and prevent him from advancing further. <margin>O</margin> For this reason, he took the surname **Fabius the Delayer** <note>original: "Fabio contatore," from the Latin "Cunctator"</note>. This strategy alone was what saved the Roman Republic, because Hannibal was not powerful enough to defeat Quintus Fabius when he remained on the defensive, nor could he proceed with any of his army without all the Roman armies following, as Fabius was always near him with a nearly equal army. Therefore, Hannibal was in great distress and manifest danger. For this reason, the Romans—first through the words of **Ennius** and later confirmed by **Virgil**—were able to say the words of Anchises: **"Where do you lead me in my weariness, O Fabii? You are that greatest one who alone restores our state to us by delaying"** <note>original: "Quo fessum rapitis fabij tu maximus ille es. Vnus qui nobis cunctando restituis rem." A quote from Virgil’s Aeneid, VI. 845–846</note>. By this, the salvation achieved through his delaying is denoted. The proof of this was shown by **Minucius**, the Master of the Horse <note>original: "maestro de militi"</note> who served under the command of Fabius. Despising and blaming Fabius's slowness, Minucius decided to fight Hannibal. Having descended into the field, he quickly realized his great error, for, surrounded by the Carthaginians, he was forced to either die or be taken prisoner in a short time. Fabius, seeing Minucius in such grave danger, turned to his soldiers and said: "Fortune has overtaken rashness no more quickly than I feared." Then, having exhorted them, he rescued Minucius, who, being liberated by the prudence of Fabius, turned to his fellow soldiers and spoke these words: ¶ **"I have often heard, soldiers, that he is the first man who counsels well on what should be done. Second is he who obeys one who counsels well. But he who knows neither how to counsel himself nor how to obey another is of the lowest intellect"** <note>original: "Saepe ego audiui milites en primum esse virum qui bene consulat quid in re sit. Secundum eum qui bene monenti obediat: qui nec ipse consulere nec alteri parere scit eum extremi ingenij esse." A famous sentiment recorded by Livy, Book XXII.29</note>. To us...

<meta>This page continues the historical and genealogical commentary on the Roman figures mentioned in Petrarch’s "Triumph of Fame." Following the discussion of the Claudian and Livian families, the text now focuses on the various branches of the Fabii and the beginning of the Cato lineage.</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>J</margin> If the first lot of mind and intellect is denied to us, let us hold the second and middle ground: while we learn to be humble <note>Latin: *impare discemus*, literally 'learn while unequal,' suggesting a period of apprenticeship or subordination to the great figures of the past</note>, let us be led by a prudent spirit; let us join our camp with **Fabius** <note>Quintus Fabius Maximus, famously known as "The Delayer" for his stalling tactics against Hannibal</note> and carry our standards into his headquarters. There I, as a father, recognize how his kindness toward us is worthy of such majesty. You indeed, soldiers, whom your own arms have protected, shall salute your patrons; and if nothing else, this day will have given us at least the glory of a grateful heart. Not only for this worthy and singular deed is Quintus Fabius praised, but for his prudence and a cleverness equal to that with which **Hannibal** had taken **Taranto**, for he recovered it <note>Taranto was a vital port city recaptured by Fabius in 209 BC</note>. Whereupon Hannibal said of him: "The Romans, too, have their own Hannibal." And from Taranto, he brought to Rome the image and statue of **Hercules**, which he placed in the Capitol. Quintus Fabius was also most observant of his promised word in every action. Thus, having made an agreement with the enemy to ransom Roman prisoners, the Senate did not approve it. Fabius then sold his own estate and ransomed them with his own money to satisfy his honor. <margin>M</margin> Afterwards, <term>M. F.</term> <note>Likely the commentator, Master Francesco, or a reference to Petrarch himself (Messer Francesco)</note> adds a triplet containing a greater number of excellent men, saying that with Fabius there was another Fabius, and two other outstanding **Catos**, the **Pauli**, the **Bruti**, two glorious **Marcelli**, and one **Marcus Regulus**, who loved the Republic and others much more than himself and his own life. Thus he says:

> ->Another Fabius; and two Catos with him;<-
> ->Two Paulis; two Bruti, two Marcelli<-
> ->Regulus, who loved Rome, and not himself;<-

<margin>Q</margin> For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it should be understood (as seen in the history of **Livy** <note>Titus Livius, the primary Roman historian for these events</note> *From the Founding of the City*, Book 2) that the family of the **Fabii** was very great, in which there were many diverse and excellent men. Foremost among them were **Quintus Fabius** and **Caeso Fabius**, brothers. When the Aequi and Veientes <note>Early Italian rivals of Rome</note> moved war against the Romans, Quintus Fabius forced the Aequi to lay down their arms. And Caeso Fabius, almost alone, preserved Roman liberty by resisting the Veientes and suppressing the discord of the Roman people caused by the envy toward **Spurius Furius**, who was his colleague. ¶ It followed that in the next year the Aequi renewed war against the people of Rome. Therefore, another **Marcus Fabius**, a most outstanding man, was elected consul. At this time, the former Quintus Fabius having been killed by the Veientes in the previous battle, the family of the Fabii alone took it upon themselves to finish that war. Under the leadership or consulship of Marcus Fabius, they achieved many victories. Finally, becoming emboldened and no longer fearing or caring for the Veientes, they were led one day into an ambush while pursuing them. When the trap was revealed, they made a worthy defense, but in the end, 306 Fabii were killed in that battle <note>The Battle of the Cremera (c. 477 BC), a legendary disaster where nearly the entire Fabia clan was wiped out</note>. Not a single man of the family remained except for one small boy, from whom **Quintus Fabius Maximus** and his other descendants originated. <margin>R</margin> ¶ After the death of the 306 Fabii, there was another Quintus Fabius [Rutilianus], who fought many wars against the Aequi and the Volsci. He was consul even against the Gauls, although things went poorly for the Romans then. Besides these, he was the first among them to be surnamed "Maximus," **Quintus Fabius Rutilianus**. While serving under **Lucio Papirio Cursor** <note>A Roman Dictator known for his legendary severity and discipline</note> against the Samnites as consul, he returned to Rome after fighting them against the Dictator's orders and putting them to flight and conquering them. For this reason, Papirius later wanted to have him put to death for his disobedience. Besides the Samnites, he conquered and subjugated the Apulians and Necerini to the Roman Empire. He triumphed over them and then over the Sabines, then the Gauls, the Umbrians, the Marsi, and the Tuscans, as **Pliny** and **Livy** (Book 10) write. <margin>S</margin> ¶ The last Fabius who occurs here is **Quintus Fabius**, the son of Fabius Maximus. How excellent he was in the army is understood through the text of Livy, especially as his father, Quintus Fabius, was so bold as to place him before **Scipio Africanus**. Wherefore, as Livy writes in the 3rd decade, Book 7, wanting to dissuade Fabius Maximus from Scipio making war in Carthage, to clear himself of any rivalry or envy toward the consul, he said these words: "For what rivalry can I have with him, who is not even the equal of my son?" <note>original: "Quae enim mihi emulatio cum eo esse potest: qui ne filio quidem meo equalis sit."</note>. This [Fabius] is now added to the judgment and free will of which [person] M.F. has intended at present in [the name] Fabius. <margin>T</margin> ¶ Consequently, for the understanding of the **Catos**, it is first necessary to know their genealogy. The first was **Marcus Porcius Cato the Censor**, from whom two sons were born. The first, in his youth, was named **Marcus Porcius Cato**, a most eloquent and worthy jurist; while he was praetor-designate, he died. **Cicero** writes of him in his book *On Old Age*. From him was born another **Marcus Porcius Cato**, surnamed the Grandson [Nepos], a most eloquent man who died in Africa with one **Quintus Metellus**. And from this Cato, finally, was born another **Marcus Cato**...

# CHAPTER TWO

<margin>V</margin>
**Cato.** Whom I know was appointed Aedile and Praetor. The <term>Censor, Cato</term> <note>Marcus Porcius Cato the Elder (234–149 BC), a Roman statesman known for his conservatism and opposition to Hellenistic influence</note> also had another son in his old age, whom he had by a young woman named <term>Salonia</term>, the daughter of one of his clients, and his mother's name was given to him as <term>Marcus Porcius Cato Salonianus</term>. From him was born another <term>Marcus Cato</term>, who died in <term>Thrace</term> while serving as praetor. From him was born the most excellent <term>Marcus Cato of Utica</term> <note>Cato the Younger (95–46 BC), a Stoic philosopher and statesman who opposed Julius Caesar</note>, and from the one of Utica was born <term>Marcus Cato</term>, who, while campaigning with <term>Brutus</term> after the killing of Caesar, was killed in <term>Macedonia</term> by <term>Mark Antony</term> and <term>Octavian</term>.

<margin>A</margin>
But among these Catos, it is not difficult to recognize which ones our <term>Master Francesco</term> <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch, the author of the "Triumphs"</note> intends, because in arms, the first, <term>Cato the Censor</term>, exceeds the one of <term>Utica</term> or the son; for under the leadership and auspices of <term>Cato the Censor</term>, the <term>Sardinians</term> were subdued while he was praetor. In his consulship, together with <term>Titus Manlius</term>, he defeated the <term>Celtiberians</term>. Having previously been a tribune under <term>Marcus Acilius Glabrio</term> in <term>Greece</term> at the pass of <term>Thermopylae</term>, he performed most glorious and worthy deeds in arms, as <term>Pliny</term> and <term>Appian of Alexandria</term> write. Thus, although he was a most distinguished and singular orator, he nevertheless proved himself equally diligent with sword in hand as with his tongue in the forum. Because of his eloquence, he obtained, after the Third Punic War, the result that Rome's rival, <term>Carthage</term>, was cast down into ruin.

<margin>X</margin>
Regarding the other two <term>Catos</term>, namely the one of <term>Utica</term> and his son: although each of them performed worthy and singular deeds in the exercise of arms, the son of Cato had the disposition and reputation of a soldier rather than a commander. Therefore, by the other Cato, we conclude it is the one of <term>Utica</term>, in addition to the <term>Censor</term>. To him, all the remnants of the <term>Pompeians</term> fled in <term>Africa</term> after the death of <term>Gnaeus Pompey</term> in <term>Egypt</term>, seeking a garrison against <term>Julius Caesar</term>. At that time, <term>Cato</term> and <term>Lucius Scipio</term> succeeded in <term>Pompey’s</term> place, as <term>Florus</term> writes. Later, when <term>Caesar</term> went against them in <term>Africa</term>, and <term>Titus Labienus</term>, <term>Scipio</term>, and <term>Juba</term> came against him to resist, Caesar finally overcame them all in a single day. <term>Cato</term>, not having taken part in that battle, fled to <term>Utica</term>; hearing of Caesar’s authority, he killed himself, so greatly did he feel ashamed that his great soul should have to be pardoned by <term>Caesar</term>, as <term>Augustine</term> writes in the *City of God*, chapter 22. These two glorious Catos may therefore deservedly follow with <term>Fabius</term> in the triumph of fame for their exercise of arms.

<margin>Y</margin>
In the third place were the two <term>Paulli</term>, namely <term>Paullus Aemilius the father</term> and <term>Paullus Aemilius the son</term>. It is to be understood that the first made memorable and famous the sad and horrendous slaughter of the <term>Romans</term> at <term>Cannae</term>. As the war with <term>Hannibal</term> continued and the term of the consulship of <term>Quintus Fabius Maximus</term> ended, the <term>Romans</term> elected <term>Paullus Aemilius</term> and <term>Terentius Varro</term> as consuls. Since <term>Fabius</term> had trapped <term>Hannibal</term> in the <term>Salernitan</term> <note>Likely a reference to the Ager Falernus, where Fabius famously trapped Hannibal</note> territory in a valley between <term>Pasiliano</term> and Mount <term>Caliculo</term>, <term>Hannibal</term> was almost reduced to ultimate despair. Then <term>Fabius</term> reminded <term>Aemilius</term> that if he wished to win, he should by no means change his strategy. <term>Aemilius</term>, recognizing the plan, followed <term>Fabius’s</term> precept and did not intend to fight in any way. But his colleague, <term>Terentius Varro</term>, a most audacious man inexperienced with the <term>African</term> fury, blamed the "delaying" <note>Referring to the strategy of *cunctatio* or stalling</note> of <term>Fabius</term> and <term>Aemilius</term>. He wrote to the <term>Senate</term> that <term>Paullus</term> did not want to win because he did not want to fight. Consequently, the <term>Senate</term> commanded the consuls to engage in battle with <term>Hannibal</term> at all costs. Coming thus to the battle, and the <term>Carthaginians</term> being forced either to die or to win, they made a most cruel slaughter of the <term>Romans</term>, where forty thousand <term>Romans</term> died and as many of the Latin name. The worthy consul <term>Paullus Aemilius</term> died there, whereas <term>Varro</term> fled with great fear and gravity. Before he died, being mortally wounded and already barely able to breathe, sitting upon a rock, a tribune named <term>Gaius Cornelius Lentulus</term> said these words to him:

> "Paullus Aemilius, you whom the gods should look upon as a man innocent of the guilt of today's disaster, take this horse while some strength remains in you. I can take you as my companion and protect you, lest you make this funeral-stricken battle even more grim by the death of a consul; and there has already been enough weeping and grief." <note>original: "Paule emili: quem uirum insontem culpe cladis hodierne dii respicere debent cape hūc equum donec tibi uirium aliquid superest: comes ego te tollere possum: ac tegere ne fune-stā hanc pugnā m morte cõsulis feceris: & si hoc lachrymarū satis: luctusq[ue] est."</note>

To these sweet and pious words, the consul <term>Paullus</term> answered kindly and with prudence, saying:

> "You indeed, Marcus Cornelius, be blessed in your virtue; but take care not to lose, through useless pity, the little time you have to escape from the hands of the enemy. Go: announce publicly to the fathers that they must fortify the city of Rome and strengthen it with garrisons before the victorious enemy arrives. Tell them privately that Fabius Aemilius was mindful of his teacher's precepts and lived by them, and now allow me to die in this slaughter of my soldiers. Do not stay to perish further, or to stand as an accuser of your colleague's consulship, as if to protect my own innocence by another's crime." <note>original: "Tu q[ui]dem. m Corneli macte virtute esto: sed caue ne frustra miserādo exiguū tẽpus e manibus hostiū euadẽdi amittas: Abi: nucia publice patribus urbẽ romanā murniant: ac priusq[ui] uictor hostis adueniat p̃ fidiis firmerit: priuatiq[ue] Fabio Emilij p̃ceptorē eius memorē extitisse & uixisse: & hūc mori me in hac strage militū meorū patere expirare. Ne tu ulterius intereas cāq[ue] cõsulatus accusator collegæ existas vt alieno crimine inocẽtiā meā ptegā."</note>

# TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>A</margin>**Aemilius Paullus** <note>Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus (c. 229–160 BC), a Roman general famous for his victory over Macedon</note> campaigned against the Iberians at the time when, during the war with **Antiochus, King of Syria**, a grave and turbulent uprising broke out in **Hesperia** <note>The Iberian Peninsula/Spain</note>. Aemilius was sent to this war not only with the praetors, as was customary, but with the **twelve axes** <note>The fasces or bundles of rods with axes carried by lictors, symbolizing the full authority of a Consul</note> so that every consular dignity might shine forth in him. Having arrived on Iberian soil, he defeated them in just two battles, in which about thirty thousand people were killed. ¶ The second war that Aemilius waged was against the **Ligurians**, a most fierce people; in a short time, he brought all their territories, lands, and vines to surrender. ¶ The last and most famous war was against **Perseus**, the son of **Philip, King of Macedonia**. This war being advanced, Aemilius principally overcame and defeated **Milione**, the duke and prefect of Perseus, along with nearly all his flourishing army. As the war subsequently progressed prosperously, he finally took the King's wife and children and led them as prisoners to **Rome** before his chariot during his triumph. But he did not wish for envious and malignant fortune to allow him to experience this glory without some sorrow. Thus, though he had four sons—of whom one was named **Scipio** and the other **Fabius** <note>These two had been adopted into the Scipio and Fabius families respectively</note>—one died at the age of sixteen, five days before his triumph; the other died three days after his triumph at the age of twelve. But Aemilius, enduring such cruel blows with a strong spirit, spoke these worthy words to the people:

> <note>original: "Cum iam saluis rebus..."</note> When, with the state now safe and sound, I saw myself brought back to you and the city filled with joy and festivity, I still held fortune in suspicion. I knew that she is not accustomed to grant anything pure to men without envy. Nor did my mind cease to fear for my Republic until this adverse misfortune first struck me. It has taken away my best sons, whom I had chosen as my only successors, in nearly continuous funerals. But now I see that you are out of danger; I believe I can place good hope in the idea that fortune will now remain without blemish for the Roman people, since she has inflicted enough envy upon me and mine for our prior prosperity.

¶ Finally, after this triumph, Aemilius Paullus was made **Censor**, but fell into a long illness. On the advice of physicians, he went to live in **Velia**, a small island very near Italy. There, three days after his arrival, having performed a sacrifice to the gods so that they might restore his health, he died happily. Finally, it should not be overlooked that Aemilius Paullus lived his life with such restraint and temperance that, although he had always worn his triumphal robes at the **Circensian games** <note>Public games held in the Circus Maximus</note> by decree of the Senate, upon his death his wife's dowry could not be repaid until his possessions were sold. ¶ Besides the two Aemilii Paulli, there was another <margin>B</margin>**Aemilius Paullus** in the time of **Caesar**, who was only a Tribune at that time; **Suetonius Tranquillus** commemorates no other deed of his. ¶ Following in the fourth place are the two **Bruti**, namely **Junius Brutus** and **Marcus Brutus**. <margin>C</margin>In my judgment, one should add a third, **Decius Brutus**, and leave it to the minds of men to decide which of them our **Master Francesco** <note>Petrarch</note> intends. Regarding **Junius Brutus**, it is known that after **Sextus Tarquinius** had corrupted and violated **Lucretia** by force, and the habits of **Tarquin the Proud** <note>Tarquinius Superbus, the last King of Rome</note> became hateful to the Roman Senate, Brutus by his own work drove Tarquin out of Rome and from power. Consequently, seeing that the name of the Tarquins was odious among the people, he arranged for **Tarquinius Collatinus**, the husband of the chaste Lucretia and a consul, to leave Rome because he was descended from the Tarquins—being the son of the sister of Tarquin the Proud. After this was done, Tarquin the Proud sent ambassadors to Rome to demand his goods. During their stay, a conspiracy was born with the youths of Rome to restore the king, among whom were the two sons of Brutus who conspired. But this conspiracy was revealed to the consul Brutus by a servant named **Vindicius**. Brutus had his sons seized and then had their heads cut off. To his servant, he gave a great sum of money, his freedom, and citizenship. <margin>D</margin>From that servant's name, the rod with which the praetor restored slaves to freedom was thereafter called the **Vindicta** <note>A rod used in the ceremony of manumission</note>. ¶ Tarquin, seeing his plan failed, even still moved a public war against the Romans with the help of **Porsena** and the people of **Chiusi**, to whom he had fled in exile. But Brutus, together with his colleague **Valerio Publicola**, who had been appointed in place of Collatinus, manfully opposed him to defend Roman liberty. <margin>E</margin>After fighting for a long time, finally, while fighting in a cruel and sharp battle, Brutus and **Aruns**, the son of Tarquin, struck one another with a powerful blow and killed each other simultaneously. ¶ **Marcus Brutus**, as we certainly stated above, was the son of **Julius Caesar** and **Servilia**, the sister of **Cato of Utica**. To recover the occupied Republic and Roman liberty, he killed Caesar in the Senate. As for his military skill, after going to **Greece**, he primarily moved a great war against **Thrace**, although the outcomes were not very successful. From there, quickly—

# SECOND CHAPTER

->triumph<-

Even still, having turned back and gathered the remains of their armies, they prepared new forces by both sea and land against **Antony** and **Octavian**. Finally, coming to battle, in all that truly pertained to him, [Brutus] remained superior; however, due to the error of **Cassius** <note>Cassius committed suicide at the Battle of Philippi because he mistakenly believed Brutus had been defeated</note>—as we certainly stated above—in the end, he remained defeated and killed himself. For this reason, he should be justly reputed as worthy and excellent, especially since he was no less greedy for letters than he was studious of liberty, as **Tullio** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> demonstrates in several different works of varying study inscribed and sent to him. 

<margin>F</margin>
**Decimus Brutus** likewise has left a record of himself, especially for having been the only one to hold out against the will and the fury of **Antony**, who, after the terrible and cruel death of **Caesar**, wished to occupy and extinguish the life of **Octavian** and the Roman Republic. But he was afterwards condemned by the Senate because he had not followed the pursuit in the rout of **Modena** <note>The Battle of Mutina, 43 BC</note>; finally, falling into Antony’s power, he was killed by a soldier named **Capenus** by Antony’s command.

<margin>G</margin>
¶ In the fifth place come the two **Marcelli**, of whom the first was named **Marcus Marcellus**. When the **Gauls** and the **Insubres** <note>A Celtic people of Cisalpine Gaul/Northern Italy</note> came against the Romans under the leadership of **Viridomarus**, their prince, he proceeded against them. After several bitter battles, he finally overcame and defeated them; then, most cruelly in single combat, he killed **Viridomarus**. He consecrated his <term>opime spoils</term> <note>original: "opime ſpoglie"; the *spolia opima*, the highest honor a Roman general could earn by killing an enemy commander in single combat</note> to **Jove** <note>original: "Ione", likely a transcription or variant for Jove/Jupiter Feretrius</note>, as **Livy** describes and **Virgil** later celebrated. 

Then the great war of **Hannibal** followed. Having almost taken the entire Roman countryside, **Marcus Marcellus** was in **Nola**. One day, making a sally from the land, he assaulted Hannibal, who was in the field. Fighting prosperously with his few men, he remained the victor and superior to Hannibal in that action. As Hannibal continued the siege, the praetor Marcellus infested the Africans with such heavy goading that Hannibal was forced to flee. Thus, Marcellus was the first of the Romans to see the back of Hannibal in flight, giving some hope of victory to the Roman Senate. 

Marcellus harassed Hannibal very often. As **Livy** writes in the seventh book of the Second Punic War, having been once overcome by the Carthaginians with about two thousand seven hundred Romans killed—among whom were two tribunes and four centurions—Marcus Marcellus rebuked and scolded his soldiers so sharply that all those who remained cried out with one voice that they would follow his every will and that he should put them to a certain test. Marcellus truly said he wished to do this; thus, the next day he came against Hannibal and attacked them, breaking them where about eight thousand Carthaginians were cruelly killed along with five elephants. For this reason, Hannibal turned to his soldiers and said of Marcus Marcellus these words: <note>original Latin: "Cũ eo nimirũ hoſte vobis res eſt: q; nec bonam nec malam ſcit ferre fortunã: nec põt. Seu vincit ferociter inſtat victis: ſeu victus eſt inſtaurat cũ victoribus certamẽ"</note> *“Truly, you have to deal with such an enemy who knows not how to bear good nor bad fortune, nor can he. If he wins, he fiercely pursues the conquered; if he is defeated, he renews the struggle with the victors.”*

During this time, almost all of **Sicily** was in the power and dominion of the Carthaginians. Marcus Marcellus went there with his armies and captured **Syracuse**, and in short order recovered the entire island and brought it back to the devotion of the Romans. Finally, having been made consuls against Hannibal, Marcus Marcellus and **Titus Quinctius Crispinus**, not allowing the Africans a single day to rest in peace, it happened that the consuls went to scout the site where Hannibal was camped. They took a small company with them; as they were returning, some of Hannibal's squadrons assaulted the consuls. Fighting there most fiercely, in the end, the glorious Marcus Marcellus was killed.

<margin>M</margin>
¶ The other **Marcus Marcellus** was he who was consul at the time of **Caesar**. Together with **Pompey**, **Cato**, **Bibulus**, and his other adversaries, he was in the civil war. Although he exercised himself greatly in the feat of arms against Caesar, nonetheless I believe he remains more famous for the clemency shown to him by Caesar after he was forced to surrender, and for the oration of **Cicero** which begins: <note>original Latin: "Diuturni ſilentij quo eram iis tẽpibus vſus. Patres conſcripti"</note> *“The long silence which I had observed in those times, O Conscript Fathers...”* In this speech, he thanked Caesar for the clemency shown to Marcellus more than for his own actions; for while he was exiled in **Athens** and Caesar had granted him return at the instance of the Senate, just as he was setting out on the way to return, he was killed by **P. Magius Cilo**, his client. 

As **Livy** writes in the fourth book of the twelfth decade (according to the fragments of **Florus**), there was also another **Claudius Marcellus**, as **Livy** truly writes in the third book of the fourth decade (according to **Lucius Florus**'s notes). He, together with **Lucius Furius Purpureo**, defeated and overcame the **Boii**, the **Insubres**, and the **Gauls**, who had once again conspired against the Romans beyond the time of Viridomarus; and from these peoples, Claudius Marcellus [celebrated a triumph].

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

->triumph<-

<margin>I</margin> Finally, there was one **Licinius Marcellus** at the time of the first **Marcellus**; he was a tribune and soldier under the **Marcus Marcellus** narrated above. He died in that great and most cruel battle when Marcellus was overcome by **Hannibal**. 

¶ It remains finally to narrate the deeds of **Regulus**, gathering them from **Pliny**, from the context of **Lucius Florus**, and from the fragments made by him from **Livy** in the second decade, books seven and eight, and likewise from **Eutropius**. Here it is primarily to be understood that, since the Romans were not in full possession of Italy but were at war with the **Salentini** <note>An ancient people of the Salento peninsula in Apulia, the "heel" of Italy</note>, **Marcus Atilius Regulus** was made consul against them; he defeated them and triumphed over them, most significantly where this last victory pertained to the acquisition of Italy. 

The Romans then desired—since they were in possession of the land of Italy and already had two seas as the borders of their dominion—to test their fortune at sea. By chance, an excellent opportunity was offered to them: because in **Sicily**, there was a war between the **Syracusans** and the **Messinese**. The Syracusans implored the help of the **Carthaginians**, while the Messinese asked for the favor <margin>K</margin> of the Romans. Because of this, the **First Punic War** <note>The first of three major wars between Rome and Carthage (264–241 BC) fought for control of Sicily and the Mediterranean</note> had its origin. Three Roman leaders had already gone into this war: namely **Appius Claudius**, **Gaius Duilius**, and **Atilius Collatinus**. 

¶ In the fourth place succeeded **Marcus Atilius Regulus**, who among the many Romans was the first leader to pass into **Africa**. While Regulus was primarily in the African sea, he fought with **Hamilcar** the Carthaginian, whom he overcame, capturing about sixty-one Carthaginian ships. After this worthy and great victory, descending onto land, he took a noble city called *Clypea* <note>An ancient Carthaginian city, now Kelibia in Tunisia</note>. And from there, in a short space of time, he took three hundred forts and two hundred thousand men who were subjected to the Roman Empire. 

¶ It seems Regulus fought not only against men, but likewise against the gods; for, as if in vengeance for Africa, there appeared near the Roman camps a most cruel and horrible serpent, which greatly infested and likewise damaged the Romans. But Regulus, victor in every other thing, overcame even the serpent. Wherefore, not without great fear and admiration, his name was spread throughout Africa; nothing else remained to do except to go and conquer **Carthage**. Seeing this, and realizing that in their own strength they were being overcome by Regulus, the Carthaginians turned to external helpers. Thus, they hired as their captain for a price **Xanthippus the Lacedaemonian** <note>A Spartan mercenary general</note>. Coming to Carthage and seeing that the Romans suffered from a scarcity of water, he devised a plan to occupy it. When he saw them sufficiently exhausted by this effect, he assaulted them, broke them, and took prisoner the distinguished and outstanding Marcus Atilius Regulus. 

<margin>L</margin> Regulus, having previously captured a great abundance and multitude of Carthaginians in the war, and now having become a prisoner himself, the Carthaginians wished to make an exchange between Regulus and their captured youth. Therefore, they deliberated to send Regulus himself as an ambassador to the Romans, first making him swear an oath that if the Romans did not consent to the pact, he would return to Carthage. Marcus Regulus obeyed. Having arrived in Rome, he showed himself to be a Roman in no gesture or custom <note>He considered himself a slave of Carthage and thus stripped of his Roman citizenship</note>; but being introduced into the Senate, he presented his embassy from the Carthaginians. After that, with a copious and urgent speech, he persuaded the Roman Senate and the people that such an exchange should not be made, nor should they even make peace. He said that he was old and the war was totally useless <note>Meaning his own life was of little value compared to the tactical advantage</note>, while the Carthaginian prisoners were young and fit for military exercise. For this reason, the Romans did not make peace, nor did they exchange the prisoners. When Regulus wished to depart and return to Carthage, his wife wanted to embrace him and the Senate told him to remain in Rome; but Regulus pushed his wife away and said these worthy words to the Senate:

> ¶ From that day in which I came into the power of the Africans, I ceased to be a Roman. Therefore, I refuse to remain in this city in which, after I have served the Africans, I cannot hold the dignity of an honest citizen. <note>original: "Ex illa die in qua in potestatem affrorum veni romanus esse desivi. Quare nego me in ea urbe mansurum: in qua postq̃ affris seruiui dignitatem honesti civis habere nō possum."</note>

Regulus then returned to Carthage. Knowing truly that the exchange had been disrupted by his own effort, they shut him in a wooden vessel surrounded entirely by very sharp nails, and they cut off his eyelids so that he would feel pain until his final breath. In that way, they miserably caused him to die. With great reason, therefore, it is well said of him that he loved others—namely, the Roman Republic—much more than he did himself and his own life. 

**Master Francesco** <note>Petrarch, the author of the original poem "The Triumphs"</note> then adds who followed after Marcus Regulus, saying that behind him he saw coming a **Curio** and a **Fabricius**, much more beautiful in their poverty—their fame being more worthy for being voluntary—than were **Midas**, King of Phrygia, and **Marcus Crassus** the Roman with their gold and riches; for those two were rebels against perpetual and singular virtue. Wherefore he says:

It concludes by contrasting the virtuous poverty of Curio and Fabricius with the corrupting wealth of Midas and Crassus.</summary>

# CHAPTER TWO

-> A Curius and a Fabricius far more beautiful <-
-> With their poverty, than Midas or Crassus <-
-> With gold; they were never rebels against virtue. <-

<insert>
¶ A fitting thing: just as Marcus Curius and Gaius Licinius Fabricius were of similar will and deeds, it is likewise right that they both proceed together in the Triumph of Fame. Thus it should be explained that the Romans...
</insert>

<margin>M</margin>
Having acquired part of the dominion in Italy, the Samnites <note>An ancient Oscan-speaking people of the Apennines who were formidable rivals to the early Roman Republic</note>—who were a very powerful people—bore great envy toward the Romans and moved to war against them. This war was marked by much variety, and several consuls were sent on the expedition: namely Gaius Veturius and Lucius Papirius, surnamed Cursor. However, the Samnites were not so subjugated by any of these men that they did not renew the war again. Therefore, the Roman people sent Marcus Curius Dentatus there. He not only defeated them but brought everything under the Roman Empire from the shore of the sea where they lived all the way to the Upper Sea <note>The Adriatic Sea</note>. During the war, when the people of Sabina rebelled against the Romans, Marcus Curius defeated them as well. And so he triumphed twice: once over the Samnites and the other over the Sabines, in one and the same consulship. In addition to these victories, Curius subjugated the Lucanians and totally drove Pyrrhus, King of the Epiroti, out of Italy. Having then returned to Rome, it was confirmed that Curius had taken so much land that it would have been a wilderness if he had not captured so many men, and he had captured so many men that they would have died of hunger if he had not taken so much land. He returned to live in his small and poor dwelling. While staying there and cooking turnips one morning, the ambassadors of the Samnites brought him a very great quantity of gold as a gift. As soon as he saw it, he rejected it, saying to the ambassadors: <term>“I prefer to eat from my earthenware and to command those who have gold.”</term> <note>original: "Malo in fictilibus meis esse: & aurum habentibus imperare."</note> A truly worthy response, suited to a most illustrious Roman. Beyond this, when Curius was accused of taking much plunder from the Samnite war, he showed the people only a single wooden chalice with which he sacrificed to the gods, swearing that he had possessed nothing else from all the spoils but that; for this reason, he was acquitted.

<margin>N</margin>
Similar poverty and self-restraint were found in Gaius Licinius Fabricius. He showed no less knowledge of the deeds of arms in the war the Romans had with Pyrrhus and the people of Taranto than Marcus Curius Dentatus did, and also in the war of the Samnites and Lucanians, from which he brought back glorious triumphs. He also wished to demonstrate his equality in the other virtue of voluntary poverty. Regarding him, Aulus Gellius writes in the *Attic Nights*, book one, that when the Samnites had also offered him—just as they had to Curius—a very great quantity of gold, he, in their presence, silently touched all his limbs and then, turning to the Samnites, said these excellent words: <term>“As long as I can resist and rule over all these limbs I have just touched, nothing will ever be lacking to me. Therefore, I will not accept money for which I have no use from those whom I know find it useful.”</term> <note>original: "Dum iis omnibus quae modo attigi membris obsistere atque imperare potero: nuq̃ quicq̃ defuturum est. Quare pecuniam qua mihi nullus est usus ab hiis quibus scio eam usui esse non accipiam."</note>

<margin>O</margin>
Similarly, when Fabricius went once as an ambassador to Pyrrhus to ransom the prisoners of war, Pyrrhus, seeing him and recognizing his poverty, offered to give him a fourth part of his ample kingdom. Fabricius, despising this, brought Pyrrhus to great admiration. But this admiration increased much more later when Fabricius, having gone as consul against him with the camps very near, Terannes of Ambracia—as Valerius writes in the sixth book, chapter five—offered to have his son give poison to Pyrrhus. Nicias, his physician, also came by night to Fabricius, offering in a similar way to bring death to Pyrrhus. Fabricius had him bound and sent back to Pyrrhus, revealing his evil intention to him and writing to him, out of respect for Terannes, that he should watch himself in eating and drinking, without explaining further. Whereupon Pyrrhus said: <term>“That is Fabricius, who can be turned from honesty with more difficulty than the sun from its course.”</term> <note>original: "ille est Fabritius: qui difficilius ab honestate quã sol a cursu suo auerti potest"</note> And immediately because of this, he left Italy and crossed into Sicily. Therefore, with great reason, Dante Alighieri in the twentieth canto of the *Purgatorio* says that he heard the purged souls say these verses in praise of Fabricius:

<margin>P</margin>
> O good Fabricius, you preferred virtue with poverty rather than possessing great riches with vice.

¶ Just as these two most excellent men were notable and beautiful with their poverty, so, by contrast, immense greed and insatiable desire made Crassus and King Midas appear filthy with their riches. It is well known that Marcus Crassus was a very rich and powerful Roman citizen and had such a vast amount of money that he could easily, from his own funds...

<summary>This page recounts the legendary lives of Marcus Curius Dentatus and Gaius Licinius Fabricius, emphasizing their incorruptibility and preference for humble living over Samnite gold or Pyrrhus's kingdom. It contrasts their Roman "beauty" in poverty with the "filth" of wealth associated with Marcus Crassus and King Midas.</summary>

# CHAPTER TWO

Fighting with them, he conquered them and crushed their pride, forcing them to beg with prayers for mercy and peace. He freed Minutius from the siege and, having returned to Rome, made him renounce the consulship, saying to him this honorable chastisement: <note>original: "Carebit prede pro te miles ex eo hoste cui quoque preda fuisti: tu Luci Quinto Minuti donec consularem animum incipias habere legatus iis legionibus praeesto"</note> "The soldier shall lack plunder because of you from that enemy to whom you yourself were nearly plunder; and you, Lucius Quinctius Minutius, until you begin to possess a consular mind, shall remain as a subordinate commander over these legions." Having achieved this victory within fifteen days, Cincinnatus, on the sixteenth day, laid down his dictatorship and returned to his fields to finish his sowing. <note>Cincinnatus is the Roman archetype of the "citizen-soldier" who leaves his plow to save the state and returns to it immediately after victory.</note> Following him is Furius Camillus: of whom Messer Francesco <note>The author refers to Petrarch, the poet of this "Triumph"</note> narrates that the great Camillus followed Cincinnatus. This Camillus appeared to be weary of living before he was ever weary of acting well and virtuously; therefore heaven strengthened him and placed him in a worthy rank of excellence so that his clear, glorious virtue led him back to Rome, from which previously a blind rage of malice and envy had disappeared and removed him. <note>Camillus had been exiled due to false accusations before being recalled to save Rome.</note> Thus it says:

<margin>
¶ Worthy and glorious fame must rightfully be attributed to Camillus, having been a vessel of so many noble and singular virtues and possessing the intelligence of a lawgiver and scholar. As Livy writes in *From the Founding of the City*, Book 5: the Roman people had already held the inhabitants of Veii under siege for ten years. At this time, many dissensions had arisen.

-> **and the great Camillus,** <-
-> **Weary of living before weary of doing good;** <-
-> **Because heaven chose him for such a high rank,** <-

-> **From where others' blind rage had removed him.** <-

The tribunician <note>Refers to the 'Tribunes of the Plebs,' political officers in Rome</note> conflicts had already led the Romans to such despair that they not only lost hope of obtaining victory, but remained in doubt of abandoning Rome altogether because of the many incursions made at times even to their very gates. <margin>Z</margin> It was, therefore, at this time that Marcus Furius Camillus was made dictator as the last hope of the Romans. He immediately enrolled a new army with the help of the Latins and Hernici, who had spontaneously offered to come to war in favor of the Romans. Leaving Rome, Camillus and his army first encountered the Capenates and the Falisci near Nepete, and then those of Fidenae. Having won these victories, he reached Veii, which he conquered and defeated most excellently; and so he ended the great siege of ten years that had been continuously maintained by the Romans against their enemies. <margin>A</margin> Having then returned to Rome, Camillus first satisfied Apollo with a tenth part of the plunder because of the vow he had made to win, and afterward he triumphed according to the custom. ¶ Again he went as consul against the Falisci—or truly as a military tribune with consular power—and as they were at the head of the resistance against Furius Camillus, they were defeated by him in battle. Their camps were taken and totally plundered, because of which it was necessary for them to stay shut inside to guard their land. Whereupon Camillus besieged them. While this harsh siege continued, a schoolmaster, to whom the education of all the adolescent sons of the Falisci was committed, wishing to ingratiate himself with Camillus, one day led those boys outside of Falerii under the guise of exercising. Step by step, he proceeded until he reached the Roman camps. Presenting himself to Camillus, he said that he was giving him those boys as prisoners, by means of whom Camillus could easily obtain victory over the city. The good Camillus—to whom all vices were highly hateful, and especially fraud and treachery—seeing the malice of this man, said: "Take him and bind his hands behind his back," and he gave a rod into the hand of each boy. Then he said to the man these words: <note>original: "Non ad simile tui: nec ad populum: nec ad imperatorem sceleratus ipse cum scelesto munere venisti..."</note> "You, a wicked man, have come with a wicked gift to a people and a commander not like yourself. Human society is formed by a pact which nature generated for both of us. There are laws of war just as there are laws of peace; we have learned to carry them out no less justly than bravely. We have arms, not against that age [childhood] which is spared even when cities are captured, but against those who are armed... I shall conquer by Roman arts: virtue, labor, and arms, just as I did at Veii." And after he had finished these words, he commanded the boys to beat him; and in such a manner, he sent him back to Falerii. The Falisci, therefore, seeing such great faith, virtue, and excellence in the Roman Camillus, concluded after mature examination that it was much better to obey such just princes and observers of such faith and clemency as the Romans were, than to have peace and government from any other republic or even from themselves. Therefore, they immediately elected ambassadors to go to the Senate to give themselves, their city, and their dominion into Roman power and will. <margin>B</margin> ¶ The ambassadors having come to Rome and being introduced before the Senate, they spoke these few and worthy words on behalf of all the Falisci.

<meta>This page continues the biography of Marcus Furius Camillus, following the previous discussion of his exile and moral character.
