# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

words. **"Enrolled Fathers, <note>The traditional address for the Roman Senate: "Patres Conscripti."</note> whom neither god nor man should envy: we have surrendered ourselves to you, having been conquered by you and your commander, believing that nothing is more beautiful for a victor than that we shall live better under your rule and our own laws. By the outcome of this war, two salutary examples have been provided to the human race. You preferred faith in war, which is present in victories. We, provoked by your faith, have voluntarily brought victory to you. We are under your jurisdiction. Send those who may receive our arms, our hostages, and our city with open gates; neither will you be dissatisfied with our loyalty, nor we with your rule."** Having thus achieved victory and returned to Rome with offerings for Delphi <note>Camillus sent a golden bowl to the Temple of Apollo at Delphi as a tithe of the spoils from the city of Veii.</note> to fulfill his vows, Camillus was honorably received by the Senate and the people with great joy and exultation. Afterward, during this time, a great discord multiplied between the Senate and the common people, because the commoners wanted to drive out Aulus Virginius and Quintus Pomponius, the tribunes from the past two years. Although they were innocent, and the Fathers and the Senate wanted to acquit them, in the end, the anger of the commoners was more powerful than the mercy of the Fathers, and they were condemned to pay a large sum of money. Therefore, Camillus spoke gravely to the commoners; as a result, after a certain Lucius Apuleius was made tribune, having already conceived a great anger against Camillus, he had him condemned to pay five hundred thousand bronze coins. <note>original: "cinquecento milia dinari di metallo" referring to the heavy bronze currency of early Rome.</note> The reason given was that he had allegedly misappropriated spoils in the Veientine war. Because Camillus could not pay such a large fine, he was forced to flee to Ardea and live in exile. At this time, it happened that the Senonian Gauls passed into Tuscany and laid siege to the city of Chiusi. Since the people of Chiusi could not defend themselves on their own, they asked the Romans for help. The Romans, consulting upon this request, finally deliberated to send ambassadors to the Gauls to tell them to peacefully lift the siege.

<margin>C</margin>
When the ambassadors arrived at the camp and delivered their message, the Gauls replied that they believed the Romans were brave men, and that they should help their friends with arms in hand rather than with a delegation; however, they would not refuse the offered peace if the Romans would give them enough land where they could comfortably live. Hearing this response, the Roman legates were moved to anger and took up arms with the Gauls. <note>Roman ambassadors traditionally held diplomatic immunity but were forbidden from fighting; by joining the battle, they violated international religious law, giving the Gauls a "just cause" for war.</note> Because of this, the Gauls turned their anger against the Romans and decided to wage war only against them. Lifting the siege of Chiusi, they marched toward Rome. To resist them, the Romans sent certain legions to the river called Allia with little order and little foresight. The Gauls, fighting with the Romans, overcame and defeated them. From there, proceeding as victors to Rome, they took the city. Seeing the Roman senators of advanced age sitting in their chairs, dressed in their most honorable robes in the halls of their palaces, the Gauls were at first moved by their venerable majesty and honored them like gods; but afterward, they killed them all, along with the rest of the people, except for those who had retreated to the Capitol. They attacked that place, but as the Gauls tried several times to capture it, they suffered many slaughterous defeats at the hands of the young Romans. While the Gauls held Rome, they began to raid the surrounding lands, especially toward Ardea, where Camillus was in exile. Because of this, he incited the Ardeans against the Gauls and assaulted them in the fields, committing a great slaughter. The people of Veii and the Romans besieged in the Capitol did the same; those Gauls who remained in Rome then reached a common agreement and elected Camillus as their leader. Camillus then took command of the armies and came against the Gauls, who had already struck a bargain with the Romans to receive a thousand pounds of gold to lift the siege. While this gold was being weighed, a proud Gaul said he wanted even more, adding the weight of his sword to the scales. <note>This refers to the famous "Vae victis" (Woe to the conquered) episode where the Gallic leader Brennus threw his sword onto the scale.</note> While they were in this dispute, Camillus arrived with the armies, fought the Gauls, and overcame and killed them all. Nor was this the only benefit Camillus provided to the city of Rome; since it had been burned and destroyed by the Gauls and the Romans wanted to abandon it to live in Veii, Camillus restrained them and had them restore Rome.

<margin>D</margin>
Afterward, as the war with the neighboring cities continued, Camillus gloriously defeated the Aequi, Volsci, Latins, Hernici, and the people of Sutrium and Nepi, and many other peoples he subjected to the Roman Republic. While a very grave plague was coming to Rome, Camillus died. He was then allotted to heaven, according to the opinion of those who attribute every effect to the heavens—especially the astrologer Posidonius—to such a worthy and excellent degree of virtue that, from where envy had driven him out, his own virtue brought him back with glory and triumph. Therefore, Titus Livy deservedly writes these worthy words about him in the seventh book of *From the Founding of the City*: **"For he was truly a unique man, a leader in every fortune: in peace and war before he went into exile; more famous in exile, either because of the longing of the city which, when captured, implored the help of the absent one, or because of the success with which, restored to his country, he restored the country itself along with him; then for thirty-five years—for he lived that long afterward—he was worthy of the title of such great glory and was held worthy to be called the second founder after Romulus, the founder of the city of Rome."**

<summary>This page details the exile of Marcus Furius Camillus, the subsequent Gallic sack of Rome, and Camillus's heroic return to defeat the invaders and rebuild the city. He is celebrated as the "Second Founder of Rome" for his military leadership and for convincing the citizens not to abandon the ruined city.</summary>

<margin>
Titus Manlius Torquatus was the son of Lucius Manlius. Because he appeared to be of very slow wit, his father had almost relegated him to a villa in the countryside. When Lucius Manlius was later accused by a certain Marcus Pomponius, Torquatus—hearing of this, as Livy writes in *From the City's Foundations*, Book 7—was moved by fatherly affection and returned to Rome. With a sword in his hand, he forced Pomponius to swear he would drop the accusation against his father. Later, when the Romans decided to wipe out the remnants of the Gauls in Italy, he was created Dictator. With Quintus Minucius and Sergio Cornelio Maluginensis as masters of the horse, Titus Manlius went with the army. There, a Gaul challenged the Roman knights to single combat. Manlius alone went out against him, fought him, and defeated him. He took a necklace <term>torques: a twisted metal neck ring worn by Gauls</term> which the enemy wore around his neck and put it on himself, thereby acquiring the name "Torquatus."

->Of the military, so it would not be blinded:<-

Later, when war broke out between the Romans and the Latins, Torquatus was elected Consul. Having to manage the war prudently alongside his colleague—since it seemed the Latins were equal in both valor and power—Manlius commanded that no one should fight without his permission. During this time, his own son went out to scout the enemy's preparations. He came with his troop near the Latin leaders, where the Tusculans were guarding the camp under a leader named Metius Geminius. This man provoked Titus Manlius (the son of Torquatus) to battle, insulting him with many biting words. Finally, Manlius, unable to endure Metius's insults, fought him, defeated him, and killed him on the field. Returning afterward with joy to his father, he spoke these words: <note>original Latin: "Ut me oēs pater tuo sanguine ortū vere referrent prouocatus equestria hec spolia capta ex hoste ceso porto."</note> **"Father, so that everyone might truly report that I am born of your blood, I bring these equestrian spoils taken from the slain enemy, having been provoked to battle."** When Torquatus heard these words, he replied with great sorrow: <note>original Latin: "Tite manli neq; iperiū consulare: neq; maiestatē paternā veritus aduersus edictū nostrū extra ordinē in hoste pugnasti. Et quantū in te fuit disciplinā militarē qua stetit ad hanc diem romana respu. soluisti..."</note> **"Titus Manlius, since you feared neither the consular authority nor the majesty of a father, and fought against our edict outside the ranks against the enemy—and insofar as it was in your power, you have dissolved the military discipline upon which the Roman Republic has stood until this day—you have brought me to this necessity: that I must either forget the Republic or forget myself and my own. We should rather be punished for our own crime than have the Republic pay for our sins with such great damage. It will be a sad example, but a healthy one for the youth of the future."** Finally, having called a lictor, he had his son bound to a stake and beheaded in his presence. This was a worthy observance of the law, certainly, however sad and bitter it may be, especially in war; for through the disregard of laws, the Republic can fall into much greater ruin. Therefore Cicero says in the first book of *On Duties*: **"The laws of war must be especially preserved in a Republic,"** as they are necessary for the common safety. Next, Messer Francesco mentions Publius Decius, both the father and the son, saying that after Torquatus, he saw both the one and the other Decius, who were equal to him, as they broke through the enemy ranks with their own chests and a hard death. He then exclaims, and rightfully so: "O fierce and pious vow, which offered and led both father and son to the same death." Thus he says:

This figure told them on behalf of the gods that their intention was for the consul of one side to be killed in the next battle, and for the army of the other side to be defeated. Therefore, after conferring in the morning about what they had seen and performing the proper sacrifices, the consuls agreed that—so the army would not lose heart—whichever side began to falter in the coming battle, that consul would vow himself to the gods and die for his country. # CHAPTER TWO

<margin>O</margin>
External wars were a very fruitful endeavor for the Roman Republic and the cause of eternal fame for Lucius Mummius. <note>Lucius Mummius Achaicus was the Roman general who destroyed Corinth in 146 BC, marking the end of the Achaean League.</note> ¶ Marcus Valerius Laevinus is deservedly considered in the second place by Master Francesco [Petrarch]. Here it is to be understood that while the Romans were waging war against the Tarentines, Pyrrhus, King of Epirus, came to the aid of Tarentum against the Romans; he brought with him a great army of men and also a large number of elephants. Marcus Laevinus <note>Consul in 280 BC during the Pyrrhic War.</note> was therefore sent against him, and with him a centurion named Cosidius. When they came to battle with Pyrrhus, the centurion Cosidius pressed Pyrrhus's army in such a way that, had it not been for the novelty of the elephants—which threw the Roman ranks into disorder and caused the frightened horses to turn back—they would have emerged as victors. In the end, Pyrrhus remained superior; but certainly, as far as it concerned Laevinus and the Roman soldiers, they fulfilled their duty in every turn of fortune. Both in winning and losing, they showed courage: for when winning they always pursued the enemy, and when losing they never turned back to flee; and after they were killed, their faces still showed their innate and admirable ferocity.

<margin>P</margin>
¶ In the third place, Attilius <note>Usually identified here as Marcus Atilius Regulus or Aulus Atilius Calatinus, heroes of the First Punic War.</note> brought better fortune to the city of Rome than Laevinus did. During the First Punic War, as Sicily was devoted to the favor of the Carthaginians, Attilius Collatinus was sent as captain of the fleet against the Carthaginians. Once he arrived in Sicily, he conquered and brought under Roman rule the noble and powerful cities of the island—primarily Etna, Lilybaeum, Agrigento, and Palermo. Then, having proceeded with very few ships against Hamilcar, the prefect and leader of Carthage who led a vast number of ships, he engaged him in battle and was superior and victorious. This immediately resulted in the entire island of Sicily becoming subject to the Roman empire.

<margin>Q</margin>
¶ Besides this Attilius, there was another, Marcus Atilius Glabrio; as Livy writes in Book 6 of the *Macedonian War* and Justin refers to in Book 31, he defeated Antiochus and drove him out of Greece, recovering the cities occupied by him; and beyond him, he also overcame the Aetolians. From his victory over Antiochus and the Aetolians, he brought back a triumph, and the utility of this work was no less than the glory it added to the Roman Republic.

<margin>R</margin>
¶ Finally, Titus Quinctius Flamininus: after the furies of the Second Punic War, the Senate decreed war against Philip, King of Macedonia. Flamininus was sent as consul against him and against Nabis, tyrant of the Lacedaemonians [Spartans]. Having arrived in Greece and continuing the war for some time against these two enemies, many cities had allied themselves with Philip and Nabis, wishing to preserve the friendship of the Greeks rather than that of the newly acquired Romans. In the end, Flamininus remained superior over both princes. Having ultimately defeated Philip, he called together all the cities of Greece that had been subject to him and commanded that they come on a designated day to hear the will of the Senate. When they had assembled, waiting in great fear for the consul's sentence, he finally—as Valerius writes in Book 4, Chapter 8—having ordered silence to be proclaimed to everyone, pronounced this sentence in a loud voice:

> The Senate and People of Rome and Quinctius Flamininus the General command that all the cities of Greece which were under the rule of King Philip shall be free and exempt from taxes. <note>original: "S.P.Q.R. & Qu. Flaminius imperator oēs græciæ vrbes q̃ sub ditiõe Philip. regis fuerūt liberas & imunes eẽ iubēt"</note>

This clemency and piety did not only confirm their spirits in loyalty to the Romans, but as this generosity was spread throughout all Greece, in a short space of time all Greece voluntarily came under the government and protection of the Romans. For these deeds, returning to Rome, Flamininus was deservedly honored by the Senate and the people with a glorious triumph lasting three entire days. Consequently, Master Francesco [Petrarch] introduces the one who followed after Titus Flamininus, saying that in that place was also he who encircled the King of Syria with a magnanimous circle. <note>This refers to the "Circle of Popilius," a famous diplomatic gesture where a Roman envoy forced a king to make a decision before stepping out of a circle drawn in the sand.</note> And then with his tongue, with his brow, and his authority, he constrained him to consent to his duty. Wherefore he says:

</margin>

<margin>T</margin>
¶ For the understanding of the preceding text, it should be known that this fourth figure described by our Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> was **Manlius Capitolinus**. When the Senone Gauls <note>A Celtic tribe from northern Italy who sacked Rome in 390 BC.</note> had taken the city of Rome, and by the counsel of the fathers all the Roman youth had run to the defense of the Capitol, defending it very manfully, it happened one night that the Gauls wanted to ascend with ladders onto the Capitol. At this, many **geese** <note>Sacred to the goddess Juno, these geese are legendary for alerting the Romans to the Gallic siege.</note> heard the commotion and began to cackle. Because of this, Manlius woke up, took his arms, and together with many Romans went out to the defense. Fighting bitterly with the Gauls, he made a most copious slaughter of them. For this reason, he was highly honored, and given a house upon the Capitol at public expense; from this deed, he was surnamed **Manlius Capitolinus**. However, Manlius, raised in pride by these honors, later sought to make himself the lord of Rome. When this was discovered by the others, he was put in prison. Later, having been released through the favor of the people, he remained persistent in his purpose; for this reason, Marcus Menenius and Quintus Publilius, then <term>Tribunes of the Plebs</term> <note>Elected officials who protected the interests of the common people.</note>, put him to death by throwing him from the **Tarpeian Rock**, which is located on the same Capitoline Hill. Beyond this, they ruined his house and forced the Manlius family to swear that in the future, no one would ever again use the surname **Capitolinus** to be compared with Manlius.

Master Francesco adds that there came he who alone defended the bridge of the Tiber against the force of all the Tuscans <note>The Etruscans</note> who were gathered wanting to capture it. Wherefore he says:

> *and he who, alone,*
> *Against all of Tuscany, held the bridge;*

<margin>V</margin>
¶ After **Tarquin the Proud** <note>The seventh and final king of Rome.</note> had been driven from Rome by Brutus, as we said above, he fled to **Porsena**, King of the Tuscans, who reigned then in the city of Chiusi. Having come to him with pleas, he moved him with reason to help him make war against the Romans. Whereupon Porsena, consenting to Tarquin, gathered a great army and came against the Romans. This event, being unexpected by the Romans, caused them such fear that they consulted on nothing else except how they should flee. While they were in this trepidation, Porsena and Tarquin arrived with the army, and they occupied the **Janiculum** <note>A hill across the Tiber from the city center.</note> almost before the Romans noticed anything.

<margin>X</margin>
¶ At that hour, by chance, guarding the <term>Sublician Bridge</term> <note>The oldest bridge in Rome, made of wood.</note> over the Tiber (which is the one that is now ruined below the Bridge of Saint Angelo) was a Roman named **Horatius Cocles** with a small company of soldiers. When they saw the enemies appear, they threw down their arms and began to flee. Horatius, seeing this and unable to sustain the battle any longer, turned to two who alone had remained with him—one named **Spurius Lartius** and the other **Herminius**—and told them to see to it that the bridge be cut away with iron and fire. He alone, as much as was permitted for one man, would sustain the fight and the impetus of the Tuscans. Putting himself forward against the soldiers at the head of the bridge, he began the battle. Fighting manfully, he held back such a multitude until finally the bridge was cut and broken. When this was known by signs given by the Romans, he turned back, and having thrown himself into the Tiber, he returned to his people with his own safety and that of the Romans.

Master Francesco then adds, saying that along with Horatius he saw another, who with laudable art and wit in the midst of the crowd and the enemy ranks, moved his worthy hand in vain; and then that same hand he burned so strongly, being angry in his mind with himself, that he felt neither the burning nor the pain. Wherefore he says:

> And he, who in the midst of the enemy host
> Moved his hand in vain; and then burned it
> So angry with himself, that he did not feel the pain;

<margin>y</margin> ¶ Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known: that after Horatius <note>Horatius Cocles, who famously defended the Sublician Bridge alone against the Etruscans.</note> returned to Rome by swimming across the Tiber, Porsena <note>Lars Porsena, the King of Clusium.</note> pitched his camp around Rome and commanded that the siege be maintained. As this was prolonged for a long time, Rome was brought to the greatest necessity and scarcity, for which reason it was necessary either that they die of hunger or surrender as prisoners to Porsena. In this state, therefore, a Roman youth named **Gaius Mucius** <note>Better known as Mucius Scaevola, or "Lefty," because of the hand he burned.</note> deliberated to die and kill the king to liberate his fatherland. Whereupon he asked license from the Senate to be able to go into the enemy camp. 

When license was granted to him, Mucius crossed the Tiber; and having arrived in the camp, he saw the scribe and priest of the king dressed in purple. Believing, therefore, by the clothing that he was King Porsena, he approached him and killed him. For this reason, Mucius was immediately captured and led before the king. The king, seeing him so young, asked him who he was. Mucius, without fear, replied with these worthy words: "I am a Roman citizen; they call me Gaius Mucius. As an enemy, I wished to kill my enemy; my courage for death is no less than it was for killing. To do and to endure brave things is the Roman way. Nor have I alone carried this spirit against you. Behind me is a long rank of those seeking the same honor." <note>original: "Romanus sum civis. C. mutium vocant: hostis hostem occidere volui: nec ad mortem minus aī est quam fuit ad cedem & facere nec pati fortia romanum est. Nec unus in te ego hos animos gessi. Logus post me ordo est idem petentium decus"</note>

The king, therefore, terrified and angered by these words, had him surrounded, threatening to burn him if he did not reveal the plots which he said were prepared against him. Mucius then extended his hand into the fire—which was stationed there to perform sacrifice—and obstinately letting it burn, he added to the king these other excellent words: "Behold, so that you may realize how cheap the body is to those who fix their eyes on great glory." <note>original: "En tibi ut sentias quam vile corpus sit ijs q magnām gloriam vident."</note> 

<margin>z</margin> ¶ Then the king, having seen this constancy, was entirely terrified; he abandoned the siege and granted peace to the Romans and safety to Mucius. Turning to him, he said: "Go, for you have dared more against yourself than against me; I would bid you be blessed in your virtue, if that virtue stood for my own country. Now, by the law of war, I dismiss you free, untouched, and unharmed." <note>original: "Abi in te m’giš ⁊ i me hostilia ausus: iuberem macte virtutis esse. Si p mea patria ista virtus staret. Nunc iure belli liberum te itactum inviolatumq hinc dimitto."</note> 

Mucius, therefore, having taken his leave from the king, returned to Rome where he was deservedly received by the people with great glory and honor. And Porsena, because of Mucius's constancy, made peace with the Romans, lifting every siege and returning with his army to Chiusi. 

Next, Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> narrates another example, saying that after Mucius follows the one who first showed himself to be a victor at sea against the Carthaginians. And with him came likewise that other one who had broken and dispersed the African ships between Sicily and Sardinia. Wherefore he says:

> And he who first appeared as victor at sea
> Against the Carthaginians; and he who broke and scattered
> Their ships between Sicily and Sardinia.

<margin>A</margin> ¶ In these verses, Messer Francesco writes of **Gaius Duilius** and **Quintus Lutatius Catulus** <note>Roman naval commanders of the First Punic War (264–241 BC).</note> proceeding deservedly with the other Romans in the triumph of Fame. Where it is to be understood: that since the Romans and Carthaginians had deliberated to bring succor and aid to the two dissenting cities in Sicily—that is, Messina and Syracuse, as we said above—this gave origin to the **First Punic War** <note>The long series of conflicts between Rome and Carthage for dominance of the Mediterranean.</note>. On the Roman side, **Gaius Duilius** was sent as captain of the fleet; and on the Carthaginian side, **Hamilcar** <note>The text uses "Milcone," likely referring to Hamilcar or Himilco.</note> was sent. 

Duilius, therefore, knowing that the Carthaginians were powerful at sea, instituted a new generation of ships, built more for battle than for a spectacle of beauty; and besides this, he added **iron anchors** <term>ancore ferree: likely referring to the *corvus*, a boarding bridge with a heavy spike used to grapple enemy ships</term> to be able to catch and link the enemies together. Coming, therefore, face to face with the Carthaginians, Duilius had the anchors thrown onto their ships, at which the Carthaginians laughed. Afterward, the Carthaginians fighting bitterly, Duilius remained the victor of the battle; and by means of the anchors, all the Carthaginians remained prisoners, except for the ship of Hamilcar, which fled and returned to Carthage. 

When Hamilcar arrived before the Carthaginian Senate and explained the disposition of the Roman fleet, they asked him what he thought should be done. The Carthaginians replied that it seemed they should fight; then Hamilcar said: "I have fought and lost." Thus he escaped the penalty of the cross <note>Crucifixion was a common punishment for failed generals in Carthage.</note> instituted by the Carthaginians for anyone who was defeated in battle at sea. 

The First Punic War having thereafter lasted many years, and having been fought very variably on both sides, each of the two powers wished to attempt to bring it to an end; each of them strove to make a final effort in the... <note>The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of the page.</note>

# CHAPTER TWO

The days and other peoples—certainly the westerners for Hercules and the northerners for Epaminondas <note>A Theban general known for his tactical genius; the text compares his northern reach to Pompey’s universal reach</note>—but Pompey alone conquered and subjected all these peoples, eastern, western, and northern, to the Roman Empire. Thus, after Sicily had first been occupied by those proscribed by Sulla, Pompey, manfully following his faction, recovered it from them. Secondly, after Gnaeus Domitius (one among the other proscribed men) along with Hiarba had occupied Numidia and taken his kingdom from Masinissa, Pompey returned to Rome and triumphed over them, being only twenty-four years of age. Succeeding this was the hard and bitter war against Sertorius <note>A Roman general who led a large-scale rebellion in Spain</note> and other proconsuls who had followed the party of Marius; Pompey drove them out and conquered them in Spain. 

And while there was a massive quantity of pirates infesting both seas <note>The Mediterranean, divided into the Tyrrhenian and Adriatic/Ionian</note> and plundering the provisions coming to Rome—which caused the Romans great distress—Pompey alone forced them all to surrender or death within sixty days. Turning then toward the East, he principally defeated King Mithridates, King of Pontus, and King Tigranes of Armenia; he forced them to surrender, and triumphing over them, he led before him the son of Tigranes, the sons of King Mithridates, and Aristobulus, King of the Jews. In that triumph, one never saw a more worthy display of pomp. Following after Mithridates and those peoples who had favored him, he conquered and overcame the Albanians, the Colchians, the Hernici, the Syrians, the Phoenicians, the Caspians, and the Bosphorans. He also conquered the Jews and those who inhabited the Red Sea, the Arabian Sea, and the Sicanian <note>Sicilian</note> Sea; he was the first Roman commander to carry Roman standards into these places. Wherefore, Pompey was deservedly superior in the civil war; he was without doubt the first among all other famous Romans. 

But nonetheless, what end he met in that war is well known through the comparison made by our poet <note>Petrarch</note> regarding the Thebans. Therefore, Master Francis <note>Petrarch</note> reasonably concludes that a long and excessive life is the worst thing, according to the opinion of Cicero in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*. There, he enumerates Priam, Metellus, and Gnaeus Pompey, who, if he had died when he was ill at Naples, would not have fallen into such great calamities and miseries. In that place, Cicero says, speaking of that illness: 

> "Would he then have departed from good things or from bad? Certainly from miserable things. For he would not have waged war with his father-in-law <note>Julius Caesar</note>; he would not have taken up arms unprepared; he would not have left his home; he would not have fled from Italy; he would not have fallen, naked, into the iron and hands of slaves after losing his army; his children would not have been wept for; all his fortunes would not be possessed by the victors." <note>original Latin: "Vtrū igit̄ si tū eēt exitus a bonis rebus an a malis excessisset certe a miseris..."</note>

And for this reason, Suetonius Tranquillus writes that it was the opinion of many that Julius Caesar wished to die at the time he was killed, fearing that in old age his glory might diminish; therefore, he despised the auguries, ignored the warnings of friends, and finally dismissed the soldiers <note>The text says "israeliti," likely a transcription error for "satelliti" (guards/satellites)</note> whom he used to lead around himself as his own guard. Master Francis then adds, saying that after Pompey, he saw another follow of his kind, who was to be, and who quickly and easily gained a reputation in the flower of his years. Whereupon he says:

<margin>
To understand the preceding verses, one should know that this man whom Master Francis describes in this place was Lucius Cornelius Sulla. Here it is understood that while Sulla was still small in swaddling clothes, there appeared to him...
</margin>

->...and I saw then <-
-> him who, for his status, quickly and easily <-
-> Had the name, and was in the flower of his years; <-

...a woman who, as Plutarch writes, said to him: "Greetings, boy, lucky for yourself and for your republic" <note>original: "Salue puer tibi & reipub. tuae fælix."</note>. And immediately after these words were spoken, she vanished. Sulla later verified this prophecy when, having forced Marius to die, he described and named himself "Felix" <note>The Lucky or The Fortunate</note> by perpetual edict. Nonetheless, among all the surnames that can be attributed to men, there is none that can be more easily removed than that of "happiness" or "fortune," since man is subject to infinite perils, the smallest of which is sufficient to take away any happy state—as Aristotle demonstrates in the first book of the *Ethics*. 

Sulla, then, primarily served as Quaestor under Gaius Marius, manfully fighting against Jugurtha, who, by the will of Bocchus, King of Mauritania, had moved great war against the Romans. In the end, this Bocchus was led to surrender Jugurtha as a prisoner to Marius. Likewise, in the Cimbric and Teutonic wars, Sulla carried himself so manfully in combat that he gave a preview of himself as a most worthy and magnanimous man.

<margin>

He even overcame the Samnites and restored the kingdom of Cappadocia to King Ariobarzanes. # CHAPTER TWO

<margin>N</margin>
...of Pompey can be understood by the universal goodwill shown to him by the people. The situation was such that, as Appian of Alexandria <note>A Roman historian of Greek origin who wrote a famous history of the Roman Civil Wars</note> writes, Caesar, in his worthy triumphs, did not wish to carry the image of Pompey upon his chariot for fear that the people might be moved against him out of respect for Pompey. On the contrary, he displayed images of those who had caused Pompey's death, which served as a relief to the Romans. ¶ The third and final interpretation is that the poet refers to Julius Caesar. For as Sallust writes when comparing Cato to Caesar, Cato sought the goodwill of the Romans through rigidity, while Caesar did so through kindness and clemency. This quality was shown by Caesar during the Battle of Pharsalus <note>The decisive battle where Caesar defeated Pompey</note> when he cried out loudly to his soldiers: "spare the citizens" <note>original: "parcite ciuibus"</note>. And according to this interpretation, the verses are introduced thus: as much as Sulla was cruel and severe in arms, so was the one who followed very kind. He adds that he does not know if he should be called a better leader or a true knight, to agree with Lucius Florus <note>A Roman historian</note>, who, writing of the Battle of Pharsalus, says of Caesar: "Caesar was a great force in that battle, acting as both general and soldier" <note>original: "multus fuit cesar in eo plio: mediūsqz inter imperatorem & militem"</note>. Let the choice now rest with the judgment of whichever of these—or indeed someone else—our Master Francesco <note>Petrarch, the author of the poem being commented upon</note> intended in these verses. But if anyone should say that since the poet has already commemorated Caesar and Pompey above, mentioning them here would be redundant, I respond that this is not true. For he only wishes to use their examples to show that Sulla's cruelty was most extreme, being equal to the immense kindness of each of them. Master Francesco then recounts another example, saying that after Sulla and indeed Valerius Corvinus came that noble Lucius Volumnius, worthy of high and excellent praise and virtue, who through good deeds suppressed the livid and malignant tumor that came from corrupt blood. Whence he says:

<margin>
Lucius Volumnius, a most distinguished Roman, being excellent in the deeds of arms, was elected consul—as Livy writes in book 10 of "From the Founding of the City"—against the Samnites and Tuscans, upon which peoples he inflicted many great slaughters.
</margin>
> Then came he who, by doing good, suppressed
> The livid, malignant tumor of blood;
> Volumnius, noble and worthy of high praise.

He brought utility to the Roman Republic, but his most fruitful action was when the pestilential influence ceased through him. Here it is to be understood that the city of Rome was gripped by a deadly plague <note>A reference to the plague of 293–291 BC</note>, in which, through the boiling of the blood and its putrefaction, nature—attempting to expel it—manifested an abscess in the emunctories <note>The lymph nodes, specifically in the armpits or groin</note>, which physicians define as a tumor against nature, as Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher</note> seems to suggest in the second part of his first book and the third of his fourth. Because of this, men died in a short time. Having tried and experienced worldly remedies and seeing they were not effective, the Romans—and especially the prudent Volumnius—judged that for true help they must turn to God as the efficient cause of this pestilential influence. This is according to the opinion of Avenzoar <note>An Arab physician from Al-Andalus</note>, who says: "the plague happens because the Lord commanded it" <note>original: "pestis contigit quia dominus mandavit"</note>. Avicenna, in the tenth book of his Metaphysics, writes in this form: "Understand the disposition of all things that occur; and I believe that God has given the plague as one of the divine scourges that descend upon cities of vice and upon injurious men" <note>original: "Intēdas dispōnē oium rerū q̄ pueniunt; & credo q̄ deus dederit pestē de flagellis diuinis q̄ descēdūt sup ciuitates flagitiorū & super hoies iniuriofos"</note>. Therefore, the Romans deliberated to send to Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine</note>, and for this, they chose ten ambassadors, among whom the first was Lucius Volumnius. ¶ When the ambassadors arrived at the temple and offered their prayers devoutly, a serpent—venerable rather than horrifying—emerged from beneath the image of Aesculapius. Proceeding slowly, it reached the Roman ship where it lay down in Volumnius’s cabin. When the Romans returned with it and reached Ostia, the serpent left the ship and entered a nearby forest. Where it stopped, the Romans built a temple in honor of Aesculapius, and at that moment, the cruel plague suddenly vanished. Since Volumnius was the advisor and worker of this deed, the benefit of having saved Rome is deservedly attributed to him. Master Francesco then adds three other examples of very valiant men, saying that after Lucius Volumnius followed Cossus, Philo, and Rutilio. Whence he says:

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>R</margin> grieving the unjust killing of the Roman ambassadors: the Romans were greatly terrified, especially by the impetus and fury of Lars Tolumnius <note>The King of the Veientes during the 5th century BCE</note>, their leader, such that they almost feared certain ruin. Therefore, as the battle was already in danger, Aulus Cornelius Cossus, seeing his soldiers and, on the other side, seeing Tolumnius riding through the front lines, spoke these words: *“Is this he who broke the human treaty and violated the law of nations? Now, if the gods wish any holy thing to remain on earth, I will offer him here as a sacrificed victim to the shades of the ambassadors.”* <note>original: "Hiccinc est ruptor federis hūani: violatorq gētiū iuris. Iam ego hic mactatã victimã: si mō sanctu quicq~ i terris eẽ dij volūt legatorū manibus dabo."</note> And then, directing his course against him, he pursued him so manfully that he killed him. He consecrated his spoils to Jupiter Feretrius <note>The god of oaths and spoils of war</note> following the example of Romulus. Immediately afterward, as the war continued, one day the people of Fidenae <note>An ancient town near Rome</note> fought against the Romans with burning torches. Cossus commanded his soldiers to remove the bridles from their horses. Then Cossus, spurring them toward the enemies, and each man attacking with such impetus, in a short space of time he overcame and conquered them. ¶ Livy writes of Philo <note>Publilius Philo, a prominent Roman general and statesman</note> in the eighth book of his history from the founding of the city. He was made consul together with Titus Aemilius Mamertinus in the war against the people of Antium, whom he defeated and conquered through industry and military discipline. He was such an outstanding man that Titus Livy, in his ninth book, when numbering the leaders who would have been fit to resist Alexander the Great <note>Livy’s famous "what if" digression regarding Alexander invading Rome</note>, recounts him among the others.

<margin>S</margin> Publilius Philo, therefore, after his first victory, was again made consul with Lucius Cornelius Lentulus. During this consulship, he passed into Greece, where he brought great glory and a triumph to the Roman Empire, as Livy shows in the eighth book of the first decade. ¶ Now, regarding the record, it should be understood that there was a Marcus Rutilus <note>C. Marcius Rutilus Censorinus</note> who, when the war in Tuscany was finished and Perugia, Cortona, and Arezzo were taken by the Romans (as Livy writes in the ninth book), was elected consul against the Samnites, who had moved for war again out of envy. From there, Rutilus took the armies and, entering Samnium <note>A region of the southern Apennines</note>, captured almost all the lands of the province by force, so that he soon forced the Samnites to surrender. After this victory, when the Hernici caused trouble for the Romans, Marcus Rutilus went against them, successfully conquered them, returned to Rome, and triumphantly celebrated his victory over them.

<margin>T</margin> ¶ The other Rutilius was Publius Rutilius <note>Rutilius Rufus, a statesman known for his honesty</note>, of whom Titus Livy speaks in the seventh decade, ninth book, according to the fragments of Florus. It is said that when he was consul together with Gaius Mucius, the Roman soldiers left to guard Asia were harassing the land tyrannically. Rutilius took it upon himself to defend it. Because of this, he incurred the great envy of the equestrian order <note>The social class of knights who controlled the law courts at the time</note>, who held the judgment and the magistracy for the recovery of extorted money <note>term: "repetunde pecunie" — a court specifically for trying provincial governors for extortion</note>. Being accused by them, Rutilius was eventually condemned to exile by the envy of the equestrian order. Through his condemnation, it seemed that the Roman Senate lost all honor and majesty. Therefore, as both of these Rutilii were most excellent men, let it be left to judgment which one our Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> intends. Next to these, the poet mentions three other distinguished and excellent men, though they were strong fighters rather than expert leaders or commanders of armies. He says that he saw going somewhat apart, removed from the rest, frequent lights of famous men, and three soldiers alone who had bruised limbs and their armor all battered and shattered. In their appearance, they seemed to be three rocks—or rather, three lightning bolts of war. One was Lucius Dentatus, the second was Marcus Sergius, and the third was Cassius Scaeva. And none of these was a successor to a lesser fame. Hence he says:

And finally, there followed him new triumphant commanders who, equal in their own virtues, had reported victory over their enemies. <margin>X</margin> Marcus Sergius was also memorable next to Lucius Dentatus regarding the excellence of a single man. For according to what Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Roman grammarian and compiler</note> writes, he was wounded in the chest three times in victorious battles. In those battles, having lost his right hand, he replaced it with one of iron; fighting with this iron hand four times in a single day in individual combat, he always remained the victor. Furthermore, after Marcus Sergius had been captured twice by Hannibal and held in chains for twenty consecutive months, he escaped. This same man was always honored with military gifts and civic crowns in whatever most atrocious and unhappy battle the Romans fought against Hannibal—at Lake Trasimene, at Trebbia, and at Cannae. And truly, he was to be considered glorious, as Solinus writes, if his descendant and heir, Catiline <note>Lucius Sergius Catilina, the famous conspirator against the Roman Republic</note>, had not blackened his nobility with condemnation and exile. <margin>Y</margin> Caesar’s centurion, Caesius Scaeva, should by right be considered equal, or truly only slightly inferior, to these two excellent men mentioned before. For as Plutarch writes in the *Life of Caesar*, and Caesar himself in his *Civil War* commentaries, Scaeva did not neglect any duty belonging to such a faithful, strong, and intrepid centurion. Hence, when Caesar had besieged Pompey at Dyrrhachium in Epirus, and had built twenty-four forts around the land, and Scaeva was left to guard one of them, Pompey broke out and was victorious that day in the fighting against Caesar's troops. Thus he captured the fort where the brave Caesius Scaeva was on guard. In this assault, then, Scaeva, manfully defending himself, received one hundred and thirty arrows in his shield; and besides this, his shoulders were pierced with many darts, and an arrow hitting him in one eye, Scaeva pulled that arrow out of his head along with the eye. In the midst of so many wounds, Scaeva continually called out to the enemies, pretending that he wanted to surrender to them. As they came toward him, and Scaeva being unable to wield his weapons, he bit them with his teeth and made them die. In this manner he defended himself so long that he was aided by many of his own men, and being carried upon their arms, he was brought back to a safe place.

<margin>Z</margin> Finally, regarding the meaning of the preceding verses, it should be known that the last verse—**BUT fame does not take away the successor**—can be explained in two ways. First, that one of these men does not take away the fame of his successor, since each of these three is famous; thus "takes away" in this explanation is the verb. The other interpretation is that the one, namely Marcus Sergius, is not a successor; this explanation follows many texts. Nevertheless, there are some texts which, in my judgment, are more appropriate, which say: *But the one [Sergius] does not take away his fame as a successor*, where Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> silently describes Marcus Sergius having lost his right hand and remaining only a successor of fame because of his worthy "leva" <note>A pun on 'leva' meaning both a lever/arm and 'to lift/remove'</note> and his left hand. And he commemorates only their father, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus: and justly so: because primarily, when the Celtiberians later rose up against the Roman people, as Livy writes in the fifth decade and Florus recounts, Tiberius Gracchus went against them, overcame them, and lived; and as a perpetual memory of himself and of his most noble family, he built a castle in the province which was called the Castle of the Gracchi. Lastly, Tiberius was elected consul against the Sardinians, whom he overcame and conquered; and he took so many as prisoners and led them away to be sold as slaves that this ignominy of the Sardinians was reduced to a common proverb, saying: *Sardinians for sale* <note>original: "Sardi venales" — a proverb used to describe something cheap or of little value because the market was flooded with Sardinian slaves</note>. Nor was Gracchus worthy of being celebrated by fame only for arms, but also for justice and piety: wherefore, as we said above, he did not allow his adversary Scipio Asiaticus to be led to prison; similarly, when his colleague Claudius had been condemned to exile, Tiberius swore to go with him if he were not acquitted, for which reason the sentence was immediately revoked. Finally, Gracchus found two serpents in his bed one night: one male and the other female. He asked the augur <note>a religious official who interpreted omens</note> what this portended: he was told that either he or his wife must die. And this depended on which serpent he killed, matching the sex of the one who was to die. For this reason, Gracchus, having heard the answer, immediately killed the male serpent, choosing rather to die himself than to be the cause of death for his worthy and beloved Cornelia. Master Francesco lastly calls Sardinia a "restless and chattering nest," which has many times made the Roman people weary in war: because according to the accounts of historians, the Romans never fought so much after complete and obtained victories as they did against the Sardinians. Wherefore, as Livy writes in the second decade and Lucius Florus, the Sardinians and Corsicans together with Hanno the Carthaginian were defeated by Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio; secondly they were overcome by Marcus Porcius Cato the Censor while he was praetor, as Pliny writes. Afterwards, as Florus testifies and Livy writes in the fifth decade, the Sardinians were defeated by various consuls who, in the end, being led to the aforementioned sale by Tiberius Gracchus, should deservedly be ascribed to him for greater glory and more perennial fame. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the "Triumph of Fame," moving from the Gracchus family to the illustrious Metellus family, examining the lives and military triumphs of several generations of Roman commanders surnamed Metellus.</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

Metellus <note>Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus (c. 210–115 BC), a Roman general and statesman</note> was the principal figure in that city <note>Rome</note> which was the head and held the empire of the entire circle of the ocean sea. He was born of most noble and honest parents with commendable and worthy gifts of body and soul. Metellus had a most eloquent and modest wife; he held the consular dignity and obtained the power of commander through great and precious triumphs. He had four excellent sons, three of whom he saw become consuls and one a triumphator <note>one who celebrates a formal victory parade</note>; he had three daughters who were most worthily married. He held and embraced his grandchildren in his lap. He never had any cause for sadness until his death, which came naturally and peacefully; he was most worthily carried to the funeral pyre with great pomp by his sons and sons-in-law. Therefore, one might reasonably conclude that he was quite happy and joyful.

<margin>B</margin>
Secondly, it should be understood that Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> was right not to definitively judge Metellus as "happy," because all our happiness and joy consists in our soul; and because that is unknown to us—according to the opinion of Aristotle and of Augustine in *The City of God*, chapter twenty-five, when he says: "No one knows what goes on in a man except the spirit of the man that is in him" <note>original Latin: "Nemo scit quid agat in homine nisi spiritus hominis qui in ipso est"</note>. Therefore, we cannot judge if any man is truly blessed within himself.

<margin>C</margin>
In the third and final place, regarding the history, it should be noted that according to Livy and Florus in the last book of the fifth decade: when the "pseudo-Philip" <note>Andriscus, a pretender to the Macedonian throne</note> went against the friends of the Romans bordering Macedonia and destroyed an army that was a Roman garrison in those places, killing the praetor Marcus Juventius, Quintus Caecilius Metellus was elected consul against him. Going to Macedonia after several battles, he finally routed and killed him; returning to Rome, he led a glorious triumph. This Philip’s proper name was first called Andriscus, but he named himself Philip; hence he was nicknamed the "pseudo-Philip." It happened afterward that the Romans sent ambassadors to the Achaeans <note>a confederation of Greek city-states</note>, who were cruelly beaten by them, causing a great injury to the Roman Senate. For this reason, it was decided in Rome that Quintus Metellus should go against them to avenge the injury received. Going there and fighting them twice, he overcame and conquered them so that only the final overthrow remained—the triumph which Lucius Mummius later brought back when he conquered Corinth. Thus Metellus, in the second battle he fought with them—where the Achaeans had help from those of Boeotia and Chalcis as far as the straits of Thermopylae—defeated them so thoroughly that their leader Critolaus killed himself out of despair, as Livy writes and Florus testifies in the second book of the seventh decade, by taking poison. Afterward, a new war broke out in Spain; Metellus went as consul against them and in a short time overcame them, particularly defeating those of Arbacia and the Celtiberians. Metellus was accustomed to always exhorting his soldiers to recover their position if they ever retreated from it. Metellus was a man of clever wit and action, and a great observer of secrets. Hence, according to Valerius Maximus, when he was asked one day by a friend what he planned to do, he replied: "I would strip off my inner tunic if I thought it knew my counsel" <note>original Latin: "Tunicam meam interiorem exuerem: si eam consilium meum scire existimarem"</note>.

<margin>G</margin>
The other Metellus was Quintus Caecilius Metellus Numidicus, who primarily conquered the "sling-bearers," almost wild men of the Balearic Islands. Thereafter he proceeded into Numidia against Jugurtha, the Roman Senate having declared war against him for the death of his brothers which he had caused. Metellus, fighting with Jugurtha, defeated and overcame him twice in battle, and afterward overran and conquered all of Numidia; thus the surname "Numidicus" was deservedly attributed to him. He was later sent into exile because he refused to swear to uphold the Gracchan laws which Lucius Appuleius Saturninus wanted to solidify only for the favor he showed to Marius. Therefore, Metellus chose to go into exile rather than consent to what was not just. Regarding this, as Livy writes in the eighth book of the seventh decade and as Florus shows, while Metellus was in exile near the city of Smyrna located in Greece, he was recalled after the death of Marius and his praetor Glaucia with the greatest honor and favor of the city of Rome.

<margin>H</margin>
The other Metellus was Quintus Metellus Pius, son of Metellus Numidicus, who was nicknamed "Pius" <note>dutiful/devoted</note> for the many tears he shed while his father was in exile so that he might be recalled. This man, when the Marsi <note>an Italic tribe</note> moved war against the Romans and while he was praetor, proceeded against them and overcame and conquered them, killing their leader whose name was Quintus Poppaedius. Thereafter, during the Sertorian War, Quintus Metellus, being proconsul and going to Spain, defeated and killed Lucius Hirtuleius, the praetor of Sertorius, along with almost his entire army. Continuing the war against Sertorius and Marcus Perpenna, Quintus Metellus defeated and conquered them twice in such a way that they were forced to flee Spain entirely. The Senate saw a sign of his great virtue and excellence when, while still a youth, he succeeded in seeking the praetorship and the pontificate; by the judgment of the Senate, he was preferred over many other men, even those who had been consuls.

# CHAPTER TWO

Metellus, having been made proconsul <note>a governor of a province acting with the authority of a consul</note>, went against them <note>the Cretans</note> and laid siege to them. He besieged a noble and powerful city called Adoniata <note>possibly a corruption of Kydonia or another Cretan city</note>; finally, as Livy writes in his tenth decade, in the sixth and seventh books, and according to Lucius Florus, Metellus defeated them. Proceeding further by force, he conquered and overcame many more noble and strong cities, among which were Knossos, Lyctus, and Cydonia <note>original: "gnonſon Litiū & Siſonia"</note>; from this, no small glory, reputation, and wealth followed for the Roman Empire. <margin>K</margin> There was another Metellus <note>Lucius Caecilius Metellus, d. 221 BC</note> of whom Livy writes in the cited place: while serving as praetor, he defeated a great multitude of pirates in Sicily; this was not the same Lucius Metellus. In addition to the deeds already narrated, it is attributed to Quintus Metellus <note>Quintus Caecilius Metellus Metellus Scipio</note> that he wished to protect the treasury against Caesar; he was also censor alongside Quintus Pompeius and counted 317,824 citizens, excluding orphans and widows. Feeling that this was too small a population, he told the Senate it seemed to him that every man should be compelled to take a wife; wherefore, at the end of his copious oration, he concluded with these worthy words:

> "If we could live without wives, citizens <note>original: "Quirites"</note>, we would certainly all be free from that trouble. But since nature has disposed that we cannot live very comfortably with them, nor at all without them, we must look to our perpetual benefit rather than our brief pleasure." <note>original Latin: "Si sine uxoribus possemus esse quirites: oes profecto ea molestia careremus. Sed qm nõ satis cõmode sine eis aut ipossibile vivere: proinde ppetue utilitati magis q̄ brevi voluptati duo cõsulendũ."</note>

<margin>L</margin> Concluding then, because of the deeds narrated above, the Metelli were most outstanding men. As the poet says, the father and sons brought to Rome the spoils of Achaia, Crete, Spain, Macedonia, and Numidia. All of these were most excellent men, and the majority of them are gracefully commemorated by Virgil in the sixth book of the *Aeneid* when he introduces Anchises showing Aeneas all his successors, and also in the eighth book when he describes Venus giving Aeneas the shield worked by Vulcan, upon which were depicted all the successes of the Roman Empire; for now, to avoid delay, we will intentionally omit Virgil’s verses. Afterward, Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> adds that after the Metelli, he saw the famous Vespasian and his beautiful and good son Titus—but not the "beautiful and wicked" Domitian. Wherefore he says:

->Then I saw Vespasian with his son,<-
->The good and the beautiful; but not the beautiful and the wicked;<-

<margin>M</margin> <margin>Vespasian, according to the writings of Suetonius Tranquillus, originated from Titus Flavius Petro, a citizen of Reate, who fought under Gnaeus Pompey in the Battle of Pharsalus and was his centurion. He was born</margin> thus, Vespasian was born under Augustus in the territory of Reate in a small castle called Falacrinae; he was raised by his grandmother, whose name was Tertulla. Once Vespasian had grown and taken the <term>toga virilis</term> <note>the "toga of manhood" assumed by Roman boys around age 14-17</note>, he came to Rome. At that time, Claudius was the fifth Roman Emperor, where, after arriving, he obtained several dignities through the favor of friends: namely, the praetorship and the aedileship. He took a wife named Flavia Domitilla, by whom Vespasian had two sons, Titus and Domitian, and one daughter; the daughter died along with the mother before Vespasian was elevated to the Empire. While Claudius was alive, Vespasian went as a legate <note>a high-ranking military officer</note> to Germany; from there he passed into Britain where, in each province after many battles, he remained with glory and victorious triumph, occupying about twenty castles in Britain and an island called Vectis <note>the Isle of Wight</note>, which he subjected to the Empire of Claudius. For this reason, he twice received the pontifical priesthood and the triumphal ornaments from Claudius. After Claudius died through the agency of Nero, and while Vespasian had already proceeded with his son Titus on the Jewish expedition—which Josephus describes copiously—Nero succeeded to the Empire. After the death of Nero, Galba, having rebelled in Spain, was called Emperor by the Roman soldiers. It then happened that Otho, who had been a very close friend to Nero, killed Galba, and the Roman soldiers called him Emperor. At that time, Vitellius was in Germany with an army; therefore, when those Roman soldiers heard of the death of Galba and the succession of Otho, they called Vitellius Emperor. Returning to Italy, Vitellius fought with Otho and forced him to kill himself, leaving Vitellius as the sole Emperor. In the eighth month of Vitellius's reign, the Roman armies in Hungary and those across the sea in Syria and Judea rebelled against him and called Vespasian Emperor. Returning to Italy against Vitellius, Vespasian captured him, Vitellius having fled quite basely out of fear; after Vespasian captured him, he had him put to death as the base and unworthy prince that he was. <margin>N</margin> Vespasian was, therefore, most expert in arms and distinguished by every other virtue. Thus, Messer Francesco rightly deserves to count him among the famous men. It remains now to narrate the reason why Messer Francesco describes Titus and not Domitian in the *Triumph of Fame*: it should be understood that Titus, because of his supreme and singular virtues, was greatly beloved by his father.

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>O</margin> ...from his father Vespasian in this form, as Suetonius <note>original: "Tranquillo," the cognomen of the historian Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus</note> writes: **Titus, the love and delight of the human race** <note>original: "Titus amor ac delitiæ generis humani"</note>. And truly such a title was fitting for him, as he demonstrated such graceful gratitude and humanity in words, in habits, and in deeds. And likewise, just as Titus was adorned with every excellence of spirit, so too was he most singularly adorned with physical beauty among all others; these qualities and most worthy gifts seemed to increase in him as his age grew. As for military exercise, while Titus was a tribune in Germany and Britain, he earned the highest praise. This is testified to by the image of the triumphal arch which can still be seen today in the city of Rome, as well as the emblem and memorable victory of Jerusalem, for which Titus was hailed as Emperor <note>a military title of acclaim at this time</note> by his soldiers; and together with his father, he administered the empire. Titus was also most clement and possessed of such benevolence that if he had passed a single day without performing some good deed, he was intensely saddened and mourned. This merit earned him praise for those worthy words expressed at dinner when no friend had been helped by him that day, saying: **"Alas, friends, I have lost a day"** <note>original: "Heu amici diem perdidi"</note>. Thus, Titus, together with his father, is deservedly celebrated for his fame by Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>. Just as Titus was excellent in virtue, so on the contrary Domitian was inclined toward vice; wherefore he was cruel, lustful, unjust, avaricious, and a persecutor of Christians and Jews. In this man, the spirit was dull; every summer day, as Suetonius <note>original: "tranquillo"</note> writes, wanting some hours of rest in which he did nothing else but kill flies, if anyone seeking an audience asked at that time if anyone was inside with Caesar, Julius Crispus <note>historical sources usually identify this as Vibius Crispus</note>, his knight, would respond: **"Not even a fly"** <note>original: "nec musca qdē"</note>. However much Domitian was physically beautiful among others, he nevertheless obscured that beauty with such filthy and horrendous vices that he was, with great reason, excluded from fame and honor by our excellent poet. Messer Francesco continues afterward with other notable examples, saying that after Vespasian and his son came those outstanding princes, Nerva and Trajan. Wherefore he says:

-> **"And the good Nerva, and Trajan, faithful princes;"** <-

<margin>P</margin> The aforementioned Domitian, son of Vespasian, practicing his detestable vices in the administration of the empire, was finally killed, as was fitting for his unjust tyranny. Wherefore, through the work of Petronius <note>original: "corniō," likely referring to Titus Petronius Secundus</note>, the Praetorian Prefect, and Parthenius <note>original: "cernio"</note>, his killers, they ensured that Nerva was elected emperor, who was a just old man adorned with every other virtue. Thus Domitian’s dream was fulfilled, which was true; but after his empire, there was to be a much more joyful state. Nerva reigned for only one year in the empire; he administered it with such justice that deservedly, after his death, by deliberation of the Sen-

<margin>Q</margin> -ate, he was enumerated among the gods. In that year, Nerva adopted Ulpius Trajan, of Spanish origin; thus, being with his father in Gaul near the city of Agrippina <note>modern-day Cologne</note> at the time of his death, he received the empire there by the universal election of the Romans. He administered it with such justice and virtue that he was deservedly to be preferred above all other Roman princes. Since many provinces had rebelled from the Roman Empire due to the injustice and intolerable tyranny of the emperors preceding Nerva—provinces which both Augustus and Tiberius had held—Trajan not only recovered those but even expanded the empire in some parts. Principally, he recovered Armenia, which the Parthians had occupied, and established it as a province. From there he proceeded into Syria, and fighting with the King of the Syrians <note>likely referring to the campaigns against the Parthians or neighboring client kings</note>, he overcame, conquered, and killed him in battle. Afterward, he received as faithful subjects to the Roman Empire the king of the Iberians, the king of the Sarmatians, the king of the Dacians, the king of the Bosporans, and the king of the Arabs. He saw Mesopotamia and made it a province, and in the likeness of a province, he confirmed Arabia. He dominated the Red Sea, and there prepared a fleet to plunder the borders of India. For so many worthy and excellent works, Trajan easily pursued every glory attributed to military discipline; yet, despite so many victories and the highest praise given to him by men, he was never lifted up in pride. Rather, he always walked, stayed, and conversed throughout Rome like a private citizen. When he was reproved by his friends for such submission, Trajan replied with these worthy words: **"I wish to be such an emperor to private citizens as I, when a private citizen, would have wished emperors to be to me."** <note>original: "Talem me imperatorē esse p̄uatis uolo q̄les ēē mihi īpatores ꝑuatus optassem"</note>

<margin>R</margin> Trajan was also a most strict observer of justice; once, while on horseback for the expedition against the Parthians, a widow took him by the bridle, saying that he should do her justice because her innocent son had been killed. Trajan replied that he would satisfy her when he returned. The widow said, "But if you do not return, who will satisfy me?" Trajan replied, "The one who succeeds me will satisfy you." Then the widow said, "You are my debtor, and truly it is a fraud on your part not to want to return that which..." <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the famous anecdote of Trajan's Justice</note>

# CHAPTER TWO

To that which you are obligated: know that the just deeds of others will never render one absolved. For the sake of justice, Trajan <note>Roman Emperor, 98–117 AD, famously noted for his fairness</note> could be drawn away from his plans; he immediately dismounted his horse and attended to no other cares until he had fully satisfied the widow's claim. Because of this deed, it is read that Saint Gregory was later so moved to compassion for Trajan that he wept for his remission until his <unclear>soul</unclear> was absolved from the laws of hell. After this, he brings forward other examples, saying that after Trajan and Nerva, there followed Aelius Hadrian and Antoninus Pius; and proceeding through a beautiful and laudable succession, finally followed Marcus Antoninus Pius <note>The author is referring to Marcus Aurelius</note>. These men possessed no less a natural desire than a will to rule. Whence he says:

->Aelius Hadrian, and his Antoninus Pius;<-
->A fair succession ending with Marcus;<-
->Who had at least the natural desire.<-

<margin>S</margin>
¶ For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it should primarily be known that Aelius Hadrian—according to the writings of Aelius Spartianus <note>A historian in the "Augustan History"</note>—was born in Adria and was the son of Aelius Hadrianus Afer, a cousin of Trajan, and of Domitilla Paulina, born at Gades <note>Modern Cádiz, Spain</note>. This Aelius Hadrian, by ancient origin, was himself also from Spain. Upon the death of Trajan, he was assumed to the empire, which he ruled with great justice and modesty. He was a man of outstanding virtue and character; he was also very learned in the Greek language no less than in Latin. He had a vast knowledge of medicine, geometry, music, painting, and sculpture, and was very dexterous and versatile in intellect. He could write, dictate, give audience, and chat with friends all at the same time. Regarding military expeditions, Hadrian was a most diligent leader toward his army and very generous and kind to his soldiers, for which reason he was much loved by them. He was cautious in starting wars; for this reason, he relinquished the Moors, the Sarmatians, the Bactrians, and Egypt, saying he was imitating the example of Cato, who had declared that the Macedonians should be free since they could not be kept in subjection. Out of envy for Trajan's glory, he also relinquished Syria, Armenia, and Mesopotamia, making them free and establishing the Euphrates River as the sole boundary and limit of the Roman Empire. Hadrian had a war with the Jews, who had rebelled against the Roman Empire and occupied Palestine; he
<margin>T</margin>
overcame and conquered them in short order, and burned Jerusalem entirely, later rebuilding it. He constructed notable buildings in Rome, among which was the Tomb of Hadrian <note>original: "moles adriani"</note>, today called by us Castel Sant’Angelo. Finally, as Hadrian also wished to relinquish Dacia and make it free, he fell into disgrace with the Senate. Consequently, when he died in the countryside, he was not enrolled among the gods <note>divinized/canonized as an emperor</note> by the Senate until Antoninus, with great difficulty and many prayers, obtained it. For this deed, Antoninus subsequently earned the surname "Pius." Hadrian, being near death and considering his passing, wrote these words:
> Little soul, wandering and charming, guest and companion of the body, where will you go now? To places pale, stiff, and naked, nor will you give your jokes as you used to. <note>original Latin: "Animus vagula blandula hospes comesq; corporis..."</note>
Hadrian died at the age of 72 and remained in the empire for about 22 years.
<margin>V</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is to be understood that upon the death of Hadrian, his son by adoption, Antoninus Pius, was assumed to the empire; though by nature he was descended as we said above. According to the writings of Julius Capitolinus, he was the son of Titus Aurelius Fulvus, born in Transalpine Gaul, and was later brought to Rome for his merits. Through many intermediate magistracies and the consular dignity, he was truly "Pius" <note>dutiful/godly</note> and so adorned with every virtue that without doubt he was equal to Nerva and considered the peer of King Numa Pompilius. Antoninus held the empire with great justice and in peace. He was of such great authority that Capitolinus describes how the King of Arabia came to help him in Rome with much more dignity and greater tribute than he had previously done for Hadrian. Likewise, the King of the Parthians, while making war against the Armenians, withdrew from the enterprise solely because of simple letters from Antoninus which commanded him to do so. Antoninus did not exercise himself in war but always lived and maintained himself in peace. When he was persuaded by friends to make war, he would respond with the worthy <term>judgment</term> <gloss>sententia</gloss> of Scipio, namely: **"I would rather save one citizen than kill a thousand enemies."** <note>original: "malo unū ciuē suare: q̄ mille hostes occidere"</note> At the end, as Capitolinus writes, he focused more on enriching the treasury without injury to anyone than on acquiring dominion. Having held the empire with tranquility and justice for about 22 years, he died at the age of 77 and was buried at his villa, which was 12 miles from Rome, from where he was deservedly numbered among the gods by the Senate.
<margin>X</margin>
¶ Succeeding him finally was Marcus Antoninus Pius <note>Marcus Aurelius</note> and his brother Lucius Annius Severus <note>Lucius Verus</note>, whose origin we have discussed at length above in the *Triumph of Love* based on the testimony of Julius Capitolinus. Born of Annius Verus and Domitia Lucilla in Rome, and having become most learned under the teachers listed above, he came into great favor and love with Antoninus Pius, who gave him...
->Faustina<-

<header>THE TRIUMPH OF FAME</header>

Because of Faustina, his daughter, and likewise because of her singular virtues, this marriage was arranged by Hadrian so that by this means he [Antoninus] would succeed to the empire, having adopted Antoninus Pius as a son, as Eutropius <note>A 4th-century Roman historian</note> writes. In this man [Marcus Aurelius] there was such virtue and perfection that he is deservedly placed before all other Roman emperors. As for military expeditions, Marcus Antoninus, together with his brother Lucius, primarily defeated the Germans; nor did he wish to triumph in any way upon returning to Rome without his brother. Afterward, when the Parthians stirred up war against the Roman Empire, and Lucius Severus <note>The author likely means Lucius Verus, Marcus Aurelius's co-emperor</note> being already dead, Marcus went against them. In a short time, he overcame and conquered them. From there, departing, he proceeded into Syria, where he gloriously defeated the noble city of Seleucia, which yielded about 400,000 prisoners. He also defeated the Marcomanni, almost on the banks of the Danube, and all the peoples situated between Illyricum and Gaul, such as the Tharisti, Hermunduli, Suebi, Lacringi, Bastarnae, and others numbered by Capitolinus <note>One of the authors of the *Augustan History*</note>; whereby he demonstrated his virtue to be no less perfect in arms than in philosophy. Having therefore reported a glorious triumph from these narrated victories, Marcus died in the 19th year of his reign at the age of 61. With him ended the worthy succession of emperors; for after Marcus, there followed in the empire Commodus Antoninus, held to be his true son, although he showed himself rather to be the son of the gladiator mentioned above. This is considered given the cruelty, supreme luxury, and avarice that were in him, as Lampridius <note>Another biographer from the *Augustan History*</note> demonstrates in his life of him. Wherefore Messer Francesco [Petrarch] proceeds no further in the "Triumph of Fame" regarding those emperors who were called Roman.

¶ Finally, it should be noted that through the paths narrated and written by the above-mentioned authors, the reason is manifest why Messer Francesco says that these aforementioned princes had no less a "natural desire" <note>This refers to the intellectual curiosity common to the "Good Emperors"</note>; for they all applied themselves to study. This labor is natural according to the opinion of the Philosopher [Aristotle] in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, who says: <term>All men by nature desire to know.</term> <note>original: "Omnes homines natura scire desiderant."</note> And Cicero writes in the first book of *On Duties*: <term>For we are all drawn and led to a desire for knowledge and science, in which we think it beautiful to excel; but to slip, to err, to be deceived, we say is evil and shameful.</term> <note>original: "Oēs enim trabimur ⁊ ducimur ad cognitiōis ⁊ sciētie cupiditatē in qua excellere pulchrum putamus: labi autem errare decipi malum ac turpe dicimus."</note> Wherefore, these aforementioned emperors have been deservedly celebrated by Fame by Messer Francesco for both types of work [military and intellectual]. Finally, the poet concludes the glorious ranks of Romans with their first ancestors and kings, saying that while he, wandering and delighted by the preceding sight, crossed further and proceeded with his eyes, he saw the great founder of the city of Rome coming, and five kings who succeeded him; but the last and sixth king <note>Tarquin the Proud</note> he saw standing on the ground, burdened by an evil weight of the gravest infamy, just as universally happens to all those who leave virtue and follow vice, taking delight in it. Whence he says:

<margin>Y</margin>
<margin>Z</margin>
-> While I, wandering, passed further with my eyes; <-
-> I saw the great founder, and the five kings: <-
-> The other was on the ground, burdened by an evil weight; <-
-> As happens to those who abandon virtue, <-

<margin>Z</margin> ¶ Wishing to repeat the origin of the city of Rome and of the ancient Romans, it is to be understood that the genealogy of Aeneas, through continuous succession, finally came to Procas, king of the Albans. Having two sons, one named Amulius and the other Numitor, as he came to death, he left the sons to reign by turns for one year each. Whereupon Amulius, who was the firstborn, began to reign, but at the end of the year, he did not wish to return the kingdom to his brother Numitor; rather, he deprived him in perpetuity and drove him out. And so that no progeny should ever arise from him, he had the son, who was named Lausus, killed; and the daughter, named Rhea Ilia, he placed in the temple of Vesta. She, having later been impregnated by Mars, gave birth at the proper time to Romulus and Remus in a single birth. Hearing of this, Amulius commanded that they be cast into the Tiber; but the water miraculously led the two infants to land where, as they were crying, a she-wolf came. She nourished and cherished them with her milk until a shepherd named Faustulus arrived. Moved by compassion, he took the little children and carried them to his wife named Laurenza <note>Acca Larentia</note> so that she might nurse them as her own children.

<margin>A</margin> ¶ Thus, when Romulus and Remus had grown, they took to raiding; and having gathered a great number of shepherds, they guided and led them almost like an army. In this state, having recognized their own origin, they came to Alba, killed Amulius, and drew Ilia, their mother, out of prison. They restored the kingdom to Numitor, their grandfather. From there, they departed from Alba and came to the banks of the Tiber, in which place they built Rome...
