...which Romulus named after himself for a better omen. Since the city had grown significantly, Romulus requested marriage alliances from the neighboring cities. Because of their pastoral origins, these requests were denied. Therefore, Romulus organized certain equestrian games to which many people came—men and women, with a great number of virgins. Seeing this crowd along with his people, Romulus proceeded to where the people were and seized all the virgins, distributing them among his Romans and taking them as wives. For this reason, a most cruel war arose between the Romans and their neighbors, primarily with the Caeninenses. Romulus defeated them and killed Acron, who was their king, reporting a victory over him and consecrating the spoils to <term>Jupiter Feretrius</term> <note>One of the oldest titles of Jupiter, to whom "spoils of honor" (spolia opima) were dedicated by a general who killed an enemy king in single combat.</note>.

<margin>B</margin>
Consequently, for a similar reason, the Sabines, under the leadership and omen of Titus Tatius, moved war against the Romans. They were seen on the Capitoline Hill through the deed and simplicity of a virgin, <term>Tarpeia</term> <note>A Roman woman who betrayed the city to the Sabines in exchange for jewelry; according to legend, she was crushed to death by their shields.</note>. Seeing this, Romulus marched against them. While the battle was raging, Hostilius, a very brave Roman fighter, was killed, causing all the Romans to flee. Seeing this, Romulus made a vow to <term>Jupiter Stator</term> <note>Jupiter "the Stayer," invoked to stop an army from retreating.</note> to build a temple if his army held their ground. In this state, the abducted Sabine women came into the midst of the armed ranks; with words and pitiful gestures, they finally reconciled their Roman husbands with the Sabines, their fathers and brothers, through pacts, articles, and common conventions. Most importantly, the Sabines were to come live in Rome and the Romans would call themselves <term>Quirites</term> <note>A name for Roman citizens in their civil capacity, derived from the Sabine word for spear.</note> after their weapons. These things being done, and Romulus having remained as ruler, one day while reviewing his people at the <term>Goat Marsh</term> <note>original: "palude caprea"</note>, he vanished and was never again seen alive among mortals. Whereupon, a rebellion immediately began between the common people and the <term>Fathers</term> <note>The original members of the Roman Senate.</note> whom he had instituted in the Senate.

<margin>C</margin>
A Roman named Julius Proculus swore he had seen Romulus ascending to heaven, and that Romulus had said these words: first, that they should adore him and call him <term>Quirinus</term> <note>The deified form of Romulus.</note>, as it was the will of the gods; and that they should abstain from rebellions because Rome, by divine will, was destined to be the head of the entire empire of the world. By his authority, the common folk were immediately quieted. Romulus was deified, and a temple was established for him on the Quirinal Hill, and he was ever after called the god Quirinus.

<margin>D</margin>
After Romulus, the <insert>next</insert> king of the Romans <note>The text refers to Numa as the "first" king following Romulus, though he is traditionally the second king of Rome.</note> was Numa Pompilius, son of Pomponio from the Sabine stronghold. He was a man of great religious devotion and most holy. Reigning without harm to anyone, and seeing the Roman people as hard and almost like iron, he instituted more sacrifices to humble them. He also established the temple and religion of the goddess <term>Vesta</term> <note>Goddess of the hearth and home.</note>, composed the priesthood, created the <term>Flamens</term> <note>Priests dedicated to specific Roman deities.</note>, and divided the year into twelve months, adding January and February. He reformed many useful and honorable laws for the Roman Republic. Whatever he did, he claimed to do by the instruction and teaching of <term>Egeria</term>, his wife, who at that time was reputed to be a goddess. Because of his holiness and goodness, no one made war against him, nor did he move war against anyone. He finally died an old man, and with great sorrow and honor, he was buried by the Romans on the Janiculum Hill.

<margin>E</margin>
The <insert>third</insert> king <note>The text numbers the kings following Romulus; Tullus Hostilius is traditionally the third king of Rome.</note> was Tullus Hostilius, a most virtuous and worthy man. Immediately upon assuming the royal dignity, he moved war against the people of Alba Longa. While Mettius Fuffetius was king in Alba, having three very strong young brothers in that land called the <term>Curiatii</term>, he trusted in them and told Hostilius that if he pleased, their war should be decided by three Romans against three of his men from Alba, so that the city whose three combatants won would remain the victor. Hostilius liked the pact, so he sent three other Roman brothers called the <term>Horatii</term> to fight for their homeland against the three Curiatii sent by Mettius for Alba. Coming to the battle, the Roman Horatii remained superior; one remained alive and the other two died, but he killed all three of the Curiatii. The result was that Mettius fell into great hatred and displeasure among the Albans for having committed their fortune and virtue to such a small fight. Realizing this, and wanting to recover his position, he incited the Veientines and the Fidenates against the Romans, offering to betray Rome. Consequently, these peoples moved war against the Romans. Hostilius requested Mettius’s help, and Mettius went there to fulfill his promise. While the Romans were in battle with the enemies, Mettius stood on a hill, not descending so as to wait for the right time for his betrayal. The Romans were in doubt and asked Hostilius what it meant that Mettius had not yet descended to the battle. Hostilius, recognizing the scheme, cried out in a loud voice that Mettius was staying in that place because he had commanded him to do so. As soon as the enemies heard this, thinking that Mettius was committing a double betrayal, they immediately fled, leaving the complete victory to the Romans. When Mettius came the following day to celebrate with Hostilius, Hostilius exposed his betrayal and immediately had him drawn and quartered.

<margin>F</margin>
The <insert>fourth</insert> king of Rome was Ancus Marcius, the son of Numa Pompilius’s daughter, similar to his grandfather in holiness and virtue.

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>G</margin> This man <note>Ancus Marcius, the fourth king of Rome.</note> in battle conquered and overcame the Latins; he added two hills to the city of Rome, namely the **Martius**—so named after him—and the **Aventine**, which, along with the rest of Rome, he caused to be enclosed by a wall. Ancus also built the port at the mouth of the Tiber <note>The port of Ostia.</note> and designated many forests as public property solely for the use of building ships. Afterward, he established many other royal works and ordinances to maintain the state; but in a short time, being overtaken by death, he could not bring everything to completion; he remained, as was previously promised, a most excellent prince.
¶ The fourth king <note>The text counts Ancus as the third in this sequence, or perhaps considers the previous page's subjects; traditionally Tarquinius Priscus is the fifth king.</note> was **Lucio Tarquino Prisco**, son of Lord Demaratus of Corinth, who, fleeing the tyranny in Greece, came to Rome. As he was entering Rome, an eagle flying by took his cloak <note>In traditional mythology, the eagle takes his cap (pileus), not his cloak.</note> and, carrying it high, finally replaced it upon him. He had a wife named **Tanaquil** who, being a prophetess, and having seen this act, told Tarquin that it portended he would hold the kingdom of Rome. Tarquin, being wealthy, acquired much goodwill and familiarity with Ancus Marcius through his money, and even held certain dignities; thus, when Ancus came to death, he left Tarquin as the guardian of his children. Because of this, as soon as Tarquin took up the guardianship, he began to innovate rituals and laws, and to govern anew, especially trusting in the augury of **Accius Navius**. The augur told him that heaven promised he could do everything he imagined doing; whereupon Tarquin asked if he thought Accius Navius could cut a stone with a razor. In testimony of his prophecy, with a single stroke, he immediately cut that hard stone with the razor. This king defeated the Latins and the Sabines in battle and triumphed over them; he surrounded the seven hills of the city of Rome with walls; then, later, through the fraud and snares of the sons of Ancus Marcius, he was cruelly murdered.

<margin>H</margin> ¶ The fifth king was **Servius Tullius**, who had been raised in the house of Tarquin. He was recognized by Tanaquil because of a flame of fire that surrounded his head <note>A famous legend where a sleeping Servius's head caught fire without harming him, signaling his future royalty.</note>, signifying that the kingdom of Rome was to come to him; she had her husband Tarquin give him one of his daughters as a wife. Therefore, when Tarquin was killed, and the rumor was great, Tanaquil went out before the people and said that Tarquin was wounded but not dead, nor even mortally wounded; she desired and commanded that until he recovered, Servius should administer his kingdom. The people remained quiet at the voice of Tanaquil, and so Servius took the lordship. Administering it most justly, he was later confirmed in the kingdom. While he reigned, he defeated the Tuscans several times and built many temples in Rome. Having two daughters of very different characters, he gave them as wives to the sons of Tarquin, who were also very different, so that each might be corrected: he gave his fierce daughter as a wife to the humble son of Tarquin, and his humble daughter to the proud Tarquin <note>Tarquinius Superbus.</note>. ¶ From which it happened that, wishing to join like natures together, **Tullia** <note>The "ferox" or fierce daughter.</note> killed her husband and saw to it that the proud Tarquin killed his wife; afterward, they took each other as spouses, content with such wicked murders; they then ordered that Servius be killed.

<margin>I</margin> After this deed was done, Tullia, hearing that her father was already dead, climbed onto a chariot to go and greet her husband, King Tarquin. Finding the body of her father Servius in the road, she commanded without horror that the chariot be driven over him. And thus ended, besides Romulus, five praiseworthy kings of the Romans; they were succeeded by **Tarquin the Proud**, who for his evil deeds was driven out of Rome by **Brutus**. He lived as an exile for a long time with Porsenna, then with his son-in-law Mamilius Octavius at Tusculum, growing old with his wife, and finally died most miserably at Cumae. Therefore, Tarquin rightly stands on the ground without being able to rise from the tomb, burdened by the heavy weight of infamy, as our **Master Francesco** <note>Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch).</note> has described.

## EXPOSITION OF THE THIRD CHAPTER OF FAME.

<margin>K</margin> ¶ All things that exceed the nature of man in his own estimation are accustomed, by common habit, to lead whoever considers them to a great marvel and high esteem of them; as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> clearly shows in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, where he says:
> <note>original Latin: "Conscij autẽ sibij ip̄is suæ ignorantiæ alios cũ aliq̃d supra seipsos dicunt admirantur."</note> *Being conscious of their own ignorance, men admire others when they say something that is above themselves.*

<margin>L</margin> For which reason, Master Francesco Petrarca, moved by this natural disposition, says in the present case that he is principally drawn to marvel at the virtue and excellence of the preceding Romans. In this chapter, the poet intends by a universal argument to treat other men of arms of various nations: those who, either for the public safety or for some other common utility, have worthily distinguished themselves in the exercise of arms. To discourse particularly on every such instance would perhaps be too long a work. For this reason, Master Francesco briefly encompasses in the present chapter the Greek, Hebrew, and Barbarian nations, joining together both men and women, provided that through some outstanding work they aided the common safety. He says, therefore, beginning the present matter, that he is full of infinite, noble, and unspeakable wonder, being taken by the...

So, from a laudable desire to gaze upon the great people of Mars—the Roman army—which was such that there was never another family like it in the world, the narrator <note>Petrarch, the author of the poem.</note> joined his own vision with the ancient writings of poets and historians. In those books are described high and excellent names, the highest honors, and most outstanding praises. And he recognized in this work of his that his own speaking <note>His poetic account.</note> had missed a very great part of the Romans, both of the men and of their deeds, as is known to anyone who has ever frequented history. While he was considering these omitted Romans, he was diverted and pulled away from that thought by the sight of the excellent pilgrims and foreign men, among whom he first recognized **Hannibal the Carthaginian**. Whence he says:

**F**ull of infinite and noble wonder,
I began to admire the good people of Mars;

The sight joined with the ancient papers,
Where the high names and supreme honors are;

<margin>M</margin>
<insert>
**C**oncerning the understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known principally that for three reasons our excellent poet speaks of and names the Romans as the "people of Mars." The first reason is because of their first progenitor and father, who was **Mars**, having been the father of Romulus and Remus, from whom all the Romans are descended. The second is because the exercise of arms—which is given and attributed to Mars—was never of such excellence in any other people as it was in the Romans. The third and last is because
</insert>

<margin>N</margin>
according to the astrologers, Mars is said to be the significator <note>The planet that governs or represents a particular group or destiny.</note> of the Romans. For these reasons, the Roman people are deservedly called the "good people of Mars." ¶ Secondly, as to the notice of **Hannibal**, little remains to be added, since his most glorious deeds were described enough above in the *Triumph of Chastity*. <note>Petrarch's previous poem in the sequence.</note> Therefore, for this present notice, let the testimony of **Livy** <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> in the third decade, book 1, suffice, where he writes of the nature of Hannibal; and also the testimony of Hannibal himself to **Scipio**, which the same Livy writes in the fourth decade, book 4. Concerning the first notice, Livy says this: *Hannibal, though possessing the greatest daring in undertaking dangers and the greatest wisdom in the midst of those dangers, never sparing any labor, nonetheless marred his great virtues with vices: inhuman cruelty, Punic treachery <term>Punic faith (Punica fides)</term> <note>A common Roman slur suggesting the Carthaginians were inherently deceitful.</note> beyond measure, no truth, no holiness, no fear of any god, no oath, no religion.* <note>original: "Hannibal cum plurimum audacie ad pericula capessenda: plurimumq[ue] consilii inter ipsa picula heret... nihil veri: nihil scti: nullius dei metus: nullum iusiurandum: nulla religio." (Livy, 21.4)</note> Through this art and Punic treachery, Hannibal, while in Italy, conquered **Taranto** by means of Nico and Philemenus; by pretending to go hunting at night, he brought the treachery of Hannibal into Taranto. And through a certain Pacuvius Calenus, he fraudulently obtained **Capua**. Hannibal also escaped the hands of **Quintus Fabius Maximus** by craft alone, placing bundles of dry branches on the heads of captured oxen and lighting them on fire at night. The beasts, moved by their own impulse and the horror they showed, caused the Romans to abandon their stations. Hannibal, having then arranged his ranks, escaped the narrow place where he was trapped under **Mount Calliculo**. He also conquered with similar craft—as **Trogus** writes and **Justin** reports in book 32—after he had fled to **Prusias**, King of Bithynia. Being made prefect of the fleet, he defeated **Eumenes**, King of Ilium <note>Actually King of Pergamum; "Ilium" refers to the region around Troy.</note>, in a sea battle by enclosing horrible snakes in earthenware jars and throwing them into Eumenes' ships. This thing generated great laughter at first, but then, due to the cruelty and horror of the snakes, they were defeated and confused, and surrendered to Hannibal. ¶ Now as to the second testimony, which Hannibal affirms of himself, 
<margin>O</margin>
Livy writes that while Hannibal was with **Antiochus**, King of Syria, **Scipio Africanus** was sent with other ambassadors to Antiochus. One day, while speaking together, Scipio asked Hannibal whom he believed was the most laudable commander who had ever lived. Hannibal replied, **Alexander the Macedonian**, because with a small beginning he conquered innumerable armies and reached the furthest lands. Scipio then asked about the second, and Hannibal replied **Pyrrhus**, King of the Epirotes, because he was the first who taught how to pitch an army <note>How to organize a military camp.</note> and no one ever knew better how to choose locations.

<margin>M</margin>
The Messenian people, the most ferocious in Greece—as Trogus Pompeius writes and Justin relates in the third book of *Concerning Foreign Wars*—established certain sacrifices on a given day. To see these, a great multitude of people gathered, among whom were many Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan</note> virgins. When the Messenians saw how beautiful they were, they abducted and raped them, causing grave injury to the Lacedaemonians; for which reason a massive war <margin>Q</margin> was incited between them. This lasted ten years, and then, ending with certain grave conditions for the Messenians, they endured in such a way for about eighty years with patience. They then renewed the second war against the Lacedaemonians. The Lacedaemonians then sent to the oracle of Apollo to know what they should do to have victory; the oracle replied to them that if they wished to win, it was necessary that they have an Athenian commander. Wherefore the Lacedaemonians sent ambassadors to Athens to humbly pray that they might be pleased to grant them a leader. The Athenians, having heard the embassy, gave them as a joke a lame poet who was then named Tyrtaeus <note>The text reads "Cirtheo," a common medieval/Renaissance corruption of the Greek name Tyrtaeus.</note>. Fighting against the Messenians three times, the Lacedaemonians were defeated, so much so that they were forced to arm their slaves and grant them liberty, giving them citizenship and offering them the wives of those who had died in battle. But seeing that the King of the Lacedaemonians remained inferior to the Messenians, he did not want to tempt the fortune of combat, but rather to withdraw and end the war with peace and endure the grave conditions of the Messenians. Because of this, Tyrtaeus began to exhort his soldiers, singing in verse that they should expose themselves to battle; in this way he stirred them so that they immediately took up arms and went against the Messenians. Fighting fiercely with them, the Lacedaemonians were ultimately superior. Thus, Tyrtaeus deservedly earned the highest praise; as much as he was less expert in the exercise of arms, he deserved more for having reported victory through his own virtue. There are some texts which say: *And that one sung in verses*, where it should not be understood as Tyrtaeus, but as Achilles; and thus it should be read together with the subsequent verse, understanding that Achilles was sung and celebrated by the divine poet Homer in his verses, especially in his *Iliad*. As our poet Petrarch testifies in the subsequent fourth triumph concerning Homer having sung the wanderings and the toil of the son of Laertes <note>Odysseus</note>, and even more clearly in that sonnet where, when Alexander reached the famous tomb of the fierce Achilles, sighing he said: "O fortunate one, who found so clear a trumpet, who wrote of you so highly!" <note>Petrarch, Rerum vulgarium fragmenta 187. Alexander the Great envied Achilles for having Homer to record his deeds.</note> And although this sentiment is more fitting to me, we will nevertheless leave it to any other more solid judgment and bring forward the example of our poet according to the first sense, saying that Achilles proceeded together with Tyrtaeus, he who had great praise and great ornaments of fame. Whence he says:

### CHAPTER THREE

<margin>S</margin>
**Leontius** <note>Likely referring to Leontius Pilatus, a 14th-century scholar who provided Greek myths to Boccaccio and Petrarch.</note> says that the name of **Achilles** is derived from *a*, which means "without," and *chilos*, which means "food"—as if he were nourished without common or natural food. <note>original: "ab a q̃ eſt ſine & chilos q̃ ẽ cibus." This is a traditional but scientifically incorrect etymology suggesting Achilles was fed on the marrow of lions and bears rather than bread.</note> Therefore, Thetis, looking one day upon what the fate of Achilles was to be, saw that he was destined to die in the Trojan War. Because of this, she secretly took him from the cave of Chiron <note>The centaur who tutored Achilles.</note> and carried him to the island of Scyros, dressed in women's clothing, to King Lycomedes, so that he might keep him among his young daughters. While staying and conversing and sleeping there with Deidamia, he impregnated her, and from her was born Pyrrhus, as we mentioned above. Later, after Helen was abducted, the Greeks, deliberating on making war against the Trojans, consulted the oracle to ask what provisions they should make to obtain victory. It replied, among other things, that they must arrange to have Achilles, because without his person it was impossible for Troy ever to be taken. From this, the Greeks diligently investigated his whereabouts and finally learned he was among the daughters of King Lycomedes. For this reason, they commanded Ulysses that, by his ingenuity, he should lead him forth. Ulysses, therefore, pretending not to know him, feigned being a merchant; he took many jewels and other feminine ornaments, and besides these, a bow with arrows and a polished suit of armor. He went to Scyros under the name of wanting to trade, where he was immediately led to the place where the girls were staying. Having spread out his merchandise before them, all the girls took and looked at the feminine ornaments. Achilles alone took and looked at the bow and the armor; by this means, Ulysses recognized him. Finally, by persuading him, they led him into the Greek army. As the Greeks proceeded to the Trojan War, Achilles performed many worthy and glorious deeds of arms. Whence, principally as Dictys of Crete <note>A legendary author believed in the Middle Ages to have been an eyewitness at Troy.</note> writes, when Agamemnon, Calchas, Menelaus, and Ulysses wished to sacrifice Iphigenia—having taken her from her mother Clytemnestra by fraud, Ulysses having written to her in the name of Agamemnon that she was to be married to Achilles—so that Neptune and the winds might be appeased for their voyage.

<margin>T</margin>
Achilles, arriving by chance at that place where they wished to perform the sacrifice and seeing this maiden weeping and commending herself to him, rescued her from them by force of arms. After she was freed, a very large hind appeared, which Achilles sacrificed to the gods in place of Iphigenia, sending word under his own name to Clytemnestra her mother, though she had been deceived and betrayed. Then, the Greeks having gathered at the island of Aulis, they proceeded to the Trojan expedition. Having arrived in Mysia, where a king named Telephus reigned (descended by ancient lineage from Hercules), he first wanted his ministers, and then he himself, to prohibit the Greeks from landing on his shore. Because of this, coming to battle, he was cruelly wounded in that place by the hands of Achilles. But later, recognizing the kinship he had with the Greeks, he received them kindly; and finally, through the works of the same Achilles and Machaon and Podalirius, the sons of Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine; his sons were the physicians of the Greek army.</note>, Telephus was restored to his former health. Arriving later on the Trojan shore, Achilles did marvelous things in arms; whence he was often able to sustain and resist the entire impetus and power of the Trojans alone, and likewise alone he many times turned them all back and followed them in flight. And Patroclus, his dearest friend, having been killed in the war by Hector—as Dictys writes—after long weeping and due funeral rites:

<margin>V</margin>
Achilles deliberated on taking total vengeance. Whence, one day when Hector had gone out to meet Queen Penthesilea (who was coming from the Amazon kingdom in favor of the Trojans), Achilles waited for him on his return at the crossing of the river Xanthus. Hector being already in the water, Achilles assailed and killed him. It is true that Dares the Trojan <note>Dares Phrygius, another supposed eyewitness whose account often contradicted the Greek versions.</note> writes that Hector was killed by Achilles in battle while he was leading a Greek king prisoner, being deprived of the protection of his shield which he had thrown behind his shoulders. Once Achilles had killed Hector, he despoiled the naked body and had it bound to his chariot; then, in vengeance and satisfaction for Patroclus, he dragged it around the walls of Troy and throughout the entire army. For several days he kept it in that form before the mound where Patroclus was buried. Later, receiving a great quantity of money, he rendered the dead body of Hector to Priam, his father. As the war continued thereafter, Achilles killed the very strong Troilus and Sarpedon of Lycia and many others of the Trojan army. Whence, deservedly, Achilles bore the name of the strongest Greek until, as we said above, he was killed by Paris through the work of Hecuba in the temple of Apollo. Master Francis <note>Petrarch.</note> then continues, saying that after Achilles, he saw two famous Trojans follow. Whence he says:

<margin>X</margin>
<margin>The two famous Trojans;</margin>

It highlights the use of medieval sources like Dictys of Crete and Dares Phrygius to provide a complete biography of the hero.</summary>

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>2</margin> Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> uses these two examples because if we look at the various whims of fortune, not only was Priam not happy or glorious, but he exceeded all others in being the most unhappy man in the world. If we consider the wisdom and prophecy of Helenus, son of Priam, and Proteus, son of Euphorbus <note>A philosopher-warrior in the Trojan cycle</note>, they surpass all others. If we look at physical beauty, Paris was the foremost among all the Trojans. But if we consider military skill, Deiphobus, Troilus, Polydamas, Aeneas, and Hector always deserve to be celebrated and praised by fame. Nevertheless—leaving aside any better judgment—according to my understanding, I affirm that the poet intended to speak of Hector and Aeneas. This is because, as Dares <note>Dares Phrygius, an author believed in the Middle Ages to have been an eyewitness to the Trojan War</note> writes, Hector, fighting many times with Achilles in single combat, continually remained superior to him, so that Achilles was always held back in battle; he alone many times forced all the Greeks to flee, as Homer testifies. Hector’s virtue and military discipline can also be clearly understood by the name "Hector" itself. According to Leonardo of Arezzo <note>Leonardo Bruni, a famous humanist scholar</note>—a man most learned in the Greek language and in our own age—agreeing with Plato in his book *On Names* <note>Plato's *Cratylus*</note>, the name means "the governor and defender of the fatherland." Virgil also openly demonstrates this in the second book of the *Aeneid*, when he introduces Hector appearing in a dream to persuade Aeneas that he must leave the city of Troy and no longer attempt to save it, because its ruin was destined by the gods and therefore could not be defended by any right hand of any human body. For if it had been possible to save it, the right hand of Hector was powerful enough to secure its safety. Thus Virgil says in the person of Aeneas, speaking of Hector:

> He said nothing, nor did he delay for my useless questions, but drawing heavy groans from the bottom of his chest: "Alas, flee, son of the goddess, and snatch yourself from these flames. The enemy has the walls; Troy falls from its high peak. Enough has been given to the fatherland and to Priam; if Pergamum <note>The citadel of Troy</note> could be defended by a right hand, it would have been defended even by this one [Hector's]." <note>original: "Ille nihil: nec me querentem vana moratur. Sed graviter gemitus imo de pectore ducens: Heu fuge nate dea teq; his ait eripe flammis. Hostis habet muros: ruit alto a culmie troia. Sat patria priamoq; datum: si pergama dextra. Defendi possent etiã hac offensa fuissent."</note>

Ovid manifests the same in his *Epistles* <note>The *Heroides*</note> when he introduces Penelope writing to Ulysses and saying:

> I imagined the violent Trojans would come against you; at the name of Hector, I always turned pale. <note>original: "In te fingebam violentos troas ituros: Nomine in Hectoreo pallida semper eram."</note>

Because of this great and singular virtue of Hector, Homer writes that Jove commanded Apollo to take care that Hector's body would never decay. This was truly done by the work and command of Priam through the power of balsam and many other mixtures, as Dares writes. Hector is also made clear and famous alongside Aeneas because of the noble people who descended from him. According to what Vincent of Beauvais <note>Vincentio gallico</note>, the historian, writes: after the fall of Troy, the lives of Helenus (son of Priam) and the sons of Hector were spared by the Greeks. They traveled to far Germany where they built the city of Sicambria; and eventually, multiplying from Francion <note>A legendary figure used to link the French monarchy to Troy</note>, the son of Hector, the noble kings of France took their origin. 

Aeneas, likewise the son of Anchises, is well known through Virgil’s poem for how much virtue he was judged to have. Nor was he overlooked by Dares the Trojan, who says he defended himself most manfully in single combat against Achilles, Diomedes, and Ajax. Since his deeds are largely well known, and his progress was narrated above in the *Triumph of Love*—and to avoid being repetitive and omitting what happened in the war against Turnus—we will write no more of him here, especially since it was already said how Virgil intended to speak of Dido and Aeneas in the *Triumph of Chastity*. Therefore, through this celebration by the poets, it seems to us that our Master Francesco meant both Hector and Aeneas—especially given the authority of Dante Alighieri in the fourth chapter of the *Inferno*. Writing of the people who inhabited the Elysian Fields <note>Dante places these virtuous pagans in Limbo</note>, Dante affirms that Hector and Aeneas were among them, saying in these verses:

> I saw Electra with many companions, among whom I recognized both Hector and Aeneas. Caesar, armed, with his hawklike eyes. <note>original: "vidi elettra con molti compagni: fra i qual visco: si Hector & Enea. Cesare armato con li occhi grifagni."</note>

From this, concluding about the two famous Trojans, I say the poet meant Hector and Aeneas. Next, Master Francesco recounts two other examples of two great Persians. Regarding this he says:

<margin>A</margin> Just as the poet's words about the Trojans can be understood in different ways, so it is with the Persians. Here, putting aside Cyrus (whom Master Francesco mentions below as the occasion arises), the title of "Great" is appropriately attributed to two men: namely Xerxes and Artaxerxes, the two well-known descendants of Darius. But because Xerxes and Artaxerxes were [great] more by the benefit of nature and fortune than by any of their own virtue, they were...

->**The two great Persians**<-

<summary>The commentator identifies the "two clear Trojans" in Petrarch’s poem as Hector and Aeneas, citing authorities like Virgil, Ovid, and Dante, and then introduces the "two great Persians" as Xerxes and Artaxerxes.</summary>

### CHAPTER THREE

They were great according to the records of history, especially those of Pompeius Trogus <note>A Roman historian of the 1st century BC whose works survive primarily through the summaries of Justin</note>, as Justin relates. For this reason, in my judgment, the poet refers in this passage to the two men named Darius: one, namely, he who was the father of Xerxes; the other, he who fought against Alexander the Great. I say, then, regarding the first <note>Darius I, also known as Darius the Great</note>, that when the kingdom of Persia was in chaos due to the wickedness of Cambyses, son of Cyrus—who had ordered the murder of his brother Smerdis—a certain Magus named Comaris managed to pass the kingdom to his brother Patizithes <note>The text calls him Horopaste, following various medieval versions of the name Gaumata</note>, after Cambyses had cruelly killed himself. A noble citizen of Persepolis named Otanes <note>Orthanes</note> strongly suspected this deception. But because the Magus was so similar to Smerdis in appearance that one could not be distinguished from the other, Otanes did not dare to attempt anything publicly. Therefore, since he had a daughter who was a consort of the king—whom she believed was Smerdis—he sent word to her that when she slept with the king, she should feel to see if he had ears, for he remembered that Cambyses had once ordered the ears of the Magus to be cut off.

The daughter, following her father's commands, searched for the ears while sleeping with the king that evening and found that the king did not have them. She reported this to her father, Otanes. Knowing clearly from this that the king was not Smerdis, the son of Cyrus, but the Magus, he conspired with the nobles of Persia to kill the Magus who was pretending to be king. Seven of them met, though Justin names only four: namely Otanes, Zopyrus, Gobryas, and Darius. Bound by an oath, they resolved to either kill the king or die. They went by night to the palace and attacked the Magi. There, Gobryas embraced the Magus, but in the darkness, he feared his companions might hit him instead of the king. Gobryas cried out that they should not hesitate to strike, even if he were killed along with the Magus. Thus, in the end, the Magi were killed. These Persian lords, having in this way avenged Smerdis and removed the Magi, deliberated among themselves how to choose a king. They came to this agreement: each of them would ride his horse to a certain designated spot, and the one whose horse neighed first at the rising of the sun would remain king among them.

<margin>B</margin>
Darius, therefore, the evening before the day of the trial, led a mare to that spot and allowed his horse to be with her. Consequently, on the following morning, when Darius arrived at that spot with the others, the horse, remembering the previous evening, neighed. By this effect, by common accord, Darius, son of Hystaspes <note>Idaspro</note>, was consecrated as king and established by the Persians. Once established in the kingdom, Darius, to demonstrate his royal virtue, took the daughter of Cyrus as his wife. He marched against Babylon, as the Assyrians had rebelled. After several battles, he finally captured it through the effort and ingenuity of Zopyrus <note>Zopyrus famously mutilated himself to trick the Babylonians into trusting him</note>. Later, incited and persuaded by Hippias, the tyrant of the Athenians, he moved war against the Greeks. Having arrived there with his armies, he was finally defeated and conquered by the efforts of the Athenians Miltiades and Themistocles and forced to flee. While he was preparing for a second war with a worthy naval fleet, he died.

<margin>C</margin>
The other Darius <note>Darius III</note> was he who fought with Alexander the Great. Since Philip, Alexander's father, had already decided to wage the Persian war and was then killed by conspirators, Alexander, succeeding him, primarily decided to follow through with the expedition of the Persian war out of reverence for his father’s order. Darius, hearing this and trusting in his riches and the great multitude of his people, decided to let Alexander enter the kingdom of Persia rather than meet him at the borders to fight. When Alexander had entered Persia, Darius met him with six hundred thousand people, as Justin writes. Fighting in the Adrastic fields <note>Likely referring to the Battle of the Granicus River</note>, Darius was defeated with a massive slaughter of Persians, from which he was forced to flee. Nevertheless, not frightened in any way by this event, Darius restored his armies once again and went against the victorious Alexander. Where, fighting together a second time, both kings showed such manliness that both were found to be cruelly wounded that day. But Darius was again inferior, and in this battle, his daughters, his wife, and his mother were captured by Alexander.

<margin>D</margin>
Ultimately, seeing that Alexander's progress seemed fated, Darius wished to submit to him. He sent ambassadors to ask for peace, offering him a portion of the kingdom and his daughter as a wife. But Alexander did not consent. Because of this, Darius turned to his final resources and decided to fight one last time. Exhorting his soldiers, as Quintus Curtius writes, he concluded with these words, saying:

> Each man's right hand will bring about either the revenge of so many evils or his own end. Indeed, if fortune is fickle, I myself am the proof of it; nor do I undeservedly expect its kinder turns. But if the gods oppose just and holy wars, it will nonetheless be permitted for brave men to die honorably. By the glory of your ancestors, I entreat you, who held the memorable kingdoms of the entire East in praise... <note>original: "Sus cuiq; dextra aut vltionem tot malor pariet aut sese. Eqdem ī versatilis fortuna sit: documētum ipse sum: nec īmerito mitiores vices eius expecto. Sed si iusta ac pia bella dii aduersantur: fortibus tamen viris licebit honeste mori. per ego vos decora maiorū: q totius oriētis regna cōmemorabilia lau le tenuere."</note>

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

...they did. By those men through whom Macedonia once paid tribute; by so many fleets of ships sent into Greece; by so many trophies of kings, I pray and beseech you: that you take up spirits worthy of your nobility and of your race, so that with the same constancy of mind with which you have tolerated past events, you may endure whatever fortune brings next. For me, certainly, either an outstanding victory will ennoble me forever, or the fight... <note>original: "Per illos uiros quibus stipendium macedoniā quondā tulit..." This is a translation of the Latin speech attributed to Darius III before his final stand against Alexander.</note> These were truly royal words of Darius and suited to his excellence. After he had spoken, he made every possible effort and final preparation, proceeding to the third battle. In this battle, he was ultimately defeated. Following the advice and assistance of his soldiers, Darius changed his purpose and fled, though he had previously been prepared to die. During this flight, his kinsmen and relatives—among whom were a certain Bessus and one Nabarzanes—conspired against Darius. First, they captured him and bound him in chains with the intent of handing him over to Alexander as a prisoner. Later, changing their minds, they struck him to death, from which he died. 

Therefore, although he was overcome by Alexander, Darius is reasonably numbered among famous men. This is because it was not a lack of virtue in him, but rather the fortune of Alexander—which is a most powerful factor in wars, as Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> affirms in his oration *On the Command of Gnaeus Pompey*—that caused Darius to fall in battle. Darius was also very observant of gratitude, which is a most excellent quality in a prince. Quintus Curtius <note>A Roman historian who wrote the "Histories of Alexander the Great"</note> demonstrates this clearly when he introduces Tyriotes, who informs Darius that his wife had been kept unharmed while in Alexander's care. Because of this, Darius said these words to the gods: "O ancestral gods, first give me a stable kingdom; then, if my time is already finished, I pray that no one else be king rather than this so just an enemy, this so merciful a victor." And finally, at his death, Darius left the vengeance for his murder to no one but Alexander, praying to the gods of the upper world and even those of the underworld that Alexander might prosper as a victorious lord, not only of Asia but of the entire world.

Next, **M.F.** <note>Likely the commentator's initials</note> adds two examples, saying that after the two great Persians followed Philip of Macedon and his son Alexander, who, rushing from Pella <note>The capital of the ancient kingdom of Macedonia</note> to the Indus with great speed, conquered and subdued various countries. Hence the poet says:

<margin>
**B**
</margin>

<margin>
To understand the preceding verses, one must primarily know that Philip of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great—according to what Trogus writes and Justin relates in the seventh book of his *History of the World* <note>original: "lib. de bellis externis," referring to the "Epitome of the Philippic History of Pompeius Trogus"</note>—was the son of Amyntas II, King of Macedonia. By his wife Eurydice, Amyntas had three sons: Alexander, Perdiccas, and this Philip. After the death of the two brothers, which was orchestrated by their mother, Philip was placed under the discipline of Epaminondas <note>A famous Theban general and statesman known for his military tactics</note> when he was given as a hostage to the Thebans by his brother Alexander during the Illyrian war. Eventually, he was made King of Macedonia. 

Being established as king at the age of twenty-two, he primarily waged war against the Athenians. Having quickly overcome and defeated them, and holding them all as prisoners, he freely released them back to their liberty. Then he turned toward the Illyrians, whom he swiftly defeated, capturing the noble city of Larissa from them. Afterward, he proceeded against the Thessalians and similarly overcame them, adding both peoples to his army. At this time, Philip took as his wife Olympias, daughter of Neoptolemus, King of the Molossians. Later, he attacked King Arybbas, his brother-in-law, who was married to Troas, the sister of Olympias, invading his kingdom. While he was besieging a city called Methone <note>The text reads "Mathona"</note>, he was blinded in one eye by an arrow. 

Afterward, when the Phocian War broke out against the Thebans under the leadership of Onomarchus <note>The text reads "Oroma co"</note>, Philip took up the cause of helping the Thebans. But the Athenians, fearing that if Philip entered Greece he would occupy their liberty, made every effort to stop him at the narrow pass of Thermopylae so he would not pass. Nevertheless, their efforts were in vain, because Philip passed through many cities of Greece, ruining them all—even those that had been under his protection. Among these, he even conquered the great Cappadocia by force. Having passed from Greece into this kingdom, Philip then proceeded against the Olynthians and soon added them to his kingdom, along with the Phocians and Dardanians, using great cruelty and treachery toward them. Then, after Philip had illicitly abused Alexander, the brother of Olympias, who was a very beautiful youth, he decided to make him king. For this reason, he waged war against Arybbas, King of Epirus, who was a very close relative of his wife, and drove him from the kingdom, investing the other Alexander as king.
</margin>

...was said. Philip <note>Philip II of Macedon (r. 359–336 BCE), the father of Alexander the Great.</note> then turned against Greece, eventually defeating the Athenians, the Thebans, the Triballi, and other peoples, whereby all of Greece came under the lordship of Philip. At this time, the Scythians were not idle in the face of Philip’s violence, but he entered Scythia and took a vast amount of plunder from them. Once the affairs of his kingdom were settled, he repudiated Olympias, the mother of Alexander the Great, and took as his wife Cleopatra, the sister of one of his prefects named Attalus. To this Attalus, along with Parmenion and Amyntas, Philip had committed the care of the war he intended to wage first against the Persians. He gave the daughter of this same Cleopatra as a wife to Alexander, the King of Epirus.

<margin>F</margin>
It happened ultimately that while a noble banquet was being celebrated, given by this Attalus, and as he was somewhat heated by food and drink, he took a most beautiful and noble Macedonian youth named Pausanias and committed an illicit sexual act with him. Not only did he use him, but he subjected him to most of the others at the banquet. When Pausanias complained of this matter to Philip and Philip took no care of it, Pausanias, in his revenge, killed him one day when Philip was forty-seven years of age. Philip being dead, his son Alexander succeeded him in the kingdom at the age of twenty. Since the Macedonians were terrified by the death of Philip, and seeing that various opinions and factions had been generated in his army, Alexander spoke so worthily to those people that, all sadness and fear being taken away, the Macedonians directed their spirit toward the empire of the whole earth. 

Alexander, wishing to begin his intentions, was opposed by his brother Caranus <note>In some historical accounts, Caranus is identified as a half-brother or rival claimant to the throne whom Alexander executed to secure his power.</note>, born of the aforementioned Cleopatra, who placed a very heavy impediment before him; for this reason, Alexander had him killed. He was then concordantly elected leader of all Greece. This general conclusion having been made by the Greek republics, not much time passed before the Athenians and the Thebans, by the persuasion of Demosthenes <note>The famous Athenian orator and staunch opponent of Macedonian expansion.</note>, rebelled against the dominion of Alexander. Thereupon, turning his arms against them, he routed and defeated them in a short time. He brought the worthy and warlike city of Thebes to total and extreme ruin, while pardoning the Athenians and those of Lampsacus through the work and prudence of the philosopher Anaximenes. Anaximenes had asked Alexander to ruin the city, knowing that Alexander had sworn *not* to do whatever Anaximenes asked him as a favor <note>Anaximenes used a clever rhetorical trick: by asking Alexander to destroy the city, he forced the king—who had sworn to do the opposite of whatever the philosopher asked—to save it.</note>, as Valerius writes in Book VII, Chapter 4. Afterward, Alexander proceeded against Darius in Persia and defeated and conquered him three times, as we said recently. In the third battle, after Darius had been killed by Bessus and Nabarzanes, as was mentioned above, Alexander stirred his soldiers to take revenge, saying these words at the end of his oration:

<margin>G</margin>
> We stand on the very threshold of victory, my soldiers; only a few fugitives and the murderers of everyone remain. This is an excellent task, by Hercules, and it shall be numbered among the first rewards of your glory; you will pass down to posterity and fame that Darius too, once an enemy—his hatred having ended after death—you wished to be treated as a nobleman, and that no one escaped your hands. Once this is perpetrated, how much more obedient do you believe the provinces will be when they realize you undertake pious wars and are angry at the crime of Bessus, not at his name? <note>original: "In ipfo limine victoriæ ftamus milites pauci nobis fugitiui..." This Latin speech is attributed to Alexander by the historian Quintus Curtius Rufus.</note>

And so, putting this into execution, he constrained both of them to die in desperation. This was a deed truly worthy and suited to a royal god. In this war, Alexander having captured Sisygambis, the mother of Darius, as well as his daughters and his wife, he maintained them with no less reverence, modesty, and love than if they had been his own mother, his own wife, and his own children. So much so that Sisygambis, having outlived Darius, killed herself when Alexander later died, so as not to remain after the great clemency he had shown her, as Justin writes in Book XIII of *The History of the World*. Nor did Alexander use less liberality toward the prisoners of Darius. Parmenion said that he should let them go for money, but Alexander sent them all back courteously to Darius, saying to Parmenion these worthy words, as Curtius writes:

> I would prefer money to glory if I were Parmenion; but now, as Alexander, I am secure from poverty and know myself to be not a merchant, but a king. I have nothing for sale; certainly, I do not sell my fortune. If it pleases you that the captives be returned, we will give them as an honorable gift rather than release them for a price. <note>original: "Ego pecuniam quā gloriā mallem si parmenio efsem..." A famous anecdote illustrating Alexander's prioritize of reputation and "glory" over material wealth.</note>

And another time, when Parmenion persuaded Alexander to attack Darius’s camp by night, Alexander replied:

> I would rather regret my victory than be ashamed of it. <note>original: "Malo me uictoriæ pœniteat q̄ uictoriæ pudeat." This reflects Alexander's refusal to use "dishonorable" stealth tactics.</note>

Therefore, prepare yourselves for battle. Once, when Alexander was ill and yet did not leave the cares of the army, it was told to him that he should rest until he was healed, to which he replied in this form:

> Slow remedies and sluggish doctors have not tested my time; it is better for me to die vigorously than to recover slowly. Therefore, if there is any work or skill in doctors, let them know I seek a remedy not so much for death as for war. <note>original: "Lenta remedia & segnes medicos non experti..."</note>

<margin>H</margin>
Alexander, having thus obtained the victory over Darius, went to the field at Gordium, a city situated in the midst of Greater and Lesser Phrygia, solely because he had heard that there was a knot there, and whoever untied it was prophesied to become the lord of all Asia. Departing from there, he went into Syria and conquered it.

# ## TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>I</margin> He overcame and then conquered and captured the great city of Tyre, and afterwards he defeated Rhodes and Cilicia; then Egypt and Alexandria. To briefly recount the peoples subjugated by him: he defeated the Illyrians, the Achaeans, the Triballi, those of Boeotia, those of Thrace, the Spartans of the Peloponnese, those of the Hellespont, and he recovered the region of Helodia <note>Likely referring to Euboea or a similar Greek region</note> which the barbarians had occupied. He defeated the Carystians, the Lydians, Cappadocia, Phrygia, Paphlagonia, Pamphylia, Phoenicia, Armenia, Persia, Media, and Parthia, and other peoples around Mount Caucasus, as Justin <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a 2nd-century Roman historian who abridged the works of Pompeius Trogus</note> writes. Ultimately, Alexander defeated Porus, the King of India, who had demanded to fight in single combat with Alexander. In the fight, Alexander defeated him and took him prisoner; but seeing him first coming against him with a massive body and mounted upon an elephant, Alexander said: "I see at last a danger equal to my spirit" <note>original: "Tantundem par animo meo periculum video"</note>. Having thus gained the victory over Porus, he graciously restored his kingdom and his life to him; and solely for perpetual memory, Alexander built two noble cities in India: namely, Nicaea and Bucephala <note>Named after his famous horse, Bucephalus</note>. In these expeditions, Alexander performed the office of a good knight no less than that of the finest commander, because in battle he was always the first to strike; in the taking of lands and in the crossing of rivers, he was always an example to all others. And once, as Curtius <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, Roman historian of Alexander</note> writes, at the fortress of the Sudrachae <note>The Malli campaign, where Alexander was severely wounded</note>, Alexander entered over the walls alone and leaped into the ground; he sustained the battle for so long that he was rescued by his men and the castle was taken. Finally, Alexander made the limit of his dominion on one side the Hyphasis <note>The modern Beas River</note>, the most noble river of India, as Solinus writes, saying: "The Hyphasis, the most noble river of India, which marked the end of the journey of Alexander the Great, as the altars placed on its bank prove" <note>original: "Hippanis nobilissimus Indiae fluvius qui alexandri magni iter terminavit sicut arae in ripa eius posite probant"</note>. And from the other side, the Indian Ocean; he then returned to Babylonia, where already the Western powers had sent ambassadors solely to give him lordship over the West. <margin>K</margin> Having at this time put to death Parmenion and his son Philotas—whereas previously he had killed at dinner Clitus, his most singular friend—he also had the philosopher Callisthenes' limbs cut off and exposed Lysimachus, his excellent nobleman, to a famished lion. Antipater, who had been the governor in Macedonia, seeing Alexander grown envious of many worthy and glorious deeds which he had performed, deliberated to have him killed with poison. For this reason, he sent his son Cassander to Babylonia with a poison so terrible that it could only be held in the hoof of a horse. Having arrived there, through the work of Iola and Philip, his brothers, who served Alexander by tasting the wine, they poisoned Alexander. When he came to death—although he had a brother, the troubled Aridaeus <note>Philip III Aridaeus, who was mentally disabled</note>, and a son by Queen Cleophis (who reigned in India near the Daedala mountains) named Alexander, and another by the Persian Barsine named Hercules, and even though his wife Roxana was pregnant—when he was asked by his noblemen whom he would appoint as his heir, setting aside all carnal affection, he only replied: "To the most worthy" <note>original: "Dignissimum"</note>. And he died immediately, being thirty-two years and one month of age. Justly, then, Alexander—having in this short course of time, only thirteen years in which he campaigned, remained the victor over so many provinces stretching from the city of Macedonia, where he was born, to the province of India—was described by our poet <note>Petrarch</note> as having conquered his undertakings "by running." He then introduces the example of Alexander of Epirus, saying that afterwards he saw another Alexander, and not far from this first Macedonian, who did not run with such speed but met with a different encounter and obstacle; exclaiming, he adds: "O Fortune, how much you cut and divide through your work the true honor from those whom you rule under your power." Whence he says:

heard the news, he rejoiced no less than at having been made King by Philip; he estimated that just as the Eastern Empire had come to Alexander the Macedonian, so Fortune had prepared for him the opportunity to possess the Western Empire. And certainly, he hoped for a prize no less worthy of glory and honor in Italy, Sicily, and Africa than Persia, Media, and the entire East. Thus, having arrived in Italy and forming a friendship with the Metapontines and Romans, he proceeded against the Bruttians and Lucanians, and after having much war with them, finally near the city of Pandosia in the kingdom, fighting...

<header>CHAPTER THREE</header>

<margin>M</margin>
...he was killed while fighting. <note>Referring to Alexander of Epirus, who died in battle in Italy, unlike his more famous nephew</note> ¶ Secondly, it is to be understood that Master Francesco <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch</note> rightly exclaims how much fortune takes away from honor and praise. For if Alexander of Epirus had gone against the Easterners, he would have obtained a glorious victory; and if Alexander the Macedonian had come to the West—as Livy writes in *History from the Founding of the City*, Book 9 <note>original: "Liu. ab urbe cōdita lib. ix."</note>—he would have found, instead of Persians, the Romans. In place of Darius, he would have faced Lucius Papirius Cursor, Publius Rutilius, Valerius Corvinus, Manlius Torquato, Lucius Volumnius, Quintus Fabius Maximus, and other outstanding leaders, and the armies that forced Italy to surrender, the Gauls to death, and the Africans to flight. Thus, Livy affirms that Alexander would have met no different a fate than Hannibal did with his fierce and powerful army. For this reason, Caesar called Pompey "lucky" when he saw Pharnaces fleeing before him, as Pompey had acquired his fame only through the cowardice of the Eastern peoples. On this subject, Quintus Curtius writes: "Who denies that extraordinary glory is more often a benefit of fortune than of virtue?" <note>original: "Quis negat eximiā quoq; gloriā sæpius fore fortunæ q virtutis esse beneficiū"</note> ¶ Lucius Florus: "How much more effective is fortune than virtue." <note>original: "Quāto efficacior est fortuna q virtus"</note> So also Caesar in the *Civil War* commentaries: "But fortune, for the most part, reserves those whom she has adorned with the most benefits for the harsher falls." <note>original: "At fortuna plerūq; quos beneficiis plurimis ornauit: eos ad duri riores casus reseruat"</note> Therefore, it can certainly be concluded that regarding Alexander of Epirus, fortune alone made him inferior in fame to the Macedonian by assigning him war in the West, while giving the Macedonian the fate of the East. Consequently, after him, Master Francesco describes Hercules, Bacchus, and Epaminondas, whom he counted together above in comparison to Pompey, saying that he saw following after Alexander the three Thebans whom he narrates in a fine group, saying with distinction: *“Like Bacchus, Hercules, and Epaminondas at Thebes.” Wherefore he says:*

<margin>N</margin>
# The three Thebans whom I spoke of in a fine group

<insert>
¶ The first of the excellent Thebans
described in this place by
our poet is Hercules, son of Jove and
Alcmene, wife of Amphitryon.
</insert>

Because of his great and marvelous deeds, the poets, historians, and other worthy authors of the Greek and Latin languages have exhausted themselves in celebrating his praises. We, desiring the greatest brevity at present, will not relate them differently than they were, but will only extend our writing to narrate part of his worthy deeds. Principally, then, since Juno was angry with Hercules and anyone descended from Jove, while he was a tiny child in the cradle with his brother Iphicles, Juno sent two serpents to devour him. Hercules, being intrepid while his brother Iphicles was terrified and crying, took them in his hands and killed them both. Later, having grown up, hearing that there was a most horrible serpent called the Hydra in the Lernaean swamp, Hercules went there and overcame it, killing at one stroke its natural heads and those that multiplied sevenfold when he cut just one. In the third place, there being in the Nemean region a most troublesome and fierce lion, Hercules, having been shown the location by a shepherd named Molorchus, went against it, captured and killed it, and by force stripped its skin, and for perpetual memory always went dressed in it. No less virtue did he show against the other Teumessian lion <note>A reference to the fox of Teumessus or perhaps a confusion with another lion labor</note>, overcoming it and striking it to the ground; and similarly, forcefully leading out the boar of the Erymanthian woods <note>original: "cinghiali de i boschi menali"</note> which was gnawing and wasting Arcadia, giving it alive first to King Eurystheus. Similarly, he brought to their deaths the hind with brazen feet <note>The Ceryneian Hind</note>, the Harpies, and the Cretan bull. Beyond this, no longer following beastly combat, Hercules overcame Achelous, the river of Calidonia <note>The river-god Achelous</note>, as we said above, obtaining as a prize his beloved Deianira. He then overcame Diomedes, the King of Thrace, who killed foreigners who came into his kingdom and fed his beasts with those bodies; and he prepared that same Diomedes as food for those animals of his. Then, leaving Greece and arriving in Libya, he found that Busiris—son of Neptune and Libya and King of the province bordering the Nile—troubled all those regions, and the prisoners he took he sacrificed to the gods. For this reason, Hercules, going against him, killed him and put all that country in peace. And in this same region, he found the giant Antaeus, son of the Earth, with whom he wrestled, finding by experience that every time he touched the ground, Antaeus's strength doubled. Therefore, Hercules, lifting him from the earth upon his arms, squeezed him so much that he made him die. ¶ Proceeding then to the West, Hercules acquired no less fame and glory, giving entry to the Ocean sea into the land. Wherefore, beyond Hispania, at the extremity of the habitable earth known to us, are two mountains: one named Calpe and the other Abyla <note>OCR: "Apinna"</note>, surnamed the Pillars of Hercules. For it is the opinion, which Solinus does not deny and Seneca affirms in his last tragedy, that Hercules... the mountain which was continuous... <note>Catchword: "continuate"</note>

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

...it was helpful to have divided and opened [the land]: through which opening the ocean gained entry and created the Mediterranean Sea. Wherefore Pomponius Mella <note>A Roman geographer of the 1st century AD</note> says these words on this subject: "Next is a mountain set forward which rises opposite Spain; they call this one Abyla and that one Calpe, the Pillars of Hercules <note>The Strait of Gibraltar; Abyla is in Africa and Calpe is the Rock of Gibraltar</note>: to both, fame adds the story of the name. That Hercules himself once divided the mountains joined by a continuous ridge, and so the ocean, previously excluded by the mass of mountains, was let in and now floods the area." <note>original: "Deide est mons pre latus que ex aduerso hyspania attollit obiectus hunc appinnā illū calpi vocant colūnas herculis: utruq̄ addit fama nōis fabulā. Hercule ipsum iūnctos olim ꝓpetuo iugo dirimiſſe collest atq̄ ita excluſum ante a mole montiū oceanū atq̄ nunc inundat admiſſum."</note> He passed beyond this into Hesperia <note>Italy or Spain, here referring to the far West</note> where Hercules went into the garden of the Hesperian maidens: and in that place, having killed the dragon guardian, he took the golden apples and left them deprived of such excellence. Afterwards in Spain, he conquered the three-bodied Geryon <note>A giant often depicted with three heads or three joined bodies</note>: and having killed him, he led his herds and sheep into Greece with great pomp and perpetual glory. Similarly, alongside the Theban <note>Likely referring to his companion in certain myths, or perhaps a reference to his own Theban origin</note>, Hercules overcame the kingdom of the Amazons, and Albion and Bergion in Gaul who blocked his path: they were killed by him near the mouth of the Rhone. Laomedon was killed at Troy. The thief Licinius <note>Possibly a variant of the bandit names encountered by Hercules</note> near the borders of Italy: and Cacus, also a thief, beneath Mount Aventine. He writes further of Hercules having overcome the centaurs who wanted to take Hippodamia from Pirithous: and beyond this, the poets affirm Hercules to have sustained the sky upon his shoulders. This matter is written in two ways: one is that Hercules, having gone into outer Spain and finding King Atlas, who was exhausted from sustaining the sky, at Atlas's request, Hercules placed his shoulders beneath it so that Atlas could turn his back. The other way is written by Anselm in the book *The Image of the World* <note>original: "Anselmo in li. de imagine mundi." Referring to a popular medieval encyclopedia attributed to Anselm of Canterbury or Honorius Augustodunensis</note>: which is that when the gods were gathered in that part above Mount Atlas, it seemed the sky was almost about to fall from too much weight: because of which Hercules, placing himself beneath it, gave great help to the already weary Atlas. Likewise, Hercules, always following virtuous works and having already overcome every worldly toil, decided to attempt a victory over Hell: from where he descended into the underworld and from there dragged out by force the three-throated Cerberus <note>The three-headed guard dog of Hades</note> and also Alcestis, the wife of Admetus, lord of Thessaly, together with Theseus his dearest friend: who had descended to the underworld with Pirithous to recover Proserpina, wanting a woman who was born of Jove; and Pirithous, having died, was detained by Pluto. Hercules then, having returned from the underworld to Thebes, conquered and killed Lycus, king of Thebes: who had wanted to force himself upon Megara, Hercules's beloved wife.

<margin>P</margin> 
Lastly, Hercules returning from Calydon with his beloved Deianira: having reached a very large river, he found the centaur Nessus: who, seeing that Deianira was beautiful, immediately fell in love with her: and believing he could deceive Hercules with fair words, he offered to carry Deianira across the river on his back. Hercules accepted the offer and placed Deianira upon the back of Nessus. Whereupon he entered the water with her and was soon on the other bank: where, as soon as they arrived, Nessus began to flee with Deianira. Seeing this, Hercules took a poisoned arrow: with which, by the strength of his powerful bow, he reached Nessus and struck him. Nessus, feeling himself wounded and knowing his death was certain, thought to avenge himself: whereupon, having set Deianira on the ground, he took his shirt, which was stained with his poisoned blood, and gave it to her, telling her to keep it: because it had this power, that whenever Hercules should fall in love with another woman, as soon as he wore it, he would be recalled to her love, setting aside every other. Deianira, hearing the words of Nessus, gave them certain faith. Wherefore she took the shirt and kept it with diligence and good guard for a long time. It happened later that Hercules fell in love with Iole, daughter of Eurytus, king of Aetolia: as soon as Deianira heard of it, she sent him the shirt: which Hercules, having put on and then exercised his body, the poison mixed with the sweat and penetrated inside through the open pores. Whence it reached his heart and caused him such pain that he decided to die entirely. Because of this, he called Philoctetes, son of Poeas, his dearest friend, and climbed up Mount Oeta: where he constructed a pyre, and placing himself upon it, had it set on fire: and in such a manner Hercules came to his death, just as we said above in the *Triumph of Love*.

<margin>Q</margin> 
Hercules is not a proper name: nor were all these things performed by a single Hercules: nor for the most part do they have any other foundation than the discretion of poets, who, wanting to extol someone in strength of body, always named him Hercules as long as he performed some excellent deed. These narrations contain many fictional things: regarding which, if one wanted to rewrite the allegories given by various authors, the writing would perhaps extend too far: and especially because the diversity of the interpreters creates no less confusion than...

# CHAPTER THREE

<margin>R</margin>
Though fables are told about him, nonetheless we read in the works of historians that the Theban Hercules <note>original: "Hercule thebano"; distinguishing the Greek hero from other legendary figures with the same name</note> defeated the Amazons and King Laomedon in battle and performed other worthy deeds, for which he should deservedly follow the others in fame. ¶ The second of the excellent Thebans was Bacchus, son of Jove <note>The text reads "Ione," likely a variant or error for Giove (Jove/Jupiter)</note>, who was in order the son of Heaven, born of the ether and eternal; he was the father of Semele, daughter of Cadmus, the King of Thebes. Regarding him, I will set aside the fables of the poets and follow Eusebius in his *Book of Times* <note>The *Chronicon* of Eusebius, a primary source for ancient chronology</note> and Justin in the twelfth book of his *Foreign Wars*. We shall say that Bacchus was Dionysus, otherwise called Liber; as he marched against the Indians, he overcame and defeated them in battle. And then, for his eternal memory, he built the city called Nysa in India upon the Indus River. When Alexander the Great reached it, he did not attack it out of reverence for Bacchus. Since he was of Theban origin and later reached India, one can clearly understand that he was most excellent in arms—especially as he was later deified and described in so many ways by the poets. We shall pass over these descriptions in silence for now, as it seems their praise should be attributed to various different things. ¶ The third and last of the three excellent Thebans was the most outstanding 
<margin>S</margin>
Epaminondas <note>A famous Theban general and statesman of the 4th century BC</note>. Concerning him, it must be understood that because of his virtues, the Thebans raised their hopes of possessing the entire empire of Greece. Desiring and seeking an opportunity to make war, they perhaps aided the Athenians against the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>. Having made Epaminondas their leader, he achieved a glorious victory, most notably through the death of Alexander the Lacedaemonian <note>Probably referring to Alexander of Pherae, an ally of the Spartans</note>, under whose leadership and auspices the Athenians had been defeated. Having achieved this victory, Epaminondas proceeded to the siege of the Lacedaemonians and finally overcame and defeated them. Later, when the Lacedaemonians had been defeated again and moved war against the Arcadians, Epaminondas went to the aid of Arcadia and once more defeated and overcame the Lacedaemonians. In that cruel battle, Epaminondas performed the duty of a soldier no less than that of a commander or leader, to the extent that while fighting he received a wound from which he died a few days later. At his death, it seemed that all dignity and glory died with him—indeed, the Theban Republic itself—since after his death the Thebans 
<margin>T</margin>
became memorable only for their disasters. Justin, in the sixth book of his *Foreign Wars*, deservedly writes these worthy words about Epaminondas:

> It was uncertain whether he was a better man or a better leader. For he sought power not for himself, but always for his country: and he was so frugal with money that he lacked the funds for his funeral. He was no more desirous of glory than of money. Indeed, all his commands were carried out even as he refused honors; he held his offices in such a way that he seemed not to receive distinction from the position, but to bestow it upon the dignity itself. <note>original: "Fuit aut(em) incertu(m) vir melior an dux fuerit. Na(m) iperiu(m) no(n) sibi: sed semp(er) patrie q(uae)siuit: z pecunie adeo parcus fuit: ut sumptus funeris defuerit. Glorie quoq(ue) no(n) cupidior q(uam) pecunie. Quippe recusanti oia iperia gesta sunt: honoresq(ue) ita gessit vt ornatu(m) no(n) accipere: sed dare ipsi dignitati uideretur."</note>

While Epaminondas was in the throes of death from his wound, and having been somewhat relieved, he asked those standing around him if his shield had remained in the hands of the enemy. When he heard that it had not, and that the Thebans had achieved a complete victory, he had the shield brought to him. Kissing and embracing it many times as the companion of his glories and labors, he expired. Gathering together the deeds and virtues of these three outstanding Thebans, the comparison made above between them and Gnaeus Pompey by our famous and worthy poet <note>Petrarch</note> is made quite clear. He then adds that after these men, he saw following in the next group Ajax, Diomedes, and Ulysses, who had too great a desire to see and search the world; wherefore he says:

<margin>V</margin>
->**In the other, Ajax; Diomedes, and Ulysses,**<-
->**who had too much desire to see the world:**<-

For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, one must first know that there were two Ajaxes. One was the Telamonian Ajax, son of Telamon, King of Salamis, and of Hesione, sister of Priam and daughter of Laomedon, King of Troy. Among the Greeks, he was most expert in arms, so bold that he alone dared to resist Hector in battle. As Dictys of Crete <note>A legendary witness to the Trojan War and purported author of a diary on the conflict</note> writes, Achilles, because of the strength of Ajax, called him his companion in almost every action. One day, while Ajax was in a turbulent battle, he encountered Hector. After fighting together for a long time, they finally recognized one another; whereupon Hector gave him a sword, and Ajax gave Hector a beautiful baldric <note>term: <term>baltheo</term> (a belt or strap worn over the shoulder to support a sword)</note>. According to Servius <note>A 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Virgil</note>, these gifts were truly fatal: because Hector, wearing that baldric, was killed by Achilles, and Ajax killed himself with that sword after losing the armor of Achilles to Ulysses by the judgment of the Greeks. Dictys of Crete nevertheless asserts that one day, Ajax, in front of the Greeks, threatened to kill Ulysses...
