# ->THE TRIUMPH OF FAME<-

<margin>X</margin>
Because Ulysses won the aforementioned arms <note>This refers to the "Judgment of Arms," a contest between Ulysses and Ajax for the armor of the fallen Achilles</note> and the Palladium <note>A sacred wooden statue of the goddess Pallas Athena that protected Troy; Ulysses and Diomedes stole it</note> was obtained against him, Ajax was found dead the following morning with many wounds. It was widely believed to be the work of Ulysses, who, after the death of Ajax, secretly departed from the army. ¶ The other Ajax was Ajax Oileus <note>Also known as Ajax the Lesser</note>, King of the Locrians, a people most warlike. As Dictys <note>original: "Ditis"; referring to Dictys of Crete, the supposed author of a popular medieval history of the Trojan War</note> testifies, while returning from the destruction of Troy, he was struck by the force of winds and lightning among the Euboean rocks. Although his ships were wrecked, he struggled to survive and swam, but ultimately died in this shipwreck. Thus Virgil, speaking through the character of Juno, who was indignant against the Trojans, says these words:

> Am I forbidden by the fates? Could Pallas burn the fleet of the Greeks <note>original: "Argiuum"</note> and submerge the men themselves in the sea because of the crime and the frenzy of one man, Ajax son of Oileus? She herself, having hurled Jove's swift fire from the clouds, scattered the ships and overturned the seas with winds. Him, breathing out flames from his pierced chest, she seized in a whirlwind and impaled on a sharp rock. <note>original: "Quippe vetor fatis. Pallaſne exurere claſſem: Argiuum..." quoting Virgil's Aeneid, Book I</note>

This wrath of Pallas fell upon Ajax for having profaned her temple during the fall of Troy with blood and lust <note>A reference to Ajax the Lesser dragging Cassandra from the sanctuary of Athena</note>. Thus, it seemed he was justly led to his death for the excesses he committed. From this, one can easily judge that the poet <note>Petrarch</note> intended to refer to Ajax Telamon <note>Ajax the Greater</note> for being magnanimous, most courageous, and distinguished by many virtues, rather than the other Ajax Oileus, who, although most warlike, was nonetheless wrath-
<margin>y</margin>
ful, most cruel, profane, and contaminated by many other vices. However, we leave this to the better and more firm judgment of others. ¶ Secondly, it is to be understood that Diomedes was the son of Tydeus and Deipyle, previously mentioned; he was a most strong man and a most fierce combatant. Going on the Trojan expedition, he was judged the most excellent among the Greeks to enter battle, second only to Achilles. Thus Virgil, in the *Aeneid*, says in the person of Aeneas:

> O Diomedes <note>original: "Tytide"; son of Tydeus</note>, bravest of the Greek race! Could I not have fallen on the Trojan fields and poured out this soul of mine by your right hand? <note>original: "O danaum fortiſſime gentis Tytide..." from Aeneid, Book I</note>

Because of his prowess and strength, it was affirmed by Homer that Diomedes wounded Mars <note>The god of war</note> in battle. Diomedes, in addition to those he killed in the Trojan War and the singular battles fought against Aeneas and Hector, finally, together with Ulysses, stole the horses of Rhesus before they could enter Troy and drink from the river Xanthus. With great industry, he also stole the Palladium. After the Trojan War ended, Diomedes wished to return to his homeland, but his wife Aegiale did not want to receive him, having been persuaded by Nauplius (father of Palamedes) to marry another man. Servius <note>A famous 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note> nonetheless affirms that Diomedes, having heard that Aegiale had committed adultery with Cyllabarus <note>original: "Cilibero"</note>, son of Sthenelus, decided not to return to her. Instead, he came to Italy where he built a city called Siponto. In this place, the poets feign that his companions were transformed into birds. According to some others, he also built Arpi and Benevento. Justin, in the twelfth book of *Foreign Wars*, affirms that the Aetolians who came with Diomedes to Italy built the city of Brindisi <note>original: "Brūduſio"</note>, where, upon his eventual death, he was reputed to be a god by his men.
<margin>z</margin>
Aristotle, nonetheless, in the book *On Marvelous Things Heard*, affirms that Diomedes was killed by Aeneas and his kingdom occupied by the Trojans. ¶ Lastly, it is to be noted that Ulysses, son of Laertes, King of Ithaca, and his wife Anticlea <note>original: "antidia"</note>, was likewise a man most practiced in arms; but in cunning and eloquence, he was to be preferred above all other Greeks. Having gone to the destruction of Troy and performed many glorious deeds in that expedition, he finally departed secretly from the army after the victory was won because of the death of Ajax, as we said recently. While he was at sea, he was seized by a desire to see different regions of the world, although others say he was forced to do so by the fury of the winds. Carrying out this purpose, he ran into most grave shipwrecks and horrendous dangers on his journey, as Homer introduces with great abundance in the *Odyssey*. But because part of his deeds are described only through fiction—to which authors attribute only moral sentiment, such as his arrival at the court of Aeolus and receiving the winds enclosed in skins <note>original: "odry"</note>, or his descent into the underworld and other similar feats—we shall presently narrate only his progress according to the testimony of Dictys of Crete and Dares the Phrygian <note>Two authors believed in the Renaissance to have written true historical accounts of the war</note>. Ulysses, having departed from Troy, came primarily to Smyrna, the homeland of the most excellent Homer, the greatest of all poets. When he arrived there and the inhabitants forbade him from their shores, Ulysses obtained a very great prize by force of arms and departed. Navigating from there, he reached the region of the Lotus-eaters.

<meta>This page continues the biography of Ulysses (Odysseus), following the dispute over Achilles' armor mentioned on page 129. # CHAPTER THREE

<margin>A</margin> The Lotophagi <note>The Lotus-eaters; in mythology, those who ate the lotus fruit forgot their homes</note>: in which place, sending some scouts to see the country, and they not returning, he [Ulysses] thought they must have been killed. Wherefore, having departed, he arrived in Sicily. ¶ In that time, two brothers, tyrants, ruled the region of Sicily. One of them was called Listrigona <note>A personification of the Laestrygonians, a race of man-eating giants</note> and the other was named Cyclops. As soon as they saw Ulysses, they robbed and imprisoned him, and killed many of his companions. Thereafter, through the work of Polyphemus and Antipitre <note>Likely Antiphates, king of the Laestrygonians</note>, Ulysses was drawn out of prison and brought somewhat into the favor of the princes. While Ulysses was thus staying at liberty in the palace, it happened that Arene, daughter of Listrigona, fell in love with Alphenore, one of Ulysses' companions. When Ulysses learned of this, he ordered an escape, and in the flight, they took the aforementioned Arene with them. But Listrigona, noticing this fraud, wanted to capture or kill Ulysses, for which reason he fled and came to Calypso and Circe with only one boat and few companions. As soon as she [Circe] saw him, she fell in love with him. Having detained him one year with her, she became pregnant by him with a son; whom she named Telegonus when he was born at the proper time. Ulysses then departed from Circe and came to Lake Avernus <note>Regarded by the Romans as the entrance to the Underworld</note>, and not staying in that place, he sailed to the island of the Sirens, where a very heavy storm of winds drove him. When he realized he had arrived there, he stopped his own ears and those of all his companions. Departing from that place, he then arrived at the whirlpools of Scylla and Charybdis, where he lost a great part of the ships he had received from Calypso and Circe. But having escaped such great danger, while he was wandering by sea, he was taken by certain Phoenician pirates. These men, later releasing Ulysses out of compassion, he returned to Circe, where she once again equipped him to return to his fatherland. Departing then from her, he sailed fortunately at last to Crete. Later, by the force of winds, he was forced to arrive in Salamis, where he was totally robbed by Telamon, father of Ajax, and narrowly escaped death <note>Telamon held a grudge because Ulysses was blamed for the death of his son, Ajax the Greater</note>. Because of this, being very poor, he was brought by two Phoenician ships to Crete to King Idomeneus. Idomeneus, having recognized Ulysses, gave him two ships and many goods and sent him to Alcinous, King of Phoenicia <note>In the Odyssey, Alcinous is King of the Phaeacians; medieval traditions often confused or substituted these names</note>. As soon as he heard the celebrated name of Ulysses, he received him gratefully and honored him worthily. While Ulysses stayed in Phoenicia, he learned through letters written to him by Penelope of the evil state of his kingdom. For this reason, he deliberated entirely on returning to Ithaca, and he prayed Alcinous that he should help him, which Alcinous did willingly and gratefully. Ulysses thus returned in this manner to his kingdom, where he was joyfully received by his people, and especially by the beloved Penelope. Having arrived there and taken vengeance on his enemies, he governed his kingdom with great justice. ¶ <margin>B</margin> It happened thereafter, not much time later, that Telegonus, having the will to go visit his dear father—Ulysses being unknown to him—departed from Circe his mother and sailing came to Ithaca. At this same time, Ulysses having seen a vision in his sleep, which was interpreted that he must die by the hands of his son, and not remembering Telegonus, he only doubted Telemachus. Therefore, because of this, he had the entrance guarded so that no one could go to him without his permission. Telegonus, having arrived at the palace, wanted to go up to see his father; but being held back by the guards and not known to them, he engaged in battle with those custodians. Having wounded a great part of them, Ulysses heard the noise, wherefore he came to that place carrying a dart in his hand. Seeing this young man wounding his men, he threw a dart at him and wounded him slightly. But Telegonus took up the dart, and not knowing Ulysses, threw it at him and wounded him mortally. When Ulysses felt this wound, remembering the vision, he suddenly made the battle stop and asked Telegonus who he was. Telegonus replied that he was the son of Ulysses and Circe, and had come to that place to see his father Ulysses. Then, hearing who he was, Ulysses embraced him and kissed him, and immediately made peace between him and Telemachus, who had come to that place armed only to take revenge for his father, telling him that this was his own flesh-and-blood brother. A few days later, Ulysses died. Therefore, he is deservedly written of in fame, both for the works done by him before the Trojan War—such as the finding of Achilles <note>Ulysses discovered Achilles hiding among women on Skyros</note> and the bringing of Iphigenia to the army—and also for what he did in the war and in the horrific battles for the theft of the Palladium from the ashes of Laomedon <note>Refers to the theft of the sacred statue from Troy, which was founded by Laomedon</note>, and for the theft of the horses of Rhesus, and likewise for the various misfortunes tolerated by him in his hard and long pilgrimage. Consequently, he adds...

### TRIUMPH OF FAME

Following this, Master Francesco <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch, the author of the poem being commented upon</note> follows the example of Nestor: saying that after Ulysses, he saw Nestor follow, who lived beyond the common custom and therefore knew much through scientific knowledge and great experience had of the things of the world. Whence he says:

<margin>A</margin>
**->Nestor, who knew so much, and lived so long:<-**

*Nestor was the son of Neleus, son of Neptune, and Chloris <note>The text says "Diodoris," a likely scribal error or variant for Chloris</note>, daughter of Amphion, king of Orchomenus. He was a most eloquent and learned man, according to the testimony of Homer in the Iliad. He lived a very long time, as Ovid demonstrates in the 12th book of the Metamorphoses, when he introduces Achilles asking Nestor and praying that he tell him in what way Caeneus turned from a woman into a man; and with whom he served, and if he was ever defeated in battle, and by whom. He then adds his answer in this form, saying:* <note>original: "Quisq; adeft narret..."</note> *"Let whoever is present tell; those whom Achilles asks. Speak, O eloquent old man, to whom our prudence [is known]. Who was Caeneus, and why turned to the opposite sex? What was your military service? In the contest of what battle were you known? By whom were you conquered, if you were conquered by any? Then the elder replied: although slow old age hinders me, and many things seen in my first years escape me, yet I remember many things. No matter remains more fixed in my heart than the many things done in war and at home; for indeed, a spacious old age has been able to make me a spectator of many works. I have lived two hundred years; now the third age is being lived."*

<margin>D</margin>
*And beyond the learning and knowledge of experienced things, which he likely had due to his long life, Nestor was a most warlike man. Whence, principally while still a youth, he made war against the Thessalians and overcame and conquered them, killing a great quantity of them, as Homer writes in the cited place. In this war, he was together with Theseus and Pirithous against the Centaurs. According to Dares <note>Dares Phrygius, a purported eyewitness to the Trojan War whose account was popular in the Middle Ages</note> and Dictys the Cretan, there were two Trojan wars: the first with Hercules and Jason against Laomedon, and then with the other Greeks against Priam. In this expedition, although he was very old—as the aforementioned historians describe—he showed such experience in battles that he was justly not to be considered inferior to many Greeks whose age was flourishing and strong. Then Master Francesco narrates Agamemnon and Menelaus, saying that behind Nestor he saw Agamemnon and Menelaus, who, having been very unhappy in their wives, nevertheless caused the cruelest quarrels and battles in the world. Whence he says:*

<margin>E</margin>
*How grave the Trojan war was, how long and how dangerous, with how much expense, with how much hardship, and with how many deaths of excellent princes, is common enough knowledge diffused by the authors who have written of it. Menelaus presided for the interest of the kidnapped Helen, and Agamemnon, by common election, was made captain and leader of the whole army by the lords of Greece. This occurred in the time of Juno, following the ritual performed when passing with a sword through a pig cut in two, signifying the East and the West, according to the account of Calchas <note>The text says "Calenas," likely referring to the seer Calchas</note>, son of Nestor, appointed by Agamemnon to observe the oath. The form of the oath was that each, having a sword in hand, would strike the middle of the pig and pass through it saying these words:* <note>original: "Iuro perpetuas cū Priamo inimicitias..."</note> *"I swear perpetual enmities with Priam; nor shall I desert the war before Ilium and all his kingdom be overturned." Justly, therefore, can it be said of them that they made great quarrels and cruel wars in the world, as was shown by love.*

**->Agamemnon, and Menelaus; who through wives<-**
**->Unfortunate, made great strife in the world:<-**

<margin>F</margin>
*But the unhappiness of Menelaus is understood clearly enough by the testimony of Dictys the Cretan, who says that after the kidnapping of Helen, Menelaus and Ulysses went to Troy to demand her back from Priam. Priam had her come into their presence and gave her full liberty if she wished to go away with Menelaus; but she, responding to Priam, said these words:* <note>original: "Nihil mihi cum Menelai matrimonio cōuenit."</note> *"Nothing of Menelaus’s marriage suits me." Whence his being joined in marriage with Helen was a great unhappiness, because as Socrates used to say:* <note>original: "Sicut nihil eſt ſuperius benigna coniuge: ita nihil infeſta muliere crudelius."</note> *"Just as nothing is superior to a kind spouse, so nothing is more cruel than a hostile woman." Wherefore, for this reason, one sees this quality quite appropriately attributed to them by our Master Francesco. Consequently, the poet brings forward another most worthy example, saying that after these...*

Leonidas the Spartan, with only four thousand fighters, opposed them in the narrows of Thermopylae <note>The narrow coastal pass where the famous battle took place in 480 BCE</note>. Seeing this, Xerxes, despising them for their small number, ordered that they be fought. Whereupon Leonidas courageously prepared himself and defended the pass by fighting for three continuous days; many Persians were killed by them. On the fourth day, Xerxes having occupied the summit of a mountain—and Leonidas having noticed it—he told three thousand four hundred of his men, who were of other Greek nations and had joined him before the general discord of Greece, to return to their own homelands and defend them. He asked that they leave him alone with his Spartans to face their common fortune. Leonidas did this because, having previously asked the oracle about the future outcome of the war, it had replied (as Justin <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian</note> writes): "Either the leader and king of the Spartans, or the city, must fall." <note>original: "Aut duci r regi sparthanoru; aut vrbi cadendum est."</note> Remaining then alone with seven hundred companions—

<margin>H</margin>
Leonidas arranged the day on which he wished to fight; and in the morning, having prepared a most noble breakfast, he exhorted his most brave fellow soldiers that they must courageously strike and assault the Persian camps that day, for if they remained victors they could not conquer more worthily than in that place; and if they had to fall, it was not possible to die more gloriously in any other. And at the end of his words he concluded (as Valerius <note>Valerius Maximus</note> writes in the third book, second chapter), saying: "Eat your breakfast, fellow soldiers, as if you are to dine among the dead below." <note>original: "Prādete cō militones tanq̄ apud inferos cenaturi."</note> And Cicero <note>The Roman orator and philosopher</note> in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: "Go forward then with a brave spirit, Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>; today perhaps we shall dine among those in the underworld." <note>original: "Pergite ergo forti animo. Lacedemony hodie apud īferos fortasse cenabimus."</note> Wherefore the Spartans, being perfectly prepared for death by Leonidas's words, entered the battle. They immediately reached Xerxes's camps; as soon as the King heard the noise, he fled cowardly, leaving the complete victory to the Spartans. In the end, wandering through the field and killing Persians while exhausted, the Spartans were nonetheless killed by the defeated Persians, falling together with their captain Leonidas. 

Afterwards, the poet adds Alcibiades after Leonidas, saying he saw Alcibiades, who very many times turned and overturned the city of Athens with his eloquence and the joyful sight of his serene face. Wherefore he says:

Alcibiades then came to Lacedaemon <note>Sparta, the rival of Athens</note> and incited them to make war on the Athenians. While he was staying in Lacedaemon, he had an affair with the wife of Agis, King of the Lacedaemonians; realizing this, Agis forced Alcibiades to flee to Tissaphernes, the prefect of Darius <note>Darius II</note>, son of Xerxes, who wanted to move war against Greece. ...which he <note>Cimon, the son of Miltiades</note> obtained with great difficulty, on the condition that he himself should wear all the chains with which Miltiades had been bound until he reached the place of his father's tomb. The worthy and pious son, consenting to this, performed the funeral rites for his beloved and dear father Miltiades while in chains. Next, Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch, the author of the poem</note> adds alongside Miltiades other Athenians who, having always acted with virtue, nevertheless experienced the harshness of their ungrateful homeland. He says that in this same company as Miltiades went **Themistocles**, **Theseus**, and **Aristides**—who, in his virtue and supreme self-restraint, was a Greek **Fabricius** <note>Gaius Fabricius Luscinus was a Roman leader famous for refusing bribes and living simply; the author calls Aristides his Greek equivalent</note>. To all of these, burial in their fatherland was equally forbidden and denied. Thus, the great vice of such ingratitude and envy makes their fame more illustrious; for nothing reveals and makes known two opposites better than a very small distance and a brief interval or minimal gap between them. And he adds that he saw along with these three mentioned above **Phocion** the Athenian, who was killed and driven out of his land, where the reward and prize received for his worthy and excellent works was very different and contrary to what he deserved. Wherefore he says:

<margin>
¶ For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, one must know that while every vice should be greatly blamed—and especially ingratitude—it is also necessary to extol and illuminate those against whom such a failing is directed. Thus the poet rightly says that the vice of others (that is, of ungrateful Athens) has illustrated the fame of **Themistocles**, **Theseus**, **Aristides**, and **Phocion**, they having always acted worthily for their country. Secondly, it is to be understood as a matter of natural reason that nothing better reveals one opposite than the nearby opposition of its contrary. This is because every contrariety exists only between qualities that can be recognized by the senses. Therefore, judgment is reserved for the senses alone, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> shows in the second book of the *Physics* when he says: **A blind man does not judge colors** <note>original: "Non enim de coloribus iudicat caecus"</note>. And because opposites can be diminished from their highest intensity and excellence by a small, medium, or large distance, they give a confused knowledge of themselves when presented to the senses in isolation. But when two opposites occur together before the judgment of the sensory power, they are grasped distinctly and clearly, both because of their diverse nature and the contrary change they produce. Therefore, our poet spoke excellently in saying that nothing better reveals two opposites than a very brief gap between them.
</margin>

-> Q R S <-

<meta>Catchword: Around</meta>

...they turned against Xerxes. Therefore, all those Greek republics being under the leadership and auspices of **Themistocles**, they gathered in the Strait of Salamis. Some of those republics wished to return to their lands and remain on the defensive; seeing this, and fearing that if they departed he would not be able to resist Xerxes, Themistocles immediately wrote a letter to Xerxes himself, persuading him to come to battle, arguing that he could capture the entire strength of the Greek nation at once in that place. He suggested that if he allowed them to depart, he would then have greater difficulty in obtaining dominion over Greece. Xerxes, therefore, not recognizing the prudence of Themistocles, and it appearing to him that the persuasions were true, moved his fleet to come to battle. Whence it happened that some cities which had already departed returned to Themistocles out of fear. Because of this, as the battle followed, the Ionians turned in favor of the Greeks and acted in such a way that Xerxes was then defeated. He was already completely surrounded when Themistocles, fearing that the Persians might rally out of desperation, opened a passage and sent word to Xerxes that he should flee before he was captured, showing him the method and the way. Xerxes, seeing this, most wretchedly put it into execution and fled away. 

Having later returned to Athens with the victory, Themistocles was, as a reward for such worthy work, banished from Athens and constrained to go into exile in Persia to the court of Xerxes, whom he had defeated. Xerxes, having received him graciously, showed him great honor. Wishing to make war on Athens for revenge, Xerxes made Themistocles his captain. But Themistocles, seeing this—not wishing to make war against his fatherland, yet not wishing to betray Xerxes who had been so meritorious toward him—resolved to satisfy everyone through death. Thus, taking poison, he died an exile outside his fatherland.

<margin>Q</margin>
Regarding **Theseus**, how many worthy works he performed for the Athenian republic was related extensively above in the *Triumph of Love*; nevertheless, he could not escape the rabid, common, and false envy by which he was driven into exile, and was constrained to live and die miserably on the island of Scyros.

<margin>R</margin>
**Aristides** was not only a preeminent Greek in deeds of arms but also a most illustrious philosopher in literature. In a single exploit, he saved all of Greece from two imminent tyrannies. For when the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> and the Athenians wished to avenge themselves in part for the injuries received from the Persians, the Lacedaemonians chose for their leader one **Pausanias**, and the Athenians chose Aristides. These two leaders having plundered and traversed much territory in Persia, Pausanias turned his mind during the war toward seizing the liberty of Greece. Whence he wrote to Xerxes, sending back all the prisoners, saying that Xerxes should help him in this, and he would give him his daughter as a wife; and so that this work should be secret, he told him to kill all the messengers he sent with letters. Whereupon Aristides, being diligent regarding the actions of Pausanias, recognized the treason; for which reason, having made it manifest, Pausanias was sent into exile and Greece was saved and freed from danger. 

Xerxes, therefore, seeing himself discovered in such a manner, later moved for war, in which he was defeated by **Cimon**. In addition to this, Aristides was truly similar to **Fabricius** <note>Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, a Roman famous for his integrity</note>, judging that no glory or utility could be attributed to the republic through fraud. Whence, as Cicero writes in the third book of *On Duties* <note>original: "Tullio nel terzo de gli officii"</note>, the Athenians having obtained victory against the Persians through the work of Themistocles, the latter said one day in the Senate that he had an excellent and beneficial plan for the Athenian republic, which he wished to manifest to only one man among them. Whereupon the Senate gave him Aristides. Themistocles said to him: that the fleet of the Lacedaemonians <term>Lacedaemonians</term> <note>The Spartans, who were at that time allies of Athens but potential rivals</note> should be totally destroyed. Aristides, having heard the opinion of Themistocles, said in the Senate—where he was awaited with great expectation—that the counsel of Themistocles was most useful, but not honorable. Therefore, the Athenians judged that what was not honorable could not even be useful. Nevertheless, the preeminent Aristides was in the end driven out by his fatherland, with whom—as Valerius writes in the fifth book, chapter three <note>original: "Vale. nel qnto li. al .iii. cap."</note>—there went into exile virtue, continence, and Greek sanctity.

<margin>S</margin>
Lastly **Phocion**, who was adorned with all the gifts that can give birth to both splendor and glory—especially liberality and clemency—was nevertheless, as Valerius writes in the same place, first put to death with great bitterness through envy by the Athenians in a most grave and Herculean trial of punishment; and then they commanded that his bones be carried outside the land of Attica and left unburied. In which land Phocion had lived with great virtue and holiness, benignly and without injury to anyone; wherefore, rightly, Master Francesco says that in this man the reward was most different from the merit that preceded it. Next, Master Francesco brings forward the example of **Pyrrhus**, saying how he saw following after Phocion the good Pyrrhus, king of Epirus. Whence he says:

# CHAPTER THREE

## CHAPTER THREE

->As I turned, I caught sight of the good Pyrrhus,<-

<margin>
Regarding the notice of the preceding verses, it is to be understood that two men named Pyrrhus have been celebrated by writers for their virtue and fame. The first was Neoptolemus, son of Deidamia and Achilles, who in his youth took the surname **Pyrrhus** because of the redness of his hair, as Plutarch writes. This man, according to <term>Dictys of Crete</term><note>Dictys and Dares (mentioned below) were believed in the Renaissance to be eyewitnesses to the Trojan War, though their texts are now considered later forgeries.</note>, having come to the destruction of Troy after the death of Achilles, was made leader of the Myrmidons. Having succeeded to his father's armor and other possessions, he demonstrated in battle that he was truly the image of Achilles. Whence, in battle, he killed Penthesilea, Queen of the Amazons, according to what <term>Dares the Phrygian</term> writes—although Dictys attributes her death to Achilles. He then killed Priam in the temple and Polyxena before his father’s tomb. But I do not believe our author [Petrarch] intended to speak of this one. The other Pyrrhus was **Pyrrhus of Epirus**, a descendant of the aforementioned Pyrrhus. Plutarch writes that among the Molossians, after Deucalion and Phaethon, this Pyrrhus (son of Achilles, also called Neoptolemus) reigned; from him all his descendants took the name of Pyrrhus. After some kings of barbaric and perverse customs, finally Tharripas reigned, and after him his son Alcetas, and after Alcetas, Arybbas, and after Arybbas, Aeacides. This Aeacides took as his wife Phthia, daughter of Menon, lord of Thessaly, by whom he fathered two daughters, one named Deidamea and the other Troas, and besides these, he had this Pyrrhus. After Aeacides died, a sedition arose among the Molossians, where they killed all the friends of Aeacides and sought to kill Pyrrhus. Because he was still a small child, he was hidden by some who sought to save him, taking him away as they fled. This flight became known and they were pursued. Nevertheless, they arrived with the small child at a very large river. Seeing people on the other bank, they wrote a letter and, tying it to a stone, threw it across, by which they made known the misfortune of Pyrrhus. Having read the letter, those people were moved to compassion; they crossed the river, took Pyrrhus, and went with him into Illyria, presenting him to King Glaucias, who reigned at that time. Glaucias, hearing his history, did not want to receive him for fear of provoking enmity, but the little Pyrrhus made so many gestures of asking him for mercy and help that Glaucias was moved to pity, received him, and had him nurtured. Pyrrhus grew up and became great and courageous in arms. He took Glaucias' daughter as his wife and, with his help, returned to Epirus and recovered his kingdom by force of arms, though he was later expelled again by his people. Pyrrhus then went to Demetrius, son of Antigonus King of Macedonia, who had Pyrrhus' sister Deidamea as his wife. With his help, he recovered his kingdom once more, and through the favor of Demetrius, he thereafter grew in great glory. Much later, when Demetrius was at war with Ptolemy, Seleucus, and Lysimachus—the chief generals of Alexander the Great—he asked for aid from his brother-in-law Pyrrhus, who went to his aid with a powerful army. Once he arrived there, casting aside every kinship and forgetting every benefit received, Pyrrhus corrupted Demetrius' men, drove him away, and took Macedonia for himself.
</margin>

<margin>V</margin>
¶ Being thus established in this kingdom, although he did not possess it for long, Pyrrhus turned his mind toward an empire of the world, but first toward the occupation of Italy. Having revealed his concept to **Cineas**, who was a man of the greatest authority in his service, Cineas sought to show him quietly that his desire was vain. He said to him: "The Romans are said to be truly outstanding in war and to rule over many bellicose nations. If the gods grant us to overcome them, what shall we do then, O Pyrrhus?" <note>original: "Egregiũ quidem bello Romani esse dicuntur: multisq; bellicosis gentibus imperare quod si eos superare dỹ nobis dederint quid tunc agemus o Pyrrhe."</note> To which question Pyrrhus replied: "Next is Sicily, a happy and populous island, easy to take through siege and the discord of its cities." <note>original: "proxima sicilia est insula fælix ac populosa capi vero facilis obsidiõe ac discordia ciuitatum."</note> Cineas then added: "You speak correctly, but will the capture of Sicily be the end of our military campaign?" <note>original: "Recte dicis sed an finis militie nobis erit Siciliam capisse."</note> Pyrrhus said: "If only God grants us victory. For we shall use these things as preludes to achieving the greatest matters. For who could keep their hands off Carthage, which Agathocles, having secretly departed from Syracuse with a great fleet, was nearly able to capture?" <note>original: "Deus modo victoria preftet. Nam iis veluti preludijs vtemur ad res maximas conficiendas. Quis enim se libis abstineat a Carthagine quam modo Agatocles clam siracusis profectus magna classe pa lo abfuit quin caperet."</note> Cineas then added: "It is so. For it is certain that with this power we will be able to recover Macedonia and certainly rule over Greece. But after everything is captured and subdued, what shall we do at last?" <note>original: "Ita est. Constat enim qd macedoniam recuperare & græciæ dominari certissime cum hac potentia licebit: sed partis omnibus atq; subactis quid faciemus tandem."</note> Pyrrhus then laughing replied: "We shall take our leisure: and enjoy happiness with daily festivities and mutual conversation." <note>original: "Otium agemus: quotidiana festiuitate mutuisq; sermõibus letitiãq; perfruemur."</note> Cineas, having had the answer he desired, finally said to Pyrrhus: "But what prevents us, O King, from enjoying that happiness and leisure now?" <note>original: "At quid vetat o rex quo minus ista letitia nunc & ocio Potius."</note>

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

> Let us enjoy this: for indeed the opportunity is before us, without labor, to possess those things which we would otherwise reach only through blood, hardships, and the dangers faced by ourselves and others. <note>original: "perfruamur: adest quippe nobis sine labore facultas eorum ad que per sanguinem molestias & pericula nostra & aliorum peruenturi sumus." This introductory quote reflects on the value of learning from history rather than through direct suffering.</note>

<margin>⁕</margin>
Pyrrhus, therefore, being more troubled than deterred by these words, went to the oracle of Apollo to ask if he would have victory against the Romans. The oracle gave him an ambiguous response, as the historian <term>Pliny</term> writes: **"I say to you, son of Aeacus, that the Romans you can defeat."** <note>original: "Aio te eacide romanos vicere posse." This is a famous double-meaning in Latin; it can mean "You can defeat the Romans" or "The Romans can defeat you."</note> Considering this, Pyrrhus came to Italy to aid the Tarentines against the Romans. In this expedition, he was helped with ships from Antigonus, King of Macedonia; with money from Antiochus, King of Syria; and with many people from Ptolemy, King of Egypt. Having arrived in Italy, the Romans sent Aulus Albinus against him in Lucania, who, after fighting fiercely with Pyrrhus, was finally overcome by him. Nevertheless, the victory of Pyrrhus was such that it was to be judged more glorious than joyful. <note>This refers to the "Pyrrhic victory," where the cost of winning is so high it feels like a defeat.</note>

<margin>X</margin>
The Romans then sent Marcus Laevinus against Pyrrhus. In the first battle, Laevinus was likewise overcome by Pyrrhus due to the terrifying nature of the elephants and the Romans' lack of familiarity with them. In that battle, looking afterward at the dead Roman knights who still retained their previous ferocity in their faces, Pyrrhus said, as <term>Florus</term> <note>Lucius Annaeus Florus, a Roman historian who summarized Roman military history.</note> attests:

> "Oh, how easy it would be to seize the empire of the world: either with me having Roman soldiers, or with me as King of the Romans." <note>original: "O quam facile erat orbis imperiū occupare: aut mihi romanis militibus aut me rege Romanis."</note>

As this war continued, Laevinus restored his armies. Eventually, through the courage of a Roman named Considius—who killed an elephant by wounding it and thus demonstrated that the others could also die—the Macedonians, Egyptians, and other peoples of Pyrrhus were defeated and conquered in the second battle. Whence Pyrrhus said his fortune was similar to that of Hercules against the Hydra in the Lernaean swamp. In this situation, Pyrrhus sought to make peace with the Romans, which they did not consent to due to the authority of **Appius Claudio Ceco** <note>Appius Claudius "the Blind," a famous Roman statesman who gave a celebrated speech against making peace with Pyrrhus while he was still on Italian soil.</note>. Thus it came to a third battle, where the consuls were Manius Curius and Fabricius. In this battle, Pyrrhus was overcome and totally forced to flee to Tarentum. Pyrrhus then departed Italy and went to Sicily, where he took Messina and the Mamertines, and finally the whole island. Once he had obtained it, contrary to his nature, he became a cruel tyrant where previously he had been mild, clement, and humane. In this state, the Carthaginians, doubting him, sent ambassadors to ask him for peace, having had war over Sicily. They offered a great number of ships and a quantity of money. To these, as <term>Plutarch</term> affirms, Pyrrhus replied with these proud words: **"There is but one way to peace: if, leaving all things in Sicily aside, you make the Libyan sea your boundary."** <note>original: "Vna est pacis via: si omissis omnibus in sicilia rebus libicum mare terminos capietis."</note> Pyrrhus finally left Sicily to go against the aforementioned King Antigonus, son of Demetrio, and against the Lacedaemonians [Spartans]. As he left, looking back often at Sicily, he said:

> "Oh, what a wrestling ground we leave here for the Carthaginians and the Romans!" <note>original: "O qualem carthaginensibus: ac romanis pro hac insula palestram reliquimus." This famously predicted the Punic Wars between Rome and Carthage.</note>

<margin>F</margin>
Having arrived in Greece, he immediately moved for war, thinking by his strength and cunning to soon possess all of Greece. But one day, while Ptolemy, son of Pyrrhus, was fighting the Spartans, he ran into the middle of the land where he was killed by the gathering of the people. When Pyrrhus learned of this, he said: **"He was killed somewhat later than I feared, or than his rashness deserved."** <note>original: "Aliquanto tardius quam timuerim: aut temeritas eius meruit occisus est."</note> Finally, having held Antigonus under siege for some time, he decided to give battle to the city [Argos]. While the battle was at its most fervent, Pyrrhus was already inside the gateway; intending to kill a Macedonian who had wounded the mother of a man who was up on the walls, she threw a roof tile onto Pyrrhus’s head, causing him to fall to the ground. Then a knight of Antigonus whose name was Zopyrus arrived and, taking Pyrrhus, cut off his head. Alcyoneus, the son of Antigonus, carried it with great joy to his father. Antigonus, who was a man of excellent and truly royal spirit, strongly rebuked his son and struck him, calling him a barbarian. He then took the head and body of Pyrrhus and gave him a magnificent burial.

<margin>Z</margin>
Alcyoneus, having been punished by his father, returned to the battle, where he found Helenus, the son of Pyrrhus, in mournful and very lowly clothes. He received him kindly and peacefully led him to Antigonus, to whom Antigonus said:

> "You have done better now than before, my son; but not even now well enough, for you have [not removed] <unclear>abiuieueris</unclear> this garment, which dishonors us who seem to have won more than it does him." <note>The sense is that the sight of the prince in rags shames the victor by showing the tragedy of the fallen house.</note>

Then, having embraced and kissed Helenus, he sent him back to Epirus and had him established as King of the province in place of his father. Thus the end of Pyrrhus was a shining example of both types of fortune [good and bad]. Next, Messer Francesco [Petrarch] narrates the example of King **Masinissa**, saying that after Pyrrhus followed the good King Masinissa, who was observant and seemed to feel it a wrong not to be numbered among the other Romans. Whence he says:

-> The good King Masinissa was of the mind, <-

<note>original: "L’buon re masinissa e gli era aviso, / D’esser senza i roman, receuer torto." These lines are from Petrarch's *Trionfo della Fama* (Triumph of Fame), Canto II.</note>

<margin>A</margin>
¶ **M**asinissa, as is seen in Titus Livy in the ninth book of the third decade, was the son of Gala, King of the Massylii. Upon his father's death, he succeeded to the kingdom. During this time, Syphax, King of the Masaesyli, having returned to the side of the Carthaginians <term>for</term> <note>original shorthand: "p̄" (per/pro)</note> the sake of having taken the aforementioned Sophonisba as his wife, defeated Masinissa and drove him from his kingdom. Because of this, Masinissa, an exile and very poor, came to the camp of Scipio Africanus; having been kindly received by him, he was made a leader of part of the army. From then on, because of this noble courtesy, Masinissa became such a partisan and friend to Scipio that he loved nothing else as much as he did Scipio alone. Therefore, Masinissa, having been received into the trust of the Romans, proceeded primarily with Scipio against Hanno, son of Barca, and killed him along with a very great number of Carthaginians. Furthermore, proceeding against Hasdrubal, son of Gisgo, he overcame him and drove him from the field, taking the spoils of his lodgings. Afterwards, as the Punic War continued, Masinissa went together with Gaius Laelius against his enemy Syphax, whom he overcame and defeated, taking him prisoner. In that same campaign they also took Cirta, his principal city, and Masinissa took Sophonisba as his wife, with 그 result that we narrated above <note>Sophonisba committed suicide by drinking poison sent by Masinissa to prevent her from being led in a Roman triumph.</note>. For this reason, Masinissa’s kingdom was restored to him, where he lived for a long time in peace, except that over border disputes he first went to judgment with the Carthaginians, and then to a fair war, which he manfully won, as Livy writes in the fifth decade, in the seventh and eighth books, according to the account of Florus. Masinissa later died at the age of ninety-two; and after he was eighty-six, he fathered a son, as Solinus and Titus Livy write in the aforementioned decade and in the last book. At his death, Masinissa left his three living sons—namely Micipsa, Gulussa, and Mastanabal—under the protection of the Romans, requesting that the division of their inheritance be made according to the judgment and will of Scipio Aemilianus. ¶ The benevolence of Masinissa toward the Romans, and especially toward the Scipios, was as great as Cicero describes in the *Dream of Scipio* when he introduces Scipio Aemilianus as having come to Masinissa in his kingdom; having embraced him, Masinissa said these worthy words:
> I give thanks to you, O highest Sun, and to you other heavenly beings, that before I depart from this life I behold in my kingdom and within these roofs Publius Cornelius Scipio, by whose very name I am refreshed; thus never from my soul does the memory of that most excellent and unconquered man depart. <note>original: "Grates tibi ago o summe sol .uobiſq reliq celites q antequā ex hac vita migro conſpicio i meo regno: & his tectis Publium Cornelium ſcipionem cuius ego ipſe noīe recreor: itaq nunquam ex aio me diſcedit illius optimi atq inuictiſſimi viri memoria." This is a famous passage from Cicero’s *Somnium Scipionis*.</note>

<margin>B</margin>
This same benevolence is likewise seen throughout the context of Livy... <note>The text here becomes slightly fragmented or refers to specific commentary structures</note> where Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> fittingly introduces Masinissa as appearing to "suffer a wrong" by not being counted alongside his Romans, whom he loved so much. Consequently, Master Francesco brings forward the example of Hiero of Syracuse, saying that as he looked fixedly here and there around Masinissa, he saw Hiero of Syracuse with him. Whence he says:

<margin>C</margin>
¶ **H**iero of Syracuse was the son of Hierocles, a noble citizen throughout all Sicily, who by ancient lineage descended from Gelon, the most ancient lord of Sicily. This Hiero, being born of a handmaiden, was rejected by his father and exposed to death as someone ignoble and as one who obscured his genealogy. Thus, while this boy was small and had no one to nourish him, a swarm of bees for several days poured honey into his mouth and, surrounding him, they nourished him. Because of this, the augurs told the father that he should raise him, for he was destined to be a most worthy king of Sicily. Once Hiero grew up and became most beautiful of body and adorned with virtue, he gave himself to the exercise of arms; thus, fighting many times in single combat, he always remained the victor. For this, he was distinguished by Pyrrhus, King of the Epiroti, with many military gifts and other ornaments. After Pyrrhus departed from Sicily, the Carthaginians moved a most cruel war; thus Hiero was first made a general against them, and afterwards, by universal consent, King of all Sicily, as Trogus shows <term>and</term> <note>original shorthand: "z" (et)</note> Justin reports in the twenty-third book of *Foreign Wars*. ¶ Following this, during the First Punic War between the Romans and the Carthaginians, Hiero, being on the side of the Carthaginians, was defeated by Appius Claudius; whence...

...thereafter he [Hiero II] always remained steadfast in his love and faith toward the Roman Republic. But Hiero <note>The text likely refers to Hieronymus of Syracuse, the grandson and successor of Hiero II, who abandoned the Roman alliance for Carthage.</note>, his son, was unlike his father, being wicked and stubborn, as Livy writes in the second decade and the fourth book. Just as he was the opposite of his father in virtue, so too was he in his actions, for he was always a manifest enemy to the Romans; and for his vices, he soon received his due reward, for he was cruelly killed by his own people, as was fitting. Afterward, the poet adds, saying that after Hiero he saw the cruel Hamilcar, who was very different from him and Masinissa in his goodwill toward the people of Rome. Therefore he says:

-> and the cruel <-

<margin>
E
To provide a clearer understanding of the preceding example, it should be understood that although there was always the greatest enmity between the Romans and the Carthaginians, no Carthaginian ever showed it as much as Hamilcar and his son Hannibal.
</margin>

Wherefore, as Valerius writes in the ninth book, third chapter: Hamilcar, having four sons—namely Hannibal, Hanno, Hasdrubal, and Mago—said he was nursing four lion cubs for the destruction and ruin of the Roman Empire. And as they reached their ninth year of age, he made them swear upon the altar in the temple to have perpetual hatred against the city of Rome. Nor did he show himself an enemy to the Romans in this act alone, but also in public speeches and military expeditions. For in the first Punic War, he was the commander of the fleet <term>fleet</term> <note>original: "classe"</note> against the Romans, although he was surpassed and defeated by Atilius Calatinus, as we said above. For this reason, our Master Francesco [Petrarch] has described him in this place as excellently divided and separated from Masinissa and Hiero. Nevertheless, some texts are found that say Hamilcar was *not* very different from them, which can be explained by the poet mentioning the physical distance in the procession of Fame. Next, our poet narrates that after Hamilcar, through his presence, he saw how King Croesus of Lydia emerged naked from the midst of the fire; and having understood through a manifest example how little a shield avails against Fortune, he says:

<margin>
F
While Belshazzar, son of Nebuchadnezzar, was reigning in Babylon, and God was angry with him for having profaned the vessels of the temple of God at the banquet he gave for his satraps and nobles, as Daniel writes in the fifth chapter...
</margin>

-> I saw him who once emerged naked from the fire, <-
-> The King of Lydia: a manifest example, <-
-> That a shield avails little against Fortune. <-

At this time, according to Eusebius and William of Nangis in his *Chronicles* <term>Chronicles</term> <note>original: "libris temporum"</note>, Cyrus, King of Persia, came against the Babylonians, to whom Croesus sent aid. As Herodotus, the very grave Greek historian, writes, Croesus sent to various oracles to ask what his future would be if he took up war against the Persians, and if his empire was to be long-lasting. Among these oracles, the one of Apollo in Greece replied with these verses: *When a mule shall sit upon the throne of the Medes, then, O sturdy Lydian, flee across the pebbly Hermus; do not stay, and do not be ashamed of being a coward.* <note>original Latin translation of the Greek oracle: "Regis apud medos mulo iam sede potito. Tunc scrupofum fugere hermium strenue lide Nec per stare: nec ignauum te esse pudendum." The "mule" refers to Cyrus the Great, who was of mixed Persian and Median descent.</note> Hearing this response, Croesus was filled with the greatest joy, thinking his empire would be perpetual, considering that a mule cannot rule in place of a man. For this reason, with a large army and a great quantity of gold, he went to Babylon to help. Cyrus, therefore, having captured Babylon and killed Belshazzar, and Croesus having fled and returned to Lydia, Cyrus proceeded against him and, fighting with him, surpassed and defeated him. Whereupon Croesus fled to a city called Sardis, which Cyrus besieged. 

Croesus had a son who was excellent in every way, except that he was mute. Having tried many medicines to make him speak to no avail, he finally sent to the Oracle of Apollo asking for his favor so that he might speak. To which Apollo replied in this form: *O King Croesus, of the Lydian race, ruler of many, you have desired much to hear the voice of your son speaking; but it would be far better for you to be without that voice in your house, for on that unhappy day he shall first speak.* <note>original: "Lide genus rex multorum ualde iscie crese e curã gnati exoptatam audisse loquentis: intra edes uocem sine qua potior tibi longe. Ille die quoniam primum infelice loquetur"</note> This predicted unhappiness befell Croesus. For seeing one day Hyroiades the Mardian, a very brave soldier of Cyrus, descending from the citadel of Sardis, and taking note of the path, he entered the land with a great quantity of Persians and took it. When they reached the palace, not recognizing Croesus, they were about to kill him. Then the mute son, out of fear and pity, said: *Man, do not kill Croesus!* <note>original: "Homo ne perimas cresum"</note> And according to Solinus, he spoke saying: *Spare my father Croesus, O Cyrus, and learn to be a good man from our misfortunes.* <note>original: "Parce patri creso cyre: z boiem te casibus disce nostris"</note> Because of this, Croesus was not killed then but

<header>CHAPTER THREE</header>

## CHAPTER THREE

<margin>G</margin>
Taken prisoner. Cyrus, therefore, having Croesus as his prisoner—and because it was said that Croesus had been a religious man—wished either to offer the first fruits of the spoils, or to fulfill a vow, or perhaps to test whether any divine spirit would deliver Croesus. He thus had him seized and stripped naked, and along with him thirteen other Lydians. He had him placed upon a great pyre, and then ordered the fire to be lit beneath it. 

Now, while Croesus still considered himself happy in his kingdom, he had many times asked Solon the Athenian which man seemed to him to be truly blessed. To this, Solon had replied: Cleobis and Biton, the sons of the Argive priestess; and Tellus the Athenian, who, being fortunate in all other things, died gloriously in a battle the Athenians fought near Eleusis <note>Original: "Ensino," likely a corruption of Eleusis</note> against their neighbors; he was buried there publicly and magnificently. Croesus, marvelling that he did not seem happy to Solon, said to him:

<margin>H</margin>
> "Athenian guest, is our happiness so utterly despised by you that you do not even consider us equal to private citizens?" <note>original: "Hospes atheniensis adeo ne tibi pro nullis contennitur nostra felicitas: vt ne priuatis qdem viris nos equarandos ducas."</note> 

To which Solon replied in this manner: "O Croesus, you ask me about human affairs, yet I know that every deity is envious and seeks to disturb our lives. In a long span of time, one sees much that no one wishes to see, and many things are suffered that one would rather not endure. We set the limit of a man’s life at seventy years. These years consist of twenty-five thousand and two hundred days, not counting the intercalary month <note>An extra month added periodically to the calendar to keep it aligned with the solar year.</note>. But if you wish for certain years to be longer because of this month, so that the seasons occur when they should, then there will be twenty-five such intercalary months over seventy years, adding five hundred days. Of all these days—which over seventy years number twenty-six thousand, two hundred and fifty—not one brings exactly the same experience as another. Thus, Croesus, man is entirely a creature of chance. 

Indeed, you seem to me to be very powerful in wealth and the king of many men. But I cannot yet call you what you asked me to call you until I hear that you have ended your life well. For the man of great riches is no more blessed than he who has enough for his daily needs, unless fortune grants him the grace to die well while still possessing all those goods. Many men are very wealthy yet not at all happy, while many who have only a modest inheritance are fortunate. Of these, the one who flows with wealth but is not happy excels the fortunate man in only two things, but the fortunate man excels the rich one in many. The rich man is better able to satisfy his desires and to endure a great misfortune if it falls upon him. The fortunate man, though lower in those two respects, excels because he has no experience of such evils; he enjoys good health, is free from misfortune, is the parent of good children, and is handsome. If, in addition to these things, he ends his life rightly, he is the one worthy of being called 'blessed.' But before he reaches his end, he should not be called blessed, only fortunate—for it is impossible for a human to possess all these things at once. Just as no single land provides everything for itself, but having one thing lacks another, and that land is best which possesses the most, so it is with the human body; no one is complete, for having one thing, it lacks another. Whoever possesses the most of these things continually, and then departs from life with a peaceful mind, he is the one who, in my judgment, deserves to be gifted with this title. One must look to the end of everything, to see how it will turn out; for God has utterly uprooted many to whom he had granted great fortunes."

<margin>I</margin>
Croesus, therefore, seeing himself placed in such great calamity and already feeling the great heat of the fire, remembered this judgment. Approving of it within himself, he cried out three times in a loud voice: "O Solon!" 

Hearing this, Cyrus, who was nearby, had him asked through interpreters what he was calling out. Croesus remained silent at the first asking, but to the second he replied: "I would rather have given a vast sum of money than that he [Solon] should speak to all tyrants as he spoke to me." The interpreters, not understanding this confused saying, forced him to speak more clearly. 

Whereupon Croesus said: "It is as if Solon, having seen all my riches, had despised them and said to me, and to all other men—and especially those who think themselves blessed—how great their folly is; for while one lives, one should not believe oneself to be happy." And so, finding himself in this misery and proving Solon's true judgment, he called the king as if he were an oracle. 

Cyrus, having understood through the interpreters what Croesus had said to them, and judging it to be true—and considering that in human life nothing can be stable—immediately commanded that the fire be extinguished and Croesus be taken down from the high pyre. But the fire had already reached the edges where Croesus was, and it could not be put out by human strength. Thereupon, Croesus, seeing by his gestures the good will of Cyrus, prayed to Apollo that if any gift he had ever offered had been accepted, the god should save him from such misfortune. 

> "Hear, Apollo, the piteous voice of Croesus." 

Immediately, even though the sky was perfectly clear, such a great abundance of water fell that the fire was totally extinguished. Croesus then descended from the pyre and was brought before Cyrus. Cyrus questioned him in this way: "Croesus, who among men persuaded you to invade my land with an army, becoming an enemy instead of a friend?" 

To which Croesus replied: "O King, I did this through your prosperous fate and my own unhappy one, at the urging of the Greek god, who impelled me to bring war upon you. For no one is so mad that he prefers war over peace."

<summary>King Croesus of Lydia is captured by Cyrus and nearly burned alive, only to be saved by the wisdom of Solon and a miraculous rainstorm from Apollo. The narrative emphasizes that true happiness cannot be judged until the end of a person's life.</summary>

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

...he should prefer; for in peace, sons bury their fathers, but in war, fathers bury their sons. <note>original: "nam in pace filii patres. in bello patres filios sepeliunt"</note> But for these things to happen, it was necessary for the demon <note>The author likely means "fate" or "fortune" here</note> to be satisfied. Therefore, Cyrus pardoned him [Croesus] entirely and restored his whole patrimony to him, as the historian Justin writes, and gave him a city called Baragom <note>Likely referring to Barene in Media, mentioned by Justin as the city Cyrus gave to Croesus</note> where, although he did not have his former abundance, he nonetheless lived in royal luxury. <insert>¶</insert> In this state, Croesus went to the oracle in Greece, having obtained permission from Cyrus. He asked if it was permitted for the gods of Greece to be liars and ungrateful, since they had urged him to go against the Persians and said he would conquer them. [The oracle replied that] it is impossible even for a god to escape the lot destined by fate. <note>original: "sortem fato destinatam defugere contingit: deo quoque est impossibile"</note> Therefore, Croesus, no longer trusting the oracle, and seeing Cyrus occupied with another province, incited the Lydians to rebel against him. But Cyrus, coming against them once more, defeated them; he had Croesus executed on a cross, and to their perpetual ignominy, he took away their arms and horses. He ordered that in their armies they should practice only debauchery and frequent taverns; <note>original: "lenocinia & tauernæ"</note> thus their lazy treachery was rightfully punished by Cyrus. Truly, Croesus was a clear example that the shield is held in vain against the blows of Fortune. For according to the Philosopher <note>A common medieval and Renaissance reference to Aristotle</note> in the second book of the *Physics*, man is totally overcome by Fortune, which is unknown to human understanding; and Fortune was even considered a deity, as was the opinion of the Romans. Thus, Lucius Lucullus, by deliberation of the Senate, built a temple in Rome to the goddess Fortune, noting that it is in vain for humans to oppose her blows with their own shields. Our Master Francesco <note>referring to Francesco Petrarch, the author of the poem being commented upon</note> continues, saying that besides Croesus, he saw Syphax, who met with a similar example and an equal misfortune. Whence he says:

->I saw Syphax, equal in a similar ruin;<-

<margin>L</margin> <insert>¶</insert> Let Syphax, king of the Masaesyli <note>The Masaesyli were a powerful Berber tribe in western Numidia (modern-day Algeria)</note>, suffice for us. His story has been made clear in the region of Numidia through many examples narrated above in the chapter on outstanding Romans and foreigners. But who might be nearly equal to Croesus is not difficult to understand: for he [Syphax] could have remained neutral between the Carthaginians and the Romans, or later preserved himself in Roman goodwill. By either action, he could have worthily maintained himself in royal life until the end of his days. Nevertheless, he wished to test Fortune by taking the side of the Carthaginians, persuaded only by the beauty of his Sophonisba. <note>Sophonisba was a Carthaginian noblewoman whose influence led Syphax to switch allegiances from Rome to Carthage</note> Thus it happened, as Livy writes in the tenth book of the third decade, that Syphax, having joined his African armies with his father-in-law Hasdrubal and coming to battle with Gaius Laelius and Masinissa, was surpassed and defeated along with the Carthaginians. He remained a prisoner and was led by C. Laelius to Rome before the Senate. He was condemned to the prison at Alba, where, living miserably in great ignominy, he was led to his death. Following this, Master Francesco adds that he saw Brennus, under whose leadership and auspices many people fell, and who later met his death beneath the Delphic temple. Whence he says:

->Brennus; under whom many people fell,<-
->And then he fell under the famous temple,<-

<margin>M</margin> <insert>¶</insert> Regarding the knowledge of the preceding verses, one should know (as Justin writes in book 23 of *The Foreign Wars*) that the population in Gaul had multiplied so much that the province could not sustain them. For this reason, they decided to go and conquer more homelands and countries by means of arms. Therefore, part of them came into Italy in the time of Camillus, as Livy writes in the fifth book *From the Founding of the City* and as we said above. Another part, following the omen of birds, went into Illyricum. Just as they had subjugated the Scordisci, they then passed into Hungary; taking it likewise for some time, they rested there. But as they multiplied once more, they went out again to acquire more regions. Some of them went to Greece, and some came into Macedonia. All the peoples there bought them off with money, except Ptolemy, King of Macedonia <note>Ptolemy Keraunos</note>, who turned to defend himself against them. Moreover, when the Dardanians offered him help, he despised them, trusting too much in himself. He did not even want there to be twenty thousand armed men. Consequently, he came to battle with Belgius, who was the leader of this part of the Gauls; he was quickly overcome and killed by him. Brennus, then, the other leader of the Gauls, hearing of Belgius's victory, departed from Greece in indignation and came into Macedonia himself to plunder...

In a short time, he [Brennus] overcame and conquered them; thus they were forced to flee into the land and defend the walls where Brennus had set up camp around them. While he was thus engaged in the siege of Macedonia, Brennus—being most greedy for plunder and lacking all religious scruple—deliberated on going to rob the temple of Apollo. The temple of Apollo, together with the city of Delphi, was situated atop Mount Parnassus, where great cliffs and deep heights surround it in such a way that the nature of the place provides no less wonder than the majesty of the temple itself. When Brennus arrived in that region, the people of the country left a great quantity of provisions in the villages, estimating—as indeed happened—that the Gauls would linger so long over that prey that the locals would have the opportunity to send for help from their friends. Having thus worked to multiply their defenders and trusting in the god Apollo, they went out to battle with Brennus. While the fight was at its most fervent, there appeared visibly a young man of marvelous beauty in the midst of two virgins, who came out of the temple of Diana and Minerva with bows in their hands. They proceeded before the Delphians, and as they fought, a massive hailstorm came down from the air, by which the Gauls were finally overcome. Brennus, having been wounded in the battle and feeling grievous pain, killed himself with a dagger in despair. **Diverse in dress.** For a greater and clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it should primarily be known how Messer Francesco says this host was "diverse in dress" to show that in this chapter he has spoken of various nations together: namely, Greeks, Barbarians, and Jews. Just as their regions are distinct, so too are their clothing and their deeds diverse. Secondly, it is to be understood that, as Messer Francesco is now to speak of the Jews, he says this group of men who followed in fame was "collected only within itself" to demonstrate that their renown and the glory attributed to them proceeded only from their own authors. This is because Justin <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian.</note> and the other writers who describe them and their origins all detract from their excellence. Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> laments this thing at the beginning of the book he wrote *On the Jewish War*. He says he wishes to speak of it because other writers have written either out of deference to the Romans or out of hatred borne against the Jews, contrary to faith and the truth of matters. Herein he reproves them and affirms that they diminish the dignity of the Romans, saying: <note>original: "Nam dum Romanos volunt magnos ostendere: iudeorum res extetenuant: & in humilitatem deyiciunt. Non autē itelligo quo nã pacto magni esse videant q parua supauerint."</note> "For while they wish to show the Romans to be great, they diminish the affairs of the Jews and cast them into lowliness. I do not understand, however, by what logic they appear great who have overcome small things." From this, it is manifest that the Jews were made famous through their own accounts.

### TRIUMPH OF FAME

...prophecy communicated to him by God: but in the exercise of arms and other noble deeds, he can be well known through the accounts in the First and Second Books of Kings <note>In many older traditions, the Books of Samuel were referred to as 1 and 2 Kings.</note> and in Chronicles, beginning at the tenth chapter. There, once the attacks made against him by Saul had ceased upon Saul's death, and David having been raised to the royal heights by all
<margin>Q</margin> Israel, he came toward the land of the Jebusites <note>The original inhabitants of Jerusalem before David's conquest.</note>, who were unwilling to receive him. ¶ David sent out a proclamation that whoever should defeat them would be made the leader of his military; for which reason Joab shortly overcame and conquered them. David chose that stronghold—which was called Zion—for the site of his dwelling; wherefore Zion was ever after called the house and the city of David. After this victory, David chose thirty most valiant men as his fellow soldiers and companions, through whom he always achieved great and glorious victories. Thus he conquered and overcame the Philistines, the Assyrians, those of Rabbah, and many other peoples described in the cited places. David then, having brought the Ark of the Covenant into Jerusalem and having constructed and built many houses—and especially his own most worthy one made of cedar wood, which had been given to him by Hiram <note>original: "Furom," a variation of Hiram.</note>, King of Tyre—felt a prick of conscience and called Nathan the prophet to him and said: "Behold, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord is under curtains" <note>original: "Ecce habito in domo cedrina. Archa autem foederis domini sub pellibus est." The text reads "sub pedibus" (under feet), likely a transcription error for "sub pellibus" (under skins/curtains).</note>. To which Nathan replied then, saying: "Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you." But later that night, God appeared in a vision to Nathan and told him to announce on His behalf that David should not build Him a house; for He had decreed that one of David's sons should be the one to build the temple He desired. Wherefore in Chronicles 17 and in 2 Kings, the text speaks in the person of God to David: "I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come forth from your body, and I will establish his kingdom; he shall build a house for my name, and I will establish his throne
<margin>R</margin> forever; I will be his father, and he shall be my son" <note>original: "Suscitabo semen tuum post te: qui egredietur de utero tuo: et firmabo regnum eius: ipse edificabit domum nomini meo: et stabiliam thronum eius usque in sempiternum: et ego ero ei in patrem: et ipse erit mihi in filium."</note>. ¶ This matter, according to the letter regarding the building of the marble temple, was fulfilled in Solomon, the son of David and of Bathsheba, who was the wife of Uriah. But according to the allegory and divine mind, the aforementioned text was fulfilled when the Divine Word, the true Son of God, established the glorious body of the Virgin Mary as a temple, when she immediately replied to the testimony of the Angel Gabriel: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word" <note>original: "Ecce ancilla domini fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum."</note>, as is written in the first chapter of Saint Luke. ### CHAPTER THREE

<margin>T</margin> ...a vestibule and a portico twenty cubits long and of a similar width. The woodwork inside the building was all made of cedar, and the whole was constructed and composed of stone of great dimensions, finished with a chisel. Inside, there was a most abundant fountain of water; there was also a surplus supplied by aqueducts, through which the blood of the animals offered in the Jewish sacrifices was washed away. Its facade faced toward the East and the rear toward the West, as Aristeas writes in the *Book on the Interpretation of the Jewish Law* <note>original: "lib. de īterpretatiõe iudaice legis"; a reference to the Letter of Aristeas, a Hellenistic work describing the Septuagint's origins and the Temple.</note>. This was the form and noble composition given by Solomon to the noble Temple of God. ¶ However, Solomon was not such an "architect" within himself as he was in this building of his own design and labor; for in the third Book of Kings <note>In the modern Bible, this is 1 Kings 11.</note> at the eleventh chapter, we read that Solomon sinned through luxury and idolatry, and died in anger without ever performing any penance. Thus, he did not know how to build his own soul in divine obedience; for which reason he was deservedly judged by our poet <note>Petrarch</note> not to be as great an architect of his soul as he was of the Temple outside. The poet then continues and enumerates those whom he saw following in fame behind Solomon, saying that he then saw the one who was so familiar with God that he spoke with Him face to face. In this, no one else in the world could boast more. Whence he says:

<margin>V</margin> > *Then he who was so familiar with God,*
> *That he spoke with Him face to face in grace;*
> *So that no other can boast of the same:*

¶ Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> describes Moses in these verses, where it is understood that he alone among all men was the one who spoke "face to face" with God, as is written in Exodus in the thirty-second chapter <note>The text cites Chapter 32, though the famous "face to face" description is primarily in Exodus 33:11.</note>. His holiness and doctrine are demonstrated thereafter by the Sacred Scriptures, and his knowledge is declared by Virgil in the sixth <note>The author likely refers to a perceived prophecy of a savior or the Sibyl in Virgil’s works, though the connection to Moses specifically is a Renaissance interpretive tradition.</note>, by Eupolemus the Greek, and by the military exercises described in the context of the Pentateuch, as well as by Artapanus <note>Hellenistic historians who wrote about Jewish history.</note>. For this reason, it is primarily important to know that the people of Israel had multiplied so greatly in Egypt that Pharaoh, fearing them, commanded Shiphrah and Puah, the Jewish midwives, that they should kill every male child. In this time Moses was born, who was beautiful beyond measure. His mother did not wish to kill him, but kept him hidden for a period of three months. As the child grew and could no longer be hidden, his mother decided to expose him to fortune; therefore, one day she took a wicker basket, placed him inside, sealed it well, and exposed him in the river. On that day, Merris <note>A traditional name for Pharaoh’s daughter in extra-biblical accounts like those of Artapanus.</note>, the daughter of Chenefres, King of Egypt—known as Pharaoh—had come down to the river to wash herself. Seeing that little basket coming through the water, she immediately had it taken and opened. Seeing the child so beautiful, and being herself sterile, she adopted him as her son.

<margin>X</margin> ¶ When Moses had grown and become a shepherd in his youth, he was one day out on Mount Horeb. God appeared to him while he was guarding the sheep in a burning bush <term>rubro</term> <note>From the Latin *rubus*, meaning bramble or bush.</note>. God called to him and told him that the affliction of His people had moved Him to pity; therefore, He wished to liberate them from the hands of the Egyptians and lead them to the land of promise, flowing and abounding with milk and honey, which was held by the Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, and Jebusites. He told Moses that He had elected him as prince and leader; therefore, he should go to Pharaoh and tell him on His behalf to release His people, as it was His will. Moses, having heard the words of God, excused himself and said he was not the kind of man Pharaoh would believe. To this, God replied that He would be with him and would make him perform great miracles. Thus, Moses trusted in God and went to Pharaoh, to whom he delivered the divine embassy. But Pharaoh's heart hardened further because of it, and he placed more burdens upon the people of God. Thus Moses was constrained to perform miracles; he entered into a contest with the magicians and turned his staff into a serpent. The magicians did the same, except that the serpent made from the staff of Aaron and Moses devoured all the serpents made from the staves of the magicians. Because of this, Moses was judged superior in this act. And finally, when the magicians could not drive away the <term>Cynife</term> <note>original: "Cynife," referring to the lice or gnats of the third plague, from the Latin *sciniphes*.</note> as Moses did, they confessed to Pharaoh that in all the works of Moses, divine power was operating and not magic. Nevertheless, not bending for these signs—Pharaoh's heart instead hardening much more—God struck the Egyptians with more plagues: namely, rotting boils, a very great hail, and finally the death of all the firstborn of Egypt. As Pharaoh still did not move from his obstinate purpose, God finally commanded Moses to prepare with all the people and flee. Having to depart from Egypt, the Hebrews, according to God's command, were told by Moses that everyone should ask the Egyptians for a loan of some silver or gold vessel; which thing, after they had...
