<margin>y</margin> He caused <term>Moses</term> <note>original: "Moyfes"</note> to depart with them by night and come as far as the <term>Red Sea</term> <note>original: "mare rosso"</note>. ¶ <term>Pharaoh</term>, noticing their flight, followed them with a very great number of his armed people. When the Jews were already nearby, <term>Moses</term> struck the sea with his rod, by which means twelve paths were immediately made there where the earth appeared to be dry. The people of Israel therefore passed the Red Sea through these twelve ways; where, at the crossing, <term>Pharaoh</term> arrived with the Egyptians. And seeing the open paths, he and his army entered into them; whereupon it happened that as soon as the Hebrews were out, the waters closed back up, so that the Egyptians all drowned in the sea. The Israelites having escaped such great danger, <term>Moses</term> came with the people into the deserts, where they were fed by <term>God</term> for forty years with quail and manna. And there <term>Moses</term> miraculously turned all the bitter waters into sweet. Then, leaving the desert and coming into the lands of the Amalekites, they fought with them; and while Moses prayed, the people always defeated <term>Amalek</term>. Finally, having led them according to the promise of <term>God</term> near Mount <term>Sinai</term>, <term>God</term> gave the Law to Moses upon that mountain, which He wished His people to observe. Descending then, <term>Moses</term>, and bringing that Law written on tablets, he found the people worshipping the golden calf; for which reason he was so strongly angered that, striking the tablets against the ground, he broke them into several pieces. Afterward, moved by compassion for the people, he prayed to <term>God</term> for their forgiveness; then he instituted laws regarding political life, ordained the priesthood, fashioned the Ark, constructed the tabernacle <note>original: "oratorio"</note>, and described the tribes according to the commandment of blessed <term>God</term>. And he climbed atop Mount <term>Nebo</term>, from where he beheld all the Promised Land; just as <term>God</term> had ordained, he finally died in that place at the age of 120 years. These works are made manifest through the narrative of the Sacred Scriptures in <term>Exodus</term>, <term>Leviticus</term>, <term>Numbers</term>, and <term>Deuteronomy</term>. Furthermore, notwithstanding the testimony of Sacred Scripture, the excellence of Moses is known through the writings of <term>Eusebius</term> in the ninth book of the *Preparation for the Gospel* <note>original: "p'paratione euangelica"</note>, where he introduces <term>Eupolemus</term> writing these worthy words about Moses:
> Moses was the wisest of men; he first handed down letters to the Jews, and from the Jews the Phoenicians received them. <note>original Latin: "moyfes sapientissimus homo fuit: litteras iudeis primum tradidit & a iudeis foenices acceperunt."</note> <term>Virgil</term> also manifests the doctrine of Moses in the sixth book of the <term>Aeneid</term>, describing Musaeus in the Elysian Fields—for so the Greeks call him, according to the testimony of <term>Eusebius</term> <note>A common Renaissance idea was that the legendary Greek poet Musaeus was actually Moses.</note>—as being more excellent than the others, saying these verses:
> "Look, his right hand takes some, his left others, as they feed upon the grass and sing a joyful hymn in a chorus. Amidst a fragrant laurel grove, where the mighty river Eridanus rolls through the woods from above. Here is the band of those who suffered wounds fighting for their fatherland. And those who were chaste priests while life remained; and pious poets who spoke things worthy of Apollo. Or those who refined life through the arts they discovered. And those who by their merits made others remember them. The temples of all these are bound with snow-white ribbons. The Sibyl spoke thus to them as they gathered round, and to Musaeus before all others—for a vast crowd held him in the center and looked up at him as he stood tall with his high shoulders: 'Tell us, happy souls, and you, best of poets! What region, what place holds Anchises? For this reason, he was worshipped in <term>Egypt</term> almost as a god; and because of his great learning, he was named <term>Mercury</term> <note>Identifying Moses with Hermes/Thoth, the Egyptian god of wisdom.</note> among them. Because of this, <term>Chenephres</term> <note>A legendary Egyptian king often identified in these accounts as the Pharaoh of the Oppression.</note>, moved by envy, so that Moses might die, sent him as a leader against the Ethiopians. Whereupon he, preparing the army, took the majority of the Jewish people, so that being inexperienced, they might die together with their leader Moses. Moses, therefore, took the armies and went on the expedition where he stayed for ten years; because the war lasted so long, he built a city in that place where they first sustained the onslaught of the Ethiopians, which he caused to be called <term>Hermopolis</term> after his own name. Then, having overcome the Ethiopians, he came into such great veneration among them that they all consented, to please him, to be circumcised. Moses, having then returned to <term>Chenephres</term> and being received by him with a joyful countenance, was again sent on other expeditions; and finally to Ethiopia with the body of <term>Dimeris</term> <note>Likely referring to Merris, his adoptive mother.</note>, telling him to bury her in that place. He went there and executed the command of <term>Chenephres</term>, and built a city in the name of his adoptive mother, which he named <term>Meroe</term>. Having recognized the snares of <term>Chenephres</term> during this expedition, Moses fled to <term>Arabia</term>, where he took as his wife <term>Raguelle</term> <note>Zipporah, daughter of Raguel/Jethro.</note>, daughter of the king of the province. <margin>D</margin> As the scripture of <term>Genesis</term> in the twelfth chapter teaches us, and for the understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known that after the death of <term>Terah</term> <note>original: "Thare"</note>, father of <term>Abraham</term>, in the region of <term>Canaan</term> <note>In the biblical account, Terah died in Haran, but the commentator follows a specific reading or tradition here.</note>, God appeared to Abraham and told him to leave the land of Canaan and go into the Land of Promise. This was done so as not to be killed by the Egyptians, as Sarah was beautiful and the Egyptians were lustful, and among them, adultery was considered a very grave sin. Wherefore it happened that, this order having been given, as soon as Sarah was seen in Egypt she was taken and led to <term>Pharaoh</term>. Because of this, God plagued Egypt; then Pharaoh, having learned the cause, with great goodwill returned Sarah to her beloved husband Abraham.

<margin>E</margin> When Abraham and his companion had come to <term>Bethel</term> <note>original: "Bethe-leem," likely a slip by the commentator or printer for Bethel, as per Genesis 13:3.</note>, the shepherds of Lot had a dispute with those of Abraham. Lot went then to dwell in <term>Sodom</term>, and Abraham in <term>Hebron</term>, very near the valley of <term>Mamre</term>. Then the men of Chedorlaomer took great plunder from Sodom and Gomorrah; and among the others, they took Lot, the brother <note>Historically, Lot was Abraham's nephew, but the text uses "fratello" (brother) here, as was common in older biblical translations.</note> of Abraham. One man, fleeing the battle, came to Abraham and announced to him the capture of Lot. For this reason, Abraham chose about three hundred of his servants and followed the victors until he reached them. And while he was returning with this victory, he met <term>Melchizedek</term>, a priest who blessed him and offered to God a sacrifice of bread and wine—a figure and a precursor to the sacrifice of today <note>A reference to the Christian Eucharist.</note>. For this reason, God later blessed Abraham and told him that as many should be blessed in his seed as there were stars in the sky and grains of sand on the shore of the sea: a great praise and singular fame. Truly, this was for Abraham in that time; but certainly much greater was that obedience of the <term>circumcision</term> and of the offering of <term>Isaac</term> his son to satisfy the commandment of God, as is written in Genesis in the twenty-second chapter. From this, not unworthily, Abraham has been placed with the other Hebrews to have followed the Triumph of Fame. <term>Messer Francesco</term> <note>Petrarch</note> then continues, saying that with Abraham was his son and the grandson to whom the game of the two brides was played: that is, of <term>Leah</term> and <term>Rachel</term>. Wherefore he says:

<margin>F</margin>
> **With him his son, and the grandson; for whom the game**
> **Was played of the two brides;**

<margin>F</margin> Running through the scripture of Genesis and searching for the deeds for which praise and fame may be appropriately attributed to Isaac, son of Abraham, and to <term>Jacob</term>, his grandson: the most excellent and most effective will be found to have been the having remained so firm in the divine precepts. This is especially true regarding Isaac, who, to satisfy the divine will and the paternal commandment, consented to die and to be sacrificed, as is written in Genesis in the twenty-second chapter. For such great obedience, through the conformity he had with God, he deserved to be numbered among the holy patriarchs.

<margin>G</margin> But Jacob, besides this disposition, is made famous by the deception done to <term>Esau</term> his brother: first for having taken his birthright for a bowl of lentils, and later the blessing through the counsel of <term>Rebecca</term> his mother, having feigned to be Esau by wrapping lamb skins on his hands so that he would appear hairy as Esau was, as is written in Genesis in the twenty-seventh chapter. Beyond this, the vision he had of the angels ascending and descending the ladder to heaven has greatly amplified his name; and certainly no less clear is he made by having wrestled with the angel, whence he obtained the name of <term>Israel</term>. For this reason, these two likewise should not be strangers to the Triumph of Fame. But what game or what deception it was...

Then Joseph said, "Now I see clearly that you are spies," and he had them seized and put in prison. On the third day, Joseph brought them out and said, "I intend to test whether what you have told me is true: therefore, let one of you remain here for now, and the others may depart, but on your next visit, bring me your youngest brother." Joseph said this to them because he desired to see <term>Benjamin</term>, who alone among the children born of <term>Rachel</term> <note>Jacob’s beloved wife; Joseph and Benjamin were her only two biological sons.</note> was his full brother. <term>Simeon</term> remained behind, and Joseph had the grain given to them; in their sacks, he had the pouches containing all their money hidden.

Afterward, upon opening the sacks of grain, they found the money, which caused them to marvel. Nonetheless, the necessity of eating later compelling them, <term>Judah</term> said to Jacob: "Father, give Benjamin to me and I promise you to return him." He spoke so much in the end that Jacob, with many tears, granted him his youngest son. These eleven brothers having left, when they were a short distance away, Joseph had them seized and brought before his presence, saying with a threatening face that they were ungrateful and had stolen the king's cup. They replied that this was not true, and that he should search thoroughly; if he found them at fault, he should punish them harshly.

<margin>K</margin>
Joseph then had the sacks searched, and at last, the cup was found in Benjamin's sack. Because of this, Joseph had him seized and gave the other brothers leave to go. But seeing this, Judah and the other brothers realized that because of the theft, Benjamin would have to remain as a slave. Each one for himself said they wished to stay in his place, so that Benjamin might obtain leave to go, solely for the love of their old father. But Joseph remained firm in his purpose until, finally, Judah moved Joseph’s soul with a long, weeping plea. Joseph, no longer able to contain himself as his tears were already overflowing, sent everyone else out of the hall except for his brothers and revealed himself to them. They embraced each other dearly with joyful faces. Afterward, the news spread, and Pharaoh heard that Joseph’s brothers had come to Egypt, which pleased him...

And to Joseph, by Pharaoh's command, was given the best land of the kingdom of Egypt for them to inhabit. There, worthily, the wise and chaste Joseph, by the will of God—as it is written in **Genesis, chapter 45**—lived for a little while far from his father. The poet then follows by saying that, extending his sight as far as his strength allowed, and looking beyond into a place where the eye no longer passes the sight of seeing: he saw the just king **Hezekiah** and the great and powerful, ruined **Samson**. Wherefore he says:

-> Then, extending my sight as far as I am able, <-
-> Looking toward where the eye does not pass beyond, <-
-> I saw the just Hezekiah and ruined Samson: <-

<margin>L</margin>
For a easier understanding of the preceding verses, it should primarily be known that **Hezekiah**, King of Judah, was the son of **Ahaz** and **Abijah**, daughter of Zechariah, son of Berechiah: and he was among all the kings of Judea one of the most just and most excellent that were among them in those times; wherefore, as a testimony of his goodness, Holy Scripture says in **2 Kings, chapter 18**, having spoken of him:

> Therefore, after him there was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor among those who were before him; he clung to the Lord and did not depart from his footsteps, and he kept the mandates which the Lord commanded Moses; wherefore the Lord was with him, and in all things to which he went forth he acted wisely. <note>original: "Itaq; post eũ non fuit similis ei de cunctis regibus Iuda: sed neq; in iis qui ante fuere & adhaesit domino: & non recessit a vestigijs eius: fecitq; mandata quae preceperat dominus Moysi vnde & erat cū eo dominus & i cūctis ad q̄ pcedebat sapiẽter se hēbat."</note>

This man, then, in the beginning of his reign, destroyed the idols and the **Bronze Serpent** <term>Bronze Serpent</term> <note>The Nehushtan, a copper snake made by Moses (Numbers 21) to heal the Israelites, which had eventually become an object of idolatrous worship.</note> of Moses, which he made for the health of the people when the Hebrews were infested by cruel serpents in the desert by the way of the Red Sea; at which, whoever looked was saved—as is written in **Numbers, chapter 21**—as a sign and <term>figure</term> <note>In biblical commentary, a "figure" or "type" is an Old Testament person or event that foreshadows a New Testament reality, in this case, the Crucifixion.</note> of those who would look upon the crucified Christ to receive true salvation. He crushed this serpent because the Jews were still offering incense to it, through which they all fell into idolatry. Afterward, Hezekiah, knowing it was not fitting for the people of God to be subject to another foreigner, rebelled against King **Sennacherib** who ruled the Assyrians, under whom the Jews had been subjugated for a long time. Beyond this, he fought the **Philistines**, overcame and conquered them, and drove them from their region. But Sennacherib, hearing of King Hezekiah's rebellion, came against him in the region of Judah, taking many lands, so much so that Hezekiah was forced to pay him tribute. But Sennacherib, not content with the tribute, sent three ambassadors to Jerusalem, whose names were **Tartan**, **Rabsaris**, and **Rabshakeh**, who told the people they should not trust in their God, nor even in Hezekiah, who was deceiving them; but that they should surrender to him before they had to experience his power.

<margin>M</margin>
Hezekiah, having heard this embassy, wept and clothed himself in sackcloth and sent **Eliakim**, his palace master, and **Shebna** his scribe to **Isaiah**, son of Amoz the prophet, to ask him to pray to God for his people, because the time of tribulation had come. Isaiah replied that he should not fear, but trust in God and go out to battle. Having received this response, Hezekiah did as the prophet told him. Wherefore he made it known to the ambassadors that he was ready to fight, which they reported to Sennacherib. Again, he wrote to Hezekiah that he should not trust in this false hope which he judged to be from his God if he wished to find mercy with him. Nevertheless, having received the letters, Hezekiah stood firm in his good purpose and made a devout prayer to God. Then, the armies having met for battle, and the day of the battle being set, the night before, the **Angel of the Lord** came against the Assyrians and killed 185,000 men. Seeing this in the morning, Sennacherib fled to Assyria, and Hezekiah was delivered from this trouble. After this victory, Hezekiah became sick unto death; wherefore he devoutly wept and commended himself to God. Moved to compassion, God sent Isaiah to him to say that on the third day he would be healed and that He had added fifteen years to the appointed time of his life. Afterward, Hezekiah lived peacefully in his kingdom and happily slept with his fathers.

<margin>N</margin>
Who **Samson** was and how he acted in most parts was largely narrated above in the *Triumph of Love*. Therefore, to repeat it further would be judged quite superfluous. Finally, it should be noted that although the verse *Looking toward where the eye does not pass beyond* is said by many to signify the great antiquity of He-

### CHAPTER THREE

Nevertheless, I believe the poet held a higher concept: that is, when looking into the **Fourth Book of Kings** <note>In the Latin Vulgate, 1 and 2 Kings are titled 3 and 4 Kings; this refers to 2 Kings in modern Bibles.</note>. Where the vision extends no further than the literal historical sense—neither moral, nor allegorical, nor anagogical <note>Anagogical interpretation relates to the spiritual or mystical sense of scripture regarding the afterlife.</note> senses being applied—he saw **Hezekiah** from the 17th to the 21st chapter. Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> narrates afterwards, saying that on this side of Hezekiah and Samson, he saw the one who made the ark so large and also that other one who constructed and built the tall and immense **Tower of Babel**, which was so burdened with sin and error. Thus he says:

->**On this side of him, he who made the great ark**<-
->**And he who then began the great tower**<-
->**Which was so burdened with sin and error:**<-

<margin>O</margin>
After the highest God—not constrained by any reason but through immense and infinite liberality—deigned to create the world and man within it; human wickedness having multiplied after the sin of our first parents, God was moved to anger and decided to send the flood upon the earth, as is written in **Genesis, chapter 6**. For which reason God called **Noah** to himself and told him to build an ark, etc., fifty cubits wide and thirty in height, and that he should enter into it with his whole family and also place there the male and female of every kind of animal. Noah obeyed God and thus constructed the ark and entered it with his family and all the animals. Then God sent the flood upon the earth, where it rained for forty continuous days and the floodgates of heaven were opened, and every living soul upon the earth died, except those whom Noah saved. Noah, recognizing then that the waters had diminished and the dry earth was revealed—after the dove sent out by him a second time brought back in its beak a green olive leaf—sent out from the ark to their own homes every animal, and God blessed them all, saying: **"Increase and multiply and fill the earth"** <note>original: "Crescite & multiplicamini & replete terram"</note>. Thus, giving effort to generation, Noah afterwards restored the world.

<margin>P</margin>
Noah had three sons: namely **Shem, Ham, and Japheth**. From Ham were born several sons, among whom was **Cush**, and from Cush was born **Nimrod** <note>Original: "Mebroth"</note>, who was robust and strong in body and began to be powerful and desire to rule. Having then arrived with the sons of Japheth in the plain of **Shinar** <note>Original: "fenaar"</note>, Nimrod, in order to rule, told the sons of Japheth that they should make bricks from the earth and build a city and a tower whose summit would reach the stars. The sons of Japheth consented and began to build, and the tower having already risen to a certain height, God wished to confound the pride of Nimrod. Since there was then only one language and only one idiom, God confused it and divided it into many languages. Wherefore, in their work, one did not understand the other, and thus it was necessary that the tower cease from proceeding further. And because of this confusion of languages, it was later called the **Tower of Babel**. Beyond the previously narrated deeds, it is to be understood for a greater knowledge of the preceding verses that the poet does not say these two were "on this side" of Hezekiah because they did not precede him in time, but because he <note>Hezekiah</note> preceded them in fame and renown, they being known only for a single deed, while he was known for many diverse ones.

<margin>Q</margin>
Lastly, it is to be noted that the Tower of Babel was laden with sin and error because it was established through pride from its beginning, and because the architects thought they could penetrate the second region of the air, which is extremely cold, and the sphere of fire, and the third region of the air, which is extremely hot—all of which was impossible. Likewise, it was laden with error because of the confusion of languages; for the workers, not understanding one another, then erred in all their work. Master Francesco then adds the famous and outstanding Maccabee, saying that he then saw that good **Judas** from whom the paternal laws could not be taken, walking in his sight bold and undefeated, like a man who voluntarily runs to his death for the sake of observing a just desire. Thus he says:

->**Then that good Judas, from whom no one could take**<-
->**His paternal laws; undefeated and bold,**<-
->**Like a man who runs to death for justice**<-

## THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

He <note>Referring to King Antiochus IV Epiphanes</note> also willed and granted, beyond the profanation of the Temple of Solomon, that the Jews should abandon their first laws and worship idols. Because many were unwilling to do this, they were butchered by his ministers and killed with various tortures. Seeing this, **Judas Maccabeus** and his brothers—the sons of **Mattathias** the priest—deliberated with their father to pursue the defense of their region. Whereupon Judas succeeded to the leadership after the death of his father Mattathias, who, while he lived, had killed the ministers of Antiochus and a Jew who had consented to them; he exhorted the people of Israel to join him in seeking vengeance for their original liberty and life. He organized them into the form of a main army and proceeded against **Apollonius**, the prince of Samaria, with whom he came to battle and killed him with a very great slaughter of his Samaritans. Having then obtained this victory, it was announced to Judas how **Seron**, a commander of the Syrian army, was coming against Israel; for which reason Judas went against him, and having comforted his men—who were hungry and fasting—with prudent words, he descended into the second battle. In this battle, Seron was defeated and killed, and his whole army was dispersed. And so, in a brief and continuous time, Judas obtained these two glorious victories.

Antiochus, having heard the fame of Judas and the destruction of his own men, decided to take revenge to the best of his power. For this reason, he gathered a very large force of armies; then, seeing that there was not enough money in his treasury to be sufficient, he went into Persia to gather more from them, and left a noble man named **Lysias**, of royal lineage, to govern his kingdom. Lysias, having remained in the kingdom, chose three leaders: namely **Ptolemy**, **Nicanor**, and **Gorgias**, and sent them against the Jews with eight thousand cavalry and forty thousand other combatants. He commanded them to burn and destroy the region of Judea. When these men had arrived near the army of the Jews, Gorgias took five thousand men for himself and came by night to assault Judas, who stood alone with three thousand for the defense of Israel. Judas, hearing of this plan, prepared himself and in the morning proceeded against Gorgias, and defeated him and turned him to flight, following him even to the other army; finding that army in disorder, he likewise defeated and conquered it. Returning with victory, he sent to Jerusalem—even though the greater part of it had been burned—to offer at the Temple twelve thousand silver drachmas for the souls of those who had died in the preceding battles. <note>This refers to 2 Maccabees 12:43, where Judas makes an offering for the fallen; the text here uses the figure of 12,000.</note>

Lysias heard the news of Judas's victory and of the flight and great slaughter of his own; for which reason, the following year, he decided to take revenge. Whence he came against Judas with five thousand cavalry and sixty thousand combatants. Judas, having seen this multitude and being not at all frightened, made a prayer to God and fought with Lysias and overcame and conquered him. Having obtained this victory, Judas returned to Jerusalem and rebuilt it in part, and purified the Temple from the defilements made by Antiochus. While they were in this state, the neighboring peoples, hearing that they had erected the altar and continued their accustomed ceremonies, conspired against them. But Judas, the glorious victor, conquered and overcame them all; among others, **Timothy**, who was the leader of the children of Ammon. He took many of their cities for himself, and among others, the city of **Ephron** and **Scythopolis**. He also conquered the treacherous sons of Esau <note>The Edomites</note>; and for several months they rested in peace. At this time, Antiochus of Syria died and was succeeded by **Demetrius Soter**, his brother <note>Historically his nephew</note> and son of the elder Antiochus, who also wished to make war with the Jews. But Judas conquered him; and for a time they composed a feigned peace. Afterward, Demetrius sent King Nicanor against Judas; he came to deceive him under the guise of peace. In the end, they fought together, where Judas and his brothers performed marvelous feats of arms, especially **Eleazar** against the elephants, killing them, which was considered a miracle. In the end, Nicanor was defeated and killed; and his head, along with his shoulder and tongue, was carried to Jerusalem by the command of Judas.

<margin>T</margin>
Judas then made a confederance with the Romans, having heard of their good fame. Regarding this confederance, Demetrius, King of Syria, moved war against Judas anew and sent two captains against him: one named **Alcimus** and the other **Bacchides**. Whereupon Judas, having prepared for defense, went against them; and while fighting and driving back the army of Bacchides, in the end, Judas was killed in battle. His death was worthily avenged by his brothers **Simon** and **Jonathan** with a great shedding of Syrian blood.

Then **Master Francesco** <note>Petrarch</note> adds, saying that after the sight of so many and such excellent men, his desire to see and understand was nearly exhausted, until a beautiful sight made him much more eager to look than he had ever been before. For he saw in a row and rank several outstanding women, among whom was **Antiope** and the beautiful, armed **Orithyia**; **Hippolyta**, sad and afflicted for her son Hippolytus, and also **Menalippe**—all queens of the Amazon kingdom. Each one was in appearance most slender and noble, so expert in arms that it was a glory for the great **Hercules** to have conquered them, when as a prize for victory, he took one sister and **Theseus** took the other. Whence he <note>Petrarch</note> says:

<margin>V</margin>
For a more rapid understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known that the women of Scythia <note>An ancient region in Eurasia</note> took up arms (as we said above in the *Triumph of Chastity*) following the loss of their husbands. They established their first two queens: Marpesia and Lampedo. While they reigned, they occupied much territory in Europe and part of Asia, where they founded Ephesus along with many other cities. Marpesia remained in those parts to guard their dominion and rule, while the others returned with glory to their kingdom. 

<margin>X</margin>
This Marpesia was killed by an onslaught of barbarians, along with a great number of her maidens. Therefore, Orithia succeeded her in the kingdom; she was to be preferred above all others for her military discipline and supreme chastity. At this time, when the other queen Lampedo died, Orithia’s sister, named Antiope, was elected in her place. Antiope remained in the kingdom, while Orithia went abroad conducting wars.

<margin>X</margin>
Through the virtue of these two excellent queens, the **Amazons** <note>A legendary tribe of warrior women</note> achieved such a high reputation that King Eurystheus, becoming envious of their glory, commanded **Hercules** to go and conquer them. When Hercules arrived in the kingdom where Antiope was—who at that time suspected nothing of war—he found her without defenses. With little battle or resistance, he captured her. There, **Menalippe** (the queen’s sister) and **Hippolita** were also taken. Hercules took the first one [Menalippe] but restored her to her sister in exchange for the queen’s armor.

<margin>Z</margin>
And **Theseus** took Hippolita, who became his legitimate wife, and in time they had a son, **Hippolytus**. She was later sorrowful and sad because—according to **Seneca** in his tragedies—Hippolytus was torn apart and killed by Theseus’s doing upon the seashore. His chariot horses were terrified by the appearance of "Phocian" sea monsters, though he was later called back from the underworld and restored to life by the work of Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine</note>, as the poets feign. But in truth, Hippolytus had been wounded by Theseus due to a false accusation made by **Phaedra**. Theseus, believing him dead, left him on the shore. A woman named **Aricia**, whom Hippolytus loved deeply, gathered him up and had him treated by Aesculapius, by whom he was healed. When Theseus heard of this, he did not wish to proceed any further against his son.

<margin>A</margin>
But Hippolytus, in order not to further experience his father’s wrath and the great wrong conceived against him, came to Italy. There he built a land and named it **Aricia** after the name of his beloved; it is a place near where the city of Rome stands today. Later, when **Aeneas** came to Italy, **Virbius** (the son of Hippolytus) departed from Aricia and came to the aid of Turnus, as **Virgil** writes in the seventh book of the *Aeneid*, saying: *The most beautiful offspring of Hippolytus shall go to war, Virbius, whom his mother Aricia sent out in his glory; raised in the noble groves of Egeria near the moist shores, where there is a rich and peaceful altar to Diana.* <note>original Latin: "Ibit a Hippoliti proles pulcherrima bello. Virbius insignem quem mater aritia misit. Eductum egregie lucis humẽtis circũ Littora pinguis vbi & placabilis ara dianæ."</note> It is for this reason that Hippolita was rightly sad and afflicted for her son.

<margin>B</margin>
Finally, it should be noted that our poet attributes no small praise and fame to the aforementioned queens by saying that it was a "glory" for Hercules to defeat them. Because Hercules was so virtuous and powerful, he could not acquire glory by winning unless his defeated enemy possessed great dignity and excellence. Orithia later demonstrated that they possessed such integrity when, with the help of **Sagylus** (King of Scythia) and his son **Panasagoras**, she wanted to avenge the oppression of her defeated sisters upon the Greeks. This might have succeeded if a dissension had not fallen between the Amazons and Panasagoras; for this reason, she was defeated by the Athenians and forced to return to her kingdom. The poet then continues, saying that in this same group he saw the widow **Tomyris**, who saw her son's death with such steadfastness, and who took such a famous revenge that she killed **Cyrus** then and kills his fame now. For since the histories still speak of his evil end and ignominious death, it seems he dies every day for his own fault; for on the day he was defeated by Tomyris, he lost all the honor he had acquired in Asia in previous times. Wherefore the poet says:

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>V</margin>
It was demonstrated extensively above in the *Triumph of Chastity*—to better understand the preceding verses—who Tomyris was and her son Spargapises, as well as who Cyrus was and the manner in which he was defeated by her; therefore, it is not necessary to repeat it. One should only consider how gracefully the poet [Petrarch] says it seems that Cyrus dies every day to his great shame, being caught by Tomyris in the same snare with which he had previously ensnared Spargapises through deceit. Messer Francesco then continues, saying that after Tomyris, he saw her who "saw Troy poorly" <note>This refers to Penthesilea, whose arrival at Troy led to her death.</note> and, together with the others, he recognized a Latin virgin who is very well known in Italy to the Trojans. > The widow; who so surely saw
> ->Her son dead, and took such vengeance,<-
> ->That she killed Cyrus, and now kills his fame.<-
> Therefore, seeing still his wicked end,
> ->It seems he dies anew to his great shame;<-
> ->So much did he lose of his name that day.<-

<margin>D</margin>
The first of these two women described by our poet in the preceding verses was Penthesilea, Queen of the Amazons. Both because of the ancient enmity held against the Greeks in the time of Theseus and Hercules, and also (according to Dares the Phrygian) because of the friendship she had with Hector, she came to the aid of the Trojans. This woman, after many battles, was finally killed by Pyrrhus; however, according to Dictys of Crete, having been brought there for a price, she came to the favor of the Trojans and, fighting one day with Achilles, she was killed by him as we mentioned above. Justin, besides these, in the second book of *Foreign Wars* <note>original: "de bellis externis," referring to the "Epitome of the Philippic History of Pompeius Trogus"</note> only commemorates that she was Queen of the Amazons and that she displayed many worthy examples of virtue in the Trojan War.

> Then I saw her, who saw Troy poorly;
> ->And among these a Latin virgin,<-
> ->Who is so well known in Italy to the Trojans.<-

<margin>E</margin>
The other Latin virgin is Camilla, daughter of Metabus. We spoke of her history quite clearly above in the *Triumph of Chastity*. Virgil describes her arrival at the war of Turnus in this manner in the seventh book of the *Aeneid*, saying: <term>Above these came Camilla of the Volscian people, leading a troop of cavalry and columns gleaming with bronze. A warrior, her feminine hands were not accustomed to the distaff or the baskets of Minerva, but the maiden was hardened to endure fierce battles and to outrun the winds with the speed of her feet.</term> <note>original Latin: "Hos super aduenit volsca de gente Camilla..."</note> Furthermore, how virtuously and manfully she conducted herself against the Trojans is clearly shown by Virgil in the eleventh book, where he introduces her speaking thus to Turnus at the beginning: <term>Turnus, if the brave may have any self-confidence, I dare and promise to meet the troop of Aeneas’s followers, and to go alone to face the Tyrrhenian horsemen. Let me be the first to attempt the dangers of war; you stay on foot by the walls and guard the city.</term> <note>original Latin: "Turne sui merito si qua est fiducia forti..."</note> For this reason, Camilla is worthily counted in the Triumph of Fame. He [Petrarch] adds that he saw, besides these, the high-minded queen who, with one braid gathered up and the other loose, ran to the seizure and capture of Babylon. Whence he says:

> Then I saw the high-minded queen,
> ->Who with one braid turned up, and the other loose<-
> ->Ran to the ruins of Babylon:<-

<margin>F</margin>
As Justin writes in the first book of *Foreign Wars*, after the death of Ninus, King of the Assyrians, he was succeeded by Semiramis, his wife. She not only preserved what she inherited from her husband but greatly increased and expanded her proud kingdom. Once established on the royal throne, she gathered new armies and went against the fierce Ethiopians, whom she overcame and defeated with great slaughter. Afterwards, turning against the Indians, she proved herself equal to any other prince, for never before had a woman entered those regions with an army. Having thus gained honor in every undertaking, she built the great city of Babylon and surrounded it with walls of baked brick joined with pitch and bitumen. While Semiramis was one day amidst royal delights, tending to her braids according to feminine custom, news was brought to her that Babylon had rebelled against her rule. Thus, having already gathered half of her braids while the others were loose and unbound, she immediately

she rose up and took up arms, and with her army, she went to Babylon. She did not gather her loose braid until she had reduced the city to her obedience. ### Then I saw Cleopatra: and each one burned
### With unworthy fire:

Because the appetite for dominating—according to the Greek sentiment written by Cicero in the third book of *On Duties*, <note>original: "De Officiis"</note> when he says: "If justice is to be violated, it must be violated for the sake of reigning" <note>original: "Si ius violandum est regnandi causa violandum est"</note>—is a natural and worthy thing. Joined to this appetite, alongside Cleopatra, were her sister Arsinoe, Agrippina (the wife of Claudius and mother of Nero), Tullia (wife of Tarquinius), <margin>M</margin> and Athaliah, who was the daughter of Ahab, King of Jerusalem, <note>Historical correction: Ahab was King of Israel; the text conflates the kingdoms.</note> and of Jezebel <note>original: "Ithobol," referring to Ethbaal's daughter</note> his wife; she was the wife of Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, as is written in the second book of Kings, chapter 11, and many others. Although these women were savage in their actions, they nevertheless agreed in this worthy desire to reign. However, some texts read "unworthy fire." Both readings can be tolerated, as Cleopatra was burned by carnal concupiscence as mentioned above. <margin>5</margin> This aforementioned vice is reduced to a famous virtue, for "the straight is the judge of itself and of the crooked," <note>original: "rectum est iudex sui & obliqui"</note> as the Philosopher [Aristotle] affirms in the first book of *On the Soul*. Hence, each of these two contrary readings can be sufficiently accommodated to the text; but the first is more learned and also more common; the other seems more conforming to the subsequent verses. And therefore he [Petrarch] adds, saying that he saw in that dance <note>original: "tresca," a lively dance, here used metaphorically for the procession</note> of women burned with worthy or unworthy fire, Zenobia, who was much more sparing of her honor than Cleopatra. She was beautiful and in her flowery and fresh age. And the more beauty and youth she possessed, the more it seemed her praise for chastity increased. And he adds that in the feminine heart of Zenobia there was such great substance and firmness that her beautiful face and her hair, bound by a helmet, caused fear in those who by nature are accustomed to despise dangers—that is, the Roman Empire, which she once attacked with arms. Though, in the end, she was a worthy prey and a most rich prize for the Italian triumph. Whence he says:

<margin>N</margin>
<margin>H</margin>
<margin>¶ Zenobia, as Trebellius Pollio writes, was Queen of the Palmyrenes, by origin descended from Ptolemy, King of Egypt. In the age of her girlhood, having given herself to the exercise of hunting, she despised marriage with any lord. Having later reached marriageable years, by the advice of her friends, she married a prince of the Palmyrenes named Odenathus. ¶ At this time, Valerian, the 31st Roman Emperor, having been taken by Shapur, King of Persia, and forced into the most vile servitude, and his son Gallienus, who was the successor to the empire, living effeminately and showing no care for his father or the empire, Odenathus...</margin>

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>K</margin> Ctesiphon: <note>The capital of the Parthian and Sasanian Empires, near modern Baghdad.</note> While Odenatus was in this state, ruling the Empire of the East, he was killed through the actions of Maeonius, his cousin, together with his son Herodes. Zenobia, therefore, having learned of the death of her husband, and having two sons of Odenatus remaining—one called Hermaniota and the other Ethimolsus <note>These names refer to Herennianus and Timolaus, the historical sons of Zenobia and Odenatus mentioned in the *Augustan History*.</note>—took up the care of the Eastern kingdom and empire. In its preservation, she demonstrated the deeds of a good knight no less than those of an excellent queen. At this time, Gallienus was killed along with his brother Valerian through the fraud of one of his generals named Aureolus. Whereupon Claudius II succeeded to the empire by the deliberation of the Senate; he was a most worthy prince, subjugated the Goths, and had a reputation for possessing the combined virtue of Trajan, the piety of Antoninus, and the diligence of Augustus. After this Claudius died at the end of two years, his brother Quintillus held the empire for seventeen days; although he was not inferior in virtue to his brother, he was nonetheless killed by the proud soldiers. To him, therefore, succeeded Aurelian. As Flavius Vopiscus <note>A historian, one of the purported authors of the *Augustan History* (*Historia Augusta*).</note> writes, having recovered the entire West, he also wished that the East, which Zenobia held, should return under his dominion, although she held it in peaceful possession for her sons. Therefore, before he attempted war, Aurelian wrote to her in this manner:

<margin>L</margin>
<margin>M</margin> ->*Aurelian, Emperor of the Roman world and Restorer of the East, to Zenobia and all others held by the alliance of war. You ought to have done voluntarily what is commanded by my letter under duress. For I command your surrender with the promise of your life being spared, on the condition that you, Zenobia, shall live with your people where I shall place you according to the judgment of the most noble Senate. Your gems, gold, silver, silk, horses, and camels you shall hand over to the Roman treasury. The rights of the Palmyrenes shall be preserved.*<- <note>original: "Aurelianus iperator romani orbis & receptor orientis..."</note>

Zenobia, therefore, having received this letter, did not diminish her worthy spirit <note>The original reads "virgine," likely a typo for "virtù" (virtue) or "vigore" (vigor).</note> in soul, words, or deeds. Therefore, she responded to Aurelian in this way:

<margin>N</margin> ->*Zenobia, Queen of the East, to Aurelian Augustus. No one until now except you has asked for what you seek in this letter. Whatever must be done in matters of war must be achieved through courage. You seek my surrender as if you did not know that Queen Cleopatra preferred to die rather than live in any rank of indignity. We do not lack the aid of the Persians, which we already expect; for us are the Saracens, for us the Armenians. The Syrian bandits defeated your army, Aurelian. If, therefore, those forces arrive in arms which are expected from all sides, you will surely set aside the arrogance with which you now command my surrender as if you were already a total victor.*<- <note>original: "Zenobia regina orientis aureliano auguſto. Nemo adhuc præter te..."</note>

After these letters were sent and received, both parties, Aurelian and Zenobia, prepared for battle. There, fighting with as much intensity as is expected of human virtue, Aurelian remained the victor. Having fought in Syria in a place called Thimmia <note>Likely the Battle of Immae, near Antioch.</note> near Antioch, the soldiers of Aurelian were already fleeing when a deity appeared who comforted them. By this strength, they returned to battle. Zenobia was defeated and taken alive. Later, when Aurelian returned, he led her before his triumph along with her chariot, which was made of silver, and upon which she once believed she would lead Rome.

<margin>O</margin> Secondly, it should be understood that Messer Francesco [Petrarch] rightly says Zenobia was "stingy of her honor." Since the highest honor of women is to abstain from the venereal act, Zenobia was most excellent in this. Although she was a girl of tender age and very beautiful, she never joined with her husband Odenatus except solely to procreate offspring. After one union, she would remain away from him long enough to clearly understand if she had become pregnant from the preceding connection. Whenever she found herself pregnant, she did not rejoin her husband until she was diligently cleansed after childbirth.

<margin>P</margin> Lastly, it should be noted that Messer Francesco says the Romans, by nature, are not accustomed to fear, but rather to despise their enemies and even dangers. In this, he does not depart from the doctrine of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> in the fourth book of the *Ethics*. Since the Romans were called the "people of Mars," as we said above at the beginning of this chapter, they were prone by particular inclination to undergo dangers. Beyond this natural fortitude, they had similar qualities: first was civil fortitude, through which they did not fear death to acquire glory and because of the penalty of the law of *postliminium* <note>A Roman legal concept regarding the recovery of rights by a person returned from captivity; here it refers to the shame of a soldier who does not die in battle.</note>. Second, they had military skill, through which they believed in the habit of winning, by which they marvelously should not fear. Nonetheless, the great virtue of Zenobia struck fear into them, as the aforementioned Vopiscus testifies. The poet then adds, saying that although for the sake of brevity he conceals many names of excellent and famous women and men, he nonetheless does not want the bold widow Judith to be among them, who, for the safety of herself and her country, made her foolish lover <note>Holofernes, the Assyrian general.</note> shorter by a head. Whence he says:

<meta>catchword: CAssai</meta>

# CHAPTER THREE

<margin>Q</margin>
It was shown quite extensively above in the *Triumph of Love* who Judith was, and how she killed Holofernes. From this, the preceding verses contain quite clear knowledge. For which reason—

> **Among the names, which in brief speaking I hide and press,**
> **Let not Judith be missing, the bold little widow,**
> **Who deprived the foolish lover of his head.**

This alone is to be understood: that although Judith was not physically in the battle from which the victory at Bethulia <note>A biblical city, the setting of the Book of Judith.</note> was acquired, she was nevertheless the efficacious cause that moved her citizens to go out and fight. Wherefore, by this work, she is deservedly numbered among the men who became famous by means of arms. Afterward, M. F. <note>Messer Francesco (Petrarch).</note> narrates—as if responding to himself for having taken such a long delay in describing the subsequent examples—saying to himself: "Now where do I leave off, that I do not recount him from whom every human history is woven and begun, and his great successor, who led his proud life into a beast-like habit?" Wherefore he says:

> **But Ninus, with whom every human history is begun,**
> **Where do I leave him? And his great successor,**
> **Whom pride led to a beast-like life?**

<margin>R</margin>
The two examples which our poet describes in the preceding verses are quite worthy of annotation and memory. Here it is to be understood that the one from whom every human history is "woven" was Ninus, King of the Assyrians. Few historians wrote of the <term>Genesis</term> <note>The first book of the Bible, traditionally attributed to Moses.</note> written by Moses; and if any other wrote of it more, as Eusebius shows in his *Preparation for the Gospel* <note>original: "de pparatione euangelica"</note>, it should not be called human history, but divine. Therefore, when Abraham reigned in his first year among the Hebrews, Ninus had reigned forty-three years in Assyria and Europe, twenty-five among the Sicyonians and the Thebans; he also began to reign among the Egyptians. It being, therefore, the custom of kings before Ninus—as Justin writes in the beginning of *On Foreign Wars* <note>original: "de bellis externis"</note>—to wage
<margin>S</margin>
wars far from their own kingdoms, they designed the glory of their works not for themselves, but for their people. Ninus was the first who made war on his neighbors; wherefore, having first taken all of Syria, and having built in it the great city called Nineveh after himself, he successively took the entire empire of the East. After he possessed it, he moved war against Zoroaster, King of the Bactrians, with whom he came to battle and was 
<margin>T</margin>
victorious and killed him. Ultimately, while going against the Egyptians, Ninus was wounded by an arrow in a battle and died. Now, concerning his successor, it is to be understood that this was Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, who for two reasons can be called the successor to Ninus, besides the temporal succession. First, because while the Empire of the Assyrians remained with Semiramis <note>The legendary queen of Babylon and widow of Ninus.</note>, she built Babylon, which union having come to Nebuchadnezzar by continuous succession. Since Semiramis was the successor to Ninus, Nebuchadnezzar likewise succeeded him. The other way is that although from Sardanapalus, the last king of the Assyrians, the empire was translated to the Medes in the person of Arbates; and after Arbates followed Sefarmo, and Medido, Cardiceas, Deioces, and Phraortes. Finally, for our purpose, Cyaxares. Nevertheless, Nebuchadnezzar in this time succeeded Ninus by occupying Syria. For while Cyaxares was reigning, Nebuchadnezzar went against Necho II of Egypt, with whom he came to battle and overcame and defeated him. Then he moved to the Euphrates, and having crossed it, he occupied all of Syria, by which possession Messer Francesco calls him the "great successor" of Ninus. After Nebuchadnezzar had Syria under his dominion, he went with war into Judea, which he plundered and burned all around. Having arrived at Jerusalem where King Jehoiachin <note>referred to here as "Ioschin."</note> reigned, as is written at the beginning of the Book of Daniel, he took it along with the King and his family, and him with many other prisoners, and with the sacred vessels of the Temple; among the others was 
<margin>V</margin>
Daniel. Being therefore elevated in pride by so many victories, Nebuchadnezzar removed his soul from God. Wherefore he had a statue made in his likeness and constrained everyone to worship it. Because Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego <note>The three Hebrew companions of Daniel.</note> did not wish to do this, he had them put into a burning furnace. God, wishing to show him that every state and lordship depends on Him, made him see a tree in a dream one night, under whose shadow many animals grazed. In this there was a royal majesty with a great multitude of servants, and He commanded his ministers to immediately cut down that tree and drive away every animal that grazed under it.
<margin>X</margin>
Nebuchadnezzar had great fear because of this vision. Wherefore, having awakened, he sent for his diviners, and having explained the dream, he asked what it signified; but they did not know how to give any interpretation of it, whereupon—

# TRIUMPH OF FAME

<meta>catchword: nivolsono</meta>

Wherefore the king sent for Daniel, to whom the king repeated the dream once more and asked for its significance. Daniel replied: "O King, you are that great tree whose power extends everywhere; and that royal majesty coming from heaven which commanded the tree to be cut down is God, whom your pride has displeased. Therefore He wishes to uproot it and demonstrate to you that He alone is the one who grants power and kingdoms. For this reason, you shall dwell together with the beasts, and your food shall be hay and grass, until seven years have passed over you." Once Nebuchadnezzar understood Daniel, he suddenly became a madman <note>original: "manimaco," a madman or one possessed by mania</note>; and fleeing away, he went into the woods, truly driven out by his own people. There, under the open sky, he lived with the beasts for seven years, until he recognized the Most High God and thanked and praised Him, as is written in Daniel, chapter four. Next, M. F. <note>Messer Francesco (Petrarch).</note> adds, saying: "Now in this writing of mine, there remains Zoroaster, who was the inventor of the magic arts." Wherefore he says:

<margin>Y</margin>
<margin>C</margin> In the discourse of historical poetry, several men named Belus are found to have been celebrated and described by means of some worthy work. The first was the son of Epiphus, son of the first Jove, and father afterward of Danaus, Aegistus, and Agenor. He—

->Where does Belus remain, the source of error,<-
->Not through his own fault; where is Zoroaster,<-
->Who was the inventor of the magic art?<-

—was a most learned man, so much so that he later deserved to have a temple built in his honor in Babylon and to be worshipped.

<margin>Z</margin>
<margin>C</margin> The second Belus was the son of Phoenix, son of Agenor; to whom the first Belus was a grandfather. He was a man most expert in arms, wherefore he conquered the Cypriots who were infesting the kingdom of Phoenicia, according to what Virgil commemorates in the first book of the *Aeneid* when he introduces Dido responding to the thanks offered by Aeneas, saying: "Then my father Belus was laying waste to rich Cyprus and, as victor, held it under his rule" <note>original: "Genitor tum belus opimam vastabat cypro & victor ditione tenebat"</note>; but M. F. intends these others.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>C</margin> The third Belus was the father of the recently mentioned Ninus. The said Ninus revered and loved him, so when he came to death, Ninus felt heavy grief for him. In his consolation, he built a temple and had an image sculpted in the likeness of Belus, his father, and placed it in the aforementioned temple. He ordained that whoever came to that temple should be pardoned for every error. Because of this, the neighboring peoples began to make sacrifice to the said image; and thus they fell into idolatry, which is the worst sin, as is written in Exodus, chapter 32.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>A</margin> It happened then that the demon, enemy of the human race, entered into the statue of Belus and began to respond to men and deceive the common people. Afterward, through the long following of this idolatry, every idol took on the name of Belus <note>Often rendered as "Baal" or "Bel" in biblical texts.</note>, as is written in the prophet Daniel. Belus was, therefore, the cause and source of a very great error, though not through his own fault, but through the fault of Ninus. For although men erred before this by worshipping the sun and the moon—as Eusebius writes on the testimony of Diodorus in the first book of the *Preparation for the Gospel* <note>original: "de præparatione evangelica"</note>, and as Virgil shows at the beginning of the *Georgics*, and Bradwardine <note>original: "Bregnardin," likely referring to Thomas Bradwardine</note> in the book *On the Cause of God against Pelagius* <note>original: "de causa dei contra pelagium"</note>—they were nonetheless excusable, because their cognition did not extend further than sensible things. And because they clearly saw that by the power of those planets, things in life were produced and prolonged in the world; which the idols did not do, and primarily not the statue of Belus.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>C</margin> Zoroaster, whom we recently said was killed by Ninus, was the King of Bactria, a man expert in arms, but more so in letters and speculative habits. Wherefore, as Justin writes at the beginning and Isidore in the *Etymologies* <note>original: "etbi-mo," referring to the Etymologiae</note>, Zoroaster was a supreme philosopher and the inventor, among his other works, of the magic arts. Solinus also writes of him in *The Wonders of the World* <note>original: "de mira. mundi"</note> that in the very hour he was born, he laughed, which was truly wonderful; especially according to the opinion of Pliny in the seventh book of the *Natural History*, where, narrating human qualities, he says among other things: "But by Hercules, such precocious laughter, and so sharp, is granted to no one before the fortieth day" <note>original: "At hercule risus precox illi acerrimus ante xl. diem nulli datur"</note>. For so many excellent qualities contained in Zoroaster, it was appropriate that he too should be numbered by the poet in the *Triumph of Fame*. Next, M. F. adds, saying: "Now where do those remain who made the bad governance of our leaders, who under a harsh and unhappy star crossed the Euphrates?" Which thing was a fierce poultice <note>original: "empiastro," meaning a medical plaster, here used metaphorically for a failed or aggravating remedy</note> to the Italian sorrows and a heavy Italian passion. Wherefore he says:

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>C</margin> As we said above in the chapter on the preceding Romans, when the Roman Empire was divided among those three men—namely Gnaeus Pompey, Julius Caesar, and Marcus Crassus—it happened that the Romans wished—

->And who of our leaders, who under a harsh star<-
->Crossed the Euphrates, and made bad governance,<-
->A fierce poultice to the Italian sorrows.<-

### CHAPTER THREE

<margin>E</margin>
They decided to wage war against the <term>Parthians</term> <note>A powerful empire in the ancient Near East, located in modern-day Iran.</note>: since that region is most abundant in gold. <term>Marcus Crassus</term> <note>A Roman general and politician known for his immense wealth and greed.</note>, out of his avarice, desired this province; having thus prepared the army, which consisted of eleven Roman legions. <term>Crassus</term> crossed the <term>Euphrates</term> at <term>Zeugma</term> <note>original: "isclisce," likely a corruption of the historical crossing point at Zeugma.</note> as he ascended, and entered the land of the <term>Parthians</term>. There were then two leaders of the <term>Parthians</term>: according to what <term>Florus</term> writes, one was named <term>Silaces</term> <note>original: "Silates."</note> and the other <term>Surenas</term> <note>original: "firenas."</note>. Although <term>Livy</term> mentions only <term>Surenas</term> in his eleventh decade, in the fourth book, according to the fragments of <term>Florus</term>, both together went against <term>Crassus</term> and killed him along with his entire army in the manner expressed above when reciting the deeds of <term>Fabricius</term> and <term>Curius</term>. This event was truly a fierce blow to <term>Italian sorrows</term> <note>Refers to the massive Roman casualty count at the Battle of Carrhae.</note>: for <term>Caesar</term> and <term>Pompey</term> would not have fought so much among themselves had each of them not been greatly inflamed by the power of <term>Crassus</term>. Deservedly, then, are these two famous men to be celebrated: having defeated and killed such a consul with so great an army. Next, <term>Messer Francesco</term> <note>Petrarch.</note> adds the example of <term>Mithridates</term>, King of <term>Pontus</term>, saying: now where do I leave the great King <term>Mithridates</term>: that eternal enemy of the Romans who, like a wanderer and a rusted fugitive, fled before them at all times, winter and summer. Wherefore he says:

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>
¶ Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known: as <term>Livy</term> writes according to what <term>Florus</term> recites from the seventh to the eleventh decade, and <term>Lucius Florus</term> himself in his compendium drawn from <term>Marcus Varro</term>, <term>Pliny</term> in the life of <term>Mithridates</term>, and <term>Justin</term> in the thirty-seventh and thirty-eighth books <term>on foreign wars</term> <note>original: "de bellis exter."</note>: that <term>Mithridates</term> was the son of <term>Mithridates</term>, King of <term>Pontus</term>. ->Enemy of the Romans; who so like a wanderer<-

<margin>F continued</margin>
<note>The text here repeats the biographical details of Mithridates' youth found in the margin above.</note> ...on foreign wars: that Mithridates was the son of Mithridates, King of Pontus. While he was a small boy—and forced to ride beyond what was appropriate for his age so that he might grow tough—his tutors tried to poison him while he was managing the horses, since his death had not occurred through such exercise. But he, realizing this, frequently took medicines resistant to poison. Besides this, having devoted himself to the exercise of hunting, he did not confine himself within walled lands. Having grown up and taken the permanent kingdom of Pontus, he went against the <term>Syrians</term>: a people until that time undefeated by anyone, and he saw and conquered them in a short time. Directing his mind then to the empire of <term>Asia</term>, he went to explore it entirely with a few companions; and having returned, he joined with <term>Nicomedes</term>, King of <term>Bithynia</term>: and together they went to conquer <term>Paphlagonia</term> <note>original: "paslagonia."</note>. Whereupon the Romans, under whose tutelage and protection <term>Paphlagonia</term> was, sent ambassadors to <term>Mithridates</term> to tell him to abstain from the enterprise already begun. But he, already being elevated in pride and believing he could defend himself against the Romans, replied that he had come into his hereditary kingdom. And <term>Nicomedes</term>, who was with <term>Mithridates</term>, wishing to delude the Roman ambassadors, said that he would restore the kingdom to the rightful king: wherefore he appointed his son <term>Philomenes</term> as King of <term>Paphlagonia</term>, changing his name and calling him <term>Paphlagonius</term>. The Romans, therefore, being strongly provoked by both deceptions, set themselves against <term>Mithridates</term>: and especially because at that time he caused the death of <term>Ariarathes</term> <note>original: "ariacte."</term>, King of <term>Cappadocia</term>, and sought also to cause the death of <term>Ariobarzanes</term> <note>original: "Aribarzā."</note>, the son who had remained under the government of the Roman Republic.

<margin>G</margin>
And <term>Mithridates</term>, judging that because of these preceding injuries done to the Romans he would have to go to war with them, joined with <term>Tigranes</term>, King of the Armenians, to be stronger in defense and offense. At this time, <term>Nicomedes</term>, King of <term>Bithynia</term>, died: for which reason <term>Mithridates</term> occupied the kingdom and drove out the son, who was also named <term>Nicomedes</term>. Beyond this, he sent <term>Archelaus</term>, his prefect, with a powerful fleet <note>original: "classe."</note>, who took all the islands of the archipelago except <term>Rhodes</term> and the land of <term>Athens</term>.

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

And seeing that he did not die by poison, and keeping him besieged inside a castle, he finally sent a servant named <term>Sithoco</term> to kill him. This <term>Sithoco</term>, as soon as he saw the presence of <term>Mithridates</term>, was so intimidated that <term>Mithridates</term> comforted him until he finally grew bold enough to kill him. And so died the great King <term>Mithridates</term>, truly the eternal enemy of the Romans, having waged war with them for sixty-six continuous years, and always fleeing before them since they truly resolved on the enterprise, although many varied victories occurred in that time. Next, <term>Messer Francesco</term> <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the author of the poem being commented upon.</note> adds, saying he will "bind many notable things, worthy deeds, and glorious facts into a small bundle," asking himself where he left King <term>Arthur</term> and three <term>Augustan Caesars</term>, of whom one was from Africa, one from Spain, and one was from Lorraine. Whence he says:

->**M**any great things I bind in a small bundle.<-
->Where is King Arthur; and three Augustan Caesars;<-
->**O**ne from Africa; one from Spain, one from Lorraine?<-
->His twelve robust men surrounded this man:<-

<margin>R</margin>
¶ Truly worthy and excellent things our poet describes concisely in the preceding verses. For their understanding, it is primarily necessary to know—as <term>William of Nangis</term> <note>A 13th-century French Benedictine chronicler.</note> writes on the authority of <term>Sigebert the Gaul</term> <note>Sigebert of Gembloux, a medieval historian.</note>—that King <term>Arthur</term> was the son of King <term>Uther Pendragon</term>, king of <term>Britain</term> (today called England). Though he was unknown and not highly regarded at that time, it was because Queen <term>Igerna</term> <note>original: "Igerda."</note>, Arthur’s mother, having been impregnated by <term>Uther Pendragon</term> in her father's house, feared that the King would not believe her and think she had committed adultery with another if she kept the child in the public eye. For this reason, when she came to labor and gave birth to Arthur, she commanded that this child be killed. ¶ But <term>Merlin</term>, who in those times was a mage and greatly loved King <term>Uther Pendragon</term>, having learned of the planned death of this child, arranged for his escape through his enchantments, setting him free and having him raised in secret. Later, when King <term>Uther Pendragon</term> died <margin>L</margin>—there being, according to common opinion, no male heir left by him, but only <margin>M</margin> a maiden named <term>Morgan</term> <note>original: "Morguen," referring to Morgan le Fay.</note>, who was a sorceress and most learned in astrology—¶ the principal inhabitants of the kingdom gathered in a church to celebrate the solemn offices. With humble prayer, they begged God to peacefully show them who should be king before it came to swords. Once the prayer was made, a great stone immediately fell from the air before the door of the temple, in the middle of which was fixed a sword with golden letters which said: **He shall be king who draws me out** <note>original Latin: "Rex erit qui me traxerit."</note>. Hearing the thud of the stone from inside the church, all the people came out; seeing the miracle and reading the letters, they gave the highest thanks to God. Wanting to proceed with the experiment, the most noble of the kingdom first tried to pull out the sword, but none of them had the strength. Then the commoners and those of lower condition began to try; among their number was Arthur, and he alone was the one for whom the stone yielded, and who drew the sword out of it. Seeing this great miracle, the people established Arthur as King of Britain without any contradiction. Once Arthur was elevated to the kingship in this manner, he allied himself with <term>Hoel</term>, Count of Brittany, and together with him, he primarily took vengeance on the <term>Saxons</term> who had occupied England. He then conquered Ireland, Flanders, Normandy, Denmark, Touraine, Anjou, and Poitou, Gascony, and part of France. Because of this, along with his worthy and singular virtues, he was greatly loved and received by the people; wherefore, as we said above in the *Triumph of Love*, he established the <term>Round Table</term> and organized the <term>knights errant</term>, by which he attained great fame and reputation. <margin>N</margin>¶ Now descending to the three Augustan Caesars: and first to the African one. # CHAPTER THREE

After the death of <term>Julianus</term> <note>Didius Julianus, the 19th Emperor, who famously bought the empire at auction from the Praetorian Guard.</note> by the hand of God, who was the 20th Roman Emperor, and that of <term>Clodius Albinus</term>, an election of several emperors was held. Julianus himself had been elected by the Roman Senate; in Germany, the army elected <term>Severus</term>; in the East and Syria, <term>Pescennius</term>; and in Gaul, <term>Clodius Albinus</term>. While things were in this state of fluctuation, Julianus drove from Rome <term>Septimius Severus</term> <note>The text here refers to a kinsman or namesake of the future emperor.</note>, who was a relative of the said Severus. Consequently, Septimius went to Severus and incited him against Julianus. Thus, while Julianus was in Italy with his
<margin>P</margin> armies, he was deposed and killed by the authority of the Senate. ¶ There remained, then, Severus, Pescennius, and Albinus in the empire. The Romans sent to their school <note>Likely referring to an oracle or a place of wisdom.</note> to ask which of them would be most beneficial to the Roman Republic to rule over them. Apollo replied:
> The dark one is best; the African is good; the white one is the worst.
> <note>original: "optimus est fuscus : bonus affer : pessimus albus." This is a pun on the candidates' names: Pescennius Niger (Dark/Black), Septimius Severus (the African), and Clodius Albinus (White).</note>

The Romans understood from this response that <term>Pescennius Niger</term> was the one who would be best for the Roman Republic, the second would be Severus, and Clodius Albinus was to be utterly rejected. And they further asked, inquiring who among them would conquer and obtain the empire; to which Apollo replied:
> The blood of the Dark One shall be poured out elsewhere; but the one from the city who shall rule the world’s storehouse shall hold the empire.
> <note>original: "Fundet sanguis alibi nigri : at antis iperium mundi penus reget urbe profectus."</note>

Having understood the response, the Senate left to Severus the peaceful possession of the West. Once he had obtained it, he did not wish to
lose time in idleness; having gathered his armies, he departed from Rome and went into Syria against Pescennius. Finally, fighting with him, he was overcome and Pescennius was defeated near a place named <term>Cyzicus</term> <note>The text writes "tizico."</note>. Afterward, he defeated the Antiochians,
<margin>Q</margin> the Parthians, the Arabs, the Jews, and likewise the Armenians. Later, going into Gaul against Albinus, he fought with him at <term>Lyon</term> <note>The text uses the Latin "lugduno."</note> upon the Rhone, and killed him with a great slaughter of his men. Returning afterward to Rome, he built many noble buildings there, among which were the <term>Severan Baths</term>, built in the likeness of those he had constructed in Antioch. ¶ Finally, as Severus approached death, <term>Aelius Spartianus</term> <note>A historian, one of the purported authors of the *Historia Augusta*.</note> writes that he left so much oil that for five years it was sufficient not only for the use of Rome, but for all of Italy. Dying in the 17th year of his reign, he spoke these worthy and final words:
> I received the Republic troubled everywhere; I leave it at peace even to the Britons—an old man, weak and sick. It will be a strong empire for my sons, the <term>Antonines</term>, if they are good; but weak if they are bad.
> <note>original: "Turbatā rēpublicā ubiq; accepi pacatā ēt britannis relinquō senex & debilis æger firmū īperiū antoninis filijs meis si bōni erunt ībecillū : si mali." Referring to his sons Caracalla and Geta.</note>
