# TRIUMPH OF FAME

<note>The text begins mid-sentence.</note>

...advancing his steps without hindrance, <term>Theodosius</term> <note>Theodosius I (the Great), the last emperor to rule over both the Eastern and Western halves of the Roman Empire.</note> arrived at Aquileia. When the two armies met in cruel battle, a wind miraculously rose toward the soldiers of <term>Maximus</term> <note>Magnus Maximus, a usurper emperor. This refers to the Battle of the Frigidus in 394 AD, where a powerful wind called the Bora famously assisted Theodosius.</note>, by which the arrows shot by Theodosius’s soldiers struck more sharply, while Maximus’s combatants lost all their momentum. Therefore, the poet <term>Claudian</term> deservedly wrote these verses about Theodosius:

> O greatly beloved of God, for whom the atmosphere itself fights,
> and the conspired winds come at the sound of the trumpets.
> <note>original: "O nimium dilecte deo cui militat æther. Et coniurati veniunt ad classica venti." From Claudian's Panegyric on the Third Consulship of the Emperor Honorius.</note>

In conclusion, Theodosius obtained a complete victory and killed Maximus in the battle. Seeing this, <term>Andragathus</term> <note>A general under Maximus who had killed Emperor Gratian.</note>, in despair, killed himself by drowning.

<margin>v</margin>
¶ In the fourth place, there are several opinions regarding the <term>Caesar of Lorraine</term> <note>A reference to a figure in Petrarch's poem. The author is debating which historical "Charles" or "Otto" Petrarch meant.</note>. Some say he was a certain Arnulf of Austria; others say <term>Frederick Barbarossa</term>; many others say <term>Otto I</term>, the first Emperor; and still others, Otto, Duke of Lorraine. Nevertheless, while always respecting better informed views, I believe that <term>Master Francesco</term> <note>Petrarch (Francesco Petrarca).</note> meant <term>Charlemagne</term>, son of King Pepin. To understand this, one must know that Charlemagne was German, as seen in the works of the canon lawyers in the chapter *Venerabile* on elections, where the text says: *The Empire was transferred from the Greeks to the Germans through the person of King Charles, son of Pepin.* <note>original: "Translatū ī īperiū est a grecis i germanos p p̄sonā caroli regis pipini filij"</note> That he was of Lorraine is clearly evidenced by <term>Sigebert of Gembloux</term> <note>A 12th-century medieval chronicler.</note>. It should be considered that during the reign of <term>Gratian</term>, many peoples and diverse nations rebelled against the Romans and decided to maintain their own kingdoms. Among these were the Huns, who elected <term>Balamber</term> as their king; the Ostrogoths, who elected one <term>Vincaro</term>; the Visigoths, who elected <term>Athalaric</term>; the Vandals, who elected <term>Modigifilus</term>; the Britons, who elected <term>Britannico</term>, the father of Maximus; and those of <term>Franconia</term>, who elected one <term>Priam</term> <note>The author is citing the medieval legend that the Franks were descended from Trojan refugees led by a King Priam.</note>. This Priam, fighting against Gratian, was defeated and killed in battle; wherefore the Franks elected three dukes: namely Marco Miro, Senone, and Genebando; and in this way, they remained for some time.

<margin>x</margin>
¶ After the death of Marco Miro, the Franks elected a king whose name was <term>Pharamond</term>. From this Pharamond was born one <term>Clodio</term>, who made war against the people of Lorraine and took the whole province, decreeing it should be the head of his kingdom. From this Clodio was born <term>Meroveus</term>; from Meroveus, <term>Childeric</term>; from Childeric, <term>Clovis</term>; from Clovis, <term>Clotaire</term>; and from Clotaire, <term>Chilperic</term>. From Chilperic was born a girl named <term>Vuitildis</term>, who was the wife of one <term>Ausbertus</term>, and he gave her his kingdom of Lorraine as a dowry. From this Ausbertus was born <term>Arnulf</term>; from Arnulf, Arnulf; and from Arnulf, <term>Ansegisel</term>; then <term>Pepin</term>; and from Pepin the Short came <term>Charles Martel</term>; from Charles Martel, Pepin; and from Pepin, <term>Charlemagne</term>. Thus it is manifest that Charlemagne was of Lorraine by ancient origin, even though it is true that Lorraine has been transformed like Britain and many other provinces. Pepin, having conquered Gaul and many other lands, died. He was succeeded by Charles, who had war principally with the Saxons, whom he subdued to their great detriment. He then defeated <term>Waifer</term> and <term>Hunald</term>, dukes of Aquitaine, whom he miserably forced to die after many battles.

¶ At this time, <term>Pope Hadrian I</term> (in the year 787), being persecuted and oppressed by the power of <term>Desiderius</term>, King of the Lombards, sent for Charlemagne for his defense. Being a most Christian man, Charles immediately came to Italy and by force and battle overcame Desiderius and <term>Arechis</term>, Duke of Benevento. While he stayed there, the Saxons rebelled against him again; for which reason he returned to France, proceeded with a new army against them, finally defeated them, and made them return to Christianity. During this delay, <term>Adelchis</term>, son of Desiderius, returned from Greece where he had previously fled, and with their help made war against Charles and the Church. Charles returned to Italy and, fighting with him, briefly overcame him and lived victoriously in battle. In this disposition of the Western state, a vision came to <term>Constantine</term> <note>Emperor Constantine VI.</note>, who ruled in Constantinople, that he should join with Charles, King of the Franks, and they should go together to the conquest of the <term>Holy Land</term> <note>The author repeats a popular medieval legend that Charlemagne went on a crusade to Jerusalem, though this never historically occurred.</note>. Therefore, Constantine signified to Charles by ambassadors the warning he had received from the Angel. Charles gratefully accepted the enterprise and, putting it into execution, they crossed the sea and took Syria and Jerusalem. From there, on his return, Charles brought back many worthy relics which are still seen today in the city of Paris. When Charles returned with great triumph from the conquest of the Holy Land, the Romans rebelled against the faith and drove from Rome <term>Pope Leo III</term>, who had been the successor to Hadrian. For this reason, Leo sent to Charles asking for favor; and Charles, desiring to satisfy the Church, returned once more to Italy and by means of arms restored the Pope to his see with great triumph. Wherefore Pope Leo gave him the dignity of the Western Empire as merit for his works.

# CHAPTER THREE

<margin>A</margin> After the King of the Goths <note>Referring to the fall of the Ostrogothic Kingdom in Italy.</note> under Totila had been dispersed, and having returned to France, [Charles] went to Hungary against the Huns and overcame them with a glorious victory. He afterwards also conquered Illyricum <note>The Roman province covering much of the Balkans.</note> and the island of England, which he brought under his dominion by treaty. During this time, Charles <note>Charlemagne (r. 768–814).</note> had a brief respite from the wars of Europe; but while he was thus staying in peace, King Agoland <note>A legendary Saracen king from the medieval "Matter of France" epics.</note> moved from Africa and came into Spain with a massive army. Hearing this, Charles went against him and, fighting with him, finally overcame and defeated him. In this war, <term>Sigebert</term> <note>Sigebert of Gembloux (c. 1030–1112), a medieval chronicler.</note> recounts the dukes and peers of Charlemagne, who are called "Paladins" by the common people. He says that first among them proceeded Turpin, Archbishop of Reims; Roland <note>Orlando</note>, son of Milo of Angers, Count of Le Mans and Lord of Blaye; Oliver, Count of Geneva; Stutus, Count of Langres; Arastanus, Duke of Brittany; Engelier, Duke of Aquitaine; Gaifier, King of Bordeaux; Galero; Galino; Solomon and Baldwin; Gondebodo, King of Frisia; Namo, Duke of Bavaria; Ogier, Duke of Dacia and Lord of Denmark; Lambert, Duke of Bourges; Samson, Duke of Burgundy; Constantine, Prefect of the Romans; Renaud of Montauban; Walter of Termes; Ginellino, twin brother to the Duke of Lorraine; Bernard of Nublis; and Ganelon of Mainz <note>The infamous traitor of the "Song of Roland".</note>. Sigebert also writes that after this victory over Agoland, Charles defeated Fiure, Prince of Navarre; and in Spain he conquered three cities: namely Augusta, Pamplona, and Lucerna. $\P$ At this time, a fierce Turk in the form of a giant also came across the Mediterranean Sea from Turkey to the city of Nájera in Spain; his name was <term>Ferragut</term> <note>A giant mentioned in the "Pseudo-Turpin Chronicle."</note>. When Charles went against him, the giant demanded single combat, in which he captured all of Charles's barons except Roland, who finally killed him in battle. Whereupon, due to the wounds he had received, the Saracens cried out loudly and came to his aid; seeing this, Charles's people entered into battle with them. In the end, as the Turks fled and the Franks pursued them toward the land, they all entered Nájera together, which they captured and recovered the prisoners. Finally, Charles went against the King of Seville and against Altumajore, King of Córdoba, whom he shortly thereafter subdued and defeated.

<margin>B</margin> $\P$ And having occupied all of Spain, he left Roland with a small company to govern the province and ensure the Spaniards received baptism. Ganelon, having remained with him and being corrupted by gold, orchestrated a betrayal so that the Christians were killed by the Spanish Saracens. Therefore, concluding according to the account of Sigebert, his robust dukes surrounded him. This title of "Caesar of Lorraine" <note>Lothoringia</note> is better attributed to Charlemagne than to King Arthur of Britain, despite Arthur's many knights-errant. Next, the poet <note>Petrarch</note> consequently speaks, saying that after the three worthy Augustan Caesars, he saw the good Duke <term>Godfrey</term> <note>Godfrey of Bouillon, a leader of the First Crusade.</note> proceeding alone, who undertook the holy enterprise and the just journey with life-giving steps. He adds, explaining what this enterprise was, saying that he made his way into Jerusalem—the "nest" of Mount Sion, which was poorly guarded by the Christians and already neglected—concerning which he [the poet] is indignant and cries out in vain. Wherefore he says:

<margin>C</margin>
> Then came alone the good Duke Godfrey,
> Who performed the holy enterprise and the just steps;
> This place, for which I am indignant and cry out in vain,
> He made in Jerusalem with his own hands
> The ill-guarded and already neglected nest.
> <note>original: "Poi venia solo il buon duce Goffredo, / Che fe l'impresa santa, ei passi iusti: / Questo; di ch'io mi sdegno; e'ndarno grido; / Fece in Hierusalem con le sue mani / Il mal guardato , & gia negletto nido." From Petrarch's "Triumph of Fame," Part II.</note>

$\P$ During the reign of Urban II in the Papacy and Henry IV in the Roman Empire, in the year of Christ 1093, <term>Kilij Arslan</term> <note>Belzeto</note>, King of the Turks, came into Greece where he caused a great slaughter of Christians; he brought ruin and fire to the greater part of the province. For this reason, the Lords of the West, awakened and incensed by a certain Peter.

<margin>D</margin>

### THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>E</margin> ¶ Once this noble army had gathered, they all harmoniously chose the excellent Godfrey <note>Godfrey of Bouillon (c. 1060–1100), a leader of the First Crusade and the first ruler of the Kingdom of Jerusalem.</note> as their duke and captain. Having taken up the staff of command, he first arrived in Greece. In that place where the river called the Pharpar <note>original: "Farfar"; likely referring to the Orontes River or a nearby tributary where the crusaders fought near Antioch.</note> flows, the Turks had gathered. Godfrey, coming to battle with them, defeated and conquered them with a very great slaughter. Proceeding then into Rum <note>original: "Romania"; referring to the Sultanate of Rum in Asia Minor (modern Turkey), not the modern nation of Romania.</note>, he fought the Turks once more on the first day of July, 1098. There, he likewise killed a great multitude of them. Having secured these two victories, they proceeded without further interval into Syria, where they took many cities. Among these were Ma'arra <note>original: "Marra"</note> and Barad <note>original: "Barrata"</note>. During the sieges, they suffered such a great lack of provisions that, as William of Nangis <note>A 13th-century French chronicler.</note> writes, the Christians were forced to eat the bodies of the Saracens. Afterward, they came to a castle near Jerusalem called Arqa <note>original: "archas"</note>, where there were most cruel battles and where many Christians died, including Anselm of Ribemont. Once that victory was won, the Christians were attacked by a great multitude of Parthians <note>A classical term used here by the author to refer to Muslim forces from the East.</note>. But the Christians overcame and defeated them, chasing them as far as Ascalon, which they also took by force of arms and the fury of battle through God’s will.

<margin>F</margin> ¶ Returning then with his victorious army, Godfrey took and captured Jerusalem by force, where many Saracens died. Once the Christians had taken the Holy Land in this manner, the princes took counsel among themselves as to who should remain as the Christian lord there; finally, by common accord, they elected Godfrey as King and Lord of all the Holy Land. When they wished to place the crown upon him, Godfrey, with a beautiful oration, refused the princes' wish to wear it; then he spoke these excellent and religious words: **"Truly I will never wear a crown of gold in that city in which Christ, the King of the world and the heavens, himself wore a crown of thorns."** <note>original Latin: "Nunq̃ profecto ego in ea urbe aureã feram in qua xp̃s rex mũdi: atq; cælorũ & ipse spineã portauit coronã."</note> Godfrey remained as Lord in Jerusalem for only the one year that he lived, ruling from those notable and worthy buildings, among which he made a worthy dwelling on Mount Sion, where the Sepulcher of Christ is located today.

<margin>G</margin> ¶ Next, it should be understood that the lordship of Jerusalem and Syria continued through Godfrey's successors until the year of our Lord 1188. In subsequent times, the Saracens caused much damage and great war against the Christians. Up until the age of our Master Francesco <note>Petrarch (1304–1374).</note>, he, as a religious person, always exhorted and persuaded Christians to avenge the offenses they had received and to reconquer Holy Jerusalem, as is clearly seen in that song: **"O BLESSED AND BEAUTIFUL ONE, awaited in heaven,"** <note>original: "O ASPETTATA in ciel beata & bella"; Petrarch’s Canzone 28, a poem urging a crusade.</note> and through those sonnets: **"NO MORE JOYFUL THAN I is seen on earth"** <note>original: "PIV di me lieta nõ si uede a terra"; Sonnet 26.</note> and **"The successor of Charles, who the hair..."** <note>original: "ET IL successor di Carlo: che la chioma"; Sonnet 27.</note>. In these, he particularly exhorts the Italians to follow Wenceslaus <note>Wenceslaus IV (1361–1419), son of Emperor Charles IV.</note>, son of Charles the 31st Emperor, who, seeing himself growing old, had this son crowned as Caesar. He likewise exhorted them to follow Urban V <note>Pope from 1362 to 1370.</note>, who returned to Italy solely to initiate the "holy passage" <note>A common medieval term for a Crusade.</note> with the help and power of the Italians in the year of Christ 1366. But the Italian princes, and even the republics, remained firm and fixed in their obstinate purpose and disturbed that enterprise, being too overcome by private passions. And therefore, Master Francesco adds in this place a worthy, just, and deserved reprimand to all Christians, calling them miserable and proud Christians: "Now go on, consuming one another, and let it not matter to you, nor give any care, that the Sepulcher of Christ is occupied and in the hands of Saracen dogs." Wherefore he says:

<margin>H</margin> ¶ Oh, how just and soul-saving is the poet’s reprimanding admonition to awaken the minds of the most unconquerable Christian princes and remind them of their pride and misery! Alas, what greater pride can there be in the world than not to care for the injuries done to such a beneficial, humble, and benign King as Christ? He, from immortal, eternal, and incomprehensible divinity, humbled himself for all of us into the form of a servant even unto death. Alas, what greater misery can there be than to let oneself be overcome by such anger and passion that one desires to shed the blood of one's own brothers? Alas, what closer or more sacred brotherhood is there than that of Christians in the union of the Catholic Church? Where should there be greater benevolence than among those who are created only in charity and love? Oh, blind minds of Christians! If religion does not move you; if the admonition of your mother, the Holy Roman Church—similar to those words Jocasta <note>In Greek mythology, the mother of Eteocles and Polynices, who killed each other in a civil war over Thebes; a classic example of fratricide.</note> gave while weeping to Polynices and Eteocles in the tragedies—does not persuade you; if nature and innate compassion do not lead you; then at least let your passions of Avarice, Pride, and Ferocity force you! Now, where could the wide sack of your greed be better filled than with the gold, the silk, and the gems [of the East]?

¶ In the year of Christ 1200, the Eastern Empire being totally lost to the <term>Christians</term>, the most Christian King of France and the most illustrious Signoria of Venice deliberated on making the passage and going across the sea. Thus putting this into execution, they came to Constantinople, took it, and appointed as Emperor the son of the previous Emperor.

At that time, Michael Palaiologos, with the help of the Genoese, recovered the Eastern Empire, from which followed a very great favor to the Christians who lived in the eastern parts. At this time there was in Babylon <note>Babylon was a common medieval term for Cairo, the seat of the Mamluk Sultanate.</note> an outstanding prince, a Sultan named Bondogar <note>Baibars (reigned 1260–1277), the Mamluk Sultan who dealt heavy blows to the Crusader states.</note>. There he caused a very great slaughter and shedding of Christian blood. From there he then came to Armenia and took the province, not without many bloody battles. But while he was on this expedition, the Syrians rebelled. Returning against them, he took the city of Antioch; and proceeding through the province against the Syrians, he was finally wounded one day in battle and carried to Damascus. There he later died of his wounds.

Because of this, it happened that Saladin easily overcame and defeated both parts, which were weakened by being divided. From which a great slaughter was made...

->THE TRIUMPH OF FAME<-

<margin>N</margin> After the slaughter of the Christians, he <note>Saladin</note> took the king and the Master of the Temple with the other worthy men of Jerusalem; he had them all cruelly killed except for the king and the Master of the Temple, whom he reserved for the glory of his triumph. For this reason, the city of Jerusalem and Acre <note>original: "Tholomaida"</note> surrendered to Saladin without a fight. In addition to his skill in arms, Saladin was a most just and liberal man, and most observant of his promises <note>original: "pole," likely a contraction for "parole" or "promesse"</note>. After he had entered Jerusalem and taken dominion, he allowed all the clergy and all the poor who could not pay the imposed tax to go free. And furthermore, there being many poor wounded knights, Saladin had them cared for from his
<margin>O</margin> own private treasury <note>term: "fisco" refers to a ruler's personal or state funds</note>. Because of this, it happened that in all those parts he was both feared and loved. Secondly, to have a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, this verse—*That one who followed Saladin from afar*—can have two different interpretations. One is that the Saracen who caused our people such shame and damage follows Saladin in fame from quite a distance; the other is that Saladin follows him. Both interpretations can be tolerated, because Saladin possessed a greater abundance of moral virtues, while the other was more glorious in victory, having defeated the Christians through his own cunning and strategy rather than through their own disorder. However, the first interpretation is more commended, especially by the authority of Dante, who commemorates Saladin in the first circle
<margin>P</margin> of Hell in the fourth Canto <note>original: "cap."</note> among the other famous men. Finally, it is to be understood that **Lancaster** is a province between Aragon and France where there was a duke who, with the help of King Edward of England, waged most cruel war for a long time against Philip, King of France, and his son John, so much so that the King of France and his son were captured in it. The name of this duke is not revealed to us beyond this generality: that is, the famous **Duke of Lancaster** <note>The commentator is geographically confused here; Lancaster is in England, though the Duke (likely Henry of Grosmont or John of Gaunt) fought extensively in France and Spain</note>. Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> concludes the end of this chapter by saying that after the sight of these last ones, he gazed in the manner of someone who raises his eyes so that he might surpass the others to see if more men famous in arms followed, in the same way he had seen earlier in this present life. And in this, he says he saw two who departed recently from this country and this life of ours. One of them was the good Sicilian king, who reached for high things and saw from afar so much that he was truly **Argus**. On the other side was his great **Colonna**, who was magnanimous, generous, constant, and secure in his every work. Whence he says:

<margin>Q</margin> Master Francesco chose—so as not to deviate from the custom of grateful men—to introduce two of his singular benefactors together with the others in the Triumph of Fame. These were **King Robert**, under the title of "Sicily this side of the lighthouse" <note>original: "cecily citra farum," referring to the Kingdom of Naples</note>, to whom he collectively attributes as much dignity as can exist in any earthly man. He says he "reached for high things," noting his excellence regarding the speculative intellect, and that he "saw from afar" and was an "Argus," by which one understands the act of prudence regarding the practical intellect. Experience truly shows these excellences in him through his peaceful possession of the kingdom and in the dedication of many books to him by various authors. **Argus**, to whom King Robert is compared, was a shepherd who had a hundred eyes, 
<margin>R</margin> whom Ovid commemorates in the first book of the *Metamorphoses* in the fable of Jove and the daughter of Inachus the river <note>Io</note>, 
<margin>S</margin> saying: *Argus had a head surrounded by a hundred eyes; from there, they took their rest in pairs by turns; the others kept watch and remained on station.* <note>original: "Centum luminibus cinctum caput argus habebat. Inde suis vicibus capiebat bina quietem. Cetera seruabant atq; in statione manebant."</note> By this, in short, prudent men are understood. The **Colonna** of Master Francesco could be either **Sciarra Colonna**, **Stefano Colonna**, **Cardinal Giovanni Colonna**, or **Matteo Palmieri** the Florentine <note>Palmieri was actually a contemporary of the commentator, not Petrarch</note>, a man still living and most learned. But it is likely that he means Stefano Colonna, in whose house in Rome he lived honorably for a long time, as we said at the beginning; how great his excellence and dignity were can be clearly understood through the virtues expressed in his praises by our excellent poet.

> *I gazed as a man who willingly steps forward;*
> *To see if anyone else appeared, such as he was*
> *Elsewhere my eyes had seen before:*
> *And I saw two, who departed only yesterday*
> *From this our age and from this country:*
> *These two closed that honored company:*
> *The good Sicilian king, who reached for high things,*
> *And saw far off: and was truly Argus;*
> *On the other side, my great Colonna,*
> *Magnanimous, noble, constant, and generous.*

<meta>This page transitions from the historical and military figures mentioned in Petrarch's "Triumph of Fame" to the fourth chapter, which focuses on the fame achieved through intellectual pursuits. It sets up a classic Renaissance debate comparing the glory of military deeds (arms) against the glory of scholarship (letters).</meta>

<page-num>138</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER FOUR</header>
<sig>SS ii</sig>

# EXPOSITION OF THE FOURTH CHAPTER OF FAME.

It is a fitting thing for noble souls <note>original: "animi pelegrini," literally "wandering souls," referring to those on a spiritual or intellectual quest</note> who desire to exalt virtue: when they see it shining in some part, they do not turn their sight from that object to anything less worthy. Instead, they fix themselves solely upon that spectacle, feeding the mind with its delicious and sweet fruits. For every thing, desiring its own perfect state, would perform a contrary operation if it were to move away from a more worthy object to the care and understanding of something of less excellence. This disposition existed in our poet <note>Petrarch</note>; having contemplated so many outstanding and excellent men who, by means of glorious military discipline, had ascended to lasting fame, he rightly begins the subsequent chapter by saying he did not know how to remove his sight from such a view. Nevertheless, in this elevation and contemplation of mind, he reasonably discussed and joined—as something not foreign to this triumph of fame—the consideration of another quality by which men rise in both fame and honor: which is literary knowledge and the exercise of study in the acquisition of the sciences <note>term: "scientie" refers to the organized branches of knowledge or scholarly disciplines</note>. Therefore, as the universal subject of the present chapter, Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> intends to treat Fame, the fourth state of the soul, in a more specific consideration: namely, according to how it is attributed to men by means of letters and sufficient studies. But in this place, a necessary and worthy doubt arises: for what reason does Messer Francesco attribute more fame to the exercise of arms than to that of letters?

<margin>T</margin>
<margin>V</margin>
Since many reasons seem to suggest the contrary, we—borrowing the syllogistic form <note>the formal structure of a logical argument consisting of two premises and a conclusion</note> from the dialecticians <note>logicians</note>—shall bring forth some of them. Thus, the first is: whatever thing contains greater perfection within itself, to that also should greater praise be attributed; but the sciences are more perfect than the military art. Therefore, they deserve much greater commendation. The first part of our assumption is manifest, and the second is clearly proven. For the goods of the soul are, among all others, the most perfect and the highest goods. Therefore, since these are acquired through the exercise of letters and study, it seems one is forced to concede that such study is fitting of more praise than any other operation.

<margin>X</margin>
¶ The second reason is: nothing which falls largely under the dominion and power of Fortune <note>the personification of luck or chance</note> deserves more glory than those worthy habits that are totally alien to Fortune; but military service consists largely in the service and favor of Fortune. And scientific habits are safe from Fortune; therefore, military service and arms cannot exceed the joyful sciences in fame. Likewise, the first part of our assumption is very well known. It is stated most strongly by the sentence of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the book *On Good Fortune* <note>original: "lib. de bona fortuna"</note>, where he says there is the least intellect where Fortune dominates the most. The other part is clearly written by Cicero in his *Oration for Gnaeus Pompey* <note>original: "oratione pro. GN. Pompeo"</note>; by Lucan, by Caesar, by Lucius Florus, by Quintus Curtius, and by Suetonius Tranquillus. By this reason, it is not only concluded that military service does not exceed letters, but it seems to suggest that it should be totally alien to all praise.

<margin>Y</margin>
¶ The third reason is: nothing which is repugnant to the nature of man and his universal inclination can be more worthy than that through which man is naturally led to his ordained end; but the military art is repugnant to the nature of man. And letters lead him to his ultimate happiness, which is the contemplation of abstract substances; therefore, military service does not deserve more fame than scientific letters. Again, the first part of our assumption is most evident, and the second is proven: for military service is a force that tears apart human company and natural mutual benevolence, toward which man is naturally inclined, as [Aristotle] writes in the first book of the *Politics* and the eighth book of the *Ethics*. Whereas studies are the efficient cause of this benevolence through divine and admirable philosophy, as Cicero <note>original: "Tullio"</note> demonstrates in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*. Therefore, it seems that without any doubt, letters ought to precede the deeds of arms in fame.

<margin>A</margin>
¶ The fourth and final reason is: every quality is more worthy if it produces a more excellent effect; but the sciences produce the most perfect state, which is happiness; arms produce only a temporary prize; therefore, the sciences are far more worthy than the military art. The first part of our assumption is known by itself. And the second is declared by Aristotle in the tenth book of the *Ethics*, and by Averroes in the prologue to the *Physics*, and by Cicero in the book *On Friendship* <note>original: "libro de amicitia"</note>, where he places wisdom before friendship, and that before all other things. Therefore, concluding the exercise of study shows itself more worthy than the command of arms. Cicero consents to this in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations* when he says that philosophy is nothing other than a true gift and an invention of the gods, and nothing in this world is sweeter than lettered leisure <note>original: "ocio lrato," referring to *otium litteratum* or the productive leisure of the scholar</note>. And Aristotle likewise in the—

<summary>This page introduces the fourth chapter of Petrarch's "Triumph of Fame," focusing on intellectual achievement. The commentator presents a series of logical arguments (the "Paragone" of arms vs. letters) to debate why scholarly study might be more deserving of fame than military conquest.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch's "Triumph of Fame," specifically addressing the debate between the glory of military life ("Arms") and the glory of scholarship ("Letters"). The previous page introduced the fourth chapter of Petrarch's poem, which shifts focus to intellectual figures.</meta>

# ## TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>B •</margin>
First, in *On the Soul* <note>original: "de lanimā," referring to Aristotle's *De Anima*</note> and in the works of Boethius, it is said that the sciences <note>term: "scientie" here refers to systematic knowledge or academic disciplines</note> are among the number of honorable goods. Wherefore Cicero, not without merit, said in the first book of *On Duties*: *Let arms yield to the toga: let the laurel yield to the tongue.* <note>original: "Cedant arma togae: concedat laurea linguae." This is a famous quote where Cicero argues that civil oratory and law are superior to military force.</note> For these reasons, it would seem that it was no small error for the poet <note>Petrarch</note> to have placed armed men before other men of science. We, nevertheless, not departing from the poet's intention, will confess the truth—even though we are deeply indebted to the philosophers—by saying that in terms of fame, arms must be superior to letters. To prove this conclusion, we will first show its truth through a single reason; thereafter, we will respond to the contrary arguments. *For the dispute requires these two things.* <note>original: "Hec enim duo exigit disputatio."</note> As Averroes describes in the first and fifth books of *On Natural Hearing* <note>Aristotle's *Physics*</note>: Let this be the reason: whatever good is public and universal is much more worthy of honor and praise than a good that is private and particular. Military discipline and action are a public and universal good, while the sciences and studies are particular goods. Therefore, military discipline is more worthy of praise than any other faculty or private science.

The first part of our assumption is declared by Aristotle in the first book of the *Ethics*, where, comparing the public good to the private, he says and affirms these appropriate words: *It is lovely indeed for a single man, but it is more beautiful and more divine for a nation and for city-states.* <note>original: "Amabile quidem et uni soli pulcrius tamen ac diuinius genti ciuitatibusque."</note> And Cicero, in the first book of *On Duties*, says: *But the life of those in retirement is easier, safer, and less heavy or troublesome to others; however, the life of those who have applied themselves to the republic and to performing great deeds is more fruitful for the human race and more suited to renown and greatness.* <note>original: "Sed facilior et tutior minus aliis grauis aut molesta uita ociosorum fructuosior autem hominum generi ad claritatem amplitudinemque aptior eorum qui se ad rempublicam: et ad magnas res gerendas accommodauerunt."</note> But the second part is affirmed by Cicero in the same book when he speaks demonstrating the purpose of warlike exercise: *Therefore, wars are to be undertaken for this reason: so that one may live in peace without injury.* <note>original: "Quare suscipienda quidem bella sunt: ut sine iniuria in pace viuatur."</note>

Which dignity and excellence of arms was demonstrated even in fact and in experience when, as Livy writes in the seventh book of *From the Founding of the City*, a great opening <note>a chasm or pit</note> appeared in the middle of Rome which, in order to be closed, demanded the best thing that the Roman Republic possessed. Marcus Curtius, interpreting this "best thing" to be men-at-arms, mounted on horseback and threw himself into it; wherefore that cave immediately closed itself. This reason is further confirmed because that thing which, through its virtue, draws men most into discussion should proceed first in fame—fame being nothing other than the virtues attributed by men to preceding works. Because the exercise of arms cannot be performed out of sight and away from common notice (as studies are, for which such community often acts as a great hindrance), military deeds draw men to discussion more than those of letters. And for this reason, not without merit, Aristotle in the second book of the *Politics* does not number speculative men among the essential parts of the republic, where he affirms the military <note>original: "militi"</note> to be the third part. And Plato divides his republic into only two parts: namely, the judges and the men of arms. For this reason, the text of the legal scholars in the *Institutes of Justice and Law* says, putting arms first: *It is necessary for the imperial majesty not only to be decorated with arms, but also to be armed with laws, so that it may rightly govern both times of war and of peace.* <note>original: "imperatoriam maiestatem non solum armis decoratam: verum et legibus oportet esse armatam ut vtrunque tempus et bellorum et pacis recte possit gubernare."</note> Therefore, concluding with Aristotle in the first book of the *Politics*: just as arms make an unjust man most cruel and shameful, so they make the virtuous man worthy, glorious, and more excellent than any other.

<margin>C •</margin>
¶ Now, to respond to the contrary arguments, it is only necessary to make one presupposition: that political happiness consists in the act of prudence, as Aristotle demonstrates in the first book of the *Ethics* when he says happiness is the operation of the highest virtue, which is prudence—this being the moderator and the reason of all things that can be done, and in which all other virtues are joined. This opinion is also declared by Egidio <note>Giles of Rome</note> in the first part of *The Governance of Princes*, in chapter twelve. To this foundation, he adds that the military service for which men are attributed fame should be considered in its perfect state—just as the perfection of letters is equal to it—and that it must conform to a right will. For if the will were depraved, no praise should be given to the man either through arms or through letters, as Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> presupposes here in this glorious triumph of fame.

¶ Secondly, according to this foundation, it is replied to the first argument that not only scientific habits should be called the goods of the soul, but also the moral virtues, as is seen in the first book of the *Ethics* when the philosopher says: *Since goods are divided in three ways, and some are called external and others of the soul and of the body: we call the goods of the soul the most principal and the greatest goods; and we place the acts and operations of the soul among them.* <note>original: "Cum ergo tripliciter diuidantur bona et alia externa dicantur alia animi et corporis: bona animi principalissima dicimus ac maxime bona: Actus uero et operationes animales cum esse ponimus."</note> Among these, prudence holds the first place. And that is divided into individual, familial, political, governing, and military prudence, as if into five different species. Therefore, military discipline itself is contained among the goods of the soul, just like the sciences. Wherefore, in this respect, it is equal to them ...

Using authorities like Aristotle, Cicero, and the legend of Marcus Curtius, the commentator concludes that military discipline is a moral virtue and a species of Prudence, making it a "good of the soul" equal or superior to academic study.</summary>

# CHAPTER FOUR

<sig>SS iij</sig>
<meta>Catchword: Petier.</meta>

# CHAPTER FOUR

<margin>B</margin>
...it exceeds them because those sciences serve a particular good, while the military profession <note>original: "militia"</note> serves a universal good, which is far more worthy and excellent. Furthermore, the military profession excels the speculative sciences in the breadth of its dignity, because it necessarily encompasses the goods of the body, the goods of fortune, and all the moral virtues which work together to direct its operation. This is taught by Tully <note>The common Renaissance name for Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> in the first book of *On Duties*, where he says:
> **To rush headlong into battle and fight hand-to-hand with the enemy is something monstrous and like wild beasts; but when time and necessity demand it, one must fight hand-to-hand, and death is to be preferred to slavery and disgrace.** <note>original: "Temere aut in acie versari & manu cō hoste cōfligere: immanne quidē & beluarum simile est: sed cū tps necessitasq; postulat decertandum manu est: & mors seruituti turpitudiniq; anteponenda"</note>

Beyond these, he describes many other observances as necessary for virtuous combat.

<margin>F</margin>
Regarding the second reason, I say that it is not military prudence <note>term: "prudētia militare" — the practical wisdom and strategic foresight of a commander</note> but only the outcome of the act of battle that is in the power of Fortune. Since battle is a specific event, a thousand singular cases and dispositions entirely unknown to the human intellect can converge upon it; therefore, only the outcome is subject to the ministry of Fortune. Yet who doubts that, in terms of military discipline, Marcus Marcellus <note>A Roman general famous for his service in the Punic Wars</note> was superior to Hannibal, even though he was later killed by the Africans? Similarly, Brutus and Cassius were inferior to Octavian and Antony only by Fortune in the outcome of the war. Caesar was overcome by Pompey at Dyrrachium, and in Spain he once thought of killing himself; yet by the clemency and kindness of Pompey, he was not destroyed in the aforementioned conflict. There would be many examples to bring to our purpose—such as those of Pyrrhus, Darius, and many others—which we will omit for the present to keep the writing brief.

<margin>G</margin>
Therefore, in conclusion, military prudence overcomes Fortune by using diligence in establishing encampments, in the ordering of the ranks, and in attacking the enemy, so that nothing can intervene against the intention of the captain or leader of the army. To Cicero, one responds that prosperous Fortune is a universal aid in specific matters. But science is not measured according to its outcome. And if anyone should say that even the sciences sometimes perish in this same misfortune: let Archimedes, Aeschylus, Philemon, and Euripides suffice as examples and as proof of our intent; each of them died by Fortune solely because of their devotion to their studies and scientific letters. <note>Archimedes was killed by a soldier while drawing geometric figures; Aeschylus was allegedly killed by a falling tortoise; these are standard humanist examples of "scholarly" deaths.</note>

<margin>H</margin>
To the third reason, it is replied that a just war does not destroy human benevolence but is instituted only to oppose injury and to defend what is possessed in peace from external incursions. This matter is easily understood by the name given to the military by Plato: he calls them "fighters of war" <note>original: "pugnatores belli"</note>. Thus, arms and the military art are instituted only for defense, which is a matter of natural law <note>term: "iure naturali" — laws considered inherent to human nature and discoverable by reason</note> according to Tully in the first book of *On Duties* and the legal scholars in the laws of the *Digest*. This defense obliges us so strongly for our fatherland that it lawfully breaks even the love of a son and the benevolence of a father; so much so that if one kills the other solely for the end of saving the Republic, he is justly worthy of reward, as the legal text says. And to Cicero, one responds that military prudence is no less contained under the philosophy of which he speaks than the speculative sciences, because he says that philosophy was the inventor of laws and the bond of cities. Thus Cicero says in his oration *In Defense of Aulus Cluentius Habitus*, speaking of the laws:
> **For this is the bond of this dignity which we enjoy in the Republic; this is the foundation of liberty, this is the source of equity. As our bodies are without a mind, so a city without law cannot use its members and parts.** <note>original: "Hoc enī vinculum est huius dignitatis q fruimur in republica: hoc fundamētū libertatis: his fons eqtatis corpora nostra sine mēte sic ciuitas sine lege suis mēbris & partibus vti non pōt."</note>

And Aristotle in the second book of the *Politics* says: **Where laws do not prevail, there is no Republic.** <note>original: "Vbi leges non preualent nō est respu."</note> For those laws would be of no value if there were no one to make them be observed, as the text expresses: **For the law is of little use in a city unless there are those who can govern the laws.** <note>original: "Parū ē enī ius i ciuitate eē nisi sint q iura regere possint."</note> And Cicero, in the same oration cited above: **The magistrates are the ministers of the laws.** <note>original: "Ministri legū magistratus sunt."</note> Therefore, since the law is maintained by means of arms, for this reason arms exceed the speculative sciences, in which one only attends to the well-being of a particular individual.

<margin>I</margin>
To the fourth and final reason, it is replied (as we said above in our premise) that political happiness is acquired no less through the act of prudence than contemplative happiness is through the habit of wisdom, and through the union of the active intellect with the potential intellect, according to what Averroes writes in the third book of *On the Soul*. Nor are the acts of virtue less honorable goods than the habits of the sciences, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> writes at the end of the *Ethics*; and philosophy, which is a gift from God, comprises the moral no less than the natural. Hence Socrates drew philosophy down from heaven and placed it in the city, as Tully himself affirms. And the sweetness of literary leisure is only considered in respect to other particular cares, and not in respect to the public; a thing which Tully demonstrates at the end of the first book of *On Duties* when he says:
> **For who is so eager in perceiving and understanding the nature of things that, if while he is treating and contemplating...** <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

# TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>R</margin> <note>This Latin passage paraphrases Cicero's *On Duties* (I, 153-154)</note> Even if a man were occupied with things most worthy of knowledge <note>original: "res cognitione dignissimas"</note>, if a sudden danger or crisis of the fatherland were presented which he could assist, he should leave and cast aside all those studies, even if he believed he could count the stars or measure the magnitude of the world. From this, it is shown clearly enough to be an answer to the arguments we brought forth above. But as for what Cicero wrote: **"Let arms yield to the toga; let the laurel yield to the tongue"** <note>original: "Cedant arma togae: concedat Laurea linguae"</note> and **"arms are of little value abroad unless there is counsel at home,"** <note>original: "foris parvi sunt arma nisi sint consilium domi"</note> as well as his other discussion in the first book of *On Duties* where he wishes to show as false the opinion of those who say that military matters are to be preferred to civil ones: this does not contradict our purpose. For we concede that judges and the prudent are always the primary part and much more worthy of the republic, just as Aristotle also confirms in the second book of his *Politics* and similar things in the third or fourth rank. But we are not speaking of these at present, but only of the speculative habits of the sciences, over which judgment and dominion are reserved for civil discipline, as one reads at the beginning and in the fifth book of the *Ethics*. Therefore, concluding that our poet is free of any error, it was right that he described the famous men of arms before the men of speculation. Having resolved this doubt, it remains now to descend to the particular exposition of the text. Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> says at the beginning of the present chapter that he did not know how to take his eyes from such a sight of so many worthy and excellent men, when, being lost in this thought, he heard someone say: "O Messer Francesco, now turn your mind to the other side of human operation; for you will see that praise, fame, and honor can well be acquired through means other than arms." And he adds that at this he turned and saw Plato, who in that troop of speculative men went closest to the mark of human intelligence. To which mark he attains, to whom it is given and permitted by heaven. Whence he says:

# CHAPTER FOUR OF FAME

<margin>L</margin> <gloss>Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should primarily be known that because of the aforementioned harmony between our spirit and its worthy objects, Messer Francesco says he did not know how to take his eyes from the worthy sight of the armed men; this is because through the exercise of arms, more than any other human operation, praise, glory, and triumph are acquired. Whence spirits should deservedly always be intent upon that with great diligence. Secondly, it should be understood that Messer Francesco says that while in this thought and desire to know the armed men, he heard a voice telling him to turn and set his mind to the other side, where he would also see that in this life one acquires merit, and not only through arms. He does not further explain by whom this was spoken, in order to demonstrate a hidden understanding that results in us by means of a fury <note>term: "furore" — in the Renaissance sense of 'divine frenzy' or inspired poetic madness</note> and an angelic commotion. How this occurs we will explain more extensively in the subsequent Triumph <note>The Triumph of Divinity</note>, as it is the place more expressly treated by Messer Francesco.</gloss>

> **I was unable to take myself from such a sight;**
> **When I heard: "Turn your mind to the other side;**
> **For praise is well-acquired through other than arms."**
> **I turned to the left hand, and saw Plato;**
> **Who in that troop went closest to the mark;**
> **To which he attains, to whom it is given from heaven:**
> **Aristotle then, full of high genius:**
> **Pythagoras, who first humbly**
> **Called Philosophy by its worthy name:**

<margin>M</margin> In the third place it is to be noted: that Messer Francesco says Plato went closest to the mark which is attained by those to whom it is given by heaven; because he was of the opinion that every operation of ours was led by the celestial bodies, or at least that they provided a very great inclination, as we shall strive to demonstrate more clearly in the course of this chapter shortly below. In the fourth place, it seems right to repeat that, seeing the poet strive for brevity in what he can follow, we shall do the same as much as we are able. Only and briefly, we shall strive to recount the fatherland, the parents, the opinions, and the sayings of the subsequent philosophers.

<meta>This page continues the transition from the active, military life to the speculative, philosophical life. Having established that the "active" life is essential for the state but the "speculative" life achieves a different kind of fame, the commentator now introduces the first and most "divine" of the philosophers: Plato.</meta>

### CHAPTER FOUR

...we shall strive to bring forward; we shall leave the other deeds of their lives to be recounted by the excellence of Diogenes Laertius <note>A 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers</note>, so as not to weave the web any further than that which was shown to be warped by our poet regarding the acquisition of scientific fame.

<margin>N</margin> ¶ Finally, it is to be considered that **Plato** was an Athenian, the son of one Ariston and of Perictione <note>original: "pitiona: overo petona"</note>, as Laertius writes, who by maternal origin descended from Solon <note>The famous Athenian lawmaker</note>, or from his lineage. For Dropides, his brother, fathered one Critias; and Critias fathered Caleschrus; and Caleschrus fathered Glaucon; and Glaucon fathered Perictione. Plato, therefore, was his surname, having first been named Aristocles after his grandfather; the reason for this surname, according to Alexander the Greek, was the shapely habit of his body <note>Plato means "broad," likely referring to his shoulders or forehead</note>, and according to Neanthes, his eloquence and marvelous freedom of speech.

His father, wishing Plato to devote himself to letters, decided to give him to **Socrates**. Three days before Plato was brought to him, Socrates had seen in a dream a swan growing in his lap, which then took wing and, flying high, expressed the sweetest songs. Valerius Maximus also writes in the first book, chapter four, that while Plato was a tiny infant in the cradle, certain bees came and distilled honey into his mouth—a sign and omen of his future eloquence.

Devoting himself to letters, Plato became so excellent that he overshadowed his fellow students under Socrates. Nor did he skip any place or journey <margin>O</margin> where he thought he might acquire some doctrine without wishing to go there. Thus, he primarily went to search for the origin of the Nile, by which means, having arrived in Egypt, he learned arithmetic and astrology. From there, he later came to Italy solely to hear Archytas of Tarentum. Afterward, he passed into Sicily to contemplate Mount Etna and its fire. He later returned to Athens to better devote himself to speculation; as Jerome writes in *Against Jovinian*, he chose the Academy, a location not only desolate but unhealthy, so that the constant cares of illness might mortify the fire of lust.

Plato reached such perfection that he was deservedly called the "god of philosophers." Cicero also writes in his praise in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: **"I always except Plato, outstanding in genius and diligence, [even though] Aristotle is far above all others"** <note>original: "Aristotelem longe oībus Platonem semper excipio prestans igenio: ac diligentia"</note>. By these words, it is understood clearly enough how great Plato's excellence must have been. But Augustine shows it even more clearly in the tenth book of *The City of God*, chapter one, saying: **"For we have chosen the Platonists as deservedly the most noble of all philosophers"** <note>original: "Elegimus enim Platonicos omnium philosophorum merito nobilissimos"</note>. And in the eighth book he said: **"Aristotle, a man of excellent genius, yet unequal to the eloquence of Plato"** <note>original: "Aristoteles vir excellentis ingenii: Platonis tamen elogo impar"</note>.

Marcus Fabius Quintilian also writes in praise of Plato in the tenth book of *The Education of the Orator*: **"Who doubts that Plato is foremost, whether in the sharpness of debate or a certain divine and Homeric faculty of speaking? For he rises much above prose—which the Greeks call 'pedestrian'—so that he seems to me to be instructed not by human genius, but by a kind of Delphic oracle"** <note>original: "Quis dubitat platonem esse praecipuum siue acumine differendi: siue eloquendi facultate diuina quadam & homerica... vt mihi non hominis ingenio: sed quodam delphico videatur oraculo instructus"</note>. With this opinion, that of Tully [Cicero] in *On the Orator*, addressed to Brutus, is in agreement: **"He stood out by far among all who ever wrote or spoke, foremost in gravity"** <note>original: "Longe omnium quicumque scripserunt aut locuti sunt extitit & grauitate princeps"</note>. Finally, Eusebius, in the tenth book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter two, says of Plato: **"Plato then, a man of superior nature, truly sent by the divine, left no part of philosophy imperfect"** <note>original: "Plato deinde vir natura prestantior vere diuinitus missus nullam partem philosophie imperfectam reliqt"</note>. Through these authorities, it is understood that Plato deservedly ascended to the summit of the speculative intellect.

<margin>P</margin> ¶ Now, regarding Platonic opinions, it should be known that concerning **God**, as Eusebius shows in the thirteenth book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter eight, Plato spoke very diversely. At first, he said that He was the maker and creator of all the world, unique, most perfect, and immutable, as is read in the eighth book of *The City of God*. Afterward, he fell into the pestiferous error of idolatry, whence he used to call the Delphic Apollo the "paternal interpreter of grace," and he wished a cock to be sacrificed to Aesculapius <note>Plato's famous last words in the *Phaedo*</note>, and he approved many other wicked superstitions. <margin>Q</margin> Likewise, he posited that demons were eternal and derived from the divine mind and nature.

¶ Regarding the **human soul**, he imagined it to be a self-moving eternal number of the most subtle nature, as is written in the first book of *On the Soul*. He divided the soul into three parts: namely, the rational, the vital, and the concupiscible <note>The parts dealing with reason, spirit/life-force, and physical desire</note>, as Tully shows in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*. He said primarily that it was a "number" because he imagined number to concur as a principle in the generation of things; but because he judged the soul eternal, he concluded it was not *made* of number, but *was* itself a number. He then said that it moved itself, considering that it moves the body, and every quality and perfection of the effect must be present much more greatly in its cause. ¶ Eusebius also writes at the same...

->TRIUMPH OF FAME<-

<meta>Catchword: Aristotle</meta>

# TRIUMPH OF FAME

...the tenth book, chapter ten <note>likely referring to the "Myth of Er" in Book 10 of Plato's Republic</note>, that Plato said souls, after their separation from the body, wandered until they were reunited, and in those times inhabited various bodies of brute animals. According to how their actions in life had been conformable to the nature of those animals: if in life a man had been given to lust <note>original: "voluptà"</note>, upon his departure he entered into a donkey or a pig; if he had been rapacious, he entered into an eagle or a wolf or similar animals; if he had been prudent, he entered into ants or bees, and sometimes into other creatures. Sometimes Plato says that souls departing from the body immediately fly to heaven, and at other times he subjects them to divine justice, saying that if they had acted well, they stayed a thousand years in heaven; then they were permitted to choose any state that pleased them and was not repugnant to them. If they had acted badly, they stayed a thousand years underground to be purged; then, once purged, they returned to the world. Yet another version <note>original: "altra voluntà"</note> Plato expressed was that good souls who had been in the world would, after their separation, perpetually inhabit heaven, and the wicked would be eternally tormented in hell. From this, it is manifest that Plato spoke diversely concerning our soul. Plato also wrote of the heavens, saying it was fitting to adore them and to express vows to them, as Eusebius <note>A 4th-century Christian historian and bishop</note> shows in the same book concerning the "Supreme Good." He said that this was an "Idea" through whose participation every other thing was good. Hence, by positing "Ideas"—which were universal species, abstract and separate from particulars—he moved toward saving the <term>univocal generation</term> <note>The biological concept that like produces like (e.g., humans produce humans)</note> of animals and especially of men; and also to establish that the object of human sciences is eternal. Finally, as Cicero <note>original: "il pono" likely referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> writes in the second book of the *Politics* and Eusebius confirms in the aforementioned book in the twelfth chapter, Plato wished his Republic to be in such unity that women and possessions were held in common; and that females should be trained in the works of war; and that the city should be divided into twelve tribes, and the entire civil community should then be divided into two parts: judges and defenders of the war.

<margin>S</margin> Plato also wrote more worthy thoughts. Whence Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo</note> in the eighth book of the *City of God*, chapter eight, says the Platonists stated that the "light of all things to be learned is that very same God by whom all things were made" <note>original: "Platonici lumē oīum esse dixerunt ad discēda oīa eundē ipm deum a quo facta sunt oīa"</note>. Valerius Maximus <note>A 1st-century Roman author of anecdotes</note> in the eighth book, first chapter, writes that when Plato was angry with a servant, he told Speusippus, his nephew, to beat him, fearing that he himself could not diligently maintain the proper measure of vengeance while being gravely angry at the servant's crime; he estimated it would be unseemly if the punishment from Plato, together with the fault of the servant, merited equal reproach. And so as not to proceed at too great a length, we will refer only to a few sayings; for in his *Book of Laws* he says: "A sleeping man is worth nothing" <note>original: "Dormiēs nemo nullius pcii est"</note>; and "Truth is sweeter to hear than all things that are said" <note>original: "veritas auditu suauior oibus q dicunt"</note>. There is also no small custom in this. Besides these, there are almost infinite notable sayings of Plato transcribed by Cicero <note>original: "Tullio"</note> in his various books, and Diogenes Laertius writes of them quite diffusely; therefore, we will refer to no more of them for the present.

<margin>T</margin> Plato died at the age of eighty years, in the thirteenth year of the reign of Philip of Macedon, father of Alexander. In his books, according to the testimony of moderns, he said many things through fictions <note>referring to his use of allegories and dialogues</note>, always remaining within the true understanding, for which he is judged almost by consensus to be the first among all other philosophers.

<margin>V</margin> Next, the poet adds, saying that after Plato he saw **Aristotle** coming, full of high, great, and notable genius. Whence he says: *Aristotle then, full of high genius.* Aristotle, as Laertius writes, was from the village of Stagira, which was very near to Athens, the son of one Nicomachus and of Phaestiade his wife. This Nicomachus was by origin descended from Nicomachus, the son of Machaon, the son of Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine</note>, as Hermippus testifies. From there, Aristotle, having reached the age of seventeen and being learned in eloquence, gave himself to philosophy. He labored for three years under Socrates <note>Historical tradition usually places Aristotle only with Plato; the commentator may be conflating the succession</note> and then twenty under Plato; in which he became so perfect that he was deservedly called—as we said above—excellent over all other Greeks, except Plato. Averroes <note>A 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> of Córdoba, nevertheless, presumes much more of Aristotle than Cicero does. Whence he writes of him in this manner in the prologue of the *Physics*: "The name of the author is Aristotle, son of Nicomachus, the wisest of the Greeks, who composed many books in this art, and in Logic, and in Metaphysics; he himself discovered and completed them. These three arts he discovered; whatever is found written by the ancients is not worthy to be a part of this art, nor a principle, nor an ambiguity, let alone a principle of essence. He completed them: for none of those who followed him up to this time found in his words any error of any magnitude. That such a disposition is found in a single individual is miraculous and extraordinary. Therefore, the quality found in this man deserves to be called divine rather than human." <note>original: "Nomē autem auctoris est aristotiles... Ergo qlits reperta fuit i isto homine meretur potius dici diuinus q; bumanus"</note>. He confirms this same thing in the third book *On the Soul* and the first *On Generation*, where he says that Aristotle was the ultimate perfection of human nature. Whence he is deservedly judged a rule, an example, and the father of philosophy by those who love it, as Diogenes Laertius writes of Aristotle.

## CHAPTER FOUR

Aristotle attributes moderate praise to him <note>likely referring to the transition from Plato to Aristotle or perhaps a specific contemporary</note>, saying: "For in all things he possessed the highest zeal and industry, and flourished with an incredible abundance of invention." <note>original Latin: "cunctis eni in rebus summo studio atq; industria fuit iuventionisq; incredibili copia uiguit"</note> Quintilian also, in the tenth book of *The Education of the Orator*, enumerating the philosophers whose readings increase oratorical skill, says of Aristotle: "I am uncertain whether I should consider him more famous for his knowledge of things, the abundance of his writings, the sweetness of his speech, the sharpness of his inventions, or the variety of his works." <note>original Latin: "quod Aristotelē quē dubito an sciā rerum: an scriptorū copia: an eloquendi suavitate an inventionum acumine: an varietate operū clariorē putē"</note>

<margin>X</margin>
¶ Regarding the opinions of Aristotle, first concerning God, he said that He is a simple, unique, and eternal substance; as he demonstrates in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* when he says:
> Where indeed plurality is evil, there is therefore one ruler; <note>original Latin: "Quā qdem pluralitas mala est: unus est ergo princeps"</note>

And he proves this ruler to be entirely immobile <note>the "Unmoved Mover" concept</note> in the eighth book of the *Physics*; and that He understands and delights in His own intellection in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*. From this, he uniquely demonstrated the extent of the Divine Trinity, which would be an easy thing to recognize by joining several of his opinions together. He also said that God is the object of happiness in the tenth book of the *Ethics*, and the creator and maker of the universe in the book *On the Nature of the Gods*; and in the book *On the World* addressed to Alexander, confirming this opinion, he wrote these words:
> For it is necessary to consider this regarding God: that he is indeed the strongest in power, most glorious in appearance, immortal in life, and most powerful in virtue. Therefore, although invisible to every visible nature, he is made manifest by his works. For all passions—those in the air, those in the water, and those upon the earth—are truly said to be the works of God. <note>original Latin: "Oportet .n. hoc de Deo cōfiderare..."</note>

He also attributed the heavens to God as His seat, as is manifest in the same book and in the first book of *On the Heavens*.

<margin>Y</margin>
¶ As for the soul, as Cicero writes in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, this philosopher said in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original Latin: "de aia"</note> that it is a "first perfection" <note><term>first perfection</term> or 'entelechy,' the realization or form of a living body</note> of a natural and organic body. But he held that the human soul could be simple and incorruptible with two powers: one active, which purifies the <term>phantasms</term> <note>mental images or sensory impressions</note>, and the other passive, in which intellection resides. However, what happened to the soul after death he did not express very clearly; although Tacitus <note>likely a citation error in the original manuscript, perhaps referring to a commentator like Eustratius</note> in the first book of the *Ethics* sufficiently demonstrates that souls are reserved in places of happiness or misery when he defines how the prosperous or adverse fortunes of those surviving after a death should be compared. Regarding the heavens, as clearly seen in the first book of *On the Heavens* and the eighth book of the *Physics*, he affirmed there to be a <term>Prime Mover</term> <note>the first source of motion in the universe</note> and a simple body, separate and diverse from elemental nature, more perfect than other material things, but of less dignity than the abstract substances. He said the principles of natural things were a confused subject which he called <term>matter</term>, and a perfection and distinct act which he named <term>form</term>; besides these two, <term>privation</term> <note>the absence of a form in a subject that could potentially have it</note> could also be a principle. And this is because they are intrinsic and essential; but for extrinsic principles, he added the <term>end</term> <note>purpose or goal</note> and the <term>efficient</term> <note>the cause that brings something about</note>. From this results the number of the four causes expressed above at the beginning of the book, which entire process is seen openly in the first and second books of the *Physics* according to the second and fifth books of the *Metaphysics*.

<margin>Z</margin>
¶ Aristotle divided his Republic into six parts: Judges, Priests, Soldiers, the Wealthy, Artisans, and Farmers. In other areas, he similarly contradicted Plato, such as regarding the <term>Ideas</term> <note>Plato’s Theory of Forms, which Aristotle famously critiqued</note>, as one reads in the second book of the *Politics*. Aristotle wrote as many worthy opinions as there are propositions expressed by him. Hence, in his *Life*, Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, a 3rd-century biographer of philosophers</note> writes these excellent sayings:
> Education is an ornament in prosperity and a refuge in adversity. Discipline is the best provision for old age; for one gains this from philosophy: to do without being commanded what most do out of fear of the laws. Vices are sufficient for a miserable and unhappy life. <note>original Latin: "Eruditio iter prospera est ornamentum..."</note>

Aristotle also writes in the *Economics* concerning the state of man in the active life:
> Nothing can be better for a man than for husband and wife to govern the home with equal harmony. <note>original Latin: "Nihil .n. hoī potest esse melius..."</note>

Which true and excellent opinion I not only understand now through reason, but I know and affirm it through experience, by means of the innate modesty, most chaste benevolence, diligence, joyful modesty, and most helpful conversation of my dearest and beloved consort, **Mariana Ilicina**. He also attests in the first book of the *Politics* these worthy words:
> Man is the best of animals, but when separated from law and justice, he is the worst of all. The most cruel thing is injustice holding weapons. <note>original Latin: "Optimum aīalium homo est..."</note>

And in the third book of the *Ethics* he says: "Every wicked man is ignorant of what he ought to do and what he ought to avoid." <note>original Latin: "Ignorātia .oīs flagitiosus..."</note> In the fourth: "For it is the duty of virtue itself to bestow benefits rather than receive them, and to do honorable things rather than shameful ones." <note>original Latin: "Est eni ipsius virtutis offim..."</note> Finally, in the sixth he writes: "For it is impossible for anyone to be prudent unless he is good." <note>original Latin: "Impossibile est eni prudentem esse..."</note> Aristotle, therefore, as Laertius writes, was held in the highest reputation by Philip of Macedon, where he was the teacher of Alexander the Great. He established the Peripatetic sect in Athens—philosophers so named from their habit of walking. Finally, seeing Socrates <note>The author likely means Aristotle’s own departure to avoid the fate of Socrates</note> put to death in Athens because he blamed their idolatry, he departed and went to Chalcis, where he died at the age of sixty-two. His genius was so sublime that from that time until our own day, he has become more glorious through every age.

### THE TRIUMPH OF FAME
<meta>Google Digitized watermark at bottom right</meta>
<meta>Handwritten note '7pk' or '771' at top left</meta>

<margin>A</margin>Arioso. <note>This may be a stylistic label or a reference to a specific commentator's voice.</note> ¶ Master Francesco <note>referring to the author, Francesco Petrarch</note> subsequently adds, saying that after Aristotle, he saw Pythagoras follow: who, principally with humility, called philosophers by a worthy and appropriate name. Regarding Pythagoras, who first humbly named philosophy with a worthy name, as Justin writes in the twentieth book of *Foreign Wars* <note>original Latin: "de bellis externis"</note>: he was from the island of Samos, the son of a merchant named Demaratus. Wishing, therefore, to dedicate himself to the speculative sciences, he went principally to Egypt to learn the mathematical sciences. From there, he later passed into Babylonia solely to grasp astrological knowledge. He then came to stay in Macedonia and Crete to contemplate the laws of Lycurgus, of Minos, and of the other Greek republics. From Greece, Pythagoras then came to Italy in the region of Crotone; for which reason, as Augustine writes in the eighth book of *The City of God*, chapter two, Pythagoras was the beginning of Italian philosophy. Pythagoras then gave himself totally to the contemplative life, wherefore in the same book Augustine says:

> Since the study of wisdom consists in action and contemplation, one part of it can be called active and the other contemplative; of which the active pertains to leading a life, and the contemplative to perceiving the causes of nature and the simplest truth. Socrates is remembered to have excelled in the active. Pythagoras, however, insisted more on the contemplative with the powers of intelligence he could muster. <note>original Latin: "cum studium sapietie i actione & contemplatione versetur: vna de vna pars eius actiua altera contemplatiua dici potest: quarum actiua ad agēdam vitam ptinet contemplatiua ad pspiciendas nature causas & simplicissimam veritatē: Socrates i actiua excelluisse memoratur. Pythagoras vero magis contemplatiue qbus potuit itelligentie viribus istititisse"</note>

Cicero also, in the book *On Old Age*, calls Pythagoras the prince of philosophers. And Boethius, in *The Art of Music*, affirms Pythagoras to have been its author. Wherefore Isidore writes thus in the third book of the *Etymologies*: <margin>B</margin>

> The Greeks name Pythagoras as the first to have written down the discipline of numbers; it was finally set in order and spread by Nicomachus, which Apuleius first, and then Boethius, translated for the Latins. <note>original Latin: "Numeri disciplinam apud grecos primum Pythagoram nuncupant: perfcripsisse ad demum a Nicomacho diffusus fuisse dispositam quā apud latinos pmus apuleius: ac deinde Boetius transtulerunt."</note>

¶ Regarding his opinions: first, Pythagoras said, as is written in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, that the principles of natural things are finite and infinite number. And thus every natural thing was produced from number as if from a material cause. But in this Pythagoras differed from Plato: for Plato said that number was a principle through the participation made of it by natural things, while Pythagoras said it was through the imitation of number in the substance of natural things. Regarding the soul, he held the same, saying that it was composed of numbers, as Cicero writes in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, when it is separated from the body. Pythagoras said the soul was immortal and transferred itself into different bodies; wherefore, as Ovid writes in the fifteenth book of the *Metamorphoses*, Pythagoras affirmed of himself that he had been Euphorbus, a Trojan knight, and in that cruel war he had been killed. <margin>C</margin> Later, in that time when Pythagoras was found, the soul was that of a ruler governing the entire universal world, which a frivolous person would never oppose in the republic. ¶ He judged only one thing necessary: namely, friendship. Wherefore his disciples were bound by his doctrine to expose themselves to death for one another. For this reason, Pythias and Damon—as Valerius writes in the fourth book, seventh chapter, and Cicero in the third book of *On Duties*—observed the institute and precept of their master Pythagoras, exposing themselves to death for one another, becoming a guarantor for the life of the other before Dionysius of Syracuse. Dionysius, wishing to put one of them to death, was asked for the grace of allowing him to return to his homeland to dispose of his inheritance, after which he would return and give a guarantee for this. Dionysius consented to this request, and thus the friend entered prison for him. When the appointed day for the execution arrived, the friend returned to Dionysius and demanded his own execution and the release of his friend. <margin>D</margin> Seeing this with great wonder, Dionysius pardoned each of them and asked them to accept him as a third member in their friendship. ¶ Thereafter, Pythagoras having arrived one day before Leon, Prince of the Phliasians—as Cicero writes in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*—and having disputed some things very excellently, Leon asked him what his art or profession was. Pythagoras replied that he knew no art, but was truly a philosopher. Pythagoras spoke this name out of great humility, and it was truly a worthy and fitting name for philosophers. Here it should be understood that before the time of Pythagoras, studious men called themselves "wise men" <note>referring to the Greek "Sophoi"</note>. This name was too arrogant, as wisdom is the habit through which the causes of all things, human and divine, are comprehended, <margin>E</margin> as is written in the second book of *On Duties*, the sixth of the *Ethics*, and in the *Metaphysics*. Such a habit is impossible for men to possess. ¶ And therefore, Pythagoras, as this name seemed proud to him, called them truly "philosophers": that is, lovers of wisdom. Thus, this name is worthy and appropriate, as he demonstrates.
