# CHAPTER FOUR

<margin>F</margin>
Augustine shows this in the eighth book of *The City of God*, in the first chapter, saying: <note>original Latin: "Philosophorum nomen si latine interpretetur: amorem sapientie significat..."</note> *“If the name of ‘philosophers’ is translated into Latin, it signifies the ‘love of wisdom.’ Furthermore, if wisdom is God through whom all things were made, as divine authority and truth demonstrate, then the true philosopher is a lover of God.”* Because of this, we always direct our nine universal powers—namely, our will and intellect—toward God as the infinite good and the highest truth. Therefore, men should worthily be called philosophers because of this inclination. 

¶ Pythagoras wrote many worthy sentences, some of which we will report here first: <note>These are "Golden Verses" or traditional maxims attributed to Pythagoras.</note> *“In every way, one must flee and cut away: sickness from the body, ignorance from the soul, excess from the belly, sedition from the city, discord from the home, and intemperance from all things in common.”* *“The end of anger is the beginning of repentance.”* *“He is not free whom a proud spirit inflames.”* *“He knows not how to speak who knows not how to keep silent.”* *“A man, if he is at his best, proves himself by his affections.”* *“Riches are to be despised which are lost by generosity and rot through stinginess.”* 

Finally, Pythagoras departed from Leonte and came to Metapontum, where he died. He was held in such great veneration that he was considered divine by the people, and they turned his own house into a temple.

Afterward, Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch</note> brings forward his poem, saying that after Pythagoras, he saw Socrates follow, then Xenophon, and that bold old man of poetic frenzy, Homer, to whom the Muses were such close friends and familiars that Argos, Mycenae, and Troy are famous because of him and have come into great light. This Homer, the poet adds, was the one who sang of the wanderings and toils of Ulysses, son of Laertes, and of Achilles, son of the goddess Thetis. He was the first painter on paper of ancient memories. Whence he says:

<margin>G</margin>
<margin>Socrates, as Laertius writes, was the son of one Sophroniscus, a stone-worker, and of Phaenarete, his midwife wife. He was born in a village called Alopeke within the Athenian jurisdiction. Socrates, therefore, as Plato especially notes, did not overlook any place he could go, provided he knew that doctrine was taught there. But because the things of the earth...</margin>

...seeing that things beneath the heavens were always in a state of continuous flux, and that those things above the heavens were hidden from our senses and could not be understood except through probable opinion, he said that there is no natural science. Therefore, because of this, he turned entirely to the philosophy of morals. For this reason, Aristotle writes of him in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, saying: <note>original Latin: "socrate vero circa moralia negociante: & de tota natura nihil."</note> *“Socrates, however, occupied himself with moral matters, and not at all with the whole of nature.”* 

And on this subject, Laertius also says of Socrates: *“Noticing that the fruit of natural speculation was nothing, he found that nothing was necessary for the duties of life except ethics. Philosophizing daily about this both in workshops and in public, he urged that those things rather should be sought which instruct morals and whose use is necessary for us at home. From here, indeed, by the testimony of Homer, good and evil are born.”* 

Isidore also, in the *Etymologies*, confirms the same, saying: *“Socrates was the first to establish Ethics to correct and compose morals, and he directed all his study toward the discussion of living well, dividing it into four virtues: namely, prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance.”* <note>These are the four Cardinal Virtues: Wisdom/Prudence, Courage/Fortitude, Justice, and Moderation/Temperance.</note>

<margin>H</margin>
Finally, Cicero, confirming the same sentiment, says in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: *“Socrates, however, was the first to call philosophy down from heaven, and placed it in cities, and introduced it into homes, and compelled it to inquire about life and morals, and good and evil things.”* 

Regarding the opinions Socrates imagined about God, as Eusebius shows in the fourteenth book of *The Preparation for the Gospel* and in the sixth chapter, he held that God is the unique, uniform, and most perfect Good and Intelligence, upon whom everything and every tiny preparation of ours is dependent. He said the human soul is immortal, and after its separation from the body, it is subject to divine justice according to the works performed in life, as we said above by the testimony of Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*. He said the world is a common fatherland, and he established that the Republic ought to be as Plato described, and united with it.

...sentences in addition to those that Cicero <note>original: "Tullio"</note> wrote in *On Old Age*, the *Tusculan Disputations*, and *On Duties*, and in his other works. Among the first: *“Consider the eyes and ears of the common crowd to be bad witnesses; one should pray to the gods only for this: that they grant what is good. For we often seek in prayer that which it would have been better not to have obtained. Indeed, the virtue of youth is ‘nothing in excess’; what fortune has granted, let justice temper; what justice finds, let moderation govern. For you will always be able to deceive fame, but never your conscience. He who is not ashamed of his fault doubles his sin. If you doubt anything, do not do it; rather, flee what has been denied by the judgment of the soul; if you act well, you will help yourself.”* Socrates died in the prisons of Athens because he criticized their idolatry, at the age of eighty years according to Cicero in *On Old Age*, but according to Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, a biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> at seventy years, the Athenians having condemned him to die by poison. They later grieved so much for his death that they condemned to exile all those who had been the cause of it, and some they put to a cruel death; and they erected a statue for the eternal memory of Socrates. Thus his great merits became known.

¶ Xenophon, a worthy and outstanding philosopher, was the son of one named Gryllus, born in a fortress called Erchia <note>original: "Archieo"</note> near Athens and under its jurisdiction. He was of a very beautiful body and, in his character and intellect, eager for every praiseworthy study. One day, as Xenophon was walking through a narrow alley in Athens, he was met in that narrow passage by Socrates. Socrates, wanting to prevent him from passing further, blocked his way and asked him where he intended to go. Xenophon replied that he wanted to go where good and learned men were to be found. To which Socrates added: "Then follow me and learn." And Xenophon, being invited, obeyed. Xenophon was not only a clear and distinguished philosopher but an excellent and eloquent orator. Regarding him, Quintilian says in the tenth book of the *Institutes of Oratory*: *“Xenophon does not fall short for me, but is to be placed among the philosophers.”* And he adds what I commemorate: *“That unaffected pleasantness of Xenophon, which no affectation could ever achieve, as if he had fashioned the very language of the Graces.”* Valerius Maximus in the fifth book, last chapter, says: *“Xenophon, as far as Socratic discipline is concerned, is next to Plato in the rank of happy and blessed fertility.”* Diogenes Laertius conforms to the aforementioned opinions, saying that *“he called Xenophon the 'Attic Muse' because of the sweetness of his eloquence and his incredible facility.”* Regarding his opinions, he differed in nothing from his teacher Socrates; for he imitated him <term>to the fingernail</term> <note>original: "ad unguem," an idiom meaning "perfectly" or "to the highest degree of polish."</note> as Laertius writes. Xenophon was very constant, magnanimous, and a great observer of justice. For this reason, while he was sacrificing one day in Corinth, he received news at that moment that his son—who was named Gryllus after his father—had died in battle. He endured this with the greatest patience, nor did he stop the practice of sacrificing for this reason; he only removed a crown he had on his head. But hearing how his son had been killed while fighting manfully among the enemies, he put the crown back on, rejoicing more in his son's virtue, worthy name, and acquired fame than he was sad for his bitter death. ¶ Xenophon wrote many notable sayings, among which was this: having been one day greatly insulted with dishonest words, he only replied: *“You have devoted your study to speaking evil. I, however, with my conscience as witness, have learned to despise insults.”* Xenophon died in Corinth in the ninetieth <note>original: ".xxxix." is likely a scribe's error for "lxxxx" (90), as Xenophon lived to an old age; however, the text reads thirty-nine.</note> year of his praiseworthy life.

¶ Homer was a most excellent poet among all others who ever lived in Greece. His dignity can easily be known by considering that many homelands in Greece went to arms only for Homer, each claiming he had been a citizen of theirs. Thus Cicero says in the oration *For the Poet Archias*: *“The Colophonians say Homer is their citizen; the Chians claim him as their own; the Salaminians reclaim him; the Smyrnaeans, however, confirm he is theirs, and so they even dedicated a shrine to him in their city.”* Many others besides fight and contend among themselves for this. And Marcus Tullius [Cicero] adds in the same oration the judgment of Alexander the Great, who judged Achilles happy only because he had Homer to sing his praises. Quintilian also describes the praise of Homer in the tenth book of the *Institutes of Oratory*: *“Just as all the force of springs and the course of rivers take their beginning from the Ocean, so Homer gave the example and origin to all parts of eloquence. No one has surpassed him in sublimity for great things, nor in propriety for small things; he is at once joyful and grave, pleasant and serious, admirable both for his abundance and his brevity; he is most eminent not only for poetic but for oratorical virtue. For, to say nothing of his praises, exhortations, and consolations, does not the ninth book, which contains the embassy sent to Achilles, or the contention between the leaders in the first book, or all the opinions expressed in the second book, explain the arts of legal disputes and counsels?”* And a little further down he adds: *“Truly, he has without doubt left everyone, in every kind of eloquence, far behind him.”*

### CHAPTER FOUR

<margin>O</margin>
...he left behind the most excellent Heroic works. Now, concerning his opinions, Homer felt primarily about God according to the Greek custom and the plurality of gods; wherefore Helinand <note>Hélinand of Froidmont, a medieval monk and writer known for his chronicles.</note> writes that because Homer affirmed that the gods fought among themselves, he was considered insane. Perhaps this critic did not realize that vernacular poets often use fiction and refer to the opinions of others rather than affirming things as their own.

<margin>P</margin>
Homer wrote of the Trojan War, the praises of Achilles, and the wanderings of Ulysses; he was among the first to give origin to history. Homer died, as written in the *Policraticus* <note>A work on political philosophy by John of Salisbury.</note>, at the age of 108. Walking one day along the seashore, he encountered certain fishermen who proposed this enigma to him: *“What we caught we do not have; what we did not catch we do have.”* <note>original: "Quot cepimus non habemus: quot vero non cadimus habemus." This is a famous classical riddle about lice; the fishermen "had" the lice they couldn't catch (on their bodies) and "didn't have" the ones they caught and threw away.</note> Considering this, and being unable to comprehend it with his mind, Homer perished from anger and the agony of the thought. The poet follows this by saying that near Homer followed the Mantuan, Virgil, who in the heroic style jousts with him as an equal in eloquence, invention, and poetic fantasy. Wherefore he says:

<margin>Q</margin>
->Hand in hand with him, singing, comes<-
->The Mantuan, who jousts as his equal;<-

Virgil—as Servius <note>A famous 4th-century commentator on Virgil.</note> writes at the beginning of the *Bucolics*—was the son of Maro Virgil, a potter <term>potter</term><note>original: "figulo." Ancient biographies often claimed Virgil's father was a humble artisan or potter.</note>, and of Maia his wife, citizens of Mantua. He willingly gave himself to studies, principally in Verona, then in Milan, and finally practiced in Naples. Having served in the military under Asinius Pollio and Maecenas, who were very dear to Octavian [Augustus], he was intensely loved by the Emperor. Quintilian writes these worthy words about Virgil in the tenth book of his *Education of an Orator*, having spoken of the Greeks: *“Just as among them Homer is the standard, so among us Virgil has provided the most auspicious beginning; for of all the poets of this genre, Greek or Roman, he undoubtedly holds the place closest to Homer. Indeed, I recall these words from Domitius Afer when I was a young man: when I asked him which poet he believed came closest to Homer, he said, 'Virgil is second, yet closer to the first than he is to the third.' And by Hercules, though we must yield to that celestial and immortal nature of Homer, there is more care and diligence in Virgil, perhaps because he had to labor harder; what we lack in eminence we perhaps make up for in consistency. All others follow far behind.”* <note>original: "Ita ut apud illos Homerus: sic apud nos Virg. auspicacissimum dederit exordium... Ceteri omnes longe sequentur."</note> Propertius also describes Virgil with this greatest praise: *“Yield, Roman writers; yield, Greeks! Something greater than the Iliad is being born.”* <note>original: "Cedite Romani scriptores. cedite Grai. Nescio quid maius nascitur iliade."</note>

<margin>R</margin>
Regarding his opinions, anyone who carefully considers his sayings will find that Virgil held there to be one omnipotent and lone God. Thus, in the fifth book of the *Aeneid*, introducing Aeneas invoking Jove after his ships were set on fire by the work of Juno, he says: *“Then pious Aeneas tore the robe from his shoulders and called the gods for help, stretching out his palms: 'Omnipotent Jupiter, if you do not yet utterly hate the Trojans, if your ancient piety regards human labors, grant that the fleet may escape the flame.'”* <note>original: "Tum pius eneas humeris abscindere veste... os flammam evadere classi."</note> And in the tenth book, introducing Venus speaking to Jove, he says: *“O Father, O eternal power of men and gods! For what other power can there be that we might now implore?”* <note>original: "O pater o hominum divumque eterna potestas... iplorare queamus."</note> Concerning the universe and our souls, Virgil holds them to be eternal, as he demonstrates in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*; and he says that heaven is the seat of God and the generative cause of earthly things, as is clearly seen in the tenth book of the *Aeneid* and the first of the *Georgics*.

<margin>S</margin>
Virgil wrote as many noble sayings as there are almost verses in his three principal works, setting aside his other minor poems. Thus, primarily against the proud, he says in the first book of the *Aeneid*: *“If you despise the human race and mortal arms, yet expect the gods to be mindful of right and wrong.”* <note>original: "Si genus humanum & mortalia tenitis arma. At sperate deos memores fandi atque nefandi."</note> And in the sixth: *“Be warned: learn justice and do not slight the gods.”* <note>original: "Discite iustitiam moniti & non tenere divos."</note> Virgil exhorted children to paternal reverence when he introduced Aeneas speaking to Anchises during the ruin of Troy, saying: *“Come then, dear father, place yourself upon my neck; I shall support you on my shoulders, and that labor will not weigh me down. However things fall out, there shall be one common danger and one salvation for us both. Let little Iulus be my companion, and let my wife follow our footsteps at a distance.”* <note>original: "Ergo age care pater cervici imponere nostræ... longe servet vestigia coniunx."</note> He also demonstrates how great the love of one's country should be when he says: *“In my madness I take up arms; there is little purpose in arms, but my spirit burns to gather a band for war and rush to the citadel. Fury and anger drive my mind headlong, and it occurs to me that it is beautiful to die in arms.”* <note>original: "Arma amens capio... Pulchrumque mori succurrit in armis."</note> Ultimately, one must conclude that he described every gesture and work of virtue, as is known throughout his books.

<margin>T</margin>
Virgil died at the age of 52 in Taranto; afterward, his bones were carried with glory to Naples, where it is still believed they rest. Consequently, <term>M.F.</term> <note>Likely referring to the commentator or the poet Petrarch's narrator.</note> brings forth Cicero <note>original: "Cicerone"</note> after Virgil, saying that after him he saw one pass who scattered flowers along the way upon the grass; and this was that Marco Tullio [Cicero], in whom it is clearly shown how much the faculty of eloquence has flowers and also fruits. He and Virgil together are truly the eyes and the light of the Latin tongue. Wherefore he says:

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

->And one, at whose passing the grass flowered:<-
## **This is that Marcus Tullius, in whom is shown**
## **Clearly, how much eloquence has fruits and flowers;**
## **These are the eyes of our language.**

---

<margin>V</margin> ¶ **Marcus Tullius Cicero, as Plutarch writes,** was from Arpinum, the son of a noble man descended from an ancient line from Tullius, King of the Volsci, and Helvia <note>The OCR reads "Olbia," but Cicero's mother was Helvia.</note>, his beloved and dearest lady. From his tender age, by devoting himself to the exercise of study, he rose to such glory and reputation that he deservedly won the palm of eloquence. Concerning him, Plutarch writes that in Athens, under several teachers, he learned Greek letters in due time. Later, having arrived at Rhodes at the persuasion of Apollonius, the Greek philosopher and orator, he declaimed in the Greek language. By this act, he drew all his listeners to the greatest admiration and compelled them to praise him highly. At the end, after a long silence, Apollonius spoke these words regarding Cicero:

> I indeed praise and admire you, Cicero. However, the reason I remained silent for so long while others were finishing their speeches is due to a certain sorrow and pity. For I was reflecting to myself on the former times—how the Greeks flourished above all other nations in arms, the governance of public affairs, and domestic institutions. In these matters, the Romans have now long since surpassed us, taking the prize by the confession of all through their true and incredible virtue. Only one thing remained: the glory of learning and eloquence. Now, through you, I see even this being taken from us and transferred to the Romans, so that nothing of special praise is left among our people.

<margin>X</margin> ¶ No less does **Quintilian, in the tenth book of his *Institutes of Oratory*,** describe the primary praises of Cicero, saying: Marcus Tullius, having devoted himself entirely to the imitation of the Greeks, seems to me to have expressed the power of Demosthenes, the abundance of Plato, and the sweetness of Socrates. Indeed, he did not just achieve the best of each through study, but rather brought forth most—or rather all—virtues from himself through the most blessed fertility of his immortal genius. For he does not merely collect rainwater, as Pindar says, but overflows from a living spring, born by a certain gift of providence so that eloquence might test all its powers within him. For who can teach more diligently or move an audience more vehemently? To whom did such sweetness ever belong? You would believe that he commands the very things he extorts from the listener; and when he strikes the judge down with his force, the judge does not seem to be carried away, but to follow willingly. In all he says, there is such authority that one is ashamed to disagree; he brings not the zeal of an advocate, but the reliability of a witness or a judge. While among all these qualities—which any other man could scarcely achieve individually even with the most intense care—his words flow without effort. His speech carries with it a most happy facility, even though nothing is more beautiful to hear. For this reason, he was not undeservedly said by the men of his time "to reign in the courts." Among posterity, he achieved the same status: so that the name "Cicero" is no longer the name of a man, but of eloquence itself. Therefore, let us look to him; let him be the example set before us. Let a man know he has made progress when he finds that Cicero pleases him greatly.

<margin>y</margin> ¶ Regarding the opinions of Tullius <note>Tullius is Marcus Tullius Cicero's family name; medieval and Renaissance writers often referred to him as "Tullius" or "Tully."</note> concerning God, the world, and the soul, it is not necessary to report further. This is because, by the testimony of Cicero himself, he was an Academic <term>Academic: A follower of the Skeptic school of philosophy at the Platonic Academy, who argued that certain knowledge is impossible and one should follow the most probable argument.</term>, whose profession is to affirm nothing, but to defend every contrary side at will, provided it is probable. Whence he says in the third book of *On Duties*: **"For our Academy gives us great license, so that whatever appears most probable, we may defend by our own right."** And so **Augustine, in the fourth book of *The City of God*,** in chapter thirty, while reserving the palm of eloquence for Tullius, diminishes his authority in all other things, saying: *Cicero the augur mocks auguries and rebukes men who moderate their life's counsel by the voices of crows and ravens; but this Academic, who contends that all things are uncertain, is unworthy to have any authority in these matters.* However, even if the works of Cicero do not show us assertive doctrine, the "fruits and flowers" of eloquence are clearly seen in them. Regarding this, **Quintilian says in the second book of his *Institutes of Oratory*:** *And by Hercules, that god who is the prince, the parent of things and the maker of the world, separated humans from other animals by no greater gift than the faculty of speech.* Since this faculty was supreme in Cicero, the most noble ornament of man is deservedly made known through him.

<margin>Z</margin> ¶ Cicero wrote as many worthy maxims and moral sayings as there are expressions and words in his books. Leaving aside those inserted throughout his books, I wish to report only some of his sayings from the orations. Primarily, in the first oration against Catiline <note>Catiline was a Roman senator who led a conspiracy to overthrow the government; Cicero's speeches against him are masterpieces of political rhetoric.</note>, he says: *Just as men sick with a heavy disease, when they are tossed by heat and fever, seem at first to be relieved if they drink cold water, but afterward are afflicted much more heavily and vehemently.* And in the third: *But if those two days on which we are preserved are no less joyful and illustrious to us—because the joy of safety is certain, while the condition of birth is uncertain, and because we are born without sensing it...*

<meta>catchword: scimur (we are known)</meta>

### CHAPTER FOUR
144

<margin>In the fourth [against Catiline] he says:</margin>
¶ We are made through pleasure, but we are preserved through virtue. For neither can a shameful death happen to a brave man, nor an untimely one to a man of consular rank, nor a miserable one to a wise man. <margin>In the same speech:</margin> However, those among the number of citizens who, corrupted by some madness, have once begun to be enemies of their country: when you have repelled them from the destruction of the republic, you can neither restrain them by force nor appease them by kindness. In addition to these, in the first of the *Philippics* <note>The *Philippics* were a series of speeches Cicero delivered attacking Mark Antony.</note> he says: No one is happy who lives under such a condition that he may be killed not only with impunity, but even with the highest glory for his killer. <margin>In the second:</margin> Things ill-gotten are ill-lost. Is it not, then, a thousand times better to die than to be unable to live in one’s own city without the protection of arms? Peace is tranquil liberty; slavery is the worst of all evils, to be repelled not only by war, but even by death. <margin>In the 7th:</margin> But even recently, it was the highest praise for men of consular rank to be watchful, to think, to be present in spirit, and always to be either doing or saying something for the sake of the republic. <margin>In the 11th:</margin> It is the nature of any man to err; but of no one except a fool to persevere in error. <margin>In the last [the 14th]:</margin> For as a race is surpassed by a race, so in brave men, virtue is surpassed by virtue. It would be long and tedious to run through all of Tullius’s orations to report those grave and excellent sentiments. And therefore, out of the many that exist, let these few written above suffice. ¶ Cicero died on the seashore near Astura, killed by the soldiers of Mark Antony led by one Pompilius <note>Historical sources usually identify him as Popilius Laenas, a man Cicero had previously defended in court.</note>, whom Cicero had once defended in a trial for his life. As Plutarch shows us at the end of his life, the grass flowered where Tullius walked as a sign and omen of the ultimate perfection and vitality of his oratorical faculty. The poet then narrates, saying that after Cicero came Demosthenes, who was entirely without hope of obtaining the first place among orators; and in his appearance, he showed he was not content with the honor given to him by being placed second; and in his movement, he truly seemed like a great flash of lightning, all ignited with the flame of fire. Wherefore he says:

<margin>¶ **Demosthenes:** As Plutarch writes, he was the son of Demosthenes the Athenian, called a "maker of knives" <note>original: "Maceopio," a corruption of the Greek *machaeropoios*</note> because he worked with blades in Athens; and his mother was the daughter of one Gylon and a barbarian woman, as Aeschines used to reproach Demosthenes. This man, then, desiring infinitely from a tender age to pursue learning—especially the faculty of oratory—devoted all his study and diligence to it with the greatest care. So much so that he became known throughout all Greece as the most illustrious and distinguished orator, as is written by Valerius Maximus in his eighth book, and by Plutarch in his *Life* of him, and likewise in the *Policraticus*. Concerning him, Cicero deservedly writes these words in *On Famous Orators*:</margin>

->Afterwards came Demosthenes, who was<-
->Now beyond the hope of the first place;<-
->Not well content with second honors,<-
->He seemed a great lightning bolt, all of fire.<-

For he is clearly perfect, and nothing is lacking in him. You would easily say that Demosthenes lacks nothing; nothing could be found more acutely in the cases he wrote; nothing, so to speak, was so subtle or crafty that he did not see it; nothing could be said more precisely or clearly to make it more polished; nothing was out of step, nothing uninspired, nothing unadorned by the weight of words or sentiments that could be more elevated. <margin>G</margin> ¶ Quintilian also, in the tenth book of the *Education of the Orator*, says of Demosthenes: A huge band of orators follows; although one age produced ten at once in Athens, Demosthenes was by far the chief among them, and was almost the very law of oratory. There is such force in him, everything is so dense, and stretched as if by certain sinews; there is nothing idle in his style of speaking, such that nothing is missing in him. Nor will you find anything redundant. <margin>H</margin> Aeschines also, as is written in the *Compendium of the Lives and Manners of Philosophers*, used to say of Demosthenes: Whoever had considered the sharpest vigor of his eyes, the terrible weight of his expression, the sound of his voice accommodated to every single word, and the most effective movements of his body, would surely recognize that although nothing can be added to his written work, a great part of Demosthenes is missing when he is read rather than heard. <margin>D</margin> There is no more to report regarding the opinions of Demosthenes, as he was not one of the natural philosophers, but only an excellent orator. ¶ He nevertheless wrote many worthy and notable sayings. First: A friend is not one who does not share in one's fortune. Also: You will speak well if you say nothing except what you know well. Truth separates the character of the free man from the slave; lying mixes the slave and the free man together. Finally, going into exile, he turned his face toward Athens and said:

> O Pallas, guardian of cities, why do you delight in three most hostile beasts: the owl, the dragon, and the people?

<margin>E</margin> ¶ Demosthenes died through the actions of Antipater <note>Antipater was a powerful Macedonian general and a successor to Alexander the Great.</note>, who had seized the liberty of the Athenians. He died in the temple of Neptune in Calauria, already mature in years, on the 16th of July, as Plutarch writes, by taking poison which he had always kept with him in a reed <note>A hollow "calamus" or writing quill used to hide the poison.</note> for whatever outcome fortune might bring. He resolved to do this because an actor of tragedies named Archias wanted to bring him back alive by force to Antipater. Master Francesco <note>Petrarch, the author of the original poem.</note> adds, saying that along with Demosthenes, he saw Aeschines coming, who could feel and understand how much he was diminished and hoarse when compared to the great "thunder" of the orator Demosthenes. Thus he says:

<margin>F</margin> ¶ Just as Diogenes Laertius writes that there were eight men, each of whom was named Aeschines, the third one he lists is the one intended here by our Master Francesco. This Aeschines, then, was the rival of Demosthenes, a worthy and outstanding orator and philosopher in his own right. Concerning him, Cicero continues his praise of Demosthenes by saying: *Next to him was Aeschines* <note>original: "Huic proximus Aeschines fuit."</note>.

> Let Aeschines say it, who could hear it,
> When near his thunder he felt himself grow hoarse.

<margin>G</margin> ¶ And Quintilian likewise adds this to the context cited above: *Aeschines is fuller and more expansive, and seems grander the less restrained he is. However, he has more flesh but fewer muscles* <note>original Latin: "Plenior Aeschines et magis fusus..." From Quintilian’s *Institutes of Oratory*. He uses a physical metaphor to say Aeschines is more ornate but less powerful than Demosthenes.</note>. Aeschines, then, by his learning was made a citizen of Athens solely for having composed a tragedy. Regarding him, Augustine says in *The City of God*, chapter 11: *Aeschines and Aristodemus were granted the Athenian citizenship because of their production of tragedies.* He frequently came into conflict with Demosthenes, most notably once in the case of Ctesiphon, in which Demosthenes was judged superior and Aeschines far less eloquent. For this reason, he left Athens in great indignation and went to Rhodes. There, at the request of the people, he recited his own speech and the one Demosthenes had given in Athens for the aforementioned case. When the Rhodians were moved to great admiration and praised Demosthenes most highly, Aeschines said—as Pliny writes in the second book of his letters to his nephew—*What if you had heard that beast himself speaking?* <note>original: "Quid si bestiam illam perorantem audivissetis." A famous tribute to his rival's delivery.</note> He did not wish to remain silent regarding the great dignity Demosthenes possessed in expressing appropriate actions. His opinions, like those of Demosthenes, are not to be overlooked, as he was more eloquent than speculative.

<margin>H</margin> ¶ Aeschines wrote several noble sayings, as one reads in the oration of Leonardo of Arezzo <note>Leonardo Bruni (1370–1444), a famous humanist scholar.</note>, a most eloquent man, which he translated into Latin. This was written against Ctesiphon, who was a dear friend to Demosthenes. He says first: *For he who hates his own children and is a bad father can never be a good governor of the people. He who is bad in private can never be good in public. He who is wicked at home will be virtuous nowhere, whether in his homeland or on an embassy; for he has changed his location, but not his character.*

<margin>I</margin> ¶ Aeschines also died in a very long and mature old age. Master Francesco then follows by saying that he cannot now recount in order where this or that man of letters was seen, or which went before or followed behind. This is because, beholding such and so great a crowd and thinking upon it, the number was countless; and furthermore, his eye and thought strayed from his intended order. At this point, he adds that he saw Solon, who planted the most useful plant—which today is so poorly cultivated and still produces such bad and pestilential fruit—and with him were the other six in whom all Greece boasts and glories. Thus he says:

<margin>R</margin> ¶ Concerning the understanding of the preceding verses, it is important to know primarily that the poet is right to say he cannot recount this multitude in order: first, because of the great number of learned men; and second, because it is difficult to know who should precede the other in fame. Solon, then, who is numbered among this company, is first recounted by our Master Francesco. As Laertius writes, he was the son of Execestides of the kingdom of Salamis. This man, desiring to achieve—

> I cannot recount in order,
> 	This one or that, where I saw them or when;
> 	And which went before, and which followed after:
> For thinking of innumerable things,
> 	And beholding such and so great a crowd,
> 	The eye and the thought went straying.
> I saw Solon, who planted the useful plant;
> 	Which, if ill-cultivated, produces ill fruit;
> 	With the other six, of whom Greece boasts.

It concludes by introducing Solon and the Seven Sages of Greece, using the metaphor of a "useful plant" for the laws and wisdom they provided.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of famous Greeks in Petrarch's "Triumph of Fame." Following the discussion of the orators Demosthenes and Aeschines, the author introduces Solon, the great Athenian lawgiver, who is the first of the Seven Sages featured in this section.</meta>

## CHAPTER FOUR

To achieve his learning, he did not overlook any region where he could engage in scholarly exercise. Having reached the highest perfection, he never ceased to do things that were useful to the republic. In times past, there had been cruel wars between the Athenians and the Megarians over the region of Salamis <note>An island near Athens; its possession was vital for controlling the Saronic Gulf.</note>, to the point that both republics had prohibited anyone from speaking of it further under penalty of death. Solon, recognizing that this province was extremely useful to the Athenians, feigned for a long time to be a fool. Then one day, through gestures and acts of folly, he began to speak in the forum to the people about the recovery of Salamis. He did not finish his speech before the Athenians, incited by him, took up arms and began the campaign, obtaining it with victory and honor, from which the Athenian republic gained great utility. This simulated folly of Solon was truly a supreme prudence, highly profitable to all Athenians.

But certainly, his most worthy work was when he led them to live under the most useful plant of the laws, which brought forth the worthy fruit of the Roman laws written in the Twelve Tables <note>The foundation of Roman law, traditionally said to have been influenced by a commission sent to Greece to study the laws of Solon.</note> and others which had their dependence on them. From these is constituted today the sacred and venerable body of civil law <term>Corpus Iuris Civilis</term>, as one reads in the Digest, on the origin of law <note>original: "l.ij. ff. de origi. iur." Referring to Book 1, Title 2 of the Digest of Justinian.</note>. The utility of these laws can be well known through the text of the legal experts in the Digest, under the title "On Laws," where it says: "Law is a common precept, the counsel of wise men, the restraint of crimes committed voluntarily or through ignorance, and the common promise of the republic" <note>original: "Lex est cõe preceptum sapientium virorum consultum delictorum quae sponte vel ignorantia fuerit coertio: communis reipub. sponsio"</note>. 

And in the law named for Demosthenes under the same title, the text says: "Law is indeed a discovery and a gift of God; the dogma of all wise men; the correction of voluntary and involuntary sins; and the common covenant of the city according to which all those in the city ought to live" <note>original: "Lex est inuentio quidem & donum dei. Dogma autem omnium sapientium. Correctio autem voluntariorum & non voluntariorum peccatorum. Ciuitatis autẽ cõpositio cõmunis sm quã omnes decet viuere qui in ciuitate sunt."</note>. And in the same text, by the authority of Chrysippus the Stoic <note>A leading Stoic philosopher known for his work on logic and ethics.</note>, it adds: "Law is the knowledge of all things human and divine. It must stand over both the good and the bad, and be a prince and a leader. It is the rule of the just and the unjust, and of those things which are social by nature; the commander of what must be done, and the prohibitor of what must not be done" <note>original: "Lex est omnium rerum & humanaru & diuinarum notitia. Oportet autẽ eam prestare bonis & malis & principem & ducem esse secundum hoc. Regula est iustorum & iniustorum & eorum quae natura ciuilis sunt: preceptrix quidem faciendorum: prohibitrix autem non faciendorum."</note>.

Aristotle also, in the fifth book of the *Ethics*, says regarding the utility of laws and their perfection: "For laws provide for all things, aiming at the common utility of all" <note>original: "Leges enim prouident in omnibus coniectantes aut cõmunẽ omniũ utilitatem"</note>. And Cicero, in the *Philippics*, in the tenth oration, writes these words: "For law is nothing other than right reason drawn from the divine mind of the gods, commanding what is honorable and forbidding the contrary" <note>original: "Est enim lex nihil aliud nisi recta & a numine deorum tracta oratio: imperans honesta: prohibensq: contraria."</note>. The fruits that are born of these laws are very well expressed in the text of the law itself, where it says: "The power of the law is this: to command, to forbid, to permit, and to punish" <note>original: "Legis virtus haec est: imperare vetare permittere & punire."</note>. And in the law on justice, it says: "The precepts of law are: to live honestly, to injure no one, and to give everyone their due" <note>original: "Iuris precepta sunt honesta viuere: alterum non laedere: ius suũ vnicuique tribuere"</note>. This most useful plant is the unique bond and foundation of every well-constituted republic.

<margin>L</margin> ¶ Already in the time of our Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, and even in the time of Solon himself, this was quite poorly cultivated. This is shown by Solon's answer when he was asked what law was; he replied: "Law is a spider's web: because if anything weak falls into it, it is caught; but anything heavy and strong breaks the web and passes through" <note>original: "Lex est aranea tela: quia si in ea inciderit quid debile retinetur: graue autem ac validum pertransit tela rescissa"</note>. From this, the philosopher [Aristotle] clearly demonstrates in the second book of the *Politics*, and Cicero in the third book of *On Duties*, how many evils are born from the non-observance of laws. This non-observance is that wicked and perverse "cultivation" contributed to the laws, from which is born the division between what is honorable and what is useful, as noted in the fifth book of the *Ethics*; and Cicero shows it to us in the book *On Duties* when he says: "Wherefore the error of dishonest men, when it seizes upon something that seems useful, immediately separates it from what is honorable. From this come daggers, from this come poisons, from this come false wills, from this come thefts and embezzlements; the plundering and robbing of allies and citizens; and from this comes the unbearable power of excessive wealth" <note>original: "Quare error hominum non proborum cum aliquid quod vtile visum est arripuit id cõtinuo secernit ab honesto: hinc sicce: hinc venena: hinc falsi testamenti nascuntur: hinc furta: hinc peculatus. Expilationes: direptiones sociorum & ciuium hinc opum nimiarum potentiae non ferendae."</note>. Finally, in free cities, there arises the desire for kingship, than which nothing more foul or hideous can be imagined. From this legal invalidity also arises sedition, discord, the robbery of the lesser people, and ultimately internal wars and the ruin of the empire, as Otho showed in a single word, saying: "When obedience perishes, the empire also dies" <note>original: "Per eunte obsequio imperium quoq; interdít." From Tacitus, *Histories*.</note>. How much this was true in the Italian republics and lordships is well known through the writers of the annals of Italian history, especially by Matteo Palmeri <note>Matteo Palmieri (1406–1475), a Florentine humanist and historian.</note> of Florence, a most prolific man of our times. 

Of Solon, therefore, Cicero writes these words in the book *On Old Age*: "And we saw Solon boasting in his verses, saying that he becomes an old man by daily learning something new" <note>original: "Et solonem vidimus gloriantem versibus qui se quotidie denuo aliquid adiscentem dicit senem fieri."</note>. Justin also, in his second book of *Foreign Wars*, and Laertius in his *Life*, also say of Solon: "Solon was anxious, therefore, lest by remaining silent he would consult too little for the republic, or by speaking out he would bring sudden madness upon himself; by the grace of which he was going to do what was forbidden, rather than merely speak of it" <note>original: "Sollicitus ergo solon ne aut tacẽdo parũ reipu. cõsulere: aut censendo dementiam sibi subita simulati..." Referring to his feigned madness to save Salamis.</note>.

<summary>This page discusses Solon of Athens, focusing on his strategic feigning of madness to reclaim Salamis and his foundational role as a lawgiver whose work influenced Roman law. It defines the nature and necessity of law through various classical authorities and warns of the societal ruin that follows when laws are ignored.</summary>
<keywords>Solon, Athens, Salamis, Law, Twelve Tables, Digest, Aristotle, Cicero, Chrysippus, Matteo Palmieri, Justice, Civil Law</keywords>

--- Page 620 ---
<meta>This page continues the biography of Solon of Athens, specifically his use of feigned madness to influence political policy, and begins the account of Thales of Miletus, the first of the Seven Sages of Greece.</meta>

-># THE TRIUMPH OF FAME<-

He went out in public dressed hideously in the manner of a madman. Having gathered a crowd of people so that he might better hide his plan, he began to persuade the people with verses unusual for him. He influenced the minds of all such that, following his example, they decided upon war against the Megarians. Valerius Maximus writes of a similar sentiment in Book 2, in the chapter on study, and adds that when Solon was near death, he heard his friends debating. Thereupon he raised himself up and listened to their dispute. When asked why he stood up with such great physical discomfort to himself, he replied: <note>original: "Vt cum istud de quo disputatis perceperim moriar."</note> *“So that when I have understood that which you are debating, I may die.”* From this one can clearly understand with what a fervent soul Solon went about acquiring knowledge.

<margin>M</margin>
Regarding his opinions, he felt rightly concerning the simple being of God and the reverence worthy and due to Him. He believed the world to be perpetual and the soul immortal. Among other things, he said—as written in the first book of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics.</note>, by Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, author of "Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers."</note> in his biography, and in Herodotus, as we cited above in the preceding chapter—that no one in this world could be called happy, for fortune holds dominion over us until death. Therefore, if any state were to be called happiness, it should be attributed either to knowledge, to death, or to universal fame. Thus, when he was asked by Croesus, King of Lydia, whom he judged to be happy in this world, he replied: Tellus the Athenian, then Cleobis and Biton <note>Solon's famous answer to Croesus: Tellus died for his city, and the brothers Cleobis and Biton died peacefully after a great act of filial piety. This taught the king that wealth does not equal happiness.</note>, and the other things which are on everyone’s lips.

<margin>N</margin>
Solon wrote several most worthy maxims, and first: *“If anyone does not nourish his parents, let him be ignoble and obscure. He who pursues idleness should be liable to accusation by anyone who wishes. Do not take what you did not set down. If a ruler is caught drunk, he must be punished with death. Seal your speech with silence, and your silence with the proper time. Consider virtue and probity more faithful than an oath. Do not lie. Do not be quick to acquire friends, but be careful of rejecting those you have acquired. Rule only when you have first learned to be ruled. Give counsel not for what is most pleasant, but for what is best. Follow the mind and reason as your guide; do not contend with the great. Honor God, and revere your parents above all else.”*

<margin>O</margin>
Finally, Solon died in Cyprus at the age of eighty years. He commanded his people that his body be burned and his ashes scattered across the whole land of the region of Salamis.

<margin>P</margin>
Secondly, it is to be understood that of the other six of whom Greece boasts, the first was Thales of Miletus. The second was Chilon of Lacedaemon. The third was Pittacus of Mitylene; the fourth, Bias of Priene; the fifth, Cleobulus of Lydia; and the sixth and last, Periander of Corinth. As for the specific report of each, it is understood first that Thales of Miletus was the son (according to Herodotus and Democritus, as Laertius confirms) of Examyas and Cleobulina his wife, but by ancient origin descended from Cadmus and Agenor, kings of Phoenicia. This man, then, by the testimony of Plato, was called the first wise man of Greece. He first disputed natural philosophy and described astronomical calculations, whereby he divided the year into three hundred and sixty-five days and six hours. He wished always to live in poverty and in study. When this was once held against him as a reproach, he showed that it was an easy thing for a philosopher to grow rich. Thus, as Jerome of Rhodes writes, Thales saw through astrology that the following year there would be a very great abundance of olives. He borrowed money from friends and bought up the rights to the presses; through this, in the following year, Thales gained a very great quantity of gold, which he then freely distributed and returned once more to his poor way of living. He was diligent toward his republic, and through his diligence, he preserved its liberty from Croesus. Laertius also writes of him that while contemplating the stars one time, he fell into a ditch that was before him; whereupon he was rebuked by an old domestic servant in this manner: <note>original: "Qua ratione o thales que in cœlis sunt te comprehensurum arbitraris qui ea quæ sunt ante oculos uidere nō uales."</note> *“By what reason, O Thales, do you think you will grasp what is in the heavens, you who are not able to see what is before your eyes?”*

<margin>Q</margin>
Concerning his opinions, Thales principally said—as Aristotle writes in the first book of the *Physics* and *Metaphysics*, Augustine in *The City of God* (Book 8), and Eusebius in the fourteenth book of *Preparation for the Gospel*—that water is the principle of all things that can be generated or corrupted, seeing that everything, especially living things, is nourished by moisture. He said our soul is immortal, and the world is animated and full of spirits, made and created by God. And furthermore, it is most beautiful as Laertius writes, but according to Eusebius in the aforementioned book, Thales said the world is God because of its comprehension of all celestial and earthly things.

<margin>R</margin>
Thales wrote several notable sayings, and first: *“Many words are not the sign of a prudent mind. Whatever support you provide to your parents, expect the same from your children. Necessity is the strongest of all things, for it overcomes everything. Time is the wisest, for it finds out everything. God is the oldest of all things, for He is unbegotten. An old tyrant is the most difficult thing. Happy is he who is healthy in body, wealthy in fortune, and [tranquil in mind].* <note>The Latin "ignauus aut imperitus" (lazy or unlearned) in the OCR likely reflects a scribal error or a specific editorial tradition; most classical sources for this Thales quote read "well-educated in mind."</note> *We should be mindful of friends both present and absent. Best and most justly...”*

<summary>This page recounts the final deeds and death of Solon, including his famous maxims on civic duty, and introduces Thales of Miletus as the first of the Seven Sages, highlighting his scientific achievements and philosophical views on water as the primary element.</summary>
<keywords>Solon, Thales of Miletus, Seven Sages of Greece, Croesus, philosophy, astronomy, ancient maxims, Miletus, ethics</keywords>

--- Page 621 ---
<meta>This page continues the biographies of the Seven Sages of Greece, concluding the life of Thales of Miletus and providing accounts of Chilon of Lacedaemon and Pittacus of Mytilene.</meta>

->### CHAPTER FOUR<-

...and we shall live most justly if we ourselves do not do those things which we blame in others. Thales was also accustomed to thank God most highly for three things. First, for being born a human and not a beast; second, a man and not a woman; third, a Greek and not a barbarian <note>In antiquity, "barbarian" referred to anyone who did not speak Greek or share Greek culture.</note>. And in every matter, he said that a man ought to strive to know himself, as we said at the beginning of this book.

<margin>S</margin>
Thales died at the age of seventy-eight according to Apollodorus, and at the age of ninety according to Socrates. Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, the primary source for the lives of ancient philosophers.</note> tolerates these differing opinions as being both possible and equally evident to everyone.

<margin>T</margin>
Chilon of Lacedaemon <note>Sparta.</note>, as Laertius writes, was the son of Damagetus and was the second in Greece to be granted the surname of "Sage." He, as it is written in the *Policraticus* <note>A work by John of Salisbury regarding government and philosophy.</note>, while going to Corinth as an ambassador to forge a league between the Corinthians and the Spartans, found those who were in charge of the magistracy playing at tables <note>Games of chance involving dice and boards.</note>. He returned without delivering his embassy, saying that he did not wish to contaminate the glory of the Spartans with players of tables.

<margin>V</margin>
This Chilon was an excellent philosopher. Nevertheless, he practiced poetry more, especially singing elegiac verses, for which reason no more of his specific opinions are known; rather, it is read only in a general sense that he upheld the ancestral laws of Sparta. Chilon also observed such brevity of speech that Aristagoras, as Laertius testifies, called every instance of brief speech "Chilonian." Thus, speaking of him, he says: <note>original: "Erat in loquẽdo breuis atq; ob ea rẽ aristagoras milesius hūc loquendi morẽ Chiloniū appellat."</note> *“He was brief in speaking, and for that reason Aristagoras of Miletus called this style of speaking 'Chilonian'.”* One day, when Chilon was asked by Aesop <note>The famous author of fables.</note> what Jupiter was doing, he replied: "He humbles the high and exalts the humble." This response could not have been more prudent, more true, or more appropriate. Likewise, when asked how the learned differ from the ignorant, he replied with nothing other than: "Good hope." From this one can understand that he held our soul to be immortal. Being asked again to say what thing was most difficult for us to do, he replied: <note>original: "archana reticere: ocium recte disponere: iiuriasq; posse tollerare."</note> *“To keep secrets; to organize leisure rightly; and to be able to tolerate injuries.”*

<margin>X</margin>
Besides these, Chilon wrote many worthy <term>maxims</term> <note>original: "snie", a contraction of "sententie".</note> and <term>precepts</term> <note>original: "prĩa", likely "praecepta".</note>: *“Always hold your tongue, but especially at a banquet. No one should be threatened, for that is womanly. Marry a modest wife with small finery. Honor old age and observe yourself. Choose loss rather than shameful profit, for the former hurts but once, while the latter hurts always. A strong man ought to be gentle, so that his neighbors do not fear him so much as they revere him. One must not permit the tongue to outrun the mind. Anger must be overcome in all ways. Where there is a guarantee, loss is not far behind.”*

<margin>y</margin>
Chilon died in the city of Pisa in Greece while embracing his son, who had been crowned victor in the Olympic wrestling matches. As far as can be guessed, he died of joy, being quite old and naturally weak.

<margin>z</margin>
Pittacus of Mytilene, Laertius writes, was the son of Hyrradius (or Heradius) of Thrace, and because of his learning, he was also numbered among the other Seven Sages of Greece. Although he was a man of letters and study, he was nonetheless no less excellent in the feat of arms. Thus, when the Mytileneans were at war with the Athenians, Pittacus took up arms and went against the enemies of his country. Fighting in single combat with Phrynon, the leader of the Athenians, he overcame him, and they later obtained a complete victory. For this reason, the Mytileneans by common accord gave him the principality and established him as their lord. Pittacus administered this office so well that he composed laws and external defenses, fortifying the republic in honest, just, and political living. Having done this, he resigned the lordship and the magistracy, as Laertius writes, having held it for ten years. Pittacus was adorned with every moral virtue, especially clemency and gentleness.

<margin>A</margin>
Regarding this, Laertius writes that after his son had been killed in Cyme, and the murderer was captured by the Cumans and brought to Pittacus, Pittacus pardoned him. Another time, having captured another of his greatest enemies, he likewise pardoned him. Thus the text says: <note>original: "a cumanis vero victum homicidam ad pittacum missum atq; ab eo pena fuisse absolutum dicente indulgentiam penitentie esse pferendam..."</note> *“From the Cumans, the defeated murderer was sent to Pittacus, and was released from punishment by him, Pittacus saying that mercy is to be preferred to punishment. Heraclitus asserts that he held Alcaeus captive and set him free, saying that forgiveness is better than vengeance.”* After resigning his leadership, Pittacus wished to live poorly, and therefore he refused a great quantity of money which <term>King Croesus</term> <note>original: "cre sore", likely a typo for "Creso re".</note> of Lydia wished to give him.

<margin>B*</margin>
He wrote many worthy <term>maxims</term> <note>original: "snie"</note>, feeling rightly concerning our soul, even though regarding God he posited many of His other qualities, attributing them all to Him. Thus: *“It is difficult to be good. Power shows the man. The best of all things is to do well. The outcome of future events is obscure. The earth is faithful, but the sea is unfaithful. It is the part of a prudent man to provide for future adversities so they do not happen; it is the part of the brave to bear them with an even mind when they do occur. What you intend to do, do not brag about; for if you fail to do it, you will be mocked.”*

<summary>This page concludes the biography of Thales of Miletus and details the lives, moral teachings, and political achievements of Chilon of Lacedaemon and Pittacus of Mytilene, two of the Seven Sages of Greece.</summary>
<keywords>Thales of Miletus, Chilon of Lacedaemon, Pittacus of Mytilene, Seven Sages of Greece, Laconic speech, clemency, ancient philosophy, Spartan laws, Mytilene</keywords>

<meta>catchword: Periander</meta>
<sig>C</sig>

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

...return what you have received. Do not speak ill of a friend, nor even of an enemy. Cultivate piety, be frugal, love modesty, and strive for truth. Guard your faith, skill, dexterity, fellowship, and diligence. Having taken up the bow and arrows and the carrying-quiver, one should by no means attack a man; for wood speaks nothing faithful <note>A philosophical warning against relying on weapons or violence over the strength of the soul</note>, as long as a double sense sits deep within the body.

<margin>C</margin>

<margin>D</margin> ¶ Pittacus died at the age of sixty in Lesbos where he was buried, and upon his tomb this single word was written: "Know thy time" <note>original: *te pus nosce*, likely a corruption of *tempus nosce*—a call to recognize the right moment for action</note>.

¶ Bias of Priene, according to what Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius</note> writes, was the son of a man named Teutamus. He was so excellent and supreme in study that he was placed before all the other six sages of Greece by Satyrus, the great Greek writer.

<margin>E</margin> ¶ This man, therefore, both through his natural disposition and also through the exercise of study, was a most prudent man. For this reason, when a certain Alyattes <note>King of Lydia</note> besieged Priene, and the city was in extreme need of provisions, Bias had two mules fattened and ordered that they be sent out to be captured by the enemies as if by chance. When they were led to the camp, they caused everyone to marvel, and especially the king, who judged that the rumor of the city being in such need was not true. To be certain, he sent a scout into the land to learn of the state and condition of the place. Bias, knowing this, had mounds of sand placed in many parts of the city and covered them with grain. Having seen this, the scout returned to the king and said there was a great abundance of grain in the land; for which reason Alyattes lifted the siege and departed. Thus, by the prudence of Bias alone, his homeland of Priene was saved. Valerius Maximus also writes of him in the seventh book, third chapter, and Cicero in the *Paradoxes*, where his great praise is seen, saying: "I will often praise that wise Bias, as I believe he is named among the seven sages of Greece; for when the enemy had captured his homeland Priene and the others were fleeing such that they carried away many of their things, when he was warned by someone to do the same, he said, 'Indeed, I am doing it. For I carry all my things with me'" <note>original: *Omnia mea mecum porto*. This famous phrase indicates that true wealth lies in one's character and knowledge, which cannot be stolen.</note>.

<margin>F</margin> ¶ Besides this, Bias was most observant of friendship and left behind many worthy sayings. First: "For he is exceedingly unhappy who cannot bear unhappiness." "Whatever you set out to do, take it up with hesitation and deliberation." "Do not praise an unworthy man for the sake of his riches." "Whatever good you do, attribute it to the gods." "Do not speak quickly, for it is a sign of madness." "Acquire wisdom as provision for yourself from youth to old age, for that alone is a certain and true possession." Finally, when Bias was asked what was difficult, he replied: "To bear the changing of things for the worse." And another time, when a most audacious and impious man asked Bias what piety was, Bias did not answer him. When the man asked why he remained silent in such a way, Bias replied: "Because you ask about things that do not pertain to you."

<margin>G</margin> Another time, while Bias was sailing, a great storm arose at sea. The sailors with a loud voice offered prayers to the gods for their safety. To whom Bias said: "Be silent, lest they sense that you are sailing here" <note>original: *filete ne uos hic illi nauigare sentiant*. A witty, biting remark suggesting that if the gods realized such wicked men were on the boat, they would surely sink it.</note>.

<margin>H</margin> ¶ Bias died quite old in this manner, as Laertius writes: after having been an advocate in a case and having spoken, while resting in the lap of one of his grandsons, once the sentence was given in favor of his client, he was found dead. Whereupon the people of Priene built a temple in his honor and everlasting memory.

¶ Cleobulus the philosopher was a worthy man from Caria, or truly from Lindos, as Laertius confirms. He was the son of one Euagoras and descended from the ancient lineage of Hercules. Being perfectly distinguished in learning, character, and beauty of body, he was also counted among the seven sages of Greece. This man, therefore, to increase his value through the search for learning, traveled to Egypt—which was the source of almost all wisdom <note>Ancient Greeks often viewed Egypt as the cradle of philosophy and science</note>—wherever there was something that could provide any knowledge; from there he became a most learned and singular philosopher. He had a daughter named Cleobulina, who was also excellent, especially in the poetic art. Laertius writes of Cleobulus that he described the year in this manner: "There is one father, and he has twelve sons, and each of them has thirty daughters of beautiful and varied appearance. For some are white, others are black; they are indeed immortal, and yet they all die" <note>A riddle where the father is the Year, the sons are the Months, and the daughters are the Days and Nights.</note>.

<margin>I</margin> ¶ Cleobulus also wrote many worthy moral sayings, as Laertius clearly shows in his life. First: "Friends should be cherished with benefits so they become closer; enemies, however, so they become friends." "Before you leave home, consider what you are to do; again, when you return, reflect on what you have done." "The body must be properly exercised." "One ought to be more studious of listening than of speaking." "To have a laudable tongue is a property of virtue." "Be far from vice." "Injustice is to be fled." "Choose a wife equal to yourself, for if you marry one more distinguished than you, you will have masters for in-laws." "Learn to bear the changes of fortune bravely."

¶ Cleobulus died at the age of seventy, for whom at his tomb, in his perpetual praise, his works were described in an epigram.

<page-num>147</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER FOUR</header>

# CHAPTER FOUR

<margin>K</margin>
¶ **Periander of Corinth**, the last of the philosophers counted among the seven: as Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, a biographer of ancient philosophers</note> writes, he was the son of a man named Cypselus. Having reached old age through his practices and studies, and knowing he was near death, he resolved that his grave should never be found, so as not to wait for the final natural decay. For this reason, one day he spoke to two young men on a solitary road, telling them that at the first hour of the coming night, they should kill the first person they found on that path and then bury him secretly. Then, he led four men to the same place and told them that at the second hour of the night, they should kill and likewise cautiously bury whoever they found on that road. After this, he came and led a greater number of men, telling them to do the same at the third hour. It followed that on the next night, Periander, walking on that road at the first hour, was killed and buried by the first two. Then those two were killed by the four, and the four by those of the larger number. Thus it happened that the place where Periander was buried remained unknown to every man from that time on, just as he had desired.

<margin>L</margin>
¶ Periander wrote several notable maxims; first: *We must not act for the sake of money* <note>original: "Non pecuniarum gratia agendum est"</note>. *In prosperous times be moderate; in adverse times be prudent.* *Show yourself the same to friends even in their misfortunes.* *Keep whatever you have promised.* *In conversation, take care not to reveal secrets.* *Punish not only those who sin, but those who desire to sin.* Besides his letters and study, Periander was intent on the business of ruling Corinth; concerning this, Laertius writes these words: *He was the first to walk surrounded by armed guards and he transformed the magistracy into a tyranny.*

<margin>M</margin>
¶ Periander died at the age of eighty in the manner described above. Concluding then, Greece rightly boasts of these seven men, they having been so worthy and excellent, as our Master Francesco <note>Petrarch (Francesco Petrarca)</note> has consequently described. Next, our poet narrates a greater number of men most excellent in doctrine and letters—no less so than the preceding Greeks—as he saw our Latin people led by the third great Roman light, which the more it is gazed upon, the more clearly it shines and resplends. Wherefore he says:

<margin>N</margin>
-> Here I saw our people led by <-
-> Varro, the third great Roman light; <-
-> Who the more I look at him, the more he shines: <-

¶ Marcus Varro was a most distinguished Roman citizen, a most eloquent man, most abundant in history, and a worthy philosopher and theologian together. As Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville</note> testifies in his *Etymologies*, Varro wrote a vast number of books. Among those still known are: *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, *On the Ages of the City*, *On Antiquities*, *On the Selected Gods*, and *On Agriculture*. Therefore, the poet appropriately says he is a light that shines more the more one looks at it. Augustine <note>Saint Augustine</note> writes in the fourth book of *The City of God*, chapter thirty-one, these fitting words about Varro: *Marcus Varro, the most acute and learned man, saw that the gods were but the sun and the stars; he perceived what God was: those who believed God to be the soul governing the world through motion and reason.* And the same Varro adds more holily and modestly that the gods should be worshipped without images, a matter to which the Jewish people are witnesses. Nor was he moved to this only by the custom of the Jewish people, but by reason, saying that the greatest Jove is incomprehensible. And therefore, he should not have an image, as the same Augustine testifies in the previously cited book and in the ninth chapter; from which one can clearly understand that he perfectly understood the unity, simplicity, and infinite incomprehensibility of the divine.

<margin>O</margin>
¶ Concerning our soul, he said that it was immortal, and while it was joined with the body, Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius, author of "Attic Nights"</note> called it—and said it was—of a divine nature, as Augustine shows in the same book. He says heaven is our home and the world is eternal.

<margin>P</margin>
¶ He also wrote many worthy maxims in various books and in different places. And first, in the book *To Atticus the Listener*: *To be wise against everyone is to be foolish.* *Give feigned thanks to an unwilling giver; for what is given by force should not be considered a gift, but plunder.* *He who is asked for a favor hurts once, but he who is not asked hurts twice.* <note>Suggesting that an unasked favor creates a double debt or social complication</note> *If you wish to test a friend, become unfortunate.* *Let no one think that which is outside himself belongs to him.* *For no one is miserable except he who believes himself to be.* *No loss is graver to a scholar than that of time.* *It is a mark of flattery when praise precedes a request.* Through these authorities and maxims, one can easily understand how the words written about Varro by Quintilian <note>A Roman educator and rhetorician</note> in the tenth book of the *Education of the Orator* apply, where he says: *Varro, the most learned of the Romans, wrote many...*

While the previous page concluded the Seven Sages of Greece and introduced the first Roman light, Marcus Varro, this page explores the lives and legacies of the historians Sallust and Livy, as well as the beginning of an account of Pliny the Elder.</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME
74

...he composed many books and was most learned, being highly skilled in the Latin language, all of antiquity, and our historical deeds.

<margin>Q</margin> ¶ **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar</note> died at a very advanced age; and after his end, he was deservedly celebrated by writers for his fame. Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch, the author of the poem being commented upon</note> then follows by saying that together with Varro, he saw **Sallust** <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus</note> coming after. Whence he says:

<margin>R</margin> ¶ **Sallust** was an outstanding and worthy Roman citizen, a most learned man, and a most famous historian. His learning, elegance, and skill in speaking can be seen very clearly through his written works on the conspiracy and death of **Catiline** and the **Jugurthine War** <note>Two of Sallust's major historical monographs</note>; for which reason Quintilian <note>A famous Roman educator and rhetorician</note> rightly wrote these words of him:

->**Sallust:**<-

> But do not yield history to the Greeks: nor would I fear to set Sallust against **Thucydides** <note>original: "At non historia cesseris graecis: nec opponere Thucididi Salustium verear." Thucydides was the gold standard of Greek historical writing.</note>.

And beyond this, by the universal conclusion of both ancient and modern writers, the first place among all those who have written history is deservedly given to Sallust. ¶ Sallust wrote many worthy maxims, and first:

<margin>S</margin>
> It seems more correct to me to seek glory by the resources of the intellect than of physical strength. And since the life we enjoy is itself brief, the glory of riches and beauty is fleeting and fragile; but virtue is held clear and eternal. Before you begin, there is need of deliberation, and when you have deliberated, there is need of timely action. It is a beautiful thing to do well for the republic; even to speak well is not without value. But indeed, fortune rules in every matter: it celebrates or obscures all things according to its whim rather than the truth. The guide and commander of the life of mortals is the mind <note>original: "Mihi rectius esse videtur ingenii quam virium opibus gloriam quaerere..." These are famous excerpts from the prefaces of Sallust’s histories.</note>.

<margin>T</margin> There are nevertheless some who attribute that title of "Third Great Roman Light" to Sallust, because he wrote the entire Roman history, counting Cicero as the first, Varro the second, and Sallust the third. Nevertheless, considering the Roman custom that Rome was the common homeland of everyone, **Virgil** <note>The epic poet of the Aeneid</note> ought not to be removed from the Roman name; and so, according to this reasoning, Virgil was the first, Cicero the second, and Varro the third Roman light described by Master Francesco. Master Francesco then narrates, saying that step by step with Sallust came one whom he once envied, and he saw him with a crooked and then a straight mind: that is, the great Paduan, **Titus Livy**. Whence he says:

<margin>V</margin> ¶ How great the dignity of the Paduan **Titus Livy** is can be understood not only through his works but through the nickname given to him, being called the "Golden Ocean" and "River of Eloquence." Furthermore, there are the words of Quintilian written of him in the tenth book of the *Institutes of Oratory* in this form:

->And with him, step by step,<-
->One who envied him and saw the wrong:<-
->That is the great Titus Livy of Padua.<-

> Titus Livy is of wonderful joy in his narration and of the clearest brightness, and in his speeches he is eloquent beyond what can be described. Thus they say everything is suited to the facts and the persons: but as for the emotions, especially the sweeter ones, to speak most sparingly: no historian has commanded them more. Therefore, he achieved that immortal speed of Sallust through different virtues <note>original: "Titum Livium cum i narràdo mire iocunditatis..." Quintilian is comparing the styles of the two greatest Roman historians.</note>. Through these words, one can well understand how gracefully Master Francesco has described the matter.

<margin>X</margin> Master Francesco described Titus Livy as having carried envy toward Sallust. ¶ Titus Livy wrote 140 books on the deeds of the Romans <note>Historically, 142 books are recorded, though many are lost</note>, divided into 14 **decades** <term>decades: groups of ten books</term>, beginning from the origin of Rome until the time of Augustus, where the last war he writes of is that of Drusus against the Germans. In that context are almost infinite notable sayings of his, of which we have gathered a small number, and first:

> Fortune is to be trusted least when it is greatest. It rarely happens to men that they are given good fortune and a good mind at the same time. A certain peace is better and safer than a hoped-for victory. To despair at the last is the help of the republic; the honorable yields to the useful. This is the nature of the multitude: they either serve humbly or rule proudly; they know neither how to moderately despise liberty, which is in the middle, nor how to hold it. Many things that are difficult by nature are unraveled by counsel. Therefore, those whom fear does not hold must be won over by benefit and grace. A small fire has often stirred up a great conflagration. Anger without strength is vain. By experience, it has been seen that fortune favors the brave <note>original: "Maxie cuiq; fortunae minime credendù est..." A collection of Livy’s most famous philosophical and political observations.</note>.

<margin>Y</margin> Titus Livy died in Padua in the fourth year of Tiberius Caesar at the age of about 80. His tomb and his dignity are manifest in Padua even to this day. Next, Master Francesco introduces **Pliny the Veronese** <note>Pliny the Elder</note> after Titus Livy, saying that while he was looking at Livy, he suddenly saw and noticed Pliny, a neighbor by the location of their homelands, who was very diligent in writing but little mindful of his death. Whence he says:
