<header>CHAPTER FOUR</header>

## **While I was looking, suddenly I caught sight**
## **Of that Veronese Pliny, his neighbor** <note>original: "suo vicino." Likely referring to his proximity in the procession to other Roman authors like Catullus or Vitruvius.</note>
## **Wise in writing much, but little in death.**

<margin>Z</margin>
¶ There were two Plinys, each of whom is called Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (the Elder) and Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus (the Younger)</note>, namely the uncle and the nephew. Between them there was a great similarity regarding their writing and great difference regarding their deaths. Pliny the Younger, the nephew, coming principally to Rome, attained many degrees of dignity, most notably the proconsulship of Africa and the praetorship of Spain. While there, he wrote to Trajan Augustus <note>Emperor Trajan, reigned 98–117 AD</note>, who was persecuting the Christians, in their favor, saying they lived under Roman laws and only worshipped the crucified Christ—a thing which did not contradict those laws. Therefore, because of Pliny’s letters, Trajan did not want the Christians to be killed, as Eusebius of Caesarea <note>An early Christian historian and bishop</note> writes in his *Ecclesiastical History*.

<margin>A</margin>
¶ This Pliny wrote a history from the beginning of the world until his own times in 78 books <note>The text here attributes a massive history to the Younger, though most of his surviving fame rests on his *Letters*</note>, in which he imitates his uncle, as he himself asserts in the fifth book of his letters to Capito, in the eighth epistle. He also wrote *On Illustrious Men* and *On the Three Parts of the World*, and one volume of most worthy letters. He died as an old man in Rome of a natural death, and the poet does not intend to speak of him here.

<margin>B</margin>
¶ The other Pliny mentioned above was the uncle of the aforementioned Pliny. He was from Verona, as he himself demonstrates in the introduction to his *Natural History*, where he says that Valerius Catullus <note>The famous Roman lyric poet</note> was his fellow countryman. But in Suetonius Tranquillus's book *On Illustrious Men*, this Pliny is called "the New" because he lived for a large part of his life in Como, and also near Lake Como, where he had a great abundance of possessions, as the previously mentioned Pliny shows in the fourth book of his letters, in the last epistle to Licinius. This Pliny was a most studious man and a great writer of excellent things; hence he wrote the Roman histories from the beginning of Rome until his own times in 38 books, and the *Natural History* in 37 books, where, in the text, he demonstrates his belief that our soul dies with the body.

<margin>C</margin>
¶ He also wrote nearly finished notable sayings, of which it is enough to refer only to the lamentation made by him regarding human nature at the beginning of the seventh book of the *Natural History*, where he says:

> The world and its lands, nations, seas, famous islands, and cities are arranged in this manner: the nature of living creatures within it is hardly less significant in any part of its contemplation. Since the human mind cannot investigate everything, the beginning is rightly given to man, for whose sake nature seems to have produced all other things. Yet she did so at a great and cruel price against such gifts, so that it is not easy to judge whether she was a better parent or a harsher stepmother to man. Above all, man is the only creature that she covers with resources not his own; to others, she gives various coverings: shells, barks, hides, thorns, fleece, bristles, hair, down, feathers, scales, and wool. She protects even the trunks and trees from cold and heat, sometimes with a double layer of bark. Man alone she casts out naked on the bare ground on his birthday, immediately to wailing and weeping. No other among so many animals is prone to tears, and these right at the very beginning of life. But by Hercules, laughter is denied him, even as a precocious or quick thing, before his fortieth day from this first light. No wild beasts born among us are received with chains or the binding of all their limbs; and yet, born into such unhappiness, the animal destined to rule the others lies with hands and feet bound, weeping. He begins his life with punishments for the single fault of being born. Alas, the madness of those who, considering these beginnings, think they were born for pride! The first hope of strength and the first gift of time makes him like a quadruped. When does man walk? When does he have a voice? When is his mouth firm for food? How long does the top of his head throb—the sign of extreme weakness in all animals? Then there are so many diseases and so many medicines devised against evils, and even these are constantly defeated by new ailments. Other creatures sense their own nature: some use their swiftness, others their swift flight, others their ability to swim. Man knows nothing without being taught: neither how to speak, nor walk, nor eat. In short, by nature's will, he can do nothing spontaneously except cry. Thus, many have existed who judged it best not to be born, or to be abolished as quickly as possible. To one living creature alone is grief given; to one, luxury, and indeed in innumerable ways and through every limb; to one, ambition; to one, avarice; to one, an immense desire for living; to one, superstition; to one, a care for burial, and even for what comes after him. To none is life more fragile; to none is the lust for all things greater; to none is fear more confused; to none is rage more piercing. Finally, other animals live properly within their own kind: we see them flock together and stand against those unlike them. The lion's ferocity does not fight against its own kind. The bite of serpents does not seek out serpents; nor indeed do the monsters and fish of the sea vent their rage except against different species. But by Hercules, for man, most evils come from his fellow man.

<margin>D</margin>
¶ Pliny died in this way, as Suetonius Tranquillus writes and Pliny [the Younger] in the fifth book in the letter to Cornelius Tacitus <note>The famous Roman historian. The letter actually describes the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD</note>, while he was prefect of the fleet at Misenum, etc.

<header>TRIUMPHS OF FAME</header>

<meta>catchword: neither Menia</meta>

### THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>S</margin>
On the Kalends of November <note>The first day of November</note> a cloud in the likeness of a tree came out of the abyss of Mount Vesuvius, which is below Naples and called the mountain of Somma. His sister, then, announced this rising of the cloud to Pliny, who was at his studies. Coming to see it, he decided to climb the mountain to contemplate the place where those dense and black vapors were emerging. While he was on his way, a fury of wind arose, and the mountain began to vomit forth burning flames and to breathe out a sulfurous odor very troublesome to the sense of smell. Pliny, having been enveloped by the dusty storm while between two servants, fell to the ground, suffocated and dead—although Suetonius says that at his own request he was killed by one of his servants. Pliny was therefore somewhat unwise in his dying, because he could have left with the galleys and made himself safe from the maritime storm. Being exhorted to this effect by the governor of the ships, he did not wish to agree, but responded as Pliny writes: *Fortune favors the bold* <note>original: "Fortes fortuna iuuat"</note>. Thus, by his stubbornness, he was led to his end. Consequently, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch, the author of the poem being commented upon</note> brings forward Plotinus after Pliny, saying that he later saw Plotinus the great Platonist, who, believing he could live safely in leisure, was nonetheless overtaken by his fierce and immovable destiny. This destiny had grown with him in life even from his mother's womb, and therefore no foresight was of any use to him against it. Thus he says:

<margin>¶ For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, three things are to be diligently considered: first, what destiny is and how various writers have already spoken of it. Second, in what way Plotinus was overtaken by his fierce destiny. Third and last, in what way, while presupposing destiny, Master Francesco saves the praise of virtuous action. As to the first, one must know...</margin>

> **T** hen I saw the great Platonist Plotinus;
> **Who** believing he could live safely in leisure
> **Overtaken** was by his fierce destiny;
> **W** hich came with him from the maternal womb;
> **A** nd therefore providence there was of no avail;

<margin>E</margin>
...that among the ancients "destiny" and "fate" are taken for the same thing, which is principally defined by Tullio <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> in his book *On Divination* as being an invariable order, saying: *I call "Fate" that which the Greeks call "Himarmene," that is, the order and series of causes, since one cause begets another from itself; it is the eternal truth flowing from all eternity.* <note>original: "Fatum id appello quod greci himarmenē. i. ordinem seriemq; cārum..."</note> From this definition it follows that every action of ours is necessitated by superior causes. Apuleius of Madaura and Hermes Trismegistus in the book *On the Nature of the Gods* conform to this definition; they also describe fate thus: *Fate is the complexity of causes depending on providence and the first cause.* The astrologers Phrynichus and Posidonius felt the same, except that they attributed the operation of the effects to the sun, the moon, and the stars; hence Phrynichus says: *Fate is the collection of causes drawing power and efficacy from the movements of the stars.* To this definition, Ptolemy added necessary immutability, saying: *Fate is the immovable power of the constellations.* Seneca, besides these, in his book *On Natural Questions*, citing Cetina the priest, attributes this fatal order to the will, counsel, and premeditation of God. Thus concluding that every event is necessary, he says: *Fate is the necessity of all things and actions which no force can break, coming from Jove’s disposition and the defined counsel of the gods.* This same necessity was approved by all the Gentiles <note>Non-Christians/Pagans</note> through the opinion of Homer and Apollo. Hence, as Eusebius writes in the sixth book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, when Apollo was asked how long his temple should last, he responded by prophesying its ruin in these verses: *Then also this temple, struck by terrifying lightning, shall burn; the immovable order of the fates stands. It is far better to endure whatever happens. The Sisters <note>The Three Fates/Parcae</note> have established this with a fixed and stable law, for whatever the king of Olympus weaves into the spindles of the Fates must be certain, stable, and forever inviolable.* And Homer explained with briefer words that there is no contingency, but absolute necessity, saying: *There is no one who can escape or turn away the fixed laws of the Fates.* Moved by this authority, Seneca said again in his tragedy *Oedipus* regarding this matter: *Believe in the fates; we are driven by the fates. Anxious cares cannot change the threads of the spindle; whatever we of the mortal race suffer, whatever we do, comes from above.* Ovid, likewise in the *Metamorphoses*, introducing Jove speaking to Venus, says: *Do you alone think you can move insuperable fate?* And Virgil, in the first book of the *Aeneid*, confirming the same, says in the person of Jove to Venus:
<margin>C</margin>
*Spare your fear, Cytherea <note>An epithet for Venus</note>; the fates of your people remain unmoved for you. You shall see the city and the promised walls of Lavinium...*

# CHAPTER FOUR

...the walls [of Lavinium]; and you shall bear the great-hearted Aeneas on high to the stars of heaven; nor does my purpose change <note>original: "neq; me snĩa vertit". These are quotes from Virgil’s Aeneid, Books 1 and 6, regarding the destined future of Rome.</note>. 1. in the .vi. [Book 6].

Cease to hope that the decrees of the gods can be shifted by prayer <note>original: "Desine fata deũ flecti sperare p̄cando". A famous line from Aeneid 6.376.</note>. Therefore, in conclusion, it is quite clearly seen what fate was according to the opinion of the ancients: how it must necessitate even human operations. However, the truth of the Catholic Church disagrees with this false and rigid opinion, instead approving the opinion of the Stoics; they said some causes operate by necessity, and others are exempt from it, as Augustine writes in the fifth book of *The City of God*, in the seventh chapter. Among these contingent <note>events that happen by chance or choice rather than necessity</note> causes can be fortune and our own will. But as for what fortune was, the Romans differed greatly from Aristotle in the second book of the *Physics*; for they believed it to be a deity ruling and disposing of these external things. Thus, to provoke its favor, they established a temple through Lucullus under the name of Felicity <note>original: "felicita"; here meaning prosperity or good luck</note>. However that may be, they agree in this: that fortune does not operate by necessity.

But beyond the Stoics, it is demonstrated by our theologians that nothing except the intrinsic operations of the Divine—such as generating and breathing forth <note>Technical theological terms for the internal life of the Trinity: the generation of the Son and the spiration of the Holy Spirit.</note>—is necessary. Hence every creature is produced from nothing into being by the mere liberality of the divine will. For this reason, the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, whose "Sentences" was the standard medieval textbook of theology.</note> in the first book, from the 38th to the 41st distinction, says that fate—or rather destiny, or predestination according to the fantasy of the ancients—is only the foreknowledge of God with His good pleasure. This, denoting the external creature as an object, imposes no necessity, as the creature is variable; and the definition of the knowledge of a thing follows the variation of the knowable thing, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> writes at the end of the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*. Wherefore Boethius, learnedly in the fourth book of *The Consolation of Philosophy*, says that fate is nothing other than an inherent disposition of mutable things, through which divine providence connects all things in their order, saying: *Fate is a disposition inherent in changeable things, by which Providence knits each one into its own ranks* <note>original: "Fatũ est inherens rebus mobilibus dispositiō p̄ quã prouidentia queq; suis nectit ordinibus"</note>. By these words, it is manifest that fate only implies an order of causes to effects without imposing any other necessity.

<margin>G</margin> Now as for the second point, it should be understood that Plotinus was a worthy and distinguished man, born in Alexandria of Egypt, the son of a sculptor, small of body and not very well-formed. He was primarily a disciple of Ammonius of Alexandria <note>Ammonius Saccas, the influential teacher of Neoplatonism.</note>, under whom he studied for eleven years alongside Origen and Lysimachus. Then he went to Persia and India solely to learn the magical arts; later he came to Rome at the age of forty. He was a man of the highest constancy, sobriety, and justice; for the sake of chastity, he never wished to involve himself in the knot of marriage. Plotinus was such a great champion of Platonic doctrine that the poet rightly calls him "the great Platonist Plotinus." Regarding him, Hermes <note>Possibly a reference to a Hermetic source or a misidentified biographer.</note> writes: *Plotinus, a singular philosopher, what parts of philosophy did he not touch? Since his life followed his doctrine; distinguished, since that which he taught was shown not by another's example but by his own example of virtue.* Macrobius likewise, in *The Dream of Scipio*, says: *But Plotinus, the prince among professors of philosophy along with Plato, in his book on virtues, arranges their grades in order with a true and natural reason for their division.*

<margin>H</margin> *There are four types of virtues,* he says. *Of these, the first are called political; the second, purgative <note>purifying</note>; the third, of the already purified; the fourth, exemplary.* Regarding his opinions, he primarily said that God is the author of nature and from Him proceeds every being, life, and intelligence; and that the world was created by Him. He made our soul more noble than the angels and said that it has no more excellent superior above it than that of God, as we said above in the *Triumph of Death* according to the opinion of Saint Augustine. Plotinus wrote several notable sayings, and first: *The prudence of the political man is to direct everything he thinks and does according to the norm of reason, and to do nothing except what is right and laudable, and to foresee human acts as if before divine judges.* *It is the part of Fortitude to drive the soul above the fear of danger, to fear nothing except shameful things, and to bear bravely both adversity and prosperity.* *It is the part of Temperance to desire nothing to be repented of, to exceed the law of moderation in nothing, and to tame desire under the yoke of reason.* *It is the part of Justice to preserve for each one what is his own.* From Justice come innocence, friendship, concord, piety, religion, affection, and humanity. By these virtues, a good man is made first a ruler of himself and then of the republic, governing human affairs justly and with foresight without abandoning them.

Ultimately, while dying in Rome, a great many men died from a plague, as did all of Plotinus's friends; and he himself was afflicted with a great infirmity, namely spasms, hoarseness, and blindness. For this reason, thinking he might recover if he went to live in a remote place, he had himself carried to a villa in the countryside belonging to one of his disciples named Zethus; there, as soon as he arrived, he died within a few days. As he was dying, Plotinus turned to Eustochius the physician and said: *The divine that is in us, O Eustochius, I am returning to that divine which is in the universe* <note>original: "Diuinū quod in nobis est o eustochi in id quod in vniuerso est diuinum sum reuerti"</note>. Plotinus died at the age of sixty-six and wrote many books on moral and natural philosophy and theology.

It then provides a biography of the philosopher Plotinus, detailing his education in Alexandria, his ascetic life in Rome, and his system of the four cardinal virtues.</summary>

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>13.</margin>
<margin>K</margin>
...among the theologians. There are, nonetheless, some others of no small authority who say that Plotinus, seeing that the things of the world were for the most part under the government and protection of Fortune, and wishing to avoid her blows, went to live a solitary life, believing he would live in great peace in such a place. But in this state, Plotinus became completely filled with leprosy; because of this, irritated with himself by the weariness of the sickness, he died in great distress. Thus, it was concluded that this had been his destiny, which he carried from his mother's womb. This is because this sickness—as William of Piacenza <note>Guglielmo da Saliceto (c. 1210–1277), a famous Italian surgeon and physician.</note> writes in the third book of his *Practice*—is generated, among other causes, at the beginning of conception when the human seed is mixed with the menstrual blood of the woman during intercourse. Others refer this destiny only to his death, which was destined to be deprived of peace and rest. ¶ In the third and last place, a difficult and worthy doubt occurs to us: in what way is human providence compatible with the necessity of destiny? Messer Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch), the author of the *Triumphs* being commented upon here.</note> shows this providence in this place, and in that sonnet: **The high column and the green laurel are broken.** And: *The evil presses me and I fear the worst.* Also the praises and commendations of virtuous operations, which the poet described in the *Triumph of Chastity*, and which he presupposes in this *Triumph of Fame*. But in what form does he resolve the contradiction that seems to exist in these parts and others? For there he affirms the freedom of the will <term>libertà de lo arbitrio: the theological concept that humans have the power to choose their actions despite divine foreknowledge</term>, as in that song: **In the sweet time of my early age,** but more clearly in the *Last Triumph*, and in that song: **I go thinking, and a thought assails me.**

<margin>L</margin>
¶ Responding complexly to these doubts, I say that there are two ways it is clearly seen that praise for their actions is appropriate for men, even though there is predestination and necessity in all our works. One way is that if it were so—that man were necessitated to such a work—this force is totally hidden from his understanding. Since it was not apparent to him, by conforming himself in this respect with good pleasure toward those works which are defined as good, and as far as it lies within him still striving to perform them, it is a fitting thing that he should be praised for such an effect. And this is what belongs to everyone to do while they live because, 

<margin>M</margin>
as the text of the legal scholars says in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de regulis iuris". A reference to the "Rules of Law" in Justinian's Digest.</note>: **In doubt, the more favorable interpretations are always to be preferred.** <note>original: "Semper i dubio benigniora sunt preferenda."</note> ¶ The second way is that just as a person who is predestined or foreknown <note>prescito: those God knows will not be saved</note> can be "not predestined" if we make the proposition in the divided sense <note>A technical term in scholastic logic ("sensus divisus") used to distinguish between a necessity of the thing itself and the necessity of the statement.</note>. Thus, this necessity, being dependent on a future thing, is not absolute. And therefore, it can be non-necessitated. Wherefore one must always reasonably act well, and that operation should deservedly be praised and extolled. But if someone should say: "then the necessary thing is contingent, being able indifferently to be and not to be," I respond that this does not follow from the stated opinion. For this word "necessity" in a proposition of the divided sense (where this verb "can" is the principal) signifies everything and stands for that which is necessary or truly can be such, according to the rules of logical ampliation <note>A logical term for extending the reference of a term to include past, future, or possible things.</note>. And if one were to cite the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the third book of the *Physics*, who says that in eternal things power does not differ from being, it is said that this authority should be understood in the composite sense and not the divided sense: that is, if it is possible for something to be eternal, it is eternal; for if it were understood otherwise, a thousand inconveniences would follow.

<margin>N</margin>
¶ Aside from the two aforementioned ways, one can also save Messer Francesco’s position according to the opinion of Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher who argued that fate and free will could coexist.</note>, which we will state below in its proper place. Similarly, one can also say that Messer Francesco intends that human providence has no place or any power to repair death—as Plotinus intended to do—and our powerlessness against death sits very well with the freedom of the will. Many holy men seem to support this interpretation. Wherefore, first, Job in the fourteenth chapter <note>The OCR says "xiij", but the quote is from Job 14:5.</note> says: 
> The days of man are short; the number of his months is with you. You have set his limits which cannot be passed. <note>original: "Breues dies hominis sunt: & numerus mensium apud te est. Constituisti terminos eius qui preteriri non possunt."</note>

Similarly, Saint Jerome in his letter to Heliodorus says: 
> We must therefore meditate in our minds on what we will eventually be, for whether we wish it or not, it cannot be far away. <note>original: "Debemus igitur & nos animo premeditari quid aliquando futuri sumus: & quod velimus noli mus abesse longius non potest"</note>

The same was written by Saint Gregory in the *Moralia*, in the twelfth chapter, saying: 
> Although almighty God ordains that time for each person's death when their life ends, it is also established how long they live in this mortal life. <note>original: "Quamuis omnipotens deus illud tẽpus vniuscuiusq; ad mortem precipiat quo eius vita terminatur: statutum quoq; est quantum i ipsa vita mortali temporaliter viuat."</note>

<margin>O</margin>
¶ Finally, the text of the Decretum <note>original: "xxiij. questione quarta". A reference to Canon Law.</note> says in the chapter *Nebuchadnezzar*: 
> Although we know most certainly that no one will live beyond the limit set for them by God, nevertheless we appropriately provide medicine to all the sick. <note>original: "Quam uis certissime sciamus neminem vltra terminum sibi prefixum a deo esse uicturum: tamen oibus languentibus non incongrue medemur."</note>

We do not, however, say...

# CHAPTER FOUR

A person cannot lengthen their life through their own power; for the opposite happened to Hezekiah <note>King Hezekiah of Judah, who according to the Bible (Isaiah 38) was granted fifteen additional years of life by God.</note> as we said above in the previous chapter. Therefore, providence is of no use against death, which accompanies us immediately from our birth. Thus, both doubts raised above in the preceding verses are clearly resolved. Messer Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch).</note> then continues, saying that after Plotinus, he saw Crassus, Antony, and Hortensius follow; then Sergio Galba and Calvus Licinius, who, together with Asinius Pollio, raised his brow with pride against Cicero, arming their tongues against him and seeking a reputation for themselves that was unworthy and totally false. Wherefore he says:

->Then Crassus, Antony, Hortensius, Galba, and<-
->With Pollio; Calvus, who rose in such pride,<-
->Who armed their tongues against the man of Arpino;<- <note>Cicero, who was born in Arpinum.</note>
->The two of them seeking unworthy and false fame.<-

<margin>F</margin>
¶ Cornelius Tacitus writes in the book *On Famous Orators* <note>Actually referring to the *Dialogus de oratoribus*, often attributed to Tacitus.</note> for the understanding of the preceding verses, that each of the aforementioned men listed by Messer Francesco were clear and distinguished orators. And Cicero likewise confirms the same in his own *On Famous Orators*. Speaking primarily of Crassus, he says: "We have accepted Publius Crassus as a highly approved orator in nearly those same times, as he was strong in natural talent and study, and even had some domestic training." <note>original: *Publiū Crassum valde probatū oratorem i eisdē fere tēporibus accepimus q r̄ ingenio valuit & studio & habuit quasdām etiam domesticas disciplinas.*</note> And in the *Paradoxes* he says: "For what is the value of that copious rather than wise speech of the most eloquent Crassus: 'snatch us from slavery'?" <note>original: *Quid. n. valet illa eloquentissimi viri crassi copiosa magis quā sapiens oratio eripite nos a seruitute:*</note> By these sayings, it is understood quite clearly how deservedly Crassus was numbered by Messer Francesco in the triumph of fame.

<margin>Q</margin>
¶ Likewise, Cicero writes of Antony in *On the Orator* addressing Brutus, saying these words: "They were superior and suited to every genre. I speak of Crassus and Antony." And in *On Famous Orators* he says: "So now we come to Antony and Crassus. For I think these orators were the greatest, in whom for the first time the Latin abundance of speech equaled the glory of the Greeks. Everything came to Antony's mind in its proper place where it could accomplish and prevail the most; just as a general places his cavalry, infantry, and light-armored troops, so Antony placed the parts of his speech in the most opportune locations." <note>original: *Sic nunc ad Antoniū crassum peruenimus... ut ab imperatore equites pedites leuis armatura sic ab illo in maxime opportunis orationis partibus collocabantur.*</note> Quintilian also commemorates this Antony in the seventh book of the *Education of the Orator* as a clear and excellent orator. Therefore, with great reason, our graceful poet has described him as famous alongside Crassus.

<margin>R</margin>
¶ Next, as to how great the excellence of Hortensius was, Cicero demonstrated it clearly in the prologue of the book *On Famous Orators* when he says that the most learned voice of Hortensius would have been worthy of all Greek and Latin listeners.

<margin>S</margin>
¶ Nor does Cicero omit, in the same book, the worthy praises of Sergio Galba; but of him he writes these worthy words: "But among these, being a little older than the others, Sergio Galba was without controversy the leader in eloquence. And indeed, he was the first among the Latins to handle those proper and, as it were, legitimate works of orators." <note>original: *Sed inter hos ætate paulū his antecedens sine controuersia Sergius Galba eloquentia prestitit...*</note> Thus, these others are appropriately described here and celebrated with the other famous men.

<margin>T</margin>
¶ Great was the excellence of the preceding orators, but certainly no less was that of Calvus Licinius, had he not been prevented by death in his youth. Cicero shows this quite clearly in *On Famous Orators* when he says: "Mention must be made, as it seems to me, of two young men who, if they had lived longer, would have achieved great praise in eloquence. Brutus said: 'I think you mean Gaius Curio and Gaius Licinius Calvus.' You think rightly; one of whom spoke with such probability, and wanted his words to be so easy and free, sometimes sharp and certainly full of frequent sentiments, that nothing could be more ornate or more ready." <note>original: *q̄ q̄ facienda mentio est vt quidem mihi videtur duorum adolescentium...*</note> Therefore, Calvus has rightly not been separated from the other orators, who in their time and today have been worthy of singular fame.

<margin>V</margin>
¶ Finally, how great the excellence of Asinius Pollio was is understood not only by the high opinion Octavius <note>The Emperor Augustus.</note> held of him, but also by the words written by Quintilian in the tenth book of the *Education of the Orator*, saying: "I find much in Asinius Pollio of the highest diligence, so much so that to some he even seems to have enough of both counsel and spirit, but he is so far from the shine and pleasantness of Cicero that he could be seen as belonging to a prior century." <note>original: *Multa in Asinio Pollione inuenio summæ diligentis... longe abest vt videri possit secondo prior.*</note> This man, therefore, both because of his learning and also because of the power he had with Augustus, seemed to think his own glory was diminished if Cicero's was not lowered.

<margin>X</margin>
¶ Thus, together with Calvus, he began to attack Cicero; wherefore they wrote many letters to him, imposing great and most heavy slanders upon him.

Just as Cornelius Tacitus shows in the book *On Famous Orators* <note>Referring to the *Dialogus de oratoribus*, a work on the decline of eloquence.</note> when he speaks, introducing Messalla Corvinus <note>A prominent Roman general and author, friend of Horace and Tibullus.</note> as the speaker: "Calvus is more concise, Asinius more rhythmic, Caesar more splendid, Caelius more bitter, Brutus more grave, Cicero more vehement, fuller, and more powerful. Yet all of them possess the same sanctity of eloquence. So that if you were to take up the books of all of them at once, you would find, despite their differing talents, a certain similarity of judgment and volume of thought." <note>original Latin: "Acstrictior caluus: numerosior asinius: spelēdidior Cesar amarior celefus: grauior Brutus: uehementior: plenior & valentior Cicero. Oēs tn̄ e.ndē sanctitatē eloquentiæ ferunt. Ut si omnium pariter libros in manum sumpseris quis in diuersis ingenijs esse quandā iudicij ac voluminis similitudinem & cogitationē."</note> For as to the fact that they disparaged one another, and that some of their letters contain mutual malice, this is not a fault of the orators, but of men. For I believe that Calvus, Asinius, and Cicero himself were accustomed to envy, spite, and were affected by the other vices of human infirmity. For this reason, concluding that not without cause, Asinius Pollio was inserted with the other orators by the poet in his praise in the preceding verses. Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarch.</note> then adds two notable historians of the Greek nation, saying that after these Roman orators, he saw Thucydides approach, who well distinguishes the places and times of the wars fought. And also the most powerful deeds of the combatants, and particularly which field is stained and by whose blood. And together with him was Herodotus, judged—and deservedly so—the father of Greek history. Wherefore he says:

<margin>☞</margin>
¶ How great the dignity and worthy praise of Thucydides is can be clearly enough understood from what Cicero, Quintilian, and Aulus Gellius write of him. Thus, he is deservedly judged to be the greatest light upon the famous deeds and magnanimous acts of the Greek nation. Regarding him, Cicero says principally in *On Famous Orators*: "You would do best to imitate Thucydides if you intend to write history, not if you intend to argue legal cases. For Thucydides was a sincere and grand announcer of deeds performed." <note>original Latin: "Tucididē imitare optime si historiā scribere non si causas dicere cogites. Tucidides. n. rerū gestarum pronūciator sincerus & grandis fuit."</note> To these words Aulus Gellius adds in the first book of *Attic Nights*, saying: "Thucydides, the most grave author of Greek history." <note>original Latin: "Auctor historiæ græcæ grauis-simus Tucidides."</note> Quintilian agrees with him, writing: "Thucydides is sweet and candid." <note>original Latin: "Tucidides dulcis & candidus."</note> And he then continues in praise of Herodotus, adding these words: "And Herodotus is flowing; the former [Thucydides] is excited, the latter [Herodotus] is relaxed; the former is better in his passions, the former in public speeches, the latter in conversations; the former in force, the latter in charm." <note>original Latin: "& effusus Heredot?: ille concitatus: hic remissus affectib’ melior: ille contionibus: hic sermonibus: ille vi: hic voluntate."</note>

<margin>☞</margin>
¶ Hence his sufficiency is quite apparent. But it is much better known through the context of his history, which describes Greek affairs beginning from the causes for which wars were stirred up between the Phoenicians, the Assyrians, and the Greeks themselves. Such as in that abduction of Europa, daughter of Agenor, carried out by Jove; then that of Medea and Helen; and proceeding thus, he writes down to the times of Xerxes, where about 1,338 years converged from these beginnings. He describes these wars with such elegance that he is deservedly called by our poet and by other writers "Herodotus, father of Greek history." Master Francesco then recounts whom he saw following behind Herodotus, saying that he saw the noble geometer Euclid depicted all over with triangles, circles, and square shapes. Wherefore he says:

<margin>A</margin>

<margin>V</margin>
—having given himself at first to the study of natural philosophy, and especially following Parmenides, he judged that the understanding man could acquire was very small in comparison to the vast and diverse nature of things. For this reason, he left this study and gave himself entirely to moral philosophy. Having then for some time attended to this morality, he saw that it was an uncertain and specific kind of knowledge, since moral matters have their being through laws and customs rather than by nature. Therefore, he abandoned following them and, desiring the mathematical sciences, he followed them through practice, recognizing them to be in the first degree of human certainty. As Averroes <note>The influential Andalusian philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> writes in the second book of the *Metaphysics*, he followed them until his final breath, especially Geometry. ...that this [imagination] had been the cause of such an effect, the woman having strongly imagined it at the time of conception. Looking then upon the husband and the relatives, they found it to be exactly as she told them.

<margin>I</margin> <margin>Hippocrates. Wherefore by this ingenuity that woman was absolved from every suspicion.</margin> Hippocrates wrote several books in medicine: namely, *The Prognostics*, *Regimen in Acute Diseases*, *Epidemics*, *On Law*, *On the Nature of the Fetus*, and many others; among which were the excellent *Aphorisms*, so designated by the independence of one sentence from the next <note>The Aphorisms are famous for being short, pithy statements of medical truth</note>. From which one clearly understands how useful this work is through its renown; for it is seen to contain every part included in the definition of medicine given by Avicenna in the first book <note>Avicenna was a Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard medieval textbook</note>, and by Isidore in the fourth book of the *Etymologies*, where at the beginning he says: <note>original: "Medicina est quæ corporis vel tuetur vel restaurat salutem."</note> Medicine is that which either protects or restores the health of the body.

<margin>K</margin> ¶ Hippocrates truly felt that God, concerning His being, was simple and the author of all worldly things, making the manner of them eternal. But the soul: as Macrobius writes in *The Dream of Scipio*, he said it was a thin and most subtle spirit diffused throughout the whole body. Wherefore he tacitly described it as mortal. Many notable sayings and opinions are attributed to Hippocrates. <note>The following are translated from Latin maxims</note> Poverty that is secure is more choiceworthy than fear with riches. He will indeed avoid indigence who will be content with that which is modest. He who wishes to be entirely free of what he cannot have, let him not desire it; likewise, he who wishes to possess what he desires, let him crave what he can easily obtain.

<margin>L</margin> ¶ Hippocrates died in extreme old age, being ninety-five years old. Next, Master F. <note>Francesco Petrarch, the author of the poem</note> introduces Aesculapius and Apollo after Hippocrates: saying that for a very long time he saw Apollo and Aesculapius above him; they were so closed off and encompassed by the distance of time that his sight could hardly comprehend them, so much had their names become entangled and obscured by great age. Wherefore he says:

<margin>M</margin> ¶ It is a manifest thing that there were two Apollos: each of them had knowledge of medicine; one was the son of Vulcan, first son of Heaven; the other was the son of Jupiter and Latona, whose son was Aesculapius.

Wherefore Isidore says in the fourth book of the *Etymologies*: <note>original: "Medicinæ autem artis auctor ac reptor apud grecos perhibetur Apollo. But the ancient opinion sufficiently demonstrates that each of these was most excellent in the art: one of them became a God; the other had the power to recall Hippolytus and a god <note>perhaps referring to a hero or divine spirit</note> from hell; nevertheless, their antiquity is so great that they have remained among us more as fabulous fictions than as true and clear history.

<margin>N</margin> ¶ Only in a confused way, then, can we conclude that they were excellent men and most learned physicians. To see and know him there was such a crowd of people that Galen could only proceed through Rome in any place with great difficulty.

# CHAPTER FOUR

## CHAPTER FOUR

<margin>V</margin>
...profit, they neglect the necessary studies of the liberal arts, without which medicine is totally imperfect, just as the "Conciliator" <note>Peter of Abano (c. 1257–1316), a famous physician and philosopher whose work "Conciliator" sought to reconcile the differences between philosophy and medicine</note> shows at the beginning of his book of differences. Hence, the medical schools <note>original: "sette", referring to the ancient medical sects like the Methodists or Dogmatists</note> are confused, and in truth, they should be called neither unskilled nor methodical nor rational. This is a very effective cause for the ruining of medicine. But certainly, the fault is much greater, and the error of princes and other republics leads more effectively to its ruin; they make no distinction between skilled physicians and pure "experimenters" <note>those who rely solely on trial and error without theoretical knowledge</note> who are governed only by fortune. Hence, they often give more credit and reward to a simple experiment that succeeded by the benefit of nature—correcting the error of the unskilled person—than to many equal treatments performed by physicians according to reason and the medical canons. From this, it follows that the necessary diligence of medicine is abandoned, and everyone runs to perform "notomy" <note>anatomy or dissection</note> on human bodies to clarify the power of a single medicine <note>original: "simplice," a term for a medicinal herb or single-ingredient drug</note>. Oh, how the due and laudable fear written by Hippocrates in the first aphorism is lost! Where he says: "Experience is deceptive" <note>original Latin: "Experimentum fallax"</note>. And Galen explains: "Deceptive, that is, hazardous, because of the noble seed upon which one must work; for that is the human body." How neglected also is the diligence described by the authoritative verses which require proper care, saying: "These things must be considered by the physician wishing to cure: Art, age, strength, region, complexion, form; death and symptoms, fullness, time, and custom" <note>original: "Hec sūt pensanda medico curare volenti. Ars ætas virtus regio cōplexio forma. Mors & sinthoma repletio tps & vsus."</note>. Now, is it not permitted today—indeed, even lawful—for hermit monks and craftsmen to treat any grave case, including peasants and those who never had any knowledge of letters <note>meaning they were illiterate in Latin, the language of medical science</note>? Are not physicians today blamed, and the unskilled publicly and privately commended? Is not more credit given today to a young and inexperienced quack <note>original: "parabolan," from the Greek for "reckless," often used for those who took risks with patients' lives</note> than to an old, practiced, and restrained physician? O blind ignorance! O foolish credulity! Truly today one can conclude that medicine is for the most part in the hands of public and private "Pharmacopolists" <note>drug-sellers or apothecaries</note>. One must, however, have compassion for the common people: first, for their ignorance, by which they do not know the learned from the unskilled; second, because the poor commoners, fed on dreams and fables, bear the penalty for the error committed, remaining exhausted of their money or their life. I do not say, however, that there are not some most excellent and worthy physicians, and some most prudent lords and grateful republics. For their public works in nourishing and exalting studies give true testimony of their most illustrious and magnificent virtue, and also of the dignity and sufficiency of their physicians.

<margin>Q</margin>
> Galen wrote several worthy sentences: first, "Knowledge does not benefit the senseless, nor does sense benefit him who does not use it." <note>original: "Sciā insensato nō prodest neq; ei qui eo nō vtitur pdest sensus."</note> "A man is able to direct any of his actions when he has come to know himself. This is the mark of excellent wisdom: for a man to have knowledge of himself, and not be deceived by the love he has for himself, thinking himself good when he is not. Just as a man gravely ill does not stop insisting on medicines as long as he lives so that he may attain health—which he cannot fully reach—so it behooves us to add to the health of our souls, and to join goodness to goodness, even if we cannot reach the state of a giant and wise soul."

<margin>R</margin>
Galen died a natural death, quite ancient and mature in age. Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> follows after, saying that after Galen, he saw Anaxarchus follow, and saw how manly and intrepid he was. Wherefore he says:

<margin>S</margin>
->I saw Anaxarchus, intrepid and manly;<-

Anaxarchus, as Laertius writes, was a famous and outstanding philosopher from Abdera. Valerius, in the third book, third chapter, clearly demonstrates his intrepid manliness, as does Laertius himself when describing his worthy life. Principally, when Anaxarchus was at dinner with Alexander [the Great], and Nicocreon, the tyrant of Cyprus—who was also at the dinner—was his enemy. Alexander asked Anaxarchus if the banquet had been perfect in every part. To which he replied, looking fixedly at Nicocreon, these words: "Everything is magnificent, O King. But truly, the head of a certain Satrap should have been served" <note>original: "Cuncta per magnifice o rex. Verum oportebat iam caput Satrape cuiusdam apponi." By "Satrap," Anaxarchus was insulting the tyrant Nicocreon to his face.</note>. By these words, Nicocreon was moved to the greatest anger and enmity against Anaxarchus. For this reason, after the death of Alexander, Nicocreon had Anaxarchus seized and put into a large mortar <note>original: "pila," a stone vessel for grinding</note> and had him beaten with iron mallets. But the intrepid philosopher continually said to the tyrant: "Pound, pound the vessel of Anaxarchus, for you do not grind Anaxarchus himself" <note>original: "Tunde tunde anaxarchi vasculuminam anaxarchum nihil teris"</note>. Incensed by this, Nicocreon commanded that his tongue be cut out; hearing this command, Anaxarchus bit it off with his teeth and spat it in the tyrant's face.

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>V</margin> ¶ When he was once being worshipped as an idol, he bled from a wound. Anaxarchus, seeing that blood, demonstrated its nature by saying: *Surely this was not divine blood* <note>original: "Hic nempe diuinus sanguis non erat"</note>. In this way, he silently responded to the insolence and superstition of Alexander of Macedon. ¶ Anaxarchus was called "The Happy" because of the liberty and constancy of his soul. Furthermore, it was never heard that he complained of any bodily pain; for this reason, he has truly been nicknamed "manly and intrepid" by our poet <note>Petrarch</note>. Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> then adds that after Anaxarchus follows Xenocrates, who always remained more solid and continent than a stone. No force could ever turn him toward any vile act or operation. Thus he says:

->And Xenocrates, more solid than a rock;<-
->Whom no force could turn toward a base act.<-

<margin>X</margin> ¶ Xenocrates, as Diogenes Laertius writes, was a Chalcedonian, the son of one Agathenor, and a disciple of Plato. He lived with such continence, modesty, and gravity that he drew the admiration and envy of the Athenian people. Whenever he passed through the streets, the crowds would run to make way for him. At that same time in Athens, there was a notorious courtesan named Phryne, who offered a bet that she could strip Xenocrates of his chastity. She was promised a very great reward if she could do it. She went to Xenocrates and humbly prayed that he would let her sleep with him for one night. Xenocrates consented. Nevertheless, despite her presence and her lascivious and lustful incitements, Xenocrates moved no more than if he had truly been made of marble. Thus, having been deluded by his resistance, Phryne replied: she had slept that night not with a man, but with a statue.

<margin>Y</margin> ¶ Another time, Xenocrates's disciples, wanting to test his chastity, placed another courtesan in his bed one night, no less lascivious than the aforementioned Phryne, whose name was Lais. When Xenocrates felt the incitement of lust, he rose from the bed and <note>The text here implies he harmed his own genitals—likely by burning—to use physical pain to extinguish sexual desire, a common legend of his extreme asceticism</note> acted upon his own genitals. Truly, he gave such evident and infallible proof of himself that it is rightly written that no force could compel him to sin.

<margin>Z</margin> ¶ Xenocrates was held in such great veneration by the Athenians that they believed his testimony alone, without requiring an oath. He valued money no more than was necessary for his basic needs. When a great quantity of it was sent to him as a gift by Alexander, he took only a tiny portion and sent the rest back. Another time, when Antipater sent a gift, Xenocrates, having no need for it, sent it all back. One day, while Xenocrates was reading the usual lessons to his disciples, a youth named Polemo (as Valerius Maximus writes), who was of lost and wicked character, entered the school to mock Xenocrates. Noticing this, Xenocrates set aside the subject he was treating and began to speak of morality and conduct. He spoke so worthily and effectively that Polemo’s nature was transformed; before he left, he became Xenocrates's disciple, and later a famous and distinguished philosopher.

<margin>A</margin> ¶ Xenocrates wrote many works, as Laertius attests. He said our soul was "a self-moving number," as Macrobius shows in his commentary on the *Dream of Scipio*, and Cicero in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*. To Xenocrates belongs that golden maxim: *I have indeed sometimes repented of speaking, but never of keeping silent* <note>original: "Me quidem fuisse locutum aliquando pœnituit: tacuisse vero nunquam"</note>. Another time, when he was being insulted with words by one Bion in Athens, he said: *I will not answer you; for Tragedy does not deign to answer Comedy when provoked by her* <note>original: "Non tibi respondeo equidem: nam neque tragedia comediã cum ab ea lacesfitur responsione dignatur"</note>.

<margin>B</margin> ¶ Xenocrates died at quite a mature age, to the great sorrow and loss of the Chalcedonians and Athenians. The poet then narrates and adds that after Xenocrates, he saw Archimedes standing in contemplation, though with his face lowered and fixed toward the earth. Thus he says:

->I saw Archimedes standing with his face lowered;<-

<margin>C</margin> ¶ <term>ARCHIMEDES</term> <note>A Greek mathematician, physicist, and engineer from Syracuse (c. 287–212 BCE), famous for his contributions to geometry and his defensive war machines</note> was a Syracusan, as Livy shows in the fifth book of the third decade. He was a most learned man and a perfect geometer. Through his industry, when the Romans had held Syracuse under siege for a long time (as one reads in the same book of Livy), he saved the city and protected it from the pressure of Marcus Marcellus. But finally, one day when the Romans launched an assault, they took the land by force and gave it over to the soldiers for plunder. On that day, Archimedes was in his house, demonstrating certain mathematical conclusions by marking them on the ground. It happened by chance that a centurion entered Archimedes's house and, finding him intent on the aforementioned demonstration, asked him who he was. Archimedes answered nothing to his question, but only said... <note>The text breaks off, but the traditional story concludes with Archimedes telling the soldier, "Do not disturb my circles," before being killed</note>

<summary>This page illustrates the virtue of philosophical constancy through the lives of Anaxarchus and Xenocrates, emphasizing their resistance to temptation and worldly power, before introducing Archimedes as an example of total intellectual absorption.</summary>
<keywords>Anaxarchus, Xenocrates, Phryne, Lais, Polemo, Archimedes, Petrarch, Stoicism, Chastity, Syracuse, Geometry, Ancient Philosophy</keywords>

alone. He said, turning to him: "I beg you, do not disturb this circle" <note>original: "Noli obsecro istum disturbare circulum"</note>. Because of these words, the centurion, believing he was being mocked, killed him. Marcellus was intensely grieved by this, especially because he had commanded on that day that no harm should be done to Archimedes. ¶ Archimedes wrote on the *squaring of the circle* <note>The mathematical challenge of constructing a square with the same area as a given circle</note>, which, even if it can be known, was still not known in his time; Aristotle likewise wrote and affirmed that this had occurred. Following Archimedes, our Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> says that he then saw Democritus walking thoughtfully, who by his own will was deprived of gold, light, and sight. Wherefore he says:

->And Democritus walking all thoughtful<-
->By his own will deprived of light and gold.<-

<margin>E</margin>
**V**arious opinions exist regarding whose son Democritus of Abdera was. Some said he was the son of Hegesistratus, others of Athenocritus, and others of Damasippus, as Diogenes Laertius shows in his *Life*. Nevertheless, there is agreement that everyone says Democritus was a worthy and outstanding philosopher, most studious, and observant of speculation. Democritus, therefore, principally desiring to understand whatever could be learned, did not fail to travel to any land where there was anyone who taught doctrine. For this reason, he even reached India solely for the fame of the Gymnosophists <note>A sect of ancient Indian philosophers who practiced asceticism and went naked, known to the Greeks as "naked philosophers"</note>. As Aulus Gellius writes in the *Attic Nights* and Valerius Maximus in the seventh book, chapter seven, Democritus had a father so abundant in riches that he alone could have easily provided provisions for the entire army of Xerxes. Nevertheless, to better devote himself to his studies, Democritus took only a very small part of the inheritance and gave the remainder to his homeland. By choice, he lived poorly. <margin>F</margin> ¶ Democritus went to study in Athens, where he never made himself known, simply to flee from all pomp and pride. And in that place, to better attend to his speculations, he deprived himself of his sight—although some others say he blinded himself so as not to see prosperity come to the wicked. Some also claim he did it because he said he could not look upon women without lust. Democritus increased the magic arts—as Isidore writes in the eighth book of the *Etymologies*—which from the time of Zoroaster until his own had much diminished. He was most constant against insulting words, as Seneca shows in his letters to Lucilius. Democritus held the opinion that atoms are the beginning of every thing, as one reads in the book *On the Ends of Goods and Evils*, in *On Fate*, and in the *Tusculan Disputations* by Cicero, in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, and in *On the Soul* and *On Generation* by Aristotle. Likewise, in the fourteenth book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, Eusebius writes of him thus: 
> *Democritus, whom Epicurus follows, asserts the principle of things to be certain very small bodies, which he calls atoms; these are cognizable by reason, solid, neither generated nor corruptible, superior to every structure, and cannot be altered.* <note>original: "Democritus quem epicurus sequitur principium rerum asserit corpuscula quaedam minutissima: quas athomos appellat ratione cognoscibiles solidas non generabiles nec corruptibiles omni factura superiores: quae alterari non possunt."</note> 
Laertius confirms this same thing and adds that he said they were infinite, with which Cicero seems to agree in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations* when he says: 
> *For let us dismiss that great man Democritus, who produces the mind from certain smooth and round bodies by some fortuitous collision. For there is nothing among those people that the crowd of atoms does not produce.* <note>original: "Democritum enim magnum illum quidem virum & leuibus & rotundis corpusculis efficientem animum concursu quodam fortuito obmittamus. Nihil enim est apō istos: quod non athomorum turba conficiat."</note> 
<margin>G</margin> Regarding God, Democritus said that God was the soul of the world and had the form of a ball of fire, as Eusebius testifies in the same book. He also posited the existence of the vacuum <note>the void</note>, through which the atoms move. <margin>H</margin> ¶ Because of this, he said there were infinite worlds being generated infinite times, as is read in the same place; and such generation happens by chance, as is written in the eighth book of the *Physics*. ¶ Democritus wrote several worthy works in which many notable sayings are inserted: first, *Speech is the shadow of work* <note>original: "Sermo est operis umbra"</note>. ¶ *One man to me is worth the whole people, and the whole people worth but one* <note>original: "unus mihi pro populo est: et populus pro uno"</note>. <margin>I</margin> *A soft life is a dead sea. The unlearned man has only silence from the learned. Frugality is a remedy for necessity and the medicine of losses.* <note>original: "Vita mollis mare mortuum est. Indoctus solum silentium ex doctis habet. Parcitas necessitatis remedium est medicina damnorum."</note> ¶ Democritus died in the time of Hermippus at a very great age, by natural exhaustion. The poet then narrates, saying that after Democritus, in following the Triumph of Fame, he saw Hippias, the old man who was once bold enough to say in Athens that he knew everything. Wherefore he says:

->I saw Hippias; and the old man who once dared<-
->To say, "I know everything";<-

<margin>R</margin>
**H**ippias has left no more notice of himself to us than that he was a worthy and outstanding orator, numbered by Cicero in *On Famous Orators*, where Petrarch writes...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of ancient thinkers featured in Petrarch’s "Triumph of Fame." Following the previous discussion of the polymath Hippias of Elis, the text now focuses on the legendary orator Gorgias of Leontini, the skeptical philosopher Arcesilaus, and the "obscure" Heraclitus.</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

Tully <note>The Roman statesman and orator Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> says these words of him: "But as it was understood how much power an accurate speech might have, many masters of speaking suddenly emerged, such as Gorgias of Leontini, Thrasymachus of Chalcedon, Protagoras of Abdera, Prodicus of Chios, and Hippias of Elis" <note>original: "Sed vt itellectũ ẽ quãtã vim hẽret accurata ẽ facta quodãmõ oratio: tã et magistri dicẽdi multi subito extiterũt. tã Leontinus gorgias Trasymacus calcedonius p̃tagoras abderites p̃dicus Chius hyppias heleus."</note>. But the bold little old man was Gorgias of Leontini, of whom Tully writes in his book *On Old Age* that he lived one hundred and seven years. Wherefore he is rightly called a "little old man." Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville</note>, Quintilian, and Tully write of Gorgias that he was among the first inventors of the faculty of oratory. Furthermore, Saint Jerome, writing against Jovinian, says that he wrote a book on concord for the Greeks with the greatest morality. Thus, one day in the assembly at Athens, Gorgias told all the learned men <margin>L</margin> that he was prepared to answer on whatever subject anyone wished to dispute. ¶ When Gorgias had already reached extreme old age, he was asked by someone for what reason he took such pleasure in being alive; he replied with these worthy words: "Because I have nothing for which to accuse my old age" <note>original: "Quia nihil hẽo quo senectutẽ meã accusem"</note>. It is likely that Gorgias wrote many notable sayings, among which has come to our notice that which he said <margin>M</margin> while dying: namely, that he wished to abandon life just as he was beginning to know. ¶ Gorgias was the teacher of Isocrates, who was a distinguished rhetorician, as Quintilian and Tully demonstrate; he died an old man at the age written above, and after his death, the Athenians made for him a golden statue in perpetual memory. Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> continues, saying that after Gorgias, he saw Arcesilaus <note>The text uses "Archefilao," referring to Arcesilaus, the founder of the Second or Middle Academy</note> very doubtful and uncertain of every thing. Wherefore he says:

->And then certain of nothing,<-
->But Arcesilaus, doubtful of every thing.<-

<margin>N</margin> ¶ Arcesilaus, as Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, author of "Lives of the Eminent Philosophers"</note> writes, was a Pitanean, the son of one Seuthes or Scythes; he was the author of the Academic sect, although other writers, especially Augustine in the eighth book of *The City of God*, attribute it to Archelaus of Miletus. This man, therefore, considering that our knowledge could only concern probable things, always argued on both sides of any subject, reducing it to the custom that Plato had first written in the form of a dialogue. Besides this, Arcesilaus was not only a philosopher, but a distinguished orator and excellent poet. For this reason, he never went to sleep or rose from bed without first having read some part of Homer. When Arcesilaus disputed, especially in natural philosophy, he always said in his affirmations: "I think so, indeed" <note>original: "Arbitror eqdẽ"</note>. Nor did he ever show more certainty than that. He was excellent in invention, and he adapted himself optimally to human operations at every time. He was an excellent mathematician, very liberal, and a benefactor to his friends; for once, wishing to give certain golden vases to a friend who did not want to accept them, he lent them to him, and then, when the friend was forced by necessity and could not return them to Arcesilaus, he graciously gave them all to him as a gift. Another time, another friend named Ctesibius being ill and feeling ashamed to ask Arcesilaus for help, Arcesilaus, noticing this, secretly placed a bag of gold coins under his pillow; when Ctesibius found it, he said: "This is the play of Arcesilaus" <note>original: "Archesilai hic ludus est."</note>. <margin>O</margin> ¶ Arcesilaus wrote several notable sayings, starting with: "The sons of the fierce are accustomed to speak wickedly and shamelessly; but the speech of the grave lacked a nurse" <note>This is a difficult passage regarding the nature of speech and character</note>. "The passage of the winds is hidden even from birds, unless a storm is present." Finally, when Arcesilaus was asked for what reason many philosophers went over to the Epicurean sect and no one ever left it, he replied: "Because from men, eunuchs are made; but from eunuchs, men are never made" <note>original: "q̃z fape ex viris galli fiũt. ex gallis aũt viri nũquã." A metaphor suggesting that while one can lose their philosophical vigor and become a pleasure-seeker (Epicurean), one who has abandoned rigor cannot regain it.</note>. Once, Arcesilaus composed certain verses in a very inept manner to be said to a potter. Because of this, he went among his vases <margin>P</margin> and, breaking them all, said: "You corrupt my things, and I shall destroy yours" <note>original: "Tu mea corrumpis ego tua dissipabo."</note>. ¶ Arcesilaus died at quite an old age; nor did he ever want a wife or to father children, as Laertius clearly writes in his life. Afterward, Master Francesco adds, saying that after Arcesilaus he saw Heraclitus, "covered" in his speech <margin>Q</margin> and his sentences. Wherefore he says:

->I saw in his sayings Heraclitus, covered;<-

¶ Heraclitus, called by the surname "the Dark" <note>His Greek epithet "Skoteinos" refers to the difficulty and obscurity of his philosophical prose</note>, was a worthy and excellent Asian philosopher who, in describing his world, made so much difficulty that he was rightly said to move in darkness. Heraclitus held the opinion that fire was the principle of all mundane things, as Aristotle describes in the first book of the *Physics*, the *Metaphysics*, and likewise in *On the Soul*; he even said that the gods were all made of fire. Wherefore Eusebius, in the fourteenth book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, writes thus of Heraclitus: "Heraclitus and Hippasus of Metapontum believed fire to be the principle of things, by whose extinction all other things are born" <note>original: "Heraclitus vero z hippasus methapontinus ignẽ eẽ pricipiũ rerũ putauerunt quo extincto cetera gignuntur"</note>.

<summary>This page details the lives and philosophies of Gorgias of Leontini, known for his longevity and oratory; Arcesilaus, the Academic skeptic who argued both sides of every issue; and Heraclitus "the Dark," who proposed fire as the fundamental element of the universe.</summary>

### CHAPTER FOUR

<margin>R</margin> They are governed and shaped. Therefore, the principle of all things is fire, because from it all things are made and into it they are eventually resolved. ¶ Regarding God, he <note>Heraclitus of Ephesus</note> said that He and the heavens and the stars are made of fire and that they are gods, confirming in this the opinion of the Stoics. Our soul, as Macrobius writes in *The Dream of Scipio*, he defined thus: *the soul is a spark of stellar essence* <note>original: "anima est scitilla stellaris essentie"</note>; although Heraclides Ponticus said it was only light.

<margin>S</margin> ¶ Heraclitus wrote these two sayings among others: *One day is equal to all* <note>The OCR reads "pax" (peace), but the philosophical fragment by Heraclitus is "par" (equal), meaning every day is of the same nature.</note>. *Into the same river we twice descend and do not descend* <note>original: "Vnus dies pax oium est i eundem fluuium bis descēdimus & non descēdimus." This is Heraclitus’s most famous doctrine on the ever-changing nature of reality.</note>. ¶ Heraclitus died quite an old man, and after his death, he retained the surname "the Obscure." ¶ Next, Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch, the author of the poem being commented upon</note> speaks of Diogenes the Cynic after Heraclitus, saying that he saw him coming, in his deeds and actions, much more "open" than shame would allow. Wherefore he says:

<margin>V</margin>
->And Diogenes the Cynic in his deeds<-
->Far more open than shame would allow:<-

<margin>¶ Diogenes the Cynic, as Diogenes Laertius writes, was a native of Sinope, the son of one Icesius, a money-changer, who at first gave himself to the counterfeiting of coins; for which reason he was sent into exile. And he, by the counsel of the Oracle of Apollo, came to Athens where, having seen the philosopher Antisthenes, he gave himself to him as a disciple. Although he was driven away by him many times, in the end Diogenes obtained his wish through humility; for when Antisthenes took a staff and wanted to strike him, Diogenes bowed his head and said: *Yield, for you will not find a staff so hard that you can keep me away from you as long as you have something to say* <note>original: "Cede non enī ita durum baculum reperies q me abste quamdiu aliqd dixeris arcere possis"</note>. Thus Diogenes, from a counterfeiter of nature, became a philosopher and a member of the sect of the Cynics, who observed only the law of nature, judging every other law to be superfluous. For his house and dwelling, he lived in a barrel <note>The famous "tub" of Diogenes</note>, which he always turned according to the sun’s rays. It was his opinion that all wealth beyond daily use was superfluous, and he said every pleasure was blameworthy. Therefore, Seneca writes of him in the sixth book of *On Benefits*: *Diogenes was more powerful than Alexander who possessed all things; for it was more that Diogenes would not receive than what Alexander himself could give* <note>original: "potentior fuit Diogenes alexandro oīa possidente: plus enī erat q̄ Diogenes nollet accipere: quam q̄ ipse dare"</note>. Cicero confirms this same thing in the *Tusculan Disputations*, as does Valerius Maximus in his fourth book. Regarding how Diogenes and the Cynics were "more open than shame would allow" in their behavior, Saint Augustine demonstrates this well in the fourteenth book of *The City of God* <note>The OCR says "xiij" (13), but this discussion is in Book 14</note> when he says, speaking of the Cynics: *against human modesty, they put forward a foul and imprudent opinion* <note>original: "contra humanam uerecundiā imundam iprudentēq̄ sn̄iam proferebant"</note>; and he adds: *nevertheless, natural shame conquered the opinion of this error* <note>original: "Vicit tn̄ pudor naturalis opinionē huius erroris"</note>.</margin>

¶ Regarding his opinions, <margin>X</margin> Diogenes primarily imagined the principle of all things to be air, as is described by the Probus in several places, by Augustine in the seventh book of *The City of God*, and by Eusebius in the thirteenth book of *Preparation for the Gospel*, which says this of Anaximenes: *Anaximenes the Milesian indeed thought the principle of things was air, from which he contended all things are made and into which they are resolved; for he says even our soul is air: for this contains us; and spirit and air cherish the whole world* <note>Anaximenes' theory of "pneuma" or life-breath. The text here conflates Diogenes of Sinope with the natural philosopher Diogenes of Apollonia.</note>. Adding to these words in the seventh book of *The City of God*, Augustine declares what the primary opinion of Diogenes was, saying: *Augustine says that Diogenes, a student of Anaximenes, says all things consist of air, not disagreeing with the opinion of his teacher.* Diogenes was also a man of great patience; once, when a certain Lentulus spat in his face in mockery, he said no more to him nor was he moved, except to say: *O Lentulus, tell those who deny you have a mouth that they are mistaken.*

<margin>Y</margin> ¶ Diogenes performed many notable gestures and wrote many moral sayings, as can be seen in Laertius, so much so that Alexander the Macedonian often said that if he were not Alexander, he would have desired to be Diogenes. Among his primary sayings: *the honeyed snare* <note>Likely referring to the trap of worldly pleasures</note>; *avarice is the citadel of all evils* <note>original: "cupiditatē arcē oium eē malorum"</note>. He also indicates that *the bad tongue is better than the one it slanders; for conscience overcomes whatever evil the tongue has fashioned.* And in his letter to Polyxides he says: *he who is good is commended through himself.* In the letter to Aragesilaus: *one thing at least is most certain in us: corruption follows generation.* In the same: *I admonish you not to be wise above what is human.* In the letter to Acratetes: *It is certainly least safe for you to linger where you do not find those like yourself.* In the letter to Metrodorus: *For him who hastens by a short path to happiness, the company of women is useful.* ¶ *All things are of the gods; the gods are masters of all things. But wise men are friends to the gods. All things are common among friends; therefore, all things belong to the wise.* In the letter to Timocrates: *Poverty is a detriment to no one, but malice is.* In the letter to the same: *You threaten me with the sting of the Spanish fly, that is, death; you do not understand that in this way you rather discourage me; for those who care for us exact the aid of evils and the deserved punishment. And from the living indeed simply, but from the dead tenfold.* In the letter to Amonimus: *Leave riches to those who wander from the right path. Therefore, when we do not meditate on death, a more troublesome end of life is to be expected; but where we have meditated on the best meditation, life is sweet and death is not at all troublesome, and the way is very easy.*

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>Z</margin> ¶ Diogenes died at a very old age, and in death he did not wish for his body to be buried. Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> then adds, saying that after Diogenes he saw coming him who, joyful in spirit and without any distress, saw his fields uncultivated and ruined, being burdened with other rewards of worthy knowledge, through which he believed the terms of such an exchange had been enviable for him. Wherefore he says:

<margin>A</margin> ¶ The worthy and excellent philosopher described by our poet in the preceding verses is Anaxagoras of Clazomene, son of one Hegesibulus (or perhaps Eubulus) and a disciple of Anaximenes, as Laertius writes. This man, then, being 

->And he who, happy, saw his fields ruined<-
->And deserted, burdened with other rewards,<-
->Believing he had made an enviable bargain.<-

exceedingly rich, especially in land, neglected everything: he gave himself to studies, distributing a very large part of his patrimony to his relatives. And Anaxagoras delighted in studies so much that he turned his thought to nothing else; for which reason, being one day sharply rebuked for having no care or diligence for his country, Anaxagoras extended his arm and, pointing to the sky, replied: "Indeed, I have a care for my country, and a great one indeed" <note>original: "Mihi vero patrie cura & quidem summa est"</note>. Valerius also writes in Book 8, Chapter 7, that having returned to his homeland of Clazomene after a long time, he was reproached because his possessions were uncultivated; wherefore he replied, extending his hand and showing them: "I would not be safe unless these had perished" <note>original: "Non ego saluus essem nisi iste perissent." Anaxagoras suggests that his material ruin was the price of his intellectual and spiritual salvation.</note>.

<margin>B</margin> ¶ Concerning his opinions, as is written in the first book of the *Physics*, Anaxagoras primarily imagined that the principles of natural things are infinite, and every effect is confused among the other principles and reasons, likewise confused: which then, in the process of generation, are separated by the operation of the Divine Intellect. Wherefore Eusebius, in the 13th book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, writes these words concerning Anaxagoras: "He is said to be the first of all the Greeks to assert that the Intellect <note>The concept of "Nous" or Mind as a cosmic organizing force.</note> is the cause of all things; he who, for the love of philosophizing, is said to have left his fields uncultivated. He first judged the efficient cause to be rational. For all things were confused together, he says, but the Intellect reduced them from confusion into orders. It is indeed worthy of admiration that, because he spoke thus, the Athenians nearly overwhelmed him with stones, because he did not worship the sun but the Creator of the sun" <note>original: "Primus autem grecorum omnium anaxagoram fertur intellectum rerum omnium causam asseruisse... non solem sed solis creatorem venerabatur."</note>.

<margin>C</margin> ¶ Anaxagoras said many notable sayings in response to others; for when he was primarily asked for what reason he was born, he replied: "For the sake of observing the heavens, and the sun, and the moon" <note>original: "Inspiciendi cœli causa & solis & lune"</note>. At another time, when he said he did not care to be buried in his homeland, and one of his friends was indignant at this, Anaxagoras said: "Be of good spirit, for the descent to the underworld is the same from everywhere" <note>original: "Bono animo esto idem. enim undique in infernum descensus est"</note>. When another told him how he was deprived of Athens, he replied: "Not I of them, but they of me" <note>original: "Non ego illis sed illi me"</note>. Finally, when the death of his only son was announced to him, he replied: "You announce nothing new or unexpected: for I knew that he, born of me, was mortal" <note>original: "Nil nouum aut iexpectatum nuntias: ego enim illum ex me natum sciebam esse mortalem."</note>.

<margin>D</margin> ¶ Anaxagoras died at the age of seventy-two years. But how he died, there is a great difference of opinion; for Hermippus says he died in prison in Athens because he said the sun, which the Athenians worshipped, was a fiery stone and not a god. Others say that for this saying Anaxagoras was acquitted through the work of Themistocles and departed from Athens and went to Lampsacus, where he died a natural death and was honorably buried by the people of Lampsacus in that place. Messer Francesco then narrates, saying that in that place with the other famous men, he saw the curious Dicaearchus. Wherefore he says:

<margin>E</margin> ¶ Dicaearchus—or Clitarchus <note>The commentator notes a potential confusion in the manuscript or tradition between Dicaearchus (the philosopher/geographer) and Clitarchus (the historian of Alexander the Great).</note>—is no longer known to us except as a curious historian; but there is a mistake here, for Cicero writes of him

->There was the curious Dicaearchus.<-

in *On Famous Orators*, and for our purpose, these words: "Since it is granted to rhetoricians to lie in histories so that they may say something more passionately; for just as you now do regarding Coriolanus, so Clitarchus and so Stratocles invented things about Themistocles" <note>original: "Quoniam quidem concessum est rethoribus ementiri in hystoriis... clytarci probatur ingenium fides infamatur"</note>. And Quintilian in the tenth book of the *Institution of the Orator* says: "The talent of Clitarchus is approved, but his trustworthiness is defamed." There are nonetheless some <note>The OCR "bibi" is likely a typo for "viri" (men) or "libri" (books).</note> who say not Clitarchus but Dicaearchus, of whom Tully <note>Cicero</note> says in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: "Let us indeed pass over Dicaearchus with Aristoxenus, his contemporary, and with his disciple, truly learned men, one of whom <note>Aristoxenus, who believed the soul was merely a harmony of the body.</note> seems never to have felt grief because he did not perceive himself to have a soul; the other is delighted by his own..."
