# THE TRIUMPH OF TIME

<margin>P</margin>
By treating the science and the method of knowing, we see how dialectic <term>dialectic: the formal art of logical argument and investigation</term> is necessary for the acquisition of other sciences. To this purpose, Albertus Magnus <note>Albert the Great, a prominent 13th-century theologian and scientist</note> agrees in the first book of *On the Soul*, where he calls dialectic the instrument of all other sciences. Thus, Al-Farabi <note>A 10th-century Islamic philosopher known in the West as Alpharabius</note>, defining it, says: "Logic is the language of the sciences" <note>original: "Logica est lingua scientiarum"</note>. This definition agrees with Hali Abbate <note>Ali ibn Abbas al-Majusi, a famous Persian physician</note> when he says of logic: "Logic is the scales of words or a useful tool for the arts" <note>original: "Logica est verborum libra o i vtilis arti"</note>.

<margin>Q</margin>
¶ Nor does Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle</note> deviate from this opinion in his commentary on the *Categories* where, defining logic, he says: "Logic is the organic part of all philosophy, defending us from the aforementioned evils and from falsehoods in speculative matters" <note>original: "Logica est pars organica totius philosophiæ defendẽs nos a malis predictis & a falsis in speculatiuis"</note>. Through these definitions, everything is made clear: that one should not be called a "good scientist" merely for the knowledge of logic. And because Averroes <note>The 12th-century Cordoban philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle</note>, in the first book of the *Physics*, notes that dialectic is the art of disputing, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> fittingly says that logicians are clear-minded not for their knowledge, but only for contending and disputing. But if someone should say that Aristotle, in the first book of the *Topics*, affirms dialectic to be the "science of sciences and art of arts," I say that statement is more an expression of common practice than his own true opinion; or rather, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> understands the causal predication through identity—that is, dialectic is the way or principle of the sciences and the arts. This was, therefore, a very large crowd of dialecticians, among whom the first was Par-

<margin>R</margin>
menides, a disciple of Xenophanes and the author and inventor of this worthy knowledge. He, fleeing all human company, lived on the cliffs of Mount Caucasus, where it is said he discovered logic. Or truly, the first was Clitomachus of Chalcedon, to whom this invention is attributed by other writers. ¶ These authors were followed by later dialecticians: namely Alexinus, Al-Farabi, Simplicius, Al-Ghazali, Porphyry, William of Heytesbury <note>Hentisber</note>, Ralph Strode <note>Strodo</note>, and John Went <note>venistore</note>, Albert the German, Richard Ferabrich <note>Ferrabric</note>, and Richard Swineshead <note>Sumpfret</note>, Peter of Spain, and the subtle Peter of Mantua;

<margin>S</margin>
Ockham, Walter Burley, and the excellent moderns Paolo della Pergola and Paul of Venice. ¶ But certainly, none of these juniors can be counted as equal to their fellow disciple and most illustrious teacher, Alessandro of Siena <note>Alessandro Sermoneta, a major 15th-century Italian logician</note>. How great his subtlety and sharpness of wit, his dexterity of speech, and his happiness of invention is clearly understood in the marvelous and sublime compendium of his exposition on the *Consequences* of Ralph Strode and William of Heytesbury; it was dedicated to us through his unspeakable humanity and benevolence. Nor does he claim less praise in the natural and medicinal doctrines, in which—explaining every doubt, refuting every falsehood, and demonstrating every number most elegantly—he has written many works. His disciple has followed in his footsteps so closely that in disputing, reading, or writing, he appears no different from the teacher except in his body and outward appearance. Master Francesco then continues, saying that after this group he saw Carneades, so elegant and dexterous in his speech and so diligent and alert in his studies, that when he spoke, one could hardly discern what was true or what was false, so quick was he in explaining words. Wherefore, living a long time, he placed his care, the wide vein of his talent, and his diligence into reconciling the opposing arts which "literary fury" leads to war. Nevertheless, he could not do it; for just as the arts grew, so grew envy, which—together with knowledge—scattered its poisons into hearts already swollen with pride. Wherefore he says:

<margin>T Carneades, as Diogenes Laertius writes, was a Cyrenean, the son of one named Philocomus. His doctrine is commemorated by Tully (Cicero) in the fourth of the *Tusculan Disputations* when he relates that Carneades affirmed that no pain could fall upon a wise man. But his speed of understanding and his versatile wit are fittingly described by Eusebius in the 13th book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, citing Numenius in these appropriate words: "Carneades," he says, "renewed the custom of Arcesilaus by contradicting everyone, and now here, and now there, now affirming, now denying, he distracted everyone with the volatility of his oration; and having found a subject..." <note>original: "Carneades inquit morem Archesilai renouauit omnibus cõtradicens & huc: atq̃ illuc nunc affirmando: nunc negãdo volubilitate orationis omnis distrahens: cumq̃ rem nactus"</note></margin>

<margin>V</margin>

From there, a great controversy having arisen at that time against the various philosophical sects, Carneades strove to bring them to harmony; but his successors afterward—more for the sake of the honor of their name than for the defense of the truth—still persisted in those dissensions, indicating it to be

<margin>X</margin>

<margin>Y</margin>
¶ Just as Aristotle writes in the first book of *On the Soul* and Cicero confirms, the first among all the philosophers to affirm the soul was immortal was Pherecydes of Syria <note>Usually referred to as Pherecydes of Syros</note>, who was the son of a man named Badone. Nor was Pherecydes only the author of this position—by which man is raised in the hope of a future life—but he was also the first who wrote on the nature of the gods, as Laertius shows. And he had, besides this, such clear knowledge of the future that seeing a ship at sea he immediately predicted it would perish, and so it happened; and likewise, tasting the water of a spring, he predicted that three days hence a very great earthquake would follow.

<margin>Z</margin>
Against this famous opinion, then, in the time of Epicurus, he armed himself and fought many times, striving to prove our soul dies together with the body. ¶ Epicurus was an Athenian, son of Neocles and Chaerestrate his wife; he imagined the soul to be a mixture of fire, air, and spirit—as Macrobius writes in *The Dream of Scipio*. Because of this materiality, he concluded it was mortal and corruptible; and also because he held the opinion that God is idle and does not care for worldly things. For this reason, he attributed all power to the celestial spheres, and affirmed that only material things could be produced from them, which in the end must necessarily be corrupted. Epicurus moved to affirm this with many arguments, which we have cited at another time in our exposition of Cicero's *Paradoxes*.

<margin>✤</margin>
¶ Epicurus said the supreme good <term>supreme good: the ultimate goal or "summum bonum" of human life</term> was the pleasure of the mind according to Lactantius, and of the body according to Aristotle in the *Ethics* and Cicero in the first book of *On Ends* and in the *Paradoxes*. He viewed pleasure in general as the cause of the inner man according to Augustine in the 19th book of *The City of God*, who seems to consider this view vile compared to other virtues, as it commands each virtue to work only for the sake of pleasure. We, nonetheless, believe that neither of these was the true opinion of Epicurus, but that he had a more refined concept, which we explained elsewhere. We will narrate it, God granting, in the exposition of the sonnets, where we will show Epicurus to have been a very good man and very temperate, as Jerome writes in *On Illustrious Men*, Galen in the third book of *On Regimen*, and Cicero in the second book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, where he says:
> Epicurus comes, a man not at all bad: or rather a most excellent man who reminds us how much he understands. <note>original: "Venit Epicurus homo minime malus: vel potius uir optimus im monet quantū intelligat"</note>
This same thing is confirmed by Laertius in the *Life of Epicurus*, responding to those who speak dishonestly of Epicurus; and I hope it is a just thing to save and not blame his sayings, especially when they are not properly considered. Epicurus affirms, as Eusebius writes in the 14th book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, that the gods have the form of men—a thing which is only comprehensible by reason to our intellect. Whence Eusebius says:
> Epicurus says the gods have the form of men; whom they perceive not by sense on account of the thinness of their nature, but by reason. <note>original: "Epicurus deos hōium formā habere: quīs nō sensu ꝓpter tenuitatē naturæ sed rōne ꝓcipiant."</note>

<margin>B</margin>
¶ Lastly, as for the na- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; "na-" likely begins "natura" (nature)</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Epicurus’s reputation. The previous page concluded with a transition to Epicurus after the account of Carneades, examining his philosophical errors regarding the soul.</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF FAME

In understanding the diverse points of view, it should be noted that the aforementioned proposition is a matter so famous to his light that it can be explained in two ways. One is that if he had held the soul to be immortal—as Pherecydes did—it would have been a thing very famous and worthy for his light and glory. The other is that, having described how things are corrupted and having defined pleasure as the highest good, and this opinion having been rejected by everyone, Epicurus became both famous and notorious for it. Therefore, for the present, we will refer to Epicurus no further, but we will save ourselves for the exposition of that sonnet: *Gluttony, sleep, and idle pillows* <note>original: "La gola il fomno & le ociofe piumae"; this is the opening line of Petrarch's Sonnet 7, used here to critique Epicurean indulgence</note> where we will strive to demonstrate every foundation and reason of Epicurus for his well-being. # CHAPTER FOUR

### CHAPTER FOUR

> Then with a great warp-beam, and with a wondrous spindle,
> I saw a subtle web: it was Chrysippus.

<margin>I</margin>
**Chrysippus of Tarsus** <note>Though born in Soli, he is often associated with Tarsus; he was the third head of the Stoic school and its most prolific systematizer</note> was the son of one Apollonius and a disciple of Zeno the Stoic, or rather of Cleanthes. As Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, biographer of the Greek philosophers</note> writes, he was most excellent in the faculty of oratory, perfect in philosophy, and sublime in the discipline of dialectic <note>the art of logical argumentation</note>, so much so that if the gods themselves used logic, they would use none other than that of Chrysippus. Chrysippus therefore wrote a great multitude of books; as Laertius shows, among which—having lived to the age of 80 years—he composed one for which a very long life is necessary to understand. As Valerius Maximus writes in his eighth book and seventh chapter, this was the *Book of Fate*. Wanting to recount the opinion of Chrysippus, he says it was expressed thus by Lucilius: <note>referring to the debates on fate found in the works of Cicero and others</note> what fate is, and that it is not the necessity of the arrival of future things, wanting to be a middle ground between two ancient opinions. Of these, one said there was no necessity for the future. The other posited that every thing came about by necessity. To demonstrate his opinion, Chrysippus made two foundations: one was that every stated proposition is by necessity either true or false. The other foundation was that among efficient causes <note>the agents that bring something about</note>, some were principal and powerful, and some others were merely "disposing" <note>proximate or contributory</note>. Wherefore, by the first foundation, he concluded that there is fate because, in saying "tomorrow the sun will be bright," today this proposition is by necessity true or false, because it is necessary that such an effect proceeds or does not proceed from a powerful efficient cause. But in saying "tomorrow Caesar will go to the plaza," this proposition is today true or false, but *contingently* <note>depending on chance or choice</note>; because for such an effect, efficient causes that are not principal concur, but rather urging or merely disposing causes.

<margin>L</margin>
Chrysippus therefore attributed "being fatal" <note>destined</note> to the statement itself, and gave "contingency" to the concurrence of disposing causes. He also brought forth the example of the **Cylinder**: which, being first moved by its cause, only had its movement [from outside], but not its "rollability" <note>its capacity to keep rolling</note>, because that depends only on the [shape of the] internal cause. Truly this is a subtle web in which the dialecticians entangle themselves in the second [book] of *On Interpretation* <note>Aristotle’s *De Interpretatione*</note>, the naturalists in the second of the *Physics*, and the moralists, jurists, canon lawyers, theologians, and metaphysicians, and whatever other sect of philosophers, provided they consider the providence of God in the way that Chrysippus himself involved others in such matter. Whence Tully <note>Cicero</note> rightly says in his book *On Fate* these appropriate words:
> But to me at least, there have been two opinions of the ancient philosophers: one of those who thought all things happened by fate, so that this fate brought necessity, in which opinion Democritus, Heraclitus, Empedocles, and Aristides were. The other of those for whom the voluntary movements of the mind seemed to be without any fate. Chrysippus, like an honorary arbiter, is said to have wanted a middle path. But he applies himself to those who want the mind freed from the motions of necessity rather than [to the others]; while he uses his own words, he slips into such difficulties that he confirms the necessity of fate against his will. <note>original Latin: "At mihi quidem fuerunt duae sententiae veterum philosophorum..."</note>

<margin>M</margin>
It was therefore Chrysippus the Stoic to whom those worthy opinions are attributed which Tully disputes in the *Paradoxes* <note>Cicero's *Stoic Paradoxes*</note>; he died at the age of 83 years, leaving behind a singular fame and reputation. Afterward, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> narrates, saying that he saw the father of the Stoics raised on high: that is, Zeno, who, to make his meaning clear, showed the open palm and the clenched and closed fist. Wherefore he says:

<margin>N</margin>
> Of the Stoics the father, raised on high,
> To make his view clear, I saw Zeno
> Show the open palm, and the closed fist.

**Zeno of Citium in Cyprus**, son of one Mnaseas <note>OCR reads "musaico" or "demeo," likely corruptions of Mnaseas</note>, a distinguished philosopher and disciple of Crates, was the father and author of the Stoic sect as Laertius writes. He was of such veneration among the Athenians that they crowned him with a golden crown and deposited the keys of their city with him, as the same Laertius testifies. Zeno, therefore, regarding our purpose—as Cicero recites in *On the Orator* to Brutus—wanting to show the difference between dialectic and rhetoric, demonstrated rhetoric by figuring the open palm of the hand, and figured dialectic by clenching the fist. Whence Tully says: Zeno used to demonstrate with his hand what interest there was between the faculty of dialectic and rhetoric. For when he made a fist with compressed fingers, he said dialectic was of that sort. But when he had spread them and dilated his hand, he said eloquence was similar to that palm. <note>original Latin: "Zenoque manu demonstrare solebat quid inter dialecticam & rhetoricam facultatem interesset..."</note> Likewise Zeno was the first of the Stoics who, against the ancient custom of philosophers, described in papers and reduced to doctrine the reasons

# TRIUMPH OF FAME

<margin>O</margin> From the foundations of the Stoic position: where wandering opinion—pulled through many and diverse viewpoints—is drawn toward the truth: that is, to always act with virtue and reason according to the rigor of the Stoic maxim: *that is, a small fault is as a great one* <note>original: "parva quidem est ut magna culpa"; a core Stoic belief that all sins or errors are fundamentally equal in their deviation from reason</note>. Certainly, no other maxim is more fruitful for living well, as Cicero testifies in his *Paradoxes*. And this is said according to the texts that describe his "gentle web woven on paper," which draws wandering opinion to the truth. And then he turned his eyes elsewhere. Zeno wrote several notable sayings, among which these two were most excellent: *let the speech which you alone have heard be buried with you* <note>original: "sepultus sit apud te sermo quem tu solus audieris"; an exhortation to keep secrets and maintain silence</note> and *recognize that a wicked man speaking sweetly is your snare* <note>original: "malum hominem blande loquentem agnosce tuum laqueum esse"</note>. Finally, as Seneca writes in his book *On Tranquillity of Mind*:

<margin>P</margin> When it was told to Zeno that all his wealth had been submerged in the sea, he replied: *Fortune commands me to practice philosophy with less baggage* <note>original: "Iubet me fortuna expeditius philosophari"; a famous example of Stoic indifference to material loss</note>. ¶ Zeno died at the age of one hundred and seven; he was buried with great glory and honor. Lastly, it should be known that another meaning—perhaps even more fitting—could be attributed to the end of this triumph and chapter according to the present textual writing: that the poet concluded with the example of Cleanthes after his master Zeno. He says that finally he saw Cleanthes: who, to fix his beautiful intention, arranged and described in his "gentle web" wandering opinion drawn through many and diverse viewpoints toward the truth: that is, to always act with virtue and

<margin>Q</margin> reason through the rigor of the Stoic maxim: ending and leaving off speaking of them further. Wherefore he says:

<margin>¶ Cleanthes, son of Phanias, was from the city of Assos, located in the region of Asia not far from Adramyttium. He was a worthy student and disciple of Zeno the Stoic, whom Cleanthes succeeded in his school after his death, which Zeno left to Chrysippus, his disciple</margin>

->Cleanthes wove his gentle web<-

As Strabo <note>Ancient Greek geographer and historian</note> narrates, Cleanthes was quite poor in means. He went to Athens with only four drachmas of money, devoting himself to philosophy under his teacher Zeno. He studied with great hardship due to his poverty, so much so that it was necessary for him at times to work for hire; in the nighttime, he would draw water from wells to water others' gardens to sustain his life and to be able to hear his master's lessons during the day. For this reason, he was called **Phreandorce**: the well-drawer <note>term: Phreandorce; likely a corruption of the Greek 'Phreantlos', meaning one who draws water from a well</note>.

<margin>R</margin> ¶ Once, being brought to judgment to give an account of how he lived so robustly and in such good condition while being so poor, Cleanthes brought as witnesses the gardener who paid him for the water he used to irrigate his garden, and a woman for whom he used to bolt or sift flour. Whereupon he was acquitted. For this reason, the citizens wanted to give him ten minae <note>a unit of currency</note>, though Zeno would not allow him to accept them. And some say that Antigonus, who was his listener, gave him three thousand minae. Once, when asked why he drew water from wells, he replied that he did it not only to draw water, but why should he not also dig the earth and water it for the love of philosophy? And Zeno, his teacher, exhorted him to such exercise, knowing that he acquired his living through his own labor. And sometimes Zeno would have him bring his money into the midst of his friends and family, saying that Cleanthes could nourish another if he wished—unlike those who truly have the means to nourish themselves but seek from others the things necessary for their use of life. In truth, these things cause more remorse in those who practice philosophy. For this reason, Cleanthes was called the second Hercules. He was very studious, although he was of a heavy and slow intellect; but he overcame that slowness with his great study and diligence. He wrote many beautiful and worthy works, as Laertius narrates. Wherefore Cicero names him several times in his works, and Petrarch also in his Latin works. And Valerius Maximus, speaking of him, says these worthy words: *For with twofold labor you occupied the span of a single century, making it uncertain whether you were more praiseworthy as a student or a teacher* <note>original: "Duplici enim labore unius seculi spatium occupasti incertum reddendo discipulus ne an preceptor esses laudabilior"</note>.

<margin>S</margin> ¶ He lived ninety-nine years, having been a listener to Zeno for fifteen or seventeen years, and teaching his own disciples all the while. He died in this manner: one of his gums having become infected, the doctors ordered him to go two days without eating anything. He did so and recovered, but wanting to continue the diet and abstinence against the will of the doctors, he passed away—though some say he brought about his own death for the love of the next life. In conclusion, one can very clearly see how great our poet’s intelligence was in having enumerated so many men and demonstrated a full understanding of each of them. Having touched upon every philosophical sect, every kind of study, and every part of philosophy in recounting these worthy and excellent...

->**CHAPTER FOUR**<-

<meta>catchword: go.</meta>

Most excellent learned men: the hour is now appropriate to proceed no further with them, but to turn our eyes elsewhere to speculate and see how all the preceding dispositions are obscured by Time. Thus, it is truly determined that something other than fame must be the true object of our will.

# EXPLANATION OF THE TRIUMPH OF TIME.

<margin>X</margin>
**L**et us observe that the human species contains two natures within itself, as not only evident reason shows and irrefutable authorities agree, but experience—the mistress of all things—persuades us openly and without any doubt. By this experience, we understand one of these natures to be immortal and celestial, and the other to be fragile and corruptible in a short time. Nevertheless, while they live together, each of these is overcome by a weak nature; however, because human diligence can fall ill, it has come to the aid of both by finding medicine. Therefore, as the constitution changes, transforms, and the continuity dissolves—from which illnesses result in us—human ingenuity has provided a remedy for each of these conditions. But when our soul, departing from its health, becomes morbid and infirm, its sickness is not said to be caused by the destruction of the aforementioned natures, but by the stain of vice and the perversion of the upright will. Therefore, no physical power, herbal beverage <note>original: "berberno"; likely referring to medicinal potions or syrups</note>, or dietary observations <note>original: "obseruantie di dieterno"; following a prescribed medical diet</note> can restore it to health; only the practice of virtue, delight in it, and perseverance within it can lead the soul to true convalescence. 

¶ For this reason, the dark diligence of men is appropriately criticized; for, by attending only to the well-being of the body, they neglect the soul, where all our intention and diligence ought to reside. Because of this, our Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch), the author of the poem being commented upon</note>, wishing in the present triumph to recall us to the proper care, demonstrates herein the fifth state of the soul: its departure from the body with which it was united in the world. From this, we can understand that in nothing pertaining to worldly states can the health of the soul consist. Therefore, it is great prudence to direct our will and intellect toward that glory and circumspect fame which depends upon itself and not upon other men. The poet, having in the preceding triumph demonstrated clearly enough that through the death of the body men live more worthily with glory by means of fame among the people of the world, does this so that no one may be persuaded that fame is the ultimate end to be desired by the human soul. Therefore, in the present triumph and chapter, he describes how such fame and worldly glory—like all other earthly things contained and revolved by the heavens—must fail through the length of time. 

¶ And therefore, he intends, through the universal argument and subject of this triumph, to treat the vanity of fame as the fifth state of the soul, which is acquired by men through virtuous operations extending to worldly objects. Because this effect is interrupted by the daily resolution of time, the poet strives to demonstrate such a wicked succession and ebb that it truly seems that the beginning and the end of each thing occur almost together. Wishing, then, to narrate this true and indubitable judgment, and to wake us from the lazy sleep in which we slumber for earthly delights, he introduces—with graceful poetic invention—the Sun, who laments and is angry within himself that the fame of men is so long-lasting. Thus, he becomes enraged against that fame and prepares for war. He says, then, that the Sun, with his beloved and preceding Aurora <note>The goddess of the dawn</note> having left her golden inn, girt with his lovely and shining rays so quickly and with such velocity that you would have said he had only just been placed and raised a little above the hemisphere—just as is the custom of wise and prudent men—looked around himself and said to himself:

->“What are you doing now? What are you thinking? Certainly, it behooves you to have more<-
->care for yourself; for if one has lived famous and glorious up-<-
->on the earth and, by dying, does not depart from his fame,<-
->what then will become of the universal law that<-
->heaven established and fixed among us? Truly,<-
->it is necessary to be...<-

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the "Triumph of Time," the fourth section of Petrarch’s poem. In the previous pages, the poet described the "Triumph of Fame," where great men and women achieved a form of earthly immortality through their deeds. Now, the tone shifts as Time—represented by the Sun—becomes envious of human reputation and asserts the natural law that everything which begins must also end.</meta>

<page-num>159</page-num>

->**CHAPTER FOUR**<-

->**THE FOURTH TRIUMPH: TIME**<-

<margin>Y</margin> <margin>It was an ancient opinion, custom, and habit of excellent poets to always describe, under the shadowed veil of poetry, that which is doctrine and elegant morality. Our graceful and worthy poet Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> observes this here. It should be understood that not without reason does the poet introduce the sun proceeding in indignation against men, solely to show that human fame rebels against natural laws. Therefore Virgil, as we said above, writes that Fame was produced by the Earth, irritated by the wrath of the gods. Here one must consider that celestial bodies were reputed as gods by the ancient pagans, as one reads in Eusebius <note>A 4th-century historian and bishop</note> in the first book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, in the first book of the *Georgics*, in the first book of *The City of God* against Pelagius, and Cicero in the first book of *On the Nature of the Gods*, where he says these worthy words: "We have already declared that there are gods, whose remarkable power and illustrious face we see: the Sun and the Moon and the wandering stars." <note>original: "Declarauimus iam deos esse: quorū i fignem vim e illustrem faciē videmus Solē e Lunam vagas stellas"</note> This is confirmed by Deuteronomy 17 when it says, speaking in the person of God angry against the Jews: "They go and serve foreign gods and adore the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which I did not command." <note>original: "vēvadant e seruiant dijs alienis vt adorēt solē e lunam: e oēm militiā cæli que non pcepiti"</note> Furthermore, because their influence over our bodies is called "wrath" by the poets, they induce great alteration and finally death; and therefore men—nicknamed "earth"—raised up Fame as if in vengeance for their assigned death. Wherefore the poet describes the gods (signified by the celestial bodies) as operating no less against fame than they previously did against the life of man.</margin>

**I**n the golden dwelling, 
with the Dawn before him,
the Sun emerged so quickly, 
girt with rays,
that you would have said 
he had only just lain down.
Having risen a little, 
as wise men do,
he looked around him 
and said to himself:
"What are you thinking now within me? 
What further care do I have?
Behold: if a famous man 
lives on earth,
and does not depart 
through death because of his fame,
what will become of the law 
that heaven fixed?"

<margin>Z</margin> <margin>And because the sun among all the stars is the best known and of the greatest power—wherefore the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>, by the authority of Homer at the end of the second book *On the Soul* (according to the division of books made by Averroes) and at the beginning of the third (according to the division of Egidius <note>Giles of Rome, a 13th-century philosopher</note>), calls him "the father of men and of gods"—for this reason Master Francesco introduces the sun as the one most indignant at this mortal fame. Secondly, it is to be noted, as written in the first book *On the Heavens*, that by natural necessity whatever thing has a beginning must inevitably have an end at some time. Therefore, based on this foundation, one clearly sees the sun being reasonably angry against fame: for if men lived on account of it, glory would endure and this necessity of an end would be removed. Man would have had a beginning without having an end if he remained alive through fame; thus the law which heaven fixed and established would be entirely in vain. That law states that whatever receives variation from heaven could in no way be eternal. Whence Solomon in Ecclesiastes 3 concludes that nothing under the sun can be perpetual. And therefore our poet fittingly depicts the sun preparing to wage war against fame, using his celerity and quick rising with the Dawn before him. This celerity necessarily precedes the sun, as it is a whiteness born in the air like a splendor through the reflection of the solar rays in the denser parts of the sky.</margin>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>Finally, it is to be understood that Master Francesco describes the sun after its birth, and having risen somewhat above the hemisphere, conducting this reasoning with himself to demonstrate when it is that the sun has the most power over us as it moves: and this is the closer it approaches the line of the mid-heaven <note>the meridian</note>. Wherefore neither in its setting, nor in the night, nor in its rising does it have as much power as from the third to the ninth hour <note>the canonical hours of Terce and None, roughly 9 a.m. to 3 p.m.</note>. The poet also describes the sun first lamenting the overthrow of the universal law of heaven rather than for himself or his own injury, as he does in the following verses, to show how much more one should be moved by the observance of public honor and common things than by private and personal ones. Whence he deservedly concludes that if one does not depart through death [his fame...]</margin>

The accompanying commentary explains the philosophical and biblical foundations for why all earthly things must eventually perish.</summary>

-># THE TRIUMPH OF TIME <-

<margin>B</margin>
...his fame acquires on earth. What then will become of the law fixed and confirmed by heaven? It would be as if it were nothing. Finally, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> says that the sun has departed so swiftly from his **golden dwelling** <note>original: "albergo aureo"</note>; this is because at the rising and setting of the sun, due to the terrestrial vapors that sit between the sun and our eyes, it appears that the horizon is a **saffron color** <note>croceo; a reddish-yellow hue</note>, as we shall discuss more broadly a little further below. There are, nonetheless, some texts which say "the dwelling of the Bull" <note>original: "tauro albergo," referring to the zodiac sign Taurus</note> with the dawn before it; I believe these are corrupted, because as the sun circles the heavens, it remains steady in the sign of Taurus for a period of thirty days, according to its number of thirty degrees. Therefore, it is not necessary for it to "exit" its Taurine dwelling simply to rise above the hemisphere. Having thus described the sun, the poet shows it to be so moved by the universal statute of heaven that it follows by grieving for itself particularly, saying that if the fame of mortal men grows by dying—in which death it ought to be extinguished—then the sun certainly sees its own glorious excellences being brought to an end in a short time, a thing for which it grieves and feels resentment. Thus, what greater injury can it expect, or what worse can happen to it? Or what does the sun possess in heaven more than a man on earth? To the eternal Creator, the sun would ask as a most singular grace to be equal to such a man. Whence he says:

> And if mortal fame grows by dying,
>   Which should have been extinguished shortly; I see
>   Our excellences at their end; for which I grieve.
> What more is expected? Or what could be worse?
>   What more have I in heaven than a man on earth,
>   To whom, by grace, I ask to be equal?

<margin>C</margin>
The sun grieves and laments with good reason when—even though it is the proper nature of all other things upon the earth to pass away—the fame of men does not fail. Regarding this understanding, one must know that although the sun is perpetual in the future and incorruptible by nature, it is nonetheless an inanimate body, distinct in essence from the elements, as is proven in the first book of *On the Heavens and the World* <note>Aristotle’s "De Caelo," a foundational text for medieval science</note>. Therefore, the **rational soul** <note>term: "anima ragionevole" — the highest part of the human soul according to medieval philosophy, capable of intellect and reason</note> of a man, through its participation in that reason, is much more perfect than the solar body, if only man were not subjected to mortality and the finite measure of time. Consequently, if he were to become immortal and incorruptible through fame, he would undoubtedly exceed the excellence of the sun. For this reason, it seems the sun rightly grieves in this regard, and deservedly strives to extinguish that fame simply to avoid losing its own dignity. Secondly, it should be understood that fame, by right, ought to be extinguished upon a man's death. Since the "final cause" <note>the purpose for which something exists</note> has ceased, it is likely that all effects of the other causes ordained toward it should also cease, as is written in the second book of the *Physics*, the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*, and by the legal experts in the **Law "Oratio" in the Digest regarding betrothals** <note>original: "l. oratio. ff. de spōsali"; a reference to the Corpus Iuris Civilis</note>. Since virtue or its operation is the cause of glory and fame, into which it is ultimately resolved, then when those actions and their use cease through the death of the man, fame consequently ought to cease as well. Therefore, the sun appropriately affirms that its own excellences would come to an end if, without ever failing, a man's fame were to grow upon his death.

<margin>D</margin>
Finally, it must be considered that with a just and reasonable desire, the sun would wish to be equal to a famous man, and that nothing would have more than he if he remained eternal through fame. For in the sun, five qualities are considered: first, it is eternal; second, noble; third, bright; fourth, generative; and fifth and finally, many praises are attributed to it by men. In these things, man would either equal or exceed the sun. Regarding everlasting duration, man would be equal to the sun both because of the soul (which he contains within himself and is immortal by nature) and also because of fame after death. But in terms of the mobility of a great space, man would exceed the sun: this refers to human souls—as is the universal conclusion of theologians—and not only the souls, but the **glorified bodies** <note>term: "corpi glorificati" — the perfected, resurrected bodies of the blessed, which were believed to possess supernatural qualities like extreme speed and brightness</note> which are most agile. Thus, the velocity of the sun is not so great that the speed of the soul and the glorified body is not much greater. Furthermore, the sun is mobile only in a circle, as is proven in the second book of *On the Heavens*; yet the soul surpasses it, and not only the soul, but the glorified body and even the mortal body, by moving in every different direction of site and disposition. Man also surpasses it in brightness, because the light of a virtuous soul separated from the body is much...

<meta>catchword: ...is much [more]</meta>

and much greater and more intense than that of the sun: according to what we said above regarding the opinion of theologians in the *Triumph of Death*. In the fourth place, the soul equals it—indeed, by far surpasses it—concerning the production of effects: for all those things which the sun produces are material and perishable in a short space of time; but the soul produces special effects of much greater perfection and dignity, such as intellection and love, joy, possession, and fruition. <margin>E</margin> ¶ Lastly, if the fame of man were to endure forever, it would greatly exceed the sun even in praise and honor; for if this eternal fame remained in the world, the sun would possess nothing more in heaven than men would achieve upon the earth. By these artful verses of the poet, we can clearly understand him to be speaking of the state of the soul compared to the existence of men, which is much inferior, just as we said at the beginning. Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> then adds the angry words of the sun regarding its revolving and swift movement, saying that it said within itself: "Ah, weary me! With how much study and diligence do I feed, groom, adorn, and whip four horses in the great ocean, which are most swift in their course; and nevertheless, it does not seem that I can tame or extinguish the fame of a single mortal man. Truly, this is a most grave injury, fit to provoke wrath and not a joke, and for this vanity to happen to me even if I were in heaven not only the first planet, but the second or third." Wherefore he says:

->Four horses with how much care I groom,<-
->I feed in the ocean, and spur, and whip;<-
->And yet the fame of a mortal I do not tame.<-
->An injury for anger, and not for joking,<-
->To have this happen to me: even if I were in heaven<-
->Not, I say, the first; but the second or third.<-

<margin>F</margin> ¶ Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known that the poet does not depart from the opinion of the natural philosophers in describing four horses for the sun's chariot; for they distinguished its course over our hemisphere into four parts. The first is its birth into appearance. The second is its elevation. The third is its declining and rising <note>likely referring to the arc of the afternoon</note>. The fifth <note>This is likely a scribal error for "fourth"</note> and last is its setting and its ascent. Following this opinion, Ovid in the third <note>The description actually appears in Book 2 of the Metamorphoses</note> book of the *Metamorphoses*, having described the palace of the sun and its habit and worthy ornament, <margin>G</margin> ¶ then describes the horses that guide it and names them according to the aforementioned opinion, saying: *Meanwhile the swift horses of the sun, Pyroeis, Eous, and Aethon, and the fourth, Phlegon, fill the air with flaming neighs and strike the barriers with their hooves.* <note>original: "Interea volucres pyrous eous & ethon solis equi: quartusq; phlegon binnitibus auras flammigeris implent: pedibusq; repagula pulsant."</note> Where **Pyrous** is interpreted as "red" and at its birth; which occurs because the sun appears red when it begins to rise, because during the night vapors have multiplied. Since these are dense and thick above the horizons, they cause the sun's rays to reflect. From the clarity of the rays and the opacity of the vapors, the ruddy color results, which is a middle color between extremes, closer to darkness than to light. The second, **Eous**, is interpreted as "splendid"; the reason is that since the sun has risen above the hemisphere, by its power and its heat it has dissolved the vapors in the air; thus no obstacle remains by which the sun's rays are altered from their light and natural splendor. Therefore, at that hour, the sun is more lucid and shining than at any other. <margin>H</margin> The third, **Ethon**, is interpreted as "burning," and the reason is that since the sun has already reached the height of heaven and is beginning to decline, it has made a longer stay above the hemisphere while having its greatest power; and therefore, in this hour, the air is more heated than at any other hour of the day. ¶ And for this reason, according to the opinion of Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and physician (c. 980–1037)</note> in the first [part] of the first [book], he responds to the problem of why there is much greater heat in July and August than in May and June, even though in the former time the sun is in a more direct aspect and more elevated above our hemisphere. The fourth and last, **Phlegon**, is interpreted as "loving the earth"; the reason is that as the sun declines toward the setting, it descends toward the earth in a view as eager as if it loved it. And therefore, painters, when depicting the horses of the sun, paint the first red, the second white, the third saffron-colored <note>term: croceo; a deep yellow-orange</note>, and the fourth dark. <margin>I</margin> ¶ There are, concerning these verses, some others who say that the four horses are not the four hours of the day, but the four seasons of the year: namely Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter; which opinion is tolerable. Fulgentius <note>A late antique mythographer</note>, nonetheless, says we [consider] the horses of the sun...

of the sun by other names, insofar as the meaning allows: namely Erythraeus, Actaeon, Lampas, and Philogeus. <note>These are the four horses of the Sun's chariot in classical mythology, representing different qualities of sunlight.</note> Secondly, it is to be understood that the poet describes the sun feeding, taming, and spurring these four horses in the ocean to demonstrate how the ocean sea surrounds the earth, at least from one perspective of its location. Thus, when the eye is on dry land and the ocean is all around—extending toward the east, the west, the south, and the north so far that the horizon is formed in the waters—it appears to our eyes that the sun rises from the ocean and sets in the ocean. And because it makes its course through the other <term>hemisphere</term> <note>Half of the celestial or terrestrial sphere</note> out of sight, some imagine the earth on the other side to be covered by water, according to the text of Genesis at the beginning. This text seems to suggest that at the creation, water covered the earth, and then by the drying of it, the earth appeared, saying: *God also said: let the waters that are under the heaven be gathered together into one place. And he adds: and let the dry land appear.* <note>original: "Dixit quoq; deus congregentur aquæ q̄ sub cælo sunt in vnum locū. Et sogguonge: & appareat arida." from Genesis 1:9.</note> And from these words, they take the argument to say that only this small part of the earth which we inhabit is uncovered by water; therefore, as the sun travels through the other hemisphere, it always seems to proceed through the ocean. Aristotle, nevertheless, in the first book of *On the Heavens*, does not seem to agree with this opinion. Rather, he imagines the <term>antipodes</term> <note>People or places on the opposite side of the earth.</note> according to the testimony of some who say they have already proceeded so far toward the antarctic pole that the other pole is raised to the height of a lance, as the <term>Conciliator</term> <note>Pietro d'Abano (c. 1257–1315), a famous philosopher and physician known for his work "Conciliator differentiarum philosophorum et medicorum."</note> testifies in his *Differences*.

<margin>R</margin>
Lastly, it should be noted, as we said at the beginning above, that the sun is said for several reasons to be the first planet of the heaven, and especially because it is defined by philosophers and astrologers that no other planet has any light or glow of its own, but only receives it from the sun, reflecting its rays as if from a denser part of the sky. Aristotle shows this in the second book of *On the Heavens* where, defining the star, he says: *Indeed, a star is a denser part of the heaven.* <note>original: "Sigdē. n. stella ē densior pars cæli."</note> And therefore Ovid, in the beginning of the second book of the *Metamorphoses*, considering this natural quality, describes the sun's royal chamber in such a form that it is supported by sublime columns. By these, we understand the "world-machine" to be supported by the discord of the four elements according to the opinion of Empedocles, over which the sun presides. For, as Aristotle writes in the first book of the *Meteorologica*, this inferior world must be governed by the power of the superior bodies, and especially by means of their light and their influence; wherefore, being the prince and leader of all celestial light, the sun is attributed the leadership of the world's governance.

<margin>L</margin>
Wherefore, in proof of this opinion, Cicero says in *The Dream of Scipio*: *Then the sun occupies nearly the middle region, the leader and prince and moderator of the other lights.* <note>original: "foeinde subterme- diam fere regionē sol obtinet dux & prīceps moderator luminū reliquorū."</note> And Macrobius, explaining this passage, writes these words: *He is the leader because he precedes all in the majesty of light; he is the prince because he stands out so much that, because he alone appears as such, he is called "Sol."* <note>original: "Dux ergo est qa oīs luminis maiestate precedit prīceps: ga ita eminet vt propterea quod talis solus appareat sol vocetur." The name "Sol" was historically and incorrectly linked to "Solus," meaning alone.</note> Also, the sun is the moderator and distinguisher of the hours. Wherefore they were described by poets as being his daughters, and assigned to the care and preparation of his chariot. Thus, if he is angry and speaks of receiving injury from the eternal fame of men, and that his excellence is being diminished, it is not without reason. The poet then continues and narrates the effect which he said the sun's wrath and anger should follow, saying that for the aforementioned reasons, it is necessary that all his zeal and will act against the fame of men; and that for his flight and swift race, he doubles his "vanes"—that is, his feathers—inasmuch as he bears envy toward men and no longer hides or conceals it. Among these men, it sometimes happens that one, after a thousand years, and another thousand, and another thousand, is much clearer and more famous than in life; and yet the sun, for all his perpetual labors, gains nothing more than he had at first. This is because he was already such and equal from the beginning, before the earth was either established or firm, rotating by night and revolving around it through the round path of his sphere, which is infinite. Wherefore he says:

<margin>M</margin>
For a clearer and more open understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known that our Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> in this place introduces the sun protesting that he bears envy toward men, and that his zeal descends against them, to express more clearly the effectiveness of his operation against the permanence and duration of men, following the example of the scripture:

> Now it is necessary that all my zeal be kindled,
> So that for my flight, anger doubles my wings.
> For I bear envy toward men, and I do not hide it:
> Of whom I see some after a thousand years,
> And thousands more, clearer than they were in life,
> While I gain nothing but perpetual labors.

->**Such I am; as I was before the earth**<-
->**Was established; rotating day and night**<-
->**Through the circular path which is infinite.**<-

In the Sacred Scripture, in the sixth chapter of Genesis, when expressing the gravity of the sin of men in the person of God, it says: *I repent that I have made man.* <note>original: "Penitet me fecisse homine," from Genesis 6:6.</note> And in Saint Mark, in the thirteenth chapter, the Savior says to the same purpose: *The Son of man indeed goes as it is written of him. But woe to that man by whom the Son of man shall be betrayed. It were better for him if that man had not been born.* <note>original: "Et filius quidem hominis vadit sicut scriptum est de eo. Ve autem homini illi per quem filius hominis tradetur. Bonum erat ei si natus non fuisset homo ille." from Mark 14:21 (though the text cites chapter 13).</note>

<margin>N</margin>
¶ Where it is manifest, nevertheless, that neither repentance nor privation can fall upon God; and that in being, no good can intervene <note>This refers to the philosophical idea that existence itself is a good, and "not being" cannot be "better."</note> as is approved and popularized by the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> and the Commentator <note>Averroes</note> at the end of the *Physics*, and by almost all the doctors of the Church. Secondly, it is to be understood that the Sun only gains more of its perpetual toils: for it acquires no more praise, nor more fame, nor more eternity than it had from the beginning when it was created by God on the fourth day, as is written at the beginning of Genesis. And the poet <note>Petrarch</note> calls the days of the sun "perpetual toils" because they are long-lasting, or rather according to the opinion of the Philosopher in the eighth book of the *Physics*, who demonstrates through natural foundations that the movement of the sun is eternal. But the sun remains as it was before the earth was established as the domicile of man. For although the earth was created on the first day by God, and the sun on the fourth, it was not however ordained and established for the use of man until after the sin of our first parents.

<margin>O</margin>
¶ And therefore, as seen in the process of Scripture at the beginning of Genesis, when God proposed man to all the things created on earth, He did not propose him to the earth itself, nor did He yet place him upon it. But He placed him in the Paradise of Delights, from which He later cast him out and settled him on the earth. And therefore Bruno, <note>Likely Bruno of Segni, a medieval exegete.</note> in his exposition of Genesis, says the earth is named from the use of "treading" <note>Connecting the word "terra" (earth) to the Latin "terere" (to rub or tread) or "calcaria" (treading/trampling).</note>—being rotated by all the oxen and also trampled by all the other animals. And in this way it is manifest: that the sun began first to encircle the earth before the earth was established and firm for the sustenance of man. And therefore Ovid, at the beginning of the *Metamorphoses*, expressing this sentiment, says when speaking of the time of confusion and chaos:
> *Wherever there was earth, there was also weight and air: Thus*
> *the earth was unstable, the water unnavigable: Lacking light, no form remained for the air.* <note>original: "Quaqu' erat & tellus illic & pondus & aer : Sic erat instabilis tellus : innabilis unda : Lucis egens aeri nulli sua forma manebat." from Ovid's Metamorphoses, Book I.</note>
Wherefore it can rightly be concluded that the sun moved before the earth was named "stable."

<margin>P</margin>
¶ Lastly, it should be noted that Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> says the sun rotates day and night through the circular road which is infinite. For the understanding of this, it must be known that the movement of the sun is most regulated and uniform: because it does not wander like the other planets through eccentric circles and epicycles, <term>ventrosifma</term> <note>This likely refers to a "bulging" or non-uniform path</note> but with all-encompassing uniformity. Therefore, it is necessary that its sphere and the path through which it proceeds be perfectly spherical and round. From which it follows that it is infinite, because in a circle (as the mathematicians write and is expressed in the first book of *On the Heavens*) no part is given as preceding and none as following. But each of these is both the beginning and the end. And therefore, to circular motion no distinct final term is given which would be the <term>rest</term> <note>original: "qeie" for "quiete"</note> of the body moved circularly. And for this reason, the circle is said to be an infinite distance: not because it contains an infinite quantity, but because of the privation of a positive boundary; which in a circular body is not found such that, being an end and boundary, it cannot also be the beginning of that same quantity. Therefore, not having this type of end within it, it remains "privatively infinite."

<margin>Q</margin>
¶ He then "redoubles his wings" <note>Petrarch uses the word "vanni," an archaic term for flight-feathers or wings.</note> in his course to demonstrate the great velocity of his continuous turning, almost bearing envy toward mortal men upon seeing that he cannot annihilate their fame, which makes them immortal and perpetual. The "vanni" are thus the secondary feathers in the wings of the eagle, almost called "knives" because with them eagles have great power in flight. Therefore he said it was necessary in his turning to fly and "redouble the wings"—that is, the feathers—to run more swiftly than he did before. Messer Francesco, having made this prelude in the preceding verses, continues describing the operation of his actions which he did after he finished speaking; saying that the sun, after these words, resumed its course with the greatest indignation, much faster and with greater celerity than a falcon moves when it descends furiously from the height of the air toward its prey. Indeed, much more so: to the point that it is not possible for thought to follow the flight, much less for the tongue or poetic style to explain it. For which reason, he looks upon it with the greatest fear. Wherefore he says:

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s "Triumph of Time," specifically exploring the terrifying speed of the Sun’s movement and how this realization diminishes the perceived value of human life. The catchword "Che assai" bridges to the next section of the commentary.</meta>

### THE TRIUMPH OF TIME

<margin>R</margin>
¶ Just how great the speed of the sun’s course is can be well understood through the comparison made by our Master Francesco <note>Messer Francesco refers to the poet Petrarch.</note>—not because that comparison is entirely true in every way, but certainly because it is very fitting. For, as Averroes says in the second book of *On the Soul*, we do not look for literal proof in examples, but for a clear illustration. And Aristotle says to this purpose in the first book of the *Prior Analytics*: *For we set forth examples not so that it should be thus, but so that those who learn may perceive.* <note>original: "Exēpla enim ponimus non ut ita sit sed ut sentiant qui adiscunt"</note> For this reason, the poet then adds, to explain the truth of this speed, that not only could the tongue not express it, but even thought cannot comprehend it. This is a most true sentiment, for one cannot imagine any certain speed so fast that an even swifter movement could not be infinitely possible.

->After he had said this, feeling disdain,<-
->He resumed his course much more swiftly<-
->Than a hawk flying from on high toward its prey.<-
->More, I say: no thought could ever<-
->Follow his flight, let alone tongue or pen;<-
->So that I gazed back at him with great fear.<-

<margin>S</margin>
¶ Master Francesco says quite rightly, then, that he regarded the Sun's course with fear. Every steady and disciplined intellect should consider it with dread, since that movement is the cause of the changing of all things. Furthermore, since the life of man is contained within finite time, and death is entirely hidden from the human intellect, one must fear such a rapid course, as it leads us to a state where our power to act is taken away—a place where justice is rigid and there is no merit of one's own to invoke mercy. The poet follows this by describing the effect that seeing this solar speed had on him: he says that after considering such celerity and the movement of the celestial bodies, he held our living to be of much greater worthlessness than he had previously held it to be noble and refined. Whence he says:

<margin>T</margin>
->Then I held our living to be vile<-
->Because of its wonderful speed,<-
->Far more than before I held it noble:<-

¶ Truly, the life of man can be judged vile and ignoble, being subject to as many calamities and miseries as the swift movement and dominion of the eternal spheres <note>The "eternal spheres" refers to the celestial bodies in the Ptolemaic system which were believed to influence earthly events.</note> bring upon it. The primary cause of this is change itself, through which nothing can have a lasting presence longer than a single indivisible moment. This is because man is continuously varying and transforming. The Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> defines this in the third book of the *Physics* as an alteration from a previous state; and fittingly, Jacob called this life of ours a "pilgrimage" because of its continuous flowing away. As it is written in Genesis, chapter 47, when Pharaoh said to Jacob, "How many are the days of the years of your life?" he replied: *The days of the pilgrimage of my life are one hundred and thirty years; they are few and evil.* <note>original: "dies pegrinationis uite mee . c . xxx . annorū sunt parui & mali," from Genesis 47:9.</note> Likewise, Job, knowing the deficiency and misery of our life, said in the seventh chapter: *Remember that my life is wind, and it shall not return; my eye shall not see good things.* <note>original: "Memento quia uētus est uita mea & non reuertetur: oculus meus ut uideat bona," from Job 7:7.</note> And in the fourteenth chapter he adds: *Man born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries; who comes forth like a flower and flees like a shadow.* <note>original: "homo natus de muliere breui uiuēs tempore repletus multis miserijs qui quasi flos egreditur & fugit uelut umbra," from Job 14:1-2.</note> ¶ Nor is this vileness of living understood only through the lack of present delight, but through the many and inevitable causes from which toil and trouble come to man. Alas, how many are the sicknesses of the body! How many immense passions of the soul! How many slaughters, ruins, punishments, tears, and shipwrecks! How many prisons and other conditions to which man is subjected, so that it is necessary for trouble to be continually added to his soul. And even if all the aforementioned things were taken away, who can restrain the envy of men? From this envy comes calumny <note><term>Calumny</term>: the making of false and defamatory statements about someone in order to damage their reputation.</note>, which caused such bitterness to Apelles <note>Apelles of Kos was a renowned painter of Ancient Greece, famous for a painting titled "Calumny" inspired by a false accusation against him.</note> in the time of Alexander the Great. Speaking of this, Solomon says in the seventh chapter of Ecclesiastes: *Calumny disturbs the wise man and destroys the strength of his heart.* <note>original: "calumnia conturbat sapientem & perdet robur cordis illius," from Ecclesiastes 7:7.</note> But even if this calumny is moved out of the way and set aside, in the end this great speed leads us so quickly to death that one can hardly have time to consider the way in which man is continually dying. Master Francesco writes the same in that song, **SO WEAK IS** the thread on which I hold, when he says at the beginning of the second stanza: **TIME PASSES AND THE HOURS** are so ready **to complete the journey.**

# CHAPTER ONE

I do not have enough time even to think about how I am rushing toward death: this being an irreparable loss that time produces for us. For this reason, then, this earthly life is deservedly judged vile and abject. Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> then offers a moral and indubitable sign, saying that it seemed to him a marvelous vanity to place and fix one's heart on things that time presses upon and quickly brings to an end. For while a man, believing he possesses them, clings to them and gathers them more tightly, they pass away all the more and show themselves to be fleeting. Hence he says:

<margin>X</margin>
->And it seemed to me a marvelous vanity<-
->To fix the heart on things that time presses,<-
->Which, while you hold them tighter, are gone.<-

¶ Just how infallible and true the aforementioned sentiment of our poet is, Solomon demonstrates quite clearly at the beginning of *Ecclesiastes*. There, every temporal thing—first sought after, then possessed according to one's will—is nothing other than vanity of vanities and affliction of spirit. If one did not believe this to be true, then let him speak for a moment, he who considers himself most secure and certain in possessing temporal things: what thing is lost more quickly than physical beauty and health? What could be surrounded by more hostile causes than those? Oh, how in a tiny moment accumulated riches, kingdoms, children, and worldly delights are lost! <margin>Y</margin> ¶ Oh, what pleasure or consolation is there that not only lasts, but *can* last longer than an <term>indivisible instant</term>? <note>In medieval philosophy, the "indivisible instant" refers to a point in time so small it cannot be divided, emphasizing the fleeting nature of the present.</note> And certainly with great reason: I hope that just as it is written in the fourth book of the *Physics*, regarding time and the things that flow through time, nothing is "present" to us except the divisible moment connecting the past time with that which is future. Therefore, whoever places his hope in those things has no certainty that they can last even a single whole day. This is because fortune rules over them; wherefore Cicero, in his *Paradoxes* against Publius Clodius, describes our theme in this manner: *For him whose every hope, reason, and thought depends on fortune, nothing can be certain, and he can have no assurance that anything will remain his for even a single day.* <note>original Latin: "Cui vero omnis spes & ratio & cogitatio omnis pendet ex fortuna. huic nihil potest esse certi: nihilque quod habeat exploratum sibi permãsurum vnam diem."</note> It would be quite long and tedious to try to bring forward examples of those who, in a short span of time, have lost their very being and seen their status changed, not only in temporal goods, but even in fame, glory, and public opinion. The poet then follows this up with an excellent teaching and a "golden sentence" regarding this disposition of our being, saying that whoever fears for his state should take good care to solidify it while he still has the full power of his <term>will</term> <note>original: "arbitrio," referring to the faculty of free choice</note> to place and found his hope in a stable place and in a firm and lasting thing. Hence he says:

<margin>Z</margin>
->Therefore, whoever cares for or fears for his state,<-
->Let him take good care, while his will is intact,<-
->To found his hope in a stable place.<-

¶ This is certainly a life-saving document which our Master Francesco has expressed for us in the preceding verses. For its understanding, one must know that our <term>will</term> <note>arbitrio</note> is nothing other than a power to be able to choose or not choose the object represented by the intellect to our desire. That this is free is shown clearly enough by the <term>Master of Sentences</term> <note>Peter Lombard, a 12th-century theologian whose "Sentences" was the standard textbook for theology.</note> in the second book at the 15th distinction, and much more briefly in the process of the *City of God* against Pelagius. <note>Refers to St. Augustine’s "De Civitate Dei" and his defense of grace against the Pelagian heresy regarding free will.</note> This freedom is lost in two ways: one is through natural death, which, once arrived, prevents one from acting or choosing; and of this the poet speaks in the preceding verses. The other way is when men, through habit, form an unchangeable character—as we said above in the *Triumph of Love*—and as Jeremiah speaks to the point in chapter 13, saying: *If the Ethiopian can change his skin and the leopard his spots, then you also can do good, who have learned to do evil.* <note>original Latin: "Si mutare potest ethiops pellem suam & pardus varietates suas & vos poteritis benefacere cũ didiceritis malum."</note> <margin>A</margin> ¶ Similarly, Aristotle in the third book of the *Ethics* says the same thing in confirmation: *For a sick man will not become healthy just because he wishes it, if it happens that he is sick of his own accord through intemperance and lack of discipline, having ignored the doctor's orders. At that time, it was possible for him not to be sick, but now it is no longer possible—just as no one can pull back a stone once it has been thrown. Yet it was in his power to take it up and throw it. For the beginning was in him; thus, it was possible for the unjust and wicked man from the start...* <note>original Latin: "Non eni aegrotans si vult sanus fiet: si ita contingat vt sponte egrotet per incontinentiam atque lasciniam preceptis medicorum aduersatus. Tunc ergo licebat illi non egrotare: sed nunc non amplius licet te quemadmodum nec emissum lapidem quis retinere potest. Erat tamen in illo capere ipsum atque emittere. Pricipium enim erat i ipso sic iniusto & flagitioso licebat ab initio tali"</note>

This sudden and continuous succession is described by Solomon in the third chapter of *Ecclesiastes*, when he enumerates the times of every contrary operation as being near to one another, saying:

> A time to be born and a time to die; a time to plant and a time to uproot what was planted; a time to kill and a time to heal. <note>original: "Tempus nascendi & tēpus moriēdi. tēpus plātādi & tēpus euellēdi. Quod plātātū ē: tēpus occidendi: & tēpus sanādi." Ecclesiastes 3:2-3.</note>

> Nothing in the whole world stays the same. All things flow, and every image is formed in a wandering state: even time itself glides on with constant motion, not unlike a river; for neither a river nor the swift hour can stand still. But as wave is pushed by wave, and the one coming on both presses and is pressed by the one before it, so times fly and follow alike. And they are always new; for what was before is left behind, and what was not comes to be, and all moments are renewed. <note>original: "Nihil est toto qd stet in orbe... momētāq; cuncta nouant." Ovid, Metamorphoses XV, 177-185.</note>

From which it remains manifest, by the opinions introduced above, that the speed of time is so great that there can be almost no distinction between any effects that occur in a contrary manner. Consequently, the poet then excites and calls upon dead men to consider and comprehend this truth, following the worthy customs of those who, having erred, do not remain obstinate in their error, but confess it and repent for having done such a deed. He says that although the preceding sentence seems quite marvelous, nevertheless, anyone who looks straight at the truth with a firm, perceptive, and upright judgment will see that it is exactly as he has written—even though the poet himself did not see it in the time of his youth. Regarding this, he grows heated and angry against himself. Wherefore he says:

<margin>F</margin>

Wherefore everyone should rightly understand that time is thus proportioned within us. And for this reason, in our brief and fugitive space of living, we should dispose our mind and works toward achieving the end for which human nature was produced in the world by the eternal God. And therefore our poet justly reproaches himself and is angry at himself for not having recognized this speed; and he exhorts others to consider it with a more firm and mature judgment. He then adds what the means was by which he was led to such perfect negligence, saying that his hope [was in] vain desires. # THE TRIUMPH OF TIME

*...that no one is a better judge: no one is a more effective comparison than that of the author's conscience to draw back or exhort himself according to the disposition of past or present operations. To demonstrate this proof, Cicero says in the second book of the Tusculan Disputations:* > You must use your own judgment: if you please yourself by approving what is right, you will not only have conquered yourself—which I was just advising—but everyone and everything. <note>original: "Tuo tibi indicio vtendum est: tibi: si recta probanti placebis: tu non modo te viceris: quod pauloante pcipiebam: sed omnes & omnia."</note> *And a little further down he adds:* > For all good deeds wish to be placed in the light; yet no theater for virtue is greater than the conscience. <note>original: "Omnia enim benefacta in lucem collocari volunt: sed tamen nullum theatrum virtuti conscientia maius est."</note>

<margin>H</margin>
*Our poet proves the same sentiment in that sonnet:* **FROM the Tyrrhenian sea to the left bank.** <note>A reference to Petrarch's Sonnet 208</note> *Where he says in the turn of the ninth verse:* **Alone where I was among thickets and hills. I was ashamed of myself, for to a noble heart, this much is enough and I wanted no other spur.** ¶ *Where it is manifest: that to a rectified soul, which now confirms itself with the conscience, nothing is more necessary to induce it to work for the good, nor even to draw it back from evil operations; nor does it take delight in anything more than itself, nor prize any other glory; but as the apostle says speaking to all Christians in the second [letter] to the Corinthians in the first chapter, saying:* > For this is your glory, the testimony of your conscience. <note>original: "Haec .n. est gloria vestra testimonium cõsciẽtie vestre." Referring to 2 Corinthians 1:12</note>

*So the human soul speaks to itself, establishing all its dignity and honor to be faith in the conscience and the testimony of its purity. Having described the work which man must do wishing to reduce himself to virtuous operating, the poet now adds the effect that follows such examination and recognition of oneself according to the right judgment of the conscience, saying that he prepares himself for his end as much as he can, thinking at every hour of his brief living: in which in the morning he finds himself a child, and now in the evening sees himself an old man. Whence he says:*

<margin>I</margin>
<margin>¶ How worthy and health-giving an effect the poet shows us toward our granted end; for whoever considers well, no more laudable operation can exist among mortals, nor even a more secure preparation for future glory, than—having seen that death is inevitable for man—to dispose oneself optimally through one's own self-knowledge and the knowledge of one's brief life and the swift transit of men which each must necessarily make from this world to the future life; to which effect Jerome teaches us optimally writing to Heliodorus when he says:</margin>

->And as much as I can, I prepare for the end<-
->Thinking of my brief life: in which<-
->This morning I was a child, and now I am old.<-

> It is Plato's opinion that the entire life of a wise man is a meditation on death. We must therefore also premeditate in our minds what we will one day be: and that which, whether we like it or not, cannot be very far off. <note>original: "Platonis sentẽtia est omnem sapiẽtis vitam meditationem esse mortis. Debemus ergo & nos animo premeditari quid aliquando futuri sumus: & quod velimus nolimus abesse longius non potest." A common Renaissance citation attributed to St. Jerome's letters.</note>

*Similarly Seneca, in the nineteenth epistle to Lucilius, explains the aforementioned sentiment with brief words, demonstrating that man ought to prepare himself for the end and dispose himself optimally for the last breath of life, saying:* > We have lived in the river; let us die in the port. <note>original: "In flumine viximus: moriamur in portu."</note>

<margin>K</margin>
¶ *But how great this speed is—in which man is transformed almost suddenly from a child into an old man—Cicero shows clearly enough in the first book of the Tusculan Disputations through a worthy and appropriate comparison, saying:* > At the river Hypanis, which flows from the direction of Europe into the Black Sea, Aristotle says that certain little beasts are born that live for only one day. Therefore, among these, one that died at the eighth hour died at an advanced age; while one that died at sunset was decrepit, all the more so if it were a summer day. Compare our longest life with eternity: we will be found in almost the same brevity as those little beasts. <note>original: "Apud hypanim fluuium... Aristoteles ait bestiolas quasdam nasci: quae vnum diem viuant... Confer nostram longissimam etatem cum eternitate..."</note>

*Deservedly, then, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, whose mirror of conscience was bright and polished, prepared and positioned himself for death; and he thought and considered the brief space of our life, in which thought he truly concluded that in the morning he had been a child, and then in the evening an old man, demonstrating how brief is the space and the course of our life. Consequently, Master Francesco deplores the error of wretched mortals, who estimate life to be long, and in it say they find rest, sport, and consolation, saying:* **Alas, what is more, or what can be judged longer than this mortal life than one very small day? Which truly is nothing other than a cloud, both brief and cold, full of trouble and torments. Alas, to whom can she seem beautiful?** *since in her human hope is worth nothing; nevertheless, the error of men is so great that every joy is expected here; here wretched mortals grow proud and lift their heads; nonetheless, none of them knows when they are living or truly when they die. Whence he says:*

<meta>This page continues the philosophical reflection on the passage of time. While the previous page established the conscience as the ultimate "theater" or judge of a person's life, this page moves into the first chapter of the "Triumph of Time," focusing on the extreme brevity of human existence when compared to the vastness of history.
