# CHAPTER ONE

<sig>XX iij</sig>

> What is mortal life more than a single day,
> Cloudy, brief, cold, and full of sorrow?
> That may appear beautiful but is worth nothing:
> Here is human hope, and here is joy:
> Here miserable mortals raise their heads;
> And no one knows how long they live, or when they die.

<margin>L</margin>
¶ The brevity and speed of human life is taught not only by the authorities cited here, but is demonstrated by universal experience. From this, one must truly conclude that life lasts no longer than a single, very brief day. To understand this, one must know that "brief" and "long" are terms used by comparison. For instance, the life of **Nestor** <note>A legendary Greek king said to have lived for three generations.</note> was called brief in respect to that of **Methuselah** <note>The biblical figure reported to have lived 969 years.</note>, even though compared to others it is said to be quite long. And if someone today were to live one hundred years, their life would be judged brief in comparison to Nestor, whereas compared to modern lifespans it would be considered very long. Therefore, if this common span of living is compared to the entire course of the world from the beginning to the end—

<margin>M</margin>
¶ Who can doubt that the longest life possible at present should not even be called the length of a single day? And in this brief time, how many are the troubles, and how many the afflictions! Let the man who considers himself most happy bear witness to this truth. **Cicero** <note>Referred to in the text by his middle name, Tullio.</note> gives us a very good understanding of this in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations* through the example of **Dionysius of Syracuse**. Dionysius, being judged happy by **Damocles**, placed Damocles in his own seat at a banquet and hung a sword over his head by a single horsehair (as we mentioned in the *Triumph of Love*). From this, Damocles understood how many hidden cares and troubles reign in the minds of powerful men. Similarly, just as in our lives hopes are false and thoughts are vain, and human labors are spent in vain, I do not doubt that each person can be a most just judge of this for themselves.

<margin>N</margin>
¶ O miserable, truly miserable mortals! Why place all your joy and hope in the world? Why become so proud and forget your origin? For what is a human being in the whole of their progress but foul seed, a foul mind, and the food and nourishment of worms? Because of this, **Democritus**, in order to repress human pride, very often went to visit the tombs of the dead. There, considering how humble our final end is, he taught us in his works to conform ourselves to that reality. Let the infinitely proud person, then, consider and well-estimate their origin; let them set aside their haughty behavior and well-recognize their inevitable end. And let them clearly understand that while life lasts, they cannot know when they are truly living or truly dying; because while sleeping we race toward death, while waking we race toward death, while laughing we go toward death, while crying we proceed toward death. In short, in every action, one approaches death. Consequently, **Master Francesco** <note>Petrarch, the author of the poem.</note> brings forward the example of himself to demonstrate what follows from such a consideration of human life. Having examined it with good and mature judgment, he says that having considered the state and process of our life, he recognized the flight of his own living—and not only his, but that of all men—noting how swift it was. He saw clearly in the turning and fleeing of the sun that the manifest ruin of the world proceeds from it. Whence he says:

> I see the flight of my life is swift,
> Or rather everyone's; and in the sun's fleeing
> The ruin of the world is manifest.

<margin>O</margin>
¶ Since the law and universal statute of dying—and of the long-lasting and effective operations of the heavens upon us—is common to every earthly thing, and especially to man, as **Ovid** writes at the beginning of the tenth book of the *Metamorphoses*, saying: > Sooner or later we hasten to one home. We all tend here, this is our final dwelling; and you hold the longest reign over the human race. <note>original: "Serius aut citius sedẽ speramus ad unã. Tendimus huc oẽs hec est domus ultima nosq. Hūni generis lōgisima regna tenetis." Note that the OCR "speramus" (we expect) is a variation of the standard Ovidian "properamus" (we hasten).</note> It is a reasonable thing that the intellect, knowing its own progress, should also understand the same for all others. And in a similar way, seeing these celestial revolutions and movements bring great alterations to the elemental things, it also understands that there must be a universal ruin of the wor— <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("mondo") at the end of the page.</note>

<summary>This page introduces Petrarch's "Triumph of Time," providing a commentary on the fleeting nature of human life. It emphasizes that death is a universal law and that human pride is vanity given our humble origins and inevitable end.</summary>

<sig>P</sig>
<sig>Q</sig>
<sig>R</sig>

sidering: because, just as it is the common opinion of philosophers, the movement of the heavens is ordered toward the preservation of the universe as its ultimate goal. Hence, if that movement were to lessen or end, it would have been produced by nature in vain; likewise, the preservation of this world, in the form it is currently arranged, must eventually fail.

<margin>P</margin>
¶ And therefore, the poet adds a worthy rebuke to the young, who are less diligent in this consideration than their needs require—and even to those of old age—saying: "Go on then, you young people, continue to comfort yourselves with your fables and do not think of death. Measure time with a long yardstick, for it seems vast to you, as you expect to reach old age." Oh, I warn you that it would be much better to think about the fact that you must die: for a wound that is foreseen hurts far less than one that strikes unexpectedly amidst pleasures and delights. But perhaps it happens that as I rebuke you in this way, my words are scattered in vain. And if that is so, I assure you that you are too afflicted by a heavy and deathly <term>lethargy</term> <note>original: "lethargo." In a medical and philosophical sense, this refers to a state of spiritual stupor or indifference to the soul's health.</note>. For the hours, the days, and even the months and years all fly together in a very brief moment, after which, with little interval, all of us—old and young, children and the elderly—must seek and inhabit "other countries" <note>A poetic metaphor for the afterlife or the state beyond mortal existence.</note>. Therefore, do not allow a callous to form around your heart against the truth, as you have been accustomed to in the past. Instead, turn your eyes toward the path of truth while your faults and sins can still be amended, and do not wait for death to release and shoot its persistent and deadly bow. Do not act like the common folk; for certainly, the ranks and multitude of the foolish and ignorant are an infinite number. Hence he says:

> Now go, comfort yourselves in your fables,
> You young ones, and measure out time as if it were vast:
> But a foreseen wound hurts much less.
> Perhaps I scatter my words in vain:
> But I announce to you, that you are afflicted
> By a heavy and deathly <term>lethargy</term>:
> For the hours, days, years, and months fly,
> Together with a very brief interval.
> We all have to seek other countries.
> Do not form a callous on your heart against the truth,
> As you are used to doing: instead, turn your eyes,
> While you can still amend your faults.
> Do not wait for death to strike its bow,
> As most people do: for certainly
> Infinite is the army of fools.

<margin>Q</margin>
¶ For a clearer understanding of this excellent and health-giving rebuke and the fruitful instruction contained in the preceding verses, one must first know that human nature is almost universally seized by a negligence in considering future things. As **Quintus Curtius** <note>A Roman historian, likely referring to his "History of Alexander the Great."</note> elegantly writes: *Nature has poorly provided for human minds, because we mostly weigh the things that have passed rather than those to come* <note>original: "Male humanis ingenijs natura consuluit quod plerunque non futura sed transacta perpendimus."</note>. But this forgetfulness arises most sharply during prosperity and the abundance of goods, whether those goods come from nature or from fortune. Regarding this, the aforementioned **Quintus Curtius** adds these words: *In prosperous times, there is an excessive forgetfulness of human fragility* <note>original: "Fragilitatis humane nimia in prosperis rebus oblitio est."</note>. And **Titus Livy** <note>The famous Roman historian (Livy).</note>, confirming the same in his book on the Second Punic War, writes: *For it almost always happens that success creates negligence* <note>original: "Ferme enim fit ut secundae res negligentiam creent."</note>. And elsewhere in the same book he says: *But if the Gods were to give a sound mind along with good fortune, we would consider not only what has come but what is yet to come* <note>original: "Quod si in secundis rebus bonam quoque mentem darent Dij: non solum ea que venissent: sed que ventura essent putaremus."</note>. And therefore he concludes near the end, saying: *Indeed, it rarely happens to men that both good fortune and a sound mind are given together* <note>original: "Raro qdem contingit hominibus bonam fortunam: bonāq; mentem dari."</note>.

<margin>R</margin>
¶ And if this negligence occurs at any age, it is especially prevalent in the years of youth. For children, just as they do not recognize the good, they likewise do not understand the evil; therefore, this forgetfulness is not counted as a failing or sin for them. Similarly, the elderly are forced to consider death, if not by anything else, then at least by their age and experience. Thus, only the young remain to be rebuked for this negligence. The reason is that their natural strength reigns within them, and because of their lack of experience, they have not yet been deceived by fortune; for this reason, they do not conform themselves to the actions that would be appropriate for...

### CHAPTER ONE

...the mysteries of death. They measure time broadly and judge death to be far distant from them; thus they follow worldly delights, not considering what fortune can give to them. As Livy writes in the previously cited book, Hannibal said to the young Scipio: "One whom fortune has never abandoned considers the chances of uncertain events rashly." <note>original: "Incertæ temere casuum reputat: quem fortuna nunquā recepit." From Livy’s *Ab Urbe Condita*, Book 30.</note> And therefore, appropriately, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> accuses them of being afflicted by a heavy <term>lethargy</term>, which is a sickness, as physicians write. Through this ailment, the third ventricle of the brain becomes stained, and one falls into a forgetfulness of all past things; this passion is named for the River Lethe of the underworld, from which souls carried by Charon come to lose every memory of the things of the world. Therefore, to flee this excess and this failing, the poet calls the young back to the knowledge of themselves: to have to consent to the truth, not to create a hard callus around the heart, and to premeditate upon death, so that when it eventually comes by necessity, it does not seem as harsh as it would if it came unconsidered.

<margin>S</margin>
And therefore, to this same effect, Persius of Volterra <note>A Roman satirist (34–62 AD) known for his difficult but moralistic poetry.</note>, satirizing in his third satire, condemns our carelessness and negligence in these verses, saying: "Learn, O wretched ones, and know the causes of things. What are we, and for what kind of life are we born? What order is given to us? Where is the easy turn around the goalpost, and from where does it come? What is the limit for silver? What is it right to wish for? What use has the rough-minted coin? How much is it fitting to bestow upon one's country and dear kin? Whom did God command you to be, and in what part of human affairs have you been placed?" <note>original: "DISCITE et o miseri: causas cognoscite rerum..." Persius, *Satires*, 3.66-73.</note> It is therefore a fitting thing, as the poet teaches us in this valley of miseries and in this prison <note>original: "ergastulo." A Roman term for a private prison for slaves; here used metaphorically for the body or the worldly life of sin.</note> that incites lechery and sin, to turn one's eyes toward true <term>penitence</term>, through which one is purged and their stain is taken away. This time for penitence lasts as long as life continues, as determined by the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160), whose *Sentences* was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> in the fourth book, distinction 20, following the opinion of Pope Saint Leo.

<margin>T</margin>
<margin>V</margin>
Nevertheless, it is not a safe path to lead oneself to repent only "on the pillow" <note>An idiom for deathbed repentance.</note>, because there is great danger for the state of the soul since the man is then unfit to make satisfaction through works. Therefore, showing the way, Augustine says on this subject in a sermon on penitence: "If anyone placed in ultimate necessity wishes to receive penitence and is reconciled and departs from here, I confess to you that we deny no one what he asks, but we do not presume that he exits well. If he departs securely, I do not know. We can give penitence, but security we cannot. Do I say he will be damned? No; but neither do I say he will be liberated." <note>original: "Si quis positus in ultimam necessitatem..." A common medieval attribution to St. Augustine regarding the uncertainty of deathbed conversions.</note> If you wish, therefore, to be freed from doubt, perform your penitence while you are healthy, because you performed it at a time when you were able to sin. "For if you wish to perform penitence only when you can no longer sin, your sins have left you, not you them." Therefore, one should not only not wait for death to burst forth, but should act so that—as far as our intellect can know—it does not even draw near to us. The ignorant and foolish masses do the precise contrary of this, for in following their folly they can be judged infinite. As Solomon writes in the first chapter of Ecclesiastes, saying: "The perverse are hard to correct, and the number of fools is infinite." <note>original: "Perversi difficile corriguntur: & stultorum infinitus est numerus." Ecclesiastes 1:15.</note> In this consideration, then, we must think that in a short space of time all created souls, having departed from their bodies by the force of death, have to seek different countries, which are distinct among themselves. For some are taken up to heaven, some submerged in hell, and some others detained by the hands of divine justice in a third place called <term>purgatory</term>. We shall persuasively argue for the existence of this place with reason in the subsequent and final Triumph, against the opinion of the obstinate and heretical Viraldo <note>likely Vigilantius, a 4th-century priest who opposed the veneration of relics and prayers for the dead, or a similar medieval dissenter.</note> and whoever might wish to follow him through blindness of mind or hardness of heart.

<margin>X</margin>
<margin>Y</margin>
But in this place, a doubt is usually raised by elevated minds: for what reason did Master Francesco, wishing in this Triumph to demonstrate that Time overcomes the Fame of men, only narrate and conclude up to this point that the process of our life is brief and subject to many dangers that can cut it short? To this doubt, it is answered that our poet established this opinion up to here with great artistry and reason; for fame has its origin only from the virtuous works performed by men in the world. And since our life is the cause of those works—and there being no quality more perfect in the effect than in the cause, as Averroes <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> affirms in the eighth book of the *Metaphysics*—since our life is brief and can fail through a small harm, we must not persuade ourselves that the fame which is its effect is eternal.

<margin>Z</margin>
Our Master Francesco having therefore up to this point demonstrated that the swiftness of time has overcome the life of men...

<page-num>134</page-num>
-> # THE TRIUMPH OF TIME <-

The poet determines from this moment forward that Time itself will eventually conquer and darken the fame acquired during this present life. He says that since he had seen in the past, and now clearly sees in the present, the flight and sudden escape of the **great planet** <note>The Sun, which in the Ptolemaic system was considered a planet whose movement dictated the passage of time.</note> in the sky—through which he has suffered the greatest losses and deceptions—looking even more closely, he saw a group of people walking very quietly, fearing neither Time nor its rapid velocity. This group and company were under the protection and guard of **historians** and also of **poets**. Thus he says:

> After I had seen, and see clearly
> the flight and the escape of the great planet;
> From which I have suffered much harm and deception.
> I saw a people walking very quietly
> Without fearing Time, or its rage;
> For a historian or poet held them in guard.

<margin>A</margin> ¶ Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known that Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> intends by this "people" whom he says do not fear time nor its most cruel rage to be those men who are dead and celebrated by **fame**. He writes that they proceed in silence to demonstrate how they have been occupied by death. For this reason, they no longer care for anything belonging to the present life, nor are they any longer subject to the celestial revolutions; therefore, they no longer fear Time or its rapid and swift circuit. They are then placed in the guard of poets and historians, since each of these authors records and describes the virtuous deeds performed by men in the present life. And therefore, they endure and are guarded by these authors for as long as the books of histories and poems written by them endure.

<margin>B</margin> ¶ And although the poet and the historian write differently—because the poet invents <note>original: "fingere," meaning to use poetic license or allegory</note> certain things to better explain certain effects of the soul, while the historian writes only what is truthfully contained in history—nevertheless, they agree in this: that each truly records the virtuous works through which fame is acquired in this world. Master Francesco then adds what the condition of the dead and famous is in respect to living men, saying that it seems they are much more envied than any other generation upon the earth. The reason is that they, by their own efforts and through their virtuous works, were raised to the glorious value of fame, escaping from the **common cage** <note>A metaphor for the physical body or the mundane limitations of ordinary life.</note> and from this earthly dwelling and the common life of the unskilled masses. Thus he says:

> It seems there is more envy for them than for others:
> For they have raised themselves in flight
> Escaping out of the common cage.

<margin>C</margin> ¶ Anyone who diligently considers the description of Envy given by Ovid at the end of the second book of the *Metamorphoses* <note>Ovid describes Envy (Invidia) as a withered, venomous creature living in a dark, sunless cave.</note> will see quite reasonably in this passage why our elegant poet described famous men as being victims of envy. This is because Envy is primarily described as dwelling in subterranean caves where the light of the sun never penetrates, pale and obscure, wrapped in dense gloom. Thus, virtuous and famous men come to possess qualities in life and death that are contrary to this; by distancing themselves from the nature of idle men, they excite the minds of the latter and move them to envy.

<margin>D</margin> ¶ There is, therefore, nothing more contrary to envy than the fame of men; because fame always extends into the light of the sun, and every day it becomes clearer and better known. Therefore, those who cannot acquire fame through their own virtue are first provoked to admiration by the examples of others, and then to envy.

<margin>E</margin> ¶ Secondly, the greatest envy is directed toward the dead and famous because when a person finds themselves in some danger or strange adversity, they consider that the men of the past are exempt from worldly misfortunes; thus they judge the state of the dead to be much better than the present life. And therefore, envy is felt then, just as Virgil clearly shows in the first book of the *Aeneid*, when he introduces **Aeneas** in his great wandering, lamenting and saying... <note>Aeneas famously laments that those who died at Troy were luckier than he, as they are at peace while he suffers at sea.</note>

<summary>This page explains Petrarch's vision of famous figures from history who, protected by the writings of poets and historians, appear to defy the destructive power of Time. It also explores the philosophical reasons why the living feel envy toward the famous dead, referencing Ovid's personification of Envy and Virgil's Aeneas.</summary>

...saying: "At once the limbs of Aeneas are loosened by a cold chill. He groans and, stretching both palms toward the stars, speaks such words: 'O three and four times blessed are those whose lot it was to perish before the faces of their fathers beneath the high walls of Troy! O Diomedes, bravest of the Greek race! Why could I not have fallen on the Trojan fields and breathed out this soul by your right hand?'" <note>original: "Extemplo eneæ ſoluvntur..." This is a quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (Book I, 92-98), where the hero Aeneas, caught in a storm, wishes he had died a glorious death in battle rather than perishing at sea.</note>

Thus, because famous men have been withdrawn from worldly dangers by death, the poet writes that they do not care for time, and they are envied more than others. 

¶ Now, since Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> has narrated who those are who proceed in fame with quiet and silence—that fame being unalterable by celestial revolutions—and because of this they do not care for time, he adds and fully demonstrates that the hope of anyone who believes that the aforementioned fame should be eternal is entirely in vain. Describing the length of time, he shows that it extinguishes fame no less than its speed, along with the celestial influences that first exterminated life. He says that he who alone among all the planets shines <note>The Sun</note> prepared himself with much greater force and took up a much more rapid flight; and in this speed, the barley for his steeds was doubled <note>A metaphor for feeding horses more grain to increase their speed and power.</note>. And besides this, the Queen—whom we said in the previous Triumph was mortal glory and fame—already wanted to separate herself and "divorce" some of those who were with her in her worthy troop and company. Therefore he says:

<margin>
FOR a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it should primarily be known that, as we said a little while ago, no other planet in the sky possesses its own light except the Sun. The others only shine through the reflection of the solar rays that reverberate upon them, as if they were the denser parts of the sky. Secondly, it should be understood that the poet appropriately says the Sun prepares itself with greater force against fame than it had previously done against the lives of men, and that it has "doubled the barley" for its steeds. This is to imply that human life is much more easily consumed by the slightest celestial operation than is human fame.
</margin>

> Against these, he who alone shines,
> Prepared himself with greater force;
> And took up a more rapid flight:
> For his steeds, the barley was doubled:
> And the queen, of whom I spoke above;
> Already wished to divorce herself from some of hers.

And therefore it is necessary for the Sun to double, triple, quadruple, and multiply its revolutions to extinguish the name and glory of men, more so than to take away their present life. This is because to take away life, it is enough to subject a man to various and diverse adversities; but to obscure fame, nothing is needed but the length of time. And therefore, to express these qualities, he says the Sun has doubled the barley for its steeds and taken a more rapid flight. The flight of the Sun—through which its turning continues—is more absolute than that which merely deprives men of life. 

¶ Lastly, it is to be noted that the poet adds that Fame (figured above as a Queen) wished to separate herself from some. This demonstrates that, through the long passage of time, the books of the ancient writers have been corrupted and the memory of many most excellent men has failed. This can be understood in our own age, in which many histories are seen to be lost, as is evident in the works of Quintilian, Curtius, Cornelius Tacitus, Justin, Sallust, Livy, and many other historians of the Latin language. Thus, the fame of many is already beginning to be buried, and nothing remains outside the grave but their names; their works are already overtaken by the earth and obscured by time, and are totally entombed. Therefore, from such people, the worldly Queen Fame wishes to make a "divorce," a separation, and a departure. 

After our Master Francesco saw the Sun had taken a swifter course and prepared itself with a harder war against the fame of men, he adds—maintaining a laudable modesty—certain most worthy and golden <term>maxims</term> <gloss>sententiae</gloss>, saying that he had heard them said. But he does not know how to report from whom he heard them; he only wrote them down having understood them.

<summary>This page discusses Petrarch's "Triumph of Time," explaining how the Sun (as the driver of Time) accelerates to destroy human Fame, which is more resilient than life but still vulnerable to the "doubled" speed of time and the loss of historical texts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch's "Triumph of Time." Having established that human fame is fleeting, the commentator now examines Petrarch’s specific metaphors for oblivion—the "privet flower" and the "abyss"—and the role of divine inspiration in the poet's work.</meta>

...written to be reduced into two lessons. The first of these was that in these worldly effects, those things truly and properly called <term>privet flowers</term><note>The Italian *ligustri* refers to the white flowers of the privet plant, which bloom beautifully but wither very quickly, serving as a classic metaphor for the fragility of youth and fame.</note> are the deep and vast abysses of a blind and shadowed oblivion. Thus he says:

<margin>I</margin> ¶ The glorious Plato writes—giving a clearer notice of the preceding verses regarding the origins of <term>frenzies</term><note>The author refers to the Platonic concept of *furor* or divine madness/inspiration.</note>—that one type comes from earthly things: a thing truly most base and shameful, which Cicero also reproaches in the second book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, because it most often arises from bodily pain or passion of the soul. This quality should not befall a wise man. The second type is divine frenzy, and this is divided into prophecy, mystery, love, and poetry. Therefore, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, wishing in every act to maintain proper custom and modesty, does not claim this for himself; rather, he attributes the expression of these grave and indubitable thoughts to such a frenzy. And for this reason, he says he heard them said, but does not know by whom: because this frenzy is distilled and works within us secretly and in an unknown manner.

->I heard it said, I know not by whom, but I wrote the words;<-
->In these human affairs, to speak truly of privet flowers,<-
->Are the dark abysses of blind oblivion.<-

<margin>K</margin> ¶ Secondly, it is to be understood that worldly effects are appropriately nicknamed "privet flowers" because privets are white little flowers with very little moisture. For this reason, they very quickly become drooping and withered. Thus Virgil, in the *Eclogues*, wishing to express the fading of youthful beauty, introduces the shepherd Corydon speaking to Alexis and saying these words: *"O handsome boy, trust not too much in your color. The white privet flowers fall; the dark hyacinths are gathered."* <note>original: "O formose puer nimium ne crede colori. Alba ligustra cadunt . vaccinia nigra leguntur." from Virgil's Eclogue II, 17-18.</note>

<margin>L</margin> ¶ Lastly, it must be considered that in these worldly effects, nothing spreads further than oblivion. Experience teaches us this when we consider what a great number of men have passed away, and of how few any notice has remained to us. Wishing to demonstrate this blind oblivion, Solomon says at the beginning of *Ecclesiastes*: *"There is nothing new under the sun; nor is anyone able to say: 'Behold, this is new'; for it has already preceded us in the ages that were before us. There is no memory of earlier things. But neither will there be any remembrance of those things which are to come afterward among those who shall be in the latest times."* <note>original: "Nihil sub sole novum... erit recordatio apud eos qui futuri sunt nouißimi." A translation of Ecclesiastes 1:9-11.</note> ¶ Justly, therefore, we can affirm that in this world there are deep abysses of blind oblivion. Master Francesco then narrates the second sentiment, which he says he heard said by he knows not whom: that the sun will turn not only individual years, but even <term>lustra</term><note>A period of five years.</note> and the century—which is the victor over every famous, outstanding, and most celebrated man. Likewise, it will turn the lustra and see those who are presently reputed as illustrious turn into vanity, without fame, name, or recognition. As proof of this sentiment, he adds, saying: How many were clear and famous between the river Peneus and the river Hebrus, who have partly faded and partly will soon diminish? How many also on the river Xanthus? And how many still in the valley near the river Tiber? Thus he says:

<margin>M</margin> ¶ Concerning the understanding of the preceding verses, it is to be known principally that the <term>lustrum</term> is defined by writers of the Latin language to signify a period of five years, which had its origin in the counting of five years performed by the people of Rome. Thus our poet intends to argue that the sun is not only fit to prescribe a single year, but also the lustra and any other complication of years. Through this revolution and divinity, the century that encompasses them becomes the superior ruler of every celebrated man, no matter how much he is exalted by fame and made worthy by learned writers. From this, it follows that in future centuries, many who are today both famous and illustrious must return to vanity and lack of fame.

->The sun will turn not only years, but lustra,<-
->And centuries, the victors over every mind;<-
->And it will see the fading away of these illustrious ones.<-
->How many were famous between the Peneus and the Hebrus?<-
->Who have diminished or will soon diminish.<-
->How many on the Xanthus, and how many in the valley of the Tiber?<-

<margin>N</margin> ¶ Secondly, it is to be understood that Master Francesco adduces an excellent example of those who are already obscured between the Hebrus and the Peneus, and on the river Xanthus, and in the valley of the Tiber:

# CHAPTER ONE

[Page 167]

<margin>O</margin> Hebrus: which nonetheless were once most noted and clear by fame. ¶ Where it must be considered <margin>P</margin> that by the first, he intends the famous Greeks: because the River Peneus irrigates and runs through Thessaly, which lies toward the south contiguous with Macedonia; and the River Hebrus runs through Thrace, which is near the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note> and Constantinople. ¶ Thus, between these two rivers are contained Macedonia, Thrace, and Thessaly, which are near the lands of Attica and Boeotia. Therefore, let each one consider for themselves how many men were famous in this site among the Macedonians, Thracians, Thessalians, Athenians, and Thebans. And nonetheless, very many of those have been entirely removed from fame, and many others are on the way to being extinguished. ¶ By the second, the poet intends the prized Trojans; because the River Xanthus passed through the middle of Troy. <margin>Q</margin> Hence Virgil, in the first book of the *Aeneid*, commemorates it when he narrates that Aeneas saw, within the temple of Carthage, all the Trojan wars painted in order, and among other things, Diomedes when he steals the horses of Rhesus, which had the property that if they drank from the River Xanthus, Troy could no longer be lost. Hence Virgil says: *He recognizes the tears, and more, the tents betrayed by sleep. Diomedes ravaged them with great slaughter, bloody, and turned the fiery horses away toward the camp before they could taste the fodder of Troy and drink of Xanthus.* <note>original: "Agnoscit lacbrymas īmo que prodita somno. Tytides multa ua stabat cede cruentus. Ardentesq; auertit equos ī castra priusq̄. Pabula gustassent troie xantū q; bibissent." — Virgil, Aeneid I.469-473.</note> ¶ By the third and last, Master Francesco <note>The poet Petrarch</note> intends the glorious Romans; because the <margin>R</margin> river which is contiguous to Rome—although it was first named *Albula* for the whiteness of the water—was later called the *Tiber* after Tiberinus, king of the Albans, who drowned within it; later, among the common people through the corruption of the word, it was always called and named the *Tevere*. ¶ Therefore, how famous the Romans <margin>S</margin> and Trojans once were! And yet, they are greatly obscured in fame by the length of time, a very clear argument for which is understood in the discourse of histories, in which oftentimes only the names of some are seen remaining to our notice. Master Francesco then adduces another worthy <term>sentiment</term><note>Italian: *sententia*; a formal thought or philosophical maxim.</note>, which he intends by saying that he heard it said that the fame of mortal men was like a doubtful and unstable clear sky in winter, which a very tiny mist breaks and obscures. And because of this, a great and very long span of time is a great, bitter, and deadly poison to great and excellent names. Thus he says:

<margin>T</margin>
->*A doubtful winter, unstable and clear,*<-
->*Is your fame, and a little mist breaks it;*<-
->*Great time is a great poison to great names.*<-

¶ How rightly this worthy comparison and sentiment is expressed by our poet, and how great is the vanity of those who prize the fame remaining after them as the highest good: it is easier to understand it with the mind than to narrate it with the tongue, because mist and clouds do not more quickly break and disturb the serenity of the sky than a slight cause takes away or disturbs the fame of men in the world. ¶ Now, is it not <margin>V</margin> true that a small voice produced by a base and ignoble person spreads in such a way that it calls into doubt what many other most excellent men have affirmed as true? And likewise a strange opinion, a false interpretation, a personal disbelief, almost totally extinguishes the fame and ancient opinion of others. ¶ Now, is the entire and <margin>X</margin> worthy chastity of Penelope not almost called into doubt? Only by the opinion of Lycophron, the Greek poet, who affirms that she gave her body to all the <term>barons</term><note>The suitors of the Odyssey.</note> who asked her during the absence of Ulysses. Likewise, have the opinions about Aeneas and Turnus not been so diverse that one cannot distinguish which of them was superior to the other? It being the opinion of many that Aeneas was either killed at the River Numicus or forced by Turnus to throw himself into the river and drown in it. ¶ Nonetheless, Virgil affirms in the twelfth book that Turnus was killed in battle by <margin>Y</margin> Aeneas. A very great abundance of similar examples exists in the histories of the Latin language, which we shall omit for the sake of brevity; for even if these causes did not interrupt fame, Time—which is the poison of great names—must necessarily subdue and extinguish it. The poet continues, narrating another excellent sentiment, saying that beyond these referred sentiments, he once heard it said that all our greatnesses and all our pomps pass away and return to nothing. And similarly, lordships come to an end and kingdoms fail; and in the end, Time cuts off and interrupts even the most solid mortal part. Thus he says:

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s "Triumph of Time," transitioning from the specific geography of fame (rivers like the Peneus and Xanthus) to the broader philosophical and historical reality that all earthly power, regardless of its location, is eventually consumed by time.</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF TIME

->Your triumphs and your pomps pass away;<-
->Lordships pass; kingdoms pass;<-
->Time interrupts every mortal thing.<-

<margin>Z</margin>
¶ For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, one must know that the nature of all things enclosed within the element of fire <note>The "sublunary world," or everything on Earth beneath the heavens, which medieval science believed was subject to decay</note> was ordained from the beginning of the world to suffer transformation and, eventually, to come to an end. Not without reason is this earthly region named by philosophers as a "sphere" of things tending toward their end, because within it are placed the equal elements which contain within themselves their own primary contrary qualities.

<margin>A</margin>
¶ From this, by natural conclusion, it can be understood that our pomps and greatness, depending solely on earthly things, are in a short space of time—by the revolution of the years—fleeting and transitory. Likewise, this applies to states, lordships, and kingdoms. Even if this were not understood through natural reason based on the continuous action of opposites, experience at the very least demonstrates its necessity.

<margin>¶</margin>
Alas, consider well: where now is the greatness of Octavian? Where are the triumphs of Caesar, or the glory of Alexander the Great of Macedon? Where is the reputation of Pyrrhus of Epirus? Where is the pomp of Darius, the riches of Antiochus, or the singular virtues of Epaminondas? Where are the highest and worthy praises of Philopoemen? Where is the great Babylon, the powerful Carthage, or the proud Troy? Where is the warlike Thebes, the just Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>, or the studious Athens?

<margin>B</margin>
¶ Where, in the end, is triumphant Rome? All have passed away; some are leveled to the earth in such a way that no trace remains. Others are so changed from their former state that they retain no likeness of their ancient beauty.

<margin>¶</margin>
Alas, look with a steady and fixed intellect upon noble Italy alone: to what state have the great multitude of peoples—once glorious and powerful in their own right—been reduced? The Samnites, the Volsci, the Latins, the Sabines, the Caecinenses, the Falisci, the Bruttii, the Lucani, the Hernici, the Salentines: all are changed, all are extinguished and brought low, their names and kingdoms lost.

<margin>C</margin>
¶ Alas, let us consider the progress of Greek power: how one kingdom and one lordship has extinguished the other. We begin with those from whom their glorious dominion took its start. As <term>Justin</term> <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a 2nd-century Roman historian</note> writes, at the beginning of kingdoms, power was held by the Assyrians in the time of Ninus, who was the first King to use the subjugated provinces as a dominion. The Assyrians lasted about 1,350 years. Afterward, they were extinguished and overthrown by the Medes. Nor did the Medes prolong their reign much longer, for after almost 200 years, they were conquered and subjugated by the Persians. The Persians, too, did not reign eternally; after nearly the same amount of time, they were overcome and occupied by the Greeks. The Greeks were of no different nature, nor could they flee from coming to an end; in a short space of time, they were constrained by the Romans to serve.

<margin>D</margin>
¶ What shall be said of the kingdom of the Chaldeans? What of the Hebrews? What of the Sicyonians, the Argives, the Egyptians, the Tyrians, the Lydians, or the Trojans? Nothing other than what is said of the other kingdoms: that they failed, were confused, extinguished, and ultimately eradicated. Nor have only monarchies and kingdoms suffered this variation, but even established republics. The Athenians, having acquired almost every island between the Chelidonian Islands and the Black Sea, held their power for barely 72 years before they were overcome by the Lacedaemonians. The Lacedaemonians, having acquired all the Peloponnese as far as Macedonia, were in a short time subjugated by the Thebans. Nor were the Thebans perpetual in their dominion, for in the end—and not long from their beginning—they were defeated by the fierce Macedonians. Finally, the Macedonians, there being no republic in Greece that could further resist them, vanished within 30 years due to their own internal and mutual feuds.

<margin>E</margin>
¶ I will remain silent regarding the republic of Carthage, and that of the Locrians among our Italians. I will pass over the Campani, the Retines, the Herculaneans, the Tusculans, and innumerable other Italian republics. Let only the soul of Rome, and Pisa and Genoa, serve as our examples; their power was manifest in every part of the world. Even today, the barbarian nations tremble with pain and fear at the mere mention of their names, remembering their past and excellent victories.

<margin>F</margin>
¶ Therefore, our ancient ancestors, understanding perfectly that such great variation and change proceeds from nothing and returns to nothing, ascribed this to Saturn. Saturn is interpreted as Time, who devours his own children and then vomits them up. Concerning him, <term>Cicero</term> <note>The Roman statesman and philosopher Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> says, to demonstrate this consumption wrought by time: *He is called Saturn because he is saturated with years; he is imagined to eat his children because age consumes the spans of time and is insatiably filled by the years that have passed.* <note>original: "Saturnus autem appellatus: eo quod saturetur annis: edere autem natos fingitur: quia consumit aetas temporis spacia: annisque preteritis insatiabiliter expletur."</note> And so, by Saturn eating his children, we are meant to understand this great length of time...

# THE TRIUMPH OF TIME

...to enter and obscure everything. Therefore, Ovid, in the fifteenth book of the *Metamorphoses* <note>original: "methamorphoseo"</note>, comprehending this very thing, explains it gracefully and with excellent learning in these verses:

> Time, devourer of all things, and you, envious age, you destroy everything, and with the teeth of time, you gradually consume all things in a slow death. <note>Latin: *Tempus edax rerum tuq; inuidiosa vetustas. Omnia destruitis vitiataq; dentibus eui. Paulatim lenta consumitis omnia morte.*</note>

Led by this very same foundation, the wise Solomon—as we noted above at the beginning in the third chapter of Ecclesiastes—said:

> Everything has its time, and all things under heaven pass away in their seasons. <note>Latin: *Omnis tempus habet: & spatiis suis transeunt vniuersa sub caelo.*</note>

And Cicero, in his tenth *Philippic* <note>A series of speeches Cicero gave attacking Mark Antony</note>, says on this same subject:

> For nothing flourishes forever; age succeeds age. <note>Latin: *Nihil . n . semper floret aetas succedit etati.*</note>

<margin>G</margin>
From this, appropriately and with great reason, one can conclude that nothing in this world—not youth, nor wealth, nor lordship, nor bodily health, nor wisdom, nor life, nor fame—can escape the ruin and dominion of Time. Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch (Francesco Petrarca), the author of the poem being commented upon</note> then adds the next sentiment, saying that it must also be said that from those who are less good—and not to those who are more worthy—is taken away not only the outward body, which Time dissolves in a very brief space, but beyond this, their eloquence, their works, and their talents. Whence he says:

<margin>H</margin>
->And taken from the less good, it is not given to the more worthy;<-
->And not only the outward form does time dissolve;<-
->But your eloquences and your talents.<-

<margin>I</margin>
In the preceding verses, our graceful poet wishes to silently sweep away a vain hope and fantasy held by many: those who persuade themselves that through any minimal knowledge of letters they can acquire immortal fame. He says that for those who are less good and less worthy, everything is taken away at once in death—not just the body, but the works of their talent and their eloquence. And likewise their studies, although this does not happen to the more worthy; for a certain time after death, their fame is prolonged. These aforementioned verses can also be interpreted otherwise: that is, for those who have been less good in works pertaining to the political life or the Christian religion, their body, their fame, and their learning are taken away together. But those who have been more worthy, making themselves dignified by doing good—because they are restored among the blessed spirits—their fame is always very well known among them for their deeds among men at least, even though the body has been taken from them in the present life. The poet finally concludes with the last sentiment, which he says pertains to this examination of the intellect, saying that the voice, continuing further, said that as Time flees—as shown above—it leads and turns the world with it; it never stops nor ever returns. Nor does it ever seem to cease working against men until it has led them back to their beginning and made them return to a little dust. Whence he says:

<margin>K</margin>
->So fleeing, it turns the world with it;<-
->Nor does it ever rest, or stop, or return,<-
->Until it has led us back into a little dust.<-

<margin>L</margin>
Among all the recounted sentiments, none is more worthy or more fruitful for the salvation of man than this one, which our Messer Francesco has expressed with such grace in the preceding verses. To understand this, one must know that our first and true perfection consists mostly in understanding the truth, which certainly cannot be grasped if first a man does not strive to know himself, as we said at the beginning. To this self-knowledge, nothing leads more quickly than the universal natural law: that everything which has a beginning must return to that beginning; and after this, to see and understand that our ultimate end and final conversion is dust and earth. Whence we can truly conclude that our beginning was earth, and we ourselves likewise are earth. Understanding this truth, and even knowing it, the ancient Egyptians <note>original: "egyptii"</note>, in perpetual memory of their earthy and muddy origin, used to hold in their hands in their sacrifices live grass gathered in the marshes—as if it were close and akin to our nature. Likewise, the neighboring Ethiopians <note>original: "Ethio"</note> testify to this same thing, who among the other praises of their homeland that they claim for themselves, say they were the first men to be born from the earth. This <term>opinion</term> <note>original: "snia," an abbreviation for the Latin *sententia*</note> undoubtedly...

It emphasizes that human life begins as earth and must return to dust, a truth the author claims was recognized by ancient Egyptians and Ethiopians.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s "Triumph of Time." Having established that all physical things decay, the commentator now uses biblical and classical authority to prove that humanity’s very substance—earth and clay—is destined to return to its origin, despite the temporary illusions of worldly fame.</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF TIME

<margin>V</margin> It is truly affirmed by Moses—as we said above regarding the beginning of Genesis—that God formed man from "earthly mud" <note>original: "limo terreno"</note> and breathed into him the spirit of life. From this, I believe without a doubt, came the argument for the celebrated fable of Prometheus fashioning man. Nor was this only the opinion of the Hebrews, Christians, Egyptians, and Ethiopians; but Parmenides first, then Hesiod <note>original: "Exiodo"</note>, and afterward Archelaus of Miletus and Zeno of Elea—most illustrious philosophers—said that the earth was the principle of every thing produced in the world. Hence, man is primarily a tiller, cultivator, and inhabitant of the earth. **Therefore Isaiah speaks best in his sixty-fourth chapter**, demonstrating our earthly nature by speaking toward God and saying: *“And now, Lord, you are our father; we are the clay, and you are our maker; and we are all the work of your hands.”* <note>original Latin: "Et nūc dñe pater noster es tu: nos autem lutum: tu factor noster & opera manuū tuarum omnes."</note> Jeremiah also deplores this same fact in the last chapter of his *Lamentations*, showing us to be entirely mud, saying: *“The precious sons of Zion, once clothed in gold, how they are now regarded as earthen vessels, the work of the hands of the potter!”* <note>original Latin: "Filij syō iclyti amicti auro: quōmodo reputati sunt in vasa terrea opus manuū figuli?"</note> But certainly he explains it much more clearly in the twenty-second chapter when, speaking and prophesying universally to all men and showing them to be of earthly existence, he says: *“Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord.”* <note>original Latin: "Terra terra audi uerbum dñi."</note>

<margin>N</margin> What opinion, then, is more certain and true than that men are earth? It is observed by the opinions of the Gentiles, celebrated by philosophers, pronounced by poets, and approved by experience. Rightly, then, Time and the Sun do not cease to revolve and transmute this human nature until they have led us back to our origin and our beginning, which is but a tiny bit of dust. Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> now responds to a silent objection of the ignorant—those who, seeing that the fame of many men has been prolonged, cannot believe that fame is subject to Time. He says that it should be no marvel, since human glory has such a multitude of "horns" <note>An idiom for many-faceted strengths or pretensions</note>; if it takes a little longer than the usual failing of other things to break them all, let whoever wishes think or speak as they like, and let the common people imagine what they will; for if our life were not so brief and did not fail so quickly, we would certainly see all those glories return to smoke and dust. Thus he says:

<margin>O</margin> For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, one must primarily know that the multitude of writers is so great, and the diligence of men in acquiring honor is so vast, that everyone—wishing to prove their own genius—takes it upon themselves to describe histories or even to compose poems. From this, both they and those they celebrate acquire praise, reputation, and glory, which causes this worldly fame to be somewhat prolonged. And this is especially because men, seeing themselves die so soon, strive through these intellectual exercises to achieve a longer-lasting name. Whereas, if their life were more enduring, we would see—before it ended—that in a short time much of the great fame of excellent men would return to smoke as books were lost or corroded.

<margin>P</margin> And secondly, if life were longer, men would care less about prolonging themselves through fame, since they would be satisfied by the length of their own life. Having expressed these excellent sentiments up to this point, Messer Francesco now adds what he did next, what state he entered, and what object then appeared to him. He says that having heard this worthy and grave reasoning, he gave it full and indubitable faith. For it is one's duty never to contradict the truth in any part, but to render to it faith and belief. And so, doing this, the poet—in the considerations and thoughts that followed—saw all our glory to be like snow held against the rays of the sun. And he consequently saw Time, in its rotation, bring back with it such and so many prizes of mortal names and fame that he truly considered fame and reputation to be of no value—although the common and coarse people do not know or believe this, and cannot comprehend it. Thus he says:

-> Now, because human glory has so many horns, <-
-> It is no great wonder if to break them <-
-> One lingers a bit beyond the usual custom, <-
-> But whatever the common crowd thinks or speaks, <-
-> If our living were not so brief, <-
-> Soon you would see them return to dust. <-

It explains that worldly fame only seems to endure because human life is so short; if we lived longer, we would see even the greatest reputations crumble like "snow in the sun."</summary>

# CHAPTER ONE

<margin>
Q
¶ One cannot, nor should one, nor does one want to doubt that the dignity and excellence of the truth is such that it should not be resisted in any way. This is not difficult to understand, as truth, wherever it is found, is the work of the Holy Spirit. Christ himself affirms that he is the supreme truth; and besides this, there is the excellent teaching of Jesus Sirach <note>Also known as the Book of Ecclesiasticus.</note> in the fourth chapter of the Ecclesiasticus.
</margin>

> *Hearing this, because one must never*
> *Oppose the truth, but give it perfect faith,*
> *Let all our glory go like snow in the sun;*
> *And I saw time leading away such prey*
> *Of your names; that I held them for nothing,*
> *Though the people do not know this, nor believe it.*

where it says: <term>“Do not contradict the word of truth in any way.”</term> <note>original Latin: "Non contradicas verbo veritatis ullo modo."</note> And in chapter thirty-seven it is written: <term>“Before all works, let a true word go before you.”</term> <note>original Latin: "ante omnia opera verbum verax precedat te."</note> Aristotle confirms this same thing in the first book of his *Ethics* when he said that truth is to be preferred over friendship. In his seventh book, along with Cicero in his book *On Friendship*, he attributes great dignity to truth, especially when speaking against his father and teacher, Plato, saying: <term>“But for the defense of the truth, it is necessary to oppose even one’s own [friends]; this is perhaps more expected of philosophers; for since both are friends, it is a pious duty to prefer the truth in honor.”</term> <note>original Latin: "Sed pro defensione veritatis etiam propria oppugnare oportere..." – This is the source of the famous phrase "Plato is my friend, but truth is a better friend."</note> <margin>R</margin> ¶ And by observing this excellent principle, the poet confesses the truth and affirms that all our glory vanishes through the course of time. Deservedly, then, this "prey" of names and fame is led away by time and the swift passing of the years. On this point, Cicero, in *The Dream of Scipio*, introducing Scipio Africanus speaking to his grandson Emiliano, writes these worthy words relevant to our purpose: <term>“You see indeed in what narrow limits your glory seeks to spread itself; and as for those who speak of you, how long will they speak? Even if the future generations of men desire to pass down the praises of each of us received from our fathers to their descendants, yet because of the floods and fires of the earth—which must happen at certain times—we are unable to achieve even long-lasting glory, let alone eternal glory.”</term> <note>original Latin: "Cernit profecto quantis in angustijs se vestra gloria dilatari velit..."</note> And near the end, a little further down, he adds: <term>“All that talk is hemmed in by the narrowness of those regions you see; it was never everlasting for anyone; it is buried by the death of men and extinguished by the oblivion of posterity.”</term> <note>original Latin: "Sermo autem omnis ille angustijs cingitur..."</note> <margin>S</margin> ¶ Therefore, in truth, what greater foolishness can we commit than to hope for a thing whose destruction is inevitable? It cannot be repaired by any worldly power, nor can it help us in any part, neither in life nor in death, being an external thing irrelevant to our nature and the salvation of the soul. But if someone should say: "Should good fame then be despised for this reason?" I do not say this; but I do affirm that it should not be desired beyond what is due. That is, fame should be loved in respect to its cause, which is to act holily and virtuously. Thus, virtue should not be valued for the sake of worldly glory and fame; but on the contrary, fame and a worldly name should be desired for the sake of the virtue from which they are born. <margin>T</margin> ¶ The poet then exclaims against the common people, who do not know or believe that the turning of time must obscure fame, saying: "O how blind and vain they are; and how the common people feed and play in the wind, nurturing themselves on a false opinion, judging that dying in old age is much more to be desired than dying in infancy or in the first cradle." O how many are those who died happy in their swaddling clothes, and how many are the miserable ones who died in extreme old age! Indeed, it is the opinion of some that only those are blessed who are never born into the world or have never been. Hence he says:

<margin>
V
¶ Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it is primarily important to know that the reasoning and foundation of the common people for determining and saying that length of life is a good is this: that living is a good because it is an effect of nature, and nature always intends the good, being regulated by an intelligence that does not err...
</margin>

> *Blind people; who always play in the wind,*
> *And feed themselves on false opinions,*
> *Praising death in old age more than in the cradle.*
> *How many happy ones have already died in swaddling clothes;*
> *How many miserable in extreme old age?*
> *Someone says: blessed is he who is not born.*

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s "Triumph of Time." The previous page established truth as the highest value, citing Aristotle and Cicero to argue that the vanity of worldly fame must yield to the reality of time’s passage. The text now moves into a philosophical debate regarding whether a long life or an early death is more beneficial to the human soul.</meta>

->THE TRIUMPH OF TIME<-

# THE TRIUMPH OF TIME

...wherefore, the longer one participates in a good thing, the more praiseworthy that state is. Furthermore, since fame is a good and desirable thing, and cannot be acquired if a man's life is not prolonged, for these reasons living until old age is <margin>X</margin> determined by the common people to be much better than dying in swaddling clothes <note>A common Renaissance idiom for infancy.</note>. 

But how much this opinion is founded on error is not difficult to understand. For it must be presupposed as a foundation that every good and every human delight of man is to be judged with respect to the soul, as the ultimate end and a thing much more perfect, according to the doctrine of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> in the sixth book of the *Politics*, who says: <term>“Everything that is imperfect exists for the sake of that which is better.”</term> <note>original Latin: "omne enim quod imperfectum est: est melioris gratia."</note> From which foundation it follows that once the delight of the soul is seen and possessed, one should not care for that of the body; because if the body, as a distinct part, were to join with the pleasure of the soul, being deformed, it would have to diminish it; as is the rule finally demonstrated by the Calculator <note>Richard Swineshead, a 14th-century English mathematician and philosopher nicknamed "The Calculator" for his work on logic and physics.</note> and <margin>Y</margin> taken by others as a foundation. 

This most true presupposition standing—first according to the opinion of Plato and many Gentiles <note>In this context, "Gentiles" refers to the pre-Christian pagan philosophers.</note>, which is that the eternal soul descends from heaven and returns to heaven always filled with the same habits—it is manifest that by death in swaddling clothes one first achieves the supreme good of the soul, which is to return to heaven and contemplate divine things. And afterwards one escapes the miseries and troubles in which one participates during the process of life through the contagion of the body; wherefore it is much better to participate in the same good without suffering any punishment or distress than to possess the same thing complicated with bitterness. 

And if we still wish to subject the soul to divine justice because of sin, as Virgil describes in the seventh <note>Likely an error in the original text; Virgil describes the purification of souls in Book VI of the *Aeneid*.</note>, it is still better to judge dying in that age where sin does not occur. This same thing is indubitable in the Christian religion: for the voluntary passion of Christ acquired so much merit for our souls that through baptism, purging original sin, they are in such a state of innocence that dying then, a small thing <unclear>suffices for the</unclear> penance in Purgatory in satisfaction for the sin of Adam transmitted to us; as if by a swift passage, they immediately fly to heaven. There they escape every grave danger of sin which they might <margin>Z</margin> acquire through the length of living. 

Wherefore it is a very well-known thing for these reasons: that dying in swaddling clothes is much better and safer than prolonging a miserable and calamitous life. And therefore Cicero, comprehending this sentiment, confirms it to be true through many examples. Thus, in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, he tells of Hegesias the Cyrenaic, who, through express and effective reasons—arguing that prolonging life was the worst thing—induced so many men to kill themselves that teaching that doctrine was forbidden to him in his kingdom by Ptolemy, King of Egypt. To which Cicero adds his own opinion in these words: <term>“Certainly, if we had died sooner, death would have taken us from evils, not from goods.”</term> <note>original Latin: "Certe si ante obissemus: mors nos a malis: non a bonis obtraxisset."</note> And then he enumerates how many troubles happened to Metellus, Priam, and Pompey. All of which he says they would have escaped if they had died in their swaddling clothes or at least in their youth. 

And finally he introduces the <margin>A</margin> example of Cleobis and Biton, sons of the priestess Argia; who, having been pious toward their mother in having carried her on their shoulders to the temple, and she, for this piety, having prayed to the goddess that she grant them the greatest reward that can be given to men—they, having dined with their mother and then gone to sleep, were found dead the next morning. Then Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> adds that this same thing happened by their own prayer to Trophonius and Agamedes. Having built a temple to Apollo, and asking him for the reward that was the best among all others that could ever happen to all other men, after the prayer, on the third day they were found dead. 

By these <margin>B</margin> examples, then, according to the context of Tully, it is argued that if death is that best thing that can happen to men in the world, then the sooner it is achieved, the greater the happiness must be esteemed. Therefore, a death that occurs in swaddling clothes is much more to be judged happy than one which arrives in extreme old age. 

It also seems likewise <margin>C</margin> that Cicero does not reprove the sentiment of Silenus; who, being captured by Midas, King of Illyria, having nothing else to ransom himself with but his learning, told the king some excellent precepts. One: that the best thing that could happen to a man was not to be born. The other: that the next best thing to not being born was to die immediately. Wherefore Tully says: <term>“A certain story is also told of Silenus, who...”</term> <note>original Latin: "Fertur etiam de sileno fabella quaedam: que..."</note>

<summary>This page presents a philosophical and theological argument that an early death (infancy) is preferable to a long life, as it preserves the soul's purity and grants quicker access to heaven. The author synthesizes Christian doctrine on baptism with classical examples from Cicero and Greek mythology to illustrate that life is primarily a source of misery and potential sin.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Petrarch’s "Triumph of Time," specifically addressing the argument that a long life is a blessing. The previous page established that the soul’s well-being is the ultimate measure of any "good." Here, the author provides classical and scriptural counter-arguments, suggesting that an early death is often preferable to a long, miserable life, and that worldly fame is merely a fleeting "second death."</meta>

# CHAPTER ONE

<margin>D</margin>
...when <note>The text refers to the satyr Silenus, a companion of the god Dionysus.</note> had been captured by Midas, it is written that he gave the king this gift in exchange for his release: he taught him that for a man not to be born is by far the best thing; or, [the next best] is to die as soon as possible. <note>original Latin: "sum a Mida captus esset: hoc ei muneris pro sua missione dedisse scribitur: docuisse regē non nasci homiē longe optimum est: est primum aut quā primū mori."</note> This same point is confirmed by the poet **Euripides**, who teaches us to weep at the birth of men and to sing at their death. And likewise, *Crantor* <note>original: "Erātore," likely referring to the Academic philosopher Crantor, famous for his treatise "On Grief."</note>, consoling *Theramenes* <note>original: "Termāeo elysio."</note> on the death of his son, writes these verses: **Ignorant men wander in their minds through life. [Euthynous] <note>original: "Euchinous."</note> possesses death as a gift of the fates. Thus it was more useful for life to be finished, both for you and for him.** 

Nevertheless, if these witnesses were to be suspected in this cause because of religion, let us at least accept the judgment of **Job**, who was a simple and just man, fearing God and turning away from evil deeds. Considering the condition of human misery and lamenting to God, he says in the tenth chapter: **Why did you bring me out of the womb? Oh, that I had been consumed so that no eye had seen me! I should have been as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the tomb.** <note>Job 10:18-19.</note> And in the third chapter, he seems to have concluded the same, saying: **May the day perish on which I was born, and the night in which it was said, "A man is conceived."** <note>Job 3:3.</note>

<margin>E</margin>
Through these words, we can clearly enough comprehend how miserable and calamitous is this length and prolongation of life. It remains now only to respond to the arguments which are built in confusion due to the ambiguity of this term "to live." For by "to live" we can understand only the existence of animated things, according to what **Aristotle** writes in the second book of *On the Soul* when he says: **To live is the being of living things.** <note>original Latin: "Viuere viuētibus est esse."</note> And yet, by "to live" we can understand not only "being," but the duration and prolongation of it.

<margin>F</margin>
I say then that the first kind of "living" is a good and is to be desired, but not the second—not any more than what might be the will of God. Nor do wild beasts and men, in fleeing death, defend the "length" of living; rather, they only teach us to maintain "being" through the natural appetite found in all things, both rational and irrational. Secondary to this is the way in which fame is a good and is to be desired, as has been made quite manifest above. Thus, the answer to the second argument remains quite clear. 

Afterward, *Messer Francesco* <note>Petrarch.</note> brings a more manifest declaration through a noble question, saying: "Come now, tell me; let the crowd, accustomed to the greatest errors, answer. Behold, after a long age and a great prolongation of life, let the name be clear and famous; what is this fame in the end, that is so prized, so sought after, and so greatly praised?" Wherefore he says:

> But for the crowd accustomed to great errors
> After a long age, let the name be clear;
> What is this then, that is so prized?

<margin>G</margin>
<margin>Think a little, with mature examination, upon this wise and noble question: who is more greedy and desirous of this smoke and thin mist of the world? He who can answer truly and with justice will see clearly that he is constrained to confess that fame is nothing other than an easy and swift path to perdition. He will answer that worldly glory is nothing other than a means, very often, to make oneself unhappy when it is desired in a disordered way. This is what happened to Brutus, who for the glory of just government killed his own sons, whereby he became unhappy, as **Virgil** demonstrates in the sixth book, saying: **And the proud soul of the avenger Brutus: to see the rods of office regained? This man, as consul, will be the first to receive the authority and the cruel axes; and the father will call his sons, who are stirring up new wars, to punishment for the sake of beautiful liberty—unhappy man.** <note>Aeneid 6.817-822. Brutus helped expel the Tarquin kings from Rome but executed his own sons for conspiring to bring them back.</note></margin>

<margin>H</margin>
And therefore, in confirmation of this, **Augustine** says in the fifth book of *The City of God*: **For the desire for glory is better resisted, without a doubt, than it is believed; each person is more like God as they are cleaner of this filth.** <note>original Latin: "Glorie enim cupiditati melius resistitur sine dubitatiōe quā credatur: tanto quisq; est deo similior: quanto z hac immunditia mundior."</note> Because of this, in the thirteenth chapter of the same book, he teaches us to set aside this perverse appetite, saying: **Take away the boasting; what are men but men?** <note>original Latin: "Tolle iactantiam quid homines sunt nisi homines?"</note> 

What is it, then, that is so highly prized? What is this that is so esteemed? Certainly, it is nothing other than fables, wind, shadows, and confused dreams. Therefore, the poet finally adds that this time—greedy and miserly with mortal fame—conquers so much; turning itself around with the revolving of the heavens, it takes back [what it gave]. This thing called fame is nothing other than a "second death," nor can any remedy be found or given for this any more than for death itself. For these reasons, time in this way leads glory away and triumphs over the names of men, over fame, and likewise over the world. Wherefore he says:

--- Page 670 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Petrarch’s "Triumph of Time," shifting from the inevitability of decay to the final "Triumph of Divinity." The previous text explored how human life and fame are ultimately erased by the passage of years. Here, the commentator concludes the section on Time and introduces the final section of the work, which addresses the eternal nature of God and the soul's ultimate destination.</meta>

->TRIUMPH OF TIME<-

# THE TRIUMPH OF TIME

<margin>I</margin>
So great is the doctrine enclosed in these verses and their life-saving warning: that whoever wishes to turn their mind toward understanding the truth will see that they contain every rule and every form of living. Therefore:

> So much does greedy time conquer and take back:
> It is called fame; and it is a second death;
> Nor against the first is there any defense:
> Thus time triumphs over names and the world.

Through these lines, it is affirmed as a truth that humans cannot create any effective defense against either physical death or the eventual loss of worldly fame. Understanding that the human soul is immortal and was produced for blessedness as its ultimate goal, it follows that this goal should be reasonably loved. No one can be happy if they do not first enjoy the thing they love. For this reason, these verses show that nothing pertaining to the physical life of man or the fame acquired in the world can be the cause of our salvation. Since each of these things is shown by the cited verses to fail irremediably, they signal to us that it is necessary to seek another object—one that perpetually gladdens the intellect and perfects the mind. If we wish to seek this, we find in the fifteenth chapter of *The City of God* <note>A foundational work of Christian philosophy by St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD).</note> that this object is God. Speaking of this, Augustine says: *For it is God who makes us happy, which is the true wealth of minds.* <note>original Latin: "Deus eni felices facit que est mentium vera opulentia."</note> Once mortal things are neglected, fame is despised, and death is no longer feared, the soul returns to find its likeness: the one by whose infinite mercy its species was first created to enjoy and possess eternal nature.

## EXPOSITION ON THE TRIUMPH OF DIVINITY

<margin>K</margin>
The abyss and the depth of Holy Scripture brings such great confusion and such great wonder to the minds of men that the eyes of the intellect, blinded and confused, leave one stunned on the path of seeking. This is especially true when a man strives to investigate those things which exceed reasonable sobriety and the capacity of our intellect. Just as the light of the sun leads to greater blindness for those who stare at it most stubbornly, so the intellectual light clouds the mind of those who try to extend themselves further than their strengths can understand. Therefore, I understand with great reason that I should now be restrained from proceeding further. Because the matter described in the following "Triumph" by our poet <note>Referring to Francesco Petrarch, the author of the "Triumphs."</note> is of such a nature that it can neither be comprehended by the intellect nor appropriately explained by the tongue; yet it determines the nature of eternity and the universal divine judgment which must precede it.

<margin>L</margin>
I would certainly suspend my work and no longer be so bold as to provide an exposition, but three reasons force me to follow through against my own judgment and will. The first is because the Holy Scripture and the doctrine contained in this present Triumph are of such a nature and disposition by divine grace that in its sea the lamb may walk and the elephant may swim. <note>A classic theological metaphor: the Bible is simple enough for the "lamb" (the simple believer) to navigate, yet deep enough for the "elephant" (the great scholar) to find a challenge.</note> Therefore, even the lowliness of my small wit will manifest as much as it can comprehend, leaving the high and deep speculations to those men whose intellect flies like an eagle above the mountain peaks. The second reason is to not leave these "vigils" <note>The author refers to his scholarly labors as "vigils," or late-night studies.</note> of ours interrupted; rather, it is the universal desire of all ordered appetites to bring our work, with every strength and diligence, to that proper end to which the small capacity of our weak intellect can lead us. The third and final reason is the trust placed in my soul by the hope I have in the humanity and mercy of those who will read these things.

<margin>M</margin>
For I believe they will judge that this was not audacity or temerity on my part, but rather a burning desire to communicate my labors to others as best I can. Strengthened and confirmed by these reasons, we shall begin the exposition of this worthy, admirable, and glorious Triumph, placed by our poet in the sixth and final position. The human soul, which has already been noted above to vary in five states, can provide an account of itself to this world since it is united to the body and has consented to the empire of appetite and reason. From there, it is separated by death, celebrated by fame, and finally obscured by the length of time...

<summary>The author transitions from the "Triumph of Time," which erases worldly fame, to the "Triumph of Divinity," acknowledging the difficulty of explaining the eternal and divine. He justifies his commentary by arguing that spiritual truths are accessible to both the simple and the learned.</summary>
