<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final sequence of Petrarch’s "Triumphs." Having concluded the "Triumph of Time," the text now transitions to the "Triumph of Eternity," which the commentator identifies as the "sixth state" of the soul—the ultimate immutability after the Final Judgment.</meta>

# CHAPTER ONE

To the most high day of divine judgment, which is followed by all-encompassing eternity, the soul is led to the state of **immutability** <term>immutability: a state of being unchangeable and eternal</term>. In this state, having been reunited with the body by divine will, it is necessary that—based on previous merits—it either dwells forever in heaven or, because of past sins, is perpetually tormented in hell. This occurs through the virtue, efficacy, and power of that fair sentence and just judgment which the eternal Judge must pass upon men. He, who liberated us from the demon with his own blood, left and wrote down in his deeds, operations, and words a complete path and a life-saving law. Whoever proceeds by this law is led to the eternal life restored to us through his death; and whoever deviates from it wanders without hope into the abyss of death, which kills living sinners without end and torments the dead. Therefore, the final subject of this triumph is the **sixth state** <note>Petrarch’s poem is structured in six "Triumphs": Love, Chastity, Death, Fame, Time, and finally Eternity.</note> of the perpetual soul, which it must attain after it has been judged by God.

<margin>N</margin> ¶ Here, Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch (1304–1374), the author of the poem.</note> introduces eternity and infinite measure to dominate and extinguish Time, just as in the previous triumph he described Time overcoming and taking away all the fame of men. From this, by showing that every "transmutation" <note>In this context, the shifting and changing nature of earthly life.</note> must cease, he teaches those who consider it well to dispose themselves toward eternal salvation. He suggests that without any doubt, whoever observes these discrete precepts can be assured that the cruel, horrendous, and terrible sentence will not fall upon them. 

Because there are three foundations upon which our salvation consists—namely **Faith, Hope, and Charity**—the Apostle <note>St. Paul the Apostle.</note> says when exhorting the Corinthians in chapter 13: *And now remain Faith, Hope, and Charity, these three.* <note>original Latin: "Nunc autem manet Fides Spes & Charitas haec tria"</note> Through this, Messer Francesco demonstrates that these three virtues are within him, since he has been turned away from the error of the world and called back to have faith, to hope, and to love God in order to be happy. As Augustine testifies in the eighth book of *The City of God*, chapter two, when he says: *He is the True God with whom alone, in whom alone, and from whom alone the rational and intellectual soul is blessed.* <note>original Latin: "Verus deus est cum quo solo & in quo solo & de quo solo anima rationalis & intellectualis beata est." The OCR "Vetus" (Ancient) is likely a transcription error for "Verus" (True).</note> Since the first door to enter into divine grace is Faith, as the Apostle shows in Hebrews 11 when he says: *Without faith it is impossible to please God* <note>original Latin: "Sine fide impossibile est deo placere"</note>; for this reason, Messer Francesco says principally that he has placed his faith in God alone, since man can trust in nothing else of this world.

->As befits a religious and prudent soul, giving a beginning to<-
->his subject matter, Messer Francesco says that since<-
->he saw nothing else comprised within the<-
->circumference of heaven that was<-
->stable or firm, having turned back into himself and<-
->to his own knowledge, wisely<-
->asking himself, he says in his<-
->song: "In whom can I trust<-
->from now on?" Thus<-

<header>CHAPTER ONE</header>
<sig>iiy</sig>

# THE TRIUMPH OF DIVINITY.

<margin>O</margin>
After I saw that under heaven there is
no thing 
stable and firm; completely dismayed, 
I turned and said: "Look in whom 
you place your trust!"

<margin>O</margin>
¶ The preceding verses contain life-saving instruction <note>original: *saluifero documento*. The commentator views Petrarch's poetry as a moral and spiritual guide.</note>. To understand them, one must know that to seek out and investigate the discourse and experience of worldly things is a work of **prudence**, provided they are tested with measure and careful examination. Solomon himself testified to having done this at the beginning of *Ecclesiastes* <note>Ecclesiastes 1:13: "I applied my mind to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done under heaven."</note>. This was also the life's work of the **philosophers**: to find and conclude that God is entirely immobile and the Supreme Good, seeing that every other thing is mutable and subject to change. From this, they concluded that such things could not be the "Supreme." <margin>P</margin> Therefore, the prudent man should exercise himself in this examination; having found the ultimate end and the highest good, he must fix himself upon it and never look back, just like Lot’s wife <note>A biblical reference to Genesis 19:26; looking back at the worldly city of Sodom resulted in her destruction, symbolizing a soul returning to sin or worldly vanity.</note>. Nor should he stop at any transmutable thing until he reaches that which is entirely permanent, which is God. The poet demonstrates that he followed this process in the previous verses: he did not remain fixed in any mutable thing, but, dismayed by them, he asks himself with fear upon what object he should now place his faith. Having made such a worthy and just inquiry—one might almost call it a self-reprimand—the poet responds appropriately, as befits the perfection of a soul, saying that he now has no faith except in that Lord who never failed His promise to those who have placed their faith in Him. Thus he says:

<margin>Q</margin>
I replied: "In the Lord, who has never 
failed a promise to those who trust in Him."

<margin>Q</margin>
¶ A wise, golden, and celebrated response! How could our poet have responded better or more appropriately than to trust in Him who never fails a promise made to the faithful? That is, in our Redeemer and head, Jesus Christ. Oh, let man consider how great the maintenance of divine promises has been from the beginning! In the beginning, He created us to possess everlasting delights. Then, when the blind ignorance of our ancestors <note>Adam and Eve</note> caused them to be justly deprived of original divine justice through their error, did not the **Divine Word** <term>the Word</term> <note>original: *verbo diuino*. In Christian theology, the "Word" (Logos) refers to Jesus Christ as the second person of the Trinity.</note> humble Himself to the earth, come in the flesh, submit to human suffering, and obey death at the hands of ungrateful sinners? O Divine Love! Nothing other than love led Him to die. Who, then, can doubt that His promises, founded in love, will be fulfilled? Who can reasonably believe them to be fallacious? Certainly no one, unless they possess a clouded and depraved intellect. "Divine love does not permit Him to be without fruit," <note>original: *Diuinus amor no pmitit eum ſine germine eſſe* from Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Divine Names*.</note> and this love is directed toward the salvation of the whole earth. Zephaniah declares this in the third chapter, saying: *"For in the fire of my jealousy all the earth shall be devoured: for then I will restore to the people a chosen lip, so that they may all call upon the name of the Lord and serve Him with one shoulder."* <note>original: *In igne enim zeli mei devorabitur omnis terra...* Zephaniah 3:8-9.</note> Furthermore, did not Christ Jesus Himself promise this same love with His own mouth in Saint Matthew, chapter 11, when He says: *"Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you"*? <note>original: *Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis...* Matthew 11:28.</note> and in Saint John, chapter 6: *"He who comes to me I will not cast out."* <note>original: *Eum qui ad me veniet non eyciam foras.* John 6:37.</note> Does He not affirm Himself to be the Good Shepherd, who lays down His life for His sheep? The Apostle Paul also confirms the same, exhorting the Ephesians in the fourth chapter <note>Though cited as chapter 4, this quote is from Ephesians 2:19-21.</note> when he says: *"Now you are no longer guests and strangers, but you are citizens with the saints and members of God's household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone: in whom the whole structure, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord."* <margin>R</margin> Christ, therefore, is He in whom we, along with our poet, must have faith. Christ maintains His promises; Christ assists our weak being in such a way that we might deservedly say with Saint Ambrose: *"Christ has become all things to us: if you burn with fever, He is a fountain; if you have a wound, He is a doctor; if you fear death, He is life; if you need help, He is strength; if you seek food, He is nourishment."* <note>original: *Oia nobis factus ē chriſtus...* This famous passage from St. Ambrose emphasizes Christ's total sufficiency for human needs.</note> Therefore, putting aside earthly things, the poet invites us to have faith in Christ. He then adds...

The text draws heavily on the Bible (Solomon, Zephaniah, Matthew, John, Paul) and Church Fathers (Dionysius, Ambrose) to reinforce the reliability of divine love.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on the Triumph of Divinity to the Triumph of Time. <header>THE TRIUMPH OF TIME</header>

# THE TRIUMPH OF TIME

*summary: [The poet] determines from this hour forward that Time itself conquers and darkens the fame acquired from the present life, saying that since he had seen in the past and saw clearly in the present the flight and sudden escape of the great planet of the sun <note>In the Ptolemaic system, the Sun was considered a planet whose movement measured the passage of time.</note>, through which he has received the greatest harms and deceptions; looking again intently, he saw a people walking very quietly, fearing neither time nor its rapid velocity. This people and company were under the protection and guard of historians and also of poets. Whence he says:*

<margin>A</margin> *¶ Concerning the understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known that Messer Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch), the author of the poem.</note> intends by this "people"—whom he says do not fear time nor its most cruel rage—those men who are dead and celebrated through fame. Thus he writes that they proceed with silence to demonstrate how they have been occupied by death. Therefore, for this reason, they no longer care for anything that pertains to the present life, nor are they further subjected to the celestial revolutions <note>The movement of the spheres/planets which governs time and physical change.</note>; therefore they no longer fear time nor its rapid and swift circling. They are then given into the guard of poets and historians, since each of these authors records and describes the virtuous deeds performed by men in the present life.*

> **After I had seen, and see clearly,**
> **the flying and the fleeing of the great planet;**
> **whence I have suffered much harm and deception.**
> **I saw a people walking very quietly**
> **Without fear of time or its rage;**
> **For a historian or a poet had them in their guard.**

<margin>B</margin> *And therefore they endure and are guarded by them for as long as the books of histories and poems written by them endure. ¶ And although the poet and the historian write differently—because the poet feigns certain things <note>Uses metaphor or allegory.</note> to better explain certain effects of the soul, and the historian writes only that which is contained in the truth of history—nonetheless, they agree in this: that each truly records the virtuous works through which fame is acquired in this world. Messer Francesco then adds what the disposition of the dead and famous men is in respect to living men, saying that it seems they are much more envied than any other generation upon the earth. The reason is that through their own virtuous deeds they have raised themselves to the glorious value of fame, emerging from the common cage of this earthly dwelling and the common life of the unskilled masses. Whence he says:*

<margin>C</margin> *¶ Whoever diligently considers the description of Envy given by Ovid at the end of the second book of the Metamorphoses <note>Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.760-832, where Envy is depicted as a withered, venomous creature in a sunless cave.</note> will see with good reason in this place that our elegant poet has described how envy is borne toward famous men.*

> **Of them it seems more envy is felt than for others:**
> **For by themselves they have taken flight**
> **Emerging from the common cage.**

*Envy is primarily described as inhabiting subterranean caves, where the light of the sun does not penetrate in any way, pale and obscure, wrapped in dense mist. Therefore, virtuous and famous men come to possess contrary qualities in life and in death; by distancing themselves from the nature of <margin>D</margin> lazy men, they excite their minds and move them to envy. ¶ There is, therefore, nothing more contrary to envy than the fame of men; for fame always extends itself into the sunlight, and every day becomes clearer and more known. Thus, those who cannot acquire fame through their own virtue are first provoked to admiration by the examples of others, <margin>E</margin> and then to envy. ¶ Secondly, the greatest envy is borne toward the dead and famous; for when one finds oneself in some danger or strange adversity, one considers that men of the past are exempt from worldly misfortunes. Thus, one judges their state to be much better than the present life, and therefore envy is borne toward them. Just as in the first book of the Aeneid, Virgil clearly shows when he introduces Aeneas in his great wandering, lamenting and saying:* <note>The text cuts off here, but refers to Aeneas's speech in Aeneid 1.94-96: "O thrice and four times happy, those who had the luck to die before their fathers' eyes below the walls of Troy!"</note>

<header>CHAPTER ONE</header>

### CHAPTER ONE

...saying: *Immediately Aeneas’s limbs are loosened with cold. He groans, and stretching both palms to the stars, he speaks thus: "O thrice and four times blessed, whose lot it was to die before the faces of their fathers under the high walls of Troy! O Diomedes, bravest of the Grecian race! Why could I not have fallen on the Trojan plains and poured out this soul by your right hand?"* <note>original: "Extemplo eneæ soluuntur frigore mẽbra..." from Virgil's Aeneid, Book I. Aeneas laments that he did not die a glorious death in battle, which would have secured his fame, rather than perishing in a nameless shipwreck.</note> Since famous men are withdrawn from worldly dangers by death, the poet describes them as no longer caring for time, and notes that they are envied more than others <note>Death "freezes" a person's reputation, protecting it from further worldly mistakes, yet this very permanence makes the living envious of the dead's secure fame.</note>.

<margin>F</margin> Now, since Master Francesco <note>Petrarch, the author.</note> has narrated who those are who proceed quietly and in silence—for their fame is not altered by the celestial revolutions <note>The movement of the planets which dictates the passage of time on Earth.</note>—and because they do not care for time, he adds and demonstrates that the hope of those who believe the aforementioned fame will be eternal is totally in vain. He describes how the length of time extinguishes fame no less than its speed, combined with the operations of the heavens, had previously exterminated life. He says that the one who alone shines among all the planets <note>The Sun.</note> prepared himself with much greater force and resumed an even swifter flight; in this speed, the barley and the fodder for his steeds were doubled <note>A classical metaphor: to make the Sun’s chariot move faster across the sky, its horses are given more food.</note>. And besides this, the Queen—whom we called glorious mortal Fame in the previous Triumph—already wished to separate herself and "divorce" some of those who were with her in her worthy rank and company. Whence he says:

> Against these, he who alone shines,
> Prepared himself with greater effort,
> And resumed a more swift flight:
> For his steeds, the barley was doubled:
> And the queen, of whom I spoke above,
> Already wished to divorce some of her own.

<margin>G</margin> For a clear understanding of the preceding verses, it should primarily be known that, as we said a little while ago, no other planet in the sky possesses its own light except the sun. All others only shine through the reflection of the solar rays that reverberate upon them and the other stars, as if upon the denser parts of the heaven. Secondly, it is to be understood that the poet appropriately says the sun prepares with "greater effort" against Fame than it did previously against the life of men. He says he "doubled the barley" for his steeds to make us understand that human life is much more easily eaten and consumed by even the smallest celestial operation than is his fame. Therefore, it is necessary for the sun to double, triple, quadruple, and multiply its revolutions to extinguish the name and glory of men, compared to what is needed to take away their present life. While it only takes a small change in physical conditions to destroy a life, to obscure fame requires nothing but the vast length of time. Therefore, to express these qualities, he says the sun doubled the barley for his steeds and took a more "expedited flight," the flight of the sun being nothing other than its continuous turning which eventually deprives men of their legacy.

<margin>H</margin> Lastly, it should be noted that the poet adds that Fame—portrayed above as a queen—wished to separate herself from some to demonstrate that, due to the long duration of time, the books of the ancient writers have been corrupted and the knowledge of many most excellent men has failed. This can be seen in our own age, in which many histories are found to be lost, as is understood regarding the works of <term>Quintilian</term><note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, Roman rhetorician.</note>, <term>Curtius</term><note>Quintus Curtius Rufus, historian of Alexander the Great.</note>, <term>Cornelius Tacitus</term><note>Roman historian known for his Annals and Histories.</note>, <term>Justinus</term><note>Latin historian.</note>, <term>Sallust</term><note>Roman historian.</note>, <term>Titus Livius</term><note>Livy, whose massive history of Rome survived only in fragments.</note>, and many other historians of the Latin language. Thus, the fame of many is already beginning to be buried; nothing remains outside the sepulcher except their names, while their works are already consumed by the earth and obscured by time, being totally entombed. Therefore, from such as these, the worldly queen Fame wishes to make a divorce, separation, and departure. After our Master Francesco saw that the sun had resumed a swifter course and prepared for a harder war against the fame of men, he adds—preserving a laudable modesty—certain most worthy and "golden" sentences, saying he had heard them said. He does not report from whom he heard them, but having understood them, he wrote them down.

He wrote and reduced to doctrine. Of these, the first was that in these worldly effects, those things truly and properly called <term>privets</term><note>original: "ligustri"; a type of white-flowered shrub used as a metaphor for fleeting, fragile beauty.</note> are the deep and widest abysses of a blind and shadowed oblivion. <margin>I</margin>
The glorious Plato writes for a clearer understanding of the preceding verses where the generations of <term>fury</term><note>Plato’s concept of "divine madness" or inspiration (theia mania).</note> reside: one which comes from earthly things, a thing truly of blame and shameful, which Cicero also censures in the third book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, because most of the time it arises from pain of the body or passion of the soul. This quality should not fall upon a wise man. The second generation is divine fury, and this is divided into prophecy, mystery, love, and poetry. Hence Master Francesco <note>Petrarch.</note>, wishing in his every act to preserve proper custom and inspiration, attributes the expression of these grave and indubitable maxims to such a fury. And therefore he says he heard them said, but knows not by whom: because this fury is distilled and works within us in a hidden and unknown way.

->I heard it said, I know not by whom, but I wrote the word;<-
->In these human things, properly called privets,<-
->Dark abysses of blind oblivion.<-

<margin>K</margin>
Secondly, it is to be understood that worldly effects are appropriately named privets: because privets are white flowers with very little moisture. Thus they very quickly become languid and withered. Hence Virgil, in his *Bucolics* <note>The *Eclogues*.</note>, wishing to express how youthful beauty fails, introduces the shepherd Corydon speaking to Alexis and saying these words: *O beautiful boy, trust not too much in your color. The white privets fall, the dark hyacinths are gathered.* <note>original: "O formose puer nimium ne crede colori. Alba ligustra cadunt-vacinia nigra leguntur." from Virgil's Eclogues II, 17-18.</note> Finally, it is to be considered that in these worldly effects nothing spreads further than oblivion. Experience teaches us this by considering how great a number of men have passed away, and of how few the memory has remained to us. Wishing to demonstrate this blind oblivion, Solomon says at the beginning of *Ecclesiastes*: *Nothing is new under the sun; nor can anyone say: "Behold, this is new"; for it has already preceded us in the ages that were before us. There is no memory of the former things. But neither shall there be any remembrance of those things that are to come hereafter among those who shall follow.* <note>original: "Nihil sub sole novum..." paraphrasing Ecclesiastes 1:9-11.</note>

<margin>L</margin>
Rightly, then, can we affirm that in this world there are deep abysses of blind oblivion. Master Francesco then recounts the second maxim which he says he heard and knows not from whom, which is that the sun will turn not only individual years, but even <term>lustra</term><note>A period of five years.</note> and the century—which is the victor over every famous, outstanding, and most celebrated man. Likewise, it will turn the lustra and will see those who are presently reputed as illustrious become vain and without fame, name, or recognition. And as proof of this maxim, he adds, saying: "How many were clear and famous between the river Peneus and the river Hebrus <note>Rivers in Greece and Thrace, symbolizing the ancient world.</note>, of whom some have faded and some will soon fail; how many also on the river Xanthus <note>A river near Troy.</note>, and how many still in the valley near the river Tiber <note>The river of Rome.</note>?" Thus he says:

Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it is to be known primarily that the <term>lustrum</term> is defined by writers of the Latin language to signify a period of five years, which had its origin in the counting of five years performed by the people of Rome. Hence our poet intends to argue that the sun is not only fit to consume a year, but even the lus-

->The sun will turn not just years, but lustra,<-
->And centuries, victors over every mind;<-
->And it will see the vanity of these illustrious ones.<-
->How many were famous between Peneus and Hebrus?<-
->Who have faded or will soon fade.<-
->How many on the Xanthus, and how many in the valley of the Tiber?<-

<margin>N</margin>
-tra and every other combination of years; through which revolution and divinity, the century that encompasses them becomes the superior ruler of every celebrated man, however much he may be exalted by fame and made worthy by learned writers. From which, in future centuries, many who are today both famous and illustrious must become vain and without fame. Secondly, it is to be understood that Master Francesco brings forth an excellent example of those who are already obscured between the Hebrus and the Peneus, and on the river Xanthus, and in the valley of the Tiber.

And through the length of time, their fame having been greatly obscured, a very clear argument of this is understood in reviewing histories, in which often the names of some are the only things seen remaining to our knowledge. Then Master Francesco introduces the other sentiment, which he intended by saying that he heard it said that the fame of mortal men was like a doubtful and unstable clear sky in winter, which a very tiny mist breaks and obscures. And because of this, a great and very long span of time is a great, bitter, and deadly poison to great and excellent names. Wherefore he says:

->A doubtful, unstable, and clear winter<-
->Is your fame, and a little mist breaks it;<-
->And great time is great poison to great names.<-

<margin>T</margin> ¶ How rightly this worthy comparison and sentiment is expressed by our poet, and how great is the vanity of those who prize the fame remaining after them as the highest good: it is easier to understand with the mind than to narrate with the tongue. For just as the mist and the clouds break and disturb the serenity of the sky, so a slight cause takes away all or disturbs the fame of men in the world. <margin>V</margin> ¶ Now, is it not true that a small rumor produced by a vile and ignoble person spreads in such a way that it calls into doubt what many other most excellent men have affirmed as true? And likewise, a strange opinion, a false interpretation, or one's own incredulity almost totally extinguishes the ancient fame and opinion of others. <margin>X</margin> ¶ Now, is not the entire and worthy chastity of Penelope almost called into doubt? Only by the opinion of Lycophron, the Greek poet, who affirms she had sexual relations with all the barons who asked her during the absence of Ulysses. Likewise, have opinions not been so diverse concerning Aeneas and Turnus that one cannot distinguish which of them was superior to the other? It being the opinion of many that Aeneas, above the river Numicus, was either killed or forced by everything to throw himself into the river and drown therein. <margin>Y</margin> ¶ Nonetheless, Virgil affirms in the twelfth book that Turnus was killed in battle by Aeneas. There is a very great abundance of similar examples in the histories of the Latin language which, for the sake of brevity, we shall omit; for if these causes do not interrupt fame, time—which is the poison of great names—must necessarily master and extinguish it. The poet continues by narrating another excellent sentiment, saying that beyond these reported sentiments, he already heard it said that all our greatnesses and all our pomp pass away and return to nothing. And similarly, lordships end and kingdoms fail; and finally, time cuts short and interrupts whatever seems to be the most solid mortal thing. Wherefore he says:

> Your triumphs pass, and your pomps:
> Lordships pass; kingdoms pass:
> Time interrupts every mortal thing.

<margin>Z</margin> ¶ For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known that the nature of all things enclosed within the element of fire <note>The "sublunary sphere," which according to ancient and medieval science, was the region of the universe subject to change and decay.</note> was decreed from the beginning of the world to suffer transformation, and at some point to come to an end. Wherefore, not without reason, this worldly region is named by philosophers the "sphere of active and passive things," because within it are placed the elements which, though equal, contain within themselves the primary opposing qualities.

<margin>A</margin> ¶ From this, by natural conclusion, it can be understood that our pomps and greatnesses, depending only on earthly things, are in a short space of time—through the revolution of time—fleeting and transitory. Likewise, states, lordships, and kingdoms; for if this were not understood to be founded upon the natural reason of constant opposing action, experience at least demonstrates it by necessity. Alas, consider well where the greatness of Octavian <note>Augustus Caesar.</note> is at present? The triumphs of Caesar? The glory of Alexander the Macedonian? The reputation of Pyrrhus of Epirus? Where is the pomp of Darius? The riches of Antiochus? The singular virtues of Epaminondas? The supreme and worthy praises of Philopoemen? <note>Epaminondas and Philopoemen were famous Greek generals celebrated for their integrity and military skill.</note> Where is the great Babylon? The power of Carthage? Proud Troy? Where is warlike Thebes? Just Lacedaemon <note>Sparta.</note>? Studious Athens?

<margin>B</margin> ¶ Where, in the end, is triumphant Rome? All have passed away; some leveled to the earth so that no trace remains; others so changed from their former state that they retain no resemblance to their ancient beauty. Alas, look with a steady intellect upon noble Italy alone: where have the great multitude of peoples—once glorious and powerful in themselves—been reduced? The Samnites, Volsci, Latins, Sabines, Caecinenses, Falisci, Bruttians, Lucanians, Hernici, Salentinians: all are changed, all are extinguished, their names humbled and their kingdoms lost.

<margin>C</margin> ¶ Alas, let us consider the process of Greek power: how one kingdom and one lordship has extinguished the other. And first, beginning with those where their glorious dominion took its start: principally, as Justin <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian.</note> writes, at the beginning of kingdoms, power was among the Assyrians in the time of Ninus, who was the first King to maintain dominion over subjugated provinces. The Assyrians lasted about 1,350 years. Then they were extinguished and confounded by the Medes; nor did the Medes remain long in the kingdom, for after nearly 200 years they were defeated and subjugated by the Persians. The Persians likewise did not rule eternally, but being overcome in roughly the same amount of time, they were occupied by the Greeks. Nor were the Greeks of a different nature, nor could they escape coming to an end; in a short space of time, they were forced into servitude by the Romans.

<margin>D</margin> ¶ What shall be said of the kingdom of the Chaldeans? What of the Hebrews? What of the Sicyonians? What of the Argives? What of the Egyptians? What of the Tyrians? What of the Lydians? Of the Trojans? Nothing other than that same thing said of the other kingdoms: that they have failed, been confounded, extinguished, and ultimately uprooted. Nor have only monarchies and kingdoms suffered this variation, but even established republics. For the Athenians, having acquired almost every island between the Pamphylian Sea and that of the Pontus <note>The Black Sea.</note>, had scarcely seventy-two years of space before they were put to flight by the Lacedaemonians. And the Lacedaemonians, having acquired all the Peloponnese as far as Macedonia, were in a short time subjugated by the Thebans. Nor were the Thebans perpetual in their dominion, for in the end, and not far from their beginning, they were defeated by the fierce Macedonians. The Macedonians finally, there being no other republic in Greece to resist them, vanished within thirty years due to their own mutual feuds.

<margin>E</margin> ¶ I am silent regarding the republic of Carthage, and that among our Italians of Locri. I am silent regarding the Campanians, the Tarentines, the Herculaneans, the Tusculans, and innumerable other Italian republics. Let only soul-nourishing Rome, Pisa, and Genoa be examples for us, whose power was manifest in every part of the world.

<margin>F</margin> ¶ Note even today that the barbarian nations, merely by hearing the name of their past excellent victories remembered, still tremble with grief and fear. ¶ Therefore, this great variation and permutation—proceeding from nothing and returning to nothing—our ancient ancestors, understanding it perfectly, ascribed to Saturn. He is interpreted as Time, who devours his own children. Regarding him, Cicero says, to demonstrate this assumption made about time: **"He was called Saturn, however, because he is saturated with years; and he is imagined to devour his offspring because age consumes the reaches of time, and is insatiably filled by the years that have passed."** <note>original: "Saturnus autem appellatus : eo q saturetur annis : edere autem natos fingitur : quia consumit ætas temporis spatia : annisq; preteritis insatiabiliter expletur." From Cicero's *De Natura Deorum*.</note> And so, by Saturn eating his children, we ought to understand this length of time with its tra <unclear>ce</unclear>...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the inevitable power of Time. ### CHAPTER 2, PART 1

[...to en]ter and obscure everything: and therefore Ovid, in the fifteenth book of the *Metamorphoses*, understanding this same truth, explains it gracefully and with excellent learning in these verses:

> Time, the devourer of all things, and you, envious Old Age, you destroy everything and, with the teeth of time, little by little, you consume everything with a slow death. <note>original Latin: "Tempus edax rerum..." from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* 15.234-236. A classic poetic expression of the "all-consuming" nature of time.</note>

Induced by this same foundation, the wise Solomon—as we noted above at the beginning in the third chapter of *Ecclesiastes*—said:

> Everything has its time, and all things under heaven pass away in their allotted space. <note>original Latin: "Omnis tempus habet..." from Ecclesiastes 3:1. This biblical reference reinforces the idea that human life is subject to divine timing and eventual decay.</note>

And Cicero, in the *Philippics* and the tenth oration, says on the same subject:

<margin>G</margin>
> Nothing flourishes forever; age succeeds age. <note>original Latin: "Nihil enim semper floret..." from Cicero's Tenth Philippic.</note>

From which we can appropriately and with great reason conclude that nothing in this world—not youth, nor wealth, nor lordship, nor physical strength, nor wisdom, nor life, nor fame—can escape the ruin and dominion of Time. Next, Messer Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarca, the author of the poem being commented upon.</note> adds the other sentiment, saying that he also heard it said that to those who are less good—and not even to those who are more worthy—is taken away not only the external body (which Time dissolves very quickly), but beyond this, their eloquence, their works, and their genius. Wherefore he says:

<margin>H</margin>
> And taken from the less good, not given to the more worthy;
> And not only does Time dissolve the outward appearance;
> But your eloquence and your works of genius.

<margin>I</margin> In the preceding verses, our graceful poet intends to silently strip away a vain hope and fantasy held by many, who persuade themselves that through even the slightest knowledge of letters they can acquire immortal fame. He says that for those who are less good and less worthy, when they are suddenly taken by death, not only is the body gone, but so are their works of genius and their eloquence. 

And likewise their studies, although this does not happen to the "more worthy" in the same way; for a certain time after death, their fame is prolonged. These aforementioned verses can also be interpreted another way: that for those who were less good in works pertaining to the <term>political life</term> <note>Active service to the state or community.</note> or the Christian religion, their body, fame, and learning are all taken away together. But those who were more worthy—making themselves worthy through good deeds—are restored among the Blessed Spirits; their fame remains very well known among those spirits because of their deeds among men in the world, even though their body was taken from them in this present life. 

Finally, the poet concludes with the last sentiment, which he heard regarding this dictate of the intellect, saying that as Time continues to flee—as shown above—it leads and turns the world with it; it never rests, nor does it ever return. Nor does it ever seem to cease working against men, until it has led them back to their beginning and made them return to a little bit of dust. Wherefore he says:

<margin>K</margin>
> Thus, fleeing, it turns the world with it;
> It never rests, nor stops, nor returns,
> Until it has led you back to a little dust.

None among all the narrated sentiments is more worthy or more fruitful for the salvation of man than this one, which our Messer Francesco has expressed with such grace in the preceding verses. To understand this, one must know that our first and true perfection consists mostly in understanding the truth. This truth certainly cannot be grasped unless man first—as we said at the beginning—strives to know himself. 

Nothing leads to this knowledge more quickly than the universal natural law: that everything which has a beginning must return to that same beginning. Following this, one must see and understand that our final end and ultimate conversion is dust and earth. 

<margin>L</margin> Wherefore we can truly conclude that our beginning was earth, and we ourselves are likewise earth. Understanding this truth, the ancient Egyptians—to keep a perpetual memory of their terrestrial and muddy origin—used to hold live grass gathered from the marshes in their hands during their sacrifices, as if it were close and akin to our nature. The neighboring Ethiopians testify to this same thing; among the various praises they attribute to their homeland, they say they were the first men to be born from the earth. This sentiment undoubtedly...

# ## THE TRIUMPH OF TIME

<margin>V</margin>
Similarly, it is affirmed by Moses: as we said above regarding the beginning of Genesis, when he affirms that God formed man from the clay of the earth and breathed into him the spirit of life. From this, I undoubtedly believe, the celebrated fable of Prometheus took its argument regarding the fashioning of man. <note>Prometheus was the Titan in Greek mythology said to have shaped the first humans out of clay.</note> Nor was this the opinion only of the Hebrews and the Egyptian and Ethiopian Christians; Parmenides <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher.</note> was among the first, then Hesiod, and later Archelaus of Miletus and Zeno of Elea—most illustrious philosophers—who said that the earth was the beginning of everything produced in the world. For this reason, it is principally the beginning of man, as he is the first inhabitant, tiller, and dweller of the earth. Excellent, then, is the way Isaiah 63 demonstrates our earthly nature, speaking toward God and saying: *And now, O Lord, you are our father; we are the clay, and you are our maker; and we are all the work of your hands.* <note>original Latin: "Et nunc domine pater noster es tu: nos autem lutum: tu factor noster & opera manuum tuarum omnes." This is actually Isaiah 64:8.</note> Jeremiah also deplores this same fact in the last chapter of his Lamentations, demonstrating that we are entirely clay, saying: *The noble sons of Zion, clothed in gold: how are they regarded as earthen vessels, the work of the potter's hands?* <note>original Latin: "Filii syon inclyti amicti auro: quomodo reputati sunt in vasa terrea opus manuum figuli?" (Lamentations 4:2).</note> But certainly he explains it much more clearly in chapter 13, <note>Actually Jeremiah 22:29.</note> when speaking and prophesying universally to men, demonstrating to them that they are earthly beings, saying: *Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord.* <note>original Latin: "Terra terra audi verbum domini."</note> What opinion, then, is more certain and true than that men are

<margin>N</margin>
earth? This is observed by pagan opinions, celebrated by philosophers, pronounced by poets, and approved by experience. Rightly, then, Time and the sun do not cease to revolve and transmute this human nature until they have led us back to our origin and our beginning: equals, and made of the tiniest dust. Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch.</note> now responds at the end to a silent objection from the ignorant; those who, seeing that the fame of many men is so prolonged, cannot believe that it is subject to Time. He says that it should be no marvel, as human glory has such a multitude of "horns" <note>The "horns" of glory refer to the many different branches or foundations of a person's reputation which Time must break down one by one.</note> that if it stays a bit beyond the usual to break them all, it nonetheless follows the custom of all other things in failing. But let whoever wishes think or speak, and let the common people imagine what they will: if our life were not so brief and did not fail so quickly, we would certainly see all those glories return to smoke and dust. Whence he says:

<margin>O</margin>
<margin>For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, one must primarily know that the multitude of writers is so great, and the diligence of men to acquire honor so high, that everyone wishing to prove their own genius takes up either the writing of histories or the composing of poems. From this, they acquire praise, reputation, and glory both for themselves and for those they celebrate; through this, it happens that this worldly fame is somewhat prolonged. And this is especially because men, seeing they must die so soon, strive through these exercises to achieve a longer-lasting name. Whereas if their lives were longer, it would follow that we would see—in a short time, through the loss of books and the corrosion of the ages—even the greatest fame of excellent men turn to smoke.</margin>

> ->Now because human glory has so many horns,<-
> ->It is no great wonder if to break them<-
> ->It lingers a bit beyond the usual,<-
> ->But whatever the common people think or say,<-
> ->If our life were not so brief,<-
> ->Soon you would see them return to dust.<-

<margin>P</margin>
And secondly, if life were longer, men would care less about prolonging themselves through fame, because they would be satisfied within themselves by the length of their lives. Having now expressed these excellent sentiments narrated thus far, Messer Francesco adds what he himself did, what state he came to be in, and what object he then seemed to see. He says that having heard this so worthy and grave reasoning, he gave it full and indubitable faith. Because it is one’s duty not to contradict the truth in any part, but to give it faith and belief. And so, the poet, in the considerations and thoughts that followed, saw all our glory to be like shadows, or rather, set against the rays of the sun. And he consequently saw Time remaining with him in its rotation, carrying such and so many prizes of names and mortal fames that he truly judged fame and names to be of no value—although the common and coarse people do not know or believe this, and cannot understand it. Whence he says:

> **I say this, because one must not oppose**

<margin>Q</margin> ¶ One should not, cannot, and must not doubt that the dignity and excellence of truth is such that one should never resist it. This is not difficult to understand: for truth, wherever it may be, is the work of the Holy Spirit; and Christ affirms that He Himself is the highest truth. This is also the excellent teaching of Jesus son of Sirach in *Ecclesiasticus*, in the fourth chapter, where it says: *Do not contradict the word of truth in any way.* <note>original Latin: "Non contradicas verbo veritatis ullo modo." Found in Ecclesiasticus 4:30.</note> And in the thirty-seventh chapter it is written: *Before all works, let a true word go before you.* <note>original Latin: "ante omnia opera verbum verax precedat te." Found in Ecclesiasticus 37:20.</note> Aristotle confirms this in the first book of the *Ethics* when he said that truth is to be preferred over friendship. <note>A reference to Aristotle's famous sentiment that while he loved his teacher Plato, he loved the truth more.</note> Cicero also attributes great dignity to this in his book *On Friendship*, especially when speaking against his teacher Plato, saying: *But for the defense of the truth, it is necessary to oppose even one’s own friends: it must be thought that this is perhaps especially required of philosophers; for since both are friends, it is a pious duty to prefer truth in honor.* <note>original Latin: "Sed pro defensione veritatis etiam propria oppugnare oportere: prefertim philosophos forsan magis extimandum est: nam cum ambo sint amici pium est veritatem in honore preferre."</note>

<margin>R</margin> ¶ And following and preserving this excellent principle, the poet <note>Petrarch</note> confesses the truth: he affirms that all our glory vanishes through the course of time. Deservedly, then, time and the swift passing of the years carry away these spoils of names and fame. Hence Cicero, in *The Dream of Scipio*, introducing Scipio Africanus speaking to his grandson Aemilianus, writes these worthy words for our purpose: *He sees indeed within what narrow bounds your glory wishes to expand; and as for those who speak of you, how long will they continue to do so? Indeed, even if future generations should desire to pass down the praises of each of us from their fathers to their descendants, nevertheless, because of the floods and fires of the earth—which must happen at certain times—we are unable to achieve a glory that is not only not eternal, but not even long-lasting.* <note>original Latin: "Cernit profecto quantis in angustijs se vestra gloria dilatari velit: ipsi autem qui de vobis loquuntur quamdiu loquentur? quin etiam si cupiat proles illa futurorum hominum: deinceps vniuscuiusq; nostrum laudes patribus acceptas posteris procedere. Tamen propter eluuiões exustionesque terrarum: quas accidere tempore certo necesse est: non modo non æternam: sed ne diuturnam quidem assequi gloriam possumus." From Cicero’s Somnium Scipionis, part of De Re Publica.</note> And near the end, further down, he adds: *All such speech is hemmed in by the narrowness of those regions which you see; it has never been everlasting for anyone; it is overwhelmed by the death of men and extinguished by the oblivion of posterity.* <note>original Latin: "Sermo autem omnis ille angustijs cingitur iis regionum: quas vides: nec unquam de ullo perennis fuit & obruitur hominum iteritu & obliuioe posteritatis extinguitur."</note>

<margin>S</margin> ¶ Therefore, in truth, what greater foolishness can we commit than to hope for something whose destruction is inevitable? It cannot be repaired by any worldly power, nor can it help us in any way, neither in life nor in death, as it is something external and irrelevant to our nature and to the health of the soul. But if someone should say: "Does this mean that good fame should be despised for this reason?" I do not say that; rather, I affirm that one should not desire it more than is due. That is, one should love fame out of respect for its cause: which is to act holily and virtuously. Thus, one should not value virtue for the sake of worldly glory and fame; but on the contrary, worldly fame and name should be desired for the sake of the virtue from which they are born.

<margin>T</margin> ¶ The poet then subsequently exclaims against the common people, who do not know or believe that the turning of time must obscure fame, saying: <margin>Look how blind and vain they are: how much they feed and play in the wind, nurturing themselves on a false opinion. The common folk judge that dying in old age is much more to be desired than dying in infancy or in the first cradle. Oh, how many are those who died happy in their swaddling clothes, and how many are the miserable ones who died in extreme old age? And it is even the opinion of some that only those are blessed who are never born into the world or have never existed. Hence he says:</margin>

> **Blind; which always plays in the wind,**
> **And feeds itself on false opinions,**
> **Praising death in old age more than in the cradle.**
> **How many happy ones have already died in swaddling clothes;**
> **How many miserable ones in the depths of old age?**
> **Some say, blessed is he who is not born.**

<margin>V</margin> ¶ Regarding the understanding of the preceding verses, it should primarily be known that the reasoning and foundation of common men in determining and saying that longevity of life is a good thing is this: that living is good and an effect of nature, and nature always intends the good, being regulated by an unerring intelligence...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Petrarch’s "Triumph of Time," expanding on the idea that human life is a fleeting misery and that a "long life" is often a burden rather than a blessing, contrasting the soul's eternal nature with the body's decay.</meta>

-># THE TRIUMPH OF TIME<-

<margin>X</margin>
Hence, the longer one participates in "the good," the more laudable that state is considered. Beyond this, since fame is a good and desirable thing, and cannot be acquired unless a man’s life is prolonged, the common people have determined for these reasons that living until old age is much better than dying in swaddling clothes <note>A common Renaissance idiom for infancy.</note>. However, it is not difficult to understand how deeply this opinion is founded in error. ¶ Here, one must presuppose the foundation that every "good" and every human delight of man must be judged in respect to the soul, as the soul is the ultimate goal and a much more perfect thing, according to the doctrine of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle was almost always referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> in the sixth book of the *Politics*, where he says: *Everything that is imperfect exists for the sake of something better.* <note>original Latin: "omne enim quod imperfectum est: est melioris gratia."</note> From this foundation, it follows that once the delight of the soul is seen and possessed, one should not care for the delight of the body. For if the body’s pleasure—as a separate and lesser part—were to unite with the pleasure of the soul, it would only diminish it because of its own deformity; this is a rule recently demonstrated by "the Calculator" <note>Richard Swineshead (active c. 1340–1354), a mathematician and logician at Oxford known as "The Calculator" for his complex calculations regarding qualitative change.</note> and taken by others as a fundamental principle.

<margin>Y</margin>
¶ This being a most true presupposition, we turn first to the opinion of Plato and many of the Gentiles <note>Non-Christian classical authors.</note>, which is that the eternal soul descends from heaven and returns to heaven, always filled with the same habits. It is clear that by dying in infancy, one first achieves the soul's highest good, which is to return to heaven and contemplate divine things. Furthermore, one escapes the miseries and troubles that one participates in during the course of life through the contagion of the body. Therefore, it is much better to participate in that same good without suffering any punishment or toil than to possess it mixed with bitterness. And if we wish to subject the soul to divine justice because of sin—as Virgil describes in the seventh book <note>The author likely refers to the *Aeneid*, specifically Book VI, which discusses the purification of souls, though the text cites Book VII.</note>—it is still better to judge death at an age where sin does not occur. This same point is beyond doubt in the Christian religion; for the voluntary Passion of Christ acquired such merit for our souls that, through baptism purging original sin, infants are in such a state of innocence that if they die then, they satisfy the penalty for the sin of Adam infused in us with only a small stay in Purgatory. They fly almost immediately to heaven in a swift passage. Thus, they escape every grave danger of sin that might arise through a long life.

<margin>Z</margin>
¶ Hence, it is a well-known thing for these reasons: that dying in infancy is much better and safer than prolonging a miserable and calamitous life. Cicero, understanding this sentiment, confirms it as true through many examples. In the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, he says that Hegesias of Cyrene <note>A Greek philosopher who argued that life was so full of suffering that happiness was impossible.</note>, through the express and effective reasons he had for why prolonging life was the worst thing, induced so many men to kill themselves that King Ptolemy of Egypt prohibited him from teaching that doctrine in his kingdom. To this, Cicero adds his own opinion with these words: *Certainly, if we had died sooner, death would have taken us from evils, not from goods.* <note>original Latin: "Certe si ante obissemus: mors nos a malis: non a bonis obtraxisset." Found in Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* 1.35.86.</note> From there, he enumerates how many troubles befell Metellus, Priam, and Pompey. He says all of them would have escaped these troubles if they had died in their swaddling clothes, or at least in their youth.

<margin>A</margin>
¶ At the end, he introduces the example of Cleobis and Biton, sons of the priestess Argia. Because they had been pious toward their mother, having carried her on their shoulders to the temple, she prayed to the goddess to grant them the greatest reward that can be given to men. After they had dined with their mother and gone to sleep, they were found dead the next morning. Then Cicero adds that this same thing happened to Trophonius and Agamedes by their own prayer. Having built a temple to Apollo, they asked him for the reward that was best among all things that could ever happen to men. After their prayer, on the third day, they were found dead.

<margin>B</margin>
¶ By these examples, according to Cicero's text, it is argued that if death is the best thing that can happen in the world to men, then the sooner it is achieved, the greater the happiness must be esteemed. Therefore, a death occurring in infancy is to be judged as much more happy than one that arrives in extreme old age.

<margin>C</margin>
¶ It also seems that Cicero does not reject the sentiment of Silenus. When he was captured by Midas, King of Illyria <note>Though usually associated with Phrygia, the text places Midas in Illyria.</note>, and having nothing else with which to ransom himself but his wisdom, he gave the king excellent precepts. One was that the best thing that could happen to a man was not to be born. The other was that the next best thing to not being born was to die immediately. Whence Cicero says: *A certain fable is also told concerning Silenus, who...* <note>original Latin: "Fertur etiam de sileno fabella quaedam."</note>

### CHAPTER ONE

<margin>D</margin>
...and when Midas <note>The mythical king of Phrygia, famous for his "golden touch."</note> was captured, it is written that this wisdom was given as a gift for his release: he taught the King that it is by far the best thing for a man not to be born at all; the next best is to die as soon as possible <note>original Latin: "non nasci homiẽ longe optimum est: est primum aut quā primū mori." This pessimistic trope was common in Greek philosophy.</note>. ¶ The poet Euripides confirms this same idea; he teaches us to weep at the birth of men and to sing at their death. Likewise, Crantor <note>A Greek Academic philosopher (c. 300 BCE) famous for his treatise "On Grief."</note>, while consoling Elysius of Terina on the death of his son, wrote these verses:
> Men wander in life with ignorant minds.
> Euchenon enjoys death as a gift of the fates.
> Thus it was more useful for his life to end, for him and for you.
Lest these testimonies be suspected in this cause because of their pagan origin, let us at least accept the judgment of Job <note>The biblical figure characterized by his suffering and patience.</note>. He was a simple, righteous man who feared God and turned away from evil. Considering the condition of human misery and lamenting to God, he says these words in the tenth chapter:
> Why did you bring me out of the womb? Oh, that I had been consumed so that no eye might see me! I should have been as if I had not been, carried from the womb to the tomb. <note>original Latin: "Quare de vulua eduxisti me..."</note>
And in the third chapter, he seems to have concluded the same, saying:
> May the day perish in which I was born, and the voice that said, "A man is conceived."

<margin>E</margin>
¶ By these words, we can clearly enough comprehend how miserable and calamitous this length and prolongation of life is. It remains now only to respond to the arguments which are constructed in confusion due to the double meaning of the term "living." For by "living," we can mean only the *being* of animate things, as Aristotle <note>The "Philosopher" mentioned on the previous page.</note> writes in the second book of *On the Soul* when he says:
> To live, for living things, is to be. <note>original Latin: "Viuere viuentibus est esse."</note>
And yet, by "living," we can understand not only *being* but also the longevity and prolongation of that being.

<margin>F</margin>
¶ I say, therefore, that the first kind of living is good and is to be desired, but the second is not, unless it be the will of God. Nor do beasts and men defend the length of life when they flee death; rather, they only show that they maintain their *being* through the natural appetite shared by all rational and irrational things. Secondly, we must consider how fame is a good and is to be desired, as has been made quite manifest above. Thus, the answer to the second argument remains clear. Afterward, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch, the author of the *Triumphs*.</note> brings forth a noble question for a more manifest declaration, saying: "Come now, tell me, and let the crowd accustomed to great errors answer. Behold, after a long age and a great prolongation of life, the name shall be clear and famous—yet what is this fame in the end, that is so prized, so sought after, and so greatly praised?" Wherefore he says:

<margin>G</margin>
->But for the crowd accustomed to great errors<-
->After long age the name shall be clear;<-
->What is this, then, that is so prized?<-

¶ Oh, think a little with mature examination on this wise and noble question: who is more greedy and desirous of this smoke and thin mist of the world? Whoever can answer him with truth and justice will see clearly that they are forced to confess that fame is nothing other than an easy and swift path to perdition. Thus, they will answer that worldly glory is nothing other than a means, very often, to make oneself unhappy when it is desired in an inordinate way. This is what happened to Brutus <note>Lucius Junius Brutus, a founder of the Roman Republic.</note>, who for the glory of just government killed his own sons; thus he became unhappy, as Virgil demonstrates in the sixth book <note>The *Aeneid*, Book VI.</note>, saying:
> And the proud soul of the avenger Brutus: to see the recovered fasces? As consul, he shall be the first to receive the authority and the cruel axes; and the father, for the sake of beautiful liberty, shall call his sons to punishment for stirring up new wars—unhappy man! <note>original Latin: "Animamque superbam Vltoris Bruti..."</note>

<margin>H</margin>
¶ And therefore, in confirmation of this, Augustine says in the fifth book of *The City of God*:
> Without doubt, the desire for glory is better resisted than believed; the more one is clean of this uncleanness, the more one is like God. <note>original Latin: "Glorie enim cupiditati melius resistitur..."</note>
And because of this, in the thirteenth chapter of the same book, he teaches us to cast off this perverse appetite, saying:
> Take away your boasting; what are men but men?
What is this, then, that is so prized? What is this that is so highly esteemed? Certainly, it is nothing other than fables, wind, shadows, and confused dreams. Therefore, the poet finally adds that this time—greedy and stingy regarding mortal fame—conquers so much, and by revolving around the turning of the heavens, it takes back so much that what is called "fame" is nothing other than a second death. No remedy can be found or given for this any more than for death itself. For these reasons, time in this form leads glory away and triumphs over the names of men, over fame, and likewise over the world. Wherefore he says:

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Petrarch’s "Triumph of Time" and begins the "Triumph of Divinity." The previous page established the vanity of human life through the examples of Midas and Job; here, the author argues that only God provides true permanence.</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF TIME

<margin>I</margin>
¶ So great is the doctrine enclosed in these verses for their health-giving warning: that whoever wishes to turn their mind to understanding the truth will see that they contain every rule and every form of living. For this reason:

->Greedy time conquers and takes back so much:<-
->It is called fame; and it is a second death;<-
->Nor is there any more defense against it than against the first:<-
->Thus time triumphs over names and the world.<-

Because through these verses it is affirmed as the truth that against bodily death, and even against the loss of worldly fame, no effective defense can be mounted by men. Thus, understanding that his soul is immortal and was produced for blessedness as its ultimate end, man should reasonably love that end, for no one can be happy unless they first enjoy the thing they love. Because of this, these verses show that nothing pertaining to the bodily life of man, nor to the fame acquired in the world, can be the cause of our salvation. Since each of these is shown by the aforementioned verses to inevitably fail, they signal to us that it is necessary to seek another object which perpetually gladdens the intellect and makes the mind perfect. If we wish to seek this, we shall find in *The City of God* <note>St. Augustine’s seminal work, *De Civitate Dei*, written in the 5th century.</note> in chapter 15, that this object is God, of whom Augustine speaks, saying:
> For God indeed makes us happy, he who is the true wealth of minds. <note>original Latin: "Deus enim felices facit que est mentium vera opulentia."</note>
Therefore, having neglected mortal things, having despised even fame, and not caring for death, let the soul return to find its like: the one who, through infinite mercy, created its form in the beginning to enjoy and possess his eternal nature.

### EXPOSITION OF THE TRIUMPH OF DIVINITY.

<margin>K</margin>
**L**O, the abyss and the depth of Holy Scripture brings such and so much confusion and such great wonder to the minds of men that the eyes of the intellect, blinded and confused, leave one stunned in the path of seeking. This is especially true when, beyond the faculty and capacity of our intellect, man still strives to investigate those things which exceed reasonable sobriety. Just as the light of the sun leads to greater blindness for the one who stares most persistently into it, so the intellectual light obscures the mind of the one who strives to extend himself further than his strengths allow him to understand. Therefore, I rightly understand that I am now held back from proceeding any further, since this matter described in the following triumph by our poet is of such a nature that it can neither be comprehended by the intellect nor adequately explained by the tongue. For it determines matters of eternity and the universal divine judgment which must precede it.

<margin>L</margin>
¶ I would therefore certainly suspend my work, nor would I be so bold as to explain further, but three reasons force me to continue against my own judgment and will. The first is because the Holy Scripture and doctrine contained in the present triumph is of such a nature and disposition by divine grace that in its ocean the lamb may walk and the elephant may swim. <note>A traditional metaphor for the Bible: shallow enough for the simple to navigate but deep enough for the greatest scholars.</note> Therefore, the lowliness of my small wit will be made as manifest as can be understood, leaving the high and profound speculations to those men whose intellect flies like an eagle above the mountain peaks.

The second reason is so as not to leave these vigils of ours interrupted, but rather—as is the universal desire of all orderly appetites—to bring it with all our strength and diligence to that proper end to which the small capacity of our weak intellect can lead us.

<margin>M</margin>
The third and last reason is the confidence placed in my soul by the hope I have in the humanity and mercy of those who will read these words. For I estimate they will judge that this was not audacity or temerity on my part, but rather a burning desire to want to communicate my labors to others as best I can.

¶ Comforted and confirmed by these reasons, we shall give a beginning to the exposition of this worthy, admirable, and glorious triumph placed by our poet in the final position. The human soul, which has already been noted above as varying in five states, can provide its account to this world after it is united to the body and the empire of appetite and reason has consented. From there, it is separated by death, celebrated by fame, and at last obscured by the length of time, ending that day...

# CHAPTER ONE

<warning>Faded text in some areas; ink bleed-through from the reverse page.</warning>

...to the day of divine judgment, which is followed by all-encompassing eternity, already leading to the state of invariability <note>The state of the soul after death where no further change or repentance is possible.</note>: in which the soul, being reunited to the body by divine will, is necessarily either gladdened forever in heaven for previous merits or perpetually tortured in hell for past sins. This occurs by the virtue, efficacy, and power of that equitable sentence and just judgment which the eternal judge must render to men. He—who liberated us from the demon with his own blood—left and wrote in his deeds, operations, and words a complete path and a health-giving law. By this law, whoever proceeds is led to the eternity restored to us by his death; and whoever deviates from it passes without hope into the abyss of death, which kills living sinners without end and torments the dead. Therefore, the final subject of this triumph is the sixth state of the soul, which is perpetual, and which the soul must acquire after it has been judged by God. 

¶ Here, Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch), the author of the *Triumphs*.</note> introduces eternity to dominate and extinguish time with infinite measure, just as in the previous triumph he described time overcoming and taking away all human fame. From this, by showing that all transmutation <note>Change or decay.</note> must fail, he teaches anyone who considers it well how to dispose themselves in the world toward eternal salvation. Without any doubt, whoever observes these discrete precepts can be assured that the cruel, horrendous, and terrible sentence will not apply to them. 

And because there are three foundations upon which our salvation consists—namely faith, hope, and charity—the Apostle <note>St. Paul.</note> says when exhorting the Corinthians in chapter 13: 
<margin>N</margin>
> But now faith, hope, and charity, these three, remain. <note>original Latin: "Nunc autem manet Fides Spes & Charitas haec tria"</note>
Through this, Master Francesco demonstrates that these three virtues are in him, since he was confused by the error of the world and called back to have faith, to hope, and to love God in order to be happy. This is as Augustine testifies in the *City of God*, book 8, chapter 2, when he says: 
> He is the old God with whom alone, in whom alone, and from whom alone the rational and intellectual soul is blessed. <note>original Latin: "Vetus deus est cum quo solo & in quo solo & de quo solo anima rationalis & intellectualis beata est." While the text reads "Vetus" (Old), Augustine typically uses "Verus" (True) in this context.</note>
Therefore, because the first door to enter divine grace is faith—as the Apostle shows in Hebrews 11 when he says: 
> Without faith it is impossible to please God <note>original Latin: "Sine fide ipos sibile est deo placere"</note>
—for this reason, Master Francesco says principally that he has placed his faith in God alone. Since man cannot easily trust in anything of the world, and as is fitting for a religious and prudent soul, Master Francesco, giving a beginning to his subject, says that after he saw nothing contained within the circumference of heaven <note>The physical universe or the spheres of the stars.</note> that was stable or firm, he turned back to himself and to his own knowledge. Wisely questioning himself, he says: "In what do you trust henceforth?"

<margin>O</margin> ¶ These preceding verses contain a health-giving teaching. To understand this, one must know that the discourse and experience of searching and investigating worldly things is a work of prudence, provided they are tested with measure and careful examination. Solomon testified to having done this himself at the beginning of the book of Ecclesiastes. This was also the life's work of the philosophers: to find and conclude that God is entirely unmoving and the supreme good, seeing that every other thing is changeable and subject to alteration. Therefore, they concluded that such things could not be the highest good. <margin>P</margin> In this examination, then, the prudent man must exercise himself. Having found the ultimate end and the highest good, he must fix himself upon it and never look back, like the wife of Lot <note>A biblical reference to Lot's wife, who turned into a pillar of salt for looking back at the destruction of Sodom; here used as a metaphor for looking back at worldly distractions.</note>. Nor should he stop at any changeable thing until he reaches that which is entirely permanent, which is God. This process is what the poet shows he has performed in the preceding verses. He does not find himself settled in any changeable thing; rather, dismayed by them, he asks himself with fear: in what object <gloss>from now on</gloss> should he place his faith? Having thus asked himself such a worthy and just question—almost a self-reproach—he responds appropriately, as befits the perfection of a soul, saying that from now on he has no faith except in that Lord who never failed his promise to those who have placed their faith in him. Thus he says:

-> I replied, in the Lord; who never failed <-
-> His promise to those who trust in him: <-

<margin>Q</margin> ¶ A wise, golden, and celebrated response! Indeed, where could one respond better or more appropriately than our poet has responded: to trust in him who never fails his promise to those who give their faith to him—our redeemer and head, Jesus Christ. Consider how much God has maintained his divine promises from the beginning, when he created us to possess everlasting delights. Even after the blind ignorance of our first parents <note>Adam and Eve.</note> caused us to be justly deprived of original divine justice by their error, did the Divine Word not deign to humble himself to the earth? Did he not come in the flesh to submit himself to human penalties and obey death at the hands of ungrateful sinners? O, divine love! Nothing other than love led him to die. Who, then, can doubt that his promises, founded in love, will be fulfilled? Who can reasonably believe them to be fallacious? Certainly no one, except for a clouded and depraved intellect. "Divine love does not permit him to be without offspring," says Dionysius in *On the Divine Names* <note>Original Latin: "Diuinus amor nō pmit tit eum sine germine esse." Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.</note>; this love is directed toward the salvation of the whole earth. Zephaniah declares this in the third chapter, saying: "For in the fire of my jealousy all the earth shall be devoured: for then I will restore to the people a chosen lip, that they may all call upon the name of the Lord, and serve him with one shoulder" <note>Original Latin: "In igne enim zeli mei deuorabitur omnis terra: qia tunc reddam populis labium electum: vt inuocent oēs nomē domini: & seruiant ei humero vno." (Zephaniah 3:8-9).</note>. Furthermore, Christ Jesus himself affirms this same love with his own mouth, promising in the eleventh chapter of Saint Matthew: "Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh <gloss>you</gloss>" <note>Matthew 11:28.</note>. And in Saint John <gloss>in the sixth chapter</gloss>: "The one who comes to me I will not cast out" <note>John 6:37.</note>. Does he not affirm himself to be the good shepherd, who lays down his life for his sheep? The apostle Paul also confirms the same, exhorting the Ephesians in the second chapter: "Now you are no longer guests and strangers, but you are citizens with the saints and members of God's household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone, in whom the whole building, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord" <note>Ephesians 2:19-21.</note>. <margin>R</margin> Christ, therefore, is the one in whom we, along with our poet, must have faith. Christ keeps his promises; Christ assists our weak being in such a way that, with Saint Ambrose, we might deservedly say: "Christ is made all <gloss>things for us</gloss>: if you burn with fever, he is a fountain; if you have a wound, he is a doctor; if you fear death, he is life; if you need help, he is strength; if you seek food, he is nourishment" <note>Original Latin: "Oia nobis factus ē christus: si febribus estuas: fons ē: si vulnus habes: medicus est: si morte times: vita est: si auxilio indiges: virtus est: si cibū qris: alimentū est."</note>. Therefore, setting aside earthly things, the poet invites us to have faith in Christ. Next, M.F. <note>Messer Francesco (Petrarch).</note> adds the effect that arises...
