# THE TRIUMPH OF DIVINITY

And so, when prudence has found that in which it must have faith, it recognizes that the things loved in the past were not a foundation of faith, but of errors; not a harbor of safety, but a wide road to perdition. Saying that now, having placed his trust only in that Lord whose promises do not fail, he clearly sees and knows that the world has mocked and cheated him. He further sees now what he once was; he sees how time passes away—or rather, how it flies. At this, he would like to grieve, but he knows not who to blame other than himself, because the fault is entirely his own; for at a better hour and much earlier he should have opened his eyes to understand the truth, rather than delaying until the end of his old age. To tell the truth and confess his debt, he is now too much subject to the years and the turning of age and time. Wherefore he says:

> But I see well that the world has mocked me,
> And I feel what I am and what I was;
> And I see time go by, or rather fly;
> And I would like to grieve, but I know not for whom:
> For the fault is purely mine; since more in time <note>In this context, "more in time" (*più per tempo*) means "earlier" or "sooner."</note>
> I should have opened my eyes, and not delayed until the end:
> For to tell the truth, I am already too much aged;

<margin>s</margin> For a swifter understanding of the preceding verses, one must know what "the Philosopher" <note>A standard medieval and Renaissance reference to Aristotle.</note> says in the second book of *On the Heavens* and the fifth book of the *Ethics*: one contrary is the comparison and the means of knowing the other, and the nature of one's essence is more clearly seen and known through its opposite. Therefore, the poet skillfully introduces the idea that, having trusted in Christ, he realizes the world has deceived him, because Christ and the world are opposites. This is written in the Gospel of Saint John, in the fourteenth chapter, when Christ said: "For the prince of this world comes, and in me he has nothing" <note>original: *Venit enim princeps mundi huius: & in me non habet quicquam*</note>; and in the sixteenth chapter, speaking to the apostles, He said: "In the world you shall have distress: but have confidence, for I have overcome the world" <note>original: *In mundo pressuram habetis: sed confidite quia ego vici mundum*</note>. Therefore, all worldly things that offer us delight are to our own deception, if the necessary restraint of reason is not applied to our desires for them. Wherefore the Apostle <note>Refers to Saint Paul.</note> reminds us that we must guard ourselves against these things, saying in the second chapter of Colossians: "See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of this world and not according to Christ" <note>original: *Videte ne quis uos decipiat per philosophiam & inanem fallaciam secundum traditionem hominum secundum elementa mundi huius & non secundum Christum*</note>.

<margin>t</margin> Secondly, it should be understood that when a man recognizes how the sweetness of the world has deceived him in such a manner, he recognizes what he was in the past—and how much he is to be blamed—and he also understands what he is in the present. Through the sting of conscience, he would like to grieve; and beginning to blame worldly things as the causes of his past life and errors, he concludes in the end that the fault is purely his own. Because he could have used his <term>free will</term> <note>The theological concept of *libero arbitrio*, the capacity of humans to make choices between good and evil.</note> to look back sooner and recall himself to the true vision, if he finds himself in old age without having amended his ways, he should blame no one but himself. This is what the poet affirms he is doing in the preceding verses.

<margin>v</margin> Lastly, it should be noted that when a man recognizes his state—and not before old age—he has lived too long in sin. Because it is necessary to perform the required penance to take away one's guilt, a man at that age is unsuited for it, both because of his diminished physical nature and the short remaining span of life. Therefore, a man should perceive his errors in good time, and realize how many snares the devil has set for us in this world. Having thus shown in the aforementioned verses the just self-reproach given by "our Master Francesco" <note>The commentator refers to the author, Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch), with a title of respect.</note> for having delayed in knowing God and his own condition, he now wishes to make known that a man should never deprive himself of hope while he is alive. Instead, he should consider at every hour that the arms of divine mercy are always open to whoever returns from sin to God. He says that since divine graces were never late in helping those who have invoked them piously and with a contrite heart, he also hopes in them, that they will perform high, worthy, and wondrous works within him. Wherefore he says:

<margin>x</margin> > But divine graces were never late:
> In them I hope, that they will yet perform in me
> High and wondrous works.

Just as it is manifest through the teaching of Paul the Apostle to the Hebrews in the eleventh chapter that there cannot be faith without hope, when he says: "Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen" <note>original: *Fides est substantia rerum sperandarum argumentū non apparentiū*</note>. So our Master Francesco, having shown in the preceding verses that faith is within him, now describes himself as having...

# CHAPTER ONE

We should have no less hope in the mercy of God; for this same principle teaches us that divine grace is never denied to any person who turns to penance for their past errors, if they humbly ask it of God. Christ makes this manifest in Saint Matthew, chapter 18, when Saint Peter asked if he should forgive a sinner seven times; He replied: <note>Matthew 18:22</note> I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven. And in Saint Luke, chapter 15, regarding the conversion of the sinner, it is written: *Rejoice with me: for I have found what was lost.* <note>original: "Congratulamini mihi: quia inueni quod perierat." Luke 15:6</note> Oh, how great then is the hope that should rise within us, understanding that the most high God never desires the death of a sinner, but rather his life and his conversion; and beyond this, knowing that mercy is more acceptable to Him than the offerings and sacrifices of foolish men. In the proper course of our life, then, by faith believing rightly in God—for as Augustine says in the fifth book of *The City of God*, chapter 7: *One lives badly if one does not believe rightly about God.* <note>original: "Male enim viuitur si de deo non bene credit."</note>

<margin>y</margin>
¶ It is also undoubtedly necessary to hope in order to achieve salvation, as our graceful poet <note>Petrarch</note> has shown us. Nor is this only a precept of the Christian religion; for Quintilian, in the twelfth book of the *Institutes of Oratory*, demonstrates that this same hope must be held when he says: *For there is never any time that is too late for a right will.* <note>original: "Nunquam enim tempus ullum est rectæ voluntatis serum." The OCR reads "feru," a common mistake for the long "s" in "serum" (late).</note> To which purpose Seneca says in his tragedies: *The path to good morals is never too late.* <note>original: "Nunquam sera est ad bonos mores via."</note> Wherefore we can deservedly conclude that divine graces were never too late for us, provided they are asked for with a straight and pure will. Where faith and our hope are joined with a proper connection, it is necessary that most ardent charity <note>In this context, "charity" (caritas) refers to the highest form of Christian love.</note> not be separated from them; because, since future good is expected through hope, the soul cannot be divided from the love of the Giver of such good—especially when, through true liberality and courtesy, and not constrained by any benefit received, He grants what He gives to the one who receives it.

<margin>z</margin>
¶ Therefore, we can conclude that since the poet has shown that faith and hope were in him, charity was also present; which he shows below that he holds toward the supreme good when he says in that verse: "O what grace it would be if I ever obtain it." And thus, having described these three virtues in him, and having shown what our disposition should be in reconciling ourselves with God, he consequently describes a reasonable thought which arises in the minds of the faithful: considering that these worldly things must necessarily end one day, and what the state of natural things will be after the course and the revolving of the heavens have finished, and the generation, corruption, and alteration of things have ceased. He says that, having thus spoken and responded within himself (as was narrated in the preceding verses), he thought about what end these things would have—things that the heavens, after their long and swift turning and governing, cannot maintain as perpetual in this state in which they currently are. Wherefore he says:

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>It is a fitting thing that every perfectible effect should always be intent upon its perfection: just as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> writes at the end of the first book of the *Physics*. Therefore, since the perfection of our intellect is the understanding of divine operations insofar as we can understand those things as participants...</margin>

By this, the poet said he was drawn back to thinking about the end of the celestial circulations. Having been elevated to such a high and excellent thought, Messer <note>A title of respect, like "Master."</note> Francesco adds what he seemed to comprehend with his mind in this consideration, saying: that while his intellect went deeper into itself, he seemed to see a new world being renewed in an eternal age—immobile and unchangeable. And he similarly seemed to see this heaven undone, together with its stars and the sun; and likewise the sea and the earth and all the other elements risen again, one after the other, much more beautiful, more joyful, and more noble. # THE TRIUMPH OF DIVINITY
<meta>Catchword: dominion</meta>

<margin>▲</margin> For clearer evidence of the preceding verses, it should be known: that the poet affirms this world must be undone and another generated, far more noble.

-> With its stars; even the earth and the sea <-
-> And remake one more beautiful and more joyful. <-

¶ This "beautiful remake" conforms in its conclusion to the ideas of Empedocles, Democritus, and Plato, as well as to Christian doctrine; however, their ways of speaking and their positions differ. For Empedocles says that in a certain span of time, the elements run together into one confusion and one chaos, and thus the world is destroyed; and afterwards he affirms that those same elements separate, and the world is generated anew. This occurs through the power of the heavenly intelligences and the arrangement of the celestial bodies; and just as a better influence reigns in that generation, so the world is made more beautiful and perfect than it was in previous times. Ovid seems to confirm this kind of manufacturing at the beginning of the *Metamorphoses*, as is well known to those who look at his verses.

<margin>D</margin> ¶ But Democritus had a different fantasy than Empedocles: for, positing that atoms are the principles of all natural things and judging the world to be a natural effect, he says that things are generated by the congregation of atoms moving inordinately—as one sees in the sun's rays. Because of this, he said the world was produced by chance.

<margin>E</margin> ¶ Plato the Athenian, for the most part following Pythagoras, said the world must be renewed in every complete circulation of the eighth sphere <note>the sphere of the fixed stars</note>, varying from the aforementioned philosophers by positing that the same effects return to the world exactly according to the same celestial revolutions.

<margin>F</margin> ¶ Virgil seems to agree with this opinion in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*; where, having spoken of the souls that have passed to the Elysian Fields, he says:

> Each of us suffers his own spirit <note>the "manes" or afterlife fate</note>; then we are sent through wide Elysium, and a few of us hold the joyful fields. Until a long day, in the cycle of time, has removed the hardened stain and left pure the ethereal sense and the fire of simple air. All these, when they have turned the wheel for a thousand years, God calls in a great troop to the river Lethe. So that, surely, being unmindful, they may revisit the upper reaches and begin again to wish to return into bodies. So Anchises had spoken. <note>original: "Quisq; suos patimur manes: exinde per amplum. Mittimur elysium... Rursus & icipiẽt in corpora velle reuerti. Dixerat anchises."</note>

<margin>G</margin> ¶ The <term>opinion</term> <note>original: snia (sententia)</note> of these <term>philosophers</term> <note>original: ph'i (philosophi)</note> is true regarding the fact that this world must be renewed, but it is frivolous and false in assigning the method. Therefore, the most holy Catholic faith—an effect of the Holy Spirit illuminated by God, the author of nature—posits that on the day of the universal judgment that must take place, this heaven and the sun and the moon must shine sevenfold. This occurs after this region of the living is first undone and burned by fire, as Isaiah clearly pronounces in chapter 30 when he says the light of celestial bodies must be rendered similar to that light which they had in the seven days before the sin of our first parents, saying:

> And the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days. <note>original: "Et erit lux lune sicut lux solis: & lux solis erit septempliter sicut lux septẽ dierũ"</note>

They lost this light through the sin committed by man. The Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, a primary medieval theologian</note> also affirms in the third book, distinction 38, that the heaven will stand still and move no more. He says this on the authority of Zechariah. From this, Isidore <note>of Seville</note> concludes that then the heaven will receive the reward for its great flight by standing immobile and no longer circling.

<margin>H</margin> ¶ Reason demonstrates, beyond this, that the age of the renewed heaven will be eternal; because the end for which man was created will have already been achieved, and judgment will have been given and ordered for him. Thus, no cause will remain by which the world could or should be renewed anymore. Therefore, the vision of our Messer Francesco Petrarch is true and approved by our theologians: namely, that after the final revolution of the heaven, the world, the heaven, the sun, and the stars must be undone and changed, and made much more beautiful in a perfect, immutable, and infinite age. Messer Francesco then adds and narrates what he saw with great wonder following this renewal of the world, saying that he marveled exceedingly when he saw the heaven rest on "one foot" <note>stand still</note> along with the sun, which had never ceased turning from the day it was created. For only with its turning and running did everything vary and change. He saw, beyond this, its three parts <note>likely past, present, and future</note> restricted to one; and that one was so firm that in its turning it no longer hurried as it used to. Consequently, he saw that there was no longer a distinction of time into past and future, nor was time divided into "before" and "after"—which variation causes our life to be filled with infirmity and bitterness. Instead, it stood in the likeness and form of the earth, bare and totally deprived of grass. Wherefore he says:

<margin>I</margin> ¶ For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it should primarily be known—as Peter of Tarantasia <note>theologian and later Pope Innocent V</note> writes in the fourth book of the *Sentences* at distinction 48—that since before the judg—

-> What wonder did I have? When I saw <-
-> Stay on one foot he who never stood still; <-
-> But running alone, changed everything. <-

# CHAPTER ONE

<margin>The universal judgment is arranged by divine justice so that the world may be purged by fire. Some say this will happen through the gathering of superior and inferior fires, just as the flood occurred through the downpour of celestial and earthly waters. Others say the fire will be ignited by the reflection of the sun’s rays upon these earthly bodies, which—</margin>

> **And I saw its three parts restricted**
> **Into one alone, and that one to be firm;**
> **So that, as it was wont, it no longer hastens:**
> **And as if on earth naked of grass and desolate,**
> **There is neither "above" nor "ever," neither "before" nor "behind,"**
> **Which make life bitter, varied, and weak.**

—by their nature are solid, similar to the solar reflection made in a concave mirror where experience shows that nearby objects are suddenly set ablaze. Others, however, say that the power of heaven—which currently restrains the <term>sphere of fire</term> <note>In the Aristotelian cosmos, the sphere of fire sat between the earth's atmosphere and the moon</note> so that it does not overflow and burn—will be relaxed. Therefore, after this combustion, heaven will be renewed and transmuted from the qualities suited to human corruption. Its immobility will follow, for the heavens currently move for no other purpose than the conservation of the world in this state until it pleases God to change it. Thus, when that purpose is removed, the movement of the heavens will likewise be removed. Therefore, heaven will then be fixed upon one point: that is, one immobile point where at present its two "feet" are fixed—the North Pole and the South Pole. For the intellect cannot imagine a spherical body remaining fixed upon one point while moving circularly toward—

<margin>K</margin>
—any other site. Secondly, it should be understood that the poet attributes the fact of "never having stopped since the day of creation" to the sun rather than to the heaven itself. This seems to be suggested by Holy Scripture at the beginning of Genesis, where, speaking of the creation of our mobile heaven (which is that of the fixed stars), it says nothing more than: <note>original: "Dixit quog; deus fiat firmamētū..."</note> *God also said: "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters." And God made the firmament, and divided the waters that were under the firmament from those that were above the firmament, and it was so. And God called the firmament Heaven, and the evening and the morning were the second day.* In these words, it is clear that no reason is expressed as to why this heaven should move. Therefore, it stood firm and immobile until the day the first parents sinned. But in the creation of the sun, He expressed the purpose for which it moved immediately, which was to illuminate the moon so she might preside over the night, as the text says: <note>original: "Dixit autē deus fiat luminaria..."</note> *And God said: "Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide the day and the night, and let them be for signs, and seasons, and days, and years." And it follows: "And God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night."* From this, it is manifest that the sun began to move immediately upon being created. This movement and path, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the second book of *On Generation and Corruption* and the second book of the *Physics* (as we have said elsewhere), is the efficient cause of every variation that occurs in the world.

<margin>L</margin>
In the third place, it should be considered that in the heaven and the sun (which can generally be understood of either), there are three qualities through which they alter and produce these various worldly effects: namely, light, <term>influence</term> <note>the astrological power believed to flow from stars to earth</note>, and movement. Of these three qualities, only light will remain after the Judgment; movement and all influence will cease. This is because the purpose for which they currently influence and move will have passed away. And therefore the poet rightly says that "its three parts"—that is, of the sun or the heaven, which are influence, brightness, and motion—will be "restricted to one alone": namely, to light, and that light will remain still. These preceding verses can also be interpreted as referring only to the sun, saying that its three parts—light, heat, and generative power—will be restricted to one: light, which will remain immobile. The poet says with good reason that those three parts will be restricted to one, rather than saying they will be taken away.

<margin>M</margin>
For these powers will not be lacking in the sun as a potential quality, but only in their operation, except for light, which will be more intense than it is now, as Isaiah shows us above. Finally, it should be noted that the poet says time will be like a "land naked of grass" to demonstrate its uniformity. Just as land where there is no grass does not appear varied but seems entirely similar and uniform, as experience teaches us when it is cultivated and furrowed. Therefore, there will no longer be "before" or "behind," since these differences arise only from the movement of heaven, as Aristotle shows in the fourth book of the *Physics* and the text of Genesis cited above.

<margin>N</margin>
Nevertheless, some texts are found that say "Down here the earth is naked of grass and desolate," which can easily be reconciled; for because of the scorching of the fire—

# THE TRIUMPH OF DIVINITY

Before the fire, the earth must return to its first origin and nature, of which the text of Genesis says: <note>original: "Terra autem erat inanis & vacua"</note> *The earth was without form and void.* Therefore, concluding that once the movement of the heavens is removed after the Judgment, the "was"—that is, the past—and the "will be"—that is, the future—will be taken away. It is these diversities of time that make our life seem bitter to us, and make it also infirm, weak, and fleeting. 

Afterward, Master Francesco <note>Messer Francesco Petrarch, the author of the poems being commented upon.</note> narrates what he further understood by contemplating with his mind, saying that by passing and penetrating with his thought and consideration of future things after the Day of Judgment—just as the sun penetrates through a pane of glass, or rather much more so, because nothing holds back thought as glass partially holds back the sun—he saw a Supreme Good without any company of evil, which only time mixes and produces for us. And demonstrating, as we said above, the act of burning charity, he exclaims, adding what a grace he considers to have been granted to him if he obtains the favor of being led into its possession. Whence he says:

<margin>O</margin>
<gloss>Having up to this point described the incomprehensible eternity which must follow after the Judgment, our poet now sees time confused and every other finite measure ended; he sees within it, without any present evil, the Supreme Good, who is the most high Ruler and Disposer of the order of the universe with everlasting laws. Most powerful God is seen clearly—</gloss>

> ->Thought passes through, just as the sun through glass;<-
> ->Rather, much more; for nothing holds it back:<-
> ->O, what grace will be mine if I ever obtain it:<-
> ->That I may see the Supreme Good present there,<-
> ->And not any evil; which only time mixes<-
> ->And departs with it, and with it comes.<-

—clearly, he has not separated himself from the opinion of Claudian <note>Claudius Claudianus (c. 370–404 AD), the last great Latin poet of antiquity.</note>, a worthy and excellent poet, who, considering eternity, describes it thus in these verses: <note>original: "Est ignota procul nostraeque impar vigat menti. Vix adeunda dijs annorum squallida mater. Immensum speluncam aevi que tempora vasto. Suppeditat reuocatque sinus: complectitur antrum Omnia: quae placido consumit numine serpens perpetuum viret squamis: caudaque reducto Ore vorat tacito relegens exordia lapsu. Vestibulum custos vultu longæva decoro ante fores natura sedet: cunctisq̃ uolantēs dependent mēbris aĩes mansura verendus scribit iura senex: numeros qui diuidit astris: Et cursus stabiles que moras: quibus oīa viuunt: Ac perunt: fixis cum legibus ille recenset."</note> *Far off, unknown, and beyond the reach of our minds, is the mother of years, scarce accessible even to the gods. A vast cave of ages provides and recalls time from its great lap. The cavern encompasses all things; a serpent, forever green with scales, consumes them with its calm power, devouring its tail with its mouth, retracing its beginnings in silent passage. At the threshold sits Nature, aged but of beautiful countenance; souls hang from her limbs, ready to fly. A venerable old man [Aeon/Eternity] writes the laws that shall endure: he divides the numbers of the stars, their stable courses and their delays, by which all things live and perish; he reviews them all with fixed laws.*

<margin>P</margin>
Secondly, for the understanding of the preceding verses, it should be understood that although after the Day of Judgment the two cities—that is, the one of Christ and the other of the Devil—will be full, nevertheless the poet here only commemorates the glory of the blessed. For by understanding that glory, one also understands the <term>disposition of the damned</term> <note>The state or arrangement of those condemned to hell.</note>, as is drawn from <term>the Philosopher</term> <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), whose works formed the basis of Renaissance university education.</note> in the first book of *On the Soul*, where he says: <note>original: "Rectum est index sui atque obliqui"</note> *The straight is the judge of itself and of the crooked.* 

He says, therefore, that he saw here a Supreme Good without any other evil, which only time mixes and brings, as his thought penetrates just as the sun passes through glass—and even much more. For it must be understood that the light of the sun is of such subtlety that it penetrates and passes through certain <term>pores</term> <note>original: "perosta" (porosità), referring to microscopic gaps in the material structure.</note> which are in the glass; but the intellect does not pass through pores nor any other obstacle, and therefore it reaches every object, however remote or hidden, provided the will to know is directed toward it. 

Similarly, it should also be considered that after the Day of Judgment, our bodies being glorified,

<margin>Q</margin>
the invalidity and infirm nature of our <term>sensitive powers</term> <note>The physical senses (sight, hearing, etc.) as opposed to the pure intellect.</note> will be taken away, and they will remain in their perfect being, enjoying God then "face to face," as the Apostle <note>Saint Paul the Apostle.</note> shows when speaking of the <term>beatific vision</term> <note>The ultimate direct self-communication of God to the individual person.</note>, saying: <note>original: "Vidimus nunc per speculum in enigmate: tunc autem facie ad faciem."</note> *Now we see through a glass darkly; but then face to face.* 

Thus we shall possess the Supreme Good without any mixture of evil, which only time produces for you. Here the poet takes the quality for the subject: that is, "time" for the heaven that turns, because God in Himself cannot be the cause of any evil, being supreme perfection. And therefore John says in the first chapter, speaking of God:

<margin>R</margin>
<note>original: "Sine ipso factum est nihil"</note> *Without Him nothing was made.* Where the theologians, in their glosses, say: <note>original: "nihil, id est, peccatum"</note> *Nothing—that is, sin.* 

Therefore, although God is the first cause of all things, as is proved by Aristotle in the second book of the *Metaphysics*, and as Augustine shows in the seventh book of *On the Trinity*, He nevertheless moves things only as the Beloved and Desired, and as the ultimate end—as is written in the first book of *On the Heavens* and the twelfth of the *Metaphysics*. Because of this, efficacy is attributed to the heavens as His instrument and secondary cause. Whence the philosopher in the first book of the *Metaphysics* affirms that this inferior world is effectively governed by the heavens. Therefore, when the heavens no longer move after the Judgment, the secondary causes will universally cease to act, and only the First Cause will remain, from which nothing but good can possibly proceed. Appropri- <meta>catchword: -ately</meta>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s "Triumph of Divinity." The previous page discussed the cessation of time and the end of the world’s changing nature. # CHAPTER ONE

Therefore the poet correctly affirms: saying that evil comes with time and departs with it, time being an accident of the heaven <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that does not belong to the essence of a thing; here, it refers to time being a byproduct of the movement of the celestial spheres.</note> as we said above by the authority of the philosopher. Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> then adds a privative effect <note>A result defined by the absence of something—in this case, the absence of motion.</note> which must necessarily follow the stillness of the heaven, saying that after the Judgment the sun will no longer have as its dwelling and zodiacal circle the place where the signs of Taurus and Pisces are located; for it is through the varying movement through these houses and signs that all our labor is now born, now dies, now grows, and now diminishes.

> The sun shall have no lodging in Taurus or Pisces;
> Through whose variation our labor grows,
> Now is born, now dies, and now wanes.

<margin>S</margin>
¶ As we said at the beginning for the understanding of the preceding verses, in the seventh sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note> a circle is designated, contained between two tropics where the winter and summer solstices occur when the sun reaches them. This is called the zodiac, divided into twelve parts called signs by the astrologers, named for their resemblance to the creatures counted within them. Therefore, through this circle, or rather beneath it, the sun moves, passing through the twelve signs in the time of one year. From this movement, according to the properties and temperament of those signs, the sun generates various qualities and dispositions in us and in the world. However, since the sun must stop after the Day of Judgment and no longer move in a circle, it will no longer have Taurus as its lodging (which it enters on the 11th or 12th of April), nor will it enter Pisces (which it enters in February, on the same days of the month), nor any other sign in the zodiac which it enters according to the proportion of its entry into the sign of Aries in March at the beginning of the year.

<margin>T</margin>
¶ But if anyone should ask here: if the sun stops moving, where will it stop? In which sign will it remain? I respond that the sun will not move from the sphere where it is, nor will the parts of the zodiac change; only the qualities proportioned to human corruption will cease. The sun will stand still in the sign of Aries, and likely at the fifteenth degree, since God ought to choose for Judgment the same day He chose for the Incarnation and Death <note>Traditional medieval theology often held that the world was created, the Annunciation occurred, and Christ died on the same calendar date, often identified as March 25th, when the sun is in Aries.</note>—though the truth of this remains always with our Salvation and with those who understand better and more soundly. For as Augustine says: *It is better to doubt concerning hidden things than to argue about uncertain things* <note>original: "Melius est dubitare de occultis quam litigare de incertis"</note>, as the Master reports in the fourth book of the *Sentences* at the final distinction <note>Refers to Peter Lombard, the "Master of the Sentences," a standard medieval theological textbook.</note>. Therefore, Messer Francesco, having reached eternal glory, the Supreme Good, infinite beatitude, and every kind of happiness in his thought, exclaims worthily regarding the state of the "comprehensores" <note>A theological term for those who have reached heaven and "grasp" or see God directly.</note> and blessed souls, saying: "O blessed spirits, how happy are those who find themselves established in that rank, and those who likewise will find that their names shall then be in eternal memory." Whence he says:

> Blessed spirits, who in the supreme choir
> Will be found, or are found, in such a rank,
> That their name shall be in eternal memory.

<margin>V</margin>
¶ O worthy and excellent memory! O most singular fame of the blessed souls! How worthy is our author and the historian, God the Father Almighty, who celebrates your names and your deeds! Let Dictys of Crete and Dares the Phrygian be silent; let Eutropius be silent together with Paul Orosius; let Sextus Rufus, Pliny with Lucius Florus, Justin, and Euclid the historian be silent; let Aelius Spartianus, Aelius Lampridius, and Flavius Vopiscus be silent; let Trebellius Pollio, Julius Capitolinus, Valerius Maximus, and Julius Frontinus be silent; let Ammianus Marcellinus, Cornelius Tacitus, and Diodorus Siculus be silent; let Servilius Romanus, Aufidius Bassus, and Herodian be silent; let Quintus Curtius, Herodotus, and Appian of Alexandria be silent; let Suetonius Tranquillus, Polybius, and Trogus Pompeius be silent; and finally, let Titus Livy be silent, and Plutarch with Sallust be hushed. Let Caesar and Varro fall into silence in comparison to the Divine Historian <note>The commentator provides an exhaustive list of famous Greek and Roman historians to emphasize that their records of human empires are nothing compared to God's record of the saved.</note>, who has written the deeds of the blessed according to the divine will and intellect, predefining and rewarding us according to our works. He does not merely note general things like other writers, but every tiny gesture, thought, or word; for He has written the Book of Life, of which Moses speaks in Exodus chapter 32, Isaiah in chapter 8, Daniel in chapter 11, and John in the Apocalypse, chapter 20.

<margin>X</margin>
¶ This Book of Life, therefore, wherein all meritorious works are written, shall stand forever open before the blessed for their glory. Thus, in eternity, as each spirit looks upon the good works of the others in this exchange of contemplation, they shall all remain in each other’s perpetual memory.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s "Triumph of Divinity." The previous page discussed the end of celestial movement and the cessation of time. This page shifts focus to the soul's journey through the "torrent of life" and the distinction between worldly goods and eternal happiness.</meta>

# TRIUMPH OF DIVINITY

The poet exclaims in the same manner. Messer Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> speaks regarding the state of wayfarers <note>A theological term for people currently living their lives on earth as a journey toward the afterlife.</note>, saying truly how happy is he who, through his good works, finds the way and the ford to safely cross this craggy and rapid torrent named life—which to many ignorant people is pleasing and delightful. Thus he says:

<margin>y</margin>
¶ Because when a thing is ordered toward some end, it is appropriately named after that end: wherefore on this subject the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the second book of the *Physics*: generation is nature, because it tends toward nature <note>original: "generatio est natura quia cuius i naturam." This suggests that the process of becoming (generation) is defined by the essence or "nature" it eventually achieves.</note>.

->O happy is he who finds the ford<-
->Of this craggy and rapid torrent;<-
->Which is named life, and to many is pleasing.<-

Therefore, since we and our lives are ordered toward perpetual happiness, a life can deservedly be called happy when it adapts itself to achieve its end—which is the possession of the celestial homeland—upon departing from this life, which is so dear and so much craved by common men. This life is a most rapid torrent; it is impossible to imagine water flowing in a river, however fast it may be, that is not infinitely slower than the transit of our worldly life.

<margin>Z</margin>
¶ Therefore, whatever certain velocity might be granted, the present life passes infinitely faster; nor is a blink of an eye so quick that every temporal delight and pleasure has not passed away in even less time. 

O happy, then, and truly happy are those who, in such velocity and in such a deep sea of passion, know how to find the ford of abstinence from carnal delights and cross this river of earthly life with the white robe of pure innocence—the robe entrusted to us by the Holy Church, which we must carry before the tribunal of Christ, according to the vision of John in the seventh chapter of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, when he saw that great multitude standing before the throne in the sight of the Lamb without blemish, all clothed and adorned in white robes. 

Afterward, Messer Francesco, having in the preceding verses deservedly praised the state of the blessed and the <term>just</term> <note>Those living in a state of grace</note> who proceed in grace, he now deplores the miserable condition of common folk. These people ignorantly believe that things dominated by time can bring us happiness or peace, saying: "O wretched common people, totally blind to the light of the intellect, who still place their hope in this world in things that time carries away and cuts short with such fury and suddenness." Wherefore he says:

->Wretched, the common and blind folk;<-
->Who place their hopes here in such things<-
->That time carries away so suddenly.<-

<margin>A</margin>
¶ For clearer evidence of the preceding verses, it should be known that "goods"—as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> writes in the first book of the *Ethics*—are distinguished into three kinds: namely, goods of the soul, goods of the body, and goods of fortune. It is likewise a most manifest thing that hope has as its object a good, albeit a future one. Thus it happens that common men imagine that whenever they possess goods of the body and goods of fortune, they are blessed. Some others, not having the light of the holy faith, believe that the goods of the soul—and especially the habit of <term>wisdom</term> <note>Theoretical or worldly knowledge</note> (which is the noblest of all others, as Aristotle writes in the sixth book of the *Ethics*, and Cicero in the second book of *On Duties* and in *On Friendship*)—are what make us happy. 

How false this imagination and opinion is regarding the first group has been demonstrated at length above; and to the second group, speaking of worldly wisdom, Solomon openly shows them to be in error. Wherefore in the second chapter of Ecclesiastes, wishing to show that human wisdom is dominated by time, he says these words: "The wise man shall not be remembered forever, any more than the fool; and all things in the days to come shall be covered with oblivion" <note>original: "Non . n . erit memoria sapientis similiter & stulti in ppetuum: & futura tēpora obliuione cuncta pariter operient." A translation of Ecclesiastes 2:16.</note>. From this it remains manifest that true beatitude is not in such objects. And therefore those who, so believing, think to make themselves happy by their possessions, are truly wretched, for they always remain and live in error.

<margin>B</margin>
¶ Having thus far shown the falsity of the opinions of the common folk, Messer Francesco now, with an honest and deserved reprimand, describes what the true object is—that in which our intellect and will find rest, and where every happiness is truly placed—saying: "O mortals, sick and weak of intellect, or truly deaf and blind of mind!" 

¶ You are poor in counsel and in reasonings [concerning] Him who governs the world solely by a nod of His brow, and who quiets the elements or disturbs them according to His will. To His intelligence and wisdom, not only I, an earthly creature, cannot reach or attain, but even the angels are satisfied in their desire just to see one thousandth part of His perfection.

<summary>This page discusses the metaphor of life as a rapid, dangerous torrent and contrasts the "white robe" of spiritual innocence with the fleeting nature of worldly goods. It uses the authority of Aristotle, Cicero, and Solomon to argue that neither physical wealth nor human wisdom can provide lasting happiness compared to the divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Petrarch’s "Triumph of Divinity." The previous page concluded with the rapid passage of time and the pursuit of eternal happiness. This page identifies God as the ultimate object of human intellect and desire, defending Petrarch’s poetic style through theological and philosophical authorities.</meta>

# CHAPTER ONE

...its perfection, and in this they are thirsty and attentive. This, therefore, is He who ought to be our object; this is what we must seek to understand and this alone we must propose as the end of our investigation. Wherefore he says:

<margin>C ¶ Fifthly, the elegance and the learning of our excellent poet <note>Petrarch</note> are demonstrated even more by the ignorance of those who frequently reprimand him. This is most clearly shown where it is understood that the "imperfect construction" for which he is slandered in these verses is not without reason and is described with great foundation. For, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> writes in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*, the most well-known truths and evident principles are recognized only if the terms are understood. Therefore, we, knowing how much is implied by</margin>

->O truly deaf, naked, and frail,<-
->Poor in argument and in counsel,<-
->Wholly sick, and miserable mortals.<-
->He who governs the world with a brow alone,<-
->Who disturbs and quiets the elements,<-
->To whose knowledge not only do I not attain,<-
->But the angels are glad and content<-
->To see but one of a thousand parts,<-
->And in this they remain desirous and intent.<-

this term "He who governs the world with a brow," we will immediately understand Him to be the object that we must both love and understand, without it needing to be further affirmed or expressed. In God alone, therefore, consists the fulfillment of our <term>beatitude</term> <note>Supreme blessedness or happiness.</note>, which the common people—poor and naked of judgment—do not understand, thinking instead that it is placed elsewhere.

<margin>D</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is to be understood that God is infinite, as the Philosopher shows in the first book of *On the Heavens*, in *On Good Fortune*, and in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* where he says: *For he moves through infinite time, and a finite thing does not have infinite power* <note>original: "Mouet .n. per tēpus infinitum & non habet potentiam infinitā finitum."</note>. And Saint Anselm confirms this, as do Athanasius and John of Damascus in his sentences, saying: *God is a beginning without beginning, the first principle, uncreated, unbegotten, eternal, infinite, powerful over infinite things* <note>original: "Deus est sine principio principium primum increatum ingenitū æternū infinitum ad infinita potens."</note>. Similarly, <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic.</note> also says: *God is an intellectual sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere* <note>original: "Deus spera intellectualis cui' centrum vbiq; est circumferētia vero nusq̄;."</note>. And finally, the prophet David in Psalm 147 <note>The text cites Psalm 134, but the quote "magnitudinis eius non est finis" is from Psalm 145/144.</note> says: *of his greatness there is no end* <note>original: "magnitudinis eius non est finis."</note>. For this reason, He is not comprehensible by a created intellect, as every creature has only a defined perfection and is not capable of containing an infinite object. Wherefore John of Damascus, in the place cited, excellently adds: *For no one has seen God except the only-begotten Son, who was eternally in the bosom of the Father* <note>original: "Nemo .n deum vidit nisi unigenitus fili' qui i sinu patris æternaliter fuit."</note>. And Isaiah, confirming the same in the 40th chapter, says: *The eternal God, who created the ends of the earth, will not faint nor grow weary, and there is no searching out of his wisdom* <note>original: "Deus sempiternus q creauit terminus terræ nō deficiet neq; laborabit nec est inuestigatio sapientiæ eius."</note>.

<margin>E</margin>
¶ Therefore, because of this, the angels remain content to understand even a tiny part of the divine essence: by the understanding of which they judge themselves to be blessed and every desire of theirs to be filled. Let mortals, then, understand this: here let them direct their every desire; let each seek this as the end and rest of their labors. For as Augustine says in the 17th book <note>Likely referring to the 15th book of *De Trinitate*.</note> of *On the Trinity*: *Eternal life consists in that contemplation in which God will be seen not for punishment, but for everlasting joy* <note>original: "Vita eterna est in illa contēplatione in qua deus non ad pœnam videbitur .sed ad gaudium sempiternum."</note>. And Christ himself teaches us this in Saint John in the 17th chapter <note>OCR says xvj (16), but it is John 17:3.</note> when he said: *For this is eternal life, that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent* <note>original: "Hæc enim est vita æterna vt cognoscant te verū deum: quem misisti Iesum Christum."</note>. Mortals are therefore to be judged naked and deprived of all intelligence if they persuade themselves in any way that they can perfectly hope for or understand anything without the proper knowledge of God, in whom is placed the principle and light of all our knowing and understanding. Wherefore Plato rightly said, as Augustine reports in the seventh book of *The City of God*, chapter seven: *The light suited for learning all things is God himself, by whom all things were made* <note>original: "Lumē accōmodatū ad discēdū omnia ē ipse deus a quo facta sunt oia."</note>. Therefore, our mind, soul, and heart should always be turned toward him.

<margin>F</margin>
¶ Having now shown in the preceding verses what the true object of our intellect is—whereby the vanity of every other science pertaining to the <term>speculative life</term> <note>The life of contemplation and study.</note> is made known—the poet consequently reproves the obscure diligence and the clouded discourse of human prudence concerning temporal things pertaining to the <term>political life</term> <note>The life of action and worldly affairs.</note>, saying: "O vain and wandering mind, always fasting and empty at the end of your labor, why do you give yourself so many worries?" Seeing as a single small hour clears away and undoes all that work which was gathered with labor over many years; and especially because that which presses upon the thought and burdens the soul—that is, the "just past," the "now present," the "yesterday morning," the "yesterday evening," and every other distinction of time—will all pass away just as if they were a shadow. Wherefore he says:

# CHAPTER ONE

By placing a greater number of blessed spirits, he says that Lady Laura was much more blessed than the others. For an understanding of this, it must be known that the most high God—a just judge and no respecter of persons—will reward each person with glory and salvation according to the merits of their preceding life. This we have said many times above, especially on the authority of John in the Apocalypse, chapter 20, and Isaiah, chapter 28. The means, therefore, by which this glory and salvation are acquired are sacred baptism and faith, as Christ testifies in Saint Matthew <note>While the text attributes this to Matthew, the quote "He who believes and is baptized shall be saved" is found in Mark 16:16.</note>, saying: *He who believes and is baptized shall be saved.* <note>original: "Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit saluus erit."</note> Secondly, it should be noted that by "M. L." <note>Madonna Laura</note>, as we said from the beginning, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> intends to describe those people who govern themselves with reason and religion, as was demonstrated by him in his worthy *Triumphs of Chastity* and of *Death*. ¶ Lastly, it should be noted that according to the final conclusion of the theologians—especially Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> in the *Second Part of the Second Part* <note>Summa Theologica, II-II</note>, question 1—Christians are saved through faith in three ways. Some are saved in the faith of the universal church; these are the unlearned people <note>original: "idioti," referring to those without formal education or theological training.</note> who do not have a distinct knowledge of those things which are necessary to believe, but ultimately believe what the Church believes. Some others are saved in the faith of their fathers and mothers; these are the children who die, for whom godparents promise faith to God at the font. The third group who are saved are the adults who, through their own faith, are well-learned and expert in those things that must be done to conform themselves to the will of God. Such people, represented by the poet through Laura, will be much more blessed than the others, having merited more than the others. By this, the poet quietly invites us to pursue this greater glory, and yet gives hope to the others who cannot raise themselves to the contemplation of divine things by their own power, placing them among the blessed, though with lesser glory. ¶ Laura, therefore, more glorious in heaven because of her merits, was taken by death and removed far from her natural term. This is because she died at the age of thirty-five, whereas the common term of living reaches the age of seventy. Thus, Laura was taken and her life subtracted in the middle of her life's course, as our Master Francesco demonstrates in that sonnet when he says: *In her most beautiful and flowering age, when Love is accustomed to have the most power in us, leaving her earthly husk on the earth.* By these verses, the poet describes the aforementioned age. Then, the poet consequently continues and introduces an effect that will follow for the blessed souls: namely, the appearance of their good and holy works. He says that then, after the Day of Judgment, the angelic, honest, and distinct words of Laura and the chaste and virtuous thoughts that nature placed and located in her youthful and wise heart will be apparent before the sight of all the blessed. Where he says:

<margin>¶ For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, it should be known that in the state of blessed glory—so that there may be no cause for envy or any other human scandal, but rather a completely affectionate and burning charity in every soul—each person will see their reward </margin>

> Then the angelic garbs shall appear,
> And the honest words, and the chaste thoughts,
> Which nature placed in her youthful heart.

corresponding to their preceding merit. For a person earns merit in the present life in three ways: through words, through thoughts, and through deeds. Just as, conversely, one sins in these same three ways. Therefore, the poet expresses that Laura’s words and thoughts will be known, remaining silent about her deeds as they are a most well-known thing. ¶ He then adds another effect that must be present and follow after the Judgment: which is that the dead, resurrected and glorified, will return to their most flowering age. Thus, Laura’s beautiful face will be seen in the place where Love held him bound for so long. Because of this, everything being known in the sight of all the blessed, he says he will be pointed out among them and it will be said: "Behold the one who always wept in life and in death for Laura; and nonetheless, in his weeping, this man was more blessed than any other lover ever was in any laughter or other amorous pleasure." Wherefore he says:

<margin>¶ As it is an easy thing to understand from the context of the preceding verses, our poet assumes two things in them: one is that the dead must rise again; the other is the blessed rising again.</margin>

> So many faces, which time and death have ruined,
> Shall return to their most flowering state;
> And it shall be seen where Love, you bound me.

# THE TRIUMPH OF DIVINITY

...in the most flourishing age, which is said to be the age that Christ was <note>Referring to the traditional belief that the resurrected will appear to be about 33 years old, the age of Christ at his death.</note>. Concerning this, our sacred theologians persuade us by a great number of effective reasons; however, for the present, we shall be content only with—

-> Wherefore I shall be pointed out by finger, <-
-> Behold, he who always wept, and in his weeping <-
-> Was more blessed than the laughter of any other: <-
<note>These lines are from Petrarch’s "Triumph of Divinity," where the poet describes his own transformation and future state among the blessed.</note>

<margin>C</margin> —two reasons, for the understanding of which it must first be presupposed that God is just. This is demonstrated by the Apostle to the Ephesians, chapter 6, when he says that with God there is no respect of persons <note>original: "acceptiōe di p̄sone," from Ephesians 6:9, meaning God does not show favoritism based on status.</note>, and the prophet David writes the same in Psalm 7 when he says: **God is a just and strong judge.** <note>original: "Deus iudex iustus & fortis."</note> And in Psalm 10: **For the Lord is just and has loved justice; his face has beheld equity.** <note>original: "Qm̄ iustus dn̄s iustitiā dilexit eqtatem vidit vultus eius."</note> And in Psalm 144: **The Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works.** <note>original: "Iustus dn̄s in ōibus viis suis sanctus in opi bus suis."</note> He affirms this same thing in Psalm 18, Psalm 49, and Psalm 46. This is also confirmed by the gloss on the law of justice in the Digest <term>ff. de iustitia z iure<gloss>A reference to the Digest of Justinian, the foundation of medieval Roman law.</gloss></term>. ¶ Secondly, it must be presupposed that whatever commits a sin must be judged and punished by God. From these two presuppositions, a primary reason is deduced: since both the soul and the body sinned together in the individual Adam in his transgression against the law and commandment of God, for this reason both the soul and the body must be punished by God if His infinite justice is to be maintained. For this reason, experience teaches us that many sinners come to death without suffering any penalty in the body; therefore, it is necessary that the body must rise again to duly suffer that penalty after the Day of Judgment which was worthy of the sin it committed.

<margin>D</margin> ¶ But if anyone should say that the penalty of the body is its incineration <note>The process of the body turning to dust/ash after death.</note>, I say this is an error, because where there is no sensation, there can be no penalty. Therefore, that is not a penalty of the human body, but the dissolution of the corpse, which was once the body and an essential part of the man. For the second reason, it is presupposed that we are members united in the mystical body to our own head, Jesus Christ. This presupposition the Apostle explains in Ephesians, chapter 6 <note>Actually Ephesians 5:30.</note>, when he says, speaking of Christ and of us: **For we are members of his body and of his bones.** <note>original: "Quare mēbra sumus corporis eius & de ossibus eius."</note> And Christ in Saint John, chapter 17, confirming the same, said while speaking to the Father: **The love which you gave me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one: I in you and you in me.** <note>original: "Charitatē quā dedisti mihi dedi eis ut sint unus sicut & nos unū sumus ego ī te & tu ī me." The author uses "Charitatem" (charity/love) where most Latin Bibles use "claritatem" (glory).</note> From this presupposition arises the other reason, which is this: Christ rose, therefore we shall rise. This consequence is necessary by virtue of the scientific principle: that is, concerning anything, either the one or the other of two contradictories is true, and of no thing are both true <note>The Principle of Excluded Middle.</note>. Whence, if we did not rise again, it would be necessary to say either that of the same mystical body "rising" and "not rising" were both true (which is impossible), or else that Christ had merit and was not true God—a thing which is a divine error even to imagine and is forbidden to everyone.

<margin>E</margin> ¶ The resurrection of the dead is then confirmed by the sacred eloquence of the divine prophets; wherefore principally Hosea in chapter 13, speaking in the person of Christ, says: **O death, I will be your death.** <note>original: "O mors ego ero mors tua."</note> This thing cannot be—that is, that death should die—unless those who are dead rise in a state which will never again be subject to death. David the prophet also shows this purpose in Psalm 4 when he speaks thus: **I slept and took my rest, and I rose up, because the Lord has taken me.** <note>original: "Ego dormiui z soporatus sum & resurrexi qz dn̄s suscepit me."</note> The hope of Martha in Saint John, chapter 11, confirmed the same when she said to Christ: **I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection on the last day.** <note>original: "Scio quod resurget ī resurrectiōe in nouissimo die."</note> Judas Maccabeus, also hoping for the resurrection, sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to the temple in Jerusalem to offer for the sins of the dead, as is written in the second book of Maccabees. Let us now pass over Ezekiel in chapter 37 and Micah in chapter 7; let us pass over Job and the Gospel, so as not to make any more concordant testimonies in this cause, for which we have no doubt. But as to whether Christ rose again—if Jewish perfidy and heretical depravity do not believe the prophets who announced it to the apostles (who walked, reasoned, and ate with Him after He was raised, and testified to it)—let them believe at least their own writer Josephus in the book of *Antiquities of the Jews*, which certainly confounds every error. He says this of Christ: **Now there was about this time Jesus, a wise man, if it be lawful to call him a man. For he was a doer of wonderful works, a teacher of all those men who receive the truth with pleasure. He drew over to him both many of the Jews and many of the Gentiles. He was the Christ; and when Pilate, at the suggestion of the principal men amongst us, had condemned him to the cross, those that loved him at the first did not forsake him. For he appeared to them alive again the third day, as the divine prophets had foretold these and ten thousand other wonderful things concerning him.** <note>original: "Fuit aūt iisdem tp̄ibus Iesus sapiens vir..." This is the famous "Testimonium Flavianum," a passage in Josephus's history that mentions Jesus. Modern scholars debate its total authenticity, but it was used as a primary proof in the Renaissance.</note> Where then can the Jew rightfully flee? Where the heretic? Where the Sadducee who denies the resurrection? Nowhere more securely than to the bosom of the Holy Church, and there repent and confess his error.

<margin>F</margin> ¶ Lastly, the second thing introduced by our poet must be understood: that is, that the bodies of the blessed, in rising again, will return to their most flourishing state; and this is the conclusion.

# CHAPTER ONE

G
It is the common conclusion of all the theologians in the fourth book of the *Sentences* <note>Referring to the *Sentences* of Peter Lombard, the standard medieval textbook of theology.</note> at the final distinction where they say that all the blessed shall rise again in the age of Christ, which was the age He had attained when He earned merit [through the Passion], being thirty-two years and three months from His birth. This will be for two probable reasons. The first is because, as the blessed were conformed to Christ in their works during life, it is fitting that they should also be conformed to Him in glory. The second reason is because, since the blessed must take up every perfection, they must not lack the perfection of age, which is the midpoint of consistency called by physicians the "age of beauty" <note>original: "ætas pulchritudinis"</note>, which Christ chose for His death so that, this age being more flourishing than any other, He might feel so much more pain in His death. In this regard, then, Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> adds that the beautiful face of Laura will be seen again, and he says of himself how much he was blessed in his weeping, so as to conform to the opinion of Augustine in book 5 of *The City of God* at the final chapter, where he says:

¶ Miserable is he to whom it was permitted to sin. <note>original: "Miſerum cui peccare licebat."</note>

Wherefore, by contrast, one can be called blessed to whom sinning is not permitted, just as happened to our Master Francesco who, wishing to look upon the beauty of Laura with too much delight and too immoderately, was prohibited from doing so by her chastity and prudence. Because of this he grieved and wept, in which weeping he was much more to be considered blessed than other lovers in their joyful laughter for the possession of the object they loved here below without measure. These verses can also be interpreted otherwise: namely, that Master Francesco wishes to make Laura's beauty exceedingly excellent, saying it was so great that it was a greater beatitude to gaze upon her and always weep for her—not being able to possess her—than to love another woman and have every desired pleasure from her. As he himself testifies in that sonnet, "Cruel star, if heaven has power over us," where at the end, speaking to Love, he says: *Yet it consoles me that to languish for her is better than to rejoice in another, and you swear it to me by the hour and your arrow; and I believe you.* This interpretation is tolerable, but the first is, in my judgment, more consistent with the context of the material. Master Francesco continues thereafter, adding an effect appropriate to the blessed souls, saying that she—for whom he also sings in his poems, always weeping and remembering her after death—will have the greatest wonder at herself, feeling herself given the prize of perfection and glory among the blessed souls. Wherefore he says:

<margin>The poet intends in the preceding verses (though he names only Laura) to describe—as we have said many times—through her person all those good people who by their own faith and virtuous work shall acquire heaven. Lady Laura, therefore, and these</margin>

<meta>This page continues the theological commentary on Petrarch's *Triumph of Eternity*, transitioning from the physical state of the resurrected to the celestial hierarchy of angels and the nature of the final judgment.</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF DIVINITY

<margin>K</margin>
In the ninth distinction <note>A reference to the divisions in Peter Lombard's *Sentences*, a standard medieval theological textbook.</note>, it is explained that the order of the angels is divided into three hierarchies, and each hierarchy into three choirs of angels. These are named according to the gifts of grace granted to them by the Most High God. 

The first and highest hierarchy is the most worthy and is divided into: **Seraphim**, who are interpreted as "burning with charity"; **Cherubim**, who are interpreted as "full of intelligence and wisdom"; and **Thrones**, who are so called because they are seats, being so filled with grace that God seems to rest or sit within them. 

The second hierarchy is divided into **Dominations**, and angels who exceed in **Virtue**, then **Principalities** and **Powers**. To these is committed the government or the order of the heavens and the conservation of the universe. The **Principalities** are so named because they are set over the disposal of particular worldly matters subject to them. The **Powers** are so called because they have the power to enact all supernatural effects in the world. 

Of the third and final hierarchy, the first are the **Virtues** <note>The author's classification of Virtues in both the second and third hierarchy reflects a variation in traditional angelic lore.</note>, through whom great signs, portents, and miracles are performed. The second are the **Archangels**, through whom the future events of greater significance are announced to the world. The third and last are called **Angels**, who announce common matters to humanity.

Secondly, it should be known that when the Universal Judgment occurs, it is a very great and hidden secret. No one knows it except the Eternal Father, as Christ testifies in Saint Matthew, affirming it in the twenty-fourth chapter, and in Saint Mark in the fourteenth chapter, when he speaks of the Day of Judgment: *But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but the Father alone* <note>original: "De die aut illa & hora nemo scit neq; āgeli cœlorū nisi pater solus"</note>. However, many judge that Christ meant the lower angels of the second and third hierarchies, and not the first, who possess the fullness of intelligence. This seems to be the opinion of Saint Gregory, even though the Master <note>Peter Lombard</note> in the cited passage interprets it otherwise. His saying is judged thus: that the Seraphim, through their charity, have as much intelligence as the Cherubim, since they are always assisting God. This is the opinion Master Francesco <note>Petrarch</note> affirms in that place.

->To such a high secret, he who approaches<-
->I believe draws near:<-

<margin>L</margin>
Lastly, it should be noted that the poet in these verses describes a very great praise of **L.** <note>Laura, Petrarch's muse</note>. He says that through her merits she has ascended to the first hierarchy of angels. And whether the Cherubim or Seraphim look upon her, their intelligence shines through this great secret, which is given to those who come closest to the most faithful companions of God. These are the angels placed in the first hierarchy: Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones. Nevertheless, Master Francesco believes the time of judgment is drawing near, and certainly not without reason. For through the signs of Christ in the cited passages, and in Saint Luke in the twenty-first chapter, he assigns signs such as universal wars, pestilences, famines, defects of the moon and celestial bodies, great hatred, and other signs that must immediately precede the judgment. Any sound intellect can easily understand that the day of the Universal Judgment should not be very distant from us.

<margin>M</margin>
Master Francesco then narrates what must actually be done on the day of judgment before the Just Judge. He says that then the human conscience shall give an account of "true gains"—those which came from the grace of God and our merits—and also of the "false deeds" of blind cupidity and insatiable avarice. At that time, all these will be known to have been "works of spiders"—that is, subtle and fragile—or "works of spiders" in the sense of works made for one's own perdition. This is like what Arachne did when she contested her skill against Pallas <note>Athena</note>, where in her tapestry Arachne depicted the sins of the gods; for this reason, she was turned into that worm which is still called *aranea* <note>Latin for spider. The story comes from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*.</note>. And he adds that then it will be seen how much care is presently placed in vain regarding the acquisition of earthly things, and how in vain men exhaust themselves and sweat to acquire worldly abundance. And how, in the end, believing they possess these delights and pleasures forever, people find themselves deceived and deluded. Wherefore he says:

<margin>N</margin>
What the acquisition of "true gains" made by the soul in glorified heaven might be has been made quite clear above. But now, with great reason in these verses, Master Francesco, wishing to show the disposition of the reprobate <note>The damned or those rejected by God.</note>, takes his beginning from avarice. He says how an account of "false gains" will be made before God; for, as the Apostle writes to Timothy in the fourth chapter, avarice is the foundation and root of every other sin. Wherefore he says: *For the root of all evils is greed; which some reaching after have erred from the law and pierced themselves through with many sorrows* <note>original: "radix. n. omniū malorū ē cupiditas. quā quidem appetentes errauerunt a lege: e īseruerunt se doloribus multis"</note>. To this same purpose, Quintus Curtius <note>A Roman historian.</note> also speaks.

->and of gains<-
->True, and of false, an account shall be made:<-
->For then all shall be as spider's webs.<-
->It will be seen, how much care is placed in vain:<-
->And how in vain one tires, and sweats,<-
->How people are deceived.<-

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the finality of the Last Judgment, transitioning from the description of the angelic hierarchies to the ethical rejection of worldly wealth and the transparency of the human conscience before the Divine Judge.</meta>

# CHAPTER ONE

<margin>O</margin>
Nothing is forbidden to greed. For this reason, the ancient philosophers **Crates the Theban**, **Zeno**, **Thales of Miletus**, **Anaxagoras of Clazomenae**, **Diogenes the Cynic**, **Bias of Priene**, and many others also mentioned above, always repudiated riches as the cause of many troubles and vices. And **Lycurgus the Spartan**, as **Justinian** shows in his laws, removed all use of gold and silver as the source of every evil and scandal. Finally, regarding the vanity of human cares, their vain labor, and their deception, let the sentiment of **Solomon** written at the beginning of <term>Ecclesiastes</term> <note>The text uses "Ecclesiastico," but refers to the opening of Ecclesiastes.</note> be sufficient: *Vanity of vanities: and all is vanity* <note>original: "vanitas vanitatum: & omnia vanitas"</note>. And likewise the sentiment of **Empedocles**, who said that the most principal and honorable thing in all the variety found in the world is to despise the flux of moving, falling, and transitory things. Therefore, all those who have hoped in these things in the present life will rightfully find themselves deceived; together with **Boethius** in the second book of the *Consolation*, they will weep for their losses, saying in verse to themselves: *Alas, who was that first man who dug out the weights of covered gold and the gems that wished to remain hidden—precious dangers?* <note>original: "Heu primus quis fuit ille Auri qui pondera tecti: Gẽmasq; latere volentes Preciosa pericula fodit?"</note>. And so, just as they will find themselves deceived in the end, they also provoke divine justice to rightfully exasperate and punish them according to the vanity of their thoughts. Next follows another disposition of souls for the judgment: which is that every human work shall be most known and clear, saying that in that day, before the sight of God, there shall be no secret that closes or covers the minds of men, but every conscience, whether bright or dark, will be naked and open before the whole world on that day.

<margin>P</margin>
<margin>¶ Divine justice and divine goodness intend to omit nothing that might procure glory for worthy souls; and conversely, to offer confusion and pain to damned sinners: because good works and</margin>
->There shall be no secret that covers or closes:<-
->Every conscience, whether bright or dark, shall be<-
->Before the whole world, open and naked;<-

<margin>Q</margin>
affections of the conscience will serve to honor glorious souls and confound the wicked together with their iniquity, which they will see present before them. For this reason, the Most High wills that on the day of judgment every conscience be seen: just as the Apostle instructs us even now in the second [letter] to the **Corinthians** <note>The manuscript erroneously cites Romans; the quote is from 2 Corinthians 5:10.</note> in the 5th chapter when he says: *For we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive the proper things of the body according as he has done, whether good or evil* <note>original: "Omnes. n. nos māifestari oportet ante tribunal Christi ut referat unus qf q: propria corporis prout gessit siue bonum siue malum"</note>. And in **Romans** in the 13th [chapter] he adds: *So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God* <note>original: "Itaque unusqfque pro se rōnẽ reddet deo"</note>. ¶ This same sentiment was expressed by **Christ** in Saint **Matthew** in the 10th [chapter], saying to everyone: *For nothing is hidden that shall not be revealed, and secret that shall not be known* <note>original: "Nihil enim optum est quod non reueletur & occultū quod non sciatur"</note>. Therefore, Holy Mother Church, on the morning of the Commemoration of the Dead, sings in that sequence *Dies Irae* <note>A famous medieval Latin hymn describing the "Day of Wrath" and the Last Judgment.</note> these verses relevant to our purpose: *The written book shall be brought forth in which all is contained, by which the world shall be judged. Therefore when the judge sits, whatever is hidden shall appear. Nothing shall remain unpunished* <note>original: "Liber scriptus proferẽtur in quo totū continetur: unde mundus iudicetur. iudex ergo cū sedebit qcquid latet apparēbit. Nil iultū remanebit."</note>. Hence it is necessary that at some time the obstinate souls receive shame and harm for their hidden evil works. Thus he says:

justice. To understand this, it is necessary to repeat a little from the beginning the divine operations: where it is primarily to be understood that **God**, having created man so that he might understand, love, possess, and enjoy Him—as is written at the beginning of the second [book] of the *Sentences*—and having furthermore established for him the penalty of death, both spiritual of the soul and of the body, for transgressing His commandments; hence the text says in **Genesis** in the 2nd chapter: *Eat of every tree of paradise; but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat.
