<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding divine justice, transitioning from a critique of worldly vanity and greed to the necessity of the Incarnation and the logical requirement for a final Universal Judgment of both body and soul.</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF DIVINITY

...will it cost you? where the scripture and the prophet are clearly seen in Psalm 6 <note>The author refers to the text of the Psalms to support the immortality of the soul.</note>:
> For there is no death of the soul. <note>original: "Quoniá ná no é morte de laia." The term "laia" is an archaic or dialectal contraction of "l'anima" (the soul).</note>

<margin>S</margin> ¶ Therefore, since the death of the soul is nothing other than an alienation from God, it was necessary either that God be frustrated in his own end and instituted purpose, or that man be reassumed and restored from his great sin. Because this sin was infinite—since the magnitude of a sin is measured by the object against whom it is committed <note>A common medieval theological argument: because sin is committed against an infinite God, the offense itself is infinite.</note>, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> shows in the fifth book of the *Ethics* and Cicero in the *Paradoxes*—therefore, man's sin could not be redeemed by the work of any creature. Indeed, it was not possible for all created things together to satisfy even the smallest part of it. Thus, by the power of divine justice, since a penalty must be paid for the expiation of every sin, it was necessary that a penalty be paid to take away the sin of man. And since no one other than God himself could remove the infinite offense of sin—an infinite merit being necessary, which no creature was fit to acquire—it was therefore necessary that if God wished to redeem man, he himself must suffer the penalty. Since he could not suffer in his own divine essence, it was necessary for him to take on a <term>passible nature</term> <note>A nature capable of feeling pain and suffering.</note>. And for this reason, the Divine Word came to be incarnated through the burning love and infinite charity held for man. And so Christ Jesus is born into the world, true God and true man, as Ezekiel demonstrates by his proof made to know the secrets of the heart, saying in the twenty-first chapter:
> It is not the divination of demons, but the judgment of God. <note>original: "Non est demonum diuinatio: sed dei iudicium."</note>

Likewise, the other prophecies, all of which were verified in Christ, confirm this.

<margin>T</margin> ¶ Finally, the seal [of his divinity] is his having raised the dead in his own name. This is an operation that God says belongs only to himself; hence in <term>Deuteronomy</term> <note>The text cites chapter 27, but the quote is from Deuteronomy 32:39.</note>:
> I will kill and I will make to live: see that I am alone and there is no other God besides me. <note>original: "Ego occidam & ego viuere faciam: videte q̃d ego sum solus r non t alius deus p̃ter me"</note>

so says the text. And therefore Christ, wishing to demonstrate that he was God—not like Elisha in the fourth book of Kings <note>2 Kings 4 in modern Bibles.</note> who called upon the name of God—but in his own name, he raised the son of the widow, saying in Saint Luke, chapter seven:
> Young man, I say to you, arise. <note>original: "adolescens tibi dico surge"</note>

Christ, therefore, God and man, born and incarnated in the world to redeem human nature from the sin of the first parents, was prepared to endure his passion and pay the penalty established by divine justice as compensation for sin. He did this so that his passion would be sufficient not only for past sins, but he also established new laws for future ones, through the observance of which man could attain eternal life. Therefore, he instituted baptism, faith, the Eucharist, and many other laws, as is known through the account of the Gospel texts. Nevertheless, he left the same penalty for sin: namely, bodily and spiritual death. For these various foundations, then, and for three reasons, Christ is proven to have to come to judge the world. The first is: that since God has redeemed us from the death of the body and the soul, the body must at some time return to life, and then judgment must be given of it by Christ according to the works done, whether in conformity with or contrary to the laws he gave; otherwise, it would be necessary to say that the passion of Christ had not been sufficient to take away the penalty incurred by our sin. The second reason is that a just and prudent prince who desires the observance of his laws, as Christ was, must wish at some time to give his judgment according to them, so that he did not give them in vain for the people to observe. Thus, Christ having given the laws, as was presupposed above, he must therefore at some time come to make a universal judgment according to them. But if anyone should say this is not necessary because as soon as a man is dead—or if he does not believe—he is already judged, according to what Saint John writes in the third chapter when he says:
> He who has not believed is already judged. <note>original: "Qui non crediderit iam iudicatus est"</note>

I respond by saying that this is true regarding the partial judgment of the soul and the respective fitness for the universal judgment to be made of the whole "composite" <note>The "composite" refers to the human person as a union of both body and soul.</note> and natural subject; but it is not yet so regarding the actual sentence which Christ must give over men, since he gave his laws to be observed by men, not only by the soul, as is manifest. The third and final reason is founded upon the text of Saint Matthew in the seventh chapter, when Christ said:
> With that measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you. <note>original: "In illa mensura qua metiemini remetietur & vobis"</note>

Therefore, since everyone in this world has their due measure of works, it is necessary by the words of Christ that he should be judged another time in the universal judgment, so that we do not suggest any lack in the divine intelligence by having his operations multiply many times for only one end. ¶ That this universal judgment must be performed was foretold by the prophet David in Psalm 95 when he said:
> Then all the trees of the forest shall rejoice before the face of the Lord because he comes: because he comes to judge the earth. <note>original: "tunc exultabüt oia ligna siluarum a facie domini quia venit: quonia venit iudicare terram"</note>

Isaiah also in the third chapter confirms the same, saying:
> He stands to judge. <note>original: "Stat ad iudicandum"</note>

It provides three rational proofs for why a final judgment of both body and soul must occur to validate Christ's laws and the resurrection.</summary>

Likewise, the mercy of God embraces the good to be cherished, just as the severity of God seizes the wicked to be punished. It indeed pleased divine providence to prepare good things in the future for the righteous which the unrighteous would not enjoy, and evils for the wicked by which the good would not be tortured. However, He willed that these temporal goods and evils be common to both, so that goods might not be sought by the greedy—since the wicked are also seen to possess them—nor should evils be shamefully avoided, with which even the good are often afflicted. It matters greatly, however, what the use of these things is, whether they be called prosperous or adverse; for the good man is neither puffed up by temporal goods nor broken by evils. The wicked man, however, is punished with this kind of unhappiness because he is corrupted by happiness. Nevertheless, God often shows His hand more evidently in distributing these things; for if every sin were now punished with manifest penalty, it would be thought that nothing was reserved for the final judgment. Conversely, if the divinity now punished no sin openly, no divine providence would be believed in. Similarly, in favorable things, if God did not grant them with most evident generosity to some who ask, we would not say that these things pertain to Him. Likewise, if He gave them to everyone who asked, we would think that He should be served only for the sake of such rewards, and such service would not make us pious, but rather greedy and avaricious." <note>This long passage from St. Augustine explains why bad things happen to good people and vice versa: it proves that a final, perfect judgment must happen later to balance the scales.</note> Through these words, it is clearly understood that in this world, God only partially rewards the good and reserves the full completion for the final judgment. # THE TRIUMPH OF DIVINITY

<margin>A</margin> ¶ O unquenchable avarice: o insatiable greed: o blind abyss or wide pit of perdition: o how much you are always contrary to God. By understanding this, it is to be known that among all vices, none is seen to be more opposed to the infinite liberality <note>Liberality here refers to the theological concept of God's boundless generosity and grace.</note> of God than cruel avarice, in the presence of which every other love is extinguished except for the love of gold. O enemy of Christ, it is not enough for you to possess dominion, it is not enough for you to possess land, it is not enough for you to possess riches: it is not enough for you to possess the gold for which you continually exhaust yourself. Alas, let the miser consider the works of Christ, which ought to be our instruction; let him see how He not only commanded the apostles that they should not accumulate, but even that they should not be anxious for their daily food. Alas, let every miser hear, understand, and consider well how avarice provides no pleasure, nor does it yet provide any utility; it is the cause of eternal loss and certain punishment. Regarding the first two points, 

->And you will see in that brief comparison,<-
->That there, to the proud, gold and land<-
->Have been a harm and not an advantage:<-

<header>CHAPTER SIX FIRST</header>

# CHAPTER SIX

By practicing human diligence and using worldly goods well and moderately—over which man has been placed as a steward—and by following Christ with all one’s heart, a person can wait for the Day of Judgment with security and hear that joyful voice:

> "Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you." <note>Original Latin: "Venite benedicti patris mei possidete paratum vobis regnum" (Matthew 25:34).</note>

From there, alongside the angels and other saints, one will be a perpetual citizen of heaven. Master Francesco <note>Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch), the 14th-century Italian poet whose work is being analyzed here.</note> then adds the specific places of these six states of the soul, which he has demonstrated in his progression. He says that these five aforementioned triumphs symbolize the five universal variations of the soul: namely, the state of the sensory appetite <note>The "sensory appetite" refers to physical desires and emotions.</note> symbolized by Cupid under a <term>poetic veil</term> <note>A "poetic veil" is an allegorical device where a poet hides spiritual truths under fictional characters or stories.</note>; the dominion of reason symbolized by Lady Laura; the state of death; the state of fame; and the state of time. We have seen and known these five on earth. But this sixth one—Eternity, following the Judgment—we shall see again up there in heaven in blessed glory, through the infinite grace and permission of God. Hence he says:

<margin>P</margin>
->These five triumphs down here on earth<-
->We have seen; and at the end the sixth,<-
->God permitting, we shall see up there;<-

¶ Because the fragility of the world and other things subject to the governance of the heavens are of such a nature that they are in no way capable of eternity, only the presence of God—when He reveals Himself as an object without any other intermediary—can produce that measure in us, or rather, His all-encompassing perfection. Therefore, the poet appropriately says that we shall see this sixth triumph of Eternity in heaven, having seen these others down here on earth, where it is necessary for every produced thing to fail and come to its end. And therefore he adds that in that state of eternal measure, time will undo itself, and even death—so cruel and greedy in its empire—will be dead along with time. Hence he says:

<margin>G</margin>
->And time undoes everything so quickly;<-
->And death, in its reign so greedy;<-
->Both she and he will be dead together:<-

¶ As we have said several times in the preceding process, after the Day of Judgment, death and time shall cease. It is to be understood that Eternity is a state in which no further change can occur. Because when change is taken away, successive things are taken away; and consequently, time is taken away first, as it is the primary cause of every succession of flow and variation. Likewise, death is taken away, for death is nothing other than a condition where our soul can be separated from the body. Since after the Day of Judgment the heavens will remain in eternal stillness and the soul will be in perpetual union with the body, the poet appropriately says that in that state, death will be dead along with time.

<margin>H</margin>
¶ Afterward, our Master Francesco repeats for a third time the clear, eternal, and invariable fame which the blessed souls will have in celestial glory after the Day of Judgment. He says that those who in this present life merited clear fame and most glorious praise—which time extinguished and obscured in this world—and even their graceful faces and other bodily beauties, which first age and then death made pale, will return to that state then more beautiful than ever. They will leave behind their dark and gloomy appearances, and their horrid and pale likenesses, along with blind and dark oblivion, to fierce and impetuous death. Similarly, the days, which were "thieves" <note>The poet calls days "thieves" because they stealthily steal away a person's youth and time.</note> moving swiftly in their most beautiful and flowering age, will reassume an immortal and unchangeable beauty with a stable, infinite fame. But first, before all those who go to be made clear again within Purgatory from the stains contracted through human fragility, there will be her whom the world calls back through the poet’s tongue and his weary pen <note>A reference to Laura, Petrarch's muse, whom he immortalized in his writing.</note>, and whom heaven itself yearns and desires to see whole again with a glorified body. Hence he says:

<margin>I</margin>
->And those who earned clear fame,<-
->Which time extinguished, and the lovely, graceful faces,<-

¶ For a clearer understanding of the preceding verses, one must primarily know how Master Francesco, as we said above, sets out to express the effect—

<margin>L</margin> supreme glory. Finally, it is to be noted that Master Francesco, wishing—according to the nature of grateful lovers—to extol his Lady Laura with the highest praise, says she will be the first among all those who go to "remake themselves." Here it must be considered that Master Francesco is affirming the existence of Purgatory, where souls go to be remade and are transformed from that state and disposition in which they are found when they pass from this life to the next—which is to have in themselves some stain of sin, by means of which everyone is prohibited from immediate entry into the celestial homeland. Wishing, therefore, as much as my small wit has understood, to show that the said place of Purgatory exists against the heretical depravity of Waldo, <note>Peter Waldo (c. 1140–1218), the founder of the Waldensians, a movement that was declared heretical by the Catholic Church, partly for denying the existence of Purgatory.</note> it must first be understood that the kingdom of heaven and the wedding of eternal life are of such a nature that they do not allow anyone to enter the delicious tables without the wedding garment of innocence and purity, as 

<margin>M</margin> Saint Matthew testifies in [chapter] 11. <note>Specifically Matthew 22:11–13 regarding the wedding garment.</note> Secondly, it must be presupposed that even if the just man did not fall seven times a day into sin, he cannot avoid having the stain of <term>original sin</term> <note>The Christian doctrine that humans inherit a tainted nature and a proclivity toward sin from the first humans.</note> as was expressed above. For this, it is necessary that satisfaction be made to divine justice through punishment. And if someone should say that the Passion of Christ was a sufficient means to restore the sin committed and that its effect was to take away eternal damnation, and furthermore that baptism purges away all the stain contracted from Adam, the answer is that this is true regarding the guilt, but not regarding the obligation of the punishment. Although in infants who die without baptism this [punishment] is not one of physical sense, but only of loss <note>A reference to "poena damni" (the loss of the vision of God) vs "poena sensus" (the physical suffering of Purgatory or Hell).</note>; nevertheless, in those who are washed in the baptismal font, because the punishment of loss falls upon them, it is changed into a plenary and complete satisfaction through

<margin>N</margin> punishment of the senses, however small it may be. ¶ In the third place, it must be presupposed that although a man may be a sinner, if he returns to true repentance before he sees death, he may be safe from the pains of hell, as Christ testifies in Saint John in the 5th chapter when He says: 

> Truly, truly, I say to you, that he who hears my word and believes in Him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but shall pass from death into life. <note>original: "Amen amen dico vobis quia qui verbum meum audit & credit ei qui misit me habet vitam eternam: & in iudicium non venit sed transibit a morte in vitam" (John 5:24).</note>

And in the third [chapter] He says: 

> For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that everyone who believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life. <note>original: "Sic deus dilexit mundum: ut filium suum unigenitum daret: ut omnis qui in ipso crediderit non pereat: sed habeat vitam eternam" (John 3:16).</note>

And in Saint Matthew in the 9th [chapter], confirming the point, it is written: **I desire mercy and not sacrifice. For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.** <note>original: "Misericordiam volo & non sacrificium. Non enim veni vocare iustos sed peccatores ad penitentiam" (Matthew 9:13).</note> This same mercy 

<margin>O</margin> is understood when God is willing to forgive the sinner seventy-seven times; where a determined and finite number is put for an indeterminate and infinite one. ¶ In the fourth and last place, it is presupposed that distributive divine justice must distribute [rewards and punishments] according to various merits. This is not only known through the doctrine of the holy doctors, but also through the philosophers, orators, and poets, as has been made clear in part in the process above. By these four foundations, then, one can conclude by two effective reasons that everyone goes to Purgatory to be remade. The first, taking two [examples]: one just man, in whom there has never been mortal sin, but only venial falls according to human frailty; and another who has been a very great sinner but converted...

It explains that while baptism removes the guilt of sin, divine justice still requires a "satisfaction" or punishment before the soul can enter heaven.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological discourse on the final state of the soul, specifically addressing the necessity of Purgatory. It follows the previous discussion on the resurrection of the body and the attainment of eternal glory, now refining the distinction between those who die in a state of perfect righteousness and those who die in a state of grace but still owe a debt of temporal punishment.</meta>

<page-num>683</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER ONE</header>
<sig>P</sig>
<sig>Q</sig>
<sig>R</sig>

...died in a state of pardon and grace: and both of these died on one and the same day. In this case, it is asked whether these two ascend to heaven equally at the same time or not. If one responds that they do: then the faith and contrition of the sinner alone would be as meritorious as the faith and righteous works of the just man. This contradicts the fourth supposition and the universal opinion of theologians who place a distinction of degrees of bliss <note>Theologians like Thomas Aquinas argued that while all in Heaven see God, they do so with varying degrees of clarity or "intensity" based on their merit and capacity.</note> in heaven. This distinction would necessarily be removed if unequal works were rewarded equally. But if someone were to say that such a diversity of glory arises in the lesser part because of having sinned more—even though at the end he was converted and repentant—this is false and erroneous. For it would be necessary to concede that the judgment for sin was the diminution of glory and not the imposition of punishment. 

However, if it is granted that those two do not go to eternal life equally, but one goes some time before the other, then it is asked of the one who remains whether he descends to hell. And if one says yes, then the third supposition and the words of Christ are false: because that person does not have eternal life and does not pass from death to life, but falls into a most wretched and everlasting death; and his penance would not have been fruitful, because in hell **there is no redemption.** <note>original: "nulla est redemptio." A common theological maxim stating that after death, there is no further opportunity for repentance or salvation for those in Hell.</note> 

If one responds no, then it is asked whether—the sinner being then in a state of not being able to possess heaven with that current disposition—he must always remain uniform in that state, never ascending to celestial glory or changing from such a state to true innocence. If one says no, then the former would never enter heaven, and consequently, Christ died in vain for sinners to give them eternal life. If one says yes to the second option, then it is necessary that, being no longer able to satisfy through works, he satisfies through the punishment of pain in Purgatory. Wherefore, by this first reason, it is necessary to concede that Purgatory exists and that souls are purged before they ascend to eternal life.

¶ The other reason is that it is necessary for little children who die after baptism to purge the stain and the "dirty garment" of the soul. Therefore, much more so are adults obligated to such purgation. That it is necessary for little children to be purged of sin is shown by this: that they are born with original sin. Thus, being unable to ascend to heaven with that stain according to the first supposition, it is necessary that they leave it behind. One asks, then: do they satisfy the obligation of sin through their own operation, or through the Passion of Christ by means of the instrument of sacred baptism, or truly through the passion of punishment? The first cannot be said in any way, as they are at an age unfit for meritorious works. 

But if one says the second, then the Passion of Christ—not being of less virtue regarding other sins than regarding original sin—and furthermore, the sacraments of confession and extreme unction, would not be of less efficacy and virtue than baptism. Thus, at the death of sinners, these should make them exempt from every punishment. This is shown to be totally false by the first reason, because it would be necessary to say that they immediately ascended to heaven, the converted and penitent sinner just like the righteous man who always lived justly.

¶ Therefore, it is necessary to concede the third part of the division: that is, that little children satisfy the obligation through the passion of punishment—though it be the very smallest amount in an imperceptible time—in the place of Purgatory. This state of Purgatory is demonstrated by Christ in Saint Matthew [chapter 18] <note>The text reads "al. lxvij," likely a reference to a specific sermon or legal citation system rather than the modern chapter number.</note> when, from the similitude of the kingdom of heaven to a temporal king who wished to settle accounts with his servants, he placed his servant in the hands of the torturers until he should pay the entire debt. Earlier, it had been shown that the king had pardoned him the sale of himself, his wife, and his children. Since the debt of sin cannot be entirely paid in this world, it is necessary for Purgatory to be granted, where the debt is fully satisfied to divine justice. 

This same point is shown by Saint Paul in Philippians 2, when he says: **He became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross; wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, and those on earth, and those under the earth.** <note>original: "Factus est obediens usque ad mortem... terrestrium & infernorum."</note> Wherefore, if those in the "underworlds" <note>original: "infernorum." In this context, the author interprets the "under the earth" inhabitants as those in Purgatory, as they are the ones capable of bowing in prayer/submission, unlike the damned.</note> bow down to God, then they are not in the Hell [of the damned] where there is no redemption; for those in that place blaspheme God every day. As Dante Alighieri says at the beginning of the *Inferno* when he writes: *they blaspheme the divine power here.* <note>A reference to Dante's *Inferno*, Canto III, where the damned blaspheme God, their parents, and the human race.</note>

¶ This sentence is also seen manifestly in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 3, <note>OCR reads "xiij" (13), but the quote is from Peter's speech in Acts 3.</note> when Saint Peter says to the Jews: **Repent and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord, and he shall send Jesus Christ, who before was preached unto you: whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of his holy prophets since the world began.** <note>original: "Convertimini & poenitemini... seculo prophetarum."</note> Therefore, if the time of restitution and the time of refreshing is to come, the souls are in supplications and in punishments with confirmed hope of salvation. We conclude together with Virgil in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*, and with our poet <note>Likely Petrarch, as the book is a commentary on his *Triumphs*.</note>: that the place of Purgatory is where souls go to remake themselves and change from all their stains, so that they may return to the first innocence in which they were created from the beginning. ¶ Finally, it is to be noted most greatly...

<summary>This page presents a theological defense of Purgatory, arguing that it is a logical necessity for satisfying divine justice and distinguishing between the merits of the lifelong righteous and the newly repentant. It supports this using biblical citations from Matthew, Acts, and Philippians, alongside literary references to Dante and Virgil.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Petrarch's "Triumph of Divinity" and begins the author’s formal dedication and concluding apologies. It transitions from the theological contemplation of Laura’s resurrection to the translator's personal humble submission to his patron.</meta>

# THE TRIUMPH OF DIVINITY
<meta>Catchword: [so that he] may have</meta>

<margin>S</margin>
It is to the greatest praise of **Madonna Laura** <note>Petrarch’s idealized muse, often interpreted in these commentaries as a bridge between earthly beauty and divine virtue.</note> to say that heaven yearns to see her again with her body on earth. It is as if to demonstrate that the other blessed souls in heaven are drawn to the greatest wonder by the beauty of her soul, as is shown in this sonnet. And the angels are chosen for the blessed souls; from this, it is reasonably provoked that they wish to see her again with her glorified body, in whose presence the soul will be bright. From this, the poet silently concludes that the corporal and mental beauty of Laura is more outstanding and worthy than any other in heaven. Finally, our **Messer Francesco** <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the author of the *Triumphs*.</note>, having demonstrated the excellence and beauty of Laura, concludes what the duties of every prudent intellect should be. Even if in youth one has sometimes looked with delight upon the beauty and manners of some noble lady, he demonstrates that one should consider her without [sinful] pleasure; this will be a greater and more perfect state, and one of greater clarity, to see her in heaven with the blessed souls. He says this through the example of himself: that near the bank of a river which rises in the **Cevennes** <note>The original text uses "Gebenna," referring to the Cevennes mountain range in France where the Rhone originates.</note>, Love gave him a very great war for this lady of his. And he adds, exclaiming: **O happy stone!** Which encloses and covers that beautiful face. If he who beheld her in her earthly beauty was truly to be considered blessed, what will it be then to see her again with her glorified body, assumed into celestial glory? It is as if he responds: "eternal happiness." Whence he says:

<margin>T</margin>
It is a very well-known and great thing that the affection of the poet toward his beloved **Madonna Laura** was such that even when he was reduced to true penance and in his declining age, the memory of her still signaled the accustomed war of love to his heart. Nevertheless, he demonstrates afterwards that—notwithstanding that—he has turned his mind only to considering the beauty of Laura, no longer through the senses but through the intellect in blessed glory; and thus he silently admonishes us.

> ->By the bank of a river, which rises in the Cevennes,<-
> ->Love gave me such a long war for her sake;<-
> ->That the memory still strikes my heart.<-
> ->Happy stone, that encloses the beautiful face:<-
> ->For after she has taken up her beautiful veil <gloss>her body</gloss> again;<-
> ->If he was blessed, who saw her on earth;<-
> ->Now what will it be then to see her again in heaven?<-

<margin>V</margin>
Every lover ought to cast aside transitory pleasures and desire only the eternal ones. It should be understood that by the bank of the river that rises in the Cevennes, he intends to describe the city of **Avignon**, through which the **Rhone** passes. This river rises, as **Suetonius Tranquillus** <note>A Roman historian; the commentator is citing him to provide geographical authority.</note> writes in the *Life of Caesar*, in the mountain contiguous to the Pyrenees that divide Italy from Provence, which is called **Gebenna** <note>The Cevennes</note>, where there is a lake near a land called **Geneva**; and the aforementioned river Rhone runs through part of Provence, then goes through France and passes through the city of Avignon, where Love, by means of **Madonna Laura**, made **Messer Francesco** feel such a bitter war.

<margin>Y</margin>
He says finally that the stone which covers the beautiful face of Laura in the sepulcher is "happy," according to the custom of **Plutarch** <note>The text says "Potarcos," likely a corruption of Plutarch, or perhaps a reference to a specific Aristotelian commentator.</note> written in the second book of *Physics* by the poet. According to this view, just as inanimate things were dedicated to more worthy or less worthy exercises, so he said they were "unhappy" or "happy." And thus ends the exposition of the *Triumphs* of the glorious poet **Messer Francesco Petrarch**, according to the requirement of the talent of me, **Bernardo Ilicino** <note>Bernardo Ilicino (c. 1410–1492), a physician and philosopher who wrote one of the most famous commentaries on Petrarch.</note>, student of medicine and philosophy. For which, may infinite thanks be to Him who has granted me to finish it, and who lives without the overshadowing of change. Forever and ever. Amen. <note>original: "Per infinita secula seculorum. Amen."</note>

<margin>Z</margin>
<insert>E</insert> <note>The ornate initial 'E' begins the author’s formal address to his patron.</note> Since now, most illustrious prince, with the help of God, the little boat of my talent has finished its furrowing and shading according to my small power, and has already arrived and withdrawn into port, I see it is necessary for me to offer an excuse. If anyone, beyond my intended purpose, attributes something to me for which I could justly be reproved: for perhaps it will be said by someone that I have dared, with temerity and presumption, to wish to open the mind to that prince. To him—because of the greatness of his talent and his actions—not only **Lombardy** but **Italy** and foreign nations look, as if to the oracle of **Apollo** and the wise **Minerva**, solely for his just and prudent government. To him, no sentence, no doctrine, no private or public opinion can be unknown, unattempted, or obscure, because of the great sharpness of his clear intellect and his very great and universal experience of worldly things. Some others will persuade themselves that I believe I have brought some new doctrine to this exposition of mine, never before imagined or expressed by others. Whence they will say I am less attentive, incautious, and little practiced in the readings of others. Some others, perhaps in no less number, will say that I have gone astray from the subject and against the intention of the poet—

# CHAPTER ONE
<note>While the header indicates "Chapter One," this page actually functions as the formal conclusion and epilogue to the entire work.</note>

Z

...having uprooted the <unclear>doubts</unclear>, [I have] expanded his verses and the subject matter: wherefore they may suffice, and everyone should consider me less than intelligent. Now, Most Illustrious Prince, I confess that I am to be reproached as human frailty allows; but certainly, in these matters, no error occurs, because I know how much wisdom, intelligence, prudence, and excellence you provide—O, you—an experienced and most glorious prince. This excellence is as widespread as it can be among all those who are led and regulated by him, and even among those who might wish to resist his dominion. Alas, where can there be more intelligence, more constancy, more justice, more wisdom, and more of every virtue and habit worthy of commendation and praise than in a most happy prince? Upon him, all the eyes of his faithful people, those bordering his domain, and foreigners and pilgrims are turned; all his actions are subjected to judgment and censure, and by infinite good men, they are highly praised. 

It was not, therefore, my intention to want to "educate education" itself; but since fortune has granted my weak being no other way to demonstrate to you, my Lord, how great my faith, sincerity, and obedience are toward your Lordship, I decided at least that these labors of mine should be a testament and witness of my service toward your most illustrious Lordship. Just as my conscience testifies this to itself, so I desire through this attestation of mine to make it known and manifest to others. 

As for the second objection, I respond that my understanding is not so confused that I do not have a true judgment of myself. Wherefore, I concede that I have brought forward nothing new that has not been previously narrated and described by others. But just like one who, in a noble and bountiful meadow of flowers, gathers those produced by nature and, joining them together and weaving a bound garland, is said to have fabricated something new; so I say I have done, having, through the gathering of the doctrines of others, collected together these my "vigils" <note>A term often used by scholars to describe long nights of study and writing.</note> into a form more easily noticed and more understood regarding our graceful poet. 

As for the third objection, I say first that the work of the poet itself responds for me. Then, there is the authority of **Giovanni da Certaldo** <note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), the famous author of the Decameron and a close friend/disciple of Petrarch.</note>, the most observant disciple of **Messer Francesco** <note>Francesco Petrarch.</note>, who attributes so much to the poet that I judge myself to be diminished in every part. Therefore, Most Illustrious Prince, everyone can be persuaded that nothing else induced me to compose these vigils other than to demonstrate love toward the poet and to take the burden of labor from many who delight in him. And to your most illustrious Lordship, to demonstrate faith, service, and dedication, which I desire and pray may be happy according to your will, and the will of those who love you most, desire, and work to maintain you in glory forever and ever. <note>original: "in infinita secula seculorum"</note> Amen.
